title: Preface
text: Preface [Introduction] A plurisubharmonic function is the several-variable analogue of a subharmonic function: an upper semicontinuous function whose restriction to every complex line is subharmonic. Such functions arise as local potentials of closed positive currents, as weights of singular Hermitian metrics on line bundles and as solutions of complex Monge–Ampère equations. They may take the value $-\infty $, and much of the geometric information they carry is concentrated in their singularities. Pluripotential theory studies these functions, the nonlinear measures they define, and the ways in which their singularities can be measured and compared. This book develops the foundations of the theory from the beginning. It is written as a companion to Part I of Singularities in global pluripotential theory [ XiaSampleBook ] , and its purpose is to give complete proofs of the analytic results on which that text relies. We start from classical potential theory in $\mathbb R^ d$ and end with the machinery behind non-pluripolar products, singularity envelopes, relative energy and the ample toric setting. The chapters are arranged in the order in which the proofs depend on one another: weighted holomorphic estimates come before multiplier ideals, regularization comes before the study of global positive classes, and the Monge–Ampère operator on bounded functions comes before any product involving unbounded potentials.

title: From distributions to pointwise potentials
text: From distributions to pointwise potentials A locally integrable function has distributional derivatives of every order, but as a distribution it cannot see its values on a set of measure zero. Potential theory recovers these values from mean-value inequalities. If the distributional Laplacian of a function is a positive measure, the function has a canonical subharmonic representative, whose value at each point is the limit of its averages over small balls. Harmonic replacement on balls then controls maxima, boundary values and upper envelopes. The exceptional sets that occur in these constructions are measured by capacity rather than by Lebesgue measure. For this reason measure theory, the Dirichlet problem, energy and the fine topology together form the first part of the book. In several variables a further difficulty appears. Plurisubharmonicity requires the submean inequality on every complex line, and an upper bound obtained separately on each line need not be uniform on a neighborhood. The Fourier and incidence estimates of chapter 6 provide this uniformity. With them we show in theorem 8.1.3 that upper semicontinuity is automatic for a function that is subharmonic on every complex line, and we identify plurisubharmonic functions with the canonical representatives of distributions whose complex Hessian is positive. Compactness and envelope arguments can therefore be carried out for genuine functions, not only for almost-everywhere classes.

title: Two ways of measuring a singularity
text: Two ways of measuring a singularity The first way is local and holomorphic. The Lelong number of a plurisubharmonic function measures its logarithmic concentration at a point, while its multiplier ideals record which holomorphic functions remain square integrable against the corresponding exponential weight. The proofs that multiplier ideals are coherent, and that integrability persists after a small increase of the weight, rely on holomorphic extension. Weighted $L^2$ estimates for the $\bar\partial $ operator are the basic tool: they correct the error introduced by a cutoff function, prescribe values along slices and produce the holomorphic functions used in approximation. Potentials with analytic singularities, defined by finitely many holomorphic functions, make the resulting growth explicit; on a resolution of singularities it is described by divisors. The second way is nonlinear. For locally bounded plurisubharmonic functions, Bedford and Taylor defined the exterior products of their curvature currents and proved that these products are continuous along decreasing sequences. For an unbounded function one first truncates the potential and then discards the part of the product carried by its pole set. When the products obtained in this way have locally bounded mass, their limit is the non-pluripolar product. This operation can lose mass, and the relation between this loss and the singularities of the potentials is one of the central themes of the global theory. The two measurements need not agree. Using an atom-free probability measure carried by a polar Cantor set (proposition 4.2.4 ), we construct in example 15.3.8 a potential on the projective line whose Lelong numbers all vanish and whose multiplier ideals are all trivial, but whose non-pluripolar mass is zero. This example, which is [ Example 6.1.3 , XiaSampleBook ] , shows that neither Lelong numbers nor multiplier ideals can replace the mass theory developed in the later chapters.

title: Global potentials and envelopes
text: Global potentials and envelopes On a compact Kähler manifold, a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form fixes a cohomology class, and a potential changes the current within that class. Local positivity must now be reconciled with this global constraint. Elliptic theory for the scalar Laplacian provides global potentials, and compactness and approximation describe pseudo-effective and big classes, including their boundary behavior. Singular Hermitian metrics express the same positivity in the language of line bundles. An envelope is the largest admissible potential lying below a given obstacle. When an additional constraint on the singularities is imposed, the envelope selects a canonical representative of that constraint. Its Monge–Ampère measure is carried by the set where the envelope touches the obstacle, but proving this requires local replacement arguments and careful passages to the limit. Relative capacities and integration by parts then lead to the relative energy, to Monge–Ampère equations with prescribed singularities and to Perron segments joining two potentials. As an application we prove in theorem 17.5.3 the identity between ceilings and singularity envelopes of [ Theorem 1.2 , PSWZ26 ] in every big class, together with the idempotence of the singularity envelope; the case of zero mass is obtained from positive-mass perturbations together with a uniform estimate of their tails. Finally, convex duality and real Monge–Ampère measures provide the corresponding foundations for invariant potentials on the open torus, and the projective toric manifold of a Delzant polytope, with its sections and the Guillemin metric, provides the ample toric setting.

title: Prerequisites and how to read this book
text: Prerequisites and how to read this book We assume undergraduate real analysis, including the differential calculus of several real variables (in particular the inverse and implicit function theorems), Lebesgue integration with its convergence theorems and the change of variables formula, linear algebra, point-set topology and the elementary theory of holomorphic functions of one variable. Distribution theory, the functional analysis needed for weighted estimates and elliptic equations, holomorphic functions of several variables, the commutative algebra used for ideals of holomorphic germs, complex differential geometry and convex analysis are developed in the text. 1 establishes the linear theory and the theory of exceptional sets; 2 develops the local complex theory and then passes to singular potentials on compact manifolds. Each part opens with a short introduction describing its chapters. Chapter A collects the facts about complex spaces, normalization and modifications that are needed for multiplier ideals and resolutions; it can be consulted when these tools first appear. Two existence theorems are used without proof: the resolution of singularities of complex spaces and the principalization of coherent ideals. They are stated precisely as theorem A.5.4 , theorem A.5.5 , and every consequence of them used in the book is proved. The historical and bibliographical notes in chapter B give the sources of the results and the precise versions of the cited works, with references to the corresponding statements in the text. Our notation and normalizations follow [ XiaSampleBook ] . The global conventions are listed on the following pages; all other notation is introduced where it is first needed. A few definitions and constructions of [ XiaSampleBook ] are repeated here when a complete argument requires them, while the classification of singularities and its applications are left to that book.

title: Conventions
text: Conventions In the whole book, we adopt the following conventions: A complex space is always assumed to be reduced , paracompact and Hausdorff . A modification of a complex space $X$ is a proper bimeromorphic morphism $\pi \colon Y\rightarrow X$ that is locally obtained from a finite composition of blow-ups with smooth centers. A subnet of a net refers to a Willard subnet. More precisely, if $f\colon I\rightarrow X$ and $f'\colon I'\rightarrow X$ are nets, namely, maps from directed sets $I$ and $I'$ to the same set $X$, we say $f'$ is a subnet of $f$ if there is an increasing final function $h\colon I'\rightarrow I$ such that $f\circ h=f'$. A domain in $\mathbb {R}^ d$ or $\mathbb {C}^ n$ refers to a connected open subset. A complex manifold is assumed to be paracompact. A submanifold of a complex manifold means a closed complex submanifold. A neighborhood is not necessarily open. The set $\mathbb {N}$ of natural numbers includes $0$. Increasing functions and decreasing functions are not necessarily strictly monotone. Positive forms are not necessarily strictly positive. The function $\mathbb {R}\ni x \mapsto x^2$ is convex instead of concave. This is different from the convention in [ CLS11 ] . We say a positive measure $\mu $ on a measurable space $X$ is carried by a measurable subset $Y$ if $\mu (X\setminus Y)=0$. $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ means $(2\pi )^{-1}\mathrm{i}\partial \overline{\partial }$. We also use the following notation throughout the book. The indicator function of a set $E$ is denoted by $\mathbf1_ E$. For subsets $A$ and $B$ of a topological space, $A\Subset B$ means that the closure of $A$ is a compact subset of $B$; we then say that $A$ is relatively compact in $B$. The closure, interior and boundary of a set $E$ in its ambient space are denoted by $\overline E$, $\operatorname{Int}E$ and $\partial E$. The support of a function, measure, distribution or current is denoted by $\operatorname{Supp}$. For an open set $\Omega $ in $\mathbb R^ d$ or in a manifold, $C^ k(\Omega )$ is the space of $k$ times continuously differentiable functions, where $0\leq k\leq \infty $, and $C^ k_ c(\Omega )$ is its subspace of functions with compact support. We write $L^ p_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$ for the functions whose restrictions to compact subsets of $\Omega $ are $p$-integrable. The imaginary unit is $\mathrm{i}$, and $\operatorname{Re}z$ and $\operatorname{Im}z$ are the real and imaginary parts of a complex number $z$.

title: Potential theory
text: 1 Potential theory

title: Introduction to Part I
text: Introduction to Part I This part develops the potential theory of the Laplacian on open subsets of $\mathbb R^ d$, as far as it is needed for the complex theory of 2 . A potential can be described in three ways: by its distributional derivatives, by its mean values, and by the measure that records its singularities. Each description is suited to different operations, namely weak limits, pointwise comparison and the analysis of poles. Our main task is to pass between these descriptions while keeping control of the exceptional sets produced by limits and envelopes. Measures and distributions come first (chapter 1 ), because the curvature currents of later chapters have measures as coefficients. We prove that positive linear functionals are given by measures, approximate distributions by smooth functions through convolution, and establish the compactness principles used to extract weak limits. Harmonic functions (chapter 2 ) are the comparison functions of the theory. The Poisson kernel solves the Dirichlet problem on a ball; on a general bounded domain, Perron's method produces a harmonic function in the interior, and barriers decide whether it attains the prescribed boundary values. Subharmonic functions (chapter 3 ) are obtained by replacing the mean-value equality by an inequality. Their distributional Laplacians are positive measures, and a subharmonic function is determined at every point by its almost-everywhere class. This correspondence is indispensable for upper envelopes: the pointwise supremum of a family and its upper semicontinuous regularization may differ, and one must know where. The Riesz decomposition splits a subharmonic function into a harmonic part and the potential of its Laplacian, which links comparison arguments with energy. Capacity (chapter 4 ) measures the size of a set by the potentials it can support. A set of Lebesgue measure zero can have positive capacity, whereas a polar set carries no nonzero measure of finite energy. Equilibrium potentials connect this distinction with comparison arguments. The fine topology (chapter 5 ) is the coarsest topology that makes all subharmonic functions continuous. The reduction of a nonnegative superharmonic function on a set is the infimum of the nonnegative superharmonic functions that dominate it there, and balayage sweeps a measure onto a compact set while preserving its potential quasi-everywhere on that set. These constructions explain why the exceptional sets of potential theory can be discarded only when they have capacity zero, and not merely when they have Lebesgue measure zero. The last chapter of this part (chapter 6 ) prepares the passage to several complex variables. Before subharmonicity along complex lines can produce a plurisubharmonic function, upper bounds along individual lines must be made uniform. An energy estimate, the Fourier transform and a projection argument provide this uniformity. The same Fourier methods give $L^ p$ estimates for second derivatives. The two results serve different purposes in 2 : the incidence estimate provides the local upper bounds that identify the pointwise representative of a plurisubharmonic function, while the second-derivative estimates control the Monge–Ampère measure of an envelope lying below a nonsmooth obstacle.

title: Measures and distributions
text: 1 Measures and distributions The potentials studied in this book are seldom differentiable. On $\mathbb R^2$, for instance, the function $\log |x|$ tends to $-\infty $ at the origin, yet its Laplacian has a precise meaning: it is $2\pi $ times the Dirac mass at the origin (proposition 2.2.1 ). Such statements are made rigorous by differentiating in the weak sense, that is, by moving derivatives onto smooth compactly supported test functions through integration by parts. The derivatives obtained in this way are distributions. For subharmonic functions, and later for plurisubharmonic ones, the relevant second derivatives are positive distributions, and a positive distribution is a measure. The measure attached to a potential records where its mass lies, including the mass concentrated at its singularities; measures and distributions are therefore the basic language of potential theory. Throughout this chapter, $\Omega $ is an open subset of $\mathbb R^ d$, where $d\geq 1$. The first section introduces Radon measures and signed Radon measures and recalls, with short proofs that fix our conventions, the parts of Lebesgue integration that we use. The core of the chapter consists of two facts: the Riesz representation theorem (theorem 1.2.2 ), which identifies positive linear functionals on compactly supported continuous functions with Radon measures, and the regularization of distributions by convolution with a smooth kernel, which commutes with derivatives and preserves positivity (proposition 1.4.3 ). Together they show that positive distributions are measures (theorem 1.4.5 ). Since limits of potentials lead to limits of measures, we then study weak convergence and compactness of measures, for sequences and, where sequences do not suffice, for nets. The last section constructs bounded densities and proves the Lebesgue differentiation theorem; as an application, a continuous function with locally bounded distributional Hessian has a second-order Taylor expansion almost everywhere (proposition 1.7.5 ). Historical remarks and references for this chapter are collected in section B.1 .

title: Radon measures and integration
text:
1.1 Radon measures and integration Unless stated otherwise, all measures in this chapter are positive, that is, they take values in $[0,\infty ]$. We use the Lebesgue integral, defined first for nonnegative simple functions and then, for a nonnegative measurable function, as the supremum of the integrals of the simple functions below it. Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R^ d$ is denoted by $\mathrm dx$, and the Lebesgue measure of a measurable set $E\subset \mathbb R^ d$ by $|E|$. The Borel $\sigma $-algebra of $\Omega $ is the smallest $\sigma $-algebra containing the open subsets of $\Omega $, and a Borel measure on $\Omega $ is a measure defined on it. A measure on a measurable space $X$ is $\sigma $-finite if $X$ is a countable union of measurable sets of finite measure. We write $C(\Omega )=C^0(\Omega )$ and $C_ c(\Omega )=C^0_ c(\Omega )$. Their elements may be real- or complex-valued; the real-valued functions in $C_ c(\Omega )$ form the space $C_ c(\Omega ,\mathbb R)$, which we use whenever positivity is involved. Definition 1.1.1 . A Radon measure on $\Omega $ is a Borel measure $\mu $ on $\Omega $ which is finite on compact sets and satisfies, for every Borel set $E\subset \Omega $, \[  \mu (E)=\inf _{E\subset U,\  U	ext{ open}}\mu (U) =\sup _{K\subset E,\  K	ext{ compact}}\mu (K).  \] The two equalities are called outer and inner regularity of $\mu $. A measurable function is locally integrable with respect to $\mu $ if its absolute value has finite integral over every compact subset of $\Omega $. The support $\operatorname{Supp}\mu $ of a Radon measure $\mu $ is the set of points of $\Omega $ all of whose open neighborhoods have positive measure. Its complement $\Omega \setminus \operatorname{Supp}\mu $ is the union of all open subsets of $\Omega $ of measure zero, so it is open and $\operatorname{Supp}\mu $ is relatively closed in $\Omega $. Moreover $\mu (\Omega \setminus \operatorname{Supp}\mu )=0$ by inner regularity, because every compact subset of $\Omega \setminus \operatorname{Supp}\mu $ is covered by finitely many open sets of measure zero. We shall often use a compact exhaustion of $\Omega $, that is, a sequence of compact sets $K_ j\subset \Omega $, $j\geq 1$, with $K_ j\subset \operatorname{Int}K_{j+1}$ for every $j$ and $ igcup _ j\operatorname{Int}K_ j=\Omega $. For example, \[  K_ j=\{ x\in \Omega :|x|\leq j,\  \operatorname {dist}(x,\mathbb R^ d\setminus \Omega )\geq j^{-1}\} ,  \] where $\operatorname {dist}(x,\varnothing )=+\infty $ if $\Omega =\mathbb R^ d$. Indeed, $K_ j$ is closed and bounded, hence compact. It lies in the open set $\{ x:|x|<j+1,\  \operatorname {dist}(x,\mathbb R^ d\setminus \Omega )>(j+1)^{-1}\} $, which is contained in $K_{j+1}$, and every point of $\Omega $ lies in $\operatorname{Int}K_ j$ for all large $j$. If $K\subset \Omega $ is compact and $U\subset \Omega $ is an open set containing $K$, a cutoff function for $K$ in $U$ is a continuous function $\eta \colon \Omega 	o [0,1]$ such that $\eta =1$ on $K$ and $\operatorname{Supp}\eta $ is a compact subset of $U$. Such functions exist. If $K=\varnothing $, take $\eta =0$; otherwise choose $\delta >0$ with $2\delta <\operatorname {dist}(K,\mathbb R^ d\setminus U)$, so that $V=\{ x:\operatorname {dist}(x,K)<\delta \} $ is an open set whose closure is a compact subset of $U$, and put \[  \eta (x)= rac{\operatorname {dist}(x,\mathbb R^ d\setminus V)}{\operatorname {dist}(x,\mathbb R^ d\setminus V)+\operatorname {dist}(x,K)}.  \] The denominator never vanishes, since the first term is positive on $V\supset K$ and the second is positive off $K$; moreover $\eta =1$ on $K$ and $\eta =0$ outside $V$. Smooth cutoff functions are constructed in lemma 1.4.1 . Proposition 1.1.2 . Let $\mu $ be a Borel measure on $\Omega $ which is finite on compact subsets. Then $\mu $ is a Radon measure. In particular, $\mu $ is $\sigma $-finite. Proof. Assume first that $\mu (\Omega )<\infty $, and let $F\subset \Omega $ be relatively closed; we may assume that $F
eq \varnothing $. The open sets $U_ j=\{ x\in \Omega :\operatorname {dist}(x,F)<j^{-1}\} $ decrease to $F$, so $\mu (U_ j)	o \mu (F)$ because $\mu $ is finite. Hence $F$ can be approximated in measure from outside by open sets. Passing to complements, every open set can be approximated from inside by relatively closed sets. Let $\mathcal A$ be the class of Borel sets $E$ such that for every $\varepsilon >0$ there are an open set $U$ and a relatively closed set $F$ with $F\subset E\subset U$ and $\mu (U\setminus F)<\varepsilon $. We have just seen that $\mathcal A$ contains the relatively closed sets, and $\mathcal A$ is closed under complements because the condition is symmetric. To see that $\mathcal A$ is closed under countable unions, let $E= igcup _ jE_ j$ with $E_ j\in \mathcal A$, and choose $F_ j\subset E_ j\subset U_ j$ with $\mu (U_ j\setminus F_ j)<\varepsilon 2^{-j}$. The open set $U= igcup _ jU_ j$ satisfies $\mu (U\setminus E)<\varepsilon $. Since $\mu ( igcup _{j\leq N}E_ j)	o \mu (E)$, there is $N$ such that the relatively closed set $F= igcup _{j\leq N}F_ j$ satisfies $\mu (E\setminus F)\leq \mu (E\setminus  igcup _{j\leq N}E_ j)+\sum _{j\leq N}\mu (E_ j\setminus F_ j)<2\varepsilon $, and hence $\mu (U\setminus F)<3\varepsilon $. Thus $\mathcal A$ is a $\sigma $-algebra containing the open sets, so it contains every Borel set $E$. If $F\subset E$ is relatively closed and $(K_ j)$ is a compact exhaustion of $\Omega $, then the sets $F\cap K_ j$ are compact and $\mu (F\setminus K_ j)	o 0$. Hence every Borel set can be approximated in measure from outside by open sets and from inside by compact sets. In general, let $(K_ j)$ be a compact exhaustion of $\Omega $, put $K_0=\varnothing $, and let $V_ j=\operatorname{Int}K_{j+1}$. The measures $\mu _ j(E)=\mu (E\cap V_ j)$ are finite, hence Radon by the first part. For inner regularity, let $E$ be a Borel set and $\varepsilon >0$. A compact set $K\subset E$ with $\mu _ j(E\setminus K)<\varepsilon $ satisfies $\mu (K)\geq \mu _ j(K)>\mu (E\cap V_ j)-\varepsilon $, and $\mu (E\cap V_ j)	o \mu (E)$ as $j	o \infty $. For outer regularity, note that the Borel sets $B_ j=K_ j\setminus K_{j-1}$ partition $\Omega $ and that $E\cap B_ j\subset V_ j$. By outer regularity of $\mu _ j$ there is an open set $O_ j\subset V_ j$ containing $E\cap B_ j$ with $\mu (O_ j\setminus (E\cap B_ j))<\varepsilon 2^{-j}$; it suffices to intersect an approximating open set with $V_ j$. Then $O= igcup _ jO_ j$ is an open set containing $E$ with $\mu (O\setminus E)<\varepsilon $. Finally, $\mu $ is $\sigma $-finite because $\Omega = igcup _ jK_ j$ and each $\mu (K_ j)$ is finite. $\square$ Proposition 1.1.3 . Let $(X,\mu )$ be a measure space and let $f_ j$, $j\geq 1$, be measurable functions on $X$. If $f_ j\geq 0$ and $f_ j\uparrow f$ pointwise, then $\int f_ j\, \mathrm d\mu \uparrow \int f\, \mathrm d\mu $. If $f_ j\geq 0$ for every $j$, then \[  \int \varliminf _ j f_ j\, \mathrm d\mu \leq \varliminf _ j\int f_ j\, \mathrm d\mu .  \] If the $f_ j$ are real or complex, converge almost everywhere to a measurable function $f$, and satisfy $|f_ j|\leq g$ for an integrable function $g$, then $f$ is integrable and $\int |f_ j-f|\, \mathrm d\mu 	o 0$. Proof. (1) The integrals $\int f_ j\, \mathrm d\mu $ increase and are bounded by $\int f\, \mathrm d\mu $, so we must show that their limit is at least $\int f\, \mathrm d\mu $. Let $s\leq f$ be a nonnegative simple function and $0<t<1$. The measurable sets $E_ j=\{ f_ j\geq ts\} $ increase with $j$, and their union contains $\{ s>0\} $, since $f(x)\geq s(x)>ts(x)$ there. Applying continuity from below to the sets $E_ j\cap \{ s=a\} $ for the finitely many values $a$ of $s$, we obtain \[  \lim _ j\int f_ j\, \mathrm d\mu \geq \lim _ jt\int _{E_ j}s\, \mathrm d\mu =t\int s\, \mathrm d\mu .  \] Taking the supremum over $s$ and then letting $t\uparrow 1$ proves (1); infinite integrals are allowed. (2) The functions $g_ j=\inf _{k\geq j}f_ k$ are measurable, they increase to $\varliminf _ jf_ j$, and $\int g_ j\, \mathrm d\mu \leq \int f_ k\, \mathrm d\mu $ for every $k\geq j$. Applying (1) to $(g_ j)$ gives (2). (3) Letting $j	o \infty $ in $|f_ j|\leq g$ gives $|f|\leq g$ almost everywhere, so $f$ is integrable. The functions $2g-|f_ j-f|$ are nonnegative almost everywhere, and (2), applied after a modification on a null set, gives \[  \int 2g\, \mathrm d\mu \leq \varliminf _ j\int  igl (2g-|f_ j-f| igr )\, \mathrm d\mu =\int 2g\, \mathrm d\mu -\varlimsup _ j\int |f_ j-f|\, \mathrm d\mu .  \] Since $\int 2g\, \mathrm d\mu <\infty $, it follows that $\int |f_ j-f|\, \mathrm d\mu 	o 0$. $\square$ Assertions (1), (2) and (3) are the monotone convergence theorem, Fatou's lemma and the dominated convergence theorem. They concern sequences and fail for nets. For instance, the indicator functions of the finite subsets of $[0,1]$, directed by inclusion, form an increasing net of Borel functions with supremum $\mathbf1_{[0,1]}$; each of them has Lebesgue integral zero, while the supremum has integral one. The supremum of an increasing net of measurable functions need not even be measurable: if $A\subset \mathbb R$ is not Lebesgue measurable, the indicator functions of the finite subsets of $A$ increase to $\mathbf1_ A$. Where nets occur later, the passage to the limit therefore requires a separate argument. Sets that are not Lebesgue measurable exist. Choose a set $V\subset [0,1)$ containing exactly one point of each coset $x+\mathbb Q$ of the rational numbers. The translates $V+q$, $q\in \mathbb Q\cap (-1,1)$, are contained in $(-1,2)$, and they are pairwise disjoint, because two points of $V$ with rational difference coincide. They cover $[0,1)$, since every $x\in [0,1)$ differs from the point of $V$ in its coset by a rational number in $(-1,1)$. If $V$ were measurable, translation invariance of Lebesgue measure would give $1\leq \sum _ q|V|\leq 3$, which is impossible for a countably infinite sum of equal terms. Lemma 1.1.4 (Jensen's inequality) . Let $(X,P)$ be a probability space, let $I\subset \mathbb R$ be an open interval, let $\varphi \colon I	o \mathbb R$ be convex, and let $f\colon X	o I$ be an integrable function. Then $\int f\, \mathrm dP\in I$, the function $\varphi \circ f$ is measurable, its negative part is integrable, and \[  \varphi \Bigl (\int f\, \mathrm dP\Bigr )\leq \int \varphi \circ f\, \mathrm dP.  \] Proof. For $u<v$ in $I$ put $s(u,v)=(\varphi (v)-\varphi (u))/(v-u)$. If $u<v<w$ lie in $I$, then $v=\lambda u+(1-\lambda )w$ with $\lambda =(w-v)/(w-u)\in (0,1)$, and the convexity inequality $\varphi (v)\leq \lambda \varphi (u)+(1-\lambda )\varphi (w)$ is equivalent to each of the inequalities $s(u,v)\leq s(u,w)$ and $s(u,w)\leq s(v,w)$. Hence $s(u,v)$ is nondecreasing in each of its two arguments. Consequently, if $[x,y]\subset I$ and $x'<x$, $y'>y$ are points of $I$, then $s(x',x)\leq s(u,v)\leq s(y,y')$ whenever $x\leq u<v\leq y$, so $\varphi $ is Lipschitz on $[x,y]$. In particular, $\varphi $ is continuous, and $\varphi \circ f$ is measurable. Let $a=\int f\, \mathrm dP$. If $I$ has a finite left endpoint $\alpha $, then $f-\alpha >0$ on $X$, so one of the sets $\{ f-\alpha >1/k\} $, which increase to $X$, has positive measure, and therefore $a-\alpha =\int (f-\alpha )\, \mathrm dP>0$. In the same way, $a$ is smaller than a finite right endpoint of $I$; thus $a\in I$. For $u<a<w$ in $I$ we have $s(u,a)\leq s(u,w)\leq s(a,w)$, so $c=\sup _{u<a}s(u,a)$ is finite and $c\leq s(a,w)$ for every $w>a$. Hence $\varphi (y)\geq \varphi (a)+c(y-a)$ for every $y\in I$: for $y<a$ this is the inequality $s(y,a)\leq c$, and for $y>a$ it is $s(a,y)\geq c$. It follows that $\varphi \circ f\geq \varphi (a)+c(f-a)$, where the right side is integrable. Therefore the negative part of $\varphi \circ f$ is integrable, and since $\int (f-a)\, \mathrm dP=0$, integration gives $\int \varphi \circ f\, \mathrm dP\geq \varphi (a)$. $\square$ Let $(X,\mathcal M)$ and $(Y,\mathcal N)$ be measurable spaces, and let $\Phi \colon X	o Y$ be measurable, that is, $\Phi ^{-1}(E)\in \mathcal M$ for every $E\in \mathcal N$. The image of a measure $\mu $ on $X$ under $\Phi $ is the measure $\Phi _*\mu (E)=\mu (\Phi ^{-1}(E))$ on $Y$; it is countably additive because preimages preserve disjoint unions. For every $\mathcal N$-measurable function $f\geq 0$ on $Y$, \[  \int _ Yf\, \mathrm d\Phi _*\mu =\int _ Xf\circ \Phi \, \mathrm d\mu .  \] This holds for indicator functions by definition, hence for simple functions by linearity, and for general $f$ by monotone convergence, applied to simple functions $s_ k\uparrow f$ and to $s_ k\circ \Phi \uparrow f\circ \Phi $. Consequently, a function $f$ is integrable with respect to $\Phi _*\mu $ if and only if $f\circ \Phi $ is integrable with respect to $\mu $, and then the identity still holds. Lemma 1.1.5 . Let $\mu $ be a $\sigma $-finite measure on a measurable space $X$. Then every family of pairwise disjoint measurable subsets of $X$ of positive measure is countable. Proof. Write $X= igcup _ mX_ m$ with measurable sets $X_ m$ of finite measure. Every member $E$ of the family satisfies $\mu (E\cap X_ m)\geq 1/k$ for some $m$ and some integer $k\geq 1$. For fixed $m$ and $k$, at most $k\mu (X_ m)$ members have this property, because the corresponding sets $E\cap X_ m$ are pairwise disjoint subsets of $X_ m$. Hence the family is a countable union of finite subfamilies. $\square$ In particular, a $\sigma $-finite Borel measure has at most countably many atoms, that is, points of positive measure. If $\mu $ is a Radon measure on $\Omega $, which is $\sigma $-finite by proposition 1.1.2 , and $a\in \mathbb R^ d$, then $\mu (\Omega \cap \{ x:|x-a|=r\} )=0$ for all but countably many radii $r>0$, since these sets are pairwise disjoint. Uniqueness questions for measures, and the construction of product measures, rest on the following lemma. Lemma 1.1.6 . Let $\mathcal P$ be a nonempty family of subsets of a set $Z$ which is closed under finite intersections, and let $\sigma (\mathcal P)$ be the $\sigma $-algebra generated by $\mathcal P$. Every family of subsets of $Z$ which contains $\mathcal P$ and is closed under complements and countable disjoint unions contains $\sigma (\mathcal P)$. Let $\lambda $ and $\lambda '$ be finite measures on a $\sigma $-algebra containing $\sigma (\mathcal P)$. If $\lambda (Z)=\lambda '(Z)$ and $\lambda (A)=\lambda '(A)$ for every $A\in \mathcal P$, then $\lambda (E)=\lambda '(E)$ for every $E\in \sigma (\mathcal P)$. Proof. (1) Let $\mathcal L$ be the intersection of all families of subsets of $Z$ which contain $\mathcal P$ and are closed under complements and countable disjoint unions; it is the smallest such family. It contains $Z=A\cup (Z\setminus A)$ for any $A\in \mathcal P$. If $B\subset A$ belong to $\mathcal L$, so does $A\setminus B$, the complement of the disjoint union of $Z\setminus A$ and $B$. For $A\in \mathcal P$, the sets $B\in \mathcal L$ with $A\cap B\in \mathcal L$ form a family which contains $\mathcal P$ and is closed under countable disjoint unions and under complements, because $A\cap (Z\setminus B)=A\setminus (A\cap B)$; hence it equals $\mathcal L$. Thus $A\cap B\in \mathcal L$ whenever $A\in \mathcal P$ and $B\in \mathcal L$. Repeating the argument with $A\in \mathcal L$ shows that $\mathcal L$ is closed under finite intersections. Writing a countable union $ igcup _ jA_ j$ of members of $\mathcal L$ as the disjoint union of the sets $A_ j\cap (Z\setminus A_1)\cap \cdots \cap (Z\setminus A_{j-1})$, we see that $\mathcal L$ is a $\sigma $-algebra. Hence $\sigma (\mathcal P)\subset \mathcal L$, and $\mathcal L$ is contained in every family as in (1). (2) The sets $E\in \sigma (\mathcal P)$ with $\lambda (E)=\lambda '(E)$ form a family which contains $\mathcal P$, is closed under countable disjoint unions by countable additivity, and is closed under complements because $\lambda (Z\setminus E)=\lambda (Z)-\lambda (E)$ and $\lambda '(Z\setminus E)=\lambda '(Z)-\lambda '(E)$ are differences of finite numbers. By (1), this family is all of $\sigma (\mathcal P)$. $\square$ Assertion (1) is Dynkin's $\pi $–$\lambda $ theorem. Proposition 1.1.7 . Let $(X,\mu )$ and $(Y,

To apply them to Borel functions on products of topological spaces, we need to compare the Borel $\sigma $-algebra of a product with the product of the Borel $\sigma $-algebras. Lemma 1.1.8 . Let $Z_1$ and $Z_2$ be separable metric spaces, and give $Z_1	imes Z_2$ the product topology. Then the Borel $\sigma $-algebra of $Z_1	imes Z_2$ is the $\sigma $-algebra generated by the products $A_1	imes A_2$ of Borel sets $A_1\subset Z_1$ and $A_2\subset Z_2$. Consequently, every Borel function on $Z_1	imes Z_2$ is measurable for the product of the Borel $\sigma $-algebras of $Z_1$ and $Z_2$, and Tonelli's and Fubini's theorems apply to it whenever $Z_1$ and $Z_2$ carry $\sigma $-finite Borel measures. Proof. Let $p_1$ and $p_2$ be the projections of $Z_1	imes Z_2$ onto its factors. For $i=1,2$, the sets $E\subset Z_ i$ with $p_ i^{-1}(E)$ Borel form a $\sigma $-algebra which contains the open sets, because $p_ i$ is continuous; hence it contains all Borel sets. Thus $A_1	imes A_2=p_1^{-1}(A_1)\cap p_2^{-1}(A_2)$ is Borel whenever $A_1$ and $A_2$ are Borel. Conversely, we may assume that $Z_1$ and $Z_2$ are nonempty, and we choose countable dense subsets $D_1\subset Z_1$ and $D_2\subset Z_2$. Let $W\subset Z_1	imes Z_2$ be open and $(z_1,z_2)\in W$. There is $r>0$ with $B(z_1,r)	imes B(z_2,r)\subset W$, where $B(z_ i,r)$ is the open ball in $Z_ i$. Choose $a_ i\in D_ i$ with $\operatorname {dist}(a_ i,z_ i)<r/3$ and a rational number $q\in (r/3,2r/3)$; then $z_ i\in B(a_ i,q)\subset B(z_ i,r)$ by the triangle inequality. Hence $W$ is the union of those of the countably many products $B(a_1,q_1)	imes B(a_2,q_2)$, with $a_ i\in D_ i$ and positive rational $q_ i$, that are contained in $W$. Each of them is a product of open sets, so every open subset of $Z_1	imes Z_2$, and therefore every Borel subset, belongs to the $\sigma $-algebra generated by the products of Borel sets. $\square$ In particular, the Borel $\sigma $-algebra of $\mathbb R^{d_1+d_2}=\mathbb R^{d_1}	imes \mathbb R^{d_2}$ is the product of the Borel $\sigma $-algebras of the factors. On Borel sets, Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R^{d_1+d_2}$ is the product of the Lebesgue measures on the factors. Indeed, both measures assign to a product of half-open boxes the product of their volumes. These products are closed under finite intersections, and they generate the Borel $\sigma $-algebra, since every open set is a countable union of half-open boxes. By lemma 1.1.6 (2), the two measures agree on the Borel subsets of every box $[-N,N)^{d_1+d_2}$, hence on all Borel sets. Recall that the completion of a measure $\lambda $ on a $\sigma $-algebra $\mathcal A$ is its extension to the $\sigma $-algebra of all sets $E\cup N'$, where $E\in \mathcal A$ and $N'$ is contained in a $\lambda $-null set of $\mathcal A$; Lebesgue measure is the completion of its restriction to the Borel sets. A function $f$ which is measurable for the completion agrees $\lambda $-almost everywhere with an $\mathcal A$-measurable function $g$. Indeed, approximate $f$ pointwise by simple functions measurable for the completion. Replace each of their level sets by a set of $\mathcal A$ contained in it and differing from it only inside a $\lambda $-null set of $\mathcal A$, and let $g$ be the pointwise limit of the modified simple functions outside the countable union of these null sets, and $0$ on that union. In particular, every Lebesgue measurable function on $\Omega $ agrees almost everywhere with a Borel function, and in integrals with respect to Lebesgue measure we may use Borel representatives; for instance, if $v$ is a Borel function on $\mathbb R^ d$, then $(x,y)\mapsto v(x-y)$ is a Borel function on $\mathbb R^ d	imes \mathbb R^ d$. Tonelli's and Fubini's theorems are often applied to functions that are only measurable for the completion of $\mu 	imes 
u $; statements about almost every section of such a function refer to a product-measurable representative. Let $\alpha $ and $ eta $ be Radon measures on $\Omega $. The difference $\sigma =\alpha - eta $ is defined on the relatively compact Borel subsets of $\Omega $, and on all Borel subsets if $\alpha $ and $ eta $ are finite. We call $\sigma $ a real signed Radon measure, and a finite real signed measure if $\alpha $ and $ eta $ are finite. The total variation of $\sigma $ is \[  |\sigma |(A)=\sup _{A= igsqcup _{i=1}^ m A_ i}\sum _{i=1}^ m|\sigma (A_ i)|,  \] where $A$ is a relatively compact Borel set and the supremum is taken over all finite partitions of $A$ into Borel sets. Since $|\sigma (A_ i)|\leq \alpha (A_ i)+ eta (A_ i)$, we have $|\sigma |\leq \alpha + eta $. We show that $|\sigma |$ is countably additive on the relatively compact Borel sets. It is finitely additive: if $A=A'\sqcup A''$, combining partitions of $A'$ and $A''$ gives $|\sigma |(A)\geq |\sigma |(A')+|\sigma |(A'')$, and intersecting a partition of $A$ with $A'$ and $A''$ gives the reverse inequality by the triangle inequality. If $A$ is the union of disjoint Borel sets $A_ j$, finite additivity and monotonicity give $|\sigma |(A)\geq \sum _ j|\sigma |(A_ j)$. Conversely, for every finite partition $A= igsqcup _ iB_ i$, countable additivity of $\sigma $ gives $\sum _ i|\sigma (B_ i)|\leq \sum _ i\sum _ j|\sigma (B_ i\cap A_ j)|\leq \sum _ j|\sigma |(A_ j)$. This argument uses only the countable additivity of $\sigma $ on relatively compact Borel sets, the bound $|\sigma |\leq \alpha + eta $ and the triangle inequality. To extend $|\sigma |$ to all Borel sets, let $(K_ j)$ be a compact exhaustion of $\Omega $ and $K_0=\varnothing $. The relatively compact Borel sets $B_ j=K_ j\setminus K_{j-1}$ partition $\Omega $, and we put $|\sigma |(E)=\sum _ j|\sigma |(E\cap B_ j)$ for Borel sets $E\subset \Omega $. This extension is countably additive, by rearrangement of double series of nonnegative terms, and it agrees with the previous definition on relatively compact sets by countable additivity there. It is bounded by $\alpha + eta $, hence finite on compact sets, so it is a Radon measure by proposition 1.1.2 . In the same way, the set functions $\sigma ^\pm =(|\sigma |\pm \sigma )/2$, which are nonnegative because $|\sigma (A)|\leq |\sigma |(A)$, extend to Radon measures, and $\sigma =\sigma ^+-\sigma ^-$ and $|\sigma |=\sigma ^++\sigma ^-$ on relatively compact Borel sets. For a Borel function $f$ which is integrable with respect to $|\sigma |$, for instance a bounded Borel function with compact support, we put $\int f\, \mathrm d\sigma =\int f\, \mathrm d\sigma ^+-\int f\, \mathrm d\sigma ^-$. The measures $\sigma ^++ eta $ and $\alpha +\sigma ^-$ agree on relatively compact Borel sets, hence on all Borel sets, so $\int f\, \mathrm d\sigma =\int f\, \mathrm d\alpha -\int f\, \mathrm d eta $ whenever $f$ is integrable with respect to $\alpha + eta $. The inequality $|\int f\, \mathrm d\sigma |\leq \int |f|\, \mathrm d|\sigma |$ holds for simple $f$ because $|\sigma ^+(A)-\sigma ^-(A)|\leq |\sigma |(A)$, and in general by approximation with simple functions $s_ k	o f$, $|s_ k|\leq |f|$, and dominated convergence. In this way, convergence theorems and iterated integrals for signed measures reduce to the positive case.

title: Radon measure
text: Definition 1.1.1 . A Radon measure on $\Omega $ is a Borel measure $\mu $ on $\Omega $ which is finite on compact sets and satisfies, for every Borel set $E\subset \Omega $, \[  \mu (E)=\inf _{E\subset U,\  U\text{ open}}\mu (U) =\sup _{K\subset E,\  K\text{ compact}}\mu (K).  \] The two equalities are called outer and inner regularity of $\mu $. A measurable function is locally integrable with respect to $\mu $ if its absolute value has finite integral over every compact subset of $\Omega $.

title: Borel regularity
text: Proposition 1.1.2 . Let $\mu $ be a Borel measure on $\Omega $ which is finite on compact subsets. Then $\mu $ is a Radon measure. In particular, $\mu $ is $\sigma $-finite. Proof. Assume first that $\mu (\Omega )<\infty $, and let $F\subset \Omega $ be relatively closed; we may assume that $F\neq \varnothing $. The open sets $U_ j=\{ x\in \Omega :\operatorname {dist}(x,F)<j^{-1}\} $ decrease to $F$, so $\mu (U_ j)\to \mu (F)$ because $\mu $ is finite. Hence $F$ can be approximated in measure from outside by open sets. Passing to complements, every open set can be approximated from inside by relatively closed sets. Let $\mathcal A$ be the class of Borel sets $E$ such that for every $\varepsilon >0$ there are an open set $U$ and a relatively closed set $F$ with $F\subset E\subset U$ and $\mu (U\setminus F)<\varepsilon $. We have just seen that $\mathcal A$ contains the relatively closed sets, and $\mathcal A$ is closed under complements because the condition is symmetric. To see that $\mathcal A$ is closed under countable unions, let $E=\bigcup _ jE_ j$ with $E_ j\in \mathcal A$, and choose $F_ j\subset E_ j\subset U_ j$ with $\mu (U_ j\setminus F_ j)<\varepsilon 2^{-j}$. The open set $U=\bigcup _ jU_ j$ satisfies $\mu (U\setminus E)<\varepsilon $. Since $\mu (\bigcup _{j\leq N}E_ j)\to \mu (E)$, there is $N$ such that the relatively closed set $F=\bigcup _{j\leq N}F_ j$ satisfies $\mu (E\setminus F)\leq \mu (E\setminus \bigcup _{j\leq N}E_ j)+\sum _{j\leq N}\mu (E_ j\setminus F_ j)<2\varepsilon $, and hence $\mu (U\setminus F)<3\varepsilon $. Thus $\mathcal A$ is a $\sigma $-algebra containing the open sets, so it contains every Borel set $E$. If $F\subset E$ is relatively closed and $(K_ j)$ is a compact exhaustion of $\Omega $, then the sets $F\cap K_ j$ are compact and $\mu (F\setminus K_ j)\to 0$. Hence every Borel set can be approximated in measure from outside by open sets and from inside by compact sets. In general, let $(K_ j)$ be a compact exhaustion of $\Omega $, put $K_0=\varnothing $, and let $V_ j=\operatorname{Int}K_{j+1}$. The measures $\mu _ j(E)=\mu (E\cap V_ j)$ are finite, hence Radon by the first part. For inner regularity, let $E$ be a Borel set and $\varepsilon >0$. A compact set $K\subset E$ with $\mu _ j(E\setminus K)<\varepsilon $ satisfies $\mu (K)\geq \mu _ j(K)>\mu (E\cap V_ j)-\varepsilon $, and $\mu (E\cap V_ j)\to \mu (E)$ as $j\to \infty $. For outer regularity, note that the Borel sets $B_ j=K_ j\setminus K_{j-1}$ partition $\Omega $ and that $E\cap B_ j\subset V_ j$. By outer regularity of $\mu _ j$ there is an open set $O_ j\subset V_ j$ containing $E\cap B_ j$ with $\mu (O_ j\setminus (E\cap B_ j))<\varepsilon 2^{-j}$; it suffices to intersect an approximating open set with $V_ j$. Then $O=\bigcup _ jO_ j$ is an open set containing $E$ with $\mu (O\setminus E)<\varepsilon $. Finally, $\mu $ is $\sigma $-finite because $\Omega =\bigcup _ jK_ j$ and each $\mu (K_ j)$ is finite. $\square$

title: Integral limits
text: Proposition 1.1.3 . Let $(X,\mu )$ be a measure space and let $f_ j$, $j\geq 1$, be measurable functions on $X$. If $f_ j\geq 0$ and $f_ j\uparrow f$ pointwise, then $\int f_ j\, \mathrm d\mu \uparrow \int f\, \mathrm d\mu $. If $f_ j\geq 0$ for every $j$, then \[  \int \varliminf _ j f_ j\, \mathrm d\mu \leq \varliminf _ j\int f_ j\, \mathrm d\mu .  \] If the $f_ j$ are real or complex, converge almost everywhere to a measurable function $f$, and satisfy $|f_ j|\leq g$ for an integrable function $g$, then $f$ is integrable and $\int |f_ j-f|\, \mathrm d\mu \to 0$. Proof. (1) The integrals $\int f_ j\, \mathrm d\mu $ increase and are bounded by $\int f\, \mathrm d\mu $, so we must show that their limit is at least $\int f\, \mathrm d\mu $. Let $s\leq f$ be a nonnegative simple function and $0<t<1$. The measurable sets $E_ j=\{ f_ j\geq ts\} $ increase with $j$, and their union contains $\{ s>0\} $, since $f(x)\geq s(x)>ts(x)$ there. Applying continuity from below to the sets $E_ j\cap \{ s=a\} $ for the finitely many values $a$ of $s$, we obtain \[  \lim _ j\int f_ j\, \mathrm d\mu \geq \lim _ jt\int _{E_ j}s\, \mathrm d\mu =t\int s\, \mathrm d\mu .  \] Taking the supremum over $s$ and then letting $t\uparrow 1$ proves (1); infinite integrals are allowed. (2) The functions $g_ j=\inf _{k\geq j}f_ k$ are measurable, they increase to $\varliminf _ jf_ j$, and $\int g_ j\, \mathrm d\mu \leq \int f_ k\, \mathrm d\mu $ for every $k\geq j$. Applying (1) to $(g_ j)$ gives (2). (3) Letting $j\to \infty $ in $|f_ j|\leq g$ gives $|f|\leq g$ almost everywhere, so $f$ is integrable. The functions $2g-|f_ j-f|$ are nonnegative almost everywhere, and (2), applied after a modification on a null set, gives \[  \int 2g\, \mathrm d\mu \leq \varliminf _ j\int \bigl (2g-|f_ j-f|\bigr )\, \mathrm d\mu =\int 2g\, \mathrm d\mu -\varlimsup _ j\int |f_ j-f|\, \mathrm d\mu .  \] Since $\int 2g\, \mathrm d\mu <\infty $, it follows that $\int |f_ j-f|\, \mathrm d\mu \to 0$. $\square$

title: Jensen's inequality
text: Lemma 1.1.4 (Jensen's inequality) . Let $(X,P)$ be a probability space, let $I\subset \mathbb R$ be an open interval, let $\varphi \colon I\to \mathbb R$ be convex, and let $f\colon X\to I$ be an integrable function. Then $\int f\, \mathrm dP\in I$, the function $\varphi \circ f$ is measurable, its negative part is integrable, and \[  \varphi \Bigl (\int f\, \mathrm dP\Bigr )\leq \int \varphi \circ f\, \mathrm dP.  \] Proof. For $u<v$ in $I$ put $s(u,v)=(\varphi (v)-\varphi (u))/(v-u)$. If $u<v<w$ lie in $I$, then $v=\lambda u+(1-\lambda )w$ with $\lambda =(w-v)/(w-u)\in (0,1)$, and the convexity inequality $\varphi (v)\leq \lambda \varphi (u)+(1-\lambda )\varphi (w)$ is equivalent to each of the inequalities $s(u,v)\leq s(u,w)$ and $s(u,w)\leq s(v,w)$. Hence $s(u,v)$ is nondecreasing in each of its two arguments. Consequently, if $[x,y]\subset I$ and $x'<x$, $y'>y$ are points of $I$, then $s(x',x)\leq s(u,v)\leq s(y,y')$ whenever $x\leq u<v\leq y$, so $\varphi $ is Lipschitz on $[x,y]$. In particular, $\varphi $ is continuous, and $\varphi \circ f$ is measurable. Let $a=\int f\, \mathrm dP$. If $I$ has a finite left endpoint $\alpha $, then $f-\alpha >0$ on $X$, so one of the sets $\{ f-\alpha >1/k\} $, which increase to $X$, has positive measure, and therefore $a-\alpha =\int (f-\alpha )\, \mathrm dP>0$. In the same way, $a$ is smaller than a finite right endpoint of $I$; thus $a\in I$. For $u<a<w$ in $I$ we have $s(u,a)\leq s(u,w)\leq s(a,w)$, so $c=\sup _{u<a}s(u,a)$ is finite and $c\leq s(a,w)$ for every $w>a$. Hence $\varphi (y)\geq \varphi (a)+c(y-a)$ for every $y\in I$: for $y<a$ this is the inequality $s(y,a)\leq c$, and for $y>a$ it is $s(a,y)\geq c$. It follows that $\varphi \circ f\geq \varphi (a)+c(f-a)$, where the right side is integrable. Therefore the negative part of $\varphi \circ f$ is integrable, and since $\int (f-a)\, \mathrm dP=0$, integration gives $\int \varphi \circ f\, \mathrm dP\geq \varphi (a)$. $\square$

title: Disjoint positive countable
text: Lemma 1.1.5 . Let $\mu $ be a $\sigma $-finite measure on a measurable space $X$. Then every family of pairwise disjoint measurable subsets of $X$ of positive measure is countable. Proof. Write $X=\bigcup _ mX_ m$ with measurable sets $X_ m$ of finite measure. Every member $E$ of the family satisfies $\mu (E\cap X_ m)\geq 1/k$ for some $m$ and some integer $k\geq 1$. For fixed $m$ and $k$, at most $k\mu (X_ m)$ members have this property, because the corresponding sets $E\cap X_ m$ are pairwise disjoint subsets of $X_ m$. Hence the family is a countable union of finite subfamilies. $\square$

title: Pi lambda
text: Lemma 1.1.6 . Let $\mathcal P$ be a nonempty family of subsets of a set $Z$ which is closed under finite intersections, and let $\sigma (\mathcal P)$ be the $\sigma $-algebra generated by $\mathcal P$. Every family of subsets of $Z$ which contains $\mathcal P$ and is closed under complements and countable disjoint unions contains $\sigma (\mathcal P)$. Let $\lambda $ and $\lambda '$ be finite measures on a $\sigma $-algebra containing $\sigma (\mathcal P)$. If $\lambda (Z)=\lambda '(Z)$ and $\lambda (A)=\lambda '(A)$ for every $A\in \mathcal P$, then $\lambda (E)=\lambda '(E)$ for every $E\in \sigma (\mathcal P)$. Proof. (1) Let $\mathcal L$ be the intersection of all families of subsets of $Z$ which contain $\mathcal P$ and are closed under complements and countable disjoint unions; it is the smallest such family. It contains $Z=A\cup (Z\setminus A)$ for any $A\in \mathcal P$. If $B\subset A$ belong to $\mathcal L$, so does $A\setminus B$, the complement of the disjoint union of $Z\setminus A$ and $B$. For $A\in \mathcal P$, the sets $B\in \mathcal L$ with $A\cap B\in \mathcal L$ form a family which contains $\mathcal P$ and is closed under countable disjoint unions and under complements, because $A\cap (Z\setminus B)=A\setminus (A\cap B)$; hence it equals $\mathcal L$. Thus $A\cap B\in \mathcal L$ whenever $A\in \mathcal P$ and $B\in \mathcal L$. Repeating the argument with $A\in \mathcal L$ shows that $\mathcal L$ is closed under finite intersections. Writing a countable union $\bigcup _ jA_ j$ of members of $\mathcal L$ as the disjoint union of the sets $A_ j\cap (Z\setminus A_1)\cap \cdots \cap (Z\setminus A_{j-1})$, we see that $\mathcal L$ is a $\sigma $-algebra. Hence $\sigma (\mathcal P)\subset \mathcal L$, and $\mathcal L$ is contained in every family as in (1). (2) The sets $E\in \sigma (\mathcal P)$ with $\lambda (E)=\lambda '(E)$ form a family which contains $\mathcal P$, is closed under countable disjoint unions by countable additivity, and is closed under complements because $\lambda (Z\setminus E)=\lambda (Z)-\lambda (E)$ and $\lambda '(Z\setminus E)=\lambda '(Z)-\lambda '(E)$ are differences of finite numbers. By (1), this family is all of $\sigma (\mathcal P)$. $\square$

title: Borel product separable
text: Lemma 1.1.8 . Let $Z_1$ and $Z_2$ be separable metric spaces, and give $Z_1\times Z_2$ the product topology. Then the Borel $\sigma $-algebra of $Z_1\times Z_2$ is the $\sigma $-algebra generated by the products $A_1\times A_2$ of Borel sets $A_1\subset Z_1$ and $A_2\subset Z_2$. Consequently, every Borel function on $Z_1\times Z_2$ is measurable for the product of the Borel $\sigma $-algebras of $Z_1$ and $Z_2$, and Tonelli's and Fubini's theorems apply to it whenever $Z_1$ and $Z_2$ carry $\sigma $-finite Borel measures. Proof. Let $p_1$ and $p_2$ be the projections of $Z_1\times Z_2$ onto its factors. For $i=1,2$, the sets $E\subset Z_ i$ with $p_ i^{-1}(E)$ Borel form a $\sigma $-algebra which contains the open sets, because $p_ i$ is continuous; hence it contains all Borel sets. Thus $A_1\times A_2=p_1^{-1}(A_1)\cap p_2^{-1}(A_2)$ is Borel whenever $A_1$ and $A_2$ are Borel. Conversely, we may assume that $Z_1$ and $Z_2$ are nonempty, and we choose countable dense subsets $D_1\subset Z_1$ and $D_2\subset Z_2$. Let $W\subset Z_1\times Z_2$ be open and $(z_1,z_2)\in W$. There is $r>0$ with $B(z_1,r)\times B(z_2,r)\subset W$, where $B(z_ i,r)$ is the open ball in $Z_ i$. Choose $a_ i\in D_ i$ with $\operatorname {dist}(a_ i,z_ i)<r/3$ and a rational number $q\in (r/3,2r/3)$; then $z_ i\in B(a_ i,q)\subset B(z_ i,r)$ by the triangle inequality. Hence $W$ is the union of those of the countably many products $B(a_1,q_1)\times B(a_2,q_2)$, with $a_ i\in D_ i$ and positive rational $q_ i$, that are contained in $W$. Each of them is a product of open sets, so every open subset of $Z_1\times Z_2$, and therefore every Borel subset, belongs to the $\sigma $-algebra generated by the products of Borel sets. $\square$

title: Positive linear functionals
text:
1.2 Positive linear functionals A linear functional $L\colon C_ c(\Omega ,\mathbb R)	o \mathbb R$ is positive if $L(f)\geq 0$ whenever $f\geq 0$. Integration against a Radon measure is the basic example, and the Riesz representation theorem below shows that there are no others. Positivity alone gives a local bound. Let $K\subset \Omega $ be compact and let $\eta $ be a cutoff function for $K$ in $\Omega $. If $f\in C_ c(\Omega ,\mathbb R)$ and $\operatorname{Supp}f\subset K$, then $\| f\| _\infty \eta \pm f\geq 0$, and therefore 1.1  egin{equation} \label{eq:positive-functional-bound} |L(f)|\leq L(\eta )\| f\| _\infty ,\qquad \operatorname{Supp}f\subset K, \end{equation} where the constant $L(\eta )$ depends on $K$ but not on $f$. The measure representing $L$ is obtained from an outer measure. Recall that an outer measure on a set $X$ is a function $m^*$ from the subsets of $X$ to $[0,\infty ]$ such that $m^*(\varnothing )=0$, $m^*(A)\leq m^*(B)$ whenever $A\subset B$, and $m^*( igcup _ jA_ j)\leq \sum _ jm^*(A_ j)$ for every sequence of subsets. A set $F\subset X$ is $m^*$-measurable if $m^*(E)=m^*(E\cap F)+m^*(E\setminus F)$ for every $E\subset X$. For subsets $A,B$ of a metric space, $\operatorname {dist}(A,B)$ is the infimum of the distances between points of $A$ and of $B$, and $+\infty $ if $A$ or $B$ is empty. Lemma 1.2.1 . Let $m^*$ be an outer measure on a metric space $X$ such that \[  m^*(A\cup B)=m^*(A)+m^*(B)\quad 	ext{whenever }\operatorname {dist}(A,B)>0.  \] Then every Borel subset of $X$ is $m^*$-measurable, and the restriction of $m^*$ to the Borel sets is a measure. Proof. We first show that the $m^*$-measurable sets form a $\sigma $-algebra on which $m^*$ is countably additive. The definition is symmetric in $F$ and $X\setminus F$, so complements of measurable sets are measurable. If $F$ and $G$ are measurable and $E\subset X$, splitting $E$ by $F$ and then $E\cap F$ by $G$ gives \[   egin{split}  m^*(E)& =m^*(E\cap F\cap G)+m^*((E\cap F)\setminus G)+m^*(E\setminus F)\ & \geq m^*(E\cap F\cap G)+m^*(E\setminus (F\cap G)), \end{split}  \] where the inequality follows from subadditivity, since $E\setminus (F\cap G)=((E\cap F)\setminus G)\cup (E\setminus F)$. The reverse inequality is again subadditivity, so $F\cap G$ is measurable. If $F_1,F_2,\ldots $ are disjoint measurable sets with union $F$, splitting $E$ successively by $F_1,\ldots ,F_ N$ gives \[  m^*(E)=\sum _{j=1}^ Nm^*(E\cap F_ j)+m^*\Bigl (E\setminus  igcup _{j=1}^ NF_ j\Bigr )\geq \sum _{j=1}^ Nm^*(E\cap F_ j)+m^*(E\setminus F).  \] Letting $N	o \infty $ and using subadditivity, we obtain $m^*(E)\geq m^*(E\cap F)+m^*(E\setminus F)$, so $F$ is measurable, and the choice $E=F$ gives $m^*(F)=\sum _ jm^*(F_ j)$. As every countable union of measurable sets is a disjoint union of measurable sets, this proves the claim. It remains to show that every nonempty closed set $F\subset X$ is measurable. By subadditivity, we only need $m^*(E)\geq m^*(E\cap F)+m^*(E\setminus F)$, and only for sets $E\subset X$ with $m^*(E)<\infty $. For $N\geq 1$ put $E_ N=\{ x\in E:\operatorname {dist}(x,F)\geq N^{-1}\} $. Since $\operatorname {dist}(E\cap F,E_ N)\geq N^{-1}$, the hypothesis gives $m^*(E)\geq m^*(E\cap F)+m^*(E_ N)$, and it suffices to show that $m^*(E_ N)	o m^*(E\setminus F)$. Consider the layers \[  A_ k=\{ x\in E:(k+1)^{-1}\leq \operatorname {dist}(x,F)<k^{-1}\} ,\qquad k\geq 1.  \] Since $\operatorname {dist}(\cdot ,F)$ is $1$-Lipschitz, $\operatorname {dist}(A_ k,A_{k'})\geq (k+1)^{-1}-(k+2)^{-1}>0$ whenever $k'\geq k+2$. Hence finitely many layers whose indices have the same parity are pairwise at positive distance, and repeated use of the hypothesis shows that the sum of their outer measures is at most $m^*(E)$. Consequently $\sum _ km^*(A_ k)\leq 2m^*(E)<\infty $. Since $F$ is closed, $E\setminus F\subset E_ N\cup  igcup _{k\geq N}A_ k$, and therefore \[  m^*(E_ N)\leq m^*(E\setminus F)\leq m^*(E_ N)+\sum _{k\geq N}m^*(A_ k).  \] The tails of the convergent series tend to zero, so $m^*(E_ N)	o m^*(E\setminus F)$. Thus the $\sigma $-algebra of $m^*$-measurable sets contains the closed sets, and hence all Borel sets. $\square$ This is Carathéodory's criterion for metric outer measures. Theorem 1.2.2 (Riesz representation) . Let $L$ be a positive linear functional on $C_ c(\Omega ,\mathbb R)$. Then there is a unique Radon measure $\mu $ on $\Omega $ such that $L(f)=\int f\, \mathrm d\mu $ for every $f\in C_ c(\Omega ,\mathbb R)$. Proof. We construct $\mu $ from a metric outer measure (lemma 1.2.1 ) and identify $L$ with integration against $\mu $ by slicing functions into level sets. Call $f$ admissible for an open set $U\subset \Omega $ if $f\in C_ c(\Omega ,\mathbb R)$, $0\leq f\leq 1$ and $\operatorname{Supp}f\subset U$, and put \[  m(U)=\sup \{ L(f):f	ext{ admissible for }U\} .  \] Then $m(\varnothing )=0$, and $m$ is monotone. Step 1: $m$ is countably subadditive on open sets and additive on disjoint ones. Let $U_1,U_2,\ldots $ be open and let $f$ be admissible for $U= igcup _ jU_ j$. Covering $\operatorname{Supp}f$ by finitely many open balls whose closures lie in some $U_ j$, we find $n$ and compact, possibly empty, sets $K_ j\subset U_ j$, $1\leq j\leq n$, which cover $\operatorname{Supp}f$. If $\eta _ j$ is a cutoff function for $K_ j$ in $U_ j$, then $\eta =\sum _{j=1}^ n\eta _ j\geq 1$ on $\operatorname{Supp}f$, so $\eta >0$ on an open neighborhood $W$ of $\operatorname{Supp}f$. The functions $f_ j$ equal to $f\eta _ j/\eta $ on $W$ and to $0$ on $\Omega \setminus \operatorname{Supp}f$ are continuous, since both formulas give $0$ where these open sets overlap; moreover $0\leq f_ j\leq f$, $\operatorname{Supp}f_ j\subset U_ j$ and $\sum _ jf_ j=f$. Hence $L(f)=\sum _{j=1}^ nL(f_ j)\leq \sum _ jm(U_ j)$, and so $m(U)\leq \sum _ jm(U_ j)$. If the $U_ j$ are pairwise disjoint and $h_ j$ is admissible for $U_ j$, then the $h_ j$ have disjoint supports, so $\sum _{j\leq N}h_ j$ is admissible for $U$; taking suprema shows that $m$ is countably additive on disjoint open sets. Step 2: construction of $\mu $. For $A\subset \Omega $ put $m^*(A)=\inf \{ m(U):U\supset A	ext{ open}\} $. Then $m^*(U)=m(U)$ for open $U$ by monotonicity of $m$. If $\sum _ jm^*(A_ j)<\infty $ (otherwise there is nothing to prove) and $\varepsilon >0$, open sets $U_ j\supset A_ j$ with $m(U_ j)<m^*(A_ j)+\varepsilon 2^{-j}$ give $m^*( igcup _ jA_ j)\leq \sum _ jm^*(A_ j)+\varepsilon $ by Step 1. Thus $m^*$ is an outer measure. Let $A,B\subset \Omega $ be nonempty with $\operatorname {dist}(A,B)=2r>0$, and let $W\supset A\cup B$ be open. The sets $W\cap \{ \operatorname {dist}(\cdot ,A)<r\} $ and $W\cap \{ \operatorname {dist}(\cdot ,B)<r\} $ are open neighborhoods of $A$ and $B$ in $W$, which are disjoint by the triangle inequality, so Step 1 gives $m(W)\geq m^*(A)+m^*(B)$. Taking the infimum over $W$, we obtain the hypothesis of lemma 1.2.1 (if $A$ or $B$ is empty, it holds because $m^*(\varnothing )=0$), and that lemma yields a Borel measure $\mu $ with $\mu (U)=m(U)$ for open $U$. It remains to show that $\mu $ is finite on compact sets. Every compact set $K\subset \Omega $ has a relatively compact open neighborhood $V$ in $\Omega $, for instance the set $V$ used in the construction of cutoff functions in section 1.1 . If $\eta $ is a cutoff function for $\overline V$ in $\Omega $, then ( 1.1 ) gives $L(f)\leq L(\eta )$ for every $f$ admissible for $V$, so $\mu (K)\leq m(V)\leq L(\eta )<\infty $. By proposition 1.1.2 , $\mu $ is a Radon measure. Step 3: $L(f)=\int f\, \mathrm d\mu $. By linearity, it suffices to treat $f\geq 0$ with $M=\| f\| _\infty >0$. Fix an integer $N\geq 1$, put $\delta =M/N$, and let $U_ k=\{ f>k\delta \} $ for $k\geq 0$, so that $\mu (U_ k)\leq \mu (\operatorname{Supp}f)<\infty $. If $h_ k$ is admissible for $U_ k$, $1\leq k\leq N$, then $h_ k\leq \mathbf1_{U_ k}$, and since at most $f(x)/\delta $ indices $k\geq 1$ satisfy $f(x)>k\delta $, we have $\delta \sum _{k=1}^ Nh_ k\leq \delta \sum _{k=1}^ N\mathbf1_{U_ k}\leq f$. Positivity of $L$ and the supremum over the $h_ k$ give the lower bound \[  \delta \sum _{k=1}^ N\mu (U_ k)\leq L(f).  \] For an upper bound, put $g_ k=\min \{ 1,\max \{ 0,f/\delta -(k-1)\} \} $ for $1\leq k\leq N$; these are continuous with values in $[0,1]$, and $f=\delta \sum _{k=1}^ Ng_ k$. If $\eta $ is a cutoff function for $\operatorname{Supp}f$ in $\Omega $, then $g_1\leq \eta $, so $L(g_1)\leq L(\eta )$. For $k\geq 2$, $g_ k$ vanishes outside the compact set $\{ f\geq (k-1)\delta \} \subset U_{k-2}$, so it is admissible for $U_{k-2}$ and $L(g_ k)\leq \mu (U_{k-2})$. Consequently \[  L(f)\leq \delta L(\eta )+\delta \sum _{k=2}^ N\mu (U_{k-2}),  \] and the upper bound exceeds the lower bound by \[  \delta L(\eta )+\delta  igl (\mu (U_0)-\mu (U_{N-1})-\mu (U_ N) igr )\leq \delta  igl (L(\eta )+\mu (\operatorname{Supp}f) igr ).  \] On the other hand, the simple function $s_ N=\delta \sum _{k=1}^ N\mathbf1_{U_ k}$ satisfies $0\leq f-s_ N\leq \delta $ and vanishes outside $\operatorname{Supp}f$, so $\int f\, \mathrm d\mu $ exceeds the lower bound $\int s_ N\, \mathrm d\mu $ by at most $\delta \mu (\operatorname{Supp}f)$. Hence $|L(f)-\int f\, \mathrm d\mu |\leq \delta (L(\eta )+\mu (\operatorname{Supp}f))$, and letting $N	o \infty $ gives $L(f)=\int f\, \mathrm d\mu $. Step 4: uniqueness. Let $
u $ be any Radon measure on $\Omega $ and $U\subset \Omega $ open. If $K\subset U$ is compact and $\eta $ is a cutoff function for $K$ in $U$, then $
u (K)\leq \int \eta \, \mathrm d
u \leq 
u (U)$, so inner regularity gives 1.4  egin{equation} \label{eq:measure-open-tests} 
u (U)=\sup \left\{ \int f\, \mathrm d
u :0\leq f\leq 1,\  f\in C_ c(\Omega ),\  \operatorname{Supp}f\subset Uight\} . \end{equation} Hence two Radon measures inducing the same functional agree on open sets, and by outer regularity on all Borel sets. $\square$ Proposition 1.2.3 . Let $\mu $ be a Radon measure on $\Omega $ and let $1\leq p<\infty $. Then $C_ c(\Omega )$ is dense in $L^ p(\mu )$. Proof. Let $u\in L^ p(\mu )$ and let $(K_ j)$ be a compact exhaustion of $\Omega $. The functions $u\mathbf1_{K_ j\cap \{ |u|\leq j\} }$ converge to $u$ in $L^ p(\mu )$ by dominated convergence (proposition 1.1.3 ), so it suffices to approximate a bounded Borel function $v$ vanishing outside a compact set $K$. A uniform approximation of $\operatorname{Re}v$ and $\operatorname{Im}v$ by simple functions vanishing outside $K$, with error $\delta $, has $L^ p(\mu )$ error at most $2\delta \mu (K)^{1/p}$; we are thus reduced to indicator functions $\mathbf1_ E$ of Borel sets $E\subset K$. Given $\varepsilon >0$, regularity of $\mu $ gives a compact set $K'\subset E$ and an open set $U\supset E$ with $\mu (U\setminus K')<\varepsilon $. A cutoff function $\eta $ for $K'$ in $U$ satisfies $|\eta -\mathbf1_ E|\leq \mathbf1_{U\setminus K'}$, so $\| \eta -\mathbf1_ E\| _{L^ p(\mu )}^ p<\varepsilon $. $\square$

title: Positive functional bound
text: 1.1 \begin{equation} \label{eq:positive-functional-bound} |L(f)|\leq L(\eta )\| f\| _\infty ,\qquad \operatorname{Supp}f\subset K, \end{equation}

title: Metric outer measure
text: Lemma 1.2.1 . Let $m^*$ be an outer measure on a metric space $X$ such that \[  m^*(A\cup B)=m^*(A)+m^*(B)\quad \text{whenever }\operatorname {dist}(A,B)>0.  \] Then every Borel subset of $X$ is $m^*$-measurable, and the restriction of $m^*$ to the Borel sets is a measure. Proof. We first show that the $m^*$-measurable sets form a $\sigma $-algebra on which $m^*$ is countably additive. The definition is symmetric in $F$ and $X\setminus F$, so complements of measurable sets are measurable. If $F$ and $G$ are measurable and $E\subset X$, splitting $E$ by $F$ and then $E\cap F$ by $G$ gives \[  \begin{split}  m^*(E)& =m^*(E\cap F\cap G)+m^*((E\cap F)\setminus G)+m^*(E\setminus F)\\ & \geq m^*(E\cap F\cap G)+m^*(E\setminus (F\cap G)), \end{split}  \] where the inequality follows from subadditivity, since $E\setminus (F\cap G)=((E\cap F)\setminus G)\cup (E\setminus F)$. The reverse inequality is again subadditivity, so $F\cap G$ is measurable. If $F_1,F_2,\ldots $ are disjoint measurable sets with union $F$, splitting $E$ successively by $F_1,\ldots ,F_ N$ gives \[  m^*(E)=\sum _{j=1}^ Nm^*(E\cap F_ j)+m^*\Bigl (E\setminus \bigcup _{j=1}^ NF_ j\Bigr )\geq \sum _{j=1}^ Nm^*(E\cap F_ j)+m^*(E\setminus F).  \] Letting $N\to \infty $ and using subadditivity, we obtain $m^*(E)\geq m^*(E\cap F)+m^*(E\setminus F)$, so $F$ is measurable, and the choice $E=F$ gives $m^*(F)=\sum _ jm^*(F_ j)$. As every countable union of measurable sets is a disjoint union of measurable sets, this proves the claim. It remains to show that every nonempty closed set $F\subset X$ is measurable. By subadditivity, we only need $m^*(E)\geq m^*(E\cap F)+m^*(E\setminus F)$, and only for sets $E\subset X$ with $m^*(E)<\infty $. For $N\geq 1$ put $E_ N=\{ x\in E:\operatorname {dist}(x,F)\geq N^{-1}\} $. Since $\operatorname {dist}(E\cap F,E_ N)\geq N^{-1}$, the hypothesis gives $m^*(E)\geq m^*(E\cap F)+m^*(E_ N)$, and it suffices to show that $m^*(E_ N)\to m^*(E\setminus F)$. Consider the layers \[  A_ k=\{ x\in E:(k+1)^{-1}\leq \operatorname {dist}(x,F)<k^{-1}\} ,\qquad k\geq 1.  \] Since $\operatorname {dist}(\cdot ,F)$ is $1$-Lipschitz, $\operatorname {dist}(A_ k,A_{k'})\geq (k+1)^{-1}-(k+2)^{-1}>0$ whenever $k'\geq k+2$. Hence finitely many layers whose indices have the same parity are pairwise at positive distance, and repeated use of the hypothesis shows that the sum of their outer measures is at most $m^*(E)$. Consequently $\sum _ km^*(A_ k)\leq 2m^*(E)<\infty $. Since $F$ is closed, $E\setminus F\subset E_ N\cup \bigcup _{k\geq N}A_ k$, and therefore \[  m^*(E_ N)\leq m^*(E\setminus F)\leq m^*(E_ N)+\sum _{k\geq N}m^*(A_ k).  \] The tails of the convergent series tend to zero, so $m^*(E_ N)\to m^*(E\setminus F)$. Thus the $\sigma $-algebra of $m^*$-measurable sets contains the closed sets, and hence all Borel sets. $\square$

title: Riesz representation
text:
Theorem 1.2.2 (Riesz representation) . Let $L$ be a positive linear functional on $C_ c(\Omega ,\mathbb R)$. Then there is a unique Radon measure $\mu $ on $\Omega $ such that $L(f)=\int f\, \mathrm d\mu $ for every $f\in C_ c(\Omega ,\mathbb R)$. Proof. We construct $\mu $ from a metric outer measure (lemma 1.2.1 ) and identify $L$ with integration against $\mu $ by slicing functions into level sets. Call $f$ admissible for an open set $U\subset \Omega $ if $f\in C_ c(\Omega ,\mathbb R)$, $0\leq f\leq 1$ and $\operatorname{Supp}f\subset U$, and put \[  m(U)=\sup \{ L(f):f	ext{ admissible for }U\} .  \] Then $m(\varnothing )=0$, and $m$ is monotone. Step 1: $m$ is countably subadditive on open sets and additive on disjoint ones. Let $U_1,U_2,\ldots $ be open and let $f$ be admissible for $U= igcup _ jU_ j$. Covering $\operatorname{Supp}f$ by finitely many open balls whose closures lie in some $U_ j$, we find $n$ and compact, possibly empty, sets $K_ j\subset U_ j$, $1\leq j\leq n$, which cover $\operatorname{Supp}f$. If $\eta _ j$ is a cutoff function for $K_ j$ in $U_ j$, then $\eta =\sum _{j=1}^ n\eta _ j\geq 1$ on $\operatorname{Supp}f$, so $\eta >0$ on an open neighborhood $W$ of $\operatorname{Supp}f$. The functions $f_ j$ equal to $f\eta _ j/\eta $ on $W$ and to $0$ on $\Omega \setminus \operatorname{Supp}f$ are continuous, since both formulas give $0$ where these open sets overlap; moreover $0\leq f_ j\leq f$, $\operatorname{Supp}f_ j\subset U_ j$ and $\sum _ jf_ j=f$. Hence $L(f)=\sum _{j=1}^ nL(f_ j)\leq \sum _ jm(U_ j)$, and so $m(U)\leq \sum _ jm(U_ j)$. If the $U_ j$ are pairwise disjoint and $h_ j$ is admissible for $U_ j$, then the $h_ j$ have disjoint supports, so $\sum _{j\leq N}h_ j$ is admissible for $U$; taking suprema shows that $m$ is countably additive on disjoint open sets. Step 2: construction of $\mu $. For $A\subset \Omega $ put $m^*(A)=\inf \{ m(U):U\supset A	ext{ open}\} $. Then $m^*(U)=m(U)$ for open $U$ by monotonicity of $m$. If $\sum _ jm^*(A_ j)<\infty $ (otherwise there is nothing to prove) and $\varepsilon >0$, open sets $U_ j\supset A_ j$ with $m(U_ j)<m^*(A_ j)+\varepsilon 2^{-j}$ give $m^*( igcup _ jA_ j)\leq \sum _ jm^*(A_ j)+\varepsilon $ by Step 1. Thus $m^*$ is an outer measure. Let $A,B\subset \Omega $ be nonempty with $\operatorname {dist}(A,B)=2r>0$, and let $W\supset A\cup B$ be open. The sets $W\cap \{ \operatorname {dist}(\cdot ,A)<r\} $ and $W\cap \{ \operatorname {dist}(\cdot ,B)<r\} $ are open neighborhoods of $A$ and $B$ in $W$, which are disjoint by the triangle inequality, so Step 1 gives $m(W)\geq m^*(A)+m^*(B)$. Taking the infimum over $W$, we obtain the hypothesis of lemma 1.2.1 (if $A$ or $B$ is empty, it holds because $m^*(\varnothing )=0$), and that lemma yields a Borel measure $\mu $ with $\mu (U)=m(U)$ for open $U$. It remains to show that $\mu $ is finite on compact sets. Every compact set $K\subset \Omega $ has a relatively compact open neighborhood $V$ in $\Omega $, for instance the set $V$ used in the construction of cutoff functions in section 1.1 . If $\eta $ is a cutoff function for $\overline V$ in $\Omega $, then ( 1.1 ) gives $L(f)\leq L(\eta )$ for every $f$ admissible for $V$, so $\mu (K)\leq m(V)\leq L(\eta )<\infty $. By proposition 1.1.2 , $\mu $ is a Radon measure. Step 3: $L(f)=\int f\, \mathrm d\mu $. By linearity, it suffices to treat $f\geq 0$ with $M=\| f\| _\infty >0$. Fix an integer $N\geq 1$, put $\delta =M/N$, and let $U_ k=\{ f>k\delta \} $ for $k\geq 0$, so that $\mu (U_ k)\leq \mu (\operatorname{Supp}f)<\infty $. If $h_ k$ is admissible for $U_ k$, $1\leq k\leq N$, then $h_ k\leq \mathbf1_{U_ k}$, and since at most $f(x)/\delta $ indices $k\geq 1$ satisfy $f(x)>k\delta $, we have $\delta \sum _{k=1}^ Nh_ k\leq \delta \sum _{k=1}^ N\mathbf1_{U_ k}\leq f$. Positivity of $L$ and the supremum over the $h_ k$ give the lower bound \[  \delta \sum _{k=1}^ N\mu (U_ k)\leq L(f).  \] For an upper bound, put $g_ k=\min \{ 1,\max \{ 0,f/\delta -(k-1)\} \} $ for $1\leq k\leq N$; these are continuous with values in $[0,1]$, and $f=\delta \sum _{k=1}^ Ng_ k$. If $\eta $ is a cutoff function for $\operatorname{Supp}f$ in $\Omega $, then $g_1\leq \eta $, so $L(g_1)\leq L(\eta )$. For $k\geq 2$, $g_ k$ vanishes outside the compact set $\{ f\geq (k-1)\delta \} \subset U_{k-2}$, so it is admissible for $U_{k-2}$ and $L(g_ k)\leq \mu (U_{k-2})$. Consequently \[  L(f)\leq \delta L(\eta )+\delta \sum _{k=2}^ N\mu (U_{k-2}),  \] and the upper bound exceeds the lower bound by \[  \delta L(\eta )+\delta  igl (\mu (U_0)-\mu (U_{N-1})-\mu (U_ N) igr )\leq \delta  igl (L(\eta )+\mu (\operatorname{Supp}f) igr ).  \] On the other hand, the simple function $s_ N=\delta \sum _{k=1}^ N\mathbf1_{U_ k}$ satisfies $0\leq f-s_ N\leq \delta $ and vanishes outside $\operatorname{Supp}f$, so $\int f\, \mathrm d\mu $ exceeds the lower bound $\int s_ N\, \mathrm d\mu $ by at most $\delta \mu (\operatorname{Supp}f)$. Hence $|L(f)-\int f\, \mathrm d\mu |\leq \delta (L(\eta )+\mu (\operatorname{Supp}f))$, and letting $N	o \infty $ gives $L(f)=\int f\, \mathrm d\mu $. Step 4: uniqueness. Let $
