title: Continuous density
text: Proposition 1.2.3 . Let $\mu $ be a Radon measure on $\Omega $ and let $1\leq p<\infty $. Then $C_ c(\Omega )$ is dense in $L^ p(\mu )$. Proof. Let $u\in L^ p(\mu )$ and let $(K_ j)$ be a compact exhaustion of $\Omega $. The functions $u\mathbf1_{K_ j\cap \{ |u|\leq j\} }$ converge to $u$ in $L^ p(\mu )$ by dominated convergence (proposition 1.1.3 ), so it suffices to approximate a bounded Borel function $v$ vanishing outside a compact set $K$. A uniform approximation of $\operatorname{Re}v$ and $\operatorname{Im}v$ by simple functions vanishing outside $K$, with error $\delta $, has $L^ p(\mu )$ error at most $2\delta \mu (K)^{1/p}$; we are thus reduced to indicator functions $\mathbf1_ E$ of Borel sets $E\subset K$. Given $\varepsilon >0$, regularity of $\mu $ gives a compact set $K'\subset E$ and an open set $U\supset E$ with $\mu (U\setminus K')<\varepsilon $. A cutoff function $\eta $ for $K'$ in $U$ satisfies $|\eta -\mathbf1_ E|\leq \mathbf1_{U\setminus K'}$, so $\| \eta -\mathbf1_ E\| _{L^ p(\mu )}^ p<\varepsilon $. $\square$

title: Test functions and distributions
text: 1.3 Test functions and distributions A locally integrable function need not be differentiable, but integration by parts shows how its derivatives should act: if $u\in C^1(\Omega )$ and $\chi $ is smooth with compact support in $\Omega $, then $\int (\partial _ ju)\chi \, \mathrm dx=-\int u\, \partial _ j\chi \, \mathrm dx$, and the right side makes sense for every locally integrable $u$. Distributions are the continuous linear functionals on such functions $\chi $. A test function on $\Omega $ is an element of $C_ c^\infty (\Omega )$. For a nonempty compact set $K\subset \Omega $, let $\mathcal D_ K(\Omega )$ be the space of test functions supported in $K$. A multi-index is an element $\alpha =(\alpha _1,\ldots ,\alpha _ d)\in \mathbb N^ d$; we write $|\alpha |=\alpha _1+\cdots +\alpha _ d$ and $\partial ^\alpha =\partial _{x_1}^{\alpha _1}\cdots \partial _{x_ d}^{\alpha _ d}$. We give $\mathcal D_ K(\Omega )$ the topology defined by the seminorms \[  p_{K,m}(\chi )=\max _{|\alpha |\leq m}\sup _{x\in K}|\partial ^\alpha \chi (x)|,\qquad m\in \mathbb N,  \] and $\mathcal D(\Omega )=C_ c^\infty (\Omega )$ the topology defined by all seminorms on $C_ c^\infty (\Omega )$ whose restriction to every $\mathcal D_ K(\Omega )$ is continuous. Here a family $\mathcal S$ of seminorms on a complex vector space $E$ defines the topology in which a set $G\subset E$ is open if for every $\chi _0\in G$ there are $q_1,\ldots ,q_ k\in \mathcal S$ and $r>0$ with $\{ \chi :q_ l(\chi -\chi _0)<r\text{ for }1\leq l\leq k\} \subset G$. A net $(\chi _ i)$ in $E$ converges to $\chi $ for this topology whenever $q(\chi _ i-\chi )\to 0$ for every $q\in \mathcal S$, because every neighborhood of $\chi $ contains a set of the above form. A seminorm $q$ on $E$ is continuous if and only if there are $q_1,\ldots ,q_ k\in \mathcal S$ and $C\geq 0$ with $q\leq C\max _ lq_ l$. Indeed, if $q$ is continuous, the open set $\{ q<1\} $ contains a set $\{ \chi :q_ l(\chi )<r\text{ for }l\leq k\} $. For $\chi \in E$ with $M=\max _ lq_ l(\chi )>0$, the vector $r\chi /(2M)$ belongs to this set, so $q(\chi )<2M/r$; if $M=0$, then $t\chi $ belongs to it for every $t>0$, so $q(\chi )=0$. Conversely, such a bound gives $|q(\chi )-q(\chi _0)|\leq q(\chi -\chi _0)\leq C\max _ lq_ l(\chi -\chi _0)$, and $q$ is continuous. The same argument, applied to $q=|T|$, shows that a linear functional $T$ on $E$ is continuous if and only if $|T|\leq C\max _ lq_ l$ for some $q_1,\ldots ,q_ k\in \mathcal S$ and $C\geq 0$. Since $p_{K,m}$ increases with $m$, a seminorm on $\mathcal D_ K(\Omega )$ is therefore continuous if and only if it is bounded by a constant multiple of a single $p_{K,m}$. In particular, let test functions $\chi _ j$ be supported in a fixed compact set $K$, and suppose that $\partial ^\alpha \chi _ j\to \partial ^\alpha \chi $ uniformly for every $\alpha $. Then $\chi $ is supported in $K$, and every seminorm $q$ defining the topology of $\mathcal D(\Omega )$ satisfies $q(\chi _ j-\chi )\leq Cp_{K,m}(\chi _ j-\chi )\to 0$ for suitable $C$ and $m$; hence $\chi _ j\to \chi $ in $\mathcal D(\Omega )$. Definition 1.3.1 . A distribution on $\Omega $ is a complex linear functional $\chi \mapsto \langle T,\chi \rangle $ on $C_ c^\infty (\Omega )$ such that for each nonempty compact set $K\subset \Omega $ there are $C>0$ and $m\in \mathbb N$ with \[  |\langle T,\chi \rangle |\leq C p_{K,m}(\chi )\qquad \text{for all }\chi \in \mathcal D_ K(\Omega ).  \] A distribution $T$ is real if $\langle T,\chi \rangle $ is real for every real test function $\chi $, and a real distribution is positive if $\langle T,\chi \rangle \geq 0$ for every nonnegative test function $\chi $. The space of distributions on $\Omega $ is denoted by $\mathcal D'(\Omega )$. The constants $C$ and $m$ may depend on $K$. The estimate is equivalent to continuity of $T$ on $\mathcal D(\Omega )$. Indeed, the maximum of finitely many seminorms whose restrictions to every $\mathcal D_ K(\Omega )$ are continuous is again such a seminorm, so by the criterion above, $T$ is continuous if and only if $|T|\leq Cq$ for a single seminorm $q$ defining the topology of $\mathcal D(\Omega )$. If $T$ is continuous, the restriction of this $q$ to $\mathcal D_ K(\Omega )$ is continuous, hence bounded by a multiple of some $p_{K,m}$, and the estimate follows. Conversely, under the estimate, the restriction of the seminorm $\chi \mapsto |\langle T,\chi \rangle |$ to every $\mathcal D_ K(\Omega )$ is continuous, so this seminorm is one of those defining the topology of $\mathcal D(\Omega )$, and $T$ is continuous. A locally integrable function $u$ defines a distribution by $\langle u,\chi \rangle =\int _\Omega u\chi \, \mathrm d x$; on $\mathcal D_ K(\Omega )$ the estimate holds with $m=0$ and $C=1+\int _ K|u|\, \mathrm d x$. Likewise, a Radon measure defines a distribution by integration (theorem 1.4.5 ). These pairings are bilinear, without complex conjugation; other conventions are compared in section B.1 . Changing $u$ on a null set does not change its distribution, and conversely, by proposition 1.4.3 below, the distribution determines $u$ up to equality almost everywhere. A distribution $T$ vanishes on an open set $U\subset \Omega $ if $\langle T,\chi \rangle =0$ whenever $\operatorname{Supp}\chi \subset U$, and its support $\operatorname{Supp}T$ is the complement in $\Omega $ of the union of all open sets on which $T$ vanishes. For a multi-index $\alpha $, the distributional derivative of $T\in \mathcal D'(\Omega )$ is defined by \[  \langle \partial ^\alpha T,\chi \rangle =(-1)^{|\alpha |}\langle T,\partial ^\alpha \chi \rangle .  \] Since $p_{K,m}(\partial ^\alpha \chi )\leq p_{K,m+|\alpha |}(\chi )$, an estimate of order $m$ for $T$ on $\mathcal D_ K(\Omega )$ gives one of order $m+|\alpha |$ for $\partial ^\alpha T$. By integration by parts, this definition agrees with the classical derivative for smooth functions. If $a\in C^\infty (\Omega )$, the product $aT$ is defined by $\langle aT,\chi \rangle =\langle T,a\chi \rangle $; it is a distribution because Leibniz's formula bounds the derivatives of $a\chi $ on $K$ by those of $\chi $. Unwinding the definitions gives $\partial _ j(aT)=a\partial _ jT+(\partial _ ja)T$. Example 1.3.2 . For $x\in \Omega $, the Dirac measure $\delta _ x$ assigns $1$ to Borel sets containing $x$ and $0$ to the others; as a distribution, $\langle \delta _ x,\chi \rangle =\chi (x)$. In one real dimension, with $0\in \Omega $, we have $\langle \delta '_0,\chi \rangle =-\chi '(0)$. This distribution is not given by integration against a real signed Radon measure in the sense of section 1.1 . Indeed, let $\theta $ be a test function with $\theta (0)=1$, for instance a multiple of the function $\rho _\varepsilon $ of section 1.4 with $\varepsilon $ small. The test functions $\theta (x)\sin (nx)$ are bounded by $\sup |\theta |$ and supported in $\operatorname{Supp}\theta $, while their pairings with $\delta '_0$ equal $-\theta (0)n\cos 0-\theta '(0)\sin 0=-n$. Integration against a real signed Radon measure $\sigma $ would bound these pairings by $\sup |\theta |\cdot |\sigma |(\operatorname{Supp}\theta )$, since $|\int f\, \mathrm d\sigma |\leq \int |f|\, \mathrm d|\sigma |$.

title: Distributions
text: Definition 1.3.1 . A distribution on $\Omega $ is a complex linear functional $\chi \mapsto \langle T,\chi \rangle $ on $C_ c^\infty (\Omega )$ such that for each nonempty compact set $K\subset \Omega $ there are $C>0$ and $m\in \mathbb N$ with \[  |\langle T,\chi \rangle |\leq C p_{K,m}(\chi )\qquad \text{for all }\chi \in \mathcal D_ K(\Omega ).  \] A distribution $T$ is real if $\langle T,\chi \rangle $ is real for every real test function $\chi $, and a real distribution is positive if $\langle T,\chi \rangle \geq 0$ for every nonnegative test function $\chi $. The space of distributions on $\Omega $ is denoted by $\mathcal D'(\Omega )$.

title: Dirac derivative
text: Example 1.3.2 . For $x\in \Omega $, the Dirac measure $\delta _ x$ assigns $1$ to Borel sets containing $x$ and $0$ to the others; as a distribution, $\langle \delta _ x,\chi \rangle =\chi (x)$. In one real dimension, with $0\in \Omega $, we have $\langle \delta '_0,\chi \rangle =-\chi '(0)$. This distribution is not given by integration against a real signed Radon measure in the sense of section 1.1 . Indeed, let $\theta $ be a test function with $\theta (0)=1$, for instance a multiple of the function $\rho _\varepsilon $ of section 1.4 with $\varepsilon $ small. The test functions $\theta (x)\sin (nx)$ are bounded by $\sup |\theta |$ and supported in $\operatorname{Supp}\theta $, while their pairings with $\delta '_0$ equal $-\theta (0)n\cos 0-\theta '(0)\sin 0=-n$. Integration against a real signed Radon measure $\sigma $ would bound these pairings by $\sup |\theta |\cdot |\sigma |(\operatorname{Supp}\theta )$, since $|\int f\, \mathrm d\sigma |\leq \int |f|\, \mathrm d|\sigma |$.

title: Convolution and mollifiers
text:
1.4 Convolution and mollifiers Mollification, that is, convolution with a smooth kernel of small support, is our basic tool for approximating functions and distributions by smooth functions. The convolution of two functions $f$ and $g$ on $\mathbb R^ d$ is \[  (f*g)(x)=\int _{\mathbb R^ d}f(y)g(x-y)\, \mathrm dy,  \] defined at every point $x$ at which the integral exists. As kernel we take \[  ho (x)= egin{cases} c\exp (-(1-|x|^2)^{-1}),& |x|<1,\ 0,& |x|\geq 1,\end{cases} \qquad \int _{\mathbb R^ d}ho \, \mathrm d x=1,  \] where the constant $c>0$ normalizes the integral. Inside the unit ball, each partial derivative of $ho $ is a polynomial in $x$ and $(1-|x|^2)^{-1}$ times $\exp (-(1-|x|^2)^{-1})$, and hence tends to zero at the unit sphere, because $t^ k\mathrm e^{-t}	o 0$ as $t	o \infty $. Since a coordinate line meets the sphere in at most two points, the mean value theorem on coordinate segments shows inductively that all partial derivatives of $ho $ exist on $\mathbb R^ d$, vanish on the sphere and are continuous. Thus $ho $ is a nonnegative function in $C_ c^\infty (\mathbb R^ d)$; it is radial, that is, $ho (x)$ depends only on $|x|$, and in particular it is even. We write $B(x,r)=\{ y\in \mathbb R^ d:|y-x|<r\} $ for the open ball with center $x$ and radius $r>0$; its closure $\overline{B(x,r)}=\{ y\in \mathbb R^ d:|y-x|\leq r\} $ is the closed ball. For $\varepsilon >0$ the function $ho _\varepsilon (x)=\varepsilon ^{-d}ho (x/\varepsilon )$ is radial, has integral $1$ and is supported in $\overline{B(0,\varepsilon )}$. We call $ho $ and the functions $ho _\varepsilon $ mollifiers. Put \[  \Omega _\varepsilon =\{ x\in \Omega :\operatorname {dist}(x,\mathbb R^ d\setminus \Omega )>\varepsilon \} .  \] For $u\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$, extended by zero outside $\Omega $, the mollification of $u$ is \[  u_\varepsilon (x)=(u*ho _\varepsilon )(x)=\int _\Omega u(y)ho _\varepsilon (x-y)\, \mathrm d y,\qquad x\in \Omega _\varepsilon .  \] The mollification $u_\varepsilon $ is smooth on $\Omega _\varepsilon $. To see this, let $\psi \in C_ c^\infty (\mathbb R^ d)$ be supported in $\overline{B(0,\varepsilon )}$, fix $x\in \Omega _\varepsilon $, and let $L\subset \Omega _\varepsilon $ be a closed ball about $x$. For $x'\in L$, only points $y$ of the compact set $L'=\{ y:\operatorname {dist}(y,L)\leq \varepsilon \} $ contribute to $(u*\psi )(x')$. Every point of $L'$ lies within distance $\varepsilon $ of a point of $L$, so $L'\subset \Omega $, and $u$ is integrable on $L'$. Hence $|(u*\psi )(x')-(u*\psi )(x)|\leq \sup _ y|\psi (x'-y)-\psi (x-y)|\int _{L'}|u|\, \mathrm dy$ for $x'\in L$, so $u*\psi $ is continuous at $x$ by the uniform continuity of $\psi $. Moreover, if $e_ j$ denotes the $j$th coordinate unit vector, the mean value theorem and the uniform continuity of $\partial _ j\psi $ show that $t^{-1}(\psi (x+te_ j-y)-\psi (x-y))	o \partial _ j\psi (x-y)$ uniformly in $y$ as $t	o 0$. Integrating against $u$ over $L'$, we obtain $\partial _ j(u*\psi )(x)=(u*\partial _ j\psi )(x)$. Applying this to $\psi =\partial ^\alpha ho _\varepsilon $, we find by induction on $|\alpha |$ that $u_\varepsilon \in C^\infty (\Omega _\varepsilon )$ and $\partial ^\alpha u_\varepsilon =u*\partial ^\alpha ho _\varepsilon $. Lemma 1.4.1 . In the following assertions, limits are taken as $\varepsilon 	o 0$. If $u\in C(\Omega )$, then $u_\varepsilon 	o u$ uniformly on every compact subset of $\Omega $. Let $1\leq p<\infty $. Translation is continuous in $L^ p(\mathbb R^ d)$: if $v\in L^ p(\mathbb R^ d)$, then $\| v(\cdot -h)-v\| _ p	o 0$ as $h	o 0$. If $u\in L^ p_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$, then $u_\varepsilon 	o u$ in $L^ p(K)$ for every compact set $K\subset \Omega $. If $\chi \in C_ c^\infty (\Omega )$ is extended by zero to $\mathbb R^ d$, then for small $\varepsilon $ the functions $\chi *ho _\varepsilon $ are supported in a fixed compact subset of $\Omega $, and $\partial ^\alpha (\chi *ho _\varepsilon )	o \partial ^\alpha \chi $ uniformly for every multi-index $\alpha $. If $K\subset U\subset \Omega $ with $K$ compact and $U$ open, there is a smooth cutoff function for $K$ in $U$ which equals $1$ on a neighborhood of $K$. If $f\in C_ c(\Omega )$ is extended by zero to $\mathbb R^ d$, then for small $\varepsilon $ the functions $f*ho _\varepsilon $ are test functions supported in a fixed compact subset of $\Omega $, and they converge uniformly to $f$. Consequently, $C_ c^\infty (\Omega )$ is dense in $L^ p(\mu )$ for every Radon measure $\mu $ on $\Omega $ and every $1\leq p<\infty $. Proof. (1) Since $\int ho _\varepsilon =1$, we have for $x\in \Omega _\varepsilon $ \[  |u_\varepsilon (x)-u(x)|\leq \int |u(x-h)-u(x)|ho _\varepsilon (h)\, \mathrm dh\leq \sup _{|h|\leq \varepsilon }|u(x-h)-u(x)|.  \] If $K\subset \Omega $ is compact, choose $\delta >0$ with $K'=\{ x:\operatorname {dist}(x,K)\leq \delta \} \subset \Omega $. For $\varepsilon <\delta $ we have $K\subset \Omega _\varepsilon $, because the closed ball of radius $\delta $ about each point of $K$ lies in $\Omega $, and the bound tends to zero uniformly on $K$ by the uniform continuity of $u$ on the compact set $K'$. (2) We first prove the continuity of translation. For $v\in C_ c(\mathbb R^ d)$ it follows from uniform continuity, since the functions $v(\cdot -h)$, $|h|\leq 1$, are supported in a fixed compact set; the general case follows by approximating $v$ in $L^ p$ by such functions (proposition 1.2.3 for Lebesgue measure), since translation preserves the $L^ p$ norm. Since $\int ho _\varepsilon =1$, we have $v*ho _\varepsilon (x)-v(x)=\int (v(x-h)-v(x))ho _\varepsilon (h)\, \mathrm dh$. Hence, by the triangle inequality and Jensen's inequality (lemma 1.1.4 ) for the convex function $t\mapsto |t|^ p$ on $\mathbb R$, applied to the function $h\mapsto |v(x-h)-v(x)|$, which is integrable for the probability measure $ho _\varepsilon (h)\, \mathrm dh$ because $|v|\leq 1+|v|^ p$, we obtain \[  |v*ho _\varepsilon (x)-v(x)|^ p\leq \int |v(x-h)-v(x)|^ pho _\varepsilon (h)\, \mathrm dh\qquad 	ext{for every }x.  \] We may take $v$ to be a Borel function, so that the integrand is a Borel function of $(x,h)$. Integrating in $x$ and using Tonelli's theorem, we obtain \[  \| v*ho _\varepsilon -v\| _ p^ p \leq \int ho _\varepsilon (h)\| v(\cdot -h)-v\| _ p^ p\, \mathrm d h\leq \sup _{|h|\leq \varepsilon }\| v(\cdot -h)-v\| _ p^ p	o 0.  \] Now let $u\in L^ p_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$ and $K\subset \Omega $ compact, choose $\delta >0$ with $\{ x:\operatorname {dist}(x,K)\leq 2\delta \} \subset \Omega $, and let $v\in L^ p(\mathbb R^ d)$ equal $u$ on $W=\{ x:\operatorname {dist}(x,K)<2\delta \} $ and $0$ elsewhere. For $\varepsilon <\delta $, the values of $u_\varepsilon $ on $K$ only involve $u$ on $W$, so $\| u_\varepsilon -u\| _{L^ p(K)}\leq \| v*ho _\varepsilon -v\| _ p	o 0$. (3) The function $\chi *ho _\varepsilon $ vanishes outside the set of points at distance at most $\varepsilon $ from $\operatorname{Supp}\chi $, which is a compact subset of $\Omega $ for small $\varepsilon $. Differentiation under the integral sign gives $\partial ^\alpha (\chi *ho _\varepsilon )=(\partial ^\alpha \chi )*ho _\varepsilon $, and the bound displayed in (1), applied on $\mathbb R^ d$ to the uniformly continuous function $\partial ^\alpha \chi $ in place of $u$, proves uniform convergence. (4) Choose $\delta >0$ with $3\delta <\operatorname {dist}(K,\mathbb R^ d\setminus U)$, and let $\eta $ be a cutoff function for $\{ x:\operatorname {dist}(x,K)\leq 2\delta \} $ in $\{ x:\operatorname {dist}(x,K)<3\delta \} $. If $\varepsilon <\delta $ is smaller than the distance from $\operatorname{Supp}\eta $ to $\mathbb R^ d\setminus U$, then $\eta *ho _\varepsilon $ is smooth with values in $[0,1]$ and compact support in $U$, and it equals $1$ on $\{ x:\operatorname {dist}(x,K)<\delta \} $, where the average only involves points at which $\eta =1$. (5) The support statement is proved as in (3), the functions $f*ho _\varepsilon $ are smooth by differentiation under the integral sign, and uniform convergence follows from (1) applied on $\mathbb R^ d$, since all these functions vanish outside a fixed compact set. If $g\in L^ p(\mu )$, choose $f\in C_ c(\Omega )$ close to $g$ in $L^ p(\mu )$ by proposition 1.2.3 . If all $f*ho _\varepsilon $ are supported in the compact set $L$, then so is their uniform limit $f$, and $\| f*ho _\varepsilon -f\| _{L^ p(\mu )}\leq \sup |f*ho _\varepsilon -f|\, \mu (L)^{1/p}	o 0$. $\square$ Smooth cutoff functions yield partitions of unity, which localize test functions and distributions. Lemma 1.4.2 . Let $K\subset \Omega $ be compact, and let $U_1,\ldots ,U_ n\subset \Omega $ be open sets covering $K$. Then there are smooth functions $\eta _ j\colon \Omega 	o [0,1]$ with compact support in $U_ j$, $1\leq j\leq n$, such that $\sum _ j\eta _ j\leq 1$ on $\Omega $ and $\sum _ j\eta _ j=1$ on a neighborhood of $K$. Consequently, every test function $\chi $ with $\operatorname{Supp}\chi \subset U_1\cup \cdots \cup U_ n$ is the sum of the test functions $\chi \eta _ j$, which are supported in $U_ j$ and are nonnegative if $\chi $ is nonnegative. In particular, a distribution on $\Omega $ that vanishes on each member of a family of open subsets of $\Omega $ vanishes on their union. Proof. For every $x\in K$ choose an index $j(x)$ with $x\in U_{j(x)}$ and a radius $r_ x>0$ with $\overline{B(x,r_ x)}\subset U_{j(x)}$. Finitely many of the balls $B(x,r_ x)$ cover $K$; let $L_ j$ be the union of the closures of those among them with $j(x)=j$. Then $L_ j$ is a compact, possibly empty, subset of $U_ j$, and $K\subset L_1\cup \cdots \cup L_ n$. By lemma 1.4.1 (4), there are smooth cutoff functions $\psi _ j$ for $L_ j$ in $U_ j$ which equal $1$ on neighborhoods $V_ j$ of $L_ j$. Put $\eta _1=\psi _1$ and $\eta _ j=\psi _ j(1-\psi _1)\cdots (1-\psi _{j-1})$ for $2\leq j\leq n$. These functions are smooth with values in $[0,1]$, and $\operatorname{Supp}\eta _ j\subset \operatorname{Supp}\psi _ j$ is a compact subset of $U_ j$. By induction on $n$, \[  \sum _{j=1}^ n\eta _ j=1-\prod _{j=1}^ n(1-\psi _ j),  \] which takes values in $[0,1]$ and equals $1$ on the neighborhood $V_1\cup \cdots \cup V_ n$ of $K$. If $\chi $ is a test function with $\operatorname{Supp}\chi \subset U_1\cup \cdots \cup U_ n$, we apply this to $K=\operatorname{Supp}\chi $; then $\chi =\sum _ j\chi \eta _ j$, and $\operatorname{Supp}(\chi \eta _ j)\subset \operatorname{Supp}\eta _ j$ is a compact subset of $U_ j$. Finally, let a distribution $T$ vanish on each member of a family of open subsets of $\Omega $, and let $\chi $ be a test function supported in their union. The compact set $\operatorname{Supp}\chi $ is covered by finitely many members $U_1,\ldots ,U_ n$ of the family, and the decomposition $\chi =\sum _ j\chi \eta _ j$ just obtained gives $\langle T,\chi angle =\sum _ j\langle T,\chi \eta _ jangle =0$. $\square$ By the last assertion of lemma 1.4.2 , every distribution $T$ vanishes on $\Omega \setminus \operatorname{Supp}T$. A distribution is mollified by letting it act on the translated kernel. Let $T\in \mathcal D'(\Omega )$, let $s>0$, and let $\phi \in C_ c^\infty (\mathbb R^ d)$ be supported in $\overline{B(0,s)}$. If $x\in \Omega _ s$, then $\phi (x-\cdot )$ is a test function on $\Omega $, supported in $\overline{B(x,s)}$, and we put \[  (T*\phi )(x)=\langle T,\phi (x-\cdot )angle ,\qquad x\in \Omega _ s.  \] For $T$ given by $u\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$, this is the convolution $u*\phi $ of $u$, extended by zero, with $\phi $. The function $T_\varepsilon =T*ho _\varepsilon $ is called the mollification of $T$; for $T$ given by $u$, it is the mollification $u_\varepsilon $ of $u$. Proposition 1.4.3 . Let $T\in \mathcal D'(\Omega )$ and $\varepsilon >0$, and let $T_\varepsilon (x)=\langle T,ho _\varepsilon (x-\cdot )angle $ for $x\in \Omega _\varepsilon $. If $s>0$ and $\phi \in C_ c^\infty (\mathbb R^ d)$ is supported in $\overline{B(0,s)}$, then $T*\phi $ is smooth on $\Omega _ s$, and $\partial ^\alpha (T*\phi )=T*\partial ^\alpha \phi =(\partial ^\alpha T)*\phi $ for every multi-index $\alpha $. In particular, $T_\varepsilon $ is smooth on $\Omega _\varepsilon $, and $\partial ^\alpha T_\varepsilon =(\partial ^\alpha T)_\varepsilon $. title: Mollifier density
text: Lemma 1.4.1 . In the following assertions, limits are taken as $\varepsilon \to 0$. If $u\in C(\Omega )$, then $u_\varepsilon \to u$ uniformly on every compact subset of $\Omega $. Let $1\leq p<\infty $. Translation is continuous in $L^ p(\mathbb R^ d)$: if $v\in L^ p(\mathbb R^ d)$, then $\| v(\cdot -h)-v\| _ p\to 0$ as $h\to 0$. If $u\in L^ p_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$, then $u_\varepsilon \to u$ in $L^ p(K)$ for every compact set $K\subset \Omega $. If $\chi \in C_ c^\infty (\Omega )$ is extended by zero to $\mathbb R^ d$, then for small $\varepsilon $ the functions $\chi *\rho _\varepsilon $ are supported in a fixed compact subset of $\Omega $, and $\partial ^\alpha (\chi *\rho _\varepsilon )\to \partial ^\alpha \chi $ uniformly for every multi-index $\alpha $. If $K\subset U\subset \Omega $ with $K$ compact and $U$ open, there is a smooth cutoff function for $K$ in $U$ which equals $1$ on a neighborhood of $K$. If $f\in C_ c(\Omega )$ is extended by zero to $\mathbb R^ d$, then for small $\varepsilon $ the functions $f*\rho _\varepsilon $ are test functions supported in a fixed compact subset of $\Omega $, and they converge uniformly to $f$. Consequently, $C_ c^\infty (\Omega )$ is dense in $L^ p(\mu )$ for every Radon measure $\mu $ on $\Omega $ and every $1\leq p<\infty $. Proof. (1) Since $\int \rho _\varepsilon =1$, we have for $x\in \Omega _\varepsilon $ \[  |u_\varepsilon (x)-u(x)|\leq \int |u(x-h)-u(x)|\rho _\varepsilon (h)\, \mathrm dh\leq \sup _{|h|\leq \varepsilon }|u(x-h)-u(x)|.  \] If $K\subset \Omega $ is compact, choose $\delta >0$ with $K'=\{ x:\operatorname {dist}(x,K)\leq \delta \} \subset \Omega $. For $\varepsilon <\delta $ we have $K\subset \Omega _\varepsilon $, because the closed ball of radius $\delta $ about each point of $K$ lies in $\Omega $, and the bound tends to zero uniformly on $K$ by the uniform continuity of $u$ on the compact set $K'$. (2) We first prove the continuity of translation. For $v\in C_ c(\mathbb R^ d)$ it follows from uniform continuity, since the functions $v(\cdot -h)$, $|h|\leq 1$, are supported in a fixed compact set; the general case follows by approximating $v$ in $L^ p$ by such functions (proposition 1.2.3 for Lebesgue measure), since translation preserves the $L^ p$ norm. Since $\int \rho _\varepsilon =1$, we have $v*\rho _\varepsilon (x)-v(x)=\int (v(x-h)-v(x))\rho _\varepsilon (h)\, \mathrm dh$. Hence, by the triangle inequality and Jensen's inequality (lemma 1.1.4 ) for the convex function $t\mapsto |t|^ p$ on $\mathbb R$, applied to the function $h\mapsto |v(x-h)-v(x)|$, which is integrable for the probability measure $\rho _\varepsilon (h)\, \mathrm dh$ because $|v|\leq 1+|v|^ p$, we obtain \[  |v*\rho _\varepsilon (x)-v(x)|^ p\leq \int |v(x-h)-v(x)|^ p\rho _\varepsilon (h)\, \mathrm dh\qquad \text{for every }x.  \] We may take $v$ to be a Borel function, so that the integrand is a Borel function of $(x,h)$. For $\varepsilon <\delta $, the values of $u_\varepsilon $ on $K$ only involve $u$ on $W$, so $\| u_\varepsilon -u\| _{L^ p(K)}\leq \| v*\rho _\varepsilon -v\| _ p\to 0$. (4) Choose $\delta >0$ with $3\delta <\operatorname {dist}(K,\mathbb R^ d\setminus U)$, and let $\eta $ be a cutoff function for $\{ x:\operatorname {dist}(x,K)\leq 2\delta \} $ in $\{ x:\operatorname {dist}(x,K)<3\delta \} $. (5) The support statement is proved as in (3), the functions $f*\rho _\varepsilon $ are smooth by differentiation under the integral sign, and uniform convergence follows from (1) applied on $\mathbb R^ d$, since all these functions vanish outside a fixed compact set. If $g\in L^ p(\mu )$, choose $f\in C_ c(\Omega )$ close to $g$ in $L^ p(\mu )$ by proposition 1.2.3 . If all $f*\rho _\varepsilon $ are supported in the compact set $L$, then so is their uniform limit $f$, and $\| f*\rho _\varepsilon -f\| _{L^ p(\mu )}\leq \sup |f*\rho _\varepsilon -f|\, \mu (L)^{1/p}\to 0$. $\square$

title: Smooth partition unity
text: Lemma 1.4.2 . Let $K\subset \Omega $ be compact, and let $U_1,\ldots ,U_ n\subset \Omega $ be open sets covering $K$. Then there are smooth functions $\eta _ j\colon \Omega \to [0,1]$ with compact support in $U_ j$, $1\leq j\leq n$, such that $\sum _ j\eta _ j\leq 1$ on $\Omega $ and $\sum _ j\eta _ j=1$ on a neighborhood of $K$. Consequently, every test function $\chi $ with $\operatorname{Supp}\chi \subset U_1\cup \cdots \cup U_ n$ is the sum of the test functions $\chi \eta _ j$, which are supported in $U_ j$ and are nonnegative if $\chi $ is nonnegative. In particular, a distribution on $\Omega $ that vanishes on each member of a family of open subsets of $\Omega $ vanishes on their union. Proof. For every $x\in K$ choose an index $j(x)$ with $x\in U_{j(x)}$ and a radius $r_ x>0$ with $\overline{B(x,r_ x)}\subset U_{j(x)}$. Finitely many of the balls $B(x,r_ x)$ cover $K$; let $L_ j$ be the union of the closures of those among them with $j(x)=j$. Then $L_ j$ is a compact, possibly empty, subset of $U_ j$, and $K\subset L_1\cup \cdots \cup L_ n$. By lemma 1.4.1 (4), there are smooth cutoff functions $\psi _ j$ for $L_ j$ in $U_ j$ which equal $1$ on neighborhoods $V_ j$ of $L_ j$. Put $\eta _1=\psi _1$ and $\eta _ j=\psi _ j(1-\psi _1)\cdots (1-\psi _{j-1})$ for $2\leq j\leq n$. These functions are smooth with values in $[0,1]$, and $\operatorname{Supp}\eta _ j\subset \operatorname{Supp}\psi _ j$ is a compact subset of $U_ j$. By induction on $n$, \[  \sum _{j=1}^ n\eta _ j=1-\prod _{j=1}^ n(1-\psi _ j),  \] which takes values in $[0,1]$ and equals $1$ on the neighborhood $V_1\cup \cdots \cup V_ n$ of $K$. If $\chi $ is a test function with $\operatorname{Supp}\chi \subset U_1\cup \cdots \cup U_ n$, we apply this to $K=\operatorname{Supp}\chi $; then $\chi =\sum _ j\chi \eta _ j$, and $\operatorname{Supp}(\chi \eta _ j)\subset \operatorname{Supp}\eta _ j$ is a compact subset of $U_ j$. Finally, let a distribution $T$ vanish on each member of a family of open subsets of $\Omega $, and let $\chi $ be a test function supported in their union. The compact set $\operatorname{Supp}\chi $ is covered by finitely many members $U_1,\ldots ,U_ n$ of the family, and the decomposition $\chi =\sum _ j\chi \eta _ j$ just obtained gives $\langle T,\chi \rangle =\sum _ j\langle T,\chi \eta _ j\rangle =0$. $\square$

title: Zero gradient constant
text: Corollary 1.4.4 . Let $T\in \mathcal D'(\Omega )$ satisfy $\partial _ jT=0$ for $1\leq j\leq d$. Then $T$ is given by a locally constant function on $\Omega $. If $\Omega $ is connected, $T$ is a constant function. Proof. Let $B$ be an open ball with $\overline B\subset \Omega $, and fix $\theta \in C_ c^\infty (B)$ with $\int \theta \, \mathrm dx=1$, for instance a translate of $\rho _ s$ with $s>0$ small. If $f\geq 0$, then $f*\rho _\varepsilon \geq 0$, so $\Lambda (f)\geq 0$. By theorem 1.2.2 , there is a Radon measure $\mu $ with $\Lambda (f)=\int f\, \mathrm d\mu $. For a real test function $\chi $, the constant sequence $\chi _ k=\chi $ shows that $\Lambda (\chi )=\langle T,\chi \rangle $; applying this to $\operatorname{Re}\chi $ and $\operatorname{Im}\chi $ gives $\langle T,\chi \rangle =\int \chi \, \mathrm d\mu $ for all test functions. The measure $\mu $ is unique by proposition 1.4.3 (4). Conversely, if $\mu $ is a Radon measure, then $|\int \chi \, \mathrm d\mu |\leq (1+\mu (K))p_{K,0}(\chi )$ for $\chi \in \mathcal D_ K(\Omega )$, so integration against $\mu $ is a distribution, and it is positive. $\square$

title: Weak convergence of measures
text: 1.5 Weak convergence of measures The families of measures whose limits we shall need are not always sequences, so we work with nets. A directed set is a nonempty set $I$ with a preorder $\leq $ in which every two elements have a common upper bound. A net $(x_ i)_{i\in I}$ in a topological space $X$ is a map $i\mapsto x_ i$ from a directed set $I$ to $X$; it converges to $x\in X$ if for every neighborhood $U$ of $x$ there is $i_0\in I$ with $x_ i\in U$ for all $i\geq i_0$. For a net $(a_ i)$ in $[-\infty ,\infty ]$, $\varliminf _ i a_ i=\sup _{i_0}\inf _{i\geq i_0}a_ i$ and $\varlimsup _ i a_ i=\inf _{i_0}\sup _{i\geq i_0}a_ i$. The weak topology on $\mathcal D'(\Omega )$ is the weakest topology for which all maps $T\mapsto \langle T,\chi \rangle $, $\chi \in C_ c^\infty (\Omega )$, are continuous. A set containing $T$ is a neighborhood of $T$ for this topology if and only if it contains a set $\{ S:|\langle S-T,\chi _ l\rangle |<r\text{ for }1\leq l\leq k\} $ with finitely many test functions $\chi _ l$ and $r>0$. Since the index set of a net is directed, it follows that a net $(T_ i)$ converges to $T$ exactly when $\langle T_ i,\chi \rangle \to \langle T,\chi \rangle $ for every test function $\chi $, and we then say that $T_ i\to T$ in the sense of distributions. Likewise, the vague topology on the set of Radon measures on $\Omega $ is the weakest topology for which all maps $\mu \mapsto \int f\, \mathrm d\mu $, $f\in C_ c(\Omega )$, are continuous. For the same reason, a net $(\mu _ i)$ converges to $\mu $ in this topology, and we say that $\mu _ i\to \mu $ vaguely, if and only if $\int f\, \mathrm d\mu _ i\to \int f\, \mathrm d\mu $ for every $f\in C_ c(\Omega )$. A net of finite Radon measures converges narrowly to a finite Radon measure $\mu $ if the same holds for every bounded continuous function $f$ on $\Omega $. Narrow convergence implies vague convergence, but the converse fails, because mass can escape to infinity or to the boundary of $\Omega $ (example 1.5.4 ). Proposition 1.5.1 . Let $(T_ i)$ be a net of positive distributions on $\Omega $ converging in the sense of distributions to $T\in \mathcal D'(\Omega )$. Then $T$ is positive, and the Radon measures associated with the $T_ i$ by theorem 1.4.5 converge vaguely to the Radon measure associated with $T$. Conversely, if a net of Radon measures converges vaguely, the associated distributions converge in the sense of distributions. Proof. For a nonnegative test function $\chi $, the numbers $\langle T_ i,\chi \rangle $ are nonnegative, hence so is their limit $\langle T,\chi \rangle $; likewise $\langle T,\chi \rangle $ is real for real $\chi $. Thus $T$ is positive, and $T$ and the $T_ i$ are given by Radon measures $\mu $ and $\mu _ i$. Let $f\in C_ c(\Omega )$. By lemma 1.4.1 (5), $f$ is the uniform limit of test functions supported in a fixed compact set $L$; in particular, $f$ vanishes outside $L$. If $\eta $ is a smooth cutoff function for $L$ in $\Omega $, then $\mu _ i(L)\leq \langle T_ i,\eta \rangle \to \langle T,\eta \rangle $. A convergent net of real numbers need not be bounded, but it is bounded from some index on; hence there is $i_0$ with $\mu _ i(L)\leq C=\langle T,\eta \rangle +1$ for $i\geq i_0$, and also $\mu (L)\leq \langle T,\eta \rangle <C$. For every test function $\chi $ supported in $L$ and every $i\geq i_0$, \[  \left|\int f\, \mathrm d\mu _ i-\int f\, \mathrm d\mu \right|\leq 2C\| f-\chi \| _\infty +|\langle T_ i,\chi \rangle -\langle T,\chi \rangle |,  \] so $\varlimsup _ i|\int f\, \mathrm d\mu _ i-\int f\, \mathrm d\mu |\leq 2C\| f-\chi \| _\infty $, which can be made arbitrarily small. Hence $\mu _ i\to \mu $ vaguely. The converse holds because test functions belong to $C_ c(\Omega )$. $\square$ Thus, by the uniqueness in theorem 1.4.5 , a net of Radon measures converges vaguely to a Radon measure if and only if it converges to it in the sense of distributions. In 2 , where measures appear as currents of top degree, this mode of convergence is called weak convergence. Proposition 1.5.2 . Let $(\mu _ i)$ be a net of Radon measures on $\Omega $ converging vaguely to a Radon measure $\mu $. Then for every open set $U\subset \Omega $ and every compact set $K\subset \Omega $, \[  \mu (U)\leq \varliminf _ i\mu _ i(U),\qquad \varlimsup _ i\mu _ i(K)\leq \mu (K).  \] Consequently, if $E\Subset \Omega $ is a Borel set with $\mu (\partial E)=0$, then $\mu _ i(E)\to \mu (E)$. Proof. If $f\in C_ c(\Omega )$, $0\leq f\leq 1$ and $\operatorname{Supp}f\subset U$, then $\int f\, \mathrm d\mu =\lim _ i\int f\, \mathrm d\mu _ i\leq \varliminf _ i\mu _ i(U)$; taking the supremum over such $f$ and using ( 1.4 ) gives the first inequality. For the second, let $\varepsilon >0$, choose by outer regularity an open set $V\supset K$ with $\mu (V)<\mu (K)+\varepsilon $, and let $\eta $ be a cutoff function for $K$ in $V$. Then $\mu _ i(K)\leq \int \eta \, \mathrm d\mu _ i\to \int \eta \, \mathrm d\mu \leq \mu (V)$, so $\varlimsup _ i\mu _ i(K)\leq \mu (K)+\varepsilon $. Finally, for $E$ as in the last assertion, the closure $\overline E$ is a compact subset of $\Omega $, and $\overline E\setminus \operatorname{Int}E=\partial E$ is $\mu $-null, so $\mu (\operatorname{Int}E)=\mu (E)=\mu (\overline E)$. Since $\mu _ i(\operatorname{Int}E)\leq \mu _ i(E)\leq \mu _ i(\overline E)$, the two inequalities, applied to $\operatorname{Int}E$ and $\overline E$, give \[  \mu (E)=\mu (\operatorname{Int}E)\leq \varliminf _ i\mu _ i(E)\leq \varlimsup _ i\mu _ i(E)\leq \mu (\overline E)=\mu (E).  \] $\square$ Proposition 1.5.3 . Let $(\mu _ i)$ be a net of finite Radon measures on $\Omega $ converging vaguely to $\mu $. Suppose that the net is eventually uniformly tight: for every $\varepsilon >0$ there are a compact set $K\subset \Omega $ and an index $i_0$ such that $\mu _ i(\Omega \setminus K)<\varepsilon $ for all $i\geq i_0$. Then $\mu $ is finite and $\mu _ i\to \mu $ narrowly. In particular, $\mu _ i(\Omega )\to \mu (\Omega )$. Proof. Let $\varepsilon >0$, and choose $K$ and $i_0$ as above. Since $\Omega \setminus K$ is open, proposition 1.5.2 gives $\mu (\Omega \setminus K)\leq \varepsilon $, and since $\mu (K)<\infty $, the measure $\mu $ is finite. Let $f$ be a bounded continuous function on $\Omega $ and $\eta $ a cutoff function for $K$ in $\Omega $. Then $f\eta \in C_ c(\Omega )$, so $\int f\eta \, \mathrm d\mu _ i\to \int f\eta \, \mathrm d\mu $, while $1-\eta $ takes values in $[0,1]$ and vanishes on $K$, so that for $i\geq i_0$ \[  \left|\int f(1-\eta )\, \mathrm d\mu _ i\right|\leq \| f\| _\infty \varepsilon , \qquad \left|\int f(1-\eta )\, \mathrm d\mu \right|\leq \| f\| _\infty \varepsilon .  \] Hence $\varlimsup _ i|\int f\, \mathrm d\mu _ i-\int f\, \mathrm d\mu |\leq 2\| f\| _\infty \varepsilon $. Letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ proves narrow convergence, and $f=1$ gives the last assertion. $\square$ Example 1.5.4 . On $\mathbb R$, the Dirac measures $\delta _ j$, $j\geq 1$, converge vaguely to zero, since every $f\in C_ c(\mathbb R)$ vanishes at $j$ for large $j$; yet each has total mass one. On $\Omega =(0,1)$ the measures $\delta _{1/j}$, $j\geq 2$, behave in the same way, the mass escaping through the boundary point $0$, which does not belong to $\Omega $. Neither sequence is eventually uniformly tight: a compact subset of $\mathbb R$ does not contain $j$ for large $j$, and a compact subset of $(0,1)$ does not contain $1/j$ for large $j$, so the mass outside a fixed compact set is eventually equal to one. Theorem 1.5.5 . Let $(\mu _ j)$ be a sequence of Radon measures on $\Omega $ such that $\sup _ j\mu _ j(K)<\infty $ for every compact set $K\subset \Omega $. Then $(\mu _ j)$ has a vaguely convergent subsequence. If, moreover, the $\mu _ j$ are finite and the sequence is eventually uniformly tight, then it has a narrowly convergent subsequence with a finite limit. Proof. Step 1: a countable dense family. Let $\varphi (t)=\max \{ 0,1-|t|\} $, so that $\sum _{n\in \mathbb Z}\varphi (t-n)=1$ for $t\in \mathbb R$. For $k\geq 1$ and $n\in \mathbb Z^ d$ put $\varphi _{k,n}(x)=\prod _{l=1}^ d\varphi (2^ kx_ l-n_ l)$. These are nonnegative continuous functions with $\sum _ n\varphi _{k,n}=1$, and $\varphi _{k,n}(x)\neq 0$ only if $|x-2^{-k}n|_\infty <2^{-k}$, where $|\cdot |_\infty $ is the maximum norm. Let $\mathcal F$ be the countable family of all finite sums $\sum _ nq_ n\varphi _{k,n}$, $k\geq 1$, with rational coefficients $q_ n$, whose support is a compact subset of $\Omega $. Given $f\in C_ c(\Omega ,\mathbb R)$, extended by zero to $\mathbb R^ d$, choose rational numbers $q_{k,n}$ with $|q_{k,n}-f(2^{-k}n)|\leq 2^{-k}$ and $q_{k,n}=0$ if $f(2^{-k}n)=0$, and put $f_ k=\sum _ nq_{k,n}\varphi _{k,n}$. Then \[  |f_ k(x)-f(x)|\leq \sum _ n|q_{k,n}-f(x)|\varphi _{k,n}(x)\leq 2^{-k}+\sup \{ |f(y)-f(x)|:|y-x|_\infty <2^{-k}\} ,  \] which tends to zero uniformly in $x$ because $f$ is uniformly continuous. Moreover, $f_ k$ vanishes at points of $|\cdot |_\infty $-distance more than $2^{-k}$ from $\operatorname{Supp}f$, so for large $k$ all the $f_ k$ belong to $\mathcal F$ and are supported in a fixed compact set $L\subset \Omega $. Step 2: diagonal extraction. Enumerate $\mathcal F=\{ g_1,g_2,\ldots \} $. For each $l$, the numbers $\int g_ l\, \mathrm d\mu _ j$ are bounded by $\| g_ l\| _\infty \sup _ j\mu _ j(\operatorname{Supp}g_ l)$. Choosing successively convergent subsequences for $g_1,g_2,\ldots $ and passing to the diagonal subsequence, we find $(\mu _{j_ k})$ such that $\int g_ l\, \mathrm d\mu _{j_ k}$ converges for every $l$. If $f\in C_ c(\Omega ,\mathbb R)$ and $L$, $f_ m$ are as in Step 1, then with $C_ L=\sup _ j\mu _ j(L)$, \[  \left|\int f\, \mathrm d\mu _{j_ k}-\int f\, \mathrm d\mu _{j_{k'}}\right|\leq 2C_ L\| f-f_ m\| _\infty +\left|\int f_ m\, \mathrm d\mu _{j_ k}-\int f_ m\, \mathrm d\mu _{j_{k'}}\right|,  \] so $(\int f\, \mathrm d\mu _{j_ k})_ k$ is a Cauchy sequence. Its limit is a positive linear functional of $f$, hence integration against a Radon measure $\mu $ by theorem 1.2.2 , and $\mu _{j_ k}\to \mu $ vaguely; complex $f$ are handled by linearity. If the sequence is eventually uniformly tight, so is every subsequence, and proposition 1.5.3 gives the last assertion. $\square$

title: Positive distribution convergence
text: Proposition 1.5.1 . Let $(T_ i)$ be a net of positive distributions on $\Omega $ converging in the sense of distributions to $T\in \mathcal D'(\Omega )$. Then $T$ is positive, and the Radon measures associated with the $T_ i$ by theorem 1.4.5 converge vaguely to the Radon measure associated with $T$. For a nonnegative test function $\chi $, the numbers $\langle T_ i,\chi \rangle $ are nonnegative, hence so is their limit $\langle T,\chi \rangle $; likewise $\langle T,\chi \rangle $ is real for real $\chi $. If $\eta $ is a smooth cutoff function for $L$ in $\Omega $, then $\mu _ i(L)\leq \langle T_ i,\eta \rangle \to \langle T,\eta \rangle $. title: Vague set inequalities
text: Proposition 1.5.2 . Let $(\mu _ i)$ be a net of Radon measures on $\Omega $ converging vaguely to a Radon measure $\mu $. Then for every open set $U\subset \Omega $ and every compact set $K\subset \Omega $, \[  \mu (U)\leq \varliminf _ i\mu _ i(U),\qquad \varlimsup _ i\mu _ i(K)\leq \mu (K).  \] Consequently, if $E\Subset \Omega $ is a Borel set with $\mu (\partial E)=0$, then $\mu _ i(E)\to \mu (E)$. Proof. If $f\in C_ c(\Omega )$, $0\leq f\leq 1$ and $\operatorname{Supp}f\subset U$, then $\int f\, \mathrm d\mu =\lim _ i\int f\, \mathrm d\mu _ i\leq \varliminf _ i\mu _ i(U)$; taking the supremum over such $f$ and using ( 1.4 ) gives the first inequality. For the second, let $\varepsilon >0$, choose by outer regularity an open set $V\supset K$ with $\mu (V)<\mu (K)+\varepsilon $, and let $\eta $ be a cutoff function for $K$ in $V$. Since $\mu _ i(\operatorname{Int}E)\leq \mu _ i(E)\leq \mu _ i(\overline E)$, the two inequalities, applied to $\operatorname{Int}E$ and $\overline E$, give \[  \mu (E)=\mu (\operatorname{Int}E)\leq \varliminf _ i\mu _ i(E)\leq \varlimsup _ i\mu _ i(E)\leq \mu (\overline E)=\mu (E).  \] $\square$

title: Tight vague narrow
text: Proposition 1.5.3 . Let $(\mu _ i)$ be a net of finite Radon measures on $\Omega $ converging vaguely to $\mu $. Suppose that the net is eventually uniformly tight: for every $\varepsilon >0$ there are a compact set $K\subset \Omega $ and an index $i_0$ such that $\mu _ i(\Omega \setminus K)<\varepsilon $ for all $i\geq i_0$. Then $\mu $ is finite and $\mu _ i\to \mu $ narrowly. In particular, $\mu _ i(\Omega )\to \mu (\Omega )$. Proof. Let $\varepsilon >0$, and choose $K$ and $i_0$ as above. Letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ proves narrow convergence, and $f=1$ gives the last assertion. $\square$

title: Escaping mass
text: Example 1.5.4 . On $\mathbb R$, the Dirac measures $\delta _ j$, $j\geq 1$, converge vaguely to zero, since every $f\in C_ c(\mathbb R)$ vanishes at $j$ for large $j$; yet each has total mass one. title: Local measure selection

title: Nets and compactness
text:
1.6 Nets and compactness In a general topological space, compactness cannot be tested with sequences alone. For instance, the product $[0,1]^{[0,1]}$ of copies of $[0,1]$, whose points are the functions $[0,1]	o [0,1]$, is compact by Tychonoff's theorem (lemma 1.6.2 below), and convergence of a sequence in it is pointwise convergence. Let $f_ n(t)=\lfloor 2^ ntfloor -2\lfloor 2^{n-1}tfloor $ be the $n$th binary digit of $t$. Given $n_1<n_2<\cdots $, the number $t=\sum _{k	ext{ even}}2^{-n_ k}$ has a binary expansion with infinitely many zeros, whose digit at the place $n_ k$ is $1$ for even $k$ and $0$ for odd $k$. Hence $f_{n_ k}(t)$ alternates between $1$ and $0$, and no subsequence of $(f_ n)$ converges. For nets, subnets take the place of subsequences. Recall from the Conventions that subnets are Willard subnets: if $(x_ i)_{i\in I}$ is a net and $h\colon J	o I$ is an increasing map from a directed set $J$ which is final, meaning that for every $i_0\in I$ there is $j_0\in J$ with $h(j)\geq i_0$ for all $j\geq j_0$, then $(x_{h(j)})_{j\in J}$ is a subnet of $(x_ i)$. Every subnet of a net converging to $x$ converges to $x$: given a neighborhood $U$ of $x$, choose $i_0$ with $x_ i\in U$ for $i\geq i_0$, and then $j_0$ as in the definition of finality. Proposition 1.6.1 . A topological space $X$ is compact if and only if every net in $X$ has a convergent Willard subnet. Proof. Suppose that $X$ is compact, and let $(x_ i)_{i\in I}$ be a net in $X$. The closures $T_{i_0}$ of the tails $\{ x_ i:i\geq i_0\} $ have the finite intersection property, since finitely many of them contain the tail of a common upper bound of their indices. As $X$ is compact, they have a common point $x$; otherwise their complements would form an open cover without a finite subcover. Thus every neighborhood of $x$ meets every tail of the net. We now construct a subnet converging to $x$. Let $J$ be the set of triples $(i,U,k)$ with $i,k\in I$, $k\geq i$, $U$ an open neighborhood of $x$ and $x_ k\in U$, preordered by \[  (i,U,k)\leq (i',U',k')\quad 	ext{if }i\leq i',\  U'\subset U,\  k\leq k'.  \] It contains $(i,X,i)$ for every $i$, and it is directed: given two triples $(i_1,U_1,k_1)$ and $(i_2,U_2,k_2)$, choose $i\geq i_1,i_2,k_1,k_2$, put $U=U_1\cap U_2$, and choose $k\geq i$ with $x_ k\in U$, which is possible because $U$ meets the tail of $i$; then $(i,U,k)$ dominates both triples. The map $h(i,U,k)=k$ is increasing, and it is final because $(i,U,k)\geq (i_0,X,i_0)$ implies $k\geq i_0$. The subnet $(x_{h(j)})_{j\in J}$ converges to $x$: if $V$ is a neighborhood of $x$, choose an open neighborhood $U\subset V$ of $x$ and a triple $(i,U,k)\in J$; then $x_{k'}\in U'\subset V$ for every $(i',U',k')\geq (i,U,k)$. Conversely, suppose that $X$ is not compact, and let $\mathcal U$ be an open cover without a finite subcover. The finite subfamilies $F\subset \mathcal U$, ordered by inclusion, form a directed set, and we may choose points $x_ F
otin  igcup F$. If a subnet $(x_{h(j)})_{j\in J}$ converged to a point $x$, let $U\in \mathcal U$ contain $x$. Then $x_{h(j)}\in U$ for all large $j$, while finality gives $h(j)\supset \{ U\} $, and hence $x_{h(j)}
otin U$, for all large $j$. Since $J$ is directed, some $j$ satisfies both conditions, a contradiction. $\square$ Lemma 1.6.2 . A product of compact topological spaces is compact in the product topology. Proof. This is Tychonoff's theorem; we prove it with ultrafilters, using the axiom of choice in the form of Zorn's lemma. A filter on a set $Z$ is a family $\mathcal F$ of subsets of $Z$ such that $Z\in \mathcal F$, $\varnothing 
otin \mathcal F$, and $\mathcal F$ is closed under finite intersections and under passing to supersets. An ultrafilter is a filter which is maximal for inclusion. Since the union of a chain of filters containing a given filter is again a filter, Zorn's lemma shows that every filter is contained in an ultrafilter. A filter $\mathcal U$ on $Z$ is an ultrafilter if and only if, for every $A\subset Z$, either $A\in \mathcal U$ or $Z\setminus A\in \mathcal U$. Indeed, let $\mathcal U$ be an ultrafilter and $A\subset Z$. If $A$ meets every member of $\mathcal U$, the sets containing some $U\cap A$ with $U\in \mathcal U$ form a filter containing $\mathcal U$ and $A$, so $A\in \mathcal U$ by maximality; otherwise some $U\in \mathcal U$ is disjoint from $A$, and $Z\setminus A\supset U$ belongs to $\mathcal U$. Conversely, if $\mathcal U$ has this property, a strictly larger filter would contain some $A
otin \mathcal U$ together with $Z\setminus A$, hence $\varnothing $. A filter on a topological space $Z$ converges to $z$ if every neighborhood of $z$ belongs to it. We show that $Z$ is compact if and only if every ultrafilter on $Z$ converges. If $Z$ is compact and $\mathcal U$ is an ultrafilter, the closures of the members of $\mathcal U$ have the finite intersection property and hence a common point $z$. If an open neighborhood $N$ of $z$ were not in $\mathcal U$, the closed set $Z\setminus N$ would belong to $\mathcal U$. Since $z$ lies in the closure of every member of $\mathcal U$, this would give $z\in Z\setminus N$, which is absurd. Hence $\mathcal U$ converges to $z$. Conversely, suppose that every ultrafilter converges, and let $\mathcal C$ be a family of closed sets with the finite intersection property. The sets containing a finite intersection of members of $\mathcal C$ form a filter, which lies in an ultrafilter $\mathcal U$ converging to some $z$. If $z
otin C$ for some $C\in \mathcal C$, then both $C$ and its complement, a neighborhood of $z$, would belong to $\mathcal U$. Hence $z$ lies in every member of $\mathcal C$, and $Z$ is compact. Now let $Z=\prod _\alpha X_\alpha $ with compact factors and projections $p_\alpha $; if some $X_\alpha $ is empty, so is $Z$, and there is nothing to prove. Let $\mathcal U$ be an ultrafilter on $Z$. For each $\alpha $, the family $\{ A\subset X_\alpha :p_\alpha ^{-1}(A)\in \mathcal U\} $ is a filter with the property characterizing ultrafilters, hence an ultrafilter, and since $X_\alpha $ is compact it converges to some $z_\alpha \in X_\alpha $. Put $z=(z_\alpha )$. A basic neighborhood $ igcap _{l=1}^ np_{\alpha _ l}^{-1}(V_ l)$ of $z$, with $V_ l$ a neighborhood of $z_{\alpha _ l}$, is a finite intersection of members of $\mathcal U$, so every neighborhood of $z$ belongs to $\mathcal U$. Thus every ultrafilter on $Z$ converges, and $Z$ is compact. $\square$ Theorem 1.6.3 . Let $(K_ r)_{r\geq 1}$ be a compact exhaustion of $\Omega $. For each $r$, let $\chi _ r\in C_ c(\Omega )$ be a nonnegative function equal to $1$ on $K_ r$, and let $0\leq M_ r<\infty $. Then \[  \mathcal M=\left\{ \mu 	ext{ Radon measure on }\Omega :\int \chi _ r\, \mathrm d\mu \leq M_ r	ext{ for every }right\}   \] is compact in the vague topology. In particular, every net in $\mathcal M$ has a Willard subnet converging vaguely to an element of $\mathcal M$. Proof. We embed $\mathcal M$ homeomorphically onto a closed subset of a product of compact intervals. For $f\in C_ c(\Omega ,\mathbb R)$, choose $r(f)$ with $\operatorname{Supp}f\subset K_{r(f)}$; this is possible because $\operatorname{Supp}f$ is compact and the open sets $\operatorname{Int}K_ r$ increase to $\Omega $. For $\mu \in \mathcal M$ we have $|f|\leq \| f\| _\infty \chi _{r(f)}$, so $\int f\, \mathrm d\mu $ lies in $I_ f=[-M_{r(f)}\| f\| _\infty ,M_{r(f)}\| f\| _\infty ]$. The product $P=\prod _ fI_ f$ over all $f\in C_ c(\Omega ,\mathbb R)$ is compact by lemma 1.6.2 . The map $\Phi \colon \mathcal M	o P$, $\Phi (\mu )=(\int f\, \mathrm d\mu )_ f$, is injective by the uniqueness in theorem 1.2.2 , and it is a homeomorphism onto its image. Indeed, since $\int f\, \mathrm d\mu =\int \operatorname{Re}f\, \mathrm d\mu +\mathrm i\int \operatorname{Im}f\, \mathrm d\mu $, the vague topology on $\mathcal M$ is the weakest topology for which the maps $\mu \mapsto \int f\, \mathrm d\mu $ with real $f$ are continuous. The subspace topology of $\Phi (\mathcal M)$ is the weakest topology for which the restrictions of the coordinate projections are continuous, and $\Phi $ intertwines these two families of maps. The image consists of the points $(a_ f)\in P$ such that $a_{sf+tg}=sa_ f+ta_ g$ for all $f,g$ and real $s,t$, $a_ f\geq 0$ whenever $f\geq 0$, and $a_{\chi _ r}\leq M_ r$ for every $r$: a point satisfying these conditions defines a positive linear functional on $C_ c(\Omega ,\mathbb R)$, which by theorem 1.2.2 is integration against a Radon measure belonging to $\mathcal M$. Each condition involves finitely many coordinates and is closed, so $\Phi (\mathcal M)$ is closed in $P$ and hence compact. Therefore $\mathcal M$ is vaguely compact, and the assertion about nets follows from proposition 1.6.1 . $\square$ Proposition 1.6.4 (Arzelà–Ascoli) . Let $K$ be a compact metric space, and let $\mathcal F\subset C(K)$ be equicontinuous and pointwise bounded, that is, $\sup _{f\in \mathcal F}|f(x)|<\infty $ for every $x\in K$. Then $\mathcal F$ is relatively compact for the uniform topology. In particular, every sequence in $\mathcal F$ has a uniformly convergent subsequence. Proof. We may assume that $K
eq \varnothing $. Let $\varepsilon >0$. By equicontinuity, every $x\in K$ is the center of an open ball on which $|f-f(x)|<\varepsilon $ for all $f\in \mathcal F$; by compactness, $K$ is covered by finitely many such balls $B_ l$ with centers $x_ l$, $1\leq l\leq N$. Then every $f\in \mathcal F$ is bounded on $K$ by $M=\varepsilon +\max _ l\sup _{g\in \mathcal F}|g(x_ l)|$, which is finite by pointwise boundedness. Let $G$ be a finite set of scalars such that every scalar of absolute value at most $M$ lies at distance less than $\varepsilon $ from some element of $G$. For each map $\gamma \colon \{ 1,\ldots ,N\} 	o G$, the functions $f\in \mathcal F$ with $|f(x_ l)-\gamma (l)|<\varepsilon $ for all $l$ form a set $\mathcal F_\gamma $, and these finitely many sets cover $\mathcal F$. If $f,g\in \mathcal F_\gamma $ and $y\in B_ l$, then \[  |f(y)-g(y)|\leq |f(y)-f(x_ l)|+|f(x_ l)-g(x_ l)|+|g(x_ l)-g(y)|<4\varepsilon .  \] Choosing one function in each nonempty $\mathcal F_\gamma $, we obtain a finite set within uniform distance $4\varepsilon $ of $\mathcal F$, and hence within $5\varepsilon $ of its closure $\overline{\mathcal F}$ in $C(K)$. Thus $\overline{\mathcal F}$ is totally bounded. It is also complete, because $C(K)$ is complete for the uniform metric: a uniform Cauchy sequence converges pointwise, and the limit is continuous since the convergence is uniform. A complete and totally bounded metric space $Y$ is sequentially compact and compact. Given a sequence in $Y$, cover $Y$ by finitely many sets of diameter less than $1$ and keep one containing infinitely many terms. Cover it by finitely many sets of diameter less than $1/2$, keep one containing infinitely many of those terms, and so on. A diagonal choice gives a Cauchy subsequence, which converges because $Y$ is complete. Suppose now that an open cover of $Y$ had no finite subcover, and put $S_0=Y$. Covering $S_{n-1}$ by finitely many subsets of diameter less than $1/n$, we see that one of them, $S_ n$, is not covered by finitely many members of the cover, since otherwise $S_{n-1}$ would be. This gives nested nonempty sets $S_1\supset S_2\supset \cdots $ with $\operatorname {diam}S_ n<1/n$, none of which is covered by finitely many members of the cover. Points $y_ n\in S_ n$ form a Cauchy sequence with a limit $y$. If the open ball of radius $s$ about $y$ in $Y$ lies in a member $U$ of the cover, then $S_ n$ lies in this ball, and hence in $U$, as soon as $1/n+\operatorname {dist}(y_ n,y)<s$, a contradiction. Hence $\overline{\mathcal F}$ is compact, and every sequence in $\mathcal F$ has a uniformly convergent subsequence. $\square$

title: Compact net characterization
text: Proposition 1.6.1 . A topological space $X$ is compact if and only if every net in $X$ has a convergent Willard subnet. Proof. Suppose that $X$ is compact, and let $(x_ i)_{i\in I}$ be a net in $X$. The closures $T_{i_0}$ of the tails $\{ x_ i:i\geq i_0\} $ have the finite intersection property, since finitely many of them contain the tail of a common upper bound of their indices. As $X$ is compact, they have a common point $x$; otherwise their complements would form an open cover without a finite subcover. Thus every neighborhood of $x$ meets every tail of the net. We now construct a subnet converging to $x$. Let $J$ be the set of triples $(i,U,k)$ with $i,k\in I$, $k\geq i$, $U$ an open neighborhood of $x$ and $x_ k\in U$, preordered by \[  (i,U,k)\leq (i',U',k')\quad \text{if }i\leq i',\  U'\subset U,\  k\leq k'.  \] It contains $(i,X,i)$ for every $i$, and it is directed: given two triples $(i_1,U_1,k_1)$ and $(i_2,U_2,k_2)$, choose $i\geq i_1,i_2,k_1,k_2$, put $U=U_1\cap U_2$, and choose $k\geq i$ with $x_ k\in U$, which is possible because $U$ meets the tail of $i$; then $(i,U,k)$ dominates both triples. The map $h(i,U,k)=k$ is increasing, and it is final because $(i,U,k)\geq (i_0,X,i_0)$ implies $k\geq i_0$. The subnet $(x_{h(j)})_{j\in J}$ converges to $x$: if $V$ is a neighborhood of $x$, choose an open neighborhood $U\subset V$ of $x$ and a triple $(i,U,k)\in J$; then $x_{k'}\in U'\subset V$ for every $(i',U',k')\geq (i,U,k)$. Conversely, suppose that $X$ is not compact, and let $\mathcal U$ be an open cover without a finite subcover. The finite subfamilies $F\subset \mathcal U$, ordered by inclusion, form a directed set, and we may choose points $x_ F\notin \bigcup F$. If a subnet $(x_{h(j)})_{j\in J}$ converged to a point $x$, let $U\in \mathcal U$ contain $x$. Then $x_{h(j)}\in U$ for all large $j$, while finality gives $h(j)\supset \{ U\} $, and hence $x_{h(j)}\notin U$, for all large $j$. Since $J$ is directed, some $j$ satisfies both conditions, a contradiction. $\square$

title: Compact product
text:
Lemma 1.6.2 . A product of compact topological spaces is compact in the product topology. Proof. This is Tychonoff's theorem; we prove it with ultrafilters, using the axiom of choice in the form of Zorn's lemma. A filter on a set $Z$ is a family $\mathcal F$ of subsets of $Z$ such that $Z\in \mathcal F$, $\varnothing 
otin \mathcal F$, and $\mathcal F$ is closed under finite intersections and under passing to supersets. An ultrafilter is a filter which is maximal for inclusion. Since the union of a chain of filters containing a given filter is again a filter, Zorn's lemma shows that every filter is contained in an ultrafilter. A filter $\mathcal U$ on $Z$ is an ultrafilter if and only if, for every $A\subset Z$, either $A\in \mathcal U$ or $Z\setminus A\in \mathcal U$. Indeed, let $\mathcal U$ be an ultrafilter and $A\subset Z$. If $A$ meets every member of $\mathcal U$, the sets containing some $U\cap A$ with $U\in \mathcal U$ form a filter containing $\mathcal U$ and $A$, so $A\in \mathcal U$ by maximality; otherwise some $U\in \mathcal U$ is disjoint from $A$, and $Z\setminus A\supset U$ belongs to $\mathcal U$. Conversely, if $\mathcal U$ has this property, a strictly larger filter would contain some $A
otin \mathcal U$ together with $Z\setminus A$, hence $\varnothing $. A filter on a topological space $Z$ converges to $z$ if every neighborhood of $z$ belongs to it. We show that $Z$ is compact if and only if every ultrafilter on $Z$ converges. If $Z$ is compact and $\mathcal U$ is an ultrafilter, the closures of the members of $\mathcal U$ have the finite intersection property and hence a common point $z$. If an open neighborhood $N$ of $z$ were not in $\mathcal U$, the closed set $Z\setminus N$ would belong to $\mathcal U$. Since $z$ lies in the closure of every member of $\mathcal U$, this would give $z\in Z\setminus N$, which is absurd. Hence $\mathcal U$ converges to $z$. Conversely, suppose that every ultrafilter converges, and let $\mathcal C$ be a family of closed sets with the finite intersection property. The sets containing a finite intersection of members of $\mathcal C$ form a filter, which lies in an ultrafilter $\mathcal U$ converging to some $z$. If $z
otin C$ for some $C\in \mathcal C$, then both $C$ and its complement, a neighborhood of $z$, would belong to $\mathcal U$. Hence $z$ lies in every member of $\mathcal C$, and $Z$ is compact. Now let $Z=\prod _\alpha X_\alpha $ with compact factors and projections $p_\alpha $; if some $X_\alpha $ is empty, so is $Z$, and there is nothing to prove. Let $\mathcal U$ be an ultrafilter on $Z$. For each $\alpha $, the family $\{ A\subset X_\alpha :p_\alpha ^{-1}(A)\in \mathcal U\} $ is a filter with the property characterizing ultrafilters, hence an ultrafilter, and since $X_\alpha $ is compact it converges to some $z_\alpha \in X_\alpha $. Put $z=(z_\alpha )$. A basic neighborhood $ igcap _{l=1}^ np_{\alpha _ l}^{-1}(V_ l)$ of $z$, with $V_ l$ a neighborhood of $z_{\alpha _ l}$, is a finite intersection of members of $\mathcal U$, so every neighborhood of $z$ belongs to $\mathcal U$. Thus every ultrafilter on $Z$ converges, and $Z$ is compact. $\square$

title: Arzelà–Ascoli

title: Densities and differentiation of integrals
text:

u $. When $

Together with a Poincaré inequality on cubes, these results relate a distributional Hessian to a pointwise second-order expansion (proposition 1.7.5 ), and they will later describe the coefficients of positive currents. For a Radon measure $

u $ be a Radon measure on $\Omega $, and let $T$ be a real distribution on $\Omega $. If there is a constant $C\geq 0$ with $|\langle T,\chi angle |\leq C\int \chi \, \mathrm d

title: Lebesgue differentiation
text: Theorem 1.7.3 (Lebesgue differentiation) . Let $f$ be a locally integrable function on $\Omega $. Then almost every $x\in \Omega $ is a Lebesgue point of $f$, that is, $f(x)$ is finite and \[  \lim _{r\downarrow 0}\frac1{|Q(x,r)|} \int _{Q(x,r)}|f(y)-f(x)|\, \mathrm dy=0, \qquad Q(x,r)=x+(-r,r)^ d.  \] At every Lebesgue point $x$ of $f$, the mollifications satisfy $f_\varepsilon (x)\to f(x)$ as $\varepsilon \to 0$. Proof. We prove a maximal inequality on $\mathbb R^ d$, deduce the theorem for integrable functions by approximation with continuous ones, and then localize. The set $N$ where $f$ is infinite is a null set. Changing $f$ to $0$ on $N$ changes neither the averages in the statement nor the values $f(x)$ for $x\notin N$, so the modified function has the same Lebesgue points outside $N$ and the same mollifications. We may therefore assume that $f$ is finite everywhere. Consider first $f\in L^1(\mathbb R^ d)$, and define its maximal function $Mf(x)$ as the supremum over $r>0$ of the averages of $|f|$ over $Q(x,r)$. For fixed $r$, the average of $|f|$ over $Q(x,r)$ depends continuously on $x$, because $\int _{Q(x,r)}|f|$ and $\int _{Q(x',r)}|f|$ differ by at most $\| f(\cdot +x-x')-f\| _1$, which tends to zero as $x'\to x$ by the continuity of translation in $L^1$ (lemma 1.4.1 (2)). As a supremum of continuous functions, $Mf$ is lower semicontinuous, so $\{ Mf>t\} $ is open. We claim the maximal inequality \[  |\{ Mf>t\} |\le \frac{3^ d}{t}\| f\| _1,\qquad t>0.  \] By inner regularity of Lebesgue measure, it suffices to bound $|L|$ for compact $L\subset \{ Mf>t\} $. Each point of $L$ is the center of an open cube over which the average of $|f|$ exceeds $t$, and finitely many of these cubes cover $L$. Select one of largest side length, discard all cubes meeting it, and repeat with the remaining ones. The selected cubes are disjoint, and each discarded cube meets a selected cube of at least the same side length, so it lies in the concentric cube with three times that side length. These enlarged cubes cover $L$, and therefore $|L|$ is at most $3^ d$ times the total volume of the selected cubes, which is less than $t^{-1}\| f\| _1$. Now let $g\in C_ c(\mathbb R^ d)$. For every $x$ and $r$, \[  \begin{split}  \frac1{|Q(x,r)|}\int _{Q(x,r)}|f(y)-f(x)|\, \mathrm dy\leq {}& M(f-g)(x)+|g(x)-f(x)|\\ & +\frac1{|Q(x,r)|}\int _{Q(x,r)}|g(y)-g(x)|\, \mathrm dy, \end{split}  \] and the last term tends to zero as $r\downarrow 0$ because $g$ is continuous at $x$. Hence the upper limit $\Lambda f(x)$ of the left side satisfies $\Lambda f\leq M(f-g)+|f-g|$, and for $t>0$ the set $\{ \Lambda f>2t\} $ is contained in $\{ M(f-g)>t\} \cup \{ |f-g|>t\} $, whose measure is at most $(3^ d+1)t^{-1}\| f-g\| _1$ by the maximal inequality and Chebyshev's inequality. By proposition 1.2.3 , $\| f-g\| _1$ can be made arbitrarily small, so $\{ \Lambda f>2t\} $ is contained in measurable sets of arbitrarily small measure and is therefore a null set. Letting $t$ run through the positive rationals shows that $\Lambda f=0$ almost everywhere. Next, let $f$ be locally integrable on $\Omega $, and let $(K_ j)$ be a compact exhaustion of $\Omega $. The function equal to $f$ on $\operatorname{Int}K_{j+1}$ and to $0$ elsewhere belongs to $L^1(\mathbb R^ d)$, and for $x\in \operatorname{Int}K_ j$ and small $r$ the averages in the statement are the same for $f$ and for this function. Hence almost every point of each $\operatorname{Int}K_ j$, and therefore of $\Omega $, is a Lebesgue point of $f$. Finally, let $x$ be a Lebesgue point of $f$ and let $\varepsilon >0$ be so small that $x\in \Omega _\varepsilon $. The function $\rho _\varepsilon (x-\cdot )$ is bounded by $\varepsilon ^{-d}\sup \rho =2^ d\sup \rho /|Q(x,\varepsilon )|$ and vanishes outside $B(x,\varepsilon )\subset Q(x,\varepsilon )$. Since $\int \rho _\varepsilon =1$, \[  \begin{split}  |f_\varepsilon (x)-f(x)|& =\left|\int (f(y)-f(x))\rho _\varepsilon (x-y)\, \mathrm dy\right|\\ & \leq \frac{2^ d\sup \rho }{|Q(x,\varepsilon )|}\int _{Q(x,\varepsilon )}|f(y)-f(x)|\, \mathrm dy, \end{split}  \] which tends to zero as $\varepsilon \to 0$. $\square$

title: Weak poincare cube
text: Lemma 1.7.4 . Let $Q\subset \mathbb R^ d$ be a closed cube of side length $l$, and let $F$ be a locally integrable function on an open neighborhood $V$ of $Q$ whose distributional first derivatives $\partial _ kF$ on $V$ are locally integrable. Put $F_ Q=|Q|^{-1}\int _ QF\, \mathrm dx$. Then \[  \int _ Q|F-F_ Q|\, \mathrm dx\le l\sum _{k=1}^ d\int _ Q|\partial _ kF|\, \mathrm dx.  \] The same assertion holds componentwise for vector-valued $F$. Proof. Suppose first that $F$ is continuously differentiable near $Q$. For $x,y\in Q$, the points $z^{(k)}=(y_1,\ldots ,y_ k,x_{k+1},\ldots ,x_ d)$, $0\leq k\leq d$, lead from $x$ to $y$ by changing one coordinate at a time. If $I_ k$ is the $k$th side interval of $Q$, the fundamental theorem of calculus gives \[  |F(y)-F(x)|\leq \sum _{k=1}^ d\int _{I_ k}|\partial _ kF(y_1,\ldots ,y_{k-1},t,x_{k+1},\ldots ,x_ d)|\, \mathrm dt.  \] Integrate over $(x,y)\in Q\times Q$. The $k$th term does not depend on the $d+1$ coordinates $x_1,\ldots ,x_ k,y_ k,\ldots ,y_ d$, which contribute a factor $l^{d+1}$, and integration over the remaining coordinates and $t$ gives $\int _ Q|\partial _ kF|\, \mathrm dx$. Since $|F(x)-F_ Q|\leq |Q|^{-1}\int _ Q|F(x)-F(y)|\, \mathrm dy$ and $|Q|=l^ d$, the inequality follows. In general, the mollifications $F_\varepsilon $ are smooth on $V_\varepsilon =\{ x\in V:\operatorname {dist}(x,\mathbb R^ d\setminus V)>\varepsilon \} $, which is a neighborhood of $Q$ for small $\varepsilon $. By lemma 1.4.1 (2) and proposition 1.4.3 (1), $F_\varepsilon \to F$ and $\partial _ kF_\varepsilon =(\partial _ kF)_\varepsilon \to \partial _ kF$ in $L^1(Q)$. Since $|(F_\varepsilon )_ Q-F_ Q|\leq |Q|^{-1}\| F_\varepsilon -F\| _{L^1(Q)}$, the left sides of the inequality for $F_\varepsilon $ and for $F$ differ by at most $2\| F_\varepsilon -F\| _{L^1(Q)}$, and the inequality for $F_\varepsilon $ passes to the limit. $\square$

title: Bounded hessian taylor

Proposition 1.7.5 . Let $f\colon \Omega 	o \mathbb R$ be continuous, and suppose that its real distributional Hessian has locally bounded measurable coefficients, that is, $\partial _ a\partial _ bf=A_{ab}$ for measurable functions $A_{ab}$ on $\Omega $ that are bounded on compact sets, $1\leq a,b\leq d$. Then $f\in C^{1,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$: its first derivatives exist and are locally Lipschitz. More precisely, if $V\subset \Omega $ is a convex open set and $|A_{ab}|\leq C$ almost everywhere on $V$ for all $a$ and $b$, then $

More precisely, it suffices that every ball $B\Subset \Omega $ carry smooth functions $f_ j$ which converge to $f$ in the sense of distributions on $B$ and whose second derivatives are bounded on $B$ uniformly in $j$. Applying proposition 1.6.4 successively to the components of the maps $

Covering $\Omega $ by such balls $B$, we conclude that $f\in C^1(\Omega )$ and that its distributional first derivatives coincide with the continuous functions $\partial _ af$ on each such ball, hence on $\Omega $ by the last assertion of lemma 1.4.2 . Consequently, $\partial _ af_\varepsilon =(\partial _ af)_\varepsilon 	o \partial _ af$ uniformly on compact subsets of $\Omega $, by lemma 1.4.1 (1). Step 2: the Lipschitz bound. Let $V\subset \Omega $ be convex and open with $|A_{ab}|\leq C$ almost everywhere on $V$, and let $x,y\in V$. The segment $[x,y]$ is a compact subset of $V$; choose $\delta >0$ smaller than its distance to $\mathbb R^ d\setminus V$. For $\varepsilon <\delta $ and $z\in [x,y]$, the closed ball $\overline{B(z,\varepsilon )}$ lies in $V$, so $z\in \Omega _\varepsilon $ and $|\partial _ a\partial _ bf_\varepsilon (z)|=|(A_{ab}*ho _\varepsilon )(z)|\leq C$. As in Step 1, $|

By theorem 1.7.3 , almost every point of $\Omega $ is a common Lebesgue point of the functions $A_{ab}$. Let $x$ be such a point, let $Q=(-1,1)^ d$, and choose $r_0>0$ with $x+3r_0\overline Q\subset \Omega $. The functions $|A_{ab}|$ are bounded on the compact set $x+3r_0\overline Q$ by some constant $C$, so by Step 2, $

The function $z\mapsto \psi ((z-x)/r)$ is a test function on $\Omega $, and the distributional derivative $\partial _ b$ of the continuous function $\partial _ af$ is $\partial _ b\partial _ af=\partial _ a\partial _ bf=A_{ab}$, since partial derivatives of distributions commute. Hence the change of variables $z=x+ry$ gives \[   egin{split}  \int  rac{\partial _ af(x+ry)}r\, \partial _ b\psi (y)\, \mathrm dy& =r^{-d}\int \partial _ af(z)\, \partial _{z_ b} igl [\psi ((z-x)/r) igr ]\, \mathrm dz\ & =-\int A_{ab}(x+ry)\psi (y)\, \mathrm dy. \end{split}  \] Thus $\partial _{y_ b}(G_ r)_ a(y)=A_{ab}(x+ry)-A_{ab}(x)$ in the sense of distributions on $2Q$, and since $x$ is a Lebesgue point, \[  \int _ Q|A_{ab}(x+ry)-A_{ab}(x)|\, \mathrm dy= rac1{r^ d}\int _{Q(x,r)}|A_{ab}(z)-A_{ab}(x)|\, \mathrm dz	o 0\qquad (r\downarrow 0).  \] Lemma 1.7.4 , applied on the cube $\overline Q$ of side length $2$ to each component of $G_ r$, gives \[  \int _ Q|G_ r-(G_ r)_ Q|\, \mathrm dy\leq 2\sum _{a,b}\int _ Q|A_{ab}(x+ry)-A_{ab}(x)|\, \mathrm dy	o 0\qquad (r\downarrow 0).  \] We deduce that $\sup _{\overline Q}|G_ r-(G_ r)_ Q|	o 0$. Otherwise there would be $\kappa >0$, radii $r_ k	o 0$ and points $y_ k\in \overline Q$ with $|G_{r_ k}(y_ k)-(G_{r_ k})_ Q|\geq \kappa $, and by the common Lipschitz bound, $|G_{r_ k}-(G_{r_ k})_ Q|\geq \kappa /2$ on $Q\cap B(y_ k,\kappa /(2\Lambda ))$.
