title: Harmonic functions and the Dirichlet problem
topic: Harmonic functions and the Dirichlet problem
text: 2 Harmonic functions and the Dirichlet problem Harmonic functions are the solutions of the Laplace equation $\Delta h=0$. In potential theory they play the role that affine functions play for convex functions: the subharmonic functions of chapter 3 are studied by comparison with them, and the fundamental solution of the Laplacian, together with the Green functions obtained from it by harmonic corrections, defines the potentials and energies of chapter 4 , chapter 5 . Unless stated otherwise, $\Omega $ denotes an open subset of $\mathbb R^ d$, where $d\geq 1$. We begin with mean values. After introducing surface measure, polar coordinates and the divergence theorem on balls, we show that a continuous function is harmonic exactly when its value at the center of every closed ball in its domain equals its mean over the boundary sphere (theorem 2.1.2 ). Averaging against a mollifier then shows that harmonic functions are smooth, with interior estimates for all their derivatives. A distribution in the sense of chapter 1 need not have pointwise values; nevertheless, Weyl's lemma (theorem 2.1.4 ) shows that a distribution with vanishing Laplacian is a smooth harmonic function. The fundamental solution of the Laplacian (proposition 2.2.1 ) fixes the sign conventions for all later potentials. The Dirichlet problem asks for a harmonic function with prescribed continuous boundary values. On a ball it is solved explicitly by the Poisson integral (theorem 2.3.1 ), whose kernel also yields the Harnack inequalities and the compactness of families of nonnegative harmonic functions. On a general bounded open set there is no such formula, and we use Perron's method instead. The candidate solution is the pointwise supremum of all continuous subsolutions whose boundary values do not exceed the data; replacing a subsolution on a small ball by the Poisson integral of its values shows that this envelope is harmonic (theorem 2.4.2 ). The envelope also depends linearly on the data (theorem 2.4.4 ). A boundary point is regular if the envelope attains the prescribed value there for all data. Regularity is decided by the existence of a barrier, which need only be constructed near the point (theorem 2.4.6 , proposition 2.4.7 ); for $d\geq 2$, regularity fails at the center of a punctured ball. When every boundary point is regular, the solution operator is integration against harmonic measure, and correcting the fundamental solution by the harmonic function with the same boundary values gives the Green function (theorem 2.5.2 ). Historical remarks and references for this chapter are collected in section B.2 .

title: The Laplacian and mean values
topic: Harmonic functions and the Dirichlet problem
text:
2.1 The Laplacian and mean values Recall from section 1.4 that $B(x,r)$ is the open ball with center $x$ and radius $r>0$; its closure $\overline{B(x,r)}$ is the closed ball. We write $S^{d-1}=\{ y\in \mathbb R^ d:|y|=1\} $ for the unit sphere. The Laplacian is $\Delta =\sum _{j=1}^ d\partial _{x_ j}^2$. A real function $h\in C^2(\Omega )$ is harmonic if $\Delta h=0$, and a complex function is harmonic if its real and imaginary parts are harmonic. In dimension one the harmonic functions are the functions that are affine on each component interval of $\Omega $, because $h''=0$ on an interval forces $h'$ to be constant there. We define surface measure on the unit sphere through the Lebesgue measure of cones: for a Borel set $A\subset S^{d-1}$ put \[  S(A)=d\,  igl |\{ t\omega :0<t<1,\  \omega \in A\}  igr |.  \] The cone over $A$ is the inverse image of $A$ under the continuous map $y\mapsto y/|y|$ on $B(0,1)\setminus \{ 0\} $, so it is a Borel set; moreover, the cone over a countable union is the union of the cones, and cones over disjoint sets are disjoint. Hence $S$ is a finite Borel measure on $S^{d-1}$, the surface measure . It is invariant under every orthogonal transformation $Q$ of $\mathbb R^ d$: the cone over $QA$ is the image under $Q$ of the cone over $A$, and Lebesgue measure is invariant under orthogonal transformations. By linearity and monotone convergence (proposition 1.1.3 ), it follows that $\int _{S^{d-1}}g\circ Q\, \mathrm dS=\int _{S^{d-1}}g\, \mathrm dS$ for every nonnegative or integrable Borel function $g$. We write $s_{d-1}=S(S^{d-1})$ for the area of the unit sphere, so that the unit ball has volume $s_{d-1}/d$. For instance, $s_0=2$, because $S$ is counting measure on $S^0=\{ \pm 1\} $, and $s_1=2\pi $, because the unit disc has area $\pi $. On a sphere $\partial B(x,r)$ we use the measure obtained by translation and dilation, again denoted $\mathrm dS$: \[  \int _{\partial B(x,r)}g\, \mathrm dS=r^{d-1}\int _{S^{d-1}}g(x+r\omega )\, \mathrm dS(\omega ).  \] Next we express Lebesgue measure in polar coordinates. Let $0\leq a<b$ and let $A\subset S^{d-1}$ be a Borel set. By dilation, the cone $\{ t\omega :0<t<b,\  \omega \in A\} $ has Lebesgue measure $b^ dS(A)/d$. The set $\{ t\omega :0<t\leq a,\  \omega \in A\} $ is the intersection of the decreasing cones $\{ t\omega :0<t<a+1/n,\  \omega \in A\} $, so its measure is $\lim _ n(a+1/n)^ dS(A)/d=a^ dS(A)/d$. Subtracting and translating, we find that for every $x\in \mathbb R^ d$ the annular sector $\{ x+t\omega :a<t<b,\  \omega \in A\} $ has Lebesgue measure \[   rac{(b^ d-a^ d)S(A)}{d}=S(A)\int _ a^ bt^{d-1}\, \mathrm dt.  \] Now fix $x\in \mathbb R^ d$ and $R>0$, let $\lambda $ be the measure $t^{d-1}\, \mathrm dt$ on the Borel sets of $(0,R)$, and let $\Phi (t,\omega )=x+t\omega $. The map $\Phi $ is a homeomorphism from $(0,R)	imes S^{d-1}$ onto $Z=B(x,R)\setminus \{ x\} $, with inverse $y\mapsto (|y-x|,(y-x)/|y-x|)$, and the annular sectors with center $x$ contained in $Z$ are the images under $\Phi $ of the rectangles $(a,b)	imes A$ with $b\leq R$. These sectors generate the Borel $\sigma $-algebra of $Z$. Indeed, the sets $(a,b)	imes (S^{d-1}\cap B(\omega ,q))$, where $0<a<b<R$ are rational, $\omega $ runs through a countable dense subset of $S^{d-1}$ and $q$ through the positive rationals, form a countable base of the topology of $(0,R)	imes S^{d-1}$. Hence every open subset of $Z$ is a countable union of their images, which are sectors. The sets $E\subset Z$ for which $\Phi ^{-1}(E)$ belongs to the product $\sigma $-algebra form a $\sigma $-algebra containing the sectors, and hence all Borel subsets of $Z$. Consequently $\mu (E)=(\lambda 	imes S)(\Phi ^{-1}(E))$ defines a finite Borel measure $\mu $ on $Z$, and $\mu $ agrees with Lebesgue measure on the sectors. The sectors are closed under finite intersections, and $Z$ itself is a sector, so the two finite measures agree on every Borel subset of $Z$ by part (2) of lemma 1.1.6 . Hence $\int _ Zf\, \mathrm dy=\int f\circ \Phi \, \mathrm d(\lambda 	imes S)$ for indicator functions of Borel sets, by linearity for nonnegative simple Borel functions, and by monotone convergence (proposition 1.1.3 ) for all nonnegative Borel functions $f$. Since the point $x$ is a Lebesgue null set, Tonelli's theorem (proposition 1.1.7 ) yields the formula of integration in polar coordinates 2.1  egin{equation} \label{eq:polar-coordinates} \int _{B(x,R)}f(y)\, \mathrm d y =\int _0^ R r^{d-1}\int _{S^{d-1}}f(x+r\omega )\, \mathrm d S(\omega )\, \mathrm d r \end{equation} for every nonnegative Borel function $f$ on $B(x,R)$. Applying it to the positive and negative parts of $\operatorname{Re}f$ and $\operatorname{Im}f$ and using Fubini's theorem, we obtain ( 2.1 ) for every Borel function $f$ which is integrable on $B(x,R)$. Letting $R	o \infty $ and using monotone convergence, we see that ( 2.1 ) also holds with $R=\infty $, where $B(x,\infty )=\mathbb R^ d$. In particular, every sphere $\partial B(x,r)$ is a Lebesgue null set, since its indicator function vanishes at $x+t\omega $ unless $t=r$. Next we prove the divergence theorem on balls. Let $B=B(c,R)$, let $
u (y)=(y-c)/R$ be the outward unit normal on $\partial B$, and let $F=(F_1,\ldots ,F_ d)$ be a $C^1$ vector field on an open neighborhood $U$ of $\overline B$, with divergence $\operatorname {div}F=\sum _{j=1}^ d\partial _ jF_ j$. Then 2.2  egin{equation} \label{eq:ball-divergence} \int _ B\operatorname {div}F\, \mathrm dy=\int _{\partial B}F\cdot 
u \, \mathrm dS. \end{equation} It suffices to prove, for each $j$, that $\int _ B\partial _ jF_ j\, \mathrm dy=\int _{\partial B}F_ j
u _ j\, \mathrm dS$. To do so, we approximate $\mathbf1_ B$ by smooth radial cutoff functions $\chi _\varepsilon $ and integrate $\partial _ j(F_ j\chi _\varepsilon )$ over $\mathbb R^ d$. Let $0<\varepsilon <R$, and let $\psi _\varepsilon $ be a smooth nonnegative function on $\mathbb R$ with support in $[R-\varepsilon ,R]$ and integral one, for instance a translate and dilate of the mollifier $ho $ of section 1.4 in dimension one. The function $	heta _\varepsilon (t)=\int _ t^\infty \psi _\varepsilon (s)\, \mathrm ds$ is smooth with values in $[0,1]$, equals $1$ for $t\leq R-\varepsilon $ and $0$ for $t\geq R$, and satisfies $	heta _\varepsilon '=-\psi _\varepsilon $. Hence $\chi _\varepsilon (y)=	heta _\varepsilon (|y-c|)$ is smooth on $\mathbb R^ d$, because $|y-c|$ is smooth for $y
eq c$ and $\chi _\varepsilon =1$ on $B(c,R-\varepsilon )$. Moreover, $\chi _\varepsilon $ vanishes outside $\overline B$, and \[  \partial _ j\chi _\varepsilon (y)=-\psi _\varepsilon (|y-c|)\,  rac{y_ j-c_ j}{|y-c|}\qquad (y
eq c).  \] The function $F_ j\chi _\varepsilon $, extended by zero outside $U$, is a $C^1$ function with compact support on $\mathbb R^ d$, because it is $C^1$ on $U$ and vanishes on the open set $\mathbb R^ d\setminus \overline B$. On the left, $\chi _\varepsilon 	o \mathbf1_ B$ pointwise and $|\chi _\varepsilon \partial _ jF_ j|\leq |\partial _ jF_ j|\mathbf1_{\overline B}$, so by dominated convergence the left side tends to $\int _ B\partial _ jF_ j\, \mathrm dy$. u (c+R\omega )=\omega $, so the definition of surface measure on $\partial B$ gives $g(R)=\int _{\partial B}F_ j
u _ j\, \mathrm dS$. Summing over $j$ proves ( 2.2 ). We also need the corresponding identity on an annulus. Let $0<r<R$, and let $F$ be a $C^1$ vector field on an open neighborhood $U$ of the closed annulus $\{ r\leq |y-c|\leq R\} $. Choose a smooth function $\eta $ with compact support in $U$ which equals one near the annulus (lemma 1.4.1 (4)). Then $\eta F$, extended by zero outside $U$, is a $C^1$ vector field on $\mathbb R^ d$, and it equals $F$ near the closed annulus. We apply ( 2.2 ) to $\eta F$ on $B(c,R)$ and on $B(c,r)$ and subtract. On the left we obtain the integral of $\operatorname {div}(\eta F)$ over $\{ r\leq |y-c|<R\} $, which is the integral of $\operatorname {div}F$ over the open annulus, because the sphere $\partial B(c,r)$ is a Lebesgue null set. Hence 2.3  egin{equation} \label{eq:annulus-divergence} \int _{r<|y-c|<R}\operatorname {div}F\, \mathrm dy=\int _{\partial B(c,R)}F\cdot 
u \, \mathrm dS-\int _{\partial B(c,r)}F\cdot 
u \, \mathrm dS, \end{equation} where $
u (y)=(y-c)/|y-c|$ on both spheres. For a continuous function $u$ on $\Omega $ and a closed ball $\overline{B(x,r)}\subset \Omega $, we write \[  M_ u(x,r)= rac{1}{s_{d-1}}\int _{S^{d-1}}u(x+r\omega )\, \mathrm d S(\omega )  \] for the spherical mean of $u$ over the sphere $\partial B(x,r)$. We say that $u$ has the sphere mean-value property if $u(x)=M_ u(x,r)$ for every closed ball $\overline{B(x,r)}\subset \Omega $, and the ball mean-value property if $u(x)=|B(x,r)|^{-1}\int _{B(x,r)}u\, \mathrm dy$ for every such ball. Proposition 2.1.1 . Let $u\in C^2(\Omega )$ and $\overline{B(x,R)}\subset \Omega $. Then, for $0<r<R$, 2.4  egin{equation} \label{eq:spherical-mean-derivative}  rac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm d r}M_ u(x,r) = rac{1}{s_{d-1}r^{d-1}}\int _{B(x,r)}\Delta u(y)\, \mathrm d y. \end{equation} In particular, harmonic functions have both the sphere and the ball mean-value properties. Proof. Fix $0<r<R$. For $\omega \in S^{d-1}$ and small $h
eq 0$, the fundamental theorem of calculus gives \[   rac{u(x+(r+h)\omega )-u(x+r\omega )}{h}=\int _0^1
abla u(x+(r+sh)\omega )\cdot \omega \, \mathrm ds.  \] Since $
abla u$ is uniformly continuous on the compact set $\overline{B(x,R)}$, these difference quotients converge to $
abla u(x+r\omega )\cdot \omega $ uniformly in $\omega $ as $h	o 0$. Integrating over the finite measure space $(S^{d-1},S)$ and using the definition of surface measure on $\partial B(x,r)$, where $
u (x+r\omega )=\omega $, we obtain \[   rac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm d r}M_ u(x,r)= rac{1}{s_{d-1}}\int _{S^{d-1}}
abla u(x+r\omega )\cdot \omega \, \mathrm dS(\omega )= rac{1}{s_{d-1}r^{d-1}}\int _{\partial B(x,r)}
abla u\cdot 
u \, \mathrm dS.  \] Applying ( 2.2 ) on $B(x,r)$ to $F=
abla u$, which is $C^1$ on $\Omega $ with divergence $\Delta u$, gives ( 2.4 ). Now let $u$ be harmonic. Then $M_ u(x,\cdot )$ has zero derivative, and hence is constant, on $(0,R)$. Since $|M_ u(x,r)-u(x)|\leq \max _{|y-x|=r}|u(y)-u(x)|$, which tends to zero as $r\downarrow 0$ because $u$ is continuous at $x$, the constant is $u(x)$. If $\overline{B(x,r)}\subset \Omega $, then the compact set $\overline{B(x,r)}$ has positive distance from the closed set $\mathbb R^ d\setminus \Omega $, so there is $R>r$ with $\overline{B(x,R)}\subset \Omega $, and therefore $u(x)=M_ u(x,r)$; this is the sphere mean-value property. Since $M_ u(x,t)=u(x)$ for $0<t\leq r$, ( 2.1 ) gives $\int _{B(x,r)}u\, \mathrm dy=s_{d-1}r^ du(x)/d=|B(x,r)|\, u(x)$, which is the ball mean-value property. $\square$ Theorem 2.1.2 . A continuous function on $\Omega $ is harmonic if and only if it has the sphere mean-value property. Every harmonic function is smooth. If $h$ is harmonic on $\Omega $ and $\overline{B(x,r)}\subset \Omega $, then for every multi-index $\alpha $, 2.5  egin{equation} \label{eq:harmonic-interior-derivatives} |\partial ^\alpha h(x)|\leq C_{d,\alpha }r^{-d-|\alpha |}\int _{B(x,r)}|h(y)|\, \mathrm d y, \end{equation} where the constant $C_{d,\alpha }$ depends only on $d$ and $\alpha $. Moreover, every harmonic function $h$ on $\Omega $ satisfies $h*ho _\varepsilon =h$ on $\Omega _\varepsilon $ for every $\varepsilon >0$, where $ho _\varepsilon $ and $\Omega _\varepsilon $ are as in section 1.4 . Proof. As in section 1.4 , we write $u_\varepsilon =u*ho _\varepsilon $. Let $u$ be continuous with the sphere mean-value property, and let $\overline{B(x,\varepsilon )}\subset \Omega $. The compact set $\overline{B(x,\varepsilon )}$ has positive distance from $\mathbb R^ d\setminus \Omega $, so $x\in \Omega _\varepsilon $, and $M_ u(x,r)=u(x)$ for $0<r\leq \varepsilon $. Since $ho $ is radial, we may write $ho _\varepsilon (y)=\phi _\varepsilon (|y|)$; as $ho _\varepsilon $ is even and vanishes outside $B(0,\varepsilon )$, ( 2.1 ) gives 2.6  egin{equation} \label{eq:mean-value-mollifier}  egin{split}  u_\varepsilon (x)& =\int _{B(0,\varepsilon )}u(x+y)ho _\varepsilon (y)\, \mathrm dy=s_{d-1}\int _0^\varepsilon r^{d-1}\phi _\varepsilon (r)M_ u(x,r)\, \mathrm dr\ & =u(x)\, s_{d-1}\int _0^\varepsilon r^{d-1}\phi _\varepsilon (r)\, \mathrm dr=u(x)\int _{\mathbb R^ d}ho _\varepsilon \, \mathrm dy=u(x). \end{split} \end{equation} Every point of $\Omega _\varepsilon $ is the center of such a closed ball, so $u=u_\varepsilon $ on the open set $\Omega _\varepsilon $, and $u_\varepsilon $ is smooth there (section 1.4 ). As $\Omega $ is the union of the sets $\Omega _\varepsilon $, the function $u$ is smooth. Next we show that $\Delta u=0$. Fix $x\in \Omega $. Taylor's formula gives \[  u(x+r\omega )=u(x)+r\sum _ j\partial _ ju(x)\, \omega _ j+ rac{r^2}{2}\sum _{j,k}\partial _ j\partial _ ku(x)\, \omega _ j\omega _ k+o(r^2),  \] uniformly in $\omega \in S^{d-1}$. We average over the sphere. The reflections $\omega \mapsto -\omega $ and $\omega _ j\mapsto -\omega _ j$ preserve $S$, so $\int \omega _ j\, \mathrm dS=0$ and $\int \omega _ j\omega _ k\, \mathrm dS=0$ for $j
eq k$. Permutations of the coordinates also preserve $S$, so the integrals $\int \omega _ j^2\, \mathrm dS$ are all equal, and their sum is $s_{d-1}$ because $\sum _ j\omega _ j^2=1$. Hence \[  M_ u(x,r)=u(x)+ rac{r^2}{2d}\Delta u(x)+o(r^2).  \] Since $M_ u(x,r)=u(x)$ for all small $r$, it follows that $\Delta u(x)=0$. Thus $u$ is harmonic. Conversely, harmonic functions have the sphere mean-value property by proposition 2.1.1 ; in particular they are smooth, and they satisfy $h=h_\varepsilon =h*ho _\varepsilon $ on $\Omega _\varepsilon $ by the first part of the proof. Now let $h$ be harmonic and $\overline{B(x,r)}\subset \Omega $. Then $x$ lies in the open set $\Omega _ r$, and $h=h_ r$ on $\Omega _ r$ by the first part of the proof. By the differentiation formula $\partial ^\alpha h_ r=h*\partial ^\alpha ho _ r$ of section 1.4 , and since $\partial ^\alpha ho _ r$ vanishes outside $B(0,r)$, we get \[  \partial ^\alpha h(x)=\int _{B(x,r)} h(y)\, (\partial ^\alpha ho _ r)(x-y)\, \mathrm d y.  \] Since $\partial ^\alpha ho _ r(z)=r^{-d-|\alpha |}(\partial ^\alpha ho )(z/r)$, this proves ( 2.5 ) with $C_{d,\alpha }=\sup |\partial ^\alpha ho |$, where $ho $ is the mollifier on $\mathbb R^ d$ fixed in section 1.4 . $\square$ Proposition 2.1.3 . Let $h$ be a real harmonic function on an open set $D\subset \mathbb R^ d$. If $D$ is connected and $h$ attains its maximum or its minimum over $D$ at a point of $D$, then $h$ is constant. If $D$ is bounded and $\varlimsup _{D
i x	o \zeta }h(x)\leq 0$ for every $\zeta \in \partial D$, then $h\leq 0$ on $D$. Consequently, a harmonic function on a bounded open set which is continuous on its closure is determined by its boundary values. Proof. For the first assertion, suppose that $h$ attains its maximum $m$ at a point of $D$, and let $E=\{ x\in D:h(x)=m\} $. This set is nonempty and closed in $D$. If $x\in E$ and $\overline{B(x,r)}\subset D$, the ball mean-value property gives $\int _{B(x,r)}(m-h)\, \mathrm dy=0$. The integrand is continuous and nonnegative, so it vanishes on $B(x,r)$. Thus $E$ is open, and $E=D$ by connectedness. For the minimum, apply this to $-h$. For the second assertion, let $\varepsilon >0$, and suppose that $h>\varepsilon $ somewhere in $D$; we derive a contradiction. Each $\zeta \in \partial D$ has a ball $B(\zeta ,r_\zeta )$ such that $h<\varepsilon $ on $D\cap B(\zeta ,r_\zeta )$. Since $D$ is bounded, $\partial D$ is compact, and finitely many of these balls cover it; let $W$ be their union. Then $K=\overline D\setminus W=D\setminus W$ is compact. Since $h<\varepsilon $ on $D\setminus K=D\cap W$, the set $K$ is nonempty. The maximum of $h$ over $K$ is attained at some point $x_0$, and $h(x_0)>\varepsilon $; hence $h(x_0)$ is also the maximum of $h$ over $D$. Let $D_0$ be the component of $D$ containing $x_0$; it is open, because every point of $D$ lies in a ball contained in $D$, and balls are connected. By the first assertion, $h=h(x_0)$ on $D_0$. Since $\mathbb R^ d$ is connected and $D_0$ is a nonempty, bounded, open subset, $D_0$ is not closed, so it has a boundary point $\zeta $. This point does not lie in $D$: otherwise the component of $D$ containing $\zeta $ would be an open neighborhood of $\zeta $, so it would meet $D_0$ and hence equal $D_0$, which does not contain its boundary point $\zeta $. Thus $\zeta \in \partial D$ and $\varlimsup _{D
i x	o \zeta }h(x)\geq h(x_0)>0$, contradicting the hypothesis. Hence $h\leq \varepsilon $ on $D$, and letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ gives $h\leq 0$. Let $T\in \mathcal D'(\Omega )$ satisfy $\Delta T=0$. Then there is a unique smooth harmonic function $h$ on $\Omega $ such that $\langle T,\chi angle =\int _\Omega h\chi \, \mathrm dx$ for every $\chi \in C_ c^\infty (\Omega )$. Recall from section 1.4 that $(T*\phi )(y)=\langle T,\phi (y-\cdot )angle $ for a test function $\phi $ on $\mathbb R^ d$ supported in $\overline{B(0,s)}$ and $y\in \Omega _ s$, and that $T_\varepsilon =T*ho _\varepsilon $. By part (1) of proposition 1.4.3 , $T*\phi $ is smooth on $\Omega _ s$ and $\partial ^\alpha (T*\phi )=T*\partial ^\alpha \phi $; moreover $\Delta T_\varepsilon =(\Delta T)_\varepsilon =0$, so $T_\varepsilon $ is a smooth harmonic function on $\Omega _\varepsilon $. We show that $T_\varepsilon $ converges to the required $h$, locally uniformly with all derivatives, by writing $T_\varepsilon =T*(ho _\varepsilon *ho _ r)$ near each point for a fixed $r>0$. Fix $x\in \Omega $ and $r>0$ with $\overline{B(x,3r)}\subset \Omega $, and let $0<\varepsilon <r$. Since $\operatorname {dist}(x,\mathbb R^ d\setminus \Omega )>3r$, every point of $B(x,2r)$ has distance greater than $r$ from $\mathbb R^ d\setminus \Omega $, and every point of $B(x,r)$ has distance greater than $2r$; thus $B(x,2r)\subset \Omega _\varepsilon $ and $B(x,r)\subset \Omega _{2r}$. Let $y\in B(x,r)$. The closed ball $\overline{B(y,r)}$ lies in $B(x,2r)$, where $T_\varepsilon $ is harmonic, so the last assertion of theorem 2.1.2 , applied to $T_\varepsilon $ on $B(x,2r)$, gives $T_\varepsilon (y)=\int T_\varepsilon (z)ho _ r(y-z)\, \mathrm dz$. The test function $\chi =ho _ r(y-\cdot )$ is supported in $\overline{B(y,r)}\subset \Omega _\varepsilon $, so ( 1.7 ) gives $T_\varepsilon (y)=\langle T,\chi *ho _\varepsilon angle $. Substituting $z=w+v$ and using that $ho _\varepsilon $ is even, we find  egin{align*}  (\chi *ho _\varepsilon )(w)& =\int ho _ r(y-z)ho _\varepsilon (w-z)\, \mathrm dz\ & =\int ho _\varepsilon (v)ho _ r(y-w-v)\, \mathrm dv=(ho _\varepsilon *ho _ r)(y-w). \end{align*} The function $ho _\varepsilon *ho _ r$ is a test function supported in $\overline{B(0,\varepsilon +r)}\subset \overline{B(0,2r)}$, so we have shown that \[  T_\varepsilon =T*(ho _\varepsilon *ho _ r)\qquad 	ext{on }B(x,r).  \] Since $ho _\varepsilon *ho _ r=ho _ r*ho _\varepsilon $, part (3) of lemma 1.4.1 , applied on $\mathbb R^ d$ to $ho _ r$, shows that $\partial ^\alpha (ho _\varepsilon *ho _ r)	o \partial ^\alpha ho _ r$ uniformly for every multi-index $\alpha $ as $\varepsilon 	o 0$. Let $C$ and $m$ be the constants of definition 1.3.1 for $T$ and the compact set $\overline{B(x,3r)}$, which contains the supports of $(ho _\varepsilon *ho _ r)(y-\cdot )$ and $ho _ r(y-\cdot )$ for $y\in B(x,r)$. For $y\in B(x,r)$ and a multi-index $\alpha $, the difference $\partial ^\alpha T_\varepsilon (y)-\partial ^\alpha (T*ho _ r)(y)$ is the pairing of $T$ with $w\mapsto \psi (y-w)$, where $\psi =\partial ^\alpha (ho _\varepsilon *ho _ r-ho _ r)$, and the derivatives of order $ eta $ of this test function are $\pm (\partial ^ eta \psi )(y-w)$. Hence \[  \sup _{y\in B(x,r)} igl |\partial ^\alpha T_\varepsilon (y)-\partial ^\alpha (T*ho _ r)(y) igr | \leq C\max _{| eta |\leq m}\sup  igl |\partial ^{\alpha + eta }(ho _\varepsilon *ho _ r-ho _ r) igr |,  \] which tends to zero. Thus $T_\varepsilon 	o T*ho _ r$ on $B(x,r)$, uniformly with all derivatives. Every point of $\Omega $ is the center of such a ball. Therefore $h(y)=\lim _{\varepsilon 	o 0}T_\varepsilon (y)$ exists for every $y\in \Omega $, and on each ball $B(x,r)$ as above it equals $T*ho _ r$ and is the limit of $T_\varepsilon $ uniformly with all derivatives. Thus $h$ is smooth and $\Delta h=\lim _{\varepsilon 	o 0}\Delta T_\varepsilon =0$. Every compact subset of $\Omega $ is covered by finitely many of these balls, so $T_\varepsilon 	o h$ uniformly on compact sets, and part (2) of proposition 1.4.3 gives $\int h\chi \, \mathrm dx=\lim _{\varepsilon 	o 0}\int T_\varepsilon \chi \, \mathrm dx=\langle T,\chi angle $ for every test function $\chi $. If two continuous functions define the same distribution, they agree almost everywhere by part (4) of proposition 1.4.3 , and hence everywhere, since nonempty open sets have positive measure. This proves uniqueness. Finally, if $T$ is given by a locally integrable function $u$, then $u$ and $h$ define the same distribution, so $u=h$ almost everywhere by the same proposition. $\square$

title: Harmonic mean characterization
topic: Harmonic functions and the Dirichlet problem
text: Theorem 2.1.2 . A continuous function on $\Omega $ is harmonic if and only if it has the sphere mean-value property. Every harmonic function is smooth. If $h$ is harmonic on $\Omega $ and $\overline{B(x,r)}\subset \Omega $, then for every multi-index $\alpha $, 2.5 \begin{equation} \label{eq:harmonic-interior-derivatives} |\partial ^\alpha h(x)|\leq C_{d,\alpha }r^{-d-|\alpha |}\int _{B(x,r)}|h(y)|\, \mathrm d y, \end{equation} where the constant $C_{d,\alpha }$ depends only on $d$ and $\alpha $. Moreover, every harmonic function $h$ on $\Omega $ satisfies $h*\rho _\varepsilon =h$ on $\Omega _\varepsilon $ for every $\varepsilon >0$, where $\rho _\varepsilon $ and $\Omega _\varepsilon $ are as in section 1.4 . Proof. As in section 1.4 , we write $u_\varepsilon =u*\rho _\varepsilon $. Let $u$ be continuous with the sphere mean-value property, and let $\overline{B(x,\varepsilon )}\subset \Omega $. The compact set $\overline{B(x,\varepsilon )}$ has positive distance from $\mathbb R^ d\setminus \Omega $, so $x\in \Omega _\varepsilon $, and $M_ u(x,r)=u(x)$ for $0<r\leq \varepsilon $. Since $\rho $ is radial, we may write $\rho _\varepsilon (y)=\phi _\varepsilon (|y|)$; as $\rho _\varepsilon $ is even and vanishes outside $B(0,\varepsilon )$, ( 2.1 ) gives 2.6 \begin{equation} \label{eq:mean-value-mollifier} \begin{split}  u_\varepsilon (x)& =\int _{B(0,\varepsilon )}u(x+y)\rho _\varepsilon (y)\, \mathrm dy=s_{d-1}\int _0^\varepsilon r^{d-1}\phi _\varepsilon (r)M_ u(x,r)\, \mathrm dr\\ & =u(x)\, s_{d-1}\int _0^\varepsilon r^{d-1}\phi _\varepsilon (r)\, \mathrm dr=u(x)\int _{\mathbb R^ d}\rho _\varepsilon \, \mathrm dy=u(x). \end{split} \end{equation} Every point of $\Omega _\varepsilon $ is the center of such a closed ball, so $u=u_\varepsilon $ on the open set $\Omega _\varepsilon $, and $u_\varepsilon $ is smooth there (section 1.4 ). As $\Omega $ is the union of the sets $\Omega _\varepsilon $, the function $u$ is smooth. Next we show that $\Delta u=0$. Fix $x\in \Omega $. Taylor's formula gives \[  u(x+r\omega )=u(x)+r\sum _ j\partial _ ju(x)\, \omega _ j+\frac{r^2}{2}\sum _{j,k}\partial _ j\partial _ ku(x)\, \omega _ j\omega _ k+o(r^2),  \] uniformly in $\omega \in S^{d-1}$. We average over the sphere. The reflections $\omega \mapsto -\omega $ and $\omega _ j\mapsto -\omega _ j$ preserve $S$, so $\int \omega _ j\, \mathrm dS=0$ and $\int \omega _ j\omega _ k\, \mathrm dS=0$ for $j\neq k$. Permutations of the coordinates also preserve $S$, so the integrals $\int \omega _ j^2\, \mathrm dS$ are all equal, and their sum is $s_{d-1}$ because $\sum _ j\omega _ j^2=1$. Hence \[  M_ u(x,r)=u(x)+\frac{r^2}{2d}\Delta u(x)+o(r^2).  \] Since $M_ u(x,r)=u(x)$ for all small $r$, it follows that $\Delta u(x)=0$. Thus $u$ is harmonic. Conversely, harmonic functions have the sphere mean-value property by proposition 2.1.1 ; in particular they are smooth, and they satisfy $h=h_\varepsilon =h*\rho _\varepsilon $ on $\Omega _\varepsilon $ by the first part of the proof. Now let $h$ be harmonic and $\overline{B(x,r)}\subset \Omega $. Then $x$ lies in the open set $\Omega _ r$, and $h=h_ r$ on $\Omega _ r$ by the first part of the proof. By the differentiation formula $\partial ^\alpha h_ r=h*\partial ^\alpha \rho _ r$ of section 1.4 , and since $\partial ^\alpha \rho _ r$ vanishes outside $B(0,r)$, we get \[  \partial ^\alpha h(x)=\int _{B(x,r)} h(y)\, (\partial ^\alpha \rho _ r)(x-y)\, \mathrm d y.  \] Since $\partial ^\alpha \rho _ r(z)=r^{-d-|\alpha |}(\partial ^\alpha \rho )(z/r)$, this proves ( 2.5 ) with $C_{d,\alpha }=\sup |\partial ^\alpha \rho |$, where $\rho $ is the mollifier on $\mathbb R^ d$ fixed in section 1.4 . $\square$

title: Harmonic maximum
topic: Harmonic functions and the Dirichlet problem
text: Proposition 2.1.3 . Let $h$ be a real harmonic function on an open set $D\subset \mathbb R^ d$. If $D$ is connected and $h$ attains its maximum or its minimum over $D$ at a point of $D$, then $h$ is constant. If $D$ is bounded and $\varlimsup _{D\ni x\to \zeta }h(x)\leq 0$ for every $\zeta \in \partial D$, then $h\leq 0$ on $D$. Consequently, a harmonic function on a bounded open set which is continuous on its closure is determined by its boundary values. Proof. For the first assertion, suppose that $h$ attains its maximum $m$ at a point of $D$, and let $E=\{ x\in D:h(x)=m\} $. This set is nonempty and closed in $D$. If $x\in E$ and $\overline{B(x,r)}\subset D$, the ball mean-value property gives $\int _{B(x,r)}(m-h)\, \mathrm dy=0$. The integrand is continuous and nonnegative, so it vanishes on $B(x,r)$. Thus $E$ is open, and $E=D$ by connectedness. For the minimum, apply this to $-h$. For the second assertion, let $\varepsilon >0$, and suppose that $h>\varepsilon $ somewhere in $D$; we derive a contradiction. Each $\zeta \in \partial D$ has a ball $B(\zeta ,r_\zeta )$ such that $h<\varepsilon $ on $D\cap B(\zeta ,r_\zeta )$. Since $D$ is bounded, $\partial D$ is compact, and finitely many of these balls cover it; let $W$ be their union. Then $K=\overline D\setminus W=D\setminus W$ is compact. Since $h<\varepsilon $ on $D\setminus K=D\cap W$, the set $K$ is nonempty. The maximum of $h$ over $K$ is attained at some point $x_0$, and $h(x_0)>\varepsilon $; hence $h(x_0)$ is also the maximum of $h$ over $D$. Let $D_0$ be the component of $D$ containing $x_0$; it is open, because every point of $D$ lies in a ball contained in $D$, and balls are connected. By the first assertion, $h=h(x_0)$ on $D_0$. Since $\mathbb R^ d$ is connected and $D_0$ is a nonempty, bounded, open subset, $D_0$ is not closed, so it has a boundary point $\zeta $. This point does not lie in $D$: otherwise the component of $D$ containing $\zeta $ would be an open neighborhood of $\zeta $, so it would meet $D_0$ and hence equal $D_0$, which does not contain its boundary point $\zeta $. Thus $\zeta \in \partial D$ and $\varlimsup _{D\ni x\to \zeta }h(x)\geq h(x_0)>0$, contradicting the hypothesis. Hence $h\leq \varepsilon $ on $D$, and letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ gives $h\leq 0$. Finally, if two harmonic functions on a bounded open set are continuous on its closure and agree on its boundary, apply the second assertion to the real and imaginary parts of their difference and of its negative. $\square$

title: Weyl's lemma
topic: Harmonic functions and the Dirichlet problem
text: Theorem 2.1.4 (Weyl's lemma) . Let $T\in \mathcal D'(\Omega )$ satisfy $\Delta T=0$. Then there is a unique smooth harmonic function $h$ on $\Omega $ such that $\langle T,\chi \rangle =\int _\Omega h\chi \, \mathrm dx$ for every $\chi \in C_ c^\infty (\Omega )$. In particular, a locally integrable function whose distributional Laplacian vanishes agrees almost everywhere with a harmonic function. Proof. Recall from section 1.4 that $(T*\phi )(y)=\langle T,\phi (y-\cdot )\rangle $ for a test function $\phi $ on $\mathbb R^ d$ supported in $\overline{B(0,s)}$ and $y\in \Omega _ s$, and that $T_\varepsilon =T*\rho _\varepsilon $. By part (1) of proposition 1.4.3 , $T*\phi $ is smooth on $\Omega _ s$ and $\partial ^\alpha (T*\phi )=T*\partial ^\alpha \phi $; moreover $\Delta T_\varepsilon =(\Delta T)_\varepsilon =0$, so $T_\varepsilon $ is a smooth harmonic function on $\Omega _\varepsilon $. We show that $T_\varepsilon $ converges to the required $h$, locally uniformly with all derivatives, by writing $T_\varepsilon =T*(\rho _\varepsilon *\rho _ r)$ near each point for a fixed $r>0$. Fix $x\in \Omega $ and $r>0$ with $\overline{B(x,3r)}\subset \Omega $, and let $0<\varepsilon <r$. Since $\operatorname {dist}(x,\mathbb R^ d\setminus \Omega )>3r$, every point of $B(x,2r)$ has distance greater than $r$ from $\mathbb R^ d\setminus \Omega $, and every point of $B(x,r)$ has distance greater than $2r$; thus $B(x,2r)\subset \Omega _\varepsilon $ and $B(x,r)\subset \Omega _{2r}$. Let $y\in B(x,r)$. The closed ball $\overline{B(y,r)}$ lies in $B(x,2r)$, where $T_\varepsilon $ is harmonic, so the last assertion of theorem 2.1.2 , applied to $T_\varepsilon $ on $B(x,2r)$, gives $T_\varepsilon (y)=\int T_\varepsilon (z)\rho _ r(y-z)\, \mathrm dz$. The test function $\chi =\rho _ r(y-\cdot )$ is supported in $\overline{B(y,r)}\subset \Omega _\varepsilon $, so ( 1.7 ) gives $T_\varepsilon (y)=\langle T,\chi *\rho _\varepsilon \rangle $. Substituting $z=w+v$ and using that $\rho _\varepsilon $ is even, we find \begin{align*}  (\chi *\rho _\varepsilon )(w)& =\int \rho _ r(y-z)\rho _\varepsilon (w-z)\, \mathrm dz\\ & =\int \rho _\varepsilon (v)\rho _ r(y-w-v)\, \mathrm dv=(\rho _\varepsilon *\rho _ r)(y-w). \end{align*} The function $\rho _\varepsilon *\rho _ r$ is a test function supported in $\overline{B(0,\varepsilon +r)}\subset \overline{B(0,2r)}$, so we have shown that \[  T_\varepsilon =T*(\rho _\varepsilon *\rho _ r)\qquad \text{on }B(x,r).  \] Since $\rho _\varepsilon *\rho _ r=\rho _ r*\rho _\varepsilon $, part (3) of lemma 1.4.1 , applied on $\mathbb R^ d$ to $\rho _ r$, shows that $\partial ^\alpha (\rho _\varepsilon *\rho _ r)\to \partial ^\alpha \rho _ r$ uniformly for every multi-index $\alpha $ as $\varepsilon \to 0$. Let $C$ and $m$ be the constants of definition 1.3.1 for $T$ and the compact set $\overline{B(x,3r)}$, which contains the supports of $(\rho _\varepsilon *\rho _ r)(y-\cdot )$ and $\rho _ r(y-\cdot )$ for $y\in B(x,r)$. For $y\in B(x,r)$ and a multi-index $\alpha $, the difference $\partial ^\alpha T_\varepsilon (y)-\partial ^\alpha (T*\rho _ r)(y)$ is the pairing of $T$ with $w\mapsto \psi (y-w)$, where $\psi =\partial ^\alpha (\rho _\varepsilon *\rho _ r-\rho _ r)$, and the derivatives of order $\beta $ of this test function are $\pm (\partial ^\beta \psi )(y-w)$. Hence \[  \sup _{y\in B(x,r)}\bigl |\partial ^\alpha T_\varepsilon (y)-\partial ^\alpha (T*\rho _ r)(y)\bigr | \leq C\max _{|\beta |\leq m}\sup \bigl |\partial ^{\alpha +\beta }(\rho _\varepsilon *\rho _ r-\rho _ r)\bigr |,  \] which tends to zero. Thus $T_\varepsilon \to T*\rho _ r$ on $B(x,r)$, uniformly with all derivatives. Every point of $\Omega $ is the center of such a ball. Therefore $h(y)=\lim _{\varepsilon \to 0}T_\varepsilon (y)$ exists for every $y\in \Omega $, and on each ball $B(x,r)$ as above it equals $T*\rho _ r$ and is the limit of $T_\varepsilon $ uniformly with all derivatives. Thus $h$ is smooth and $\Delta h=\lim _{\varepsilon \to 0}\Delta T_\varepsilon =0$. Every compact subset of $\Omega $ is covered by finitely many of these balls, so $T_\varepsilon \to h$ uniformly on compact sets, and part (2) of proposition 1.4.3 gives $\int h\chi \, \mathrm dx=\lim _{\varepsilon \to 0}\int T_\varepsilon \chi \, \mathrm dx=\langle T,\chi \rangle $ for every test function $\chi $. If two continuous functions define the same distribution, they agree almost everywhere by part (4) of proposition 1.4.3 , and hence everywhere, since nonempty open sets have positive measure. This proves uniqueness. Finally, if $T$ is given by a locally integrable function $u$, then $u$ and $h$ define the same distribution, so $u=h$ almost everywhere by the same proposition. $\square$

2.3 Poisson kernels and Harnack inequalities Let $D\subset \mathbb R^ d$ be a bounded open set. The Dirichlet problem on $D$ asks, for a given $f\in C(\partial D)$, for a function $h$ which is harmonic on $D$ and continuous on $\overline D$ with $h=f$ on $\partial D$. By proposition 2.1.3 it has at most one solution. On a ball $B=B(c,R)$ the solution is given by an explicit integral formula: for $x\in B$ and $\zeta \in \partial B$ put 2.14  egin{equation} \label{eq:ball-poisson-kernel} P_ B(x,\zeta )= rac{R^2-|x-c|^2}{s_{d-1}R|x-\zeta |^ d}. \end{equation} This is the Poisson kernel of $B$. In dimension one, $B=(a,b)$, the boundary $\partial B=\{ a,b\} $ carries counting measure and $s_0=2$, so that $P_ B(x,a)=(b-x)/(b-a)$ and $P_ B(x,b)=(x-a)/(b-a)$; the Poisson integral below is then the affine interpolation of the two endpoint values. Theorem 2.3.1 . Let $B$ be a ball and $f\in C(\partial B)$. The Poisson integral \[  H_ Bf(x)=\int _{\partial B}P_ B(x,\zeta )f(\zeta )\, \mathrm d S(\zeta ),\qquad x\in B,  \] is the unique harmonic function on $B$ which extends continuously to $\overline B$ with boundary values $f$. The kernel is positive, and $\int _{\partial B}P_ B(x,\zeta )\, \mathrm dS(\zeta )=1$ for every $x\in B$. The operator $H_ B$ is linear, preserves order, and satisfies $\sup _ B|H_ Bf|\leq \max _{\partial B}|f|$. Every function harmonic on a neighborhood of $\overline B$ is the Poisson integral of its restriction to $\partial B$. Proof. If $d=1$ and $B=(a,b)$, then $H_ Bf$ is the affine function with the values $f(a)$ and $f(b)$ at the endpoints, as noted above. It is harmonic on $B$ and extends continuously to $\overline B$ with boundary values $f$, and the kernel is positive with $P_ B(x,a)+P_ B(x,b)=1$. The remaining assertions are proved below in all dimensions. Now let $d\geq 2$; after a translation we may assume that $c=0$. Fix $\zeta \in \partial B$ and put $A(x)=R^2-|x|^2$ and $t(x)=|x-\zeta |$ for $x
eq \zeta $. We have $
abla A=-2x$, $\Delta A=-2d$ and $
abla t^{-d}=-dt^{-d-2}(x-\zeta )$, and ( 2.13 ), applied to $F(t)=t^{-d}$ after translating $\zeta $ to the origin, gives $\Delta t^{-d}= igl (d(d+1)-d(d-1) igr )t^{-d-2}=2dt^{-d-2}$. By the product rule $\Delta (At^{-d})=(\Delta A)t^{-d}+2
abla A\cdot 
abla t^{-d}+A\Delta t^{-d}$, and since $t^2=|x|^2-2x\cdot \zeta +|\zeta |^2$, \[  \Delta (At^{-d})=2dt^{-d-2} igl (-t^2+2x\cdot (x-\zeta )+R^2-|x|^2 igr )=2dt^{-d-2}(R^2-|\zeta |^2)=0.  \] Thus $P_ B(\cdot ,\zeta )$ is harmonic on $B$ for every $\zeta \in \partial B$. Every partial derivative $\partial _ x^\alpha P_ B(x,\zeta )$ is continuous on $B	imes \partial B$, hence bounded on $K	imes \partial B$ for each compact set $K\subset B$, where $|x-\zeta |\geq \operatorname {dist}(K,\partial B)>0$. By the mean value theorem and dominated convergence on the finite measure space $(\partial B,S)$, we may therefore differentiate under the integral sign any number of times, so $H_ Bf$ is smooth on $B$ and $\Delta H_ Bf(x)=\int _{\partial B}\Delta _ xP_ B(x,\zeta )f(\zeta )\, \mathrm dS(\zeta )=0$. Next we show that the kernel has integral one. Taking $f=1$, we see that $I(x)=\int _{\partial B}P_ B(x,\zeta )\, \mathrm dS(\zeta )$ is harmonic on $B$. It is also radial. Indeed, $P_ B(Qx,Q\zeta )=P_ B(x,\zeta )$ for every orthogonal transformation $Q$, and surface measure on $\partial B$ is invariant under $Q$, so $I(Qx)=I(x)$. Moreover, if $|x|=|x'|$ and $x
eq x'$, the orthogonal reflection $y\mapsto y-2(y\cdot e)e$ with $e=(x-x')/|x-x'|$ maps $x$ to $x'$. Hence $I(x)=F(|x|)$, where $F(r)=I(re_1)$ is smooth on $(-R,R)$ and $e_1$ is the first coordinate vector. By ( 2.13 ), $(r^{d-1}F'(r))'=0$ on $(0,R)$, so $r^{d-1}F'(r)$ is constant there. Since $F'$ is bounded near $0$ and $d\geq 2$, this constant is $\lim _{r	o 0}r^{d-1}F'(r)=0$. Hence $F$ is constant on $(0,R)$, and since $I$ is continuous at the origin, $I$ is constant on $B$, with value $I(0)=R^2\cdot s_{d-1}R^{d-1}/(s_{d-1}R\cdot R^ d)=1$. For the boundary behavior, fix $\zeta _0\in \partial B$ and $\varepsilon >0$, and choose $\delta >0$ such that $|f(\zeta )-f(\zeta _0)|<\varepsilon $ for $\zeta \in \partial B$ with $|\zeta -\zeta _0|<\delta $. Since the kernel is positive with integral one,  egin{align*}  |H_ Bf(x)-f(\zeta _0)|& \leq \int _{\partial B}P_ B(x,\zeta )|f(\zeta )-f(\zeta _0)|\, \mathrm dS(\zeta )\ & \leq \varepsilon +2\max _{\partial B}|f|\int _{\{ \zeta \in \partial B:|\zeta -\zeta _0|\geq \delta \} }P_ B(x,\zeta )\, \mathrm dS(\zeta ). \end{align*} If $|x-\zeta _0|<\delta /2$, then $|x-\zeta |\geq \delta /2$ in the last integral, so $P_ B(x,\zeta )\leq (R^2-|x-c|^2)/(s_{d-1}R(\delta /2)^ d)$ there, and the integral is at most $R^{d-2}(2/\delta )^ d(R^2-|x-c|^2)$. This tends to zero as $x	o \zeta _0$, because $|\zeta _0-c|=R$. Hence $\varlimsup _{x	o \zeta _0}|H_ Bf(x)-f(\zeta _0)|\leq \varepsilon $ for every $\varepsilon >0$. Since $f$ is continuous on $\partial B$, it follows that the function equal to $H_ Bf$ on $B$ and to $f$ on $\partial B$ is continuous on $\overline B$. Finally, if $h$ is harmonic on a neighborhood of $\overline B$, then $h$ and $H_ B(h|_{\partial B})$ are harmonic on $B$, continuous on $\overline B$ and equal on $\partial B$, so they coincide. $\square$ We often regard $H_ Bf$ as the continuous function on $\overline B$ which equals $f$ on $\partial B$. Proposition 2.3.2 . Let $h\geq 0$ be harmonic on $B(0,R)$, let $x\in B(0,R)$ and put $r=|x|$. Then 2.15  egin{equation} \label{eq:harnack-ball}  rac{R^{d-2}(R-r)}{(R+r)^{d-1}}h(0) \leq h(x)\leq  rac{R^{d-2}(R+r)}{(R-r)^{d-1}}h(0). \end{equation} A nonnegative harmonic function on a domain is either positive everywhere or identically zero. Let $\Omega $ be a domain, $K\subset \Omega $ compact and $x_0\in \Omega $. Then there is a constant $C=C(K,x_0,\Omega )>0$ such that \[  \sup _ K h\leq C h(x_0)  \] for every nonnegative harmonic function $h$ on $\Omega $. Proof. (1) Let $r<R'<R$. By theorem 2.3.1 on $B(0,R')$, both $h(x)$ and $h(0)$ are integrals of the nonnegative boundary values of $h$ against the Poisson kernel. For $|\zeta |=R'$ we have $R'-r\leq |x-\zeta |\leq R'+r$, so the ratio \[   rac{P_{B(0,R')}(x,\zeta )}{P_{B(0,R')}(0,\zeta )}= rac{R'^{d-2}(R'^2-r^2)}{|x-\zeta |^ d}  \] lies between the two coefficients in ( 2.15 ) with $R'$ in place of $R$. Integrating and letting $R'\uparrow R$ gives ( 2.15 ). (2) If a nonnegative harmonic function on a domain vanishes at a point, it attains its minimum there and is identically zero by proposition 2.1.3 . (3) We first apply (1), after a translation, to a ball $B(a,2t)\subset \Omega $: for $y\in B(a,t)$ we have $r=|y-a|<t$, and the right inequality in ( 2.15 ) on $B(a,2t)$ gives \[  h(y)\leq  rac{(2t)^{d-2}(2t+r)}{(2t-r)^{d-1}}h(a)\leq  rac{(2t)^{d-2}\cdot 3t}{t^{d-1}}h(a)=C_0h(a),\qquad C_0=3\cdot 2^{d-2}.  \] Now let $y\in \Omega $. Since $\Omega $ is connected, $y$ can be joined to $x_0$ by a polygonal path in $\Omega $: the set of points that can be so joined is open, and so is its complement in $\Omega $, because balls are convex. The path is compact, so there is $t>0$ with $B(z,2t)\subset \Omega $ for every point $z$ of the path. Choose points $x_0=p_0,p_1,\ldots ,p_ N=y$ along the path with $|p_{i+1}-p_ i|<t$. Applying the ball estimate on $B(p_ i,2t)$ for $i=0,\ldots ,N-1$ gives $h(y)\leq C_0^ Nh(x_0)$, and once more on $B(y,2t)$ gives $h\leq C_0^{N+1}h(x_0)$ on $B(y,t)$. Here $t$ and $N$ depend on $y$, $x_0$ and $\Omega $, but not on $h$. Finitely many of the balls $B(y,t)$, $y\in K$, cover $K$, and the largest of the corresponding constants $C_0^{N+1}$ is the required $C$. $\square$ A sequence of smooth functions on an open set $D\subset \mathbb R^ d$ converges to $g$ in $C^\infty $ on compact subsets if, for every multi-index $\alpha $, the derivatives $\partial ^\alpha $ of its terms converge to $\partial ^\alpha g$ uniformly on compact subsets of $D$. Corollary 2.3.3 . Let $D\subset \mathbb R^ d$ be a domain. Every sequence of nonnegative harmonic functions on $D$ which is bounded at one point of $D$ has a subsequence converging in $C^\infty $ on compact subsets; the limit is harmonic. An increasing sequence of harmonic functions on $D$ either converges in $C^\infty $ on compact subsets to a finite harmonic function, or tends to $+\infty $ uniformly on compact subsets. A decreasing sequence of harmonic functions on $D$ either converges in $C^\infty $ on compact subsets to a finite harmonic function, or tends to $-\infty $ uniformly on compact subsets. Proof. Let $h_ j\geq 0$ be harmonic on $D$ with $h_ j(x_0)\leq M$ for some $x_0\in D$. By proposition 2.3.2 (3), $h_ j\leq C(K_\delta ,x_0,D)M$ on $K_\delta $ for all $j$, and ( 2.5 ) with radius $\delta $ then bounds each derivative $\partial ^\alpha h_ j$ on $K$ uniformly in $j$. Taking for $K$ a closed ball in $D$ and applying this bound to the first derivatives of $\partial ^\alpha h_ j$, we see that the functions $\partial ^\alpha h_ j$ are uniformly Lipschitz on every closed ball in $D$, and hence equicontinuous on compact subsets of $D$. Let $K_ m$ be the sets of the compact exhaustion of $D$ constructed in section 1.1 ; every compact subset of $D$ lies in some $K_ m$. Applying proposition 1.6.4 on each $K_ m$ and making a diagonal extraction over all $m$ and all multi-indices $\alpha $, we obtain a subsequence along which every $\partial ^\alpha h_ j$ converges uniformly on compact subsets of $D$, say to $g_\alpha $. To identify the limits, let $e_ k$ be the $k$th standard basis vector. Passing to the uniform limit in \[  \partial ^\alpha h_ j(y+te_ k)-\partial ^\alpha h_ j(y)=\int _0^ t\partial ^{\alpha +e_ k}h_ j(y+se_ k)\, \mathrm ds,  \] which holds whenever the segment from $y$ to $y+te_ k$ lies in $D$, we find that $\partial _ kg_\alpha =g_{\alpha +e_ k}$. By induction, $g=g_0$ is smooth with $\partial ^\alpha g=g_\alpha $, so the subsequence converges to $g$ in $C^\infty $ on compact subsets, and $\Delta g=\lim _ j\Delta h_ j=0$. This proves the first assertion. Indeed, if $B(a,2t)\subset D$ and $y\in B(a,t)$, then $r=|y-a|<t$, and the left inequality in ( 2.15 ) on $B(a,2t)$ gives $h(y)\geq (2t)^{d-2}(2t-r)(2t+r)^{1-d}h(a)\geq c_0h(a)$ with $c_0=2^{d-2}3^{1-d}$. Cover $K$ by finitely many balls $B(a_ k,t_ k)$ with $B(a_ k,2t_ k)\subset D$. Proposition 2.3.2 (3), applied to the compact set $\{ x_0\} $ and the base point $a_ k$, gives $h(x_0)\leq C_ kh(a_ k)$. Hence $h\geq (c_0/\max _ kC_ k)h(x_0)$ on $K$. Now let $(h_ j)$ be increasing and fix $x_0\in D$. The functions $h_ j-h_1$ are nonnegative and harmonic. If $h_ j(x_0)$ is bounded, the first assertion applies to every subsequence of $(h_ j-h_1)$. Since the sequence increases and, by proposition 2.3.2 (3), is bounded on compact sets, it has a finite pointwise limit, and every subsequence has a further subsequence converging in $C^\infty $ on compact subsets to this limit. Hence the whole sequence converges in $C^\infty $ on compact subsets, and the limit is a finite harmonic function. If $h_ j(x_0)	o +\infty $, the lower Harnack bound gives $h_ j-h_1\geq c(h_ j(x_0)-h_1(x_0))$ on each compact $K$, and since $h_1$ is bounded on $K$, $h_ j	o +\infty $ uniformly on $K$. For a decreasing sequence, apply this to $(-h_ j)$. $\square$ Corollary 2.3.4 . A real harmonic function on $\mathbb R^ d$ which is bounded above or bounded below is constant. Proof. After changing the sign and adding a constant, we may assume that the function $h$ is nonnegative. Fix $x\in \mathbb R^ d$ and put $r=|x|$. For $R>r$, ( 2.15 ) on $B(0,R)$ gives $c_ Rh(0)\leq h(x)\leq C_ Rh(0)$, where the coefficients $c_ R$ and $C_ R$ of ( 2.15 ) tend to one as $R	o \infty $. Letting $R	o \infty $ gives $h(x)=h(0)$. Hence $h$ is constant. $\square$

Every sequence of nonnegative harmonic functions on $D$ which is bounded at one point of $D$ has a subsequence converging in $C^\infty $ on compact subsets; the limit is harmonic. An increasing sequence of harmonic functions on $D$ either converges in $C^\infty $ on compact subsets to a finite harmonic function, or tends to $+\infty $ uniformly on compact subsets. A decreasing sequence of harmonic functions on $D$ either converges in $C^\infty $ on compact subsets to a finite harmonic function, or tends to $-\infty $ uniformly on compact subsets. Proof. Let $h_ j\geq 0$ be harmonic on $D$ with $h_ j(x_0)\leq M$ for some $x_0\in D$. Let $K\subset D$ be compact and choose $\delta >0$ such that $K_\delta =\{ y:\operatorname {dist}(y,K)\leq \delta \} $ is contained in $D$. By proposition 2.3.2 (3), $h_ j\leq C(K_\delta ,x_0,D)M$ on $K_\delta $ for all $j$, and ( 2.5 ) with radius $\delta $ then bounds each derivative $\partial ^\alpha h_ j$ on $K$ uniformly in $j$. Taking for $K$ a closed ball in $D$ and applying this bound to the first derivatives of $\partial ^\alpha h_ j$, we see that the functions $\partial ^\alpha h_ j$ are uniformly Lipschitz on every closed ball in $D$, and hence equicontinuous on compact subsets of $D$. Let $K_ m$ be the sets of the compact exhaustion of $D$ constructed in section 1.1 ; every compact subset of $D$ lies in some $K_ m$. Applying proposition 1.6.4 on each $K_ m$ and making a diagonal extraction over all $m$ and all multi-indices $\alpha $, we obtain a subsequence along which every $\partial ^\alpha h_ j$ converges uniformly on compact subsets of $D$, say to $g_\alpha $. To identify the limits, let $e_ k$ be the $k$th standard basis vector. Passing to the uniform limit in \[  \partial ^\alpha h_ j(y+te_ k)-\partial ^\alpha h_ j(y)=\int _0^ t\partial ^{\alpha +e_ k}h_ j(y+se_ k)\, \mathrm ds,  \] which holds whenever the segment from $y$ to $y+te_ k$ lies in $D$, we find that $\partial _ kg_\alpha =g_{\alpha +e_ k}$. By induction, $g=g_0$ is smooth with $\partial ^\alpha g=g_\alpha $, so the subsequence converges to $g$ in $C^\infty $ on compact subsets, and $\Delta g=\lim _ j\Delta h_ j=0$. This proves the first assertion. We also need a lower Harnack bound: for compact $K\subset D$ and $x_0\in D$ there is $c>0$ such that $h\geq c\, h(x_0)$ on $K$ for every nonnegative harmonic $h$ on $D$. Indeed, if $B(a,2t)\subset D$ and $y\in B(a,t)$, then $r=|y-a|<t$, and the left inequality in ( 2.15 ) on $B(a,2t)$ gives $h(y)\geq (2t)^{d-2}(2t-r)(2t+r)^{1-d}h(a)\geq c_0h(a)$ with $c_0=2^{d-2}3^{1-d}$. Cover $K$ by finitely many balls $B(a_ k,t_ k)$ with $B(a_ k,2t_ k)\subset D$. Proposition 2.3.2 (3), applied to the compact set $\{ x_0\} $ and the base point $a_ k$, gives $h(x_0)\leq C_ kh(a_ k)$. Hence $h\geq (c_0/\max _ kC_ k)h(x_0)$ on $K$. Now let $(h_ j)$ be increasing and fix $x_0\in D$. The functions $h_ j-h_1$ are nonnegative and harmonic. If $h_ j(x_0)$ is bounded, the first assertion applies to every subsequence of $(h_ j-h_1)$. Since the sequence increases and, by proposition 2.3.2 (3), is bounded on compact sets, it has a finite pointwise limit, and every subsequence has a further subsequence converging in $C^\infty $ on compact subsets to this limit. Hence the whole sequence converges in $C^\infty $ on compact subsets, and the limit is a finite harmonic function. If $h_ j(x_0)\to +\infty $, the lower Harnack bound gives $h_ j-h_1\geq c(h_ j(x_0)-h_1(x_0))$ on each compact $K$, and since $h_1$ is bounded on $K$, $h_ j\to +\infty $ uniformly on $K$. For a decreasing sequence, apply this to $(-h_ j)$. $\square$
