text: Corollary 2.3.4 . A real harmonic function on $\mathbb R^ d$ which is bounded above or bounded below is constant. Proof. After changing the sign and adding a constant, we may assume that the function $h$ is nonnegative. Fix $x\in \mathbb R^ d$ and put $r=|x|$. For $R>r$, ( 2.15 ) on $B(0,R)$ gives $c_ Rh(0)\leq h(x)\leq C_ Rh(0)$, where the coefficients $c_ R$ and $C_ R$ of ( 2.15 ) tend to one as $R\to \infty $. Letting $R\to \infty $ gives $h(x)=h(0)$. Hence $h$ is constant. $\square$

title: Perron envelopes and boundary barriers
topic: Harmonic functions and the Dirichlet problem
text:
2.4 Perron envelopes and boundary barriers We now solve the Dirichlet problem on a general bounded open set by Perron's method, and we characterize by barriers the boundary points at which the solution attains the prescribed values. Throughout this section $\Omega $ is a nonempty bounded open set, and all functions and boundary data are real-valued. The boundary $\partial \Omega $ is compact, and it is nonempty: otherwise $\Omega $ would be a nonempty proper subset of the connected space $\mathbb R^ d$ which is both open and closed. Let $D$ be an open set. A continuous subsolution on $D$ is a continuous function $v\colon D	o \mathbb R$ such that $v\leq H_ B(v|_{\partial B})$ on $B$ for every ball $B$ with $\overline B\subset D$. A function $w$ is a continuous supersolution if $-w$ is a continuous subsolution. Harmonic functions are both, by the Poisson representation in theorem 2.3.1 . At the center $c$ of $B=B(c,r)$ the Poisson kernel equals $(s_{d-1}r^{d-1})^{-1}$, so a continuous subsolution satisfies the sphere submean inequality $v(c)\leq M_ v(c,r)$ whenever $\overline{B(c,r)}\subset D$. Conversely, a continuous function $v$ on $D$ such that every $c\in D$ satisfies $v(c)\leq M_ v(c,r)$ for all sufficiently small $r>0$ is a continuous subsolution. The proof rests on the identity $M_{|\cdot |^2}(c,r)=|c|^2+r^2$ for the mean of $|y|^2$ over the sphere $\partial B(c,r)$, which holds because $|c+r\omega |^2=|c|^2+2r\, c\cdot \omega +r^2$ and $\int _{S^{d-1}}\omega \, \mathrm dS(\omega )=0$, by the invariance of $S$ under $\omega \mapsto -\omega $. To prove the claim, let $B$ be a ball with $\overline B\subset D$, let $H$ be the Poisson integral of $v|_{\partial B}$, regarded as a continuous function on $\overline B$, and for $\varepsilon >0$ put $w(y)=v(y)-H(y)+\varepsilon |y|^2$. Since $M_ H(c,r)=H(c)$ whenever $\overline{B(c,r)}\subset B$ (proposition 2.1.1 ), we obtain $w(c)\leq M_ w(c,r)-\varepsilon r^2$ for every $c\in B$ and all small $r>0$. Hence the continuous function $w$ cannot attain its maximum over the compact set $\overline B$ at a point $c\in B$, for we would then have $M_ w(c,r)\leq w(c)$ for all small $r$. The maximum is therefore attained on $\partial B$, where $H=v$ and hence $w(y)=\varepsilon |y|^2$. Thus $v-H\leq \varepsilon \max _{\overline B}|y|^2$ on $B$, and letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ gives $v\leq H$. In particular, being a continuous subsolution is a local property: if every point of $D$ has an open neighborhood on which $v$ is a continuous subsolution, then $v$ is a continuous subsolution on $D$. Moreover, a real-valued continuous function is subharmonic in the sense of definition 3.1.1 exactly when every point $c$ satisfies $v(c)\leq M_ v(c,r)$ for all small $r>0$, so the continuous subsolutions are exactly the real-valued continuous subharmonic functions. These functions are stable under the usual operations. If $v_1$ and $v_2$ are continuous subsolutions, then so is $\max \{ v_1,v_2\} $, because $H_ B$ preserves order, so that $v_ i\leq H_ B(v_ i|_{\partial B})\leq H_ B(\max \{ v_1,v_2\} |_{\partial B})$. Sums and multiples by nonnegative constants of continuous subsolutions are continuous subsolutions, by linearity of $H_ B$, and so is $v-h$ for every harmonic $h$, because $h=H_ B(h|_{\partial B})$ on $B$. Correspondingly, the minimum of two continuous supersolutions is a continuous supersolution. Finally, a real function $v\in C^2(D)$ with $\Delta v\geq 0$ is a continuous subsolution. Indeed, if $\overline{B(c,R)}\subset D$, then by ( 2.4 ) the mean $M_ v(c,r)$ is nondecreasing in $r\in (0,R)$, and it tends to $v(c)$ as $r\downarrow 0$ because $v$ is continuous at $c$; hence $v(c)\leq M_ v(c,r)$ for $0<r<R$, and the converse statement above applies. Lemma 2.4.1 . Let $D$ be a bounded open set and $v$ a continuous subsolution on $D$. If $\varlimsup _{D
i x	o \zeta }v(x)\leq 0$ for every $\zeta \in \partial D$, then $v\leq 0$ on $D$. Moreover, if $B$ is a ball with $\overline B\subset D$, then the function $v^ B$ which equals $H_ B(v|_{\partial B})$ on $B$ and $v$ on $D\setminus B$ is a continuous subsolution on $D$ with $v^ B\geq v$. Proof. For the first assertion we may assume that $D
eq \varnothing $. Let $\varepsilon >0$, and put $w(y)=v(y)+\varepsilon |y|^2$ for $y\in D$. If $\overline{B(c,r)}\subset D$, then $v(c)\leq M_ v(c,r)$, and the identity $M_{|\cdot |^2}(c,r)=|c|^2+r^2$ gives $w(c)\leq M_ w(c,r)-\varepsilon r^2$. Consequently $w$ does not attain its supremum over $D$ at any point $c\in D$, for we would then have $M_ w(c,r)\leq w(c)$ for small $r$. Choose $x_ k\in D$ with $w(x_ k)	o \sup _ Dw$. Since $D$ is bounded, we may assume, after passing to a subsequence, that $x_ k$ converges to a point $p\in \overline D$. If $p$ were in $D$, the continuity of $w$ would give $w(p)=\sup _ Dw$, which we have excluded. Hence $p\in \partial D$. Since $\sup _ Dw=\lim _ k igl (v(x_ k)+\varepsilon |x_ k|^2 igr )$, the hypothesis gives $\sup _ Dw\leq \varlimsup _{D
i x	o p}v(x)+\varepsilon |p|^2\leq \varepsilon \max _{\overline D}|y|^2$. Thus $v\leq w\leq \varepsilon \max _{\overline D}|y|^2$ on $D$, and letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ gives $v\leq 0$. For the second assertion, $v^ B$ is harmonic on $B$ and equals $v$ on $D\setminus B$; it is continuous at the points of $\partial B$ because $H_ B(v|_{\partial B})$ extends continuously to $v$ on $\partial B$ (theorem 2.3.1 ). Moreover $v^ B\geq v$, because $v\leq H_ B(v|_{\partial B})$ on $B$. To verify the subsolution inequality, let $A$ be a ball with $\overline A\subset D$, and let $H=H_ A(v^ B|_{\partial A})$, regarded as a continuous function on $\overline A$. Since $v\leq v^ B$ and $H_ A$ preserves order, $v\leq H_ A(v|_{\partial A})\leq H$ on $A$; the same inequality holds on $\partial A$, where $H=v^ B\geq v$. On the open set $A\cap B$, the function $v^ B-H$ is harmonic, and it is continuous on the closure of $A\cap B$. A boundary point $\zeta $ of $A\cap B$ lies either on $\partial A$, where $v^ B(\zeta )=H(\zeta )$, or in $A\cap \partial B$, where $v^ B(\zeta )=v(\zeta )\leq H(\zeta )$. By part (2) of proposition 2.1.3 , applied to $v^ B-H$ on the bounded open set $A\cap B$, we get $v^ B\leq H$ on $A\cap B$. On $A\setminus B$ we have $v^ B=v\leq H$. Hence $v^ B\leq H_ A(v^ B|_{\partial A})$ on $A$, which is the subsolution inequality for $v^ B$ on $A$. $\square$ We call $v^ B$ the harmonic lifting of $v$ on $B$. For $f\in C(\partial \Omega )$, let $\mathcal S_ f$ be the set of continuous subsolutions $v$ on $\Omega $ such that $\varlimsup _{\Omega 
i x	o \zeta }v(x)\leq f(\zeta )$ for every $\zeta \in \partial \Omega $. The lower Perron envelope of $f$ is \[  U_ f(x)=\sup _{v\in \mathcal S_ f}v(x),\qquad x\in \Omega .  \] The constant $\min _{\partial \Omega }f$ belongs to $\mathcal S_ f$, and every $v\in \mathcal S_ f$ satisfies $v\leq \max _{\partial \Omega }f$, by lemma 2.4.1 applied to $v-\max _{\partial \Omega }f$. Theorem 2.4.2 . Let $f\in C(\partial \Omega )$. Then $U_ f$ is harmonic on $\Omega $ and $\min _{\partial \Omega }f\leq U_ f\leq \max _{\partial \Omega }f$. If a harmonic function on $\Omega $ extends continuously to $\overline\Omega $ with boundary values $f$, then it equals $U_ f$. Proof. The bounds for $U_ f$ were proved above. To prove harmonicity, fix a ball $B$ with $\overline B\subset \Omega $ and a point $x_0\in B$; we show that $U_ f$ agrees on $B$ with a harmonic function. If $v\in \mathcal S_ f$, its harmonic lifting $v^ B$ on $B$ is a continuous subsolution by lemma 2.4.1 , and it coincides with $v$ near $\partial \Omega $ because $\overline B$ is a compact subset of $\Omega $; hence $v^ B\in \mathcal S_ f$. Choose $v_ j\in \mathcal S_ f$ with $v_ j(x_0)	o U_ f(x_0)$, and put $w_ j=\max \{ v_1,\ldots ,v_ j,\min _{\partial \Omega }f\} $. Then $(w_ j)$ is an increasing sequence in $\mathcal S_ f$ with values in $[\min _{\partial \Omega }f,\max _{\partial \Omega }f]$, and $w_ j(x_0)	o U_ f(x_0)$ because $v_ j\leq w_ j\leq U_ f$. The liftings $w_ j^ B$ belong to $\mathcal S_ f$ and satisfy $w_ j\leq w_ j^ B\leq U_ f$. On $B$ they are harmonic, increase with $j$ because $H_ B$ preserves order, and are bounded by $\max _{\partial \Omega }f$. By part (2) of corollary 2.3.3 , applied on the domain $B$ to this sequence, which is bounded above, they converge on $B$ to a harmonic function $h$, and $h\leq U_ f$ on $B$, while $h(x_0)=U_ f(x_0)$. Now let $v\in \mathcal S_ f$ be arbitrary. The same argument applied to the increasing sequence $\max \{ w_ j,v\} \in \mathcal S_ f$ shows that the liftings $(\max \{ w_ j,v\} )^ B$ increase on $B$ to a harmonic function $k$. Since these liftings dominate $w_ j^ B$ and $v$ and lie in $\mathcal S_ f$, we have $h\leq k\leq U_ f$ and $k\geq v$ on $B$. In particular $k(x_0)\leq U_ f(x_0)=h(x_0)$, so the nonnegative harmonic function $k-h$ on $B$ vanishes at $x_0$ and therefore vanishes identically, by proposition 2.3.2 (2). Hence $v\leq h$ on $B$. Taking the supremum over $v\in \mathcal S_ f$ gives $U_ f\leq h$, so $U_ f=h$ on $B$. Since $B$ was arbitrary, $U_ f$ is harmonic on $\Omega $. Finally, let $H$ be harmonic on $\Omega $ and continuous on $\overline\Omega $ with $H=f$ on $\partial \Omega $. Then $H\in \mathcal S_ f$, so $H\leq U_ f$. Conversely, for $v\in \mathcal S_ f$ the function $v-H$ is a continuous subsolution with $\varlimsup _{x	o \zeta }(v-H)(x)\leq 0$ at every $\zeta \in \partial \Omega $, so $v\leq H$ by lemma 2.4.1 . Hence $U_ f=H$. $\square$ The upper Perron envelope is $V_ f=-U_{-f}$. Equivalently, $V_ f$ is the pointwise infimum of the set $-\mathcal S_{-f}$, which consists of the continuous supersolutions $w$ on $\Omega $ with $\varliminf _{\Omega 
i x	o \zeta }w(x)\geq f(\zeta )$ for every $\zeta \in \partial \Omega $. If $v\in \mathcal S_ f$ and $w\in -\mathcal S_{-f}$, then $v-w$ is a continuous subsolution with $\varlimsup _{x	o \zeta }(v-w)(x)\leq f(\zeta )-f(\zeta )=0$ at every $\zeta \in \partial \Omega $, so $v\leq w$ by lemma 2.4.1 . Hence $U_ f\leq V_ f$. To prove equality, we first treat data that extend smoothly to a neighborhood of $\overline\Omega $ and then approximate, using the following lemma. Lemma 2.4.3 . Let $K\subset \mathbb R^ d$ be compact and $f\in C(K)$. Then $f$ is the uniform limit on $K$ of restrictions to $K$ of functions in $C_ c^\infty (\mathbb R^ d)$, which can be taken real-valued if $f$ is real-valued. Proof. We may assume that $K
eq \varnothing $. Let $\delta >0$. By compactness there are points $\zeta _1,\ldots ,\zeta _ N\in K$ with $K\subset  igcup _ iB(\zeta _ i,\delta )$. Put $\chi _ i(x)=ho ((x-\zeta _ i)/(2\delta ))$, where $ho $ is the mollifier of section 1.4 ; this function is smooth, positive on $B(\zeta _ i,2\delta )$ and zero outside it. The function $\sigma =\sum _ i\chi _ i$ is positive on the open set $W= igcup _ iB(\zeta _ i,2\delta )\supset K$. Choose a smooth function $\eta $ with compact support in $W$ which equals one near $K$ (lemma 1.4.1 (4)), and put \[  F=\eta \,  rac{\sum _ if(\zeta _ i)\chi _ i}{\sigma },  \] extended by zero outside $W$. This is a smooth function with compact support on $\mathbb R^ d$, because it is smooth on $W$, where $\sigma >0$, and vanishes on the open set $\mathbb R^ d\setminus \operatorname{Supp}\eta $; it is real-valued if $f$ is. For $\zeta \in K$ we have $\eta (\zeta )=1$, so $F(\zeta )$ is a convex combination of values $f(\zeta _ i)$ with $|\zeta _ i-\zeta |<2\delta $, and therefore $|F(\zeta )-f(\zeta )|\leq \sup \{ |f(y)-f(y')|:y,y'\in K,\  |y-y'|<2\delta \} $. By the uniform continuity of $f$ on the compact set $K$, this bound tends to zero as $\delta 	o 0$. $\square$ Theorem 2.4.4 . For every $f\in C(\partial \Omega )$ we have $U_ f=V_ f$. The resulting map $f\mapsto U_ f$ from $C(\partial \Omega )$ to harmonic functions on $\Omega $ is linear and positive, and it is a contraction for the supremum norm: $\sup _\Omega |U_ f|\leq \max _{\partial \Omega }|f|$. Proof. Write $\| f\| =\max _{\partial \Omega }|f|$, and let $\mathcal R$ be the set of $f\in C(\partial \Omega )$ with $U_ f=V_ f$. We show that $\mathcal R$ is a closed linear subspace of $C(\partial \Omega )$ containing a dense subset. Step 1: $\mathcal R$ is a closed linear subspace, and $f\mapsto U_ f$ is linear on it. If $v\in \mathcal S_ f$ and $w\in \mathcal S_ g$, then $v+w\in \mathcal S_{f+g}$; taking suprema over $v$ and $w$ at a fixed point gives $U_ f+U_ g\leq U_{f+g}$. Applying this to $-f$ and $-g$ and changing signs gives $V_{f+g}\leq V_ f+V_ g$. Together with the inequality $U_{f+g}\leq V_{f+g}$ proved above, we obtain \[  U_ f+U_ g\leq U_{f+g}\leq V_{f+g}\leq V_ f+V_ g.  \] Moreover $\mathcal S_{tf}=t\, \mathcal S_ f$ for $t>0$, so $U_{tf}=tU_ f$ and $V_{tf}=tV_ f$, while $U_{-f}=-V_ f$ and $V_{-f}=-U_ f$ by definition. Also $U_0=0$, because $0\in \mathcal S_0$ and every member of $\mathcal S_0$ is nonpositive by lemma 2.4.1 ; hence $V_0=-U_0=0$ and $0\in \mathcal R$. Consequently, if $f,g\in \mathcal R$, the display forces $U_{f+g}=V_{f+g}=U_ f+U_ g$, and $tf\in \mathcal R$ for every real $t$. Thus $\mathcal R$ is a linear subspace, and $f\mapsto U_ f$ is linear on it. To see that $\mathcal R$ is closed, we first show that $U_ f$ and $V_ f$ depend $1$-Lipschitz continuously on $f$ for the supremum norm. If $f\leq g$, then $\mathcal S_ f\subset \mathcal S_ g$ and hence $U_ f\leq U_ g$; and $\mathcal S_{f+t}=\mathcal S_ f+t$ for constants $t$, so $U_{f+t}=U_ f+t$. Since $f\leq g+\| f-g\| $, we get $U_ f\leq U_ g+\| f-g\| $, and by symmetry $|U_ f-U_ g|\leq \| f-g\| $; as $V_ f=-U_{-f}$ and $V_ g=-U_{-g}$, also $|V_ f-V_ g|\leq \| f-g\| $. If $f_ n\in \mathcal R$ converge uniformly to $f$, then $0\leq V_ f-U_ f\leq |V_ f-V_{f_ n}|+|U_{f_ n}-U_ f|\leq 2\| f-f_ n\| 	o 0$, so $f\in \mathcal R$. Hence $\mathcal R$ is closed. Step 2: $\mathcal R$ contains the restriction to $\partial \Omega $ of every real smooth function on a neighborhood of $\overline\Omega $. Suppose first that $F$ is a real smooth function on a neighborhood of $\overline\Omega $ with $\Delta F\geq 0$ there. Then $F$ is a continuous subsolution on $\Omega $, and $F(x)	o F(\zeta )$ as $\Omega 
i x	o \zeta \in \partial \Omega $, so $F\in \mathcal S_{F|_{\partial \Omega }}$ and $U_{F|_{\partial \Omega }}\geq F$. Consequently the harmonic function $U_{F|_{\partial \Omega }}$ satisfies $\varliminf _{x	o \zeta }U_{F|_{\partial \Omega }}(x)\geq F(\zeta )$ at every $\zeta \in \partial \Omega $, so it belongs to $-\mathcal S_{-F|_{\partial \Omega }}$ and $V_{F|_{\partial \Omega }}\leq U_{F|_{\partial \Omega }}$. Thus $F|_{\partial \Omega }\in \mathcal R$. Now let $F$ be an arbitrary real smooth function on an open neighborhood $W$ of $\overline\Omega $, and choose $\delta >0$ such that the compact set $L=\{ x:\operatorname {dist}(x,\overline\Omega )\leq \delta \} $ lies in $W$. Since $\Delta F$ is continuous, hence bounded below, on $L$, there is a constant $A\geq 0$ with $\Delta F+2dA\geq 0$ on $L$. As $\Delta (A|x|^2)=2dA$, both $F+A|x|^2$ and $A|x|^2$ are smooth with nonnegative Laplacian on the open neighborhood $\{ x:\operatorname {dist}(x,\overline\Omega )<\delta \} $ of $\overline\Omega $. By the first case their restrictions to $\partial \Omega $ lie in $\mathcal R$, and by Step 1 so does the restriction of their difference $F$. Step 3: these restrictions are dense in $C(\partial \Omega )$. This is lemma 2.4.3 , applied to real-valued functions on the compact set $\partial \Omega $. By Steps 1–3, $\mathcal R=C(\partial \Omega )$, and $f\mapsto U_ f$ is linear. By Step 1 it preserves order and satisfies $|U_ f-U_ g|\leq \| f-g\| $. Since $U_0=0$, it follows that $U_ f\geq 0$ whenever $f\geq 0$, and that $|U_ f|\leq \| f\| $. $\square$ Definition 2.4.5 . A boundary point $\xi \in \partial \Omega $ is regular if $U_ f(x)	o f(\xi )$ as $\Omega 
i x	o \xi $, for every $f\in C(\partial \Omega )$. A barrier at $\xi $ is a positive continuous supersolution $b$ on $\Omega $ such that $b(x)	o 0$ as $x	o \xi $ and, for every neighborhood $N$ of $\xi $ with $\Omega \setminus N
eq \varnothing $, \[  \inf _{\Omega \setminus N}b>0.  \] Theorem 2.4.6 . A boundary point of $\Omega $ is regular if and only if it has a barrier. If every boundary point of $\Omega $ is regular, then for every $f\in C(\partial \Omega )$ the Perron envelope $U_ f$ is the unique harmonic function on $\Omega $ which extends continuously to $\overline\Omega $ with boundary values $f$. If $\xi \in \partial \Omega $ and there is a ball $B(a,r)$ with $\overline{B(a,r)}\cap \overline\Omega =\{ \xi \} $, then $\xi $ has a barrier. Proof. Suppose that $b$ is a barrier at $\xi $, and let $f\in C(\partial \Omega )$ and $\varepsilon >0$. We show that $|U_ f-f(\xi )|\leq \varepsilon +Cb$ on $\Omega $ for a suitable constant $C$. Choose $\delta >0$ such that $|f(\zeta )-f(\xi )|<\varepsilon $ for all $\zeta \in \partial \Omega $ with $|\zeta -\xi |<2\delta $, and put $c=\inf _{\Omega \setminus B(\xi ,\delta )}b>0$; if $\Omega \subset B(\xi ,\delta )$, then $|\zeta -\xi |\leq \delta $ for every $\zeta \in \partial \Omega $, and we put $c=1$. If $\zeta \in \partial \Omega $ and $|\zeta -\xi |\geq 2\delta $, then $\Omega \cap B(\zeta ,\delta )$ lies outside $B(\xi ,\delta )$, so $\varliminf _{x	o \zeta }b(x)\geq c$. Let $M=\max _{\partial \Omega }|f|$ and fix $C\geq 2M/c$, which depends on $f$, $\varepsilon $ and $b$. We claim that, for every $\zeta \in \partial \Omega $, \[  \varlimsup _{x	o \zeta } igl (f(\xi )-\varepsilon -Cb(x) igr )\leq f(\zeta )\leq \varliminf _{x	o \zeta } igl (f(\xi )+\varepsilon +Cb(x) igr ).  \] If $|\zeta -\xi |<2\delta $, this holds because $b>0$ and $f(\xi )-\varepsilon <f(\zeta )<f(\xi )+\varepsilon $. If $|\zeta -\xi |\geq 2\delta $, it holds because $f(\xi )-Cc\leq M-2M\leq f(\zeta )$ and $f(\xi )+Cc\geq -M+2M\geq f(\zeta )$. Hence the continuous subsolution $f(\xi )-\varepsilon -Cb$ belongs to $\mathcal S_ f$, and the continuous supersolution $f(\xi )+\varepsilon +Cb$ belongs to $-\mathcal S_{-f}$, so that it dominates every member of $\mathcal S_ f$, as shown after theorem 2.4.2 . Therefore $|U_ f-f(\xi )|\leq \varepsilon +Cb$ on $\Omega $. Letting $x	o \xi $ and then $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ shows that $U_ f(x)	o f(\xi )$. Thus $\xi $ is regular. Conversely, let $\xi $ be regular, and take the boundary function $f(\zeta )=|\zeta -\xi |$. The smooth function $v(x)=|x-\xi |^2/\operatorname {diam}\Omega $ satisfies $\Delta v\geq 0$, and $v\leq f$ on $\partial \Omega $ because $|\zeta -\xi |\leq \operatorname {diam}\overline\Omega =\operatorname {diam}\Omega $ for $\zeta \in \partial \Omega $; hence $v\in \mathcal S_ f$. Thus $b=U_ f$ is harmonic by theorem 2.4.2 , and hence a continuous supersolution, with $b\geq |x-\xi |^2/\operatorname {diam}\Omega $. In particular $b$ is positive on $\Omega $, and if $N$ is a neighborhood of $\xi $ containing a ball $B(\xi ,t)$, then $\inf _{\Omega \setminus N}b\geq t^2/\operatorname {diam}\Omega >0$. By regularity, $b(x)	o f(\xi )=0$ as $x	o \xi $. Hence $b$ is a barrier. Now suppose that every boundary point is regular, and let $f\in C(\partial \Omega )$. Then $U_ f$ is harmonic on $\Omega $ by theorem 2.4.2 . By regularity and the continuity of $f$ on $\partial \Omega $, the function equal to $U_ f$ on $\Omega $ and to $f$ on $\partial \Omega $ is continuous on $\overline\Omega $. Uniqueness follows from proposition 2.1.3 . Finally, suppose that $\overline{B(a,r)}\cap \overline\Omega =\{ \xi \} $. Then $|\xi -a|=r$, since otherwise the open ball $B(a,r)$ would be a neighborhood of $\xi $ and would therefore contain points of $\Omega $, which differ from $\xi 
otin \Omega $. In particular $a
otin \overline\Omega $, and every point of $\overline\Omega \setminus \{ \xi \} $ satisfies $|x-a|>r$. Put \[  b(x)= egin{cases}  |x-a|-r,& d=1,\  \log (|x-a|/r),& d=2,\  r^{2-d}-|x-a|^{2-d},& d\geq 3. \end{cases}  \] For $d\geq 2$ this is harmonic on $\mathbb R^ d\setminus \{ a\} $ by proposition 2.2.1 , being a positive multiple of $E_ d(x-a)$ plus a constant. In dimension one, each component of $\Omega $ is an open interval disjoint from $[a-r,a+r]$, so it lies on one side of this interval; hence $|x-a|$ is affine on each component, and $b$ is harmonic on $\Omega $ as well. In all dimensions $b$ is an increasing function of $|x-a|$ which vanishes when $|x-a|=r$, so it is continuous on the compact set $\overline\Omega $, positive on $\overline\Omega \setminus \{ \xi \} $ and zero at $\xi $. Hence $b(x)	o 0$ as $x	o \xi $, and if $N$ is a neighborhood of $\xi $ with $\Omega \setminus N
eq \varnothing $, the infimum of $b$ over the nonempty compact set $\overline\Omega \setminus \operatorname{Int}N$ is attained and positive. Thus $b$ is a barrier at $\xi $. $\square$ It is often easier to construct a barrier only near $\xi $; the next proposition shows that this suffices. Proposition 2.4.7 . Let $\xi \in \partial \Omega $ and let $W$ be an open neighborhood of $\xi $. Suppose that $b$ is a positive continuous supersolution on $\Omega \cap W$ which extends continuously to $\overline\Omega \cap W$, and that the extension vanishes at $\xi $ but nowhere else on $\overline\Omega \cap W$. Then $\xi $ is regular. Proof. Choose $r>0$ with $\overline{B(\xi ,2r)}\subset W$ and $0<t<r$. The set $L=\overline\Omega \cap \{ r-t\leq |x-\xi |\leq r+t\} $ is compact, and $b$ is positive and continuous on it, so there is $c>0$ with $b\geq 2c$ on $L$ (if $L$ is empty, any $c>0$ will do). Define $	ilde b=\min \{ b,c\} $ on $\Omega \cap B(\xi ,r)$ and $	ilde b=c$ on $\Omega \setminus B(\xi ,r)$. Since $b\geq 2c$ on $L$, we have $	ilde b=\min \{ b,c\} $ on $\Omega \cap B(\xi ,r+t)$ and $	ilde b=c$ on $\Omega \setminus \overline{B(\xi ,r)}$. These two open sets cover $\Omega $, and on each of them $	ilde b$ is a continuous supersolution, being a minimum of two continuous supersolutions or a constant. By the locality of the subsolution property, noted after the definition of continuous subsolutions, $	ilde b$ is a continuous supersolution on $\Omega $. The function $	ilde b$ is positive, and it tends to zero at $\xi $, because $0<	ilde b\leq b$ on $\Omega \cap B(\xi ,r)$ and the extension of $b$ vanishes at $\xi $. If $N$ is a neighborhood of $\xi $, then $	ilde b\geq c$ on $\Omega \setminus B(\xi ,r)$, while on $(\Omega \cap B(\xi ,r))\setminus N$ it is at least the minimum of $c$ and of $b$ over the compact set $(\overline\Omega \cap \overline{B(\xi ,r)})\setminus \operatorname{Int}N$, on which $b$ is positive. Hence $	ilde b$ is a barrier at $\xi $, and theorem 2.4.6 shows that $\xi $ is regular. $\square$ Example 2.4.8 . Let $d\geq 2$. The punctured ball $\Omega =B(0,1)\setminus \{ 0\} $ is a bounded domain with boundary $S^{d-1}\cup \{ 0\} $, and the origin is an irregular boundary point, that is, a boundary point that is not regular. The punctured ball is connected, because it is the image of $(0,1)	imes S^{d-1}$ under the continuous map $(t,\omega )\mapsto t\omega $ and the sphere $S^{d-1}$ is path-connected when $d\geq 2$. Indeed, two points $\omega ,\omega '$ with $\omega '
eq -\omega $ are joined by the path $s\mapsto ((1-s)\omega +s\omega ')/|(1-s)\omega +s\omega '|$, $0\leq s\leq 1$, whose denominator does not vanish, and two antipodal points can be joined through a unit vector orthogonal to them, which exists because $d\geq 2$. To see that the origin is irregular, let $f$ equal one at the origin and zero on $S^{d-1}$; it is continuous on $\partial \Omega $ because the origin is an isolated point of $\partial \Omega $. Let $g(x)=\Gamma _ d(x)-\Gamma _ d(e_1)$, that is, $g(x)=(2\pi )^{-1}\log (1/|x|)$ if $d=2$ and $g(x)=((d-2)s_{d-1})^{-1}(|x|^{2-d}-1)$ if $d\geq 3$. This function is harmonic on $\mathbb R^ d\setminus \{ 0\} $ by proposition 2.2.1 , it vanishes on $S^{d-1}$, and it tends to $+\infty $ at the origin. Let $v\in \mathcal S_ f$ and $\varepsilon >0$; recall that $v\leq \max _{\partial \Omega }f=1$. For every sufficiently small $\delta \in (0,1)$ we have $\varepsilon g\geq 1$ on the sphere $|x|=\delta $. On the annulus $D=\{ \delta <|x|<1\} $, the function $v-\varepsilon g$ is a continuous subsolution; it is continuous and nonpositive on the inner sphere $|x|=\delta $, and its upper limit at every point of $S^{d-1}$ is at most $f=0$, because $g$ is continuous with value $0$ there. By lemma 2.4.1 , $v\leq \varepsilon g$ on $D$. Letting $\delta \downarrow 0$ and then $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ gives $v\leq 0$ on $\Omega $. Since $0\in \mathcal S_ f$, the Perron envelope $U_ f$ vanishes identically, so it does not tend to $f(0)=1$ at the origin. In dimension one the situation is different: the bounded open set $(-1,0)\cup (0,1)$ has boundary $\{ -1,0,1\} $. If $f$ is a function on this boundary, the function which is affine on each of the two intervals with the boundary values given by $f$ is harmonic and extends continuously to $[-1,1]$ with boundary values $f$, so it equals $U_ f$ by theorem 2.4.2 . Hence the origin is a regular boundary point of $(-1,0)\cup (0,1)$.

title: Subsolution comparison
topic: Harmonic functions and the Dirichlet problem
text:
Lemma 2.4.1 . Let $D$ be a bounded open set and $v$ a continuous subsolution on $D$. If $\varlimsup _{D
i x	o \zeta }v(x)\leq 0$ for every $\zeta \in \partial D$, then $v\leq 0$ on $D$. Moreover, if $B$ is a ball with $\overline B\subset D$, then the function $v^ B$ which equals $H_ B(v|_{\partial B})$ on $B$ and $v$ on $D\setminus B$ is a continuous subsolution on $D$ with $v^ B\geq v$. Proof. For the first assertion we may assume that $D
eq \varnothing $. Let $\varepsilon >0$, and put $w(y)=v(y)+\varepsilon |y|^2$ for $y\in D$. If $\overline{B(c,r)}\subset D$, then $v(c)\leq M_ v(c,r)$, and the identity $M_{|\cdot |^2}(c,r)=|c|^2+r^2$ gives $w(c)\leq M_ w(c,r)-\varepsilon r^2$. Consequently $w$ does not attain its supremum over $D$ at any point $c\in D$, for we would then have $M_ w(c,r)\leq w(c)$ for small $r$. Choose $x_ k\in D$ with $w(x_ k)	o \sup _ Dw$. Since $D$ is bounded, we may assume, after passing to a subsequence, that $x_ k$ converges to a point $p\in \overline D$. If $p$ were in $D$, the continuity of $w$ would give $w(p)=\sup _ Dw$, which we have excluded. Hence $p\in \partial D$. Since $\sup _ Dw=\lim _ k igl (v(x_ k)+\varepsilon |x_ k|^2 igr )$, the hypothesis gives $\sup _ Dw\leq \varlimsup _{D
i x	o p}v(x)+\varepsilon |p|^2\leq \varepsilon \max _{\overline D}|y|^2$. Thus $v\leq w\leq \varepsilon \max _{\overline D}|y|^2$ on $D$, and letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ gives $v\leq 0$. For the second assertion, $v^ B$ is harmonic on $B$ and equals $v$ on $D\setminus B$; it is continuous at the points of $\partial B$ because $H_ B(v|_{\partial B})$ extends continuously to $v$ on $\partial B$ (theorem 2.3.1 ). Moreover $v^ B\geq v$, because $v\leq H_ B(v|_{\partial B})$ on $B$. To verify the subsolution inequality, let $A$ be a ball with $\overline A\subset D$, and let $H=H_ A(v^ B|_{\partial A})$, regarded as a continuous function on $\overline A$. Since $v\leq v^ B$ and $H_ A$ preserves order, $v\leq H_ A(v|_{\partial A})\leq H$ on $A$; the same inequality holds on $\partial A$, where $H=v^ B\geq v$. On the open set $A\cap B$, the function $v^ B-H$ is harmonic, and it is continuous on the closure of $A\cap B$. A boundary point $\zeta $ of $A\cap B$ lies either on $\partial A$, where $v^ B(\zeta )=H(\zeta )$, or in $A\cap \partial B$, where $v^ B(\zeta )=v(\zeta )\leq H(\zeta )$. By part (2) of proposition 2.1.3 , applied to $v^ B-H$ on the bounded open set $A\cap B$, we get $v^ B\leq H$ on $A\cap B$. On $A\setminus B$ we have $v^ B=v\leq H$. Hence $v^ B\leq H_ A(v^ B|_{\partial A})$ on $A$, which is the subsolution inequality for $v^ B$ on $A$. $\square$

title: Perron harmonic
topic: Harmonic functions and the Dirichlet problem
text: Theorem 2.4.2 . Let $f\in C(\partial \Omega )$. Then $U_ f$ is harmonic on $\Omega $ and $\min _{\partial \Omega }f\leq U_ f\leq \max _{\partial \Omega }f$. If a harmonic function on $\Omega $ extends continuously to $\overline\Omega $ with boundary values $f$, then it equals $U_ f$. Proof. The bounds for $U_ f$ were proved above. To prove harmonicity, fix a ball $B$ with $\overline B\subset \Omega $ and a point $x_0\in B$; we show that $U_ f$ agrees on $B$ with a harmonic function. If $v\in \mathcal S_ f$, its harmonic lifting $v^ B$ on $B$ is a continuous subsolution by lemma 2.4.1 , and it coincides with $v$ near $\partial \Omega $ because $\overline B$ is a compact subset of $\Omega $; hence $v^ B\in \mathcal S_ f$. Choose $v_ j\in \mathcal S_ f$ with $v_ j(x_0)\to U_ f(x_0)$, and put $w_ j=\max \{ v_1,\ldots ,v_ j,\min _{\partial \Omega }f\} $. Then $(w_ j)$ is an increasing sequence in $\mathcal S_ f$ with values in $[\min _{\partial \Omega }f,\max _{\partial \Omega }f]$, and $w_ j(x_0)\to U_ f(x_0)$ because $v_ j\leq w_ j\leq U_ f$. The liftings $w_ j^ B$ belong to $\mathcal S_ f$ and satisfy $w_ j\leq w_ j^ B\leq U_ f$. On $B$ they are harmonic, increase with $j$ because $H_ B$ preserves order, and are bounded by $\max _{\partial \Omega }f$. By part (2) of corollary 2.3.3 , applied on the domain $B$ to this sequence, which is bounded above, they converge on $B$ to a harmonic function $h$, and $h\leq U_ f$ on $B$, while $h(x_0)=U_ f(x_0)$. Now let $v\in \mathcal S_ f$ be arbitrary. The same argument applied to the increasing sequence $\max \{ w_ j,v\} \in \mathcal S_ f$ shows that the liftings $(\max \{ w_ j,v\} )^ B$ increase on $B$ to a harmonic function $k$. Since these liftings dominate $w_ j^ B$ and $v$ and lie in $\mathcal S_ f$, we have $h\leq k\leq U_ f$ and $k\geq v$ on $B$. In particular $k(x_0)\leq U_ f(x_0)=h(x_0)$, so the nonnegative harmonic function $k-h$ on $B$ vanishes at $x_0$ and therefore vanishes identically, by proposition 2.3.2 (2). Hence $v\leq h$ on $B$. Taking the supremum over $v\in \mathcal S_ f$ gives $U_ f\leq h$, so $U_ f=h$ on $B$. Since $B$ was arbitrary, $U_ f$ is harmonic on $\Omega $. Finally, let $H$ be harmonic on $\Omega $ and continuous on $\overline\Omega $ with $H=f$ on $\partial \Omega $. Then $H\in \mathcal S_ f$, so $H\leq U_ f$. Conversely, for $v\in \mathcal S_ f$ the function $v-H$ is a continuous subsolution with $\varlimsup _{x\to \zeta }(v-H)(x)\leq 0$ at every $\zeta \in \partial \Omega $, so $v\leq H$ by lemma 2.4.1 . Hence $U_ f=H$. $\square$

title: Compact smooth approximation
topic: Harmonic functions and the Dirichlet problem
text: Lemma 2.4.3 . Let $K\subset \mathbb R^ d$ be compact and $f\in C(K)$. Then $f$ is the uniform limit on $K$ of restrictions to $K$ of functions in $C_ c^\infty (\mathbb R^ d)$, which can be taken real-valued if $f$ is real-valued. Proof. We may assume that $K\neq \varnothing $. Let $\delta >0$. By compactness there are points $\zeta _1,\ldots ,\zeta _ N\in K$ with $K\subset \bigcup _ iB(\zeta _ i,\delta )$. Put $\chi _ i(x)=\rho ((x-\zeta _ i)/(2\delta ))$, where $\rho $ is the mollifier of section 1.4 ; this function is smooth, positive on $B(\zeta _ i,2\delta )$ and zero outside it. The function $\sigma =\sum _ i\chi _ i$ is positive on the open set $W=\bigcup _ iB(\zeta _ i,2\delta )\supset K$. Choose a smooth function $\eta $ with compact support in $W$ which equals one near $K$ (lemma 1.4.1 (4)), and put \[  F=\eta \, \frac{\sum _ if(\zeta _ i)\chi _ i}{\sigma },  \] extended by zero outside $W$. This is a smooth function with compact support on $\mathbb R^ d$, because it is smooth on $W$, where $\sigma >0$, and vanishes on the open set $\mathbb R^ d\setminus \operatorname{Supp}\eta $; it is real-valued if $f$ is. For $\zeta \in K$ we have $\eta (\zeta )=1$, so $F(\zeta )$ is a convex combination of values $f(\zeta _ i)$ with $|\zeta _ i-\zeta |<2\delta $, and therefore $|F(\zeta )-f(\zeta )|\leq \sup \{ |f(y)-f(y')|:y,y'\in K,\  |y-y'|<2\delta \} $. By the uniform continuity of $f$ on the compact set $K$, this bound tends to zero as $\delta \to 0$. $\square$

title: Perron resolutivity
topic: Harmonic functions and the Dirichlet problem
text: Theorem 2.4.4 . For every $f\in C(\partial \Omega )$ we have $U_ f=V_ f$. The resulting map $f\mapsto U_ f$ from $C(\partial \Omega )$ to harmonic functions on $\Omega $ is linear and positive, and it is a contraction for the supremum norm: $\sup _\Omega |U_ f|\leq \max _{\partial \Omega }|f|$. Proof. Write $\| f\| =\max _{\partial \Omega }|f|$, and let $\mathcal R$ be the set of $f\in C(\partial \Omega )$ with $U_ f=V_ f$. We show that $\mathcal R$ is a closed linear subspace of $C(\partial \Omega )$ containing a dense subset. Step 1: $\mathcal R$ is a closed linear subspace, and $f\mapsto U_ f$ is linear on it. If $v\in \mathcal S_ f$ and $w\in \mathcal S_ g$, then $v+w\in \mathcal S_{f+g}$; taking suprema over $v$ and $w$ at a fixed point gives $U_ f+U_ g\leq U_{f+g}$. Applying this to $-f$ and $-g$ and changing signs gives $V_{f+g}\leq V_ f+V_ g$. Together with the inequality $U_{f+g}\leq V_{f+g}$ proved above, we obtain \[  U_ f+U_ g\leq U_{f+g}\leq V_{f+g}\leq V_ f+V_ g.  \] Moreover $\mathcal S_{tf}=t\, \mathcal S_ f$ for $t>0$, so $U_{tf}=tU_ f$ and $V_{tf}=tV_ f$, while $U_{-f}=-V_ f$ and $V_{-f}=-U_ f$ by definition. Also $U_0=0$, because $0\in \mathcal S_0$ and every member of $\mathcal S_0$ is nonpositive by lemma 2.4.1 ; hence $V_0=-U_0=0$ and $0\in \mathcal R$. Consequently, if $f,g\in \mathcal R$, the display forces $U_{f+g}=V_{f+g}=U_ f+U_ g$, and $tf\in \mathcal R$ for every real $t$. Thus $\mathcal R$ is a linear subspace, and $f\mapsto U_ f$ is linear on it. To see that $\mathcal R$ is closed, we first show that $U_ f$ and $V_ f$ depend $1$-Lipschitz continuously on $f$ for the supremum norm. If $f\leq g$, then $\mathcal S_ f\subset \mathcal S_ g$ and hence $U_ f\leq U_ g$; and $\mathcal S_{f+t}=\mathcal S_ f+t$ for constants $t$, so $U_{f+t}=U_ f+t$. Since $f\leq g+\| f-g\| $, we get $U_ f\leq U_ g+\| f-g\| $, and by symmetry $|U_ f-U_ g|\leq \| f-g\| $; as $V_ f=-U_{-f}$ and $V_ g=-U_{-g}$, also $|V_ f-V_ g|\leq \| f-g\| $. If $f_ n\in \mathcal R$ converge uniformly to $f$, then $0\leq V_ f-U_ f\leq |V_ f-V_{f_ n}|+|U_{f_ n}-U_ f|\leq 2\| f-f_ n\| \to 0$, so $f\in \mathcal R$. Hence $\mathcal R$ is closed. Step 2: $\mathcal R$ contains the restriction to $\partial \Omega $ of every real smooth function on a neighborhood of $\overline\Omega $. Suppose first that $F$ is a real smooth function on a neighborhood of $\overline\Omega $ with $\Delta F\geq 0$ there. Then $F$ is a continuous subsolution on $\Omega $, and $F(x)\to F(\zeta )$ as $\Omega \ni x\to \zeta \in \partial \Omega $, so $F\in \mathcal S_{F|_{\partial \Omega }}$ and $U_{F|_{\partial \Omega }}\geq F$. Consequently the harmonic function $U_{F|_{\partial \Omega }}$ satisfies $\varliminf _{x\to \zeta }U_{F|_{\partial \Omega }}(x)\geq F(\zeta )$ at every $\zeta \in \partial \Omega $, so it belongs to $-\mathcal S_{-F|_{\partial \Omega }}$ and $V_{F|_{\partial \Omega }}\leq U_{F|_{\partial \Omega }}$. Thus $F|_{\partial \Omega }\in \mathcal R$. Now let $F$ be an arbitrary real smooth function on an open neighborhood $W$ of $\overline\Omega $, and choose $\delta >0$ such that the compact set $L=\{ x:\operatorname {dist}(x,\overline\Omega )\leq \delta \} $ lies in $W$. Since $\Delta F$ is continuous, hence bounded below, on $L$, there is a constant $A\geq 0$ with $\Delta F+2dA\geq 0$ on $L$. As $\Delta (A|x|^2)=2dA$, both $F+A|x|^2$ and $A|x|^2$ are smooth with nonnegative Laplacian on the open neighborhood $\{ x:\operatorname {dist}(x,\overline\Omega )<\delta \} $ of $\overline\Omega $. By the first case their restrictions to $\partial \Omega $ lie in $\mathcal R$, and by Step 1 so does the restriction of their difference $F$. Step 3: these restrictions are dense in $C(\partial \Omega )$. This is lemma 2.4.3 , applied to real-valued functions on the compact set $\partial \Omega $. By Steps 1–3, $\mathcal R=C(\partial \Omega )$, and $f\mapsto U_ f$ is linear. By Step 1 it preserves order and satisfies $|U_ f-U_ g|\leq \| f-g\| $. Since $U_0=0$, it follows that $U_ f\geq 0$ whenever $f\geq 0$, and that $|U_ f|\leq \| f\| $. $\square$

title: Boundary barrier
topic: Harmonic functions and the Dirichlet problem
text: Definition 2.4.5 . A boundary point $\xi \in \partial \Omega $ is regular if $U_ f(x)\to f(\xi )$ as $\Omega \ni x\to \xi $, for every $f\in C(\partial \Omega )$. A barrier at $\xi $ is a positive continuous supersolution $b$ on $\Omega $ such that $b(x)\to 0$ as $x\to \xi $ and, for every neighborhood $N$ of $\xi $ with $\Omega \setminus N\neq \varnothing $, \[  \inf _{\Omega \setminus N}b>0.  \]

title: Barrier regularity
topic: Harmonic functions and the Dirichlet problem
text:
Theorem 2.4.6 . A boundary point of $\Omega $ is regular if and only if it has a barrier. If every boundary point of $\Omega $ is regular, then for every $f\in C(\partial \Omega )$ the Perron envelope $U_ f$ is the unique harmonic function on $\Omega $ which extends continuously to $\overline\Omega $ with boundary values $f$. If $\xi \in \partial \Omega $ and there is a ball $B(a,r)$ with $\overline{B(a,r)}\cap \overline\Omega =\{ \xi \} $, then $\xi $ has a barrier. Proof. Suppose that $b$ is a barrier at $\xi $, and let $f\in C(\partial \Omega )$ and $\varepsilon >0$. We show that $|U_ f-f(\xi )|\leq \varepsilon +Cb$ on $\Omega $ for a suitable constant $C$. Choose $\delta >0$ such that $|f(\zeta )-f(\xi )|<\varepsilon $ for all $\zeta \in \partial \Omega $ with $|\zeta -\xi |<2\delta $, and put $c=\inf _{\Omega \setminus B(\xi ,\delta )}b>0$; if $\Omega \subset B(\xi ,\delta )$, then $|\zeta -\xi |\leq \delta $ for every $\zeta \in \partial \Omega $, and we put $c=1$. If $\zeta \in \partial \Omega $ and $|\zeta -\xi |\geq 2\delta $, then $\Omega \cap B(\zeta ,\delta )$ lies outside $B(\xi ,\delta )$, so $\varliminf _{x	o \zeta }b(x)\geq c$. Let $M=\max _{\partial \Omega }|f|$ and fix $C\geq 2M/c$, which depends on $f$, $\varepsilon $ and $b$. We claim that, for every $\zeta \in \partial \Omega $, \[  \varlimsup _{x	o \zeta } igl (f(\xi )-\varepsilon -Cb(x) igr )\leq f(\zeta )\leq \varliminf _{x	o \zeta } igl (f(\xi )+\varepsilon +Cb(x) igr ).  \] If $|\zeta -\xi |<2\delta $, this holds because $b>0$ and $f(\xi )-\varepsilon <f(\zeta )<f(\xi )+\varepsilon $. If $|\zeta -\xi |\geq 2\delta $, it holds because $f(\xi )-Cc\leq M-2M\leq f(\zeta )$ and $f(\xi )+Cc\geq -M+2M\geq f(\zeta )$. Hence the continuous subsolution $f(\xi )-\varepsilon -Cb$ belongs to $\mathcal S_ f$, and the continuous supersolution $f(\xi )+\varepsilon +Cb$ belongs to $-\mathcal S_{-f}$, so that it dominates every member of $\mathcal S_ f$, as shown after theorem 2.4.2 . Therefore $|U_ f-f(\xi )|\leq \varepsilon +Cb$ on $\Omega $. Letting $x	o \xi $ and then $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ shows that $U_ f(x)	o f(\xi )$. Thus $\xi $ is regular. Conversely, let $\xi $ be regular, and take the boundary function $f(\zeta )=|\zeta -\xi |$. The smooth function $v(x)=|x-\xi |^2/\operatorname {diam}\Omega $ satisfies $\Delta v\geq 0$, and $v\leq f$ on $\partial \Omega $ because $|\zeta -\xi |\leq \operatorname {diam}\overline\Omega =\operatorname {diam}\Omega $ for $\zeta \in \partial \Omega $; hence $v\in \mathcal S_ f$. Thus $b=U_ f$ is harmonic by theorem 2.4.2 , and hence a continuous supersolution, with $b\geq |x-\xi |^2/\operatorname {diam}\Omega $. In particular $b$ is positive on $\Omega $, and if $N$ is a neighborhood of $\xi $ containing a ball $B(\xi ,t)$, then $\inf _{\Omega \setminus N}b\geq t^2/\operatorname {diam}\Omega >0$. By regularity, $b(x)	o f(\xi )=0$ as $x	o \xi $. Hence $b$ is a barrier. Now suppose that every boundary point is regular, and let $f\in C(\partial \Omega )$. Then $U_ f$ is harmonic on $\Omega $ by theorem 2.4.2 . By regularity and the continuity of $f$ on $\partial \Omega $, the function equal to $U_ f$ on $\Omega $ and to $f$ on $\partial \Omega $ is continuous on $\overline\Omega $. Uniqueness follows from proposition 2.1.3 . Finally, suppose that $\overline{B(a,r)}\cap \overline\Omega =\{ \xi \} $. Then $|\xi -a|=r$, since otherwise the open ball $B(a,r)$ would be a neighborhood of $\xi $ and would therefore contain points of $\Omega $, which differ from $\xi 
otin \Omega $. In particular $a
otin \overline\Omega $, and every point of $\overline\Omega \setminus \{ \xi \} $ satisfies $|x-a|>r$. Put \[  b(x)= egin{cases}  |x-a|-r,& d=1,\  \log (|x-a|/r),& d=2,\  r^{2-d}-|x-a|^{2-d},& d\geq 3. \end{cases}  \] For $d\geq 2$ this is harmonic on $\mathbb R^ d\setminus \{ a\} $ by proposition 2.2.1 , being a positive multiple of $E_ d(x-a)$ plus a constant. In dimension one, each component of $\Omega $ is an open interval disjoint from $[a-r,a+r]$, so it lies on one side of this interval; hence $|x-a|$ is affine on each component, and $b$ is harmonic on $\Omega $ as well. In all dimensions $b$ is an increasing function of $|x-a|$ which vanishes when $|x-a|=r$, so it is continuous on the compact set $\overline\Omega $, positive on $\overline\Omega \setminus \{ \xi \} $ and zero at $\xi $. Hence $b(x)	o 0$ as $x	o \xi $, and if $N$ is a neighborhood of $\xi $ with $\Omega \setminus N
eq \varnothing $, the infimum of $b$ over the nonempty compact set $\overline\Omega \setminus \operatorname{Int}N$ is attained and positive. Thus $b$ is a barrier at $\xi $. $\square$

title: Local barrier
topic: Harmonic functions and the Dirichlet problem
text: Proposition 2.4.7 . Let $\xi \in \partial \Omega $ and let $W$ be an open neighborhood of $\xi $. Suppose that $b$ is a positive continuous supersolution on $\Omega \cap W$ which extends continuously to $\overline\Omega \cap W$, and that the extension vanishes at $\xi $ but nowhere else on $\overline\Omega \cap W$. Then $\xi $ is regular. Proof. Choose $r>0$ with $\overline{B(\xi ,2r)}\subset W$ and $0<t<r$. The set $L=\overline\Omega \cap \{ r-t\leq |x-\xi |\leq r+t\} $ is compact, and $b$ is positive and continuous on it, so there is $c>0$ with $b\geq 2c$ on $L$ (if $L$ is empty, any $c>0$ will do). Define $\tilde b=\min \{ b,c\} $ on $\Omega \cap B(\xi ,r)$ and $\tilde b=c$ on $\Omega \setminus B(\xi ,r)$. Since $b\geq 2c$ on $L$, we have $\tilde b=\min \{ b,c\} $ on $\Omega \cap B(\xi ,r+t)$ and $\tilde b=c$ on $\Omega \setminus \overline{B(\xi ,r)}$. These two open sets cover $\Omega $, and on each of them $\tilde b$ is a continuous supersolution, being a minimum of two continuous supersolutions or a constant. By the locality of the subsolution property, noted after the definition of continuous subsolutions, $\tilde b$ is a continuous supersolution on $\Omega $. The function $\tilde b$ is positive, and it tends to zero at $\xi $, because $0<\tilde b\leq b$ on $\Omega \cap B(\xi ,r)$ and the extension of $b$ vanishes at $\xi $. If $N$ is a neighborhood of $\xi $, then $\tilde b\geq c$ on $\Omega \setminus B(\xi ,r)$, while on $(\Omega \cap B(\xi ,r))\setminus N$ it is at least the minimum of $c$ and of $b$ over the compact set $(\overline\Omega \cap \overline{B(\xi ,r)})\setminus \operatorname{Int}N$, on which $b$ is positive. Hence $\tilde b$ is a barrier at $\xi $, and theorem 2.4.6 shows that $\xi $ is regular. $\square$

title: Punctured ball irregular
topic: Harmonic functions and the Dirichlet problem
text: Example 2.4.8 . Let $d\geq 2$. The punctured ball $\Omega =B(0,1)\setminus \{ 0\} $ is a bounded domain with boundary $S^{d-1}\cup \{ 0\} $, and the origin is an irregular boundary point, that is, a boundary point that is not regular. The punctured ball is connected, because it is the image of $(0,1)\times S^{d-1}$ under the continuous map $(t,\omega )\mapsto t\omega $ and the sphere $S^{d-1}$ is path-connected when $d\geq 2$. Indeed, two points $\omega ,\omega '$ with $\omega '\neq -\omega $ are joined by the path $s\mapsto ((1-s)\omega +s\omega ')/|(1-s)\omega +s\omega '|$, $0\leq s\leq 1$, whose denominator does not vanish, and two antipodal points can be joined through a unit vector orthogonal to them, which exists because $d\geq 2$. To see that the origin is irregular, let $f$ equal one at the origin and zero on $S^{d-1}$; it is continuous on $\partial \Omega $ because the origin is an isolated point of $\partial \Omega $. Let $g(x)=\Gamma _ d(x)-\Gamma _ d(e_1)$, that is, $g(x)=(2\pi )^{-1}\log (1/|x|)$ if $d=2$ and $g(x)=((d-2)s_{d-1})^{-1}(|x|^{2-d}-1)$ if $d\geq 3$. This function is harmonic on $\mathbb R^ d\setminus \{ 0\} $ by proposition 2.2.1 , it vanishes on $S^{d-1}$, and it tends to $+\infty $ at the origin. Let $v\in \mathcal S_ f$ and $\varepsilon >0$; recall that $v\leq \max _{\partial \Omega }f=1$. For every sufficiently small $\delta \in (0,1)$ we have $\varepsilon g\geq 1$ on the sphere $|x|=\delta $. On the annulus $D=\{ \delta <|x|<1\} $, the function $v-\varepsilon g$ is a continuous subsolution; it is continuous and nonpositive on the inner sphere $|x|=\delta $, and its upper limit at every point of $S^{d-1}$ is at most $f=0$, because $g$ is continuous with value $0$ there. By lemma 2.4.1 , $v\leq \varepsilon g$ on $D$. Letting $\delta \downarrow 0$ and then $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ gives $v\leq 0$ on $\Omega $. Since $0\in \mathcal S_ f$, the Perron envelope $U_ f$ vanishes identically, so it does not tend to $f(0)=1$ at the origin. In dimension one the situation is different: the bounded open set $(-1,0)\cup (0,1)$ has boundary $\{ -1,0,1\} $. If $f$ is a function on this boundary, the function which is affine on each of the two intervals with the boundary values given by $f$ is harmonic and extends continuously to $[-1,1]$ with boundary values $f$, so it equals $U_ f$ by theorem 2.4.2 . Hence the origin is a regular boundary point of $(-1,0)\cup (0,1)$.

2.5 Harmonic measure and Green functions A nonempty bounded open set is called regular if all its boundary points are regular in the sense of definition 2.4.5 . Balls are regular, by the first and the last assertion of theorem 2.4.6 : for $\zeta \in \partial B(c,R)$, the closed ball $\overline{B(2\zeta -c,R)}$ meets $\overline{B(c,R)}$ only at $\zeta $. Indeed, $\zeta $ is the midpoint of $c$ and $2\zeta -c$, so every $y\in \mathbb R^ d$ satisfies $|y-c|^2+|y-(2\zeta -c)|^2=2|y-\zeta |^2+2R^2$, and if $y$ lies in both closed balls, the left side is at most $2R^2$, whence $y=\zeta $. In this section $\Omega $ is a regular bounded open set. For real $f\in C(\partial \Omega )$ we write $H_\Omega f$ for the unique harmonic function on $\Omega $ which extends continuously to $\overline\Omega $ with boundary values $f$ (theorem 2.4.6 ). By uniqueness, $H_\Omega $ is linear, and by proposition 2.1.3 it preserves order and satisfies $\sup _\Omega |H_\Omega f|\leq \max _{\partial \Omega }|f|$. For complex boundary data we put $H_\Omega (f+\mathrm i g)=H_\Omega f+\mathrm i H_\Omega g$, where $f$ and $g$ are real and continuous. When $\Omega $ is a ball, $H_\Omega $ is the Poisson integral of theorem 2.3.1 , again by uniqueness. Proposition 2.5.1 . For every $x\in \Omega $ there is a unique Borel probability measure $\omega _ x=\omega _ x^\Omega $ on $\partial \Omega $ such that \[  H_\Omega f(x)=\int _{\partial \Omega }f\, \mathrm d\omega _ x,\qquad f\in C(\partial \Omega ).  \] For each $f\in C(\partial \Omega )$, the function $x\mapsto \int f\, \mathrm d\omega _ x$ is harmonic on $\Omega $. If $\Omega $ is a ball, then $\mathrm d\omega _ x=P_\Omega (x,\cdot )\, \mathrm dS$. Proof. The map $g\mapsto H_\Omega (g|_{\partial \Omega })(x)$ is a positive linear functional on $C_ c(\mathbb R^ d,\mathbb R)$, so by theorem 1.2.2 it is integration against a Radon measure $\mu $ on $\mathbb R^ d$. If $g\in C_ c(\mathbb R^ d)$ is supported in the open set $\mathbb R^ d\setminus \partial \Omega $, then $g|_{\partial \Omega }=0$ and $\int g\, \mathrm d\mu =0$; by ( 1.4 ), $\mu (\mathbb R^ d\setminus \partial \Omega )=0$. If $\eta \in C_ c(\mathbb R^ d)$ equals one on the compact set $\partial \Omega $, then $\mu (\mathbb R^ d)=\mu (\partial \Omega )=\int \eta \, \mathrm d\mu =H_\Omega 1(x)=1$. Let $\omega _ x$ be the restriction of $\mu $ to the Borel subsets of $\partial \Omega $; it is a probability measure. Every $f\in C(\partial \Omega )$ is a uniform limit of restrictions of functions in $C_ c(\mathbb R^ d)$, by lemma 2.4.3 . Both sides of the asserted identity are continuous for uniform convergence on $\partial \Omega $, the right side because $\omega _ x$ is finite and the left side because $|H_\Omega f|\leq \max _{\partial \Omega }|f|$. Hence the identity holds for real $f$, and by linearity for complex $f$. If $\omega '$ is another Borel probability measure on $\partial \Omega $ with the same property, then $\omega _ x$ and $\omega '$, extended by zero to $\mathbb R^ d$, are finite Borel measures, hence Radon measures by proposition 1.1.2 , with the same integrals against every $g\in C_ c(\mathbb R^ d)$. The uniqueness assertion of theorem 1.2.2 gives $\omega '=\omega _ x$. The function $x\mapsto \int f\, \mathrm d\omega _ x=H_\Omega f(x)$ is harmonic by the definition of $H_\Omega $. If $\Omega $ is a ball, $P_\Omega (x,\cdot )\, \mathrm dS$ is a Borel probability measure on $\partial \Omega $ with the required property, by theorem 2.3.1 , so it equals $\omega _ x$. $\square$ The probability measure $\omega _ x$ is called the harmonic measure of $\Omega $ at $x$. When $\Omega $ is a ball centered at $x$, it is normalized surface measure on $\partial \Omega $; in general it depends on $x$. Theorem 2.5.2 . Let $\Omega $ be a bounded regular domain. For $x\in \Omega $, define the Green function of $\Omega $ by \[  G_\Omega (x,y)=\Gamma _ d(y-x)-H_\Omega (\Gamma _ d(\cdot -x)|_{\partial \Omega })(y),\qquad y\in \Omega ,  \] so that $G_\Omega (x,x)=\Gamma _ d(0)=+\infty $ when $d\geq 2$. For every $x\in \Omega $, the function $G_\Omega (x,\cdot )$ is positive on $\Omega $, harmonic on $\Omega \setminus \{ x\} $ and locally integrable on $\Omega $, it satisfies $-\Delta _ yG_\Omega (x,\cdot )=\delta _ x$ in the sense of distributions on $\Omega $, and $G_\Omega (x,y)	o 0$ as $y$ tends to any point of $\partial \Omega $. These properties determine $G_\Omega (x,y)$ uniquely for $y
eq x$. If $d=1$ and $\Omega =(a,b)$, then \[  G_{(a,b)}(x,y)= rac{(\min \{ x,y\} -a)(b-\max \{ x,y\} )}{b-a},\qquad x,y\in (a,b).  \] Green functions are monotone in the domain: if $D'\subset D''$ are bounded regular domains, then $G_{D'}(x,y)\leq G_{D''}(x,y)$ for all $x,y\in D'$. Let $D_1\subset D_2\subset \cdots $ be bounded regular domains whose union $D$ is a bounded regular domain. Then for $x
eq y$ in $D$, the values $G_{D_ j}(x,y)$, defined once $x,y\in D_ j$, increase to $G_ D(x,y)$, and for fixed $x$ the convergence holds in $C^\infty $ on compact subsets of $D\setminus \{ x\} $, as functions of $y$. Proof. (1) Fix $x\in \Omega $ and let $\gamma =\Gamma _ d(\cdot -x)|_{\partial \Omega }$, which is continuous because $\Gamma _ d(\cdot -x)$ is continuous on $\mathbb R^ d\setminus \{ x\} $. The function $H_\Omega \gamma $ is harmonic on $\Omega $, and $\Gamma _ d(\cdot -x)$ is harmonic on $\mathbb R^ d\setminus \{ x\} $ by proposition 2.2.1 , so $G_\Omega (x,\cdot )$ is harmonic on $\Omega \setminus \{ x\} $. By the same proposition, $\Gamma _ d(\cdot -x)$ is locally integrable, and for every test function $\chi $ on $\Omega $, which we extend by zero to $\mathbb R^ d$, \[  \int \Gamma _ d(y-x)\Delta \chi (y)\, \mathrm dy=-\int E_ d(z)(\Delta \chi )(x+z)\, \mathrm dz=-\langle \Delta E_ d,\chi (x+\cdot )angle =-\chi (x).  \] Since $H_\Omega \gamma $ is smooth on $\Omega $ with $\Delta H_\Omega \gamma =0$, integration by parts gives $\int H_\Omega \gamma \, \Delta \chi \, \mathrm dy=0$. Hence $G_\Omega (x,\cdot )$ is locally integrable on $\Omega $ and $\langle -\Delta _ yG_\Omega (x,\cdot ),\chi angle =\chi (x)$, that is, $-\Delta _ yG_\Omega (x,\cdot )=\delta _ x$. As $y	o \zeta \in \partial \Omega $, both $\Gamma _ d(y-x)$ and $H_\Omega \gamma (y)$ tend to $\gamma (\zeta )$, so $G_\Omega (x,y)	o 0$. At a point $\zeta \in \partial \Omega $ its upper limit is at most $\gamma (\zeta )-\gamma (\zeta )=0$, and on $\partial B(x,\varepsilon )$ it is continuous and nonpositive. By lemma 2.4.1 , $v\leq \Gamma _ d(\cdot -x)$ on $\Omega \setminus \overline{B(x,\varepsilon )}$, and letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ gives the claim. Strict positivity follows from the minimum principle, because $\Omega \setminus \{ x\} $ is connected when $d\geq 2$. To see this, let $y_0,y_1\in \Omega \setminus \{ x\} $. They can be joined by a polygonal path $p\colon [0,1]	o \Omega $, because the points of the domain $\Omega $ that can be joined to $y_0$ by a polygonal path in $\Omega $ form an open set whose complement in $\Omega $ is also open, balls being convex. Suppose that $p$ passes through $x$, and choose $r>0$ with $\overline{B(x,r)}\subset \Omega $ and $r<\min \{ |y_0-x|,|y_1-x|\} $. By the intermediate value theorem, the closed set of times $t$ with $|p(t)-x|=r$ is nonempty; let $t_1$ and $t_2$ be its smallest and largest elements. Then $|p(t)-x|>r$ for $t<t_1$ and for $t>t_2$, and replacing $p$ on $[t_1,t_2]$ by a path from $p(t_1)$ to $p(t_2)$ in the sphere $\partial B(x,r)$, which is path-connected because $d\geq 2$ (example 2.4.8 ), we obtain a path from $y_0$ to $y_1$ in $\Omega \setminus \{ x\} $. Now if $G_\Omega (x,\cdot )$ vanished at some point of the domain $\Omega \setminus \{ x\} $, it would attain its minimum there, and part (1) of proposition 2.1.3 would make it identically zero on $\Omega \setminus \{ x\} $, contradicting $G_\Omega (x,y)	o +\infty $ as $y	o x$. Hence $G_\Omega (x,\cdot )>0$. For uniqueness, let $G'$ be another function with the stated properties. The locally integrable function $G_\Omega (x,\cdot )-G'$ has vanishing distributional Laplacian on $\Omega $, so by theorem 2.1.4 it agrees almost everywhere with a harmonic function $h$ on $\Omega $. Away from $x$, the functions $G_\Omega (x,\cdot )$ and $G'$ are harmonic, so their difference is continuous there and therefore equals $h$ everywhere on $\Omega \setminus \{ x\} $. Then $h$ is real and has zero boundary limits, because $G_\Omega (x,\cdot )$ and $G'$ do, and $h=0$ by proposition 2.1.3 , applied to $h$ and to $-h$. This argument does not use positivity, and it applies in every dimension. (2) Let $d=1$, $\Omega =(a,b)$ and $x\in (a,b)$, and let $g(y)$ denote the right side of the formula in (2). The function $g$ is continuous, positive on $(a,b)$, and tends to zero at $a$ and $b$. It is affine on each side of $x$, with slope $g'_-=(b-x)/(b-a)$ on $(a,x)$ and $g'_+=-(x-a)/(b-a)$ on $(x,b)$, so $g'_+-g'_-=-1$. For a test function $\chi $ on $(a,b)$, an integration by parts on each of the intervals $(a,x)$ and $(x,b)$, on which $g'$ is constant, gives \[  \int _ a^ bg\chi ''\, \mathrm dy= igl (g(x)\chi '(x)-g'_-\chi (x) igr )+ igl (-g(x)\chi '(x)+g'_+\chi (x) igr )=-\chi (x),  \] so $-g''=\delta _ x$ in the sense of distributions. Moreover $g$ is harmonic on $(a,b)\setminus \{ x\} $. By the uniqueness argument just given, $g$ coincides with $G_{(a,b)}(x,\cdot )$ on $(a,b)\setminus \{ x\} $, and also at $x$, since both functions are continuous there. This proves (2), and with it the positivity in (1) when $d=1$. (3) Let $D'\subset D''$ be bounded regular domains and $x\in D'$. On $D'\setminus \{ x\} $ the fundamental solutions cancel, and \[  G_{D''}(x,\cdot )-G_{D'}(x,\cdot )=H_{D'}(\Gamma _ d(\cdot -x)|_{\partial D'})-H_{D''}(\Gamma _ d(\cdot -x)|_{\partial D''}),  \] which is harmonic on all of $D'$. By proposition 2.1.3 , applied to its negative, this harmonic function is nonnegative on $D'$, so $G_{D'}(x,y)\leq G_{D''}(x,y)$ for $y\in D'\setminus \{ x\} $. For $y=x$, both sides are $+\infty $ if $d\geq 2$; if $d=1$, the display also holds at $y=x$, so the inequality holds there as well. Put $h_ j=H_{D_ j}(\Gamma _ d(\cdot -x)|_{\partial D_ j})$ and $h=H_ D(\Gamma _ d(\cdot -x)|_{\partial D})$; we show that $h_ j$ decreases to $h$ in $C^\infty $ on compact subsets of $D$. On $B$ the functions $h_ j$ then form a decreasing sequence of harmonic functions bounded below by $h$, and part (3) of corollary 2.3.3 shows that they converge in $C^\infty $ on compact subsets of $B$ to a finite harmonic function. Every compact subset of $D$ is covered by finitely many balls $B(a,s)$ with $\overline{B(a,2s)}\subset D$, and $\overline{B(a,s)}$ is a compact subset of $B(a,2s)$; hence $h_ j	o h_\infty $ in $C^\infty $ on compact subsets of $D$. eq x$. Moreover $h_ j-h	o 0$ in $C^\infty $ on compact subsets of $D$, and $G_{D_ j}(x,\cdot )-G_ D(x,\cdot )=h-h_ j$ on $D_ j\setminus \{ x\} $; since every compact subset of $D\setminus \{ x\} $ lies in $D_ j$ for large $j$, $G_{D_ j}(x,\cdot )	o G_ D(x,\cdot )$ in $C^\infty $ on compact subsets of $D\setminus \{ x\} $. $\square$

Moreover $g$ is harmonic on $(a,b)\setminus \{ x\} $. By the uniqueness argument just given, $g$ coincides with $G_{(a,b)}(x,\cdot )$ on $(a,b)\setminus \{ x\} $, and also at $x$, since both functions are continuous there. This proves (2), and with it the positivity in (1) when $d=1$. (3) Let $D'\subset D''$ be bounded regular domains and $x\in D'$. On $D'\setminus \{ x\} $ the fundamental solutions cancel, and \[  G_{D''}(x,\cdot )-G_{D'}(x,\cdot )=H_{D'}(\Gamma _ d(\cdot -x)|_{\partial D'})-H_{D''}(\Gamma _ d(\cdot -x)|_{\partial D''}),  \] which is harmonic on all of $D'$. At every $\zeta \in \partial D'$ its lower limit is nonnegative, because $G_{D'}(x,y)	o 0$ as $y	o \zeta $ and $G_{D''}(x,y)\geq 0$. By proposition 2.1.3 , applied to its negative, this harmonic function is nonnegative on $D'$, so $G_{D'}(x,y)\leq G_{D''}(x,y)$ for $y\in D'\setminus \{ x\} $. For $y=x$, both sides are $+\infty $ if $d\geq 2$; if $d=1$, the display also holds at $y=x$, so the inequality holds there as well. (4) Let $D_ j$ and $D$ be as in the statement, fix $x\in D$, and consider only $j$ large enough that $x\in D_ j$. Put $h_ j=H_{D_ j}(\Gamma _ d(\cdot -x)|_{\partial D_ j})$ and $h=H_ D(\Gamma _ d(\cdot -x)|_{\partial D})$; we show that $h_ j$ decreases to $h$ in $C^\infty $ on compact subsets of $D$. By (3), $G_{D_ j}(x,\cdot )\leq G_{D_{j+1}}(x,\cdot )\leq G_ D(x,\cdot )$ on $D_ j\setminus \{ x\} $, that is, $h_ j\geq h_{j+1}\geq h$ there, and also at $x$, since these functions are continuous at $x$. Let $B$ be a ball with $\overline B\subset D$. The compact set $\overline B$ is covered by the increasing open sets $D_ j$, so $\overline B\subset D_ j$ for all large $j$. On $B$ the functions $h_ j$ then form a decreasing sequence of harmonic functions bounded below by $h$, and part (3) of corollary 2.3.3 shows that they converge in $C^\infty $ on compact subsets of $B$ to a finite harmonic function. These local limits are pointwise limits, so they define a harmonic function $h_\infty $ on $D$. Every compact subset of $D$ is covered by finitely many balls $B(a,s)$ with $\overline{B(a,2s)}\subset D$, and $\overline{B(a,s)}$ is a compact subset of $B(a,2s)$; hence $h_ j	o h_\infty $ in $C^\infty $ on compact subsets of $D$. It remains to show that $h_\infty =h$. The function $\Gamma _ d(\cdot -x)-h_\infty $ is the pointwise limit of $G_{D_ j}(x,\cdot )$, so it lies between $0$ and $G_ D(x,\cdot )$. Therefore the harmonic function $h_\infty -h=G_ D(x,\cdot )-(\Gamma _ d(\cdot -x)-h_\infty )$ satisfies $0\leq h_\infty -h\leq G_ D(x,\cdot )$ on $D\setminus \{ x\} $, so it has zero boundary limits and vanishes by proposition 2.1.3 . Thus $h_ j	o h$, which means that $G_{D_ j}(x,y)$ increases to $G_ D(x,y)$ for every $y
eq x$. Moreover $h_ j-h	o 0$ in $C^\infty $ on compact subsets of $D$, and $G_{D_ j}(x,\cdot )-G_ D(x,\cdot )=h-h_ j$ on $D_ j\setminus \{ x\} $; since every compact subset of $D\setminus \{ x\} $ lies in $D_ j$ for large $j$, $G_{D_ j}(x,\cdot )	o G_ D(x,\cdot )$ in $C^\infty $ on compact subsets of $D\setminus \{ x\} $. $\square$

title: Subharmonic functions
text: 3 Subharmonic functions Subharmonic functions are, roughly speaking, the functions $u$ with $\Delta u\geq 0$. They are the real-variable model for the plurisubharmonic functions of 2 , and they include the potentials $E_ d*\nu $ of positive measures $\nu $, which are studied further in chapter 4 . The condition $\Delta u\geq 0$ cannot be imposed in the classical sense, because the most important examples are singular: for $d\geq 2$ the fundamental solution $E_ d$ of proposition 2.2.1 tends to $-\infty $ at the origin. We therefore define subharmonicity pointwise, by upper semicontinuity and a submean inequality on small spheres, and we allow the value $-\infty $. Throughout the chapter, $\Omega $ is an open subset of $\mathbb R^ d$ and $d\geq 1$. From the submean inequality we first derive the comparison principle and the monotonicity of spherical means. We then show that locally integrable subharmonic functions correspond exactly to real distributions with positive Laplacian (theorem 3.2.2 ). No pointwise information is lost in passing to the distribution: the value of a subharmonic function at each point is the limit of its ball averages, and every real distribution with positive Laplacian has exactly one subharmonic representative, its canonical representative. This allows us to pass between pointwise and almost-everywhere statements, and it leads to the Riesz decomposition of a subharmonic function into a potential and a harmonic function. The last three sections concern limits and their exceptional sets. A sequence of subharmonic functions on a domain that is uniformly bounded above on compact sets either tends to $-\infty $ locally uniformly or has a subsequence converging in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$, and by Hartogs' lemma the limit controls the sequence from above, uniformly on compact sets. The pointwise supremum of a family of subharmonic functions need not be upper semicontinuous; with Choquet's countable selection lemma we show that its upper semicontinuous regularization is subharmonic and differs from it only on a Lebesgue null set. Finally, we introduce polar sets, which lie locally in the pole set $\{ \psi =-\infty \} $ of a subharmonic function $\psi $ that is not identically $-\infty $, and prove that relatively closed polar sets are removable for subharmonic functions that are bounded above near them. Historical remarks and references for this chapter are collected in section B.3 .

title: Mean inequalities and comparison
text:
3.1 Mean inequalities and comparison Recall that a function $u\colon \Omega 	o [-\infty ,\infty )$ is upper semicontinuous if the set $\{ u<a\} $ is open for every $a\in \mathbb R$; equivalently, $\varlimsup _{y	o x}u(y)\leq u(x)$ for every $x\in \Omega $. Such a function is Borel measurable, because the sets $\{ u<a\} $ are open. It is bounded above on every compact set $K\subset \Omega $, because the increasing open sets $\{ u<n\} $, $n\in \mathbb N$, cover $K$, so that one of them contains $K$. A similar covering argument shows that $u$ attains its maximum on every nonempty compact set $K$: otherwise the open sets $\{ u<a\} $ with $a<\sup _ Ku$ would cover $K$, and a finite subcover would give $\sup _ Ku<\sup _ Ku$. The same arguments apply to upper semicontinuous functions on any compact metric space. We shall often integrate upper semicontinuous functions over products. Subsets $X$ and $Y$ of Euclidean spaces are separable metric spaces, so by lemma 1.1.8 every Borel function on $X	imes Y$ is measurable for the product of the Borel $\sigma $-algebras of $X$ and $Y$. Hence Tonelli's and Fubini's theorems (proposition 1.1.7 ) apply to Borel functions on such products. As in section 2.1 , $\mathrm dS$ denotes surface measure on the unit sphere $S^{d-1}$, and $s_{d-1}$ is its total mass. Definition 3.1.1 . A function $u\colon \Omega 	o [-\infty ,\infty )$ is subharmonic if it is upper semicontinuous and every $x\in \Omega $ admits an $r_ x>0$ with $\overline{B(x,r_ x)}\subset \Omega $ such that 3.1  egin{equation} \label{eq:subharmonic-submean} u(x)\leq  rac{1}{s_{d-1}}\int _{S^{d-1}}u(x+r\omega )\, \mathrm d S(\omega )\qquad 	ext{for }0<r<r_ x. \end{equation} The function identically equal to $-\infty $ is subharmonic. We write $\mathrm{SH}(\Omega )$ for the set of subharmonic functions on $\Omega $. A function $v$ is superharmonic if $-v$ is subharmonic. As for continuous functions in section 2.1 , we denote the right-hand side of ( 3.1 ) by $M_ u(x,r)$, the spherical mean of $u$ over $\partial B(x,r)$, for every upper semicontinuous $u$ and every $r>0$ with $\overline{B(x,r)}\subset \Omega $. It is well defined in $[-\infty ,\infty )$, since $u$ is Borel measurable and bounded above on the compact sphere $x+rS^{d-1}$. Subharmonicity is a local property: a function is subharmonic on $\Omega $ if every point of $\Omega $ has an open neighborhood on which it is subharmonic. Indeed, upper semicontinuity is a local condition, and if $u$ is subharmonic on an open neighborhood $W\subset \Omega $ of $x$, then a radius $r_ x$ as in definition 3.1.1 for $u|_ W$, with $\overline{B(x,r_ x)}\subset W$, also serves for $u$ on $\Omega $. By proposition 2.1.1 , every real harmonic function on $\Omega $ is subharmonic. To compare subharmonic functions with harmonic functions on balls, we shall approximate upper semicontinuous boundary values from above by continuous functions. Lemma 3.1.2 . Let $X$ be a metric space and let $f\colon X	o [-\infty ,\infty )$ be upper semicontinuous and bounded above; the latter holds automatically if $X$ is compact. Then $f$ is the pointwise limit of a decreasing sequence of bounded, real-valued continuous functions $f_ n$ on $X$. For every finite Borel measure $\mu $ on $X$, the integrals $\int _ Xf_ n\, \mathrm d\mu $ decrease to $\int _ Xf\, \mathrm d\mu \in [-\infty ,\infty )$. Proof. Since $f$ is bounded above, we can choose a positive integer $n_0>\sup _ Xf$. For $n\geq n_0$ and $x\in X$ put \[  f_ n(x)=\sup _{y\in X} igl (\max \{ f(y),-n\} -n\operatorname {dist}(x,y) igr ).  \] Taking $y=x$ gives $f_ n(x)\geq \max \{ f(x),-n\} \geq f(x)$, and $f_ n\leq \max \{ \sup _ Xf,-n\} <n_0$. Thus $-n\leq f_ n<n_0$, so $f_ n$ is real-valued and bounded, and as a supremum of $n$-Lipschitz functions of $x$ it is $n$-Lipschitz. Both $\max \{ f(y),-n\} $ and $-n\operatorname {dist}(x,y)$ decrease as $n$ increases, so the sequence $(f_ n)$ is decreasing. We show that $f_ n(x)	o f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Otherwise there is a real number $c$ with $\lim _ nf_ n(x)>c>f(x)$. For each $n$ choose $y_ n\in X$ with $\max \{ f(y_ n),-n\} -n\operatorname {dist}(x,y_ n)>c$. Then $n\operatorname {dist}(x,y_ n)<n_0-c$, so $y_ n	o x$. Moreover $\max \{ f(y_ n),-n\} >c$, which forces $f(y_ n)>c$ as soon as $n>-c$. On the other hand, $\{ f<c\} $ is an open neighborhood of $x$ by upper semicontinuity, so it contains $y_ n$ for all large $n$. This contradiction proves that $f_ n\downarrow f$. Finally, the nonnegative functions $n_0-f_ n$ increase to $n_0-f$, so the monotone convergence theorem gives $\int (n_0-f_ n)\, \mathrm d\mu \uparrow \int (n_0-f)\, \mathrm d\mu $. Subtracting these integrals from the finite number $n_0\mu (X)$ proves the assertion about the integrals of $f_ n$. $\square$ Theorem 3.1.3 . Let $u\in \mathrm{SH}(\Omega )$. Let $D\subset \Omega $ be a bounded open set, and let $h$ be a real function which is harmonic on $D$ and continuous on $\overline D$. If \[  \varlimsup _{D
i x	o \zeta }u(x)\leq h(\zeta )\qquad 	ext{for every }\zeta \in \partial D,  \] then $u\leq h$ on $D$. Let $x\in \Omega $ and $\overline{B(x,R)}\subset \Omega $. Then the spherical mean $M_ u(x,r)$ increases with $r\in (0,R]$ and decreases to $u(x)$ as $r\downarrow 0$. Moreover, \[  u(x)\leq  rac{1}{|B(x,R)|}\int _{B(x,R)}u(y)\, \mathrm d y.  \] Conversely, an upper semicontinuous function $u\colon \Omega 	o [-\infty ,\infty )$ is subharmonic if assertion (1) holds for $u$ whenever $D$ is a ball with $\overline D\subset \Omega $. Proof. We begin with (1). Fix $\varepsilon >0$ and consider the upper semicontinuous function $w(y)=u(y)-h(y)+\varepsilon |y|^2$ on $D$. For $x\in D$ and small $r>0$ we have $M_ h(x,r)=h(x)$ by proposition 2.1.1 , and $M_{|\cdot |^2}(x,r)=|x|^2+r^2$ by the identity for spherical means of $|y|^2$ proved in section 2.4 . Together with ( 3.1 ) this gives \[  M_ w(x,r)\geq w(x)+\varepsilon r^2  \] for every $x\in D$ and every sufficiently small $r>0$. Consequently, $w$ cannot attain a finite maximum over $D$ at a point $x\in D$, since we would then have $M_ w(x,r)\leq w(x)$ for small $r$. Now let $\delta >0$. Because $h$ is continuous on $\overline D$, the boundary hypothesis gives $\varlimsup _{D
i x	o \zeta }(u-h)(x)\leq 0$, so every $\zeta \in \partial D$ has an open neighborhood $N_\zeta $ with $u-h<\delta $ on $N_\zeta \cap D$. Finitely many of these neighborhoods cover the compact set $\partial D$. If $N$ denotes their union, then $K=\overline D\setminus N$ is a compact subset of $D$. Put $c=\delta +\varepsilon \sup _{y\in \overline D}|y|^2$, so that $w<c$ on $D\setminus K$. If $w$ took a value larger than $c$, then $\sup _ Dw=\sup _ Kw$ would be a finite maximum attained at a point of $K$, which we have just excluded. Hence $u-h\leq w\leq c$ on $D$, and letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ and $\delta \downarrow 0$ gives $u\leq h$. For (2), let $B=B(x,R)$. By lemma 3.1.2 there are continuous functions $f_ n$ on $\partial B$ that decrease to $u|_{\partial B}$. Let $H_ n=H_ Bf_ n$ be their Poisson integrals; by theorem 2.3.1 , $H_ n$ is harmonic on $B$ and continuous on $\overline B$ with boundary values $f_ n$. For $\zeta \in \partial B$, upper semicontinuity gives $\varlimsup _{B
i y	o \zeta }u(y)\leq u(\zeta )\leq f_ n(\zeta )$, so (1) yields $u\leq H_ n$ on $B$. The value of a Poisson integral at the center of the ball is the mean of its boundary values, because $P_ B(x,\cdot )$ is the constant $(s_{d-1}R^{d-1})^{-1}$ by ( 2.14 ). Using also the mean-value property of $H_ n$, we obtain for $0<r<R$ \[  u(x)\leq H_ n(x)=M_{f_ n}(x,R),\qquad M_ u(x,r)\leq M_{H_ n}(x,r)=H_ n(x)=M_{f_ n}(x,R).  \] By lemma 3.1.2 , applied to surface measure on $\partial B$, $M_{f_ n}(x,R)$ decreases to $M_ u(x,R)$. Therefore $u(x)\leq M_ u(x,R)$, and $M_ u(x,r)\leq M_ u(x,R)$ for $0<r<R$. As $R$ may be replaced by any smaller radius, $M_ u(x,\cdot )$ is increasing on $(0,R]$. Moreover, $u(x)\leq M_ u(x,r)\leq \sup _{\partial B(x,r)}u$, and the upper limit of the right-hand side as $r\downarrow 0$ is at most $u(x)$ by upper semicontinuity; hence $M_ u(x,r)$ decreases to $u(x)$ as $r\downarrow 0$. Finally, let $M$ be a real upper bound for $u$ on $\overline B$. Integration in polar coordinates ( 2.1 ), applied to the nonnegative function $M-u$, and the substitution $r=Rt$ give 3.2  egin{equation} \label{eq:ball-average-spherical-means}  rac{1}{|B|}\int _ Bu(y)\, \mathrm d y= rac{d}{R^ d}\int _0^ Rr^{d-1}M_ u(x,r)\, \mathrm d r=d\int _0^1t^{d-1}M_ u(x,Rt)\, \mathrm d t, \end{equation} where all integrals lie in $[-\infty ,\infty )$; here we used $|B|=s_{d-1}R^ d/d$. Since $M_ u(x,r)\geq u(x)$ for $0<r\leq R$ and $d\int _0^1t^{d-1}\, \mathrm dt=1$, the right-hand side is at least $u(x)$. The proof of (2) used the subharmonicity of $u$ only through (1) for the ball $B$. Hence, if $u$ is upper semicontinuous and satisfies (1) for all balls $B$ with $\overline B\subset \Omega $, then $u(x)\leq M_ u(x,R)$ whenever $\overline{B(x,R)}\subset \Omega $, so $u$ is subharmonic. $\square$ We call the first assertion of theorem 3.1.3 the comparison principle. Applied with $\Omega =D$, it holds for every bounded open set $D$ and every $u\in \mathrm{SH}(D)$, even when $u$ is not defined near $\partial D$. Elementary operations preserve subharmonicity. If $u,v\in \mathrm{SH}(\Omega )$ and $c\geq 0$, then $u+v$, $cu$ and $\max \{ u,v\} $ are subharmonic; here we use the convention $0\cdot (-\infty )=0$, so that $0\cdot u$ is the zero function. Indeed, these functions are upper semicontinuous: $\{ cu<a\} =\{ u<a/c\} $ if $c>0$, $\{ \max \{ u,v\} <a\} =\{ u<a\} \cap \{ v<a\} $, and if $u(x)+v(x)<a$, we can choose real numbers $s>u(x)$ and $t>v(x)$ with $s+t\leq a$, so that $u+v<a$ on the open neighborhood $\{ u<s\} \cap \{ v<t\} $ of $x$. The identities $M_{u+v}=M_ u+M_ v$ and $M_{cu}=cM_ u$, together with the inequality $M_{\max \{ u,v\} }\geq \max \{ M_ u,M_ v\} $, give the submean inequality at $x$ for all radii smaller than the radii $r_ x$ for $u$ and for $v$. In particular, adding a real harmonic function to a subharmonic function produces a subharmonic function. Proposition 3.1.4 . Let $u\in \mathrm{SH}(\Omega )$. If $\Omega $ is connected and $u$ attains its maximum over $\Omega $, then $u$ is constant. If $\Omega $ is bounded and $\varlimsup _{\Omega 
i x	o \zeta }u(x)\leq 0$ for every $\zeta \in \partial \Omega $, then $u\leq 0$ on $\Omega $. Proof. Let $m=\max _\Omega u$. If $m=-\infty $, then $u$ is identically $-\infty $, so assume that $m$ is finite, and let $E=\{ u=m\} =\{ u\geq m\} $. This set is nonempty, and it is closed in $\Omega $ because $u$ is upper semicontinuous. Let $x\in E$. For every sufficiently small $r>0$, ( 3.1 ) gives $m=u(x)\leq M_ u(x,r)\leq m$, so \[  \int _{S^{d-1}} igl (m-u(x+r\omega ) igr )\, \mathrm dS(\omega )=0.  \] Suppose that $u(x+r\omega _0)<a<m$ for some $\omega _0\in S^{d-1}$ and some real number $a$. By upper semicontinuity, the set $A=\{ \omega \in S^{d-1}:u(x+r\omega )<a\} $ is relatively open in $S^{d-1}$, and it contains $\omega _0$. The cone $\{ t\omega :0<t<1,\  \omega \in A\} $ is the inverse image of $A$ under the continuous map $y\mapsto y/|y|$ on $B(0,1)\setminus \{ 0\} $, so it is a nonempty open set, and therefore $S(A)>0$ by the definition of surface measure in section 2.1 . Since $m-u(x+r\omega )>m-a>0$ for $\omega \in A$, the integral above would be at least $(m-a)S(A)>0$, a contradiction. Hence $u=m$ on every sufficiently small sphere centered at $x$, and $E$ contains a ball around $x$. Thus $E$ is open and closed in $\Omega $, and $E=\Omega $ because $\Omega $ is connected. The second assertion is the comparison principle on the bounded open set $D=\Omega $ with $h=0$, in the form noted after theorem 3.1.3 . $\square$ Proposition 3.1.5 . Let $u\in \mathrm{SH}(\Omega )$. On each connected component of $\Omega $, either $u$ is identically $-\infty $, or $u$ is locally integrable and hence finite almost everywhere. Proof. Let $x\in \Omega $ with $u(x)>-\infty $, and let $\overline{B(x,r)}\subset \Omega $. If $M$ is a real upper bound for $u$ on $B(x,r)$, the ball submean inequality of theorem 3.1.3 gives \[  \int _{B(x,r)}(M-u)\, \mathrm d y\leq |B(x,r)|\, (M-u(x))<\infty .  \] Since $M-u\geq 0$, it follows that $u$ is integrable on $B(x,r)$. Now let $\Omega '$ be a connected component of $\Omega $ on which $u$ is not identically $-\infty $, and let $Y$ be the set of points of $\Omega '$ that have a neighborhood on which $u$ is integrable. Then $Y$ is open, and it is nonempty by the first paragraph. Let $y\in \Omega '$ lie in the closure of $Y$, and choose $r>0$ with $\overline{B(y,3r)}\subset \Omega $. The set $Y\cap B(y,r)$ contains a point $z$, and $u$ is integrable on an open neighborhood $U$ of $z$; hence $u$ is finite almost everywhere on the nonempty open set $U\cap B(y,r)$, which has positive measure, and there is a point $x\in B(y,r)$ with $u(x)>-\infty $. Since $|x-y|<r$, the ball $B(x,2r)$ contains $y$ and its closure lies in $\overline{B(y,3r)}\subset \Omega $. By the first paragraph, $u$ is integrable on $B(x,2r)$, hence $y\in Y$. Thus $Y$ is also closed in $\Omega '$, and $Y=\Omega '$ because $\Omega '$ is connected. Finally, a locally integrable function is finite almost everywhere. $\square$ A subharmonic function on a domain is called nontrivial if it is not identically $-\infty $; by proposition 3.1.5 , the nontrivial subharmonic functions on a domain are exactly the locally integrable ones. The set $\{ u=-\infty \} $ is called the pole set of $u$. In particular, the pole set of a nontrivial subharmonic function on a domain has Lebesgue measure zero. Theorem 3.1.6 . Let $(u_ j)$ be a decreasing sequence in $\mathrm{SH}(\Omega )$ with pointwise limit $u$. Then $u\in \mathrm{SH}(\Omega )$. On each connected component $\Omega '$ of $\Omega $, either $u$ is identically $-\infty $ and $u_ j	o -\infty $ uniformly on compact subsets of $\Omega '$, or $u$ is locally integrable on $\Omega '$ and $u_ j	o u$ in $L^1$ on compact subsets of $\Omega '$. Proof. The limit $u$ is upper semicontinuous, since $\{ u<a\} = igcup _ j\{ u_ j<a\} $ is open for every real $a$. Let $x\in \Omega $ and $\overline{B(x,r)}\subset \Omega $. By theorem 3.1.3 , $u_ j(x)\leq M_{u_ j}(x,r)$ for every $j$. If $M$ is a real upper bound for $u_1$ on $\partial B(x,r)$, the nonnegative functions $M-u_ j$ increase to $M-u$ on this sphere, so the monotone convergence theorem gives $M_{u_ j}(x,r)\downarrow M_ u(x,r)$. Hence $u(x)\leq u_ j(x)\leq M_{u_ j}(x,r)$ for all $j$, and in the limit $u(x)\leq M_ u(x,r)$. Thus $u$ is subharmonic. Let $\Omega '$ be a connected component of $\Omega $. By proposition 3.1.5 , $u$ is either identically $-\infty $ or locally integrable on $\Omega '$. In the first case, fix a compact set $K\subset \Omega '$ and a real number $A$. The open sets $\{ u_ j<-A\} $ increase with $j$ and cover $\Omega '$, because $u_ j(x)\downarrow -\infty $ for every $x\in \Omega '$. Finitely many of them, and hence one of them, cover $K$; thus $u_ j<-A$ on $K$ for all large $j$. In the second case, $u_1\geq u$ is not identically $-\infty $ on $\Omega '$ and is therefore locally integrable there as well. Then $0\leq u_ j-u\leq u_1-u$ almost everywhere on $\Omega '$, and $u_ j-u	o 0$ wherever $u$ is finite, so dominated convergence gives $\int _ K(u_ j-u)\, \mathrm d x	o 0$ for every compact $K\subset \Omega '$. $\square$
