text: Theorem 7.2.5 . Let $T$ be a positive current of bidegree $(p,p)$ on a complex manifold $X$ of dimension $n$. Then $T$ is real and of order zero. More precisely, in every coordinate chart the coefficient measures of $T=\sum _{|I|=|J|=p}T_{IJ}\, \mathrm dz_ I\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ J$ satisfy \[  |T_{IJ}|\leq C_{n,p}\, \mu _ T,  \] where $\mu _ T$ is the trace measure and $C_{n,p}$ depends only on $n$ and $p$. Moreover, suppose that $X$ has a countable basis, and let $(T_ j)$ be a sequence of positive currents of bidegree $(p,p)$ whose trace measures are locally uniformly bounded: $\sup _ j\mu _{T_ j}(K)<\infty $ for every compact subset $K$ of every chart. Then a subsequence converges weakly to a positive current, which is closed if all $T_ j$ are closed. Proof. Fix a chart and put $q=n-p$. By proposition 7.2.1 , $\beta ^ q$ is an interior point of the cone of strongly positive $(q,q)$-forms. Hence for every constant real $(q,q)$-form $\tau $ there is $C_\tau >0$ such that the forms $C_\tau \beta ^ q\pm \tau $ are strongly positive. For a nonnegative test function $\chi $, the forms $\chi (C_\tau \beta ^ q\pm \tau )$ are strongly positive test forms, so positivity of $T$ gives $T(\chi (C_\tau \beta ^ q\pm \tau ))\geq 0$. Therefore $T(\chi \tau )$ is real and \[  |T(\chi \tau )|\le C_\tau \mu _ T(\chi ).  \] The distributions $C_\tau \mu _ T\pm T(\, \cdot \, \tau )$ are nonnegative on nonnegative test functions, hence positive Radon measures by the remark after definition 7.2.4 and theorem 1.4.5 . Consequently $S_\tau =T(\, \cdot \, \tau )$ is a real signed Radon measure, the difference of the positive measures $(C_\tau \mu _ T\pm S_\tau )/2$, and $|S_\tau (A)|\leq C_\tau \mu _ T(A)$ for every relatively compact Borel set $A$, so that $|S_\tau |\leq C_\tau \mu _ T$. Choose real constant $(q,q)$-forms $\tau _1,\ldots ,\tau _ N$ forming a basis of the real $(q,q)$-forms; they also form a complex basis of all constant $(q,q)$-forms, and they can be chosen depending only on $n$ and $p$. Up to a constant factor depending only on $n$, $I$ and $J$, the coefficient $T_{IJ}$ is the distribution $\chi \mapsto T(\chi \, \mathrm dz_{I^ c}\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_{J^ c})$, where $I^ c$ and $J^ c$ are the complementary multi-indices. Expanding $\mathrm dz_{I^ c}\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_{J^ c}=\sum _ rc_ r\tau _ r$, we see that $T_{IJ}$ is a fixed complex linear combination of the measures $S_{\tau _ r}$, and the coefficient bound follows from $|S_{\tau _ r}|\leq C_{\tau _ r}\mu _ T$. To prove that $T$ is real, let $\varphi $ be a test form supported in the chart; only its $(q,q)$-component contributes, and we write it as $\sum _ rf_ r\tau _ r$ with complex test functions $f_ r$. Since $T(f\tau _ r)=\int f\, \mathrm dS_{\tau _ r}$ is real for real $f$, we obtain $T(\bar\varphi )=\overline{T(\varphi )}$, and a partition of unity extends this identity to all test forms. Now let $X$ have a countable basis, and let $(T_ j)$ be as in the statement. Then $X$ is covered by countably many charts $U_1,U_2,\ldots $: for each basic open set contained in some chart, choose one such chart. On $U_1$ the positive Radon measures $C_{\tau _ r}\mu _{T_ j}\pm S^ j_{\tau _ r}$, where $S^ j_\tau =T_ j(\, \cdot \, \tau )$, have mass at most $2C_{\tau _ r}\sup _ j\mu _{T_ j}(K)$ on every compact $K\subset U_1$. Applying theorem 1.5.5 successively to these finitely many sequences, we find a subsequence along which all of them converge vaguely on $U_1$; then each $S^ j_{\tau _ r}$ converges vaguely, and $T_ j(\varphi )$ converges for every test form $\varphi $ supported in $U_1$. Repeating the extraction for $U_2,U_3,\ldots $ and passing to the diagonal subsequence, we may assume that $T_ j(\varphi )$ converges for every test form $\varphi $ supported in some $U_ k$. A partition of unity subordinate to $(U_ k)$ writes every test form as a finite sum of such forms, so $T(\varphi )=\lim _ jT_ j(\varphi )$ exists for every test form $\varphi $. The functional $T$ is linear, and it is a current. Indeed, if $\varphi =\sum _ rf_ r\tau _ r$ is supported in a compact set $K\subset U_ k$, then $|T_ j(\varphi )|\leq \sum _ rC_{\tau _ r}\| f_ r\| _\infty \sup _ i\mu _{T_ i}(K)$ for all $j$, and this bound passes to the limit. On compact subsets of the intersection of two charts, the coefficients of a form in the two charts are related by a matrix of continuous functions. Hence, covering a compact subset of an arbitrary chart by finitely many $U_ k$ and using a partition of unity, we obtain the estimate in the definition of a current, with $m=0$. Thus $T_ j\to T$ weakly. If $\varphi $ is a strongly positive test form, then $T(\varphi )=\lim _ jT_ j(\varphi )\geq 0$; and if all $T_ j$ are closed, then $T(\mathrm d\psi )=\lim _ jT_ j(\mathrm d\psi )=0$ for every test form $\psi $. $\square$

title: Current gluing
topic: Complex differential forms and positive currents
text: Lemma 7.2.6 . Let $(W_ a)_{a\in A}$ be an open cover of $X$, and for each $a$ let $T_ a$ be a current of degree $k$ on $W_ a$, such that $T_ a$ and $T_ b$ agree on $W_ a\cap W_ b$ for all $a,b\in A$. Then there is a unique current $T$ of degree $k$ on $X$ which agrees with $T_ a$ on $W_ a$ for every $a$. If all $T_ a$ have bidegree $(p,q)$, then so has $T$; if all $T_ a$ are closed, then so is $T$; and if $p=q$ and all $T_ a$ are positive, then so is $T$. Proof. If two currents on $X$ agree with $T_ a$ on $W_ a$ for every $a$, their difference vanishes on every $W_ a$, hence on $X$, since a current that vanishes on each member of a family of open sets vanishes on their union, as shown at the beginning of this section. For existence, choose a partition of unity $(\chi _ c)_{c\in C}$ with compact supports subordinate to the cover (proposition 7.1.3 ), and for each $c$ an index $a(c)$ with $\operatorname{Supp}\chi _ c\subset W_{a(c)}$. For a test form $\varphi $ of degree $2n-k$ on $X$, only finitely many $\chi _ c$ are not identically zero on the compact set $\operatorname{Supp}\varphi $, and $\chi _ c\varphi $ is a test form supported in $W_{a(c)}$; we put \[  T(\varphi )=\sum _ cT_{a(c)}(\chi _ c\varphi ).  \] This is a linear functional, and it is a current. Indeed, let $K$ be a compact subset of a chart domain $U$. Only finitely many indices $c_1,\ldots ,c_ N$ have $\chi _{c_ i}\not\equiv 0$ on $K$, and for test forms $\varphi $ supported in $K$ the form $\chi _{c_ i}\varphi $ is supported in the compact subset $K\cap \operatorname{Supp}\chi _{c_ i}$ of the chart domain $U\cap W_{a(c_ i)}$ of $W_{a(c_ i)}$. By the Leibniz rule, its seminorms $p_{K,m}$ are bounded by a constant times those of $\varphi $, so the estimates for the currents $T_{a(c_ i)}$ give the estimate in the definition of a current for $T$. If $\varphi $ is supported in some $W_ b$, then each $\chi _ c\varphi $ is supported in $W_{a(c)}\cap W_ b$, where $T_{a(c)}$ and $T_ b$ agree, so that $T(\varphi )=\sum _ cT_ b(\chi _ c\varphi )=T_ b(\varphi )$. Thus $T$ agrees with $T_ b$ on $W_ b$. Multiplication by $\chi _ c$ preserves bidegrees, and $\chi _ c\varphi $ is strongly positive at every point if $\varphi $ is, because $\chi _ c\geq 0$; so the assertions about bidegrees and positivity follow from the formula for $T(\varphi )$. Finally, if all $T_ a$ are closed and $\psi $ is a test form supported in $W_ a$, then so is $\mathrm d\psi $, and $(\mathrm dT)(\psi )=(-1)^{k+1}T(\mathrm d\psi )=(-1)^{k+1}T_ a(\mathrm d\psi )=(\mathrm dT_ a)(\psi )=0$; hence $\mathrm dT$ vanishes on every $W_ a$, and therefore $\mathrm dT=0$. $\square$

title: Submanifold current
topic: Complex differential forms and positive currents
text: Example 7.2.7 . Let $Z$ be a complex submanifold of $X$ of dimension $r$, with its complex orientation. Then \[  [Z](\varphi )=\int _ Z\varphi |_ Z  \] defines a closed positive current of bidegree $(n-r,n-r)$ on $X$, the current of integration over $Z$. Since $Z$ is closed, $Z\cap \operatorname{Supp}\varphi $ is compact for every test form $\varphi $, so the integral is defined. In a chart in which $Z=\{ z_{r+1}=\cdots =z_ n=0\} $, the value $[Z](\varphi )$ is a constant times the integral over this coordinate plane of the coefficient of $\mathrm dz_ I\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ I$ in $\varphi $, where $I=(1,\ldots ,r)$, because the pullbacks of $\mathrm dz_ j$ and $\mathrm d\bar z_ j$ to $Z$ vanish for $j>r$. Hence $[Z]$ is a current, and its coefficients in such a chart are constant multiples of Lebesgue measure on the plane. Since $[Z]$ vanishes on $X\setminus Z$, the charts of this kind and the charts contained in $X\setminus Z$ form an atlas in which $[Z]$ has measure coefficients, and $[Z]$ is a current of order zero. If $\varphi $ is strongly positive, so is its pullback $\varphi |_ Z$ to $Z$, which is therefore a nonnegative multiple of the volume form of $Z$ at each point (proposition 7.2.1 ); thus $[Z](\varphi )\geq 0$. Finally, since pullback commutes with $\mathrm d$ by ( 7.3 ), $[Z](\mathrm d\psi )=\int _ Z\mathrm d(\psi |_ Z)=0$ by proposition 7.1.3 applied on $Z$ when $r\geq 1$; when $r=0$ the current $[Z]$ has degree $2n$, and $\mathrm d[Z]=0$ because currents of degree $2n+1$ are zero.

title: Local potentials for closed (1,1)-currents
topic: Complex differential forms and positive currents
text: 7.3 Local potentials for closed $(1,1)$-currents Coordinate computations in this section take place on an open set $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ with $n\geq 1$, for instance a coordinate domain. By theorem 7.2.5 , a positive $(1,1)$-current on $\Omega $ is real and has measure coefficients. We normalize them as \[  T=\frac{\mathrm{i}}{2\pi }\sum _{j,k}t_{j\bar k}\, \mathrm{d}z_ j\wedge \mathrm{d}\bar z_ k,  \] so that $T=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ means $t_{j\bar k}=u_{j\bar k}$, by ( 7.5 ). Positivity of $T$ is expressed by the following matrix criterion. The coefficient matrix $(t_{j\bar k})$ is Hermitian, that is, $t_{k\bar j}=\overline{t_{j\bar k}}$, because $T$ is real, and it is positive semidefinite in the distributional sense: $\sum _{j,k}t_{j\bar k}\xi _ j\bar\xi _ k$ is a positive measure for every $\xi \in \mathbb C^ n$. To see this, we may assume that $|\xi |=1$ and choose a unitary matrix $U$ whose first row is $\bar\xi $. In the coordinates $w=Uz$ the coefficient of $\mathrm dw_1\wedge \mathrm d\bar w_1$ in $T$ is $(\mathrm i/2\pi )\sum _{j,k}t_{j\bar k}\xi _ j\bar\xi _ k$, and evaluating $T$ on the strongly positive test forms $\chi \bigwedge _{j\geq 2}(\mathrm i\mathrm dw_ j\wedge \mathrm d\bar w_ j)$ with $\chi \geq 0$ gives a positive constant times $\langle \sum _{j,k}t_{j\bar k}\xi _ j\bar\xi _ k,\chi \rangle $, which is therefore nonnegative. Conversely, a real $(1,1)$-current whose coefficient matrix is positive semidefinite in this sense is positive. For smooth coefficients this is the $(1,1)$-case discussed after proposition 7.2.1 . In general the mollified currents $T_\varepsilon $ have pointwise positive semidefinite coefficient matrices, because mollifications of positive measures are nonnegative (proposition 1.4.3 ); hence they are positive, and so is their weak limit $T$. Taking for $\xi $ the coordinate vectors, we see that every diagonal coefficient $t_{j\bar j}$, and hence the trace $\mu =\sum _ jt_{j\bar j}$, is a positive measure; expanding $\beta ^{n-1}$ shows that the trace measure of $T$ is $T\wedge \beta ^{n-1}=((n-1)!/\pi )\, \mu $. Since $\partial T$ and $\bar\partial T$ are computed by differentiating the coefficients, $T$ is closed if and only if 7.9 \begin{equation} \label{eq:closed-hessian-coefficients} \partial _{z_ l}t_{j\bar k}=\partial _{z_ j}t_{l\bar k},\qquad \partial _{\bar z_ l}t_{j\bar k}=\partial _{\bar z_ k}t_{j\bar l} \qquad \text{for all }j,k,l. \end{equation} The construction of local potentials uses the following smooth local exactness results, which we prove by explicit integral formulas. Lemma 7.3.1 . Let $\Delta \subset \mathbb C^ n$, $n\geq 1$, be a polydisc, and let $g$ be a smooth $(0,1)$-form on $\Delta $ with $\bar\partial g=0$. Then for every polydisc $\Delta '\Subset \Delta $ there is a smooth function $f$ on $\Delta '$ with $\bar\partial f=g$. Moreover, every smooth real closed $(1,1)$-form $R$ on an open subset of $\mathbb C^ n$ is locally of the form $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$: each point has a neighborhood on which $R=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$ for a smooth real function $v$. Finally, every smooth closed $k$-form $\gamma $ with $k\geq 1$, with real or complex coefficients, on a ball $B\subset \mathbb C^ n=\mathbb R^{2n}$ is exact on $B$: $\gamma =\mathrm d\alpha $ for a smooth $(k-1)$-form $\alpha $ on $B$, which is real if $\gamma $ is real. Proof. We solve the $\bar\partial $-equation in one variable by a Cauchy integral, then on a polydisc one variable at a time, and combine it with the Poincaré lemma. Step 1: one variable. The function $K(z)=1/(\pi z)$ on $\mathbb C$ is locally integrable, and $\partial _{\bar z}K=\delta _0$ in the sense of distributions. Indeed, for a test function $\varphi $, dominated convergence gives $\langle \partial _{\bar z}K,\varphi \rangle =-\pi ^{-1}\lim _{\varepsilon \to 0}\int _{|z|>\varepsilon }(\partial _{\bar z}\varphi /z)\, \mathrm dV_2$. In polar coordinates $z=r\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\vartheta }$ we have $\partial _{\bar z}=\frac12\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\vartheta }(\partial _ r+\frac{\mathrm i}r\partial _\vartheta )$ and $\mathrm dV_2=r\, \mathrm dr\, \mathrm d\vartheta $. Hence, by Fubini's theorem, \[  \int _{|z|>\varepsilon }\frac{\partial _{\bar z}\varphi }{z}\, \mathrm dV_2=\frac12\int _\varepsilon ^\infty \! \! \int _0^{2\pi }\Big(\partial _ r\varphi +\frac{\mathrm i}r\partial _\vartheta \varphi \Big)\, \mathrm d\vartheta \, \mathrm dr=-\frac12\int _0^{2\pi }\varphi (\varepsilon \mathrm e^{\mathrm i\vartheta })\, \mathrm d\vartheta ,  \] because $\int _0^{2\pi }\partial _\vartheta \varphi \, \mathrm d\vartheta =0$ by periodicity and $\int _\varepsilon ^\infty \partial _ r\varphi \, \mathrm dr=-\varphi (\varepsilon \mathrm e^{\mathrm i\vartheta })$, $\varphi $ having compact support. As $\varepsilon \to 0$, the right-hand side tends to $-\pi \varphi (0)$, since $\varphi $ is continuous at $0$; so $\langle \partial _{\bar z}K,\varphi \rangle =\varphi (0)$. Consequently, for a smooth function $a$ with compact support in $\mathbb C$, the function \[  f(z)=\frac1\pi \int _{\mathbb C}\frac{a(\zeta )}{z-\zeta }\, \mathrm dV_2(\zeta )=\frac1\pi \int _{\mathbb C}\frac{a(z-w)}{w}\, \mathrm dV_2(w)  \] is smooth, since in the second expression all derivatives may be taken under the integral sign by dominated convergence, and $\partial _{\bar z}f(z)=\int K(w)(\partial _{\bar z}a)(z-w)\, \mathrm dV_2(w)=\langle \partial _{\bar w}K,a(z-\cdot )\rangle =a(z)$, because $\partial _{\bar w}[a(z-w)]=-(\partial _{\bar z}a)(z-w)$. More generally, let $a(\zeta ,s)$ be smooth on $\mathbb C\times S$, where $S$ is an open subset of some $\mathbb R^ N$, and suppose that $a$ vanishes for $\zeta $ outside a fixed compact set. Then $f(z,s)=\pi ^{-1}\int a(z-w,s)w^{-1}\, \mathrm dV_2(w)$ is smooth on $\mathbb C\times S$, and it is holomorphic in those complex parameters in which $a$ is holomorphic, again by differentiation under the integral sign: for $(z,s)$ in a compact set, the integrand vanishes for $w$ outside a fixed bounded set, and its derivatives are bounded by constants times the integrable function $|w|^{-1}$. Step 2: the $\bar\partial $-equation on a polydisc. Write $\Delta =\Delta _1\times \cdots \times \Delta _ n$ and $\Delta '=\Delta '_1\times \cdots \times \Delta '_ n$, and write $g=\sum _ ja_ j\, \mathrm d\bar z_ j$. For each $j$ choose a smooth function $\chi _ j$ with compact support in $\Delta _ j$ that equals one on an open neighborhood $D_ j$ of $\overline{\Delta '_ j}$ (lemma 1.4.1 ), and put $P_ k=D_1\times \cdots \times D_ k\times \Delta _{k+1}\times \cdots \times \Delta _ n$. We construct smooth functions $f_1,\ldots ,f_ n$ such that, for $k=0,\ldots ,n$, the $\bar\partial $-closed form $g^{(k)}=g-\bar\partial (f_1+\cdots +f_ k)=\sum _ ja^{(k)}_ j\mathrm d\bar z_ j$ satisfies $a^{(k)}_ j=0$ on $P_ k$ for $j\leq k$. For $k=0$ there is nothing to prove. Let $k\geq 1$. Since $g^{(k-1)}$ is $\bar\partial $-closed, $\partial _{\bar z_ i}a^{(k-1)}_ j=\partial _{\bar z_ j}a^{(k-1)}_ i=0$ on $P_{k-1}$ for $i<k$; thus the coefficients of $g^{(k-1)}$ are holomorphic in $z_1,\ldots ,z_{k-1}$ there. Define \[  f_ k(z)=\frac1\pi \int _{\mathbb C}\frac{\chi _ k(\zeta )\, a^{(k-1)}_ k(z_1,\ldots ,z_{k-1},\zeta ,z_{k+1},\ldots ,z_ n)}{z_ k-\zeta }\, \mathrm dV_2(\zeta ).  \] By Step 1, applied with the parameters $z_ i$, $i\neq k$, the function $f_ k$ is smooth on $\Delta $ and holomorphic in $z_1,\ldots ,z_{k-1}$ on $P_{k-1}$, and $\partial _{\bar z_ k}f_ k=\chi _ ka^{(k-1)}_ k=a^{(k-1)}_ k$ on $P_ k$. Hence $g^{(k)}=g^{(k-1)}-\bar\partial f_ k$ has the required property. For $k=n$ we obtain $g=\bar\partial (f_1+\cdots +f_ n)$ on $P_ n\supset \Delta '$. Step 3: the Poincaré lemma and real closed $(1,1)$-forms. In this step we write points of $\mathbb C^ n=\mathbb R^{2n}$ as $x=(x_1,\ldots ,x_{2n})$, and we may assume that $R$ is defined on a ball $B$ centered at $0$. For a smooth $k$-form $\gamma $ on $B$, $k\geq 1$, define the $(k-1)$-form $H\gamma $ by \[  (H\gamma )_ x(v_1,\ldots ,v_{k-1}) =\int _0^1t^{k-1}\gamma _{tx}(x,v_1,\ldots ,v_{k-1})\, \mathrm{d}t,  \] where $x$ is regarded as a tangent vector at $tx\in B$; the form $H\gamma $ is smooth, by differentiation under the integral sign. We claim that $\mathrm{d}H\gamma +H\mathrm{d}\gamma =\gamma $. Since both sides are linear in $\gamma $, it suffices to verify this for $\gamma =c\, \mathrm dx_ I$ with $|I|=k$. Let $\iota _ x$ denote contraction with $x$, and write $\partial _ l=\partial /\partial x_ l$. Then $H\gamma =F\, \iota _ x\mathrm dx_ I$ with $F(x)=\int _0^1t^{k-1}c(tx)\, \mathrm dt$, and $H\mathrm d\gamma =\sum _ l\partial _ lF\, \iota _ x(\mathrm dx_ l\wedge \mathrm dx_ I)$, because $\partial _ lF(x)=\int _0^1t^ k(\partial _ lc)(tx)\, \mathrm dt$. Using $\mathrm d(\iota _ x\mathrm dx_ I)=k\, \mathrm dx_ I$ and $\iota _ x(\mathrm dx_ l\wedge \mathrm dx_ I)=x_ l\, \mathrm dx_ I-\mathrm dx_ l\wedge \iota _ x\mathrm dx_ I$, we find \[  \mathrm dH\gamma +H\mathrm d\gamma =\Big(kF+\sum _ lx_ l\partial _ lF\Big)\mathrm dx_ I=\int _0^1\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\big (t^ kc(tx)\big )\, \mathrm dt\, \mathrm dx_ I=\gamma ,  \] where we used that $t^ kc(tx)$ vanishes at $t=0$, since $k\geq 1$. In particular, a closed $k$-form $\gamma $ on $B$ satisfies $\gamma =\mathrm d(H\gamma )$, and $H\gamma $ is real if $\gamma $ is real; after a translation this proves the last assertion of the lemma for every ball. Applied to the closed real $2$-form $R$, this gives $R=\mathrm d\alpha $ with the real $1$-form $\alpha =HR$. Since $\alpha $ is real, $\alpha ^{1,0}=\overline{\alpha ^{0,1}}$. The $(0,2)$-component of $\mathrm d\alpha =R$ is $\bar\partial \alpha ^{0,1}=0$, so by Step 2, applied to a polydisc in $B$ centered at $0$, there is a smooth function $f$ with $\alpha ^{0,1}=\bar\partial f$ on a smaller polydisc; then $\alpha ^{1,0}=\partial \bar f$. Hence \[  R=\mathrm d\alpha =\bar\partial \partial \bar f+\partial \bar\partial f=\partial \bar\partial (f-\bar f)=2\mathrm{i}\partial \bar\partial \operatorname{Im}f =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(4\pi \operatorname{Im}f),  \] and $v=4\pi \operatorname{Im}f$ has the required properties. $\square$ Theorem 7.3.2 . Let $T$ be a closed positive $(1,1)$-current on a complex manifold of positive dimension. Every point has a coordinate neighborhood $U$ on which $T=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ for a real function $u\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$. Since $\Delta u=4\sum _ ju_{j\bar j}\geq 0$ by the matrix criterion, the class of $u$ has a canonical subharmonic representative in the coordinates of $U$ (theorem 3.2.2 ), which we call a canonical local potential of $T$. Two canonical local potentials $u$ and $\widetilde u$ of $T$ on the same coordinate neighborhood differ by a smooth pluriharmonic function $h$, that is, a real smooth function with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h=0$: we have $\widetilde u=u+h$ at every point. Proof. Fix a point and a coordinate chart around it, identified with an open set $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$, and write $T$ as above with trace $\mu =\sum _ jt_{j\bar j}$, a positive Radon measure on $\Omega $. Choose a test function $\chi $ on $\Omega $ with $0\leq \chi \leq 1$ that equals one on a neighborhood $W$ of the point (lemma 1.4.1 ), and let $E_{2n}$ be the fundamental solution of proposition 2.2.1 . By proposition 3.2.1 , the function $u_0=4E_{2n}*(\chi \mu )$ is locally integrable and subharmonic, and $\Delta u_0=4\chi \mu $; in particular $\Delta u_0=4\mu $ on $W$. The current $R=T-\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_0$ on $W$ is real and closed, and its coefficients $r_{j\bar k}=t_{j\bar k}-(u_0)_{j\bar k}$ have trace $\sum _ lr_{l\bar l}=\mu -\Delta u_0/4=0$, by ( 7.5 ). Using both relations ( 7.9 ) for $R$, we find \[  \tfrac 14\Delta r_{j\bar k} =\sum _ l\partial _{z_ l}\partial _{\bar z_ l}r_{j\bar k} =\sum _ l\partial _{\bar z_ k}\partial _{z_ l}r_{j\bar l} =\partial _{z_ j}\partial _{\bar z_ k}\sum _ l r_{l\bar l}=0.  \] By Weyl's lemma (theorem 2.1.4 ) every coefficient $r_{j\bar k}$ is smooth, so $R$ is a smooth real closed $(1,1)$-form on $W$. By lemma 7.3.1 , $R=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$ on a coordinate neighborhood $U\subset W$ of the point, with $v$ smooth and real. Then $u=u_0+v$ satisfies $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=T$ on $U$. Moreover $\Delta v=4\sum _ lr_{l\bar l}=0$, so $v$ is harmonic. Since the sum of a subharmonic function and a real harmonic function is subharmonic (see the discussion following theorem 3.1.3 ), $u$ is a locally integrable subharmonic function. By the uniqueness in theorem 3.2.2 , it is the canonical subharmonic representative of its class. Now let $u$ and $\widetilde u$ be canonical local potentials of $T$ on the same coordinate neighborhood $U$. Their classes in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$ differ by a real distribution with vanishing complex Hessian, hence with vanishing Laplacian. By Weyl's lemma, this difference is a smooth real harmonic function $h$, and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h=0$. Hence, as above, $u+h$ is a locally integrable subharmonic function, and it agrees almost everywhere with $\widetilde u$. By the uniqueness in theorem 3.2.2 , $\widetilde u=u+h$ at every point of $U$, including the points where $u=-\infty $. $\square$ A smooth real function $h$ is pluriharmonic if and only if it is locally the real part of a holomorphic function. If $h=\operatorname{Re}g$ with $g$ holomorphic, then $\bar\partial g=0$ and $\partial \bar g=\overline{\bar\partial g}=0$, so $\partial \bar\partial h=\frac12(\partial \bar\partial g-\bar\partial \partial \bar g)=0$. Conversely, suppose that $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h=0$ on a ball $B$, which after a translation is centered at $0$. The $(1,0)$-form $\partial h=\sum _ jh_{z_ j}\mathrm dz_ j$ has holomorphic coefficients, since $\partial _{\bar z_ k}h_{z_ j}=h_{j\bar k}=0$, and it is closed, since $\partial _{z_ k}h_{z_ j}$ is symmetric in $j$ and $k$. The function \[  g(z)=2\int _0^1\sum _ j z_ jh_{z_ j}(tz)\, \mathrm{d}t  \] is holomorphic on $B$, by differentiation under the integral sign. Since the functions $h_{z_ k}$ are holomorphic, the chain rule and the symmetry give \begin{align*}  \partial _{z_ k}g(z)& =2\int _0^1\Big(h_{z_ k}(tz)+t\sum _ jz_ j(\partial _{z_ j}h_{z_ k})(tz)\Big)\mathrm dt\\ & =2\int _0^1\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\big (th_{z_ k}(tz)\big )\, \mathrm dt=2h_{z_ k}(z). \end{align*} Hence $\partial (\operatorname{Re}g-h)=\frac12\partial g-\partial h=0$. Since $\operatorname{Re}g-h$ is real, also $\bar\partial (\operatorname{Re}g-h)=0$. Thus its gradient vanishes, so $\operatorname{Re}g-h$ is constant on the ball $B$ (corollary 1.4.4 ); subtracting this constant from $g$ gives $h=\operatorname{Re}g$ on $B$. In particular, if $f$ is holomorphic and nowhere zero, then $\log |f|^2$ is pluriharmonic: near each point $z_0$, a branch of the logarithm on a disc around $f(z_0)$ not containing $0$ gives a holomorphic function $L$ with $\mathrm e^ L=f$, and $\log |f|^2=2\operatorname{Re}L$. Proposition 7.3.3 . Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb {C}^ n$, $n\geq 1$, be open, and let $u$ be the canonical subharmonic representative of a real function in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\ge 0$. Let $D\subset \mathbb {C}^ m$, $m\ge 1$, be open and let $F\colon D\to \Omega $ be holomorphic. Then on each connected component of $D$ the composition $u\circ F$ is either identically $-\infty $, or locally integrable and subharmonic with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u\circ F)\geq 0$. In particular, the restriction of $u$ to each connected component of the intersection of $\Omega $ with an affine complex line has this alternative. Proof. We first work near a point. Fix $w_0\in D$, a ball $B\Subset \Omega $ centered at $F(w_0)$, and a connected open neighborhood $W$ of $w_0$ with $F(W)\subset B$. The mollifications $u_\varepsilon =u*\rho _\varepsilon $, with the radial mollifier $\rho _\varepsilon $ of section 1.4 , are defined on $B$ for small $\varepsilon $, and by ( 3.3 ) they decrease pointwise to $u$ as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. Their complex Hessians are positive semidefinite at every point: for $\xi \in \mathbb C^ n$, the function $\sum _{j,k}(u_\varepsilon )_{j\bar k}\xi _ j\bar\xi _ k$ is the mollification of the positive measure $\sum _{j,k}u_{j\bar k}\xi _ j\bar\xi _ k$ (matrix criterion), hence nonnegative by proposition 1.4.3 . Since $F$ is holomorphic, the chain rule gives \[  (u_\varepsilon \circ F)_{a\bar b} =\sum _{j,k}(u_\varepsilon )_{j\bar k}(F)\,  \frac{\partial F_ j}{\partial w_ a}\,  \overline{\frac{\partial F_ k}{\partial w_ b}},  \] so the complex Hessian of $u_\varepsilon \circ F$ is positive semidefinite, and in particular its Laplacian is nonnegative. A smooth function with nonnegative Laplacian is subharmonic, because by proposition 2.1.1 its spherical means increase with the radius and tend to its value at the center. Thus, along a sequence $\varepsilon _ k\downarrow 0$, the smooth subharmonic functions $u_{\varepsilon _ k}\circ F$ decrease to $u\circ F$ on $W$. By theorem 3.1.6 , $u\circ F$ is subharmonic on $W$, and it is either identically $-\infty $ there or locally integrable, in which case $u_{\varepsilon _ k}\circ F\to u\circ F$ in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(W)$. In the second case the currents $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u_{\varepsilon _ k}\circ F)$, which are positive by the matrix criterion, converge weakly to $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u\circ F)$, and positivity passes to the limit; so $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u\circ F)\geq 0$ on $W$. It remains to pass from these neighborhoods to the connected components of $D$. Let $D_0$ be a component and let $A$ be the set of points of $D_0$ having a neighborhood on which $u\circ F\equiv -\infty $. The set $A$ is open. It is also closed in $D_0$: if $w_0\in D_0$ lies in the closure of $A$, the connected neighborhood $W$ of $w_0$ constructed above meets $A$, so $u\circ F=-\infty $ on a nonempty open subset of $W$; since a locally integrable function is finite almost everywhere, the alternative on $W$ forces $u\circ F\equiv -\infty $ on $W$, and $w_0\in A$. Hence either $A=D_0$, or $A=\varnothing $; in the latter case $u\circ F$ is locally integrable and subharmonic with positive complex Hessian near every point of $D_0$, hence on $D_0$. $\square$ Applied to holomorphic changes of coordinates, proposition 7.3.3 shows that the canonical subharmonic representative of a class with positive complex Hessian does not depend on the chart. Here we use that the current $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ of a locally integrable function $u$, given by $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)(\varphi )=\int u\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $, is defined without reference to coordinates, and that in every chart its coefficients are $(\mathrm i/2\pi )u_{j\bar k}$, as computed in section 7.2 . Now let $F$ be a biholomorphic map between open subsets of $\mathbb C^ n$. Since $u$ is finite almost everywhere and biholomorphic maps preserve Lebesgue null sets, $u\circ F$ is not identically $-\infty $ on any component; hence it is locally integrable and subharmonic, and it represents the composition of the class of $u$ with $F$. By the uniqueness in theorem 3.2.2 , it is the canonical representative in the new coordinates. In particular, canonical local potentials of a closed positive $(1,1)$-current are well defined on open subsets of the manifold, and by theorem 7.3.2 any two of them differ by a smooth pluriharmonic function on the intersection of their domains.

title: Closed hessian coefficients
topic: Complex differential forms and positive currents
text: 7.9 \begin{equation} \label{eq:closed-hessian-coefficients} \partial _{z_ l}t_{j\bar k}=\partial _{z_ j}t_{l\bar k},\qquad \partial _{\bar z_ l}t_{j\bar k}=\partial _{\bar z_ k}t_{j\bar l} \qquad \text{for all }j,k,l. \end{equation}

title: Smooth dbar poincare
topic: Complex differential forms and positive currents
text: Lemma 7.3.1 . Let $\Delta \subset \mathbb C^ n$, $n\geq 1$, be a polydisc, and let $g$ be a smooth $(0,1)$-form on $\Delta $ with $\bar\partial g=0$. Then for every polydisc $\Delta '\Subset \Delta $ there is a smooth function $f$ on $\Delta '$ with $\bar\partial f=g$. Moreover, every smooth real closed $(1,1)$-form $R$ on an open subset of $\mathbb C^ n$ is locally of the form $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$: each point has a neighborhood on which $R=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$ for a smooth real function $v$. Finally, every smooth closed $k$-form $\gamma $ with $k\geq 1$, with real or complex coefficients, on a ball $B\subset \mathbb C^ n=\mathbb R^{2n}$ is exact on $B$: $\gamma =\mathrm d\alpha $ for a smooth $(k-1)$-form $\alpha $ on $B$, which is real if $\gamma $ is real. Proof. We solve the $\bar\partial $-equation in one variable by a Cauchy integral, then on a polydisc one variable at a time, and combine it with the Poincaré lemma. Step 1: one variable. The function $K(z)=1/(\pi z)$ on $\mathbb C$ is locally integrable, and $\partial _{\bar z}K=\delta _0$ in the sense of distributions. Indeed, for a test function $\varphi $, dominated convergence gives $\langle \partial _{\bar z}K,\varphi \rangle =-\pi ^{-1}\lim _{\varepsilon \to 0}\int _{|z|>\varepsilon }(\partial _{\bar z}\varphi /z)\, \mathrm dV_2$. In polar coordinates $z=r\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\vartheta }$ we have $\partial _{\bar z}=\frac12\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\vartheta }(\partial _ r+\frac{\mathrm i}r\partial _\vartheta )$ and $\mathrm dV_2=r\, \mathrm dr\, \mathrm d\vartheta $. Hence, by Fubini's theorem, \[  \int _{|z|>\varepsilon }\frac{\partial _{\bar z}\varphi }{z}\, \mathrm dV_2=\frac12\int _\varepsilon ^\infty \! \! \int _0^{2\pi }\Big(\partial _ r\varphi +\frac{\mathrm i}r\partial _\vartheta \varphi \Big)\, \mathrm d\vartheta \, \mathrm dr=-\frac12\int _0^{2\pi }\varphi (\varepsilon \mathrm e^{\mathrm i\vartheta })\, \mathrm d\vartheta ,  \] because $\int _0^{2\pi }\partial _\vartheta \varphi \, \mathrm d\vartheta =0$ by periodicity and $\int _\varepsilon ^\infty \partial _ r\varphi \, \mathrm dr=-\varphi (\varepsilon \mathrm e^{\mathrm i\vartheta })$, $\varphi $ having compact support. As $\varepsilon \to 0$, the right-hand side tends to $-\pi \varphi (0)$, since $\varphi $ is continuous at $0$; so $\langle \partial _{\bar z}K,\varphi \rangle =\varphi (0)$. Consequently, for a smooth function $a$ with compact support in $\mathbb C$, the function \[  f(z)=\frac1\pi \int _{\mathbb C}\frac{a(\zeta )}{z-\zeta }\, \mathrm dV_2(\zeta )=\frac1\pi \int _{\mathbb C}\frac{a(z-w)}{w}\, \mathrm dV_2(w)  \] is smooth, since in the second expression all derivatives may be taken under the integral sign by dominated convergence, and $\partial _{\bar z}f(z)=\int K(w)(\partial _{\bar z}a)(z-w)\, \mathrm dV_2(w)=\langle \partial _{\bar w}K,a(z-\cdot )\rangle =a(z)$, because $\partial _{\bar w}[a(z-w)]=-(\partial _{\bar z}a)(z-w)$. More generally, let $a(\zeta ,s)$ be smooth on $\mathbb C\times S$, where $S$ is an open subset of some $\mathbb R^ N$, and suppose that $a$ vanishes for $\zeta $ outside a fixed compact set. Then $f(z,s)=\pi ^{-1}\int a(z-w,s)w^{-1}\, \mathrm dV_2(w)$ is smooth on $\mathbb C\times S$, and it is holomorphic in those complex parameters in which $a$ is holomorphic, again by differentiation under the integral sign: for $(z,s)$ in a compact set, the integrand vanishes for $w$ outside a fixed bounded set, and its derivatives are bounded by constants times the integrable function $|w|^{-1}$. Step 2: the $\bar\partial $-equation on a polydisc. Write $\Delta =\Delta _1\times \cdots \times \Delta _ n$ and $\Delta '=\Delta '_1\times \cdots \times \Delta '_ n$, and write $g=\sum _ ja_ j\, \mathrm d\bar z_ j$. For each $j$ choose a smooth function $\chi _ j$ with compact support in $\Delta _ j$ that equals one on an open neighborhood $D_ j$ of $\overline{\Delta '_ j}$ (lemma 1.4.1 ), and put $P_ k=D_1\times \cdots \times D_ k\times \Delta _{k+1}\times \cdots \times \Delta _ n$. We construct smooth functions $f_1,\ldots ,f_ n$ such that, for $k=0,\ldots ,n$, the $\bar\partial $-closed form $g^{(k)}=g-\bar\partial (f_1+\cdots +f_ k)=\sum _ ja^{(k)}_ j\mathrm d\bar z_ j$ satisfies $a^{(k)}_ j=0$ on $P_ k$ for $j\leq k$. For $k=0$ there is nothing to prove. Let $k\geq 1$. Since $g^{(k-1)}$ is $\bar\partial $-closed, $\partial _{\bar z_ i}a^{(k-1)}_ j=\partial _{\bar z_ j}a^{(k-1)}_ i=0$ on $P_{k-1}$ for $i<k$; thus the coefficients of $g^{(k-1)}$ are holomorphic in $z_1,\ldots ,z_{k-1}$ there. Define \[  f_ k(z)=\frac1\pi \int _{\mathbb C}\frac{\chi _ k(\zeta )\, a^{(k-1)}_ k(z_1,\ldots ,z_{k-1},\zeta ,z_{k+1},\ldots ,z_ n)}{z_ k-\zeta }\, \mathrm dV_2(\zeta ).  \] By Step 1, applied with the parameters $z_ i$, $i\neq k$, the function $f_ k$ is smooth on $\Delta $ and holomorphic in $z_1,\ldots ,z_{k-1}$ on $P_{k-1}$, and $\partial _{\bar z_ k}f_ k=\chi _ ka^{(k-1)}_ k=a^{(k-1)}_ k$ on $P_ k$. Hence $g^{(k)}=g^{(k-1)}-\bar\partial f_ k$ has the required property. For $k=n$ we obtain $g=\bar\partial (f_1+\cdots +f_ n)$ on $P_ n\supset \Delta '$. Step 3: the Poincaré lemma and real closed $(1,1)$-forms. In this step we write points of $\mathbb C^ n=\mathbb R^{2n}$ as $x=(x_1,\ldots ,x_{2n})$, and we may assume that $R$ is defined on a ball $B$ centered at $0$. For a smooth $k$-form $\gamma $ on $B$, $k\geq 1$, define the $(k-1)$-form $H\gamma $ by \[  (H\gamma )_ x(v_1,\ldots ,v_{k-1}) =\int _0^1t^{k-1}\gamma _{tx}(x,v_1,\ldots ,v_{k-1})\, \mathrm{d}t,  \] where $x$ is regarded as a tangent vector at $tx\in B$; the form $H\gamma $ is smooth, by differentiation under the integral sign. We claim that $\mathrm{d}H\gamma +H\mathrm{d}\gamma =\gamma $. Since both sides are linear in $\gamma $, it suffices to verify this for $\gamma =c\, \mathrm dx_ I$ with $|I|=k$. Let $\iota _ x$ denote contraction with $x$, and write $\partial _ l=\partial /\partial x_ l$. Then $H\gamma =F\, \iota _ x\mathrm dx_ I$ with $F(x)=\int _0^1t^{k-1}c(tx)\, \mathrm dt$, and $H\mathrm d\gamma =\sum _ l\partial _ lF\, \iota _ x(\mathrm dx_ l\wedge \mathrm dx_ I)$, because $\partial _ lF(x)=\int _0^1t^ k(\partial _ lc)(tx)\, \mathrm dt$. Using $\mathrm d(\iota _ x\mathrm dx_ I)=k\, \mathrm dx_ I$ and $\iota _ x(\mathrm dx_ l\wedge \mathrm dx_ I)=x_ l\, \mathrm dx_ I-\mathrm dx_ l\wedge \iota _ x\mathrm dx_ I$, we find \[  \mathrm dH\gamma +H\mathrm d\gamma =\Big(kF+\sum _ lx_ l\partial _ lF\Big)\mathrm dx_ I=\int _0^1\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\big (t^ kc(tx)\big )\, \mathrm dt\, \mathrm dx_ I=\gamma ,  \] where we used that $t^ kc(tx)$ vanishes at $t=0$, since $k\geq 1$. In particular, a closed $k$-form $\gamma $ on $B$ satisfies $\gamma =\mathrm d(H\gamma )$, and $H\gamma $ is real if $\gamma $ is real; after a translation this proves the last assertion of the lemma for every ball. Applied to the closed real $2$-form $R$, this gives $R=\mathrm d\alpha $ with the real $1$-form $\alpha =HR$. Since $\alpha $ is real, $\alpha ^{1,0}=\overline{\alpha ^{0,1}}$. The $(0,2)$-component of $\mathrm d\alpha =R$ is $\bar\partial \alpha ^{0,1}=0$, so by Step 2, applied to a polydisc in $B$ centered at $0$, there is a smooth function $f$ with $\alpha ^{0,1}=\bar\partial f$ on a smaller polydisc; then $\alpha ^{1,0}=\partial \bar f$. Hence \[  R=\mathrm d\alpha =\bar\partial \partial \bar f+\partial \bar\partial f=\partial \bar\partial (f-\bar f)=2\mathrm{i}\partial \bar\partial \operatorname{Im}f =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(4\pi \operatorname{Im}f),  \] and $v=4\pi \operatorname{Im}f$ has the required properties. $\square$

title: Local positive current potential
topic: Complex differential forms and positive currents
text: Theorem 7.3.2 . Let $T$ be a closed positive $(1,1)$-current on a complex manifold of positive dimension. Every point has a coordinate neighborhood $U$ on which $T=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ for a real function $u\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$. Since $\Delta u=4\sum _ ju_{j\bar j}\geq 0$ by the matrix criterion, the class of $u$ has a canonical subharmonic representative in the coordinates of $U$ (theorem 3.2.2 ), which we call a canonical local potential of $T$. Two canonical local potentials $u$ and $\widetilde u$ of $T$ on the same coordinate neighborhood differ by a smooth pluriharmonic function $h$, that is, a real smooth function with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h=0$: we have $\widetilde u=u+h$ at every point. Proof. Fix a point and a coordinate chart around it, identified with an open set $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$, and write $T$ as above with trace $\mu =\sum _ jt_{j\bar j}$, a positive Radon measure on $\Omega $. Choose a test function $\chi $ on $\Omega $ with $0\leq \chi \leq 1$ that equals one on a neighborhood $W$ of the point (lemma 1.4.1 ), and let $E_{2n}$ be the fundamental solution of proposition 2.2.1 . By proposition 3.2.1 , the function $u_0=4E_{2n}*(\chi \mu )$ is locally integrable and subharmonic, and $\Delta u_0=4\chi \mu $; in particular $\Delta u_0=4\mu $ on $W$. The current $R=T-\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_0$ on $W$ is real and closed, and its coefficients $r_{j\bar k}=t_{j\bar k}-(u_0)_{j\bar k}$ have trace $\sum _ lr_{l\bar l}=\mu -\Delta u_0/4=0$, by ( 7.5 ). Using both relations ( 7.9 ) for $R$, we find \[  \tfrac 14\Delta r_{j\bar k} =\sum _ l\partial _{z_ l}\partial _{\bar z_ l}r_{j\bar k} =\sum _ l\partial _{\bar z_ k}\partial _{z_ l}r_{j\bar l} =\partial _{z_ j}\partial _{\bar z_ k}\sum _ l r_{l\bar l}=0.  \] By Weyl's lemma (theorem 2.1.4 ) every coefficient $r_{j\bar k}$ is smooth, so $R$ is a smooth real closed $(1,1)$-form on $W$. By lemma 7.3.1 , $R=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$ on a coordinate neighborhood $U\subset W$ of the point, with $v$ smooth and real. Then $u=u_0+v$ satisfies $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=T$ on $U$. Moreover $\Delta v=4\sum _ lr_{l\bar l}=0$, so $v$ is harmonic. Since the sum of a subharmonic function and a real harmonic function is subharmonic (see the discussion following theorem 3.1.3 ), $u$ is a locally integrable subharmonic function. By the uniqueness in theorem 3.2.2 , it is the canonical subharmonic representative of its class. Now let $u$ and $\widetilde u$ be canonical local potentials of $T$ on the same coordinate neighborhood $U$. Their classes in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$ differ by a real distribution with vanishing complex Hessian, hence with vanishing Laplacian. By Weyl's lemma, this difference is a smooth real harmonic function $h$, and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h=0$. Hence, as above, $u+h$ is a locally integrable subharmonic function, and it agrees almost everywhere with $\widetilde u$. By the uniqueness in theorem 3.2.2 , $\widetilde u=u+h$ at every point of $U$, including the points where $u=-\infty $. $\square$

title: Positive hessian holomorphic composition
topic: Complex differential forms and positive currents
text: Proposition 7.3.3 . Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb {C}^ n$, $n\geq 1$, be open, and let $u$ be the canonical subharmonic representative of a real function in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\ge 0$. Let $D\subset \mathbb {C}^ m$, $m\ge 1$, be open and let $F\colon D\to \Omega $ be holomorphic. Then on each connected component of $D$ the composition $u\circ F$ is either identically $-\infty $, or locally integrable and subharmonic with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u\circ F)\geq 0$. In particular, the restriction of $u$ to each connected component of the intersection of $\Omega $ with an affine complex line has this alternative. Proof. We first work near a point. Fix $w_0\in D$, a ball $B\Subset \Omega $ centered at $F(w_0)$, and a connected open neighborhood $W$ of $w_0$ with $F(W)\subset B$. The mollifications $u_\varepsilon =u*\rho _\varepsilon $, with the radial mollifier $\rho _\varepsilon $ of section 1.4 , are defined on $B$ for small $\varepsilon $, and by ( 3.3 ) they decrease pointwise to $u$ as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. Their complex Hessians are positive semidefinite at every point: for $\xi \in \mathbb C^ n$, the function $\sum _{j,k}(u_\varepsilon )_{j\bar k}\xi _ j\bar\xi _ k$ is the mollification of the positive measure $\sum _{j,k}u_{j\bar k}\xi _ j\bar\xi _ k$ (matrix criterion), hence nonnegative by proposition 1.4.3 . Since $F$ is holomorphic, the chain rule gives \[  (u_\varepsilon \circ F)_{a\bar b} =\sum _{j,k}(u_\varepsilon )_{j\bar k}(F)\,  \frac{\partial F_ j}{\partial w_ a}\,  \overline{\frac{\partial F_ k}{\partial w_ b}},  \] so the complex Hessian of $u_\varepsilon \circ F$ is positive semidefinite, and in particular its Laplacian is nonnegative. A smooth function with nonnegative Laplacian is subharmonic, because by proposition 2.1.1 its spherical means increase with the radius and tend to its value at the center. Thus, along a sequence $\varepsilon _ k\downarrow 0$, the smooth subharmonic functions $u_{\varepsilon _ k}\circ F$ decrease to $u\circ F$ on $W$. By theorem 3.1.6 , $u\circ F$ is subharmonic on $W$, and it is either identically $-\infty $ there or locally integrable, in which case $u_{\varepsilon _ k}\circ F\to u\circ F$ in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(W)$. In the second case the currents $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u_{\varepsilon _ k}\circ F)$, which are positive by the matrix criterion, converge weakly to $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u\circ F)$, and positivity passes to the limit; so $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u\circ F)\geq 0$ on $W$. It remains to pass from these neighborhoods to the connected components of $D$. Let $D_0$ be a component and let $A$ be the set of points of $D_0$ having a neighborhood on which $u\circ F\equiv -\infty $. The set $A$ is open. It is also closed in $D_0$: if $w_0\in D_0$ lies in the closure of $A$, the connected neighborhood $W$ of $w_0$ constructed above meets $A$, so $u\circ F=-\infty $ on a nonempty open subset of $W$; since a locally integrable function is finite almost everywhere, the alternative on $W$ forces $u\circ F\equiv -\infty $ on $W$, and $w_0\in A$. Hence either $A=D_0$, or $A=\varnothing $; in the latter case $u\circ F$ is locally integrable and subharmonic with positive complex Hessian near every point of $D_0$, hence on $D_0$. $\square$

title: Holomorphic zeros and the Poincaré–Lelong formula
topic: Complex differential forms and positive currents
text:
7.4 Holomorphic zeros and the Poincaré–Lelong formula Let $f$ be a holomorphic function on a domain in $\mathbb C^ n$, not identically zero. Away from the zero set of $f$, the function $\log |f|^2$ is pluriharmonic, so the current $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |f|^2$ is supported on the zero set. We show that it is the current of integration over the zero set, each smooth sheet counted with the vanishing order of $f$ along it. The main difficulty is the singular part of the zero set, where several sheets may meet. Using the Weierstrass preparation theorem in several directions, we show that in suitable linear coordinates this part lies over a Lebesgue null set in every coordinate projection, which is enough to see that it carries no mass. Lemma 7.4.1 . Let $f$ be a holomorphic function on a domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$, $n\ge 1$, that is not identically zero. Then the zero set of $f$ has Lebesgue measure zero. Let $P\subset \Omega $ be a polydisc, let $1\leq j\leq n$, and write $P=P'	imes D$ and points of $P$ as $(z',z_ j)$, where $D\subset \mathbb C$ is a disc in the variable $z_ j$ and $z'$ consists of the other coordinates. Then the set of points $z'\in P'$ such that $z_ j\mapsto f(z',z_ j)$ vanishes identically on $D$ is a Lebesgue null subset of $\mathbb C^{n-1}$; for $n=1$ it is empty. Moreover, for every zero $a$ of $f$ there is a complex linear coordinate system centered at $a$ such that $f$ does not vanish identically on any of the coordinate axes through $a$. Proof. We prove the first two assertions together by induction on $n$. For $n=1$, every zero of $f$ is isolated: at a zero $a$, the Taylor expansion has a first nonzero term $c(z-a)^ m$, since otherwise $f$ would vanish near $a$ and hence on $\Omega $ by the identity theorem; so $f(z)=(z-a)^ mg(z)$ with $g(a)
eq 0$. Hence the zero set meets every compact subset of $\Omega $ in a finite set, and since $\Omega $ is a countable union of compact sets, it is countable, hence null. Moreover, $f$ does not vanish identically on a disc $D\subset \Omega $, by the identity theorem, which proves the second assertion for $n=1$. Let $n\geq 2$, and let $P=P'	imes D$ be as in the statement; after permuting the coordinates, which preserves Lebesgue measure, we may assume that $j=n$, and we write $w=z_ n$ and $w_0$ for the center of $D$. The functions $c_ k(z')=\partial _ w^ kf(z',w_0)/k!$ are holomorphic on $P'$, and, by the one-variable Taylor expansion of $w\mapsto f(z',w)$ on the disc $D$ centered at $w_0$, this function vanishes identically on $D$ if and only if all $c_ k(z')$ vanish. Since $f$ does not vanish identically on the nonempty open set $P$, by the identity theorem, some $c_ k$ is not identically zero on the polydisc $P'$, and its zero set $N\subset P'$ is null by the first assertion in dimension $n-1$. This proves the second assertion in dimension $n$, since the set in question is contained in $N$. For $z'
otin N$, the zero set of $w\mapsto f(z',w)$ in $D$ is null by the case $n=1$. By Tonelli's theorem, applied to the indicator function of the relatively closed zero set of $f$ in $P$, this zero set is null; and countably many such polydiscs, for instance those with rational centers and radii contained in $\Omega $, cover $\Omega $. For the last assertion, translate $a$ to the origin and let $P_ m$ be the first nonzero term of the homogeneous expansion of $f$ at $0$; it exists because $f$ does not vanish identically near $0$, and $m\geq 1$ because $f(0)=0$. The set $\{ P_ m
eq 0\} $ is open and dense in $\mathbb C^ n$, because a polynomial vanishing on a nonempty open set is zero: its derivatives at a point $b$ of that set vanish, and the polynomial is the sum of its finite Taylor expansion at $b$. Choose $v_1\in \{ P_ m
eq 0\} $, and inductively $v_ j\in \{ P_ m
eq 0\} $ outside the linear span of $v_1,\ldots ,v_{j-1}$; this is possible because the complement of a proper linear subspace is open and dense, and the intersection of two dense open sets is dense. Then $v_1,\ldots ,v_ n$ is a basis, and $f(tv_ j)=t^ mP_ m(v_ j)+O(t^{m+1})$ by ( 7.2 ), so $t\mapsto f(tv_ j)$ does not vanish identically near $t=0$. Taking $v_1,\ldots ,v_ n$ as coordinate axes proves the assertion. $\square$ Theorem 7.4.2 (Weierstrass preparation) . Let $f$ be holomorphic on a neighborhood $U$ of $0$ in $\mathbb {C}^{n-1}	imes \mathbb {C}$, $n\geq 1$, and suppose that $w\mapsto f(0,w)$ has a zero of order $m\ge 1$ at $w=0$. Then there are polydiscs $P'	imes \{ |w|<ho \} \subset U$ centered at $0$ with arbitrarily small radii, and numbers $ho _1\in (0,ho )$, such that on $P'	imes \{ |w|<ho \} $ \[  f(z',w)=g(z',w)W(z',w),\qquad W=w^ m+a_1(z')w^{m-1}+\cdots +a_ m(z'),  \] where $g$ is holomorphic and nowhere zero, the coefficients $a_ j$ are holomorphic on $P'$ with $a_ j(0)=0$, and for every $z'\in P'$ the $m$ roots of $W(z',\cdot )$ lie in $\{ |w|<ho _1\} $. Proof. Since the zeros of $f(0,\cdot )$ are isolated, there is $ho _0>0$ such that $\{ 0\} 	imes \{ |w|\leq ho _0\} \subset U$ and $f(0,w)
eq 0$ for $0<|w|\leq ho _0$. Let $0<ho <ho _0$, and choose $ho _1<ho <ho _2\leq ho _0$. Then $f(0,w)
eq 0$ on the compact annulus $\{ ho _1\leq |w|\leq ho _2\} $. Since $|f(0,\cdot )|$ has a positive minimum on this annulus and $f$ is uniformly continuous on a compact neighborhood of $\{ 0\} 	imes \{ ho _1\leq |w|\leq ho _2\} $ in $U$, there is a polydisc $P'$ centered at $0$, as small as we wish, such that $P'	imes \{ |w|\leq ho _2\} \subset U$ and $f(z',w)
eq 0$ for $z'\in P'$ and $ho _1\leq |w|\leq ho _2$. By the argument principle, the number of zeros of $f(z',\cdot )$ in $\{ |w|<ho \} $, counted with multiplicity, is \[   rac{1}{2\pi \mathrm{i}}\int _{|w|=ho } rac{f_ w(z',w)}{f(z',w)}\, \mathrm{d}w,  \] a continuous integer-valued function of $z'$ on the connected set $P'$; hence it equals its value $m$ at $z'=0$. Denote these zeros by $\lambda _1(z'),\ldots ,\lambda _ m(z')$, in any order; they lie in $\{ |w|<ho _1\} $. By the residue theorem, their power sums are \[  p_ k(z')=\sum _{l=1}^ m\lambda _ l(z')^ k= rac{1}{2\pi \mathrm{i}}\int _{|w|=ho } w^ k rac{f_ w(z',w)}{f(z',w)}\, \mathrm{d}w,\qquad 1\leq k\leq m,  \] which are holomorphic functions on $P'$, by differentiation under the integral sign. The elementary symmetric functions $e_ k$ of the roots satisfy Newton's identities \[  ke_ k=\sum _{j=1}^ k(-1)^{j-1}e_{k-j}p_ j,\qquad e_0=1.  \] To prove them, put $E(t)=\prod _ l(1+t\lambda _ l)=\sum _ ke_ kt^ k$ and compare the coefficients of $t^{k-1}$ in $E'(t)=E(t)\sum _{j\geq 1}(-1)^{j-1}p_ jt^{j-1}$, which is the expansion of the logarithmic derivative $E'/E=\sum _ l\lambda _ l/(1+t\lambda _ l)$. By induction on $k$, every $e_ k$ is holomorphic on $P'$. Hence $W(z',w)=\prod _ l(w-\lambda _ l(z'))$ is a monic polynomial in $w$ with holomorphic coefficients $a_ k=(-1)^ ke_ k$, and $a_ k(0)=0$ because all $\lambda _ l(0)=0$. It remains to show that $f/W$ extends to a nowhere vanishing holomorphic function on $P'	imes \{ |w|<ho \} $. For fixed $z'\in P'$, the functions $f(z',\cdot )$ and $W(z',\cdot )$ have the same zeros, with the same multiplicities, in $\{ |w|<ho _2\} $; so $f/W$ and $W/f$ extend to holomorphic functions of $w$ there. On the annulus $\{ ho _1<|w|<ho _2\} $ both quotients are holomorphic in $(z',w)$. The Cauchy integral \[  G(z',w)= rac{1}{2\pi \mathrm i}\int _{|\zeta |=ho } rac{(f/W)(z',\zeta )}{\zeta -w}\, \mathrm d\zeta ,\qquad |w|<ho ,  \] is holomorphic in $(z',w)$, by differentiation under the integral sign, and equals $f/W$ by Cauchy's formula in $w$. Defining $\widetilde G$ in the same way from $W/f$, we obtain $G\widetilde G=1$. Thus $g=G$ is holomorphic and nowhere zero, and $f=gW$. $\square$ Proposition 7.4.3 . Let $f$ be holomorphic on a domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$, $n\geq 1$, and not identically zero, and put $\log |f|^2=-\infty $ on the zero set of $f$. Then $\log |f|^2$ is locally integrable, it is the canonical subharmonic representative of its class, and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |f|^2\geq 0$. Moreover, let $P\subset \Omega $ be a polydisc, let $1\leq j\leq n$, and write points of $P$ as $(z',z_ j)$, where $z'$ consists of the coordinates other than $z_ j$. Then for every test function $\varphi $ on $P$, 7.10  egin{equation} \label{eq:logarithm-coordinate-slices}  ig \langle (\log |f|^2)_{j ar j},\varphi  ig angle =\pi \int _{\mathbb {C}^{n-1}}\sum _{a:\, f(z',a)=0} m(z',a)\varphi (z',a)\, \mathrm{d}V_{2n-2}(z'), \end{equation} where the sum runs over the zeros $a$ of $z_ j\mapsto f(z',z_ j)$ in the fiber of $P$ over $z'$, and $m(z',a)$ is the order of that zero; the integrand is defined outside the null set of those $z'$ over which $f$ vanishes identically on the fiber. In particular, if $\pi _ j$ is the projection of $P$ omitting $z_ j$, the positive measure $(\log |f|^2)_{j ar j}$ gives zero mass to $\pi _ j^{-1}(N)$ for every Lebesgue null set $N$. Proof. Local integrability. Near a point where $f
eq 0$, the function $\log |f|^2$ is smooth. Let $a$ be a zero of $f$. After a translation and a complex-linear change of coordinates, which preserve local integrability, we may assume that $a=0$ and that $f(0,w)$ does not vanish identically in the last variable $w$ (lemma 7.4.1 ). Then $f(0,\cdot )$ has a zero of some order $m\geq 1$ at $0$, and by theorem 7.4.2 , $f=gW$ on a polydisc $P'	imes \{ |w|<ho \} $, where $g$ is a holomorphic unit and $W(z',w)=\prod _{l=1}^ m(w-\lambda _ l(z'))$ with all roots in $\{ |w|<ho _1\} $ for some $ho _1<ho $. Choose $r\in (ho _1,ho )$ and replace $P'$ by a smaller concentric polydisc with compact closure in $P'$; since $g$ is continuous and nowhere zero, $\log |g|^2$ is then bounded on $P'	imes \{ |w|<r\} $. For $|\lambda |\leq ho _1$ we have \[  \int _{|w|<r} ig |\log |w-\lambda | ig |\, \mathrm{d}V_2(w)\le C,  \] with $C$ independent of $\lambda $: the positive part of $\log |w-\lambda |$ is at most $\max \{ \log (r+ho _1),0\} $, and after the translation $\zeta =w-\lambda $ the integral of its negative part is at most $\int _{|\zeta |<1}(-\log |\zeta |)\, \mathrm dV_2(\zeta )$. Since $|\log |W(z',w)||\leq \sum _ l|\log |w-\lambda _ l(z')||$, it follows that $\int _{|w|<r}|\log |W(z',w)||\, \mathrm dV_2(w)\leq mC$ for every $z'\in P'$. (The estimate holds for each fiber separately, so we need not choose the roots as measurable functions of $z'$.) By Tonelli's theorem $\log |W|^2$, and hence $\log |f|^2$, is integrable on $P'	imes \{ |w|<r\} $, a neighborhood of $a=0$. The slice formula. For $n=1$, example 3.2.4 gives $\Delta \log |f|^2=4\pi \sum _ am(a)\delta _ a$ locally, that is, $(\log |f|^2)_{z ar z}=\pi \sum _ am(a)\delta _ a$; this is ( 7.10 ) with $\mathbb C^0$ a point. In general, write $P=P'	imes D$ with $D$ a disc in the variable $z_ j$. By lemma 7.4.1 , the set $N_0$ of points $z'\in P'$ over which $f$ vanishes identically on $D$ is null. By Fubini's theorem,  egin{align*}   ig \langle (\log |f|^2)_{j ar j},\varphi  ig angle & =\int _ P\log |f|^2\, \partial _{z_ j}\partial _{ ar z_ j}\varphi \, \mathrm dV_{2n}\ & =\int _{P'}\Big(\int _ D\log |f(z',w)|^2\, \partial _ w\partial _{ ar w}\varphi (z',w)\, \mathrm dV_2(w)\Big)\mathrm dV_{2n-2}(z'), \end{align*} the inner integral being an integrable function of $z'$. For $z'
otin N_0$, the one-variable case applied to $f(z',\cdot )$ on $D$ shows that the inner integral equals $\pi \sum _ am(z',a)\varphi (z',a)$. This proves ( 7.10 ); the integrand on the right is measurable and integrable, being equal almost everywhere to the inner integral. Positivity. By ( 7.10 ), $(\log |f|^2)_{j ar j}$ is nonnegative on nonnegative test functions supported in polydiscs contained in $\Omega $, hence on all nonnegative test functions, which are finite sums of such functions by lemma 1.4.2 . This holds in every system of complex linear coordinates, since $f$ remains holomorphic after a linear change of coordinates. Applying this after a unitary change of coordinates, as in the matrix criterion of section 7.3 , we see that $\sum _{j,k}(\log |f|^2)_{j ar k}\xi _ j ar\xi _ k$ is a positive measure for every $\xi \in \mathbb C^ n$. By the matrix criterion, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |f|^2\geq 0$, and by theorem 7.2.5 its coefficients are measures. Null sets. Let $
u =(\log |f|^2)_{j ar j}$ on $P=P'	imes D$, and let $\eta \geq 0$ be a test function on $D$. By ( 7.10 ), for every nonnegative test function $\psi $ on $P'$, \[  \int _ P\psi (z')\eta (z_ j)\, \mathrm d
u =\int _{P'}\psi \, h_\eta \, \mathrm dV_{2n-2},\qquad h_\eta (z')=\pi \sum _ am(z',a)\eta (a)\geq 0.  \] Both sides define positive Radon measures on $P'$ in $\psi $, the function $h_\eta $ being locally integrable by the identity itself. By the uniqueness in theorem 1.4.5 , the image measure $A\mapsto \int _{\pi _ j^{-1}(A)}\eta \, \mathrm d
u $ of $\eta 
u $ under $\pi _ j$ is therefore $h_\eta \, \mathrm dV_{2n-2}$. Every null set is contained in a Borel null set, by outer regularity of Lebesgue measure, so we may assume that $N$ is a Borel set. Then $\int _{\pi _ j^{-1}(N)}\eta \, \mathrm d
u =\int _ Nh_\eta \, \mathrm dV_{2n-2}=0$. Letting $\eta $ increase to $1$ on $D$ along a sequence, we obtain $
u (\pi _ j^{-1}(N))=0$ by monotone convergence. The canonical representative. The trace of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |f|^2$ is positive, so by theorem 3.2.2 the class of $\log |f|^2$ has a canonical subharmonic representative $v$, given by the limits of ball averages in ( 3.3 ). At a point where $f
eq 0$, the function $\log |f|^2$ is continuous, so $v$ agrees with it there. At a zero $a$, there is $C$ with $|f(z)|\leq C|z-a|$ near $a$, since $f$ is smooth and $f(a)=0$; hence the average of $\log |f|^2$ over $B(a,r)$ is at most $\log C^2+2\log r$, which tends to $-\infty $ as $r	o 0$. Thus $v(a)=-\infty =\log |f(a)|^2$, and $v=\log |f|^2$ everywhere. $\square$ To describe $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |f|^2$, let $f$ be as in proposition 7.4.3 , and consider the zero set $V=f^{-1}(0)$. Its regular part $V_{\mathrm{reg}}$ is the set of points $p\in V$ having a neighborhood on which \[  f=g\, a^ m,\qquad g
e 0,\quad \mathrm{d}a
e 0,\quad m\ge 1,  \] with $a$ and $g$ holomorphic. In a chart around $p$ we have $\mathrm da=\sum _ k\partial _{z_ k}a\, \mathrm dz_ k$, so the complex Jacobian matrix of $a$ at $p$ is a nonzero row, and proposition 7.1.2 (2), applied with $r=1$, shows that $a$ is the first coordinate of a holomorphic chart near $p$, in which $V=\{ a=0\} $ is a coordinate hyperplane. The integer $m$ depends only on $f$ and $p$. Indeed, let $f=\widetilde g\, \widetilde a^{\widetilde m}$ be a second such representation near $p$. Since $g$ and $\widetilde g$ do not vanish and $m,\widetilde m\geq 1$, both $a$ and $\widetilde a$ vanish exactly on $V$ near $p$. We use holomorphic coordinates $(t,x')$ centered at $p$ with $t=a$, defined on a polydisc. Since $\widetilde a(0,x')=0$, we have $\widetilde a(t,x')=t\, b(t,x')$ with the holomorphic function $b(t,x')=\int _0^1\partial _ t\widetilde a(st,x')\, \mathrm ds$, and $\mathrm d\widetilde a_ p=b(p)\, \mathrm da_ p$, so that $b(p)
eq 0$. On the line $x'=0$, the function $t\mapsto f(t,0)$ is $g(t,0)t^ m$ and also $\widetilde g(t,0)b(t,0)^{\widetilde m}t^{\widetilde m}$, with nonvanishing factors in front of the powers of $t$ near $t=0$; comparing the orders of vanishing at $t=0$ gives $\widetilde m=m$. We call $m$ the multiplicity, or transverse vanishing order, of $f$ along $V$ at $p$; it is locally constant on $V_{\mathrm{reg}}$. The set $V_{\mathrm{reg}}$ is open in $V$, so $S=V\setminus V_{\mathrm{reg}}$ is closed, and $V_{\mathrm{reg}}$ is a complex hypersurface, that is, a submanifold of dimension $n-1$, of the open set $\Omega \setminus S$. These definitions are local and invariant under holomorphic changes of coordinates, so they apply equally to holomorphic functions on complex manifolds. Lemma 7.4.4 . Let $f$ be as in proposition 7.4.3 , and let $z_0$ be a zero of $f$. There are complex linear coordinates centered at $z_0$ and a polydisc $P$ centered at $z_0$ such that, for every $j=1,\ldots ,n$, the projection $\pi _ j$ of $P$ omitting the coordinate $z_ j$ satisfies $S\cap P\subset \pi _ j^{-1}(N_ j)$ for a Lebesgue null set $N_ j$. Proof. Choose coordinates as in lemma 7.4.1 , so that $f$ does not vanish identically on any coordinate axis through $z_0=0$. Fix $j$, and write points as $(z',w)$ with $w=z_ j$. By theorem 7.4.2 in the variable $w$, there is a polydisc $P_ j=P'_ j	imes \{ |w|<ho \} $ in the domain of $f$ on which $f=gW$, where $g$ is a holomorphic unit and $W$ is a monic polynomial in $w$ of some degree $m\geq 1$ whose coefficients are holomorphic on $P'_ j$ and whose roots lie in $\{ |w|<ho _1\} $ for some $ho _1<ho $. We shall find a holomorphic function $h$ on $P'_ j$, not identically zero, such that every zero of $f$ in $P_ j$ lying over $\{ h
eq 0\} $ belongs to $V_{\mathrm{reg}}$. Then $S\cap P_ j\subset \pi _ j^{-1}(N_ j)$ with $N_ j=\{ h=0\} $, which is null by lemma 7.4.1 if $n\geq 2$, and empty if $n=1$, when $P'_ j$ is a point. Any polydisc $P$ centered at $0$ and contained in $P_1\cap \cdots \cap P_ n$ then has the required property. For $z'\in P'_ j$, let $\lambda _1(z'),\ldots ,\lambda _ m(z')$ be the roots of $W(z',\cdot )$, repeated according to multiplicity, and put $p_ k(z')=\sum _ l\lambda _ l(z')^ k$ for $k\geq 0$. By the residue theorem, \[  p_ k(z')= rac1{2\pi \mathrm i}\int _{|w|=ho '}w^ k rac{\partial _ wW(z',w)}{W(z',w)}\, \mathrm dw\qquad (ho _1<ho '<ho ),  \] so $p_ k$ is holomorphic on $P'_ j$, by differentiation under the integral sign. Let $s$ be the largest number of distinct roots of $W(z',\cdot )$ for $z'\in P'_ j$, and let $h$ be the determinant of the $s	imes s$ matrix $(p_{a+b})_{0\leq a,b\leq s-1}$; it is holomorphic on $P'_ j$. For fixed $z'$, this matrix is $A^{\mathsf T}A$, where $A$ is the $m	imes s$ matrix with entries $A_{la}=\lambda _ l^ a$. To compute $h(z')$, note that the $b$th column of $A^{\mathsf T}A$ is $\sum _ l\lambda _ l^ bv_ l$, where $v_ l=(\lambda _ l^0,\ldots ,\lambda _ l^{s-1})$ is the $l$th row of $A$. Expanding the determinant by multilinearity in the columns, discarding the terms in which some $v_ l$ occurs twice, and grouping the remaining terms according to the set $L$ of indices that occur, we find that each group contributes $(\det A_ L)^2$. Indeed, if $L=\{ l_1<\cdots <l_ s\} $, the terms of this group are indexed by the permutations $\pi $ of $\{ 1,\ldots ,s\} $, the term of $\pi $ taking $\lambda _{l_{\pi (b+1)}}^ bv_{l_{\pi (b+1)}}$ from the $b$th column. Reordering the columns multiplies the determinant by $\operatorname {sign}(\pi )$, so the group contributes $\det A_ L\sum _\pi \operatorname {sign}(\pi )\prod _{b=0}^{s-1}\lambda _{l_{\pi (b+1)}}^ b$, and this sum is the Leibniz expansion of $\det A_ L$. Thus we obtain the Cauchy–Binet formula \[  h(z')=\det (A^{\mathsf T}A)=\sum _ L(\det A_ L)^2=\sum _ L\prod _{l<l',\  l,l'\in L}(\lambda _ l-\lambda _{l'})^2,  \] where $L$ runs over the $s$-element subsets of $\{ 1,\ldots ,m\} $, $A_ L$ is the square matrix formed by the rows of $A$ with indices in $L$, and the last equality is the Vandermonde formula. If $W(z',\cdot )$ has fewer than $s$ distinct roots, every set $L$ contains two indices with equal roots, and $h(z')=0$. If $W(z',\cdot )$ has exactly $s$ distinct roots $\mu _1,\ldots ,\mu _ s$, of multiplicities $k_1,\ldots ,k_ s$, then the nonzero terms are those of the $k_1\cdots k_ s$ sets $L$ containing exactly one index of each root, and each of them equals $\prod _{c<c'}(\mu _ c-\mu _{c'})^2
eq 0$; hence $h(z')
eq 0$. By the choice of $s$, the function $h$ is not identically zero. Now let $h(z'_0)
eq 0$, and let $(z'_0,w_0)\in P_ j$ be a zero of $f$. Then $W(z'_0,w_0)=0$, since $g$ is a unit, and $W(z'_0,\cdot )$ has exactly $s$ distinct roots $\mu _1,\ldots ,\mu _ s$, of multiplicities $k_1,\ldots ,k_ s$; say $w_0=\mu _1$. Choose disjoint closed discs $E_ c$ centered at $\mu _ c$ in $\{ |w|<ho \} $, and a connected neighborhood $Y$ of $z'_0$ in $P'_ j$ such that $W(z',\cdot )$ has no zeros on the boundary circles $\partial E_ c$ for $z'\in Y$; this is possible because $W(z'_0,\cdot )$ has no zeros on these compact circles and $W$ is continuous. By the argument principle, the number of roots of $W(z',\cdot )$ in $E_ c$, counted with multiplicity, is $(2\pi \mathrm i)^{-1}\int _{\partial E_ c}\partial _ wW/W\, \mathrm dw$, a continuous integer-valued function on $Y$, hence equal to $k_ c$. Thus each $E_ c$ contains at least one root of $W(z',\cdot )$. Since $W(z',\cdot )$ has at most $s$ distinct roots, each $E_ c$ contains exactly one, $\mu _ c(z')$, of multiplicity $k_ c$, and since $k_1+\cdots +k_ s=m$, there are no other roots. By the residue theorem, \[  \mu _ c(z')= rac1{2\pi \mathrm ik_ c}\int _{\partial E_ c}w\,  rac{\partial _ wW(z',w)}{W(z',w)}\, \mathrm dw,  \] which is holomorphic on $Y$, and $W(z',w)=\prod _ c(w-\mu _ c(z'))^{k_ c}$ for $z'\in Y$, both sides being monic polynomials in $w$ with the same roots and multiplicities. Near $(z'_0,w_0)$ the function $U=\prod _{c\geq 2}(w-\mu _ c(z'))^{k_ c}$ does not vanish, so $f=(gU)(w-\mu _1(z'))^{k_1}$, where $gU$ is a holomorphic unit and $\mathrm d(w-\mu _1(z'))
eq 0$. That is, $(z'_0,w_0)\in V_{\mathrm{reg}}$. $\square$ Theorem 7.4.5 (Poincaré–Lelong) . Let $f$ be a holomorphic function on a complex manifold $X$ that is not identically zero on any connected component of $X$, and let $V$, $V_{\mathrm{reg}}$ and $S$ be as above. Then the current $m[V_{\mathrm{reg}}]$ on $X\setminus S$, the integration over $V_{\mathrm{reg}}$ weighted by the multiplicity $m$, has locally finite mass near $S$: its coefficient measures have finite total variation on $K\setminus S$ for every compact subset $K$ of a chart. Extending its coefficient measures by zero on $S$, we obtain a closed positive $(1,1)$-current $[\operatorname{div}(f)]$ on $X$, and 7.11  egin{equation} \label{eq:poincare-lelong-normalized} \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |f|^2=[\operatorname{div}(f)]. \end{equation} Proof. If $X$ has dimension zero, then $f$ has no zeros and both sides vanish. Let $X$ have dimension $n\geq 1$. The set of points near which $f$ vanishes identically is open, and it is closed by the identity theorem, applied in connected coordinate neighborhoods; since $f$ does not vanish identically on any component of $X$, this set is empty. Hence proposition 7.4.3 applies in every connected chart: the function $\log |f|^2$ is locally integrable, and $T=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |f|^2$, given by $T(\varphi )=\int _ X\log |f|^2\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $ independently of coordinates, is a positive current with measure coefficients. It is closed because $\mathrm d\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}=\mathrm d\mathrm d\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}=0$. We show that $T$ gives zero mass to $S$ and agrees with $m[V_{\mathrm{reg}}]$ outside $S$. Step 1: $T$ gives $S$ zero mass. Let $x_0\in S$, and choose coordinates and a polydisc $P$ centered at $x_0$ as in lemma 7.4.4 . For each $j$, the last assertion of proposition 7.4.3 shows that the diagonal coefficient $(\log |f|^2)_{j ar j}$ vanishes on $S\cap P\subset \pi _ j^{-1}(N_ j)$. By the computation of the trace measure in section 7.3 , the sum of these diagonal coefficients is a positive multiple of the trace measure of $T$ in these coordinates, which therefore vanishes on $S\cap P$; by theorem 7.2.5 so do all coefficient measures of $T$ in these coordinates. By ( 7.8 ), the vanishing of the coefficient measures on a Borel set does not depend on the chart. Every compact subset of $S\cap U$, for a chart $U$, is covered by finitely many such polydiscs $P$, so by inner regularity all coefficient measures of $T$ vanish on $S\cap U$. Step 2: $T=m[V_{\mathrm{reg}}]$ on $X\setminus S$. Since $T$ is defined without reference to coordinates, we may compute it in any holomorphic coordinates. Away from $V$ the function $\log |f|^2$ is pluriharmonic, so $T=0$ there. Near a point $p\in V_{\mathrm{reg}}$ write $f=g\, a^ m$ as above, and use holomorphic coordinates $(t,x')$ with $t=a$. Then $\log |f|^2=\log |g|^2+m\log |t|^2$, where $\log |g|^2$ is pluriharmonic. In one variable, $\partial _ t\partial _{ ar t}\log |t|^2=\pi \delta _0$ by example 3.2.4 . Since $\log |t|^2$ does not depend on $x'$, Fubini's theorem shows that its distributional derivatives involving $x'$ or $ ar x'$ vanish and that $\langle (\log |t|^2)_{t ar t},\psi angle =\pi \int \psi (0,x')\, \mathrm dV_{2n-2}(x')$ for test functions $\psi $; thus $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |t|^2=(\mathrm i/2\pi )(\log |t|^2)_{t ar t}\, \mathrm dt\wedge \mathrm d ar t$. Let $\varphi $ be a test form of bidegree $(n-1,n-1)$, and let $\varphi _0=c(t,x') igwedge _ l( rac{\mathrm i}2\mathrm dx'_ l\wedge \mathrm d ar x'_ l)$ be its component without $\mathrm dt$ and $\mathrm d ar t$, the only one that contributes. Since $(\mathrm i/2\pi )\, \mathrm dt\wedge \mathrm d ar t\wedge \varphi _0=\pi ^{-1}c\, \mathrm dV_{2n}$, we obtain \[  (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |t|^2)(\varphi )=\int c(0,x')\, \mathrm dV_{2n-2}(x')=\int _{\{ t=0\} }\varphi |_{\{ t=0\} },  \] that is, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |t|^2=[\{ t=0\} ]$ in the sense of example 7.2.7 , the hypersurface carrying its complex orientation. Therefore $T=m[V_{\mathrm{reg}}]$ near $p$. Step 3: extension across $S$. Let $U$ be a chart and $K\subset U$ compact. By Step 2, the trace measure of the positive current $m[V_{\mathrm{reg}}]$ on $U\setminus S$ is the restriction of $\mu _ T$, so its mass on $K\setminus S$ is at most $\mu _ T(K)<\infty $. By the coefficient bound of theorem 7.2.5 , applied on $U\setminus S$, the coefficient measures of $m[V_{\mathrm{reg}}]$, a positive current of bidegree $(1,1)$, have total variation at most $C_{n,1}\mu _ T(K)$ on $K\setminus S$. Hence they extend by zero on $S$ to complex Radon measures on $U$. Indeed, each coefficient measure $\sigma $ is a complex combination of the positive and negative variations of $\operatorname{Re}\sigma $ and $\operatorname{Im}\sigma $, which are positive Radon measures on $U\setminus S$ bounded by $|\sigma |$; extended by zero on $S$, they become Borel measures on $U$ that are finite on compact sets, hence Radon by proposition 1.1.2 . By Step 2 the coefficient measures of $T$ agree with those of $m[V_{\mathrm{reg}}]$ on $U\setminus S$, and by Step 1 they vanish on $S$. Thus the extensions by zero are the coefficient measures of the current $T$ of order zero; we denote this current by $[\operatorname{div}(f)]$. This proves ( 7.11 ), and $[\operatorname{div}(f)]=T$ is positive and closed. $\square$ Example 7.4.6 . Let $1\leq r\leq n$ and $f(z)=z_1^{a_1}\cdots z_ r^{a_ r}$ on $\mathbb C^ n$, with positive integers $a_ j$. Then $\log |f|^2=\sum _ ja_ j\log |z_ j|^2$ everywhere, both sides being $-\infty $ on the zero set, and theorem 7.4.5 applied to each $z_ j$ gives $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |f|^2=\sum _{j=1}^ r a_ j[\{ z_ j=0\} ]$ on all of $\mathbb C^ n$, including the intersections of the coordinate hyperplanes. More generally, let $g$ and $h$ be holomorphic and not identically zero on a connected coordinate neighborhood. The function $\log |g|^2-\log |h|^2$, defined outside the null set where $g$ or $h$ vanishes, is locally integrable, and its complex Hessian is $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\log |g|^2-\log |h|^2)=[\operatorname{div}(g)]-[\operatorname{div}(h)]$. This current depends only on the quotient $g/h$: if $g',h'$ is another such pair with $gh'=g'h$, the two logarithmic differences agree almost everywhere, hence as distributions. We regard the difference only as an element of $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$; in particular, it is assigned no values at the common zeros of $g$ and $h$.

title: Holomorphic zero null
topic: Complex differential forms and positive currents
text:
Lemma 7.4.1 . Let $f$ be a holomorphic function on a domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$, $n\ge 1$, that is not identically zero. Then the zero set of $f$ has Lebesgue measure zero. Let $P\subset \Omega $ be a polydisc, let $1\leq j\leq n$, and write $P=P'	imes D$ and points of $P$ as $(z',z_ j)$, where $D\subset \mathbb C$ is a disc in the variable $z_ j$ and $z'$ consists of the other coordinates. Then the set of points $z'\in P'$ such that $z_ j\mapsto f(z',z_ j)$ vanishes identically on $D$ is a Lebesgue null subset of $\mathbb C^{n-1}$; for $n=1$ it is empty. Moreover, for every zero $a$ of $f$ there is a complex linear coordinate system centered at $a$ such that $f$ does not vanish identically on any of the coordinate axes through $a$. Proof. We prove the first two assertions together by induction on $n$. For $n=1$, every zero of $f$ is isolated: at a zero $a$, the Taylor expansion has a first nonzero term $c(z-a)^ m$, since otherwise $f$ would vanish near $a$ and hence on $\Omega $ by the identity theorem; so $f(z)=(z-a)^ mg(z)$ with $g(a)
eq 0$. Hence the zero set meets every compact subset of $\Omega $ in a finite set, and since $\Omega $ is a countable union of compact sets, it is countable, hence null. Moreover, $f$ does not vanish identically on a disc $D\subset \Omega $, by the identity theorem, which proves the second assertion for $n=1$. Let $n\geq 2$, and let $P=P'	imes D$ be as in the statement; after permuting the coordinates, which preserves Lebesgue measure, we may assume that $j=n$, and we write $w=z_ n$ and $w_0$ for the center of $D$. The functions $c_ k(z')=\partial _ w^ kf(z',w_0)/k!$ are holomorphic on $P'$, and, by the one-variable Taylor expansion of $w\mapsto f(z',w)$ on the disc $D$ centered at $w_0$, this function vanishes identically on $D$ if and only if all $c_ k(z')$ vanish. Since $f$ does not vanish identically on the nonempty open set $P$, by the identity theorem, some $c_ k$ is not identically zero on the polydisc $P'$, and its zero set $N\subset P'$ is null by the first assertion in dimension $n-1$. This proves the second assertion in dimension $n$, since the set in question is contained in $N$. For $z'
otin N$, the zero set of $w\mapsto f(z',w)$ in $D$ is null by the case $n=1$. By Tonelli's theorem, applied to the indicator function of the relatively closed zero set of $f$ in $P$, this zero set is null; and countably many such polydiscs, for instance those with rational centers and radii contained in $\Omega $, cover $\Omega $. For the last assertion, translate $a$ to the origin and let $P_ m$ be the first nonzero term of the homogeneous expansion of $f$ at $0$; it exists because $f$ does not vanish identically near $0$, and $m\geq 1$ because $f(0)=0$. The set $\{ P_ m
eq 0\} $ is open and dense in $\mathbb C^ n$, because a polynomial vanishing on a nonempty open set is zero: its derivatives at a point $b$ of that set vanish, and the polynomial is the sum of its finite Taylor expansion at $b$. Choose $v_1\in \{ P_ m
eq 0\} $, and inductively $v_ j\in \{ P_ m
eq 0\} $ outside the linear span of $v_1,\ldots ,v_{j-1}$; this is possible because the complement of a proper linear subspace is open and dense, and the intersection of two dense open sets is dense. Then $v_1,\ldots ,v_ n$ is a basis, and $f(tv_ j)=t^ mP_ m(v_ j)+O(t^{m+1})$ by ( 7.2 ), so $t\mapsto f(tv_ j)$ does not vanish identically near $t=0$. Taking $v_1,\ldots ,v_ n$ as coordinate axes proves the assertion. $\square$

title: Weierstrass preparation
topic: Complex differential forms and positive currents
text:
Theorem 7.4.2 (Weierstrass preparation) . Let $f$ be holomorphic on a neighborhood $U$ of $0$ in $\mathbb {C}^{n-1}	imes \mathbb {C}$, $n\geq 1$, and suppose that $w\mapsto f(0,w)$ has a zero of order $m\ge 1$ at $w=0$. Then there are polydiscs $P'	imes \{ |w|<ho \} \subset U$ centered at $0$ with arbitrarily small radii, and numbers $ho _1\in (0,ho )$, such that on $P'	imes \{ |w|<ho \} $ \[  f(z',w)=g(z',w)W(z',w),\qquad W=w^ m+a_1(z')w^{m-1}+\cdots +a_ m(z'),  \] where $g$ is holomorphic and nowhere zero, the coefficients $a_ j$ are holomorphic on $P'$ with $a_ j(0)=0$, and for every $z'\in P'$ the $m$ roots of $W(z',\cdot )$ lie in $\{ |w|<ho _1\} $. Proof. Since the zeros of $f(0,\cdot )$ are isolated, there is $ho _0>0$ such that $\{ 0\} 	imes \{ |w|\leq ho _0\} \subset U$ and $f(0,w)
eq 0$ for $0<|w|\leq ho _0$. Let $0<ho <ho _0$, and choose $ho _1<ho <ho _2\leq ho _0$. Then $f(0,w)
eq 0$ on the compact annulus $\{ ho _1\leq |w|\leq ho _2\} $. Since $|f(0,\cdot )|$ has a positive minimum on this annulus and $f$ is uniformly continuous on a compact neighborhood of $\{ 0\} 	imes \{ ho _1\leq |w|\leq ho _2\} $ in $U$, there is a polydisc $P'$ centered at $0$, as small as we wish, such that $P'	imes \{ |w|\leq ho _2\} \subset U$ and $f(z',w)
eq 0$ for $z'\in P'$ and $ho _1\leq |w|\leq ho _2$. By the argument principle, the number of zeros of $f(z',\cdot )$ in $\{ |w|<ho \} $, counted with multiplicity, is \[   rac{1}{2\pi \mathrm{i}}\int _{|w|=ho } rac{f_ w(z',w)}{f(z',w)}\, \mathrm{d}w,  \] a continuous integer-valued function of $z'$ on the connected set $P'$; hence it equals its value $m$ at $z'=0$. Denote these zeros by $\lambda _1(z'),\ldots ,\lambda _ m(z')$, in any order; they lie in $\{ |w|<ho _1\} $. By the residue theorem, their power sums are \[  p_ k(z')=\sum _{l=1}^ m\lambda _ l(z')^ k= rac{1}{2\pi \mathrm{i}}\int _{|w|=ho } w^ k rac{f_ w(z',w)}{f(z',w)}\, \mathrm{d}w,\qquad 1\leq k\leq m,  \] which are holomorphic functions on $P'$, by differentiation under the integral sign. The elementary symmetric functions $e_ k$ of the roots satisfy Newton's identities \[  ke_ k=\sum _{j=1}^ k(-1)^{j-1}e_{k-j}p_ j,\qquad e_0=1.  \] To prove them, put $E(t)=\prod _ l(1+t\lambda _ l)=\sum _ ke_ kt^ k$ and compare the coefficients of $t^{k-1}$ in $E'(t)=E(t)\sum _{j\geq 1}(-1)^{j-1}p_ jt^{j-1}$, which is the expansion of the logarithmic derivative $E'/E=\sum _ l\lambda _ l/(1+t\lambda _ l)$. By induction on $k$, every $e_ k$ is holomorphic on $P'$. Hence $W(z',w)=\prod _ l(w-\lambda _ l(z'))$ is a monic polynomial in $w$ with holomorphic coefficients $a_ k=(-1)^ ke_ k$, and $a_ k(0)=0$ because all $\lambda _ l(0)=0$. It remains to show that $f/W$ extends to a nowhere vanishing holomorphic function on $P'	imes \{ |w|<ho \} $. For fixed $z'\in P'$, the functions $f(z',\cdot )$ and $W(z',\cdot )$ have the same zeros, with the same multiplicities, in $\{ |w|<ho _2\} $; so $f/W$ and $W/f$ extend to holomorphic functions of $w$ there. On the annulus $\{ ho _1<|w|<ho _2\} $ both quotients are holomorphic in $(z',w)$. The Cauchy integral \[  G(z',w)= rac{1}{2\pi \mathrm i}\int _{|\zeta |=ho } rac{(f/W)(z',\zeta )}{\zeta -w}\, \mathrm d\zeta ,\qquad |w|<ho ,  \] is holomorphic in $(z',w)$, by differentiation under the integral sign, and equals $f/W$ by Cauchy's formula in $w$. Defining $\widetilde G$ in the same way from $W/f$, we obtain $G\widetilde G=1$. Thus $g=G$ is holomorphic and nowhere zero, and $f=gW$. $\square$

title: Holomorphic logarithm hessian
topic: Complex differential forms and positive currents
text:
Proposition 7.4.3 . Let $f$ be holomorphic on a domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$, $n\geq 1$, and not identically zero, and put $\log |f|^2=-\infty $ on the zero set of $f$. Then $\log |f|^2$ is locally integrable, it is the canonical subharmonic representative of its class, and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |f|^2\geq 0$. Moreover, let $P\subset \Omega $ be a polydisc, let $1\leq j\leq n$, and write points of $P$ as $(z',z_ j)$, where $z'$ consists of the coordinates other than $z_ j$. Then for every test function $\varphi $ on $P$, 7.10  egin{equation} \label{eq:logarithm-coordinate-slices}  ig \langle (\log |f|^2)_{j ar j},\varphi  ig angle =\pi \int _{\mathbb {C}^{n-1}}\sum _{a:\, f(z',a)=0} m(z',a)\varphi (z',a)\, \mathrm{d}V_{2n-2}(z'), \end{equation} where the sum runs over the zeros $a$ of $z_ j\mapsto f(z',z_ j)$ in the fiber of $P$ over $z'$, and $m(z',a)$ is the order of that zero; the integrand is defined outside the null set of those $z'$ over which $f$ vanishes identically on the fiber. In particular, if $\pi _ j$ is the projection of $P$ omitting $z_ j$, the positive measure $(\log |f|^2)_{j ar j}$ gives zero mass to $\pi _ j^{-1}(N)$ for every Lebesgue null set $N$. Proof. Local integrability. Near a point where $f
eq 0$, the function $\log |f|^2$ is smooth. Let $a$ be a zero of $f$.
