Since $L_ j$ is a complex line, $c_ j=x_ j+\langle p-x_ j,e_ jangle e_ j$ and $\langle c_ j-p,e_ jangle =0$ for the Hermitian inner product, so $\operatorname{Re}\langle c_ j-p,se_ jangle =0$ and $|c_ j+se_ j-p|^2=|c_ j-p|^2+|s|^2$ for $s\in \mathbb {C}$. Hence $L_ j\cap \partial B$ is the circle $\{ c_ j+ho _ j\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}	heta }e_ j\} $ with $ho _ j=(r^2-|c_ j-p|^2)^{1/2}	o r$. Since $|c_ j+ho _ j\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}	heta }e_ j-p-r\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}	heta }e|\leq |c_ j-p|+|ho _ j-r|+r|e_ j-e|$, these circles converge uniformly in $	heta $ to $\Gamma =\{ p+r\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}	heta }e\} $. The distance from the compact set $\Gamma $ to the closed complement of the open set $O$ is positive, so the circles lie in $O$ for large $j$. For such $j$, the closed disc $\Delta _ j=L_ j\cap \overline B$ lies in $\Omega \setminus S$, and the restriction of $u$ to the connected component of $L_ j\cap (\Omega \setminus S)$ containing $\Delta _ j$ is subharmonic or identically $-\infty $. Its values on the boundary circle of $\Delta _ j$ are less than $C+1$, so the maximum principle, that is, theorem 3.1.3 with the constant harmonic function $C+1$, gives $u\leq C+1$ on $\Delta _ j$. Since $x_ j\in B\cap L_ j\subset \Delta _ j$, this gives $u(x_ j)\leq C+1$, contradicting $u(x_ j)	o +\infty $. Hence $u$ is bounded above near every point of $S$. Step 2: the subharmonic extension. By lemma 8.4.2 (1), every compact set $S\cap \overline B$ as above is real polar. Countably many such sets cover $S$, so $S$ is real polar by proposition 4.2.3 . By Step 1 and the upper semicontinuity of $u$ on $\Omega \setminus S$, the function $u$ is bounded above on $K\setminus S$ for every compact $K\subset \Omega $. Moreover $u$ is subharmonic on $\Omega \setminus S$ by theorem 8.2.1 . By theorem 3.5.2 , $u$ has a subharmonic extension $\widetilde u$ to $\Omega $, given on $S$ by the upper-limit formula. Since $S$ is Lebesgue null and $u$ is finite almost everywhere on $\Omega \setminus S$, the function $\widetilde u$ is not identically $-\infty $ on the domain $\Omega $, so it is locally integrable. Step 3: $\widetilde u$ is plurisubharmonic. We verify the hypothesis of lemma 8.1.2 for the locally integrable function $\widetilde u$. Fix a unit vector $a\in \mathbb {C}^ n$ and a nonnegative $\chi \in C^\infty _ c(\Omega )$, and write $z=v+ta$ with $v\in (\mathbb {C}a)^\perp $ and $t\in \mathbb {C}$, as in that lemma. The compact set $S\cap \operatorname{Supp}\chi $ is $\mathcal H^{2n-3}$-null, since it is covered by finitely many of the sets $S\cap \overline B$ of the first paragraph, so by lemma 8.4.2 (3) its orthogonal projection onto $(\mathbb {C}a)^\perp $ is Lebesgue null. For $v$ outside this projection, the line $\{ v+ta:t\in \mathbb {C}\} $ meets $\operatorname{Supp}\chi $ only in $\Omega \setminus S$. Thus the open set $G_ v=\{ t:v+ta\in \Omega \setminus S\} $ contains $K_ v=\{ t:v+ta\in \operatorname{Supp}\chi \} $, and its connected components are the connected components of an affine complex-line section of $\Omega \setminus S$, on each of which the restriction of $\widetilde u=u$ is subharmonic or identically $-\infty $. As $a$ and $\chi $ are arbitrary, lemma 8.1.2 gives $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\widetilde u\geq 0$. Since $\widetilde u$ is a locally integrable subharmonic function, it is the canonical representative of its class, and it is plurisubharmonic by theorem 8.2.1 . Uniqueness follows from the same theorem, since two plurisubharmonic extensions agree outside the Lebesgue null set $S$. $\square$

title: Psh bounded zero extension
text:
Theorem 8.4.1 . Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb {C}^ n$ be a domain, $n\ge 1$, and let $S\subset \Omega $ be relatively closed. Assume that every point of $S$ has a connected neighborhood $W\subset \Omega $ with a holomorphic function $f
ot\equiv 0$ on $W$ such that $S\cap W\subset \{ f=0\} $. Let $u$ be a plurisubharmonic function on $\Omega \setminus S$ that is locally bounded above near $S$, that is, every point of $S$ has a neighborhood $W$ such that $u$ is bounded above on $W\setminus S$. Then $u$ has a unique plurisubharmonic extension $\widetilde u$ to $\Omega $, and its value at $x\in S$ is \[  \widetilde u(x)=\varlimsup _{\Omega \setminus S
i y	o x}u(y).  \] Proof. Define $\widetilde u$ by $u$ on $\Omega \setminus S$ and by the displayed formula on $S$. Since plurisubharmonicity is a local property, it suffices to show that every point $x_0\in S$ has a neighborhood on which $\widetilde u$ is plurisubharmonic; uniqueness is proved at the end. By hypothesis there are a connected neighborhood $W_0$ of $x_0$ with a holomorphic function $f
ot\equiv 0$ on $W_0$ such that $S\cap W_0\subset \{ f=0\} $, and a neighborhood $W_1$ of $x_0$ such that $u$ is bounded above on $W_1\setminus S$. Choose a ball $W$ about $x_0$ with $\overline W\subset W_0\cap W_1$. By the identity theorem, $f$ does not vanish identically on $W$, and $u$ is bounded above on $W\setminus S$. Multiplying $f$ by a nonzero constant, we may assume that $|f|\leq 1$, that is, $\log |f|^2\le 0$, on $W$. For $\varepsilon >0$ define $u_\varepsilon $ on $W$ by \[  u_\varepsilon =u+\varepsilon \log |f|^2\quad 	ext{on }W\setminus S,\qquad u_\varepsilon =-\infty \quad 	ext{on }S\cap W.  \] Step 1: $u_\varepsilon \in \mathrm{PSH}(W)$. At a point $x\in S\cap W$ we have $f(x)=0$, so $\log |f(y)|^2	o -\infty $ as $y	o x$, while $u$ is bounded above near $x$; hence $u_\varepsilon (y)	o -\infty $ as $y	o x$, and $u_\varepsilon $ is upper semicontinuous at $x$. On $W\setminus S$, $u_\varepsilon $ is upper semicontinuous as a sum of upper semicontinuous functions. Now let $\Lambda $ be a connected component of $L\cap W$ for an affine complex line $L$. If $f$ vanishes identically on $\Lambda $, then $u_\varepsilon \equiv -\infty $ on $\Lambda $. Otherwise the zeros of $f$ on the connected set $\Lambda $ are isolated, by the identity theorem in one variable. Since $S$ is relatively closed, $A=S\cap \Lambda $ is therefore a closed discrete subset of $\Lambda $, hence countable, because each of the countably many compact sets exhausting $\Lambda $ contains only finitely many of its points. It is polar, because points are polar in the plane and countable unions of polar sets are polar by proposition 4.2.3 . Each connected component of $\Lambda \setminus A$ is a connected subset of $L\cap (\Omega \setminus S)$ and therefore lies in a connected component of this line section, on which the restriction of $u$ is subharmonic or identically $-\infty $. Hence the restriction of $u$ to $\Lambda \setminus A$ is subharmonic, the constant $-\infty $ being subharmonic. The function $\log |f|^2$ is subharmonic on $\Lambda $ by example 3.2.4 . Thus $u_\varepsilon $ is subharmonic on $\Lambda \setminus A$, and it is bounded above there by $\sup _{W\setminus S}u$, because $\log |f|^2\leq 0$. By theorem 3.5.2 , it has a subharmonic extension to $\Lambda $ whose value at $x\in A$ is $\varlimsup _{\Lambda \setminus A
i y	o x}u_\varepsilon (y)=-\infty $, which is the value of $u_\varepsilon $ at $x$. Hence the restriction of $u_\varepsilon $ to $\Lambda $ is subharmonic. Finally, $u_\varepsilon $ is not identically $-\infty $, because $u$ is finite almost everywhere on $W\setminus S$ and $\{ f=0\} $ is Lebesgue null by lemma 7.4.1 . Thus $u_\varepsilon \in \mathrm{PSH}(W)$. Step 2: the extension. As $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ the functions $u_\varepsilon $ increase, because $\log |f|^2\leq 0$, and they are bounded above on $W$ by $\sup _{W\setminus S}u$. Let $F=\sup _{\varepsilon >0}u_\varepsilon $. By theorem 8.3.2 , $F^*\in \mathrm{PSH}(W)$ and $F^*=F$ almost everywhere. Since $F=u$ outside the null set $\{ f=0\} $, we get $F^*=u$ almost everywhere on $W\setminus S$; both functions are locally integrable and subharmonic there, so $F^*=u$ everywhere on $W\setminus S$ by theorem 3.2.2 . It remains to show that $F^*=\widetilde u$ on $S\cap W$, which is Lebesgue null as a subset of $\{ f=0\} $. Let $x\in S\cap W$. Since $F^*=u$ on $W\setminus S$, the upper semicontinuity of $F^*$ gives $\widetilde u(x)=\varlimsup _{W\setminus S
i y	o x}u(y)\leq F^*(x)$. Conversely, for small $r>0$ the ball submean inequality for $F^*$ gives $F^*(x)\leq |B(x,r)|^{-1}\int _{B(x,r)\setminus S}F^*\, \mathrm dV\leq \sup _{B(x,r)\setminus S}u$, because removing the null set $S$ does not change the integral, and letting $r	o 0$ gives $F^*(x)\leq \widetilde u(x)$. Hence $\widetilde u=F^*$ on $W$, and $\widetilde u$ is plurisubharmonic on $W$. Uniqueness. The set $S$ is Lebesgue null, since it is covered by countably many neighborhoods $W$ as in the hypothesis and $S\cap W\subset \{ f=0\} $ is null. Two plurisubharmonic extensions of $u$ therefore agree almost everywhere, and hence everywhere by theorem 8.2.1 . $\square$

title: Small set polar directions
text:
Lemma 8.4.2 . Let $n\ge 2$ and let $K\subset \mathbb {C}^ n$ be a compact $\mathcal H^{2n-3}$-null set. Then: $K$ is real polar; for every $x\in \mathbb {C}^ n$, the set of directions from $x$ of the points of $K\setminus \{ x\} $ has $\sigma $-measure zero; the orthogonal projection of $K$ onto any complex hyperplane is Lebesgue null. Proof. (1) Suppose that $K$ is not polar. By theorem 4.3.3 , $K$ carries a nonzero positive measure of finite energy; dividing it by its mass, we obtain a probability measure $\mu $ on $K$ of finite energy $I(\mu )$ for the Newtonian kernel $k(x,y)=|x-y|^{2-2n}/((2n-2)s_{2n-1})$ of section 4.1 in $\mathbb R^{2n}$. Its potential $U^\mu $ is lower semicontinuous, and it is finite $\mu $-almost everywhere because $\int U^\mu \, \mathrm d\mu =I(\mu )<\infty $. The sets $E_ M=K\cap \{ U^\mu \le M\} $, $M\in \mathbb N$, are compact, because $U^\mu $ is lower semicontinuous, and they increase to a set of full $\mu $-measure; hence $\mu (E_ M)>0$ for $M$ large enough. Let $
u $ be the restriction of $\mu $ to $E_ M$. For $a\in E_ M$ and $r>0$, \[   rac{r^{2-2n}\, 
u (B(a,r))}{(2n-2)s_{2n-1}}\leq \int _{B(a,r)}k(a,y)\, \mathrm d
u (y)\leq U^\mu (a)\leq M,  \] so $
u (B(a,r))\le C_ nMr^{2n-2}$ with $C_ n=(2n-2)s_{2n-1}$. Now cover $E_ M$ by balls $B(c_ l,r_ l)$ with $r_ l<1$ and $\sum _ lr_ l^{2n-3}<\eta $, and discard those not meeting $E_ M$. Each remaining ball lies in $B(a_ l,2r_ l)$ for some $a_ l\in E_ M$, so \[  
u (E_ M)\leq \sum _ l
u (B(a_ l,2r_ l))\leq 2^{2n-2}C_ nM\sum _ lr_ l^{2n-2}\leq 2^{2n-2}C_ nM\eta ,  \] where we used $r_ l<1$. Since $\eta >0$ is arbitrary, $
u (E_ M)=0$, a contradiction. Hence $K$ is polar. (2) Fix $x$. For $m\geq 1$ the set $K_ m=K\cap \{ |y-x|\geq 1/m\} $ is compact and $\mathcal H^{2n-3}$-null, and $K\setminus \{ x\} = igcup _ mK_ m$. The direction map $\Phi (y)=[y-x]$ is Lipschitz on $K_ m$. Indeed, $\Phi (y)=[(y-x)/|y-x|]$. The normalization $y\mapsto (y-x)/|y-x|$ has Lipschitz constant at most $2m$ on $\{ |y-x|\geq 1/m\} $: for nonzero vectors $a,b$, \[  \Bigl | rac a{|a|}- rac b{|b|}\Bigr |\leq  rac{|a-b|}{|a|}+|b|\, \Bigl | rac1{|a|}- rac1{|b|}\Bigr |= rac{|a-b|+ igl ||b|-|a| igr |}{|a|}\leq  rac{2|a-b|}{|a|},  \] and we apply this with $a=y-x$, $b=y'-x$ and $|a|\geq 1/m$. The Hopf map is Lipschitz with constant $\pi /2$ for the metric $d$. Indeed, let $e,e'$ be unit vectors and $\delta =\arccos \operatorname{Re}\langle e,e'angle \in [0,\pi ]$ their spherical distance. Since $d$ is the minimum of the spherical distance over the unit representatives (section 6.3 ), we have $d([e],[e'])\leq \delta $. Moreover $|e-e'|^2=2-2\cos \delta =4\sin ^2(\delta /2)$, and $\sin s\geq 2s/\pi $ for $0\leq s\leq \pi /2$, so $|e-e'|\geq 2\delta /\pi $. Hence \[  d([e],[e'])\leq \delta \leq 	frac \pi 2|e-e'|.  \] Since Lipschitz images of $\mathcal H^{2n-3}$-null sets are $\mathcal H^{2n-3}$-null, the compact set $\Phi (K_ m)$ is $\mathcal H^{2n-3}$-null in $(\mathbb P^{n-1}(\mathbb C),d)$. Cover it by balls of radii $r_ l<1$ with $\sum _ lr_ l^{2n-3}<\eta $. By lemma 6.3.2 , and since $r_ l<1$, we have $\sigma (\Phi (K_ m))\leq \sum _ lr_ l^{2n-2}<\eta $, so $\sigma (\Phi (K_ m))=0$. Hence the set of directions $\Phi (K\setminus \{ x\} )= igcup _ m\Phi (K_ m)$ is a Borel set of $\sigma $-measure zero. (3) An orthogonal projection onto a complex hyperplane $H\cong \mathbb R^{2n-2}$ is $1$-Lipschitz. Hence the projection of $K$ is $\mathcal H^{2n-3}$-null in $H$, and therefore Lebesgue null because $2n-3<2n-2$. $\square$

title: Psh small set extension
text: Theorem 8.4.3 . Let $n\ge 2$, let $\Omega \subset \mathbb {C}^ n$ be a domain, and let $S\subset \Omega $ be relatively closed and locally $\mathcal H^{2n-3}$-null, that is, every point of $S$ has a neighborhood $W$ such that $S\cap W$ is $\mathcal H^{2n-3}$-null. Then every plurisubharmonic function on $\Omega \setminus S$ extends uniquely to a plurisubharmonic function on $\Omega $, given on $S$ by the same upper-limit formula as in theorem 8.4.1 . Proof. Let $u$ be a plurisubharmonic function on $\Omega \setminus S$. For every closed ball $\overline B\subset \Omega $, the compact set $S\cap \overline B$ is covered by finitely many neighborhoods $W$ as in the hypothesis, and is therefore $\mathcal H^{2n-3}$-null. Step 1: $u$ is locally bounded above near $S$. Fix $p\in S$ and $r>0$ with $\overline B=\overline{B(p,r)}\subset \Omega $, and write $B=B(p,r)$. By lemma 8.4.2 (2) applied with $x=p$, almost every complex line through $p$ meets $S\cap \overline B$ only at $p$; fix such a line $L=\{ p+te:t\in \mathbb {C}\} $, with $|e|=1$. The circle $\Gamma =L\cap \partial B$ is a compact subset of $\Omega \setminus S$, so the upper semicontinuous function $u$ is bounded above on $\Gamma $ by a finite constant $C$, and the open set $O=\{ y\in \Omega \setminus S:u(y)<C+1\} $ contains $\Gamma $. Suppose that $u$ is not bounded above near $p$. Then there are points $x_ j\in B\setminus S$ with $x_ j\to p$ and $u(x_ j)\to +\infty $. For each $j$, lemma 8.4.2 (2) applied with $x=x_ j$ shows that the directions of the lines through $x_ j$ meeting $S\cap \overline B$ form a $\sigma $-null set. Every nonempty open ball in $\mathbb P^{n-1}(\mathbb C)$ has positive $\sigma $-measure by lemma 6.3.2 , so the complement of this null set is dense. We can therefore choose directions $\xi _ j$ outside this null set with $d(\xi _ j,[e])<1/j$. Since $d$ is the minimum of the spherical distance over the unit representatives, $\xi _ j$ has a unit representative $e_ j$ whose spherical distance to $e$ is less than $1/j$, and then $|e_ j-e|<1/j$, because a chord is shorter than the arc. Thus $e_ j\to e$, and the lines $L_ j=\{ x_ j+te_ j:t\in \mathbb {C}\} $ do not meet $S\cap \overline B$. We claim that $L_ j\cap \partial B\subset O$ for all large $j$. Let $c_ j$ be the point of $L_ j$ closest to $p$, that is, the orthogonal projection of $p$ to $L_ j$; then $|c_ j-p|\leq |x_ j-p|\to 0$. Since $L_ j$ is a complex line, $c_ j=x_ j+\langle p-x_ j,e_ j\rangle e_ j$ and $\langle c_ j-p,e_ j\rangle =0$ for the Hermitian inner product, so $\operatorname{Re}\langle c_ j-p,se_ j\rangle =0$ and $|c_ j+se_ j-p|^2=|c_ j-p|^2+|s|^2$ for $s\in \mathbb {C}$. Hence $L_ j\cap \partial B$ is the circle $\{ c_ j+\rho _ j\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta }e_ j\} $ with $\rho _ j=(r^2-|c_ j-p|^2)^{1/2}\to r$. Since $|c_ j+\rho _ j\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta }e_ j-p-r\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta }e|\leq |c_ j-p|+|\rho _ j-r|+r|e_ j-e|$, these circles converge uniformly in $\theta $ to $\Gamma =\{ p+r\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta }e\} $. The distance from the compact set $\Gamma $ to the closed complement of the open set $O$ is positive, so the circles lie in $O$ for large $j$. For such $j$, the closed disc $\Delta _ j=L_ j\cap \overline B$ lies in $\Omega \setminus S$, and the restriction of $u$ to the connected component of $L_ j\cap (\Omega \setminus S)$ containing $\Delta _ j$ is subharmonic or identically $-\infty $. Its values on the boundary circle of $\Delta _ j$ are less than $C+1$, so the maximum principle, that is, theorem 3.1.3 with the constant harmonic function $C+1$, gives $u\leq C+1$ on $\Delta _ j$. Since $x_ j\in B\cap L_ j\subset \Delta _ j$, this gives $u(x_ j)\leq C+1$, contradicting $u(x_ j)\to +\infty $. Hence $u$ is bounded above near every point of $S$. Step 2: the subharmonic extension. By lemma 8.4.2 (1), every compact set $S\cap \overline B$ as above is real polar. Countably many such sets cover $S$, so $S$ is real polar by proposition 4.2.3 . By Step 1 and the upper semicontinuity of $u$ on $\Omega \setminus S$, the function $u$ is bounded above on $K\setminus S$ for every compact $K\subset \Omega $. Moreover $u$ is subharmonic on $\Omega \setminus S$ by theorem 8.2.1 . By theorem 3.5.2 , $u$ has a subharmonic extension $\widetilde u$ to $\Omega $, given on $S$ by the upper-limit formula. Since $S$ is Lebesgue null and $u$ is finite almost everywhere on $\Omega \setminus S$, the function $\widetilde u$ is not identically $-\infty $ on the domain $\Omega $, so it is locally integrable. Step 3: $\widetilde u$ is plurisubharmonic. We verify the hypothesis of lemma 8.1.2 for the locally integrable function $\widetilde u$. Fix a unit vector $a\in \mathbb {C}^ n$ and a nonnegative $\chi \in C^\infty _ c(\Omega )$, and write $z=v+ta$ with $v\in (\mathbb {C}a)^\perp $ and $t\in \mathbb {C}$, as in that lemma. The compact set $S\cap \operatorname{Supp}\chi $ is $\mathcal H^{2n-3}$-null, since it is covered by finitely many of the sets $S\cap \overline B$ of the first paragraph, so by lemma 8.4.2 (3) its orthogonal projection onto $(\mathbb {C}a)^\perp $ is Lebesgue null. For $v$ outside this projection, the line $\{ v+ta:t\in \mathbb {C}\} $ meets $\operatorname{Supp}\chi $ only in $\Omega \setminus S$. Thus the open set $G_ v=\{ t:v+ta\in \Omega \setminus S\} $ contains $K_ v=\{ t:v+ta\in \operatorname{Supp}\chi \} $, and its connected components are the connected components of an affine complex-line section of $\Omega \setminus S$, on each of which the restriction of $\widetilde u=u$ is subharmonic or identically $-\infty $. As $a$ and $\chi $ are arbitrary, lemma 8.1.2 gives $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\widetilde u\geq 0$. Since $\widetilde u$ is a locally integrable subharmonic function, it is the canonical representative of its class, and it is plurisubharmonic by theorem 8.2.1 . Uniqueness follows from the same theorem, since two plurisubharmonic extensions agree outside the Lebesgue null set $S$. $\square$

title: Kiselman's minimum principle
text:
8.5 Kiselman's minimum principle An infimum of plurisubharmonic functions need not be plurisubharmonic. For instance, the function $v(z,w)=|w|^2+2\operatorname{Re}(zw)=|w+\bar z|^2-|z|^2$ is plurisubharmonic on $\mathbb {C}^2$, since $2\operatorname{Re}(zw)$ is pluriharmonic, but $\inf _{w\in \mathbb {C}}v(z,w)=-|z|^2$ is not. Kiselman's minimum principle shows that, under convexity assumptions on the domain, the infimum is plurisubharmonic or identically $-\infty $ if it is taken only over the real parts of some variables and the function does not depend on their imaginary parts. The reason is visible for a smooth function $u(z,w)$ that depends only on $z$ and $\operatorname{Re}w$. Its complex Hessian in $w$ is a quarter of its real Hessian in $\operatorname{Re}w$, and at a nondegenerate minimum over $\operatorname{Re}w$, the complex Hessian of the infimum is the Schur complement of the $w$-block in the complex Hessian of $u$, which is positive semidefinite. Throughout this section, points of $\mathbb {C}^ m\times \mathbb {C}^ k$ are written $(z,w)$, and $w=t+\mathrm{i}s$ with $t=\operatorname{Re}w$ and $s=\operatorname{Im}w$ in $\mathbb R^ k$. A set $\Omega \subset \mathbb {C}^ m\times \mathbb {C}^ k$ is invariant under imaginary translations if $(z,w+\mathrm{i}s')\in \Omega $ for all $(z,w)\in \Omega $ and $s'\in \mathbb R^ k$. A function $u$ on such a set is invariant under imaginary translations if $u(z,w+\mathrm{i}s')=u(z,w)$ for all such $(z,w)$ and $s'$, that is, if $u(z,w)$ depends only on $z$ and $\operatorname{Re}w$. For such $\Omega $ and $u$, we identify $t\in \mathbb R^ k$ with $t+\mathrm{i}0\in \mathbb {C}^ k$, so that $u(z,t)$ is defined. We write \[  V_ z=\{ t\in \mathbb R^ k:(z,t)\in \Omega \} ,\qquad \Omega _{\mathbb R}=\{ (z,t)\in \mathbb {C}^ m\times \mathbb R^ k:t\in V_ z\}   \] for the real fiber of $\Omega $ over $z\in \mathbb {C}^ m$ and the real slice of $\Omega $, and $p(\Omega )=\{ z:V_ z\neq \varnothing \} $ for the projection of $\Omega $ to $\mathbb {C}^ m$; it is the image of $\Omega $ under $(z,w)\mapsto z$, because $(z,\operatorname{Re}w)\in \Omega $ for every $(z,w)\in \Omega $ by invariance. Since this projection is continuous and open, $p(\Omega )$ is open if $\Omega $ is open, and connected if $\Omega $ is connected. Theorem 8.5.1 (Kiselman's minimum principle) . Let $m,k\ge 1$, and let $\Omega \subset \mathbb {C}^ m\times \mathbb {C}^ k$ be a domain invariant under imaginary translations whose nonempty real fibers $V_ z$ are convex. Assume that there is a plurisubharmonic function $\psi $ on $\Omega $, invariant under imaginary translations, such that for every $c\in \mathbb R$ the set \[  \{ (z,t)\in \Omega _{\mathbb R}:\psi (z,t)\le c\}   \] is compact. If $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$ is invariant under imaginary translations, then the function \[  v(z)=\inf _{t\in V_ z}u(z,t)  \] is plurisubharmonic or identically $-\infty $ on $p(\Omega )$. Proof. We first treat smooth functions with positive definite real Hessian in $t$ that tend to $+\infty $ at the boundary of the real fibers (Step 1). We then approximate $u$ by such functions on subdomains exhausting $\Omega $ (Step 2) and pass to the limit (Step 3). Step 1: a smooth case. In this step, $\Omega $ may be any open set invariant under imaginary translations whose real fibers are convex. Suppose that $u$ is smooth and plurisubharmonic, invariant under imaginary translations, and that for every $z\in p(\Omega )$ the function $t\mapsto u(z,t)$ has positive definite real Hessian on $V_ z$ and tends to $+\infty $ at the boundary of $V_ z$ and, if $V_ z$ is unbounded, as $|t|\to \infty $. We show that $v$ is plurisubharmonic on each connected component of $p(\Omega )$. Fix $z\in p(\Omega )$ and put $f(t)=u(z,t)$ for $t\in V_ z$. Since its Hessian is positive definite, $f$ is strictly convex on every segment in the open convex set $V_ z$, hence on $V_ z$. Its sublevel sets $\{ t\in V_ z:f(t)\leq c\} $ are compact: they are bounded, because $f\to +\infty $ as $|t|\to \infty $ when $V_ z$ is unbounded, and the limit in $\mathbb R^ k$ of a convergent sequence in such a set cannot lie on the boundary of $V_ z$, because $f\to +\infty $ there, so it lies in $V_ z$ and, since $f$ is continuous on $V_ z$, in the sublevel set. Hence $f$ attains its minimum on the nonempty set $V_ z$, and by strict convexity at a unique point $g(z)$. This point is the only critical point of $f$: if $\nabla f(t_1)=0$, then the convex function $s\mapsto f(t_1+s(t_2-t_1))$ has derivative zero at $s=0$, hence $f(t_2)\geq f(t_1)$ for every $t_2\in V_ z$, and $t_1=g(z)$. Fix $z_0\in p(\Omega )$. Since the $t$-Hessian is invertible, the implicit function theorem gives a smooth solution $t=G(z)$ of $\partial _ tu(z,t)=0$ near $z_0$ with $G(z_0)=g(z_0)$, and $G=g$ near $z_0$ because $g(z)$ is the only critical point. Hence $g$ and $v(z)=u(z,g(z))$ are smooth on $p(\Omega )$. At the point $(z,g(z))$, let $H=(\partial ^2u/\partial t_ a\partial t_ b)$, $B=(\partial ^2u/\partial z_ j\partial t_ a)$ and $C=(\partial ^2u/\partial z_ j\partial \bar z_ l)$. Thus $H$ is a real symmetric positive definite $k\times k$ matrix and $B$ is a complex $m\times k$ matrix; since $u$ is real, $(\partial ^2u/\partial t_ a\partial \bar z_ j)=B^*$, the conjugate transpose of $B$. Differentiating the identity $\partial _ tu(z,g(z))=0$ with respect to $\bar z$ gives $B^*+Hg_{\bar z}=0$, where $g_{\bar z}=(\partial g_ a/\partial \bar z_ j)$; hence $g_{\bar z}=-H^{-1}B^*$. By the chain rule and the same identity, $v_{z_ j}(z)=u_{z_ j}(z,g(z))$, and differentiating once more with respect to $\bar z$ gives \[  v_{z\bar z}=C+Bg_{\bar z}=C-BH^{-1}B^*.  \] On the other hand, for functions of $z$ and $\operatorname{Re}w$ we have $\partial _{w_ a}=\partial _{\bar w_ a}=\frac12\partial _{t_ a}$. Hence the complex Hessian of $u$ with respect to $(z,w)$, which is positive semidefinite by proposition 8.2.2 (1), is \[  \begin{pmatrix}  C

& B/2

\\  B^*/2

& H/4

\end{pmatrix}\ge 0.  \] Evaluating the associated Hermitian quadratic form at $(\xi ,-2H^{-1}B^*\xi )$, $\xi \in \mathbb {C}^ m$, gives $\xi ^*(C-BH^{-1}B^*)\xi \geq 0$. Thus $v_{z\bar z}\geq 0$, and the smooth function $v$ is plurisubharmonic on each component of $p(\Omega )$ by proposition 8.2.2 (1). Step 2: regularization. Now let $u$ be as in the theorem. For $\varepsilon >0$ let $u_\varepsilon =u*\rho _\varepsilon $ and $\psi _\varepsilon =\psi *\rho _\varepsilon $ on $\Omega _\varepsilon =\{ x\in \Omega :\operatorname {dist}(x,\mathbb {C}^{m+k}\setminus \Omega )>\varepsilon \} $, where $\rho _\varepsilon $ is the radial mollifier of section 1.4 . Imaginary translations are isometries preserving $\Omega $, and convolution commutes with translations, so $\Omega _\varepsilon $, $u_\varepsilon $ and $\psi _\varepsilon $ are invariant under imaginary translations. By proposition 8.2.2 , the functions $u_\varepsilon $ and $\psi _\varepsilon $ are smooth and plurisubharmonic on each connected component of $\Omega _\varepsilon $, so their complex Hessians are positive semidefinite at every point, and they decrease to $u$ and $\psi $ as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$; in particular $u_\varepsilon \geq u$ and $\psi _\varepsilon \geq \psi $. The real fibers of $\Omega _\varepsilon $ are convex. Indeed, $(z,t)\in \Omega _\varepsilon $ if and only if the closed ball of radius $\varepsilon $ about $(z,t)$ lies in $\Omega $ (if it does, its distance to the closed complement of $\Omega $ is positive, because it is compact); by invariance this means that $(z+y,t+y')\in \Omega _{\mathbb R}$ for all $(y,y')\in \mathbb {C}^ m\times \mathbb R^ k$ with $|y|^2+|y'|^2\leq \varepsilon ^2$. Hence the real fiber of $\Omega _\varepsilon $ over $z$ is the intersection of the convex sets $V_{z+y}-y'$ over these $(y,y')$. Moreover, on each real fiber of $\Omega _\varepsilon $ the function $t\mapsto \psi _\varepsilon (z,t)$ is convex, since by invariance its real Hessian is four times the complex Hessian of $\psi _\varepsilon $ in $w$, which is positive semidefinite, and a smooth function with positive semidefinite Hessian on an open convex set is convex along every segment. For $c\in \mathbb R$ let $K_ c=\{ (z,t)\in \Omega _{\mathbb R}:\psi (z,t)\le c\} $; it is a compact subset of $\Omega $. Choose $\varepsilon _ j\downarrow 0$, $j\geq 1$, such that $\operatorname {dist}(K_{j+1},\mathbb {C}^{m+k}\setminus \Omega )>4\varepsilon _ j$ whenever $K_{j+1}\neq \varnothing $. Since $\psi $ and the distance to the complement of $\Omega $ are invariant under imaginary translations, the same bound holds for the set $\{ x\in \Omega :\psi (x)\leq j+1\} =K_{j+1}+\mathrm{i}\mathbb R^ k$. Define \[  G_ j=\{ (z,w)\in \Omega _{\varepsilon _ j}:\psi _{\varepsilon _ j}(z,w)<j\} ,\qquad U_ j=u_{\varepsilon _ j}+\frac{|\operatorname{Re}w|^2}{j} +\frac{1}{j-\psi _{\varepsilon _ j}}\quad \text{on }G_ j.  \] The open set $G_ j$ is invariant under imaginary translations, and its real fiber over $z$ is a sublevel set of the convex function $\psi _{\varepsilon _ j}(z,\, \cdot \, )$ on the convex real fiber of $\Omega _{\varepsilon _ j}$, hence convex. Since $\psi \leq \psi _{\varepsilon _ j}$, the real slice of $G_ j$ is contained in the compact set $K_ j\subset K_{j+1}$, which lies in $\Omega _{\varepsilon _ j}$ at positive distance from its complement. Consequently, for each $z$, the closure of the real fiber of $G_ j$ over $z$ is a compact subset of the real fiber of $\Omega _{\varepsilon _ j}$, and $\psi _{\varepsilon _ j}(z,\, \cdot \, )=j$ on its boundary. The function $U_ j$ is smooth, plurisubharmonic and invariant under imaginary translations. Indeed, by the chain rule the complex Hessian of $1/(j-\psi _{\varepsilon _ j})$ has the entries \[  \frac{(\psi _{\varepsilon _ j})_{a\bar b}}{(j-\psi _{\varepsilon _ j})^2} +\frac{2(\psi _{\varepsilon _ j})_ a(\psi _{\varepsilon _ j})_{\bar b}}{(j-\psi _{\varepsilon _ j})^3},  \] where the subscripts denote derivatives with respect to the coordinates of $(z,w)$. Since $j-\psi _{\varepsilon _ j}>0$ on $G_ j$ and $(\psi _{\varepsilon _ j})_{\bar b}=\overline{(\psi _{\varepsilon _ j})_ b}$, this matrix is the sum of positive multiples of the complex Hessian of $\psi _{\varepsilon _ j}$ and of a positive semidefinite matrix of rank at most one, hence positive semidefinite. Moreover, $|\operatorname{Re}w|^2$ has the positive semidefinite complex Hessian in $(z,w)$ given by the diagonal matrix with entries $0$ in the $z$-directions and $\frac12$ in the $w$-directions. Hence $U_ j$ is plurisubharmonic on each connected component of $G_ j$, by proposition 8.2.2 (1). The real $t$-Hessian of $U_ j$ is positive definite: the $t$-Hessians of $u_{\varepsilon _ j}$ and $1/(j-\psi _{\varepsilon _ j})$ are positive semidefinite, as for $\psi _\varepsilon $ above, and that of $|t|^2/j$ is $(2/j)I$. On each real fiber of $G_ j$, which is bounded, $U_ j(z,t)\to +\infty $ at the boundary, because $1/(j-\psi _{\varepsilon _ j})\to +\infty $ there while the other two terms are bounded below on the compact closure of the fiber. Hence Step 1 applies to $U_ j$ on $G_ j$, and \[  v_ j(z)=\inf \{ U_ j(z,t):(z,t)\in G_ j\}   \] is plurisubharmonic on each connected component of $p(G_ j)$. Step 3: passage to the limit. The sets $G_ j$ increase to $\Omega $. Indeed, $\varepsilon _{j+1}\leq \varepsilon _ j$ gives $\Omega _{\varepsilon _ j}\subset \Omega _{\varepsilon _{j+1}}$ and $\psi _{\varepsilon _{j+1}}\leq \psi _{\varepsilon _ j}<j<j+1$ on $G_ j$. Every point $x\in \Omega $ lies in $\Omega _{\varepsilon _ j}$ for large $j$, and $\psi _{\varepsilon _ j}(x)\to \psi (x)<\infty $, so $x\in G_ j$ for large $j$. On $G_ j$ we have $U_{j+1}\leq U_ j$, since $u_{\varepsilon _{j+1}}\leq u_{\varepsilon _ j}$, $|\operatorname{Re}w|^2/(j+1)\leq |\operatorname{Re}w|^2/j$ and $0<j-\psi _{\varepsilon _ j}\leq j+1-\psi _{\varepsilon _{j+1}}$. Hence the functions $v_ j$ decrease on the increasing open sets $p(G_ j)$. They satisfy $v_ j\geq v$, since $U_ j\geq u_{\varepsilon _ j}\geq u$. Conversely, let $z\in p(\Omega )$ and $t\in V_ z$. Then $(z,t)\in G_ j$ for large $j$, and $U_ j(z,t)\to u(z,t)$, also when $u(z,t)=-\infty $, because $u_{\varepsilon _ j}(z,t)\to u(z,t)$ and the other two terms tend to zero. Hence $\lim _ jv_ j(z)\leq u(z,t)$ for every $t\in V_ z$, and therefore $v_ j\downarrow v$ on $p(\Omega )$. Let $B'\Subset p(\Omega )$ be a ball. Since $\overline{B'}$ is compact and covered by the increasing open sets $p(G_ j)$, we have $B'\subset p(G_ j)$ for large $j$, and the $v_ j$ with such $j$ form a decreasing sequence of plurisubharmonic functions on $B'$. By theorem 8.3.1 , $v$ is plurisubharmonic or identically $-\infty $ on $B'$. Since every point of the connected open set $p(\Omega )$ lies in such a ball, lemma 8.2.4 shows that $v$ is plurisubharmonic or identically $-\infty $ on $p(\Omega )$; this proves the theorem. $\square$ Corollary 8.5.2 . Let $m,k\geq 1$, let $D\subset \mathbb {C}^ m$ be a domain and let $V\subset \mathbb {R}^ k$ be a nonempty open convex set. If $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(D\times (V+\mathrm{i}\mathbb {R}^ k))$ is invariant under imaginary translations, then the function $z\mapsto \inf _{t\in V}u(z,t)$ is plurisubharmonic or identically $-\infty $ on $D$. The same holds for $z\mapsto \inf _{t\in V}(u(z,t)-\ell (t))$, for every real affine function $\ell $ on $\mathbb R^ k$. Proof. It suffices to prove the assertion on every ball $B(z_0,r)\Subset D$: since $D$ is connected, lemma 8.2.4 then gives it on $D$. We construct a function $\psi $ as in theorem 8.5.1 for the domain $B(z_0,r)\times (V+\mathrm{i}\mathbb R^ k)$, which is invariant under imaginary translations and has real fibers $V$. We first need a continuous convex function $b\geq 0$ on $V$ with compact sublevel sets. If $V=\mathbb R^ k$, take $b(t)=|t|^2$. Otherwise let $\delta (t)=\operatorname {dist}(t,\mathbb {R}^ k\setminus V)$, which is continuous and positive on $V$. It is concave on $V$: if the balls $B(t_1,r_1)$ and $B(t_2,r_2)$ lie in $V$ and $0\leq \lambda \leq 1$, then by convexity $V$ contains $\lambda B(t_1,r_1)+(1-\lambda )B(t_2,r_2)=B(\lambda t_1+(1-\lambda )t_2,\lambda r_1+(1-\lambda )r_2)$, so $\delta (\lambda t_1+(1-\lambda )t_2)\geq \lambda r_1+(1-\lambda )r_2$, and letting $r_ i\uparrow \delta (t_ i)$ gives concavity. Consequently $1/\delta $ is convex: since $x\mapsto 1/x$ is decreasing and convex on $(0,\infty )$, \[  \frac1{\delta (\lambda t_1+(1-\lambda )t_2)}\leq \frac1{\lambda \delta (t_1)+(1-\lambda )\delta (t_2)}\leq \frac\lambda {\delta (t_1)}+\frac{1-\lambda }{\delta (t_2)}.  \] Put $b(t)=|t|^2+1/\delta (t)$. For $c>0$ the set $\{ b\leq c\} $ is closed in $V$ and contained in the compact set $\{ t:|t|^2\leq c,\  \delta (t)\geq 1/c\} \subset V$, hence compact. A continuous convex function $f$ on $V$ defines a plurisubharmonic function $f(\operatorname{Re}w)$ on every domain of the form $D'\times (V+\mathrm{i}\mathbb R^ k)$. Indeed, $f(\operatorname{Re}w)$ is continuous, and its restriction to an affine complex line is $f\circ A$ for a real affine map $A$ from an open subset of $\mathbb {C}$ to $V$. If the closed disc of radius $r$ about $\zeta _0$ lies in the domain of $A$, then, since $A$ is affine, $A(\zeta _0)$ is the midpoint of $A(\zeta _0+r\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta })$ and $A(\zeta _0-r\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta })$ for every $\theta $, and the convexity of $f$ gives \[  f(A(\zeta _0))\leq \tfrac 12\bigl (f(A(\zeta _0+r\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta }))+f(A(\zeta _0-r\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta }))\bigr ).  \] Averaging over $\theta \in [0,2\pi ]$, we obtain the submean inequality for the continuous function $f\circ A$ on this circle. Now put $\psi (z,w)=(r^2-|z-z_0|^2)^{-1}+b(\operatorname{Re}w)$. This function is continuous, positive and invariant under imaginary translations. It is plurisubharmonic as a sum of two plurisubharmonic functions (proposition 8.2.5 ). The second term is plurisubharmonic by the preceding paragraph. For the first, $x\mapsto (r^2-x)^{-1}$ is convex and increasing on $(-\infty ,r^2)$ and $|z-z_0|^2$ has the complex Hessian $I$, so by the chain rule the complex Hessian of $(r^2-|z-z_0|^2)^{-1}$ is positive semidefinite, and proposition 8.2.2 (1) applies. For $c>0$, the set $\{ (z,t)\in B(z_0,r)\times V:\psi (z,t)\leq c\} $ is closed in $B(z_0,r)\times V$ and, since both terms of $\psi $ are nonnegative, contained in the compact set $\{ |z-z_0|^2\leq r^2-1/c\} \times \{ b\leq c\} $; it is therefore compact, and for $c\leq 0$ it is empty. Hence theorem 8.5.1 applies on $B(z_0,r)\times (V+\mathrm{i}\mathbb R^ k)$, and shows that $\inf _{t\in V}u(z,t)$ is plurisubharmonic or identically $-\infty $ on $B(z_0,r)$. Finally, if $\ell $ is real affine, then $\ell (\operatorname{Re}w)$ is the real part of a complex affine function of $w$. Hence $-\ell (\operatorname{Re}w)$ is smooth with vanishing complex Hessian, so it is plurisubharmonic by proposition 8.2.2 (1), and $u-\ell (\operatorname{Re}w)$ is plurisubharmonic by proposition 8.2.5 . It is invariant under imaginary translations, and the first part applies to it. $\square$

title: Kiselman's minimum principle
text:
Theorem 8.5.1 (Kiselman's minimum principle) . Let $m,k\ge 1$, and let $\Omega \subset \mathbb {C}^ m\times \mathbb {C}^ k$ be a domain invariant under imaginary translations whose nonempty real fibers $V_ z$ are convex. Assume that there is a plurisubharmonic function $\psi $ on $\Omega $, invariant under imaginary translations, such that for every $c\in \mathbb R$ the set \[  \{ (z,t)\in \Omega _{\mathbb R}:\psi (z,t)\le c\}   \] is compact. If $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$ is invariant under imaginary translations, then the function \[  v(z)=\inf _{t\in V_ z}u(z,t)  \] is plurisubharmonic or identically $-\infty $ on $p(\Omega )$. Proof. We first treat smooth functions with positive definite real Hessian in $t$ that tend to $+\infty $ at the boundary of the real fibers (Step 1). We then approximate $u$ by such functions on subdomains exhausting $\Omega $ (Step 2) and pass to the limit (Step 3). Step 1: a smooth case. In this step, $\Omega $ may be any open set invariant under imaginary translations whose real fibers are convex. Suppose that $u$ is smooth and plurisubharmonic, invariant under imaginary translations, and that for every $z\in p(\Omega )$ the function $t\mapsto u(z,t)$ has positive definite real Hessian on $V_ z$ and tends to $+\infty $ at the boundary of $V_ z$ and, if $V_ z$ is unbounded, as $|t|\to \infty $. We show that $v$ is plurisubharmonic on each connected component of $p(\Omega )$. Fix $z\in p(\Omega )$ and put $f(t)=u(z,t)$ for $t\in V_ z$. Since its Hessian is positive definite, $f$ is strictly convex on every segment in the open convex set $V_ z$, hence on $V_ z$. Its sublevel sets $\{ t\in V_ z:f(t)\leq c\} $ are compact: they are bounded, because $f\to +\infty $ as $|t|\to \infty $ when $V_ z$ is unbounded, and the limit in $\mathbb R^ k$ of a convergent sequence in such a set cannot lie on the boundary of $V_ z$, because $f\to +\infty $ there, so it lies in $V_ z$ and, since $f$ is continuous on $V_ z$, in the sublevel set. Hence $f$ attains its minimum on the nonempty set $V_ z$, and by strict convexity at a unique point $g(z)$. This point is the only critical point of $f$: if $\nabla f(t_1)=0$, then the convex function $s\mapsto f(t_1+s(t_2-t_1))$ has derivative zero at $s=0$, hence $f(t_2)\geq f(t_1)$ for every $t_2\in V_ z$, and $t_1=g(z)$. Fix $z_0\in p(\Omega )$. Since the $t$-Hessian is invertible, the implicit function theorem gives a smooth solution $t=G(z)$ of $\partial _ tu(z,t)=0$ near $z_0$ with $G(z_0)=g(z_0)$, and $G=g$ near $z_0$ because $g(z)$ is the only critical point. Hence $g$ and $v(z)=u(z,g(z))$ are smooth on $p(\Omega )$. At the point $(z,g(z))$, let $H=(\partial ^2u/\partial t_ a\partial t_ b)$, $B=(\partial ^2u/\partial z_ j\partial t_ a)$ and $C=(\partial ^2u/\partial z_ j\partial \bar z_ l)$. Thus $H$ is a real symmetric positive definite $k\times k$ matrix and $B$ is a complex $m\times k$ matrix; since $u$ is real, $(\partial ^2u/\partial t_ a\partial \bar z_ j)=B^*$, the conjugate transpose of $B$. Differentiating the identity $\partial _ tu(z,g(z))=0$ with respect to $\bar z$ gives $B^*+Hg_{\bar z}=0$, where $g_{\bar z}=(\partial g_ a/\partial \bar z_ j)$; hence $g_{\bar z}=-H^{-1}B^*$. By the chain rule and the same identity, $v_{z_ j}(z)=u_{z_ j}(z,g(z))$, and differentiating once more with respect to $\bar z$ gives \[  v_{z\bar z}=C+Bg_{\bar z}=C-BH^{-1}B^*.  \] On the other hand, for functions of $z$ and $\operatorname{Re}w$ we have $\partial _{w_ a}=\partial _{\bar w_ a}=\frac12\partial _{t_ a}$. Hence the complex Hessian of $u$ with respect to $(z,w)$, which is positive semidefinite by proposition 8.2.2 (1), is \[  \begin{pmatrix}  C

& B/2

\\  B^*/2

& H/4

\end{pmatrix}\ge 0.  \] Evaluating the associated Hermitian quadratic form at $(\xi ,-2H^{-1}B^*\xi )$, $\xi \in \mathbb {C}^ m$, gives $\xi ^*(C-BH^{-1}B^*)\xi \geq 0$. Thus $v_{z\bar z}\geq 0$, and the smooth function $v$ is plurisubharmonic on each component of $p(\Omega )$ by proposition 8.2.2 (1). Step 2: regularization. Now let $u$ be as in the theorem. For $\varepsilon >0$ let $u_\varepsilon =u*\rho _\varepsilon $ and $\psi _\varepsilon =\psi *\rho _\varepsilon $ on $\Omega _\varepsilon =\{ x\in \Omega :\operatorname {dist}(x,\mathbb {C}^{m+k}\setminus \Omega )>\varepsilon \} $, where $\rho _\varepsilon $ is the radial mollifier of section 1.4 . Imaginary translations are isometries preserving $\Omega $, and convolution commutes with translations, so $\Omega _\varepsilon $, $u_\varepsilon $ and $\psi _\varepsilon $ are invariant under imaginary translations. By proposition 8.2.2 , the functions $u_\varepsilon $ and $\psi _\varepsilon $ are smooth and plurisubharmonic on each connected component of $\Omega _\varepsilon $, so their complex Hessians are positive semidefinite at every point, and they decrease to $u$ and $\psi $ as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$; in particular $u_\varepsilon \geq u$ and $\psi _\varepsilon \geq \psi $. The real fibers of $\Omega _\varepsilon $ are convex. Indeed, $(z,t)\in \Omega _\varepsilon $ if and only if the closed ball of radius $\varepsilon $ about $(z,t)$ lies in $\Omega $ (if it does, its distance to the closed complement of $\Omega $ is positive, because it is compact); by invariance this means that $(z+y,t+y')\in \Omega _{\mathbb R}$ for all $(y,y')\in \mathbb {C}^ m\times \mathbb R^ k$ with $|y|^2+|y'|^2\leq \varepsilon ^2$. Hence the real fiber of $\Omega _\varepsilon $ over $z$ is the intersection of the convex sets $V_{z+y}-y'$ over these $(y,y')$. Moreover, on each real fiber of $\Omega _\varepsilon $ the function $t\mapsto \psi _\varepsilon (z,t)$ is convex, since by invariance its real Hessian is four times the complex Hessian of $\psi _\varepsilon $ in $w$, which is positive semidefinite, and a smooth function with positive semidefinite Hessian on an open convex set is convex along every segment. For $c\in \mathbb R$ let $K_ c=\{ (z,t)\in \Omega _{\mathbb R}:\psi (z,t)\le c\} $; it is a compact subset of $\Omega $. Choose $\varepsilon _ j\downarrow 0$, $j\geq 1$, such that $\operatorname {dist}(K_{j+1},\mathbb {C}^{m+k}\setminus \Omega )>4\varepsilon _ j$ whenever $K_{j+1}\neq \varnothing $. Since $\psi $ and the distance to the complement of $\Omega $ are invariant under imaginary translations, the same bound holds for the set $\{ x\in \Omega :\psi (x)\leq j+1\} =K_{j+1}+\mathrm{i}\mathbb R^ k$. Define \[  G_ j=\{ (z,w)\in \Omega _{\varepsilon _ j}:\psi _{\varepsilon _ j}(z,w)<j\} ,\qquad U_ j=u_{\varepsilon _ j}+\frac{|\operatorname{Re}w|^2}{j} +\frac{1}{j-\psi _{\varepsilon _ j}}\quad \text{on }G_ j.  \] The open set $G_ j$ is invariant under imaginary translations, and its real fiber over $z$ is a sublevel set of the convex function $\psi _{\varepsilon _ j}(z,\, \cdot \, )$ on the convex real fiber of $\Omega _{\varepsilon _ j}$, hence convex. Since $\psi \leq \psi _{\varepsilon _ j}$, the real slice of $G_ j$ is contained in the compact set $K_ j\subset K_{j+1}$, which lies in $\Omega _{\varepsilon _ j}$ at positive distance from its complement. Consequently, for each $z$, the closure of the real fiber of $G_ j$ over $z$ is a compact subset of the real fiber of $\Omega _{\varepsilon _ j}$, and $\psi _{\varepsilon _ j}(z,\, \cdot \, )=j$ on its boundary. The function $U_ j$ is smooth, plurisubharmonic and invariant under imaginary translations. Indeed, by the chain rule the complex Hessian of $1/(j-\psi _{\varepsilon _ j})$ has the entries \[  \frac{(\psi _{\varepsilon _ j})_{a\bar b}}{(j-\psi _{\varepsilon _ j})^2} +\frac{2(\psi _{\varepsilon _ j})_ a(\psi _{\varepsilon _ j})_{\bar b}}{(j-\psi _{\varepsilon _ j})^3},  \] where the subscripts denote derivatives with respect to the coordinates of $(z,w)$. Since $j-\psi _{\varepsilon _ j}>0$ on $G_ j$ and $(\psi _{\varepsilon _ j})_{\bar b}=\overline{(\psi _{\varepsilon _ j})_ b}$, this matrix is the sum of positive multiples of the complex Hessian of $\psi _{\varepsilon _ j}$ and of a positive semidefinite matrix of rank at most one, hence positive semidefinite. Moreover, $|\operatorname{Re}w|^2$ has the positive semidefinite complex Hessian in $(z,w)$ given by the diagonal matrix with entries $0$ in the $z$-directions and $\frac12$ in the $w$-directions. Hence $U_ j$ is plurisubharmonic on each connected component of $G_ j$, by proposition 8.2.2 (1). The real $t$-Hessian of $U_ j$ is positive definite: the $t$-Hessians of $u_{\varepsilon _ j}$ and $1/(j-\psi _{\varepsilon _ j})$ are positive semidefinite, as for $\psi _\varepsilon $ above, and that of $|t|^2/j$ is $(2/j)I$. On each real fiber of $G_ j$, which is bounded, $U_ j(z,t)\to +\infty $ at the boundary, because $1/(j-\psi _{\varepsilon _ j})\to +\infty $ there while the other two terms are bounded below on the compact closure of the fiber. Hence Step 1 applies to $U_ j$ on $G_ j$, and \[  v_ j(z)=\inf \{ U_ j(z,t):(z,t)\in G_ j\}   \] is plurisubharmonic on each connected component of $p(G_ j)$. Step 3: passage to the limit. The sets $G_ j$ increase to $\Omega $. Indeed, $\varepsilon _{j+1}\leq \varepsilon _ j$ gives $\Omega _{\varepsilon _ j}\subset \Omega _{\varepsilon _{j+1}}$ and $\psi _{\varepsilon _{j+1}}\leq \psi _{\varepsilon _ j}<j<j+1$ on $G_ j$. Every point $x\in \Omega $ lies in $\Omega _{\varepsilon _ j}$ for large $j$, and $\psi _{\varepsilon _ j}(x)\to \psi (x)<\infty $, so $x\in G_ j$ for large $j$. On $G_ j$ we have $U_{j+1}\leq U_ j$, since $u_{\varepsilon _{j+1}}\leq u_{\varepsilon _ j}$, $|\operatorname{Re}w|^2/(j+1)\leq |\operatorname{Re}w|^2/j$ and $0<j-\psi _{\varepsilon _ j}\leq j+1-\psi _{\varepsilon _{j+1}}$. Hence the functions $v_ j$ decrease on the increasing open sets $p(G_ j)$. They satisfy $v_ j\geq v$, since $U_ j\geq u_{\varepsilon _ j}\geq u$. Conversely, let $z\in p(\Omega )$ and $t\in V_ z$. Then $(z,t)\in G_ j$ for large $j$, and $U_ j(z,t)\to u(z,t)$, also when $u(z,t)=-\infty $, because $u_{\varepsilon _ j}(z,t)\to u(z,t)$ and the other two terms tend to zero. Hence $\lim _ jv_ j(z)\leq u(z,t)$ for every $t\in V_ z$, and therefore $v_ j\downarrow v$ on $p(\Omega )$. Let $B'\Subset p(\Omega )$ be a ball. Since $\overline{B'}$ is compact and covered by the increasing open sets $p(G_ j)$, we have $B'\subset p(G_ j)$ for large $j$, and the $v_ j$ with such $j$ form a decreasing sequence of plurisubharmonic functions on $B'$. By theorem 8.3.1 , $v$ is plurisubharmonic or identically $-\infty $ on $B'$. Since every point of the connected open set $p(\Omega )$ lies in such a ball, lemma 8.2.4 shows that $v$ is plurisubharmonic or identically $-\infty $ on $p(\Omega )$; this proves the theorem. $\square$

title: Kiselman product tube
text: Corollary 8.5.2 . Let $m,k\geq 1$, let $D\subset \mathbb {C}^ m$ be a domain and let $V\subset \mathbb {R}^ k$ be a nonempty open convex set. If $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(D\times (V+\mathrm{i}\mathbb {R}^ k))$ is invariant under imaginary translations, then the function $z\mapsto \inf _{t\in V}u(z,t)$ is plurisubharmonic or identically $-\infty $ on $D$. The same holds for $z\mapsto \inf _{t\in V}(u(z,t)-\ell (t))$, for every real affine function $\ell $ on $\mathbb R^ k$. Proof. It suffices to prove the assertion on every ball $B(z_0,r)\Subset D$: since $D$ is connected, lemma 8.2.4 then gives it on $D$. We construct a function $\psi $ as in theorem 8.5.1 for the domain $B(z_0,r)\times (V+\mathrm{i}\mathbb R^ k)$, which is invariant under imaginary translations and has real fibers $V$. We first need a continuous convex function $b\geq 0$ on $V$ with compact sublevel sets. If $V=\mathbb R^ k$, take $b(t)=|t|^2$. Otherwise let $\delta (t)=\operatorname {dist}(t,\mathbb {R}^ k\setminus V)$, which is continuous and positive on $V$. It is concave on $V$: if the balls $B(t_1,r_1)$ and $B(t_2,r_2)$ lie in $V$ and $0\leq \lambda \leq 1$, then by convexity $V$ contains $\lambda B(t_1,r_1)+(1-\lambda )B(t_2,r_2)=B(\lambda t_1+(1-\lambda )t_2,\lambda r_1+(1-\lambda )r_2)$, so $\delta (\lambda t_1+(1-\lambda )t_2)\geq \lambda r_1+(1-\lambda )r_2$, and letting $r_ i\uparrow \delta (t_ i)$ gives concavity. Consequently $1/\delta $ is convex: since $x\mapsto 1/x$ is decreasing and convex on $(0,\infty )$, \[  \frac1{\delta (\lambda t_1+(1-\lambda )t_2)}\leq \frac1{\lambda \delta (t_1)+(1-\lambda )\delta (t_2)}\leq \frac\lambda {\delta (t_1)}+\frac{1-\lambda }{\delta (t_2)}.  \] Put $b(t)=|t|^2+1/\delta (t)$. For $c>0$ the set $\{ b\leq c\} $ is closed in $V$ and contained in the compact set $\{ t:|t|^2\leq c,\  \delta (t)\geq 1/c\} \subset V$, hence compact. A continuous convex function $f$ on $V$ defines a plurisubharmonic function $f(\operatorname{Re}w)$ on every domain of the form $D'\times (V+\mathrm{i}\mathbb R^ k)$. Indeed, $f(\operatorname{Re}w)$ is continuous, and its restriction to an affine complex line is $f\circ A$ for a real affine map $A$ from an open subset of $\mathbb {C}$ to $V$. If the closed disc of radius $r$ about $\zeta _0$ lies in the domain of $A$, then, since $A$ is affine, $A(\zeta _0)$ is the midpoint of $A(\zeta _0+r\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta })$ and $A(\zeta _0-r\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta })$ for every $\theta $, and the convexity of $f$ gives \[  f(A(\zeta _0))\leq \tfrac 12\bigl (f(A(\zeta _0+r\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta }))+f(A(\zeta _0-r\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta }))\bigr ).  \] Averaging over $\theta \in [0,2\pi ]$, we obtain the submean inequality for the continuous function $f\circ A$ on this circle. Now put $\psi (z,w)=(r^2-|z-z_0|^2)^{-1}+b(\operatorname{Re}w)$. This function is continuous, positive and invariant under imaginary translations. It is plurisubharmonic as a sum of two plurisubharmonic functions (proposition 8.2.5 ). The second term is plurisubharmonic by the preceding paragraph. For the first, $x\mapsto (r^2-x)^{-1}$ is convex and increasing on $(-\infty ,r^2)$ and $|z-z_0|^2$ has the complex Hessian $I$, so by the chain rule the complex Hessian of $(r^2-|z-z_0|^2)^{-1}$ is positive semidefinite, and proposition 8.2.2 (1) applies. For $c>0$, the set $\{ (z,t)\in B(z_0,r)\times V:\psi (z,t)\leq c\} $ is closed in $B(z_0,r)\times V$ and, since both terms of $\psi $ are nonnegative, contained in the compact set $\{ |z-z_0|^2\leq r^2-1/c\} \times \{ b\leq c\} $; it is therefore compact, and for $c\leq 0$ it is empty. Hence theorem 8.5.1 applies on $B(z_0,r)\times (V+\mathrm{i}\mathbb R^ k)$, and shows that $\inf _{t\in V}u(z,t)$ is plurisubharmonic or identically $-\infty $ on $B(z_0,r)$. Finally, if $\ell $ is real affine, then $\ell (\operatorname{Re}w)$ is the real part of a complex affine function of $w$. Hence $-\ell (\operatorname{Re}w)$ is smooth with vanishing complex Hessian, so it is plurisubharmonic by proposition 8.2.2 (1), and $u-\ell (\operatorname{Re}w)$ is plurisubharmonic by proposition 8.2.5 . It is invariant under imaginary translations, and the first part applies to it. $\square$

title: Bedford–Taylor products and local capacity
text: 9 Bedford–Taylor products and local capacity Let $u$ be a plurisubharmonic function on an open set $\Omega \subset \mathbb {C}^ n$. By theorem 8.2.1 , $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ is a closed positive $(1,1)$-current, but in general its coefficients are only measures. Since products of measures have no general meaning, the exterior powers of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ cannot be formed by multiplying coefficients. For $u\in C^2(\Omega )$ the top power is the Monge–Ampère measure $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n=n!\, \pi ^{-n}\det (u_{j\bar k})\, \mathrm{d}V_{2n}$. This fully nonlinear expression in the second derivatives of $u$ plays in pluripotential theory the role that the Laplacian plays in classical potential theory. Bedford and Taylor showed that for locally bounded $u$ these powers can be defined by induction, and so can the mixed products $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q\wedge T$ with a closed positive current $T$. Indeed, since $T$ has measure coefficients and $u$ is a locally bounded Borel function, the product $uT$ makes sense, and one puts $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\wedge T=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(uT)$. This chapter develops the local theory of these products, whose factors are always locally bounded; products of unbounded potentials are treated in chapter 15 . The first two sections establish the basic properties of the products: positivity, the Chern–Levine–Nirenberg mass bounds, continuity along decreasing sequences and symmetry (theorem 9.2.5 ), and the comparison principle. The products then define the Monge–Ampère capacity, a complex analogue of the relative capacity of chapter 4 . Locally, pole sets of plurisubharmonic functions have outer capacity zero; plurisubharmonic functions are quasi-continuous with respect to this capacity, and the products are continuous under convergence in capacity and along increasing sequences. Solving the homogeneous Monge–Ampère equation on a ball, we show that a locally bounded plurisubharmonic function is maximal if and only if its Monge–Ampère measure vanishes. These are the tools with which chapter 10 characterizes pluripolar sets. The remaining sections, needed for non-pluripolar products and envelopes on compact manifolds in chapter 15 , chapter 16 , solve the equation $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n=\mu $ on a ball for increasingly singular measures $\mu $: continuous densities, bounded densities, and finally compactly supported measures dominated by the Monge–Ampère measure of a bounded plurisubharmonic function. The main application is a lower bound for mixed products: if $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ i)^ n\geq f_ i\mu $ for $1\le i\le n$, then $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ n\geq (f_1\cdots f_ n)^{1/n}\mu $ (theorem 9.11.1 ). The chapter closes with the locality of complex Hessians on contact sets and a chain rule for gradients against positive currents. Historical remarks and references for this chapter are collected in section B.9 .

title: Bounded potentials and recursive products
text: 9.1 Bounded potentials and recursive products Throughout this section and the next, $\Omega \subset \mathbb {C}^ n$ is open, $n\ge 1$, and $T$ is a closed positive current on $\Omega $ of bidimension $(r,r)$, where $0\le r\le n$ is an integer; thus $T$ has bidegree $(n-r,n-r)$. Let $\beta =(\mathrm{i}/2)\sum _ j\mathrm{d}z_ j\wedge \mathrm{d}\bar z_ j$ be the form of ( 7.4 ). For a positive current $S$ of bidimension $(s,s)$ on $\Omega $ and a compact set $K\subset \Omega $ we write \[  \| S\| _ K=\int _ KS\wedge \frac{\beta ^ s}{s!}  \] for the mass of $S$ on $K$; it is $1/s!$ times the value on $K$ of the trace measure of $S$ (definition 7.2.4 ). By theorem 7.2.5 , $S$ is a current of order zero, and the total variations of its coefficient measures are bounded by a constant multiple, depending only on $n$ and $s$, of its trace measure. Since plurisubharmonic functions are upper semicontinuous, they are bounded above on compact sets; hence a plurisubharmonic function is locally bounded if and only if it is bounded below on compact sets. Definition 9.1.1 . Suppose that $r\ge 1$, and let $u$ be a locally bounded plurisubharmonic function on $\Omega $. Let $uT$ be the current of order zero obtained by multiplying the coefficient measures of $T$ by the locally bounded Borel function $u$ (section 7.2 ), and define \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\wedge T=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(uT).  \] For an integer $1\le q\le r$ and locally bounded plurisubharmonic functions $u_1,\ldots ,u_ q$ on $\Omega $, define recursively \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q\wedge T =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\bigl (u_1\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_2\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q\wedge T\bigr ).  \] Here $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_2\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q\wedge T$ is a closed positive current, hence of order zero, by proposition 9.1.2 below applied to $q-1$ factors; so its product with $u_1$ is defined as before. The product with no factors is $T$. When $T=1$ (so that $r=n$), $q=n$ and $u_1=\cdots =u_ n=u$, the resulting positive current of bidegree $(n,n)$ is a positive measure, the Monge–Ampère measure $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n$ of $u$. Proposition 9.1.2 . Every product $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q\wedge T$ of definition 9.1.1 is a closed positive current, and it has the following properties. If $u_1,\ldots ,u_ q$ are smooth, it coincides with the exterior product of the smooth forms $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j$ with $T$. The construction is local: if $u_ j=v_ j$ for every $j$ and $T=T'$ on an open set $U\subset \Omega $, then the two products agree on $U$. It is additive and positively homogeneous in each $u_ j$ and in $T$, whenever the summands are locally bounded plurisubharmonic functions, respectively closed positive currents of bidimension $(r,r)$, and it does not change if a real constant is added to some $u_ j$. If $\gamma $ is a smooth closed form of bidegree $(s,s)$, $q\le r-s$, such that $T\wedge \gamma $ is positive (for instance, $\gamma $ strongly positive), then \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q\wedge (T\wedge \gamma )=(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q\wedge T)\wedge \gamma .  \] It is invariant under biholomorphic maps: if $F\colon \Omega '\to \Omega $ is biholomorphic and $F^*$ denotes the pullback of currents of proposition 7.5.2 , then \[  F^*\bigl (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q\wedge T\bigr )=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u_1\circ F)\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u_ q\circ F)\wedge F^*T.  \] Proof. We first record two consequences of the Leibniz rule of section 7.2 . Let $R$ be a current of even degree on an open subset of $\mathbb C^ n$ such that $\partial R=\bar\partial R=0$; this holds if $R$ is closed and of pure bidegree. If $f$ is a smooth function, then $\mathrm d(fR)=\mathrm df\wedge R$ and $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}(fR)=\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}f\wedge R$, and applying $\mathrm d$ to the latter gives 9.1 \begin{equation} \label{eq:bt-smooth-factor-leibniz} \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(fR)=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f\wedge R. \end{equation} If $\gamma $ is a smooth closed form of pure bidegree, then $\partial \gamma $ and $\bar\partial \gamma $ are the components of $\mathrm d\gamma =0$ of two different bidegrees, so they vanish, and the Leibniz rule gives $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(R'\wedge \gamma )=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}R'\wedge \gamma $ for every current $R'$. We now prove positivity and closedness, first for a single factor $u$. By proposition 8.2.2 , the regularizations $u_\varepsilon =u*\rho _\varepsilon $ by the radial mollifiers of section 1.4 are smooth plurisubharmonic functions on $\Omega _\varepsilon $ with positive semidefinite complex Hessians, and they decrease to $u$ as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. On each compact set the $u_\varepsilon $ are bounded uniformly in $\varepsilon $, because $u\le u_\varepsilon \le u_{\varepsilon _0}$ for $\varepsilon \le \varepsilon _0$ and $u$ is locally bounded. Dominated convergence with respect to the total variations of the coefficient measures of $T$ therefore gives $u_\varepsilon T\to uT$ weakly. By ( 9.1 ), $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u_\varepsilon T)=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\varepsilon \wedge T$. Since weak and strong positivity agree in bidegree $(1,1)$ (section 7.2 ), the positive smooth form $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\varepsilon $ is strongly positive, so its product with the positive current $T$ is positive; it is also closed. As $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ is continuous for weak convergence, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\varepsilon \wedge T\to \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(uT)$ weakly, and positivity and closedness pass to the limit. Thus $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\wedge T$ is positive and closed. Applying this with $T$ replaced by the closed positive current $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_2\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q\wedge T$, we obtain the first assertion by induction on $q$. (1) If the $u_ j$ are smooth, ( 9.1 ) shows at each step of the recursion that the product is the exterior product of smooth forms with $T$. (2), (3) The definition uses only multiplication of coefficient measures by functions and the operator $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$; both operations are local and linear, and no product of two measures occurs. This gives locality, and additivity and positive homogeneity in $u_1$ and in $T$; for the other factors they follow by induction on $q$, since multiplication by $u_1$ and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ are linear. If $c$ is a constant and $R=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_2\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q\wedge T$, then $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}((u_1+c)R)=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u_1R)+c\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}R=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u_1R)$, since $R$ is closed; for the other factors the invariance under constants follows again by induction. (4) The product $T\wedge \gamma $ is closed, and multiplication of coefficient measures by $u_1$ commutes with the exterior product by $\gamma $. By the identity $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(R'\wedge \gamma )=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}R'\wedge \gamma $ and induction on $q$, every step of the recursion commutes with $\wedge \gamma $. (5) The pullback $F^*T$ is closed and positive and commutes with $\partial $ and $\bar\partial $, hence with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ (proposition 7.5.2 ), and the functions $u_ j\circ F$ are locally bounded and plurisubharmonic (proposition 8.2.3 ). We claim that $F^*(uT)=(u\circ F)F^*T$ for a locally bounded plurisubharmonic $u$. For a smooth function $f$ we have $F^*(fT)=(f\circ F)F^*T$: both sides are weakly continuous in $T$, they agree when $T$ is smooth, and on every relatively compact open subset of $\Omega $ the current $T$ is the weak limit of its smooth regularizations (discussion following theorem 7.2.5 ). Applying this to the regularizations $u_\varepsilon $ on relatively compact open subsets, and letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, we obtain the claim: $u_\varepsilon T\to uT$ as shown above, so $F^*(u_\varepsilon T)\to F^*(uT)$, while $(u_\varepsilon \circ F)F^*T\to (u\circ F)F^*T$ by dominated convergence with respect to the coefficient measures of the positive current $F^*T$. Consequently every step of the recursion commutes with $F^*$, which proves (5). In particular, by (2) and (5), products of locally bounded plurisubharmonic functions with closed positive currents on a complex manifold can be computed in holomorphic charts: the products defined in two charts agree on their overlap. $\square$ Let $u\in C^2(\Omega )$ be real, and write $a_{jk}=u_{j\bar k}$, so that $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=\frac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }\sum _{j,k}a_{jk}\, \mathrm dz_ j\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ k$ by ( 7.5 ). The $2$-forms $\alpha _{jk}=\mathrm dz_ j\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ k$ commute with each other, and $\alpha _{j_1k_1}\wedge \cdots \wedge \alpha _{j_ nk_ n}=0$ unless $(j_1,\ldots ,j_ n)$ and $(k_1,\ldots ,k_ n)$ are permutations of $(1,\ldots ,n)$. If $j_ i=\sigma (i)$ and $k_ i=\tau (i)$ for permutations $\sigma ,\tau $, we may reorder the commuting factors so that the first indices increase; with $\kappa =\tau \circ \sigma ^{-1}$ we get $\mathrm dz_1\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_{\kappa (1)}\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm dz_ n\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_{\kappa (n)}$, and permuting the $1$-forms $\mathrm d\bar z_{\kappa (i)}$ among themselves gives the sign $\operatorname {sgn}\kappa $. Hence \[  \Bigl (\sum _{j,k}a_{jk}\alpha _{jk}\Bigr )^ n =\sum _{\sigma ,\tau }\prod _{i=1}^ na_{\sigma (i)\tau (i)}\, \operatorname {sgn}(\tau \sigma ^{-1})\, \bigwedge _{j=1}^ n\alpha _{jj} =n!\det (a_{jk})\bigwedge _{j=1}^ n\alpha _{jj},  \] because for each of the $n!$ permutations $\sigma $ the sum over $\tau $ is $\sum _\kappa \operatorname {sgn}\kappa \prod _ ja_{j\kappa (j)}=\det (a_{jk})$. Since $\mathrm{i}\, \mathrm{d}z_ j\wedge \mathrm{d}\bar z_ j=2\, \mathrm{d}x_ j\wedge \mathrm{d}y_ j$, we have $\bigwedge _ j(\mathrm i\alpha _{jj})=2^ n\mathrm dV_{2n}$, and therefore 9.2 \begin{equation} \label{eq:bt-determinant-normalization} (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n=\Bigl (\frac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }\Bigr )^ nn!\det (u_{j\bar k})\bigwedge _{j=1}^ n\alpha _{jj}=\frac{n!}{\pi ^ n}\det (u_{j\bar k})\, \mathrm{d}V_{2n}. \end{equation} Here $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n$ is the exterior power of the continuous form $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$; when $u$ is smooth and plurisubharmonic, it is the Monge–Ampère measure of $u$, by proposition 9.1.2 (1), and the same holds for plurisubharmonic $u\in C^2(\Omega )$ (see the remark after proposition 9.1.4 ). In particular $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|z|^2=\frac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }\sum _ j\mathrm dz_ j\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ j=\beta /\pi $ and $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|z|^2)^ n=n!\pi ^{-n}\, \mathrm dV_{2n}$. (The formula also holds for $n=0$: the empty product is the constant $1$, and both sides are the unit mass $\mathrm{d}V_0$ on the point $\mathbb C^0$.) Theorem 9.1.3 (Chern–Levine–Nirenberg) . Let $K,L\subset \Omega $ be compact sets with $K\subset \operatorname{Int}L$, and let $0\le q\le r$ be an integer. There is a constant $C_{K,L,q}$, depending only on $K$, $L$, $n$ and $q$, such that \[  \| \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q\wedge T\| _ K \le C_{K,L,q}\| T\| _ L\prod _{j=1}^ q\| u_ j\| _{L^\infty (L)}  \] for every closed positive current $T$ of bidimension $(r,r)$ on $\Omega $ and all locally bounded plurisubharmonic functions $u_1,\ldots ,u_ q$ on $\Omega $. Here $\| u_ j\| _{L^\infty (L)}=\sup _ L|u_ j|$ is the pointwise supremum. Proof. For $q=0$ the estimate holds with constant $1$, since $K\subset L$. Let $q=1$ and write $u=u_1$. By lemma 1.4.1 there is a smooth function $0\le \chi \le 1$ with compact support in $\operatorname{Int}L$ which equals $1$ on a neighborhood of $K$; it depends only on $K$ and $L$. Since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\wedge T\wedge \beta ^{r-1}$ is a positive measure, $\beta $ is closed, and $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}S)(\chi )=S(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi )$ for currents $S$ of bidimension $(1,1)$, we have \[  \begin{aligned}  \int _ K\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\wedge T\wedge \beta ^{r-1} & \le \int \chi \, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(uT)\wedge \beta ^{r-1} =\bigl (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(uT\wedge \beta ^{r-1})\bigr )(\chi )\\ & =\int uT\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi \wedge \beta ^{r-1} \le C\| u\| _{L^\infty (L)}\| T\| _ L. \end{aligned}  \] The form $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi \wedge \beta ^{r-1}$ is smooth with support in $L$, though in general not positive; its coefficients are bounded by a constant depending only on $\chi $ and $n$. The last inequality therefore holds because the total variations of the coefficient measures of $T$ on $L$ are bounded by a constant multiple of $\| T\| _ L$, the multiple depending only on $n$ and $r$ (theorem 7.2.5 ). Dividing by $(r-1)!$ and taking the largest of the constants obtained for $r=1,\ldots ,n$, we obtain the case $q=1$ with a constant depending only on $K$, $L$ and $n$. For $q>1$, let $\delta >0$ be the distance from $K$ to $\mathbb C^ n\setminus \operatorname{Int}L$ (if $K=\varnothing $ there is nothing to prove), and put $L_ j=\{ z:\operatorname {dist}(z,K)\le j\delta /(q+1)\} $ for $0\le j<q$ and $L_ q=L$. These are compact sets, depending only on $K$, $L$ and $q$, with $K=L_0$ and $L_{j-1}\subset \operatorname{Int}L_ j$ for $1\le j\le q$. By proposition 9.1.2 , the currents $S_ j=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{j+1}\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q\wedge T$, $0\le j\le q$, are positive and closed, and $S_{j-1}=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j\wedge S_ j$. The case $q=1$, applied to $S_ j$ and the pair $L_{j-1}\subset \operatorname{Int}L_ j$, gives $\| S_{j-1}\| _{L_{j-1}}\le C_ j\| u_ j\| _{L^\infty (L)}\| S_ j\| _{L_ j}$ for $j=1,\ldots ,q$, since $\| u_ j\| _{L^\infty (L_ j)}\le \| u_ j\| _{L^\infty (L)}$. Combining these $q$ inequalities, we obtain the estimate with $C_{K,L,q}=C_1\cdots C_ q$. $\square$ For continuous potentials, uniform convergence is enough to pass to the limit in the products. Proposition 9.1.4 . Let $T_ k\to T$ weakly, where $T_ k$ and $T$ are closed positive currents on $\Omega $ of bidimension $(r,r)$, and let $0\le q\le r$. For $1\le j\le q$, let $(u_{j,k})_{k\ge 1}$ be locally bounded plurisubharmonic functions on $\Omega $ converging locally uniformly, as $k\to \infty $, to a continuous function $u_ j$, and let $(u_{0,k})_{k\ge 1}$ be locally bounded Borel functions on $\Omega $ converging locally uniformly to a continuous function $u_0$. Then $u_1,\ldots ,u_ q$ are plurisubharmonic, and \[  \begin{aligned}  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{1,k}\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{q,k}\wedge T_ k & \longrightarrow \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q\wedge T,\\  u_{0,k}\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{1,k}\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{q,k}\wedge T_ k & \longrightarrow u_0\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q\wedge T \end{aligned}  \] weakly as $k\to \infty $. Proof. We first show that $u_ j$ is plurisubharmonic for $1\le j\le q$. Since plurisubharmonicity is a local property, it suffices to prove this on every ball $W\Subset \Omega $. Choose $k_1<k_2<\cdots $ such that $|u_{j,k_ m}-u_ j|\le 2^{-m}$ on $W$, and put $w_ m=u_{j,k_ m}+3\cdot 2^{-m}$. These functions are plurisubharmonic on $W$, and they decrease, because \[  w_{m+1}\le u_ j+2^{-m-1}+3\cdot 2^{-m-1}=u_ j+2^{1-m}\le u_{j,k_ m}+2^{-m}+2^{1-m}=w_ m.  \] Their limit $u_ j$ is finite, so it is plurisubharmonic on $W$ by theorem 8.3.1 . Since the $u_{j,k}$ converge locally uniformly to continuous functions, they are bounded on each compact set uniformly in $k$. Since $T_ k\to T$ weakly, the masses $\| T_ k\| _ L$ are bounded for each compact set $L$: if $\chi \in C^\infty _ c(\Omega )$ satisfies $0\le \chi \le 1$ and $\chi =1$ on $L$, then $\| T_ k\| _ L\le T_ k(\chi \beta ^ r)/r!$, and the right-hand side converges. By theorem 9.1.3 , the masses of all the products considered below are therefore bounded on compact sets uniformly in $k$, and so are the total variations of their coefficient measures (theorem 7.2.5 ). We claim: if $S_ k\to S$ weakly, where $S_ k$ and $S$ are closed positive currents whose masses are bounded on compact sets uniformly in $k$, and if locally bounded Borel functions $v_ k$ converge locally uniformly to a continuous function $v$, then $v_ kS_ k\to vS$ weakly. Applying this to $S_ k=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{2,k}\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{q,k}\wedge T_ k$ and $v_ k=u_{1,k}$, and then $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$, which is weakly continuous, proves the first assertion by induction on $q$; the case $q=0$ is the hypothesis. The second assertion is the claim with $v_ k=u_{0,k}$. To prove the claim, fix a test form $\varphi $ with compact support $K$ and $\varepsilon >0$. By lemma 1.4.1 (1), applied to $v$ on a relatively compact open neighborhood of $K$, there is a smooth function $v_\varepsilon $ on a neighborhood of $K$ with $|v-v_\varepsilon |\le \varepsilon $ on $K$. Write \[  v_ kS_ k-vS=(v_ k-v)S_ k+(v-v_\varepsilon )S_ k +v_\varepsilon (S_ k-S)+(v_\varepsilon -v)S.  \] Evaluated on $\varphi $, a term $fS_ k$ with a bounded Borel function $f$ is at most $C_\varphi \sup _ K|f|$ times the total variation on $K$ of the coefficient measures of $S_ k$, where $C_\varphi $ bounds the coefficients of $\varphi $; the same holds for $S$. Hence the first term tends to zero, since $v_ k\to v$ uniformly on $K$; the second and fourth terms are bounded by a constant times $\varepsilon $, uniformly in $k$; and the third tends to zero as $k\to \infty $, since $v_\varepsilon \varphi $ is a test form. Letting first $k\to \infty $ and then $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ proves the claim. $\square$ If $u\in C^2(\Omega )$ is plurisubharmonic, its Monge–Ampère measure is given by ( 9.2 ). Indeed, the regularizations $u_\varepsilon $ are smooth and plurisubharmonic on $\Omega _\varepsilon $ (proposition 8.2.2 ) and converge to $u$ locally uniformly (lemma 1.4.1 (1)), and their second derivatives are the regularizations of the continuous second derivatives of $u$ (proposition 1.4.3 ), so they also converge locally uniformly. Hence $\det ((u_\varepsilon )_{j\bar k})\to \det (u_{j\bar k})$ locally uniformly. Applying ( 9.2 ) to $u_\varepsilon $ and proposition 9.1.4 on each $\Omega _{\varepsilon _0}$, along a sequence $\varepsilon _ k\downarrow 0$ with $\varepsilon _ k<\varepsilon _0$, we obtain the formula for $u$ on every $\Omega _{\varepsilon _0}$, hence on $\Omega $.

title: Bedford taylor product
text: Definition 9.1.1 . Suppose that $r\ge 1$, and let $u$ be a locally bounded plurisubharmonic function on $\Omega $. Let $uT$ be the current of order zero obtained by multiplying the coefficient measures of $T$ by the locally bounded Borel function $u$ (section 7.2 ), and define \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\wedge T=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(uT).  \] For an integer $1\le q\le r$ and locally bounded plurisubharmonic functions $u_1,\ldots ,u_ q$ on $\Omega $, define recursively \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q\wedge T =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\bigl (u_1\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_2\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q\wedge T\bigr ).  \] Here $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_2\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q\wedge T$ is a closed positive current, hence of order zero, by proposition 9.1.2 below applied to $q-1$ factors; so its product with $u_1$ is defined as before. The product with no factors is $T$. When $T=1$ (so that $r=n$), $q=n$ and $u_1=\cdots =u_ n=u$, the resulting positive current of bidegree $(n,n)$ is a positive measure, the Monge–Ampère measure $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n$ of $u$.

title: Bt positive recursion
text: Proposition 9.1.2 . Every product $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q\wedge T$ of definition 9.1.1 is a closed positive current, and it has the following properties. If $u_1,\ldots ,u_ q$ are smooth, it coincides with the exterior product of the smooth forms $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j$ with $T$. The construction is local: if $u_ j=v_ j$ for every $j$ and $T=T'$ on an open set $U\subset \Omega $, then the two products agree on $U$. It is additive and positively homogeneous in each $u_ j$ and in $T$, whenever the summands are locally bounded plurisubharmonic functions, respectively closed positive currents of bidimension $(r,r)$, and it does not change if a real constant is added to some $u_ j$. If $\gamma $ is a smooth closed form of bidegree $(s,s)$, $q\le r-s$, such that $T\wedge \gamma $ is positive (for instance, $\gamma $ strongly positive), then \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q\wedge (T\wedge \gamma )=(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q\wedge T)\wedge \gamma .  \] It is invariant under biholomorphic maps: if $F\colon \Omega '\to \Omega $ is biholomorphic and $F^*$ denotes the pullback of currents of proposition 7.5.2 , then \[  F^*\bigl (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q\wedge T\bigr )=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u_1\circ F)\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u_ q\circ F)\wedge F^*T.  \] Proof. We first record two consequences of the Leibniz rule of section 7.2 . Let $R$ be a current of even degree on an open subset of $\mathbb C^ n$ such that $\partial R=\bar\partial R=0$; this holds if $R$ is closed and of pure bidegree. If $f$ is a smooth function, then $\mathrm d(fR)=\mathrm df\wedge R$ and $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}(fR)=\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}f\wedge R$, and applying $\mathrm d$ to the latter gives 9.1 \begin{equation} \label{eq:bt-smooth-factor-leibniz} \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(fR)=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f\wedge R. \end{equation} If $\gamma $ is a smooth closed form of pure bidegree, then $\partial \gamma $ and $\bar\partial \gamma $ are the components of $\mathrm d\gamma =0$ of two different bidegrees, so they vanish, and the Leibniz rule gives $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(R'\wedge \gamma )=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}R'\wedge \gamma $ for every current $R'$. We now prove positivity and closedness, first for a single factor $u$. By proposition 8.2.2 , the regularizations $u_\varepsilon =u*\rho _\varepsilon $ by the radial mollifiers of section 1.4 are smooth plurisubharmonic functions on $\Omega _\varepsilon $ with positive semidefinite complex Hessians, and they decrease to $u$ as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. On each compact set the $u_\varepsilon $ are bounded uniformly in $\varepsilon $, because $u\le u_\varepsilon \le u_{\varepsilon _0}$ for $\varepsilon \le \varepsilon _0$ and $u$ is locally bounded. Dominated convergence with respect to the total variations of the coefficient measures of $T$ therefore gives $u_\varepsilon T\to uT$ weakly. By ( 9.1 ), $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u_\varepsilon T)=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\varepsilon \wedge T$. Since weak and strong positivity agree in bidegree $(1,1)$ (section 7.2 ), the positive smooth form $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\varepsilon $ is strongly positive, so its product with the positive current $T$ is positive; it is also closed. As $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ is continuous for weak convergence, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\varepsilon \wedge T\to \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(uT)$ weakly, and positivity and closedness pass to the limit. Thus $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\wedge T$ is positive and closed. Applying this with $T$ replaced by the closed positive current $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_2\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q\wedge T$, we obtain the first assertion by induction on $q$. (1) If the $u_ j$ are smooth, ( 9.1 ) shows at each step of the recursion that the product is the exterior product of smooth forms with $T$. (2), (3) The definition uses only multiplication of coefficient measures by functions and the operator $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$; both operations are local and linear, and no product of two measures occurs. This gives locality, and additivity and positive homogeneity in $u_1$ and in $T$; for the other factors they follow by induction on $q$, since multiplication by $u_1$ and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ are linear. If $c$ is a constant and $R=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_2\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q\wedge T$, then $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}((u_1+c)R)=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u_1R)+c\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}R=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u_1R)$, since $R$ is closed; for the other factors the invariance under constants follows again by induction. (4) The product $T\wedge \gamma $ is closed, and multiplication of coefficient measures by $u_1$ commutes with the exterior product by $\gamma $. By the identity $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(R'\wedge \gamma )=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}R'\wedge \gamma $ and induction on $q$, every step of the recursion commutes with $\wedge \gamma $. (5) The pullback $F^*T$ is closed and positive and commutes with $\partial $ and $\bar\partial $, hence with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ (proposition 7.5.2 ), and the functions $u_ j\circ F$ are locally bounded and plurisubharmonic (proposition 8.2.3 ). We claim that $F^*(uT)=(u\circ F)F^*T$ for a locally bounded plurisubharmonic $u$. For a smooth function $f$ we have $F^*(fT)=(f\circ F)F^*T$: both sides are weakly continuous in $T$, they agree when $T$ is smooth, and on every relatively compact open subset of $\Omega $ the current $T$ is the weak limit of its smooth regularizations (discussion following theorem 7.2.5 ). Applying this to the regularizations $u_\varepsilon $ on relatively compact open subsets, and letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, we obtain the claim: $u_\varepsilon T\to uT$ as shown above, so $F^*(u_\varepsilon T)\to F^*(uT)$, while $(u_\varepsilon \circ F)F^*T\to (u\circ F)F^*T$ by dominated convergence with respect to the coefficient measures of the positive current $F^*T$. Consequently every step of the recursion commutes with $F^*$, which proves (5).
