Recall from the paragraph before lemma 7.2.2 that $D(A_1,\ldots ,A_ n)$ is $1/n!$ times the coefficient of $t_1\cdots t_ n$ in $\det (\sum _ jt_ jA_ j)$; it is symmetric and real multilinear, and $D(A,\ldots ,A)=\det A$ (lemma 7.2.2 (1)). We prove the geometric-mean inequality for $D$ by means of a reverse Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, which follows from the signature of $D$ computed in lemma 7.2.3 . Convolution then extends it to locally bounded potentials as before. Lemma 9.7.5 . Let $n\geq 1$. For positive semidefinite Hermitian $n\times n$ matrices $A_1,\ldots ,A_ n$, \[  D(A_1,\ldots ,A_ n)\geq \prod _{i=1}^ n(\det A_ i)^{1/n}.  \] Proof. For $n=1$ both sides equal $A_1$. Let $n\geq 2$, and assume first that all $A_ i$ are positive definite. By lemma 7.2.2 (3), $D$ is positive on positive definite matrices. We first derive the reverse Cauchy–Schwarz inequality. Fix positive definite matrices $A_3,\ldots ,A_ n$, and consider the symmetric bilinear form \[  q(A,B)=D(A,B,A_3,\ldots ,A_ n)  \] on Hermitian matrices. Let $A,B$ be positive definite, put $c=q(A,B)/q(B,B)$ and $M=A-cB$. Then $q(M,B)=0$, so $q(M,M)\leq 0$ by lemma 7.2.3 . Since $q(M,M)=q(A,A)-q(A,B)^2/q(B,B)$, we obtain 9.32 \begin{equation} \label{eq:mixed-discriminant-reverse-cauchy} q(A,B)^2\geq q(A,A)q(B,B). \end{equation} Put $\widetilde A_ i=(\det A_ i)^{-1/n}A_ i$, so that $\det \widetilde A_ i=1$. By multilinearity it suffices to prove that $D(\widetilde A_1,\ldots ,\widetilde A_ n)\geq 1$. Consider the finitely many ordered $n$-tuples whose entries belong to the set $\{ \widetilde A_1,\ldots ,\widetilde A_ n\} $, and let $F>0$ be the smallest mixed discriminant of such a tuple. A tuple whose entries all equal $\widetilde A_ i$ has discriminant $\det \widetilde A_ i=1$, so $F\leq 1$. The multiplicity of a matrix in a tuple is the number of entries equal to it. Among the tuples with discriminant $F$, choose one for which the sum of the squares of the multiplicities is largest. Suppose that this tuple contains two different matrices $A$ and $B$. By symmetry of $D$ we may place them in the first two slots, so that $F=q(A,B)$, where $q$ is formed with the remaining entries of the tuple. Replacing the pair $(A,B)$ by $(A,A)$ or by $(B,B)$ gives tuples with discriminants $q(A,A)\geq F$ and $q(B,B)\geq F$, whereas ( 9.32 ) gives $q(A,A)q(B,B)\leq F^2$. Hence $q(A,A)=q(B,B)=F$, and both new tuples are minimizing. If $A$ and $B$ have multiplicities $r$ and $s$, the two replacements change the sum of the squared multiplicities by $2(r-s)+2$ and $2(s-r)+2$, respectively. These two numbers add up to $4$, so one of them is positive, which contradicts the choice of the tuple. Therefore all entries of the chosen tuple are equal, and $F=1$. In particular $D(\widetilde A_1,\ldots ,\widetilde A_ n)\geq 1$. Finally, for positive semidefinite $A_ i$, apply the inequality to $A_ i+\varepsilon I$ and let $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. Both sides are continuous: $D$ is a polynomial in the matrix entries, and $(\det A)^{1/n}$ is continuous on positive semidefinite matrices. $\square$ Corollary 9.7.6 . Let $u_1,\ldots ,u_ n$ be locally bounded plurisubharmonic functions on an open set $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$, $n\geq 1$, and let $f_1,\ldots ,f_ n\geq 0$ be continuous functions on $\Omega $ such that \[  (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ i)^ n\geq f_ i\eta ^ n\quad (1\leq i\leq n), \qquad \eta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|z|^2.  \] Then \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ n \geq \left(\prod _{i=1}^ n f_ i^{1/n}\right)\eta ^ n.  \] Proof. For $n=1$ this is the hypothesis, so let $n\geq 2$. Put $u_{i,\varepsilon }=u_ i*\rho _\varepsilon $, with the same radial mollifiers for all $i$. By the last assertion of proposition 9.7.3 , applied to each $u_ i$ with the density $f_ i$, \[  \det \mathcal H(u_{i,\varepsilon })\geq (f_ i^{1/n}*\rho _\varepsilon )^ n\qquad (1\leq i\leq n).  \] By ( 9.2 ), applied to the smooth function $\sum _ it_ iu_{i,\varepsilon }$, the exterior powers of smooth forms satisfy \[  \Bigl (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\sum _{i=1}^ nt_ iu_{i,\varepsilon }\Bigr )^ n=\det \Bigl (\sum _{i=1}^ nt_ i\mathcal H(u_{i,\varepsilon })\Bigr )\eta ^ n\qquad (t_1,\ldots ,t_ n\in \mathbb R).  \] Both sides are polynomials in $t_1,\ldots ,t_ n$. Since $2$-forms commute, the coefficient of $t_1\cdots t_ n$ on the left is $n!\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{1,\varepsilon }\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{n,\varepsilon }$, and on the right it is $n!\, D(\mathcal H(u_{1,\varepsilon }),\ldots ,\mathcal H(u_{n,\varepsilon }))\eta ^ n$. Since the Bedford–Taylor product of smooth functions is the exterior product of the forms $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{i,\varepsilon }$ (proposition 9.1.2 (1)), we obtain \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{1,\varepsilon }\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{n,\varepsilon } =D\bigl (\mathcal H(u_{1,\varepsilon }),\ldots ,\mathcal H(u_{n,\varepsilon })\bigr )\eta ^ n \geq \prod _{i=1}^ n(f_ i^{1/n}*\rho _\varepsilon )\, \eta ^ n,  \] where the inequality is lemma 9.7.5 , applied to the complex Hessians of the smooth plurisubharmonic functions $u_{i,\varepsilon }$, which are positive semidefinite (proposition 8.2.2 ). As $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, the density on the right converges locally uniformly to $\prod _ if_ i^{1/n}$, and the left side converges weakly to $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ n$ by theorem 9.2.5 , since $u_{i,\varepsilon }\downarrow u_ i$ for each $i$ (proposition 8.2.2 ). $\square$

title: Multifactor mixed discriminant
text: Lemma 9.7.5 . Let $n\geq 1$. For positive semidefinite Hermitian $n\times n$ matrices $A_1,\ldots ,A_ n$, \[  D(A_1,\ldots ,A_ n)\geq \prod _{i=1}^ n(\det A_ i)^{1/n}.  \] Proof. For $n=1$ both sides equal $A_1$. Let $n\geq 2$, and assume first that all $A_ i$ are positive definite. By lemma 7.2.2 (3), $D$ is positive on positive definite matrices. We first derive the reverse Cauchy–Schwarz inequality. Fix positive definite matrices $A_3,\ldots ,A_ n$, and consider the symmetric bilinear form \[  q(A,B)=D(A,B,A_3,\ldots ,A_ n)  \] on Hermitian matrices. Let $A,B$ be positive definite, put $c=q(A,B)/q(B,B)$ and $M=A-cB$. Then $q(M,B)=0$, so $q(M,M)\leq 0$ by lemma 7.2.3 . Since $q(M,M)=q(A,A)-q(A,B)^2/q(B,B)$, we obtain 9.32 \begin{equation} \label{eq:mixed-discriminant-reverse-cauchy} q(A,B)^2\geq q(A,A)q(B,B). \end{equation} Put $\widetilde A_ i=(\det A_ i)^{-1/n}A_ i$, so that $\det \widetilde A_ i=1$. By multilinearity it suffices to prove that $D(\widetilde A_1,\ldots ,\widetilde A_ n)\geq 1$. Consider the finitely many ordered $n$-tuples whose entries belong to the set $\{ \widetilde A_1,\ldots ,\widetilde A_ n\} $, and let $F>0$ be the smallest mixed discriminant of such a tuple. A tuple whose entries all equal $\widetilde A_ i$ has discriminant $\det \widetilde A_ i=1$, so $F\leq 1$. The multiplicity of a matrix in a tuple is the number of entries equal to it. Among the tuples with discriminant $F$, choose one for which the sum of the squares of the multiplicities is largest. Suppose that this tuple contains two different matrices $A$ and $B$. By symmetry of $D$ we may place them in the first two slots, so that $F=q(A,B)$, where $q$ is formed with the remaining entries of the tuple. Replacing the pair $(A,B)$ by $(A,A)$ or by $(B,B)$ gives tuples with discriminants $q(A,A)\geq F$ and $q(B,B)\geq F$, whereas ( 9.32 ) gives $q(A,A)q(B,B)\leq F^2$. Hence $q(A,A)=q(B,B)=F$, and both new tuples are minimizing. If $A$ and $B$ have multiplicities $r$ and $s$, the two replacements change the sum of the squared multiplicities by $2(r-s)+2$ and $2(s-r)+2$, respectively. These two numbers add up to $4$, so one of them is positive, which contradicts the choice of the tuple. Therefore all entries of the chosen tuple are equal, and $F=1$. In particular $D(\widetilde A_1,\ldots ,\widetilde A_ n)\geq 1$. Finally, for positive semidefinite $A_ i$, apply the inequality to $A_ i+\varepsilon I$ and let $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. Both sides are continuous: $D$ is a polynomial in the matrix entries, and $(\det A)^{1/n}$ is continuous on positive semidefinite matrices. $\square$

title: The ball Dirichlet problem with continuous density
text:
9.8 The ball Dirichlet problem with continuous density We now solve the Dirichlet problem \[  (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n=f\eta ^ n\quad 	ext{on }B,\qquad u=\varphi \quad 	ext{on }\partial B,  \] on a ball $B$, for a continuous density $f\ge 0$ and continuous boundary values $\varphi $. As for the homogeneous equation in theorem 9.6.3 , the solution is the upper envelope of subsolutions. By the linear characterization of density lower bounds in proposition 9.7.3 , subsolutions are stable under maxima, convex combinations and the addition of multiples of $|z|^2$ (lemma 9.8.1 ). Stability under maxima makes the envelope a subsolution, and stability under averages allows us to compose with the automorphisms of lemma 9.6.1 once more to bound its second differences; since a biholomorphism multiplies the density by the squared modulus of its Jacobian determinant, this factor now enters the estimate. Lemma 9.8.1 . Let $u,v$ be locally bounded plurisubharmonic functions on $\Omega $, and let $F,G\ge 0$ be continuous functions on $\Omega $ with $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n\ge F^ n\eta ^ n$ and $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n\ge G^ n\eta ^ n$. Then, for $0\le t\le 1$ and $c\ge 0$, \[   igl (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}((1-t)u+tv+c|z|^2) igr )^ n \ge  igl ((1-t)F+tG+c igr )^ n\eta ^ n.  \] Moreover, $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\max \{ u,v\} )^ n\ge \min \{ F,G\} ^ n\eta ^ n$. Proof. Let $B$ be a positive definite Hermitian matrix with $\det B=1$. By the implication from (1) to (3) in proposition 9.7.3 , $L_ Bu\ge nF$ and $L_ Bv\ge nG$ in the sense of distributions. Moreover $L_ B|z|^2=\operatorname {tr}B\ge n(\det B)^{1/n}=n$ by the arithmetic–geometric mean inequality for the eigenvalues of $B$. Hence \[  L_ B igl ((1-t)u+tv+c|z|^2 igr ) \ge n igl ((1-t)F+tG igr )+c\operatorname {tr}B \ge n igl ((1-t)F+tG+c igr ),  \] and the implication from (3) to (1), applied with the continuous density $((1-t)F+tG+c)^ n$, gives the first assertion. For the second, let $q$ be an upper test function for $\max \{ u,v\} $ at a point $x$. If $u(x)\ge v(x)$, then $q(x)=u(x)$ and $q\ge \max \{ u,v\} \ge u$ near $x$, so $q$ is an upper test function for $u$ at $x$, and the implication from (1) to (2) gives $\det \mathcal H(q)(x)\ge F(x)^ n\ge \min \{ F,G\} (x)^ n$. The case $v(x)\ge u(x)$ is symmetric. The implication from (2) to (1) now gives the assertion. $\square$ Theorem 9.8.2 . Let $B=B(a,R)\subset \mathbb C^ n$ with $n\ge 1$ and $R>0$. Let $f\in C(\overline B)$ be nonnegative, and let $\varphi \in C(\partial B)$ be real. There is a unique $H_{f,\varphi }\in \mathrm{PSH}(B)\cap C(\overline B)$ such that \[  (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H_{f,\varphi })^ n=f\eta ^ n\quad 	ext{on }B, \qquad H_{f,\varphi }|_{\partial B}=\varphi .  \] It is the pointwise supremum of the bounded plurisubharmonic functions $v$ on $B$ such that $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n\ge f\eta ^ n$ and $\varlimsup _{B
i z	o \zeta }v(z)\le \varphi (\zeta )$ for every $\zeta \in \partial B$. If $g\in C(\overline B)$ is another nonnegative density and $\chi \in C(\partial B)$ another real boundary function, then 9.33  egin{equation} \label{eq:ball-dirichlet-root-stability} \| H_{f,\varphi }-H_{g,\chi }\| _{L^\infty (B)} \le \| \varphi -\chi \| _{L^\infty (\partial B)} +R^2\| f^{1/n}-g^{1/n}\| _{L^\infty (B)}. \end{equation} If $f^{1/n}$ is the restriction of a real $C^2$ function on a neighborhood of $\overline B$ and $\varphi $ that of a real $C^2$ function on a neighborhood of $\partial B$, then $H_{f,\varphi }\in C^{1,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(B)$. Proof. For data of class $C^2$ (defined below) we show that the envelope of subsolutions is a locally $C^{1,1}$ solution (Steps 1–3). A stability estimate then gives a solution for continuous data (Step 4), and a comparison argument identifies every continuous solution with the envelope (Step 5). The affine map $	au (\xi )=a+R\xi $ carries the unit ball onto $B$. Since $|	au (\xi )|^2-R^2|\xi |^2=2R\operatorname{Re}\sum _ j\xi _ j ar a_ j+|a|^2$ is the real part of a holomorphic polynomial plus a constant, its complex Hessian vanishes, so $	au $ pulls $\eta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|z|^2$ back to $R^2\eta $ and $\eta ^ n$ back to $R^{2n}\eta ^ n$. Since Bedford–Taylor products are invariant under biholomorphisms (proposition 9.1.2 (5)), a function $u$ on $B$ satisfies $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n\ge f\eta ^ n$ if and only if $\xi \mapsto u(a+R\xi )$ satisfies the same inequality with the density $R^{2n}f(a+R\xi )$, whose $n$th root is $R^2f^{1/n}(a+R\xi )$; the same holds with equality. It therefore suffices to prove the theorem for the unit ball $B=B(0,1)$, with $R=1$ in ( 9.33 ). We write $z$ again for the variable and put \[  \psi =|z|^2-1,\qquad F=f^{1/n}.  \] In this proof a subsolution for $(f,\varphi )$ is a bounded plurisubharmonic function $v$ on $B$ with $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n\ge f\eta ^ n$ and $\varlimsup _{B
i z	o \zeta }v(z)\le \varphi (\zeta )$ for all $\zeta \in \partial B$. We say that the data $(f,\varphi )$ are of class $C^2$ if $F$ and $\varphi $ are restrictions of real $C^2$ functions on neighborhoods of $\overline B$ and $\partial B$, respectively. Step 1. The envelope of subsolutions for data of class $C^2$. Assume that $(f,\varphi )$ is of class $C^2$. We first construct a subsolution with boundary values $\varphi $. Multiplying a $C^2$ extension of $\varphi $ by a smooth cutoff function for $\partial B$ in its domain which equals one near $\partial B$ (lemma 1.4.1 (4)), we obtain a real $C^2$ function $b$ on $\mathbb C^ n$ with compact support and $b=\varphi $ on $\partial B$. Let $\lambda \ge 0$ bound the operator norm of the complex Hessian of $b$, and choose $c_0>\lambda $ with $(c_0-\lambda )^ n\ge \max _{\overline B}f$. The complex Hessian of $s=b+c_0\psi $ is at least $(c_0-\lambda )I$, so $s$ is plurisubharmonic (proposition 8.2.2 ) and $\det (s_{j ar k})\ge (c_0-\lambda )^ n\ge f$ on $B$; by the formula for plurisubharmonic $C^2$ functions at the beginning of section 9.7 , $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}s)^ n\ge f\eta ^ n$ on $B$. Moreover $s$ is continuous on $\overline B$ and equals $\varphi $ on $\partial B$; in particular, $s$ is a subsolution. On the other hand, every subsolution is subharmonic (theorem 8.2.1 ) with boundary upper limits at most $\varphi $, so the comparison principle (theorem 3.1.3 and the remark following it) bounds it above by the harmonic extension $P\varphi $ of $\varphi $, its Poisson integral (theorem 2.3.1 ). Let $H$ be the pointwise supremum of all subsolutions, so that $s\le H\le P\varphi $. By lemma 9.8.1 , the maximum of finitely many subsolutions is a subsolution. By theorem 8.3.2 , some countable family of subsolutions has the same upper semicontinuous regularization $H^*$ as the whole family, and its supremum equals $H^*$ almost everywhere. Taking finite maxima of $s$ and the members of this family, we obtain subsolutions $v_ j$ which increase to a function equal to $H^*$ almost everywhere, and $s\le v_ j\le P\varphi $. By theorem 9.5.1 , $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ j)^ n	o (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H^*)^ n$ weakly, and hence $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H^*)^ n\ge f\eta ^ n$. Since $P\varphi $ is continuous, $s\le H\le H^*\le P\varphi $; as $s$ and $P\varphi $ are continuous on $\overline B$ and equal $\varphi $ on $\partial B$, the function $H^*$ has boundary limits $\varphi $. Thus $H^*$ is a subsolution, so $H^*\le H$ and $H=H^*$. In particular, $H$ is a subsolution with $\lim _{B
i z	o \zeta }H(z)=\varphi (\zeta )$ for all $\zeta \in \partial B$. Step 2. Second differences for data of class $C^2$. We show that $H$ satisfies the hypothesis of lemma 9.6.2 on $B$. Fix a compact set $K\subset B$, and let $h_0>0$ and the automorphisms $S_{a,h}$, $a\in K$, $|h|\le h_0$, be as in lemma 9.6.1 . Thus $(a,h,z)\mapsto S_{a,h}(z)$ is smooth, and holomorphic in $z$, on an open set $O$ containing the compact set $L=K	imes \overline{B(0,h_0)}	imes \overline B$, and so is the complex Jacobian determinant $J_{a,h}(z)=\det _{\mathbb C}DS_{a,h}(z)$ of $z\mapsto S_{a,h}(z)$. Since $S_{a,0}$ is the identity, $J_{a,0}=1$ on $B$, and hence on $\overline B$, as $z\mapsto J_{a,0}(z)$ is continuous. The open set $W=\{ (a,h,z)\in O:|J_{a,h}(z)-1|<1/2\} $ therefore contains the compact set $K	imes \{ 0\} 	imes \overline B$, and hence all points within some positive distance of it; decreasing $h_0$, we may assume that $L\subset W$. Then $|J_{a,h}|^{2/n}=(J_{a,h}\overline{J_{a,h}})^{1/n}$ is smooth and positive on the neighborhood $W$ of $L$. Since $S_{a,h}$ is holomorphic, $S_{a,h}^*(\mathrm dz_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm dz_ n)=J_{a,h}\, \mathrm dz_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm dz_ n$, and the conjugate identity holds for $\mathrm d ar z_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm d ar z_ n$. As $\eta ^ n$ is a constant multiple of $\mathrm dz_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm dz_ n\wedge \mathrm d ar z_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm d ar z_ n$, it follows that $S_{a,h}^*\eta ^ n=|J_{a,h}|^2\eta ^ n$. Pulling back the inequality $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H)^ n\ge F^ n\eta ^ n$ by $S_{a,h}$, and using again the invariance of Bedford–Taylor products under biholomorphisms, we obtain \[   igl (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(H\circ S_{a,h}) igr )^ n \ge (F\circ S_{a,h})^ n|J_{a,h}|^2\eta ^ n = igl ((F\circ S_{a,h})|J_{a,h}|^{2/n} igr )^ n\eta ^ n.  \] Put \[  \Phi _{a,h}=	frac 12 igl ((F\circ S_{a,h})|J_{a,h}|^{2/n} +(F\circ S_{a,-h})|J_{a,-h}|^{2/n} igr ),  \] a nonnegative continuous function on $\overline B$. We claim that there are constants $C_1,C_2\ge 0$ such that, for all $a\in K$ and $|h|\le h_0$, \[   egin{aligned}  \Phi _{a,h}& \ge F-C_1|h|^2 & & 	ext{on }\overline B,\  	frac 12(\varphi \circ S_{a,h}+\varphi \circ S_{a,-h}) & \le \varphi +C_2|h|^2 & & 	ext{on }\partial B. \end{aligned}  \] To prove the first inequality, fix $a\in K$ and $z\in \overline B$, and consider $\gamma (h)=F(S_{a,h}(z))|J_{a,h}(z)|^{2/n}$ as a function of the real variable $h\in \mathbb C^ n=\mathbb R^{2n}$, $|h|\le h_0$. Since $S_{a,h}(\overline B)=\overline B$, $F$ is of class $C^2$ on a neighborhood of $\overline B$, and the maps $(a,h,z)\mapsto S_{a,h}(z)$ and $(a,h,z)\mapsto |J_{a,h}(z)|^{2/n}$ are smooth near the compact set $L$, the second derivatives of $\gamma $ are bounded by a constant $2C_1$ which depends neither on $a$ nor on $z$. Taylor's formula with integral remainder, applied at $h$ and at $-h$, gives $|\gamma (h)+\gamma (-h)-2\gamma (0)|\le 2C_1|h|^2$, since the first-order terms cancel. As $\gamma (0)=F(z)$, it follows that $\Phi _{a,h}(z)= rac12(\gamma (h)+\gamma (-h))\ge F(z)-C_1|h|^2$. The second inequality follows in the same way from a $C^2$ extension of $\varphi $ to a neighborhood of $\partial B$, since $S_{a,\pm h}$ map $\partial B$ onto itself and $S_{a,0}$ is the identity. The constants depend only on $K$, $h_0$, $n$ and the $C^2$ extensions of $F$ and $\varphi $. Now consider \[  V_{a,h}=	frac 12(H\circ S_{a,h}+H\circ S_{a,-h}) +C_1|h|^2\psi -C_2|h|^2.  \] Since additive constants do not change Monge–Ampère measures, lemma 9.8.1 , applied with $t=1/2$ and the quadratic term $C_1|h|^2|z|^2$, gives \[  (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V_{a,h})^ n\ge  igl (\Phi _{a,h}+C_1|h|^2 igr )^ n\eta ^ n\ge F^ n\eta ^ n=f\eta ^ n.  \] Since $S_{a,\pm h}$ preserve $\partial B$ and $H$ has boundary limits $\varphi $, the boundary limits of $V_{a,h}$ are $ rac12(\varphi \circ S_{a,h}+\varphi \circ S_{a,-h})-C_2|h|^2\le \varphi $. Thus $V_{a,h}$ is a subsolution, and $V_{a,h}\le H$. Evaluating at $a$, where $S_{a,\pm h}(a)=a\pm h$, and using $-1\le \psi (a)\le 0$, we obtain \[  H(a+h)+H(a-h)-2H(a)\le 2(C_1+C_2)|h|^2  \] for all $a\in K$ and $|h|\le h_0$; here the points $a\pm h=S_{a,\pm h}(a)$ lie in $B$. Step 3. The equation for data of class $C^2$. Since $K$ was arbitrary and $H$ is bounded and plurisubharmonic, lemma 9.6.2 applies on $B$. Thus $H$ is continuous and locally $C^{1,1}$ on $B$, and its distributional real Hessian is a locally bounded measurable matrix $A$. Almost every $x\in B$ satisfies \[  H(x+h)=H(x)+
abla H(x)\cdot h+	frac 12h^ tA(x)h+o(|h|^2)\qquad (h	o 0),  \] and the complex Hessian $(H_{j ar k})$ computed from $A$ is positive semidefinite almost everywhere and satisfies $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H)^ n=n!\pi ^{-n}\det (H_{j ar k})\, \mathrm dV_{2n}=\det (H_{j ar k})\, \eta ^ n$. Since $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H)^ n\ge f\eta ^ n$, we have $\det (H_{j ar k})\ge f$ almost everywhere, and it remains to prove the reverse inequality. Suppose, to the contrary, that $\det (H_{j ar k}(x))>f(x)$ at a point $x$ at which the Taylor expansion holds and $(H_{j ar k}(x))$ is positive semidefinite. The quadratic Taylor polynomial $Q(x+h)=H(x)+
abla H(x)\cdot h+ rac12h^ tA(x)h$ has the constant complex Hessian $(H_{j ar k}(x))$, which is positive semidefinite with positive determinant, hence positive definite. Choose $\varepsilon >0$ so small that the matrix $(H_{j ar k}(x))-\varepsilon I$ is positive definite and its determinant exceeds $f(x)$. By the continuity of $f$ and the Taylor expansion at $x$, there is $r>0$ such that $\overline{B(x,r)}\subset B$, this determinant exceeds $f$ on $B(x,r)$, and $|H-Q|<\varepsilon r^2/2$ on $\partial B(x,r)$. The function \[  q=Q-\varepsilon |z-x|^2+\varepsilon r^2/4  \] is plurisubharmonic (proposition 8.2.2 ), and $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q)^ n=\det  igl ((H_{j ar k}(x))-\varepsilon I igr )\eta ^ n\ge f\eta ^ n$ on $B(x,r)$. Moreover $q<H-\varepsilon r^2/4$ on $\partial B(x,r)$, while $q(x)=H(x)+\varepsilon r^2/4>H(x)$. Let $\widehat H=\max \{ H,q\} $ on $B(x,r)$ and $\widehat H=H$ on $B\setminus B(x,r)$. Since $q$ and $H$ are continuous and $q<H$ on the sphere $\partial B(x,r)$, we have $q<H$ on a neighborhood of this sphere. Hence $\widehat H$ is plurisubharmonic by proposition 8.2.5 , and it coincides with $H$ near $\partial B(x,r)$. On $B(x,r)$, lemma 9.8.1 , applied with $F=G=f^{1/n}$, gives $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\widehat H)^ n\ge f\eta ^ n$. Every other point of $B$ has a neighborhood on which $\widehat H=H$, so $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\widehat H)^ n\ge f\eta ^ n$ near it as well. Since every nonnegative test function on $B$ is a finite sum of nonnegative test functions supported in such neighborhoods (lemma 1.4.2 ), the inequality holds on all of $B$. Thus $\widehat H$ is a subsolution with $\widehat H(x)>H(x)$, a contradiction. Consequently $\det (H_{j ar k})=f$ almost everywhere, that is, $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H)^ n=f\eta ^ n$. As $H$ is continuous on $B$ with boundary limits $\varphi $ (Step 1), it extends to a solution in $\mathrm{PSH}(B)\cap C(\overline B)$, which is locally $C^{1,1}$ on $B$. Step 4. Stability and continuous data. Let $(f,\varphi )$ and $(g,\chi )$ be data of class $C^2$, with envelopes $H_{f,\varphi }$ and $H_{g,\chi }$ as in Step 1. Put $\delta =\| \varphi -\chi \| _{L^\infty (\partial B)}$ and $\sigma =\| f^{1/n}-g^{1/n}\| _{L^\infty (B)}$. By lemma 9.8.1 , \[   igl (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(H_{g,\chi }+\sigma \psi -\delta ) igr )^ n\ge (g^{1/n}+\sigma )^ n\eta ^ n\ge f\eta ^ n,  \] and $H_{g,\chi }+\sigma \psi -\delta $ has boundary limits $\chi -\delta \le \varphi $. It is therefore a subsolution for $(f,\varphi )$, and since $\psi \ge -1$ we get $H_{g,\chi }-\sigma -\delta \le H_{f,\varphi }$. Exchanging the roles of the two data gives ( 9.33 ) with $R=1$ for data of class $C^2$. Now let $f$ and $\varphi $ be continuous. Extend $F$ to $\mathbb C^ n$ by $F(z)=F(z/|z|)$ for $|z|>1$ and convolve with mollifiers; this gives smooth functions $F_ j\ge 0$ with $F_ j	o F$ uniformly on $\overline B$ (lemma 1.4.1 (1)). Similarly, extending $\varphi $ to a neighborhood of $\partial B$ by $\varphi (z)=\varphi (z/|z|)$ and mollifying, we obtain smooth functions $\varphi _ j$ on a neighborhood of $\partial B$ with $\varphi _ j	o \varphi $ uniformly on $\partial B$. The data $(F_ j^ n,\varphi _ j)$ are of class $C^2$, and by Steps 1–3 the corresponding envelopes $H_ j=H_{F_ j^ n,\varphi _ j}$ are solutions which are continuous on $\overline B$ with boundary values $\varphi _ j$. By the estimate just proved, \[  \| H_ j-H_ k\| _{L^\infty (B)}\le \| \varphi _ j-\varphi _ k\| _{L^\infty (\partial B)}+\| F_ j-F_ k\| _{L^\infty (B)},  \] so $(H_ j)$ is a uniform Cauchy sequence on $\overline B$. Its uniform limit $U$ is continuous on $\overline B$ and equal to $\varphi $ on $\partial B$. By proposition 9.1.4 , $U$ is plurisubharmonic on $B$ and $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H_ j)^ n	o (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U)^ n$ weakly; since $F_ j^ n	o f$ uniformly on $\overline B$, we obtain $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U)^ n=f\eta ^ n$. Step 5. The envelope, uniqueness and stability. Let $U$ be a solution of the problem that is continuous on $\overline B$, for instance the one constructed in Step 4, and let $v$ be a subsolution for $(f,\varphi )$. For $\varepsilon >0$ put $v_\varepsilon =v+\varepsilon \psi $. By lemma 9.8.1 , $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_\varepsilon )^ n\ge (F+\varepsilon )^ n\eta ^ n$, while $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U)^ n=F^ n\eta ^ n$. Since $\varliminf _{z	o \zeta }(U(z)-v_\varepsilon (z))\ge 0$ for every $\zeta \in \partial B$, the comparison principle theorem 9.2.8 gives \[  \int _{\{ U<v_\varepsilon \} }(F+\varepsilon )^ n\eta ^ n \le \int _{\{ U<v_\varepsilon \} }(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_\varepsilon )^ n \le \int _{\{ U<v_\varepsilon \} }F^ n\eta ^ n.  \] These integrals are finite, because $F$ is bounded on $B$, and $(F+\varepsilon )^ n-F^ n\ge \varepsilon ^ n$, so the Borel set $\{ U<v_\varepsilon \} $ is Lebesgue null. Hence $\max \{ U,v_\varepsilon \} =U$ almost everywhere, and the uniqueness assertion of theorem 8.2.1 gives $U\ge v_\varepsilon $ everywhere. Letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, we get $U\ge v$. Since $U$ is itself a subsolution, it is the pointwise supremum of all subsolutions. In particular, any two solutions in $\mathrm{PSH}(B)\cap C(\overline B)$ coincide with this supremum, which proves uniqueness. For data of class $C^2$ the solution is therefore the envelope of Step 1, which is locally $C^{1,1}$ by Step 3. Finally, if $(f,\varphi )$ and $(g,\chi )$ are continuous data, approximate both as in Step 4. By uniqueness, the corresponding solutions converge uniformly to $H_{f,\varphi }$ and $H_{g,\chi }$, and ( 9.33 ) for the approximating data of class $C^2$ passes to the limit. Undoing the affine change of variables proves all assertions of the theorem. $\square$

title: Continuous density subsolution algebra
text: Lemma 9.8.1 . Let $u,v$ be locally bounded plurisubharmonic functions on $\Omega $, and let $F,G\ge 0$ be continuous functions on $\Omega $ with $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n\ge F^ n\eta ^ n$ and $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n\ge G^ n\eta ^ n$. Then, for $0\le t\le 1$ and $c\ge 0$, \[  \bigl (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}((1-t)u+tv+c|z|^2)\bigr )^ n \ge \bigl ((1-t)F+tG+c\bigr )^ n\eta ^ n.  \] Moreover, $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\max \{ u,v\} )^ n\ge \min \{ F,G\} ^ n\eta ^ n$. Proof. Let $B$ be a positive definite Hermitian matrix with $\det B=1$. By the implication from (1) to (3) in proposition 9.7.3 , $L_ Bu\ge nF$ and $L_ Bv\ge nG$ in the sense of distributions. Moreover $L_ B|z|^2=\operatorname {tr}B\ge n(\det B)^{1/n}=n$ by the arithmetic–geometric mean inequality for the eigenvalues of $B$. Hence \[  L_ B\bigl ((1-t)u+tv+c|z|^2\bigr ) \ge n\bigl ((1-t)F+tG\bigr )+c\operatorname {tr}B \ge n\bigl ((1-t)F+tG+c\bigr ),  \] and the implication from (3) to (1), applied with the continuous density $((1-t)F+tG+c)^ n$, gives the first assertion. For the second, let $q$ be an upper test function for $\max \{ u,v\} $ at a point $x$. If $u(x)\ge v(x)$, then $q(x)=u(x)$ and $q\ge \max \{ u,v\} \ge u$ near $x$, so $q$ is an upper test function for $u$ at $x$, and the implication from (1) to (2) gives $\det \mathcal H(q)(x)\ge F(x)^ n\ge \min \{ F,G\} (x)^ n$. The case $v(x)\ge u(x)$ is symmetric. The implication from (2) to (1) now gives the assertion. $\square$

title: Continuous density ball dirichlet
text:
Theorem 9.8.2 . Let $B=B(a,R)\subset \mathbb C^ n$ with $n\ge 1$ and $R>0$. Let $f\in C(\overline B)$ be nonnegative, and let $\varphi \in C(\partial B)$ be real. There is a unique $H_{f,\varphi }\in \mathrm{PSH}(B)\cap C(\overline B)$ such that \[  (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H_{f,\varphi })^ n=f\eta ^ n\quad 	ext{on }B, \qquad H_{f,\varphi }|_{\partial B}=\varphi .  \] It is the pointwise supremum of the bounded plurisubharmonic functions $v$ on $B$ such that $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n\ge f\eta ^ n$ and $\varlimsup _{B
i z	o \zeta }v(z)\le \varphi (\zeta )$ for every $\zeta \in \partial B$. If $g\in C(\overline B)$ is another nonnegative density and $\chi \in C(\partial B)$ another real boundary function, then 9.33  egin{equation} \label{eq:ball-dirichlet-root-stability} \| H_{f,\varphi }-H_{g,\chi }\| _{L^\infty (B)} \le \| \varphi -\chi \| _{L^\infty (\partial B)} +R^2\| f^{1/n}-g^{1/n}\| _{L^\infty (B)}. \end{equation} If $f^{1/n}$ is the restriction of a real $C^2$ function on a neighborhood of $\overline B$ and $\varphi $ that of a real $C^2$ function on a neighborhood of $\partial B$, then $H_{f,\varphi }\in C^{1,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(B)$. Proof. For data of class $C^2$ (defined below) we show that the envelope of subsolutions is a locally $C^{1,1}$ solution (Steps 1–3). A stability estimate then gives a solution for continuous data (Step 4), and a comparison argument identifies every continuous solution with the envelope (Step 5). The affine map $	au (\xi )=a+R\xi $ carries the unit ball onto $B$. Since $|	au (\xi )|^2-R^2|\xi |^2=2R\operatorname{Re}\sum _ j\xi _ j ar a_ j+|a|^2$ is the real part of a holomorphic polynomial plus a constant, its complex Hessian vanishes, so $	au $ pulls $\eta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|z|^2$ back to $R^2\eta $ and $\eta ^ n$ back to $R^{2n}\eta ^ n$. Since Bedford–Taylor products are invariant under biholomorphisms (proposition 9.1.2 (5)), a function $u$ on $B$ satisfies $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n\ge f\eta ^ n$ if and only if $\xi \mapsto u(a+R\xi )$ satisfies the same inequality with the density $R^{2n}f(a+R\xi )$, whose $n$th root is $R^2f^{1/n}(a+R\xi )$; the same holds with equality. It therefore suffices to prove the theorem for the unit ball $B=B(0,1)$, with $R=1$ in ( 9.33 ). We write $z$ again for the variable and put \[  \psi =|z|^2-1,\qquad F=f^{1/n}.  \] In this proof a subsolution for $(f,\varphi )$ is a bounded plurisubharmonic function $v$ on $B$ with $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n\ge f\eta ^ n$ and $\varlimsup _{B
i z	o \zeta }v(z)\le \varphi (\zeta )$ for all $\zeta \in \partial B$. We say that the data $(f,\varphi )$ are of class $C^2$ if $F$ and $\varphi $ are restrictions of real $C^2$ functions on neighborhoods of $\overline B$ and $\partial B$, respectively. Step 1. The envelope of subsolutions for data of class $C^2$. Assume that $(f,\varphi )$ is of class $C^2$. We first construct a subsolution with boundary values $\varphi $. Multiplying a $C^2$ extension of $\varphi $ by a smooth cutoff function for $\partial B$ in its domain which equals one near $\partial B$ (lemma 1.4.1 (4)), we obtain a real $C^2$ function $b$ on $\mathbb C^ n$ with compact support and $b=\varphi $ on $\partial B$. Let $\lambda \ge 0$ bound the operator norm of the complex Hessian of $b$, and choose $c_0>\lambda $ with $(c_0-\lambda )^ n\ge \max _{\overline B}f$. The complex Hessian of $s=b+c_0\psi $ is at least $(c_0-\lambda )I$, so $s$ is plurisubharmonic (proposition 8.2.2 ) and $\det (s_{j ar k})\ge (c_0-\lambda )^ n\ge f$ on $B$; by the formula for plurisubharmonic $C^2$ functions at the beginning of section 9.7 , $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}s)^ n\ge f\eta ^ n$ on $B$. Moreover $s$ is continuous on $\overline B$ and equals $\varphi $ on $\partial B$; in particular, $s$ is a subsolution. On the other hand, every subsolution is subharmonic (theorem 8.2.1 ) with boundary upper limits at most $\varphi $, so the comparison principle (theorem 3.1.3 and the remark following it) bounds it above by the harmonic extension $P\varphi $ of $\varphi $, its Poisson integral (theorem 2.3.1 ). Let $H$ be the pointwise supremum of all subsolutions, so that $s\le H\le P\varphi $. By lemma 9.8.1 , the maximum of finitely many subsolutions is a subsolution. By theorem 8.3.2 , some countable family of subsolutions has the same upper semicontinuous regularization $H^*$ as the whole family, and its supremum equals $H^*$ almost everywhere. Taking finite maxima of $s$ and the members of this family, we obtain subsolutions $v_ j$ which increase to a function equal to $H^*$ almost everywhere, and $s\le v_ j\le P\varphi $. By theorem 9.5.1 , $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ j)^ n	o (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H^*)^ n$ weakly, and hence $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H^*)^ n\ge f\eta ^ n$. Since $P\varphi $ is continuous, $s\le H\le H^*\le P\varphi $; as $s$ and $P\varphi $ are continuous on $\overline B$ and equal $\varphi $ on $\partial B$, the function $H^*$ has boundary limits $\varphi $. Thus $H^*$ is a subsolution, so $H^*\le H$ and $H=H^*$. In particular, $H$ is a subsolution with $\lim _{B
i z	o \zeta }H(z)=\varphi (\zeta )$ for all $\zeta \in \partial B$. Step 2. Second differences for data of class $C^2$. We show that $H$ satisfies the hypothesis of lemma 9.6.2 on $B$. Fix a compact set $K\subset B$, and let $h_0>0$ and the automorphisms $S_{a,h}$, $a\in K$, $|h|\le h_0$, be as in lemma 9.6.1 . Thus $(a,h,z)\mapsto S_{a,h}(z)$ is smooth, and holomorphic in $z$, on an open set $O$ containing the compact set $L=K	imes \overline{B(0,h_0)}	imes \overline B$, and so is the complex Jacobian determinant $J_{a,h}(z)=\det _{\mathbb C}DS_{a,h}(z)$ of $z\mapsto S_{a,h}(z)$. Since $S_{a,0}$ is the identity, $J_{a,0}=1$ on $B$, and hence on $\overline B$, as $z\mapsto J_{a,0}(z)$ is continuous. The open set $W=\{ (a,h,z)\in O:|J_{a,h}(z)-1|<1/2\} $ therefore contains the compact set $K	imes \{ 0\} 	imes \overline B$, and hence all points within some positive distance of it; decreasing $h_0$, we may assume that $L\subset W$. Then $|J_{a,h}|^{2/n}=(J_{a,h}\overline{J_{a,h}})^{1/n}$ is smooth and positive on the neighborhood $W$ of $L$. Since $S_{a,h}$ is holomorphic, $S_{a,h}^*(\mathrm dz_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm dz_ n)=J_{a,h}\, \mathrm dz_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm dz_ n$, and the conjugate identity holds for $\mathrm d ar z_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm d ar z_ n$. As $\eta ^ n$ is a constant multiple of $\mathrm dz_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm dz_ n\wedge \mathrm d ar z_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm d ar z_ n$, it follows that $S_{a,h}^*\eta ^ n=|J_{a,h}|^2\eta ^ n$. Pulling back the inequality $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H)^ n\ge F^ n\eta ^ n$ by $S_{a,h}$, and using again the invariance of Bedford–Taylor products under biholomorphisms, we obtain \[   igl (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(H\circ S_{a,h}) igr )^ n \ge (F\circ S_{a,h})^ n|J_{a,h}|^2\eta ^ n = igl ((F\circ S_{a,h})|J_{a,h}|^{2/n} igr )^ n\eta ^ n.  \] Put \[  \Phi _{a,h}=	frac 12 igl ((F\circ S_{a,h})|J_{a,h}|^{2/n} +(F\circ S_{a,-h})|J_{a,-h}|^{2/n} igr ),  \] a nonnegative continuous function on $\overline B$. We claim that there are constants $C_1,C_2\ge 0$ such that, for all $a\in K$ and $|h|\le h_0$, \[   egin{aligned}  \Phi _{a,h}& \ge F-C_1|h|^2 & & 	ext{on }\overline B,\  	frac 12(\varphi \circ S_{a,h}+\varphi \circ S_{a,-h}) & \le \varphi +C_2|h|^2 & & 	ext{on }\partial B. \end{aligned}  \] To prove the first inequality, fix $a\in K$ and $z\in \overline B$, and consider $\gamma (h)=F(S_{a,h}(z))|J_{a,h}(z)|^{2/n}$ as a function of the real variable $h\in \mathbb C^ n=\mathbb R^{2n}$, $|h|\le h_0$. Since $S_{a,h}(\overline B)=\overline B$, $F$ is of class $C^2$ on a neighborhood of $\overline B$, and the maps $(a,h,z)\mapsto S_{a,h}(z)$ and $(a,h,z)\mapsto |J_{a,h}(z)|^{2/n}$ are smooth near the compact set $L$, the second derivatives of $\gamma $ are bounded by a constant $2C_1$ which depends neither on $a$ nor on $z$. Taylor's formula with integral remainder, applied at $h$ and at $-h$, gives $|\gamma (h)+\gamma (-h)-2\gamma (0)|\le 2C_1|h|^2$, since the first-order terms cancel. As $\gamma (0)=F(z)$, it follows that $\Phi _{a,h}(z)= rac12(\gamma (h)+\gamma (-h))\ge F(z)-C_1|h|^2$. The second inequality follows in the same way from a $C^2$ extension of $\varphi $ to a neighborhood of $\partial B$, since $S_{a,\pm h}$ map $\partial B$ onto itself and $S_{a,0}$ is the identity. The constants depend only on $K$, $h_0$, $n$ and the $C^2$ extensions of $F$ and $\varphi $. Now consider \[  V_{a,h}=	frac 12(H\circ S_{a,h}+H\circ S_{a,-h}) +C_1|h|^2\psi -C_2|h|^2.  \] Since additive constants do not change Monge–Ampère measures, lemma 9.8.1 , applied with $t=1/2$ and the quadratic term $C_1|h|^2|z|^2$, gives \[  (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V_{a,h})^ n\ge  igl (\Phi _{a,h}+C_1|h|^2 igr )^ n\eta ^ n\ge F^ n\eta ^ n=f\eta ^ n.  \] Since $S_{a,\pm h}$ preserve $\partial B$ and $H$ has boundary limits $\varphi $, the boundary limits of $V_{a,h}$ are $ rac12(\varphi \circ S_{a,h}+\varphi \circ S_{a,-h})-C_2|h|^2\le \varphi $. Thus $V_{a,h}$ is a subsolution, and $V_{a,h}\le H$. Evaluating at $a$, where $S_{a,\pm h}(a)=a\pm h$, and using $-1\le \psi (a)\le 0$, we obtain \[  H(a+h)+H(a-h)-2H(a)\le 2(C_1+C_2)|h|^2  \] for all $a\in K$ and $|h|\le h_0$; here the points $a\pm h=S_{a,\pm h}(a)$ lie in $B$. Step 3. The equation for data of class $C^2$. Since $K$ was arbitrary and $H$ is bounded and plurisubharmonic, lemma 9.6.2 applies on $B$. Thus $H$ is continuous and locally $C^{1,1}$ on $B$, and its distributional real Hessian is a locally bounded measurable matrix $A$. Almost every $x\in B$ satisfies \[  H(x+h)=H(x)+
abla H(x)\cdot h+	frac 12h^ tA(x)h+o(|h|^2)\qquad (h	o 0),  \] and the complex Hessian $(H_{j ar k})$ computed from $A$ is positive semidefinite almost everywhere and satisfies $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H)^ n=n!\pi ^{-n}\det (H_{j ar k})\, \mathrm dV_{2n}=\det (H_{j ar k})\, \eta ^ n$. Since $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H)^ n\ge f\eta ^ n$, we have $\det (H_{j ar k})\ge f$ almost everywhere, and it remains to prove the reverse inequality. Suppose, to the contrary, that $\det (H_{j ar k}(x))>f(x)$ at a point $x$ at which the Taylor expansion holds and $(H_{j ar k}(x))$ is positive semidefinite. The quadratic Taylor polynomial $Q(x+h)=H(x)+
abla H(x)\cdot h+ rac12h^ tA(x)h$ has the constant complex Hessian $(H_{j ar k}(x))$, which is positive semidefinite with positive determinant, hence positive definite. Choose $\varepsilon >0$ so small that the matrix $(H_{j ar k}(x))-\varepsilon I$ is positive definite and its determinant exceeds $f(x)$. By the continuity of $f$ and the Taylor expansion at $x$, there is $r>0$ such that $\overline{B(x,r)}\subset B$, this determinant exceeds $f$ on $B(x,r)$, and $|H-Q|<\varepsilon r^2/2$ on $\partial B(x,r)$. The function \[  q=Q-\varepsilon |z-x|^2+\varepsilon r^2/4  \] is plurisubharmonic (proposition 8.2.2 ), and $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q)^ n=\det  igl ((H_{j ar k}(x))-\varepsilon I igr )\eta ^ n\ge f\eta ^ n$ on $B(x,r)$. Moreover $q<H-\varepsilon r^2/4$ on $\partial B(x,r)$, while $q(x)=H(x)+\varepsilon r^2/4>H(x)$. Let $\widehat H=\max \{ H,q\} $ on $B(x,r)$ and $\widehat H=H$ on $B\setminus B(x,r)$. Since $q$ and $H$ are continuous and $q<H$ on the sphere $\partial B(x,r)$, we have $q<H$ on a neighborhood of this sphere. Hence $\widehat H$ is plurisubharmonic by proposition 8.2.5 , and it coincides with $H$ near $\partial B(x,r)$. On $B(x,r)$, lemma 9.8.1 , applied with $F=G=f^{1/n}$, gives $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\widehat H)^ n\ge f\eta ^ n$. Every other point of $B$ has a neighborhood on which $\widehat H=H$, so $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\widehat H)^ n\ge f\eta ^ n$ near it as well. Since every nonnegative test function on $B$ is a finite sum of nonnegative test functions supported in such neighborhoods (lemma 1.4.2 ), the inequality holds on all of $B$. Thus $\widehat H$ is a subsolution with $\widehat H(x)>H(x)$, a contradiction. Consequently $\det (H_{j ar k})=f$ almost everywhere, that is, $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H)^ n=f\eta ^ n$. As $H$ is continuous on $B$ with boundary limits $\varphi $ (Step 1), it extends to a solution in $\mathrm{PSH}(B)\cap C(\overline B)$, which is locally $C^{1,1}$ on $B$. Step 4. Stability and continuous data. Let $(f,\varphi )$ and $(g,\chi )$ be data of class $C^2$, with envelopes $H_{f,\varphi }$ and $H_{g,\chi }$ as in Step 1. Put $\delta =\| \varphi -\chi \| _{L^\infty (\partial B)}$ and $\sigma =\| f^{1/n}-g^{1/n}\| _{L^\infty (B)}$. By lemma 9.8.1 , \[   igl (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(H_{g,\chi }+\sigma \psi -\delta ) igr )^ n\ge (g^{1/n}+\sigma )^ n\eta ^ n\ge f\eta ^ n,  \] and $H_{g,\chi }+\sigma \psi -\delta $ has boundary limits $\chi -\delta \le \varphi $. It is therefore a subsolution for $(f,\varphi )$, and since $\psi \ge -1$ we get $H_{g,\chi }-\sigma -\delta \le H_{f,\varphi }$. Exchanging the roles of the two data gives ( 9.33 ) with $R=1$ for data of class $C^2$. Now let $f$ and $\varphi $ be continuous. Extend $F$ to $\mathbb C^ n$ by $F(z)=F(z/|z|)$ for $|z|>1$ and convolve with mollifiers; this gives smooth functions $F_ j\ge 0$ with $F_ j	o F$ uniformly on $\overline B$ (lemma 1.4.1 (1)). Similarly, extending $\varphi $ to a neighborhood of $\partial B$ by $\varphi (z)=\varphi (z/|z|)$ and mollifying, we obtain smooth functions $\varphi _ j$ on a neighborhood of $\partial B$ with $\varphi _ j	o \varphi $ uniformly on $\partial B$. The data $(F_ j^ n,\varphi _ j)$ are of class $C^2$, and by Steps 1–3 the corresponding envelopes $H_ j=H_{F_ j^ n,\varphi _ j}$ are solutions which are continuous on $\overline B$ with boundary values $\varphi _ j$. By the estimate just proved, \[  \| H_ j-H_ k\| _{L^\infty (B)}\le \| \varphi _ j-\varphi _ k\| _{L^\infty (\partial B)}+\| F_ j-F_ k\| _{L^\infty (B)},  \] so $(H_ j)$ is a uniform Cauchy sequence on $\overline B$. Its uniform limit $U$ is continuous on $\overline B$ and equal to $\varphi $ on $\partial B$. By proposition 9.1.4 , $U$ is plurisubharmonic on $B$ and $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H_ j)^ n	o (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U)^ n$ weakly; since $F_ j^ n	o f$ uniformly on $\overline B$, we obtain $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U)^ n=f\eta ^ n$. Step 5. The envelope, uniqueness and stability. Let $U$ be a solution of the problem that is continuous on $\overline B$, for instance the one constructed in Step 4, and let $v$ be a subsolution for $(f,\varphi )$. For $\varepsilon >0$ put $v_\varepsilon =v+\varepsilon \psi $. By lemma 9.8.1 , $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_\varepsilon )^ n\ge (F+\varepsilon )^ n\eta ^ n$, while $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U)^ n=F^ n\eta ^ n$. Since $\varliminf _{z	o \zeta }(U(z)-v_\varepsilon (z))\ge 0$ for every $\zeta \in \partial B$, the comparison principle theorem 9.2.8 gives \[  \int _{\{ U<v_\varepsilon \} }(F+\varepsilon )^ n\eta ^ n \le \int _{\{ U<v_\varepsilon \} }(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_\varepsilon )^ n \le \int _{\{ U<v_\varepsilon \} }F^ n\eta ^ n.  \] These integrals are finite, because $F$ is bounded on $B$, and $(F+\varepsilon )^ n-F^ n\ge \varepsilon ^ n$, so the Borel set $\{ U<v_\varepsilon \} $ is Lebesgue null. Hence $\max \{ U,v_\varepsilon \} =U$ almost everywhere, and the uniqueness assertion of theorem 8.2.1 gives $U\ge v_\varepsilon $ everywhere. Letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, we get $U\ge v$. Since $U$ is itself a subsolution, it is the pointwise supremum of all subsolutions. In particular, any two solutions in $\mathrm{PSH}(B)\cap C(\overline B)$ coincide with this supremum, which proves uniqueness. For data of class $C^2$ the solution is therefore the envelope of Step 1, which is locally $C^{1,1}$ by Step 3. Finally, if $(f,\varphi )$ and $(g,\chi )$ are continuous data, approximate both as in Step 4. By uniqueness, the corresponding solutions converge uniformly to $H_{f,\varphi }$ and $H_{g,\chi }$, and ( 9.33 ) for the approximating data of class $C^2$ passes to the limit. Undoing the affine change of variables proves all assertions of the theorem. $\square$

title: Ball dirichlet root stability
text: 9.33 \begin{equation} \label{eq:ball-dirichlet-root-stability} \| H_{f,\varphi }-H_{g,\chi }\| _{L^\infty (B)} \le \| \varphi -\chi \| _{L^\infty (\partial B)} +R^2\| f^{1/n}-g^{1/n}\| _{L^\infty (B)}. \end{equation}

title: Bounded measurable densities
text:
9.9 Bounded measurable densities We now allow an arbitrary bounded nonnegative measurable density $f$, approximate it by continuous densities $f_ j$ obtained by convolution, and pass to the limit in the solutions given by theorem 9.8.2 . Since $f_ j$ need not converge to $f$ uniformly, the stability estimate ( 9.33 ) is of no use here. However, the $f_ j$ have a common bound and converge in $L^1$, and we show that this suffices for convergence of the solutions in capacity. A comparison argument (lemma 9.9.1 ) bounds the capacity of the set where an approximate solution lies far below the limit in terms of the common bound and the $L^1$ convergence, while Hartogs' lemma and quasi-continuity control the set where it lies far above. The convergence theorem (theorem 9.4.8 ) then identifies the Monge–Ampère measure of the limit. Lemma 9.9.1 . Let $D\subset \mathbb C^ n$ be a bounded open set, let $u,v$ be locally bounded plurisubharmonic functions on $D$, and let $s\in \mathbb R$ and $t>0$. If $\{ u<v-s\} \Subset D$, then \[  t^ n\operatorname {Cap}_ D(\{ u<v-s-t\} ) \le \int _{\{ u<v-s\} }(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n.  \] Proof. Let $w\in \mathrm{PSH}(D)$ with $-1\le w\le 0$. Then \[  \{ u<v-s-t\} \subset \{ u<v-s+tw\} \subset \{ u<v-s\} ,  \] so the middle set is relatively compact in $D$. Hence every $x\in \partial D$ has a neighborhood on whose intersection with $D$ we have $u\ge v-s+tw$, and in particular $\varliminf _{D
i z	o x} igl (u(z)-(v(z)-s+tw(z)) igr )\ge 0$. Expanding $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v+t\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w)^ n$ by additivity and symmetry of the products (proposition 9.1.2 , theorem 9.2.5 ), and using that all the mixed products of the locally bounded plurisubharmonic functions $v$ and $w$ are positive, we get $ igl (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v-s+tw) igr )^ n\ge t^ n(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w)^ n$. title: Local comparison capacity sublevels
text: Lemma 9.9.1 . Let $D\subset \mathbb C^ n$ be a bounded open set, let $u,v$ be locally bounded plurisubharmonic functions on $D$, and let $s\in \mathbb R$ and $t>0$. If $\{ u<v-s\} \Subset D$, then \[  t^ n\operatorname {Cap}_ D(\{ u<v-s-t\} ) \le \int _{\{ u<v-s\} }(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n.  \] Proof. Let $w\in \mathrm{PSH}(D)$ with $-1\le w\le 0$. Then \[  \{ u<v-s-t\} \subset \{ u<v-s+tw\} \subset \{ u<v-s\} ,  \] so the middle set is relatively compact in $D$. Hence every $x\in \partial D$ has a neighborhood on whose intersection with $D$ we have $u\ge v-s+tw$, and in particular $\varliminf _{D\ni z\to x}\bigl (u(z)-(v(z)-s+tw(z))\bigr )\ge 0$. Expanding $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v+t\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w)^ n$ by additivity and symmetry of the products (proposition 9.1.2 , theorem 9.2.5 ), and using that all the mixed products of the locally bounded plurisubharmonic functions $v$ and $w$ are positive, we get $\bigl (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v-s+tw)\bigr )^ n\ge t^ n(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w)^ n$. The comparison principle theorem 9.2.8 , applied to $u$ and $v-s+tw$, therefore gives \[  \begin{aligned}  t^ n\int _{\{ u<v-s-t\} }(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w)^ n & \le \int _{\{ u<v-s+tw\} }\bigl (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v-s+tw)\bigr )^ n\\ & \le \int _{\{ u<v-s+tw\} }(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n \le \int _{\{ u<v-s\} }(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n. \end{aligned}  \] As $w$ ranges over these functions, $w+1$ ranges over the competitors for $\operatorname {Cap}_ D$ (definition 9.3.2 ). Taking the supremum over $w$ proves the lemma. $\square$

The resulting smooth functions $F_ j,G_ j\ge 0$ satisfy $\| F_ j-G_ j\| _{L^\infty (B)}\le \| f^{1/n}-g^{1/n}\| _{L^\infty (B)}$. Moreover $F_ j	o f^{1/n}$ and $G_ j	o g^{1/n}$ in $L^1(B)$ with a common bound, so $F_ j^ n	o f$ and $G_ j^ n	o g$ in $L^1(B)$ with a common bound. By theorem 9.8.2 , \[  \| H_{F_ j^ n,\varphi }-H_{G_ j^ n,\chi }\| _{L^\infty (B)}\le c, \qquad c=\| \varphi -\chi \| _{L^\infty (\partial B)}+R^2\| f^{1/n}-g^{1/n}\| _{L^\infty (B)}.  \] By uniqueness, $H_{F_ j^ n,\varphi }=U_{F_ j^ n,\varphi }$ and $H_{G_ j^ n,\chi }=U_{G_ j^ n,\chi }$, and by the stability just proved these functions converge in $L^1(B)$ to $U_{f,\varphi }$ and $U_{g,\chi }$. Since $|H_{F_ j^ n,\varphi }-H_{G_ j^ n,\chi }|\le c$ on $B$, the triangle inequality gives \[   igl (|U_{f,\varphi }-U_{g,\chi }|-c igr )_+\le |U_{f,\varphi }-H_{F_ j^ n,\varphi }|+|H_{G_ j^ n,\chi }-U_{g,\chi }|,  \] and integrating over $B$ and letting $j	o \infty $, we obtain $|U_{f,\varphi }-U_{g,\chi }|\le c$ almost everywhere. The uniqueness assertion of theorem 8.2.1 , applied to $\max \{ U_{f,\varphi },U_{g,\chi }+c\} $ and $U_{g,\chi }+c$, and to $\max \{ U_{g,\chi },U_{f,\varphi }+c\} $ and $U_{f,\varphi }+c$, shows that this inequality holds everywhere. $\square$

title: Local energy moments
text: 9.10 Local energy moments To solve $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n=\mu $ for a measure $\mu $ which need not be absolutely continuous, we approximate $\mu $ by the measures $\mu _ j$ obtained by averaging $\mu $ over the cubes of finer and finer grids, and we solve the equations for $\mu _ j$ by theorem 9.9.2 . Each $\mu _ j$ has a bounded density, but the bounds are not uniform in $j$, so the arguments of the preceding section do not apply. A bounded subsolution provides a substitute. If $\mu \le (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w)^ n$ for a bounded plurisubharmonic function $w$, then $\mu $ integrates the powers $(-\varphi )^ p$ of plurisubharmonic functions $\varphi $ with zero boundary values, with a bound in terms of the local energy moments $\int (-\varphi )^ p(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^ n$ (theorem 9.10.2 ). The cube averages inherit this control (proposition 9.10.3 ). In the subsections that follow, this control replaces the common density bound. It yields convergence of the energy integrals and convergence in capacity of the solutions for $\mu _ j$, and hence the solution of the Dirichlet problem for compactly supported measures $\mu $ of this kind (theorem 9.10.12 ). The section closes with an inequality for mixed energies (theorem 9.10.13 ), which is needed in section 9.11 . Throughout this section, $B\subset \mathbb C^ n$ is a ball, $n\geq 1$. Definition 9.10.1 . Let $B\subset \mathbb C^ n$, $n\geq 1$, be a ball. We denote by $\mathcal E_0(B)$ the class of bounded plurisubharmonic functions $\varphi \leq 0$ on $B$ such that \[  \lim _{B\ni z\to \zeta }\varphi (z)=0\quad (\zeta \in \partial B), \qquad \int _ B(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^ n<\infty .  \] For $\varphi \in \mathcal E_0(B)$ and real $p\geq 1$, the local energy moment of order $p$ is \[  e_ p(\varphi )=\int _ B(-\varphi )^ p(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^ n.  \] This class is due to Cegrell; see section B.9 . The zero function belongs to $\mathcal E_0(B)$. Since $\varphi $ is bounded and its Monge–Ampère measure has finite mass, every moment $e_ p(\varphi )$ is finite. Since $\partial B$ is compact, the boundary limit is uniform: for every $s>0$ there is a compact set $K_ s\subset B$ such that $\varphi >-s$ on $B\setminus K_ s$. Indeed, every $\zeta \in \partial B$ has an open neighborhood $N_\zeta $ with $\varphi >-s$ on $N_\zeta \cap B$; finitely many of these neighborhoods cover $\partial B$, and we may take for $K_ s$ the complement of their union in $\overline B$. In particular, each set $\{ \varphi \leq -s\} $, $s>0$, lies in a compact subset of $B$. Theorem 9.10.2 . Let $B\subset \mathbb C^ n$ be a ball, and let $\mu $ be a finite positive Borel measure on $B$ such that $\mu \leq (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w)^ n$ for some bounded plurisubharmonic function $w$ on $B$. Put $m=\mu (B)$ and $M=\sup _ Bw-\inf _ Bw$, and for real $p\geq 1$ put \[  \kappa _{n,p}=2^{n+p}(n+1)!M^ n, \qquad A_ p=\Bigl (1+\frac pn\Bigr )\kappa _{n,p}^{p/(n+p)}m^{n/(n+p)}.  \] Then, for every $\varphi \in \mathcal E_0(B)$, every real $p\geq 1$ and every $t>0$, 9.42 \begin{equation} \label{eq:local-energy-measure-tail} \mu (\{ \varphi <-t\} ) \leq \min \{ m,\kappa _{n,p}e_ p(\varphi )t^{-(n+p)}\} . \end{equation} Consequently, 9.43 \begin{equation} \label{eq:local-energy-measure-moment} \int _ B(-\varphi )^ p\, \mathrm d\mu \leq A_ p\, e_ p(\varphi )^{p/(n+p)}. \end{equation} The constant $A_ p$ depends only on $n$, $p$, $m$ and $M$. Proof. We prove the tail bound by applying Błocki's estimate (proposition 9.3.5 ) to truncations of $\varphi $, and then integrate it. For $s>0$ let \[  h_ s=\max \{ \varphi ,-s\} ,\qquad d_ s=h_ s-\varphi =(-\varphi -s)_+.  \] By the remark following definition 9.10.1 , there is a compact set $K_ s\subset B$ with $\varphi >-s$ on $B\setminus K_ s$, and since $K_ s$ is compact there is a ball $B_ s\Subset B$, concentric with $B$, which contains $K_ s$. Thus $h_ s=\varphi $ on $B_ s\setminus K_ s$, which is a collar of $\partial B_ s$, and $d_ s$ vanishes outside $K_ s$. The functions $\varphi $, $h_ s$ and $w$ are bounded and plurisubharmonic near $\overline{B_ s}$, $\varphi \le h_ s$, and the oscillation of $w$ on $B_ s$ is at most $M$. Błocki's estimate on $B_ s$, together with $\mu \leq (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w)^ n$, therefore gives \[  \int _ B d_ s^{n+1}\, \mathrm d\mu \leq \int _{B_ s}d_ s^{n+1}(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w)^ n \leq (n+1)!M^ n\int _{B_ s}d_ s(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^ n.  \] Now take $s=t/2$. On $\{ \varphi <-t\} $ we have $d_ s>t/2$. On the other hand, $0\le d_ s\le -\varphi $, and $d_ s=0$ where $-\varphi \le t/2$; since $p\geq 1$, we have $-\varphi \le (t/2)^{1-p}(-\varphi )^ p$ where $-\varphi >t/2$, and hence \[  \int _{B_ s}d_ s(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^ n \leq \int _{\{ -\varphi >t/2\} }(-\varphi )(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^ n \leq (t/2)^{1-p}e_ p(\varphi ).  \] Combining the two estimates and dividing by $(t/2)^{n+1}$, we obtain \[  \mu (\{ \varphi <-t\} )\le (n+1)!M^ n(t/2)^{-n-p}e_ p(\varphi )=\kappa _{n,p}e_ p(\varphi )t^{-(n+p)}.  \] Since also $\mu (\{ \varphi <-t\} )\le m$, this proves ( 9.42 ). If $m=0$, both sides of ( 9.43 ) vanish. If $\kappa _{n,p}e_ p(\varphi )=0$, then ( 9.42 ) shows that $\mu (\{ \varphi <-t\} )=0$ for every $t>0$, so the left side of ( 9.43 ) vanishes. Otherwise put \[  T=\left(\frac{\kappa _{n,p}e_ p(\varphi )}m\right)^{1/(n+p)}.  \] The first equality below is the layer-cake formula, which follows from Tonelli's theorem applied to the nonnegative function $(z,t)\mapsto pt^{p-1}\mathbf1_{\{ \varphi (z)<-t\} }$ on $B\times (0,\infty )$. Using ( 9.42 ) with the bound $m$ for $t<T$ and the second bound for $t\ge T$, we obtain \[  \begin{aligned}  \int _ B(-\varphi )^ p\, \mathrm d\mu & =p\int _0^\infty t^{p-1}\mu (\{ \varphi <-t\} )\, \mathrm dt \leq mT^ p +p\kappa _{n,p}e_ p(\varphi )\int _ T^\infty t^{-n-1}\, \mathrm dt\\ & =mT^ p+\frac pn\kappa _{n,p}e_ p(\varphi )T^{-n}. \end{aligned}  \] By the choice of $T$, \[  mT^ p=\kappa _{n,p}e_ p(\varphi )T^{-n}=\kappa _{n,p}^{p/(n+p)}m^{n/(n+p)}e_ p(\varphi )^{p/(n+p)},  \] so the right-hand side equals $(1+p/n)mT^ p=A_ pe_ p(\varphi )^{p/(n+p)}$. This proves ( 9.43 ). $\square$ We now show that the cube averages of a compactly supported measure $\mu $ as in theorem 9.10.2 satisfy the same moment estimate up to a constant depending only on $n$ and $p$. We call the solutions $U_ j$ of $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U_ j)^ n=\mu _ j$ with zero boundary values constructed in the following proposition the canonical approximants of $\mu $ (for the chosen grids). Proposition 9.10.3 . Let $\mu $, $w$, $m$ and $A_ p$ be as in theorem 9.10.2 , and assume moreover that the support $K$ of $\mu $ is a compact subset of $B$. Extend $\mu $ by zero to $\mathbb C^ n$. Let $h_ j\downarrow 0$, and for each $j$ let $\mathcal Q_ j$ be a partition of $\mathbb C^ n=\mathbb R^{2n}$ into half-open cubes of side length $h_ j$. Put \[  \mu _ j=\sum _{Q\in \mathcal Q_ j}\frac{\mu (Q)}{|Q|}\mathbf1_ Q\, \mathrm dV,  \] where $|Q|=h_ j^{2n}$ is the volume of $Q$ and $\mathrm dV=\mathrm dV_{2n}$ is Lebesgue measure. For $z\in \mathbb C^ n$ and $r>0$ let $P(z,r)=\{ \zeta \in \mathbb C^ n:|\zeta _ k-z_ k|<r,\  1\le k\le n\} $ be the polydisc of radius $r$ centered at $z$. Then $\mu _ j\to \mu $ weakly. Moreover, there are an index $j_0$ and, for every real $p\geq 1$, a constant $D_{n,p}>0$ depending only on $n$ and $p$, such that the following hold for all $j\geq j_0$ and $p\geq 1$. The measure $\mu _ j$ has a bounded density and compact support in $B$, and $\mu _ j(B)=m$. If $Q\in \mathcal Q_ j$ is a cube which meets $K$ and $z\in Q$, then $P(z,4\sqrt2\, h_ j)\subset B$, and every plurisubharmonic function $v\le 0$ on $P(z,4\sqrt2\, h_ j)$ satisfies 9.46 \begin{equation} \label{eq:canonical-grid-polydisc-average} \frac1{|Q|}\int _ Q(-v)^ p\, \mathrm dV \leq D_{n,p}(-v(z))^ p, \end{equation} where the right side is $+\infty $ if $v(z)=-\infty $. Every $\varphi \in \mathcal E_0(B)$ satisfies 9.47 \begin{equation} \label{eq:canonical-grid-energy-moment} \int _ B(-\varphi )^ p\, \mathrm d\mu _ j \leq D_{n,p}A_ p e_ p(\varphi )^{p/(n+p)}. \end{equation} The bounded plurisubharmonic solution $U_ j$ of $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U_ j)^ n=\mu _ j$ with zero boundary values, given by theorem 9.9.2 , belongs to $\mathcal E_0(B)$ and satisfies $e_ p(U_ j)\leq (D_{n,p}A_ p)^{(n+p)/n}$. Finally, the sequence $(U_ j)_{j\geq j_0}$ is relatively compact in $L^1(B)$, and the limit of every subsequence converging in $L^1(B)$ has a nonpositive plurisubharmonic representative. Proof. If $m=0$, then $\mu _ j=0$ and $U_ j=0$ for all $j$, and all assertions hold. Assume that $m>0$, put $d=\operatorname {dist}(K,\mathbb C^ n\setminus B)>0$, and choose $j_0$ such that $h_ j<d/(6\sqrt{2n})$ for $j\geq j_0$; in the rest of the proof we consider only $j\geq j_0$. Since $\mu $ is a finite Borel measure, it is a Radon measure (proposition 1.1.2 ), so $\mu $ vanishes outside its support $K$. Hence a cube $Q$ with $\mu (Q)>0$ meets $K$, and as its diameter is $\sqrt{2n}\, h_ j<d/6$, it lies in the $(d/6)$-neighborhood of $K$, which is contained in $B$. These cubes are disjoint, each has volume $h_ j^{2n}$, and they lie in a bounded set; so there are only finitely many of them. Therefore $\mu _ j$ is a finite sum of measures with constant densities on cubes contained in $B$, so it has a bounded density and compact support in $B$, and $\mu _ j(B)=\sum _ Q\mu (Q)=m$. This proves (1). For the weak convergence, let $g$ be a continuous function on $\mathbb C^ n$. Then \[  \int g\, \mathrm d\mu _ j-\int g\, \mathrm d\mu =\sum _{Q\in \mathcal Q_ j}\int _ Q\left(\frac1{|Q|}\int _ Qg\, \mathrm dV-g\right)\mathrm d\mu ,  \] and on every cube with $\mu (Q)>0$ the integrand is bounded by the modulus of continuity of $g$ at $\sqrt{2n}\, h_ j$ on the closed $(d/6)$-neighborhood of $K$. Hence the difference tends to zero. To prove (2), fix a cube $Q\in \mathcal Q_ j$ which meets $K$ and a point $z\in Q$, and put $\varrho =4\sqrt2\, h_ j$. Every point of $Q$ differs from $z$ by less than $\sqrt2\, h_ j$ in each complex coordinate, so $Q\subset P(z,\varrho /2)$. Moreover $P(z,\varrho )$ lies in the Euclidean ball of radius $4\sqrt{2n}\, h_ j$ about $z$, and $\operatorname {dist}(z,K)\le \sqrt{2n}\, h_ j$, so this polydisc lies in the $(5d/6)$-neighborhood of $K$ and hence in $B$. Let $v\le 0$ be a plurisubharmonic function on $P(z,\varrho )$; if $v(z)=-\infty $, there is nothing to prove, so we assume that $v(z)>-\infty $. The function $\zeta \mapsto v(z+\varrho \zeta )$ is plurisubharmonic and nonpositive on the unit polydisc (proposition 8.2.3 ), with the finite value $v(z)$ at the origin. The first estimate of proposition 8.3.6 , with its constant $C_{n,p}$, and the change of variables $\zeta \mapsto z+\varrho \zeta $, whose Jacobian is $\varrho ^{2n}$, give \[  \int _ Q(-v)^ p\, \mathrm dV\le \int _{P(z,\varrho /2)}(-v)^ p\, \mathrm dV\le \varrho ^{2n}C_{n,p}^ p(-v(z))^ p.  \] Since $|Q|=h_ j^{2n}$ and $(\varrho /h_ j)^{2n}=32^ n$, we obtain ( 9.46 ) with $D_{n,p}=32^ nC_{n,p}^ p$. For (3), let $\varphi \in \mathcal E_0(B)$. Since $\varphi \le 0$ is plurisubharmonic on $B$, ( 9.46 ) applies to $v=\varphi $ at every point $z$ of every cube with $\mu (Q)>0$. Integrating over $z\in Q$ with respect to $\mu $ and summing over the cubes, we obtain \[  \int _ B(-\varphi )^ p\, \mathrm d\mu _ j =\sum _{Q\in \mathcal Q_ j}\frac{\mu (Q)}{|Q|}\int _ Q(-\varphi )^ p\, \mathrm dV \leq D_{n,p}\int _ B(-\varphi )^ p\, \mathrm d\mu ,  \] and ( 9.47 ) follows from ( 9.43 ). For (4), note that $\mu _ j$ equals $f_ j\eta ^ n$ for a bounded density $f_ j\ge 0$, so the solution $U_ j$ exists by theorem 9.9.2 , applied with zero boundary values. Since $U_ j$ is subharmonic (theorem 8.2.1 ) with boundary limits $0$, the maximum principle (proposition 3.1.4 ) gives $U_ j\le 0$, and its Monge–Ampère measure has finite mass $\mu _ j(B)=m$; hence $U_ j\in \mathcal E_0(B)$. Taking $\varphi =U_ j$ in ( 9.47 ), we get \[  e_ p(U_ j)=\int _ B(-U_ j)^ p\, \mathrm d\mu _ j\le D_{n,p}A_ pe_ p(U_ j)^{p/(n+p)}.  \] If $e_ p(U_ j)>0$, dividing by $e_ p(U_ j)^{p/(n+p)}$ gives the asserted bound; if $e_ p(U_ j)=0$, there is nothing to prove. Finally write $B=B(a,R)$ and $\rho (z)=|z-a|^2-R^2$. The function $\rho $ is bounded and plurisubharmonic on $B$, and $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho )^ n=\eta ^ n=n!\pi ^{-n}\, \mathrm dV$. Applying theorem 9.10.2 to the finite measure $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho )^ n$ on $B$, with $p=2$, and using the uniform bound for $e_2(U_ j)$, we obtain $S=\sup _ j\int _ BU_ j^2\, \mathrm dV<\infty $. Since $U_ j\le 0$, theorem 8.3.4 shows that every subsequence has a further subsequence converging in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(B)$ to a plurisubharmonic function $u$; convergence to $-\infty $ is excluded by the $L^2$ bound. Exhausting $B$ by compact sets and passing to a diagonal subsequence, we may assume that $U_ j\to u$ almost everywhere on $B$, so Fatou's lemma gives $\int _ Bu^2\, \mathrm dV\le S$. For a compact set $L\subset B$, the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality gives \[  \int _{B\setminus L}|U_ j-u|\, \mathrm dV\le 2S^{1/2}|B\setminus L|^{1/2},  \] which is small when $|B\setminus L|$ is small. Since $U_ j\to u$ in $L^1(L)$, it follows that $U_ j\to u$ in $L^1(B)$ along this subsequence. In particular, if a subsequence of $(U_ j)$ converges in $L^1(B)$, its limit is represented by such a function $u$. Finally $u\le 0$ almost everywhere, hence everywhere, by the uniqueness assertion of theorem 8.2.1 applied to $\max \{ u,0\} $ and $0$. $\square$

title: Canonical grid energy control
text: Proposition 9.10.3 . Let $\mu $, $w$, $m$ and $A_ p$ be as in theorem 9.10.2 , and assume moreover that the support $K$ of $\mu $ is a compact subset of $B$. If $m=0$, then $\mu _ j=0$ and $U_ j=0$ for all $j$, and all assertions hold. Assume that $m>0$, put $d=\operatorname {dist}(K,\mathbb C^ n\setminus B)>0$, and choose $j_0$ such that $h_ j<d/(6\sqrt{2n})$ for $j\geq j_0$; in the rest of the proof we consider only $j\geq j_0$. Since $\mu $ is a finite Borel measure, it is a Radon measure (proposition 1.1.2 ), so $\mu $ vanishes outside its support $K$. Hence a cube $Q$ with $\mu (Q)>0$ meets $K$, and as its diameter is $\sqrt{2n}\, h_ j<d/6$, it lies in the $(d/6)$-neighborhood of $K$, which is contained in $B$. These cubes are disjoint, each has volume $h_ j^{2n}$, and they lie in a bounded set; so there are only finitely many of them. Therefore $\mu _ j$ is a finite sum of measures with constant densities on cubes contained in $B$, so it has a bounded density and compact support in $B$, and $\mu _ j(B)=\sum _ Q\mu (Q)=m$. This proves (1). For the weak convergence, let $g$ be a continuous function on $\mathbb C^ n$. Then \[  \int g\, \mathrm d\mu _ j-\int g\, \mathrm d\mu =\sum _{Q\in \mathcal Q_ j}\int _ Q\left(\frac1{|Q|}\int _ Qg\, \mathrm dV-g\right)\mathrm d\mu ,  \] and on every cube with $\mu (Q)>0$ the integrand is bounded by the modulus of continuity of $g$ at $\sqrt{2n}\, h_ j$ on the closed $(d/6)$-neighborhood of $K$. Hence the difference tends to zero. To prove (2), fix a cube $Q\in \mathcal Q_ j$ which meets $K$ and a point $z\in Q$, and put $\varrho =4\sqrt2\, h_ j$. Every point of $Q$ differs from $z$ by less than $\sqrt2\, h_ j$ in each complex coordinate, so $Q\subset P(z,\varrho /2)$. Moreover $P(z,\varrho )$ lies in the Euclidean ball of radius $4\sqrt{2n}\, h_ j$ about $z$, and $\operatorname {dist}(z,K)\le \sqrt{2n}\, h_ j$, so this polydisc lies in the $(5d/6)$-neighborhood of $K$ and hence in $B$. Let $v\le 0$ be a plurisubharmonic function on $P(z,\varrho )$; if $v(z)=-\infty $, there is nothing to prove, so we assume that $v(z)>-\infty $. The function $\zeta \mapsto v(z+\varrho \zeta )$ is plurisubharmonic and nonpositive on the unit polydisc (proposition 8.2.3 ), with the finite value $v(z)$ at the origin. The first estimate of proposition 8.3.6 , with its constant $C_{n,p}$, and the change of variables $\zeta \mapsto z+\varrho \zeta $, whose Jacobian is $\varrho ^{2n}$, give \[  \int _ Q(-v)^ p\, \mathrm dV\le \int _{P(z,\varrho /2)}(-v)^ p\, \mathrm dV\le \varrho ^{2n}C_{n,p}^ p(-v(z))^ p.  \] Since $|Q|=h_ j^{2n}$ and $(\varrho /h_ j)^{2n}=32^ n$, we obtain ( 9.46 ) with $D_{n,p}=32^ nC_{n,p}^ p$. For (3), let $\varphi \in \mathcal E_0(B)$. Since $\varphi \le 0$ is plurisubharmonic on $B$, ( 9.46 ) applies to $v=\varphi $ at every point $z$ of every cube with $\mu (Q)>0$. Integrating over $z\in Q$ with respect to $\mu $ and summing over the cubes, we obtain \[  \int _ B(-\varphi )^ p\, \mathrm d\mu _ j =\sum _{Q\in \mathcal Q_ j}\frac{\mu (Q)}{|Q|}\int _ Q(-\varphi )^ p\, \mathrm dV \leq D_{n,p}\int _ B(-\varphi )^ p\, \mathrm d\mu ,  \] and ( 9.47 ) follows from ( 9.43 ). For (4), note that $\mu _ j$ equals $f_ j\eta ^ n$ for a bounded density $f_ j\ge 0$, so the solution $U_ j$ exists by theorem 9.9.2 , applied with zero boundary values. Since $U_ j$ is subharmonic (theorem 8.2.1 ) with boundary limits $0$, the maximum principle (proposition 3.1.4 ) gives $U_ j\le 0$, and its Monge–Ampère measure has finite mass $\mu _ j(B)=m$; hence $U_ j\in \mathcal E_0(B)$. Taking $\varphi =U_ j$ in ( 9.47 ), we get \[  e_ p(U_ j)=\int _ B(-U_ j)^ p\, \mathrm d\mu _ j\le D_{n,p}A_ pe_ p(U_ j)^{p/(n+p)}.  \] If $e_ p(U_ j)>0$, dividing by $e_ p(U_ j)^{p/(n+p)}$ gives the asserted bound; if $e_ p(U_ j)=0$, there is nothing to prove. Finally write $B=B(a,R)$ and $\rho (z)=|z-a|^2-R^2$. The function $\rho $ is bounded and plurisubharmonic on $B$, and $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho )^ n=\eta ^ n=n!\pi ^{-n}\, \mathrm dV$. Applying theorem 9.10.2 to the finite measure $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho )^ n$ on $B$, with $p=2$, and using the uniform bound for $e_2(U_ j)$, we obtain $S=\sup _ j\int _ BU_ j^2\, \mathrm dV<\infty $. Since $U_ j\le 0$, theorem 8.3.4 shows that every subsequence has a further subsequence converging in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(B)$ to a plurisubharmonic function $u$; convergence to $-\infty $ is excluded by the $L^2$ bound. Exhausting $B$ by compact sets and passing to a diagonal subsequence, we may assume that $U_ j\to u$ almost everywhere on $B$, so Fatou's lemma gives $\int _ Bu^2\, \mathrm dV\le S$. For a compact set $L\subset B$, the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality gives \[  \int _{B\setminus L}|U_ j-u|\, \mathrm dV\le 2S^{1/2}|B\setminus L|^{1/2},  \] which is small when $|B\setminus L|$ is small. Since $U_ j\to u$ in $L^1(L)$, it follows that $U_ j\to u$ in $L^1(B)$ along this subsequence. In particular, if a subsequence of $(U_ j)$ converges in $L^1(B)$, its limit is represented by such a function $u$. Finally $u\le 0$ almost everywhere, hence everywhere, by the uniqueness assertion of theorem 8.2.1 applied to $\max \{ u,0\} $ and $0$. $\square$

Suppose that a subsequence of $(U_ j)$, relabeled $(U_ j)$ together with the corresponding measures $\mu _ j$, converges in $L^1(B)$, and let $u$ be the plurisubharmonic representative of its limit, which is nonpositive by proposition 9.10.3 . Then $u\in L^2(\mu )$ and 9.49  egin{equation} \label{eq:canonical-grid-self-integral-convergence} \int _ B|U_ j-u|\, \mathrm d\mu \longrightarrow 0, \qquad \int _ B|U_ j-u|\, \mathrm d\mu _ j\longrightarrow 0. \end{equation} In particular, \[  \int _ B U_ j(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U_ j)^ n\longrightarrow \int _ Bu\, \mathrm d\mu .  \] Proof. If $m=0$, then $\mu =\mu _ j=0$ and there is nothing to prove. We assume that $m>0$, and use the cubes $Q\in \mathcal Q_ j$, the polydiscs $P(z,r)$ and the estimate ( 9.46 ) of proposition 9.10.3 ; recall that $K$ denotes the support of $\mu $. Step 1. Convergence against the fixed measure $\mu $. By theorem 9.10.2 with $p=2$ and the uniform bound for $e_2(U_ j)$ in proposition 9.10.3 , we have $S=\sup _ j\int _ BU_ j^2\, \mathrm d\mu <\infty $. The truncations $\max \{ U_ j,-T\} $ are plurisubharmonic with values in $[-T,0]$, and they converge to $\max \{ u,-T\} $ in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(B)$, since $s\mapsto \max \{ s,-T\} $ is $1$-Lipschitz. Since $|a^2-b^2|\le 2T|a-b|$ for $a,b\in [-T,0]$, it follows that $\int \max \{ u,-T\} ^2\, \mathrm d\mu \le S$. Letting $T	o \infty $, monotone convergence gives $\int u^2\, \mathrm d\mu \le S$; in particular $u\in L^2(\mu )$, and $u$ is finite $\mu $-almost everywhere. For every measurable $v\le 0$ we have $\int _ B|v-\max \{ v,-T\} |\, \mathrm d\mu \le T^{-1}\int _ Bv^2\, \mathrm d\mu $, because $0\le \max \{ v,-T\} -v\le v^2/T$. By the monotone convergence theorem, $\sum _ k|U_{j_ k}-u|$ is $\mu $-integrable, hence finite $\mu $-almost everywhere, so $U_{j_ k}	o u$ $\mu $-almost everywhere. The absolute difference. Put $g_ j=\mathcal A_ j((U_ j-u)_+)$ on $K$. Let $z\in K$ with $u(z)>-\infty $, and let $c$ be as in Step 2. For all large $j$ we have $U_ j\le c$ and $u\le c$ on $Q_ j(z)$, so $(U_ j-u)_+\le c-u$ there, and hence $0\le g_ j(z)\le c-\mathcal A_ ju(z)$. Since $\mathcal A_ ju(z)	o u(z)$, letting $j	o \infty $ and then $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ shows that $g_ j	o 0$ $\mu $-almost everywhere. The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality and ( 9.51 ) give \[  g_ j(z)^2\leq 2\mathcal A_ j(U_ j^2)(z) +2\mathcal A_ j(u^2)(z) \leq 2D_{n,2} igl (U_ j(z)^2+u(z)^2 igr ),  \] so the $g_ j$ are bounded in $L^2(\mu )$ by Step 1. The elementary fact of Step 2 gives $\int _ Kg_ j\, \mathrm d\mu 	o 0$, and by ( 9.50 ) this integral equals $\int _ B(U_ j-u)_+\, \mathrm d\mu _ j$. Combining this with ( 9.52 ) and the identity $|U_ j-u|=2(U_ j-u)_+-(U_ j-u)$, we obtain the second convergence in ( 9.49 ). Finally, since $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U_ j)^ n=\mu _ j$, we have $\int _ BU_ j(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U_ j)^ n=\int _ B(U_ j-u)\, \mathrm d\mu _ j+\int _ Bu\, \mathrm d\mu _ j$. The first term tends to zero by the second convergence in ( 9.49 ), and by ( 9.50 ) and Step 2 the second term equals $\int _ K\mathcal A_ ju\, \mathrm d\mu $, which tends to $\int _ Bu\, \mathrm d\mu $. This proves the last assertion. $\square$

By upper semicontinuity, $v<v(z)+\varepsilon $ on a neighborhood of a closed ball $\overline{B'}\subset D$ centered at $z$, and Hartogs' lemma (theorem 8.3.4 ), applied on the connected component of $D$ containing $z$ with the constant majorant $v(z)+\varepsilon $, gives $v_ j<v(z)+\varepsilon $ on $\overline{B'}$ for all large $j$. Hence $\sup _{j\ge \ell }v_ j\le v(z)+\varepsilon $ on $B'$ for all large $\ell $, so $b_\ell (z)\le v(z)+\varepsilon $, and the decreasing limit of $b_\ell $ is at most $v$. Conversely, $b_\ell \ge v_ j$ for all $j\ge \ell $, so $(v-b_\ell )_+\le |v-v_ j|$ for $j\ge \ell $; integrating over a compact set $K\subset D$ and letting $j	o \infty $, we find that $b_\ell \ge v$ almost everywhere on $K$, hence almost everywhere on $D$. The decreasing limit of the $b_\ell $ is bounded below by $-L$, so it is plurisubharmonic by theorem 8.3.1 ; it is at most $v$ and equals $v$ almost everywhere, hence everywhere by the uniqueness of plurisubharmonic representatives, applied on each connected component of $D$. The sets $N_\ell =\{ \sup _{j\ge \ell }v_ j<b_\ell \} $ are Borel, and by corollary 9.5.2 they satisfy $\operatorname {Cap}_ D^*(N_\ell \cap K)=0$ for every compact $K\subset D$. By countable subadditivity of outer capacity (proposition 9.3.3 ), the union $N= igcup _\ell N_\ell $ has the same property, so $
u (N)=0$ by hypothesis. For $z

The argument applies to every sequence of plurisubharmonic functions with values in $[-L,L]$ that converges to $v$ in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(D)$. Step 2. Convergence of $\int v_ j\, \mathrm d

u )}.  \] Since $\mathcal C_{\ell +1}\subset \mathcal C_\ell $, the numbers $d_\ell $ increase, and they are bounded by $L\, 
u (D)^{1/2}$; let $d$ be their limit. Choose $r_\ell \in \mathcal C_\ell $ with \[  \| r_\ell \| _{L^2(
u )}^2\leq d_\ell ^2+\ell ^{-1}.  \] For $k\geq \ell $ the midpoint $(r_ k+r_\ell )/2$ belongs to the convex set $\mathcal C_\ell $, so its norm is at least $d_\ell $, and the parallelogram identity gives \[  \| r_ k-r_\ell \| _{L^2(
u )}^2 =2\| r_ k\| _{L^2(

On the other hand, the $r_{\ell _ i}$ are plurisubharmonic with values in $[-L,L]$, and $r_\ell 	o v$ in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(D)$, since $\| r_\ell -v\| _{L^1(K)}\le \sup _{j\ge \ell }\| v_ j-v\| _{L^1(K)}$ for every compact $K\subset D$. By Step 1, applied to the sequence $(r_{\ell _ i})$, we have $\varlimsup _ ir_{\ell _ i}=v$ $
