title: Canonical grid self integral convergence
text: Theorem 9.10.5 . Let $\mu $, $\mu _ j$ and $U_ j$ be as in proposition 9.10.3 . Suppose that a subsequence of $(U_ j)$, relabeled $(U_ j)$ together with the corresponding measures $\mu _ j$, converges in $L^1(B)$, and let $u$ be the plurisubharmonic representative of its limit, which is nonpositive by proposition 9.10.3 . Then $u\in L^2(\mu )$ and 9.49 \begin{equation} \label{eq:canonical-grid-self-integral-convergence} \int _ B|U_ j-u|\, \mathrm d\mu \longrightarrow 0, \qquad \int _ B|U_ j-u|\, \mathrm d\mu _ j\longrightarrow 0. \end{equation} In particular, \[  \int _ B U_ j(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U_ j)^ n\longrightarrow \int _ Bu\, \mathrm d\mu .  \] Proof. If $m=0$, then $\mu =\mu _ j=0$ and there is nothing to prove. We assume that $m>0$, and use the cubes $Q\in \mathcal Q_ j$, the polydiscs $P(z,r)$ and the estimate ( 9.46 ) of proposition 9.10.3 ; recall that $K$ denotes the support of $\mu $. Step 1. Convergence against the fixed measure $\mu $. By theorem 9.10.2 with $p=2$ and the uniform bound for $e_2(U_ j)$ in proposition 9.10.3 , we have $S=\sup _ j\int _ BU_ j^2\, \mathrm d\mu <\infty $. Fix $T>0$. The truncations $\max \{ U_ j,-T\} $ are plurisubharmonic with values in $[-T,0]$, and they converge to $\max \{ u,-T\} $ in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(B)$, since $s\mapsto \max \{ s,-T\} $ is $1$-Lipschitz. The measure $\mu $ satisfies the hypothesis of lemma 9.10.4 , because $\mu \le (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w)^ n$, so the truncations converge in $L^1(\mu )$. Since $|a^2-b^2|\le 2T|a-b|$ for $a,b\in [-T,0]$, it follows that $\int \max \{ u,-T\} ^2\, \mathrm d\mu \le S$. Letting $T\to \infty $, monotone convergence gives $\int u^2\, \mathrm d\mu \le S$; in particular $u\in L^2(\mu )$, and $u$ is finite $\mu $-almost everywhere. For every measurable $v\le 0$ we have $\int _ B|v-\max \{ v,-T\} |\, \mathrm d\mu \le T^{-1}\int _ Bv^2\, \mathrm d\mu $, because $0\le \max \{ v,-T\} -v\le v^2/T$. Applying this to $v=U_ j$ and $v=u$, and using the convergence of the truncations in $L^1(\mu )$, we get $\varlimsup _ j\int _ B|U_ j-u|\, \mathrm d\mu \le 2S/T$, and letting $T\to \infty $ proves the first convergence in ( 9.49 ). Step 2. Cube averages. For $z\in K$ let $Q_ j(z)$ be the cube of $\mathcal Q_ j$ containing $z$, and write \[  \mathcal A_ jv(z)=\frac1{|Q_ j(z)|}\int _{Q_ j(z)}v\, \mathrm dV  \] for the average over this cube of a function $v$ integrable on it. If $v$ is $\mu _ j$-integrable, then $v$ is integrable on every cube $Q$ with $\mu (Q)>0$; on a cube with $\mu (Q)=0$ on which $v$ is not integrable we set $\mathcal A_ jv=0$, which does not affect integrals against $\mu $. Since $\mu $ is carried by $K$, the definition of $\mu _ j$ gives 9.50 \begin{equation} \label{eq:canonical-grid-cell-pairing} \int _ Bv\, \mathrm d\mu _ j=\int _ K\mathcal A_ jv\, \mathrm d\mu . \end{equation} For a plurisubharmonic function $v\le 0$ on $B$ and $z\in K$, the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality for the probability measure $\mathrm dV/|Q_ j(z)|$ on $Q_ j(z)$ and ( 9.46 ) with $p=2$ give 9.51 \begin{equation} \label{eq:canonical-grid-cell-square} |\mathcal A_ jv(z)|^2 \leq \mathcal A_ j(v^2)(z)\leq D_{n,2}|v(z)|^2; \end{equation} if $v(z)=-\infty $, the right side is infinite. This applies in particular to the possibly unbounded function $u$. Fix $z\in K$ with $u(z)>-\infty $ and $\varepsilon >0$, and put $c=u(z)+2\varepsilon $. By upper semicontinuity of $u$ and Hartogs' lemma (theorem 8.3.4 ), there is a neighborhood of $z$ on which $u\le c$ and $U_ j\le c$ for all large $j$. Since the polydiscs $P(z,4\sqrt2\, h_ j)$ shrink to $z$, for $v=u$ or $v=U_ j$ and all large $j$ the function $v-c$ is plurisubharmonic and nonpositive on $P(z,4\sqrt2\, h_ j)$. Then ( 9.46 ) with $p=1$, applied to $v-c$, gives $\mathcal A_ j(c-v)(z)\le D_{n,1}(c-v(z))$, while $\mathcal A_ jv(z)\le c$ because $v\le c$ on $Q_ j(z)$. Thus, for all large $j$, \[  c-D_{n,1}(c-v(z))\leq \mathcal A_ jv(z)\leq c, \qquad v=u\  \text{or}\  v=U_ j.  \] Consequently $\mathcal A_ ju(z)\to u(z)$, and $\mathcal A_ jU_ j(z)\to u(z)$ whenever $U_ j(z)\to u(z)$. Indeed, in both cases the lower bound tends to $u(z)+2\varepsilon (1-D_{n,1})$ as $j\to \infty $, the upper bound is $u(z)+2\varepsilon $, and $\varepsilon >0$ is arbitrary. We use the following elementary fact: if Borel functions $F_ j$ on $K$ converge to zero $\mu $-almost everywhere and are bounded in $L^2(\mu )$, then $\int _ K|F_ j|\, \mathrm d\mu \to 0$. Indeed, for $\varepsilon >0$ the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality gives \[  \int _ K|F_ j|\, \mathrm d\mu \leq \varepsilon m+\| F_ j\| _{L^2(\mu )} \mu (\{ |F_ j|>\varepsilon \} )^{1/2},  \] and $\mu (\{ |F_ j|>\varepsilon \} )=\int _ K\mathbf1_{\{ |F_ j|>\varepsilon \} }\, \mathrm d\mu \to 0$ by dominated convergence; we let first $j\to \infty $ and then $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. By ( 9.51 ) and Step 1, the sequences $(\mathcal A_ jU_ j-u)$ and $(\mathcal A_ ju-u)$ are bounded in $L^2(\mu )$. Since $u$ is finite $\mu $-almost everywhere, we have shown that $\mathcal A_ ju\to u$ $\mu $-almost everywhere, so $\mathcal A_ ju\to u$ in $L^1(\mu )$ by the elementary fact. By the first convergence in ( 9.49 ), every subsequence of $(U_ j)$ has a further subsequence $(U_{j_ k})$ with $\sum _ k\int _ B|U_{j_ k}-u|\, \mathrm d\mu <\infty $. By the monotone convergence theorem, $\sum _ k|U_{j_ k}-u|$ is $\mu $-integrable, hence finite $\mu $-almost everywhere, so $U_{j_ k}\to u$ $\mu $-almost everywhere. By the pointwise convergence proved above, applied along this subsequence, $\mathcal A_{j_ k}U_{j_ k}\to u$ $\mu $-almost everywhere, and hence in $L^1(\mu )$. Consequently the whole sequence $\mathcal A_ jU_ j$ converges to $u$ in $L^1(\mu )$. The function $U_ j-u$ is $\mu _ j$-integrable, since $u$ is locally integrable and $\mu _ j$ has a bounded density with compact support. Therefore ( 9.50 ) gives 9.52 \begin{equation} \label{eq:canonical-grid-signed-integral} \int _ B(U_ j-u)\, \mathrm d\mu _ j=\int _ K(\mathcal A_ jU_ j-\mathcal A_ ju)\, \mathrm d\mu \longrightarrow 0. \end{equation} Step 3. The absolute difference. Put $g_ j=\mathcal A_ j((U_ j-u)_+)$ on $K$. Let $z\in K$ with $u(z)>-\infty $, and let $c$ be as in Step 2. For all large $j$ we have $U_ j\le c$ and $u\le c$ on $Q_ j(z)$, so $(U_ j-u)_+\le c-u$ there, and hence $0\le g_ j(z)\le c-\mathcal A_ ju(z)$. Since $\mathcal A_ ju(z)\to u(z)$, letting $j\to \infty $ and then $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ shows that $g_ j\to 0$ $\mu $-almost everywhere. The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality and ( 9.51 ) give \[  g_ j(z)^2\leq 2\mathcal A_ j(U_ j^2)(z) +2\mathcal A_ j(u^2)(z) \leq 2D_{n,2}\bigl (U_ j(z)^2+u(z)^2\bigr ),  \] so the $g_ j$ are bounded in $L^2(\mu )$ by Step 1. The elementary fact of Step 2 gives $\int _ Kg_ j\, \mathrm d\mu \to 0$, and by ( 9.50 ) this integral equals $\int _ B(U_ j-u)_+\, \mathrm d\mu _ j$. Combining this with ( 9.52 ) and the identity $|U_ j-u|=2(U_ j-u)_+-(U_ j-u)$, we obtain the second convergence in ( 9.49 ). Finally, since $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U_ j)^ n=\mu _ j$, we have $\int _ BU_ j(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U_ j)^ n=\int _ B(U_ j-u)\, \mathrm d\mu _ j+\int _ Bu\, \mathrm d\mu _ j$. The first term tends to zero by the second convergence in ( 9.49 ), and by ( 9.50 ) and Step 2 the second term equals $\int _ K\mathcal A_ ju\, \mathrm d\mu $, which tends to $\int _ Bu\, \mathrm d\mu $. This proves the last assertion. $\square$

title: Capacity convergence and truncated measures
text:
9.10.2 Capacity convergence and truncated measures In theorem 9.9.2 , a common bound for the densities forced the solutions to converge in capacity, and theorem 9.4.8 then identified the limiting equation. The canonical approximants $U_ j$ of proposition 9.10.3 have no such bound unless $\mu $ itself has a bounded density, since a bound $\mu _ j\leq M\, \mathrm dV$ for all $j$ would pass to the weak limit $\mu $; nor are the functions $U_ j$ uniformly bounded. We show that the convergence of the energy integrals in theorem 9.10.5 takes the place of the density bound once we pass to the uniformly bounded truncations $\max \{ U_ j,-T\} $, whose Monge–Ampère measures differ from $\mu _ j$ by an error controlled by the energy (lemma 9.10.7 ). Thus a subsequence of canonical approximants that converges in $L^1(B)$ also converges locally in capacity, and the Monge–Ampère measures of the truncations of its limit approximate $\mu $ in total variation (theorem 9.10.9 ). As throughout this section, $B$ is a ball in $\mathbb C^ n$, $n\geq 1$. For finite positive Borel measures $
u _1,
u _2$ on $B$ we use the total variation distance \[  \| 
u _1-
u _2\| _{\mathrm{TV}} =\sup \left\{ \left|\int _ Bf\, \mathrm d(
u _1-
u _2)ight|: f	ext{ real Borel},\  |f|\leq 1ight\} .  \] The supremum does not change if $f$ ranges only over the real functions in $C_ c(B)$ with $|f|\leq 1$. Indeed, given a real Borel function $f$ with $|f|\leq 1$, proposition 1.2.3 provides functions in $C_ c(B)$ converging to $f$ in $L^1(
u _1+
u _2)$, which we may take real by passing to real parts; clamping them to $[-1,1]$ keeps them in $C_ c(B)$ and does not increase their distance from $f$. Let $T>0$ and $\delta >0$, and let $f,g$ be functions on $B$ with values in $[-\infty ,\infty )$. Then 9.53  egin{equation} \label{eq:truncation-level-inclusions}  egin{aligned}   igl \{ \max \{ f,-T\} >\max \{ g,-T\} +\delta  igr \} & \subset \{ f>g+\delta \} ,\   igl \{ \max \{ f,-T\} <\max \{ g,-T\} -\delta  igr \} & \subset \{ f<g-\delta \} . \end{aligned} \end{equation} Indeed, at a point of the first set we have $\max \{ f,-T\} >-T$, so $f=\max \{ f,-T\} >\max \{ g,-T\} +\delta \geq g+\delta $; the second inclusion is the first with $f$ and $g$ interchanged. Consequently, truncation at a fixed level preserves convergence locally in capacity (definition 9.4.5 ): if $f_ j	o f$, then $\max \{ f_ j,-T\} 	o \max \{ f,-T\} $. Modifying a locally bounded plurisubharmonic function on a compact set does not change its total Monge–Ampère mass. Lemma 9.10.6 . Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ be open, and let $\varphi ,\psi $ be locally bounded plurisubharmonic functions on $\Omega $ which coincide outside a compact set $K\subset \Omega $. Then $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^ n$ and $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi )^ n$ agree on $\Omega \setminus K$ and assign the same finite mass to $K$. In particular $\int _\Omega (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^ n=\int _\Omega (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi )^ n$, where both sides may be infinite. Proof. The two measures agree on the open set $\Omega \setminus K$, because the products are local (proposition 9.1.2 ). For $0\leq k\leq n-1$ put $S_ k=(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^ k\wedge (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi )^{n-1-k}$. By the symmetry of the products (theorem 9.2.5 ) and definition 9.1.1 , \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\varphi S_ k)=(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^{k+1}\wedge (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi )^{n-1-k}, \qquad \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\psi S_ k)=(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^ k\wedge (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi )^{n-k},  \] so the sum over $k$ telescopes and \[  (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^ n-(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi )^ n=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}R,\qquad R=(\varphi -\psi )\sum _{k=0}^{n-1}S_ k.  \] The coefficient measures of the current $R$ of order zero vanish on $\Omega \setminus K$, so $\operatorname{Supp}R\subset K$. By lemma 1.4.1 there is $\chi \in C^\infty _ c(\Omega )$ with $0\leq \chi \leq 1$ which equals one on a neighborhood of $K$. Then $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi $ vanishes on a neighborhood of $\operatorname{Supp}R$, and therefore \[  \int \chi \, (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^ n-\int \chi \, (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi )^ n=R(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi )=0,  \] where both integrals are finite. Since $\chi =1$ on $K$ and the two measures agree on $\Omega \setminus K$, it follows that $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^ n(K)=(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi )^ n(K)<\infty $, and adding the equal masses of $\Omega \setminus K$ gives the last assertion. $\square$ Lemma 9.10.7 . Let $\varphi \in \mathcal E_0(B)$ and $T>0$, and put $\varphi _ T=\max \{ \varphi ,-T\} $. Then $\varphi _ T\in \mathcal E_0(B)$, and for every $p\geq 1$, \[  \int _ B(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ T)^ n=\int _ B(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^ n, \qquad e_ p(\varphi _ T)\leq e_ p(\varphi ),  \] 9.56  egin{equation} \label{eq:zero-boundary-truncation-variation} \| (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ T)^ n-(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^ n\| _{\mathrm{TV}} \leq 2e_ p(\varphi )T^{-p}. \end{equation} Moreover, for every Borel set $E\subset B$, 9.57  egin{equation} \label{eq:energy-measure-capacity-modulus} \int _ E(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^ n \leq T^ n\operatorname {Cap}_ B(E)+e_ p(\varphi )T^{-p}. \end{equation} Proof. Since $\varphi $ tends to zero uniformly at $\partial B$, there is an open neighborhood $V$ of $\partial B$ such that $\varphi >-T$ on $V\cap B$; there $\varphi _ T=\varphi $. Thus $\varphi _ T$ is bounded, nonpositive and plurisubharmonic, it has zero boundary values, and it coincides with $\varphi $ outside the compact set $\overline B\setminus V\subset B$. By lemma 9.10.6 , the measures $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ T)^ n$ and $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^ n$ have the same total mass, which is finite; in particular $\varphi _ T\in \mathcal E_0(B)$. Put $F_ T=\{ \varphi \leq -T\} $. By maximum locality (proposition 9.2.7 ), the two measures agree on the complement $\{ \varphi >-T\} $. Since their total masses are equal and finite, they also assign the same mass $m_ T$ to $F_ T$, and Chebyshev's inequality gives \[  m_ T\leq T^{-p}\int _{F_ T}(-\varphi )^ p(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^ n\leq e_ p(\varphi )T^{-p}.  \] As $\varphi _ T=-T$ on $F_ T$, we get \[  e_ p(\varphi _ T)=\int _{\{ \varphi >-T\} }(-\varphi )^ p(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^ n+T^ pm_ T \leq e_ p(\varphi ).  \] The two measures differ only on $F_ T$, where each has mass $m_ T$; this proves ( 9.56 ). Finally, $(\varphi _ T+T)/T$ is plurisubharmonic with values in $[0,1]$, so it is a competitor for $\operatorname {Cap}_ B$ (definition 9.3.2 ), and therefore $\int _ E(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ T)^ n\leq T^ n\operatorname {Cap}_ B(E)$. Since the two measures agree on $E\setminus F_ T$, we conclude \[  \int _ E(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^ n \leq \int _{E\setminus F_ T}(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ T)^ n+m_ T \leq T^ n\operatorname {Cap}_ B(E)+e_ p(\varphi )T^{-p}.  \] $\square$ Proposition 9.10.8 . Let $p\geq 1$. For every $\varphi \in \mathcal E_0(B)$ and every $T>0$, \[  \operatorname {Cap}_ B(\{ \varphi <-T\} ) \leq 2^{n+p}(n+1)!\, e_ p(\varphi )T^{-(n+p)}.  \] Let $\varphi _ j\in \mathcal E_0(B)$ converge in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(B)$, let $u$ be the plurisubharmonic representative of the limit (theorem 8.3.4 ), and suppose that $E_ p=\sup _ je_ p(\varphi _ j)<\infty $. For every compact set $K\subset B$ there is a constant $C_{K,p}$, depending only on $K$, $p$ and the ball $B$, such that 9.58  egin{equation} \label{eq:energy-limit-capacity-tail} \operatorname {Cap}_ B^*(K\cap \{ u<-T\} ) \leq C_{K,p}E_ p^{p/(n+p)}T^{-p}\qquad (T>0). \end{equation} In particular, $\operatorname {Cap}^*_ B(K\cap \{ u=-\infty \} )=0$ for every compact set $K\subset B$. Proof. (1) Let $h$ be a competitor for $\operatorname {Cap}_ B$, that is, $h\in \mathrm{PSH}(B)$ and $0\leq h\leq 1$. The set $\{ \varphi <-T\} $ is open, because $\varphi $ is upper semicontinuous, and it is relatively compact in $B$, because $\varphi $ has zero boundary values. Hence $
u =\mathbf1_{\{ \varphi <-T\} }(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h)^ n$ is a finite measure, and it is dominated by $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h)^ n$. The tail estimate ( 9.42 ) of theorem 9.10.2 , applied to $
u $ and $w=h$, involves the constant $\kappa _{n,p}=2^{n+p}(n+1)!M^ n$, where $M\leq 1$ is the oscillation of $h$ on $B$, but not the mass of $
u $; it gives \[  \int _{\{ \varphi <-T\} }(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h)^ n=
u (\{ \varphi <-T\} ) \leq 2^{n+p}(n+1)!\, e_ p(\varphi )T^{-(n+p)}.  \] Taking the supremum over $h$ proves (1). (2) Choose an open set $U$ and compact sets $L,L'\subset B$ with $K\subset U\Subset \operatorname{Int}L$ and $L\subset \operatorname{Int}L'$. By the Chern–Levine–Nirenberg inequality (theorem 9.1.3 , with the base current $1$ and the pair $L\subset \operatorname{Int}L'$), there is a constant $C_ L$ with $\int _ L(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h)^ n\leq C_ L$ for every competitor $h$, since $\| h\| _{L^\infty (L')}\leq 1$. The finite measure $\mathbf1_ L(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h)^ n$ is dominated by $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h)^ n$ and has mass at most $C_ L$, so the constant $A_ p$ of theorem 9.10.2 for this measure and $w=h$ is at most \[  C_{K,p}=\Bigl (1+ rac pn\Bigr ) igl (2^{n+p}(n+1)! igr )^{p/(n+p)}C_ L^{n/(n+p)}.  \] Hence the moment estimate ( 9.43 ), applied to $\varphi _ j$, gives \[  \int _ L(-\varphi _ j)^ p(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h)^ n \leq C_{K,p}E_ p^{p/(n+p)}  \] for all $j$ and all competitors $h$. We pass this bound to the limit $u$. Since the $\varphi _ j$ are nonpositive, $u\leq 0$ almost everywhere, and hence everywhere by the submean inequality. Fix $S>0$. The truncations $\max \{ \varphi _ j,-S\} $ take values in $[-S,0]$ and converge to the plurisubharmonic function $\max \{ u,-S\} $ in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(B)$, since $t\mapsto \max \{ t,-S\} $ is $1$-Lipschitz. Since $\mathbf1_ L(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h)^ n\leq (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h)^ n$, lemma 9.10.4 shows that they also converge in $L^1(\mathbf1_ L(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h)^ n)$. As $t\mapsto t^ p$ is Lipschitz on $[0,S]$ and $(-\max \{ \varphi _ j,-S\} )^ p\leq (-\varphi _ j)^ p$, it follows that \[   egin{aligned}  \int _ L(-\max \{ u,-S\} )^ p(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h)^ n & =\lim _{j	o \infty }\int _ L(-\max \{ \varphi _ j,-S\} )^ p(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h)^ n\ & \leq C_{K,p}E_ p^{p/(n+p)}. \end{aligned}  \] Letting $S	o \infty $, monotone convergence gives the same bound for $\int _ L(-u)^ p(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h)^ n$. By Chebyshev's inequality its $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h)^ n$-measure is at most $C_{K,p}E_ p^{p/(n+p)}T^{-p}$. Taking the supremum over $h$ bounds $\operatorname {Cap}_ B(U\cap \{ u<-T\} )$, and hence the outer capacity in ( 9.58 ). Finally, $K\cap \{ u=-\infty \} $ is contained in $K\cap \{ u<-T\} $ for every $T$, so letting $T	o \infty $ shows that it has zero outer capacity. $\square$ Theorem 9.10.9 . Under the hypotheses of theorem 9.10.5 , the relabeled subsequence $U_ j$ converges to $u$ locally in capacity. Moreover, let $E_2=\sup _ je_2(U_ j)$, which is finite by proposition 9.10.3 . For every $T>0$, the Monge–Ampère measure of the bounded plurisubharmonic function $u_ T=\max \{ u,-T\} $ has total mass at most $m$, and 9.61  egin{equation} \label{eq:canonical-grid-truncated-measure-limit} \| (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ T)^ n-\mu \| _{\mathrm{TV}}\leq 2E_2T^{-2}. \end{equation} Proof. We estimate the capacities of the sets where the truncation $\max \{ U_ j,-T\} $ lies far below or far above $u_ T$ (Steps 1 and 2) and deduce convergence in capacity (Step 3). The estimate for $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ T)^ n$ then follows from the convergence of the truncated measures (Step 4). Fix $T>0$ and write $a_ j=\max \{ U_ j,-T\} $ and $b=u_ T$. These plurisubharmonic functions take values in $[-T,0]$, and $a_ j	o b$ in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(B)$ because truncation is $1$-Lipschitz. By theorem 9.10.5 , $\varepsilon _ j=\int _ B|U_ j-u|\, \mathrm d\mu _ j	o 0$. Step 1. The sets where $a_ j<b-\delta $. Let $\delta >0$. The set $\{ a_ j<b-\delta /2\} $ is relatively compact in $B$, because $b\leq 0$ while $a_ j$ tends to zero at $\partial B$. Applying lemma 9.9.1 with $s=t=\delta /2$ and then Chebyshev's inequality, we obtain \[   egin{aligned}  \operatorname {Cap}_ B(\{ a_ j<b-\delta \} ) & \leq \left( rac2\delta ight)^ n\int _{\{ a_ j<b-\delta /2\} }(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a_ j)^ n\ & \leq 2^{n+1}\delta ^{-(n+1)}\int _ B(b-a_ j)_+(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a_ j)^ n. \end{aligned}  \] The weight $(b-a_ j)_+$ takes values in $[0,T]$, and it is at most $|U_ j-u|$, since truncation does not increase distances. By ( 9.56 ) with $p=2$, $\| (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a_ j)^ n-\mu _ j\| _{\mathrm{TV}}\leq 2E_2T^{-2}$, where $\mu _ j=(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U_ j)^ n$. Hence \[  \int _ B(b-a_ j)_+(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a_ j)^ n \leq \int _ B(b-a_ j)_+\, \mathrm d\mu _ j+T\cdot 2E_2T^{-2} \leq \varepsilon _ j+ rac{2E_2}T,  \] and therefore $\operatorname {Cap}_ B(\{ a_ j<b-\delta \} )\leq 2^{n+1}\delta ^{-(n+1)}(\varepsilon _ j+2E_2/T)$. Step 2. The sets where $a_ j>b+\delta $. Let $L\subset B$ be compact. By theorem 9.4.2 , for every $\sigma >0$ there is an open set $G\subset B$ with $\operatorname {Cap}_ B(G)<\sigma $ such that $b$ is continuous on $B\setminus G$. We claim that $L\cap \{ a_ j>b+\delta \} \subset G$ for all sufficiently large $j$. Let $z\in L\setminus G$. Since $b$ is upper semicontinuous, $b<b(z)+\delta /3$ on a closed ball $\overline{B(z,r)}\subset B$. Hartogs' lemma (theorem 8.3.4 ), applied to the sequence $a_ j$ with the constant majorant $b(z)+\delta /3$, gives $a_ j<b(z)+\delta /3$ on $\overline{B(z,r)}$ for all large $j$. Since $b$ is continuous on $B\setminus G$, after shrinking $r$ we also have $b>b(z)-\delta /3$ on $(L\setminus G)\cap B(z,r)$. Hence $a_ j-b<2\delta /3$ on $(L\setminus G)\cap B(z,r)$ for all large $j$. As $L\setminus G$ is compact, finitely many such balls cover it, which proves the claim. Consequently $\varlimsup _ j\operatorname {Cap}_ B(L\cap \{ a_ j>b+\delta \} )\leq \sigma $ for every $\sigma >0$, that is, $\operatorname {Cap}_ B(L\cap \{ a_ j>b+\delta \} )	o 0$. Step 3. Convergence in capacity. Let $K\subset B$ be compact, and apply Step 2 to a compact set $L\subset B$ with $K\subset \operatorname{Int}L$. The bounded functions $a_ j-b$ are quasi-continuous by theorem 9.4.2 and the remark following definition 9.4.1 . Therefore lemma 9.4.4 , together with Steps 1 and 2 applied with $\delta /2$ in place of $\delta $, gives \[   egin{aligned} & \varlimsup _{j	o \infty }\operatorname {Cap}_ B^*(K\cap \{ |a_ j-b|>\delta \} )\ & \qquad \leq \varlimsup _{j	o \infty } igl (\operatorname {Cap}_ B(L\cap \{ a_ j>b+\delta /2\} ) +\operatorname {Cap}_ B(\{ a_ j<b-\delta /2\} ) igr )\ & \qquad \leq 2^{2n+3}\delta ^{-(n+1)} rac{E_2}T. \end{aligned}  \] It remains to remove the truncation. Outside $\{ U_ j<-T\} \cup \{ u<-T\} $ we have $a_ j=U_ j$ and $b=u$. Hence both sets $K\cap \{ U_ j>u+\delta \} $ and $K\cap \{ U_ j<u-\delta \} $ in definition 9.4.5 are contained in \[   igl (K\cap \{ |a_ j-b|>\delta \}  igr )\cup \{ U_ j<-T\} \cup  igl (K\cap \{ u<-T\}  igr ).  \] By proposition 9.10.8 with $p=2$, applied in part (1) to $U_ j$, whose energy is at most $E_2$, and in part (2) to the sequence $(U_ j)$, \[  \operatorname {Cap}_ B(\{ U_ j<-T\} )\leq  rac{2^{n+2}(n+1)!\, E_2}{T^{n+2}},\qquad \operatorname {Cap}_ B^*(K\cap \{ u<-T\} )\leq  rac{C_{K,2}E_2^{2/(n+2)}}{T^2},  \] and the capacity of the open set $\{ U_ j<-T\} $ equals its outer capacity. By subadditivity of the outer capacity, the upper limits as $j	o \infty $ of the outer capacities of the two sets in definition 9.4.5 are bounded by the sum of three terms, each of which tends to zero as $T	o \infty $. Since these upper limits do not depend on $T$, they vanish. Thus $U_ j	o u$ locally in capacity. Step 4. The truncated limit measure. Fix $T>0$ again. By Step 3 and ( 9.53 ), the uniformly bounded functions $a_ j$ converge to $b$ locally in capacity, so $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a_ j)^ n	o (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ T)^ n$ weakly on $B$ by theorem 9.4.8 . By lemma 9.10.7 , each $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a_ j)^ n$ has total mass $\mu _ j(B)=m$. title: Truncation level inclusions

title: Compact perturbation mass
text: Lemma 9.10.6 . Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ be open, and let $\varphi ,\psi $ be locally bounded plurisubharmonic functions on $\Omega $ which coincide outside a compact set $K\subset \Omega $. Then $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^ n$ and $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi )^ n$ agree on $\Omega \setminus K$ and assign the same finite mass to $K$. In particular $\int _\Omega (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^ n=\int _\Omega (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi )^ n$, where both sides may be infinite. Proof. The two measures agree on the open set $\Omega \setminus K$, because the products are local (proposition 9.1.2 ). For $0\leq k\leq n-1$ put $S_ k=(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^ k\wedge (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi )^{n-1-k}$. By the symmetry of the products (theorem 9.2.5 ) and definition 9.1.1 , \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\varphi S_ k)=(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^{k+1}\wedge (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi )^{n-1-k}, \qquad \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\psi S_ k)=(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^ k\wedge (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi )^{n-k},  \] so the sum over $k$ telescopes and \[  (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^ n-(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi )^ n=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}R,\qquad R=(\varphi -\psi )\sum _{k=0}^{n-1}S_ k.  \] The coefficient measures of the current $R$ of order zero vanish on $\Omega \setminus K$, so $\operatorname{Supp}R\subset K$. By lemma 1.4.1 there is $\chi \in C^\infty _ c(\Omega )$ with $0\leq \chi \leq 1$ which equals one on a neighborhood of $K$. Then $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi $ vanishes on a neighborhood of $\operatorname{Supp}R$, and therefore \[  \int \chi \, (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^ n-\int \chi \, (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi )^ n=R(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi )=0,  \] where both integrals are finite. Since $\chi =1$ on $K$ and the two measures agree on $\Omega \setminus K$, it follows that $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^ n(K)=(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi )^ n(K)<\infty $, and adding the equal masses of $\Omega \setminus K$ gives the last assertion. $\square$

title: Zero boundary truncation mass
text: Lemma 9.10.7 . Let $\varphi \in \mathcal E_0(B)$ and $T>0$, and put $\varphi _ T=\max \{ \varphi ,-T\} $. Then $\varphi _ T\in \mathcal E_0(B)$, and for every $p\geq 1$, \[  \int _ B(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ T)^ n=\int _ B(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^ n, \qquad e_ p(\varphi _ T)\leq e_ p(\varphi ),  \] 9.56 \begin{equation} \label{eq:zero-boundary-truncation-variation} \| (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ T)^ n-(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^ n\| _{\mathrm{TV}} \leq 2e_ p(\varphi )T^{-p}. \end{equation} Moreover, for every Borel set $E\subset B$, 9.57 \begin{equation} \label{eq:energy-measure-capacity-modulus} \int _ E(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^ n \leq T^ n\operatorname {Cap}_ B(E)+e_ p(\varphi )T^{-p}. \end{equation} Proof. Since $\varphi $ tends to zero uniformly at $\partial B$, there is an open neighborhood $V$ of $\partial B$ such that $\varphi >-T$ on $V\cap B$; there $\varphi _ T=\varphi $. Thus $\varphi _ T$ is bounded, nonpositive and plurisubharmonic, it has zero boundary values, and it coincides with $\varphi $ outside the compact set $\overline B\setminus V\subset B$. By lemma 9.10.6 , the measures $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ T)^ n$ and $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^ n$ have the same total mass, which is finite; in particular $\varphi _ T\in \mathcal E_0(B)$. Put $F_ T=\{ \varphi \leq -T\} $. By maximum locality (proposition 9.2.7 ), the two measures agree on the complement $\{ \varphi >-T\} $. Since their total masses are equal and finite, they also assign the same mass $m_ T$ to $F_ T$, and Chebyshev's inequality gives \[  m_ T\leq T^{-p}\int _{F_ T}(-\varphi )^ p(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^ n\leq e_ p(\varphi )T^{-p}.  \] As $\varphi _ T=-T$ on $F_ T$, we get \[  e_ p(\varphi _ T)=\int _{\{ \varphi >-T\} }(-\varphi )^ p(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^ n+T^ pm_ T \leq e_ p(\varphi ).  \] The two measures differ only on $F_ T$, where each has mass $m_ T$; this proves ( 9.56 ). Finally, $(\varphi _ T+T)/T$ is plurisubharmonic with values in $[0,1]$, so it is a competitor for $\operatorname {Cap}_ B$ (definition 9.3.2 ), and therefore $\int _ E(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ T)^ n\leq T^ n\operatorname {Cap}_ B(E)$. Since the two measures agree on $E\setminus F_ T$, we conclude \[  \int _ E(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^ n \leq \int _{E\setminus F_ T}(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ T)^ n+m_ T \leq T^ n\operatorname {Cap}_ B(E)+e_ p(\varphi )T^{-p}.  \] $\square$

title: Zero boundary truncation variation
text: 9.56 \begin{equation} \label{eq:zero-boundary-truncation-variation} \| (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ T)^ n-(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^ n\| _{\mathrm{TV}} \leq 2e_ p(\varphi )T^{-p}. \end{equation}

title: Energy measure capacity modulus
text: 9.57 \begin{equation} \label{eq:energy-measure-capacity-modulus} \int _ E(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^ n \leq T^ n\operatorname {Cap}_ B(E)+e_ p(\varphi )T^{-p}. \end{equation}

title: Energy controlled local capacity tails
text:
Proposition 9.10.8 . Let $p\geq 1$. For every $\varphi \in \mathcal E_0(B)$ and every $T>0$, \[  \operatorname {Cap}_ B(\{ \varphi <-T\} ) \leq 2^{n+p}(n+1)!\, e_ p(\varphi )T^{-(n+p)}.  \] Let $\varphi _ j\in \mathcal E_0(B)$ converge in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(B)$, let $u$ be the plurisubharmonic representative of the limit (theorem 8.3.4 ), and suppose that $E_ p=\sup _ je_ p(\varphi _ j)<\infty $. u =\mathbf1_{\{ \varphi <-T\} }(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h)^ n$ is a finite measure, and it is dominated by $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h)^ n$. The tail estimate ( 9.42 ) of theorem 9.10.2 , applied to $
u $ and $w=h$, involves the constant $\kappa _{n,p}=2^{n+p}(n+1)!M^ n$, where $M\leq 1$ is the oscillation of $h$ on $B$, but not the mass of $
u $; it gives \[  \int _{\{ \varphi <-T\} }(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h)^ n=
u (\{ \varphi <-T\} ) \leq 2^{n+p}(n+1)!\, e_ p(\varphi )T^{-(n+p)}.  \] Taking the supremum over $h$ proves (1). We pass this bound to the limit $u$. Since the $\varphi _ j$ are nonpositive, $u\leq 0$ almost everywhere, and hence everywhere by the submean inequality. Fix $S>0$. The truncations $\max \{ \varphi _ j,-S\} $ take values in $[-S,0]$ and converge to the plurisubharmonic function $\max \{ u,-S\} $ in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(B)$, since $t\mapsto \max \{ t,-S\} $ is $1$-Lipschitz. Since $\mathbf1_ L(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h)^ n\leq (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h)^ n$, lemma 9.10.4 shows that they also converge in $L^1(\mathbf1_ L(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h)^ n)$. As $t\mapsto t^ p$ is Lipschitz on $[0,S]$ and $(-\max \{ \varphi _ j,-S\} )^ p\leq (-\varphi _ j)^ p$, it follows that \[   egin{aligned}  \int _ L(-\max \{ u,-S\} )^ p(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h)^ n & =\lim _{j	o \infty }\int _ L(-\max \{ \varphi _ j,-S\} )^ p(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h)^ n\ & \leq C_{K,p}E_ p^{p/(n+p)}. \end{aligned}  \] Letting $S	o \infty $, monotone convergence gives the same bound for $\int _ L(-u)^ p(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h)^ n$. The set $U\cap \{ u<-T\} $ is open, because $u$ is upper semicontinuous, and it contains $K\cap \{ u<-T\} $. By Chebyshev's inequality its $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h)^ n$-measure is at most $C_{K,p}E_ p^{p/(n+p)}T^{-p}$. title: Canonical grid capacity convergence
text: Theorem 9.10.9 . Under the hypotheses of theorem 9.10.5 , the relabeled subsequence $U_ j$ converges to $u$ locally in capacity. Moreover, let $E_2=\sup _ je_2(U_ j)$, which is finite by proposition 9.10.3 . For every $T>0$, the Monge–Ampère measure of the bounded plurisubharmonic function $u_ T=\max \{ u,-T\} $ has total mass at most $m$, and 9.61 \begin{equation} \label{eq:canonical-grid-truncated-measure-limit} \| (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ T)^ n-\mu \| _{\mathrm{TV}}\leq 2E_2T^{-2}. \end{equation} Proof. We estimate the capacities of the sets where the truncation $\max \{ U_ j,-T\} $ lies far below or far above $u_ T$ (Steps 1 and 2) and deduce convergence in capacity (Step 3). The estimate for $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ T)^ n$ then follows from the convergence of the truncated measures (Step 4). Fix $T>0$ and write $a_ j=\max \{ U_ j,-T\} $ and $b=u_ T$. These plurisubharmonic functions take values in $[-T,0]$, and $a_ j\to b$ in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(B)$ because truncation is $1$-Lipschitz. By theorem 9.10.5 , $\varepsilon _ j=\int _ B|U_ j-u|\, \mathrm d\mu _ j\to 0$. Step 1. The sets where $a_ j<b-\delta $. Let $\delta >0$. The set $\{ a_ j<b-\delta /2\} $ is relatively compact in $B$, because $b\leq 0$ while $a_ j$ tends to zero at $\partial B$. Applying lemma 9.9.1 with $s=t=\delta /2$ and then Chebyshev's inequality, we obtain \[  \begin{aligned}  \operatorname {Cap}_ B(\{ a_ j<b-\delta \} ) & \leq \left(\frac2\delta \right)^ n\int _{\{ a_ j<b-\delta /2\} }(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a_ j)^ n\\ & \leq 2^{n+1}\delta ^{-(n+1)}\int _ B(b-a_ j)_+(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a_ j)^ n. \end{aligned}  \] The weight $(b-a_ j)_+$ takes values in $[0,T]$, and it is at most $|U_ j-u|$, since truncation does not increase distances. By ( 9.56 ) with $p=2$, $\| (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a_ j)^ n-\mu _ j\| _{\mathrm{TV}}\leq 2E_2T^{-2}$, where $\mu _ j=(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U_ j)^ n$. Hence \[  \int _ B(b-a_ j)_+(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a_ j)^ n \leq \int _ B(b-a_ j)_+\, \mathrm d\mu _ j+T\cdot 2E_2T^{-2} \leq \varepsilon _ j+\frac{2E_2}T,  \] and therefore $\operatorname {Cap}_ B(\{ a_ j<b-\delta \} )\leq 2^{n+1}\delta ^{-(n+1)}(\varepsilon _ j+2E_2/T)$. Step 2. The sets where $a_ j>b+\delta $. Let $L\subset B$ be compact. By theorem 9.4.2 , for every $\sigma >0$ there is an open set $G\subset B$ with $\operatorname {Cap}_ B(G)<\sigma $ such that $b$ is continuous on $B\setminus G$. We claim that $L\cap \{ a_ j>b+\delta \} \subset G$ for all sufficiently large $j$. Let $z\in L\setminus G$. Since $b$ is upper semicontinuous, $b<b(z)+\delta /3$ on a closed ball $\overline{B(z,r)}\subset B$. Hartogs' lemma (theorem 8.3.4 ), applied to the sequence $a_ j$ with the constant majorant $b(z)+\delta /3$, gives $a_ j<b(z)+\delta /3$ on $\overline{B(z,r)}$ for all large $j$. Since $b$ is continuous on $B\setminus G$, after shrinking $r$ we also have $b>b(z)-\delta /3$ on $(L\setminus G)\cap B(z,r)$. Hence $a_ j-b<2\delta /3$ on $(L\setminus G)\cap B(z,r)$ for all large $j$. As $L\setminus G$ is compact, finitely many such balls cover it, which proves the claim. Consequently $\varlimsup _ j\operatorname {Cap}_ B(L\cap \{ a_ j>b+\delta \} )\leq \sigma $ for every $\sigma >0$, that is, $\operatorname {Cap}_ B(L\cap \{ a_ j>b+\delta \} )\to 0$. Step 3. Convergence in capacity. Let $K\subset B$ be compact, and apply Step 2 to a compact set $L\subset B$ with $K\subset \operatorname{Int}L$. The bounded functions $a_ j-b$ are quasi-continuous by theorem 9.4.2 and the remark following definition 9.4.1 . Therefore lemma 9.4.4 , together with Steps 1 and 2 applied with $\delta /2$ in place of $\delta $, gives \[  \begin{aligned} & \varlimsup _{j\to \infty }\operatorname {Cap}_ B^*(K\cap \{ |a_ j-b|>\delta \} )\\ & \qquad \leq \varlimsup _{j\to \infty }\bigl (\operatorname {Cap}_ B(L\cap \{ a_ j>b+\delta /2\} ) +\operatorname {Cap}_ B(\{ a_ j<b-\delta /2\} )\bigr )\\ & \qquad \leq 2^{2n+3}\delta ^{-(n+1)}\frac{E_2}T. \end{aligned}  \] It remains to remove the truncation. This proves ( 9.61 ). $\square$

If one of the asserted convergences failed for the whole sequence, some subsequence would stay away from the stated limit, and no further subsequence could converge as just described. This contradiction proves all the assertions. $\square$

u (\{ f<c\} )$ and $
u (\{ f\leq c\} )$, which are equal since $
u (\{ f=c\} )=0$. This proves ( 9.67 ). $\square$

title: Capacity controlled moving level sets
text: 9.67 \begin{equation} \label{eq:capacity-controlled-moving-level-sets} \nu _ j(\{ f_ j<c\} )\longrightarrow \nu (\{ f<c\} ). \end{equation}

title: Energy controlled fixed measure limit
text:
Corollary 9.10.11 . Let $\varphi _ j\in \mathcal E_0(B)$ with $\sup _ je_2(\varphi _ j)<\infty $ converge in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(B)$, and let $u$ be the plurisubharmonic representative of the limit (theorem 8.3.4 ). If $
u $ is a finite positive Borel measure on $B$ with $
u \leq (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w)^ n$ for some bounded $w\in \mathrm{PSH}(B)$, then $u\in L^2(
u )$ and $\varphi _ j	o u$ in $L^1(
u )$. Proof. By the moment estimate ( 9.43 ) with $p=2$, the integrals $\int _ B\varphi _ j^2\, \mathrm d
u $ are bounded uniformly in $j$. Since the $\varphi _ j$ are nonpositive, so is $u$, by the submean inequality. Fix $T>0$. By lemma 9.10.4 , the truncations $\max \{ \varphi _ j,-T\} $ converge to $\max \{ u,-T\} $ in $L^1(
u )$, and so do their squares, since squaring is Lipschitz on $[-T,0]$. Hence $\int _ B\max \{ u,-T\} ^2\, \mathrm d
u \leq \sup _ j\int _ B\varphi _ j^2\, \mathrm d
u $, and letting $T	o \infty $ shows that $u\in L^2(
u )$ with the same bound. For a function $v\leq 0$ we have $0\leq \max \{ v,-T\} -v\leq v^2/T$, so the $L^1(
u )$ distances between $\varphi _ j,u$ and their truncations are at most $T^{-1}$ times a bound independent of $j$. Letting first $j	o \infty $ and then $T	o \infty $ proves that $\varphi _ j	o u$ in $L^1(
u )$. $\square$

title: Compact bounded subsolution ball dirichlet
text:
Theorem 9.10.12 . Let $B\subset \mathbb C^ n$ be a ball, $n\geq 1$, and let $\mu $ be a finite positive Borel measure with compact support in $B$. Suppose that $\mu \leq (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w)^ n$ for some bounded $w\in \mathrm{PSH}(B)$. Then there is a unique bounded plurisubharmonic function $U$ on $B$ with \[  (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U)^ n=\mu ,\qquad \lim _{B
i z	o \zeta }U(z)=0\quad (\zeta \in \partial B).  \] It belongs to $\mathcal E_0(B)$, and it is the pointwise supremum of the bounded plurisubharmonic functions $v$ on $B$ such that $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n\geq \mu $ and $\varlimsup _{B
i z	o \zeta }v(z)\leq 0$ for every $\zeta \in \partial B$. Moreover, for every choice of grids, the whole sequence of canonical approximants $U_ j$ of $\mu $ (proposition 9.10.3 ) converges to $U$ in $L^1(B)$ and locally in capacity, and \[  \int _ B|U_ j-U|\, \mathrm d\mu +\int _ B|U_ j-U|\, \mathrm d\mu _ j\longrightarrow 0.  \] Proof. If $\mu =0$, then all $\mu _ j$ and all $U_ j$ vanish, and $U=0$ is a solution. By the maximum principle (proposition 3.1.4 ), every plurisubharmonic function on $B$ whose upper boundary limits are at most zero is nonpositive, so $U=0$ is the stated supremum, and the last assertion of theorem 9.2.8 , applied in both directions, shows that any two bounded solutions coincide. We may therefore assume that $m=\mu (B)>0$. We construct a barrier $W$ (Step 1) and, along a convergent subsequence of canonical approximants, prove that the masses of certain sublevel sets converge (Step 2). The comparison theorem then shows that the limit lies above $W$ and is a solution (Step 3), and uniqueness gives the convergence of the whole sequence (Step 4). Step 1. A barrier with zero boundary values. Write $B=B(a,R)$ and $ho (z)=|z-a|^2-R^2$, let $M=\sup _ Bw-\inf _ Bw$, and put $w_0=w-\sup _ Bw-1$, so that $-M-1\leq w_0\leq -1$. Since $\operatorname{Supp}\mu $ is a compact subset of $B$, the function $ho $ is bounded away from zero on an open neighborhood $N\Subset B$ of $\operatorname{Supp}\mu $, and we can choose $A>0$ with $Aho <-M-2$ on $N$. Put \[  W=\max \{ w_0,Aho \} ,  \] a plurisubharmonic function on $B$ (proposition 8.2.5 ). Then $W=w_0$ on $N$, while $W=Aho $ near $\partial B$, because $Aho 	o 0$ at $\partial B$ and $w_0\leq -1$. Thus $W$ is bounded and negative and has zero boundary values. By locality on the open set $N$ (proposition 9.1.2 ), $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}W)^ n=(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w)^ n\geq \mu $ there; as $\mu $ is carried by $N$, we get $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}W)^ n\geq \mu $ on $B$. For $\varepsilon >0$ put $W_\varepsilon =W+\varepsilon ho $. It equals $(A+\varepsilon )ho $ near $\partial B$, so its Monge–Ampère measure is a smooth measure there and is finite on the remaining compact part of $B$; hence it has finite total mass. Expanding $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}W+\varepsilon \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}ho )^ n$ and dropping the mixed terms, which are positive, we obtain 9.68  egin{equation} \label{eq:local-subsolution-strict-barrier} 
u _\varepsilon :=(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}W_\varepsilon )^ n \geq \mu +\varepsilon ^ n(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}ho )^ n. \end{equation} Step 2. Convergence of the masses of sublevel sets. By proposition 9.10.3 , a subsequence of the canonical approximants, still denoted $U_ j$ (together with the corresponding measures $\mu _ j$), converges in $L^1(B)$; let $u$ be the nonpositive plurisubharmonic representative of the limit. By theorem 9.10.9 , $U_ j	o u$ locally in capacity, and $E_2=\sup _ je_2(U_ j)<\infty $. By corollary 9.10.11 with $
u =
u _\varepsilon $, we have $U_ j	o u$ in $L^1(
u _\varepsilon )$ for every $\varepsilon >0$. We check that lemma 9.10.10 applies to the measures $\mu _ j$ and $\mu $. Let $K$ be the support of $\mu $ and $d=\operatorname {dist}(K,\mathbb C^ n\setminus B)>0$, and let $h_ j$ be the side lengths of the cubes defining $\mu _ j$. A cube $Q$ with $\mu _ j(Q)>0$ satisfies $\mu (Q)>0$, so it meets $K$. Since $h_ j	o 0$, after discarding finitely many indices every such cube has diameter $\sqrt{2n}\, h_ j<d/2$, and then $\mu _ j$ is supported in the compact set $K_0=\{ z:\operatorname {dist}(z,K)\leq d/2\} \subset B$, which also contains the support of $\mu $. By proposition 9.10.3 , $\mu _ j	o \mu $ weakly. By ( 9.57 ) with $p=2$, and since $\operatorname {Cap}_ B(E)\leq \operatorname {Cap}_ B^*(E)$, we have $\mu _ j(E)\leq T^ n\operatorname {Cap}_ B^*(E)+E_2T^{-2}$ for every Borel set $E\subset B$ and every $T>0$. Let $\omega (t)$ be the supremum of $\mu _ j(E)$ over all $j$ and all Borel sets $E\subset B$ with $\operatorname {Cap}_ B^*(E)\leq t$. Then $\omega $ is nondecreasing with values in $[0,m]$, and $\omega (t)\leq T^ nt+E_2T^{-2}$ for every $T>0$. Choosing first $T$ large and then $t$ small shows that $\omega (t)	o 0$ as $t\downarrow 0$. Fix $\varepsilon >0$. The level sets $\{ u-W_\varepsilon =-\delta \} $, $0<\delta <1$, are pairwise disjoint Borel sets, and $\mu +
u _\varepsilon $ is a finite measure, so by lemma 1.1.5 all but countably many of these sets are null for $\mu +
u _\varepsilon $, hence for both measures. Choose $\delta \in (0,1)$ such that $\{ u-W_\varepsilon =-\delta \} $ is null for both $\mu $ and $
u _\varepsilon $, and fix $T>\| W_\varepsilon \| _\infty +2$. Since $W_\varepsilon -\delta >-T$, the sets $\{ U_ j<W_\varepsilon -\delta \} $ and $\{ u<W_\varepsilon -\delta \} $ do not change when $U_ j$ and $u$ are replaced by $a_ j=\max \{ U_ j,-T\} $ and $b=\max \{ u,-T\} $. We apply lemma 9.10.10 to the functions $f_ j=a_ j-W_\varepsilon $ and $f=b-W_\varepsilon $, which are bounded by $T+\| W_\varepsilon \| _\infty $ and quasi-continuous by theorem 9.4.2 and the remark following definition 9.4.1 . Since $U_ j	o u$ locally in capacity, ( 9.53 ) shows that $a_ j	o b$ locally in capacity, and hence $f_ j	o f$, because $W_\varepsilon $ is finite. Moreover, $\mu (\{ f=-\delta \} )=0$ by the choice of $\delta $, since $\{ f=-\delta \} =\{ u-W_\varepsilon =-\delta \} $: indeed, $b=u$ wherever $u\geq -T$, while $u-W_\varepsilon <-2$ and $b-W_\varepsilon \leq -T+\| W_\varepsilon \| _\infty <-2$ wherever $u<-T$. Thus ( 9.67 ), with $c=-\delta $, gives \[  \mu _ j(\{ U_ j<W_\varepsilon -\delta \} ) \longrightarrow \mu (\{ u<W_\varepsilon -\delta \} ).  \] The analogous convergence holds for the fixed measure $
u _\varepsilon $. Indeed, for $s>0$, outside $\{ |U_ j-u|>s\} $, the indicators of $\{ U_ j<W_\varepsilon -\delta \} $ and $\{ u<W_\varepsilon -\delta \} $ can differ only on $\{ |u-W_\varepsilon +\delta |\leq s\} $. The $
u _\varepsilon $-mass of the first set tends to zero as $j	o \infty $, by the convergence in $L^1(
u _\varepsilon )$, and that of the second set tends to $
u _\varepsilon (\{ u-W_\varepsilon =-\delta \} )=0$ as $s\downarrow 0$. Hence \[  
u _\varepsilon (\{ U_ j<W_\varepsilon -\delta \} )\longrightarrow 
u _\varepsilon (\{ u<W_\varepsilon -\delta \} ).  \] Step 3. The limit is a bounded solution. Since $U_ j$ and $W_\varepsilon $ have zero boundary values, the difference $U_ j-(W_\varepsilon -\delta )$ has boundary limits $\delta >0$. The comparison theorem (theorem 9.2.8 ) therefore gives \[  
u _\varepsilon (\{ U_ j<W_\varepsilon -\delta \} ) \leq \mu _ j(\{ U_ j<W_\varepsilon -\delta \} ).  \] Let $j	o \infty $ and put $S=\{ u<W_\varepsilon -\delta \} $. By ( 9.68 ), \[  \mu (S)+\varepsilon ^ n\int _ S(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}ho )^ n\leq 
u _\varepsilon (S)\leq \mu (S).  \] Since $\mu (S)$ is finite, $S$ has Lebesgue measure zero. Thus $u\geq W_\varepsilon -\delta $ almost everywhere, and hence everywhere, by the uniqueness assertion of theorem 8.2.1 applied to $\max \{ u,W_\varepsilon -\delta \} $ and $u$. Letting $\delta \downarrow 0$ through admissible values and then $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, we obtain $W\leq u\leq 0$. As $W$ has zero boundary values, $u$ is bounded and has zero boundary values. For $T>\| u\| _\infty $ the truncation $\max \{ u,-T\} $ is $u$ itself, so ( 9.61 ) gives $\| (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n-\mu \| _{\mathrm{TV}}\leq 2E_2T^{-2}$ for all large $T$. Hence $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n=\mu $. In particular $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n$ has finite mass $m$, and $u\in \mathcal E_0(B)$. Step 4. Uniqueness and convergence of the whole sequence. Let $v$ be a bounded plurisubharmonic function on $B$ with $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n\geq \mu $ and upper boundary limits at most zero, and put $v_\varepsilon =v+\varepsilon ho $ for $\varepsilon >0$. As in Step 1, $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_\varepsilon )^ n\geq \mu +\varepsilon ^ n(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}ho )^ n$. Since $u-v_\varepsilon $ has nonnegative lower boundary limits, the comparison theorem, applied to $u$ and $v_\varepsilon $, gives \[  \mu (\{ u<v_\varepsilon \} ) +\varepsilon ^ n\int _{\{ u<v_\varepsilon \} }(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}ho )^ n \leq \mu (\{ u<v_\varepsilon \} ).  \] The two $\mu $-masses are finite, so the set $\{ u<v_\varepsilon \} $ is Lebesgue null. Therefore $u\geq v_\varepsilon $ everywhere, by the uniqueness assertion of theorem 8.2.1 applied to $\max \{ u,v_\varepsilon \} $ and $u$. Letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ gives $u\geq v$. Since $u$ is itself such a function, it is the pointwise supremum in the statement. Any bounded solution with zero boundary values is such a function, hence is at most $u$; exchanging the roles of the two solutions proves uniqueness. We denote the solution by $U$. Finally, by proposition 9.10.3 , every subsequence of the canonical approximants has a further subsequence converging in $L^1(B)$. By Step 3 and uniqueness, its limit is $U$, and theorem 9.10.5 , theorem 9.10.9 give the asserted convergence of the integrals and convergence in capacity along it. If one of the asserted convergences failed for the whole sequence, some subsequence would stay away from the stated limit, and no further subsequence could converge as just described. This contradiction proves all the assertions. $\square$

title: Local subsolution strict barrier
text: 9.68 \begin{equation} \label{eq:local-subsolution-strict-barrier} \nu _\varepsilon :=(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}W_\varepsilon )^ n \geq \mu +\varepsilon ^ n(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho )^ n. \end{equation}

title: Mixed energy and truncation
text: 9.10.4 Mixed energy and truncation In the next section we approximate several potentials at once by canonical approximants and pass to the limit in their mixed Monge–Ampère products. The approximants converge in capacity and have bounded energies, but we have no uniform bound for them, so theorem 9.4.8 does not apply to them directly. We therefore compare the mixed products with those of the truncated potentials, and for this we need to know that the sets where one of the potentials is very negative carry little mass of a mixed product. This follows from the mixed energy inequality of theorem 9.10.13 , which bounds a mixed energy by a constant multiple of the geometric mean of the energies $e_1$ of definition 9.10.1 . Theorem 9.10.13 . Let $u_0,\ldots ,u_ n\in \mathcal E_0(B)$. Then 9.69 \begin{equation} \label{eq:bounded-mixed-local-energy} \int _ B(-u_0)\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ n \leq C_ n\prod _{l=0}^ n e_1(u_ l)^{1/(n+1)}, \qquad C_ n=2^{n+2}. \end{equation} In particular the integral is finite, and it vanishes if one of the energies $e_1(u_ l)$ vanishes. Proof. Write $B=B(a,R)$ and $\rho (z)=|z-a|^2-R^2$. We say that $v\in \mathcal E_0(B)$ has a quadratic collar if $v=c\rho $ on a neighborhood of $\partial B$ in $B$ for some constant $c>0$. We first prove the inequality with constant one for potentials with quadratic collars (Steps 1 and 2), and then approximate arbitrary elements of $\mathcal E_0(B)$ by such potentials while keeping their energies under control (Steps 3 and 4). For functions $b_0,\ldots ,b_ n$ which either all have quadratic collars, or are smooth real functions on a neighborhood of $\overline B$ with $b_2,\ldots ,b_ n$ plurisubharmonic, put \[  I(b_0,\ldots ,b_ n) =\int _ B(-b_0)\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b_ n.  \] The integral is finite: in the first case every mixed product of the $b_ l$ is smooth near $\partial B$ and locally finite on the rest of $B$, and in the second the integrand is a smooth form on a neighborhood of $\overline B$. Step 1. Smooth functions. Let $b_0,\ldots ,b_ n$ be smooth real functions on a neighborhood of $\overline B$, with $b_2,\ldots ,b_ n$ plurisubharmonic and $b_0=0$ on $\partial B$, and put $S=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b_2\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b_ n$, with $S=1$ if $n=1$. With $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}$ as in ( 7.6 ), we claim that 9.70 \begin{equation} \label{eq:mixed-local-energy-gradient-form} I(b_0,b_1,b_2,\ldots ,b_ n) =\int _ B\mathrm db_0\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}b_1\wedge S. \end{equation} Fix a smooth function $\theta \colon \mathbb R\to [0,1]$ with $\theta =1$ on $(-\infty ,-2]$ and $\theta =0$ on $[-1,\infty )$, and put $\chi _ k=\theta (k\rho )$ for $k\geq 1$; then $\chi _ k\in C^\infty _ c(B)$. The $(2n-1)$-form $\chi _ kb_0\, \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}b_1\wedge S$ is smooth with compact support in $B$, and $S$ is closed, so proposition 7.1.3 and the Leibniz rule give \[  0=\int _ B\chi _ k\, \mathrm db_0\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}b_1\wedge S +\int _ Bb_0\, \mathrm d\chi _ k\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}b_1\wedge S +\int _ B\chi _ kb_0\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b_1\wedge S.  \] As $k\to \infty $, $\chi _ k\to 1$ pointwise on $B$, and the forms $\mathrm db_0\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}b_1\wedge S$ and $b_0\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b_1\wedge S$ have bounded coefficients on $B$; by dominated convergence, the first and the last integral tend to $\int _ B\mathrm db_0\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}b_1\wedge S$ and $-I(b_0,\ldots ,b_ n)$. In the middle integral, $\mathrm d\chi _ k=k\theta '(k\rho )\, \mathrm d\rho $ vanishes outside the set where $-2\leq k\rho \leq -1$. Let $\Lambda $ be the maximum of $|\nabla b_0|$ on $\overline B$. If $z\in B$ and $\zeta \in \partial B$ is a nearest boundary point, then $b_0(\zeta )=0$ and $|z-\zeta |=R-|z-a|$, so the mean value theorem on the segment from $z$ to $\zeta $ gives \[  |b_0(z)|\leq \Lambda (R-|z-a|)\leq \frac{\Lambda }{R}(R^2-|z-a|^2)=\frac{\Lambda }{R}|\rho (z)|.  \] Hence $|b_0\, k\theta '(k\rho )|\leq (\Lambda /R)|k\rho |\, |\theta '(k\rho )|\leq 2\Lambda \sup |\theta '|/R$ on $B$, uniformly in $k$, and $b_0\, k\theta '(k\rho )\to 0$ pointwise on $B$. Since $\mathrm d\rho \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}b_1\wedge S$ has bounded coefficients on $B$, dominated convergence shows that the middle integral tends to zero. This proves ( 9.70 ). As observed at the beginning of section 9.2 , $\mathrm db\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}c\wedge S=\mathrm dc\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}b\wedge S$ for smooth real $b,c$. Moreover, $\mathrm db\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}b=(\mathrm i/2\pi )\partial b\wedge \bar\partial b$ is a positive $(1,1)$-form, and so are the forms $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b_ l$, $l\geq 2$, since the complex Hessian of a smooth plurisubharmonic function is positive semidefinite (proposition 8.2.2 ). Positive $(1,1)$-forms are strongly positive (section 7.2 ), so by proposition 7.2.1 the $(n,n)$-form $\mathrm db\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}b\wedge S$ is a nonnegative multiple of the volume form. Consequently the real bilinear form \[  Q(b,c)=\int _ B\mathrm db\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}c\wedge S,  \] defined for smooth real functions $b,c$ on a neighborhood of $\overline B$ vanishing on $\partial B$, is symmetric and positive semidefinite, and by ( 9.70 ) we have $Q(b,c)=I(b,c,b_2,\ldots ,b_ n)$. The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality for $Q$, which follows from the nonnegativity of the quadratic polynomial $t\mapsto Q(b+tc,b+tc)$, therefore gives 9.71 \begin{equation} \label{eq:mixed-local-energy-two-slot} I(b,c,b_2,\ldots ,b_ n)^2 \leq I(b,b,b_2,\ldots ,b_ n)I(c,c,b_2,\ldots ,b_ n). \end{equation} The symmetry of $Q$ allows us to interchange the first two arguments of $I$, and the symmetry of the products allows us to permute the last $n$ arguments. Hence $I$ is symmetric in all $n+1$ arguments when they are smooth plurisubharmonic functions on a neighborhood of $\overline B$ vanishing on $\partial B$. Step 2. Quadratic collars. Let $u_0,\ldots ,u_ n$ have quadratic collars, say $u_ l=c_ l\rho $ near $\partial B$. We first show that the assertions of Step 1 persist for them. Extend each $u_ l$ by $c_ l\rho $ to a plurisubharmonic function on a neighborhood of $\overline B$. Let $\vartheta _\varepsilon $ be the radial mollifiers of section 1.4 , denoted $\rho _\varepsilon $ there; we change the letter because $\rho $ is now the quadratic function above. Because $\rho $ is a quadratic polynomial and $\vartheta _\varepsilon $ is radial, $\rho *\vartheta _\varepsilon =\rho +\gamma \varepsilon ^2$ with the constant $\gamma =\int |y|^2\vartheta _1(y)\, \mathrm dV(y)$. Hence \[  u_{l,\varepsilon }=u_ l*\vartheta _\varepsilon -c_ l\gamma \varepsilon ^2  \] equals $c_ l\rho $ on a fixed neighborhood of $\partial B$ for all small $\varepsilon $. By proposition 8.2.2 , the convolutions $u_ l*\vartheta _\varepsilon $ are smooth and plurisubharmonic on a neighborhood of $\overline B$ for small $\varepsilon $, and they decrease to $u_ l$ as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. Hence each $u_{l,\varepsilon }$, which differs from $u_ l*\vartheta _\varepsilon $ by a constant, is smooth and plurisubharmonic on a neighborhood of $\overline B$ and vanishes on $\partial B$, although the $u_{l,\varepsilon }$ need not decrease. By theorem 9.2.5 , \[  (-u_0*\vartheta _\varepsilon )\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{1,\varepsilon }\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{n,\varepsilon } \longrightarrow (-u_0)\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ n  \] weakly, and the constant $c_0\gamma \varepsilon ^2$ changes the integral against a fixed test function only by an amount tending to zero, by the local mass bounds of theorem 9.1.3 . Near $\partial B$, all the $u_{l,\varepsilon }$ and $u_ l$ coincide with $c_ l\rho $. Splitting the integrals over $B$ by a cutoff in $C_ c(B)$ which equals one outside this neighborhood of $\partial B$, we conclude that $I(u_{0,\varepsilon },\ldots ,u_{n,\varepsilon })\to I(u_0,\ldots ,u_ n)$, and likewise for every rearrangement of the potentials. Passing to the limit in the smooth case proves that $I$ is symmetric and satisfies ( 9.71 ) for potentials with quadratic collars. We now prove the inequality with constant one for these potentials. Since $u_ l=c_ l\rho $ near $\partial B$ with $c_ l>0$, the energy $e_1(u_ l)$ is positive: already its integral over a neighborhood of $\partial B$ is positive. Since $I$ is positively homogeneous of degree one in each argument and $e_1(tv)=t^{n+1}e_1(v)$ for $t>0$, both sides of the inequality are multiplied by the same factor when each $u_ l$ is replaced by $e_1(u_ l)^{-1/(n+1)}u_ l$. We may therefore assume that $e_1(u_ l)=1$ for every $l$. Consider the finitely many ordered $(n+1)$-tuples whose entries are taken from the functions $u_0,\ldots ,u_ n$, and let $F$ be the largest value of $I$ on these tuples. Since $I(u_ l,\ldots ,u_ l)=e_1(u_ l)=1$, we have $F\geq 1$. Among the tuples on which $I$ equals $F$, choose one for which the sum of the squares of the multiplicities of its distinct entries is largest. Suppose that this tuple contains two distinct functions $b$ and $c$, with multiplicities $r$ and $s$. By symmetry we may place them in the first two slots. In ( 9.71 ), the left side is $F^2$, while the two factors on the right are nonnegative values of $I$ on tuples of our family, hence at most $F$. Therefore both factors equal $F$. Replacing one entry $c$ by $b$ changes the sum of the squares of the multiplicities by $(r+1)^2+(s-1)^2-r^2-s^2=2(r-s)+2$, and replacing one entry $b$ by $c$ changes it by $2(s-r)+2$. One of these numbers is positive, which contradicts the choice of the tuple. Hence the chosen tuple consists of a single function repeated $n+1$ times, and $F=1$. In particular $I(u_0,\ldots ,u_ n)\leq 1$, which is the inequality with constant one. Step 3. Approximation with controlled energy. Let $u\in \mathcal E_0(B)$, put $m_\rho =\int _ B(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho )^ n$, and for $j\geq 1$ let \[  \delta _ j=j^{-n-1},\qquad v_ j=\max \{ u-\delta _ j,j\rho \} .  \] Since $u-\delta _ j\leq -\delta _ j$ while $j\rho >-\delta _ j$ near $\partial B$, the function $v_ j$ equals $j\rho $ on a neighborhood of $\partial B$ in $B$. Since $v_ j$ and $j\rho $ coincide outside a compact subset of $B$, lemma 9.10.6 gives $\int _ B(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ j)^ n=j^ nm_\rho $, and hence $v_ j\in \mathcal E_0(B)$. Moreover, $v_ j\to u$ uniformly on $B$. Indeed, let $s>0$, and choose a neighborhood $V$ of $\partial B$ with $u>-s$ on $V\cap B$. Since $u-\delta _ j\leq v_ j\leq 0$, we have $|v_ j-u|\leq s+\delta _ j$ on $V\cap B$. On the set $B\setminus V$, whose closure is a compact subset of $B$, the function $\rho $ is bounded away from zero and $u$ is bounded, so $j\rho <u-\delta _ j$, and hence $v_ j=u-\delta _ j$, there for all large $j$. Next we estimate $e_1(v_ j)$. Let $t>4\delta _ j$. Since $u\leq v_ j+\delta _ j$ and $v_ j\leq 0$, \[  \{ v_ j<-t\} \subset \{ u<v_ j/2-t/4\}  \subset \{ u<-t/4\} ;  \] for the first inclusion note that on $\{ v_ j<-t\} $ we have $v_ j/2<-t/2<-t/4-\delta _ j$, hence $u\leq v_ j+\delta _ j<v_ j/2-t/4$. As $u$ tends to $0$ and $v_ j/2-t/4$ tends to $-t/4$ at $\partial B$, the comparison theorem (theorem 9.2.8 ) applies to $u$ and $v_ j/2-t/4$ and gives \[  \int _{\{ v_ j<-t\} }(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ j)^ n \leq 2^ n\int _{\{ u<v_ j/2-t/4\} }\bigl (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v_ j/2)\bigr )^ n \leq 2^ n\int _{\{ u<-t/4\} }(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n.  \] For $0<t\leq 4\delta _ j$ we use the total mass $j^ nm_\rho $ instead. Integrating over $t$ by the layer-cake formula $e_1(v)=\int _0^\infty (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n(\{ v<-t\} )\, \mathrm dt$, we obtain 9.72 \begin{equation} \label{eq:quadratic-collar-energy-approximation} e_1(v_ j)\leq 4\delta _ j j^ n m_\rho +2^{n+2}e_1(u) =\frac{4m_\rho }j+C_ ne_1(u). \end{equation} Step 4. The general case. Apply the construction of Step 3 to each $u_ l$, obtaining functions $v_{l,j}\in \mathcal E_0(B)$ which equal $j\rho $ near $\partial B$. They are uniformly bounded, since $u_ l-1\leq v_{l,j}\leq 0$, and they converge uniformly, hence locally in capacity, to $u_ l$. Let $\chi \in C_ c(B)$ with $0\leq \chi \leq 1$. The weight $-u_0$ is bounded and quasi-continuous (theorem 9.4.2 ), so the weighted form of theorem 9.4.8 and Step 2 give \[  \begin{aligned}  \int _ B\chi (-u_0)\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ n & =\lim _{j\to \infty }\int _ B\chi (-v_{0,j})\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_{1,j}\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_{n,j}\\ & \leq \varlimsup _{j\to \infty }\prod _{l=0}^ ne_1(v_{l,j})^{1/(n+1)}. \end{aligned}  \] By ( 9.72 ), the right side is at most \[  \lim _{j\to \infty }\prod _{l=0}^ n\left(\frac{4m_\rho }j+C_ ne_1(u_ l)\right)^{1/(n+1)} =C_ n\prod _{l=0}^ ne_1(u_ l)^{1/(n+1)}.  \] Letting $\chi $ increase to one proves ( 9.69 ). Vanishing energies need no separate treatment, since the energies of the $v_{l,j}$ are positive. $\square$ Corollary 9.10.14 . Let $E\geq 0$, and for $1\leq l\leq n$ and $j\geq 1$ let $u_{l,j}\in \mathcal E_0(B)$ with $e_1(u_{l,j})\leq E$. Suppose that, for each $l$, $u_{l,j}\to u_ l$ locally in capacity as $j\to \infty $, where $u_ l$ is a locally bounded plurisubharmonic function on $B$. Then \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{1,j}\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{n,j} \longrightarrow \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ n  \] weakly on $B$. Proof. We compare the products with those of the truncations at a level $-T$: the latter converge by theorem 9.4.8 , and by theorem 9.10.13 the two differ by a term of order $1/T$. For $T>0$ put $a_{l,j}=\max \{ u_{l,j},-T\} $, and write \[  R_ j=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{1,j}\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{n,j},\qquad R_{j,T}=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a_{1,j}\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a_{n,j}.  \] By lemma 9.10.7 , $a_{l,j}\in \mathcal E_0(B)$ and $e_1(a_{l,j})\leq E$. For each $l$, theorem 9.10.13 with $u_0=u_{l,j}$, respectively $u_0=a_{l,j}$, gives \[  \int _ B(-u_{l,j})\, R_ j\leq C_ nE,\qquad \int _ B(-a_{l,j})\, R_{j,T}\leq C_ nE.  \] Let $D_{j,T}=\bigcup _{l=1}^ n\{ u_{l,j}\leq -T\} $. On $\{ u_{l,j}\leq -T\} $ both $-u_{l,j}$ and $-a_{l,j}$ are at least $T$, so Chebyshev's inequality gives \[  R_ j(D_{j,T})\leq nC_ nE/T,\qquad R_{j,T}(D_{j,T})\leq nC_ nE/T.  \] On the complement of $D_{j,T}$, every $u_{l,j}$ is greater than $-T$. For $0\leq k\leq n$ put \[  P_ k=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a_{1,j}\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a_{k,j}\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{k+1,j}\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{n,j},  \] so that $P_0=R_ j$ and $P_ n=R_{j,T}$. By the symmetry of the products, $P_ k=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a_{k,j}\wedge \Theta _ k$ and $P_{k-1}=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{k,j}\wedge \Theta _ k$ with the same closed positive current $\Theta _ k$ formed by the other $n-1$ factors, and maximum locality (proposition 9.2.7 with $p=1$, $u=u_{k,j}$, $v=-T$ and base current $\Theta _ k$) gives $P_ k=P_{k-1}$ on $\{ u_{k,j}>-T\} $. Hence $R_ j=R_{j,T}$ on the complement of $D_{j,T}$, and for every $\chi \in C_ c(B)$, \[  \left|\int _ B\chi \, (R_ j-R_{j,T})\right| \leq 2nC_ nE\| \chi \| _\infty /T.  \] Now fix $\chi \in C_ c(B)$, choose an open set $B'\Subset B$ containing $\operatorname{Supp}\chi $, and let $T>\max _ l\sup _{B'}|u_ l|$. By ( 9.53 ), the uniformly bounded functions $a_{l,j}$ converge to the locally bounded plurisubharmonic function $\max \{ u_ l,-T\} $ locally in capacity, and theorem 9.4.8 shows that $R_{j,T}\to \bigwedge _ l\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\max \{ u_ l,-T\} $ weakly on $B$. On $B'$ we have $\max \{ u_ l,-T\} =u_ l$, so by locality (proposition 9.1.2 ) this limit equals $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ n$ there. Consequently \[  \varlimsup _{j\to \infty }\left|\int _ B\chi \, R_ j-\int _ B\chi \, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ n\right|\leq 2nC_ nE\| \chi \| _\infty /T  \] for all large $T$, and letting $T\to \infty $ completes the proof. $\square$

title: Bounded mixed local energy
text: Theorem 9.10.13 . Let $u_0,\ldots ,u_ n\in \mathcal E_0(B)$. Then 9.69 \begin{equation} \label{eq:bounded-mixed-local-energy} \int _ B(-u_0)\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ n \leq C_ n\prod _{l=0}^ n e_1(u_ l)^{1/(n+1)}, \qquad C_ n=2^{n+2}. \end{equation} In particular the integral is finite, and it vanishes if one of the energies $e_1(u_ l)$ vanishes. Proof. Write $B=B(a,R)$ and $\rho (z)=|z-a|^2-R^2$. We say that $v\in \mathcal E_0(B)$ has a quadratic collar if $v=c\rho $ on a neighborhood of $\partial B$ in $B$ for some constant $c>0$. We first prove the inequality with constant one for potentials with quadratic collars (Steps 1 and 2), and then approximate arbitrary elements of $\mathcal E_0(B)$ by such potentials while keeping their energies under control (Steps 3 and 4). For functions $b_0,\ldots ,b_ n$ which either all have quadratic collars, or are smooth real functions on a neighborhood of $\overline B$ with $b_2,\ldots ,b_ n$ plurisubharmonic, put \[  I(b_0,\ldots ,b_ n) =\int _ B(-b_0)\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b_ n.  \] The integral is finite: in the first case every mixed product of the $b_ l$ is smooth near $\partial B$ and locally finite on the rest of $B$, and in the second the integrand is a smooth form on a neighborhood of $\overline B$. Step 1. Smooth functions. Let $b_0,\ldots ,b_ n$ be smooth real functions on a neighborhood of $\overline B$, with $b_2,\ldots ,b_ n$ plurisubharmonic and $b_0=0$ on $\partial B$, and put $S=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b_2\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b_ n$, with $S=1$ if $n=1$. With $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}$ as in ( 7.6 ), we claim that 9.70 \begin{equation} \label{eq:mixed-local-energy-gradient-form} I(b_0,b_1,b_2,\ldots ,b_ n) =\int _ B\mathrm db_0\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}b_1\wedge S. \end{equation} Fix a smooth function $\theta \colon \mathbb R\to [0,1]$ with $\theta =1$ on $(-\infty ,-2]$ and $\theta =0$ on $[-1,\infty )$, and put $\chi _ k=\theta (k\rho )$ for $k\geq 1$; then $\chi _ k\in C^\infty _ c(B)$. The $(2n-1)$-form $\chi _ kb_0\, \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}b_1\wedge S$ is smooth with compact support in $B$, and $S$ is closed, so proposition 7.1.3 and the Leibniz rule give \[  0=\int _ B\chi _ k\, \mathrm db_0\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}b_1\wedge S +\int _ Bb_0\, \mathrm d\chi _ k\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}b_1\wedge S +\int _ B\chi _ kb_0\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b_1\wedge S.  \] As $k\to \infty $, $\chi _ k\to 1$ pointwise on $B$, and the forms $\mathrm db_0\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}b_1\wedge S$ and $b_0\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b_1\wedge S$ have bounded coefficients on $B$; by dominated convergence, the first and the last integral tend to $\int _ B\mathrm db_0\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}b_1\wedge S$ and $-I(b_0,\ldots ,b_ n)$. In the middle integral, $\mathrm d\chi _ k=k\theta '(k\rho )\, \mathrm d\rho $ vanishes outside the set where $-2\leq k\rho \leq -1$. Let $\Lambda $ be the maximum of $|\nabla b_0|$ on $\overline B$. If $z\in B$ and $\zeta \in \partial B$ is a nearest boundary point, then $b_0(\zeta )=0$ and $|z-\zeta |=R-|z-a|$, so the mean value theorem on the segment from $z$ to $\zeta $ gives \[  |b_0(z)|\leq \Lambda (R-|z-a|)\leq \frac{\Lambda }{R}(R^2-|z-a|^2)=\frac{\Lambda }{R}|\rho (z)|.  \] Hence $|b_0\, k\theta '(k\rho )|\leq (\Lambda /R)|k\rho |\, |\theta '(k\rho )|\leq 2\Lambda \sup |\theta '|/R$ on $B$, uniformly in $k$, and $b_0\, k\theta '(k\rho )\to 0$ pointwise on $B$. Since $\mathrm d\rho \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}b_1\wedge S$ has bounded coefficients on $B$, dominated convergence shows that the middle integral tends to zero. This proves ( 9.70 ). As observed at the beginning of section 9.2 , $\mathrm db\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}c\wedge S=\mathrm dc\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}b\wedge S$ for smooth real $b,c$. Moreover, $\mathrm db\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}b=(\mathrm i/2\pi )\partial b\wedge \bar\partial b$ is a positive $(1,1)$-form, and so are the forms $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b_ l$, $l\geq 2$, since the complex Hessian of a smooth plurisubharmonic function is positive semidefinite (proposition 8.2.2 ). Positive $(1,1)$-forms are strongly positive (section 7.2 ), so by proposition 7.2.1 the $(n,n)$-form $\mathrm db\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}b\wedge S$ is a nonnegative multiple of the volume form. Consequently the real bilinear form \[  Q(b,c)=\int _ B\mathrm db\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}c\wedge S,  \] defined for smooth real functions $b,c$ on a neighborhood of $\overline B$ vanishing on $\partial B$, is symmetric and positive semidefinite, and by ( 9.70 ) we have $Q(b,c)=I(b,c,b_2,\ldots ,b_ n)$. The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality for $Q$, which follows from the nonnegativity of the quadratic polynomial $t\mapsto Q(b+tc,b+tc)$, therefore gives 9.71 \begin{equation} \label{eq:mixed-local-energy-two-slot} I(b,c,b_2,\ldots ,b_ n)^2 \leq I(b,b,b_2,\ldots ,b_ n)I(c,c,b_2,\ldots ,b_ n). \end{equation} The symmetry of $Q$ allows us to interchange the first two arguments of $I$, and the symmetry of the products allows us to permute the last $n$ arguments. Hence $I$ is symmetric in all $n+1$ arguments when they are smooth plurisubharmonic functions on a neighborhood of $\overline B$ vanishing on $\partial B$. Step 2. Quadratic collars. Let $u_0,\ldots ,u_ n$ have quadratic collars, say $u_ l=c_ l\rho $ near $\partial B$. We first show that the assertions of Step 1 persist for them. Extend each $u_ l$ by $c_ l\rho $ to a plurisubharmonic function on a neighborhood of $\overline B$. Let $\vartheta _\varepsilon $ be the radial mollifiers of section 1.4 , denoted $\rho _\varepsilon $ there; we change the letter because $\rho $ is now the quadratic function above. Because $\rho $ is a quadratic polynomial and $\vartheta _\varepsilon $ is radial, $\rho *\vartheta _\varepsilon =\rho +\gamma \varepsilon ^2$ with the constant $\gamma =\int |y|^2\vartheta _1(y)\, \mathrm dV(y)$. Hence \[  u_{l,\varepsilon }=u_ l*\vartheta _\varepsilon -c_ l\gamma \varepsilon ^2  \] equals $c_ l\rho $ on a fixed neighborhood of $\partial B$ for all small $\varepsilon $. By proposition 8.2.2 , the convolutions $u_ l*\vartheta _\varepsilon $ are smooth and plurisubharmonic on a neighborhood of $\overline B$ for small $\varepsilon $, and they decrease to $u_ l$ as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. Hence each $u_{l,\varepsilon }$, which differs from $u_ l*\vartheta _\varepsilon $ by a constant, is smooth and plurisubharmonic on a neighborhood of $\overline B$ and vanishes on $\partial B$, although the $u_{l,\varepsilon }$ need not decrease. By theorem 9.2.5 , \[  (-u_0*\vartheta _\varepsilon )\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{1,\varepsilon }\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{n,\varepsilon } \longrightarrow (-u_0)\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ n  \] weakly, and the constant $c_0\gamma \varepsilon ^2$ changes the integral against a fixed test function only by an amount tending to zero, by the local mass bounds of theorem 9.1.3 . Near $\partial B$, all the $u_{l,\varepsilon }$ and $u_ l$ coincide with $c_ l\rho $. Splitting the integrals over $B$ by a cutoff in $C_ c(B)$ which equals one outside this neighborhood of $\partial B$, we conclude that $I(u_{0,\varepsilon },\ldots ,u_{n,\varepsilon })\to I(u_0,\ldots ,u_ n)$, and likewise for every rearrangement of the potentials. Passing to the limit in the smooth case proves that $I$ is symmetric and satisfies ( 9.71 ) for potentials with quadratic collars. We now prove the inequality with constant one for these potentials. Since $u_ l=c_ l\rho $ near $\partial B$ with $c_ l>0$, the energy $e_1(u_ l)$ is positive: already its integral over a neighborhood of $\partial B$ is positive. Since $I$ is positively homogeneous of degree one in each argument and $e_1(tv)=t^{n+1}e_1(v)$ for $t>0$, both sides of the inequality are multiplied by the same factor when each $u_ l$ is replaced by $e_1(u_ l)^{-1/(n+1)}u_ l$. We may therefore assume that $e_1(u_ l)=1$ for every $l$. Consider the finitely many ordered $(n+1)$-tuples whose entries are taken from the functions $u_0,\ldots ,u_ n$, and let $F$ be the largest value of $I$ on these tuples. Since $I(u_ l,\ldots ,u_ l)=e_1(u_ l)=1$, we have $F\geq 1$. Among the tuples on which $I$ equals $F$, choose one for which the sum of the squares of the multiplicities of its distinct entries is largest. Suppose that this tuple contains two distinct functions $b$ and $c$, with multiplicities $r$ and $s$. By symmetry we may place them in the first two slots. In ( 9.71 ), the left side is $F^2$, while the two factors on the right are nonnegative values of $I$ on tuples of our family, hence at most $F$. Therefore both factors equal $F$. Replacing one entry $c$ by $b$ changes the sum of the squares of the multiplicities by $(r+1)^2+(s-1)^2-r^2-s^2=2(r-s)+2$, and replacing one entry $b$ by $c$ changes it by $2(s-r)+2$. One of these numbers is positive, which contradicts the choice of the tuple. Hence the chosen tuple consists of a single function repeated $n+1$ times, and $F=1$. In particular $I(u_0,\ldots ,u_ n)\leq 1$, which is the inequality with constant one. Step 3. Approximation with controlled energy. Let $u\in \mathcal E_0(B)$, put $m_\rho =\int _ B(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho )^ n$, and for $j\geq 1$ let \[  \delta _ j=j^{-n-1},\qquad v_ j=\max \{ u-\delta _ j,j\rho \} .  \] Since $u-\delta _ j\leq -\delta _ j$ while $j\rho >-\delta _ j$ near $\partial B$, the function $v_ j$ equals $j\rho $ on a neighborhood of $\partial B$ in $B$. Since $v_ j$ and $j\rho $ coincide outside a compact subset of $B$, lemma 9.10.6 gives $\int _ B(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ j)^ n=j^ nm_\rho $, and hence $v_ j\in \mathcal E_0(B)$. Moreover, $v_ j\to u$ uniformly on $B$. Indeed, let $s>0$, and choose a neighborhood $V$ of $\partial B$ with $u>-s$ on $V\cap B$. Since $u-\delta _ j\leq v_ j\leq 0$, we have $|v_ j-u|\leq s+\delta _ j$ on $V\cap B$. On the set $B\setminus V$, whose closure is a compact subset of $B$, the function $\rho $ is bounded away from zero and $u$ is bounded, so $j\rho <u-\delta _ j$, and hence $v_ j=u-\delta _ j$, there for all large $j$. Next we estimate $e_1(v_ j)$. Let $t>4\delta _ j$. Since $u\leq v_ j+\delta _ j$ and $v_ j\leq 0$, \[  \{ v_ j<-t\} \subset \{ u<v_ j/2-t/4\}  \subset \{ u<-t/4\} ;  \] for the first inclusion note that on $\{ v_ j<-t\} $ we have $v_ j/2<-t/2<-t/4-\delta _ j$, hence $u\leq v_ j+\delta _ j<v_ j/2-t/4$. As $u$ tends to $0$ and $v_ j/2-t/4$ tends to $-t/4$ at $\partial B$, the comparison theorem (theorem 9.2.8 ) applies to $u$ and $v_ j/2-t/4$ and gives \[  \int _{\{ v_ j<-t\} }(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ j)^ n \leq 2^ n\int _{\{ u<v_ j/2-t/4\} }\bigl (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v_ j/2)\bigr )^ n \leq 2^ n\int _{\{ u<-t/4\} }(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n.  \] For $0<t\leq 4\delta _ j$ we use the total mass $j^ nm_\rho $ instead. Integrating over $t$ by the layer-cake formula $e_1(v)=\int _0^\infty (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n(\{ v<-t\} )\, \mathrm dt$, we obtain 9.72 \begin{equation} \label{eq:quadratic-collar-energy-approximation} e_1(v_ j)\leq 4\delta _ j j^ n m_\rho +2^{n+2}e_1(u) =\frac{4m_\rho }j+C_ ne_1(u). \end{equation} Step 4. The general case. Apply the construction of Step 3 to each $u_ l$, obtaining functions $v_{l,j}\in \mathcal E_0(B)$ which equal $j\rho $ near $\partial B$. They are uniformly bounded, since $u_ l-1\leq v_{l,j}\leq 0$, and they converge uniformly, hence locally in capacity, to $u_ l$. Let $\chi \in C_ c(B)$ with $0\leq \chi \leq 1$. The weight $-u_0$ is bounded and quasi-continuous (theorem 9.4.2 ), so the weighted form of theorem 9.4.8 and Step 2 give \[  \begin{aligned}  \int _ B\chi (-u_0)\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ n & =\lim _{j\to \infty }\int _ B\chi (-v_{0,j})\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_{1,j}\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_{n,j}\\ & \leq \varlimsup _{j\to \infty }\prod _{l=0}^ ne_1(v_{l,j})^{1/(n+1)}. \end{aligned}  \] By ( 9.72 ), the right side is at most \[  \lim _{j\to \infty }\prod _{l=0}^ n\left(\frac{4m_\rho }j+C_ ne_1(u_ l)\right)^{1/(n+1)} =C_ n\prod _{l=0}^ ne_1(u_ l)^{1/(n+1)}.  \] Letting $\chi $ increase to one proves ( 9.69 ). Vanishing energies need no separate treatment, since the energies of the $v_{l,j}$ are positive. $\square$
