With $y=\overline{L(e)}\, e/\| e\| ^2$ this reads $L(x)=\langle x,yangle $. The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality shows that $L$ has norm at most $\| y\| $, and $L(y)=\| y\| ^2$ shows equality. If $y'$ also represents $L$, then $\langle x,y-y'angle =0$ for all $x$, and $x=y-y'$ gives $y=y'$. If $\ell $ is a bounded conjugate-linear functional, then $\overline\ell \colon x\mapsto \overline{\ell (x)}$ is a bounded linear functional with the same norm, and its representation $\overline{\ell (x)}=\langle x,yangle $ reads $\ell (x)=\langle y,xangle $. $\square$ Proposition 11.1.2 . Every bounded sequence in a Hilbert space $H$ has a weakly convergent subsequence, that is, a subsequence $(x_ j)$ for which there is $x\in H$ with $\langle x_ j,vangle 	o \langle x,vangle $ for every $v\in H$. If $(x_ j)$ converges weakly to $x$, then $\| x\| \le \varliminf _ j\| x_ j\| $. Proof. Let $(x_ j)$ be a sequence with $\| x_ j\| \le C$, and let $V$ be the closed linear span of its terms. The finite linear combinations of the $x_ j$ with coefficients in $\mathbb Q+\mathrm i\mathbb Q$ form a countable dense subset of $V$. Applying the Gram–Schmidt process to it, and discarding the vectors that depend linearly on earlier ones, we obtain a finite or countable orthonormal family $(e_ k)$ whose linear span is dense in $V$. For each $k$ the sequence $(\langle x_ j,e_ kangle )_ j$ is bounded by $C$, so by a diagonal argument we may pass to a subsequence, still denoted $(x_ j)$, such that $\langle x_ j,e_ kangle $ converges to a number $a_ k$ for every $k$. For every $N$, Bessel's inequality gives $\sum _{k\le N}|\langle x_ j,e_ kangle |^2\le C^2$; letting $j	o \infty $ and then $N	o \infty $, we get $\sum _ k|a_ k|^2\le C^2$. Since $\| \sum _{N<k\le N'}a_ ke_ k\| ^2=\sum _{N<k\le N'}|a_ k|^2$ by Pythagoras' theorem, the partial sums of the series $x=\sum _ ka_ ke_ k$ form a Cauchy sequence; the series therefore converges in the closed, hence complete, subspace $V$, and $\| x\| ^2=\sum _ k|a_ k|^2\le C^2$. By the continuity of the inner product and the orthonormality of the $e_ k$, we have $\langle x,e_ kangle =a_ k=\lim _ j\langle x_ j,e_ kangle $ for every $k$; hence $\langle x_ j,vangle 	o \langle x,vangle $ for every $v$ in the linear span of the $e_ k$. If $v\in V$ and $v'$ lies in that span with $\| v-v'\| <\delta $, then $|\langle x_ j-x,vangle |\le |\langle x_ j-x,v'angle |+2C\delta $, so the convergence extends to all $v\in V$. For an arbitrary $v\in H$, write $v=v_1+v_2$ with $v_1\in V$ and $v_2\in V^\perp $ by proposition 11.1.1 ; since $x_ j$ and $x$ lie in $V$, we get $\langle x_ j-x,vangle =\langle x_ j-x,v_1angle 	o 0$. For the last assertion we may assume that $x
e 0$. By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, $\| x\| ^2=\lim _ j\langle x_ j,xangle \le \varliminf _ j\| x_ j\| \, \| x\| $, and we divide by $\| x\| $. $\square$ Differential operators are defined only on subspaces of $L^2$ spaces, so we need the following notions. Let $H_0$ and $H_1$ be Hilbert spaces. An operator $T$ from $H_0$ to $H_1$ is a linear map $T\colon \operatorname{Dom}T	o H_1$ defined on a linear subspace $\operatorname{Dom}T\subset H_0$, its domain . We write $\ker T$ for its kernel, $\operatorname {Ran}T=T(\operatorname{Dom}T)$ for its range, and $\operatorname {Gr}T=\{ (x,Tx):x\in \operatorname{Dom}T\} $ for its graph, a subspace of the Hilbert space $H_0\oplus H_1$ with the inner product $\langle (x,y),(x',y')angle =\langle x,x'angle +\langle y,y'angle $. The operator $T$ is densely defined if $\operatorname{Dom}T$ is dense in $H_0$, and closed if $\operatorname {Gr}T$ is closed; equivalently, $x_ j\in \operatorname{Dom}T$, $x_ j	o x$ and $Tx_ j	o y$ imply $x\in \operatorname{Dom}T$ and $Tx=y$. In particular, the kernel of a closed operator is a closed subspace. If $T$ is densely defined, its Hilbert adjoint $T^*$, an operator from $H_1$ to $H_0$, is defined as follows: $y\in \operatorname{Dom}T^*$ if the linear functional $x\mapsto \langle Tx,yangle $ on $\operatorname{Dom}T$ is bounded with respect to the norm of $H_0$, and then $T^*y$ is the vector determined by \[  \langle Tx,yangle =\langle x,T^*yangle \qquad (x\in \operatorname{Dom}T).  \] This vector is well defined: since $\operatorname{Dom}T$ is dense, the functional extends uniquely to a bounded linear functional on $H_0$, which proposition 11.1.1 represents by a unique vector. Lemma 11.1.3 . Let $T$ be a densely defined operator from $H_0$ to $H_1$. Then $T^*$ is closed and $\ker T^*=(\operatorname {Ran}T)^\perp $. If $T$ is also closed, then $T^*$ is densely defined and $T^{**}=T$. Proof. If $y_ j\in \operatorname{Dom}T^*$, $y_ j	o y$ and $T^*y_ j	o w$, then for every $x\in \operatorname{Dom}T$ \[  \langle Tx,yangle =\lim _ j\langle Tx,y_ jangle =\lim _ j\langle x,T^*y_ jangle =\langle x,wangle ;  \] hence $y\in \operatorname{Dom}T^*$ and $T^*y=w$, so $T^*$ is closed. A vector $y\in H_1$ is orthogonal to $\operatorname {Ran}T$ exactly when the functional $x\mapsto \langle Tx,yangle $ vanishes, that is, when $y\in \operatorname{Dom}T^*$ and $T^*y=0$. This proves $\ker T^*=(\operatorname {Ran}T)^\perp $. In the same way, $(a,b)\in H_0\oplus H_1$ is orthogonal to $\operatorname {Gr}T$ if and only if $\langle Tx,bangle =\langle x,-aangle $ for all $x\in \operatorname{Dom}T$, so \[  (\operatorname {Gr}T)^\perp =\{ (-T^*y,y):y\in \operatorname{Dom}T^*\} .  \] Now let $T$ be closed, and let $v\in H_1$ be orthogonal to $\operatorname{Dom}T^*$. Since $\operatorname {Gr}T$ is closed, proposition 11.1.1 and the description of $(\operatorname {Gr}T)^\perp $ decompose $(0,v)$ as $(x,Tx)+(-T^*y,y)$ with $x\in \operatorname{Dom}T$ and $y\in \operatorname{Dom}T^*$. Thus $x=T^*y$ and $v=Tx+y$. Since $v$ is orthogonal to $y\in \operatorname{Dom}T^*$, we obtain \[  0=\langle v,yangle =\langle Tx,yangle +\| y\| ^2=\langle x,T^*yangle +\| y\| ^2=\| x\| ^2+\| y\| ^2,  \] so $x=y=0$ and $v=0$. Hence $\operatorname{Dom}T^*$ is dense, and $T^{**}$ is defined. Let $J\colon H_1\oplus H_0	o H_0\oplus H_1$ and $J'\colon H_0\oplus H_1	o H_1\oplus H_0$ be the unitary maps $J(b,a)=(-a,b)$ and $J'(a,b)=(-b,a)$. The description of the orthogonal complement of a graph, applied to $T$ and to the densely defined operator $T^*$, reads $(\operatorname {Gr}T)^\perp =J(\operatorname {Gr}T^*)$ and $(\operatorname {Gr}T^*)^\perp =J'(\operatorname {Gr}T^{**})$. For a closed subspace $M$ we have $(M^\perp )^\perp =M$ by proposition 11.1.1 , and unitary maps carry orthogonal complements to orthogonal complements. Therefore \[  \operatorname {Gr}T= igl ((\operatorname {Gr}T)^\perp  igr )^\perp =J igl ((\operatorname {Gr}T^*)^\perp  igr ) =JJ'(\operatorname {Gr}T^{**})=\operatorname {Gr}T^{**},  \] because $JJ'=-\mathrm{id}$ and graphs are linear subspaces. Thus $T^{**}=T$. $\square$ The next theorem, the abstract form of Hörmander's method, produces a solution of $Tu=g$ from an inequality for the adjoint operator. The second operator $S$ allows us to require the inequality only on $\operatorname{Dom}T^*\cap \operatorname{Dom}S$; in the application in section 11.3 , smooth compactly supported forms are dense in this space, and for them the inequality follows from an integration by parts. Theorem 11.1.4 . Let $H_0,H_1,H_2$ be Hilbert spaces, let $T$ from $H_0$ to $H_1$ be a closed densely defined operator, and let $S$ from $H_1$ to $H_2$ be a closed operator with $\operatorname {Ran}T\subset \ker S$. Let $g\in \ker S$ and $0\le M<\infty $, and assume that \[  |\langle g,fangle |^2\le M igl (\| T^*f\| ^2+\| Sf\| ^2 igr ) \qquad (f\in \operatorname{Dom}T^*\cap \operatorname{Dom}S).  \] Then the equation $Tu=g$ has a solution $u\in \operatorname{Dom}T$ with $\| u\| ^2\le M$. Among all solutions there is a unique one of smallest norm, and it is orthogonal to $\ker T$. Proof. Since $S$ is closed, $\ker S$ is a closed subspace, and $H_1=\ker S\oplus (\ker S)^\perp $ by proposition 11.1.1 . Since $\operatorname {Ran}T\subset \ker S$, lemma 11.1.3 gives $(\ker S)^\perp \subset (\operatorname {Ran}T)^\perp =\ker T^*$. Let $f\in \operatorname{Dom}T^*$, and write $f=f_0+f_1$ with $f_0\in \ker S$ and $f_1\in (\ker S)^\perp $. Then $f_1\in \operatorname{Dom}T^*$ and $T^*f_1=0$, so $f_0\in \operatorname{Dom}T^*\cap \operatorname{Dom}S$, $T^*f_0=T^*f$ and $Sf_0=0$. Moreover $\langle g,fangle =\langle g,f_0angle $, because $g\in \ker S$. The hypothesis applied to $f_0$ therefore gives \[  |\langle g,fangle |\le \sqrt M\, \| T^*f\| \qquad (f\in \operatorname{Dom}T^*).  \] Consequently the map $\lambda \colon T^*f\mapsto \langle g,fangle $ is well defined on $\operatorname {Ran}T^*$: if $T^*f=T^*f'$, then $|\langle g,f-f'angle |\le \sqrt M\, \| T^*(f-f')\| =0$. It is conjugate-linear and bounded by $\sqrt M$, hence uniformly continuous, so it extends uniquely to a conjugate-linear functional $	ilde\lambda $ on the closed subspace $W=\overline{\operatorname {Ran}T^*}$, again bounded by $\sqrt M$. If $P_ W$ is the orthogonal projection onto $W$, then $x\mapsto 	ilde\lambda (P_ Wx)$ is a conjugate-linear functional on $H_0$ of norm at most $\sqrt M$, because $\| P_ Wx\| \le \| x\| $. By the representation of conjugate-linear functionals in proposition 11.1.1 , there is $u\in H_0$ with $\| u\| \le \sqrt M$ and \[  \langle u,T^*fangle =\langle g,fangle \qquad (f\in \operatorname{Dom}T^*).  \] Taking complex conjugates, we get $\langle T^*f,uangle =\langle f,gangle $ for all $f\in \operatorname{Dom}T^*$. Thus the functional $f\mapsto \langle T^*f,uangle $ is bounded on $\operatorname{Dom}T^*$, so $u\in \operatorname{Dom}T^{**}$ and $T^{**}u=g$. Since $T^{**}=T$ by lemma 11.1.3 , we conclude that $u\in \operatorname{Dom}T$ and $Tu=g$. The solutions of $Tu=g$ form the affine subspace $u+\ker T$, which is closed because $\ker T$ is closed. If $P$ denotes the orthogonal projection onto $\ker T$, then $\| u+k\| ^2=\| u-Pu\| ^2+\| Pu+k\| ^2$ for $k\in \ker T$. Hence $u-Pu$ is the unique solution of smallest norm; it is orthogonal to $\ker T$, and its norm is at most $\| u\| \le \sqrt M$. $\square$

title: Hilbert projection representation
topic: Weighted L2 estimates and holomorphic extension
text:
Proposition 11.1.1 . Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space. Every nonempty closed convex subset of $H$ contains a unique point of smallest distance to a given point of $H$. If $M\subset H$ is a closed linear subspace, then $H=M\oplus M^\perp $ and $(M^\perp )^\perp =M$. Every bounded linear functional $L$ on $H$ has the form $L(x)=\langle x,yangle $ for a unique $y\in H$, and every bounded conjugate-linear functional $\ell $ on $H$ has the form $\ell (x)=\langle y,xangle $ for a unique $y\in H$; in both cases the norm of the functional is $\| y\| $. Proof. Let $C$ be a nonempty closed convex set and $x\in H$. Replacing $C$ by $C-x$, we may assume that $x=0$. Let $d=\inf _{z\in C}\| z\| $, and let $(x_ j)$ be a sequence in $C$ with $\| x_ j\| 	o d$. Since $(x_ j+x_ k)/2\in C$ by convexity, the parallelogram identity gives \[  \| x_ j-x_ k\| ^2=2\| x_ j\| ^2+2\| x_ k\| ^2 -4\| (x_ j+x_ k)/2\| ^2 \le 2\| x_ j\| ^2+2\| x_ k\| ^2-4d^2.  \] The right side tends to zero as $j,k	o \infty $, so $(x_ j)$ is a Cauchy sequence. Its limit lies in $C$, because $C$ is closed, and has norm $d$. If $x,x'\in C$ both have norm $d$, the same inequality with $x_ j=x$ and $x_ k=x'$ gives $\| x-x'\| ^2\le 0$, which proves uniqueness. Now let $M$ be a closed linear subspace and $x\in H$. Let $p$ be the point of $M$ closest to $x$, and put $r=x-p$. For $v\in M$ and $t\in \mathbb C$ we have $p+tv\in M$, and hence \[  0\le \| r-tv\| ^2-\| r\| ^2=-2\operatorname{Re} igl ( ar t\langle r,vangle  igr )+|t|^2\| v\| ^2.  \] Taking small real $t$ of both signs gives $\operatorname{Re}\langle r,vangle =0$, and taking $t\in \mathrm i\mathbb R$ gives $\operatorname{Im}\langle r,vangle =0$. Thus $r\in M^\perp $ and $x=p+r$. Since $M\cap M^\perp =\{ 0\} $, this decomposition is unique, so $H=M\oplus M^\perp $. Every element of $M$ is orthogonal to $M^\perp $, so $M\subset (M^\perp )^\perp $. Conversely, if $x\in (M^\perp )^\perp $ and $x=p+r$ as above, then $r=x-p$ lies in the linear subspace $(M^\perp )^\perp $ and in $M^\perp $, so $\| r\| ^2=\langle r,rangle =0$ and $x=p\in M$. We call $p$ the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto $M$; the map $P\colon x\mapsto p$ is linear by the uniqueness of the decomposition, and $\| Px\| \le \| x\| $, because $\| x\| ^2=\| p\| ^2+\| r\| ^2$. Finally, let $L$ be a bounded linear functional. If $L=0$ we take $y=0$. Otherwise $\ker L$ is a proper closed subspace. Choose $x_0
otin \ker L$, and let $e$ be its component in $(\ker L)^\perp $; then $e
e 0$ and $L(e)=L(x_0)
e 0$. For every $x\in H$ the vector $x-(L(x)/L(e))e$ lies in $\ker L$ and is therefore orthogonal to $e$, so that $\langle x,eangle =(L(x)/L(e))\| e\| ^2$. With $y=\overline{L(e)}\, e/\| e\| ^2$ this reads $L(x)=\langle x,yangle $. The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality shows that $L$ has norm at most $\| y\| $, and $L(y)=\| y\| ^2$ shows equality. If $y'$ also represents $L$, then $\langle x,y-y'angle =0$ for all $x$, and $x=y-y'$ gives $y=y'$. If $\ell $ is a bounded conjugate-linear functional, then $\overline\ell \colon x\mapsto \overline{\ell (x)}$ is a bounded linear functional with the same norm, and its representation $\overline{\ell (x)}=\langle x,yangle $ reads $\ell (x)=\langle y,xangle $. $\square$

title: Hilbert weak sequences
topic: Weighted L2 estimates and holomorphic extension
text: Proposition 11.1.2 . Every bounded sequence in a Hilbert space $H$ has a weakly convergent subsequence, that is, a subsequence $(x_ j)$ for which there is $x\in H$ with $\langle x_ j,v\rangle \to \langle x,v\rangle $ for every $v\in H$. If $(x_ j)$ converges weakly to $x$, then $\| x\| \le \varliminf _ j\| x_ j\| $. Proof. Let $(x_ j)$ be a sequence with $\| x_ j\| \le C$, and let $V$ be the closed linear span of its terms. The finite linear combinations of the $x_ j$ with coefficients in $\mathbb Q+\mathrm i\mathbb Q$ form a countable dense subset of $V$. Applying the Gram–Schmidt process to it, and discarding the vectors that depend linearly on earlier ones, we obtain a finite or countable orthonormal family $(e_ k)$ whose linear span is dense in $V$. For each $k$ the sequence $(\langle x_ j,e_ k\rangle )_ j$ is bounded by $C$, so by a diagonal argument we may pass to a subsequence, still denoted $(x_ j)$, such that $\langle x_ j,e_ k\rangle $ converges to a number $a_ k$ for every $k$. For every $N$, Bessel's inequality gives $\sum _{k\le N}|\langle x_ j,e_ k\rangle |^2\le C^2$; letting $j\to \infty $ and then $N\to \infty $, we get $\sum _ k|a_ k|^2\le C^2$. Since $\| \sum _{N<k\le N'}a_ ke_ k\| ^2=\sum _{N<k\le N'}|a_ k|^2$ by Pythagoras' theorem, the partial sums of the series $x=\sum _ ka_ ke_ k$ form a Cauchy sequence; the series therefore converges in the closed, hence complete, subspace $V$, and $\| x\| ^2=\sum _ k|a_ k|^2\le C^2$. By the continuity of the inner product and the orthonormality of the $e_ k$, we have $\langle x,e_ k\rangle =a_ k=\lim _ j\langle x_ j,e_ k\rangle $ for every $k$; hence $\langle x_ j,v\rangle \to \langle x,v\rangle $ for every $v$ in the linear span of the $e_ k$. If $v\in V$ and $v'$ lies in that span with $\| v-v'\| <\delta $, then $|\langle x_ j-x,v\rangle |\le |\langle x_ j-x,v'\rangle |+2C\delta $, so the convergence extends to all $v\in V$. For an arbitrary $v\in H$, write $v=v_1+v_2$ with $v_1\in V$ and $v_2\in V^\perp $ by proposition 11.1.1 ; since $x_ j$ and $x$ lie in $V$, we get $\langle x_ j-x,v\rangle =\langle x_ j-x,v_1\rangle \to 0$. For the last assertion we may assume that $x\ne 0$. By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, $\| x\| ^2=\lim _ j\langle x_ j,x\rangle \le \varliminf _ j\| x_ j\| \, \| x\| $, and we divide by $\| x\| $. $\square$

title: Closed operator adjoint
topic: Weighted L2 estimates and holomorphic extension
text: Lemma 11.1.3 . Let $T$ be a densely defined operator from $H_0$ to $H_1$. Then $T^*$ is closed and $\ker T^*=(\operatorname {Ran}T)^\perp $. If $T$ is also closed, then $T^*$ is densely defined and $T^{**}=T$. Proof. If $y_ j\in \operatorname{Dom}T^*$, $y_ j\to y$ and $T^*y_ j\to w$, then for every $x\in \operatorname{Dom}T$ \[  \langle Tx,y\rangle =\lim _ j\langle Tx,y_ j\rangle =\lim _ j\langle x,T^*y_ j\rangle =\langle x,w\rangle ;  \] hence $y\in \operatorname{Dom}T^*$ and $T^*y=w$, so $T^*$ is closed. A vector $y\in H_1$ is orthogonal to $\operatorname {Ran}T$ exactly when the functional $x\mapsto \langle Tx,y\rangle $ vanishes, that is, when $y\in \operatorname{Dom}T^*$ and $T^*y=0$. This proves $\ker T^*=(\operatorname {Ran}T)^\perp $. In the same way, $(a,b)\in H_0\oplus H_1$ is orthogonal to $\operatorname {Gr}T$ if and only if $\langle Tx,b\rangle =\langle x,-a\rangle $ for all $x\in \operatorname{Dom}T$, so \[  (\operatorname {Gr}T)^\perp =\{ (-T^*y,y):y\in \operatorname{Dom}T^*\} .  \] Now let $T$ be closed, and let $v\in H_1$ be orthogonal to $\operatorname{Dom}T^*$. Since $\operatorname {Gr}T$ is closed, proposition 11.1.1 and the description of $(\operatorname {Gr}T)^\perp $ decompose $(0,v)$ as $(x,Tx)+(-T^*y,y)$ with $x\in \operatorname{Dom}T$ and $y\in \operatorname{Dom}T^*$. Thus $x=T^*y$ and $v=Tx+y$. Since $v$ is orthogonal to $y\in \operatorname{Dom}T^*$, we obtain \[  0=\langle v,y\rangle =\langle Tx,y\rangle +\| y\| ^2=\langle x,T^*y\rangle +\| y\| ^2=\| x\| ^2+\| y\| ^2,  \] so $x=y=0$ and $v=0$. Hence $\operatorname{Dom}T^*$ is dense, and $T^{**}$ is defined. Let $J\colon H_1\oplus H_0\to H_0\oplus H_1$ and $J'\colon H_0\oplus H_1\to H_1\oplus H_0$ be the unitary maps $J(b,a)=(-a,b)$ and $J'(a,b)=(-b,a)$. The description of the orthogonal complement of a graph, applied to $T$ and to the densely defined operator $T^*$, reads $(\operatorname {Gr}T)^\perp =J(\operatorname {Gr}T^*)$ and $(\operatorname {Gr}T^*)^\perp =J'(\operatorname {Gr}T^{**})$. For a closed subspace $M$ we have $(M^\perp )^\perp =M$ by proposition 11.1.1 , and unitary maps carry orthogonal complements to orthogonal complements. Therefore \[  \operatorname {Gr}T=\bigl ((\operatorname {Gr}T)^\perp \bigr )^\perp =J\bigl ((\operatorname {Gr}T^*)^\perp \bigr ) =JJ'(\operatorname {Gr}T^{**})=\operatorname {Gr}T^{**},  \] because $JJ'=-\mathrm{id}$ and graphs are linear subspaces. Thus $T^{**}=T$. $\square$

title: Hilbert complex solvability
topic: Weighted L2 estimates and holomorphic extension
text: Theorem 11.1.4 . Let $H_0,H_1,H_2$ be Hilbert spaces, let $T$ from $H_0$ to $H_1$ be a closed densely defined operator, and let $S$ from $H_1$ to $H_2$ be a closed operator with $\operatorname {Ran}T\subset \ker S$. Let $g\in \ker S$ and $0\le M<\infty $, and assume that \[  |\langle g,f\rangle |^2\le M\bigl (\| T^*f\| ^2+\| Sf\| ^2\bigr ) \qquad (f\in \operatorname{Dom}T^*\cap \operatorname{Dom}S).  \] Then the equation $Tu=g$ has a solution $u\in \operatorname{Dom}T$ with $\| u\| ^2\le M$. Among all solutions there is a unique one of smallest norm, and it is orthogonal to $\ker T$. Proof. Since $S$ is closed, $\ker S$ is a closed subspace, and $H_1=\ker S\oplus (\ker S)^\perp $ by proposition 11.1.1 . Since $\operatorname {Ran}T\subset \ker S$, lemma 11.1.3 gives $(\ker S)^\perp \subset (\operatorname {Ran}T)^\perp =\ker T^*$. Let $f\in \operatorname{Dom}T^*$, and write $f=f_0+f_1$ with $f_0\in \ker S$ and $f_1\in (\ker S)^\perp $. Then $f_1\in \operatorname{Dom}T^*$ and $T^*f_1=0$, so $f_0\in \operatorname{Dom}T^*\cap \operatorname{Dom}S$, $T^*f_0=T^*f$ and $Sf_0=0$. Moreover $\langle g,f\rangle =\langle g,f_0\rangle $, because $g\in \ker S$. The hypothesis applied to $f_0$ therefore gives \[  |\langle g,f\rangle |\le \sqrt M\, \| T^*f\| \qquad (f\in \operatorname{Dom}T^*).  \] Consequently the map $\lambda \colon T^*f\mapsto \langle g,f\rangle $ is well defined on $\operatorname {Ran}T^*$: if $T^*f=T^*f'$, then $|\langle g,f-f'\rangle |\le \sqrt M\, \| T^*(f-f')\| =0$. It is conjugate-linear and bounded by $\sqrt M$, hence uniformly continuous, so it extends uniquely to a conjugate-linear functional $\tilde\lambda $ on the closed subspace $W=\overline{\operatorname {Ran}T^*}$, again bounded by $\sqrt M$. If $P_ W$ is the orthogonal projection onto $W$, then $x\mapsto \tilde\lambda (P_ Wx)$ is a conjugate-linear functional on $H_0$ of norm at most $\sqrt M$, because $\| P_ Wx\| \le \| x\| $. By the representation of conjugate-linear functionals in proposition 11.1.1 , there is $u\in H_0$ with $\| u\| \le \sqrt M$ and \[  \langle u,T^*f\rangle =\langle g,f\rangle \qquad (f\in \operatorname{Dom}T^*).  \] Taking complex conjugates, we get $\langle T^*f,u\rangle =\langle f,g\rangle $ for all $f\in \operatorname{Dom}T^*$. Thus the functional $f\mapsto \langle T^*f,u\rangle $ is bounded on $\operatorname{Dom}T^*$, so $u\in \operatorname{Dom}T^{**}$ and $T^{**}u=g$. Since $T^{**}=T$ by lemma 11.1.3 , we conclude that $u\in \operatorname{Dom}T$ and $Tu=g$. The solutions of $Tu=g$ form the affine subspace $u+\ker T$, which is closed because $\ker T$ is closed. If $P$ denotes the orthogonal projection onto $\ker T$, then $\| u+k\| ^2=\| u-Pu\| ^2+\| Pu+k\| ^2$ for $k\in \ker T$. Hence $u-Pu$ is the unique solution of smallest norm; it is orthogonal to $\ker T$, and its norm is at most $\| u\| \le \sqrt M$. $\square$

title: Pseudoconvexity and boundary distance
topic: Weighted L2 estimates and holomorphic extension
text:
11.2 Pseudoconvexity and boundary distance We shall prove Hörmander's estimate on open sets that are exhausted by the compact sublevel sets of a continuous plurisubharmonic function. These pseudoconvex open sets are characterized by the plurisubharmonicity of minus the logarithm of the boundary distance, and they carry smooth strictly plurisubharmonic exhaustion functions, which section 11.3 uses to localize the estimate. For $r>0$ we write $\Delta _ r=\{ t\in \mathbb C:|t|<r\} $ for the open disc of radius $r$ in $\mathbb C$, and $\Delta =\Delta _1$ for the unit disc; in this chapter the letter $\Delta $ always denotes a disc, never the Laplacian. Definition 11.2.1 . Let $n\ge 1$ and let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ be open. An exhaustion function of $\Omega $ is a function $ho \colon \Omega 	o \mathbb R$ such that the sublevel set $\{ z\in \Omega :ho (z)\le c\} $ is compact for every $c\in \mathbb R$. The open set $\Omega $ is pseudoconvex if it has a continuous plurisubharmonic exhaustion function. A continuous exhaustion function attains its minimum on each nonempty sublevel set, so it is bounded below; adding a constant, we may take it nonnegative. An open set $\Omega $ is pseudoconvex if and only if each of its connected components is. Indeed, the restriction of a continuous plurisubharmonic exhaustion function of $\Omega $ to a component is a continuous plurisubharmonic exhaustion function of that component, because the component is open and closed in $\Omega $. Conversely, the components of $\Omega $ are open, and each of them contains a point with rational real coordinates, so there are at most countably many of them, say $\Omega _1,\Omega _2,\ldots $. If $ho _ k\ge 0$ is a continuous plurisubharmonic exhaustion function of $\Omega _ k$, then the function equal to $ho _ k+k$ on $\Omega _ k$ is a continuous plurisubharmonic exhaustion function of $\Omega $: it is continuous and plurisubharmonic because the components are open, and its sublevel set $\{ \le c\} $ is the finite union of the compact sets $\{ ho _ k\le c-k\} $, $k\le c$. Recall from proposition 8.2.2 that a real function $u$ of class $C^2$ on an open set is plurisubharmonic if and only if its complex Hessian matrix $(u_{j ar k})$ is positive semidefinite at every point. Here, as in section 8.2 , a function on an open set is plurisubharmonic if it is plurisubharmonic on each connected component. Recall also, from the discussion following proposition 8.2.2 , that a function $u$ is strictly plurisubharmonic if every point has a neighborhood on which $u-\varepsilon |z|^2$ is plurisubharmonic for some $\varepsilon >0$. For smooth $u$ this means that $(u_{j ar k})$ is positive definite at every point, and then its smallest eigenvalue is a positive continuous function. To recognize plurisubharmonic functions we use the following criterion, in which the harmonic majorants in the submean inequality are restricted to real parts of polynomials. Lemma 11.2.2 . Let $U\subset \mathbb C^ N$ be open and let $v\colon U	o [-\infty ,\infty )$ be upper semicontinuous. Assume that for all $z_0\in U$ and $a\in \mathbb C^ N$ with $\{ z_0+ta:|t|\le 1\} \subset U$, and for every polynomial $P$ in one complex variable with $v(z_0+ta)\le \operatorname{Re}P(t)$ whenever $|t|=1$, we have $v(z_0)\le \operatorname{Re}P(0)$. Then \[  v(z_0)\le  rac1{2\pi }\int _0^{2\pi }v(z_0+\mathrm e^{\mathrm i	heta }a)\, \mathrm d	heta  \] for all such $z_0$ and $a$. Proof. Fix $z_0$ and $a$, and put $g(	heta )=v(z_0+\mathrm e^{\mathrm i	heta }a)$, an upper semicontinuous function on the circle. By lemma 3.1.2 there are continuous real functions $g_ m$ decreasing to $g$ whose integrals decrease to the integral of $g$, which may be $-\infty $. Fix $m$ and $\delta >0$. We approximate $g_ m$ uniformly by real trigonometric polynomials, using the Fejér kernel \[  F_ N(	heta )= rac1N\Bigl |\sum _{k=0}^{N-1}\mathrm e^{\mathrm ik	heta }\Bigr |^2=\sum _{|k|<N}\Bigl (1- rac{|k|}N\Bigr )\mathrm e^{\mathrm ik	heta },\qquad N\ge 1.  \] The two expressions agree because the product $\sum _{k,l=0}^{N-1}\mathrm e^{\mathrm i(k-l)	heta }$ contains exactly $N-|h|$ pairs $(k,l)$ with $k-l=h$, for each integer $h$ with $|h|<N$. By the first expression $F_ N\ge 0$, and summing the geometric series gives $F_ N(	heta )=\sin ^2(N	heta /2)/(N\sin ^2(	heta /2))\le 1/(N\sin ^2(	heta /2))$ for $0<|	heta |\le \pi $; by the second, $F_ N$ has integral one with respect to the normalized measure $\mathrm d	heta /(2\pi )$ on $[-\pi ,\pi ]$. Let $q_ N=g_ m*F_ N$ be the convolution with respect to $\mathrm d	heta /(2\pi )$, that is, $q_ N(	heta )= rac1{2\pi }\int _{-\pi }^{\pi }g_ m(	heta -	au )F_ N(	au )\, \mathrm d	au $. For $0<\delta '\le \pi $ let $\omega (\delta ')$ be the largest oscillation of $g_ m$ over arcs of length at most $\delta '$, which tends to zero with $\delta '$ by uniform continuity. Splitting the integral at $|	au |=\delta '$, we obtain \[  |q_ N(	heta )-g_ m(	heta )|\le  rac1{2\pi }\int _{-\pi }^{\pi }|g_ m(	heta -	au )-g_ m(	heta )|F_ N(	au )\, \mathrm d	au \le \omega (\delta ')+ rac{2\max |g_ m|}{N\sin ^2(\delta '/2)},  \] so $q_ N	o g_ m$ uniformly as $N	o \infty $. Inserting the second expression for $F_ N$ and substituting $\sigma =	heta -	au $, we see that $q_ N(	heta )=\sum _{|k|<N}c_ k\mathrm e^{\mathrm ik	heta }$ with $c_ k=(1-|k|/N) rac1{2\pi }\int _{-\pi }^{\pi }g_ m(\sigma )\mathrm e^{-\mathrm ik\sigma }\, \mathrm d\sigma $. Since $g_ m$ is real, $c_{-k}= ar c_ k$, so $q_ N(	heta )=\operatorname{Re}P(\mathrm e^{\mathrm i	heta })$ for the polynomial $P(t)=c_0+2\sum _{0<k<N}c_ kt^ k$, and $\operatorname{Re}P(0)=c_0$ is the mean of $g_ m$. Choose $N$ with $|q_ N-g_ m|<\delta $. Then $\operatorname{Re}(P(t)+\delta )\ge g_ m\ge g$ on the circle, and the hypothesis gives \[  v(z_0)\le c_0+\delta = rac1{2\pi }\int _0^{2\pi }g_ m\, \mathrm d	heta +\delta .  \] Letting $\delta 	o 0$ and then $m	o \infty $, we obtain the asserted inequality. $\square$ Richberg's lemma approximates a continuous strictly plurisubharmonic function from above by smooth strictly plurisubharmonic functions, at the cost of half of the lower bound for the complex Hessian. Convolution does this locally; the local pieces are glued by a regularized maximum. Lemma 11.2.3 (Richberg) . Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ be open, let $u$ be a continuous function on $\Omega $, and let $a>0$ be such that $u-a|z|^2$ is plurisubharmonic. Then for every continuous function $\varepsilon \colon \Omega 	o (0,\infty )$ there is a smooth function $v$ on $\Omega $ with \[  u\le v\le u+\varepsilon ,\qquad v-	frac a2|z|^2\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega ).  \] Proof. Step 1: local approximations. Let $(K_ m)_{m\ge 1}$ be a compact exhaustion of $\Omega $ (section 1.1 ), so that $K_ m\subset \operatorname{Int}K_{m+1}$ and $ igcup _ m\operatorname{Int}K_ m=\Omega $, and put $K_0=K_{-1}=\varnothing $. For each $m\ge 1$, the compact set $K_ m\setminus \operatorname{Int}K_{m-1}$ is covered by finitely many balls $B(c,r/3)$ with $c\in K_ m\setminus \operatorname{Int}K_{m-1}$ and $B(c,r)\Subset \operatorname{Int}K_{m+1}\setminus K_{m-2}$. Collecting these balls for all $m$, we obtain a sequence of balls $B_ i=B(c_ i,r_ i)\Subset \Omega $ whose inner balls $B(c_ i,r_ i/3)$ cover $\Omega $. The family $(B_ i)$ is locally finite: a compact subset of $\Omega $ lies in some $K_ m$, and a ball chosen at a stage $m'\ge m+2$ lies in the complement of $K_{m'-2}\supset K_ m$, so the compact set meets only the finitely many balls chosen at the stages $m'\le m+1$. The function $u=(u-a|z|^2)+a|z|^2$ is continuous and plurisubharmonic by proposition 8.2.5 . Let $ho _ h$, $h>0$, be the radial mollifiers of section 1.4 . By proposition 8.2.2 (2), we have $u*ho _ h\ge u$, and $(u-a|z|^2)*ho _ h=u*ho _ h-a|z|^2*ho _ h$ is smooth and plurisubharmonic, hence has positive semidefinite complex Hessian by proposition 8.2.2 (1); by lemma 1.4.1 , $u*ho _ h	o u$ locally uniformly as $h	o 0$. Since $ho _ h$ is radial, $\int yho _ h(y)\, \mathrm dV(y)=0$, and expanding $|z-y|^2=|z|^2-2\operatorname{Re}\langle z,yangle +|y|^2$ gives $|z|^2*ho _ h=|z|^2+\int |y|^2ho _ h(y)\, \mathrm dV(y)$, whose complex Hessian matrix is $I$. Hence the complex Hessian matrix of $u*ho _ h$ is at least $aI$. For each $i$ choose $\delta _ i$ with $0<\delta _ i<a/2$ and $\delta _ ir_ i^2<\min _{\overline B_ i}\varepsilon $, put $\eta _ i=\delta _ ir_ i^2/6$, and choose $h_ i>0$ so small that $u*ho _{h_ i}$ is defined near $\overline B_ i$ and satisfies $0\le u*ho _{h_ i}-u<\eta _ i$ there. Define \[  u_ i=u*ho _{h_ i}+\delta _ i igl ((2r_ i/3)^2-|z-c_ i|^2 igr ) \quad 	ext{on }B_ i.  \] The quadratic term is at least $\delta _ ir_ i^2/3=2\eta _ i$ on the inner ball $B(c_ i,r_ i/3)$, is less than $-2\eta _ i$ where $|z-c_ i|>\sqrt7\, r_ i/3$, and is at most $4\delta _ ir_ i^2/9$ everywhere. Therefore \[   egin{aligned} & u_ i>u+\eta _ i& & 	ext{on }B(c_ i,r_ i/3),\ & u_ i<u-\eta _ i& & 	ext{where }\sqrt7\, r_ i/3<|z-c_ i|<r_ i,\ & u_ i+\eta _ i<u+\varepsilon & & 	ext{on }B_ i, \end{aligned}  \] the last because $2\eta _ i+4\delta _ ir_ i^2/9=7\delta _ ir_ i^2/9<\varepsilon $ on $B_ i$. The complex Hessian matrix of $u_ i$ is at least $(a-\delta _ i)I\ge (a/2)I$. Step 2: a regularized maximum. Fix an even smooth function $	heta \ge 0$ on $\mathbb R$ with support in $(-1,1)$ and integral one, for instance the mollifier $ho _{1/2}$ of section 1.4 in dimension $d=1$. For an integer $p\ge 1$, positive numbers $\eta _1,\ldots ,\eta _ p$ and $t=(t_1,\ldots ,t_ p)\in \mathbb R^ p$, define \[  M_\eta (t)=\int _{\mathbb R^ p}\max _ i(t_ i+\eta _ i x_ i) \prod _ i	heta (x_ i)\, \mathrm dx.  \] The substitution $y_ i=\eta _ ix_ i$ and the evenness of $	heta $ show that $M_\eta $ is the convolution of the continuous function $t\mapsto \max _ it_ i$ with the smooth compactly supported function $y\mapsto \prod _ i\eta _ i^{-1}	heta (y_ i/\eta _ i)$, so $M_\eta $ is smooth by differentiation under the integral sign (section 1.4 ). It has the following properties. $M_\eta $ is convex and nondecreasing in each variable, since for fixed $x$ the function $t\mapsto \max _ i(t_ i+\eta _ ix_ i)$ is. $\max _ it_ i\le M_\eta (t)\le \max _ i(t_ i+\eta _ i)$. The upper bound holds because $|x_ i|<1$ on the support of the integrand. For the lower bound, integrate $\max _ j(t_ j+\eta _ jx_ j)\ge t_ i+\eta _ ix_ i$ and use $\int x_ i	heta (x_ i)\, \mathrm dx_ i=0$. $M_\eta (t_1+c,\ldots ,t_ p+c)=M_\eta (t)+c$ for $c\in \mathbb R$. Differentiating in $c$, together with the first property, gives $\partial M_\eta /\partial t_ i\ge 0$ and $\sum _ i\partial M_\eta /\partial t_ i=1$. If $t_ i+\eta _ i\le \max _{j
e i}(t_ j-\eta _ j)$ for some $i$, then deleting the variable $t_ i$ and the parameter $\eta _ i$ does not change the value of $M_\eta $. Indeed, for $|x_ j|<1$ we have $t_ i+\eta _ ix_ i<t_ i+\eta _ i\le \max _{j
e i}(t_ j-\eta _ j)<\max _{j
e i}(t_ j+\eta _ jx_ j)$, so the $i$-th term never realizes the maximum, and integrating out $x_ i$ removes it. For smooth real functions $w_1,\ldots ,w_ p$, the chain rule gives \[  \partial _{z_ j}\partial _{ ar z_ k}M_\eta (w)=\sum _ i rac{\partial M_\eta }{\partial t_ i}(w)\, \partial _{z_ j}\partial _{ ar z_ k}w_ i+\sum _{i,l} rac{\partial ^2M_\eta }{\partial t_ i\partial t_ l}(w)\, \partial _{z_ j}w_ i\, \overline{\partial _{z_ k}w_ l}.  \] The real Hessian matrix $G=(\partial ^2M_\eta /\partial t_ i\partial t_ l)$ is positive semidefinite, because the second derivative of the convex function $s\mapsto M_\eta (t+s	au )$ is nonnegative for every $	au \in \mathbb R^ p$. Hence the matrix given by the second sum is positive semidefinite: for $b\in \mathbb C^ n$ its quadratic form equals $\sum _{i,l}G_{il}\zeta _ i ar\zeta _ l$ with $\zeta _ i=\sum _ j\partial _{z_ j}w_ i\, b_ j$, and writing $\zeta =\xi +\mathrm i\xi '$ with $\xi ,\xi '\in \mathbb R^ p$, this is $\xi ^{\mathsf T}G\xi +\xi '^{\mathsf T}G\xi '\ge 0$ by the symmetry of $G$. Therefore, by the third property, if each $w_ i$ has complex Hessian matrix at least $(a/2)I$, so does $M_\eta (w_1,\ldots ,w_ p)$. Step 3: gluing. For $z\in \Omega $ let $I(z)=\{ i:z\in B_ i\} $, a finite nonempty set, and define $v(z)=M_\eta  igl ((u_ i(z))_{i\in I(z)} igr )$ with the parameters $(\eta _ i)_{i\in I(z)}$. We show that $v$ is smooth near a fixed point $z_0$. Let $I_0=\{ i:z_0\in B_ i\} $ and $I_1=\{ i:z_0\in \partial B_ i\} $, finite sets by local finiteness, and choose $j$ with $z_0\in B(c_ j,r_ j/3)$. There is a neighborhood $W$ of $z_0$ that is contained in $B(c_ j,r_ j/3)$ and in $B_ i$ for $i\in I_0$, that meets $\overline B_ i$ only for $i\in I_0\cup I_1$, and whose intersection with $B_ i$, for $i\in I_1$, lies in the shell $\sqrt7\, r_ i/3<|z-c_ i|<r_ i$. For $z\in W$ we have $I_0\subset I(z)\subset I_0\cup I_1$, $j\in I_0$, and every $i\in I(z)\cap I_1$ satisfies \[  u_ i(z)+\eta _ i<u(z)<u_ j(z)-\eta _ j.  \] By the fourth property of $M_\eta $, applied to these indices one at a time, $v=M_\eta  igl ((u_ i)_{i\in I_0} igr )$ on $W$, which is smooth. Thus $v$ is smooth on $\Omega $, and by Step 2 its complex Hessian matrix is at least $(a/2)I$; hence $v-	frac a2|z|^2$ is smooth with positive semidefinite complex Hessian, and so it is plurisubharmonic by proposition 8.2.2 (1). Finally, every $z$ lies in some inner ball $B(c_ j,r_ j/3)$, and the second property of $M_\eta $ gives $v(z)\ge u_ j(z)>u(z)$ and $v(z)\le \max _{i\in I(z)}(u_ i(z)+\eta _ i)<u(z)+\varepsilon (z)$. $\square$ Theorem 11.2.4 . Let $n\ge 1$ and let $\Omega \subsetneq \mathbb C^ n$ be an open set. If $\Omega $ is pseudoconvex, then $-\log \operatorname {dist}(z,\mathbb C^ n\setminus \Omega )$ is a continuous plurisubharmonic function on $\Omega $. Conversely, if this function is plurisubharmonic, then $\Omega $ is pseudoconvex. Every pseudoconvex open set in $\mathbb C^ n$ has a nonnegative smooth strictly plurisubharmonic exhaustion function. Proof. Steps 1 and 2 deduce the plurisubharmonicity of $-\log \operatorname {dist}(\cdot ,\mathbb C^ n\setminus \Omega )$ from a submean inequality for the distance to the boundary in a fixed direction; Step 3 uses this function to construct a continuous exhaustion function, which lemma 11.2.3 smooths. Step 1: distances in a fixed direction. Let $\Omega $ be pseudoconvex, with a continuous plurisubharmonic exhaustion function $ho $. For $z\in \Omega $ and $\xi \in \mathbb C^ n$ put \[  \delta (z,\xi )=\sup \{ r>0:z+\xi \Delta _ r\subset \Omega \} \in (0,\infty ],  \] so that $\delta (z,0)=\infty $. The function $\delta $ is lower semicontinuous on $\Omega 	imes \mathbb C^ n$: if $r<\delta (z,\xi )$, then the compact disc $z+\xi \overline\Delta _ r$ lies in $\Omega $, hence so does $z'+\xi '\overline\Delta _ r$ for all $(z',\xi ')$ close to $(z,\xi )$, and $\delta (z',\xi ')\ge r$ for these points. Thus $V=-\log \delta $ is an upper semicontinuous function on $\Omega 	imes \mathbb C^ n$ with values in $[-\infty ,\infty )$. We verify the hypothesis of lemma 11.2.2 for $V$ on the open set $\Omega 	imes \mathbb C^ n\subset \mathbb C^{2n}$. Let $(z_0+ta,\xi _0+tb)$, $|t|\le 1$, be a closed disc in $\Omega 	imes \mathbb C^ n$, and let $P$ be a polynomial with $V(z_0+ta,\xi _0+tb)\le \operatorname{Re}P(t)$ for $|t|=1$, that is, $\delta (z_0+ta,\xi _0+tb)\ge |\mathrm e^{-P(t)}|$. Consider the holomorphic map \[  h(t,w)=z_0+t a+w\mathrm e^{-P(t)}(\xi _0+t b),\qquad (t,w)\in \mathbb C^2.  \] We have $h(t,0)=z_0+ta\in \Omega $ for $|t|\le 1$; and $h(t,w)\in \Omega $ for $|t|=1$ and $|w|<1$, because then $|w\mathrm e^{-P(t)}|<\delta (z_0+ta,\xi _0+tb)$. Let $R$ be the supremum of the numbers $r\ge 0$ with $h(\overline\Delta 	imes \overline\Delta _ r)\subset \Omega $. Since $h(\overline\Delta 	imes \{ 0\} )$ is a compact subset of $\Omega $ and $h$ is continuous, $R>0$. We show that $R\ge 1$. Suppose that $R<1$. Then $h(\partial \Delta 	imes \overline\Delta _ R)$ is a compact subset of $\Omega $; let $c$ be the maximum of $ho $ on it. For $|w|<R$ we have $h(\overline\Delta 	imes \{ w\} )\subset \Omega $, because every radius smaller than an admissible one is admissible; since this set is compact and $h$ is continuous, there is $r'>1$ such that $t\mapsto h(t,w)$ maps the disc $\Delta _{r'}$ into $\Omega $, and hence into one connected component of $\Omega $. The function $t\mapsto ho (h(t,w))$ is finite, hence subharmonic on $\Delta _{r'}$ by proposition 8.2.3 , and it is at most $c$ on $\partial \Delta $. By upper semicontinuity, $\varlimsup _{t	o \zeta }(ho (h(t,w))-c)\le 0$ for every $\zeta \in \partial \Delta $, and the maximum principle of proposition 3.1.4 on the disc $\Delta $ gives $ho (h(t,w))\le c$ for $|t|<1$, hence for $|t|\le 1$. Thus $h(\overline\Delta 	imes \Delta _ R)$ lies in the compact set $\{ ho \le c\} $, and so does its closure $h(\overline\Delta 	imes \overline\Delta _ R)$. This compact subset of $\Omega $ has positive distance from $\mathbb C^ n\setminus \Omega $, and the uniform continuity of $h$ on compact sets gives $h(\overline\Delta 	imes \overline\Delta _{R'})\subset \Omega $ for some $R'>R$, contradicting the definition of $R$. Hence $R\ge 1$. In particular $h(0,w)=z_0+w\mathrm e^{-P(0)}\xi _0\in \Omega $ for $|w|<1$, which means that $\delta (z_0,\xi _0)\ge \mathrm e^{-\operatorname{Re}P(0)}$, that is, $V(z_0,\xi _0)\le \operatorname{Re}P(0)$. By lemma 11.2.2 , $V$ satisfies the circle submean inequality on every closed complex disc in $\Omega 	imes \mathbb C^ n$. Step 2: the boundary distance. Now let $\Omega 
e \mathbb C^ n$ and put $d(z)=\operatorname {dist}(z,\mathbb C^ n\setminus \Omega )$. For a unit vector $\xi $ we have $\delta (z,\xi )\ge d(z)$, because $z+\xi \Delta _{d(z)}$ lies in the ball $B(z,d(z))\subset \Omega $. Equality holds if $\xi $ points from $z$ to a nearest point of the closed set $\mathbb C^ n\setminus \Omega $, since that point, $z+d(z)\xi $, lies in $z+\xi \Delta _ r$ for every $r>d(z)$. Hence \[  -\log d(z)=\max _{|\xi |=1}V(z,\xi ).  \] For fixed $\xi $, the function $z\mapsto V(z,\xi )$ satisfies the circle submean inequality on every closed disc $\{ z_0+ta:|t|\le 1\} \subset \Omega $, by Step 1 with $b=0$, and it is bounded above by $-\log d$. Therefore \[  V(z_0,\xi )\le  rac1{2\pi }\int _0^{2\pi }V(z_0+\mathrm e^{\mathrm i	heta }a,\xi )\, \mathrm d	heta \le  rac1{2\pi }\int _0^{2\pi }-\log d(z_0+\mathrm e^{\mathrm i	heta }a)\, \mathrm d	heta ,  \] and taking the maximum over $\xi $ gives the submean inequality for $-\log d$. Since $d$ is positive and $1$-Lipschitz, $-\log d$ is continuous. Its restriction to each connected component of each affine complex-line section of $\Omega $ is therefore subharmonic (definition 3.1.1 ): at a point $z_0+t_0a$ of such a section, the circle means over $\{ z_0+(t_0+r\mathrm e^{\mathrm i	heta })a\} $ dominate the value for all small $r>0$. Hence $-\log d$, which is finite, is plurisubharmonic on each connected component of $\Omega $ by definition 8.1.1 , that is, on $\Omega $. Step 3: smooth exhaustion functions. Let $\Omega 
e \mathbb C^ n$ be an open set on which $-\log d$ is plurisubharmonic, and put \[  u(z)=|z|^2+\max \{ -\log d(z),0\} .  \] Then $u$ is continuous, $u-|z|^2$ is plurisubharmonic by proposition 8.2.5 , and $u$ is an exhaustion function of $\Omega $: the set $\{ u\le c\} $ is contained in the ball $\{ |z|^2\le c\} $ and in $\{ d\ge \mathrm e^{-c}\} $, so it is a closed and bounded subset of $\mathbb C^ n$ contained in $\Omega $, hence compact. In particular, $\Omega $ is pseudoconvex, which proves the converse statement. By lemma 11.2.3 with $a=1$ and $\varepsilon =1$, there is a smooth function $s$ with $u\le s\le u+1$ such that $s-|z|^2/2$ is plurisubharmonic. Then $s\ge u\ge 0$, and the complex Hessian matrix of $s$ is at least $I/2$ by proposition 8.2.2 (1) applied to $s-|z|^2/2$, so that $s$ is strictly plurisubharmonic. Moreover, since $s\ge u$, the sublevel set $\{ s\le c\} $ is a closed subset of the compact set $\{ u\le c\} $. Thus $s$ is a nonnegative smooth strictly plurisubharmonic exhaustion function. If $\Omega 
e \mathbb C^ n$ is pseudoconvex, Step 2 shows that $-\log d$ is plurisubharmonic, so this construction applies; for $\Omega =\mathbb C^ n$ we take $s=|z|^2$. $\square$ Corollary 11.2.5 . Products of pseudoconvex open sets are pseudoconvex. If $s$ is a smooth plurisubharmonic exhaustion function of an open set $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$, then each sublevel set $\{ s<c\} $, $c\in \mathbb R$, is pseudoconvex and relatively compact in $\Omega $. In particular, every pseudoconvex open set $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ is the union of an increasing sequence of pseudoconvex open sets $\Omega _ j\Subset \Omega $. Proof. Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ and $\Omega '\subset \mathbb C^ m$ be pseudoconvex, with nonnegative continuous plurisubharmonic exhaustion functions $ho $ and $ho '$. The function $(z,w)\mapsto ho (z)+ho '(w)$ is continuous and plurisubharmonic on $\Omega 	imes \Omega '$, by proposition 8.2.3 applied to the two projections and by proposition 8.2.5 . Its sublevel set $\{ \le c\} $ is a closed subset of the compact set $\{ ho \le c\} 	imes \{ ho '\le c\} $, so $\Omega 	imes \Omega '$ is pseudoconvex. Next let $s$ be as in the statement and $c\in \mathbb R$. The function $x\mapsto 1/(c-x)$ is convex and increasing on $(-\infty ,c)$, so the complex Hessian matrix of $1/(c-s)$ on the open set $\{ s<c\} $, namely $(c-s)^{-2}(s_{j ar k})+2(c-s)^{-3} igl (\partial _{z_ j}s\, \overline{\partial _{z_ k}s} igr )$ by the chain rule, is positive semidefinite. Hence $|z|^2+1/(c-s)$ is a smooth plurisubharmonic function on $\{ s<c\} $, by proposition 8.2.2 (1). For $C\le 0$ its sublevel set $\{ \le C\} $ is empty. For $C>0$ this sublevel set is closed in $\{ s<c\} $ and contained in the set $\{ s\le c-1/C\} $, which is a compact subset of $\{ s<c\} $; hence it is compact, and $\{ s<c\} $ is pseudoconvex. Moreover $\{ s<c\} $ is contained in the compact set $\{ s\le c\} $, so it is relatively compact in $\Omega $. Finally, if $\Omega $ is pseudoconvex, theorem 11.2.4 provides a smooth plurisubharmonic exhaustion function $s$, and the sets $\Omega _ j=\{ s<j\} $, $j\ge 1$, are pseudoconvex, relatively compact in $\Omega $, increasing, and have union $\Omega $. (Some of them may be empty or disconnected; definition 11.2.1 allows arbitrary open sets.) $\square$ With the boundary distance at hand, the invariant exhaustion function required in Kiselman's minimum principle exists automatically on pseudoconvex domains. Corollary 11.2.6 . Let $m,k\ge 1$, and let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ m	imes \mathbb C^ k$ be a pseudoconvex domain that is invariant under imaginary translations and whose nonempty real fibers $V_ z$ are convex, in the notation of section 8.5 . If $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$ is invariant under imaginary translations, then the function $v(z)=\inf _{t\in V_ z}u(z,t)$ is plurisubharmonic or identically $-\infty $ on $p(\Omega )$. Proof. We construct a function $\psi $ with the properties required in theorem 8.5.1 ; the corollary then follows from that theorem. If $\Omega =\mathbb C^{m+k}$, let $\psi (z,w)=|z|^2+|\operatorname{Re}w|^2$. Otherwise let $d=\operatorname {dist}(\cdot ,\mathbb C^{m+k}\setminus \Omega )$ and put \[  \psi (z,w)=|z|^2+|\operatorname{Re}w|^2+ \max \{ -\log d(z,w),0\} .  \] Imaginary translations are isometries of $\mathbb C^{m+k}$ that preserve $\Omega $ and its complement, so $d$ and $\psi $ are invariant under them. The function $\psi $ is plurisubharmonic by proposition 8.2.5 : $-\log d$ is plurisubharmonic by theorem 11.2.4 , and $|z|^2+|\operatorname{Re}w|^2$ is plurisubharmonic by proposition 8.2.2 (1), since its complex Hessian matrix is the diagonal matrix with entries $1$ in the $z$-directions and $ rac12$ in the $w$-directions, by the identity $(\operatorname{Re}w_ l)^2=	frac 12|w_ l|^2+	frac 12\operatorname{Re}(w_ l^2)$ for $1\le l\le k$. Finally, let $c\in \mathbb R$. Since $\psi $ is continuous, the set $\{ (z,t)\in \Omega _{\mathbb R}:\psi (z,t)\le c\} $ is closed in $\Omega _{\mathbb R}$. It is contained in $\{ |z|^2+|t|^2\le c\} $ and, if $\Omega 
e \mathbb C^{m+k}$, in the set $\{ d\ge \mathrm e^{-c}\} $, which is closed in $\mathbb C^{m+k}$ and contained in $\Omega $; it is therefore a closed and bounded subset of $\mathbb C^ m	imes \mathbb R^ k$, hence compact. $\square$

title: Pseudoconvex domain
topic: Weighted L2 estimates and holomorphic extension
text: Definition 11.2.1 . Let $n\ge 1$ and let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ be open. An exhaustion function of $\Omega $ is a function $\rho \colon \Omega \to \mathbb R$ such that the sublevel set $\{ z\in \Omega :\rho (z)\le c\} $ is compact for every $c\in \mathbb R$. The open set $\Omega $ is pseudoconvex if it has a continuous plurisubharmonic exhaustion function.

title: Polynomial disc comparison
topic: Weighted L2 estimates and holomorphic extension
text: Lemma 11.2.2 . Let $U\subset \mathbb C^ N$ be open and let $v\colon U\to [-\infty ,\infty )$ be upper semicontinuous. Assume that for all $z_0\in U$ and $a\in \mathbb C^ N$ with $\{ z_0+ta:|t|\le 1\} \subset U$, and for every polynomial $P$ in one complex variable with $v(z_0+ta)\le \operatorname{Re}P(t)$ whenever $|t|=1$, we have $v(z_0)\le \operatorname{Re}P(0)$. Then \[  v(z_0)\le \frac1{2\pi }\int _0^{2\pi }v(z_0+\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\theta }a)\, \mathrm d\theta  \] for all such $z_0$ and $a$. Proof. Fix $z_0$ and $a$, and put $g(\theta )=v(z_0+\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\theta }a)$, an upper semicontinuous function on the circle. By lemma 3.1.2 there are continuous real functions $g_ m$ decreasing to $g$ whose integrals decrease to the integral of $g$, which may be $-\infty $. Fix $m$ and $\delta >0$. We approximate $g_ m$ uniformly by real trigonometric polynomials, using the Fejér kernel \[  F_ N(\theta )=\frac1N\Bigl |\sum _{k=0}^{N-1}\mathrm e^{\mathrm ik\theta }\Bigr |^2=\sum _{|k|<N}\Bigl (1-\frac{|k|}N\Bigr )\mathrm e^{\mathrm ik\theta },\qquad N\ge 1.  \] The two expressions agree because the product $\sum _{k,l=0}^{N-1}\mathrm e^{\mathrm i(k-l)\theta }$ contains exactly $N-|h|$ pairs $(k,l)$ with $k-l=h$, for each integer $h$ with $|h|<N$. By the first expression $F_ N\ge 0$, and summing the geometric series gives $F_ N(\theta )=\sin ^2(N\theta /2)/(N\sin ^2(\theta /2))\le 1/(N\sin ^2(\theta /2))$ for $0<|\theta |\le \pi $; by the second, $F_ N$ has integral one with respect to the normalized measure $\mathrm d\theta /(2\pi )$ on $[-\pi ,\pi ]$. Let $q_ N=g_ m*F_ N$ be the convolution with respect to $\mathrm d\theta /(2\pi )$, that is, $q_ N(\theta )=\frac1{2\pi }\int _{-\pi }^{\pi }g_ m(\theta -\tau )F_ N(\tau )\, \mathrm d\tau $. For $0<\delta '\le \pi $ let $\omega (\delta ')$ be the largest oscillation of $g_ m$ over arcs of length at most $\delta '$, which tends to zero with $\delta '$ by uniform continuity. Splitting the integral at $|\tau |=\delta '$, we obtain \[  |q_ N(\theta )-g_ m(\theta )|\le \frac1{2\pi }\int _{-\pi }^{\pi }|g_ m(\theta -\tau )-g_ m(\theta )|F_ N(\tau )\, \mathrm d\tau \le \omega (\delta ')+\frac{2\max |g_ m|}{N\sin ^2(\delta '/2)},  \] so $q_ N\to g_ m$ uniformly as $N\to \infty $. Inserting the second expression for $F_ N$ and substituting $\sigma =\theta -\tau $, we see that $q_ N(\theta )=\sum _{|k|<N}c_ k\mathrm e^{\mathrm ik\theta }$ with $c_ k=(1-|k|/N)\frac1{2\pi }\int _{-\pi }^{\pi }g_ m(\sigma )\mathrm e^{-\mathrm ik\sigma }\, \mathrm d\sigma $. Since $g_ m$ is real, $c_{-k}=\bar c_ k$, so $q_ N(\theta )=\operatorname{Re}P(\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\theta })$ for the polynomial $P(t)=c_0+2\sum _{0<k<N}c_ kt^ k$, and $\operatorname{Re}P(0)=c_0$ is the mean of $g_ m$. Choose $N$ with $|q_ N-g_ m|<\delta $. Then $\operatorname{Re}(P(t)+\delta )\ge g_ m\ge g$ on the circle, and the hypothesis gives \[  v(z_0)\le c_0+\delta =\frac1{2\pi }\int _0^{2\pi }g_ m\, \mathrm d\theta +\delta .  \] Letting $\delta \to 0$ and then $m\to \infty $, we obtain the asserted inequality. $\square$

title: Richberg
topic: Weighted L2 estimates and holomorphic extension
text:
Lemma 11.2.3 (Richberg) . Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ be open, let $u$ be a continuous function on $\Omega $, and let $a>0$ be such that $u-a|z|^2$ is plurisubharmonic. Then for every continuous function $\varepsilon \colon \Omega 	o (0,\infty )$ there is a smooth function $v$ on $\Omega $ with \[  u\le v\le u+\varepsilon ,\qquad v-	frac a2|z|^2\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega ).  \] Proof. Step 1: local approximations. Let $(K_ m)_{m\ge 1}$ be a compact exhaustion of $\Omega $ (section 1.1 ), so that $K_ m\subset \operatorname{Int}K_{m+1}$ and $ igcup _ m\operatorname{Int}K_ m=\Omega $, and put $K_0=K_{-1}=\varnothing $. For each $m\ge 1$, the compact set $K_ m\setminus \operatorname{Int}K_{m-1}$ is covered by finitely many balls $B(c,r/3)$ with $c\in K_ m\setminus \operatorname{Int}K_{m-1}$ and $B(c,r)\Subset \operatorname{Int}K_{m+1}\setminus K_{m-2}$. Collecting these balls for all $m$, we obtain a sequence of balls $B_ i=B(c_ i,r_ i)\Subset \Omega $ whose inner balls $B(c_ i,r_ i/3)$ cover $\Omega $. The family $(B_ i)$ is locally finite: a compact subset of $\Omega $ lies in some $K_ m$, and a ball chosen at a stage $m'\ge m+2$ lies in the complement of $K_{m'-2}\supset K_ m$, so the compact set meets only the finitely many balls chosen at the stages $m'\le m+1$. The function $u=(u-a|z|^2)+a|z|^2$ is continuous and plurisubharmonic by proposition 8.2.5 . Let $ho _ h$, $h>0$, be the radial mollifiers of section 1.4 . By proposition 8.2.2 (2), we have $u*ho _ h\ge u$, and $(u-a|z|^2)*ho _ h=u*ho _ h-a|z|^2*ho _ h$ is smooth and plurisubharmonic, hence has positive semidefinite complex Hessian by proposition 8.2.2 (1); by lemma 1.4.1 , $u*ho _ h	o u$ locally uniformly as $h	o 0$. Since $ho _ h$ is radial, $\int yho _ h(y)\, \mathrm dV(y)=0$, and expanding $|z-y|^2=|z|^2-2\operatorname{Re}\langle z,yangle +|y|^2$ gives $|z|^2*ho _ h=|z|^2+\int |y|^2ho _ h(y)\, \mathrm dV(y)$, whose complex Hessian matrix is $I$. Hence the complex Hessian matrix of $u*ho _ h$ is at least $aI$. For each $i$ choose $\delta _ i$ with $0<\delta _ i<a/2$ and $\delta _ ir_ i^2<\min _{\overline B_ i}\varepsilon $, put $\eta _ i=\delta _ ir_ i^2/6$, and choose $h_ i>0$ so small that $u*ho _{h_ i}$ is defined near $\overline B_ i$ and satisfies $0\le u*ho _{h_ i}-u<\eta _ i$ there. Define \[  u_ i=u*ho _{h_ i}+\delta _ i igl ((2r_ i/3)^2-|z-c_ i|^2 igr ) \quad 	ext{on }B_ i.  \] The quadratic term is at least $\delta _ ir_ i^2/3=2\eta _ i$ on the inner ball $B(c_ i,r_ i/3)$, is less than $-2\eta _ i$ where $|z-c_ i|>\sqrt7\, r_ i/3$, and is at most $4\delta _ ir_ i^2/9$ everywhere. Therefore \[   egin{aligned} & u_ i>u+\eta _ i& & 	ext{on }B(c_ i,r_ i/3),\ & u_ i<u-\eta _ i& & 	ext{where }\sqrt7\, r_ i/3<|z-c_ i|<r_ i,\ & u_ i+\eta _ i<u+\varepsilon & & 	ext{on }B_ i, \end{aligned}  \] the last because $2\eta _ i+4\delta _ ir_ i^2/9=7\delta _ ir_ i^2/9<\varepsilon $ on $B_ i$. The complex Hessian matrix of $u_ i$ is at least $(a-\delta _ i)I\ge (a/2)I$. Step 2: a regularized maximum. Fix an even smooth function $	heta \ge 0$ on $\mathbb R$ with support in $(-1,1)$ and integral one, for instance the mollifier $ho _{1/2}$ of section 1.4 in dimension $d=1$. For an integer $p\ge 1$, positive numbers $\eta _1,\ldots ,\eta _ p$ and $t=(t_1,\ldots ,t_ p)\in \mathbb R^ p$, define \[  M_\eta (t)=\int _{\mathbb R^ p}\max _ i(t_ i+\eta _ i x_ i) \prod _ i	heta (x_ i)\, \mathrm dx.  \] The substitution $y_ i=\eta _ ix_ i$ and the evenness of $	heta $ show that $M_\eta $ is the convolution of the continuous function $t\mapsto \max _ it_ i$ with the smooth compactly supported function $y\mapsto \prod _ i\eta _ i^{-1}	heta (y_ i/\eta _ i)$, so $M_\eta $ is smooth by differentiation under the integral sign (section 1.4 ). It has the following properties. $M_\eta $ is convex and nondecreasing in each variable, since for fixed $x$ the function $t\mapsto \max _ i(t_ i+\eta _ ix_ i)$ is. $\max _ it_ i\le M_\eta (t)\le \max _ i(t_ i+\eta _ i)$. The upper bound holds because $|x_ i|<1$ on the support of the integrand. For the lower bound, integrate $\max _ j(t_ j+\eta _ jx_ j)\ge t_ i+\eta _ ix_ i$ and use $\int x_ i	heta (x_ i)\, \mathrm dx_ i=0$. $M_\eta (t_1+c,\ldots ,t_ p+c)=M_\eta (t)+c$ for $c\in \mathbb R$. Differentiating in $c$, together with the first property, gives $\partial M_\eta /\partial t_ i\ge 0$ and $\sum _ i\partial M_\eta /\partial t_ i=1$. If $t_ i+\eta _ i\le \max _{j
e i}(t_ j-\eta _ j)$ for some $i$, then deleting the variable $t_ i$ and the parameter $\eta _ i$ does not change the value of $M_\eta $. Indeed, for $|x_ j|<1$ we have $t_ i+\eta _ ix_ i<t_ i+\eta _ i\le \max _{j
e i}(t_ j-\eta _ j)<\max _{j
e i}(t_ j+\eta _ jx_ j)$, so the $i$-th term never realizes the maximum, and integrating out $x_ i$ removes it. For smooth real functions $w_1,\ldots ,w_ p$, the chain rule gives \[  \partial _{z_ j}\partial _{ ar z_ k}M_\eta (w)=\sum _ i rac{\partial M_\eta }{\partial t_ i}(w)\, \partial _{z_ j}\partial _{ ar z_ k}w_ i+\sum _{i,l} rac{\partial ^2M_\eta }{\partial t_ i\partial t_ l}(w)\, \partial _{z_ j}w_ i\, \overline{\partial _{z_ k}w_ l}.  \] The real Hessian matrix $G=(\partial ^2M_\eta /\partial t_ i\partial t_ l)$ is positive semidefinite, because the second derivative of the convex function $s\mapsto M_\eta (t+s	au )$ is nonnegative for every $	au \in \mathbb R^ p$. Hence the matrix given by the second sum is positive semidefinite: for $b\in \mathbb C^ n$ its quadratic form equals $\sum _{i,l}G_{il}\zeta _ i ar\zeta _ l$ with $\zeta _ i=\sum _ j\partial _{z_ j}w_ i\, b_ j$, and writing $\zeta =\xi +\mathrm i\xi '$ with $\xi ,\xi '\in \mathbb R^ p$, this is $\xi ^{\mathsf T}G\xi +\xi '^{\mathsf T}G\xi '\ge 0$ by the symmetry of $G$. Therefore, by the third property, if each $w_ i$ has complex Hessian matrix at least $(a/2)I$, so does $M_\eta (w_1,\ldots ,w_ p)$. Step 3: gluing. For $z\in \Omega $ let $I(z)=\{ i:z\in B_ i\} $, a finite nonempty set, and define $v(z)=M_\eta  igl ((u_ i(z))_{i\in I(z)} igr )$ with the parameters $(\eta _ i)_{i\in I(z)}$. We show that $v$ is smooth near a fixed point $z_0$. Let $I_0=\{ i:z_0\in B_ i\} $ and $I_1=\{ i:z_0\in \partial B_ i\} $, finite sets by local finiteness, and choose $j$ with $z_0\in B(c_ j,r_ j/3)$. There is a neighborhood $W$ of $z_0$ that is contained in $B(c_ j,r_ j/3)$ and in $B_ i$ for $i\in I_0$, that meets $\overline B_ i$ only for $i\in I_0\cup I_1$, and whose intersection with $B_ i$, for $i\in I_1$, lies in the shell $\sqrt7\, r_ i/3<|z-c_ i|<r_ i$. For $z\in W$ we have $I_0\subset I(z)\subset I_0\cup I_1$, $j\in I_0$, and every $i\in I(z)\cap I_1$ satisfies \[  u_ i(z)+\eta _ i<u(z)<u_ j(z)-\eta _ j.  \] By the fourth property of $M_\eta $, applied to these indices one at a time, $v=M_\eta  igl ((u_ i)_{i\in I_0} igr )$ on $W$, which is smooth. Thus $v$ is smooth on $\Omega $, and by Step 2 its complex Hessian matrix is at least $(a/2)I$; hence $v-	frac a2|z|^2$ is smooth with positive semidefinite complex Hessian, and so it is plurisubharmonic by proposition 8.2.2 (1). Finally, every $z$ lies in some inner ball $B(c_ j,r_ j/3)$, and the second property of $M_\eta $ gives $v(z)\ge u_ j(z)>u(z)$ and $v(z)\le \max _{i\in I(z)}(u_ i(z)+\eta _ i)<u(z)+\varepsilon (z)$. $\square$

title: Oka boundary distance
topic: Weighted L2 estimates and holomorphic extension
text:
Theorem 11.2.4 . Let $n\ge 1$ and let $\Omega \subsetneq \mathbb C^ n$ be an open set. If $\Omega $ is pseudoconvex, then $-\log \operatorname {dist}(z,\mathbb C^ n\setminus \Omega )$ is a continuous plurisubharmonic function on $\Omega $. Conversely, if this function is plurisubharmonic, then $\Omega $ is pseudoconvex. Every pseudoconvex open set in $\mathbb C^ n$ has a nonnegative smooth strictly plurisubharmonic exhaustion function. Proof. Steps 1 and 2 deduce the plurisubharmonicity of $-\log \operatorname {dist}(\cdot ,\mathbb C^ n\setminus \Omega )$ from a submean inequality for the distance to the boundary in a fixed direction; Step 3 uses this function to construct a continuous exhaustion function, which lemma 11.2.3 smooths. Step 1: distances in a fixed direction. Let $\Omega $ be pseudoconvex, with a continuous plurisubharmonic exhaustion function $ho $. For $z\in \Omega $ and $\xi \in \mathbb C^ n$ put \[  \delta (z,\xi )=\sup \{ r>0:z+\xi \Delta _ r\subset \Omega \} \in (0,\infty ],  \] so that $\delta (z,0)=\infty $. The function $\delta $ is lower semicontinuous on $\Omega 	imes \mathbb C^ n$: if $r<\delta (z,\xi )$, then the compact disc $z+\xi \overline\Delta _ r$ lies in $\Omega $, hence so does $z'+\xi '\overline\Delta _ r$ for all $(z',\xi ')$ close to $(z,\xi )$, and $\delta (z',\xi ')\ge r$ for these points. Thus $V=-\log \delta $ is an upper semicontinuous function on $\Omega 	imes \mathbb C^ n$ with values in $[-\infty ,\infty )$. We verify the hypothesis of lemma 11.2.2 for $V$ on the open set $\Omega 	imes \mathbb C^ n\subset \mathbb C^{2n}$. Let $(z_0+ta,\xi _0+tb)$, $|t|\le 1$, be a closed disc in $\Omega 	imes \mathbb C^ n$, and let $P$ be a polynomial with $V(z_0+ta,\xi _0+tb)\le \operatorname{Re}P(t)$ for $|t|=1$, that is, $\delta (z_0+ta,\xi _0+tb)\ge |\mathrm e^{-P(t)}|$. Consider the holomorphic map \[  h(t,w)=z_0+t a+w\mathrm e^{-P(t)}(\xi _0+t b),\qquad (t,w)\in \mathbb C^2.  \] We have $h(t,0)=z_0+ta\in \Omega $ for $|t|\le 1$; and $h(t,w)\in \Omega $ for $|t|=1$ and $|w|<1$, because then $|w\mathrm e^{-P(t)}|<\delta (z_0+ta,\xi _0+tb)$. Let $R$ be the supremum of the numbers $r\ge 0$ with $h(\overline\Delta 	imes \overline\Delta _ r)\subset \Omega $. Since $h(\overline\Delta 	imes \{ 0\} )$ is a compact subset of $\Omega $ and $h$ is continuous, $R>0$. We show that $R\ge 1$. Suppose that $R<1$. Then $h(\partial \Delta 	imes \overline\Delta _ R)$ is a compact subset of $\Omega $; let $c$ be the maximum of $ho $ on it. For $|w|<R$ we have $h(\overline\Delta 	imes \{ w\} )\subset \Omega $, because every radius smaller than an admissible one is admissible; since this set is compact and $h$ is continuous, there is $r'>1$ such that $t\mapsto h(t,w)$ maps the disc $\Delta _{r'}$ into $\Omega $, and hence into one connected component of $\Omega $. The function $t\mapsto ho (h(t,w))$ is finite, hence subharmonic on $\Delta _{r'}$ by proposition 8.2.3 , and it is at most $c$ on $\partial \Delta $. By upper semicontinuity, $\varlimsup _{t	o \zeta }(ho (h(t,w))-c)\le 0$ for every $\zeta \in \partial \Delta $, and the maximum principle of proposition 3.1.4 on the disc $\Delta $ gives $ho (h(t,w))\le c$ for $|t|<1$, hence for $|t|\le 1$. Thus $h(\overline\Delta 	imes \Delta _ R)$ lies in the compact set $\{ ho \le c\} $, and so does its closure $h(\overline\Delta 	imes \overline\Delta _ R)$. This compact subset of $\Omega $ has positive distance from $\mathbb C^ n\setminus \Omega $, and the uniform continuity of $h$ on compact sets gives $h(\overline\Delta 	imes \overline\Delta _{R'})\subset \Omega $ for some $R'>R$, contradicting the definition of $R$. Hence $R\ge 1$. In particular $h(0,w)=z_0+w\mathrm e^{-P(0)}\xi _0\in \Omega $ for $|w|<1$, which means that $\delta (z_0,\xi _0)\ge \mathrm e^{-\operatorname{Re}P(0)}$, that is, $V(z_0,\xi _0)\le \operatorname{Re}P(0)$. By lemma 11.2.2 , $V$ satisfies the circle submean inequality on every closed complex disc in $\Omega 	imes \mathbb C^ n$. Step 2: the boundary distance. Now let $\Omega 
e \mathbb C^ n$ and put $d(z)=\operatorname {dist}(z,\mathbb C^ n\setminus \Omega )$. For a unit vector $\xi $ we have $\delta (z,\xi )\ge d(z)$, because $z+\xi \Delta _{d(z)}$ lies in the ball $B(z,d(z))\subset \Omega $. Equality holds if $\xi $ points from $z$ to a nearest point of the closed set $\mathbb C^ n\setminus \Omega $, since that point, $z+d(z)\xi $, lies in $z+\xi \Delta _ r$ for every $r>d(z)$. Hence \[  -\log d(z)=\max _{|\xi |=1}V(z,\xi ).  \] For fixed $\xi $, the function $z\mapsto V(z,\xi )$ satisfies the circle submean inequality on every closed disc $\{ z_0+ta:|t|\le 1\} \subset \Omega $, by Step 1 with $b=0$, and it is bounded above by $-\log d$. Therefore \[  V(z_0,\xi )\le  rac1{2\pi }\int _0^{2\pi }V(z_0+\mathrm e^{\mathrm i	heta }a,\xi )\, \mathrm d	heta \le  rac1{2\pi }\int _0^{2\pi }-\log d(z_0+\mathrm e^{\mathrm i	heta }a)\, \mathrm d	heta ,  \] and taking the maximum over $\xi $ gives the submean inequality for $-\log d$. Since $d$ is positive and $1$-Lipschitz, $-\log d$ is continuous. Its restriction to each connected component of each affine complex-line section of $\Omega $ is therefore subharmonic (definition 3.1.1 ): at a point $z_0+t_0a$ of such a section, the circle means over $\{ z_0+(t_0+r\mathrm e^{\mathrm i	heta })a\} $ dominate the value for all small $r>0$. Hence $-\log d$, which is finite, is plurisubharmonic on each connected component of $\Omega $ by definition 8.1.1 , that is, on $\Omega $. Step 3: smooth exhaustion functions. Let $\Omega 
e \mathbb C^ n$ be an open set on which $-\log d$ is plurisubharmonic, and put \[  u(z)=|z|^2+\max \{ -\log d(z),0\} .  \] Then $u$ is continuous, $u-|z|^2$ is plurisubharmonic by proposition 8.2.5 , and $u$ is an exhaustion function of $\Omega $: the set $\{ u\le c\} $ is contained in the ball $\{ |z|^2\le c\} $ and in $\{ d\ge \mathrm e^{-c}\} $, so it is a closed and bounded subset of $\mathbb C^ n$ contained in $\Omega $, hence compact. In particular, $\Omega $ is pseudoconvex, which proves the converse statement. By lemma 11.2.3 with $a=1$ and $\varepsilon =1$, there is a smooth function $s$ with $u\le s\le u+1$ such that $s-|z|^2/2$ is plurisubharmonic. Then $s\ge u\ge 0$, and the complex Hessian matrix of $s$ is at least $I/2$ by proposition 8.2.2 (1) applied to $s-|z|^2/2$, so that $s$ is strictly plurisubharmonic. Moreover, since $s\ge u$, the sublevel set $\{ s\le c\} $ is a closed subset of the compact set $\{ u\le c\} $. Thus $s$ is a nonnegative smooth strictly plurisubharmonic exhaustion function. If $\Omega 
e \mathbb C^ n$ is pseudoconvex, Step 2 shows that $-\log d$ is plurisubharmonic, so this construction applies; for $\Omega =\mathbb C^ n$ we take $s=|z|^2$. $\square$

title: Pseudoconvex sublevels products
topic: Weighted L2 estimates and holomorphic extension
text: Corollary 11.2.5 . Products of pseudoconvex open sets are pseudoconvex. If $s$ is a smooth plurisubharmonic exhaustion function of an open set $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$, then each sublevel set $\{ s<c\} $, $c\in \mathbb R$, is pseudoconvex and relatively compact in $\Omega $. In particular, every pseudoconvex open set $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ is the union of an increasing sequence of pseudoconvex open sets $\Omega _ j\Subset \Omega $. Proof. Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ and $\Omega '\subset \mathbb C^ m$ be pseudoconvex, with nonnegative continuous plurisubharmonic exhaustion functions $\rho $ and $\rho '$. The function $(z,w)\mapsto \rho (z)+\rho '(w)$ is continuous and plurisubharmonic on $\Omega \times \Omega '$, by proposition 8.2.3 applied to the two projections and by proposition 8.2.5 . Its sublevel set $\{ \le c\} $ is a closed subset of the compact set $\{ \rho \le c\} \times \{ \rho '\le c\} $, so $\Omega \times \Omega '$ is pseudoconvex. Next let $s$ be as in the statement and $c\in \mathbb R$. The function $x\mapsto 1/(c-x)$ is convex and increasing on $(-\infty ,c)$, so the complex Hessian matrix of $1/(c-s)$ on the open set $\{ s<c\} $, namely $(c-s)^{-2}(s_{j\bar k})+2(c-s)^{-3}\bigl (\partial _{z_ j}s\, \overline{\partial _{z_ k}s}\bigr )$ by the chain rule, is positive semidefinite. Hence $|z|^2+1/(c-s)$ is a smooth plurisubharmonic function on $\{ s<c\} $, by proposition 8.2.2 (1). For $C\le 0$ its sublevel set $\{ \le C\} $ is empty. For $C>0$ this sublevel set is closed in $\{ s<c\} $ and contained in the set $\{ s\le c-1/C\} $, which is a compact subset of $\{ s<c\} $; hence it is compact, and $\{ s<c\} $ is pseudoconvex. Moreover $\{ s<c\} $ is contained in the compact set $\{ s\le c\} $, so it is relatively compact in $\Omega $. Finally, if $\Omega $ is pseudoconvex, theorem 11.2.4 provides a smooth plurisubharmonic exhaustion function $s$, and the sets $\Omega _ j=\{ s<j\} $, $j\ge 1$, are pseudoconvex, relatively compact in $\Omega $, increasing, and have union $\Omega $. (Some of them may be empty or disconnected; definition 11.2.1 allows arbitrary open sets.) $\square$

title: Kiselman pseudoconvex tube
topic: Weighted L2 estimates and holomorphic extension
text: Corollary 11.2.6 . Let $m,k\ge 1$, and let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ m\times \mathbb C^ k$ be a pseudoconvex domain that is invariant under imaginary translations and whose nonempty real fibers $V_ z$ are convex, in the notation of section 8.5 . If $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$ is invariant under imaginary translations, then the function $v(z)=\inf _{t\in V_ z}u(z,t)$ is plurisubharmonic or identically $-\infty $ on $p(\Omega )$. Proof. We construct a function $\psi $ with the properties required in theorem 8.5.1 ; the corollary then follows from that theorem. If $\Omega =\mathbb C^{m+k}$, let $\psi (z,w)=|z|^2+|\operatorname{Re}w|^2$. Otherwise let $d=\operatorname {dist}(\cdot ,\mathbb C^{m+k}\setminus \Omega )$ and put \[  \psi (z,w)=|z|^2+|\operatorname{Re}w|^2+ \max \{ -\log d(z,w),0\} .  \] Imaginary translations are isometries of $\mathbb C^{m+k}$ that preserve $\Omega $ and its complement, so $d$ and $\psi $ are invariant under them. The function $\psi $ is plurisubharmonic by proposition 8.2.5 : $-\log d$ is plurisubharmonic by theorem 11.2.4 , and $|z|^2+|\operatorname{Re}w|^2$ is plurisubharmonic by proposition 8.2.2 (1), since its complex Hessian matrix is the diagonal matrix with entries $1$ in the $z$-directions and $\frac12$ in the $w$-directions, by the identity $(\operatorname{Re}w_ l)^2=\tfrac 12|w_ l|^2+\tfrac 12\operatorname{Re}(w_ l^2)$ for $1\le l\le k$. Finally, let $c\in \mathbb R$. Since $\psi $ is continuous, the set $\{ (z,t)\in \Omega _{\mathbb R}:\psi (z,t)\le c\} $ is closed in $\Omega _{\mathbb R}$. It is contained in $\{ |z|^2+|t|^2\le c\} $ and, if $\Omega \ne \mathbb C^{m+k}$, in the set $\{ d\ge \mathrm e^{-c}\} $, which is closed in $\mathbb C^{m+k}$ and contained in $\Omega $; it is therefore a closed and bounded subset of $\mathbb C^ m\times \mathbb R^ k$, hence compact. $\square$

title: Interior density and the weighted estimate
topic: Weighted L2 estimates and holomorphic extension
text:
11.3 Interior density and the weighted estimate We now prove Hörmander's estimate, first for smooth weights (theorem 11.3.3 ) and then, by regularization, for arbitrary plurisubharmonic weights (theorem 11.3.4 ). Throughout, $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ is open, $n\ge 1$, and $\mathrm dV=\mathrm dV_{2n}$ is Lebesgue measure. For a real function $q$ of class $C^2$ we write $H_ q=(q_{j ar k})$ for its complex Hessian matrix, with $q_{j ar k}=\partial _{z_ j}\partial _{ ar z_ k}q$ as in ( 7.5 ), and we express our estimates through $H_ q$. This is the matrix denoted $\mathcal H(q)$ in section 9.7 ; we use the lighter notation here because $\mathcal H_0$, $\mathcal H_1$ and $\mathcal H_2$ will denote Hilbert spaces. By ( 7.5 ), the inequality $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q\ge \varepsilon  eta $, with $ eta $ as in ( 7.4 ), is equivalent to $H_ q\ge \pi \varepsilon I$. We also fix a smooth nonincreasing function $\kappa _0$ on $\mathbb R$ with $\kappa _0=1$ on $(-\infty ,0]$ and $\kappa _0=0$ on $[1,\infty )$. For instance, if $ho _{1/2}$ is the mollifier of section 1.4 in dimension $d=1$, then $	heta _0(x)=ho _{1/2}(x-1/2)$ is smooth and nonnegative, has integral one and vanishes outside $[0,1]$, and $\kappa _0(x)=1-\int _{-\infty }^ x	heta _0(y)\, \mathrm dy$ has these properties. The cutoff functions of one real variable used below are obtained from $\kappa _0$ by affine changes of the variable. We give $(0,1)$- and $(0,2)$-forms the pointwise norms \[  \Bigl |\sum _ jf_ j\, \mathrm d ar z_ j\Bigr |^2=\sum _ j|f_ j|^2,\qquad \Bigl |\sum _{j<k}g_{jk}\, \mathrm d ar z_ j\wedge \mathrm d ar z_ k\Bigr |^2=\sum _{j<k}|g_{jk}|^2;  \] for $n=1$ there are no nonzero $(0,2)$-forms. For a measurable function $\varphi \colon \Omega 	o [-\infty ,\infty )$, which we call a weight , we write $L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-\varphi })$ for the Hilbert space of measurable functions $u$ with $\int _\Omega |u|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi }\, \mathrm dV<\infty $, modulo null functions, with the inner product $\langle u,vangle _\varphi =\int _\Omega u ar v\, \mathrm e^{-\varphi }\, \mathrm dV$ and the norm $\| u\| _\varphi $. Similarly, $L^2_{(0,1)}(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-\varphi })$ and $L^2_{(0,2)}(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-\varphi })$ consist of the $(0,1)$- and $(0,2)$-forms $f$ with measurable coefficients and $\int _\Omega |f|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi }\, \mathrm dV<\infty $, with the analogous inner products. We write $L^2_{\mathrm{loc},(0,1)}(\Omega )$ for the $(0,1)$-forms with coefficients in $L^2_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$. The operator $ ar\partial $ is always taken in the sense of distributions. Fix smooth real functions $\varphi _1,\varphi _2,\varphi _3$ on $\Omega $ and put \[  \mathcal H_0=L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-\varphi _1}),\quad \mathcal H_1=L^2_{(0,1)}(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-\varphi _2}),\quad \mathcal H_2=L^2_{(0,2)}(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-\varphi _3}).  \] Let $T= ar\partial $ from $\mathcal H_0$ to $\mathcal H_1$ and $S= ar\partial $ from $\mathcal H_1$ to $\mathcal H_2$ be defined on their maximal domains \[  \operatorname{Dom}T=\{ u\in \mathcal H_0: ar\partial u\in \mathcal H_1\} ,\qquad \operatorname{Dom}S=\{ f\in \mathcal H_1: ar\partial f\in \mathcal H_2\} .  \] Since the weights are continuous, convergence in $\mathcal H_0$, $\mathcal H_1$ or $\mathcal H_2$ implies convergence in $L^2$ on compact sets, and hence in the sense of distributions; therefore $T$ and $S$ are closed. Since the measures $\mathrm e^{-\varphi _ k}\, \mathrm dV$ are Radon measures, lemma 1.4.1 shows that smooth compactly supported functions and forms are dense in $\mathcal H_0$ and in $\mathcal H_1$; they belong to $\operatorname{Dom}T$ and $\operatorname{Dom}S$, so $T$ and $S$ are densely defined. Finally $ ar\partial  ar\partial =0$ on distributions, so $\operatorname {Ran}T\subset \ker S$. Thus $T$ and $S$ satisfy the hypotheses on the operators in theorem 11.1.4 , with $\mathcal H_ k$ in place of $H_ k$. Let $f=\sum _ jf_ j\, \mathrm d ar z_ j\in \operatorname{Dom}T^*$. For every $u\in C^\infty _ c(\Omega )$ we have \[  \sum _ j\int _\Omega \partial _{ ar z_ j}u\; \overline{f_ j}\, \mathrm e^{-\varphi _2}\, \mathrm dV=\langle Tu,fangle _{\mathcal H_1}=\langle u,T^*fangle _{\mathcal H_0}=\int _\Omega u\, \overline{T^*f}\, \mathrm e^{-\varphi _1}\, \mathrm dV.  \] Integrating by parts on the left in the sense of distributions, we obtain $\mathrm e^{-\varphi _1}T^*f=-\sum _ j\partial _{z_ j}(f_ j\mathrm e^{-\varphi _2})$, that is, 11.4  egin{equation} \label{eq:three-weight-adjoint} T^*f=-\mathrm e^{\varphi _1-\varphi _2} \sum _ j igl (\partial _{z_ j}f_ j-(\partial _{z_ j}\varphi _2)f_ j igr ) \end{equation} in the sense of distributions. Conversely, if $f$ is a smooth compactly supported $(0,1)$-form, the same computation is valid for every $u\in \operatorname{Dom}T$, since it only pairs the distribution $ ar\partial u$ with the test form $f\mathrm e^{-\varphi _2}$; hence $f\in \operatorname{Dom}T^*$, and $T^*f$ is given by ( 11.4 ). For a general $f$, however, ( 11.4 ) describes $T^*f$ but does not characterize $\operatorname{Dom}T^*$: membership in $\operatorname{Dom}T^*$ also encodes a boundary condition, which compactly supported test functions cannot detect. The following lemma shows that this boundary condition does not matter for the estimate, provided the weights are suitably related. Lemma 11.3.1 . Let $\varphi $ and $\psi $ be smooth real functions on $\Omega $, and put $\varphi _ k=\varphi +(k-3)\psi $ for $k=1,2,3$, so that $\varphi _1=\varphi -2\psi $, $\varphi _2=\varphi -\psi $ and $\varphi _3=\varphi $. Assume that there are functions $\chi _
u \in C_ c^\infty (\Omega )$, $
u \in \mathbb N$, with $0\le \chi _
u \le 1$ and $| ar\partial \chi _
u |^2\le \mathrm e^\psi $, such that for every compact set $K\subset \Omega $ we have $\chi _
u =1$ on a neighborhood of $K$ for all large $
u $. Then, for the operators $T$ and $S$ defined by these weights, the smooth compactly supported $(0,1)$-forms are dense in $\operatorname{Dom}T^*\cap \operatorname{Dom}S$ for the graph norm $\| f\| _{\mathcal H_1}+\| T^*f\| _{\mathcal H_0}+\| Sf\| _{\mathcal H_2}$. Proof. Step 1: cutting off. Let $f\in \operatorname{Dom}T^*\cap \operatorname{Dom}S$, and write $\chi =\chi _
u $. Since $\chi $ is real, $|\partial _{z_ j}\chi |=|\partial _{ ar z_ j}\chi |$, so the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality gives $|\sum _ j(\partial _{z_ j}\chi )f_ j|^2\le | ar\partial \chi |^2|f|^2$. Lagrange's identity $\sum _{j<k}|a_ jb_ k-a_ kb_ j|^2=|a|^2|b|^2-|\sum _ ja_ j ar b_ j|^2$ gives likewise $| ar\partial \chi \wedge f|^2\le | ar\partial \chi |^2|f|^2$. Since $\varphi _1-2\varphi _2=-\varphi =-\varphi _3$ and $| ar\partial \chi |^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi }\le \mathrm e^{-\varphi _2}$, the form $ ar\partial \chi \wedge f$ lies in $\mathcal H_2$, the function $\mathrm e^{\varphi _1-\varphi _2}\sum _ j(\partial _{z_ j}\chi )f_ j$ lies in $\mathcal H_0$, and both of their squared norms are at most 11.5  egin{equation} \label{eq:three-weight-cutoff-error} \int _\Omega |f|^2| ar\partial \chi _
