On $L^2(K)$ the norm with weight $\mathrm e^{-\varphi _ k}$ is equivalent to the unweighted norm, so the subsequence also converges weakly for it, and the lower semicontinuity in proposition 11.1.2 gives \[  \int _ K|u|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi _ k}\, \mathrm dV\le \varliminf _ j\int _ K|u_ j|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi _ k}\, \mathrm dV\le \varliminf _ j\int _ K|u_ j|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi _ j}\, \mathrm dV\le M.  \] This holds for all large $k$, and $\mathrm e^{-\varphi _ k}$ increases to $\mathrm e^{-p-q}$ as $k	o \infty $; so the monotone convergence theorem gives $\int _ K|u|^2\mathrm e^{-p-q}\, \mathrm dV\le M$, and exhausting $\Omega $ by compact sets proves the estimate. The last assertion follows from the pointwise inequality $|\alpha |_{A^{-1}}^2\le \lambda ^{-1}|\alpha |^2$. $\square$ The density $\mathrm e^{-p-q}$ in theorem 11.3.4 takes values in $(0,\infty ]$. It is infinite exactly on the pole set $\{ p=-\infty \} $, which is a Lebesgue null set because $p$ is locally integrable (theorem 8.2.1 ), and it need not be locally integrable. Nevertheless, $L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-p-q})$ is a Hilbert space, and since $p+q$ is bounded above on compact sets, convergence in it implies convergence in $L^2_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$; we show both facts in the proof of lemma 11.3.5 (2) below. That lemma also provides a distinguished solution of $ ar\partial u=\alpha $ in such weighted spaces. We write $\mathcal O(\Omega )$ for the space of holomorphic functions on an open set $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$. Lemma 11.3.5 . Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ be open, $n\ge 1$. Every distribution $h$ on $\Omega $ with $ ar\partial h=0$ is a holomorphic function: there is $g\in \mathcal O(\Omega )$ with $\langle h,\chi angle =\int _\Omega g\chi \, \mathrm dV$ for every test function $\chi $. Let $\varphi \colon \Omega 	o [-\infty ,\infty )$ be a measurable function that is bounded above on every compact subset of $\Omega $. Then the elements of $L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-\varphi })$ represented by holomorphic functions form a closed subspace $\mathcal K$. Let $\alpha $ be a $(0,1)$-form with distribution coefficients such that the equation $ ar\partial u=\alpha $ has a solution in $L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-\varphi })$. Then among these solutions there is exactly one of smallest norm, and a solution is of smallest norm if and only if it is orthogonal to $\mathcal K$. Proof. (1) The real and imaginary parts of $h$, given by $\operatorname{Re}\langle h,\chi angle $ and $\operatorname{Im}\langle h,\chi angle $ for real test functions $\chi $, are real distributions. Since derivatives of distributions commute, ( 7.5 ) shows that the Laplacian of $h$ is $4\sum _ j\partial _{z_ j}\partial _{ ar z_ j}h=0$. As the Laplacian has real coefficients, the real and imaginary parts of $h$ are harmonic distributions. By Weyl's lemma (theorem 2.1.4 ) they are given by smooth functions, and hence $h$ is given by a smooth function $g$. By integration by parts, the classical derivatives $\partial _{ ar z_ j}g$ represent the distributions $\partial _{ ar z_ j}h=0$, so they vanish almost everywhere by proposition 1.4.3 (4), and hence everywhere, being continuous functions. Thus $g$ is holomorphic. (2) Let $L\subset \Omega $ be compact, and let $m_ L$ be a real upper bound for $\varphi $ on $L$. For $u\in L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-\varphi })$ we have $\int _ L|u|^2\, \mathrm dV\le \mathrm e^{m_ L}\int _ L|u|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi }\, \mathrm dV$. Hence $L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-\varphi })\subset L^2_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$, so that $ ar\partial u$ is defined in the sense of distributions, and convergence in $L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-\varphi })$ implies convergence in $L^2_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$, hence in the sense of distributions. The space $L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-\varphi })$ is a Hilbert space, by the completeness argument at the beginning of section 11.1 , applied to the positive measure $\mathrm e^{-\varphi }\, \mathrm dV$. The set $\mathcal K$ is a linear subspace. It is closed: if $g_ j\in \mathcal K$ converge to $g$ in $L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-\varphi })$, then $g_ j	o g$ in the sense of distributions, so $ ar\partial g=\lim _ j ar\partial g_ j=0$, and by (1) $g$ agrees almost everywhere with a holomorphic function, that is, $g\in \mathcal K$. Let $u_0$ be a solution of $ ar\partial u=\alpha $ in $L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-\varphi })$. By (1), an element $u$ of this space is a solution if and only if $ ar\partial (u-u_0)=0$, that is, $u-u_0\in \mathcal K$. Thus the solutions form the nonempty closed convex set $u_0+\mathcal K$, which by proposition 11.1.1 contains a unique element $u_{\min }$ of smallest norm. If a solution $u$ is orthogonal to $\mathcal K$, then $\| u+k\| ^2=\| u\| ^2+\| k\| ^2\geq \| u\| ^2$ for every $k\in \mathcal K$, so $u$ has smallest norm, that is, $u=u_{\min }$. Conversely, if $P$ is the orthogonal projection onto $\mathcal K$ (proposition 11.1.1 ), then $u_{\min }-Pu_{\min }$ is a solution orthogonal to $\mathcal K$, hence equal to $u_{\min }$; so $u_{\min }$ is orthogonal to $\mathcal K$. $\square$ The solution of smallest norm in (2) is called the minimal solution of $ ar\partial u=\alpha $ in $L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-\varphi })$.

title: Three weight density
topic: Weighted L2 estimates and holomorphic extension

Lemma 11.3.1 . Let $\varphi $ and $\psi $ be smooth real functions on $\Omega $, and put $\varphi _ k=\varphi +(k-3)\psi $ for $k=1,2,3$, so that $\varphi _1=\varphi -2\psi $, $\varphi _2=\varphi -\psi $ and $\varphi _3=\varphi $. Assume that there are functions $\chi _
u \in C_ c^\infty (\Omega )$, $
u \in \mathbb N$, with $0\le \chi _
u \le 1$ and $| ar\partial \chi _
u |^2\le \mathrm e^\psi $, such that for every compact set $K\subset \Omega $ we have $\chi _
u =1$ on a neighborhood of $K$ for all large $
u $. Then, for the operators $T$ and $S$ defined by these weights, the smooth compactly supported $(0,1)$-forms are dense in $\operatorname{Dom}T^*\cap \operatorname{Dom}S$ for the graph norm $\| f\| _{\mathcal H_1}+\| T^*f\| _{\mathcal H_0}+\| Sf\| _{\mathcal H_2}$. Proof. Step 1: cutting off. Let $f\in \operatorname{Dom}T^*\cap \operatorname{Dom}S$, and write $\chi =\chi _
u $. Since $\chi $ is real, $|\partial _{z_ j}\chi |=|\partial _{ ar z_ j}\chi |$, so the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality gives $|\sum _ j(\partial _{z_ j}\chi )f_ j|^2\le | ar\partial \chi |^2|f|^2$. Lagrange's identity $\sum _{j<k}|a_ jb_ k-a_ kb_ j|^2=|a|^2|b|^2-|\sum _ ja_ j ar b_ j|^2$ gives likewise $| ar\partial \chi \wedge f|^2\le | ar\partial \chi |^2|f|^2$. Since $\varphi _1-2\varphi _2=-\varphi =-\varphi _3$ and $| ar\partial \chi |^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi }\le \mathrm e^{-\varphi _2}$, the form $ ar\partial \chi \wedge f$ lies in $\mathcal H_2$, the function $\mathrm e^{\varphi _1-\varphi _2}\sum _ j(\partial _{z_ j}\chi )f_ j$ lies in $\mathcal H_0$, and both of their squared norms are at most 11.5  egin{equation} \label{eq:three-weight-cutoff-error} \int _\Omega |f|^2| ar\partial \chi _
u |^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi }\, \mathrm dV\le \| f\| _{\mathcal H_1}^2. \end{equation} Let $u\in \operatorname{Dom}T$. Then $\chi u\in \operatorname{Dom}T$ and $T(\chi u)=\chi Tu+u\,  ar\partial \chi $, because $u\,  ar\partial \chi \in \mathcal H_1$, the weights being bounded on the support of $\chi $. As $\chi $ is real and $\overline{\partial _{ ar z_ j}\chi }=\partial _{z_ j}\chi $, we get \[  \langle Tu,\chi fangle _{\mathcal H_1}=\langle T(\chi u),fangle _{\mathcal H_1}-\langle u\,  ar\partial \chi ,fangle _{\mathcal H_1} =\Bigl \langle u,\chi T^*f-\mathrm e^{\varphi _1-\varphi _2}\sum _ j(\partial _{z_ j}\chi )f_ j\Bigr angle _{\mathcal H_0}.  \] Hence $\chi f\in \operatorname{Dom}T^*$, and the distributional product rule shows that $\chi f\in \operatorname{Dom}S$, with \[   egin{split}  T^*(\chi f)-\chi T^*f & =-\mathrm e^{\varphi _1-\varphi _2}\sum _ j(\partial _{z_ j}\chi )f_ j,\  S(\chi f)-\chi Sf& = ar\partial \chi \wedge f. \end{split}  \] By ( 11.5 ), the squared norms of both differences are bounded by $\int |f|^2| ar\partial \chi _
u |^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi }\, \mathrm dV$. As $
u 	o \infty $, $ ar\partial \chi _
u $ tends to zero pointwise, since it vanishes near each point for large $
u $, and the integrand is dominated by the integrable function $|f|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi _2}$. By dominated convergence, both differences tend to zero. Again by dominated convergence, $\chi _
u f	o f$, $\chi _
u T^*f	o T^*f$ and $\chi _
u Sf	o Sf$. Therefore $\chi _
u f	o f$ in the graph norm. Step 2: smoothing. It remains to approximate a form $f\in \operatorname{Dom}T^*\cap \operatorname{Dom}S$ with compact support $K\subset \Omega $. By ( 11.4 ), \[  \sum _ j\partial _{z_ j}f_ j=-\mathrm e^{\varphi _2-\varphi _1}T^*f+\sum _ j(\partial _{z_ j}\varphi _2)f_ j\in L^2_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega ),  \] and $ ar\partial f=Sf\in L^2_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$. Let $f^\varepsilon =\sum _ j(f_ j*ho _\varepsilon )\, \mathrm d ar z_ j$, with $ho _\varepsilon $ the mollifier of section 1.4 ; for small $\varepsilon $ these forms are smooth and supported in a fixed compact neighborhood $K'$ of $K$ in $\Omega $. Convolution commutes with derivatives with constant coefficients (proposition 1.4.3 ), so $ ar\partial f^\varepsilon =( ar\partial f)*ho _\varepsilon $ and $\sum _ j\partial _{z_ j}f^\varepsilon _ j=(\sum _ j\partial _{z_ j}f_ j)*ho _\varepsilon $. By lemma 1.4.1 , $f^\varepsilon $, $\sum _ j\partial _{z_ j}f^\varepsilon _ j$ and $ ar\partial f^\varepsilon $ converge in $L^2(K')$ to $f$, $\sum _ j\partial _{z_ j}f_ j$ and $ ar\partial f$. Since ( 11.4 ) applies to both $f^\varepsilon $ and $f$, and its remaining coefficients are smooth, $T^*f^\varepsilon 	o T^*f$ in $L^2(K')$. The weights are bounded above and below on $K'$, so $f^\varepsilon 	o f$ in the graph norm. $\square$

title: Interior bochner identity
topic: Weighted L2 estimates and holomorphic extension
text:
Proposition 11.3.2 . Let $\varphi $ be a smooth real function on $\Omega $, and let $\delta _ j$ be the differential operator $\delta _ jg=-\partial _{z_ j}g+(\partial _{z_ j}\varphi )g$, $1\le j\le n$. Then every smooth compactly supported $(0,1)$-form $f=\sum _ jf_ j\, \mathrm d ar z_ j$ on $\Omega $ satisfies \[   egin{split} & \int \Bigl |\sum _ j\delta _ j f_ j\Bigr |^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi }\, \mathrm dV +\int | ar\partial f|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi }\, \mathrm dV\ & \qquad =\int \sum _{j,k}\varphi _{j ar k}f_ j ar f_ k\, \mathrm e^{-\varphi }\, \mathrm dV +\int \sum _{j,k}|\partial _{ ar z_ k}f_ j|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi }\, \mathrm dV. \end{split}  \] Consequently, if $\psi $ is a smooth real function and $T$ and $S$ are the operators defined by the weights $\varphi _ k=\varphi +(k-3)\psi $ of lemma 11.3.1 , then for every $t>0$ 11.10  egin{equation} \label{eq:three-weight-basic-estimate} \int \sum _{j,k}\varphi _{j ar k}f_ j ar f_ k\mathrm e^{-\varphi }\, \mathrm dV \le (1+t^{-1})\| T^*f\| _{\mathcal H_0}^2+\| Sf\| _{\mathcal H_2}^2 +(1+t)\int |f|^2| ar\partial \psi |^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi }\, \mathrm dV. \end{equation} Proof. For smooth compactly supported functions $g$ and $w$, integration by parts (Fubini's theorem and the fundamental theorem of calculus on lines) gives \[  \langle \partial _{ ar z_ j}g,wangle _\varphi =-\int g\, \partial _{ ar z_ j} igl ( ar w\mathrm e^{-\varphi } igr )\, \mathrm dV=\int g\, \overline{ igl (-\partial _{z_ j}w+(\partial _{z_ j}\varphi )w igr )}\, \mathrm e^{-\varphi }\, \mathrm dV=\langle g,\delta _ jwangle _\varphi ,  \] because $\varphi $ is real; thus $\delta _ j$ is the formal adjoint of $\partial _{ ar z_ j}$ for the inner product $\langle \cdot ,\cdot angle _\varphi $, and taking complex conjugates we also have $\langle \delta _ jw,gangle _\varphi =\langle w,\partial _{ ar z_ j}gangle _\varphi $. Since $\partial _{ ar z_ k} igl ((\partial _{z_ j}\varphi )g igr )=\varphi _{j ar k}g+(\partial _{z_ j}\varphi )\partial _{ ar z_ k}g$ and the derivatives $\partial _{z_ j}$ and $\partial _{ ar z_ k}$ commute, we obtain the commutation relation \[  \partial _{ ar z_ k}(\delta _ jg)-\delta _ j(\partial _{ ar z_ k}g)=\varphi _{j ar k}\, g.  \] By the adjoint relation, then the commutation relation, and then the conjugate adjoint relation, \[   egin{split}  \Bigl \| \sum _ j\delta _ jf_ j\Bigr \| _\varphi ^2& =\sum _{j,k}\langle \delta _ jf_ j,\delta _ kf_ kangle _\varphi =\sum _{j,k}\langle \partial _{ ar z_ k}\delta _ jf_ j,f_ kangle _\varphi \ & =\sum _{j,k}\langle \varphi _{j ar k}f_ j,f_ kangle _\varphi +\sum _{j,k}\langle \delta _ j\partial _{ ar z_ k}f_ j,f_ kangle _\varphi \ & =\int \sum _{j,k}\varphi _{j ar k}f_ j ar f_ k\mathrm e^{-\varphi }\, \mathrm dV+\sum _{j,k}\langle \partial _{ ar z_ k}f_ j,\partial _{ ar z_ j}f_ kangle _\varphi . \end{split}  \] On the other hand, $ ar\partial f=\sum _{j<k}(\partial _{ ar z_ j}f_ k-\partial _{ ar z_ k}f_ j)\, \mathrm d ar z_ j\wedge \mathrm d ar z_ k$, and expanding the squares gives \[  \|  ar\partial f\| _\varphi ^2=\sum _{j
e k}\| \partial _{ ar z_ k}f_ j\| _\varphi ^2-\sum _{j
e k}\langle \partial _{ ar z_ k}f_ j,\partial _{ ar z_ j}f_ kangle _\varphi .  \] When we add the two identities, the terms with $j
e k$ in the last sums cancel, and the remaining terms $\| \partial _{ ar z_ j}f_ j\| _\varphi ^2$ combine with $\sum _{j
e k}\| \partial _{ ar z_ k}f_ j\| _\varphi ^2$ to give $\sum _{j,k}\| \partial _{ ar z_ k}f_ j\| _\varphi ^2$. This proves the identity. For the estimate, we have $\varphi _1-\varphi _2=-\psi $ and $\partial _{z_ j}\varphi _2=\partial _{z_ j}\varphi -\partial _{z_ j}\psi $, so ( 11.4 ) reads \[  \sum _ j\delta _ jf_ j=\mathrm e^\psi T^*f+\sum _ j(\partial _{z_ j}\psi )f_ j.  \] By the elementary inequality $|x+y|^2\le (1+t^{-1})|x|^2+(1+t)|y|^2$ for $x,y\in \mathbb C$, \[  \Bigl \| \sum _ j\delta _ jf_ j\Bigr \| _\varphi ^2\le (1+t^{-1})\int |T^*f|^2\mathrm e^{2\psi -\varphi }\, \mathrm dV+(1+t)\int \Bigl |\sum _ j(\partial _{z_ j}\psi )f_ j\Bigr |^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi }\, \mathrm dV.  \] The first integral is $\| T^*f\| _{\mathcal H_0}^2$, because $\varphi _1=\varphi -2\psi $, and $|\sum _ j(\partial _{z_ j}\psi )f_ j|^2\le | ar\partial \psi |^2|f|^2$ by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, since $|\partial _{z_ j}\psi |=|\partial _{ ar z_ j}\psi |$ for real $\psi $. Moreover $\|  ar\partial f\| _\varphi ^2=\| Sf\| _{\mathcal H_2}^2$, because $\varphi _3=\varphi $. Inserting these bounds into the identity and dropping its last, nonnegative, term, we obtain ( 11.10 ). $\square$

title: Hörmander
topic: Weighted L2 estimates and holomorphic extension
text:
Theorem 11.3.3 (Hörmander) . Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ be a pseudoconvex open set, $n\ge 1$, and let $\varphi $ be a smooth plurisubharmonic function on $\Omega $. Let $\alpha $ be a $(0,1)$-form on $\Omega $ with measurable coefficients such that \[  M=\int _\Omega |\alpha |_{H_\varphi ^{-1}}^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi }\, \mathrm dV<\infty  \] and $ ar\partial \alpha =0$. Then there is $u\in L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-\varphi })$ with $ ar\partial u=\alpha $ and $\int _\Omega |u|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi }\, \mathrm dV\le M$. Proof. The idea is to modify the weight far out in $\Omega $ so that lemma 11.3.1 applies and the error term in ( 11.10 ) is absorbed by additional convexity, and then to let the modification recede to the boundary. Step 1: auxiliary functions. The matrix $H_\varphi $ is positive semidefinite because $\varphi $ is plurisubharmonic, and by the discussion preceding the theorem, applied with $A=H_\varphi $, the finiteness of $M$ implies that $\alpha \in L^2_{\mathrm{loc},(0,1)}(\Omega )$. By theorem 11.2.4 , $\Omega $ has a nonnegative smooth strictly plurisubharmonic exhaustion function $s$. Fix an integer $t\ge 1$. Let $\kappa _0$ be the function fixed at the beginning of this section, put $c_\kappa =\sup |\kappa _0'|$, and for integers $
u \ge 1$ put $\chi _
u =\kappa _0(s-t-1-
u )$. Then $0\le \chi _
u \le 1$, and $\chi _
u \in C^\infty _ c(\Omega )$, because $\{ s\le t+2+
u \} $ is compact; $\chi _
u =1$ on $\{ s\le t+1+
u \} $, hence on a neighborhood of any given compact set for large $
u $; and $ ar\partial \chi _
u =\kappa _0'(s-t-1-
u )\,  ar\partial s$ vanishes on $\{ s<t+2\} $ and satisfies $| ar\partial \chi _
u |^2\le c_\kappa ^2| ar\partial s|^2$. We put \[  \psi = igl (1-\kappa _0(s-t-1) igr )\log  igl (1+c_\kappa ^2| ar\partial s|^2 igr ).  \] Then $\psi $ is smooth and nonnegative; $\psi $ and $ ar\partial \psi $ vanish on $\{ s\le t+1\} $, since $1-\kappa _0(x-t-1)$ and its derivative vanish for $x\le t+1$; and $| ar\partial \chi _
u |^2\le \mathrm e^\psi $ for every $
u $, because $\mathrm e^\psi =1+c_\kappa ^2| ar\partial s|^2$ on $\{ s\ge t+2\} $ and $ ar\partial \chi _
u =0$ on $\{ s<t+2\} $. Next we choose a smooth convex nondecreasing function $\gamma \colon \mathbb R	o [0,\infty )$ with $\gamma =0$ on $(-\infty ,t]$ such that 11.15  egin{equation} \label{eq:hormander-convex-increase} \gamma (s)\ge 2\psi ,\qquad H_{\gamma (s)}\ge (1+t)| ar\partial \psi |^2 I, \qquad \int _\Omega |\alpha |^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi -\gamma (s)+\psi }\, \mathrm dV<\infty . \end{equation} For integers $l\ge 1$ the sets $K_ l=\{ t+l\le s\le t+l+1\} $ are compact. The smallest eigenvalue of $H_ s$ is a positive continuous function on $\Omega $ (see the discussion following proposition 8.2.2 ), so its minimum $\lambda _ l$ over $K_ l$ is positive (if $K_ l=\varnothing $, put $\lambda _ l=1$ and $m_ l=P_ l=I_ l=0$), and the numbers $m_ l=(1+t)\max _{K_ l}| ar\partial \psi |^2$, $P_ l=2\max _{K_ l}\psi $ and $I_ l=\int _{K_ l}|\alpha |^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi +\psi }\, \mathrm dV$ are finite, since $\alpha \in L^2_{\mathrm{loc},(0,1)}(\Omega )$. Choose a smooth nondecreasing function $g\colon \mathbb R	o [0,\infty )$ that vanishes on $(-\infty ,t]$ and satisfies, for every $l\ge 1$, \[  g\ge m_ l/\lambda _ l\  	ext{on }[t+l,t+l+1],\qquad \int _{t+l-1}^{t+l}g(x)\, \mathrm dx\ge \max  igl \{ P_ l,\log ^+(2^ lI_ l) igr \} .  \] For instance, let $\kappa _1(x)=1-\kappa _0(2x)$, a smooth nondecreasing function with $\kappa _1=0$ on $(-\infty ,0]$ and $\kappa _1=1$ on $[1/2,\infty )$, and put $g(x)=\sum _{l\ge 1}c_ l\kappa _1(x-t-l+1)$ with $c_ l=\max \{ m_ l/\lambda _ l,2P_ l,2\log ^+(2^ lI_ l)\} $. The sum is locally finite, since only the terms with $l<x-t+1$ are nonzero at $x$, and all its terms vanish for $x\le t$. The $l$-th term equals $c_ l$ on $[t+l-1/2,\infty )$, so $g\ge c_ l$ on $[t+l,t+l+1]$ and $\int _{t+l-1}^{t+l}g(x)\, \mathrm dx\ge c_ l/2$. Put $\gamma (x)=\int _{-\infty }^ xg(y)\, \mathrm dy$. Then $\gamma $ is smooth, nondecreasing and convex, because $\gamma '=g$ is nondecreasing, and $\gamma =0$ on $(-\infty ,t]$. Since $\Omega $ is the union of $\{ s\le t+1\} $ and the sets $K_ l$, we may check the first two conditions in ( 11.15 ) on each of these sets. On $\{ s\le t+1\} $ they hold because $\psi $ and $ ar\partial \psi $ vanish there while $\gamma \ge 0$ and $H_{\gamma (s)}\ge 0$. On $K_ l$ we have $\gamma (s)\ge \gamma (t+l)\ge P_ l\ge 2\psi $, and the chain rule \[  H_{\gamma (s)}=\gamma '(s)H_ s+\gamma ''(s) igl (\partial _{z_ j}s\, \overline{\partial _{z_ k}s} igr )_{j,k}\ge \gamma '(s)H_ s  \] gives $H_{\gamma (s)}\ge (m_ l/\lambda _ l)\lambda _ lI\ge (1+t)| ar\partial \psi |^2I$. Finally, the integral in ( 11.15 ) over the compact set $\{ s\le t+1\} $ is finite, and its integral over $K_ l$ is at most $\mathrm e^{-\gamma (t+l)}I_ l\le 2^{-l}$, because $\gamma (s)\ge \gamma (t+l)\ge \log ^+(2^ lI_ l)$ there; summing over $l$, we obtain the third condition. Step 2: the estimate. Put $\varphi _0=\varphi +\gamma (s)$ and $\varphi _ k=\varphi _0+(k-3)\psi $ for $k=1,2,3$, and let $T$ and $S$ be the corresponding operators. By the last condition in ( 11.15 ), $\alpha \in \mathcal H_1=L^2_{(0,1)}(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-\varphi _2})$, and $\alpha \in \ker S$. Let $f$ be a smooth compactly supported $(0,1)$-form. We apply ( 11.10 ) with $\varphi _0$ in place of $\varphi $ and with the integer $t$ fixed in Step 1. Since $H_{\varphi _0}=H_\varphi +H_{\gamma (s)}$, the second condition in ( 11.15 ) absorbs the last term of ( 11.10 ), and we obtain \[  \int H_\varphi [f]\, \mathrm e^{-\varphi _0}\, \mathrm dV \le (1+t^{-1})\| T^*f\| _{\mathcal H_0}^2+\| Sf\| _{\mathcal H_2}^2.  \] Moreover $\varphi -2\varphi _2=-\varphi _0-\gamma (s)+2\psi \le -\varphi _0$ by the first condition in ( 11.15 ). Since $M<\infty $, the dual energy of $\alpha $ is finite almost everywhere, and the inequality $|\sum _ j\alpha _ j ar f_ j|^2\le |\alpha |_{H_\varphi ^{-1}}^2H_\varphi [f]$ together with the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality gives \[   egin{split}  |\langle \alpha ,fangle _{\mathcal H_1}|^2 & \le \int |\alpha |_{H_\varphi ^{-1}}^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi }\, \mathrm dV\cdot \int H_\varphi [f]\, \mathrm e^{\varphi -2\varphi _2}\, \mathrm dV \le M\int H_\varphi [f]\, \mathrm e^{-\varphi _0}\, \mathrm dV\ & \le M(1+t^{-1}) igl (\| T^*f\| _{\mathcal H_0}^2+\| Sf\| _{\mathcal H_2}^2 igr ). \end{split}  \] Both sides are continuous for the graph norm of lemma 11.3.1 , whose hypotheses hold by Step 1; hence the inequality extends to all $f\in \operatorname{Dom}T^*\cap \operatorname{Dom}S$. By theorem 11.1.4 there is $u_ t\in \mathcal H_0$ with $ ar\partial u_ t=\alpha $ and $\| u_ t\| _{\mathcal H_0}^2\le M(1+t^{-1})$. On $\{ s<t\} $ both $\gamma (s)$ and $\psi $ vanish, so $\varphi _1=\varphi $ there and \[  \int _{\{ s<t\} }|u_ t|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi }\, \mathrm dV\le M(1+t^{-1}).  \] Step 3: passage to the limit. For each integer $l\ge 1$ the functions $u_ t$ with $t\ge l$ have squared norms at most $2M$ in $L^2(\{ s<l\} ,\mathrm e^{-\varphi })$. By proposition 11.1.2 and a diagonal argument, there is a sequence $t_ i	o \infty $ such that $u_{t_ i}$ converges weakly in $L^2(\{ s<l\} ,\mathrm e^{-\varphi })$ for every $l$. The limits on different sublevel sets agree on their intersections, because restriction from $\{ s<l+1\} $ to $\{ s<l\} $ is a bounded linear map, and they define a function $u$ on $\Omega $. Weak convergence in these spaces implies convergence in the sense of distributions: a test function $\chi $ has support in some set $\{ s<l\} $, and $\int u_{t_ i}\chi \, \mathrm dV=\langle u_{t_ i}, ar\chi \mathrm e^\varphi angle _\varphi $ with $ ar\chi \mathrm e^\varphi \in L^2(\{ s<l\} ,\mathrm e^{-\varphi })$. Hence $ ar\partial u=\alpha $. By the lower semicontinuity of the norm in proposition 11.1.2 , $\int _{\{ s<l\} }|u|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi }\, \mathrm dV\le \varliminf _ iM(1+t_ i^{-1})=M$ for every $l$, and the monotone convergence theorem gives $\int _\Omega |u|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi }\, \mathrm dV\le M$. $\square$

title: Hormander singular lower bound
topic: Weighted L2 estimates and holomorphic extension
text: Theorem 11.3.4 . Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ be a pseudoconvex open set, $n\ge 1$, let $p\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$, and let $q$ be a smooth real function on $\Omega $ whose complex Hessian matrix $A=H_ q$ is positive semidefinite. Let $\alpha $ be a $(0,1)$-form on $\Omega $ with measurable coefficients such that \[  M=\int _\Omega |\alpha |_{A^{-1}}^2\mathrm e^{-p-q}\, \mathrm dV<\infty  \] and $\bar\partial \alpha =0$. Then the equation $\bar\partial u=\alpha $ has a solution with $\int _\Omega |u|^2\mathrm e^{-p-q}\, \mathrm dV\le M$. In particular, if $A\ge \lambda I$ for a positive continuous function $\lambda $ on $\Omega $, then $M$ may be replaced by $\int _\Omega \lambda ^{-1}|\alpha |^2\mathrm e^{-p-q}\, \mathrm dV$. Proof. We regularize $p$ on relatively compact pseudoconvex subsets of $\Omega $, apply theorem 11.3.3 there, and pass to a weak limit. Since the weight $p+q$ is bounded above on compact sets, the discussion preceding theorem 11.3.3 shows that $\alpha \in L^2_{\mathrm{loc},(0,1)}(\Omega )$, so that $\bar\partial \alpha $ is defined. By corollary 11.2.5 there are pseudoconvex open sets $\Omega _1\subset \Omega _2\subset \cdots $ with $\Omega _ j\Subset \Omega $ and $\bigcup _ j\Omega _ j=\Omega $. Let $\rho _\varepsilon $ be the radial mollifier of section 1.4 , and choose $\varepsilon _ j\downarrow 0$ with $\varepsilon _ j<\operatorname {dist}(\overline\Omega _ j,\mathbb C^ n\setminus \Omega )$. By proposition 8.2.2 (2), $p_ j=p*\rho _{\varepsilon _ j}$ is defined, smooth and plurisubharmonic on the open neighborhood $\{ z\in \Omega :\operatorname {dist}(z,\mathbb C^ n\setminus \Omega )>\varepsilon _ j\} $ of $\overline\Omega _ j$, so its complex Hessian is positive semidefinite there, and $p_ j\downarrow p$ pointwise as $j\to \infty $. Put $\varphi _ j=p_ j+q$. Then $\varphi _ j$ is smooth with complex Hessian matrix $H_{\varphi _ j}\ge A\ge 0$ near $\overline\Omega _ j$, so it is plurisubharmonic there by proposition 8.2.2 (1), and $\varphi _ j\ge p+q$. Since the dual energy decreases when the matrix increases, \[  \int _{\Omega _ j}|\alpha |_{H_{\varphi _ j}^{-1}}^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi _ j}\, \mathrm dV \le \int _{\Omega _ j}|\alpha |_{A^{-1}}^2\mathrm e^{-p-q}\, \mathrm dV\le M.  \] By theorem 11.3.3 there is $u_ j$ on $\Omega _ j$ with $\bar\partial u_ j=\alpha $ and $\int _{\Omega _ j}|u_ j|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi _ j}\, \mathrm dV\le M$. Let $K\subset \Omega $ be compact. Then $K\subset \Omega _ k$ for some $k$, and for $j\ge k$ we have $\varphi _ j\le \varphi _ k$ on $K$, because $p_ j$ decreases. Hence $\int _ K|u_ j|^2\, \mathrm dV\le \mathrm e^{\max _ K\varphi _ k}M$ for $j\ge k$, so the sequence $(u_ j)$ is eventually bounded in $L^2(K)$ for every compact set $K$. Let $(K_ m)$ be a compact exhaustion of $\Omega $ (section 1.1 ). By proposition 11.1.2 and a diagonal argument, we find a subsequence that converges weakly in $L^2(K_ m)$ for every $m$. The weak limits are compatible, because restriction from $K_{m+1}$ to $K_ m$ is a bounded linear map, and they define a function $u\in L^2_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$; since every compact subset of $\Omega $ lies in some $K_ m$, the subsequence converges weakly to $u$ in $L^2(K)$ for every compact $K\subset \Omega $. Then $u_ j\to u$ in the sense of distributions, and $\bar\partial u=\alpha $. Now let $K\subset \Omega $ be compact, and let $k$ be so large that $K\subset \Omega _ k$. On $L^2(K)$ the norm with weight $\mathrm e^{-\varphi _ k}$ is equivalent to the unweighted norm, so the subsequence also converges weakly for it, and the lower semicontinuity in proposition 11.1.2 gives \[  \int _ K|u|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi _ k}\, \mathrm dV\le \varliminf _ j\int _ K|u_ j|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi _ k}\, \mathrm dV\le \varliminf _ j\int _ K|u_ j|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi _ j}\, \mathrm dV\le M.  \] This holds for all large $k$, and $\mathrm e^{-\varphi _ k}$ increases to $\mathrm e^{-p-q}$ as $k\to \infty $; so the monotone convergence theorem gives $\int _ K|u|^2\mathrm e^{-p-q}\, \mathrm dV\le M$, and exhausting $\Omega $ by compact sets proves the estimate. The last assertion follows from the pointwise inequality $|\alpha |_{A^{-1}}^2\le \lambda ^{-1}|\alpha |^2$. $\square$

title: Dbar closed distribution holomorphic
topic: Weighted L2 estimates and holomorphic extension
text: Lemma 11.3.5 . Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ be open, $n\ge 1$. Every distribution $h$ on $\Omega $ with $\bar\partial h=0$ is a holomorphic function: there is $g\in \mathcal O(\Omega )$ with $\langle h,\chi \rangle =\int _\Omega g\chi \, \mathrm dV$ for every test function $\chi $. Let $\varphi \colon \Omega \to [-\infty ,\infty )$ be a measurable function that is bounded above on every compact subset of $\Omega $. Then the elements of $L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-\varphi })$ represented by holomorphic functions form a closed subspace $\mathcal K$. Let $\alpha $ be a $(0,1)$-form with distribution coefficients such that the equation $\bar\partial u=\alpha $ has a solution in $L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-\varphi })$. Then among these solutions there is exactly one of smallest norm, and a solution is of smallest norm if and only if it is orthogonal to $\mathcal K$. Proof. (1) The real and imaginary parts of $h$, given by $\operatorname{Re}\langle h,\chi \rangle $ and $\operatorname{Im}\langle h,\chi \rangle $ for real test functions $\chi $, are real distributions. Since derivatives of distributions commute, ( 7.5 ) shows that the Laplacian of $h$ is $4\sum _ j\partial _{z_ j}\partial _{\bar z_ j}h=0$. As the Laplacian has real coefficients, the real and imaginary parts of $h$ are harmonic distributions. By Weyl's lemma (theorem 2.1.4 ) they are given by smooth functions, and hence $h$ is given by a smooth function $g$. By integration by parts, the classical derivatives $\partial _{\bar z_ j}g$ represent the distributions $\partial _{\bar z_ j}h=0$, so they vanish almost everywhere by proposition 1.4.3 (4), and hence everywhere, being continuous functions. Thus $g$ is holomorphic. (2) Let $L\subset \Omega $ be compact, and let $m_ L$ be a real upper bound for $\varphi $ on $L$. For $u\in L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-\varphi })$ we have $\int _ L|u|^2\, \mathrm dV\le \mathrm e^{m_ L}\int _ L|u|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi }\, \mathrm dV$. Hence $L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-\varphi })\subset L^2_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$, so that $\bar\partial u$ is defined in the sense of distributions, and convergence in $L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-\varphi })$ implies convergence in $L^2_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$, hence in the sense of distributions. The space $L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-\varphi })$ is a Hilbert space, by the completeness argument at the beginning of section 11.1 , applied to the positive measure $\mathrm e^{-\varphi }\, \mathrm dV$. The set $\mathcal K$ is a linear subspace. It is closed: if $g_ j\in \mathcal K$ converge to $g$ in $L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-\varphi })$, then $g_ j\to g$ in the sense of distributions, so $\bar\partial g=\lim _ j\bar\partial g_ j=0$, and by (1) $g$ agrees almost everywhere with a holomorphic function, that is, $g\in \mathcal K$. Let $u_0$ be a solution of $\bar\partial u=\alpha $ in $L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-\varphi })$. By (1), an element $u$ of this space is a solution if and only if $\bar\partial (u-u_0)=0$, that is, $u-u_0\in \mathcal K$. Thus the solutions form the nonempty closed convex set $u_0+\mathcal K$, which by proposition 11.1.1 contains a unique element $u_{\min }$ of smallest norm. If a solution $u$ is orthogonal to $\mathcal K$, then $\| u+k\| ^2=\| u\| ^2+\| k\| ^2\geq \| u\| ^2$ for every $k\in \mathcal K$, so $u$ has smallest norm, that is, $u=u_{\min }$. Conversely, if $P$ is the orthogonal projection onto $\mathcal K$ (proposition 11.1.1 ), then $u_{\min }-Pu_{\min }$ is a solution orthogonal to $\mathcal K$, hence equal to $u_{\min }$; so $u_{\min }$ is orthogonal to $\mathcal K$. $\square$

title: Interpolation and extension across a hyperplane
topic: Weighted L2 estimates and holomorphic extension
text:
11.4 Interpolation and extension across a hyperplane We now construct holomorphic functions with a prescribed value at a point, or a prescribed restriction to a hyperplane, and with controlled weighted norms. In both cases, a smooth function with the right values is corrected by a solution of a $ ar\partial $-equation whose weight has a singular term forcing the correction to vanish where the values are prescribed. Proposition 11.4.1 . Let $r,L>0$, let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$, $n\ge 1$, be a pseudoconvex open set of diameter at most $L$, let $a\in \mathbb C^ n$ with $B(a,2r)\subset \Omega $, and let $p\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$. If $h$ is holomorphic on $B(a,2r)$ and $\int _{B(a,2r)}|h|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV<\infty $, then there is $F\in \mathcal O(\Omega )$ such that \[  F(a)=h(a),\qquad \int _\Omega |F|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV\le C(n,r,L) \int _{B(a,2r)}|h|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV,  \] where the constant $C(n,r,L)$ depends only on $n$, $r$ and $L$, and not on $\Omega $, $p$, $h$ or $a$. Proof. Fix a smooth function $\kappa $ on $\mathbb R$ with $0\le \kappa \le 1$, $\kappa =1$ on $(-\infty ,1]$ and $\kappa =0$ on $[3/2,\infty )$, for instance $\kappa (x)=\kappa _0(2x-2)$ with the function $\kappa _0$ fixed at the beginning of section 11.3 , and put $\chi (z)=\kappa (|z-a|/r)$. Then $\chi $ is smooth, because $\kappa $ is constant near $0$; it has compact support in $B(a,2r)$, equals one on $B(a,r)$, and satisfies $| ar\partial \chi |\le c_0/r$ with $c_0=\sup |\kappa '|/2$, because $| ar\partial |z-a||=1/2$ for $z
e a$. Extend $\chi h$ by zero to $\Omega $. Then $\alpha = ar\partial (\chi h)=h\,  ar\partial \chi $ is a smooth $ ar\partial $-closed form supported in the shell $r\le |z-a|\le 2r$. The function $p+n\log |z-a|^2$ is plurisubharmonic on $\Omega $ by proposition 8.3.3 , proposition 8.2.5 . We apply theorem 11.3.4 with this function in place of $p$ and with $q=|z-a|^2$, for which $A=I$. Since $\mathrm e^{-|z-a|^2}\le 1$ and $|z-a|^{-2n}\le r^{-2n}$ on the support of $\alpha $, we obtain a solution of $ ar\partial u=\alpha $ with \[  \int _\Omega |u|^2|z-a|^{-2n}\mathrm e^{-p-|z-a|^2}\, \mathrm dV \le c_0^2r^{-2n-2}\int _{B(a,2r)}|h|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV.  \] On $B(a,r)$ we have $ ar\partial u=\alpha =0$, so $u$ is holomorphic there, by lemma 11.3.5 (1). Since $p$ is bounded above on $B(a,r)$, the factor $\mathrm e^{-p-|z-a|^2}$ is bounded below there by a positive constant. If $u(a)$ were nonzero, then $|u|$ would be bounded below by a positive constant near $a$, and the integral on the left would diverge, because $\int _{B(a,ho )}|z-a|^{-2n}\, \mathrm dV$ is a positive multiple of $\int _0^ho 	au ^{-2n}	au ^{2n-1}\, \mathrm d	au =\infty $ by integration in polar coordinates ( 2.1 ). Thus $u(a)=0$. The function $F=\chi h-u$ satisfies $ ar\partial F=0$, so it is holomorphic by the same lemma, and $F(a)=h(a)$. Since $|z-a|<L$ on $\Omega $, we have $|z-a|^{2n}\mathrm e^{|z-a|^2}\le L^{2n}\mathrm e^{L^2}$, and therefore \[  \int _\Omega |u|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV\le c_0^2L^{2n}\mathrm e^{L^2}r^{-2n-2}\int _{B(a,2r)}|h|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV.  \] Finally, $|F|^2\le 2|\chi h|^2+2|u|^2$ and $|\chi h|\le |h|\mathbf1_{B(a,2r)}$ give the assertion with $C(n,r,L)=2+2c_0^2L^{2n}\mathrm e^{L^2}r^{-2n-2}$. $\square$ For extension from a hyperplane we use the same method, with the pole $\log |z_ n|^2$ along the hyperplane $\{ z_ n=0\} $. Now, however, the cutoff must be concentrated in a thin neighborhood $\{ |z_ n|<\varepsilon \} $ of the hyperplane, and then its $ ar\partial $-derivative has size of order $\varepsilon ^{-1}$. On the support of this derivative the factor $\mathrm e^{-\log |z_ n|^2}$ of the weight has size of order $\varepsilon ^{-2}$, while the support has area of order $\varepsilon ^2$ in the normal direction. With a fixed smooth function $q$, the bound of theorem 11.3.4 is therefore of order $\varepsilon ^{-2}$. The remedy is a bounded twist of the weight. Let $\psi $ be a smooth bounded plurisubharmonic function such that the dual energy $h$ of $ ar\partial \psi $ with respect to $H_\psi $ is less than one. The next lemma gives a solution of $ ar\partial u=\alpha $ whose norm with weight $(1-h)\mathrm e^{\psi -p}$ is bounded by a multiple of $\int |\alpha |_{H_\psi ^{-1}}^2\mathrm e^{\psi -p}\, \mathrm dV$, and this integral is small if the complex Hessian of $\psi $ is large near the hyperplane. Lemma 11.4.2 . Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ be a pseudoconvex open set, $n\ge 1$, let $p\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$, and let $\psi $ be a smooth bounded plurisubharmonic function on $\Omega $. Put $A=H_\psi $ and $h=| ar\partial \psi |_{A^{-1}}^2$, where $ ar\partial \psi $ is identified with the vector $(\partial _{ ar z_ j}\psi )_ j$, and assume that $h<1$ almost everywhere. Let $\alpha $ be a $(0,1)$-form on $\Omega $ with measurable coefficients such that $E=\int _\Omega |\alpha |_{A^{-1}}^2\mathrm e^{\psi -p}\, \mathrm dV<\infty $ and $ ar\partial \alpha =0$, let $0\le a<1$, and assume that $h\le a$ almost everywhere on $\{ \alpha 
e 0\} $. Then $ ar\partial u=\alpha $ has a solution with \[  \int _\Omega (1-h)|u|^2\mathrm e^{\psi -p}\, \mathrm dV \le  rac{1+\sqrt a}{1-\sqrt a}\, E.  \] Proof. The idea is that, if $u$ is the minimal solution in $L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-p})$, then $u\mathrm e^\psi $ is the minimal solution of a twisted equation in $L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-p-\psi })$, to which we apply Hörmander's estimate. Put $m=\sup _\Omega |\psi |<\infty $. Since $\mathrm e^{-m}\le \mathrm e^{\pm \psi }\le \mathrm e^ m$, the spaces $L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-p})$ and $L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-p-\psi })$ consist of the same functions, with equivalent norms, and so contain the same holomorphic functions. By the discussion preceding theorem 11.3.3 , applied with the weight $p-\psi $, which is bounded above on compact sets, $\alpha \in L^2_{\mathrm{loc},(0,1)}(\Omega )$; so $ ar\partial \alpha $ is defined. Since $\mathrm e^{-p-\psi }\le \mathrm e^{2m}\mathrm e^{\psi -p}$, we have $\int _\Omega |\alpha |_{A^{-1}}^2\mathrm e^{-p-\psi }\, \mathrm dV\le \mathrm e^{2m}E<\infty $. Hence theorem 11.3.4 , applied with the plurisubharmonic function $p$ and the smooth function $q=\psi $, whose complex Hessian matrix $A$ is positive semidefinite, shows that the equation $ ar\partial u=\alpha $ has a solution in $L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-p-\psi })=L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-p})$. Let $u$ be the minimal solution in $L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-p})$, given by lemma 11.3.5 (2). The function $v=u\mathrm e^\psi $ belongs to $L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-p-\psi })$ and solves \[   ar\partial v= eta =(\alpha +u\,  ar\partial \psi )\mathrm e^\psi .  \] For every holomorphic $g$ in $L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-p-\psi })$ we have $\int v ar g\, \mathrm e^{-p-\psi }\, \mathrm dV=\int u ar g\, \mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV=0$, so $v$ is the minimal solution of $ ar\partial v= eta $ in $L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-p-\psi })$, by lemma 11.3.5 (2). We now estimate $v$ by theorem 11.3.4 , applied again with $p$ and $q=\psi $. The form $ eta = ar\partial v$ is $ ar\partial $-closed, and it lies in $L^2_{\mathrm{loc},(0,1)}(\Omega )$ because $\alpha $ and $u$ are locally square integrable and $\psi $ is smooth. Since $E<\infty $ and $h<1$, the dual energies of $\alpha $ and $ ar\partial \psi $ are finite almost everywhere, and at such points both vectors lie in the subspace on which the dual energy is a Hermitian quadratic form. The triangle inequality $|\alpha +u\,  ar\partial \psi |_{A^{-1}}\le |\alpha |_{A^{-1}}+|u|h^{1/2}$ therefore gives \[  \int | eta |_{A^{-1}}^2\mathrm e^{-p-\psi }\, \mathrm dV=\int |\alpha +u\,  ar\partial \psi |_{A^{-1}}^2\mathrm e^{\psi -p}\, \mathrm dV\le 2E+2\sup _\Omega \mathrm e^\psi \int |u|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV<\infty .  \] So theorem 11.3.4 yields a solution of $ ar\partial w= eta $ whose squared norm in $L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-p-\psi })$ is at most this integral, and the minimal solution $v$ has no larger norm. As $\int |v|^2\mathrm e^{-p-\psi }\, \mathrm dV=\int |u|^2\mathrm e^{\psi -p}\, \mathrm dV$, we obtain \[  \int |u|^2\mathrm e^{\psi -p}\, \mathrm dV \le \int |\alpha +u\,  ar\partial \psi |_{A^{-1}}^2\mathrm e^{\psi -p}\, \mathrm dV.  \] At almost every point, let $\langle \cdot ,\cdot angle _{A^{-1}}$ be the Hermitian inner product associated with the dual energy on the subspace where it is finite; by the polarization identity $\langle x,yangle _{A^{-1}}= rac14\sum _{k=0}^3\mathrm i^ k|x+\mathrm i^ ky|_{A^{-1}}^2$, the function $\langle \alpha , ar\partial \psi angle _{A^{-1}}$ is measurable. We expand \[  |\alpha +u\,  ar\partial \psi |_{A^{-1}}^2=|\alpha |_{A^{-1}}^2+2\operatorname{Re} igl ( ar u\langle \alpha , ar\partial \psi angle _{A^{-1}} igr )+h|u|^2, \qquad |\langle \alpha , ar\partial \psi angle _{A^{-1}}|\le |\alpha |_{A^{-1}}h^{1/2},  \] the second inequality being the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality. The function $h|u|^2\mathrm e^{\psi -p}$ is integrable, since $h<1$ almost everywhere and $u\in L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-p})$; moving its integral to the left, we find that $J=\int (1-h)|u|^2\mathrm e^{\psi -p}\, \mathrm dV$, which is finite, satisfies \[  J\le E+2\int |u|\, |\alpha |_{A^{-1}}h^{1/2}\mathrm e^{\psi -p}\, \mathrm dV.  \] If $a=0$, then $h=0$ almost everywhere on $\{ \alpha 
e 0\} $, the last integral vanishes, and $J\le E$, as claimed. Let $a>0$. The last integrand vanishes outside $\{ \alpha 
e 0\} $, where $h\le a$ and hence $h/(1-h)\le a/(1-a)$. For $t>1$, the inequality $2xy\le t^{-1}x^2+ty^2$ with $x=(1-h)^{1/2}|u|$ and $y=(h/(1-h))^{1/2}|\alpha |_{A^{-1}}$ gives there \[  2|u|\, |\alpha |_{A^{-1}}h^{1/2}\le t^{-1}(1-h)|u|^2+ rac{ta}{1-a}|\alpha |_{A^{-1}}^2.  \] Integrating, we obtain \[  J\le \left(1+ rac{ta}{1-a}ight)E+t^{-1}J.  \] Since $J$ is finite, this gives $J\le  rac t{t-1} igl (1+ rac{ta}{1-a} igr )E$. Choose $t=1+a^{-1/2}$. Then $1+ta/(1-a)=(1+\sqrt a)/(1-a)=1/(1-\sqrt a)$ and $t/(t-1)=1+\sqrt a$, so $J\le (1+\sqrt a)E/(1-\sqrt a)$. $\square$ The twisting function used for extension depends only on the normal variable. The next lemma records the one-variable calculus behind it. Lemma 11.4.3 . Let $0<\varepsilon <1/4$. For $\zeta \in \mathbb C$ with $|\zeta |<1/4$ put \[  s=-\log (|\zeta |^2+\varepsilon ^2),\qquad \eta =s+\log s,\qquad \psi _\varepsilon =-\log \eta .  \] Then $\psi _\varepsilon $ is a smooth, bounded, strictly subharmonic function on the disc $\Delta _{1/4}$. Let $h=|\partial _{ ar\zeta }\psi _\varepsilon |^2/(\psi _\varepsilon )_{\zeta  ar\zeta }$. Then \[   egin{split}  (1-h)\mathrm e^{\psi _\varepsilon }& \ge (6s^2)^{-1},\  h& \le  rac{2}{-\log (2\varepsilon ^2)}\quad 	ext{for }|\zeta |\le \varepsilon ,\   rac{\mathrm e^{\psi _\varepsilon }}{|\zeta |^2(\psi _\varepsilon )_{\zeta  ar\zeta }} & \le 25/4\quad 	ext{for }\varepsilon /2\le |\zeta |\le \varepsilon . \end{split}  \] In particular $h<1$ everywhere, and the bound for $h$ on the disc $|\zeta |\le \varepsilon $ tends to zero as $\varepsilon 	o 0$. Proof. Since $|\zeta |^2+\varepsilon ^2<1/8$, we have $s>\log 8>2$, so $\eta >s>2$ and $\psi _\varepsilon <0$ is well defined. For fixed $\varepsilon $, $s$ ranges in a bounded interval, so $\psi _\varepsilon $ is bounded; and $\psi _\varepsilon =G(|\zeta |^2)$ for a function $G$ that is smooth near $[0,1/16)$, so $\psi _\varepsilon $ is smooth. For $\zeta 
e 0$ put $x=|\zeta |^2$, $t=\log x$ and $b=x/(x+\varepsilon ^2)\in (0,1)$, and denote derivatives with respect to $t$ by primes. Then $s'=-b$ and $b'=b(1-b)$, so $s''=-b(1-b)$. With $D=1+1/s$ we have $\eta '=s'+s'/s=-bD$ and $D'=-s'/s^2=b/s^2$. Hence $\psi _\varepsilon '=-\eta '/\eta =bD/\eta $ and $\psi _\varepsilon ''=(b'D+bD')/\eta -bD\eta '/\eta ^2$, that is, \[  \psi _\varepsilon '= rac{bD}{\eta },\qquad \psi _\varepsilon ''=A+B,\quad A= rac{b^2D^2}{\eta ^2},\quad B= rac{b(1-b)D}{\eta }+ rac{b^2}{\eta s^2}>0.  \] For a function $g$ of $t=\log |\zeta |^2$ we have $\partial _{ ar\zeta }g=g'/ ar\zeta $ and $\partial _\zeta \partial _{ ar\zeta }g=g''/|\zeta |^2$. Hence $(\psi _\varepsilon )_{\zeta  ar\zeta }=\psi _\varepsilon ''/x>0$ and $h=(\psi _\varepsilon ')^2/\psi _\varepsilon ''=A/(A+B)<1$ for $\zeta 
e 0$. In general $\partial _{ ar\zeta }\psi _\varepsilon =G'(|\zeta |^2)\zeta $ and $(\psi _\varepsilon )_{\zeta  ar\zeta }=G''(|\zeta |^2)|\zeta |^2+G'(|\zeta |^2)$, so at $\zeta =0$ we have $\partial _{ ar\zeta }\psi _\varepsilon =0$ and $(\psi _\varepsilon )_{\zeta  ar\zeta }=G'(0)$, where $G'(x)=\psi _\varepsilon '/x=D/(\eta (x+\varepsilon ^2))>0$; so $(\psi _\varepsilon )_{\zeta  ar\zeta }>0$ and $h=0$ there. Thus $\psi _\varepsilon $ is strictly subharmonic, and $h<1$ everywhere. For the first estimate let $\zeta 
e 0$. Since $B\ge b^2/(\eta s^2)$, we have $A/B\le D^2s^2/\eta =(s+1)^2/\eta $, and therefore \[  (1-h)\mathrm e^{\psi _\varepsilon }= rac{B}{\eta (A+B)} \ge  rac1{\eta +(s+1)^2}\ge  rac1{6s^2},  \] because $\eta \le 2s\le 2s^2$ and $(s+1)^2\le 4s^2$ for $s\ge 1$. At $\zeta =0$ we have $(1-h)\mathrm e^{\psi _\varepsilon }=1/\eta \ge 1/(6s^2)$ as well. For the second estimate let $0<x\le \varepsilon ^2$. Then $b\le 1/2$, and $B\ge b(1-b)D/\eta $ gives \[  h\le  rac AB\le  rac{bD}{\eta (1-b)}\le  rac D\eta = rac{s+1}{s\eta }\le  rac2s,  \] since $s+1\le 2s\le 2\eta $; moreover $s\ge -\log (2\varepsilon ^2)$, because $x+\varepsilon ^2\le 2\varepsilon ^2$. Together with $h(0)=0$, this proves the second estimate. For the third, let $\varepsilon /2\le |\zeta |\le \varepsilon $. Then $1/5\le b\le 1/2$, so $\eta \psi _\varepsilon ''\ge \eta B\ge b(1-b)D\ge b(1-b)\ge 4/25$, and $\mathrm e^{\psi _\varepsilon }/(|\zeta |^2(\psi _\varepsilon )_{\zeta  ar\zeta })=1/(\eta \psi _\varepsilon '')\le 25/4$. $\square$ Theorem 11.4.4 (Ohsawa–Takegoshi) . There is an absolute constant $C$ with the following property. Let $n\ge 1$ and $R>0$, let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^{n-1}	imes \Delta _ R$ be a pseudoconvex open set, where $\Delta _ R\subset \mathbb C$ is the disc of radius $R$ centered at $0$, and let $p\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$. Put $\Omega _0=\Omega \cap \{ z_ n=0\} $, which we identify with an open subset of $\mathbb C^{n-1}$. Then every holomorphic function $f$ on $\Omega _0$ with \[  I=\int _{\Omega _0}|f|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV_{2n-2}<\infty  \] has an extension $F\in \mathcal O(\Omega )$ such that \[  F|_{\Omega _0}=f,\qquad \int _\Omega |F|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV_{2n}\le C R^2 I.  \] Here, for $n=1$, $\Omega _0$ is a point or empty, and $I$ is the weighted value of $|f|^2$ at that point, the integral with respect to the counting measure $\mathrm dV_0$. If $\Omega _0=\varnothing $ we take $F=0$. On a connected component of $\Omega _0$ on which the restriction of $p$ is identically $-\infty $, finiteness of $I$ forces $f=0$, and this component contributes zero to $I$. Proof. After a normalization, Step 1 treats smooth weights on relatively compact pseudoconvex subsets, by correcting a cutoff of $f$ with lemma 11.4.2 , lemma 11.4.3 , and Step 2 regularizes $p$ and passes to the limit. Normalization. The substitution $z_ n=4R\zeta $ maps $\mathbb C^{n-1}	imes \Delta _{1/4}$ onto $\mathbb C^{n-1}	imes \Delta _ R$, preserves the hyperplane and the integral $I$, and multiplies Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb C^ n$ by $16R^2$. Hence it suffices to show the following: if $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^{n-1}	imes \Delta _{1/4}$, then $f$ has an extension $F\in \mathcal O(\Omega )$ with $\int _\Omega |F|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV\le C_0I$ for an absolute constant $C_0$; then $C=16C_0$ works. e \varnothing $. Step 1: smooth weights on a relatively compact set. otin P$, and a subsequence would converge, $D$ being bounded, to a point $(z',0)\in \overline D$ with $z'
otin P$, which is impossible. Decreasing $\varepsilon _0$, we may also assume that $\overline P	imes \overline\Delta _{\varepsilon _0}\subset U$ and, by the uniform continuity of $\varphi $ on this compact set, that 11.22  egin{equation} \label{eq:ot-weight-comparison} \mathrm e^{-\varphi (z',\zeta )}\le 2\mathrm e^{-\varphi (z',0)}\qquad (z'\in \overline P,\  |\zeta |\le \varepsilon _0). \end{equation} Fix a smooth function $\chi $ on $\mathbb R$ with $0\le \chi \le 1$, $\chi =1$ on $(-\infty ,1/4]$ and $\chi =0$ on $[1,\infty )$, for instance $\chi (x)=\kappa _0((4x-1)/3)$ with the function $\kappa _0$ fixed at the beginning of section 11.3 , and put $c_\chi =\sup |\chi '|^2$. For $0<\varepsilon \le \varepsilon _0$ define $g_\varepsilon $ on $D$ by $g_\varepsilon (z',\zeta )=f(z')\chi (|\zeta |^2/\varepsilon ^2)$ if $z'\in P$, and $g_\varepsilon =0$ otherwise. The open sets $D\cap (P	imes \mathbb C)$ and $D\cap \{ |\zeta |>\varepsilon \} $ cover $D$ by the choice of $\varepsilon _0$, and $g_\varepsilon $ is smooth on each of them (on the second it vanishes); hence $g_\varepsilon $ is smooth on $D$, and $g_\varepsilon (z',0)=f(z')$ for $(z',0)\in D$. Since $f$ is holomorphic, \[  \alpha _\varepsilon = ar\partial g_\varepsilon =f(z')\chi '(|\zeta |^2/\varepsilon ^2)  rac{\zeta }{\varepsilon ^2}\, \mathrm d ar\zeta  \] is a $ ar\partial $-closed smooth form supported in $\{ \varepsilon /2\le |\zeta |\le \varepsilon \} $. We solve $ ar\partial u=\alpha _\varepsilon $ on $D$ by lemma 11.4.2 , with the function $\widetilde\varphi =\varphi +\log |\zeta |^2$ in place of $p$, which is plurisubharmonic on $D$ by proposition 8.3.3 , proposition 8.2.5 , and with $\psi =\psi _\varepsilon (\zeta )$ from lemma 11.4.3 , a smooth bounded function on $D$ which is plurisubharmonic by proposition 8.2.3 , applied to the projection $(z',\zeta )\mapsto \zeta $. The complex Hessian matrix $A=H_\psi $ has the single nonzero entry $(\psi _\varepsilon )_{\zeta  ar\zeta }$, so $| ar\partial \psi |_{A^{-1}}^2$ is the function $h$ of lemma 11.4.3 ; thus $h<1$, and $h\le a_\varepsilon =2/(-\log (2\varepsilon ^2))$ on $\{ \alpha _\varepsilon 
e 0\} \subset \{ |\zeta |\le \varepsilon \} $. The dual energy of $\alpha _\varepsilon $ is $|f|^2|\chi '|^2|\zeta |^2\varepsilon ^{-4}/(\psi _\varepsilon )_{\zeta  ar\zeta }$, so the third estimate of lemma 11.4.3 and $|\zeta |\le \varepsilon $ give, on its support, \[  |\alpha _\varepsilon |_{A^{-1}}^2\mathrm e^{\psi _\varepsilon -\widetilde\varphi } =|f(z')|^2|\chi '|^2\varepsilon ^{-4} rac{\mathrm e^{\psi _\varepsilon }}{(\psi _\varepsilon )_{\zeta  ar\zeta }}\mathrm e^{-\varphi } \le  rac{25}4c_\chi \varepsilon ^{-2}|f(z')|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi (z',\zeta )}.  \] By ( 11.22 ) and Fubini's theorem, since every point of the support has $z'\in P$, \[  E=\int _ D|\alpha _\varepsilon |_{A^{-1}}^2\mathrm e^{\psi -\widetilde\varphi }\, \mathrm dV \le  rac{25}4c_\chi \varepsilon ^{-2}\cdot 2\pi \varepsilon ^2I_ P= rac{25\pi }2c_\chi I_ P.  \] If $\varepsilon $ is so small that $a_\varepsilon \le 1/4$, then $(1+\sqrt{a_\varepsilon })/(1-\sqrt{a_\varepsilon })\le 3$, and lemma 11.4.2 gives $u_\varepsilon $ with $ ar\partial u_\varepsilon =\alpha _\varepsilon $ and $\int _ D(1-h)|u_\varepsilon |^2\mathrm e^{\psi _\varepsilon -\widetilde\varphi }\, \mathrm dV\le 3E$. By the first estimate of lemma 11.4.3 , $(1-h)\mathrm e^{\psi _\varepsilon }\ge 1/(6\log ^2(|\zeta |^2+\varepsilon ^2))$, and $\mathrm e^{-\widetilde\varphi }=\mathrm e^{-\varphi }|\zeta |^{-2}$. Hence, with $C_1=225\pi c_\chi $, 11.23  egin{equation} \label{eq:normal-extension-correction} \int _ D rac{|u_\varepsilon |^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi }}{ |\zeta |^2\log ^2(|\zeta |^2+\varepsilon ^2)}\, \mathrm dV \le 18E\le C_1I_ P. \end{equation} On $D\cap \{ |\zeta |<\varepsilon /2\} $ we have $ ar\partial u_\varepsilon =0$, so $u_\varepsilon $ is holomorphic there, by lemma 11.3.5 (1). Suppose that $u_\varepsilon (z'_0,0)
e 0$ for some $(z'_0,0)\in D$. On a small polydisc around this point, $|u_\varepsilon |$ is bounded below by a positive constant, $\varphi $ is bounded above, and $\log ^2(|\zeta |^2+\varepsilon ^2)\le \log ^2(\varepsilon ^2)$; so the integrand in ( 11.23 ) is at least a positive constant times $|\zeta |^{-2}$, whose integral over a disc around $\zeta =0$ diverges. This contradicts ( 11.23 ). Hence $u_\varepsilon =0$ on $D\cap \{ \zeta =0\} $, and $F_\varepsilon =g_\varepsilon -u_\varepsilon $ is holomorphic on $D$, by the same lemma, because $ ar\partial F_\varepsilon =0$; moreover $F_\varepsilon (z',0)=f(z')$. It remains to estimate $F_\varepsilon $. For $0<x=|\zeta |^2<1/16$ we have $x<x+\varepsilon ^2<1/8$, so $x\log ^2(x+\varepsilon ^2)\le x\log ^2x\le 4\mathrm e^{-2}<1$. Thus ( 11.23 ) gives $\int _ D|u_\varepsilon |^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi }\, \mathrm dV\le C_1I_ P$. By ( 11.22 ) and Fubini's theorem, $\int _ D|g_\varepsilon |^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi }\, \mathrm dV\le 2\pi \varepsilon ^2I_ P\le I_ P$. Therefore $\int _ D|F_\varepsilon |^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi }\, \mathrm dV\le 2(1+C_1)I_ P$, which is ( 11.21 ) with $C_0=2(1+C_1)$. Step 2: the general case. By corollary 11.2.5 there are pseudoconvex open sets $D_1\subset D_2\subset \cdots $ with $D_ j\Subset \Omega $ and $ igcup _ jD_ j=\Omega $. Choose $\varepsilon _ j\downarrow 0$ with $\varepsilon _ j<\operatorname {dist}(\overline D_ j,\mathbb C^ n\setminus \Omega )$, and let $ho _\varepsilon $ be the radial mollifier of section 1.4 ; then, by proposition 8.2.2 (2), $p_ j=p*ho _{\varepsilon _ j}$ is a smooth plurisubharmonic function on the open neighborhood $U_ j=\{ z\in \Omega :\operatorname {dist}(z,\mathbb C^ n\setminus \Omega )>\varepsilon _ j\} $ of $\overline D_ j$, and $p_ j\downarrow p$ pointwise. Step 1, applied to $D_ j$, $U_ j$ and $\varphi =p_ j$, gives $F_ j\in \mathcal O(D_ j)$ with $F_ j(z',0)=f(z')$ for $(z',0)\in D_ j$ and \[  \int _{D_ j}|F_ j|^2\mathrm e^{-p_ j}\, \mathrm dV\le C_0\int _{P_ j}|f(z')|^2\mathrm e^{-p_ j(z',0)}\, \mathrm dV_{2n-2}(z')\le C_0I,  \] because $p_ j\ge p$. (On a component of $\Omega _0$ on which $p(\cdot ,0)\equiv -\infty $ we have $f=0$, and the last inequality holds with the convention $0\cdot \infty =0$.) We show that a subsequence of $(F_ j)$ converges locally uniformly on $\Omega $. Let $K\subset \Omega $ be compact. Then $K\subset D_ k$ for some $k$, and for $j\ge k$ we have $p_ j\le p_ k$ on $K$, so $\int _ K|F_ j|^2\, \mathrm dV\le \mathrm e^{\max _ Kp_ k}C_0I$. It follows that $(F_ j)$ is uniformly bounded on compact subsets of $\Omega $. Indeed, for a holomorphic function $G$ the complex Hessian matrix of $|G|^2$ is $ igl (\partial _{z_\mu }G\, \overline{\partial _{z_
u }G} igr )_{\mu ,
u }$, which is positive semidefinite; so $|G|^2$ is plurisubharmonic by proposition 8.2.2 (1), and hence subharmonic by theorem 8.2.1 . If $K\subset \Omega $ is compact, $\delta >0$ and $K_\delta =\{ z:\operatorname {dist}(z,K)\le \delta \} \subset \Omega $, then the mean value inequality over balls in theorem 3.1.3 , applied to $|F_ j|^2$, gives $|F_ j(z)|^2\le |B(z,\delta )|^{-1}\int _{K_\delta }|F_ j|^2\, \mathrm dV$ for $z\in K$ and large $j$, and the right side is bounded independently of $j$ by the preceding estimate applied to $K_\delta $. Next, let $K\subset \Omega $ be compact, and choose $r>0$ such that the compact set $K'$ of points at distance at most $2\sqrt n\, r$ from $K$ lies in $\Omega $. For $z\in K'_0=\{ z:\operatorname {dist}(z,K)\le \sqrt n\, r\} $, the closed polydisc of radius $r$ centered at $z$ lies in $K'$, and the coefficient bound in ( 7.1 ) with $a=z$ gives $|\partial _{z_ l}F_ j(z)|\le r^{-1}\max _{K'}|F_ j|$ for $1\le l\le n$ and all large $j$ (those with $K'\subset D_ j$). Since $\mathrm dF_ j=\sum _ l\partial _{z_ l}F_ j\, \mathrm dz_ l$, it follows that these $F_ j$ are Lipschitz with a common constant on every ball of radius $\sqrt n\, r$ centered at a point of $K$, so the sequence $(F_ j)$ is equicontinuous on $K$ from some index on. By proposition 1.6.4 on a compact exhaustion of $\Omega $ and a diagonal argument, a subsequence converges locally uniformly on $\Omega $ to a continuous function $F$. Since $ ar\partial F_ j=0$ and $F_ j	o F$ in the sense of distributions, $ ar\partial F=0$, and $F$ is holomorphic by lemma 11.3.5 (1). Moreover $F(z',0)=\lim _ jF_ j(z',0)=f(z')$ for $z'\in \Omega _0$. Finally, let $K\subset \Omega $ be compact, and let $k$ be so large that $K\subset D_ k$. For $j\ge k$ we have $p_ j\le p_ k$ on $K$, so locally uniform convergence gives \[  \int _ K|F|^2\mathrm e^{-p_ k}\, \mathrm dV=\lim _ j\int _ K|F_ j|^2\mathrm e^{-p_ k}\, \mathrm dV\le \varliminf _ j\int _{D_ j}|F_ j|^2\mathrm e^{-p_ j}\, \mathrm dV\le C_0I.  \] This holds for all large $k$, and $\mathrm e^{-p_ k}$ increases to $\mathrm e^{-p}$ as $k	o \infty $; so the monotone convergence theorem gives $\int _ K|F|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV\le C_0I$, and exhausting $\Omega $ by compact sets gives $\int _\Omega |F|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV\le C_0I$. $\square$ Applying the theorem once for each normal direction, we obtain extension from affine subspaces of any codimension, in particular from points. Corollary 11.4.5 . Let $C$ be the constant of theorem 11.4.4 . Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$, $n\ge 1$, be a pseudoconvex open set of diameter at most $L>0$, and let $p\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$. Then for every $a\in \Omega $ with $p(a)>-\infty $ there is $F\in \mathcal O(\Omega )$ such that \[  F(a)=1,\qquad \int _\Omega |F|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV \le C^ n L^{2n}\mathrm e^{-p(a)}.  \] More generally, let $V\subset \mathbb C^ n$ be an affine complex subspace of codimension $r$, $0\le r\le n$, and let $f$ be holomorphic on $\Omega \cap V$ with finite slice norm $\int _{\Omega \cap V}|f|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV_{2n-2r}$, computed with Lebesgue measure on $V$. Then there is $F\in \mathcal O(\Omega )$ with $F|_{\Omega \cap V}=f$ and $\int _\Omega |F|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV\le C^ rL^{2r}\int _{\Omega \cap V}|f|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV_{2n-2r}$. Proof. We prove the second assertion; the first is the case $V=\{ a\} $, $r=n$ and $f=1$, whose slice norm with respect to the counting measure $\mathrm dV_0$ is $\mathrm e^{-p(a)}$. If $r=0$ we take $F=f$, and if $\Omega \cap V=\varnothing $ we take $F=0$. Assume now that $r\ge 1$ and $\Omega \cap V
e \varnothing $. Choose $b\in \Omega \cap V$ and unitary affine coordinates $w=(w_1,\ldots ,w_ n)$ on $\mathbb C^ n$ centered at $b$ with $V=\{ w_1=\cdots =w_ r=0\} $, and put $\Omega _ k=\Omega \cap \{ w_1=\cdots =w_ k=0\} $ for $0\le k\le r$, an open subset of a space isomorphic to $\mathbb C^{n-k}$. Unitary coordinates preserve Lebesgue measure. Each $\Omega _ k$ with $k<n$ is pseudoconvex: the restriction of a continuous plurisubharmonic exhaustion function of $\Omega $ to the closed subset $\Omega _ k$ of $\Omega $ is continuous and plurisubharmonic by proposition 8.2.3 , applied to the linear embedding of $\{ w_1=\cdots =w_ k=0\} $, and its sublevel sets are compact. By the discussion following definition 11.2.1 , every connected component of $\Omega _ k$ is pseudoconvex as well. Since $\Omega $ is open and has diameter at most $L$, we have $|z-b|<L$ for $z\in \Omega $ (a point $z\in \Omega $ with $|z-b|=L$ could be moved slightly away from $b$ inside $\Omega $), so the coordinate $w_ k$ takes its values in $\Delta _ L$ on $\Omega _{k-1}$. Put $f_ r=f$, let $1\le k\le r$, and assume that $f_ k\in \mathcal O(\Omega _ k)$ has finite norm $\int _{\Omega _ k}|f_ k|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV_{2n-2k}$. Let $W$ be a connected component of $\Omega _{k-1}$; ordering the coordinates as $(w_{k+1},\ldots ,w_ n,w_ k)$, we regard $W$ as an open subset of $\mathbb C^{n-k}	imes \Delta _ L$ whose slice by $\{ w_ k=0\} $ is the open subset $W\cap \Omega _ k$ of $\Omega _ k$. By proposition 8.2.3 , the restriction of $p$ to $W$ is plurisubharmonic or identically $-\infty $. In the second case $\mathrm e^{-p}=\infty $ on $W\cap \Omega _ k$, so the finiteness of the norm of $f_ k$ forces $f_ k=0$ almost everywhere on $W\cap \Omega _ k$, hence everywhere there, since $f_ k$ is continuous, and we put $f_{k-1}=0$ on $W$. In the first case, theorem 11.4.4 , applied to $W$ with normal coordinate $w_ k$, gives a holomorphic function $f_{k-1}$ on $W$ extending the restriction of $f_ k$ to $W\cap \Omega _ k$, with \[  \int _ W|f_{k-1}|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV_{2n-2k+2}\le CL^2\int _{W\cap \Omega _ k}|f_ k|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV_{2n-2k}.  \] The components $W$ are open, disjoint and cover $\Omega _{k-1}$, and the sets $W\cap \Omega _ k$ are disjoint and cover $\Omega _ k$. Hence these functions define $f_{k-1}\in \mathcal O(\Omega _{k-1})$ extending $f_ k$, and summing over $W$ gives \[  \int _{\Omega _{k-1}}|f_{k-1}|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV_{2n-2k+2}\le CL^2\int _{\Omega _ k}|f_ k|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV_{2n-2k}.  \] Proceeding in this way for $k=r,r-1,\ldots ,1$ and multiplying the $r$ estimates, we see that $F=f_0$ has the required properties. $\square$ Corollary 11.4.6 . Let $X$ be a complex manifold, let $Y\subset X$ be a complex submanifold, let $a\in Y$, and let $p$ be a plurisubharmonic function on a neighborhood of $a$ in $X$. Let $f$ be a holomorphic germ on $Y$ at $a$ such that $|f|^2\mathrm e^{-p|_ Y}$ is integrable on some neighborhood of $a$ in $Y$. Then there is a holomorphic germ $F$ on $X$ at $a$ with $F|_ Y=f$ such that $|F|^2\mathrm e^{-p}$ is integrable on some neighborhood of $a$ in $X$. Here integrability refers to smooth positive volume forms on $Y$ and $X$; since any two such forms are locally comparable, the notion does not depend on their choice. Proof. Let $k=\dim Y$ and $n=\dim X$ near $a$. By the definition of a complex submanifold (definition 7.1.1 ), there are holomorphic coordinates $w=(w',w'')\in \mathbb C^ k	imes \mathbb C^{n-k}$ centered at $a$ in which $Y=\{ w''=0\} $; by proposition 8.2.3 , $p$ is plurisubharmonic near $0$ in these coordinates. On a compact neighborhood of $a$, the densities of smooth positive volume forms with respect to coordinate Lebesgue measure are bounded above and below by positive constants. Hence we may test integrability with Lebesgue measure $\mathrm dV_{2k}$ on $Y=\mathbb C^ k	imes \{ 0\} $ and $\mathrm dV_{2n}$ in the coordinates $w$. Choose a ball $B$ around $0$ so small that $p$ is plurisubharmonic on a neighborhood of $\overline B$, that $f$ is defined on $B\cap Y$, and that $\int _{B\cap Y}|f|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV_{2k}<\infty $. The ball $B$ is a bounded pseudoconvex domain, by corollary 11.2.5 applied to the exhaustion function $|w|^2$ of $\mathbb C^ n$, and $B\cap Y$ is its intersection with the linear subspace $\{ w''=0\} $ of codimension $n-k$. By corollary 11.4.5 there is $F\in \mathcal O(B)$ with $F|_{B\cap Y}=f$ and $\int _ B|F|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV_{2n}<\infty $. (If $k=0$, the integral over $Y$ is the weighted value $|f(a)|^2\mathrm e^{-p(a)}$; if $p|_ Y$ is identically $-\infty $ near $a$, then $f=0$ and $F=0$, in accordance with the conventions of theorem 11.4.4 .) $\square$

title: Logarithmic point interpolation
topic: Weighted L2 estimates and holomorphic extension
text: Proposition 11.4.1 . Let $r,L>0$, let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$, $n\ge 1$, be a pseudoconvex open set of diameter at most $L$, let $a\in \mathbb C^ n$ with $B(a,2r)\subset \Omega $, and let $p\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$. If $h$ is holomorphic on $B(a,2r)$ and $\int _{B(a,2r)}|h|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV<\infty $, then there is $F\in \mathcal O(\Omega )$ such that \[  F(a)=h(a),\qquad \int _\Omega |F|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV\le C(n,r,L) \int _{B(a,2r)}|h|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV,  \] where the constant $C(n,r,L)$ depends only on $n$, $r$ and $L$, and not on $\Omega $, $p$, $h$ or $a$. Proof. Fix a smooth function $\kappa $ on $\mathbb R$ with $0\le \kappa \le 1$, $\kappa =1$ on $(-\infty ,1]$ and $\kappa =0$ on $[3/2,\infty )$, for instance $\kappa (x)=\kappa _0(2x-2)$ with the function $\kappa _0$ fixed at the beginning of section 11.3 , and put $\chi (z)=\kappa (|z-a|/r)$. Then $\chi $ is smooth, because $\kappa $ is constant near $0$; it has compact support in $B(a,2r)$, equals one on $B(a,r)$, and satisfies $|\bar\partial \chi |\le c_0/r$ with $c_0=\sup |\kappa '|/2$, because $|\bar\partial |z-a||=1/2$ for $z\ne a$. Extend $\chi h$ by zero to $\Omega $. Then $\alpha =\bar\partial (\chi h)=h\, \bar\partial \chi $ is a smooth $\bar\partial $-closed form supported in the shell $r\le |z-a|\le 2r$. The function $p+n\log |z-a|^2$ is plurisubharmonic on $\Omega $ by proposition 8.3.3 , proposition 8.2.5 . We apply theorem 11.3.4 with this function in place of $p$ and with $q=|z-a|^2$, for which $A=I$. Since $\mathrm e^{-|z-a|^2}\le 1$ and $|z-a|^{-2n}\le r^{-2n}$ on the support of $\alpha $, we obtain a solution of $\bar\partial u=\alpha $ with \[  \int _\Omega |u|^2|z-a|^{-2n}\mathrm e^{-p-|z-a|^2}\, \mathrm dV \le c_0^2r^{-2n-2}\int _{B(a,2r)}|h|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV.  \] On $B(a,r)$ we have $\bar\partial u=\alpha =0$, so $u$ is holomorphic there, by lemma 11.3.5 (1). Since $p$ is bounded above on $B(a,r)$, the factor $\mathrm e^{-p-|z-a|^2}$ is bounded below there by a positive constant. If $u(a)$ were nonzero, then $|u|$ would be bounded below by a positive constant near $a$, and the integral on the left would diverge, because $\int _{B(a,\rho )}|z-a|^{-2n}\, \mathrm dV$ is a positive multiple of $\int _0^\rho \tau ^{-2n}\tau ^{2n-1}\, \mathrm d\tau =\infty $ by integration in polar coordinates ( 2.1 ). Thus $u(a)=0$. The function $F=\chi h-u$ satisfies $\bar\partial F=0$, so it is holomorphic by the same lemma, and $F(a)=h(a)$. Since $|z-a|<L$ on $\Omega $, we have $|z-a|^{2n}\mathrm e^{|z-a|^2}\le L^{2n}\mathrm e^{L^2}$, and therefore \[  \int _\Omega |u|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV\le c_0^2L^{2n}\mathrm e^{L^2}r^{-2n-2}\int _{B(a,2r)}|h|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV.  \] Finally, $|F|^2\le 2|\chi h|^2+2|u|^2$ and $|\chi h|\le |h|\mathbf1_{B(a,2r)}$ give the assertion with $C(n,r,L)=2+2c_0^2L^{2n}\mathrm e^{L^2}r^{-2n-2}$. $\square$

title: Bounded weight twist
topic: Weighted L2 estimates and holomorphic extension
text:
Lemma 11.4.2 . Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ be a pseudoconvex open set, $n\ge 1$, let $p\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$, and let $\psi $ be a smooth bounded plurisubharmonic function on $\Omega $. Put $A=H_\psi $ and $h=| ar\partial \psi |_{A^{-1}}^2$, where $ ar\partial \psi $ is identified with the vector $(\partial _{ ar z_ j}\psi )_ j$, and assume that $h<1$ almost everywhere. Let $\alpha $ be a $(0,1)$-form on $\Omega $ with measurable coefficients such that $E=\int _\Omega |\alpha |_{A^{-1}}^2\mathrm e^{\psi -p}\, \mathrm dV<\infty $ and $ ar\partial \alpha =0$, let $0\le a<1$, and assume that $h\le a$ almost everywhere on $\{ \alpha 
e 0\} $. Then $ ar\partial u=\alpha $ has a solution with \[  \int _\Omega (1-h)|u|^2\mathrm e^{\psi -p}\, \mathrm dV \le  rac{1+\sqrt a}{1-\sqrt a}\, E.  \] Proof. The idea is that, if $u$ is the minimal solution in $L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-p})$, then $u\mathrm e^\psi $ is the minimal solution of a twisted equation in $L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-p-\psi })$, to which we apply Hörmander's estimate. Put $m=\sup _\Omega |\psi |<\infty $. Since $\mathrm e^{-m}\le \mathrm e^{\pm \psi }\le \mathrm e^ m$, the spaces $L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-p})$ and $L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-p-\psi })$ consist of the same functions, with equivalent norms, and so contain the same holomorphic functions. By the discussion preceding theorem 11.3.3 , applied with the weight $p-\psi $, which is bounded above on compact sets, $\alpha \in L^2_{\mathrm{loc},(0,1)}(\Omega )$; so $ ar\partial \alpha $ is defined. Since $\mathrm e^{-p-\psi }\le \mathrm e^{2m}\mathrm e^{\psi -p}$, we have $\int _\Omega |\alpha |_{A^{-1}}^2\mathrm e^{-p-\psi }\, \mathrm dV\le \mathrm e^{2m}E<\infty $. Hence theorem 11.3.4 , applied with the plurisubharmonic function $p$ and the smooth function $q=\psi $, whose complex Hessian matrix $A$ is positive semidefinite, shows that the equation $ ar\partial u=\alpha $ has a solution in $L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-p-\psi })=L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-p})$. Let $u$ be the minimal solution in $L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-p})$, given by lemma 11.3.5 (2). The function $v=u\mathrm e^\psi $ belongs to $L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-p-\psi })$ and solves \[   ar\partial v= eta =(\alpha +u\,  ar\partial \psi )\mathrm e^\psi .  \] For every holomorphic $g$ in $L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-p-\psi })$ we have $\int v ar g\, \mathrm e^{-p-\psi }\, \mathrm dV=\int u ar g\, \mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV=0$, so $v$ is the minimal solution of $ ar\partial v= eta $ in $L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-p-\psi })$, by lemma 11.3.5 (2). We now estimate $v$ by theorem 11.3.4 , applied again with $p$ and $q=\psi $. The form $ eta = ar\partial v$ is $ ar\partial $-closed, and it lies in $L^2_{\mathrm{loc},(0,1)}(\Omega )$ because $\alpha $ and $u$ are locally square integrable and $\psi $ is smooth. Since $E<\infty $ and $h<1$, the dual energies of $\alpha $ and $ ar\partial \psi $ are finite almost everywhere, and at such points both vectors lie in the subspace on which the dual energy is a Hermitian quadratic form. The triangle inequality $|\alpha +u\,  ar\partial \psi |_{A^{-1}}\le |\alpha |_{A^{-1}}+|u|h^{1/2}$ therefore gives \[  \int | eta |_{A^{-1}}^2\mathrm e^{-p-\psi }\, \mathrm dV=\int |\alpha +u\,  ar\partial \psi |_{A^{-1}}^2\mathrm e^{\psi -p}\, \mathrm dV\le 2E+2\sup _\Omega \mathrm e^\psi \int |u|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV<\infty .  \] So theorem 11.3.4 yields a solution of $ ar\partial w= eta $ whose squared norm in $L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-p-\psi })$ is at most this integral, and the minimal solution $v$ has no larger norm. As $\int |v|^2\mathrm e^{-p-\psi }\, \mathrm dV=\int |u|^2\mathrm e^{\psi -p}\, \mathrm dV$, we obtain \[  \int |u|^2\mathrm e^{\psi -p}\, \mathrm dV \le \int |\alpha +u\,  ar\partial \psi |_{A^{-1}}^2\mathrm e^{\psi -p}\, \mathrm dV.  \] At almost every point, let $\langle \cdot ,\cdot angle _{A^{-1}}$ be the Hermitian inner product associated with the dual energy on the subspace where it is finite; by the polarization identity $\langle x,yangle _{A^{-1}}= rac14\sum _{k=0}^3\mathrm i^ k|x+\mathrm i^ ky|_{A^{-1}}^2$, the function $\langle \alpha , ar\partial \psi angle _{A^{-1}}$ is measurable. We expand \[  |\alpha +u\,  ar\partial \psi |_{A^{-1}}^2=|\alpha |_{A^{-1}}^2+2\operatorname{Re} igl ( ar u\langle \alpha , ar\partial \psi angle _{A^{-1}} igr )+h|u|^2, \qquad |\langle \alpha , ar\partial \psi angle _{A^{-1}}|\le |\alpha |_{A^{-1}}h^{1/2},  \] the second inequality being the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality. The function $h|u|^2\mathrm e^{\psi -p}$ is integrable, since $h<1$ almost everywhere and $u\in L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-p})$; moving its integral to the left, we find that $J=\int (1-h)|u|^2\mathrm e^{\psi -p}\, \mathrm dV$, which is finite, satisfies \[  J\le E+2\int |u|\, |\alpha |_{A^{-1}}h^{1/2}\mathrm e^{\psi -p}\, \mathrm dV.  \] If $a=0$, then $h=0$ almost everywhere on $\{ \alpha 
e 0\} $, the last integral vanishes, and $J\le E$, as claimed. Let $a>0$. The last integrand vanishes outside $\{ \alpha 
e 0\} $, where $h\le a$ and hence $h/(1-h)\le a/(1-a)$. For $t>1$, the inequality $2xy\le t^{-1}x^2+ty^2$ with $x=(1-h)^{1/2}|u|$ and $y=(h/(1-h))^{1/2}|\alpha |_{A^{-1}}$ gives there \[  2|u|\, |\alpha |_{A^{-1}}h^{1/2}\le t^{-1}(1-h)|u|^2+ rac{ta}{1-a}|\alpha |_{A^{-1}}^2.  \] Integrating, we obtain \[  J\le \left(1+ rac{ta}{1-a}ight)E+t^{-1}J.  \] Since $J$ is finite, this gives $J\le  rac t{t-1} igl (1+ rac{ta}{1-a} igr )E$. Choose $t=1+a^{-1/2}$. Then $1+ta/(1-a)=(1+\sqrt a)/(1-a)=1/(1-\sqrt a)$ and $t/(t-1)=1+\sqrt a$, so $J\le (1+\sqrt a)E/(1-\sqrt a)$. $\square$
