Lemma 11.4.3 . Let $0<\varepsilon <1/4$. For $\zeta \in \mathbb C$ with $|\zeta |<1/4$ put \[  s=-\log (|\zeta |^2+\varepsilon ^2),\qquad \eta =s+\log s,\qquad \psi _\varepsilon =-\log \eta .  \] Then $\psi _\varepsilon $ is a smooth, bounded, strictly subharmonic function on the disc $\Delta _{1/4}$. Let $h=|\partial _{ ar\zeta }\psi _\varepsilon |^2/(\psi _\varepsilon )_{\zeta  ar\zeta }$. Then \[   egin{split}  (1-h)\mathrm e^{\psi _\varepsilon }& \ge (6s^2)^{-1},\  h& \le  rac{2}{-\log (2\varepsilon ^2)}\quad 	ext{for }|\zeta |\le \varepsilon ,\   rac{\mathrm e^{\psi _\varepsilon }}{|\zeta |^2(\psi _\varepsilon )_{\zeta  ar\zeta }} & \le 25/4\quad 	ext{for }\varepsilon /2\le |\zeta |\le \varepsilon . \end{split}  \] In particular $h<1$ everywhere, and the bound for $h$ on the disc $|\zeta |\le \varepsilon $ tends to zero as $\varepsilon 	o 0$. Proof. Since $|\zeta |^2+\varepsilon ^2<1/8$, we have $s>\log 8>2$, so $\eta >s>2$ and $\psi _\varepsilon <0$ is well defined. For fixed $\varepsilon $, $s$ ranges in a bounded interval, so $\psi _\varepsilon $ is bounded; and $\psi _\varepsilon =G(|\zeta |^2)$ for a function $G$ that is smooth near $[0,1/16)$, so $\psi _\varepsilon $ is smooth. For $\zeta 
e 0$ put $x=|\zeta |^2$, $t=\log x$ and $b=x/(x+\varepsilon ^2)\in (0,1)$, and denote derivatives with respect to $t$ by primes. Then $s'=-b$ and $b'=b(1-b)$, so $s''=-b(1-b)$. With $D=1+1/s$ we have $\eta '=s'+s'/s=-bD$ and $D'=-s'/s^2=b/s^2$. Hence $\psi _\varepsilon '=-\eta '/\eta =bD/\eta $ and $\psi _\varepsilon ''=(b'D+bD')/\eta -bD\eta '/\eta ^2$, that is, \[  \psi _\varepsilon '= rac{bD}{\eta },\qquad \psi _\varepsilon ''=A+B,\quad A= rac{b^2D^2}{\eta ^2},\quad B= rac{b(1-b)D}{\eta }+ rac{b^2}{\eta s^2}>0.  \] For a function $g$ of $t=\log |\zeta |^2$ we have $\partial _{ ar\zeta }g=g'/ ar\zeta $ and $\partial _\zeta \partial _{ ar\zeta }g=g''/|\zeta |^2$. Hence $(\psi _\varepsilon )_{\zeta  ar\zeta }=\psi _\varepsilon ''/x>0$ and $h=(\psi _\varepsilon ')^2/\psi _\varepsilon ''=A/(A+B)<1$ for $\zeta 
e 0$. In general $\partial _{ ar\zeta }\psi _\varepsilon =G'(|\zeta |^2)\zeta $ and $(\psi _\varepsilon )_{\zeta  ar\zeta }=G''(|\zeta |^2)|\zeta |^2+G'(|\zeta |^2)$, so at $\zeta =0$ we have $\partial _{ ar\zeta }\psi _\varepsilon =0$ and $(\psi _\varepsilon )_{\zeta  ar\zeta }=G'(0)$, where $G'(x)=\psi _\varepsilon '/x=D/(\eta (x+\varepsilon ^2))>0$; so $(\psi _\varepsilon )_{\zeta  ar\zeta }>0$ and $h=0$ there. Thus $\psi _\varepsilon $ is strictly subharmonic, and $h<1$ everywhere. For the first estimate let $\zeta 
e 0$. Since $B\ge b^2/(\eta s^2)$, we have $A/B\le D^2s^2/\eta =(s+1)^2/\eta $, and therefore \[  (1-h)\mathrm e^{\psi _\varepsilon }= rac{B}{\eta (A+B)} \ge  rac1{\eta +(s+1)^2}\ge  rac1{6s^2},  \] because $\eta \le 2s\le 2s^2$ and $(s+1)^2\le 4s^2$ for $s\ge 1$. At $\zeta =0$ we have $(1-h)\mathrm e^{\psi _\varepsilon }=1/\eta \ge 1/(6s^2)$ as well. For the second estimate let $0<x\le \varepsilon ^2$. Then $b\le 1/2$, and $B\ge b(1-b)D/\eta $ gives \[  h\le  rac AB\le  rac{bD}{\eta (1-b)}\le  rac D\eta = rac{s+1}{s\eta }\le  rac2s,  \] since $s+1\le 2s\le 2\eta $; moreover $s\ge -\log (2\varepsilon ^2)$, because $x+\varepsilon ^2\le 2\varepsilon ^2$. Together with $h(0)=0$, this proves the second estimate. For the third, let $\varepsilon /2\le |\zeta |\le \varepsilon $. Then $1/5\le b\le 1/2$, so $\eta \psi _\varepsilon ''\ge \eta B\ge b(1-b)D\ge b(1-b)\ge 4/25$, and $\mathrm e^{\psi _\varepsilon }/(|\zeta |^2(\psi _\varepsilon )_{\zeta  ar\zeta })=1/(\eta \psi _\varepsilon '')\le 25/4$. $\square$

title: Ohsawa–Takegoshi
topic: Weighted L2 estimates and holomorphic extension
text:
Theorem 11.4.4 (Ohsawa–Takegoshi) . There is an absolute constant $C$ with the following property. Let $n\ge 1$ and $R>0$, let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^{n-1}	imes \Delta _ R$ be a pseudoconvex open set, where $\Delta _ R\subset \mathbb C$ is the disc of radius $R$ centered at $0$, and let $p\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$. Put $\Omega _0=\Omega \cap \{ z_ n=0\} $, which we identify with an open subset of $\mathbb C^{n-1}$. Then every holomorphic function $f$ on $\Omega _0$ with \[  I=\int _{\Omega _0}|f|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV_{2n-2}<\infty  \] has an extension $F\in \mathcal O(\Omega )$ such that \[  F|_{\Omega _0}=f,\qquad \int _\Omega |F|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV_{2n}\le C R^2 I.  \] Here, for $n=1$, $\Omega _0$ is a point or empty, and $I$ is the weighted value of $|f|^2$ at that point, the integral with respect to the counting measure $\mathrm dV_0$. If $\Omega _0=\varnothing $ we take $F=0$. On a connected component of $\Omega _0$ on which the restriction of $p$ is identically $-\infty $, finiteness of $I$ forces $f=0$, and this component contributes zero to $I$. Proof. After a normalization, Step 1 treats smooth weights on relatively compact pseudoconvex subsets, by correcting a cutoff of $f$ with lemma 11.4.2 , lemma 11.4.3 , and Step 2 regularizes $p$ and passes to the limit. Normalization. The substitution $z_ n=4R\zeta $ maps $\mathbb C^{n-1}	imes \Delta _{1/4}$ onto $\mathbb C^{n-1}	imes \Delta _ R$, preserves the hyperplane and the integral $I$, and multiplies Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb C^ n$ by $16R^2$. Hence it suffices to show the following: if $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^{n-1}	imes \Delta _{1/4}$, then $f$ has an extension $F\in \mathcal O(\Omega )$ with $\int _\Omega |F|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV\le C_0I$ for an absolute constant $C_0$; then $C=16C_0$ works. From now on we write the points of $\Omega $ as $(z',\zeta )$ with $z'\in \mathbb C^{n-1}$ and $|\zeta |<1/4$; for $n=1$ the variable $z'$ is absent. We may assume $\Omega _0
e \varnothing $. Step 1: smooth weights on a relatively compact set. Let $D\Subset \Omega $ be a pseudoconvex open set, let $U\subset \Omega $ be an open neighborhood of $\overline D$, and let $\varphi $ be a smooth plurisubharmonic function on $U$. We show that there are an open set $P\Subset \Omega _0$ with $\overline P	imes \{ 0\} \subset U$ and a function $F\in \mathcal O(D)$ with $F(z',0)=f(z')$ whenever $(z',0)\in D$, such that 11.21  egin{equation} \label{eq:ot-smooth-step} \int _ D|F|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi }\, \mathrm dV\le C_0\int _ P|f(z')|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi (z',0)}\, \mathrm dV_{2n-2}(z'), \end{equation} where $C_0$ is an absolute constant; we write $I_ P$ for the integral over $P$ on the right. The set $K_0=\{ z':(z',0)\in \overline D\} $ is a compact subset of the open set $U_0=\{ z':(z',0)\in U\} \subset \Omega _0$; choose an open set $P$ with $K_0\subset P\Subset U_0$. There is $\varepsilon _0\in (0,1/4)$ such that every $(z',\zeta )\in D$ with $|\zeta |\le \varepsilon _0$ satisfies $z'\in P$: otherwise there would be points $(z'_ k,\zeta _ k)\in D$ with $\zeta _ k	o 0$ and $z'_ k
otin P$, and a subsequence would converge, $D$ being bounded, to a point $(z',0)\in \overline D$ with $z'
otin P$, which is impossible. Decreasing $\varepsilon _0$, we may also assume that $\overline P	imes \overline\Delta _{\varepsilon _0}\subset U$ and, by the uniform continuity of $\varphi $ on this compact set, that 11.22  egin{equation} \label{eq:ot-weight-comparison} \mathrm e^{-\varphi (z',\zeta )}\le 2\mathrm e^{-\varphi (z',0)}\qquad (z'\in \overline P,\  |\zeta |\le \varepsilon _0). \end{equation} Fix a smooth function $\chi $ on $\mathbb R$ with $0\le \chi \le 1$, $\chi =1$ on $(-\infty ,1/4]$ and $\chi =0$ on $[1,\infty )$, for instance $\chi (x)=\kappa _0((4x-1)/3)$ with the function $\kappa _0$ fixed at the beginning of section 11.3 , and put $c_\chi =\sup |\chi '|^2$. For $0<\varepsilon \le \varepsilon _0$ define $g_\varepsilon $ on $D$ by $g_\varepsilon (z',\zeta )=f(z')\chi (|\zeta |^2/\varepsilon ^2)$ if $z'\in P$, and $g_\varepsilon =0$ otherwise. The open sets $D\cap (P	imes \mathbb C)$ and $D\cap \{ |\zeta |>\varepsilon \} $ cover $D$ by the choice of $\varepsilon _0$, and $g_\varepsilon $ is smooth on each of them (on the second it vanishes); hence $g_\varepsilon $ is smooth on $D$, and $g_\varepsilon (z',0)=f(z')$ for $(z',0)\in D$. Since $f$ is holomorphic, \[  \alpha _\varepsilon = ar\partial g_\varepsilon =f(z')\chi '(|\zeta |^2/\varepsilon ^2)  rac{\zeta }{\varepsilon ^2}\, \mathrm d ar\zeta  \] is a $ ar\partial $-closed smooth form supported in $\{ \varepsilon /2\le |\zeta |\le \varepsilon \} $. We solve $ ar\partial u=\alpha _\varepsilon $ on $D$ by lemma 11.4.2 , with the function $\widetilde\varphi =\varphi +\log |\zeta |^2$ in place of $p$, which is plurisubharmonic on $D$ by proposition 8.3.3 , proposition 8.2.5 , and with $\psi =\psi _\varepsilon (\zeta )$ from lemma 11.4.3 , a smooth bounded function on $D$ which is plurisubharmonic by proposition 8.2.3 , applied to the projection $(z',\zeta )\mapsto \zeta $. The complex Hessian matrix $A=H_\psi $ has the single nonzero entry $(\psi _\varepsilon )_{\zeta  ar\zeta }$, so $| ar\partial \psi |_{A^{-1}}^2$ is the function $h$ of lemma 11.4.3 ; thus $h<1$, and $h\le a_\varepsilon =2/(-\log (2\varepsilon ^2))$ on $\{ \alpha _\varepsilon 
e 0\} \subset \{ |\zeta |\le \varepsilon \} $. The dual energy of $\alpha _\varepsilon $ is $|f|^2|\chi '|^2|\zeta |^2\varepsilon ^{-4}/(\psi _\varepsilon )_{\zeta  ar\zeta }$, so the third estimate of lemma 11.4.3 and $|\zeta |\le \varepsilon $ give, on its support, \[  |\alpha _\varepsilon |_{A^{-1}}^2\mathrm e^{\psi _\varepsilon -\widetilde\varphi } =|f(z')|^2|\chi '|^2\varepsilon ^{-4} rac{\mathrm e^{\psi _\varepsilon }}{(\psi _\varepsilon )_{\zeta  ar\zeta }}\mathrm e^{-\varphi } \le  rac{25}4c_\chi \varepsilon ^{-2}|f(z')|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi (z',\zeta )}.  \] By ( 11.22 ) and Fubini's theorem, since every point of the support has $z'\in P$, \[  E=\int _ D|\alpha _\varepsilon |_{A^{-1}}^2\mathrm e^{\psi -\widetilde\varphi }\, \mathrm dV \le  rac{25}4c_\chi \varepsilon ^{-2}\cdot 2\pi \varepsilon ^2I_ P= rac{25\pi }2c_\chi I_ P.  \] If $\varepsilon $ is so small that $a_\varepsilon \le 1/4$, then $(1+\sqrt{a_\varepsilon })/(1-\sqrt{a_\varepsilon })\le 3$, and lemma 11.4.2 gives $u_\varepsilon $ with $ ar\partial u_\varepsilon =\alpha _\varepsilon $ and $\int _ D(1-h)|u_\varepsilon |^2\mathrm e^{\psi _\varepsilon -\widetilde\varphi }\, \mathrm dV\le 3E$. By the first estimate of lemma 11.4.3 , $(1-h)\mathrm e^{\psi _\varepsilon }\ge 1/(6\log ^2(|\zeta |^2+\varepsilon ^2))$, and $\mathrm e^{-\widetilde\varphi }=\mathrm e^{-\varphi }|\zeta |^{-2}$. Hence, with $C_1=225\pi c_\chi $, 11.23  egin{equation} \label{eq:normal-extension-correction} \int _ D rac{|u_\varepsilon |^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi }}{ |\zeta |^2\log ^2(|\zeta |^2+\varepsilon ^2)}\, \mathrm dV \le 18E\le C_1I_ P. \end{equation} On $D\cap \{ |\zeta |<\varepsilon /2\} $ we have $ ar\partial u_\varepsilon =0$, so $u_\varepsilon $ is holomorphic there, by lemma 11.3.5 (1). Suppose that $u_\varepsilon (z'_0,0)
e 0$ for some $(z'_0,0)\in D$. On a small polydisc around this point, $|u_\varepsilon |$ is bounded below by a positive constant, $\varphi $ is bounded above, and $\log ^2(|\zeta |^2+\varepsilon ^2)\le \log ^2(\varepsilon ^2)$; so the integrand in ( 11.23 ) is at least a positive constant times $|\zeta |^{-2}$, whose integral over a disc around $\zeta =0$ diverges. This contradicts ( 11.23 ). Hence $u_\varepsilon =0$ on $D\cap \{ \zeta =0\} $, and $F_\varepsilon =g_\varepsilon -u_\varepsilon $ is holomorphic on $D$, by the same lemma, because $ ar\partial F_\varepsilon =0$; moreover $F_\varepsilon (z',0)=f(z')$. It remains to estimate $F_\varepsilon $. For $0<x=|\zeta |^2<1/16$ we have $x<x+\varepsilon ^2<1/8$, so $x\log ^2(x+\varepsilon ^2)\le x\log ^2x\le 4\mathrm e^{-2}<1$. Thus ( 11.23 ) gives $\int _ D|u_\varepsilon |^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi }\, \mathrm dV\le C_1I_ P$. By ( 11.22 ) and Fubini's theorem, $\int _ D|g_\varepsilon |^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi }\, \mathrm dV\le 2\pi \varepsilon ^2I_ P\le I_ P$. Therefore $\int _ D|F_\varepsilon |^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi }\, \mathrm dV\le 2(1+C_1)I_ P$, which is ( 11.21 ) with $C_0=2(1+C_1)$. Step 2: the general case. By corollary 11.2.5 there are pseudoconvex open sets $D_1\subset D_2\subset \cdots $ with $D_ j\Subset \Omega $ and $ igcup _ jD_ j=\Omega $. Choose $\varepsilon _ j\downarrow 0$ with $\varepsilon _ j<\operatorname {dist}(\overline D_ j,\mathbb C^ n\setminus \Omega )$, and let $ho _\varepsilon $ be the radial mollifier of section 1.4 ; then, by proposition 8.2.2 (2), $p_ j=p*ho _{\varepsilon _ j}$ is a smooth plurisubharmonic function on the open neighborhood $U_ j=\{ z\in \Omega :\operatorname {dist}(z,\mathbb C^ n\setminus \Omega )>\varepsilon _ j\} $ of $\overline D_ j$, and $p_ j\downarrow p$ pointwise. Step 1, applied to $D_ j$, $U_ j$ and $\varphi =p_ j$, gives $F_ j\in \mathcal O(D_ j)$ with $F_ j(z',0)=f(z')$ for $(z',0)\in D_ j$ and \[  \int _{D_ j}|F_ j|^2\mathrm e^{-p_ j}\, \mathrm dV\le C_0\int _{P_ j}|f(z')|^2\mathrm e^{-p_ j(z',0)}\, \mathrm dV_{2n-2}(z')\le C_0I,  \] because $p_ j\ge p$. (On a component of $\Omega _0$ on which $p(\cdot ,0)\equiv -\infty $ we have $f=0$, and the last inequality holds with the convention $0\cdot \infty =0$.) We show that a subsequence of $(F_ j)$ converges locally uniformly on $\Omega $. Let $K\subset \Omega $ be compact. Then $K\subset D_ k$ for some $k$, and for $j\ge k$ we have $p_ j\le p_ k$ on $K$, so $\int _ K|F_ j|^2\, \mathrm dV\le \mathrm e^{\max _ Kp_ k}C_0I$. It follows that $(F_ j)$ is uniformly bounded on compact subsets of $\Omega $. Indeed, for a holomorphic function $G$ the complex Hessian matrix of $|G|^2$ is $ igl (\partial _{z_\mu }G\, \overline{\partial _{z_
u }G} igr )_{\mu ,
u }$, which is positive semidefinite; so $|G|^2$ is plurisubharmonic by proposition 8.2.2 (1), and hence subharmonic by theorem 8.2.1 . If $K\subset \Omega $ is compact, $\delta >0$ and $K_\delta =\{ z:\operatorname {dist}(z,K)\le \delta \} \subset \Omega $, then the mean value inequality over balls in theorem 3.1.3 , applied to $|F_ j|^2$, gives $|F_ j(z)|^2\le |B(z,\delta )|^{-1}\int _{K_\delta }|F_ j|^2\, \mathrm dV$ for $z\in K$ and large $j$, and the right side is bounded independently of $j$ by the preceding estimate applied to $K_\delta $. Next, let $K\subset \Omega $ be compact, and choose $r>0$ such that the compact set $K'$ of points at distance at most $2\sqrt n\, r$ from $K$ lies in $\Omega $. For $z\in K'_0=\{ z:\operatorname {dist}(z,K)\le \sqrt n\, r\} $, the closed polydisc of radius $r$ centered at $z$ lies in $K'$, and the coefficient bound in ( 7.1 ) with $a=z$ gives $|\partial _{z_ l}F_ j(z)|\le r^{-1}\max _{K'}|F_ j|$ for $1\le l\le n$ and all large $j$ (those with $K'\subset D_ j$). Since $\mathrm dF_ j=\sum _ l\partial _{z_ l}F_ j\, \mathrm dz_ l$, it follows that these $F_ j$ are Lipschitz with a common constant on every ball of radius $\sqrt n\, r$ centered at a point of $K$, so the sequence $(F_ j)$ is equicontinuous on $K$ from some index on. By proposition 1.6.4 on a compact exhaustion of $\Omega $ and a diagonal argument, a subsequence converges locally uniformly on $\Omega $ to a continuous function $F$. Since $ ar\partial F_ j=0$ and $F_ j	o F$ in the sense of distributions, $ ar\partial F=0$, and $F$ is holomorphic by lemma 11.3.5 (1). Moreover $F(z',0)=\lim _ jF_ j(z',0)=f(z')$ for $z'\in \Omega _0$. Finally, let $K\subset \Omega $ be compact, and let $k$ be so large that $K\subset D_ k$. For $j\ge k$ we have $p_ j\le p_ k$ on $K$, so locally uniform convergence gives \[  \int _ K|F|^2\mathrm e^{-p_ k}\, \mathrm dV=\lim _ j\int _ K|F_ j|^2\mathrm e^{-p_ k}\, \mathrm dV\le \varliminf _ j\int _{D_ j}|F_ j|^2\mathrm e^{-p_ j}\, \mathrm dV\le C_0I.  \] This holds for all large $k$, and $\mathrm e^{-p_ k}$ increases to $\mathrm e^{-p}$ as $k	o \infty $; so the monotone convergence theorem gives $\int _ K|F|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV\le C_0I$, and exhausting $\Omega $ by compact sets gives $\int _\Omega |F|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV\le C_0I$. $\square$

topic: Weighted L2 estimates and holomorphic extension
text: Corollary 11.4.5 . Let $C$ be the constant of theorem 11.4.4 . Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$, $n\ge 1$, be a pseudoconvex open set of diameter at most $L>0$, and let $p\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$. Then for every $a\in \Omega $ with $p(a)>-\infty $ there is $F\in \mathcal O(\Omega )$ such that \[  F(a)=1,\qquad \int _\Omega |F|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV \le C^ n L^{2n}\mathrm e^{-p(a)}.  \] More generally, let $V\subset \mathbb C^ n$ be an affine complex subspace of codimension $r$, $0\le r\le n$, and let $f$ be holomorphic on $\Omega \cap V$ with finite slice norm $\int _{\Omega \cap V}|f|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV_{2n-2r}$, computed with Lebesgue measure on $V$. Then there is $F\in \mathcal O(\Omega )$ with $F|_{\Omega \cap V}=f$ and $\int _\Omega |F|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV\le C^ rL^{2r}\int _{\Omega \cap V}|f|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV_{2n-2r}$. Proof. We prove the second assertion; the first is the case $V=\{ a\} $, $r=n$ and $f=1$, whose slice norm with respect to the counting measure $\mathrm dV_0$ is $\mathrm e^{-p(a)}$. If $r=0$ we take $F=f$, and if $\Omega \cap V=\varnothing $ we take $F=0$. Assume now that $r\ge 1$ and $\Omega \cap V\ne \varnothing $. Choose $b\in \Omega \cap V$ and unitary affine coordinates $w=(w_1,\ldots ,w_ n)$ on $\mathbb C^ n$ centered at $b$ with $V=\{ w_1=\cdots =w_ r=0\} $, and put $\Omega _ k=\Omega \cap \{ w_1=\cdots =w_ k=0\} $ for $0\le k\le r$, an open subset of a space isomorphic to $\mathbb C^{n-k}$. Unitary coordinates preserve Lebesgue measure. Each $\Omega _ k$ with $k<n$ is pseudoconvex: the restriction of a continuous plurisubharmonic exhaustion function of $\Omega $ to the closed subset $\Omega _ k$ of $\Omega $ is continuous and plurisubharmonic by proposition 8.2.3 , applied to the linear embedding of $\{ w_1=\cdots =w_ k=0\} $, and its sublevel sets are compact. By the discussion following definition 11.2.1 , every connected component of $\Omega _ k$ is pseudoconvex as well. Since $\Omega $ is open and has diameter at most $L$, we have $|z-b|<L$ for $z\in \Omega $ (a point $z\in \Omega $ with $|z-b|=L$ could be moved slightly away from $b$ inside $\Omega $), so the coordinate $w_ k$ takes its values in $\Delta _ L$ on $\Omega _{k-1}$. Put $f_ r=f$, let $1\le k\le r$, and assume that $f_ k\in \mathcal O(\Omega _ k)$ has finite norm $\int _{\Omega _ k}|f_ k|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV_{2n-2k}$. Let $W$ be a connected component of $\Omega _{k-1}$; ordering the coordinates as $(w_{k+1},\ldots ,w_ n,w_ k)$, we regard $W$ as an open subset of $\mathbb C^{n-k}\times \Delta _ L$ whose slice by $\{ w_ k=0\} $ is the open subset $W\cap \Omega _ k$ of $\Omega _ k$. By proposition 8.2.3 , the restriction of $p$ to $W$ is plurisubharmonic or identically $-\infty $. In the second case $\mathrm e^{-p}=\infty $ on $W\cap \Omega _ k$, so the finiteness of the norm of $f_ k$ forces $f_ k=0$ almost everywhere on $W\cap \Omega _ k$, hence everywhere there, since $f_ k$ is continuous, and we put $f_{k-1}=0$ on $W$. In the first case, theorem 11.4.4 , applied to $W$ with normal coordinate $w_ k$, gives a holomorphic function $f_{k-1}$ on $W$ extending the restriction of $f_ k$ to $W\cap \Omega _ k$, with \[  \int _ W|f_{k-1}|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV_{2n-2k+2}\le CL^2\int _{W\cap \Omega _ k}|f_ k|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV_{2n-2k}.  \] The components $W$ are open, disjoint and cover $\Omega _{k-1}$, and the sets $W\cap \Omega _ k$ are disjoint and cover $\Omega _ k$. Hence these functions define $f_{k-1}\in \mathcal O(\Omega _{k-1})$ extending $f_ k$, and summing over $W$ gives \[  \int _{\Omega _{k-1}}|f_{k-1}|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV_{2n-2k+2}\le CL^2\int _{\Omega _ k}|f_ k|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV_{2n-2k}.  \] Proceeding in this way for $k=r,r-1,\ldots ,1$ and multiplying the $r$ estimates, we see that $F=f_0$ has the required properties. $\square$

title: Integrable germ restriction
topic: Weighted L2 estimates and holomorphic extension
text: Corollary 11.4.6 . Let $X$ be a complex manifold, let $Y\subset X$ be a complex submanifold, let $a\in Y$, and let $p$ be a plurisubharmonic function on a neighborhood of $a$ in $X$. Let $f$ be a holomorphic germ on $Y$ at $a$ such that $|f|^2\mathrm e^{-p|_ Y}$ is integrable on some neighborhood of $a$ in $Y$. Then there is a holomorphic germ $F$ on $X$ at $a$ with $F|_ Y=f$ such that $|F|^2\mathrm e^{-p}$ is integrable on some neighborhood of $a$ in $X$. Here integrability refers to smooth positive volume forms on $Y$ and $X$; since any two such forms are locally comparable, the notion does not depend on their choice. Proof. Let $k=\dim Y$ and $n=\dim X$ near $a$. By the definition of a complex submanifold (definition 7.1.1 ), there are holomorphic coordinates $w=(w',w'')\in \mathbb C^ k\times \mathbb C^{n-k}$ centered at $a$ in which $Y=\{ w''=0\} $; by proposition 8.2.3 , $p$ is plurisubharmonic near $0$ in these coordinates. On a compact neighborhood of $a$, the densities of smooth positive volume forms with respect to coordinate Lebesgue measure are bounded above and below by positive constants. Hence we may test integrability with Lebesgue measure $\mathrm dV_{2k}$ on $Y=\mathbb C^ k\times \{ 0\} $ and $\mathrm dV_{2n}$ in the coordinates $w$. Choose a ball $B$ around $0$ so small that $p$ is plurisubharmonic on a neighborhood of $\overline B$, that $f$ is defined on $B\cap Y$, and that $\int _{B\cap Y}|f|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV_{2k}<\infty $. The ball $B$ is a bounded pseudoconvex domain, by corollary 11.2.5 applied to the exhaustion function $|w|^2$ of $\mathbb C^ n$, and $B\cap Y$ is its intersection with the linear subspace $\{ w''=0\} $ of codimension $n-k$. By corollary 11.4.5 there is $F\in \mathcal O(B)$ with $F|_{B\cap Y}=f$ and $\int _ B|F|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV_{2n}<\infty $. (If $k=0$, the integral over $Y$ is the weighted value $|f(a)|^2\mathrm e^{-p(a)}$; if $p|_ Y$ is identically $-\infty $ near $a$, then $f=0$ and $F=0$, in accordance with the conventions of theorem 11.4.4 .) $\square$

title: Lelong numbers and multiplier ideals
text:
12 Lelong numbers and multiplier ideals A plurisubharmonic function can have a complicated pole set, but near each point its growth is governed by a single logarithmic rate. The Lelong number $
u (u,a)$ of a plurisubharmonic function $u$ at a point $a$ is the largest $c\geq 0$ such that $u(z)\leq c\log |z-a|^2+O(1)$ near $a$; with this normalization $
u (\log |z|^2,0)=1$. By the Jensen–Lelong formula, $
u (u,a)$ is also the limiting density at $a$ of the positive current $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$, which links the pointwise growth of $u$ with the measures studied in the preceding chapters. Lelong numbers do not, however, determine the integrability properties of a singular weight $\varphi $ (example 12.3.3 ). These are recorded by the multiplier ideal $\mathcal I(\varphi )$, which consists of the holomorphic germs $f$ for which $|f|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi }$ is locally integrable. The $L^2$ estimates and extension theorems of chapter 11 make multiplier ideals accessible. Solving a $ ar\partial $-equation with a weight that has a logarithmic pole at a point, we approximate every germ of $\mathcal I(\varphi )$, to arbitrarily high order, by holomorphic functions on a polydisc that are square integrable against $\mathrm e^{-\varphi }$; with the Krull intersection theorem and the strong Noetherian property, this shows that $\mathcal I(\varphi )$ is a coherent sheaf (theorem 12.2.7 ). Comparing the vanishing orders of the generators of $\mathcal I(m\varphi )$ with the growth of $\varphi $ (lemma 12.3.1 ), we prove Siu's theorem that the sets where the Lelong number is at least $c>0$ are analytic. The same comparison shows that $\mathrm e^{-t\varphi }$ is integrable near a point $x$ for every $t>0$ if $
u (\varphi ,x)=0$, a fact used in chapter 15 for an example on the projective line. The Ohsawa–Takegoshi theorem gives the restriction and subadditivity properties of multiplier ideals. Since its constant does not depend on the weight, it can be applied along a moving family of hyperplanes; comparing the resulting extensions on one fixed holomorphic curve, we prove that multiplier ideals are stable under increasing limits of weights and deduce the strong openness theorem $\mathcal I(\varphi )= igcup _{\varepsilon >0}\mathcal I((1+\varepsilon )\varphi )$ (corollary 12.5.4 ). The last section studies integrability on modifications. For a weight with analytic singularities, the change of variables formula on a log resolution reduces membership in the multiplier ideal to explicit one-variable integrals (theorem 12.6.5 ). For a general weight, the ideals $\mathcal I(m\varphi )$ recover the generic Lelong numbers of $\varphi $ along all prime divisors over the ambient manifold, and strong openness gives a valuative criterion for membership in $\mathcal I(\varphi )$ in which one positive parameter serves for all divisors (theorem 12.6.9 ). These results are the local foundation for comparing singularities through their multiplier ideals in later chapters. Historical remarks and references for this chapter are collected in section B.12 .

title: Logarithmic growth and the Jensen formula
text:
12.1 Logarithmic growth and the Jensen formula Proposition 12.1.1 . Let $n\geq 1$ and let $u$ be a plurisubharmonic function on a neighborhood of $a\in \mathbb C^ n$. For sufficiently negative $t$ put \[  N(t)=\sup _{|z-a|<\exp (t/2)}u(z).  \] Then $N$ is finite, nondecreasing and convex, $N(t)$ is also the supremum of $u$ over the sphere $|z-a|=\exp (t/2)$, and the limit 12.1  egin{equation} \label{eq:lelong-growth-definition} 
u (u,a)=\lim _{t	o -\infty } rac{N(t)}{t} \end{equation} exists in $[0,\infty )$; it is zero if $u(a)>-\infty $. For every $r_0>0$ such that $\overline{B(a,r_0)}$ lies in the domain of $u$, 12.2  egin{equation} \label{eq:lelong-attained-growth} u(z)\leq 
u (u,a)\log  rac{|z-a|^2}{r_0^2} +\sup _{B(a,r_0)}u,\qquad 0<|z-a|<r_0. \end{equation} Consequently $
u (u,a)$ is the largest $c\geq 0$ for which $u(z)\leq c\log |z-a|^2+O(1)$ near $a$; moreover, if $c\geq 0$ and $u(z)\leq c\log |z-a|^2+C$ for all $z$ outside a Lebesgue null set in some neighborhood of $a$, then $
u (u,a)\geq c$. The Lelong number does not change under a holomorphic change of coordinates, nor under the addition of a bounded function, provided the resulting function is plurisubharmonic. Proof. We may assume $a=0$. Let $R_*\in (0,\infty ]$ be the supremum of the radii $r$ for which $\overline{B(0,r)}$ lies in the domain of $u$; since closed balls are compact, $\overline{B(0,r)}$ lies in the domain exactly when $0<r<R_*$. For such $r$ put $S(r)=\sup _{|z|=r}u(z)$. This number is less than $+\infty $ because $u$ is upper semicontinuous and hence bounded above on the compact sphere. It is also greater than $-\infty $. Otherwise, for every unit vector $e$, the function $\zeta \mapsto u(\zeta e)$, which is subharmonic or identically $-\infty $ near the closed disc $|\zeta |\leq r$, would be $-\infty $ on the circle $|\zeta |=r$ and hence, by upper semicontinuity, have upper limits $-\infty $ there; the maximum principle (proposition 3.1.4 ), applied to $\zeta \mapsto u(\zeta e)+k$ for every $k>0$, would give $u=-\infty $ on the disc. Thus $u$ would be identically $-\infty $ on $B(0,r)$, which is impossible because $u$ is locally integrable (theorem 8.2.1 ). Let $0<r_1<r_2<r_3<R_*$, and let $h(\zeta )=A+B\log |\zeta |^2$ be the harmonic function on $\mathbb C\setminus \{ 0\} $ equal to $S(r_1)$ on $|\zeta |=r_1$ and to $S(r_3)$ on $|\zeta |=r_3$. For every unit vector $e$, the function $\zeta \mapsto u(\zeta e)-h(\zeta )$ is subharmonic or identically $-\infty $ near the closed annulus $r_1\leq |\zeta |\leq r_3$, and by upper semicontinuity its upper limits at the two boundary circles are at most $0$; by the maximum principle (proposition 3.1.4 ) it is at most $0$ on the annulus. Taking the supremum over $e$ on the circle $|\zeta |=r_2$ gives $S(r_2)\leq h(r_2)$. Since $h(r_2)$ is the value at $\log r_2^2$ of the affine function of $\log r^2$ that equals $S(r_1)$ and $S(r_3)$ at $\log r_1^2$ and $\log r_3^2$, this says that $S$ is a convex function of $\log r^2$ on $(0,R_*)$. Applying the maximum principle in the same way to $\zeta \mapsto u(\zeta e)-S(r)$ on the disc $|\zeta |\leq r$, we obtain $u(\zeta e)\leq S(r)$ for $|\zeta |\leq r$; hence $S$ is nondecreasing and $u(0)\leq S(r)$. A finite convex function on an open interval is continuous, since on a compact subinterval its difference quotients are bounded between two fixed difference quotients taken outside the subinterval. Hence $\sup _{B(0,r)}u=\sup _{ho <r}S(ho )=S(r)$, so that $N(t)=S(\mathrm e^{t/2})$ for $t<\log R_*^2$; this proves the assertions about $N$. Fix $r_0$ as in the statement and put $t_0=\log r_0^2$. Since $N$ is convex and nondecreasing on $(-\infty ,t_0]$, the difference quotients $(N(t_0)-N(t))/(t_0-t)$ are nonnegative and decrease as $t\downarrow -\infty $; let $c\in [0,\infty )$ be their limit. Writing $N(t)=N(t_0)-(t_0-t)\cdot  rac{N(t_0)-N(t)}{t_0-t}$ and dividing by $t$, we obtain $N(t)/t	o c$ as $t	o -\infty $. In particular $c$ does not depend on $t_0$, so for every fixed $s\leq t_0$ the quotients $(N(s)-N(s'))/(s-s')$ also tend to $c$ as $s'	o -\infty $. If $s'<s<t\leq t_0$, convexity gives $(N(t)-N(s))/(t-s)\geq (N(s)-N(s'))/(s-s')$; letting $s'	o -\infty $, we see that every difference quotient of $N$ on $(-\infty ,t_0]$ is at least $c$. Hence $N(t)-ct$ is nondecreasing, and $N(t)\leq c(t-t_0)+N(t_0)$ for $t<t_0$. Since $u(z)\leq S(|z|)=N(\log |z|^2)$, this is ( 12.2 ). Since $u(0)\leq S(r)$ for all $r$, we have $N(t)\geq u(0)$, hence $N(t)/t\leq u(0)/t$ for $t<0$, and $c=0$ if $u(0)>-\infty $. Conversely, if $c'\geq 0$ and $u(z)\leq c'\log |z|^2+C$ for $0<|z|<r'$, then $N(t)=S(\mathrm e^{t/2})\leq c't+C$ for all sufficiently negative $t$, and division by $t<0$ gives $c\geq c'$. This proves the characterization of $
u (u,a)$ as the largest admissible coefficient. Now let $c\geq 0$, and suppose that $u(z)\leq c\log |z|^2+C$ for all $z\in B(0,r)\setminus A$, where $\overline{B(0,r)}$ lies in the domain of $u$ and $A$ is a Lebesgue null set. Let $0<|z|<r/2$ and $0<\delta <|z|/2$. The function $u$ is subharmonic (theorem 8.2.1 ), so theorem 3.1.3 gives $u(z)\leq |B(z,\delta )|^{-1}\int _{B(z,\delta )}u\, \mathrm dV$. Every $y\in B(z,\delta )\setminus A$ satisfies $u(y)\leq c\log (|z|+\delta )^2+C$, because $c\geq 0$ and $|y|\leq |z|+\delta $; since $A$ is a null set, we obtain $u(z)\leq c\log (|z|+\delta )^2+C$. Letting $\delta \downarrow 0$, we get $u(z)\leq c\log |z|^2+C$ for $0<|z|<r/2$, and the converse part of the characterization gives $
u (u,0)\geq c$. Let $F$ be a biholomorphic map from a neighborhood of $a$ onto a neighborhood of $F(a)$; by proposition 8.2.3 , $u\circ F^{-1}$ is plurisubharmonic near $F(a)$. The maps $F$ and $F^{-1}$ are continuously differentiable, hence Lipschitz near $a$ and $F(a)$, so $\log |F(z)-F(a)|^2-\log |z-a|^2$ is bounded near $a$, $z
eq a$. Since adding a bounded function also changes $u$ by a bounded amount, in both cases the characterization just proved shows that the Lelong number is unchanged. $\square$ Definition 12.1.2 . The number $
u (u,a)$ in ( 12.1 ) is the Lelong number of $u$ at $a$. If $u$ is plurisubharmonic on a complex manifold $X$ that has positive dimension at $a$, we compute $
u (u,a)$ in a holomorphic chart at $a$; by proposition 12.1.1 the result does not depend on the chart. If $X$ has dimension zero at $a$, where plurisubharmonic functions are finite, we set $
u (u,a)=0$. For a closed positive $(1,1)$-current $T$ on $X$ we put $
u (T,a)=
u (u,a)$, where $u$ is a plurisubharmonic potential of $T$ near $a$, that is, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=T$. Such potentials exist, and two of them differ near $a$ by a smooth pluriharmonic function: by theorem 8.2.1 , the plurisubharmonic potentials of $T$ on a coordinate ball are exactly its canonical local potentials, to which theorem 7.3.2 applies. Since a smooth function is bounded near $a$, $
u (T,a)$ does not depend on the choice of the potential. The Lelong number can also be read off from the mass of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ on small balls. We use the form \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|z|^2= rac{ eta }{\pi }= rac1\pi \sum _{j=1}^ n\mathrm dx_ j\wedge \mathrm dy_ j,  \] where $ eta $ is the Euclidean Kähler form ( 7.4 ); note that $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|z-a|^2=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|z|^2$. By ( 6.2 ) with $d=2n$, and since $\Gamma (n)=(n-1)!$, the area of the unit sphere $S^{2n-1}\subset \mathbb R^{2n}$ is $s_{2n-1}=2\pi ^ n/(n-1)!$. Let $u$ be plurisubharmonic on a neighborhood of a closed ball $\overline{B(a,R)}\subset \mathbb C^ n$, $n\geq 1$. By theorem 8.2.1 , theorem 3.2.2 , $\mu =\Delta u$ is a positive Radon measure. For $0<r<R$ define 12.3  egin{equation} \label{eq:lelong-ball-density} D_ u(a,r)= rac{\mu (B(a,r))}{2s_{2n-1}r^{2n-2}} = rac1{r^{2n-2}}\int _{B(a,r)}\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\wedge (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|z|^2)^{n-1}. \end{equation} Here $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\wedge (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|z|^2)^{n-1}$ is the product of the current $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ with a smooth form, as defined in chapter 7 . To verify the second equality, assume first that $u$ is smooth. When $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|z|^2)^{n-1}$ is expanded, only the diagonal coefficients $u_{j ar j}$ of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ contribute to the product, and since $ rac{\mathrm i}{2}\mathrm dz_ j\wedge \mathrm d ar z_ j=\mathrm dx_ j\wedge \mathrm dy_ j$ and $\Delta u=4\sum _ ju_{j ar j}$, we obtain \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\wedge (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|z|^2)^{n-1}= rac{(n-1)!}{\pi ^ n}\sum _{j=1}^ nu_{j ar j}\, \mathrm dV = rac{(n-1)!}{4\pi ^ n}\Delta u\, \mathrm dV.  \] Both sides are obtained from $u$ by the same constant-coefficient differential operator, so the identity holds for every distribution $u$. Since $2s_{2n-1}=4\pi ^ n/(n-1)!$, this gives ( 12.3 ). Theorem 12.1.3 (Jensen–Lelong) . Let $n\geq 1$, $R>0$, and let $u$ be plurisubharmonic on a neighborhood of $\overline{B(a,R)}\subset \mathbb C^ n$. Then the spherical mean $M_ u(a,r)$ of $u$ over $\partial B(a,r)$ is finite for every $0<r<R$, the function $r\mapsto D_ u(a,r)$ is nondecreasing on $(0,R)$, and 12.4  egin{equation} \label{eq:euclidean-jensen-lelong} M_ u(a,r_2)-M_ u(a,r_1) =\int _{\log r_1^2}^{\log r_2^2}D_ u(a,\exp (t/2))\, \mathrm dt, \qquad 0<r_1<r_2<R. \end{equation} In particular, 12.5  egin{equation} \label{eq:lelong-density-limit} 
u (u,a)=\lim _{r\downarrow 0}D_ u(a,r) =\lim _{r\downarrow 0} rac{M_ u(a,r)}{\log r^2}. \end{equation} Proof. Step 1: smooth functions. Suppose first that $u$ is smooth. By proposition 2.1.1 in $\mathbb R^{2n}$ and the substitution $r=\mathrm e^{t/2}$, for which $\mathrm dr/\mathrm dt=r/2$, \[   rac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}M_ u(a,\mathrm e^{t/2}) = rac r2\cdot  rac{\mu (B(a,r))}{s_{2n-1}r^{2n-1}} =D_ u(a,\mathrm e^{t/2}),  \] and ( 12.4 ) follows by integration, since $\mu =\Delta u\, \mathrm dV$ has a continuous density, so that the right side is continuous in $t$. To see that $D_ u(a,\cdot )$ is nondecreasing, we show that $t\mapsto M_ u(a,\mathrm e^{t/2})$ is a convex function on $(-\infty ,\log R^2)$; the derivative of a differentiable convex function is nondecreasing. For a unit vector $\omega \in S^{2n-1}$, the function $v_\omega (\zeta )=u(a+\zeta \omega )$ is smooth on a neighborhood of the closed disc $|\zeta |\leq R$ in $\mathbb C$, and by ( 7.5 ) its Laplacian is \[  \Delta v_\omega (\zeta )=4\sum _{j,k}u_{j ar k}(a+\zeta \omega )\, \omega _ j ar\omega _ k\geq 0,  \] because the complex Hessian of the smooth plurisubharmonic function $u$ is positive semidefinite (proposition 8.2.2 (1)). Let $m_\omega (r)=(2\pi )^{-1}\int _0^{2\pi }v_\omega (r\mathrm e^{\mathrm i	heta })\, \mathrm d	heta $ be the circle means of $v_\omega $ about $0$; they are the spherical means of $v_\omega $ in $\mathbb R^2$, because surface measure on the unit circle is arc length (section 6.4 ). By proposition 2.1.1 in $\mathbb R^2$, where $s_1=2\pi $, and the same substitution, \[   rac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}m_\omega (\mathrm e^{t/2})= rac1{4\pi }\int _{|\zeta |<\mathrm e^{t/2}}\Delta v_\omega \, \mathrm dV_2,  \] which is nondecreasing in $t$ because $\Delta v_\omega \geq 0$. By the mean value theorem, a differentiable function with nondecreasing derivative is convex; so $t\mapsto m_\omega (\mathrm e^{t/2})$ is convex. Surface measure on $S^{2n-1}$ is invariant under the orthogonal transformations $\omega \mapsto \mathrm e^{\mathrm i	heta }\omega $ of $\mathbb R^{2n}$ (section 2.1 ), so $\int _{S^{2n-1}}u(a+r\omega )\, \mathrm dS(\omega )=\int _{S^{2n-1}}u(a+r\mathrm e^{\mathrm i	heta }\omega )\, \mathrm dS(\omega )$ for every $	heta $. Averaging over $	heta \in [0,2\pi ]$ and using Fubini's theorem for the continuous integrand, we obtain \[  M_ u(a,r)= rac1{s_{2n-1}}\int _{S^{2n-1}}m_\omega (r)\, \mathrm dS(\omega ),\qquad 0<r<R.  \] An average of convex functions is convex, so $t\mapsto M_ u(a,\mathrm e^{t/2})$ is convex, and $D_ u(a,\cdot )$ is nondecreasing on $(0,R)$. Step 2: approximation. For general $u$, let $u_\varepsilon =u*ho _\varepsilon $ be the regularizations of ( 3.3 ). For small $\varepsilon $ they are defined on a neighborhood of the compact set $\overline{B(a,R)}$, and by proposition 8.2.2 (2) they are smooth and plurisubharmonic there and decrease to $u$ as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. Subtracting a constant, which changes neither side of ( 12.4 ), nor $D_ u$, nor the Lelong number, we may assume $u_\varepsilon \leq 0$ on $\overline{B(a,R)}$ for all small $\varepsilon $. For $0\leq \eta <1$ put $\kappa _\eta =(1-\eta )/(1+\eta )^{2n-1}$. If $0<r<R$ and $|x-a|\leq \eta r$, the explicit formula ( 2.14 ) shows that the Poisson kernel $P$ of $B(a,r)$ satisfies $P(x,\zeta )\geq \kappa _\eta P(a,\zeta )=\kappa _\eta /(s_{2n-1}r^{2n-1})$ for $\zeta \in \partial B(a,r)$. Fix $0<r<R$ and choose $b\in B(a,r)$ with $u(b)>-\infty $, which is possible since the pole set of $u$ has measure zero; let $\eta =|b-a|/r$. By the maximum principle (proposition 3.1.4 ), applied to $u_\varepsilon $ minus the Poisson integral of its boundary values (theorem 2.3.1 ), we have $u_\varepsilon (x)\leq \int _{\partial B(a,r)}P(x,\zeta )u_\varepsilon (\zeta )\, \mathrm dS(\zeta )$ for $x\in B(a,r)$. At $x=b$, since $u_\varepsilon \leq 0$, this gives \[  u(b)\leq u_\varepsilon (b)\leq \kappa _\eta M_{u_\varepsilon }(a,r).  \] Thus the integrals of the nonnegative functions $-u_\varepsilon $ over the sphere are bounded independently of $\varepsilon $. As $-u_\varepsilon $ increases to $-u$, the monotone convergence theorem shows that $M_ u(a,r)$ is finite and $M_{u_\varepsilon }(a,r)	o M_ u(a,r)$. For fixed $x\in B(a,r)$ the kernel $P(x,\cdot )$ is positive and bounded on $\partial B(a,r)$, so the same argument, applied to the functions $-P(x,\cdot )u_\varepsilon $, lets us pass to the limit in the Poisson inequality, and we obtain $u(x)\leq \int _{\partial B(a,r)}P(x,\zeta )u(\zeta )\, \mathrm dS(\zeta )$ for $x\in B(a,r)$. Since the functions $u_\varepsilon $ decrease to the locally integrable function $u$, the monotone convergence theorem, applied to $u_{\varepsilon _0}-u_\varepsilon $ for a fixed $\varepsilon _0$, shows that $u_\varepsilon 	o u$ in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$; hence the positive measures $\Delta u_\varepsilon $ converge to $\mu $ in the sense of distributions, hence vaguely (proposition 1.5.1 ). By proposition 1.5.2 , $\Delta u_\varepsilon (B(a,r))	o \mu (B(a,r))$ for every radius $r$ with $\mu (\partial B(a,r))=0$; since the spheres $\partial B(a,r)$, $0<r<R$, are disjoint and $\mu $ is finite on $B(a,R)$, only countably many radii are excluded (lemma 1.1.5 ). Moreover, if $r_2<R$ and $\chi \in C^\infty _ c$ is a cutoff function with values in $[0,1]$, equal to one on $B(a,r_2)$, with support in a neighborhood of $\overline{B(a,R)}$ on which all $u_\varepsilon $ with small $\varepsilon $ are defined, then $\Delta u_\varepsilon (B(a,r_2))\leq \int \chi \, \Delta u_\varepsilon 	o \int \chi \, \mathrm d\mu $, so these masses are bounded uniformly in $\varepsilon $. By Step 1 each $D_{u_\varepsilon }(a,\cdot )$ is nondecreasing; letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, we see that $D_ u(a,\cdot )$ is nondecreasing on the dense set of radii with $\mu (\partial B(a,r))=0$, and hence on $(0,R)$, because $r\mapsto \mu (B(a,r))$ is left continuous. Finally, ( 12.4 ) holds for each $u_\varepsilon $ by Step 1. As $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, its left side converges to $M_ u(a,r_2)-M_ u(a,r_1)$, while the integrands on the right converge for all but countably many $t$ and are bounded uniformly in $\varepsilon $; dominated convergence gives ( 12.4 ) for $u$. Step 3: the limits. The nondecreasing nonnegative function $D_ u(a,\cdot )$ has a limit $\ell =\lim _{r\downarrow 0}D_ u(a,r)\in [0,\infty )$. Put $g(t)=M_ u(a,\mathrm e^{t/2})$ and fix $t_0<\log R^2$. Given $\delta >0$, choose $s_\delta <\min \{ t_0,0\} $ with $D_ u(a,\mathrm e^{s/2})\leq \ell +\delta $ for $s\leq s_\delta $. For $t<s_\delta $, ( 12.4 ) and the monotonicity of $D_ u(a,\cdot )$ give \[  \ell (t_0-t)\leq g(t_0)-g(t)\leq (\ell +\delta )(s_\delta -t)+(t_0-s_\delta )D_ u(a,\mathrm e^{t_0/2}).  \] Dividing by $-t>0$ and letting $t	o -\infty $, we see that all limit points of $g(t)/t$ lie in $[\ell ,\ell +\delta ]$. Hence $M_ u(a,r)/\log r^2	o \ell $ as $r\downarrow 0$. It remains to show that $\ell =
u (u,a)$. Let $0<\eta <1$. For $x\in B(a,\eta r)$, the Poisson inequality of Step 2 and the kernel bound give, since $u\leq 0$, \[  u(x)\leq \int _{\partial B(a,r)}P(x,\zeta )u(\zeta )\, \mathrm dS(\zeta ) \leq \kappa _\eta M_ u(a,r).  \] Together with $M_ u(a,r)\leq \sup _{\partial B(a,r)}u=N(\log r^2)$, where $N$ is as in proposition 12.1.1 , we obtain \[  N(\log (\eta ^2r^2))\leq \kappa _\eta M_ u(a,r), \qquad M_ u(a,r)\leq N(\log r^2).  \] We divide by $\log r^2<0$ and let $r\downarrow 0$. Since $\log (\eta ^2r^2)/\log r^2	o 1$, this gives $
u (u,a)\geq \kappa _\eta \ell $ and $\ell \geq 
u (u,a)$. Letting $\eta \downarrow 0$, so that $\kappa _\eta 	o 1$, we conclude that $\ell =
u (u,a)$, which proves ( 12.5 ). $\square$ Proposition 12.1.4 . Let $n\geq 1$, let $u$ and $v$ be plurisubharmonic on a neighborhood $U$ of $a\in \mathbb C^ n$, and let $b>0$. Then \[   egin{aligned}

u (u,a)+
u (v,a),& 
u (bu,a)& =b
u (u,a),\  
u (\max \{ u,v\} ,a)& =\min \{ 
u (u,a),
u (v,a)\} . \end{aligned}  \] If $(u_ i)_{i\in I}$ is a nonempty family of plurisubharmonic functions on $U$ that is locally uniformly bounded above, and $u=(\sup _ iu_ i)^*$, then $
u (u,a)=\inf _ i
u (u_ i,a)$. If $u_ j$, $j\geq 1$, and $u$ are plurisubharmonic on $U$, $u_ j	o u$ in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$, and $a_ j	o a$, then 12.8  egin{equation} \label{eq:lelong-upper-semicontinuity} \varlimsup _ j
u (u_ j,a_ j)\leq 
u (u,a). \end{equation} Finally, for a holomorphic germ $f
ot\equiv 0$ at $a$, $
u (\log |f|^2,a)=\operatorname {ord}_ af$, where the order $\operatorname {ord}_ af$ of $f$ at $a$ is the degree of the first nonzero homogeneous term of its Taylor expansion at $a$ (section A.1 ); moreover $
u (\log |z-a|^2,a)=1$. Proof. By ( 12.5 ), $
u (w,a)=\lim _{r\downarrow 0}M_ w(a,r)/\log r^2$ for every plurisubharmonic $w$ near $a$, and the spherical means involved are finite and linear in $w$; this proves the formulas for $u+v$ and $bu$. If $w_1\leq w_2+O(1)$ near $a$, then $
u (w_1,a)\geq 
u (w_2,a)$ by the characterization in proposition 12.1.1 ; hence $
u (\max \{ u,v\} ,a)\leq \min \{ 
u (u,a),
u (v,a)\} $. Conversely, choose $r_0>0$ with $\overline{B(a,r_0)}\subset U$. By ( 12.2 ), and since the logarithm $\log (|z-a|^2/r_0^2)$ is negative on $B(a,r_0)\setminus \{ a\} $, both $u$ and $v$, and hence $\max \{ u,v\} $, are bounded there by $c\log (|z-a|^2/r_0^2)+C$ with $c=\min \{ 
u (u,a),
u (v,a)\} $ and a constant $C$. This gives the reverse inequality. For the family, $u$ is plurisubharmonic by theorem 8.3.2 . Choose $r_0$ as above, a common upper bound $C$ for the $u_ i$ on $B(a,r_0)$, and put $c=\inf _ i
u (u_ i,a)$. By ( 12.2 ), again using that the logarithm is negative, $u_ i(z)\leq c\log (|z-a|^2/r_0^2)+C$ for $0<|z-a|<r_0$ and all $i$. The supremum of the $u_ i$ satisfies the same bound, and so does its upper semicontinuous regularization $u$ on $B(a,r_0)\setminus \{ a\} $, because the bound is continuous there. Hence $
u (u,a)\geq c$ by the characterization in proposition 12.1.1 . Conversely $u\geq u_ i$ gives $
u (u,a)\leq 
u (u_ i,a)$ for every $i$. For ( 12.8 ), note that $\Delta u_ j	o \Delta u$ in the sense of distributions, because $u_ j	o u$ in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$; hence the positive measures $\Delta u_ j$ converge vaguely to $\Delta u$ (proposition 1.5.1 ). Fix $0<r<R$ with $\overline{B(a,R)}\subset U$ and $\Delta u(\partial B(a,r))=0$, and let $0<ho <r$. Then $B(a_ j,ho )\subset B(a,r)$ for all large $j$. Letting $r\downarrow 0$ through such radii and using ( 12.5 ) proves ( 12.8 ). Finally, let $k=\operatorname {ord}_ af$, and let $P_ k

Since $|P_ k(w)|\leq c_1|w|^ k$, with equality for some $w$ on every sphere $|w|=r$, we obtain $r^ k(c_1-Cr)\leq \sup _{|w|=r}|f(a+w)|\leq r^ k(c_1+Cr)$. By proposition 12.1.1 , $N(\log r^2)$ is the supremum of $\log |f|^2$ over the sphere $|z-a|=r$, so $N(\log r^2)=k\log r^2+O(1)$ as $r\downarrow 0$, and $

title: Lelong logarithmic growth
text:
Proposition 12.1.1 . Let $n\geq 1$ and let $u$ be a plurisubharmonic function on a neighborhood of $a\in \mathbb C^ n$. For sufficiently negative $t$ put \[  N(t)=\sup _{|z-a|<\exp (t/2)}u(z).  \] Then $N$ is finite, nondecreasing and convex, $N(t)$ is also the supremum of $u$ over the sphere $|z-a|=\exp (t/2)$, and the limit 12.1  egin{equation} \label{eq:lelong-growth-definition} 
u (u,a)=\lim _{t	o -\infty } rac{N(t)}{t} \end{equation} exists in $[0,\infty )$; it is zero if $u(a)>-\infty $. For every $r_0>0$ such that $\overline{B(a,r_0)}$ lies in the domain of $u$, 12.2  egin{equation} \label{eq:lelong-attained-growth} u(z)\leq 
u (u,a)\log  rac{|z-a|^2}{r_0^2} +\sup _{B(a,r_0)}u,\qquad 0<|z-a|<r_0. \end{equation} Consequently $
u (u,a)$ is the largest $c\geq 0$ for which $u(z)\leq c\log |z-a|^2+O(1)$ near $a$; moreover, if $c\geq 0$ and $u(z)\leq c\log |z-a|^2+C$ for all $z$ outside a Lebesgue null set in some neighborhood of $a$, then $
u (u,a)\geq c$. The Lelong number does not change under a holomorphic change of coordinates, nor under the addition of a bounded function, provided the resulting function is plurisubharmonic. Proof. We may assume $a=0$. Let $R_*\in (0,\infty ]$ be the supremum of the radii $r$ for which $\overline{B(0,r)}$ lies in the domain of $u$; since closed balls are compact, $\overline{B(0,r)}$ lies in the domain exactly when $0<r<R_*$. For such $r$ put $S(r)=\sup _{|z|=r}u(z)$. This number is less than $+\infty $ because $u$ is upper semicontinuous and hence bounded above on the compact sphere. It is also greater than $-\infty $. Otherwise, for every unit vector $e$, the function $\zeta \mapsto u(\zeta e)$, which is subharmonic or identically $-\infty $ near the closed disc $|\zeta |\leq r$, would be $-\infty $ on the circle $|\zeta |=r$ and hence, by upper semicontinuity, have upper limits $-\infty $ there; the maximum principle (proposition 3.1.4 ), applied to $\zeta \mapsto u(\zeta e)+k$ for every $k>0$, would give $u=-\infty $ on the disc. Thus $u$ would be identically $-\infty $ on $B(0,r)$, which is impossible because $u$ is locally integrable (theorem 8.2.1 ). Let $0<r_1<r_2<r_3<R_*$, and let $h(\zeta )=A+B\log |\zeta |^2$ be the harmonic function on $\mathbb C\setminus \{ 0\} $ equal to $S(r_1)$ on $|\zeta |=r_1$ and to $S(r_3)$ on $|\zeta |=r_3$. For every unit vector $e$, the function $\zeta \mapsto u(\zeta e)-h(\zeta )$ is subharmonic or identically $-\infty $ near the closed annulus $r_1\leq |\zeta |\leq r_3$, and by upper semicontinuity its upper limits at the two boundary circles are at most $0$; by the maximum principle (proposition 3.1.4 ) it is at most $0$ on the annulus. Taking the supremum over $e$ on the circle $|\zeta |=r_2$ gives $S(r_2)\leq h(r_2)$. Since $h(r_2)$ is the value at $\log r_2^2$ of the affine function of $\log r^2$ that equals $S(r_1)$ and $S(r_3)$ at $\log r_1^2$ and $\log r_3^2$, this says that $S$ is a convex function of $\log r^2$ on $(0,R_*)$. Applying the maximum principle in the same way to $\zeta \mapsto u(\zeta e)-S(r)$ on the disc $|\zeta |\leq r$, we obtain $u(\zeta e)\leq S(r)$ for $|\zeta |\leq r$; hence $S$ is nondecreasing and $u(0)\leq S(r)$. A finite convex function on an open interval is continuous, since on a compact subinterval its difference quotients are bounded between two fixed difference quotients taken outside the subinterval. Hence $\sup _{B(0,r)}u=\sup _{ho <r}S(ho )=S(r)$, so that $N(t)=S(\mathrm e^{t/2})$ for $t<\log R_*^2$; this proves the assertions about $N$. Fix $r_0$ as in the statement and put $t_0=\log r_0^2$. Since $N$ is convex and nondecreasing on $(-\infty ,t_0]$, the difference quotients $(N(t_0)-N(t))/(t_0-t)$ are nonnegative and decrease as $t\downarrow -\infty $; let $c\in [0,\infty )$ be their limit. Writing $N(t)=N(t_0)-(t_0-t)\cdot  rac{N(t_0)-N(t)}{t_0-t}$ and dividing by $t$, we obtain $N(t)/t	o c$ as $t	o -\infty $. In particular $c$ does not depend on $t_0$, so for every fixed $s\leq t_0$ the quotients $(N(s)-N(s'))/(s-s')$ also tend to $c$ as $s'	o -\infty $. If $s'<s<t\leq t_0$, convexity gives $(N(t)-N(s))/(t-s)\geq (N(s)-N(s'))/(s-s')$; letting $s'	o -\infty $, we see that every difference quotient of $N$ on $(-\infty ,t_0]$ is at least $c$. Hence $N(t)-ct$ is nondecreasing, and $N(t)\leq c(t-t_0)+N(t_0)$ for $t<t_0$. Since $u(z)\leq S(|z|)=N(\log |z|^2)$, this is ( 12.2 ). Since $u(0)\leq S(r)$ for all $r$, we have $N(t)\geq u(0)$, hence $N(t)/t\leq u(0)/t$ for $t<0$, and $c=0$ if $u(0)>-\infty $. Conversely, if $c'\geq 0$ and $u(z)\leq c'\log |z|^2+C$ for $0<|z|<r'$, then $N(t)=S(\mathrm e^{t/2})\leq c't+C$ for all sufficiently negative $t$, and division by $t<0$ gives $c\geq c'$. This proves the characterization of $
u (u,a)$ as the largest admissible coefficient. Now let $c\geq 0$, and suppose that $u(z)\leq c\log |z|^2+C$ for all $z\in B(0,r)\setminus A$, where $\overline{B(0,r)}$ lies in the domain of $u$ and $A$ is a Lebesgue null set. Let $0<|z|<r/2$ and $0<\delta <|z|/2$. The function $u$ is subharmonic (theorem 8.2.1 ), so theorem 3.1.3 gives $u(z)\leq |B(z,\delta )|^{-1}\int _{B(z,\delta )}u\, \mathrm dV$. Every $y\in B(z,\delta )\setminus A$ satisfies $u(y)\leq c\log (|z|+\delta )^2+C$, because $c\geq 0$ and $|y|\leq |z|+\delta $; since $A$ is a null set, we obtain $u(z)\leq c\log (|z|+\delta )^2+C$. Letting $\delta \downarrow 0$, we get $u(z)\leq c\log |z|^2+C$ for $0<|z|<r/2$, and the converse part of the characterization gives $
u (u,0)\geq c$. Let $F$ be a biholomorphic map from a neighborhood of $a$ onto a neighborhood of $F(a)$; by proposition 8.2.3 , $u\circ F^{-1}$ is plurisubharmonic near $F(a)$. The maps $F$ and $F^{-1}$ are continuously differentiable, hence Lipschitz near $a$ and $F(a)$, so $\log |F(z)-F(a)|^2-\log |z-a|^2$ is bounded near $a$, $z
eq a$. Since adding a bounded function also changes $u$ by a bounded amount, in both cases the characterization just proved shows that the Lelong number is unchanged. $\square$

title: Lelong growth definition
text: 12.1 \begin{equation} \label{eq:lelong-growth-definition} \nu (u,a)=\lim _{t\to -\infty }\frac{N(t)}{t} \end{equation}

title: Lelong attained growth
text: 12.2 \begin{equation} \label{eq:lelong-attained-growth} u(z)\leq \nu (u,a)\log \frac{|z-a|^2}{r_0^2} +\sup _{B(a,r_0)}u,\qquad 0<|z-a|<r_0. \end{equation}

title: Lelong number
text:
Definition 12.1.2 . The number $
u (u,a)$ in ( 12.1 ) is the Lelong number of $u$ at $a$. If $u$ is plurisubharmonic on a complex manifold $X$ that has positive dimension at $a$, we compute $
u (u,a)$ in a holomorphic chart at $a$; by proposition 12.1.1 the result does not depend on the chart. If $X$ has dimension zero at $a$, where plurisubharmonic functions are finite, we set $
u (u,a)=0$. For a closed positive $(1,1)$-current $T$ on $X$ we put $
u (T,a)=
u (u,a)$, where $u$ is a plurisubharmonic potential of $T$ near $a$, that is, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=T$. Such potentials exist, and two of them differ near $a$ by a smooth pluriharmonic function: by theorem 8.2.1 , the plurisubharmonic potentials of $T$ on a coordinate ball are exactly its canonical local potentials, to which theorem 7.3.2 applies. Since a smooth function is bounded near $a$, $
u (T,a)$ does not depend on the choice of the potential.

title: Lelong ball density
text: 12.3 \begin{equation} \label{eq:lelong-ball-density} D_ u(a,r)=\frac{\mu (B(a,r))}{2s_{2n-1}r^{2n-2}} =\frac1{r^{2n-2}}\int _{B(a,r)}\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\wedge (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|z|^2)^{n-1}. \end{equation}

title: Jensen–Lelong
text:
Theorem 12.1.3 (Jensen–Lelong) . Let $n\geq 1$, $R>0$, and let $u$ be plurisubharmonic on a neighborhood of $\overline{B(a,R)}\subset \mathbb C^ n$. Then the spherical mean $M_ u(a,r)$ of $u$ over $\partial B(a,r)$ is finite for every $0<r<R$, the function $r\mapsto D_ u(a,r)$ is nondecreasing on $(0,R)$, and 12.4  egin{equation} \label{eq:euclidean-jensen-lelong} M_ u(a,r_2)-M_ u(a,r_1) =\int _{\log r_1^2}^{\log r_2^2}D_ u(a,\exp (t/2))\, \mathrm dt, \qquad 0<r_1<r_2<R. \end{equation} In particular, 12.5  egin{equation} \label{eq:lelong-density-limit} 
u (u,a)=\lim _{r\downarrow 0}D_ u(a,r) =\lim _{r\downarrow 0} rac{M_ u(a,r)}{\log r^2}. \end{equation} Proof. Step 1: smooth functions. Suppose first that $u$ is smooth. By proposition 2.1.1 in $\mathbb R^{2n}$ and the substitution $r=\mathrm e^{t/2}$, for which $\mathrm dr/\mathrm dt=r/2$, \[   rac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}M_ u(a,\mathrm e^{t/2}) = rac r2\cdot  rac{\mu (B(a,r))}{s_{2n-1}r^{2n-1}} =D_ u(a,\mathrm e^{t/2}),  \] and ( 12.4 ) follows by integration, since $\mu =\Delta u\, \mathrm dV$ has a continuous density, so that the right side is continuous in $t$. To see that $D_ u(a,\cdot )$ is nondecreasing, we show that $t\mapsto M_ u(a,\mathrm e^{t/2})$ is a convex function on $(-\infty ,\log R^2)$; the derivative of a differentiable convex function is nondecreasing. For a unit vector $\omega \in S^{2n-1}$, the function $v_\omega (\zeta )=u(a+\zeta \omega )$ is smooth on a neighborhood of the closed disc $|\zeta |\leq R$ in $\mathbb C$, and by ( 7.5 ) its Laplacian is \[  \Delta v_\omega (\zeta )=4\sum _{j,k}u_{j ar k}(a+\zeta \omega )\, \omega _ j ar\omega _ k\geq 0,  \] because the complex Hessian of the smooth plurisubharmonic function $u$ is positive semidefinite (proposition 8.2.2 (1)). Let $m_\omega (r)=(2\pi )^{-1}\int _0^{2\pi }v_\omega (r\mathrm e^{\mathrm i	heta })\, \mathrm d	heta $ be the circle means of $v_\omega $ about $0$; they are the spherical means of $v_\omega $ in $\mathbb R^2$, because surface measure on the unit circle is arc length (section 6.4 ). By proposition 2.1.1 in $\mathbb R^2$, where $s_1=2\pi $, and the same substitution, \[   rac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}m_\omega (\mathrm e^{t/2})= rac1{4\pi }\int _{|\zeta |<\mathrm e^{t/2}}\Delta v_\omega \, \mathrm dV_2,  \] which is nondecreasing in $t$ because $\Delta v_\omega \geq 0$. By the mean value theorem, a differentiable function with nondecreasing derivative is convex; so $t\mapsto m_\omega (\mathrm e^{t/2})$ is convex. Surface measure on $S^{2n-1}$ is invariant under the orthogonal transformations $\omega \mapsto \mathrm e^{\mathrm i	heta }\omega $ of $\mathbb R^{2n}$ (section 2.1 ), so $\int _{S^{2n-1}}u(a+r\omega )\, \mathrm dS(\omega )=\int _{S^{2n-1}}u(a+r\mathrm e^{\mathrm i	heta }\omega )\, \mathrm dS(\omega )$ for every $	heta $. Averaging over $	heta \in [0,2\pi ]$ and using Fubini's theorem for the continuous integrand, we obtain \[  M_ u(a,r)= rac1{s_{2n-1}}\int _{S^{2n-1}}m_\omega (r)\, \mathrm dS(\omega ),\qquad 0<r<R.  \] An average of convex functions is convex, so $t\mapsto M_ u(a,\mathrm e^{t/2})$ is convex, and $D_ u(a,\cdot )$ is nondecreasing on $(0,R)$. Step 2: approximation. For general $u$, let $u_\varepsilon =u*ho _\varepsilon $ be the regularizations of ( 3.3 ). For small $\varepsilon $ they are defined on a neighborhood of the compact set $\overline{B(a,R)}$, and by proposition 8.2.2 (2) they are smooth and plurisubharmonic there and decrease to $u$ as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. Subtracting a constant, which changes neither side of ( 12.4 ), nor $D_ u$, nor the Lelong number, we may assume $u_\varepsilon \leq 0$ on $\overline{B(a,R)}$ for all small $\varepsilon $. For $0\leq \eta <1$ put $\kappa _\eta =(1-\eta )/(1+\eta )^{2n-1}$. If $0<r<R$ and $|x-a|\leq \eta r$, the explicit formula ( 2.14 ) shows that the Poisson kernel $P$ of $B(a,r)$ satisfies $P(x,\zeta )\geq \kappa _\eta P(a,\zeta )=\kappa _\eta /(s_{2n-1}r^{2n-1})$ for $\zeta \in \partial B(a,r)$. Fix $0<r<R$ and choose $b\in B(a,r)$ with $u(b)>-\infty $, which is possible since the pole set of $u$ has measure zero; let $\eta =|b-a|/r$. By the maximum principle (proposition 3.1.4 ), applied to $u_\varepsilon $ minus the Poisson integral of its boundary values (theorem 2.3.1 ), we have $u_\varepsilon (x)\leq \int _{\partial B(a,r)}P(x,\zeta )u_\varepsilon (\zeta )\, \mathrm dS(\zeta )$ for $x\in B(a,r)$. At $x=b$, since $u_\varepsilon \leq 0$, this gives \[  u(b)\leq u_\varepsilon (b)\leq \kappa _\eta M_{u_\varepsilon }(a,r).  \] Thus the integrals of the nonnegative functions $-u_\varepsilon $ over the sphere are bounded independently of $\varepsilon $. As $-u_\varepsilon $ increases to $-u$, the monotone convergence theorem shows that $M_ u(a,r)$ is finite and $M_{u_\varepsilon }(a,r)	o M_ u(a,r)$. For fixed $x\in B(a,r)$ the kernel $P(x,\cdot )$ is positive and bounded on $\partial B(a,r)$, so the same argument, applied to the functions $-P(x,\cdot )u_\varepsilon $, lets us pass to the limit in the Poisson inequality, and we obtain $u(x)\leq \int _{\partial B(a,r)}P(x,\zeta )u(\zeta )\, \mathrm dS(\zeta )$ for $x\in B(a,r)$. Since the functions $u_\varepsilon $ decrease to the locally integrable function $u$, the monotone convergence theorem, applied to $u_{\varepsilon _0}-u_\varepsilon $ for a fixed $\varepsilon _0$, shows that $u_\varepsilon 	o u$ in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$; hence the positive measures $\Delta u_\varepsilon $ converge to $\mu $ in the sense of distributions, hence vaguely (proposition 1.5.1 ). By proposition 1.5.2 , $\Delta u_\varepsilon (B(a,r))	o \mu (B(a,r))$ for every radius $r$ with $\mu (\partial B(a,r))=0$; since the spheres $\partial B(a,r)$, $0<r<R$, are disjoint and $\mu $ is finite on $B(a,R)$, only countably many radii are excluded (lemma 1.1.5 ). Moreover, if $r_2<R$ and $\chi \in C^\infty _ c$ is a cutoff function with values in $[0,1]$, equal to one on $B(a,r_2)$, with support in a neighborhood of $\overline{B(a,R)}$ on which all $u_\varepsilon $ with small $\varepsilon $ are defined, then $\Delta u_\varepsilon (B(a,r_2))\leq \int \chi \, \Delta u_\varepsilon 	o \int \chi \, \mathrm d\mu $, so these masses are bounded uniformly in $\varepsilon $. By Step 1 each $D_{u_\varepsilon }(a,\cdot )$ is nondecreasing; letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, we see that $D_ u(a,\cdot )$ is nondecreasing on the dense set of radii with $\mu (\partial B(a,r))=0$, and hence on $(0,R)$, because $r\mapsto \mu (B(a,r))$ is left continuous. Finally, ( 12.4 ) holds for each $u_\varepsilon $ by Step 1. As $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, its left side converges to $M_ u(a,r_2)-M_ u(a,r_1)$, while the integrands on the right converge for all but countably many $t$ and are bounded uniformly in $\varepsilon $; dominated convergence gives ( 12.4 ) for $u$. Step 3: the limits. The nondecreasing nonnegative function $D_ u(a,\cdot )$ has a limit $\ell =\lim _{r\downarrow 0}D_ u(a,r)\in [0,\infty )$. Put $g(t)=M_ u(a,\mathrm e^{t/2})$ and fix $t_0<\log R^2$. Given $\delta >0$, choose $s_\delta <\min \{ t_0,0\} $ with $D_ u(a,\mathrm e^{s/2})\leq \ell +\delta $ for $s\leq s_\delta $. For $t<s_\delta $, ( 12.4 ) and the monotonicity of $D_ u(a,\cdot )$ give \[  \ell (t_0-t)\leq g(t_0)-g(t)\leq (\ell +\delta )(s_\delta -t)+(t_0-s_\delta )D_ u(a,\mathrm e^{t_0/2}).  \] Dividing by $-t>0$ and letting $t	o -\infty $, we see that all limit points of $g(t)/t$ lie in $[\ell ,\ell +\delta ]$. Hence $M_ u(a,r)/\log r^2	o \ell $ as $r\downarrow 0$. It remains to show that $\ell =
u (u,a)$. Let $0<\eta <1$. For $x\in B(a,\eta r)$, the Poisson inequality of Step 2 and the kernel bound give, since $u\leq 0$, \[  u(x)\leq \int _{\partial B(a,r)}P(x,\zeta )u(\zeta )\, \mathrm dS(\zeta ) \leq \kappa _\eta M_ u(a,r).  \] Together with $M_ u(a,r)\leq \sup _{\partial B(a,r)}u=N(\log r^2)$, where $N$ is as in proposition 12.1.1 , we obtain \[  N(\log (\eta ^2r^2))\leq \kappa _\eta M_ u(a,r), \qquad M_ u(a,r)\leq N(\log r^2).  \] We divide by $\log r^2<0$ and let $r\downarrow 0$. title: Coherent ideals from weighted integrability
text:
12.2 Coherent ideals from weighted integrability From now on $X$ denotes a complex manifold, and $n\geq 0$ its dimension at the point under consideration. We also narrow a term of chapter 11 : a weight on $X$ is now a plurisubharmonic function on $X$, a special case of the measurable weights of section 11.3 ; in particular, a weight is not identically $-\infty $ on any connected component of $X$. Restrictions of weights to submanifolds may be identically $-\infty $ on some components, and definition 12.2.5 allows this case. Local integrability on $X$ refers to Lebesgue measure in holomorphic charts, or equivalently to any smooth positive volume form, since the densities of two such measures with respect to each other are bounded above and below by positive constants on compact subsets of a chart. To pass from a Hilbert space of holomorphic functions to a coherent ideal sheaf we need two facts from local algebra, the Krull intersection theorem and the strong Noetherian property of coherent sheaves. We prove them first, the second by induction on the dimension with the help of Weierstrass polynomials. Lemma 12.2.1 . Let $x\in X$, let $R=\mathcal O_{X,x}$ with maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$, and let $E$ be a submodule of a finitely generated $R$-module $F$. Then \[   igcap _{k\geq 1}(E+\mathfrak m^ kF)=E.  \] In particular, if a sequence of holomorphic functions on a neighborhood of $x$ converges locally uniformly and the germs at $x$ of all its members belong to an ideal $J\subset R$, then the germ of the limit belongs to $J$. Proof. We derive the intersection formula from the Artin–Rees lemma, after collecting the facts about Noetherian rings that we need. A commutative ring $A$ is Noetherian if all its ideals are finitely generated. Let $A$ be Noetherian. (i) Every submodule $N$ of $A^ r$, $r\geq 1$, is finitely generated. For $r=1$ this is the definition. Let $r\geq 2$. The last coordinates of the elements of $N$ form an ideal of $A$; choose $v_1,\ldots ,v_ q\in N$ whose last coordinates generate it, and, by induction on $r$, finitely many generators of the submodule $N\cap (A^{r-1}	imes \{ 0\} )$, which is a submodule of $A^{r-1}$. If $v\in N$, subtracting from $v$ a combination of the $v_ i$ with the same last coordinate leaves an element of $N\cap (A^{r-1}	imes \{ 0\} )$; hence these finitely many elements generate $N$. (ii) Every submodule $N$ of a finitely generated $A$-module $M$ is finitely generated. Indeed, let $\pi \colon A^ r	o M$ map the standard basis to generators of $M$. By (i), the submodule $\pi ^{-1}(N)$ of $A^ r$ is finitely generated, and the images of its generators generate $N=\pi (\pi ^{-1}(N))$. (iii) The polynomial ring $A[t]$ is Noetherian (Hilbert's basis theorem). Let $I\subset A[t]$ be a nonzero ideal. The leading coefficients of the nonzero elements of $I$, together with $0$, form an ideal of $A$: if $f,g\in I$ have degrees $d\leq e$ and leading coefficients $a,b$ with $a+b
eq 0$, then $t^{e-d}f+g\in I$ has leading coefficient $a+b$, and if $c\in A$ with $ca
eq 0$, then $cf\in I$ has leading coefficient $ca$. Choose $p_1,\ldots ,p_ k\in I$ whose leading coefficients generate this ideal, and let $d_0$ be the largest of their degrees. If $f\in I$ has degree $d\geq d_0$, its leading coefficient is $\sum _ ia_ ic_ i$ for some $a_ i\in A$, where $c_ i$ is the leading coefficient of $p_ i$, and $f-\sum _ ia_ it^{d-\deg p_ i}p_ i$ is an element of $I$ of smaller degree. Repeating this, we see that $f$ differs from an element of $I\cap (A+At+\cdots +At^{d_0-1})$ by an element of the ideal generated by $p_1,\ldots ,p_ k$. The set $I\cap (A+At+\cdots +At^{d_0-1})$ is a submodule of the $A$-module $A+At+\cdots +At^{d_0-1}\cong A^{d_0}$, finitely generated by (i). Hence $I$ is generated by $p_1,\ldots ,p_ k$ and finitely many further elements. (iv) If $I\subset A$ is an ideal, then $A/I$ is Noetherian, since the ideals of $A/I$ are the images of the ideals of $A$ containing $I$. Hence, by (iii) and induction on the number of variables, every quotient of a polynomial ring in finitely many variables over $A$ is Noetherian. All this applies to $A=R$, which is Noetherian by proposition A.1.2 , since a holomorphic chart at $x$ identifies $R$ with $\mathcal O_ n$. Next we prove the Artin–Rees lemma. If $\mathfrak m=0$, which happens only in dimension zero, the lemma is trivial; so let $\mathfrak m
eq 0$, and choose generators $\xi _1,\ldots ,\xi _ p$ of $\mathfrak m$. Consider the subring $\mathcal R= igoplus _{k\geq 0}\mathfrak m^ kt^ k$ of $R[t]$, consisting of the polynomials whose coefficient of $t^ k$ lies in $\mathfrak m^ k$, where $\mathfrak m^0=R$. Since $\mathfrak m^ k$ is generated by the monomials of degree $k$ in $\xi _1,\ldots ,\xi _ p$, the ring $\mathcal R$ is the image of the homomorphism $R[T_1,\ldots ,T_ p]	o R[t]$, $T_ i\mapsto \xi _ it$, and it is Noetherian by (iii) and (iv). In the $\mathcal R$-module of polynomials in $t$ with coefficients in $F$, consider the submodule $ igoplus _{k\geq 0}\mathfrak m^ kFt^ k$. It is generated over $\mathcal R$ by generators of $F$ placed in degree zero, and it contains the submodule $\mathcal E= igoplus _{k\geq 0}(E\cap \mathfrak m^ kF)t^ k$, because $\mathfrak m^ j(E\cap \mathfrak m^ kF)\subset E\cap \mathfrak m^{j+k}F$. By (ii), $\mathcal E$ is finitely generated. The homogeneous components of the elements of $\mathcal E$ again belong to $\mathcal E$, so the homogeneous components of finitely many generators generate $\mathcal E$; let these be $e_1t^{d_1},\ldots ,e_ lt^{d_ l}$ with $e_ i\in E\cap \mathfrak m^{d_ i}F$, and let $s=\max _ id_ i$. For $k\geq s$ this gives the Artin–Rees equality \[  E\cap \mathfrak m^ kF=\mathfrak m^{k-s}(E\cap \mathfrak m^ sF).  \] Indeed, let $y\in E\cap \mathfrak m^ kF$, and write $yt^ k=\sum _ iho _ ie_ it^{d_ i}$ with $ho _ i\in \mathcal R$. Comparing the coefficients of $t^ k$, we may replace each $ho _ i$ by its term of degree $k-d_ i$, which is $a_ it^{k-d_ i}$ with $a_ i\in \mathfrak m^{k-d_ i}$. Thus $y=\sum _ ia_ ie_ i$, where $a_ i\in \mathfrak m^{k-d_ i}=\mathfrak m^{k-s}\mathfrak m^{s-d_ i}$ and $\mathfrak m^{s-d_ i}e_ i\subset E\cap \mathfrak m^ sF$; hence $y\in \mathfrak m^{k-s}(E\cap \mathfrak m^ sF)$. The reverse inclusion is immediate. Now let $Q$ be a finitely generated $R$-module and $G= igcap _ k\mathfrak m^ kQ$. By (ii), $G$ is finitely generated. Let $s$ be the index of the Artin–Rees equality for $G\subset Q$. Since $G\subset \mathfrak m^ kQ$ for all $k$, this equality with $k=s+1$ gives $G=G\cap \mathfrak m^{s+1}Q=\mathfrak m(G\cap \mathfrak m^ sQ)=\mathfrak mG$. If $g_1,\ldots ,g_ r$ generate $G$, write $g_ i=\sum _ ja_{ij}g_ j$ with $a_{ij}\in \mathfrak m$. Multiplying this system of equations by the adjugate of the matrix $(\delta _{ij}-a_{ij})$ gives $\det (\delta _{ij}-a_{ij})\, g_ i=0$ for every $i$. Expanding the determinant, we see that it is congruent to $1$ modulo $\mathfrak m$, hence a unit of the local ring $R$, and therefore $G=0$. Applied to $Q=F/E$, for which $\mathfrak m^ kQ=(E+\mathfrak m^ kF)/E$, this proves the intersection formula. For the last assertion, let $f_ l	o f$ locally uniformly near $x$, with germs $f_ l\in J$, and work in a holomorphic chart centered at $x$. By section A.1 , a germ belongs to $\mathfrak m^ k$ if and only if its Taylor coefficients of order less than $k$ vanish; hence these coefficients identify $R/\mathfrak m^ k$ with a finite-dimensional vector space. By the integral formula for the coefficients in ( 7.1 ), the Taylor coefficients of $f_ l$ at $x$ converge to those of $f$, so the images of the $f_ l$ in $R/\mathfrak m^ k$ converge to the image of $f$. The image of $J$ there is a linear subspace of a finite-dimensional vector space, hence closed, so $f\in J+\mathfrak m^ k$ for every $k$. The intersection formula with $F=R$ and $E=J$ gives $f\in J$. $\square$ Recall from section A.1 that a sheaf of ideals $\mathcal I\subset \mathcal O_ X$ is locally finitely generated if every point has a neighborhood $U$ with sections $g_1,\ldots ,g_ r\in \mathcal I(U)$ whose germs generate $\mathcal I_ y$ for every $y\in U$. For such sheaves the identity theorem takes the following form. Lemma 12.2.2 . Let $\mathcal I$ be a locally finitely generated sheaf of ideals on a connected complex manifold $W$. If $\mathcal I_ y=0$ for some $y\in W$, then $\mathcal I_ z=0$ for every $z\in W$. Proof. The set of points $z$ with $\mathcal I_ z=0$ is open: near such a point, choose sections $g_1,\ldots ,g_ r$ generating all stalks of $\mathcal I$ on a neighborhood; their germs at $z$ vanish, so they vanish on a neighborhood $U'$ of $z$, and $\mathcal I$ has zero stalks on $U'$. The set of points with $\mathcal I_ z
eq 0$ is open as well: a section with nonzero germ at $z$, defined on a connected neighborhood of $z$, has nonzero germs at all points of this neighborhood, by the identity theorem. Since $W$ is connected, one of the two sets is empty. $\square$ In the proof of the strong Noetherian property we reduce the number of variables by the following finiteness lemma for Weierstrass polynomials. For an open set $W'\subset \mathbb C^{n-1}$, a disc $\Delta \subset \mathbb C$, the projection $\pi \colon W'	imes \Delta 	o W'$, and a sheaf $\mathcal G$ of $\mathcal O_{W'	imes \Delta }$-modules, the direct image $\pi _*\mathcal G$ is the sheaf $V'\mapsto \mathcal G(V'	imes \Delta )$ on $W'$; it is a sheaf of $\mathcal O_{W'}$-modules, a holomorphic function $c$ on $V'$ acting by multiplication with $c\circ \pi $. Lemma 12.2.3 . Let $n\geq 1$, let $W'\subset \mathbb C^{n-1}$ be open, let $\Delta =\{ w\in \mathbb C:|w|<r\} $, and let \[  P(z',w)=w^\mu +a_1(z')w^{\mu -1}+\cdots +a_\mu (z'),\qquad \mu \geq 1,  \] with $a_1,\ldots ,a_\mu $ holomorphic on $W'$, such that for some $ho <r$ all roots of $P(z',\cdot )$, $z'\in W'$, lie in the disc $|w|\leq ho $. Put $D=W'	imes \Delta $ and $Z=\{ P=0\} \subset D$, let $\pi \colon D	o W'$ be the projection, and let $P\mathcal O_ D$ be the ideal generated by $P$. Let $\mathcal G$ be a sheaf of $\mathcal O_ D$-modules with $\mathcal G_ z=0$ for $z\in D\setminus Z$. Then for every $b\in W'$ the map \[  (\pi _*\mathcal G)_ b	o  igoplus _{z\in Z\cap \pi ^{-1}(b)}\mathcal G_ z,  \] which sends the germ at $b$ of a section over $V'	imes \Delta $ to its germs at the points of the fiber, is bijective. The morphism $\Phi \colon \mathcal O_{W'}^\mu 	o \pi _*(\mathcal O_ D/P\mathcal O_ D)$ that sends $(c_0,\ldots ,c_{\mu -1})$ to the class of $\sum _ kc_ kw^ k$ is an isomorphism. Let $\mathcal I\subset \mathcal O_ D$ be a coherent ideal with $P\in \mathcal I(D)$, and let $\mathcal I/P\mathcal O_ D$ denote its image in $\mathcal O_ D/P\mathcal O_ D$. Then $\mathcal M(\mathcal I)=\Phi ^{-1}(\pi _*(\mathcal I/P\mathcal O_ D))$ is a coherent subsheaf of $\mathcal O_{W'}^\mu $. If $\mathcal I'$ is a second such ideal and $\mathcal M(\mathcal I)=\mathcal M(\mathcal I')$ on an open set $V'\subset W'$, then $\mathcal I=\mathcal I'$ on $V'	imes \Delta $. Proof. For $z'\in W'$, the polynomial $P(z',\cdot )$ has at most $\mu $ roots, all in $\Delta $; so the fibers of $Z$ over $W'$ are finite. We first describe $Z$ near a fiber. Let $b\in W'$, let $w_1,\ldots ,w_ l$ be the distinct roots of $P(b,\cdot )$, and put $z_ i=(b,w_ i)$. Let $\delta >0$ be so small that the closed discs $|w-w_ i|\leq 2\delta $ are pairwise disjoint and contained in $\Delta $. The function $|P|$ is continuous and positive on the compact set $\{ b\} 	imes K$, where $K=\{ |w|\leq ho \} \setminus  igcup _ i\{ |w-w_ i|<\delta \} $; hence it is positive on $V_ b	imes K$ for a neighborhood $V_ b$ of $b$, and for $z'\in V_ b$ all roots of $P(z',\cdot )$ lie in $ igcup _ i\{ |w-w_ i|<\delta \} $. Put $B_ i=V_ b	imes \{ |w-w_ i|<2\delta \} $. These open sets are pairwise disjoint, and $Z\cap (V_ b	imes \Delta )\subset  igcup _ iB_ i$. Moreover, given neighborhoods $N_ i$ of the points $z_ i$, we can achieve $V_ b	imes \{ |w-w_ i|\leq 2\delta \} \subset N_ i$ for all $i$: first decrease $\delta $ so that $\{ b\} 	imes \{ |w-w_ i|\leq 2\delta \} \subset N_ i$, and then decrease $V_ b$, using the compactness of these discs. We call such $\delta $ and $V_ b$ adapted to $b$; a smaller neighborhood of $b$ remains adapted. (1) Let $s$ be a section of $\mathcal G$ over $V'	imes \Delta $ whose germs at all the $z_ i$ vanish. Then $s$ vanishes on neighborhoods $N_ i$ of the $z_ i$; choose $\delta $ and $V_ b\subset V'$ adapted to $b$ with $B_ i\subset N_ i$. The open sets $B_1,\ldots ,B_ l$ and $(V_ b	imes \Delta )\setminus Z$ cover $V_ b	imes \Delta $, and $s$ vanishes on each of them, on the last one because all stalks of $\mathcal G$ vanish there. Hence $s=0$ on $V_ b	imes \Delta $, and the map is injective. Conversely, let $g_ i\in \mathcal G_{z_ i}$ be given, represented by sections $t_ i$ on neighborhoods $N_ i$ of the $z_ i$, and choose $\delta $ and $V_ b$ adapted to $b$ with $B_ i\subset N_ i$. On the open cover of $V_ b	imes \Delta $ formed by the $B_ i$ and $(V_ b	imes \Delta )\setminus Z$, consider the sections $t_ i|_{B_ i}$ and $0$. They agree on the overlaps: the $B_ i$ are pairwise disjoint, and $t_ i$ vanishes on $B_ i\setminus Z$, since $\mathcal G$ has zero stalks there. Gluing them, we obtain a section over $V_ b	imes \Delta $ with germs $g_ i$ at the $z_ i$. Hence the map is surjective. (2) The map $\Phi $ is a morphism of sheaves of $\mathcal O_{W'}$-modules. It is injective on sections: suppose that the class of $R=\sum _{k<\mu }c_ kw^ k$ vanishes on $V'	imes \Delta $, and let $z'\in V'$. If $w_0$ is a root of $P(z',\cdot )$ of multiplicity $m$, then $R=Pq$ near $(z',w_0)$ with $q$ holomorphic, so the polynomial $R(z',\cdot )=P(z',\cdot )q(z',\cdot )$ vanishes to order at least $m$ at $w_0$. Thus $R(z',\cdot )$, a polynomial of degree less than $\mu $, has at least $\mu $ zeros counted with multiplicity, and therefore vanishes; that is, $c_ k(z')=0$ for all $k$. To prove surjectivity on stalks, let $s$ be a section of $\mathcal O_ D/P\mathcal O_ D$ over $V'	imes \Delta $ and $b\in V'$. Near each $z_ i$, $s$ is the class of a holomorphic function $f_ i$ on a neighborhood $N_ i$ of $z_ i$. Choose $\delta $ and $V_ b\subset V'$ adapted to $b$ with $V_ b	imes \{ |w-w_ i|\leq 2\delta \} \subset N_ i$. On the circles $|\zeta -w_ i|=2\delta $ the function $P(z',\zeta )$ does not vanish for $z'\in V_ b$, since these circles have distance at least $\delta $ from all roots. For $z'\in V_ b$ and $w\in \mathbb C$ put \[  R(z',w)= rac1{2\pi \mathrm i}\sum _{i=1}^ l\int _{|\zeta -w_ i|=2\delta }  rac{f_ i(z',\zeta )}{P(z',\zeta )}\,  rac{P(z',\zeta )-P(z',w)}{\zeta -w}\, \mathrm d\zeta .  \] The difference quotient is a polynomial in $w$ of degree $\mu -1$ whose coefficients are polynomials in $\zeta $ and in the $a_ k(z')$; hence $R$ is a polynomial in $w$ of degree less than $\mu $ whose coefficients are holomorphic on $V_ b$, by differentiation under the integral sign. For $z'\in V_ b$ and $|w-w_ i|<2\delta $ put \[  q_ i(z',w)= rac1{2\pi \mathrm i}\sum _{j=1}^ l\int _{|\zeta -w_ j|=2\delta } rac{f_ j(z',\zeta )}{P(z',\zeta )(\zeta -w)}\, \mathrm d\zeta ,  \] a holomorphic function on $B_ i$. Adding the two integrals, we obtain \[  P(z',w)q_ i(z',w)+R(z',w)= rac1{2\pi \mathrm i}\sum _{j=1}^ l\int _{|\zeta -w_ j|=2\delta } rac{f_ j(z',\zeta )}{\zeta -w}\, \mathrm d\zeta =f_ i(z',w),  \] since the term $j=i$ equals $f_ i(z',w)$ by Cauchy's formula, and the terms $j
eq i$ vanish by Cauchy's theorem, the point $w$ lying outside the closed disc $|\zeta -w_ j|\leq 2\delta $. Hence $f_ i\equiv R$ modulo $P$ on $B_ i$, so $s$ and the class of $R$ agree on each $B_ i$; on $(V_ b	imes \Delta )\setminus Z$ both vanish, since $P$ is a unit there. Thus $s=\Phi (c)$ on $V_ b	imes \Delta $, where $c$ is the tuple of coefficients of $R$. Being injective, and surjective on all stalks, $\Phi $ is an isomorphism. (3) The sheaf $\mathcal M(\mathcal I)$ is a subsheaf of $\mathcal O_{W'}$-modules of $\mathcal O_{W'}^\mu $. Since $\mathcal O_{W'}$ is coherent (theorem A.1.5 ), the last assertion of lemma A.1.4 shows that it suffices to prove that $\mathcal M(\mathcal I)$ is locally finitely generated. Note that $\mathcal I/P\mathcal O_ D$ has zero stalks off $Z$, because $P$ is a unit there; so (1) applies to it as well as to $\mathcal O_ D/P\mathcal O_ D$. Fix $b\in W'$, with $z_ i$ as above. Since $\mathcal I$ is coherent, there are neighborhoods $N_ i$ of $z_ i$ and sections $f_{i1},\ldots ,f_{i\kappa }$ of $\mathcal I$ over $N_ i$ generating all stalks of $\mathcal I$ on $N_ i$.
