u (\psi ,0)=1$ by proposition 12.1.4 . For $|z_2|\leq 1$ we have $\varphi \leq \psi $, so $
u (\varphi ,0)\geq 1$; conversely, the supremum of $\varphi $ over the ball $|z|<\mathrm e^{t/2}$ is at least $\sup _{|z_1|<\mathrm e^{t/2}}\log |z_1|^2=t$, so $
u (\varphi ,0)\leq 1$ by ( 12.1 ). Nevertheless $\mathcal I( rac32\psi )_0
eq \mathcal I( rac32\varphi )_0$. Indeed, $\mathrm e^{-3\psi /2}=|z|^{-3}$ is integrable near $0\in \mathbb R^4$ by polar coordinates, since $\int _0^ rt^{-3}t^3\, \mathrm dt<\infty $; so $\mathcal I( rac32\psi )_0=\mathcal O_{\mathbb C^2,0}$. On the other hand, on the set $A_\delta =\{ 0<|z_2|<\delta ,\  |z_1|<|z_2|^2\} $ we have $|z_1|^2+|z_2|^4<2|z_2|^4$, hence $\mathrm e^{-3\varphi /2}>2^{-3/2}|z_2|^{-6}$, and by Fubini's theorem \[  \int _{A_\delta }\mathrm e^{-3\varphi /2}\, \mathrm dV\geq 2^{-3/2}\int _{0<|z_2|<\delta }\pi |z_2|^4\, |z_2|^{-6}\, \mathrm dV_2(z_2)=2^{-3/2}\pi \int _0^\delta 2\pi t^{-1}\, \mathrm dt=\infty .  \] Since every neighborhood of $0$ contains $A_\delta $ for small $\delta >0$, the function $\mathrm e^{-3\varphi /2}$ is not integrable near $0$, and $1
otin \mathcal I( rac32\varphi )_0$.

title: Siu
text:
Theorem 12.3.4 (Siu) . Let $\varphi $ be a weight on $X$ and let $c>0$. Then \[  E_ c(\varphi )=\{ x\in X:
u (\varphi ,x)\geq c\}   \] is an analytic subset of $X$, and its intersection with every connected component of $X$ of positive dimension is a proper subset of that component. The same holds for the Lelong numbers of a closed positive $(1,1)$-current on $X$. Proof. Lelong numbers vanish on components of dimension zero, so we may assume that $X$ is connected of dimension $n\geq 1$. We describe $E_ c(\varphi )$ as an intersection of analytic sets defined by the orders of the ideals $\mathcal I(m\varphi )$ and then show that such an intersection is analytic. Let $\mathfrak a$ be a coherent ideal and $k$ an integer. The set of points $y$ where $\operatorname {ord}_ y\mathfrak a\geq k$ (with $\operatorname {ord}_ y\mathfrak a=\infty $ if $\mathfrak a_ y=0$) is analytic. Indeed, let $g_1,\ldots ,g_ r$ generate $\mathfrak a$ on a coordinate neighborhood $W$. A germ has order at least $k$ at $y$ if and only if its derivatives of order less than $k$ vanish at $y$, since these derivatives are multiples of its Taylor coefficients, by ( 7.1 ). Hence for $y\in W$ we have $\operatorname {ord}_ y\mathfrak a\geq k$ if and only if $\partial ^\alpha g_ i(y)=0$ for all $i$ and all $|\alpha |<k$: the condition is necessary because the $g_ i$ belong to $\mathfrak a_ y$, and sufficient because, by the Leibniz rule, every element $\sum _ ih_ ig_ i$ then vanishes to order at least $k$ at $y$. This is a finite system of holomorphic equations, and for $k\leq 0$ the set is all of $W$. By ( 12.12 ), 12.13  egin{equation} \label{eq:siu-as-jet-intersection} E_ c(\varphi )= igcap _{m\geq 1} \left\{ x:\operatorname {ord}_ x\mathcal I(m\varphi ) \geq \lfloor mc-nfloor +1ight\} . \end{equation} Indeed, if $
u (\varphi ,x)\geq c$, the lower bound in ( 12.12 ) gives the integer inequality $\operatorname {ord}_ x\mathcal I(m\varphi )>mc-n$, that is, $\operatorname {ord}_ x\mathcal I(m\varphi )\geq \lfloor mc-nfloor +1$, for every $m$. If $
u (\varphi ,x)<c$, the upper bound gives $\operatorname {ord}_ x\mathcal I(m\varphi )\leq m
u (\varphi ,x)\leq mc-n<\lfloor mc-nfloor +1$ as soon as $m(c-
u (\varphi ,x))\geq n$. Thus $E_ c(\varphi )$ is an intersection of analytic subsets of $X$. An arbitrary intersection $A= igcap _\lambda A_\lambda $ of analytic subsets of $X$ is analytic. Since $A$ is closed, it suffices to show that each $p\in A$ has a neighborhood $W$ such that $A\cap W$ is the intersection of $W$ with finitely many of the $A_\lambda $. Let $I_\lambda \subset \mathcal O_{X,p}$ be the ideal generated by the germs at $p$ of local defining functions of $A_\lambda $. By proposition A.1.2 the sum $\sum _\lambda I_\lambda $ is finitely generated, so it equals $I_{\lambda _1}+\cdots +I_{\lambda _ q}$ for finitely many indices; put $B=A_{\lambda _1}\cap \cdots \cap A_{\lambda _ q}$. Every local defining function of each $A_\lambda $ is then a combination of defining functions of $A_{\lambda _1},\ldots ,A_{\lambda _ q}$ near $p$, so $A_\lambda $ contains a neighborhood of $p$ in $B$. This neighborhood may depend on $\lambda $, and we now remove this dependence. By corollary A.2.13 , the irreducible components of the analytic set $B$ form a locally finite family; so some neighborhood $N$ of $p$ meets only finitely many of them. Let $B_1,\ldots ,B_ l$ be those that contain $p$. The union of the other components meeting $N$ is closed and does not contain $p$, so there is an open neighborhood $W'\subset N$ of $p$ with $B\cap W'\subset B_1\cup \cdots \cup B_ l$. Fix $\lambda $ and $i$. The regular locus $(B_ i)_{\mathrm{reg}}$ is a connected manifold, dense in $B_ i$ (corollary A.2.13 ), and its analytic subset $A_\lambda \cap (B_ i)_{\mathrm{reg}}$ has nonempty interior in it, because $A_\lambda $ contains a neighborhood of $p$ in $B_ i$ and $p$ lies in the closure of $(B_ i)_{\mathrm{reg}}$. By lemma A.1.6 , $A_\lambda \cap (B_ i)_{\mathrm{reg}}$ is therefore all of $(B_ i)_{\mathrm{reg}}$, and $B_ i\subset A_\lambda $ because $A_\lambda $ is closed. Therefore $B\cap W'\subset A_\lambda $ for every $\lambda $, and $A\cap W'=B\cap W'$. Applied to ( 12.13 ), this shows that $E_ c(\varphi )$ is analytic. By proposition 12.1.1 , $
u (\varphi ,x)=0$ at every point where $\varphi (x)>-\infty $. Thus $E_ c(\varphi )$ is contained in the pole set of $\varphi $, which has measure zero because $\varphi $ is locally integrable (theorem 8.2.1 ), and therefore has no interior points; so $E_ c(\varphi )
eq X$. Finally, let $T$ be a closed positive $(1,1)$-current on $X$. Every point of $X$ at which $X$ has positive dimension has a coordinate ball $U$ on which $T=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ with $u$ plurisubharmonic, and $
u (T,y)=
u (u,y)$ for $y\in U$ (definition 12.1.2 ). By what we have proved, applied to the weight $u$ on $U$, the set $\{ y\in U:
u (T,y)\geq c\} $ is an analytic subset of $U$ with empty interior. Since the components of $X$ of dimension zero do not meet $\{ y:
u (T,y)\geq c\} $, and analyticity is a local property, this set is an analytic subset of $X$ whose intersection with every component of positive dimension is proper. $\square$

title: Siu as jet intersection
text: 12.13 \begin{equation} \label{eq:siu-as-jet-intersection} E_ c(\varphi )=\bigcap _{m\geq 1} \left\{ x:\operatorname {ord}_ x\mathcal I(m\varphi ) \geq \lfloor mc-n\rfloor +1\right\} . \end{equation}

title: Generic divisorial lelong
text:
Proposition 12.3.5 . Let $\varphi $ be a weight on $X$ and let $Z\subset X$ be an irreducible analytic subset. The generic Lelong number of $\varphi $ along $Z$ is \[  
u (\varphi ,Z)=\inf _{x\in Z}
u (\varphi ,x).  \] It is attained at every point of $Z$ outside a countable union of proper analytic subsets of $Z$. Moreover, the complement in $Z$ of every countable union of proper analytic subsets of $Z$ is dense in $Z$; in particular, $
u (\varphi ,Z)$ is attained on a dense subset of $Z$. The same definition and conclusions apply to the Lelong numbers of a closed positive $(1,1)$-current $T$ on $X$, and give the generic Lelong number $
u (T,Z)$. If $\pi \colon Y	o X$ is a smooth model of $X$ (section A.7 ), that is, a proper bimeromorphic holomorphic map from a complex manifold $Y$, and $E\subset Y$ is a prime divisor, that is, an irreducible hypersurface, we define \[  
u (\varphi ,E)=
u (\varphi \circ \pi ,E).  \] This number depends only on the prime divisor over $X$ represented by $E$ (definition A.7.4 ), not on the model. Proof. Put $\lambda =
u (\varphi ,Z)$. For every integer $j\geq 1$, theorem 12.3.4 shows that $Z\cap E_{\lambda +1/j}(\varphi )$ is an analytic subset of $Z$, and it is a proper subset by the definition of $\lambda $. At every point of $Z$ outside the union of these sets, $
u (\varphi ,x)<\lambda +1/j$ for all $j$, hence $
u (\varphi ,x)=\lambda $. We now show that the complement in $Z$ of an arbitrary countable union of proper analytic subsets of $Z$ is dense in $Z$; applied to the sets $Z\cap E_{\lambda +1/j}(\varphi )$, this shows that $
u (\varphi ,Z)$ is attained on a dense subset of $Z$. The density is clear if $Z$ is a point, for then the proper analytic subsets of $Z$ are empty. Let $\dim Z>0$. By corollary A.2.13 , applied to the family consisting of $Z$ alone, $Z$ is an irreducible component of itself; so its regular locus $Z_{\mathrm{reg}}$ is a connected manifold, dense in $Z$. Let $B$ be a proper analytic subset of $Z$. Then $B\cap Z_{\mathrm{reg}}$ is an analytic subset of $Z_{\mathrm{reg}}$, and it is proper, since otherwise the closed set $B$ would contain the closure $Z$ of $Z_{\mathrm{reg}}$. By lemma A.1.6 , every point of $B\cap Z_{\mathrm{reg}}$ has a connected open neighborhood $U$ in $Z_{\mathrm{reg}}$ with a holomorphic function $g
ot\equiv 0$ on $U$ such that $B\cap U\subset \{ g=0\} $; shrinking $U$ to a coordinate ball, on which $g
ot\equiv 0$ by the identity theorem, we see from lemma 7.4.1 that $B\cap U$ is a null set in the chart. Covering a chart $N$ of $Z_{\mathrm{reg}}$ by countably many such balls and by open sets disjoint from $B$, we see that $B\cap N$ is a null set. Consequently, a countable union of proper analytic subsets of $Z$ meets every chart of $Z_{\mathrm{reg}}$ in a null set, which has no interior points. Its complement is therefore dense in $Z_{\mathrm{reg}}$, and hence in $Z$. For a closed positive $(1,1)$-current the same argument applies, since theorem 12.3.4 holds for its Lelong numbers. For the second assertion, note first that $\varphi \circ \pi $ is a weight on $Y$: by proposition 8.2.3 it is plurisubharmonic or identically $-\infty $ on each component of $Y$, and the second alternative is excluded. Indeed, since $\pi $ is bimeromorphic (section A.3 ), there is a nowhere dense analytic subset $A\subset X$ such that $\pi ^{-1}(A)$ is nowhere dense in $Y$ and $\pi $ maps $Y\setminus \pi ^{-1}(A)$ biholomorphically onto $X\setminus A$. If $\varphi \circ \pi $ were identically $-\infty $ on a component $Y_0$ of $Y$, then $\varphi $ would be $-\infty $ on the nonempty open set $\pi (Y_0\setminus \pi ^{-1}(A))$, which is impossible because $\varphi $ is locally integrable. Now let $E\subset Y$ and $E'\subset Y'$ be prime divisors on smooth models $\pi \colon Y	o X$ and $\pi '\colon Y'	o X$ that represent the same prime divisor over $X$, and let $ho \colon Y''	o Y$ and $ho '\colon Y''	o Y'$ be maps from a common smooth model on which the strict transforms of $E$ and $E'$ coincide, say with $E''$. By proposition A.7.3 , $ho $ is biholomorphic over $Y\setminus S$ for an analytic subset $S\subset Y$ of codimension at least two, so it maps the nonempty open subset $E''\cap ho ^{-1}(Y\setminus S)$ of $E''$ onto the nonempty open subset $E\setminus S$ of $E$, and $
u (\varphi \circ \pi \circ ho ,q)=
u (\varphi \circ \pi ,ho (q))$ for $q$ in this set, because Lelong numbers are invariant under biholomorphisms (proposition 12.1.1 ). By the first part, the generic value along $E$ is attained on a dense subset of $E$, so it equals the infimum of the Lelong numbers over any nonempty open subset of $E$; the same holds for $E''$. Hence $
u (\varphi \circ \pi ,E)=
u (\varphi \circ \pi \circ ho ,E'')$. The same argument for $ho '$ gives $
u (\varphi \circ \pi ',E')=
u (\varphi \circ \pi \circ ho ,E'')$, since $\pi \circ ho =\pi '\circ ho '$. $\square$

title: Generic lelong uniform growth
text:
Proposition 12.3.6 . Let $\varphi $ be a weight on $X$, let $Z\subset X$ be a connected closed complex submanifold of positive codimension, which is an irreducible analytic subset by corollary A.2.13 , and let $z=(z',z'')$ be local coordinates near a point of $Z$ in which $Z=\{ z'=0\} $. Then near that point \[  \varphi (z)\leq 
u (\varphi ,Z)\log |z'|^2+C,\qquad z'
eq 0,  \] for a constant $C$, and no bound of this form with a coefficient larger than $
u (\varphi ,Z)$ holds near any point of $Z$. If $\pi \colon Y	o X$ is the blowup of a point $x$ at which $X$ has positive dimension (proposition A.5.3 ), and $E=\pi ^{-1}(x)$, then $
u (\varphi ,E)=
u (\varphi ,x)$. Proof. Let $p\in Z$ be the given point and $\lambda =
u (\varphi ,Z)$. Choose $r_0>0$, a constant $C$ and a neighborhood $W$ of $p$ in $Z$ such that for every $y\in W$ the closed ball $\overline{B(y,r_0)}$ lies in the coordinate domain and $\varphi \leq C$ on it. By ( 12.2 ) at $y$, we have $\varphi (z)\leq 
u (\varphi ,y)\log (|z-y|^2/r_0^2)+C$ for $0<|z-y|<r_0$. Take $z=(z',z'')$ with $y=(0,z'')\in W$ and $0<|z'|<r_0$. Then $|z-y|=|z'|$, the logarithm is negative and $
u (\varphi ,y)\geq \lambda $, so $\varphi (z)\leq \lambda \log |z'|^2-\lambda \log r_0^2+C$. This is the asserted bound, with a constant independent of $z''$. Conversely, suppose that $\varphi (z)\leq c\log |z'|^2+C'$ for $z'
eq 0$ near a point $q$ of $Z$, where we may assume $c\geq 0$. For $y\in Z$ near $q$ we have $|z'|\leq |z-y|$, so $\varphi (z)\leq c\log |z-y|^2+C'$ for $z
otin Z$ near $y$. Since $Z=\{ z'=0\} $ is a Lebesgue null set in the chart, proposition 12.1.1 gives $
u (\varphi ,y)\geq c$. By proposition 12.3.5 there are points $y$ arbitrarily close to $q$ with $
u (\varphi ,y)=\lambda $, so $c\leq \lambda $. Now let $\pi $ be the blowup of $x$, and let $n=\dim _ xX$. If $n=1$, then $\pi $ is the identity and $E=\{ x\} $, so there is nothing to prove. Let $n\geq 2$ and choose coordinates centered at $x$. The blowup is covered by $n$ charts; in the $k$th chart, $z_ k=w_ k$ and $z_ j=w_ kw_ j$ for $j
eq k$, so that \[  |z|^2=|w_ k|^2\Bigl (1+\sum _{j
eq k}|w_ j|^2\Bigr ),\qquad E=\{ w_ k=0\} .  \] By ( 12.2 ), $\varphi \leq 
u (\varphi ,x)\log |z|^2+C$ near $x$. Pulling back, we get $\varphi \circ \pi \leq 
u (\varphi ,x)\log |w_ k|^2+C'$ on compact subsets of the $k$th chart near $E$; since $|w_ k|$ is at most the distance to any point of $E$ in that chart, $
u (\varphi \circ \pi ,q)\geq 
u (\varphi ,x)$ for every $q\in E$, and $
u (\varphi ,E)\geq 
u (\varphi ,x)$. Conversely, $E\cong \mathbb P^{n-1}$ is a compact connected submanifold of $Y$, so the first part of the proposition, applied to the weight $\varphi \circ \pi $ and $E$, gives $\varphi \circ \pi \leq 
u (\varphi ,E)\log |w_ k|^2+C$ near each point of $E$, in the coordinates of a chart containing it. Cover $E$ by finitely many such neighborhoods, on each of which $\log |w_ k|^2-\log |z|^2$ is bounded. Since $\pi $ is proper, the inverse image of a small neighborhood of $x$ lies in their union, so $\varphi (z)\leq 
u (\varphi ,E)\log |z|^2+C''$ near $x$, for $z
eq x$. Hence $
u (\varphi ,E)\leq 
u (\varphi ,x)$. $\square$

title: Restriction, products and integral closure
text: 12.4 Restriction, products and integral closure The Ohsawa–Takegoshi theorem and the Hilbert spaces of theorem 12.2.7 determine how multiplier ideals behave under restriction, products and holomorphic pullback; we also show that multiplier ideals are integrally closed. For a holomorphic map $f\colon X\to Y$ and a coherent ideal $\mathfrak a\subset \mathcal O_ Y$, we denote by $f^{-1}\mathfrak a\cdot \mathcal O_ X$ the ideal of $\mathcal O_ X$ generated by the compositions $g\circ f$ of local sections $g$ of $\mathfrak a$; it is locally generated by the compositions of local generators of $\mathfrak a$ with $f$. It is the ideal written $\mathfrak a\mathcal O_ X$ in section A.5 ; we keep $f$ in the notation when several maps occur. For a complex submanifold $Z\subset X$ with ideal sheaf $\mathcal I_ Z$ and an ideal $\mathfrak a\subset \mathcal O_ X$, the restriction of $\mathfrak a$ to $Z$ is the image \[  \mathfrak a|_ Z^{\mathrm{im}} =\mathfrak a/(\mathfrak a\cap \mathcal I_ Z)\subset \mathcal O_ X/\mathcal I_ Z=\mathcal O_ Z,  \] that is, the ideal of restrictions $g|_ Z$ of local sections $g$ of $\mathfrak a$. Here $\mathcal O_ X/\mathcal I_ Z$ is identified with $\mathcal O_ Z$ through restriction: in local coordinates $(v,w)$ with $Z=\{ w=0\} $, every holomorphic function on $Z$ is the restriction of a function independent of $w$, and a function vanishing on $Z$ belongs to $\mathcal I_ Z$ by definition. We use the image rather than the tensor product $\mathfrak a\otimes _{\mathcal O_ X}\mathcal O_ Z$, whose natural map to $\mathcal O_ Z$ need not be injective. For instance, for $X=\mathbb C$, $Z=\{ 0\} $ and $\mathfrak a=(z)$, the element $z\otimes 1$ of the stalk at $0$ is mapped to $z|_ Z=0$, but it is not zero, since $(zf,g)\mapsto f(0)g(0)$ is a well-defined $\mathcal O_{X,0}$-balanced bilinear map $\mathfrak a_0\times \mathcal O_{Z,0}\to \mathbb C$ with value $1$ at $(z,1)$. Theorem 12.4.1 . Let $Z\subset X$ be a complex submanifold and $\varphi $ a weight on $X$. Then 12.14 \begin{equation} \label{eq:multiplier-restriction} \mathcal I(\varphi |_ Z)\subset \mathcal I(\varphi )|_ Z^{\mathrm{im}}; \end{equation} on a connected component of $Z$ on which $\varphi |_ Z\equiv -\infty $, the left side is zero. If $\varphi _1$ and $\varphi _2$ are weights on complex manifolds $X_1$ and $X_2$, and $p_ i\colon X_1\times X_2\to X_ i$ are the projections, then 12.15 \begin{equation} \label{eq:multiplier-external-product} \mathcal I(\varphi _1\circ p_1+\varphi _2\circ p_2) =(p_1^{-1}\mathcal I(\varphi _1)\cdot \mathcal O) (p_2^{-1}\mathcal I(\varphi _2)\cdot \mathcal O). \end{equation} In particular, for weights $\varphi $ and $\psi $ on $X$, 12.16 \begin{equation} \label{eq:multiplier-subadditivity} \mathcal I(\varphi +\psi )\subset \mathcal I(\varphi )\mathcal I(\psi ). \end{equation} Proof. The inclusion ( 12.14 ) is a restatement of corollary 11.4.6 : if $f\in \mathcal I(\varphi |_ Z)_ x$, that corollary provides a holomorphic germ $F$ at $x$ with $F|_ Z=f$ and $F\in \mathcal I(\varphi )_ x$. The product formula is local. Near a point $(x_1,x_2)$ we choose bounded polydiscs $\Omega _ i$ around $x_ i$ in charts of $X_ i$ on which $\varphi _ i$ is bounded above; subtracting constants, which changes none of the multiplier ideals, we may assume that $\varphi _1,\varphi _2\leq 0$. We write $\Phi =\varphi _1\circ p_1+\varphi _2\circ p_2$, a nonpositive weight on the polydisc $\Omega _1\times \Omega _2$. Let $(e_ j)$ and $(g_ k)$ be orthonormal bases of $\mathcal H_{\varphi _1}(\Omega _1)$ and $\mathcal H_{\varphi _2}(\Omega _2)$, which exist by theorem 12.2.7 (2). By Fubini's theorem the functions $e_ j(z)g_ k(w)$ form an orthonormal family in $\mathcal H_\Phi (\Omega _1\times \Omega _2)$. We show that its linear span is dense. Let $F\in \mathcal H_\Phi (\Omega _1\times \Omega _2)$. By Fubini's theorem, for almost every $w\in \Omega _2$ we have $\varphi _2(w)>-\infty $ and $F(\cdot ,w)\in \mathcal H_{\varphi _1}(\Omega _1)$, and for such $w$ we put \[  a_ j(w)=\int _{\Omega _1}F(z,w)\overline{e_ j(z)} \mathrm e^{-\varphi _1(z)}\, \mathrm dV_ z.  \] We claim that each $a_ j$ agrees almost everywhere with an element of $\mathcal H_{\varphi _2}(\Omega _2)$ of norm at most $\| F\| _\Phi $. Choose compact sets $K_\ell \uparrow \Omega _1$ and put $E_\ell =K_\ell \cap \{ \mathrm e^{-\varphi _1}\leq \ell \} $; these sets increase and exhaust $\Omega _1$ up to the pole set of $\varphi _1$, which has measure zero. The function $a_{j,\ell }$ obtained by integrating over $E_\ell $ instead of $\Omega _1$ is holomorphic on $\Omega _2$. Indeed, let $L\subset \Omega _2$ be compact. For $z\in E_\ell \subset K_\ell $ and $w\in L$, the integrand $F(z,w)\overline{e_ j(z)}\mathrm e^{-\varphi _1(z)}$ and all its partial derivatives in $w$ are bounded, because $F$ and its derivatives are continuous on $K_\ell \times L$, $e_ j$ is bounded on $K_\ell $, and $\mathrm e^{-\varphi _1}\leq \ell $ on $E_\ell $. Hence we may differentiate under the integral sign any number of times: $a_{j,\ell }$ is smooth, and $\partial a_{j,\ell }/\partial \bar w_ m=0$ for all $m$, because $F$ is holomorphic in $w$. By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality in $z$, followed by integration in $w$ against $\mathrm e^{-\varphi _2}$, \[  \| a_ j-a_{j,\ell }\| _{\varphi _2}^2 \leq \| F\| _\Phi ^2 \int _{\Omega _1\setminus E_\ell }|e_ j|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi _1}\, \mathrm dV_ z \longrightarrow 0  \] by dominated convergence, since the sets $\Omega _1\setminus E_\ell $ decrease to a null set and $|e_ j|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi _1}$ is integrable. Since $\varphi _2\leq 0$, the holomorphic functions $a_{j,\ell }$ therefore converge to $a_ j$ in $L^2(\Omega _2)$, and hence in the sense of distributions; so $\bar\partial a_ j=0$, and $a_ j$ agrees almost everywhere with a holomorphic function, by lemma 11.3.5 (1). The same Cauchy–Schwarz estimate over all of $\Omega _1$ gives $\| a_ j\| _{\varphi _2}\leq \| F\| _\Phi $, which proves the claim. Now suppose that $F$ is orthogonal to all the products $e_ jg_ k$. By Fubini's theorem, whose use is justified by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, $\langle a_ j,g_ k\rangle _{\varphi _2}=\langle F,e_ jg_ k\rangle _\Phi =0$ for all $k$. Since the linear span of the $g_ k$ is dense in $\mathcal H_{\varphi _2}(\Omega _2)$, the element $a_ j$ of this space is orthogonal to itself, so $a_ j=0$ almost everywhere, for every $j$. Hence for almost every $w$ all the coefficients $\langle F(\cdot ,w),e_ j\rangle _{\varphi _1}$ vanish, and $F(\cdot ,w)=0$, because $F(\cdot ,w)$ is the limit of the partial sums of its expansion (theorem 12.2.7 (2)). Thus $F=0$ almost everywhere, and therefore everywhere, since $F$ is continuous. Consequently, the closure $M$ of the linear span of the products $e_ jg_ k$ satisfies $M^\perp =0$, and $M=\mathcal H_\Phi (\Omega _1\times \Omega _2)$ by proposition 11.1.1 . We can now prove ( 12.15 ). Denote its right side by $\mathfrak b$; it is the ideal generated by the products $(f_1\circ p_1)(f_2\circ p_2)$ of local sections $f_ i$ of $\mathcal I(\varphi _ i)$. Each product $e_ jg_ k$ is a section of $\mathfrak b$. Every $F\in \mathcal H_\Phi (\Omega _1\times \Omega _2)$ is the norm limit, hence by ( 12.9 ) the locally uniform limit, of a sequence of finite linear combinations of these products, so its germs lie in $\mathfrak b$ by lemma 12.2.1 . Since $\mathcal I(\Phi )$ is generated by the germs of the elements of $\mathcal H_\Phi (\Omega _1\times \Omega _2)$ (theorem 12.2.7 (3)), we obtain $\mathcal I(\Phi )\subset \mathfrak b$. Conversely, if $|f_ i|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi _ i}$ is integrable near $x_ i$ for $i=1,2$, then $|f_1(z)f_2(w)|^2\mathrm e^{-\Phi (z,w)}$ is integrable near $(x_1,x_2)$ by Fubini's theorem; since $\mathcal I(\Phi )$ is an ideal, $\mathfrak b\subset \mathcal I(\Phi )$. Finally, let $\varphi $ and $\psi $ be weights on $X$, and apply ( 12.14 ) to the weight $\varphi \circ p_1+\psi \circ p_2$ on $X\times X$ and the diagonal, which we identify with $X$. The restriction of the weight is $\varphi +\psi $, and by ( 12.15 ) the restriction of its multiplier ideal is generated by the products $f_1f_2$ of local sections $f_1$ of $\mathcal I(\varphi )$ and $f_2$ of $\mathcal I(\psi )$, that is, it equals $\mathcal I(\varphi )\mathcal I(\psi )$. This proves ( 12.16 ). $\square$ Corollary 12.4.2 . Let $f\colon X\to Y$ be a holomorphic map of complex manifolds and $\varphi $ a weight on $Y$. Then \[  \mathcal I(\varphi \circ f)\subset f^{-1}\mathcal I(\varphi )\cdot \mathcal O_ X,  \] with equality if $f$ is a submersion. On a connected component of $X$ on which $\varphi \circ f\equiv -\infty $, the left side is zero. Proof. Suppose first that $f$ is a submersion, and let $a\in X$. Choose holomorphic coordinates $y$ on $Y$ centered at $f(a)$. Since the differential of $f$ at $a$ is surjective, the complex Jacobian matrix at $a$ of the components of $y\circ f$, computed in a chart of $X$, has rank $\dim _{f(a)}Y$. By the holomorphic inverse function theorem (proposition 7.1.2 (3)), these components are the first coordinates of a holomorphic chart $(z,w)=(y\circ f,w)$ of $X$ near $a$. In these coordinates $f$ is the projection $(z,w)\mapsto z$. Thus $\varphi \circ f=\varphi \circ p_1+0\circ p_2$, and ( 12.15 ), together with $\mathcal I(0)=\mathcal O$, gives $\mathcal I(\varphi \circ f)=p_1^{-1}\mathcal I(\varphi )\cdot \mathcal O=f^{-1}\mathcal I(\varphi )\cdot \mathcal O_ X$. In general, the graph $\Gamma =\{ (x,f(x))\} $ is a complex submanifold of $X\times Y$, since in local coordinates $(x,y)$ the functions $(x,y-f(x))$ are holomorphic coordinates in which $\Gamma =\{ y-f(x)=0\} $; and $\iota (x)=(x,f(x))$ is a biholomorphism of $X$ onto $\Gamma $. The projection $q\colon X\times Y\to Y$ is a submersion, so $\mathcal I(\varphi \circ q)=q^{-1}\mathcal I(\varphi )\cdot \mathcal O_{X\times Y}$ by the first case. Since $\varphi \circ q\circ \iota =\varphi \circ f$, ( 12.14 ) applied to $\Gamma $ gives $\mathcal I(\varphi \circ f)\subset (q^{-1}\mathcal I(\varphi )\cdot \mathcal O_{X\times Y})|_\Gamma ^{\mathrm{im}}$ after transport by $\iota $. The right side is generated by the functions $g\circ q\circ \iota =g\circ f$ with $g$ a local section of $\mathcal I(\varphi )$, so it equals $f^{-1}\mathcal I(\varphi )\cdot \mathcal O_ X$. $\square$ Proposition 12.4.3 . Every multiplier ideal is integrally closed: if a germ $F\in \mathcal O_{X,x}$ satisfies an equation $F^ d+a_1F^{d-1}+\cdots +a_ d=0$ with $a_ j\in \mathcal I(\varphi )_ x^ j$, then $F\in \mathcal I(\varphi )_ x$. More explicitly, if $g_1,\ldots ,g_ r\in \mathcal I(\varphi )_ x$ and a holomorphic germ $F$ satisfies $|F|\leq C(\sum _ j|g_ j|^2)^{1/2}$ near $x$ for a constant $C$, then $F\in \mathcal I(\varphi )_ x$. Proof. The second assertion is immediate, since $|F|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi }\leq C^2\sum _ j|g_ j|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi }$ near $x$. For the first, choose generators $g_1,\ldots ,g_ r$ of $\mathcal I(\varphi )_ x$ (theorem 12.2.7 ), representatives of the $g_ j$, of $F$ and of the $a_ j$ on a common neighborhood, and put $|g|=(\sum _ j|g_ j|^2)^{1/2}$. Each $a_ j$ is a finite sum of products of $j$ generators with holomorphic coefficients, which are bounded on a smaller neighborhood; hence $|a_ j|\leq C_ j|g|^ j$ there. At a point where $|g|>0$, put $\lambda =|F|/|g|$. Dividing the equation by $|g|^ d$ gives $\lambda ^ d\leq \sum _ jC_ j\lambda ^{d-j}$, which forces $\lambda \leq C$ with $C=\max \{ 1,\sum _ jC_ j\} $. At a point where $|g|=0$, all the $a_ j$ vanish, so $F^ d=0$ and $F=0$. Thus $|F|\leq C|g|$ near $x$, and the second assertion applies. $\square$

title: Multiplier restriction subadditivity
text: Theorem 12.4.1 . Let $Z\subset X$ be a complex submanifold and $\varphi $ a weight on $X$. Then 12.14 \begin{equation} \label{eq:multiplier-restriction} \mathcal I(\varphi |_ Z)\subset \mathcal I(\varphi )|_ Z^{\mathrm{im}}; \end{equation} on a connected component of $Z$ on which $\varphi |_ Z\equiv -\infty $, the left side is zero. If $\varphi _1$ and $\varphi _2$ are weights on complex manifolds $X_1$ and $X_2$, and $p_ i\colon X_1\times X_2\to X_ i$ are the projections, then 12.15 \begin{equation} \label{eq:multiplier-external-product} \mathcal I(\varphi _1\circ p_1+\varphi _2\circ p_2) =(p_1^{-1}\mathcal I(\varphi _1)\cdot \mathcal O) (p_2^{-1}\mathcal I(\varphi _2)\cdot \mathcal O). \end{equation} In particular, for weights $\varphi $ and $\psi $ on $X$, 12.16 \begin{equation} \label{eq:multiplier-subadditivity} \mathcal I(\varphi +\psi )\subset \mathcal I(\varphi )\mathcal I(\psi ). \end{equation} Proof. The inclusion ( 12.14 ) is a restatement of corollary 11.4.6 : if $f\in \mathcal I(\varphi |_ Z)_ x$, that corollary provides a holomorphic germ $F$ at $x$ with $F|_ Z=f$ and $F\in \mathcal I(\varphi )_ x$. The product formula is local. Near a point $(x_1,x_2)$ we choose bounded polydiscs $\Omega _ i$ around $x_ i$ in charts of $X_ i$ on which $\varphi _ i$ is bounded above; subtracting constants, which changes none of the multiplier ideals, we may assume that $\varphi _1,\varphi _2\leq 0$. We write $\Phi =\varphi _1\circ p_1+\varphi _2\circ p_2$, a nonpositive weight on the polydisc $\Omega _1\times \Omega _2$. Let $(e_ j)$ and $(g_ k)$ be orthonormal bases of $\mathcal H_{\varphi _1}(\Omega _1)$ and $\mathcal H_{\varphi _2}(\Omega _2)$, which exist by theorem 12.2.7 (2). By Fubini's theorem the functions $e_ j(z)g_ k(w)$ form an orthonormal family in $\mathcal H_\Phi (\Omega _1\times \Omega _2)$. We show that its linear span is dense. Let $F\in \mathcal H_\Phi (\Omega _1\times \Omega _2)$. By Fubini's theorem, for almost every $w\in \Omega _2$ we have $\varphi _2(w)>-\infty $ and $F(\cdot ,w)\in \mathcal H_{\varphi _1}(\Omega _1)$, and for such $w$ we put \[  a_ j(w)=\int _{\Omega _1}F(z,w)\overline{e_ j(z)} \mathrm e^{-\varphi _1(z)}\, \mathrm dV_ z.  \] We claim that each $a_ j$ agrees almost everywhere with an element of $\mathcal H_{\varphi _2}(\Omega _2)$ of norm at most $\| F\| _\Phi $. Choose compact sets $K_\ell \uparrow \Omega _1$ and put $E_\ell =K_\ell \cap \{ \mathrm e^{-\varphi _1}\leq \ell \} $; these sets increase and exhaust $\Omega _1$ up to the pole set of $\varphi _1$, which has measure zero. The function $a_{j,\ell }$ obtained by integrating over $E_\ell $ instead of $\Omega _1$ is holomorphic on $\Omega _2$. Indeed, let $L\subset \Omega _2$ be compact. For $z\in E_\ell \subset K_\ell $ and $w\in L$, the integrand $F(z,w)\overline{e_ j(z)}\mathrm e^{-\varphi _1(z)}$ and all its partial derivatives in $w$ are bounded, because $F$ and its derivatives are continuous on $K_\ell \times L$, $e_ j$ is bounded on $K_\ell $, and $\mathrm e^{-\varphi _1}\leq \ell $ on $E_\ell $. Hence we may differentiate under the integral sign any number of times: $a_{j,\ell }$ is smooth, and $\partial a_{j,\ell }/\partial \bar w_ m=0$ for all $m$, because $F$ is holomorphic in $w$. By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality in $z$, followed by integration in $w$ against $\mathrm e^{-\varphi _2}$, \[  \| a_ j-a_{j,\ell }\| _{\varphi _2}^2 \leq \| F\| _\Phi ^2 \int _{\Omega _1\setminus E_\ell }|e_ j|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi _1}\, \mathrm dV_ z \longrightarrow 0  \] by dominated convergence, since the sets $\Omega _1\setminus E_\ell $ decrease to a null set and $|e_ j|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi _1}$ is integrable. Since $\varphi _2\leq 0$, the holomorphic functions $a_{j,\ell }$ therefore converge to $a_ j$ in $L^2(\Omega _2)$, and hence in the sense of distributions; so $\bar\partial a_ j=0$, and $a_ j$ agrees almost everywhere with a holomorphic function, by lemma 11.3.5 (1). The same Cauchy–Schwarz estimate over all of $\Omega _1$ gives $\| a_ j\| _{\varphi _2}\leq \| F\| _\Phi $, which proves the claim. Now suppose that $F$ is orthogonal to all the products $e_ jg_ k$. By Fubini's theorem, whose use is justified by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, $\langle a_ j,g_ k\rangle _{\varphi _2}=\langle F,e_ jg_ k\rangle _\Phi =0$ for all $k$. Since the linear span of the $g_ k$ is dense in $\mathcal H_{\varphi _2}(\Omega _2)$, the element $a_ j$ of this space is orthogonal to itself, so $a_ j=0$ almost everywhere, for every $j$. Hence for almost every $w$ all the coefficients $\langle F(\cdot ,w),e_ j\rangle _{\varphi _1}$ vanish, and $F(\cdot ,w)=0$, because $F(\cdot ,w)$ is the limit of the partial sums of its expansion (theorem 12.2.7 (2)). Thus $F=0$ almost everywhere, and therefore everywhere, since $F$ is continuous. Consequently, the closure $M$ of the linear span of the products $e_ jg_ k$ satisfies $M^\perp =0$, and $M=\mathcal H_\Phi (\Omega _1\times \Omega _2)$ by proposition 11.1.1 . We can now prove ( 12.15 ). Denote its right side by $\mathfrak b$; it is the ideal generated by the products $(f_1\circ p_1)(f_2\circ p_2)$ of local sections $f_ i$ of $\mathcal I(\varphi _ i)$. Each product $e_ jg_ k$ is a section of $\mathfrak b$. Every $F\in \mathcal H_\Phi (\Omega _1\times \Omega _2)$ is the norm limit, hence by ( 12.9 ) the locally uniform limit, of a sequence of finite linear combinations of these products, so its germs lie in $\mathfrak b$ by lemma 12.2.1 . Since $\mathcal I(\Phi )$ is generated by the germs of the elements of $\mathcal H_\Phi (\Omega _1\times \Omega _2)$ (theorem 12.2.7 (3)), we obtain $\mathcal I(\Phi )\subset \mathfrak b$. Conversely, if $|f_ i|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi _ i}$ is integrable near $x_ i$ for $i=1,2$, then $|f_1(z)f_2(w)|^2\mathrm e^{-\Phi (z,w)}$ is integrable near $(x_1,x_2)$ by Fubini's theorem; since $\mathcal I(\Phi )$ is an ideal, $\mathfrak b\subset \mathcal I(\Phi )$. Finally, let $\varphi $ and $\psi $ be weights on $X$, and apply ( 12.14 ) to the weight $\varphi \circ p_1+\psi \circ p_2$ on $X\times X$ and the diagonal, which we identify with $X$. The restriction of the weight is $\varphi +\psi $, and by ( 12.15 ) the restriction of its multiplier ideal is generated by the products $f_1f_2$ of local sections $f_1$ of $\mathcal I(\varphi )$ and $f_2$ of $\mathcal I(\psi )$, that is, it equals $\mathcal I(\varphi )\mathcal I(\psi )$. This proves ( 12.16 ). $\square$

title: Multiplier holomorphic pullback
text: Corollary 12.4.2 . Let $f\colon X\to Y$ be a holomorphic map of complex manifolds and $\varphi $ a weight on $Y$. Then \[  \mathcal I(\varphi \circ f)\subset f^{-1}\mathcal I(\varphi )\cdot \mathcal O_ X,  \] with equality if $f$ is a submersion. On a connected component of $X$ on which $\varphi \circ f\equiv -\infty $, the left side is zero. Proof. Suppose first that $f$ is a submersion, and let $a\in X$. Choose holomorphic coordinates $y$ on $Y$ centered at $f(a)$. Since the differential of $f$ at $a$ is surjective, the complex Jacobian matrix at $a$ of the components of $y\circ f$, computed in a chart of $X$, has rank $\dim _{f(a)}Y$. By the holomorphic inverse function theorem (proposition 7.1.2 (3)), these components are the first coordinates of a holomorphic chart $(z,w)=(y\circ f,w)$ of $X$ near $a$. In these coordinates $f$ is the projection $(z,w)\mapsto z$. Thus $\varphi \circ f=\varphi \circ p_1+0\circ p_2$, and ( 12.15 ), together with $\mathcal I(0)=\mathcal O$, gives $\mathcal I(\varphi \circ f)=p_1^{-1}\mathcal I(\varphi )\cdot \mathcal O=f^{-1}\mathcal I(\varphi )\cdot \mathcal O_ X$. In general, the graph $\Gamma =\{ (x,f(x))\} $ is a complex submanifold of $X\times Y$, since in local coordinates $(x,y)$ the functions $(x,y-f(x))$ are holomorphic coordinates in which $\Gamma =\{ y-f(x)=0\} $; and $\iota (x)=(x,f(x))$ is a biholomorphism of $X$ onto $\Gamma $. The projection $q\colon X\times Y\to Y$ is a submersion, so $\mathcal I(\varphi \circ q)=q^{-1}\mathcal I(\varphi )\cdot \mathcal O_{X\times Y}$ by the first case. Since $\varphi \circ q\circ \iota =\varphi \circ f$, ( 12.14 ) applied to $\Gamma $ gives $\mathcal I(\varphi \circ f)\subset (q^{-1}\mathcal I(\varphi )\cdot \mathcal O_{X\times Y})|_\Gamma ^{\mathrm{im}}$ after transport by $\iota $. The right side is generated by the functions $g\circ q\circ \iota =g\circ f$ with $g$ a local section of $\mathcal I(\varphi )$, so it equals $f^{-1}\mathcal I(\varphi )\cdot \mathcal O_ X$. $\square$

12.5 Strong openness by extension from moving slices The constant in the Ohsawa–Takegoshi theorem (theorem 11.4.4 ) depends only on the width of the normal direction, not on the weight. This uniformity allows us to extend a germ from a sequence of parallel hyperplanes approaching a point, with weights that vary along the sequence. If a germ were not in the expected ideal, we would obtain extensions whose norms are too small to be compatible with their behavior along a fixed holomorphic curve. The two lemmas below provide this curve and the corresponding norm estimate. Lemma 12.5.1 . If $0<|a|<r$ and $H\in \mathcal O(\Omega )$ satisfies \[  H(a,\cdot )=F(a,\cdot )	ext{ on }P,\qquad (H/F)\circ \gamma 	ext{ is holomorphic at }0	ext{ with value }0,  \] then 12.17  egin{equation} \label{eq:curve-extension-norm-lower-bound} \int _\Omega |H|^2\, \mathrm dV\geq c|a|^{-2}. \end{equation} For $n=1$, the polydisc $P$ is a point and carries counting measure. Proof. We bound the norm of $H$ from below by a weighted norm of $H\circ \gamma $ on a disc, and then use that $H\circ \gamma =F\circ \gamma $ at the points $t$ with $t^ q=a$. Choose $ho >0$ with $ho ^ q<R$ such that $\gamma $ is defined on a neighborhood of the closed disc $|t|\leq ho $, $F\circ \gamma $ has no zeros for $0<|t|\leq ho $, and, since $\gamma $ is continuous with $\gamma (0)=0$, $(\gamma _2(t),\ldots ,\gamma _ n(t))$ lies in a fixed polydisc $P'\Subset P$ centered at $0$ for $|t|\leq ho $. Let $\delta >0$ be half the distance from $P'$ to the complement of $P$. For $0<|z_1|<ho ^ q$, each of the $q$ points $\gamma (t)$ with $t^ q=z_1$ has the form $(z_1,w)$ with $w\in P'$, and ( 12.9 ) for the holomorphic function $H(z_1,\cdot )$ on the ball $B(w,\delta )\subset P$ gives $|H(z_1,w)|^2\leq C_\delta \int _ P|H(z_1,w')|^2\, \mathrm dV(w')$, where $C_\delta ^{-1}$ is the volume of a ball of radius $\delta $ in $\mathbb C^{n-1}$. Summing over the $q$ points, we obtain $\sum _{t^ q=z_1}|H(\gamma (t))|^2\leq qC_\delta \int _ P|H(z_1,w')|^2\, \mathrm dV(w')$. Now we integrate over $|z_1|<ho ^ q$. The map $t\mapsto t^ q$ maps each of the $q$ half-open sectors $\{ 0<|t|<ho ,\  2\pi k/q\leq \arg t<2\pi (k+1)/q\} $ bijectively onto the punctured disc $0<|z_1|<ho ^ q$, and on the interior of the sector it is a diffeomorphism onto the complement of a ray, with real Jacobian $|qt^{q-1}|^2$. By the change of variables formula, applied on each sector, $\int _{|t|<ho }\Phi (t)q^2|t|^{2q-2}\, \mathrm dV_2(t)=\int _{|z_1|<ho ^ q}\sum _{t^ q=z_1}\Phi (t)\, \mathrm dV_2(z_1)$ for every nonnegative measurable $\Phi $. Since $\Delta _{ho ^ q}	imes P\subset \Omega $, it follows that \[  \int _\Omega |H|^2\, \mathrm dV \geq c_0\int _{|t|<ho }|H(\gamma (t))|^2 q^2|t|^{2q-2}\, \mathrm dV_2(t)  \] with $c_0=1/(qC_\delta )$. This function is holomorphic for $0<|t|<ho $, because $F\circ \gamma $ has no zeros there, and by hypothesis it extends holomorphically across $0$ with $h(0)=0$; thus $h(t)=\sum _{\ell \geq 1}h_\ell t^\ell $ for $|t|<ho $. Then $H\circ \gamma =t^ mvh$, and $|v|$ is bounded below by a positive constant on the compact disc $|t|\leq ho $, being continuous and without zeros there. On each circle $|t|=s<ho $ the power series of $h$ converges uniformly, and the monomials $t^\ell $ are orthogonal there, so $\int _0^{2\pi }|h(s\mathrm e^{\mathrm i	heta })|^2\, \mathrm d	heta =2\pi \sum _\ell |h_\ell |^2s^{2\ell }$. Now let $0<|a|<ho ^ q$. For each of the $q$ roots $b$ of $b^ q=a$, the point $\gamma (b)$ lies on the slice $\{ z_1=a\} $, where $H=F$, and $F(\gamma (b))

We take for $N$ the union of three sets: the set where $G=\infty $; the set of $a$ for which one of the countably many functions $\varphi (a,\cdot )$, $\psi _ j(a,\cdot )$ is identically $-\infty $ on $P_0$; and the set of $a$ for which $\psi _ j(a,\cdot )	o \varphi (a,\cdot )$ fails on a subset of $P_0$ of positive measure. The first set is null because $G$ is integrable, and the other two are null by Fubini's theorem, because pole sets of weights have measure zero and $\psi _ j	o \varphi $ almost everywhere. Then the functions $\psi _ j(a_ i,\cdot )$ and $\varphi (a_ i,\cdot )$ are weights on $P_0$ (proposition 8.2.3 ), and the former increase to the latter almost everywhere on $P_0$. Moreover $G(a_ i)>0$ for all large $i$, because $F(a_ i,\cdot )$ does not vanish identically on $P_0$: for small $|a_ i|$, the slice $\{ a_ i\} 	imes P_0$ contains the points $\gamma (b)$ with $b^ q=a_ i$, at which $F
eq 0$. Discarding finitely many terms, we assume that this holds for all $i$. Step 3: integrability on a fixed inner slice. Fix $i$. Since $G(a_ i)<\infty $, the germ of $F(a_ i,\cdot )$ at every point of $P_0$ belongs to $\mathcal I(\varphi (a_ i,\cdot ))$. By the induction hypothesis, applied on $P_0$, each point of the compact set $\overline P\subset P_0$ has a neighborhood on which $|F(a_ i,\cdot )|^2\mathrm e^{-\psi _ j(a_ i,\cdot )}$ is integrable for some $j$. Covering $\overline P$ by finitely many such neighborhoods and using that the $\psi _ j$ increase, we find one index $j$ for which $\int _ P|F(a_ i,w)|^2\mathrm e^{-\psi _ j(a_ i,w)}\, \mathrm dV_ w<\infty $. For larger $j$ these integrands decrease and converge almost everywhere to $|F(a_ i,\cdot )|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi (a_ i,\cdot )}$, so by dominated convergence their integrals over $P$ converge to a number at most $G(a_ i)$. Since $G(a_ i)>0$, we can choose an index $j_ i$ with \[  \int _ P|F(a_ i,w)|^2\mathrm e^{-\psi _{j_ i}(a_ i,w)}\, \mathrm dV_ w \leq 2G(a_ i).  \] The polydisc $P$ does not depend on $i$; this is what makes the estimates of the next step uniform. Step 4: extension and contradiction. For large $i$ we have $|a_ i|<\min \{ r,R\} $, so that the normal coordinate $z_1-a_ i$ takes values in a disc of radius $2R$ on $\Omega $. The polydisc $\Omega $ is pseudoconvex by corollary 11.2.5 , being a product of discs, each of which is a sublevel set of a function $|\zeta -\zeta _0|^2$ on $\mathbb C$. Applying theorem 11.4.4 , after reordering the coordinates, with the normal coordinate $z_1-a_ i$, the radius $2R$ and the weight $\psi _{j_ i}$, and using the last display of Step 3, we obtain $H_ i\in \mathcal O(\Omega )$ with $H_ i(a_ i,\cdot )=F(a_ i,\cdot )$ on $P$ and \[  \int _\Omega |H_ i|^2\mathrm e^{-\psi _{j_ i}}\, \mathrm dV\leq 8C_0R^2G(a_ i),  \] where $C_0$ is the absolute constant of that theorem. In particular the germ of $H_ i$ at $0$ lies in $\mathcal I(\psi _{j_ i})_0\subset J$, so $H_ i=\sum _ lb_ lg_ l$ near $0$ with holomorphic $b_ l$, and $(H_ i/F)\circ \gamma =\sum _ l(b_ l\circ \gamma )\cdot (g_ l/F)\circ \gamma $ extends holomorphically across $t=0$ with value $0$. Since $\psi _{j_ i}\leq 0$, the last display also bounds $\int _\Omega |H_ i|^2\, \mathrm dV$. Now lemma 12.5.2 gives $c|a_ i|^{-2}\leq 8C_0R^2G(a_ i)$ for all large $i$, contradicting $|a_ i|^2G(a_ i)	o 0$. Hence $F\in J$, which proves ( 12.18 ). Finally, $\mathcal I(\varphi )_ x$ is generated by finitely many germs, which by ( 12.18 ) all lie in $\mathcal I(\psi _ j)_ x$ for one index $j$. Then $\mathcal I(\varphi )_ x\subset \mathcal I(\psi _ j)_ x$, and equality holds for this and every later index, since the ideals increase and are contained in $\mathcal I(\varphi )_ x$. $\square$

title: Strong openness
text: Corollary 12.5.4 (Strong openness) . Let $\varphi $ and $\chi $ be weights on $X$, and let $x\in X$. Then 12.19 \begin{equation} \label{eq:strong-openness} \mathcal I(\varphi )_ x=\bigcup _{\varepsilon >0} \mathcal I((1+\varepsilon )\varphi )_ x \end{equation} and, more generally, \[  \mathcal I(\varphi )_ x=\bigcup _{\varepsilon >0} \mathcal I(\varphi +\varepsilon \chi )_ x.  \] Moreover, there is a single $\varepsilon >0$ with $\mathcal I((1+\varepsilon )\varphi )_ x=\mathcal I(\varphi )_ x$, and similarly a single $\varepsilon >0$ with $\mathcal I(\varphi +\varepsilon \chi )_ x=\mathcal I(\varphi )_ x$. Proof. The assertions are local. On a relatively compact neighborhood of $x$ the weights are bounded above, and subtracting constants we may assume $\varphi \leq 0$ and $\chi \leq 0$ there; this changes $(1+\varepsilon )\varphi $ and $\varphi +\varepsilon \chi $ only by bounded amounts and hence changes none of the ideals. Then $(1+\varepsilon )\varphi $ and $\varphi +\varepsilon \chi $ decrease as $\varepsilon $ increases, so the corresponding ideals decrease with $\varepsilon $ and are contained in $\mathcal I(\varphi )_ x$. The sequences $(1+1/j)\varphi $ and $\varphi +\chi /j$ increase with $j$ and converge to $\varphi $ wherever $\varphi $ and $\chi $ are finite, hence almost everywhere. By theorem 12.5.3 , $\mathcal I((1+1/j)\varphi )_ x=\mathcal I(\varphi )_ x$ and $\mathcal I(\varphi +\chi /j)_ x=\mathcal I(\varphi )_ x$ for all large $j$, which proves both assertions. $\square$

title: Multiplier monomial threshold
text: Example 12.5.5 . Let $c\geq 0$ and $\varphi =c\log |z|^2$ on a disc around $0\in \mathbb C$, where $\varphi =0$ if $c=0$. A germ of order $k$ at $0$ is $z^ k$ times a unit, so by polar coordinates it belongs to $\mathcal I(\varphi )_0$ if and only if $\int _0^ rt^{2k-2c+1}\, \mathrm dt<\infty $, that is, $k+1>c$. Hence $\mathcal I(\varphi )=(z^{\lfloor c\rfloor })$. When $c$ is a positive integer, the germ $z^{c-1}$ just fails, because the radial integral diverges logarithmically. This strict threshold shows why theorem 12.5.3 concerns increasing sequences: on the unit disc, the weights $\varphi _ j=(1-1/j)\log |z|^2$, $j\geq 2$, decrease to $\log |z|^2$, yet $\mathcal I(\varphi _ j)=\mathcal O$ for every $j$, whereas $\mathcal I(\log |z|^2)=(z)$.

title: Birational change of variables and logarithmic thresholds
text:
12.6 Birational change of variables and logarithmic thresholds On a modification of $X$, the change of variables formula turns membership in a multiplier ideal into an integrability condition twisted by the Jacobian (proposition 12.6.4 ), which becomes explicit on a log resolution. Let $\pi \colon Y	o X$ be a proper bimeromorphic holomorphic map between complex manifolds of dimension $n$. Thus there is a nowhere dense analytic subset $A\subset X$ such that $\pi ^{-1}(A)$ is nowhere dense in $Y$ and $\pi $ maps $Y\setminus \pi ^{-1}(A)$ biholomorphically onto $X\setminus A$ (section A.3 ). In local coordinates $w$ on $Y$ and $z$ on $X$, the complex Jacobian determinant $J_\pi =\det (\partial z_ i/\partial w_ j)$ is holomorphic, and it does not vanish identically on any nonempty open set, since it has no zeros on the dense open set $Y\setminus \pi ^{-1}(A)$. By the chain rule, a change of coordinates on either side multiplies $J_\pi $ by a nowhere vanishing holomorphic function; equivalently, $\pi ^*(\mathrm dz_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm dz_ n)=J_\pi \, \mathrm dw_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm dw_ n$. Hence the functions $J_\pi $ are the local equations of an effective Cartier divisor $K_{Y/X}$ on $Y$ (section A.5 ), the relative canonical divisor , and $\mathcal O_ Y(K_{Y/X})$ is generated locally by $J_\pi ^{-1}$. We measure the vanishing of holomorphic functions along hypersurfaces as follows. Let $E\subset Y$ be a prime divisor, that is, an irreducible hypersurface. By corollary A.2.13 , applied to the family consisting of $E$ alone, its regular locus $E_{\mathrm{reg}}$ is a connected manifold, dense in $E$. Let $p\in E_{\mathrm{reg}}$, choose coordinates $w=(w_1,w')$ at $p$ with $E=\{ w_1=0\} $ near $p$, and let $h$ be holomorphic near $p$. The order of $h$ along $E$ at $p$ is the supremum, in $\{ 0,1,2,\ldots \} \cup \{ +\infty \} $, of the integers $k\geq 0$ such that $h$ is divisible by $w_1^ k$ near $p$, that is, $h=w_1^ kh_1$ near $p$ with $h_1$ holomorphic. By the next lemma, it does not depend on the coordinates, and for a function defined near $E$ it does not depend on the point of $E_{\mathrm{reg}}$. Lemma 12.6.1 . Let $E$ be a prime divisor on a complex manifold $Y$, let $p\in E_{\mathrm{reg}}$, let $w=(w_1,w')$ be holomorphic coordinates at $p$ with $E=\{ w_1=0\} $ near $p$, and let $h$ be holomorphic near $p$. Let $\Delta =\Delta _1	imes \Delta '$ be a polydisc centered at $p$, where $\Delta _1$ is a disc in the $w_1$-plane, so small that $E\cap \Delta =\{ w_1=0\} \cap \Delta $ and that ( 7.1 ) gives the expansion \[  h=\sum _{l\geq 0}a_ l(w')w_1^ l\quad 	ext{on }\Delta ,\qquad a_ l(w')= rac1{l!}\partial _{w_1}^ lh(0,w'),  \] where the functions $a_ l$ are holomorphic on $\Delta '$. Let $k\geq 0$ be an integer. If $h$ is divisible by $w_1^ k$ near some point of $E\cap \Delta $, then $a_ l=0$ for all $l<k$; conversely, if $a_ l=0$ for all $l<k$, then $h$ is divisible by $w_1^ k$ near $p$. In particular, a holomorphic function that vanishes on $E$ near $p$ is divisible by $w_1$ near $p$, and if $	ilde w=(	ilde w_1,	ilde w')$ are other coordinates at $p$ with $E=\{ 	ilde w_1=0\} $ near $p$, then $	ilde w_1$ is a unit times $w_1$ near $p$. The order of $h$ along $E$ at $p$ does not depend on the coordinates. It is the smallest $l$ with $a_ l
eq 0$, and it is $+\infty $ if and only if $h$ vanishes near $p$. In particular, $h$ is not divisible by $w_1$ near $p$ if and only if $h(0,\cdot )$ does not vanish identically near $p$. Moreover, the order of $h$ along $E$ is the same at all points of $E\cap \Delta $. If $h$ is holomorphic on a neighborhood of $E$, then its order along $E$ is the same at all points of $E_{\mathrm{reg}}$. Orders add under products: if $g$ is also holomorphic near $p$, then the order of $hg$ along $E$ at $p$ is the sum of the orders of $h$ and $g$. Proof. (1) If $h=w_1^ kh_1$ near a point $(0,w'_0)$ of $E\cap \Delta $, with $h_1$ holomorphic, then the Leibniz rule gives $\partial _{w_1}^ lh(0,w')=0$ for $l<k$ and $w'$ near $w'_0$; so $a_ l=0$ near $w'_0$, and hence on the connected set $\Delta '$ by the identity theorem. Conversely, if $a_ l=0$ for $l<k$, then $h=w_1^ k\sum _{l\geq k}a_ lw_1^{l-k}$ near $p$; the last series is obtained from the Taylor series of $h$ at $p$ by lowering the exponent of $w_1$ in each term by $k$, so it converges on the same polydiscs and defines a holomorphic function (section A.1 ). If $h$ vanishes on $E$ near $p$, then $a_0=h(0,\cdot )$ vanishes near the center of $\Delta '$, hence on $\Delta '$, and the case $k=1$ shows that $h$ is divisible by $w_1$ near $p$. Applying this to $	ilde w_1$, and to $w_1$ with the roles of the two coordinate systems exchanged, we obtain $	ilde w_1=c\, w_1$ and $w_1=	ilde c\, 	ilde w_1$ near $p$ with holomorphic $c$ and $	ilde c$. Then $c	ilde c=1$ off $E$; since the continuous function $c	ilde c$ equals $1$ on the dense set $\{ w_1
eq 0\} $, it equals $1$ near $p$, and $c$ is a unit. (2) By (1), $h$ is divisible by $w_1^ k$ near $p$ if and only if it is divisible by $	ilde w_1^ k$ near $p$, so the order does not depend on the coordinates. Let $k_0$ be the smallest $l$ with $a_ l
eq 0$, and $k_0=+\infty $ if all $a_ l$ vanish. By (1), $h$ is divisible by $w_1^ k$ near $p$ if and only if $k\leq k_0$, so the order of $h$ along $E$ at $p$ is $k_0$. If all $a_ l$ vanish, then $h=0$ on $\Delta $; conversely, if $h$ vanishes near $p$, then all $a_ l$ vanish near the center of $\Delta '$, hence on $\Delta '$. The case $k_0=0$ gives the assertion about $h(0,\cdot )=a_0$, because $a_0$ vanishes identically on $\Delta '$ if and only if it vanishes near the center of $\Delta '$. Finally, let $q=(0,w'_ q)\in E\cap \Delta $. The coordinates $w$ are also coordinates at $q$ with $E=\{ w_1=0\} $ near $q$, and by their formula the coefficients of the expansion of $h$ on a small polydisc centered at $q$ are the restrictions of the same functions $a_ l$. Since $\Delta '$ is connected, $a_ l$ vanishes near $w'_ q$ if and only if it vanishes on $\Delta '$, by the identity theorem. Hence the orders of $h$ along $E$ at $q$ and at $p$ are equal. (3) By the last assertion of (2), the order of $h$ along $E$ is a locally constant function on $E_{\mathrm{reg}}$, which is connected (corollary A.2.13 ). Hence it is constant. (4) Shrinking $\Delta $, we may assume that $g$ is defined on $\Delta $; let $b_ j$ and $e_ m$ be the coefficients of the expansions of $g$ and $hg$ on $\Delta $. By the Leibniz rule, $e_ m=\sum _{i+j=m}a_ ib_ j$. If $h$ or $g$ has infinite order, then $hg$ vanishes near $p$ and has infinite order by (2). Otherwise let $k$ and $l$ be the orders of $h$ and $g$. Then $e_ m=0$ for $m<k+l$, because each term $a_ ib_ j$ with $i+j<k+l$ has $i<k$ or $j<l$, and $e_{k+l}=a_ kb_ l$. Since $a_ k$ and $b_ l$ are not identically zero and the ring of holomorphic functions on the connected set $\Delta '$ is an integral domain, by the identity theorem, $e_{k+l}
eq 0$. By (2), the order of $hg$ is $k+l$. $\square$ If $h$ is holomorphic on a neighborhood of $E$, we call the common value in lemma 12.6.1 (3) the order $\operatorname {ord}_ Eh$ of $h$ along $E$. The order of $J_\pi $ along a prime divisor $E\subset Y$ is defined in the same way, because local Jacobians differ by units, which have order zero, and orders add under products (lemma 12.6.1 (4)); it is the coefficient $\operatorname {ord}_ EK_{Y/X}$ of $E$ in $K_{Y/X}$. For divisors with simple normal crossings support we use local monomial equations. Lemma 12.6.2 . Let $w$ be holomorphic coordinates centered at a point $p$ of a complex manifold, let $0\leq \ell \leq n$, and let $h$ be holomorphic near $p$, not identically zero near $p$, with zero set near $p$ contained in $\{ w_1\cdots w_\ell =0\} $. For $i\leq \ell $ let $k_ i$ be the largest integer such that $h$ is divisible by $w_ i^{k_ i}$ near $p$. Then $h=u\prod _{i\leq \ell }w_ i^{k_ i}$ near $p$, with $u$ holomorphic and $u(p)
eq 0$. Moreover, a holomorphic function near $p$ that is divisible by $w_ i^{a_ i}$ near $p$ for each $i\leq \ell $ is divisible by $\prod _{i\leq \ell }w_ i^{a_ i}$. Proof. Let $g=\sum _\alpha c_\alpha w^\alpha $ be the power series at $p$ of a holomorphic function, as in ( 7.1 ). If $g=w_ i^ ag'$ near $p$, then multiplying the series of $g'$ by $w_ i^ a$ shows that $c_\alpha =0$ whenever $\alpha _ i<a$. Conversely, if $c_\alpha =0$ whenever $\alpha _ i<a_ i$ for some $i\leq \ell $, then $g=\prod _ iw_ i^{a_ i}\cdot \sum _\alpha c_\alpha w^{\alpha -\sum _ ia_ ie_ i}$, where $e_ i$ is the $i$th unit vector, and the last series converges on the same polydiscs as that of $g$. This proves the last assertion, and it shows that $k_ i<\infty $, since otherwise all $c_\alpha $ of $h$ would vanish. Hence $h=u\prod _{i\leq \ell }w_ i^{k_ i}$ with $u$ holomorphic near $p$, and $u$ is not divisible by any $w_ i$, $i\leq \ell $, by the maximality of $k_ i$. It remains to show that $u(p)
eq 0$. Suppose, to the contrary, that $u(p)=0$. The zero set of $u$ near $p$ lies in that of $h$, hence in $\{ w_1\cdots w_\ell =0\} $; so $\ell \geq 1$. We work in the coordinates $w$, with $p=0$. Let $P$ be the first nonzero homogeneous term of $u$; it has positive degree $m$. Choose $v\in \mathbb C^ n$ with $P(v)
eq 0$ and $v_ i
eq 0$ for all $i$, which is possible since the polynomial $P(v)v_1\cdots v_ n$ is not identically zero. Then $t\mapsto u(tv)$ has a zero of order $m$ at $t=0$; choose $\varepsilon >0$ such that it has no other zeros in $|t|\leq \varepsilon $, and such that all points $y+tv$ considered below lie in the neighborhood of $0$ where the hypothesis on the zero set holds. Since $(y,t)\mapsto u(y+tv)$ is continuous and does not vanish on the compact set $\{ 0\} 	imes \{ |t|=\varepsilon \} $, there is a connected neighborhood $N$ of $0$ such that $u(y+tv)
eq 0$ for $y\in N$ and $|t|=\varepsilon $. By the argument principle, the number of zeros of $t\mapsto u(y+tv)$ in $|t|<\varepsilon $, counted with multiplicity, is \[   rac1{2\pi \mathrm i}\int _{|t|=\varepsilon } rac{\partial _ t[u(y+tv)]}{u(y+tv)}\, \mathrm dt,  \] a continuous integer-valued function of $y\in N$; it equals $m\geq 1$ at $y=0$, hence everywhere on $N$. So for every $y\in N$ there is $t$ with $u(y+tv)=0$, and then $y_ i+tv_ i=0$ for some $i\leq \ell $, that is, $u(\sigma _ i(y))=0$ for the linear projection $\sigma _ i(y)=y-(y_ i/v_ i)v$ onto the hyperplane $H_ i=\{ y_ i=0\} $. Hence the product of the holomorphic functions $u\circ \sigma _ i$, $i\leq \ell $, vanishes on $N$. If none of them vanished identically on $N$, each would be nonzero on a dense open subset of $N$, by the identity theorem, and so would be their product. Thus some $u\circ \sigma _ i$ vanishes on $N$; since $\sigma _ i(y)=y$ for $y\in H_ i$, the function $u$ vanishes on $H_ i\cap N$, which is a neighborhood of $0$ in $H_ i$. By the first paragraph, applied with $a=1$, $u$ is then divisible by $w_ i$ near $0$: all coefficients $c_\alpha $ of $u$ with $\alpha _ i=0$ vanish, since they are the coefficients of the restriction of $u$ to $H_ i$. This contradiction shows that $u(p)
eq 0$. $\square$ Let $D$ be an effective divisor on $Y$ with simple normal crossings support, and let $E_1,E_2,\ldots $ be the irreducible components of its support; they are smooth, and connected because their regular loci are (corollary A.2.13 ). Near a point $p$ choose coordinates $w$ in which the support of $D$ is $\{ w_1\cdots w_\ell =0\} $, with $E_ i=\{ w_ i=0\} $ for the components through $p$. By lemma 12.6.2 , a local equation of $D$ at $p$ is a unit times $\prod _{i\leq \ell }w_ i^{d_ i}$, where $d_ i\geq 1$ is its order along $E_ i$. Two local equations differ by a unit on the overlap of their domains, so $d_ i$ does not depend on the point of $E_ i$; it is the multiplicity of $E_ i$ in $D$, and we write $D=\sum _ id_ iE_ i$. Conversely, for integers $a_ i\geq 0$ we write $\sum _ ia_ iE_ i$ for the effective divisor whose local equations are the monomials $\prod _{i\leq \ell }w_ i^{a_ i}$. If $A$ and $B$ are effective divisors on $Y$ with local equations $s_ A$ and $s_ B$, then $\mathcal O_ Y(A-B)=\mathcal O_ Y(A)\mathcal O_ Y(-B)$ is the sheaf of functions on the complement of the support of $A$ that are locally of the form $g\, s_ B/s_ A$ with $g$ holomorphic. Definition 12.6.3 . Let $E\subset Y$ be a prime divisor. Its center on $X$ is $\pi (E)$, which is an analytic subset of $X$ by theorem A.6.2 ; it is connected, because $E$ is. Let $f$ be a holomorphic function on an open set $V\subset X$ containing the center, and let $V_0$ be the connected component of $V$ containing it. If $f$ vanishes identically on $V_0$, for instance if $f=0$, we set $\operatorname {ord}_ Ef=+\infty $. Otherwise $f\circ \pi $ does not vanish identically on any nonempty open subset of $\pi ^{-1}(V_0)$, because such a set contains a nonempty open set mapped biholomorphically onto an open subset of $V_0$, on which $f$ does not vanish identically by the identity theorem; since $E\subset \pi ^{-1}(V_0)$, the order of $f$ along $E$ is $\operatorname {ord}_ Ef=\operatorname {ord}_ E(f\circ \pi )<\infty $. This order along a divisor differs from the order at a point of proposition 12.1.4 , although the two agree for the exceptional divisor of the blowup of a point (example 12.6.10 ). For a holomorphic germ $f$ at a point $x$, this defines $\operatorname {ord}_ Ef$ for the prime divisors $E$ on smooth models of open neighborhoods of $x$ on which $f$ is defined; this is how orders of germs enter the results below. The log discrepancy of $E$ is \[  A_ X(E)=1+\operatorname {ord}_ E K_{Y/X},  \] where $\operatorname {ord}_ EK_{Y/X}=\operatorname {ord}_ EJ_\pi $ is the coefficient of $E$ in $K_{Y/X}$. Since $J_\pi $ is holomorphic, $A_ X(E)\geq 1$, and a prime divisor on $X$ itself, with $\pi $ the identity, has log discrepancy one. The center, the order and the log discrepancy depend only on the prime divisor over $X$ represented by $E$. To see that these notions depend only on the prime divisor over $X$, let $ho \colon Y'	o Y$ be a map from a common smooth model and $E'$ the strict transform of $E$. By proposition A.7.3 , $ho $ is biholomorphic over $Y\setminus S$ for an analytic subset $S$ of codimension at least two, and it maps the nonempty open subset $E'\cap ho ^{-1}(Y\setminus S)$ of $E'$ isomorphically onto the dense open subset $E\setminus S$ of $E$; hence $ho (E')=E$, since $ho (E')$ is closed by properness. At a point $q'$ of $E'\cap ho ^{-1}(Y\setminus S)$ that is regular on $E'$ and maps to a regular point of $E$, the biholomorphism $ho $ near $q'$ transforms local equations of $E$ into local equations of $E'$, so $\operatorname {ord}_{E'}(f\circ \pi \circ ho )=\operatorname {ord}_ E(f\circ \pi )$ and $\operatorname {ord}_{E'}(J_\pi \circ ho )=\operatorname {ord}_ EJ_\pi $, while $J_ho $ does not vanish near $q'$. By the chain rule $J_{\pi \circ ho }=(J_\pi \circ ho )J_ho $, and since orders add under products (lemma 12.6.1 (4)), $\operatorname {ord}_{E'}K_{Y'/X}=\operatorname {ord}_ EK_{Y/X}$. Thus $E'$ has the same center $\pi (ho (E'))=\pi (E)$ as $E$, and the same orders and log discrepancy. Since two representatives of the same prime divisor over $X$ have the same strict transform on a common smooth model, this proves the claim. Proposition 12.6.4 . Let $\varphi $ be a weight on $X$, $x\in X$, and $f\in \mathcal O_{X,x}$. Then $f\in \mathcal I(\varphi )_ x$ if and only if, near every point of the compact fiber $\pi ^{-1}(x)$, the function 12.20  egin{equation} \label{eq:birational-weighted-integrand} |f\circ \pi |^2|J_\pi |^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi \circ \pi } \end{equation} is integrable with respect to Lebesgue measure in local coordinates on $Y$. Moreover, $\pi _*\mathcal O_ Y(K_{Y/X})=\mathcal O_ X$: if $U\subset X$ is open, then every section of $\mathcal O_ Y(K_{Y/X})$ over $\pi ^{-1}(U)$, that is, every function that is locally of the form $g/J_\pi $ with $g$ holomorphic, equals $f\circ \pi $ for a unique $f\in \mathcal O(U)$. Under this identification 12.21  egin{equation} \label{eq:multiplier-birational-transform} \mathcal I(\varphi ) =\pi _* igl (\mathcal O_ Y(K_{Y/X})\mathcal I(\varphi \circ \pi ) igr ), \end{equation} where $\mathcal O_ Y(K_{Y/X})\mathcal I(\varphi \circ \pi )$ is the sheaf of functions that are locally of the form $g/J_\pi $ with $g$ a section of $\mathcal I(\varphi \circ \pi )$. Proof. By proposition A.7.3 , $\pi $ is biholomorphic over $X\setminus S$ for an analytic subset $S\subset X$ of codimension at least two; in particular $S$ is nowhere dense. The analytic subset $\pi ^{-1}(S)$ of $Y$ is nowhere dense as well, because every nonempty open subset of $Y$ contains a nonempty open set that $\pi $ maps biholomorphically onto an open subset of $X$, and such a set is not contained in $S$. Near each of their points, nowhere dense analytic subsets lie in the zero set of a holomorphic function that does not vanish identically on a connected neighborhood (section A.1 ); so $S$ and $\pi ^{-1}(S)$ are Lebesgue null sets in charts, by lemma 7.4.1 .
