Here the log resolution has no exceptional divisors, and the only condition comes from the non-exceptional component $E$; this is why theorem 12.6.5 involves all components of $D$ meeting the fiber, exceptional or not. For the blowup $\pi $ of the origin in dimension $n\geq 2$, consider the chart $z_1=w_1$, $z_ j=w_1w_ j$ for $j>1$ of proposition A.5.3 . The Jacobian matrix $(\partial z_ i/\partial w_ j)$ is lower triangular with diagonal entries $1,w_1,\ldots ,w_1$, so $J_\pi =w_1^{n-1}$, and the exceptional divisor $E=\{ w_1=0\} $ has $A_ X(E)=n$. Let $f$ be holomorphic near $0$ with homogeneous expansion $f=\sum _{k\geq k_0}P_ k$ and $P_{k_0}
eq 0$. Then $f\circ \pi (w)=\sum _{k\geq k_0}w_1^ kP_ k(1,w_2,\ldots ,w_ n)=w_1^{k_0}g(w)$ for small $w_1$ and bounded $(w_2,\ldots ,w_ n)$, where $g(0,w')=P_{k_0}(1,w')$; this polynomial is not identically zero, since $P_{k_0}(z)=z_1^{k_0}P_{k_0}(1,z_2/z_1,\ldots ,z_ n/z_1)$ for $z_1
eq 0$. Hence $\operatorname {ord}_ Ef=\operatorname {ord}_0f$. For $\varphi =c\log |z|^2$, this blowup is a log resolution of the maximal ideal, with $D=E$ and $d=1$, by proposition A.5.3 , so theorem 12.6.5 gives $f\in \mathcal I(\varphi )_0$ if and only if $\operatorname {ord}_0f+n>c$. This agrees with a direct computation in polar coordinates: since $|f(z)|\leq C|z|^{k_0}$ near $0$ by ( 7.2 ), and $\int _{S^{2n-1}}|f(t\omega )|^2\, \mathrm dS(\omega )\geq c't^{2k_0}$ for small $t>0$, with $c'>0$, by ( 12.10 ), the integral of $|f|^2|z|^{-2c}$ over a small ball $B(0,r)$ is finite if and only if $\int _0^ rt^{2k_0-2c+2n-1}\, \mathrm dt<\infty $, by ( 2.1 ), that is, if and only if $k_0+n>c$.

title: Divisor order independent
text:
Lemma 12.6.1 . Let $E$ be a prime divisor on a complex manifold $Y$, let $p\in E_{\mathrm{reg}}$, let $w=(w_1,w')$ be holomorphic coordinates at $p$ with $E=\{ w_1=0\} $ near $p$, and let $h$ be holomorphic near $p$. Let $\Delta =\Delta _1	imes \Delta '$ be a polydisc centered at $p$, where $\Delta _1$ is a disc in the $w_1$-plane, so small that $E\cap \Delta =\{ w_1=0\} \cap \Delta $ and that ( 7.1 ) gives the expansion \[  h=\sum _{l\geq 0}a_ l(w')w_1^ l\quad 	ext{on }\Delta ,\qquad a_ l(w')= rac1{l!}\partial _{w_1}^ lh(0,w'),  \] where the functions $a_ l$ are holomorphic on $\Delta '$. Let $k\geq 0$ be an integer. If $h$ is divisible by $w_1^ k$ near some point of $E\cap \Delta $, then $a_ l=0$ for all $l<k$; conversely, if $a_ l=0$ for all $l<k$, then $h$ is divisible by $w_1^ k$ near $p$. In particular, a holomorphic function that vanishes on $E$ near $p$ is divisible by $w_1$ near $p$, and if $	ilde w=(	ilde w_1,	ilde w')$ are other coordinates at $p$ with $E=\{ 	ilde w_1=0\} $ near $p$, then $	ilde w_1$ is a unit times $w_1$ near $p$. The order of $h$ along $E$ at $p$ does not depend on the coordinates. It is the smallest $l$ with $a_ l
eq 0$, and it is $+\infty $ if and only if $h$ vanishes near $p$. In particular, $h$ is not divisible by $w_1$ near $p$ if and only if $h(0,\cdot )$ does not vanish identically near $p$. Moreover, the order of $h$ along $E$ is the same at all points of $E\cap \Delta $. If $h$ is holomorphic on a neighborhood of $E$, then its order along $E$ is the same at all points of $E_{\mathrm{reg}}$. Orders add under products: if $g$ is also holomorphic near $p$, then the order of $hg$ along $E$ at $p$ is the sum of the orders of $h$ and $g$. Proof. (1) If $h=w_1^ kh_1$ near a point $(0,w'_0)$ of $E\cap \Delta $, with $h_1$ holomorphic, then the Leibniz rule gives $\partial _{w_1}^ lh(0,w')=0$ for $l<k$ and $w'$ near $w'_0$; so $a_ l=0$ near $w'_0$, and hence on the connected set $\Delta '$ by the identity theorem. Conversely, if $a_ l=0$ for $l<k$, then $h=w_1^ k\sum _{l\geq k}a_ lw_1^{l-k}$ near $p$; the last series is obtained from the Taylor series of $h$ at $p$ by lowering the exponent of $w_1$ in each term by $k$, so it converges on the same polydiscs and defines a holomorphic function (section A.1 ). If $h$ vanishes on $E$ near $p$, then $a_0=h(0,\cdot )$ vanishes near the center of $\Delta '$, hence on $\Delta '$, and the case $k=1$ shows that $h$ is divisible by $w_1$ near $p$. Applying this to $	ilde w_1$, and to $w_1$ with the roles of the two coordinate systems exchanged, we obtain $	ilde w_1=c\, w_1$ and $w_1=	ilde c\, 	ilde w_1$ near $p$ with holomorphic $c$ and $	ilde c$. Then $c	ilde c=1$ off $E$; since the continuous function $c	ilde c$ equals $1$ on the dense set $\{ w_1
eq 0\} $, it equals $1$ near $p$, and $c$ is a unit. (2) By (1), $h$ is divisible by $w_1^ k$ near $p$ if and only if it is divisible by $	ilde w_1^ k$ near $p$, so the order does not depend on the coordinates. Let $k_0$ be the smallest $l$ with $a_ l
eq 0$, and $k_0=+\infty $ if all $a_ l$ vanish. By (1), $h$ is divisible by $w_1^ k$ near $p$ if and only if $k\leq k_0$, so the order of $h$ along $E$ at $p$ is $k_0$. If all $a_ l$ vanish, then $h=0$ on $\Delta $; conversely, if $h$ vanishes near $p$, then all $a_ l$ vanish near the center of $\Delta '$, hence on $\Delta '$. The case $k_0=0$ gives the assertion about $h(0,\cdot )=a_0$, because $a_0$ vanishes identically on $\Delta '$ if and only if it vanishes near the center of $\Delta '$. Finally, let $q=(0,w'_ q)\in E\cap \Delta $. The coordinates $w$ are also coordinates at $q$ with $E=\{ w_1=0\} $ near $q$, and by their formula the coefficients of the expansion of $h$ on a small polydisc centered at $q$ are the restrictions of the same functions $a_ l$. Since $\Delta '$ is connected, $a_ l$ vanishes near $w'_ q$ if and only if it vanishes on $\Delta '$, by the identity theorem. Hence the orders of $h$ along $E$ at $q$ and at $p$ are equal. (3) By the last assertion of (2), the order of $h$ along $E$ is a locally constant function on $E_{\mathrm{reg}}$, which is connected (corollary A.2.13 ). Hence it is constant. (4) Shrinking $\Delta $, we may assume that $g$ is defined on $\Delta $; let $b_ j$ and $e_ m$ be the coefficients of the expansions of $g$ and $hg$ on $\Delta $. By the Leibniz rule, $e_ m=\sum _{i+j=m}a_ ib_ j$. If $h$ or $g$ has infinite order, then $hg$ vanishes near $p$ and has infinite order by (2). Otherwise let $k$ and $l$ be the orders of $h$ and $g$. Then $e_ m=0$ for $m<k+l$, because each term $a_ ib_ j$ with $i+j<k+l$ has $i<k$ or $j<l$, and $e_{k+l}=a_ kb_ l$. Since $a_ k$ and $b_ l$ are not identically zero and the ring of holomorphic functions on the connected set $\Delta '$ is an integral domain, by the identity theorem, $e_{k+l}
eq 0$. By (2), the order of $hg$ is $k+l$. $\square$

title: Normal crossings monomial
text:
Lemma 12.6.2 . Let $w$ be holomorphic coordinates centered at a point $p$ of a complex manifold, let $0\leq \ell \leq n$, and let $h$ be holomorphic near $p$, not identically zero near $p$, with zero set near $p$ contained in $\{ w_1\cdots w_\ell =0\} $. For $i\leq \ell $ let $k_ i$ be the largest integer such that $h$ is divisible by $w_ i^{k_ i}$ near $p$. Then $h=u\prod _{i\leq \ell }w_ i^{k_ i}$ near $p$, with $u$ holomorphic and $u(p)
eq 0$. Moreover, a holomorphic function near $p$ that is divisible by $w_ i^{a_ i}$ near $p$ for each $i\leq \ell $ is divisible by $\prod _{i\leq \ell }w_ i^{a_ i}$. Proof. Let $g=\sum _\alpha c_\alpha w^\alpha $ be the power series at $p$ of a holomorphic function, as in ( 7.1 ). If $g=w_ i^ ag'$ near $p$, then multiplying the series of $g'$ by $w_ i^ a$ shows that $c_\alpha =0$ whenever $\alpha _ i<a$. Conversely, if $c_\alpha =0$ whenever $\alpha _ i<a_ i$ for some $i\leq \ell $, then $g=\prod _ iw_ i^{a_ i}\cdot \sum _\alpha c_\alpha w^{\alpha -\sum _ ia_ ie_ i}$, where $e_ i$ is the $i$th unit vector, and the last series converges on the same polydiscs as that of $g$. This proves the last assertion, and it shows that $k_ i<\infty $, since otherwise all $c_\alpha $ of $h$ would vanish. Hence $h=u\prod _{i\leq \ell }w_ i^{k_ i}$ with $u$ holomorphic near $p$, and $u$ is not divisible by any $w_ i$, $i\leq \ell $, by the maximality of $k_ i$. It remains to show that $u(p)
eq 0$. Suppose, to the contrary, that $u(p)=0$. The zero set of $u$ near $p$ lies in that of $h$, hence in $\{ w_1\cdots w_\ell =0\} $; so $\ell \geq 1$. We work in the coordinates $w$, with $p=0$. Let $P$ be the first nonzero homogeneous term of $u$; it has positive degree $m$. Choose $v\in \mathbb C^ n$ with $P(v)
eq 0$ and $v_ i
eq 0$ for all $i$, which is possible since the polynomial $P(v)v_1\cdots v_ n$ is not identically zero. Then $t\mapsto u(tv)$ has a zero of order $m$ at $t=0$; choose $\varepsilon >0$ such that it has no other zeros in $|t|\leq \varepsilon $, and such that all points $y+tv$ considered below lie in the neighborhood of $0$ where the hypothesis on the zero set holds. Since $(y,t)\mapsto u(y+tv)$ is continuous and does not vanish on the compact set $\{ 0\} 	imes \{ |t|=\varepsilon \} $, there is a connected neighborhood $N$ of $0$ such that $u(y+tv)
eq 0$ for $y\in N$ and $|t|=\varepsilon $. By the argument principle, the number of zeros of $t\mapsto u(y+tv)$ in $|t|<\varepsilon $, counted with multiplicity, is \[   rac1{2\pi \mathrm i}\int _{|t|=\varepsilon } rac{\partial _ t[u(y+tv)]}{u(y+tv)}\, \mathrm dt,  \] a continuous integer-valued function of $y\in N$; it equals $m\geq 1$ at $y=0$, hence everywhere on $N$. So for every $y\in N$ there is $t$ with $u(y+tv)=0$, and then $y_ i+tv_ i=0$ for some $i\leq \ell $, that is, $u(\sigma _ i(y))=0$ for the linear projection $\sigma _ i(y)=y-(y_ i/v_ i)v$ onto the hyperplane $H_ i=\{ y_ i=0\} $. Hence the product of the holomorphic functions $u\circ \sigma _ i$, $i\leq \ell $, vanishes on $N$. If none of them vanished identically on $N$, each would be nonzero on a dense open subset of $N$, by the identity theorem, and so would be their product. Thus some $u\circ \sigma _ i$ vanishes on $N$; since $\sigma _ i(y)=y$ for $y\in H_ i$, the function $u$ vanishes on $H_ i\cap N$, which is a neighborhood of $0$ in $H_ i$. By the first paragraph, applied with $a=1$, $u$ is then divisible by $w_ i$ near $0$: all coefficients $c_\alpha $ of $u$ with $\alpha _ i=0$ vanish, since they are the coefficients of the restriction of $u$ to $H_ i$. This contradiction shows that $u(p)
eq 0$. $\square$

title: Divisorial order discrepancy
text: Definition 12.6.3 . Let $E\subset Y$ be a prime divisor. Its center on $X$ is $\pi (E)$, which is an analytic subset of $X$ by theorem A.6.2 ; it is connected, because $E$ is. Let $f$ be a holomorphic function on an open set $V\subset X$ containing the center, and let $V_0$ be the connected component of $V$ containing it. If $f$ vanishes identically on $V_0$, for instance if $f=0$, we set $\operatorname {ord}_ Ef=+\infty $. Otherwise $f\circ \pi $ does not vanish identically on any nonempty open subset of $\pi ^{-1}(V_0)$, because such a set contains a nonempty open set mapped biholomorphically onto an open subset of $V_0$, on which $f$ does not vanish identically by the identity theorem; since $E\subset \pi ^{-1}(V_0)$, the order of $f$ along $E$ is $\operatorname {ord}_ Ef=\operatorname {ord}_ E(f\circ \pi )<\infty $. This order along a divisor differs from the order at a point of proposition 12.1.4 , although the two agree for the exceptional divisor of the blowup of a point (example 12.6.10 ). For a holomorphic germ $f$ at a point $x$, this defines $\operatorname {ord}_ Ef$ for the prime divisors $E$ on smooth models of open neighborhoods of $x$ on which $f$ is defined; this is how orders of germs enter the results below. The log discrepancy of $E$ is \[  A_ X(E)=1+\operatorname {ord}_ E K_{Y/X},  \] where $\operatorname {ord}_ EK_{Y/X}=\operatorname {ord}_ EJ_\pi $ is the coefficient of $E$ in $K_{Y/X}$. Since $J_\pi $ is holomorphic, $A_ X(E)\geq 1$, and a prime divisor on $X$ itself, with $\pi $ the identity, has log discrepancy one. The center, the order and the log discrepancy depend only on the prime divisor over $X$ represented by $E$.

title: Birational weighted change variables
text: Proposition 12.6.4 . Let $\varphi $ be a weight on $X$, $x\in X$, and $f\in \mathcal O_{X,x}$. Then $f\in \mathcal I(\varphi )_ x$ if and only if, near every point of the compact fiber $\pi ^{-1}(x)$, the function 12.20 \begin{equation} \label{eq:birational-weighted-integrand} |f\circ \pi |^2|J_\pi |^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi \circ \pi } \end{equation} is integrable with respect to Lebesgue measure in local coordinates on $Y$. Moreover, $\pi _*\mathcal O_ Y(K_{Y/X})=\mathcal O_ X$: if $U\subset X$ is open, then every section of $\mathcal O_ Y(K_{Y/X})$ over $\pi ^{-1}(U)$, that is, every function that is locally of the form $g/J_\pi $ with $g$ holomorphic, equals $f\circ \pi $ for a unique $f\in \mathcal O(U)$. Under this identification 12.21 \begin{equation} \label{eq:multiplier-birational-transform} \mathcal I(\varphi ) =\pi _*\bigl (\mathcal O_ Y(K_{Y/X})\mathcal I(\varphi \circ \pi )\bigr ), \end{equation} where $\mathcal O_ Y(K_{Y/X})\mathcal I(\varphi \circ \pi )$ is the sheaf of functions that are locally of the form $g/J_\pi $ with $g$ a section of $\mathcal I(\varphi \circ \pi )$. Proof. By proposition A.7.3 , $\pi $ is biholomorphic over $X\setminus S$ for an analytic subset $S\subset X$ of codimension at least two; in particular $S$ is nowhere dense. The analytic subset $\pi ^{-1}(S)$ of $Y$ is nowhere dense as well, because every nonempty open subset of $Y$ contains a nonempty open set that $\pi $ maps biholomorphically onto an open subset of $X$, and such a set is not contained in $S$. Near each of their points, nowhere dense analytic subsets lie in the zero set of a holomorphic function that does not vanish identically on a connected neighborhood (section A.1 ); so $S$ and $\pi ^{-1}(S)$ are Lebesgue null sets in charts, by lemma 7.4.1 . In holomorphic coordinates the real Jacobian determinant of $\pi $, that is, the factor by which $\pi ^*$ multiplies the volume form $\mathrm dx_1\wedge \mathrm dy_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm dx_ n\wedge \mathrm dy_ n$, is $|J_\pi |^2$. Indeed, since $\frac{\mathrm i}2\mathrm dz_ j\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ j=\mathrm dx_ j\wedge \mathrm dy_ j$, this form equals $c_ n\, \mathrm dz_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm dz_ n\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ n$ with $c_ n=(\mathrm i/2)^ n(-1)^{n(n-1)/2}$, the sign coming from moving each $\mathrm dz_ j$ to the left past $\mathrm d\bar z_1,\ldots ,\mathrm d\bar z_{j-1}$, and similarly in the coordinates $w$. Since $\pi ^*(\mathrm dz_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm dz_ n)=J_\pi \, \mathrm dw_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm dw_ n$ and the conjugate identity holds for the $\mathrm d\bar z_ j$, the claim follows. The change of variables formula for nonnegative measurable functions, applied to the biholomorphism $\pi $ from $W\setminus \pi ^{-1}(S)$ onto its image, therefore gives \[  \int _{\pi (W\setminus \pi ^{-1}(S))}g\, \mathrm dV_ z =\int _ W(g\circ \pi )|J_\pi |^2\, \mathrm dV_ w  \] for every nonnegative measurable $g$ and every open set $W$ in a coordinate chart of $Y$ that is mapped into a coordinate chart of $X$, with $J_\pi $ computed in these coordinates. Now suppose that $|f|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi }$ is integrable on a coordinate neighborhood $V$ of $x$. Applying the formula with $g=|f|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi }$ to small coordinate neighborhoods $W\subset \pi ^{-1}(V)$, we see that ( 12.20 ) is integrable near every point of $\pi ^{-1}(V)$. Conversely, suppose that ( 12.20 ) is integrable near every point of $\pi ^{-1}(x)$, where $f$ is defined on a coordinate neighborhood $V_0$ of $x$. Cover the compact fiber by finitely many coordinate neighborhoods $W_1,\ldots ,W_ k\subset \pi ^{-1}(V_0)$ on which it is integrable. Since $\pi $ is proper, $\pi (Y\setminus (W_1\cup \cdots \cup W_ k))$ is closed and does not contain $x$, so there is a neighborhood $V\subset V_0$ of $x$ with $\pi ^{-1}(V)\subset W_1\cup \cdots \cup W_ k$. The sets $\pi (W_ l\setminus \pi ^{-1}(S))$ cover $V\setminus S$, and $S$ is a null set, so the formula gives $\int _ V|f|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi }\, \mathrm dV\leq \sum _ l\int _{W_ l}|f\circ \pi |^2|J_\pi |^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi \circ \pi }\, \mathrm dV_ w<\infty $. Next let $U\subset X$ be open and $h$ a section of $\mathcal O_ Y(K_{Y/X})$ over $\pi ^{-1}(U)$; we may assume that $U$ is connected. Over $U\setminus S$ the map $\pi $ is biholomorphic and $J_\pi $ has no zeros, so $h$ is holomorphic on $\pi ^{-1}(U\setminus S)$, and $h=f\circ \pi $ there for the holomorphic function $f=h\circ (\pi |_{\pi ^{-1}(U\setminus S)})^{-1}$ on $U\setminus S$, which is connected by lemma A.1.7 . If $f\not\equiv 0$, the function $\log |f|^2$ is plurisubharmonic on $U\setminus S$ (proposition 8.3.3 ), so by corollary A.2.15 it is locally bounded above near $S$; hence $f$ is locally bounded near $S$, and lemma A.1.7 extends $f$ holomorphically to $U$. Locally $h=g/J_\pi $ with $g$ holomorphic, and $g=(f\circ \pi )J_\pi $ on the dense open set $\pi ^{-1}(U\setminus S)$, hence everywhere; so $h=f\circ \pi $. The function $f$ is unique, since it is determined on $U\setminus S$, which is dense in $U$. Finally, let $U\subset X$ be open and $f\in \mathcal O(U)$. Since $\mathcal O_ Y(K_{Y/X})$ is locally generated by $J_\pi ^{-1}$, the function $f\circ \pi $ is a section of $\mathcal O_ Y(K_{Y/X})\mathcal I(\varphi \circ \pi )$ over $\pi ^{-1}(U)$ if and only if $(f\circ \pi )J_\pi $ is a section of $\mathcal I(\varphi \circ \pi )$ there, that is, if and only if ( 12.20 ) is integrable near every point of $\pi ^{-1}(U)$. By the first part, applied at every point of $U$, this holds if and only if $f$ is a section of $\mathcal I(\varphi )$ over $U$. Together with the second part, which shows that every section of the right side of ( 12.21 ) over $\pi ^{-1}(U)$ has the form $f\circ \pi $, this proves ( 12.21 ). $\square$

title: Birational weighted integrand
text: 12.20 \begin{equation} \label{eq:birational-weighted-integrand} |f\circ \pi |^2|J_\pi |^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi \circ \pi } \end{equation}

title: Multiplier birational transform
text: 12.21 \begin{equation} \label{eq:multiplier-birational-transform} \mathcal I(\varphi ) =\pi _*\bigl (\mathcal O_ Y(K_{Y/X})\mathcal I(\varphi \circ \pi )\bigr ), \end{equation}

title: Log resolution local form
text: 12.22 \begin{equation} \label{eq:log-resolution-local-form} \log \sum _{j=1}^ r|g_ j\circ \pi |^2=\sum _{i=1}^{\ell }d_ i\log |w_ i|^2+O(1)\qquad \text{near }p. \end{equation}

title: Analytic log resolution integrability
text: Theorem 12.6.5 . Let $\varphi $ be a weight on $X$ such that near $x$ \[  \varphi =c\log \left(\sum _{j=1}^ r|g_ j|^2\right)+b, \qquad c>0,\quad b\text{ bounded},  \] where the holomorphic functions $g_ j$ generate a nonzero ideal $\mathfrak a$. Let $V$ be an open neighborhood of $x$ on which this holds, and let $\pi \colon Y\to V$ be a log resolution of $\mathfrak a$ (section A.5 ), as supplied by theorem A.5.4 , theorem A.5.5 , with $\mathfrak a\mathcal O_ Y=\mathcal O_ Y(-D)$, where $D=\sum _ id_ iE_ i$ is an effective divisor with simple normal crossings support, the $E_ i$ being prime divisors and the $d_ i$ positive integers. Then a holomorphic function $f$ on $V$ belongs to $\mathcal I(\varphi )_ x$ if and only if 12.23 \begin{equation} \label{eq:analytic-strict-valuative-threshold} \operatorname {ord}_{E_ i}f+A_ X(E_ i)>c d_ i \end{equation} for every component $E_ i$ of $D$ that meets $\pi ^{-1}(x)$, exceptional or not. Since $\pi $ restricts to a log resolution of $\mathfrak a$ over every smaller open neighborhood $V'$ of $x$, the criterion applies to every germ at $x$, with the components of the restriction of $D$ to $\pi ^{-1}(V')$ in place of the $E_ i$. Equivalently, with $\lfloor cD\rfloor =\sum _ i\lfloor cd_ i\rfloor E_ i$, near $x$ 12.24 \begin{equation} \label{eq:analytic-multiplier-divisor-formula} \mathcal I(\varphi )=\pi _*\mathcal O_ Y(K_{Y/X}-\lfloor cD\rfloor ). \end{equation} For rational $c$, this computes the multiplier ideals of weights with analytic singularities (chapter 13 ). Proof. Let $p\in \pi ^{-1}(V)$, and choose coordinates $w$ at $p$ as before ( 12.22 ), so that $E_1,\ldots ,E_\ell $ are the components of $D$ through $p$ and $E_ i=\{ w_ i=0\} $ near $p$. Since $b$ is bounded, ( 12.22 ), applied to $\pi \colon Y\to V$, gives \[  \varphi \circ \pi =c\sum _{i=1}^{\ell }d_ i\log |w_ i|^2+O(1)  \] near $p$. Let $h$ be holomorphic near $p$; we decide when $|h|^2\prod _{i\leq \ell }|w_ i|^{-2cd_ i}$, or equivalently $|h|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi \circ \pi }$, is integrable near $p$. Let $k_ i$ be the order of $h$ along $E_ i$ at $p$, which is finite if $h$ does not vanish identically near $p$; if it does, the integrability is trivial and $k_ i=+\infty $. We claim that the integrability holds if and only if $k_ i+1>cd_ i$ for $i=1,\ldots ,\ell $. If these inequalities hold, write $h=\prod _ iw_ i^{k_ i}\tilde h$ with $\tilde h$ holomorphic, by lemma 12.6.2 ; the integrand is at most a constant times $\prod _ i|w_ i|^{2k_ i-2cd_ i}$, which is integrable near $p$ by Fubini's theorem and polar coordinates in each $w_ i$, since $2k_ i-2cd_ i>-2$. Conversely, suppose that $k_1+1\leq cd_1$, say, and write $h=w_1^{k_1}\tilde h$ with $\tilde h$ not divisible by $w_1$. Then $\tilde h$ does not vanish identically on $\{ w_1=0\} $ near $p$, by lemma 12.6.1 (2), so arbitrarily close to $p$ there are an open set $W'$ of points $w'=(w_2,\ldots ,w_ n)$ and $\delta ,\rho >0$ with $|\tilde h(w_1,w')|\geq \delta $ for $|w_1|<\rho $ and $w'\in W'$. There the integrand is at least a positive constant times $|w_1|^{2k_1-2cd_1}$, since the other factors $|w_ i|^{-2cd_ i}$ are bounded below; as $2k_1-2cd_1\leq -2$, its integral in $w_1$ diverges, and by Fubini's theorem the integrand is not integrable near $p$. Now let $f$ be holomorphic on $V$, and apply this to $h=(f\circ \pi )J_\pi $, with $J_\pi $ computed in local coordinates near $p$. The function $f\circ \pi $ is holomorphic on $\pi ^{-1}(V)$, which contains $E_ i$, so its order along $E_ i$ at $p$ is $\operatorname {ord}_{E_ i}f$, by lemma 12.6.1 (3) and definition 12.6.3 ; the order of $J_\pi $ along $E_ i$ at $p$ is $\operatorname {ord}_{E_ i}J_\pi $. Since orders add under products (lemma 12.6.1 (4)), $k_ i=\operatorname {ord}_{E_ i}f+\operatorname {ord}_{E_ i}J_\pi =\operatorname {ord}_{E_ i}f+A_ X(E_ i)-1$. Thus, for $p\in \pi ^{-1}(x)$, the condition at $p$ is ( 12.23 ) for the components through $p$. As $p$ ranges over $\pi ^{-1}(x)$, these are exactly the components meeting the fiber, and proposition 12.6.4 proves the first assertion. For ( 12.24 ), let $U\subset V$ be open and $f\in \mathcal O(U)$, and put $h=(f\circ \pi )J_\pi $ on $\pi ^{-1}(U)$. For an integer $k$, the strict inequality $k+1>cd_ i$ is equivalent to $k\geq \lfloor cd_ i\rfloor $. By proposition 12.6.4 and the claim, applied at every point $p\in \pi ^{-1}(U)$, we have $f\in \mathcal I(\varphi )(U)$ if and only if at every such $p$ the order of $h$ at $p$ along each component $E_ i$ through $p$ is at least $\lfloor cd_ i\rfloor $. By lemma 12.6.2 , this means that $h$ is divisible near every point of $\pi ^{-1}(U)$ by the local equation $\prod _ iw_ i^{\lfloor cd_ i\rfloor }$ of $\lfloor cD\rfloor $, that is, that $f\circ \pi =h/J_\pi $ is a section of $\mathcal O_ Y(K_{Y/X}-\lfloor cD\rfloor )$ over $\pi ^{-1}(U)$. This proves ( 12.24 ) on $V$. $\square$

title: Strict transform integrability
text: Example 12.6.10 . Let $c>0$ and $\varphi =c\log |z_1|^2$ on a polydisc in $\mathbb C^ n$. The ideal $(z_1)$ is already principal with smooth zero set, so the identity map is a log resolution, with $D=E=\{ z_1=0\} $, $d=1$ and $A_ X(E)=1$. By theorem 12.6.5 , a germ $f$ lies in $\mathcal I(\varphi )$ if and only if $\operatorname {ord}_ Ef+1>c$. Here the log resolution has no exceptional divisors, and the only condition comes from the non-exceptional component $E$; this is why theorem 12.6.5 involves all components of $D$ meeting the fiber, exceptional or not. For the blowup $\pi $ of the origin in dimension $n\geq 2$, consider the chart $z_1=w_1$, $z_ j=w_1w_ j$ for $j>1$ of proposition A.5.3 . The Jacobian matrix $(\partial z_ i/\partial w_ j)$ is lower triangular with diagonal entries $1,w_1,\ldots ,w_1$, so $J_\pi =w_1^{n-1}$, and the exceptional divisor $E=\{ w_1=0\} $ has $A_ X(E)=n$. Let $f$ be holomorphic near $0$ with homogeneous expansion $f=\sum _{k\geq k_0}P_ k$ and $P_{k_0}\neq 0$. Then $f\circ \pi (w)=\sum _{k\geq k_0}w_1^ kP_ k(1,w_2,\ldots ,w_ n)=w_1^{k_0}g(w)$ for small $w_1$ and bounded $(w_2,\ldots ,w_ n)$, where $g(0,w')=P_{k_0}(1,w')$; this polynomial is not identically zero, since $P_{k_0}(z)=z_1^{k_0}P_{k_0}(1,z_2/z_1,\ldots ,z_ n/z_1)$ for $z_1\neq 0$. Hence $\operatorname {ord}_ Ef=\operatorname {ord}_0f$. For $\varphi =c\log |z|^2$, this blowup is a log resolution of the maximal ideal, with $D=E$ and $d=1$, by proposition A.5.3 , so theorem 12.6.5 gives $f\in \mathcal I(\varphi )_0$ if and only if $\operatorname {ord}_0f+n>c$. This agrees with a direct computation in polar coordinates: since $|f(z)|\leq C|z|^{k_0}$ near $0$ by ( 7.2 ), and $\int _{S^{2n-1}}|f(t\omega )|^2\, \mathrm dS(\omega )\geq c't^{2k_0}$ for small $t>0$, with $c'>0$, by ( 12.10 ), the integral of $|f|^2|z|^{-2c}$ over a small ball $B(0,r)$ is finite if and only if $\int _0^ rt^{2k_0-2c+2n-1}\, \mathrm dt<\infty $, by ( 2.1 ), that is, if and only if $k_0+n>c$.

title: Analytic singularities and Demailly approximation
text: 13 Analytic singularities and Demailly approximation Let $u$ be a plurisubharmonic function on a domain in $\mathbb C^ n$. Convolution with a smoothing kernel approximates $u$ by smooth plurisubharmonic functions, but these approximants have lost all singularities: their Lelong numbers vanish and their multiplier ideals are trivial. Many problems require approximants whose singularities are still visible but as simple as possible, namely functions locally of the form $c\log \sum _ i|g_ i|^2+O(1)$ with holomorphic $g_ i$ and rational $c>0$; such functions are said to have analytic singularities. On a compact Kähler manifold a second difficulty appears: convolution is defined only in charts, and gluing local approximations costs positivity. This chapter presents Demailly's answer to both problems, in which convolution is replaced by weighted Bergman kernels. For $u$ plurisubharmonic on a bounded pseudoconvex domain $\Omega $ and an integer $m\geq 1$, the holomorphic functions $F$ on $\Omega $ with $\int _\Omega |F|^2\mathrm e^{-mu}<\infty $ form a Hilbert space, which generates the multiplier ideal $\mathcal I(mu)$ of chapter 12 . If $K_ m(z)$ denotes the supremum of $|F(z)|^2$ over its unit ball, then $u_ m=m^{-1}\log K_ m$ is plurisubharmonic and has analytic singularities described by $\mathcal I(mu)$. The Ohsawa–Takegoshi estimate of chapter 11 bounds $u_ m$ below by $u-O(1/m)$, and the mean-value inequality bounds it above by the supremum of $u$ over a small ball, up to an error that tends to zero as $m\to \infty $. Hence $u_ m\to u$, and the Lelong numbers of $u_ m$ differ from those of $u$ by at most $n/m$ (theorem 13.2.3 ). On a compact Kähler manifold $(X,\omega )$ we apply this construction in finitely many coordinate balls to a function $\varphi $ with $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi \geq 0$, where $\theta $ is a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form. A $\bar\partial $-estimate with a logarithmic pole shows that the kernels of two overlapping balls are comparable up to a factor that depends only on the charts (lemma 13.3.2 ). Gluing the local potentials by a maximum gives the quantitative regularization of theorem 13.3.3 , with a curvature loss of order $1/m$ and a lower bound by the generators of $\mathcal I(m\varphi )$. Gluing them instead by a sum with smooth cutoffs gives approximants $G_ m$ with gentle analytic singularities (lemma 13.4.1 ): $\exp (mG_ m)$ is smooth, and $G_ m$ has a smooth remainder on every log resolution of $\mathcal I(m\varphi )$. Comparing the kernels at the scales $m$ and $2m$ by extension from the diagonal, we show that the dyadic sequence $G_{2^ j}$, corrected by small constants, decreases to $\varphi $ and that its multiplier ideals approximate those of $\varphi $, so that it is a quasi-equisingular approximation of $\varphi $ in the sense of definition 13.4.4 (theorem 13.4.5 ). Any two quasi-equisingular approximations of $\varphi $ dominate each other up to an arbitrarily small loss in the coefficient (proposition 13.5.2 ). The first section collects the elementary properties of quasi-plurisubharmonic functions, introduces $\theta $-plurisubharmonic functions and analytic singularities, and shows, using metrics on line bundles, that blowups with smooth centers preserve the Kähler property. The last section studies the ideal of holomorphic germs $f$ with $|f|^2\leq C\mathrm e^ v$: for $v$ with analytic singularities it is coherent, and on a compact manifold the ideal attached to $kv$ contains $\mathcal I(k(1+\varepsilon )v)$ for all large $k$. Historical remarks and references for this chapter are collected in section B.13 .

title: Smooth backgrounds and analytic singularities
text:
13.1 Smooth backgrounds and analytic singularities Let $X$ be a complex manifold of dimension $n\geq 0$. Recall from section 7.5 that a Hermitian form on $X$ is a smooth real $(1,1)$-form that is strictly positive at every point, that is, the form associated with a Hermitian metric. It is a Kähler form if it is closed, and $X$ is a Kähler manifold if it carries a Kähler form. A Hermitian form $\omega $ defines a Riemannian metric on $X$ and the positive volume form $\omega ^ n/n!$. Continuous real $(1,1)$-forms are controlled by a Hermitian form on compact sets. Lemma 13.1.1 . Let $\omega $ be a Hermitian form on a complex manifold $X$, let $K\subset X$ be compact, and let $\alpha $ be a continuous real $(1,1)$-form on a neighborhood of $K$. Then there is a constant $C\geq 0$ with $\alpha \geq -C\omega $ at every point of $K$. Proof. If $K=\varnothing $ we take $C=0$. Otherwise cover $K$ by finitely many compact sets $K_\iota $, each contained in a chart and in the domain of $\alpha $, and write $\alpha =\mathrm i\sum _{j,k}a_{jk}\, \mathrm dz_ j\wedge \mathrm d ar z_ k$ and $\omega =\mathrm i\sum _{j,k}w_{jk}\, \mathrm dz_ j\wedge \mathrm d ar z_ k$ there, with Hermitian matrices $(a_{jk})$ and $(w_{jk})$. On $K_\iota $ the smallest eigenvalue of $(w_{jk})$, a continuous positive function, is at least some $c_\iota >0$, and the largest eigenvalue of $-(a_{jk})$ is at most some $M_\iota \geq 0$. Hence $(a_{jk})\geq -M_\iota I\geq -(M_\iota /c_\iota )(w_{jk})$ on $K_\iota $. By the matrix criterion for positivity (section 7.3 ), it follows that $\alpha \geq -C\omega $ on $K$ with $C=\max _\iota M_\iota /c_\iota $. $\square$ The following lemma provides smooth local potentials for smooth closed forms on whole coordinate balls, not only on small polydiscs as in lemma 7.3.1 . Lemma 13.1.2 . Let $B$ be a coordinate ball and let $	heta $ be a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form defined on a neighborhood of $\overline B$. Then there is a smooth real function $h$ on $B$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h=	heta $. Moreover, every real pluriharmonic function on a coordinate ball is, up to an additive constant, the real part of a holomorphic function on that ball. Proof. In dimension zero there is nothing to prove, so let $n\geq 1$. Choose concentric balls $B\Subset B'\Subset B''$ such that $	heta $ is defined on a neighborhood of $\overline{B''}$. By the last assertion of lemma 7.3.1 , applied to the closed real $2$-form $	heta $ on the ball $B''$, there is a smooth real one-form $\alpha $ on $B''$ with $\mathrm d\alpha =	heta $. Since $	heta $ has type $(1,1)$, the $(0,2)$-part $ ar\partial \alpha ^{0,1}$ of $\mathrm d\alpha $ vanishes. The ball $B'$ is pseudoconvex by corollary 11.2.5 , and $\alpha ^{0,1}$ is bounded on $B'$. Hence theorem 11.3.4 , applied on $B'$ with $p=0$ and $q=|z|^2$, whose complex Hessian is the identity, gives a function $f\in L^2(B')$ with $ ar\partial f=\alpha ^{0,1}$. The function $f$ is smooth. Indeed, let $y\in B'$ and choose polydiscs $P'\Subset P\Subset B'$ centered at $y$. By lemma 7.3.1 , applied to the smooth $ ar\partial $-closed form $\alpha ^{0,1}$ on $P$, there is a smooth function $f_0$ on $P'$ with $ ar\partial f_0=\alpha ^{0,1}$. Then $ ar\partial (f-f_0)=0$ on $P'$ in the sense of distributions, so $\Delta (f-f_0)=4\sum _ j\partial _{z_ j}\partial _{ ar z_ j}(f-f_0)=0$ there, and by theorem 2.1.4 the locally integrable function $f-f_0$ agrees almost everywhere on $P'$ with a smooth function. Thus $f$ agrees almost everywhere near each point with a smooth function; two such smooth functions coincide on the overlap of their domains, being continuous and equal almost everywhere, so we may take $f$ smooth on $B'$. Since $\alpha $ is real, $\alpha ^{1,0}=\overline{\alpha ^{0,1}}=\partial  ar f$, and the $(1,1)$-part of $\mathrm d\alpha =	heta $ gives \[  	heta =\partial \alpha ^{0,1}+ ar\partial \alpha ^{1,0}=\partial  ar\partial f+ ar\partial \partial  ar f=\partial  ar\partial (f- ar f)=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(4\pi \operatorname{Im}f).  \] Thus $h=4\pi \operatorname{Im}f$ has the required property on $B\subset B'$. Hence, on $\Delta $, \[  ho =\sum _\alpha \lambda _\alpha |A_\alpha w|^2=w^*\mathcal Q\, w,\qquad \mathcal Q=\sum _\alpha \lambda _\alpha A_\alpha ^*A_\alpha ,  \] where the sums run over the indices $\alpha \geq 1$ with $x_0\in V_\alpha $, and $w^*$ is the conjugate transpose of the column vector $w$. On the overlap of two charts, the local equations $t$ and $t'$ of $E$ generate the same ideal $\mathcal O_ Y(-E)$, so $t'=ut$ with $u$ holomorphic and nowhere zero. Thus $\eta $ is a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form on $Y$. It is the curvature, in the sense of definition 13.1.8 , of the metric on the line bundle $\mathcal O_ Y(-E)$ with the frame $1$ on $Y\setminus E$, the frames $t$ on the charts and the transition functions $t$ and $t'/t$, for which $|1|^2=1/(ho \circ \pi )$ and $|t|^2=1/h_ E$. On the fiber $\{ z=z_0,\  t=0\} $ we have $h_ E=	ilde v^*\mathcal Q_0	ilde v$. Since $F$ does not lie in the image of $\Lambda $, this forces $\mu =0$, so $\Lambda \xi =0$ and $\xi =0$. By the matrix criterion, the restriction of $\eta $ to each fiber of $E	o W$ is positive definite. Step 2: positivity near $E$. The form $P=\pi ^*\omega $ is a smooth closed semipositive $(1,1)$-form on $Y$. We regard the real $(1,1)$-forms $P$ and $\eta $ in a chart $(z,t,v)$ as Hermitian forms on holomorphic tangent vectors, given by their coefficient matrices, so that $P(	au ,	au )=\omega (\mathrm d\pi \, 	au ,\mathrm d\pi \, 	au )$ by the chain rule; norms of tangent vectors are taken in the coordinates of the chart. Let $V$ be spanned by the vectors $\partial /\partial v_ k$ and $H$ by the vectors $\partial /\partial z_ l$ and $\partial /\partial t$, and write $P$ and $\eta $ in block form with respect to the decomposition of the tangent space into $V$ and $H$. At points of $E$ we have $\mathrm d\pi (\partial /\partial v_ k)=t\, \partial /\partial w_ k=0$, while $\mathrm d\pi (\partial /\partial z_ l)=\partial /\partial z_ l$ and $\mathrm d\pi (\partial /\partial t)=\sum _ j	ilde v_ j\, \partial /\partial w_ j$ are linearly independent. Since $\omega $ is positive definite, $P_{HV}=0$ and $P_{HH}$ is positive definite at points of $E$, while $\eta _{VV}$ is positive definite there by Step 1. Choose finitely many compact sets $K_\iota $ whose interiors cover $E$, each contained in a chart $(z,t,v)$. The smallest eigenvalues of $P_{HH}$ and of $\eta _{VV}$ are continuous and positive on the compact sets $E\cap K_\iota $, so there are $a,c>0$ such that they exceed $2c$ and $2a$, respectively, on $E\cap K_\iota $ for every $\iota $. Let $M>0$ bound the operator norm of $\eta $ on every $K_\iota $, so that $|\eta (	au ,	au ')|\leq M|	au ||	au '|$, and choose $\ell \in (0,1]$ with $2M\ell +M\ell ^2\leq a/2$. Where $P_{HH}$ is invertible, the linear map $L=P_{HH}^{-1}P_{HV}\colon V	o H$ depends continuously on the point, and it vanishes on $E$. Completing the square, \[  P(	au ,	au )=P_{HH}(\sigma ,\sigma )+S(\xi ,\xi ),\qquad S=P_{VV}-P_{VH}P_{HH}^{-1}P_{HV},  \] and $S\geq 0$ because $P\geq 0$ (take $\zeta =-L\xi $, so that $\sigma =0$). Hence $P(	au ,	au )\geq c|\sigma |^2$. Since $	au =(\xi -L\xi )+\sigma $, \[  \eta (	au ,	au )\geq  rac a2|\xi |^2-4M|\xi ||\sigma |-M|\sigma |^2.  \] Therefore, for $\varepsilon >0$, \[  (P+\varepsilon \eta )(	au ,	au )\geq (c-\varepsilon M)|\sigma |^2+ rac{\varepsilon a}2|\xi |^2-4\varepsilon M|\xi ||\sigma |.  \] The right-hand side is a quadratic form in $(|\sigma |,|\xi |)$, which is positive definite as soon as $\varepsilon M<c$ and $(c-\varepsilon M)a>8\varepsilon M^2$; and $(\sigma ,\xi )

eq 0$. Thus $\pi ^*\omega +\varepsilon \eta $ is positive definite on the fixed neighborhood $\mathcal N$ of $E$ for all sufficiently small $\varepsilon >0$. Step 3: positivity away from $E$. On the compact set $Y\setminus \mathcal N\subset Y\setminus E$ the map $\pi $ is a local biholomorphism, so $\pi ^*\omega $ is positive definite at every point. Cover $Y\setminus \mathcal N$ by finitely many compact sets contained in charts. On each of them the smallest eigenvalue of the coefficient matrix of $\pi ^*\omega $ is bounded below by a positive constant $c'$, and the operator norm of the coefficient matrix of $\eta $ is bounded by a constant $M'$, with $c'$ and $M'$ independent of the set. Hence $\pi ^*\omega +\varepsilon \eta $ is positive definite on $Y\setminus \mathcal N$ if $\varepsilon M'<c'$. Together with Step 2, this shows that $\pi ^*\omega +\varepsilon \eta $ is positive definite on all of $Y$ for every sufficiently small $\varepsilon >0$. It is closed, since both terms are, so it is a Kähler form on $Y$. $\square$ Definition 13.1.11 . Let $X$ be a compact Kähler manifold. A quasi-plurisubharmonic function $\varphi $ on $X$ has gentle analytic singularities of type $(c,\mathfrak a)$ if it has analytic singularities of type $(c,\mathfrak a)$, the function $\exp (\varphi /c)$ is smooth on $X$, including at its zeros, and on every log resolution $\pi $ of $\mathfrak a$, with $\pi ^*\mathfrak a=\mathcal O(-D)$, one has locally \[  \varphi \circ \pi =c\log |s_ D|^2+h,\qquad h	ext{ smooth}.  \] The log resolutions in this definition are compact Kähler manifolds by proposition 13.1.10 . The smoothness of $\exp (\varphi /c)$ on $X$ and that of the remainder on the log resolutions are separate requirements. We require the local form on every log resolution, not only on one, because later proofs use it on a resolution chosen in the course of the argument. Both requirements hold if $\varphi $ has presentations ( 13.1 ) of type $(c,\mathfrak a)$ with smooth remainders $b$, since then $\exp (\varphi /c)=\mathrm e^{b/c}\sum _ i|g_ i|^2$ locally and proposition 13.1.7 applies; they also hold for the cutoff sums of lemma 13.4.1 .

title: Hermitian form comparison
text: Lemma 13.1.1 . Let $\omega $ be a Hermitian form on a complex manifold $X$, let $K\subset X$ be compact, and let $\alpha $ be a continuous real $(1,1)$-form on a neighborhood of $K$. Then there is a constant $C\geq 0$ with $\alpha \geq -C\omega $ at every point of $K$. Proof. If $K=\varnothing $ we take $C=0$. Otherwise cover $K$ by finitely many compact sets $K_\iota $, each contained in a chart and in the domain of $\alpha $, and write $\alpha =\mathrm i\sum _{j,k}a_{jk}\, \mathrm dz_ j\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ k$ and $\omega =\mathrm i\sum _{j,k}w_{jk}\, \mathrm dz_ j\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ k$ there, with Hermitian matrices $(a_{jk})$ and $(w_{jk})$. On $K_\iota $ the smallest eigenvalue of $(w_{jk})$, a continuous positive function, is at least some $c_\iota >0$, and the largest eigenvalue of $-(a_{jk})$ is at most some $M_\iota \geq 0$. Hence $(a_{jk})\geq -M_\iota I\geq -(M_\iota /c_\iota )(w_{jk})$ on $K_\iota $. By the matrix criterion for positivity (section 7.3 ), it follows that $\alpha \geq -C\omega $ on $K$ with $C=\max _\iota M_\iota /c_\iota $. $\square$

title: Smooth potential on ball
text: Lemma 13.1.2 . Let $B$ be a coordinate ball and let $\theta $ be a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form defined on a neighborhood of $\overline B$. Then there is a smooth real function $h$ on $B$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h=\theta $. Moreover, every real pluriharmonic function on a coordinate ball is, up to an additive constant, the real part of a holomorphic function on that ball. Proof. In dimension zero there is nothing to prove, so let $n\geq 1$. Choose concentric balls $B\Subset B'\Subset B''$ such that $\theta $ is defined on a neighborhood of $\overline{B''}$. By the last assertion of lemma 7.3.1 , applied to the closed real $2$-form $\theta $ on the ball $B''$, there is a smooth real one-form $\alpha $ on $B''$ with $\mathrm d\alpha =\theta $. Since $\theta $ has type $(1,1)$, the $(0,2)$-part $\bar\partial \alpha ^{0,1}$ of $\mathrm d\alpha $ vanishes. The ball $B'$ is pseudoconvex by corollary 11.2.5 , and $\alpha ^{0,1}$ is bounded on $B'$. Hence theorem 11.3.4 , applied on $B'$ with $p=0$ and $q=|z|^2$, whose complex Hessian is the identity, gives a function $f\in L^2(B')$ with $\bar\partial f=\alpha ^{0,1}$. The function $f$ is smooth. Indeed, let $y\in B'$ and choose polydiscs $P'\Subset P\Subset B'$ centered at $y$. By lemma 7.3.1 , applied to the smooth $\bar\partial $-closed form $\alpha ^{0,1}$ on $P$, there is a smooth function $f_0$ on $P'$ with $\bar\partial f_0=\alpha ^{0,1}$. Then $\bar\partial (f-f_0)=0$ on $P'$ in the sense of distributions, so $\Delta (f-f_0)=4\sum _ j\partial _{z_ j}\partial _{\bar z_ j}(f-f_0)=0$ there, and by theorem 2.1.4 the locally integrable function $f-f_0$ agrees almost everywhere on $P'$ with a smooth function. Thus $f$ agrees almost everywhere near each point with a smooth function; two such smooth functions coincide on the overlap of their domains, being continuous and equal almost everywhere, so we may take $f$ smooth on $B'$. Since $\alpha $ is real, $\alpha ^{1,0}=\overline{\alpha ^{0,1}}=\partial \bar f$, and the $(1,1)$-part of $\mathrm d\alpha =\theta $ gives \[  \theta =\partial \alpha ^{0,1}+\bar\partial \alpha ^{1,0}=\partial \bar\partial f+\bar\partial \partial \bar f=\partial \bar\partial (f-\bar f)=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(4\pi \operatorname{Im}f).  \] Thus $h=4\pi \operatorname{Im}f$ has the required property on $B\subset B'$. For the last assertion, let $h$ be real and pluriharmonic on a coordinate ball. Then $\partial h$ is a $(1,0)$-form with holomorphic coefficients, since $\bar\partial \partial h=0$, and it is closed. By the last assertion of lemma 7.3.1 , applied to the closed one-form $2\partial h$ on this ball, there is a smooth function $F$ on the whole ball with $\mathrm dF=2\partial h$. As $\mathrm dF$ has type $(1,0)$, $F$ is holomorphic, and $\mathrm d(\operatorname{Re}F)=\partial h+\bar\partial h=\mathrm dh$. Hence $h-\operatorname{Re}F$ is constant. $\square$

title: Quasi psh and theta psh
text: Definition 13.1.3 . Let $X$ be a complex manifold. A function $\varphi \colon X\to [-\infty ,\infty )$ is quasi-plurisubharmonic if it is quasi-plurisubharmonic near every point of $X$ in the sense of corollary 12.3.2 , that is, if every point of $X$ has a neighborhood $V$ on which $\varphi =u+f$ pointwise, with $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(V)$ and $f$ a smooth real function on $V$. For a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form $\theta $ on $X$ we put \[  \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )=\{ \varphi \text{ quasi-plurisubharmonic on }X:\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi \geq 0\} ,  \] and call its elements $\theta $-plurisubharmonic ( $\theta $-psh ) functions.

title: Quasi psh basic
text: Lemma 13.1.4 . Let $X$ be a complex manifold and let $\theta $ be a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form on $X$. Every quasi-plurisubharmonic function on $X$ is locally integrable, hence finite almost everywhere. If $X$ has positive dimension, a quasi-plurisubharmonic function is, at every point, the limit of its averages over small coordinate balls centered at that point. Consequently, if $\varphi $ and $\psi $ are quasi-plurisubharmonic functions on an open set $V\subset X$ with $\varphi \leq \psi $ almost everywhere on $V$, then $\varphi \leq \psi $ everywhere on $V$; in particular, two quasi-plurisubharmonic functions on $V$ that agree almost everywhere on $V$ agree everywhere on $V$. Let $V\subset X$ be open and let $h$ be a smooth real function on $V$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h=\theta $. Then a quasi-plurisubharmonic function $\varphi $ on $V$ satisfies $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi \geq 0$ on $V$ if and only if $\varphi +h$ is plurisubharmonic on $V$. If $\varphi _1,\ldots ,\varphi _ k\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, $k\geq 1$, then $\max _ i\varphi _ i\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. If $X$ is compact and $\omega $ is a Hermitian form on $X$, then for every quasi-plurisubharmonic function $\varphi $ on $X$ there is a constant $C\geq 0$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi \geq -C\omega $. Let $\omega $ be a Hermitian form on $X$, and let $\varphi \in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(X)$ satisfy $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi \geq -C\omega $ in the sense of currents for a constant $C$. Then $\varphi $ agrees almost everywhere with a quasi-plurisubharmonic function on $X$. Proof. At points where $X$ has dimension zero, which are isolated, all functions are smooth and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ vanishes, so every assertion is trivial there; we may therefore assume that $X$ has positive dimension. (1) Near each point, $\varphi =u+f$ with $u$ plurisubharmonic and $f$ smooth, and $u$ is locally integrable by theorem 8.2.1 . Moreover $u$ is subharmonic, by the same theorem, so at every point it is the limit of its averages over small balls, by ( 3.3 ); the continuous function $f$ has the same property, and hence so has $\varphi $. Now let $\varphi $ and $\psi $ be quasi-plurisubharmonic on $V$ with $\varphi \leq \psi $ almost everywhere, and let $x\in V$. Since both functions are locally integrable, their averages over small coordinate balls centered at $x$, in a chart at $x$, are finite, and those of $\varphi $ are at most those of $\psi $; letting the radius tend to zero gives $\varphi (x)\leq \psi (x)$. Applying this in both directions, we see that two quasi-plurisubharmonic functions that agree almost everywhere agree everywhere. (2) Let $\varphi $ be quasi-plurisubharmonic on $V$. If $\varphi +h$ is plurisubharmonic, then $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\varphi +h)\geq 0$ by theorem 8.2.1 . Conversely, suppose that $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\varphi +h)\geq 0$ on $V$. On a coordinate ball $B\subset V$, theorem 8.2.1 gives a plurisubharmonic function on $B$ that agrees almost everywhere with $\varphi +h$; both are quasi-plurisubharmonic on $B$, so they agree everywhere on $B$ by (1). Hence $\varphi +h$ is plurisubharmonic on $V$. (3) Let $B$ be a coordinate ball and $h$ a smooth real function on $B$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h=\theta $ (lemma 13.1.2 ). By (2) the functions $\varphi _ i+h$ are plurisubharmonic on $B$, hence so is $\max _ i\varphi _ i+h=\max _ i(\varphi _ i+h)$, by proposition 8.2.5 . Thus $\max _ i\varphi _ i$ is quasi-plurisubharmonic on $B$, and $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\max _ i\varphi _ i\geq 0$ there by (2). Such balls cover $X$. (4) By compactness there are finitely many open sets $V_\kappa \Subset V_\kappa ^+$ such that the $V_\kappa $ cover $X$ and $\varphi =u_\kappa +f_\kappa $ on $V_\kappa ^+$, with $u_\kappa $ plurisubharmonic and $f_\kappa $ smooth. By lemma 13.1.1 , applied to the compact set $\overline{V_\kappa }$ and the form $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f_\kappa $, there are constants $C_\kappa \geq 0$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f_\kappa \geq -C_\kappa \omega $ on $V_\kappa $, and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\kappa \geq 0$ by theorem 8.2.1 . Hence $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi \geq -C\omega $ with $C=\max _\kappa C_\kappa $. (5) Replacing $C$ by $\max \{ C,0\} $, we may assume that $C\geq 0$. Let $B$ be a coordinate ball whose closure lies in a chart. By lemma 13.1.1 , applied in the chart to the compact set $\overline B$, the Hermitian form $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|z|^2$ and the form $-\omega $, there is $C'$ with $\omega \leq C'\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|z|^2$ on $B$, so $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\varphi +A|z|^2)\geq 0$ on $B$ for $A=CC'$. By theorem 8.2.1 , $\varphi +A|z|^2$ agrees almost everywhere on $B$ with a plurisubharmonic function, and subtracting $A|z|^2$ gives a quasi-plurisubharmonic function $\varphi _ B$ on $B$ that agrees almost everywhere with $\varphi $. If $B'$ is a second such ball, then $\varphi _ B$ and $\varphi _{B'}$ agree almost everywhere on $B\cap B'$, and both are quasi-plurisubharmonic, so they agree everywhere on $B\cap B'$ by (1). Since such balls cover $X$, the functions $\varphi _ B$ define a quasi-plurisubharmonic function on $X$ that agrees almost everywhere with $\varphi $. $\square$

title: Rational analytic singularities
text: Definition 13.1.5 . A quasi-plurisubharmonic function $\varphi $ on $X$ has analytic singularities if every point of $X$ has a connected coordinate neighborhood $V$ on which 13.1 \begin{equation} \label{eq:rational-analytic-singularities} \varphi =c\log \sum _{i=1}^ r|g_ i|^2+b, \qquad c\in \mathbb Q_{>0},\quad b\text{ bounded}, \end{equation} where $r\geq 1$ is an integer and $g_1,\ldots ,g_ r\in \mathcal O(V)$ are not all identically zero. It has neat analytic singularities if such presentations exist with $b$ smooth. Let $c\in \mathbb Q_{>0}$ and let $\mathfrak a\subset \mathcal O_ X$ be a coherent ideal sheaf. We say that $\varphi $ has analytic singularities of type $(c,\mathfrak a)$ if presentations ( 13.1 ) exist with this coefficient $c$, where on each $V$ the functions $g_1,\ldots ,g_ r$ generate $\mathfrak a$.

title: Rational analytic singularities
text: 13.1 \begin{equation} \label{eq:rational-analytic-singularities} \varphi =c\log \sum _{i=1}^ r|g_ i|^2+b, \qquad c\in \mathbb Q_{>0},\quad b\text{ bounded}, \end{equation}

title: Analytic singularity lelong number
text:
Lemma 13.1.6 . Let $x$ be a point of a complex manifold $X$ at which $X$ has positive dimension, let $\mathfrak a\subset \mathcal O_ X$ be a coherent ideal sheaf with $\mathfrak a_ x
eq 0$, generated near $x$ by $g_1,\ldots ,g_ s$, and let $c>0$. If $w$ is quasi-plurisubharmonic near $x$ and $w=c\log \sum _ i|g_ i|^2+O(1)$ near $x$, then $
u (w,x)=c\operatorname {ord}_ x\mathfrak a$. Proof. Choose a connected coordinate neighborhood $V$ of $x$ on which the $g_ i$ are defined and generate $\mathfrak a$, on which $w=v+f$ with $v$ plurisubharmonic and $f$ smooth and bounded, and on which $|w-c\log \sum _ i|g_ i|^2|\leq M$ for a constant $M$. Let $I$ be the set of indices $i$ for which the germ of $g_ i$ at $x$ is not zero. It is not empty, since these germs generate $\mathfrak a_ x
eq 0$, and for $i
otin I$ the function $g_ i$ vanishes identically on $V$, by the identity theorem. Since $0\leq \log \sum _{i\in I}|g_ i|^2-\max _{i\in I}\log |g_ i|^2\leq \log s$, the function $v$ differs from $c\max _{i\in I}\log |g_ i|^2$ by a bounded function on $V$. The latter function is plurisubharmonic by proposition 8.3.3 , proposition 8.2.5 , so proposition 12.1.1 and proposition 12.1.4 give \[  
u (w,x)=
u (v,x)=c\, 
u \Bigl (\max _{i\in I}\log |g_ i|^2,x\Bigr )=c\min _{i\in I}\operatorname {ord}_ xg_ i=c\operatorname {ord}_ x\mathfrak a,  \] where the first equality is the definition of Lelong numbers of quasi-plurisubharmonic functions (corollary 12.3.2 ) and the last one is the description of $\operatorname {ord}_ x\mathfrak a$ by generators in section 12.3 . $\square$

title: Rational analytic operations
text: Proposition 13.1.7 . Analytic singularities are preserved by multiplication by positive rational numbers, by sums and finite maxima, and by pullback under a holomorphic map $f\colon Y\to X$ of complex manifolds whenever the composition is not identically $-\infty $ on any component of $Y$. If $\varphi $ has type $(c,\mathfrak a)$ and $\pi \colon Y\to X$ is a log resolution of $\mathfrak a$ with $\pi ^*\mathfrak a=\mathcal O_ Y(-D)$, then locally on $Y$ \[  \varphi \circ \pi =c\log |s_ D|^2+O(1),  \] and the remainder is smooth if the presentations of type $(c,\mathfrak a)$ are neat. Proof. Multiplication by $q\in \mathbb Q_{>0}$ replaces $c$ by $qc$. Sums and finite maxima of quasi-plurisubharmonic functions are quasi-plurisubharmonic. Indeed, let $\varphi _ i=u_ i+\sigma _ i$ near a point, with $u_ i$ plurisubharmonic and $\sigma _ i$ smooth. On a small coordinate ball about the point, the smooth functions $\sigma _ i+N|z|^2$ have positive semidefinite complex Hessians for a large constant $N$, hence are plurisubharmonic by proposition 8.2.2 (1). By proposition 8.2.5 , $\varphi _1+\varphi _2$ is a plurisubharmonic function minus $2N|z|^2$, and $\max _ i\varphi _ i$ is a plurisubharmonic function minus $N|z|^2$. For a sum or a maximum of two functions with analytic singularities, choose presentations about a given point, with coefficients $c$ and $d$, and a connected coordinate neighborhood $V$ of the point contained in both domains; by the identity theorem, neither tuple vanishes identically on $V$. Since $c$ and $d$ are rational, we can choose $c_0\in \mathbb Q_{>0}$ such that $c/c_0$ and $d/c_0$ are positive integers. For an integer $k\geq 1$ the multinomial formula gives \[  \Bigl (\sum _ i|g_ i|^2\Bigr )^ k=\sum _{|\alpha |=k}\Bigl |\sqrt{k!/\alpha !}\, g^\alpha \Bigr |^2,  \] again a sum of squared moduli of holomorphic functions, not all identically zero on $V$. We may therefore assume that both presentations have the coefficient $c_0$, say $c_0\log A+b$ and $c_0\log B+b'$ with $A=\sum _ i|g_ i|^2$ and $B=\sum _ l|g'_ l|^2$. The sum is $c_0\log (AB)+b+b'$, and $AB=\sum _{i,l}|g_ ig'_ l|^2$, where some product $g_ ig'_ l$ is not identically zero on the connected set $V$. For the maximum we use \[  \max (\log A,\log B)\leq \log (A+B)\leq \max (\log A,\log B)+\log 2,  \] which shows that $\max (c_0\log A+b,c_0\log B+b')$ differs from $c_0\log (A+B)$ by a bounded function. For the pullback, let $f\colon Y\to X$ be holomorphic, and suppose that $\varphi \circ f$ is not identically $-\infty $ on any connected component of $Y$. Near each point of $Y$, write $\varphi \circ f=u\circ f+\sigma \circ f$ on a connected coordinate neighborhood $W$, where $\varphi =u+\sigma $ near the image point with $u$ plurisubharmonic and $\sigma $ smooth; by proposition 8.2.3 , $u\circ f$ is plurisubharmonic or identically $-\infty $ on $W$. Let $S$ be the open set of points of $Y$ near which $\varphi \circ f$ is identically $-\infty $. If $y$ lies in the closure of $S$ and $W$ is as above for $y$, then $u\circ f=-\infty $ on the nonempty open set $W\cap S$; since plurisubharmonic functions are locally integrable, $u\circ f$ is identically $-\infty $ on $W$, so $y\in S$. Thus $S$ is open and closed, and by hypothesis it contains no component of $Y$; hence $S=\varnothing $, and $\varphi \circ f$ is quasi-plurisubharmonic. If $\varphi =c\log \sum _ i|g_ i|^2+b$ on $V$, then on every connected coordinate neighborhood $W\subset f^{-1}(V)$ we have $\varphi \circ f=c\log \sum _ i|g_ i\circ f|^2+b\circ f$, with $b\circ f$ bounded, and the functions $g_ i\circ f$ do not all vanish identically on $W$, because $S=\varnothing $. Now let $\pi $ be a log resolution of $\mathfrak a$ as in the statement. If $g_1,\ldots ,g_ r$ generate $\mathfrak a$, their pullbacks generate $\mathcal O_ Y(-D)$, so locally $g_ i\circ \pi =s_ Dh_ i$ with holomorphic $h_ i$, and $s_ D=\sum _ ik_ i(g_ i\circ \pi )$ for holomorphic $k_ i$. Since $s_ D$ is not a zero divisor, $\sum _ ik_ ih_ i=1$, so the $h_ i$ have no common zero and $\log \sum _ i|h_ i|^2$ is smooth. Hence \[  \varphi \circ \pi =c\log |s_ D|^2+c\log \sum _ i|h_ i|^2+b\circ \pi ,  \] which proves both assertions about the remainder. $\square$

title: Quadratic line bundle metric
text: Definition 13.1.8 . A holomorphic line bundle $L$ on $X$ is given by an open cover $(V_ i)$ of $X$ and local frames $e_ i$ over $V_ i$ with transition functions $e_ i=g_{ij}e_ j$ on $V_ i\cap V_ j$, where $g_{ij}$ is holomorphic and nowhere zero and $g_{ij}g_{jk}=g_{ik}$ on triple overlaps. A smooth quadratic Hermitian metric on $L$ assigns to each frame a smooth positive squared norm $|e_ i|^2$ on $V_ i$, such that $|e_ i|^2=|g_{ij}|^2|e_ j|^2$ on $V_ i\cap V_ j$. Its curvature is the closed real $(1,1)$-form equal to $-\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |e_ i|^2$ on $V_ i$.

title: Smooth line bundle metric exists
text: Lemma 13.1.9 . Let $L$ be a holomorphic line bundle on a complex manifold $X$, given by frames $e_ i$ over an open cover $(V_ i)$ with transition functions $g_{ij}$ as in definition 13.1.8 . $L$ carries a smooth quadratic Hermitian metric. The curvature of a smooth quadratic Hermitian metric on $L$ is well defined, and it is a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form on $X$. Let $h_0$ be a smooth quadratic Hermitian metric on $L$ with curvature $\eta _0$. For every smooth real function $f$ on $X$, the squared norms $|e_ i|_{h_0}^2\mathrm e^{-f}$ define a smooth quadratic Hermitian metric $h_0\mathrm e^{-f}$ on $L$, whose curvature is $\eta _0+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$. Conversely, every smooth quadratic Hermitian metric on $L$ equals $h_0\mathrm e^{-f}$ for exactly one smooth real function $f$ on $X$. Proof. (1) By proposition 7.1.3 there is a smooth partition of unity $(\chi _ a)$ subordinate to the cover $(V_ i)$; for each $a$ choose an index $k(a)$ with $\operatorname{Supp}\chi _ a\subset V_{k(a)}$, and put $\rho _ k=\sum _{k(a)=k}\chi _ a$. Since the family $(\chi _ a)$ is locally finite, each $\rho _ k$ is smooth, the family $(\rho _ k)$ is locally finite, $\sum _ k\rho _ k=1$, and $\operatorname{Supp}\rho _ k\subset V_ k$, because a locally finite union of closed sets is closed. For each $i$ put \[  |e_ i|^2=\sum _ k\rho _ k|g_{ik}|^2\qquad \text{on }V_ i,  \] where the $k$th term, defined on $V_ i\cap V_ k$, is extended by zero to the rest of $V_ i$. Each term is smooth on $V_ i$, since it is smooth on $V_ i\cap V_ k$ and vanishes on the open set $V_ i\setminus \operatorname{Supp}\rho _ k$, and these two open sets cover $V_ i$. By local finiteness, $|e_ i|^2$ is smooth on $V_ i$, and it is positive, because the $\rho _ k$ are nonnegative with sum one and every $g_{ik}$ is nowhere zero. On $V_ i\cap V_ j$, the cocycle relation $g_{ik}=g_{ij}g_{jk}$ holds on $V_ i\cap V_ j\cap V_ k$, hence wherever $\rho _ k\neq 0$, so \[  |e_ i|^2=\sum _ k\rho _ k|g_{ij}|^2|g_{jk}|^2=|g_{ij}|^2|e_ j|^2.  \] Thus these squared norms form a smooth quadratic Hermitian metric on $L$. (2) On $V_ i\cap V_ j$ we have $\log |e_ i|^2-\log |e_ j|^2=\log |g_{ij}|^2$, which is pluriharmonic, since $g_{ij}$ is holomorphic and nowhere zero (section 7.3 ). Hence the forms $-\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |e_ i|^2$ on $V_ i$ agree on the overlaps and define a $(1,1)$-form $\eta $ on $X$. It is smooth, because each $\log |e_ i|^2$ is a smooth real function. Moreover $\eta =-\mathrm d(\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\log |e_ i|^2)$ on $V_ i$, by ( 7.6 ), and $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}$ maps real forms to real forms; hence $\eta $ is real, and it is closed because $\mathrm d^2=0$. (3) The functions $|e_ i|_{h_0}^2\mathrm e^{-f}$ are smooth and positive on $V_ i$, and they satisfy the compatibility condition of definition 13.1.8 because the functions $|e_ i|_{h_0}^2$ do. The curvature of $h_0\mathrm e^{-f}$ is $-\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log \bigl (|e_ i|_{h_0}^2\mathrm e^{-f}\bigr )=-\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |e_ i|_{h_0}^2+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f=\eta _0+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$ on $V_ i$. Conversely, let $h_1$ be a smooth quadratic Hermitian metric on $L$. On $V_ i$ the function $|e_ i|_{h_1}^2/|e_ i|_{h_0}^2$ is smooth and positive, and on $V_ i\cap V_ j$ it equals $|e_ j|_{h_1}^2/|e_ j|_{h_0}^2$, since both numerator and denominator are multiplied by $|g_{ij}|^2$. Hence these quotients define a smooth positive function on $X$, which we write as $\mathrm e^{-f}$ with $f$ smooth and real; then $h_1=h_0\mathrm e^{-f}$. The function $f$ is unique, since $\mathrm e^{-f}$ must equal these quotients. $\square$

title: Kahler smooth center blowup
text:
Proposition 13.1.10 . Let $X$ be a compact Kähler manifold with Kähler form $\omega $, let $W\subset X$ be a closed submanifold of positive codimension, and let $\pi \colon Y	o X$ be the blowup of $X$ along $W$, with exceptional divisor $E=\pi ^{-1}(W)$. Then $Y$ is a compact complex manifold, and there are a smooth function $ho \colon X	o [0,\infty )$ with $ho ^{-1}(0)=W$ and a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form $\eta $ on $Y$ with $\eta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log (ho \circ \pi )$ on $Y\setminus E$, such that $\pi ^*\omega +\varepsilon \eta $ is a Kähler form on $Y$ for every sufficiently small $\varepsilon >0$. The form $\eta $ is the curvature of a smooth quadratic Hermitian metric on the line bundle $\mathcal O_ Y(-E)$, whose local frames are the function $1$ on $Y\setminus E$ and the local equations of $E$ near $E$. In particular $Y$ is a compact Kähler manifold. Consequently every log resolution of a coherent ideal on $X$, as above, is a compact Kähler manifold. Proof. By proposition A.5.3 , $Y$ is a complex manifold and $E$ is a smooth hypersurface with $\mathcal I_ W\mathcal O_ Y=\mathcal O_ Y(-E)$; moreover $Y$ is compact, since $\pi $ is proper (proposition A.5.2 ), and $\pi $ restricts to a biholomorphism $Y\setminus E	o X\setminus W$. The last assertion follows from the preceding ones by induction: since $X$ is compact, a log resolution is a composite of finitely many blowups along closed submanifolds of positive codimension, and each intermediate manifold is compact Kähler by what precedes. We construct $\eta $ as the curvature of a metric on $\mathcal O_ Y(-E)$ and show that it is positive definite along the fibers of $E	o W$ (Step 1). Since $\pi ^*\omega $ is positive in the remaining directions, $\pi ^*\omega +\varepsilon \eta $ is then positive definite near $E$ for small $\varepsilon >0$ (Step 2), and also away from $E$ (Step 3). We use the charts of proposition A.5.3 . Near a point of $W$ at which $W$ has codimension $r$, choose coordinates $(z,w)$ on $X$, $w=(w_1,\ldots ,w_ r)$, with $W=\{ w=0\} $. For each pivot $i$ the blowup has a chart with coordinates $(z,t,v)$, $v=(v_ j)_{j
eq i}$, in which \[  \pi (z,t,v)=(z,t	ilde v),\qquad 	ilde v_ i=1,\quad 	ilde v_ j=v_ j\  (j
eq i);  \] in it $E=\{ t=0\} $, and the fibers of $E	o W$ are the sets $\{ z=	ext{const},\  t=0\} $. If $r=1$ there is no variable $v$, and $\pi $ is the identity near the point. Step 1: a closed $(1,1)$-form that is positive along the fibers of $E$. Choose finitely many charts $V_1,\ldots ,V_ N$ of $X$ covering $W$, with coordinates $(z^\alpha ,w^\alpha )$ such that $W\cap V_\alpha =\{ w^\alpha =0\} $, and put $V_0=X\setminus W$. Grouping the members of a partition of unity subordinate to this cover (proposition 7.1.3 ) according to a set $V_\alpha $ containing their supports, we obtain a smooth partition of unity $(\lambda _\alpha )_{0\leq \alpha \leq N}$ on $X$ with $\operatorname{Supp}\lambda _\alpha \subset V_\alpha $. Put \[  ho =\lambda _0+\sum _{\alpha =1}^ N\lambda _\alpha |w^\alpha |^2,  \] each term extended by zero outside $V_\alpha $. This is a smooth nonnegative function on $X$ that vanishes on $W$, because $\lambda _0=0$ there, and is positive on $X\setminus W$: at a point $x
otin W$ some $\lambda _\alpha (x)$ is positive, and $w^\alpha (x)
eq 0$ if $\alpha \geq 1$. We describe $ho $ near a point $x_0\in W$, in coordinates $(z,w)$ as above on a polydisc $\Delta $ centered at $x_0$. Shrinking $\Delta $, we may assume that $\Delta $ does not meet $\operatorname{Supp}\lambda _0$, nor $\operatorname{Supp}\lambda _\alpha $ for the indices $\alpha $ with $x_0
otin V_\alpha $, and that $\Delta \subset V_\alpha $ for the others. For such an $\alpha $, each component $w^\alpha _ k$ vanishes on $W=\{ w=0\} $, so \[  w^\alpha _ k(z,w)=\sum _{l=1}^ rw_ l\int _0^1 rac{\partial w^\alpha _ k}{\partial w_ l}(z,sw)\, \mathrm ds,  \] that is, $w^\alpha =A_\alpha w$ with a holomorphic $r	imes r$ matrix $A_\alpha $ on $\Delta $. At points of $W$ the matrix $A_\alpha (z,0)=(\partial w^\alpha _ k/\partial w_ l)(z,0)$ is invertible: since $w^\alpha $ vanishes on $W$, its derivatives in the $z$-directions vanish there, and the Jacobian matrix of the coordinate change $(z,w)\mapsto (z^\alpha ,w^\alpha )$ is invertible. Hence, on $\Delta $, \[  ho =\sum _\alpha \lambda _\alpha |A_\alpha w|^2=w^*\mathcal Q\, w,\qquad \mathcal Q=\sum _\alpha \lambda _\alpha A_\alpha ^*A_\alpha ,  \] where the sums run over the indices $\alpha \geq 1$ with $x_0\in V_\alpha $, and $w^*$ is the conjugate transpose of the column vector $w$. The Hermitian matrix $\mathcal Q$ is smooth and positive semidefinite, and it is positive definite at $x_0$, because the coefficients $\lambda _\alpha (x_0)$ of the invertible matrices $A_\alpha (x_0)$ add up to one; shrinking $\Delta $, we may assume that $\mathcal Q$ is positive definite on $\Delta $. In a chart $(z,t,v)$ over $\Delta $ we obtain \[  ho \circ \pi =|t|^2h_ E,\qquad h_ E(z,t,v)=	ilde v^*\mathcal Q(z,t	ilde v)\, 	ilde v,  \] and $h_ E$ is smooth and positive, since $	ilde v
eq 0$. Define a real $(1,1)$-form $\eta $ on $Y$ by $\eta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log (ho \circ \pi )$ on $Y\setminus E$ and $\eta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log h_ E$ on each chart $(z,t,v)$ as above. These definitions agree. Off $E$ we have $\log (ho \circ \pi )=\log |t|^2+\log h_ E$, and $\log |t|^2$ is pluriharmonic there. On the overlap of two charts, the local equations $t$ and $t'$ of $E$ generate the same ideal $\mathcal O_ Y(-E)$, so $t'=ut$ with $u$ holomorphic and nowhere zero. Off $E$ the corresponding functions $h_ E$ and $h'_ E$ satisfy $\log h_ E-\log h'_ E=\log |u|^2$. Both sides are continuous on the overlap and $E$ is nowhere dense, so this identity holds on the whole overlap, and $\log |u|^2$ is pluriharmonic. Thus $\eta $ is a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form on $Y$. It is the curvature, in the sense of definition 13.1.8 , of the metric on the line bundle $\mathcal O_ Y(-E)$ with the frame $1$ on $Y\setminus E$, the frames $t$ on the charts and the transition functions $t$ and $t'/t$, for which $|1|^2=1/(ho \circ \pi )$ and $|t|^2=1/h_ E$. These squared norms are smooth and positive, and they satisfy the compatibility condition of that definition because $ho \circ \pi =|t|^2h_ E$ and $h'_ E=|t/t'|^2h_ E$. We show that $\eta $ is positive definite along the fibers of $E	o W$. Fix a point $(z_0,0,v_0)$ of $E$ in a chart, and put $\mathcal Q_0=\mathcal Q(z_0,0)$. On the fiber $\{ z=z_0,\  t=0\} $ we have $h_ E=	ilde v^*\mathcal Q_0	ilde v$. Write $\mathcal Q_0=\Gamma ^*\Gamma $ with an invertible matrix $\Gamma $, for instance the positive square root of $\mathcal Q_0$, and let $e_1,\ldots ,e_ r$ be the standard basis of $\mathbb C^ r$. Then $h_ E=|F(v)|^2$ on the fiber, where $F(v)=\Gamma 	ilde v=\Gamma e_ i+\sum _{j
eq i}v_ j\Gamma e_ j$ is an affine map whose linear part $\Lambda \xi =\sum _{j
eq i}\xi _ j\Gamma e_ j$ is injective, and $F(v)$ never lies in the image of $\Lambda $, because the columns $\Gamma e_1,\ldots ,\Gamma e_ r$ are linearly independent. Writing $\langle a,bangle =\sum _ ka_ k ar b_ k$ on $\mathbb C^ r$, we have $\partial _{ ar v_ l}|F|^2=\langle F,\Gamma e_ langle $ and $\partial _{v_ k}|F|^2=\langle \Gamma e_ k,Fangle $, so for $\xi \in \mathbb C^{r-1}$ \[  \sum _{k,l
eq i} rac{\partial ^2\log |F|^2}{\partial v_ k\partial  ar v_ l}\, \xi _ k ar\xi _ l = rac{|\Lambda \xi |^2}{|F|^2}- rac{|\langle \Lambda \xi ,Fangle |^2}{|F|^4} = rac{|F|^2|\Lambda \xi |^2-|\langle \Lambda \xi ,Fangle |^2}{|F|^4}.  \] By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality this is nonnegative, and it vanishes only if $\Lambda \xi =\mu F$ for some $\mu \in \mathbb C$. Since $F$ does not lie in the image of $\Lambda $, this forces $\mu =0$, so $\Lambda \xi =0$ and $\xi =0$. By the matrix criterion, the restriction of $\eta $ to each fiber of $E	o W$ is positive definite. Step 2: positivity near $E$. The form $P=\pi ^*\omega $ is a smooth closed semipositive $(1,1)$-form on $Y$. We regard the real $(1,1)$-forms $P$ and $\eta $ in a chart $(z,t,v)$ as Hermitian forms on holomorphic tangent vectors, given by their coefficient matrices, so that $P(	au ,	au )=\omega (\mathrm d\pi \, 	au ,\mathrm d\pi \, 	au )$ by the chain rule; norms of tangent vectors are taken in the coordinates of the chart. Let $V$ be spanned by the vectors $\partial /\partial v_ k$ and $H$ by the vectors $\partial /\partial z_ l$ and $\partial /\partial t$, and write $P$ and $\eta $ in block form with respect to the decomposition of the tangent space into $V$ and $H$. At points of $E$ we have $\mathrm d\pi (\partial /\partial v_ k)=t\, \partial /\partial w_ k=0$, while $\mathrm d\pi (\partial /\partial z_ l)=\partial /\partial z_ l$ and $\mathrm d\pi (\partial /\partial t)=\sum _ j	ilde v_ j\, \partial /\partial w_ j$ are linearly independent. Since $\omega $ is positive definite, $P_{HV}=0$ and $P_{HH}$ is positive definite at points of $E$, while $\eta _{VV}$ is positive definite there by Step 1. Choose finitely many compact sets $K_\iota $ whose interiors cover $E$, each contained in a chart $(z,t,v)$. The smallest eigenvalues of $P_{HH}$ and of $\eta _{VV}$ are continuous and positive on the compact sets $E\cap K_\iota $, so there are $a,c>0$ such that they exceed $2c$ and $2a$, respectively, on $E\cap K_\iota $ for every $\iota $. Let $M>0$ bound the operator norm of $\eta $ on every $K_\iota $, so that $|\eta (	au ,	au ')|\leq M|	au ||	au '|$, and choose $\ell \in (0,1]$ with $2M\ell +M\ell ^2\leq a/2$. Where $P_{HH}$ is invertible, the linear map $L=P_{HH}^{-1}P_{HV}\colon V	o H$ depends continuously on the point, and it vanishes on $E$. Hence every point of $E\cap K_\iota $ has a neighborhood on whose intersection with $K_\iota $ we have $P_{HH}\geq c$, $\eta _{VV}\geq a$ and $\| L\| \leq \ell $. Let $O_\iota $ be the union of these neighborhoods. Then \[  \mathcal N=\operatorname{Int}\Bigl ( igcup _\iota K_\iota \Bigr )\cap  igcap _\iota  igl (O_\iota \cup (Y\setminus K_\iota ) igr )  \] is an open neighborhood of $E$ with $\mathcal N\cap K_\iota \subset O_\iota $ for every $\iota $. On $\mathcal N\cap K_\iota $ we have, for $\xi \in V$, \[  \eta (\xi -L\xi ,\xi -L\xi )\geq  igl (a-2M\| L\| -M\| L\| ^2 igr )|\xi |^2\geq  rac a2|\xi |^2,\qquad |\xi -L\xi |\leq 2|\xi |.  \] Write a tangent vector at a point of $\mathcal N\cap K_\iota $ as $	au =\xi +\zeta $ with $\xi \in V$ and $\zeta \in H$, and put $\sigma =\zeta +L\xi \in H$. Completing the square, \[  P(	au ,	au )=P_{HH}(\sigma ,\sigma )+S(\xi ,\xi ),\qquad S=P_{VV}-P_{VH}P_{HH}^{-1}P_{HV},  \] and $S\geq 0$ because $P\geq 0$ (take $\zeta =-L\xi $, so that $\sigma =0$). Hence $P(	au ,	au )\geq c|\sigma |^2$. Since $	au =(\xi -L\xi )+\sigma $, \[  \eta (	au ,	au )\geq  rac a2|\xi |^2-4M|\xi ||\sigma |-M|\sigma |^2.  \] Therefore, for $\varepsilon >0$, \[  (P+\varepsilon \eta )(	au ,	au )\geq (c-\varepsilon M)|\sigma |^2+ rac{\varepsilon a}2|\xi |^2-4\varepsilon M|\xi ||\sigma |.  \] The right-hand side is a quadratic form in $(|\sigma |,|\xi |)$, which is positive definite as soon as $\varepsilon M<c$ and $(c-\varepsilon M)a>8\varepsilon M^2$; and $(\sigma ,\xi )
eq 0$ for $	au 
eq 0$. Thus $\pi ^*\omega +\varepsilon \eta $ is positive definite on the fixed neighborhood $\mathcal N$ of $E$ for all sufficiently small $\varepsilon >0$. Step 3: positivity away from $E$. On the compact set $Y\setminus \mathcal N\subset Y\setminus E$ the map $\pi $ is a local biholomorphism, so $\pi ^*\omega $ is positive definite at every point. Cover $Y\setminus \mathcal N$ by finitely many compact sets contained in charts. On each of them the smallest eigenvalue of the coefficient matrix of $\pi ^*\omega $ is bounded below by a positive constant $c'$, and the operator norm of the coefficient matrix of $\eta $ is bounded by a constant $M'$, with $c'$ and $M'$ independent of the set. Hence $\pi ^*\omega +\varepsilon \eta $ is positive definite on $Y\setminus \mathcal N$ if $\varepsilon M'<c'$. Together with Step 2, this shows that $\pi ^*\omega +\varepsilon \eta $ is positive definite on all of $Y$ for every sufficiently small $\varepsilon >0$. It is closed, since both terms are, so it is a Kähler form on $Y$. $\square$

title: Gentle analytic singularities
text: Definition 13.1.11 . Let $X$ be a compact Kähler manifold. A quasi-plurisubharmonic function $\varphi $ on $X$ has gentle analytic singularities of type $(c,\mathfrak a)$ if it has analytic singularities of type $(c,\mathfrak a)$, the function $\exp (\varphi /c)$ is smooth on $X$, including at its zeros, and on every log resolution $\pi $ of $\mathfrak a$, with $\pi ^*\mathfrak a=\mathcal O(-D)$, one has locally \[  \varphi \circ \pi =c\log |s_ D|^2+h,\qquad h\text{ smooth}.  \]

title: Local Bergman kernels and ideal generators
text:
13.2 Local Bergman kernels and ideal generators In this section $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$, $n\geq 1$, is a bounded pseudoconvex open set, $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$, and integrals are taken with respect to Lebesgue measure unless another measure is specified. For an integer $m\geq 1$ we put \[  H_ m=\Bigl \{ F\in \mathcal O(\Omega ):\| F\| _ m^2 =\int _\Omega |F|^2\mathrm e^{-mu}<\infty \Bigr \} ,\qquad K_ m(z)=\sup _{\| F\| _ m\leq 1}|F(z)|^2.  \] Thus $H_ m$ is the space $\mathcal H_{mu}(\Omega )$ of theorem 12.2.7 , for the complex manifold $\Omega $ and the weight $mu$, and the function $K_ m$ is the Bergman kernel of $H_ m$ on the diagonal. We need that $H_ m$ is a Hilbert space of holomorphic functions that generates the multiplier ideal $\mathcal I(mu)$, with bounded coefficients near each point. These facts were proved in chapter 12 on bounded pseudoconvex open sets, also for measures $\varrho \, \mathrm dV$ comparable with Lebesgue measure (theorem 12.2.7 , lemma 12.2.8 ), and the next lemma restates them in the notation of this section. Throughout this section, $\varrho $ denotes a measurable function on $\Omega $ with $c_\varrho \leq \varrho \leq C_\varrho $ for positive constants $c_\varrho $ and $C_\varrho $. Such measures arise in section 13.3 , where the kernels are computed with the volume form of a Kähler form. Lemma 13.2.1 . Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$, $n\geq 1$, be a bounded pseudoconvex open set, let $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$, and let $\varrho $ be a measurable function on $\Omega $ with $c_\varrho \leq \varrho \leq C_\varrho $ for positive constants $c_\varrho $ and $C_\varrho $. Put \[  \mathcal H=\Bigl \{ F\in \mathcal O(\Omega ):\| F\| ^2=\int _\Omega |F|^2\mathrm e^{-\psi }\varrho \, \mathrm dV<\infty \Bigr \} ,\qquad \langle F,Gangle =\int _\Omega F ar G\, \mathrm e^{-\psi }\varrho \, \mathrm dV.  \] For every compact set $K\subset \Omega $ there is a constant $C_ K$ such that $|F(z)|\leq C_ K\| F\| $ for all $F\in \mathcal H$ and $z\in K$. The space $\mathcal H$ is a separable Hilbert space, and it has an orthonormal basis, that is, an orthonormal family $(e_\ell )$, finite or countable, whose linear span is dense. For every such family and every $F\in \mathcal H$, the partial sums of $\sum _\ell \langle F,e_\ell angle e_\ell $ converge to $F$ in norm and locally uniformly on $\Omega $, and $\sum _\ell |\langle F,e_\ell angle |^2=\| F\| ^2$. The germs of the elements of $\mathcal H$ generate $\mathcal I(\psi )$ at every point of $\Omega $, and near each point finitely many elements of $\mathcal H$ already generate $\mathcal I(\psi )$. Let $x\in \Omega $, and let $g_1,\ldots ,g_ s\in \mathcal H$ generate $\mathcal I(\psi )$ on a neighborhood of $x$. Then there are a neighborhood $V$ of $x$ and a constant $C$ such that every $F\in \mathcal H$ can be written as $F=\sum _ ig_ ih_ i$ on $V$ with $h_ i\in \mathcal O(V)$ and $\sup _ V|h_ i|\leq C\| F\| $. Proof. We regard $\Omega $ as a complex manifold, with the single chart given by the identity map. Then $\psi $ is a weight on $\Omega $ in the sense of section 12.2 , the set $\Omega $ satisfies the hypotheses of theorem 12.2.7 , and $\mathcal H$ is the space $\mathcal H_\psi (\Omega ,\varrho )$ of that theorem, with the same inner product. Hence (1) is contained in theorem 12.2.7 (1) and (2), and (2) follows from theorem 12.2.7 (3), because an initial segment of an enumerated orthonormal basis is a finite family of elements of $\mathcal H$. Finally, (3) is the first assertion of lemma 12.2.8 , applied to the weight $\psi $ on $\Omega $. $\square$ By lemma 13.2.1 , applied with $\psi =mu$ and $\varrho =1$, the space $H_ m$ is a Hilbert space on which evaluation at each point is a bounded linear functional; in particular $K_ m$ is finite. Let $(e_\ell )$ be an orthonormal basis of $H_ m$. Then 13.2  egin{equation} \label{eq:bergman-kernel-basis} K_ m=\sum _\ell |e_\ell |^2. \end{equation} Indeed, let $F$ lie in the unit ball of $H_ m$ and put $c_\ell =\langle F,e_\ell angle $. By lemma 13.2.1 (1), $F(z)=\sum _\ell c_\ell e_\ell (z)$ and $\sum _\ell |c_\ell |^2=\| F\| _ m^2\leq 1$, so the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality gives $|F(z)|^2\leq \sum _\ell |e_\ell (z)|^2$. Conversely, for each $N$ the function $F_ N=\sum _{\ell \leq N}\overline{e_\ell (z)}e_\ell $ satisfies $F_ N(z)=\| F_ N\| _ m^2=\sum _{\ell \leq N}|e_\ell (z)|^2$; if this number is positive, then $F_ N/\| F_ N\| _ m$ lies in the unit ball, and $\sum _{\ell \leq N}|e_\ell (z)|^2=|F_ N(z)|^2/\| F_ N\| _ m^2\leq K_ m(z)$. The same argument applies to the kernel of the space defined with $\varrho \, \mathrm dV$ in place of Lebesgue measure, for an orthonormal basis of that space. Lemma 13.2.2 . The function $K_ m$ is real analytic on $\Omega $. Near each point of $\Omega $ it is bounded above and below by positive constant multiples of $\sum _ i|g_ i|^2$, where $g_1,\ldots ,g_ s$ are finitely many generators of $\mathcal I(mu)$ near that point. If $\pi \colon Y	o \Omega $ is a holomorphic map from a complex manifold $Y$ such that $\pi ^*\mathcal I(mu)=\mathcal O_ Y(-D)$ for an effective divisor $D$ on $Y$, for instance a log resolution of $\mathcal I(mu)$, then locally on $Y$ \[  K_ m\circ \pi =|s_ D|^2b_ m,\qquad b_ m	ext{ smooth and strictly positive},  \] where $s_ D$ is a local equation of $D$. The same conclusions hold if Lebesgue measure is replaced by $\varrho \, \mathrm dV$ in the definition of $H_ m$. Proof. We give the proof for the measure $\varrho \, \mathrm dV$; Lebesgue measure is the case $\varrho =1$. title: Pseudoconvex weighted bergman space
text: Lemma 13.2.1 . Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$, $n\geq 1$, be a bounded pseudoconvex open set, let $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$, and let $\varrho $ be a measurable function on $\Omega $ with $c_\varrho \leq \varrho \leq C_\varrho $ for positive constants $c_\varrho $ and $C_\varrho $. The space $\mathcal H$ is a separable Hilbert space, and it has an orthonormal basis, that is, an orthonormal family $(e_\ell )$, finite or countable, whose linear span is dense. For every such family and every $F\in \mathcal H$, the partial sums of $\sum _\ell \langle F,e_\ell \rangle e_\ell $ converge to $F$ in norm and locally uniformly on $\Omega $, and $\sum _\ell |\langle F,e_\ell \rangle |^2=\| F\| ^2$. Then there are a neighborhood $V$ of $x$ and a constant $C$ such that every $F\in \mathcal H$ can be written as $F=\sum _ ig_ ih_ i$ on $V$ with $h_ i\in \mathcal O(V)$ and $\sup _ V|h_ i|\leq C\| F\| $.
