Then $\psi $ is a weight on $\Omega $ in the sense of section 12.2 , the set $\Omega $ satisfies the hypotheses of theorem 12.2.7 , and $\mathcal H$ is the space $\mathcal H_\psi (\Omega ,\varrho )$ of that theorem, with the same inner product. Hence (1) is contained in theorem 12.2.7 (1) and (2), and (2) follows from theorem 12.2.7 (3), because an initial segment of an enumerated orthonormal basis is a finite family of elements of $\mathcal H$. Finally, (3) is the first assertion of lemma 12.2.8 , applied to the weight $\psi $ on $\Omega $. $\square$

The comparison in lemma 13.2.2 gives $u_ m=m^{-1}\log \sum _ i|g_ i|^2+O(1)$ locally, with generators $g_ i$ of $\mathcal I(mu)$; this is the asserted type. For the lower bound in ( 13.3 ), let $u(z)>-\infty $; at points of the pole set of $u$ there is nothing to prove. By corollary 11.4.5 , applied on $\Omega $ to the weight $mu$, there is $F\in H_ m$ with $F(z)=1$ and $\| F\| _ m^2\leq C_1\mathrm e^{-mu(z)}$, where $C_1$ depends only on $n$ and $L$. Hence $K_ m(z)\geq |F(z)|^2/\| F\| _ m^2\geq C_1^{-1}\mathrm e^{mu(z)}$. For the upper bound, let $\| F\| _ m\leq 1$. The mean-value inequality ( 12.9 ) of lemma 12.2.6 for $|F|^2$ on $B(z,r)$, where $|B(z,r)|=\pi ^ nr^{2n}/n!$, gives  egin{align*}  |F(z)|^2& \leq C_2r^{-2n}\int _{B(z,r)}|F|^2\ & \leq C_2r^{-2n}\exp \Bigl (m\sup _{B(z,r)}u\Bigr )\int _{B(z,r)}|F|^2\mathrm e^{-mu} \leq C_2r^{-2n}\exp \Bigl (m\sup _{B(z,r)}u\Bigr ), \end{align*} with $C_2=n!/\pi ^ n$, and taking the supremum over $F$ proves the upper bound. Now fix $z$ and $r$, and let $m	o \infty $ in ( 13.3 ): we obtain $u(z)\leq \varliminf _ mu_ m(z)\leq \varlimsup _ mu_ m(z)\leq \sup _{B(z,r)}u$. Letting $r\downarrow 0$ and using the upper semicontinuity of $u$ gives $u_ m(z)	o u(z)$, also at points of the pole set. On a compact set $K\subset \Omega $, a fixed $r<\operatorname {dist}(K,\partial \Omega )$ in the upper bound gives a uniform upper bound for all $u_ m$, while $u_ m\geq u-|\log C_1|$. Since $u\in L^1(K)$, dominated convergence gives $u_ m	o u$ in $L^1(K)$. For the Lelong numbers, let $g_1,\ldots ,g_ s$ generate $\mathcal I(mu)$ near $z$. The stalk $\mathcal I(mu)_ z$ is not zero: by the first paragraph, applied to the component of $\Omega $ containing $z$, it contains the germ of an element of $H_ m$ that does not vanish identically on that component, and this germ is not zero by the identity theorem. Since $u_ m=m^{-1}\log \sum _ i|g_ i|^2+O(1)$ near $z$, lemma 13.1.6 gives $
u (u_ m,z)=m^{-1}\operatorname {ord}_ z\mathcal I(mu)$, and ( 13.4 ) follows from lemma 12.3.1 . Finally, near each point $K_ m\leq C\sum _ i|g_ i|^2$ with $g_ i\in H_ m$, by lemma 13.2.2 , and each $|g_ i|^2\mathrm e^{-mu}$ is integrable on $\Omega $. Hence $\exp (m(u_ m-u))=K_ m\mathrm e^{-mu}$ is locally integrable. Now replace Lebesgue measure by $\varrho \, \mathrm dV$, and let $K^\varrho _ m$ be the corresponding kernel. The space of holomorphic functions is the same, and the two norms satisfy $c_\varrho \| F\| _ m^2\leq \| F\| _{m,\varrho }^2\leq C_\varrho \| F\| _ m^2$. If $\| F\| _ m\leq 1$, then $F/C_\varrho ^{1/2}$ lies in the unit ball for $\varrho $, and if $\| F\| _{m,\varrho }\leq 1$, then $c_\varrho ^{1/2}F$ lies in the unit ball for Lebesgue measure; hence \[  C_\varrho ^{-1}K_ m\leq K^\varrho _ m\leq c_\varrho ^{-1}K_ m.  \] The proof of plurisubharmonicity applies verbatim to $m^{-1}\log K^\varrho _ m$, with the unit ball taken for $\varrho $ and the continuity of $K^\varrho _ m$ given by lemma 13.2.2 . The lower and upper bounds follow from the last display, with the constants $C_\varrho C_1$ and $C_2/c_\varrho $. The convergence and the Lelong numbers then follow as before, since lemma 13.2.2 applies to $K^\varrho _ m$. Finally, $K^\varrho _ m\mathrm e^{-mu}\leq c_\varrho ^{-1}K_ m\mathrm e^{-mu}$ is locally integrable. $\square$

title: Local bergman bounds
text: 13.3 \begin{equation} \label{eq:local-bergman-bounds} u(z)-\frac{\log C_1}{m}\leq u_ m(z) \leq \sup _{B(z,r)}u+\frac1m\log \frac{C_2}{r^{2n}} \end{equation}

title: Local bergman lelong
Bergman diagonal comparison
text: Lemma 13.2.4 . Suppose that the spaces $H_ m$ are defined with respect to $\varrho \, \mathrm dV$; for instance $\varrho =1$. There is a constant $C_\Omega >0$, depending only on $n$, on a bound $L$ for the diameter of $\Omega $ and on $c_\varrho $ and $C_\varrho $, and in particular independent of $m$ and $u$, such that \[  K_{2m}\leq C_\Omega K_ m^2\qquad \text{on }\Omega .  \] Proof. We write $\| \cdot \| _ m$ for the norm of $H_ m$. By the definition of $K_ m$, every $h\in H_ m$ satisfies $|h(\zeta )|^2\leq \| h\| _ m^2K_ m(\zeta )$ for all $\zeta \in \Omega $; if $\| h\| _ m=0$, then $h$ vanishes almost everywhere, hence identically. Let $F\in H_{2m}$. We first extend $F$ from the diagonal to $\Omega \times \Omega $. By corollary 11.2.5 , $\Omega \times \Omega $ is a bounded pseudoconvex open set in $\mathbb C^{2n}$, of diameter at most $\sqrt2L$, and the function $p(z,w)=mu(z)+mu(w)$ is plurisubharmonic on it (proposition 8.2.3 , proposition 8.2.5 ). The diagonal $\Lambda =\{ (z,w)\in \mathbb C^{2n}:z=w\} $ is a complex linear subspace of codimension $n$, and the map $z\mapsto (z,z)$ multiplies Euclidean lengths by $\sqrt2$, so Lebesgue measure on $\Lambda $ corresponds to $2^ n$ times Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb C^ n$. On $\Lambda \cap (\Omega \times \Omega )$, identified with $\Omega $, the weight $p$ restricts to $2mu$, so \[  \int _{\Lambda \cap (\Omega \times \Omega )}|F|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV_{2n}=2^ n\int _\Omega |F|^2\mathrm e^{-2mu}\, \mathrm dV\leq 2^ nc_\varrho ^{-1}\| F\| _{2m}^2.  \] The extension statement of corollary 11.4.5 , applied on $\Omega \times \Omega $ to the weight $p$ and the subspace $\Lambda $, gives $G\in \mathcal O(\Omega \times \Omega )$ with $G(z,z)=F(z)$ and $\int _{\Omega \times \Omega }|G|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV_{4n}\leq C^ n(\sqrt2L)^{2n}2^ nc_\varrho ^{-1}\| F\| _{2m}^2$, where $C$ is the constant of theorem 11.4.4 . Hence \[  \| G\| ^2=\int _{\Omega \times \Omega }|G(z,w)|^2\mathrm e^{-mu(z)-mu(w)}\varrho (z)\varrho (w)\, \mathrm dV(z)\, \mathrm dV(w)\leq C_\Omega \| F\| _{2m}^2  \] with $C_\Omega =4^ nC^ nL^{2n}C_\varrho ^2/c_\varrho $. We now bound $G$ on the diagonal by $K_ m$. For $w\in \Omega $ put \[  N(w)=\int _\Omega |G(z,w)|^2\mathrm e^{-mu(z)}\varrho (z)\, \mathrm dV(z)\in [0,\infty ].  \] By Tonelli's theorem, $N$ is measurable and $\int _\Omega N(w)\mathrm e^{-mu(w)}\varrho (w)\, \mathrm dV(w)=\| G\| ^2<\infty $; since $\mathrm e^{-mu}\varrho >0$ almost everywhere, $N(w)<\infty $ for almost every $w$. For such $w$, the function $G(\cdot ,w)$ belongs to $H_ m$ with $\| G(\cdot ,w)\| _ m^2=N(w)$, so $|G(z,w)|^2\leq N(w)K_ m(z)$ for every $z$. Fix $z\in \Omega $. Integrating this inequality in $w$, we obtain \[  \int _\Omega |G(z,w)|^2\mathrm e^{-mu(w)}\varrho (w)\, \mathrm dV(w)\leq K_ m(z)\| G\| ^2,  \] so $G(z,\cdot )\in H_ m$ with $\| G(z,\cdot )\| _ m^2\leq K_ m(z)\| G\| ^2$, and therefore $|G(z,w)|^2\leq K_ m(z)K_ m(w)\| G\| ^2$ for every $w$. Taking $w=z$, \[  |F(z)|^2=|G(z,z)|^2\leq K_ m(z)^2\| G\| ^2\leq C_\Omega \| F\| _{2m}^2K_ m(z)^2.  \] Taking the supremum over the unit ball of $H_{2m}$ proves the lemma. $\square$

title: Overlap interpolation and quantitative patching
Maximum cutoff patching
text: Lemma 13.3.1 . Let $\theta $ be a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form on $X$, let $a\geq 0$, and let $v_ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(B_ j,\theta )$ for $j=1,\ldots ,J$ satisfy $v_ j\leq v_ l+a$ on $\overline{U'_ j}\cap \overline{U'_ l}$ for all $j,l$. Then the function \[  v(x)=\max _{j:\, x\in \overline{U'_ j}}\bigl (v_ j(x)+a\chi _ j(x)\bigr )  \] is quasi-plurisubharmonic on $X$ and satisfies $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\geq -aC_\chi \omega $ and $v_ j\leq v\leq v_ j+2a$ on $U_ j$. Proof. Since the $U_ i$ cover $X$, the maximum is taken over a nonempty set at every point. Fix $x_0\in X$ and choose $i$ with $x_0\in U_ i$. Indices $j$ with $x_0\notin \overline{U'_ j}$ do not occur near $x_0$. If $x_0\in \partial U'_ j$, then $\chi _ j=0$ near $x_0$, because $\chi _ j$ has compact support in $U'_ j$; so near $x_0$ the $j$th term, where it is defined, equals $v_ j\leq v_ i+a=v_ i+a\chi _ i$, since $\chi _ i=1$ on the neighborhood $U_ i$ of $x_0$. Such a term never exceeds the $i$th term and can be omitted. Hence on a small neighborhood of $x_0$, $v$ is the maximum of $v_ j+a\chi _ j$ over the fixed set of indices $j$ with $x_0\in U'_ j$. Each of these functions satisfies $\theta +aC_\chi \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v_ j+a\chi _ j)\geq 0$. Adding a local potential of the closed form $\theta +aC_\chi \omega $ on a coordinate ball about $x_0$ (lemma 13.1.2 ), which makes these functions plurisubharmonic by lemma 13.1.4 (2), and applying proposition 8.2.5 , we obtain that $v$ is quasi-plurisubharmonic near $x_0$ with $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\geq -aC_\chi \omega $. On $U_ j$ the $j$th term is $v_ j+a\geq v_ j$, and every term with index $l$ is at most $v_ l+a\leq v_ j+2a$. This proves the two bounds, also at points of the pole sets. $\square$

title: Geometry uniform kernel overlap
text: Lemma 13.3.2 . There is a constant $C_ B\geq 0$, depending only on the fixed geometry and in particular independent of $\theta $, $\varphi $ and $m$, such that \[  a_{j,m}\leq \mathrm e^{C_ B}a_{l,m}\qquad \text{on }\overline{U'_ j}\cap \overline{U'_ l}  \] for all $j,l$. In particular $a_{j,m}$ and $a_{l,m}$ have the same zeros on $\overline{U'_ j}\cap \overline{U'_ l}$, and $|v_{j,m}-v_{l,m}|\leq C_ B/m$ there outside these common zeros. Proof. Fix $j,l$ with $\overline{U'_ j}\cap \overline{U'_ l}\neq \varnothing $, and work in the coordinates of the ball $\mathcal B_{jl}$. By lemma 13.1.2 choose a smooth function $g$ on $\mathcal B_{jl}$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g=\theta $. The functions $h_ j-g$ and $h_ l-g$ are pluriharmonic on the coordinate balls $B_ j^+$ and $B_ l^+$, so by the same lemma $h_ j-g=\operatorname{Re}b_ j$ and $h_ l-g=\operatorname{Re}b_ l$ with $b_ j,b_ l$ holomorphic on these balls (the constants are absorbed into $b_ j,b_ l$). Put $u=\varphi +g$, a plurisubharmonic function on $\mathcal B_{jl}$. Since $|\mathrm e^{-mb_ j/2}|^2=\mathrm e^{-m\operatorname{Re}b_ j}$, multiplication by $\mathrm e^{-mb_ j/2}$ is an isometry from the weighted space defining $K_{j,m}$ onto the space of holomorphic functions on $B_ j$ with weight $mu$ and volume form $\omega ^ n/n!$. If $K^{mu}_{B_ j}$ denotes the Bergman kernel of the latter space, then $K^{mu}_{B_ j}=\mathrm e^{-m\operatorname{Re}b_ j}K_{j,m}$, and therefore \[  a_{j,m}=\mathrm e^{-mg}K^{mu}_{B_ j},\qquad a_{l,m}=\mathrm e^{-mg}K^{mu}_{B_ l}.  \] Hence it suffices to prove $K^{mu}_{B_ j}\leq C_0^2K^{mu}_{B_ l}$ on $\overline{U'_ j}\cap \overline{U'_ l}$ with $C_0\geq 1$ depending only on the fixed geometry. Choose a smooth function $\rho \colon X\to [0,1]$ with compact support in $B_ j\cap B_ l$, equal to one on a neighborhood of the compact set $\overline{U'_ j}\cap \overline{U'_ l}$ (proposition 7.1.3 ); this choice belongs to the fixed geometry. Let $r>0$ be the distance, in the coordinates of $\mathcal B_{jl}$, from $\overline{U'_ j}\cap \overline{U'_ l}$ to the support of $\bar\partial \rho $, and let $c>0$ and $C''$ be lower and upper bounds for the density of $\omega ^ n/n!$ with respect to Lebesgue measure on $B_ j\cup B_ l$ in these coordinates. The ball $B_ l$ is pseudoconvex also in the coordinates of $\mathcal B_{jl}$, since a biholomorphism transports a continuous plurisubharmonic exhaustion function (proposition 8.2.3 ). To compare the kernels at a point $x\in \overline{U'_ j}\cap \overline{U'_ l}$, we correct $\rho f$, for $f$ holomorphic on $B_ j$, to a holomorphic function on $B_ l$ with the same value at $x$. Let $f$ be holomorphic on $B_ j$ with norm at most one in the weighted space, and extend $\rho f$ by zero to a smooth function on $B_ l$. We apply theorem 11.3.4 on $B_ l$ to the smooth $\bar\partial $-closed form $f\bar\partial \rho $, with the plurisubharmonic function $p=mu+n\log |z-x|^2$ and the smooth function $q=|z|^2$, whose complex Hessian matrix is the identity. On the support of $\bar\partial \rho $ we have $|z-x|^{-2n}\leq r^{-2n}$, so \[  \int _{B_ l}|f\bar\partial \rho |^2\mathrm e^{-p-q}\, \mathrm dV\leq r^{-2n}\sup |\bar\partial \rho |^2\int _{B_ j}|f|^2\mathrm e^{-mu}\, \mathrm dV\leq \frac{\sup |\bar\partial \rho |^2}{cr^{2n}}.  \] Hence there is a solution of $\bar\partial w=f\bar\partial \rho $ on $B_ l$ with \[  \int _{B_ l}|w|^2|z-x|^{-2n}\mathrm e^{-mu-|z|^2}\, \mathrm dV\leq C=\frac{\sup |\bar\partial \rho |^2}{cr^{2n}},  \] and $C$ depends only on the fixed geometry. The function $|z-x|^{2n}\mathrm e^{|z|^2}$ is bounded on the bounded set $B_ l$ by a constant of the same kind, and the density of $\omega ^ n/n!$ is at most $C''$. Hence the squared weighted norm of $w$, for the weight $mu$ and the volume form $\omega ^ n/n!$, is at most a constant $C'$ depending only on the fixed geometry. Near $x$ we have $\bar\partial w=f\bar\partial \rho =0$, because $\rho =1$ there; hence $\Delta w=0$ near $x$, and by theorem 2.1.4 $w$ is smooth, hence holomorphic, near $x$. Suppose that $w(x)\neq 0$. Then $|w|^2\geq |w(x)|^2/4$ on a ball $B(x,\delta )$ on which $u\leq M$ for some constant $M$, since $u$ is upper semicontinuous, and the last integral is at least \[  \frac{|w(x)|^2}4\, \mathrm e^{-mM-\sup _{B_ l}|z|^2}\int _{B(x,\delta )}|z-x|^{-2n}\, \mathrm dV=\infty ,  \] because $\int _{B(x,\delta )}|z-x|^{-2n}\, \mathrm dV=s_{2n-1}\int _0^\delta t^{-1}\, \mathrm dt$ in polar coordinates ( 2.1 ). Hence $w(x)=0$. The function $F=\rho f-w$ satisfies $\bar\partial F=0$ on $B_ l$, so it is holomorphic by theorem 2.1.4 , and $F(x)=f(x)$. Since $0\leq \rho \leq 1$ and $\rho $ vanishes outside $B_ j$, the weighted norm of $F$ on $B_ l$ is at most $1+C'^{1/2}=C_0$. By the definition of the kernel, $|f(x)|^2=|F(x)|^2\leq C_0^2K^{mu}_{B_ l}(x)$, and taking the supremum over $f$ gives $K^{mu}_{B_ j}(x)\leq C_0^2K^{mu}_{B_ l}(x)$. No bound on $u$, $\theta $ or $m$ enters these constants. Taking $C_ B$ to be the maximum of $2\log C_0$ over the finitely many pairs $(j,l)$, with the roles of $j$ and $l$ also exchanged, proves the lemma. $\square$

title: Quantitative lower bound regularization
text: Theorem 13.3.3 . There is a constant $c>0$, depending only on $(X,\omega )$ through the fixed geometry, with the following property. Let $\theta $ be a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form on $X$, let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, and let $m\geq 1$ be an integer. Then there is a quasi-plurisubharmonic function $\varphi _ m$ on $X$ such that \[  \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ m\geq -\frac cm\omega , \qquad \varphi _ m\geq \frac1m\log \sum _ i|g_ i|^2+O(1)\quad \text{locally},  \] where the $g_ i$ are local generators of $\mathcal I(m\varphi )$. The bounded term may depend on $m$, $\theta $, $\varphi $ and the point. Proof. By lemma 13.3.2 , the functions $v_{j,m}\in \mathrm{PSH}(B_ j,\theta )$ satisfy $v_{j,m}\leq v_{l,m}+C_ B/m$ on $\overline{U'_ j}\cap \overline{U'_ l}$, also at their common zeros. Hence lemma 13.3.1 with $a=C_ B/m$ gives a quasi-plurisubharmonic function $\varphi _ m$ with $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ m\geq -(C_ BC_\chi /m)\omega $, so the first conclusion holds with $c=C_ BC_\chi $, increased if necessary to make it positive. On $U_ j$ the function $\varphi _ m$ dominates $v_{j,m}=m^{-1}\log K_{j,m}-h_ j$. Since $h_ j$ is smooth, $\mathcal I(m(\varphi +h_ j))=\mathcal I(m\varphi )$, and the comparison of lemma 13.2.2 gives $v_{j,m}\geq m^{-1}\log \sum _ i|g_ i|^2+O(1)$ near each point of $U_ j$. This proves the second conclusion. $\square$

title: Smooth cutoff sums and decreasing approximation
text:
13.4 Smooth cutoff sums and decreasing approximation The maximum in theorem 13.3.3 destroys smoothness, and that theorem does not compare the functions $\varphi _ m$ for different values of $m$. To obtain the regularity required of gentle singularities and, later, a decreasing sequence, we glue the local kernels instead by a sum with smooth cutoffs and control the curvature of its logarithm by a direct computation. We keep the notation of the previous section. Lemma 13.4.1 . Let $	heta $ be a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form on $X$, let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$, let $m\geq 1$ be an integer, and put \[  R_ m=\sum _ j\chi _ j^2a_{j,m},\qquad G_ m=m^{-1}\log R_ m,  \] each summand being extended by zero outside the support of $\chi _ j$. There is a constant $c'>0$, depending only on the fixed geometry, such that $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}G_ m\geq -(c'/m)\omega $. Moreover $R_ m$ is smooth on $X$, and $G_ m$ has gentle analytic singularities of type $(m^{-1},\mathcal I(m\varphi ))$. Let $W$ be an open subset of a complex manifold, let $N\geq 1$, and let $w_1,\ldots ,w_ N$ and $\chi _1,\ldots ,\chi _ N$ be smooth real functions on $W$ such that $S=\sum _{j=1}^ N\chi _ j^2\mathrm e^{w_ j}$ is positive on $W$. Put $\alpha _ j=\chi _ j\partial w_ j+2\partial \chi _ j$. Then, on $W$, 13.5  egin{equation} \label{eq:cutoff-sum-hessian}  egin{aligned}  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log S={}&  rac{\mathrm i}{2\pi S^2} \sum _{j<l}\mathrm e^{w_ j+w_ l} (\chi _ j\alpha _ l-\chi _ l\alpha _ j) \wedge \overline{(\chi _ j\alpha _ l-\chi _ l\alpha _ j)}\ & + rac{\sum _ j\chi _ j^2\mathrm e^{w_ j}\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ j}{S} +2 rac{\sum _ j\mathrm e^{w_ j}  igl (\chi _ j\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi _ j- rac{\mathrm i}{2\pi } \partial \chi _ j\wedge  ar\partial \chi _ j igr )}{S}, \end{aligned} \end{equation} and the first term on the right of ( 13.5 ) is a semipositive $(1,1)$-form. Proof. Step 1: proof of (2). Let $w_ j$, $\chi _ j$, $S$ and $\alpha _ j$ be as in (2), and put $f_ j=\chi _ j^2\mathrm e^{w_ j}$, so that $S=\sum _ jf_ j$. Then $\partial f_ j=\chi _ j\mathrm e^{w_ j}(\chi _ j\partial w_ j+2\partial \chi _ j)=\chi _ j\mathrm e^{w_ j}\alpha _ j$, so that $\partial S=\sum _ j\chi _ j\mathrm e^{w_ j}\alpha _ j$. Since $\chi _ j$ and $w_ j$ are real, $ ar\partial f_ j=\overline{\partial f_ j}=\chi _ j\mathrm e^{w_ j} ar\alpha _ j$ with $ ar\alpha _ j=\chi _ j ar\partial w_ j+2 ar\partial \chi _ j$, and \[   egin{aligned}  \partial  ar\partial f_ j& =\partial (\chi _ j\mathrm e^{w_ j})\wedge  ar\alpha _ j+\chi _ j\mathrm e^{w_ j}\, \partial  ar\alpha _ j\ & =\mathrm e^{w_ j} igl ((\partial \chi _ j+\chi _ j\partial w_ j)\wedge (\chi _ j ar\partial w_ j+2 ar\partial \chi _ j)\ & \qquad +\chi _ j\partial \chi _ j\wedge  ar\partial w_ j+\chi _ j^2\partial  ar\partial w_ j+2\chi _ j\partial  ar\partial \chi _ j igr )\ & =\mathrm e^{w_ j} igl (\alpha _ j\wedge  ar\alpha _ j+\chi _ j^2\partial  ar\partial w_ j+2\chi _ j\partial  ar\partial \chi _ j-2\partial \chi _ j\wedge  ar\partial \chi _ j igr ), \end{aligned}  \] where the last line follows by expanding $\alpha _ j\wedge  ar\alpha _ j=\chi _ j^2\partial w_ j\wedge  ar\partial w_ j+2\chi _ j\partial w_ j\wedge  ar\partial \chi _ j+2\chi _ j\partial \chi _ j\wedge  ar\partial w_ j+4\partial \chi _ j\wedge  ar\partial \chi _ j$. Next, $\partial  ar\partial \log S=\partial  ar\partial S/S-\partial S\wedge  ar\partial S/S^2$, and since $\sum _ l\chi _ l^2\mathrm e^{w_ l}=S$, \[  \sum _ j rac{\mathrm e^{w_ j}\alpha _ j\wedge  ar\alpha _ j}S- rac{\partial S\wedge  ar\partial S}{S^2} = rac1{S^2}\sum _{j,l}\mathrm e^{w_ j+w_ l} igl (\chi _ l^2\, \alpha _ j\wedge  ar\alpha _ j-\chi _ j\chi _ l\, \alpha _ j\wedge  ar\alpha _ l igr ).  \] In the last sum the terms with $j=l$ vanish, and for $j<l$ the terms with indices $(j,l)$ and $(l,j)$ add up to $\mathrm e^{w_ j+w_ l}(\chi _ j\alpha _ l-\chi _ l\alpha _ j)\wedge \overline{(\chi _ j\alpha _ l-\chi _ l\alpha _ j)}$. Multiplying by $\mathrm i/2\pi $ and using $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}= rac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }\partial  ar\partial $, we obtain ( 13.5 ). The first term on the right of ( 13.5 ) is semipositive, because the coefficients $\mathrm e^{w_ j+w_ l}/(2\pi S^2)$ are positive and, for a $(1,0)$-form $\gamma =\sum _ k\gamma _ k\, \mathrm dz_ k$, the coefficient matrix $(\gamma _ k ar\gamma _{k'})$ of $\mathrm i\gamma \wedge  ar\gamma $ is positive semidefinite. We now prove (1) in three steps. Step 2: a curvature estimate. By lemma 13.1.1 , applied on the compact manifold $X$ to the finitely many smooth forms below, there is a constant $A>0$, depending only on the fixed geometry, such that $\chi _ j\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi _ j- rac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }\partial \chi _ j\wedge  ar\partial \chi _ j\geq -A\omega $ for every $j$. Let $W\subset X$ be open, and for the indices $j$ with $W\cap \operatorname{Supp}\chi _ j
eq \varnothing $ let $w_ j$ be smooth real functions on $W$ such that \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ j\geq -m	heta \quad 	ext{on }W,\qquad \mathrm e^{w_ j}\leq \mathrm e^{C_ B}\mathrm e^{w_ i}\quad 	ext{on }W\cap U_ i\cap \operatorname{Supp}\chi _ j  \] for all such $i,j$. We claim that $S=\sum _ j\chi _ j^2\mathrm e^{w_ j}$ is positive on $W$ and that \[  	heta + rac1m\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log S\geq - rac{2JA\mathrm e^{C_ B}}m\omega \qquad 	ext{on }W.  \] Let $x\in W$ and choose $i$ with $x\in U_ i$. Then $\chi _ i(x)=1$, so $S(x)\geq \mathrm e^{w_ i(x)}>0$, and $\mathrm e^{w_ j}/S\leq \mathrm e^{C_ B}$ at $x$ for every $j$ with $\chi _ j(x)
eq 0$. Since $S>0$ on $W$, the identity ( 13.5 ) of (2) holds on $W$. If $\chi _ j(x)=0$, the $j$th summand of the last term in ( 13.5 ) vanishes at $x$, because the nonnegative function $\chi _ j$ attains its minimum at $x$, so that $\partial \chi _ j(x)=0$. Hence the last term is at least $-2JA\mathrm e^{C_ B}\omega $ at $x$. The coefficients $\chi _ j^2\mathrm e^{w_ j}/S$ are nonnegative with sum one, so the middle term is at least $-m	heta $, and the first term is semipositive. This proves the claim. Step 3: $G_ m$ is quasi-plurisubharmonic and satisfies the curvature bound. Since the kernels $a_{j,m}$ may vanish, we apply Step 2 to smooth approximations of $\log a_{j,m}$ and pass to the limit. Fix $x_0\in X$ and a small coordinate ball $W$ about $x_0$ such that $W\subset U'_ j$ whenever $x_0\in \operatorname{Supp}\chi _ j$, and $W\cap \operatorname{Supp}\chi _ j=\varnothing $ otherwise; then the indices $j$ with $W\cap \operatorname{Supp}\chi _ j
eq \varnothing $ are those with $x_0\in \operatorname{Supp}\chi _ j$. text: 13.5 \begin{equation} \label{eq:cutoff-sum-hessian} \begin{aligned}  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log S={}& \frac{\mathrm i}{2\pi S^2} \sum _{j<l}\mathrm e^{w_ j+w_ l} (\chi _ j\alpha _ l-\chi _ l\alpha _ j) \wedge \overline{(\chi _ j\alpha _ l-\chi _ l\alpha _ j)}\\ & +\frac{\sum _ j\chi _ j^2\mathrm e^{w_ j}\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ j}{S} +2\frac{\sum _ j\mathrm e^{w_ j} \bigl (\chi _ j\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi _ j-\frac{\mathrm i}{2\pi } \partial \chi _ j\wedge \bar\partial \chi _ j\bigr )}{S}, \end{aligned} \end{equation}

title: Integrable gap ideal transfer
text: Lemma 13.4.3 . Let $u,v$ be quasi-plurisubharmonic near a point $x$ of a complex manifold, and let $m>0$ be such that $\mathrm e^{m(v-u)}$ is integrable near $x$. If $0<\lambda <\lambda '$ and $m\geq \lambda \lambda '/(\lambda '-\lambda )$, then \[  \mathcal I(\lambda 'v)_ x\subseteq \mathcal I(\lambda u)_ x.  \] Proof. After shrinking the neighborhood we may subtract a constant from $v$ and assume $v\leq 0$; this changes neither the ideals nor the integrability of $\mathrm e^{m(v-u)}$. Put $p=\lambda '/\lambda >1$, and note that $m\geq \lambda p/(p-1)>\lambda $. Let $f\in \mathcal I(\lambda 'v)_ x$, defined on a small neighborhood on which $|f|^2\leq C$ for a constant $C$. All the following inequalities are taken outside the pole sets of $u$ and $v$, which have measure zero. Where $u\geq pv$, we have $\lambda u\geq \lambda 'v$ and hence $|f|^2\mathrm e^{-\lambda u}\leq |f|^2\mathrm e^{-\lambda 'v}$. Where $u<pv$, since $m-\lambda >0$, $v\leq 0$ and $(m-\lambda )p-m=m(p-1)-\lambda p\geq 0$, \[  (m-\lambda )u-mv\leq ((m-\lambda )p-m)v\leq 0,  \] that is, $-\lambda u\leq m(v-u)$; hence $|f|^2\mathrm e^{-\lambda u}\leq C\mathrm e^{m(v-u)}$. Both bounds are integrable near $x$, so $f\in \mathcal I(\lambda u)_ x$. $\square$

title: Quasi equisingular approximation
text: Definition 13.4.4 . Let $\theta $ be a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form on $X$ and $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. A quasi-equisingular approximation of $\varphi $ is a sequence $(\Phi _ j)_{j\geq 1}$ of quasi-plurisubharmonic functions with analytic singularities, decreasing pointwise to $\varphi $, such that $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Phi _ j\geq -\varepsilon _ j\omega $ for some numbers $\varepsilon _ j\downarrow 0$, and such that for all $0<\lambda <\lambda '$ \[  \mathcal I(\lambda '\Phi _ j)\subseteq \mathcal I(\lambda \varphi ) \quad \text{for every sufficiently large }j.  \]

title: Gentle quasi equisingular approximation
text: Theorem 13.4.5 . Let $\theta $ be a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form on $X$. Every $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ admits a quasi-equisingular approximation $(\Phi _ j)$ in which each $\Phi _ j$ has gentle analytic singularities of type $(2^{-j},\mathcal I(2^ j\varphi ))$, and which can be chosen with $\varepsilon _ j=c'2^{-j}$, where $c'$ is the constant of lemma 13.4.1 (1). Moreover $\Phi _ j\to \varphi $ in $L^1(X)$, and the Lelong numbers of $\Phi _ j$ satisfy the bounds of lemma 13.4.2 with $m=2^ j$. Proof. Put $\Phi _ j=G_{2^ j}+2D/2^ j$, with $D$ as in lemma 13.4.2 . The doubling inequality gives \[  \Phi _{j+1}=G_{2\cdot 2^ j}+\frac D{2^ j}\leq G_{2^ j}+\frac D{2^ j}+\frac D{2^ j}=\Phi _ j,  \] so the sequence is decreasing, and by lemma 13.4.2 its pointwise and $L^1$ limit is $\varphi $. Adding a constant changes neither the curvature, nor the analytic type, nor the Lelong numbers. Moreover $\exp (2^ j\Phi _ j)=\mathrm e^{2D}R_{2^ j}$ is smooth, and the remainder on a log resolution changes only by a constant. Hence $\Phi _ j$ has gentle analytic singularities of type $(2^{-j},\mathcal I(2^ j\varphi ))$ by lemma 13.4.1 (1), and $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Phi _ j\geq -c'2^{-j}\omega $. It remains to prove the inclusions of multiplier ideals. Let $0<\lambda <\lambda '$. The function $\exp (2^ j(\Phi _ j-\varphi ))=\mathrm e^{2D}\mathrm e^{2^ j(G_{2^ j}-\varphi )}$ is integrable on $X$ by lemma 13.4.2 . If $j$ is so large that $2^ j\geq \lambda \lambda '/(\lambda '-\lambda )$, then lemma 13.4.3 , with $u=\varphi $, $v=\Phi _ j$ and $m=2^ j$, gives $\mathcal I(\lambda '\Phi _ j)_ x\subseteq \mathcal I(\lambda \varphi )_ x$ at every point $x\in X$. Since this threshold for $j$ depends only on $\lambda $ and $\lambda '$, the inclusion holds as an inclusion of sheaves on $X$ for all such $j$. $\square$

title: Comparison of analytic singularities
text: 13.5 Comparison of analytic singularities For functions $u,v\colon X\to [-\infty ,\infty )$ we write $u\preceq v$, and say that $u$ is more singular than $v$, if $u\leq v+C$ on $X$ for some constant $C$. Since $X$ is compact, it suffices that every point have a neighborhood on which such an inequality holds. We now show that two quasi-equisingular approximations of the same function are comparable for $\preceq $, up to an arbitrarily small loss in the coefficient. The key is a growth estimate for the members of the multiplier ideals of a function with analytic singularities. Lemma 13.5.1 . Let $v$ be a quasi-plurisubharmonic function with analytic singularities on a compact complex manifold $X$, and let $0<\eta <1$. There is $t_0>0$ such that for every real $t\geq t_0$ and every germ $f\in \mathcal I(tv)_ x$, $x\in X$, \[  \log |f|^2\leq t(1-\eta )v+O(1)  \] near $x$, where the bounded term may depend on $f$. Moreover, for every quasi-plurisubharmonic function $u$ and every $t>0$, local generators $g_ i$ of $\mathcal I(tu)$ satisfy \[  u\leq t^{-1}\log \sum _ i|g_ i|^2+O(1).  \] Proof. For the first assertion we pull $v$ back to log resolutions of its local presentations, where theorem 12.6.5 bounds the vanishing orders of $f$ along the components of the divisor from below. Cover $X$ by finitely many open sets $V_\kappa ^+$ on which $v$ has a presentation ( 13.1 ), and choose open sets $V_\kappa \Subset V_\kappa ^+$ that still cover $X$. By theorem A.5.5 , the ideal generated by the presentation on $V_\kappa ^+$ has a log resolution $\pi _\kappa \colon Y_\kappa \to V_\kappa ^+$, a sequence of blowups that is finite over $V_\kappa $; it is proper and surjective, so $\pi _\kappa ^{-1}(\overline{V_\kappa })$ and the fibers of $\pi _\kappa $ are compact. On $Y_\kappa $ we have locally $v\circ \pi _\kappa =\sum _ Ea_ E\log |s_ E|^2+O(1)$, where $\pi _\kappa ^*(g_1,\ldots ,g_ r)=\mathcal O(-\sum _ Ed_ EE)$, $E$ runs over the components of this divisor, $s_ E$ is a local equation of $E$, and $a_ E=cd_ E>0$. Let $A_ E$ be the log discrepancy of $E$ (definition 12.6.3 ). Only finitely many components $E$ meet the compact set $\pi _\kappa ^{-1}(\overline{V_\kappa })$, so altogether there are finitely many pairs $(a_ E,A_ E)$ with $E$ meeting one of these sets. Choose $t_0>0$ with $t_0\eta a_ E\geq A_ E$ for all of them. Now let $x\in V_\kappa $, let $t\geq t_0$, and let $f\in \mathcal I(tv)_ x$ be defined on an open neighborhood $V'\subset V_\kappa $ of $x$. Near $x$ the function $tv$ differs by a smooth function from a plurisubharmonic function with the same multiplier ideal and of the form required in theorem 12.6.5 , with coefficient $tc$. We apply that theorem over $V'$, shrunk if necessary, to the log resolution obtained by restricting $\pi _\kappa $. Each component $E'$ of the restricted divisor is a connected component of $E\cap \pi _\kappa ^{-1}(V')$ for a component $E$ as above, and it has the same coefficient $d_ E$ and the same log discrepancy $A_ E$, as we show below. Since $tc\, d_ E=ta_ E$, the theorem gives \[  \operatorname {ord}_{E'}f>ta_ E-A_ E\geq t(1-\eta )a_ E  \] for every component $E'$ of the restricted divisor that meets $\pi _\kappa ^{-1}(x)$; the second inequality holds because $t\geq t_0$ and $E$ meets $\pi _\kappa ^{-1}(\overline{V_\kappa })$. The coefficient and the log discrepancy of $E'$ are those of $E$ because the vanishing orders along $E$ of a local generator of $\pi _\kappa ^*(g_1,\ldots ,g_ r)$ and of a local Jacobian determinant of $\pi _\kappa $ do not depend on the point of $E$ at which they are computed. Indeed, two local generators of this invertible ideal, like two local Jacobian determinants, differ by a unit, which has order zero along $E$; since orders add under products, they have the same order along $E$ at every point of $E$ where both are defined (lemma 12.6.1 (2),(4)). Moreover, the order along $E$ of a holomorphic function is locally constant on $E_{\mathrm{reg}}$, by the last assertion of lemma 12.6.1 (2), and $E_{\mathrm{reg}}$ is connected (corollary A.2.13 ); here $E_{\mathrm{reg}}=E$, since the components of a simple normal crossings divisor are smooth. If $f=0$ there is nothing to prove, so let $f\neq 0$. Shrinking $V'$, we may assume that $V'$ is connected; then $f$ does not vanish identically on any nonempty open subset of $V'$. Hence $f\circ \pi _\kappa $ does not vanish identically on any nonempty open subset of $\pi _\kappa ^{-1}(V')$, because $\pi _\kappa $ is a biholomorphism off the nowhere dense set $\pi _\kappa ^{-1}(V(g_1,\ldots ,g_ r))$; in particular, the orders of $f$ along the components of the restricted divisor are finite. Let $p\in \pi _\kappa ^{-1}(x)$, and choose coordinates $w$ on a neighborhood of $p$ in $\pi _\kappa ^{-1}(V')$ in which the components of the divisor through $p$ are $\{ w_ k=0\} $, $k=1,\ldots ,\ell $, with coefficients $a_ k=a_ E$ for the corresponding components $E$. Then $v\circ \pi _\kappa =\sum _ ka_ k\log |w_ k|^2+O(1)$ near $p$. For each $k$, let $E'_ k$ be the component of the restricted divisor that contains $\{ w_ k=0\} $ near $p$, and put $o_ k=\operatorname {ord}_{E'_ k}f$, an integer with $o_ k>t(1-\eta )a_ k$ by the inequality above. Since $f\circ \pi _\kappa $ is holomorphic on a neighborhood of $E'_ k$, its order along $E'_ k$ is the same at all points of the connected submanifold $E'_ k$, by lemma 12.6.1 (3); hence $f\circ \pi _\kappa $ is divisible by $w_ k^{o_ k}$ near $p$, by lemma 12.6.1 (1),(2). By the last assertion of lemma 12.6.2 , divisibility by each $w_ k^{o_ k}$ separately implies divisibility by their product: $f\circ \pi _\kappa =\prod _ kw_ k^{o_ k}\cdot h$ with $h$ holomorphic near $p$, hence bounded on a smaller neighborhood of $p$. Since $|w_ k|\leq 1$ there, we obtain $|f\circ \pi _\kappa |^2\leq C\prod _ k|w_ k|^{2t(1-\eta )a_ k}\leq C'\exp (t(1-\eta )v\circ \pi _\kappa )$. Finitely many such neighborhoods cover the compact fiber $\pi _\kappa ^{-1}(x)$, and since $\pi _\kappa $ is proper, their union contains the inverse image of a neighborhood of $x$. As $\pi _\kappa $ is surjective, the inequality $|f|^2\leq C'\exp (t(1-\eta )v)$ holds near $x$. For the second assertion, fix a point and write $u=u_0-\sigma $ near it, with $u_0$ plurisubharmonic and $\sigma $ smooth. Then $\mathcal I(tu)=\mathcal I(tu_0)$ near the point. On a bounded polydisc $\Omega $ about the point on which $u_0$ is bounded above, theorem 12.2.7 (3) provides finitely many elements of $\mathcal H_{tu_0}(\Omega )$ that generate $\mathcal I(tu_0)$ near the point, and ( 12.11 ) of lemma 12.2.8 , applied with $m=t$ to the weight $u_0$, gives $u_0\leq t^{-1}\log \sum _ i|g_ i|^2+O(1)$ for these generators. Since $\sigma $ is bounded near the point, and any two finite systems of local generators give comparable sums of squares (the remark following definition 13.1.5 ), the assertion follows. $\square$ Proposition 13.5.2 . Let $X$ be a compact complex manifold, let $\varphi $ and $\Phi $ be quasi-plurisubharmonic functions on $X$ with $\varphi \leq \Phi $, where $\Phi $ has analytic singularities, and let $(\Psi _ k)_{k\geq 1}$ be quasi-plurisubharmonic functions on $X$ such that for all $0<\lambda <\lambda '$ \[  \mathcal I(\lambda '\Psi _ k)\subseteq \mathcal I(\lambda \varphi ) \quad \text{for every sufficiently large }k.  \] Then for each $0<\varepsilon <1$, \[  \Psi _ k\preceq (1-\varepsilon )\Phi \quad \text{for every sufficiently large }k.  \] In particular, if $(X,\omega )$ is a compact Kähler manifold, $\theta $ is a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form on $X$, $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, and $(\Phi _ j)$ and $(\Psi _ k)$ are quasi-equisingular approximations of $\varphi $, then for each $j$ and each $0<\varepsilon <1$ we have $\Psi _ k\preceq (1-\varepsilon )\Phi _ j$ for every sufficiently large $k$. Proof. Choose $0<\eta <\varepsilon $ and $\delta >0$ so small that $(1-\eta )/(1+\delta )\geq 1-\varepsilon $. Fix $t\geq t_0$, where $t_0$ is given by lemma 13.5.1 for $v=\Phi $ and $\eta $. By the hypothesis on $(\Psi _ k)$, applied with $\lambda =t$ and $\lambda '=t(1+\delta )$, and since $\varphi \leq \Phi $, \[  \mathcal I(t(1+\delta )\Psi _ k) \subseteq \mathcal I(t\varphi )\subseteq \mathcal I(t\Phi )  \] for every sufficiently large $k$. Fix such a $k$ and choose local generators $g_ i$ of $\mathcal I(t(1+\delta )\Psi _ k)$ near a point of $X$. They belong to $\mathcal I(t\Phi )$, so the first part of lemma 13.5.1 gives $\log |g_ i|^2\leq t(1-\eta )\Phi +O(1)$ near the point, and hence $\log \sum _ i|g_ i|^2\leq t(1-\eta )\Phi +O(1)$. Its second part, applied to $u=\Psi _ k$ and $t(1+\delta )$, then gives \[  \Psi _ k\leq \frac1{t(1+\delta )}\log \sum _ i|g_ i|^2+O(1) \leq \frac{1-\eta }{1+\delta }\Phi +O(1).  \] The upper semicontinuous function $\Phi $ is bounded above on the compact space $X$, say by $M$. Since $\Phi -M\leq 0$ and $(1-\eta )/(1+\delta )\geq 1-\varepsilon $, we have $\frac{1-\eta }{1+\delta }(\Phi -M)\leq (1-\varepsilon )(\Phi -M)$, and therefore $\Psi _ k\leq (1-\varepsilon )\Phi +O(1)$ near every point. By compactness $\Psi _ k\preceq (1-\varepsilon )\Phi $; the constant may depend on $k$. For the last assertion, recall from definition 13.4.4 that each $\Phi _ j$ is quasi-plurisubharmonic with analytic singularities and that $\varphi \leq \Phi _ j$, since the sequence decreases to $\varphi $; and $(\Psi _ k)$ satisfies the hypothesis on the inclusions of multiplier ideals. Hence the first part applies with $\Phi =\Phi _ j$. $\square$ Example 13.5.3 . Let $u=c\log |z|^2$ on a disc about $0\in \mathbb C$, with $c>0$. A germ $z^ kh$ with $h(0)\neq 0$ lies in $\mathcal I(mu)_0$ if and only if $|z|^{2k-2mc}$ is integrable near $0$, that is, $k>mc-1$; hence $\mathcal I(mu)$ is generated by $z^{\lfloor mc\rfloor }$ (example 12.5.5 ). A potential of type $(m^{-1},\mathcal I(mu))$, such as the Bergman potential $u_ m$ of theorem 13.2.3 , is therefore $(\lfloor mc\rfloor /m)\log |z|^2+O(1)$ near $0$. Its coefficient $\lfloor mc\rfloor /m$ need not equal $c$ for any $m$, and then such an approximation does not reproduce the multiplier ideals of $u$ at a fixed scale. For instance, let $c$ be irrational, so that $\lfloor mc\rfloor /m<c$ for every $m$, and take the scale $1/c$. Since $u_ m/c$ differs by a bounded function from $c_ m\log |z|^2$ with $c_ m=\lfloor mc\rfloor /(mc)<1$, the same computation gives $\mathcal I(u_ m/c)_0=\mathcal O_0$ for every $m$, whereas $\mathcal I(u/c)_0=\mathcal I(\log |z|^2)_0$ is generated by $z$. This is why definition 13.4.4 compares two different scales $\lambda '>\lambda $ instead of requiring equality of multiplier ideals.

title: Analytic weighted integrability growth
text: Lemma 13.5.1 . Let $v$ be a quasi-plurisubharmonic function with analytic singularities on a compact complex manifold $X$, and let $0<\eta <1$. There is $t_0>0$ such that for every real $t\geq t_0$ and every germ $f\in \mathcal I(tv)_ x$, $x\in X$, \[  \log |f|^2\leq t(1-\eta )v+O(1)  \] near $x$, where the bounded term may depend on $f$. Moreover, for every quasi-plurisubharmonic function $u$ and every $t>0$, local generators $g_ i$ of $\mathcal I(tu)$ satisfy \[  u\leq t^{-1}\log \sum _ i|g_ i|^2+O(1).  \] Proof. For the first assertion we pull $v$ back to log resolutions of its local presentations, where theorem 12.6.5 bounds the vanishing orders of $f$ along the components of the divisor from below. Cover $X$ by finitely many open sets $V_\kappa ^+$ on which $v$ has a presentation ( 13.1 ), and choose open sets $V_\kappa \Subset V_\kappa ^+$ that still cover $X$. By theorem A.5.5 , the ideal generated by the presentation on $V_\kappa ^+$ has a log resolution $\pi _\kappa \colon Y_\kappa \to V_\kappa ^+$, a sequence of blowups that is finite over $V_\kappa $; it is proper and surjective, so $\pi _\kappa ^{-1}(\overline{V_\kappa })$ and the fibers of $\pi _\kappa $ are compact. On $Y_\kappa $ we have locally $v\circ \pi _\kappa =\sum _ Ea_ E\log |s_ E|^2+O(1)$, where $\pi _\kappa ^*(g_1,\ldots ,g_ r)=\mathcal O(-\sum _ Ed_ EE)$, $E$ runs over the components of this divisor, $s_ E$ is a local equation of $E$, and $a_ E=cd_ E>0$. Let $A_ E$ be the log discrepancy of $E$ (definition 12.6.3 ). Only finitely many components $E$ meet the compact set $\pi _\kappa ^{-1}(\overline{V_\kappa })$, so altogether there are finitely many pairs $(a_ E,A_ E)$ with $E$ meeting one of these sets. Choose $t_0>0$ with $t_0\eta a_ E\geq A_ E$ for all of them. Now let $x\in V_\kappa $, let $t\geq t_0$, and let $f\in \mathcal I(tv)_ x$ be defined on an open neighborhood $V'\subset V_\kappa $ of $x$. Near $x$ the function $tv$ differs by a smooth function from a plurisubharmonic function with the same multiplier ideal and of the form required in theorem 12.6.5 , with coefficient $tc$. We apply that theorem over $V'$, shrunk if necessary, to the log resolution obtained by restricting $\pi _\kappa $. Each component $E'$ of the restricted divisor is a connected component of $E\cap \pi _\kappa ^{-1}(V')$ for a component $E$ as above, and it has the same coefficient $d_ E$ and the same log discrepancy $A_ E$, as we show below. Since $tc\, d_ E=ta_ E$, the theorem gives \[  \operatorname {ord}_{E'}f>ta_ E-A_ E\geq t(1-\eta )a_ E  \] for every component $E'$ of the restricted divisor that meets $\pi _\kappa ^{-1}(x)$; the second inequality holds because $t\geq t_0$ and $E$ meets $\pi _\kappa ^{-1}(\overline{V_\kappa })$. The coefficient and the log discrepancy of $E'$ are those of $E$ because the vanishing orders along $E$ of a local generator of $\pi _\kappa ^*(g_1,\ldots ,g_ r)$ and of a local Jacobian determinant of $\pi _\kappa $ do not depend on the point of $E$ at which they are computed. Indeed, two local generators of this invertible ideal, like two local Jacobian determinants, differ by a unit, which has order zero along $E$; since orders add under products, they have the same order along $E$ at every point of $E$ where both are defined (lemma 12.6.1 (2),(4)). Moreover, the order along $E$ of a holomorphic function is locally constant on $E_{\mathrm{reg}}$, by the last assertion of lemma 12.6.1 (2), and $E_{\mathrm{reg}}$ is connected (corollary A.2.13 ); here $E_{\mathrm{reg}}=E$, since the components of a simple normal crossings divisor are smooth. If $f=0$ there is nothing to prove, so let $f\neq 0$. Shrinking $V'$, we may assume that $V'$ is connected; then $f$ does not vanish identically on any nonempty open subset of $V'$. Hence $f\circ \pi _\kappa $ does not vanish identically on any nonempty open subset of $\pi _\kappa ^{-1}(V')$, because $\pi _\kappa $ is a biholomorphism off the nowhere dense set $\pi _\kappa ^{-1}(V(g_1,\ldots ,g_ r))$; in particular, the orders of $f$ along the components of the restricted divisor are finite. Let $p\in \pi _\kappa ^{-1}(x)$, and choose coordinates $w$ on a neighborhood of $p$ in $\pi _\kappa ^{-1}(V')$ in which the components of the divisor through $p$ are $\{ w_ k=0\} $, $k=1,\ldots ,\ell $, with coefficients $a_ k=a_ E$ for the corresponding components $E$. Then $v\circ \pi _\kappa =\sum _ ka_ k\log |w_ k|^2+O(1)$ near $p$. For each $k$, let $E'_ k$ be the component of the restricted divisor that contains $\{ w_ k=0\} $ near $p$, and put $o_ k=\operatorname {ord}_{E'_ k}f$, an integer with $o_ k>t(1-\eta )a_ k$ by the inequality above. Since $f\circ \pi _\kappa $ is holomorphic on a neighborhood of $E'_ k$, its order along $E'_ k$ is the same at all points of the connected submanifold $E'_ k$, by lemma 12.6.1 (3); hence $f\circ \pi _\kappa $ is divisible by $w_ k^{o_ k}$ near $p$, by lemma 12.6.1 (1),(2). By the last assertion of lemma 12.6.2 , divisibility by each $w_ k^{o_ k}$ separately implies divisibility by their product: $f\circ \pi _\kappa =\prod _ kw_ k^{o_ k}\cdot h$ with $h$ holomorphic near $p$, hence bounded on a smaller neighborhood of $p$. Since $|w_ k|\leq 1$ there, we obtain $|f\circ \pi _\kappa |^2\leq C\prod _ k|w_ k|^{2t(1-\eta )a_ k}\leq C'\exp (t(1-\eta )v\circ \pi _\kappa )$. Finitely many such neighborhoods cover the compact fiber $\pi _\kappa ^{-1}(x)$, and since $\pi _\kappa $ is proper, their union contains the inverse image of a neighborhood of $x$. As $\pi _\kappa $ is surjective, the inequality $|f|^2\leq C'\exp (t(1-\eta )v)$ holds near $x$. For the second assertion, fix a point and write $u=u_0-\sigma $ near it, with $u_0$ plurisubharmonic and $\sigma $ smooth. Then $\mathcal I(tu)=\mathcal I(tu_0)$ near the point. On a bounded polydisc $\Omega $ about the point on which $u_0$ is bounded above, theorem 12.2.7 (3) provides finitely many elements of $\mathcal H_{tu_0}(\Omega )$ that generate $\mathcal I(tu_0)$ near the point, and ( 12.11 ) of lemma 12.2.8 , applied with $m=t$ to the weight $u_0$, gives $u_0\leq t^{-1}\log \sum _ i|g_ i|^2+O(1)$ for these generators. Since $\sigma $ is bounded near the point, and any two finite systems of local generators give comparable sums of squares (the remark following definition 13.1.5 ), the assertion follows. $\square$

title: Quasi equisingular comparison
text: Proposition 13.5.2 . Let $X$ be a compact complex manifold, let $\varphi $ and $\Phi $ be quasi-plurisubharmonic functions on $X$ with $\varphi \leq \Phi $, where $\Phi $ has analytic singularities, and let $(\Psi _ k)_{k\geq 1}$ be quasi-plurisubharmonic functions on $X$ such that for all $0<\lambda <\lambda '$ \[  \mathcal I(\lambda '\Psi _ k)\subseteq \mathcal I(\lambda \varphi ) \quad \text{for every sufficiently large }k.  \] Then for each $0<\varepsilon <1$, \[  \Psi _ k\preceq (1-\varepsilon )\Phi \quad \text{for every sufficiently large }k.  \] In particular, if $(X,\omega )$ is a compact Kähler manifold, $\theta $ is a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form on $X$, $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, and $(\Phi _ j)$ and $(\Psi _ k)$ are quasi-equisingular approximations of $\varphi $, then for each $j$ and each $0<\varepsilon <1$ we have $\Psi _ k\preceq (1-\varepsilon )\Phi _ j$ for every sufficiently large $k$. Proof. Choose $0<\eta <\varepsilon $ and $\delta >0$ so small that $(1-\eta )/(1+\delta )\geq 1-\varepsilon $. Fix $t\geq t_0$, where $t_0$ is given by lemma 13.5.1 for $v=\Phi $ and $\eta $. By the hypothesis on $(\Psi _ k)$, applied with $\lambda =t$ and $\lambda '=t(1+\delta )$, and since $\varphi \leq \Phi $, \[  \mathcal I(t(1+\delta )\Psi _ k) \subseteq \mathcal I(t\varphi )\subseteq \mathcal I(t\Phi )  \] for every sufficiently large $k$. Fix such a $k$ and choose local generators $g_ i$ of $\mathcal I(t(1+\delta )\Psi _ k)$ near a point of $X$. They belong to $\mathcal I(t\Phi )$, so the first part of lemma 13.5.1 gives $\log |g_ i|^2\leq t(1-\eta )\Phi +O(1)$ near the point, and hence $\log \sum _ i|g_ i|^2\leq t(1-\eta )\Phi +O(1)$. Its second part, applied to $u=\Psi _ k$ and $t(1+\delta )$, then gives \[  \Psi _ k\leq \frac1{t(1+\delta )}\log \sum _ i|g_ i|^2+O(1) \leq \frac{1-\eta }{1+\delta }\Phi +O(1).  \] The upper semicontinuous function $\Phi $ is bounded above on the compact space $X$, say by $M$. Since $\Phi -M\leq 0$ and $(1-\eta )/(1+\delta )\geq 1-\varepsilon $, we have $\frac{1-\eta }{1+\delta }(\Phi -M)\leq (1-\varepsilon )(\Phi -M)$, and therefore $\Psi _ k\leq (1-\varepsilon )\Phi +O(1)$ near every point. By compactness $\Psi _ k\preceq (1-\varepsilon )\Phi $; the constant may depend on $k$. For the last assertion, recall from definition 13.4.4 that each $\Phi _ j$ is quasi-plurisubharmonic with analytic singularities and that $\varphi \leq \Phi _ j$, since the sequence decreases to $\varphi $; and $(\Psi _ k)$ satisfies the hypothesis on the inclusions of multiplier ideals. Hence the first part applies with $\Phi =\Phi _ j$. $\square$

title: Analytic regularization endpoints
text: Example 13.5.3 . Let $u=c\log |z|^2$ on a disc about $0\in \mathbb C$, with $c>0$. A germ $z^ kh$ with $h(0)\neq 0$ lies in $\mathcal I(mu)_0$ if and only if $|z|^{2k-2mc}$ is integrable near $0$, that is, $k>mc-1$; hence $\mathcal I(mu)$ is generated by $z^{\lfloor mc\rfloor }$ (example 12.5.5 ). A potential of type $(m^{-1},\mathcal I(mu))$, such as the Bergman potential $u_ m$ of theorem 13.2.3 , is therefore $(\lfloor mc\rfloor /m)\log |z|^2+O(1)$ near $0$. Its coefficient $\lfloor mc\rfloor /m$ need not equal $c$ for any $m$, and then such an approximation does not reproduce the multiplier ideals of $u$ at a fixed scale. For instance, let $c$ be irrational, so that $\lfloor mc\rfloor /m<c$ for every $m$, and take the scale $1/c$. Since $u_ m/c$ differs by a bounded function from $c_ m\log |z|^2$ with $c_ m=\lfloor mc\rfloor /(mc)<1$, the same computation gives $\mathcal I(u_ m/c)_0=\mathcal O_0$ for every $m$, whereas $\mathcal I(u/c)_0=\mathcal I(\log |z|^2)_0$ is generated by $z$. This is why definition 13.4.4 compares two different scales $\lambda '>\lambda $ instead of requiring equality of multiplier ideals.

title: Bounded growth ideals

13.6 Bounded growth ideals A germ $f$ belongs to the multiplier ideal $\mathcal I(v)$ when $|f|^2\mathrm e^{-v}$ is integrable, a condition that allows $f$ to vanish to a slightly lower order than the growth of $\mathrm e^ v$ suggests. The stricter condition $|f|^2\leq C\mathrm e^ v$ defines a smaller ideal. For a weight $v$ with analytic singularities we prove that this ideal sheaf is coherent (theorem 13.6.2 ) and that, on a compact manifold, the ideal attached to $kv$ contains $\mathcal I(k(1+\varepsilon )v)$ for all large $k$ (corollary 13.6.3 ). In the proof of coherence, the condition $|f|\leq C|g|^{p/q}$ for a tuple $g$ of holomorphic functions becomes a holomorphic one: on the normalization of a root cover of a cone over the blowup of the ideal $(g)$, it is the holomorphy of a function homogeneous of weight $p$. Definition 13.6.1 . Let $v$ be a quasi-plurisubharmonic function on a complex manifold $X$. The bounded growth ideal $\mathcal I_\infty (v)$ is the sheaf of holomorphic germs $f$ satisfying \[  \log |f|^2\leq v+O(1), \quad 	ext{equivalently}\quad |f|^2\leq C\exp (v),  \] on a neighborhood of their base point, for some finite constant $C$. The zero germ belongs to $\mathcal I_\infty (v)$, and $\mathcal I_\infty (v)$ does not change if $v$ is changed by a bounded function. It is a sheaf of ideals, because $|f+g|^2\leq 2|f|^2+2|g|^2$ and holomorphic coefficients are locally bounded. It is contained in $\mathcal I(v)$, since $|f|^2\mathrm e^{-v}$ is locally bounded for $f\in \mathcal I_\infty (v)$. Theorem 13.6.2 . Let $v$ be a quasi-plurisubharmonic function with analytic singularities on a complex manifold $X$. Then $\mathcal I_\infty (v)$ is a coherent ideal sheaf. title: Analytic bounded growth ideal
text: Definition 13.6.1 . Let $v$ be a quasi-plurisubharmonic function on a complex manifold $X$. The bounded growth ideal $\mathcal I_\infty (v)$ is the sheaf of holomorphic germs $f$ satisfying \[  \log |f|^2\leq v+O(1), \quad \text{equivalently}\quad |f|^2\leq C\exp (v),  \] on a neighborhood of their base point, for some finite constant $C$.

Theorem 13.6.2 . Let $v$ be a quasi-plurisubharmonic function with analytic singularities on a complex manifold $X$. Then $\mathcal I_\infty (v)$ is a coherent ideal sheaf. Fix $x\in U$ and shrink $U$ to a connected neighborhood of $x$. If all $g_ j$ vanish identically there, then $\mathcal J_{p/q}(g)$ is the zero ideal near $x$. Conversely, let $f$ be a germ of $\mathcal J_{p/q}(g)$ at a point $x'$ with $|x'-x|<\varepsilon /2$, say $|f|\leq C_ f|g|^{p/q}$ on $\{ |z-x'|<ho \} $, and let $0<\varepsilon _1\leq \min (ho ,\varepsilon /2)$. On the part of $
u ^{-1}(W_{\varepsilon _1}(x'))$ in the dense open family, the function $f(z)t^ p$ satisfies \[  |f(z)t^ p|\leq C_ f|t^ qg(z)|^{p/q}=C_ f|a|^{p/q}.  \] It is therefore bounded, and since $Y$ is normal it extends holomorphically to $
u ^{-1}(W_{\varepsilon _1}(x'))$ by lemma A.3.4 ; the extension $h$ is homogeneous of weight $p$. By Step 5, after shrinking $\varepsilon _1$, $h$ is a combination of the functions $a^\alpha P_ es_ j$ with coefficients $k_{j,\alpha }(z)$ holomorphic near $x'$. Comparing the coefficients of $t^ p$ on the dense open family gives $f=\sum k_{j,\alpha }f_{j,\alpha }$ on $U_ i$ near $x'$, hence near $x'$, since both sides are continuous and $U_ i$ is dense. Thus the functions $f_{j,\alpha }$ generate $\mathcal J_{p/q}(g)$ on $\{ |z-x|<\varepsilon /2\} $, and $\mathcal J_{p/q}(g)$ is coherent by theorem A.1.5 , lemma A.1.4 . Finally, if $v=(p/q)\log \sum _ j|g_ j|^2+O(1)$ is a local presentation of $v$, then $\mathcal I_\infty (v)=\mathcal J_{p/q}(g)$ on its domain. Since coherence is a local property, $\mathcal I_\infty (v)$ is coherent. (If $g(x)
eq 0$, both ideals are the unit ideal near $x$; in dimension zero every finite weight gives the unit ideal.) $\square$

title: Analytic integrability bounded growth
text: Corollary 13.6.3 . Let $v$ be a quasi-plurisubharmonic function with analytic singularities on a compact complex manifold $X$. For every $\varepsilon >0$ there is $k_0>0$ such that for every real $k\geq k_0$ \[  \mathcal I(k(1+\varepsilon )v)\subseteq \mathcal I_\infty (kv).  \] Proof. Apply lemma 13.5.1 with $\eta =\varepsilon /(1+\varepsilon )$ and $t=k(1+\varepsilon )$, so that $t(1-\eta )=k$. The lemma provides one threshold $t_0$ for all germs on $X$; put $k_0=t_0/(1+\varepsilon )$. For $k\geq k_0$, every germ $f\in \mathcal I(k(1+\varepsilon )v)$ satisfies $\log |f|^2\leq kv+O(1)$ near its base point, that is, $f\in \mathcal I_\infty (kv)$. In dimension zero all these ideals are the unit ideal. $\square$

title: Global potentials and positive cohomology classes
topic: Global potentials and positive cohomology classes
text: 14 Global potentials and positive cohomology classes Let $X$ be a connected compact Kähler manifold, and let $T$ be a closed positive $(1,1)$-current on $X$. By theorem 7.3.2 , every point of $X$ has a coordinate neighborhood on which $T=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ with $u$ plurisubharmonic. On the overlap of two such neighborhoods the two local potentials differ by a pluriharmonic function, and in general no choice of the local potentials makes them agree. For instance, let $X$ have positive dimension and let $T=\omega $ be a Kähler form. A global potential $u$ would be plurisubharmonic on $X$, so it would attain its maximum, being upper semicontinuous on the compact space $X$. The set where it does so is closed, and it is also open by the maximum principle (proposition 3.1.4 ), applied on coordinate balls, where $u$ is subharmonic (theorem 8.2.1 ). Thus $u$ would be constant and $\omega =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=0$. The obstruction is the cohomology class of $T$: by the $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-lemma (theorem 14.1.7 ), if $\theta $ is a smooth closed form in the class of $T$, then $T=\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $ for a quasi-plurisubharmonic function $\varphi $ on $X$, unique up to an additive constant. We prove this by solving a Laplace equation for the trace of $T$, after developing the elliptic theory that this requires from the beginning; the same argument shows that the real $(1,1)$-cohomology of $X$ is finite dimensional. Closed positive currents in the class of $\theta $ therefore correspond, up to additive constants, to the functions in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ (definition 13.1.3 ), and the rest of the book works with such potentials. Once the additive constant is fixed by normalizing the supremum, the local compactness and integrability theorems for plurisubharmonic functions become uniform statements on $X$, and the upper envelope $V_\theta $ of the nonpositive potentials has minimal singularities. With these tools and the Demailly approximation of chapter 13 we study the positivity of a class (pseudo-effective, nef, big or Kähler) and the places where it fails. Siu's decomposition (theorem 14.3.7 ) splits off the divisorial part of a current. The minimal multiplicities of a class and its non-nef locus locate the points at which the positive currents in the class are forced to be singular, and the non-Kähler locus does the same for Kähler currents; we also compare these notions on $X$ and on a modification of $X$. A mixed version of the scalar equation gives the mixed Hodge index theorem (theorem 14.3.3 ) and inequalities between intersection numbers. The second half of the chapter concerns a holomorphic line bundle $L$ on $X$. If $h_0$ is a smooth metric on $L$ with curvature form $c_1(L,h_0)$, a singular metric $h_0\mathrm e^{-\varphi }$ with $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,c_1(L,h_0))$ is the global form of a plurisubharmonic weight; the metrics defined by finitely many holomorphic sections of powers of $L$ are examples with analytic singularities. We prove the $L^2$ estimate for $\bar\partial $ on line bundles over Kähler manifolds and combine it with the local extension theorems of chapter 11 to construct global sections with a prescribed value at a point (theorem 14.6.7 ) or a prescribed restriction to a compact submanifold (theorem 14.7.8 ), with constants that depend only on the geometry. We also describe the weighted spaces of global sections through their Bergman kernels. A related gluing construction extends strictly positive potentials from a submanifold (theorem 14.7.12 ). In the last section we leave the Kähler setting and prove Josefson's theorem on a compact complex manifold: every pluripolar set lies in the pole set of a single quasi-plurisubharmonic function (theorem 14.8.7 ). Historical remarks and references for this chapter are collected in section B.14 .

title: The trace equation and global potentials
topic: Global potentials and positive cohomology classes
text: 14.1 The trace equation and global potentials Throughout this chapter, except in section 14.8 , $(X,\omega )$ is a connected compact Kähler manifold of dimension $n\geq 1$. (In dimension zero all the notions below are trivial: $H^{1,1}(X,\mathbb R)$ and all positivity cones are $\{ 0\} $, both positivity loci are empty and normalized potentials vanish. On a disconnected compact Kähler manifold the results apply to each of its finitely many components, with normalizations imposed on each component.) The goal of this section is the $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-lemma (theorem 14.1.7 ). We first develop the Sobolev spaces of $X$ and the elliptic theory of its Laplacians (lemma 14.1.3 ), and then express the trace of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$ through the Laplacian of $f$ (lemma 14.1.6 ). Let $J$ be the complex structure of $X$. The Kähler form defines the Riemannian metric $g(v,w)=\omega (v,Jw)$ and the volume form $\mathrm dV=\omega ^ n/n!$. Forms carry the pointwise inner product induced by $g$, and the $L^2$ inner product $\langle u,v\rangle =\int _ X\langle u,v\rangle \, \mathrm dV$. The Hodge star operator is the complex-linear bundle map characterized by $u\wedge *\overline v=\langle u,v\rangle \, \mathrm dV$ for forms $u,v$ of the same degree. Explicitly, if $e_1,\ldots ,e_{2n}$ is a positively oriented orthonormal basis of the real cotangent space at a point and $I'$ denotes the increasing multi-index complementary to $I$, then $*e_ I=\varepsilon _ Ie_{I'}$, where $e_ I\wedge e_{I'}=\varepsilon _ Ie_1\wedge \cdots \wedge e_{2n}$ and $\varepsilon _ I=\pm 1$; indeed $e_ I\wedge \varepsilon _ Je_{J'}$ is $\delta _{IJ}$ times the volume form. Hence $*$ is a real isometry, and since $e_{I'}\wedge e_ I=(-1)^{k(2n-k)}e_ I\wedge e_{I'}$ for $|I|=k$, we have $**=(-1)^{k(2n-k)}=(-1)^ k$ on $k$-forms, the real dimension $2n$ being even. Now let $u$ be a $(k-1)$-form and $v$ a $k$-form, one of them with compact support. Since $\mathrm d*\overline v$ has degree $2n-k+1$, on which $**=(-1)^{k-1}$, we have $u\wedge \mathrm d*\overline v=(-1)^{k-1}u\wedge *\overline{(*\mathrm d*v)}=(-1)^{k-1}\langle u,*\mathrm d*v\rangle \, \mathrm dV$. Integrating $\mathrm d(u\wedge *\overline v)=\mathrm du\wedge *\overline v+(-1)^{k-1}u\wedge \mathrm d*\overline v$ by Stokes' formula (proposition 7.1.3 ), we obtain $\int _ X\langle \mathrm du,v\rangle \, \mathrm dV=-\int _ X\langle u,*\mathrm d*v\rangle \, \mathrm dV$. Thus the formal adjoint of $\mathrm d$ is $\mathrm d^*=-*\mathrm d*$. More generally, a linear differential operator $P$ on forms with smooth coefficients has a formal adjoint $P^*$, a differential operator of the same kind characterized by $\langle P\alpha ,\phi \rangle =\langle \alpha ,P^*\phi \rangle $ for smooth forms $\alpha ,\phi $; in a chart it is obtained by integrating by parts, and the local expressions agree on overlaps by this characterization. A distributional $k$-form is a current of degree $k$ (section 7.2 ). It is paired with smooth $k$-forms $\phi $ by $\langle u,\phi \rangle =u(*\overline\phi )$, which equals $\int _ X\langle u,\phi \rangle \, \mathrm dV$ when $u$ is a locally integrable form. For a scalar distribution $f$ and a smooth function $\chi $ the pairing reads $\langle f,\chi \rangle =f(\overline\chi \, \mathrm dV)$, and we say that $f$ has mean zero if $\langle f,1\rangle =0$. We let $P$ act on distributional forms by $\langle Pu,\phi \rangle =\langle u,P^*\phi \rangle $. For $P=\mathrm d$ this is the exterior derivative of currents, by the formula for $\mathrm d^*$; for $*$, for the exterior product with a smooth form and for its pointwise adjoint, it is the action on the distribution coefficients in local frames. Since $(PQ)^*=Q^*P^*$, and since an operator is determined by its formal adjoint, every identity between such operators that holds on smooth forms also holds on distributional forms. On functions we use the Laplace–Beltrami operator $L=\mathrm d^*\mathrm d$. For the Euclidean metric on $\mathbb R^{2n}$ we have $L=-\sum _ j\partial ^2/\partial x_ j^2$, so $L$ is the negative of the Laplacian $\Delta $ of Part I ; we use this sign convention throughout the chapter because it makes $L$ a nonnegative operator: $\int _ XfLf\, \mathrm dV=\int _ X|\mathrm df|^2\, \mathrm dV$ for smooth real $f$. On forms we use the Hodge Laplacian $\mathcal L=\mathrm d\mathrm d^*+\mathrm d^*\mathrm d$, and a form or current $u$ is harmonic if $\mathcal Lu=0$. For smooth $u$, $\langle \mathcal Lu,u\rangle =\| \mathrm du\| ^2+\| \mathrm d^*u\| ^2$, so $u$ is harmonic if and only if $\mathrm du=0$ and $\mathrm d^*u=0$. On functions $\mathcal L=L$, so for the Euclidean metric this notion of harmonic function agrees with that of section 2.1 ; on the compact connected manifold $X$, however, the only solutions of $Lf=0$ are the constants (lemma 14.1.3 ), and the harmonic objects of interest here are forms. We use the following Sobolev spaces. Choose a finite cover of $X$ by coordinate charts, frames of the bundle of differential forms over them, and smooth functions $\chi _ k\geq 0$ with compact supports in the charts and $\sum _ k\chi _ k=1$ (proposition 7.1.3 ). Using the frames, $\chi _ ku$ is a vector-valued function on $\mathbb R^{2n}$ for every form $u$. For an integer $r\geq 0$, let $H^ r$ be the completion of the space of smooth forms for the norm whose square is \[  \sum _ k\int _{\mathbb R^{2n}}(1+|\xi |^2)^ r |\widehat{\chi _ k u}(\xi )|^2\, \mathrm d\xi ,  \] and let $H^{-r}$ be the space of distributional forms $u$ for which $\phi \mapsto \langle u,\phi \rangle $ is bounded on smooth forms for the norm of $H^ r$, with the norm of this functional. By lemma 14.1.1 below, these spaces do not depend on the choices made or on $\omega $. The same notation is used for functions. Lemma 14.1.1 . Let $r,l\geq 0$ be integers. For a $\mathbb C^ N$-valued function $v$ on an open set $W\subset \mathbb R^{2n}$ whose distributional derivatives of order at most $r$ are square integrable, put $\| v\| _{(r),W}^2=\sum _{|\alpha |\leq r}\| \partial ^\alpha v\| _{L^2(W)}^2$, and $\| v\| _{(r)}=\| v\| _{(r),\mathbb R^{2n}}$. For a form $u$ of class $C^ l$, let $\| u\| _{C^ l}$ be the maximum over $k$ of the suprema on $\operatorname{Supp}\chi _ k$ of the derivatives of order at most $l$ of the coefficients of $u$ in the $k$th chart and frame. On smooth forms, the norm of $H^ r$ is equivalent to the norm $\bigl (\sum _ k\| \chi _ ku\| _{(r)}^2\bigr )^{1/2}$, and other choices of the charts, frames and cutoff functions give equivalent norms. Multiplication by a smooth function, or by a smooth endomorphism of the bundle of forms, is bounded for the norm of $H^ r$, and $\| \phi \| _{H^ r}\leq C\| \phi \| _{C^ r}$ for smooth forms $\phi $. The norm of $H^ r$ dominates a multiple of the $L^2$ norm, and the continuous extension to $H^ r$ of the identity map of smooth forms is an injective map into the space of $L^2$ forms; we regard $H^ r$ as a subspace of the $L^2$ forms. An $L^2$ form $u$ belongs to $H^ r$ if and only if, for every $k$, the distributional derivatives of order at most $r$ of $\chi _ ku$ are square integrable, and then $\bigl (\sum _ k\| \chi _ ku\| _{(r)}^2\bigr )^{1/2}$ is equivalent to $\| u\| _{H^ r}$. In particular, $H^0$ is the space of all $L^2$ forms, with an equivalent norm, and the subspace $H^ r$, with its norm up to equivalence, does not depend on the choices of the charts, frames and cutoffs. Moreover $H^{r'}\subset H^ r$ for $r\leq r'$, and if $W$ is an open set whose closure is a compact subset of a chart with a frame, then the coefficient vector of every $u\in H^ r$ on $W$ satisfies $\| u\| _{(r),W}\leq C_ W\| u\| _{H^ r}$. Let $r>l+n$. Every $u\in H^ r$ agrees almost everywhere with a form of class $C^ l$, and for this form $\| u\| _{C^ l}\leq C\| u\| _{H^ r}$. Likewise, a compactly supported $\mathbb C^ N$-valued function $v$ on $\mathbb R^{2n}$ with $\| v\| _{(r)}<\infty $ agrees almost everywhere with a function of class $C^ l$ whose derivatives of order at most $l$ are bounded by $C\| v\| _{(r)}$. Consequently, a form that lies in every $H^ r$ is smooth. For $u\in H^{-r}$ the functional $\phi \mapsto \langle u,\phi \rangle $ extends uniquely to a bounded conjugate-linear functional on $H^ r$, with norm $\| u\| _{H^{-r}}$, and every bounded conjugate-linear functional on $H^ r$ arises in this way from a unique $u\in H^{-r}$; thus $H^{-r}$ is the dual space of $H^ r$. Multiplication by smooth functions and endomorphisms is bounded on $H^{-r}$, and $H^{-r}\subset H^{-r'}$ for $r\leq r'$. The space $H^{-r}$, with its norm up to equivalence, depends neither on the choices of the charts, frames and cutoffs nor on the Kähler form $\omega $ that defines the pairing; neither does $H^ r$. Every distributional form belongs to $H^{-r}$ for some $r$. Proof. In this proof, the constants $C$ depend on $r$, $l$ and the data indicated, but not on the forms or functions involved. We first compare the coefficient vectors of a form in two charts, and then prove (1)–(5) in turn. (a) A change of charts. Let $\kappa \colon U\to \mathbb R^{2n}$ and $\kappa '\colon U'\to \mathbb R^{2n}$ be charts of $X$ with frames of the bundle of forms over $U$ and $U'$, let $K\subset U$ be compact, and let $W\subset U'$ be an open set whose closure is a compact subset of $U'$. For a smooth form $w$ that vanishes outside $K$, let $w_\kappa $ and $w_{\kappa '}$ be its coefficient vectors in the two charts and frames, the first one extended by zero to $\mathbb R^{2n}$. We claim that 14.1 \begin{equation} \label{eq:sobolev-chart-change} \| w_{\kappa '}\| _{(r),\kappa '(W)}\leq C\| w_\kappa \| _{(r)}, \end{equation} with $C$ depending on the charts, frames, $K$ and $W$. Indeed, on $\kappa '(U\cap U')$ we have $w_{\kappa '}(y)=A(y)\, w_\kappa (\tau (y))$, where $\tau =\kappa \circ \kappa '^{-1}$ and $A$ is the smooth matrix of the change of frames. By the chain rule, the Leibniz rule and induction on $|\alpha |$, \[  \partial ^\alpha w_{\kappa '}(y)=\sum _{|\beta |\leq |\alpha |}c_{\alpha \beta }(y)\, (\partial ^\beta w_\kappa )(\tau (y)),\qquad y\in \kappa '(U\cap U'),  \] where the matrices $c_{\alpha \beta }$ are polynomials in the derivatives of order at most $|\alpha |$ of $A$ and of $\tau $; they are smooth on $\kappa '(U\cap U')$ and therefore bounded on its compact subset $\kappa '(\overline W\cap K)$. Since $w$ vanishes on the open set $X\setminus K$, all derivatives of $w_{\kappa '}$ vanish on $\kappa '(W\setminus K)$, and every point of $\kappa '(W)$ lies in this set or in $\kappa '(W\cap K)$. Hence, for $|\alpha |\leq r$, \[  \begin{aligned}  \int _{\kappa '(W)}|\partial ^\alpha w_{\kappa '}|^2\, \mathrm dy & \leq C\sum _{|\beta |\leq r}\int _{\kappa '(W\cap K)}|(\partial ^\beta w_\kappa )(\tau (y))|^2\, \mathrm dy\\ & \leq C\sum _{|\beta |\leq r}\int _{\mathbb R^{2n}}|\partial ^\beta w_\kappa (x)|^2\, \mathrm dx, \end{aligned}  \] by the change of variables $x=\tau (y)$, whose Jacobian determinant $|\det D\tau ^{-1}|$ is bounded on the compact set $\kappa (\overline W\cap K)$. This proves ( 14.1 ). We also use the Leibniz rule in the following form. If $M$ is a smooth matrix-valued function on an open set $V\subset \mathbb R^{2n}$ whose derivatives of order at most $r$ are bounded on $V$, then $\| Mv\| _{(r),V}\leq C\| v\| _{(r),V}$ for smooth $v$ on $V$, with $C$ depending on these bounds. If $v$ vanishes outside a compact set $L\subset V$, it suffices that $M$ be smooth on $V$, the bounds being taken on $L$, and then $\| Mv\| _{(r)}\leq C\| v\| _{(r)}$ for the extensions by zero. (b) Proof of (1). For a test function $v$ on $\mathbb R^{2n}$ we have $\widehat{\partial ^\beta v}(\xi )=(2\pi \mathrm i\xi )^\beta \widehat v(\xi )$, and $(1+|\xi |^2)^ r=\sum _{|\beta |\leq r}c_\beta |\xi ^\beta |^2$ with positive multinomial coefficients $c_\beta $. Hence Plancherel's theorem (theorem 6.1.2 ) gives 14.4 \begin{equation} \label{eq:sobolev-fourier-derivatives} \int _{\mathbb R^{2n}}(1+|\xi |^2)^ r|\widehat v(\xi )|^2\, \mathrm d\xi =\sum _{|\beta |\leq r}c_\beta (2\pi )^{-2|\beta |}\| \partial ^\beta v\| _{L^2}^2, \end{equation} and the norm of $H^ r$ is equivalent on smooth forms to $\bigl (\sum _ k\| \chi _ ku\| _{(r)}^2\bigr )^{1/2}$. Let charts with domains $U'_ m$, frames over them, and cutoffs $\chi '_ m$ with $\sum _ m\chi '_ m=1$ be other choices, and choose open sets $W_ m$ with $\operatorname{Supp}\chi '_ m\subset W_ m$ and $\overline{W_ m}$ compact in $U'_ m$. For a smooth form $u$ we have $\chi '_ mu=\sum _ k\chi '_ m\chi _ ku$, and the form $\chi '_ m\chi _ ku$ vanishes outside the compact set $\operatorname{Supp}\chi _ k$ and outside $\operatorname{Supp}\chi '_ m\subset W_ m$. By ( 14.1 ), with $K=\operatorname{Supp}\chi _ k$ and $W=W_ m$, its norm $\| \cdot \| _{(r)}$ in the $m$th new chart is at most $C$ times its norm in the $k$th old chart, and by the Leibniz rule, applied to the factor $\chi '_ m$ on the compact set $\kappa _ k(\operatorname{Supp}\chi _ k)$, where $\kappa _ k$ is the $k$th chart, the latter is at most $C\| \chi _ ku\| _{(r)}$. Summing over $k$ and $m$, we see that the new norm is bounded by a constant times the old one, and by symmetry the two norms are equivalent. If $M$ is a smooth function or endomorphism, then $\chi _ kMu=M\chi _ ku$ vanishes outside $\operatorname{Supp}\chi _ k$, so the Leibniz rule gives $\| \chi _ kMu\| _{(r)}\leq C\| \chi _ ku\| _{(r)}$. Finally, $\| \chi _ k\phi \| _{(r)}$ is bounded, by the Leibniz rule and since $\kappa _ k(\operatorname{Supp}\chi _ k)$ has finite measure, by a constant times the suprema on $\operatorname{Supp}\chi _ k$ of the derivatives of order at most $r$ of the coefficients of $\phi $; hence $\| \phi \| _{H^ r}\leq C\| \phi \| _{C^ r}$. (c) Proof of (2). For a smooth form $u$ we have $|u|\leq \sum _ k|\chi _ ku|$ pointwise, since $\chi _ k\geq 0$ and $\sum _ k\chi _ k=1$. On the compact sets $\operatorname{Supp}\chi _ k$ the pointwise norm of forms is comparable with the Euclidean norm of the coefficient vectors, and $\mathrm dV$ with Lebesgue measure in the charts; hence $\| u\| _{L^2}\leq C\sum _ k\| \chi _ ku\| _{(0)}\leq C\| u\| _{H^ r}$, and conversely $\| \chi _ ku\| _{(0)}\leq C\| u\| _{L^2}$ because $0\leq \chi _ k\leq 1$. Therefore the identity map of smooth forms extends to a bounded map $j$ from $H^ r$ to the space of $L^2$ forms. Let $u\in H^ r$ be the limit in $H^ r$ of smooth forms $u_ i$. By (1), for every $k$ and $|\alpha |\leq r$ the functions $\partial ^\alpha (\chi _ ku_ i)$ form a Cauchy sequence in $L^2(\mathbb R^{2n})$, with a limit $g_{k,\alpha }$, while $\chi _ ku_ i\to \chi _ kj(u)$ in $L^2$. For every test function $\phi $ on $\mathbb R^{2n}$, \[  \begin{aligned}  \int g_{k,\alpha }\phi \, \mathrm dx& =\lim _ i\int \partial ^\alpha (\chi _ ku_ i)\phi \, \mathrm dx=\lim _ i(-1)^{|\alpha |}\int \chi _ ku_ i\, \partial ^\alpha \phi \, \mathrm dx\\ & =(-1)^{|\alpha |}\int \chi _ kj(u)\, \partial ^\alpha \phi \, \mathrm dx, \end{aligned}  \] so $g_{k,\alpha }$ is the distributional derivative $\partial ^\alpha (\chi _ kj(u))$. Hence these derivatives are square integrable, and $\sum _ k\| \chi _ kj(u)\| _{(r)}^2=\lim _ i\sum _ k\| \chi _ ku_ i\| _{(r)}^2$, which by (1) lies between two positive multiples of $\lim _ i\| u_ i\| _{H^ r}^2=\| u\| _{H^ r}^2$. In particular, $j(u)=0$ implies $u=0$, so $j$ is injective, and we identify $u$ with $j(u)$. This proves the first assertion, the necessity of the condition and the equivalence of the norms. Conversely, let $u$ be an $L^2$ form such that every $\chi _ ku$ has square integrable distributional derivatives of order at most $r$, and let $\rho _\varepsilon $ be the mollifier of section 1.4 . Since $\chi _ ku$ vanishes outside the compact set $\kappa _ k(\operatorname{Supp}\chi _ k)$, the functions $v_{k,\varepsilon }=\rho _\varepsilon *(\chi _ ku)$ are smooth and, for small $\varepsilon $, vanish outside a fixed compact subset $L_ k$ of $\kappa _ k(U_ k)$, where $U_ k$ is the domain of the $k$th chart; moreover $\partial ^\alpha v_{k,\varepsilon }=\rho _\varepsilon *\partial ^\alpha (\chi _ ku)$ by proposition 1.4.3 , and this converges to $\partial ^\alpha (\chi _ ku)$ in $L^2$ as $\varepsilon \to 0$, by lemma 1.4.1 , for $|\alpha |\leq r$. Let $w_{k,\varepsilon }$ be the smooth form on $X$ whose coefficient vector in the $k$th chart and frame is $v_{k,\varepsilon }$, extended by zero outside $U_ k$, and put $u_\varepsilon =\sum _ kw_{k,\varepsilon }$. Choose open sets $W_ m$ with $\operatorname{Supp}\chi _ m\subset W_ m$ and $\overline{W_ m}$ compact in $U_ m$. By ( 14.1 ), with $K=\kappa _ k^{-1}(L_ k)$ and $W=W_ m$, and by the Leibniz rule for the factor $\chi _ m$, we have $\| \chi _ m(w_{k,\varepsilon }-w_{k,\varepsilon '})\| _{(r)}\leq C\| v_{k,\varepsilon }-v_{k,\varepsilon '}\| _{(r)}$. By (1), $(u_\varepsilon )$ is therefore a Cauchy sequence in $H^ r$ as $\varepsilon \to 0$ along a sequence, and it converges in $L^2$ to $\sum _ k\chi _ ku=u$, by the comparison of pointwise norms on the compact sets $\kappa _ k^{-1}(L_ k)\cup \operatorname{Supp}\chi _ k\subset U_ k$. Hence $u\in H^ r$. For $r=0$ the condition holds for every $L^2$ form, so $H^0$ is the space of all $L^2$ forms, and its norm is equivalent to the $L^2$ norm by the first paragraph. Other choices of the charts, frames and cutoffs give, by (1), equivalent norms on smooth forms, hence the same Cauchy sequences and the same limits in $L^2$; so they give the same subspace $H^ r$ with an equivalent norm. If $r\leq r'$, then $\| \phi \| _{H^ r}\leq \| \phi \| _{H^{r'}}$ for smooth $\phi $, so every Cauchy sequence in $H^{r'}$ is a Cauchy sequence in $H^ r$ with the same limit in $L^2$; hence $H^{r'}\subset H^ r$. Finally, let $W$ be open with closure compact in a chart with a frame. For smooth $u$, we have $u=\sum _ m\chi _ mu$, and ( 14.1 ), applied to $w=\chi _ mu$ with $K=\operatorname{Supp}\chi _ m$, gives $\| u\| _{(r),W}\leq C\sum _ m\| \chi _ mu\| _{(r)}\leq C\| u\| _{H^ r}$. If $u\in H^ r$ is the limit in $H^ r$ of smooth forms $u_ i$, the coefficient vectors of the $u_ i$ on $W$ form a Cauchy sequence for $\| \cdot \| _{(r),W}$ and converge in $L^2(W)$ to that of $u$. Testing against test functions on $W$ as above, we find that their derivatives of order at most $r$ converge in $L^2(W)$ to those of the coefficient vector of $u$, and the bound passes to the limit. (d) Proof of (3). Let first $v$ be a smooth $\mathbb C^ N$-valued function with compact support, and let $|\alpha |\leq l$. The inversion formula of theorem 6.1.2 , applied to $\partial ^\alpha v$, whose Fourier transform is $(2\pi \mathrm i\xi )^\alpha \widehat v$, and the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality give \[  \begin{aligned}  \sup |\partial ^\alpha v|& \leq \int _{\mathbb R^{2n}}|2\pi \xi |^{|\alpha |}|\widehat v(\xi )|\, \mathrm d\xi \\ & \leq (2\pi )^ l\Bigl (\int _{\mathbb R^{2n}}(1+|\xi |^2)^{l-r}\, \mathrm d\xi \Bigr )^{1/2}\Bigl (\int _{\mathbb R^{2n}}(1+|\xi |^2)^ r|\widehat v(\xi )|^2\, \mathrm d\xi \Bigr )^{1/2}, \end{aligned}  \] where the first integral on the right is finite, by polar coordinates, because $2(r-l)>2n$. By ( 14.4 ), $\sup |\partial ^\alpha v|\leq C\| v\| _{(r)}$. If $v$ is only compactly supported with $\| v\| _{(r)}<\infty $, then, as in (c), the mollifications $v_\varepsilon =\rho _\varepsilon *v$ are smooth with compact support and $\| v_\varepsilon -v\| _{(r)}\to 0$ as $\varepsilon \to 0$. Along a sequence $\varepsilon _ i\to 0$, the estimate shows that the derivatives of order at most $l$ of the $v_{\varepsilon _ i}$ converge uniformly; hence the $v_{\varepsilon _ i}$ converge uniformly to a function of class $C^ l$ whose derivatives of order at most $l$ are bounded by $C\| v\| _{(r)}$. This function agrees with $v$ almost everywhere, since $v_{\varepsilon _ i}\to v$ in $L^2$ and a subsequence converges almost everywhere. Now let $u$ be a smooth form. On $\operatorname{Supp}\chi _ k$, the coefficient vector of $u$ in the $k$th chart and frame is the sum over $m$ of the coefficient vectors of the forms $\chi _ mu$. We apply the formula for $\partial ^\alpha w_{\kappa '}$ in (a) with $\kappa $ the $m$th chart, $\kappa '$ the $k$th chart and $K=\operatorname{Supp}\chi _ m$. The derivatives of the coefficient vector of $\chi _ mu$ in the $k$th chart vanish outside $\kappa _ k(\operatorname{Supp}\chi _ m)$, and the coefficients $c_{\alpha \beta }$ are bounded on the compact set $\kappa _ k(\operatorname{Supp}\chi _ k\cap \operatorname{Supp}\chi _ m)$. Hence the derivatives of order at most $l$ of this coefficient vector are bounded on $\kappa _ k(\operatorname{Supp}\chi _ k)$ by $C$ times the suprema of the derivatives of order at most $l$ of the coefficient vector of $\chi _ mu$ in the $m$th chart, and the Euclidean estimate and (1) give $\| u\| _{C^ l}\leq C\sum _ m\| \chi _ mu\| _{(r)}\leq C\| u\| _{H^ r}$. If $u\in H^ r$ is the limit in $H^ r$ of smooth forms $u_ i$, then $\| u_ i-u_{i'}\| _{C^ l}\leq C\| u_ i-u_{i'}\| _{H^ r}$, so in every chart the coefficients of the $u_ i$ and their derivatives of order at most $l$ converge uniformly on $\operatorname{Supp}\chi _ k$, and hence on the open sets $\{ \chi _ k>0\} $, which cover $X$. The limit is a form of class $C^ l$ with $\| \cdot \| _{C^ l}\leq C\| u\| _{H^ r}$, and it agrees with $u$ almost everywhere, because $u_ i\to u$ in $L^2$. Finally, if $u$ lies in every $H^ r$, then for each $l$ it agrees almost everywhere with a form of class $C^ l$; these continuous forms agree almost everywhere, hence everywhere, so $u$ agrees almost everywhere with a smooth form. (e) Proof of (4). Let $u\in H^{-r}$. Since smooth forms are dense in $H^ r$, the bounded functional $\phi \mapsto \langle u,\phi \rangle $ on smooth forms extends uniquely to a bounded conjugate-linear functional on $H^ r$, with the same norm. Conversely, let $\ell $ be a bounded conjugate-linear functional on $H^ r$. Since $*$ is a real bundle isomorphism with smooth coefficients, the formula $T(\alpha )=\ell (\overline{*^{-1}\alpha })$ defines a complex-linear functional $T$ on smooth forms. If $\alpha $ is supported in a compact subset $K$ of a chart, then, by (1) and the chain rule on the compact sets $K\cap \operatorname{Supp}\chi _ k$, we have $|T(\alpha )|\leq \| \ell \| \, \| *^{-1}\overline\alpha \| _{H^ r}\leq C\| *^{-1}\overline\alpha \| _{C^ r}\leq C_ K\sum _ Jp_{K,r}(\alpha _ J)$ in the notation of section 7.2 . Hence the components of $T$ of the various degrees are currents, and $T$ is a distributional form $u$ with $\langle u,\phi \rangle =u(*\overline\phi )=\ell (\phi )$ for smooth $\phi $. Thus $u\in H^{-r}$ and $\| u\| _{H^{-r}}=\| \ell \| $. It is unique, because $*$ maps the smooth forms onto the smooth forms, so that a distributional form is determined by its pairings with smooth forms. For a smooth function or endomorphism $M$, with pointwise adjoint $M^\dagger $, we have $\langle Mu,\phi \rangle =\langle u,M^\dagger \phi \rangle $ for distributional forms $u$ and smooth $\phi $, so $|\langle Mu,\phi \rangle |\leq \| u\| _{H^{-r}}\| M^\dagger \phi \| _{H^ r}\leq C\| u\| _{H^{-r}}\| \phi \| _{H^ r}$ by (1). The inclusion $H^{-r}\subset H^{-r'}$ for $r\leq r'$ follows from $\| \phi \| _{H^ r}\leq \| \phi \| _{H^{r'}}$, and by (1) other choices of the charts, frames and cutoffs change the norm of $H^ r$ on smooth forms, and hence $H^{-r}$, only up to equivalence.
