Lemma 14.1.3 . On $X$ the following hold. Every distributional form $u$ with $\mathcal Lu=0$ is smooth, and the space of harmonic forms is finite dimensional. For every scalar distribution $a$ of mean zero there is a unique distribution $f$ of mean zero with $Lf=a$. If $a$ is smooth, then $f$ is smooth, and if $a$ is real, then $f$ is real. For every constant $c>0$, the operator $\mathcal L+c$ is a bijection of the space of distributional forms onto itself, and it maps $H^{r+2}$ isomorphically onto $H^ r$ for every integer $r$. There is a constant $C$ such that $\| v\| _{L^2}\leq C\| \mathrm dv\| _{L^2}$ for every scalar function $v\in H^1$ of mean zero. Proof. Throughout, we use the properties of the spaces $H^ r$ proved in lemma 14.1.1 . We show that the inclusion $H^1\subset L^2$ is compact, prove Gårding's inequality, solve the equation $(\mathcal L+c)v=b$ weakly with the Riesz representation theorem, and obtain the regularity of the solution from lemma 14.1.2 . This gives (3); we then prove (1), (4) and (2) in turn. Step 1: the inclusion $H^1\subset L^2$ is compact. Let $(u_ j)$ be bounded in $H^1$, fix $k$, and put $v_ j=\chi _ ku_ j$, a coefficient vector in the $k$th chart that vanishes outside a fixed compact set $S$. For $R>0$, the part of $\widehat{v_ j}$ on $|\xi |>R$ has $L^2$ norm at most $R^{-1}\| v_ j\| _{H^1}\leq C/R$. The inverse Fourier transforms $w_{j,R}$ of the parts on $|\xi |\leq R$ are uniformly bounded with uniformly bounded derivatives, by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality on the ball $|\xi |\leq R$, so by the Arzelà–Ascoli theorem (proposition 1.6.4 ) a subsequence converges uniformly on $S$. Since $v_ j$ vanishes outside $S$, \[  \| v_ j-v_ i\| _{L^2}\leq \| w_{j,R}-w_{i,R}\| _{L^2(S)}+2CR^{-1}.  \] A diagonal subsequence over $R=1,2,\ldots $ is therefore Cauchy in $L^2$. Repeating this for the finitely many charts and using $u_ j=\sum _ k\chi _ ku_ j$ proves compactness. Step 2: Gårding's inequality. We first compute $\mathcal L$ in a chart with real coordinates $x_1,\ldots ,x_{2n}$ and the coordinate frame $\mathrm dx_ I$ of the forms. Let $(g^{ij})$ be the inverse of the matrix $(g(\partial _ i,\partial _ j))$, so that $g^{ij}$ is the inner product of $\mathrm dx_ i$ and $\mathrm dx_ j$, write the pointwise inner product of forms as $\sum _{I,J}G_{IJ}u_ I\overline{v_ J}$ and the volume form as $ho \, \mathrm dx$, and let $\epsilon _ i$ be the exterior multiplication by $\mathrm dx_ i$ and $\epsilon _ i^\dagger $ its pointwise adjoint. If $e_1,\ldots ,e_{2n}$ is an orthonormal basis of the cotangent space at a point, then exterior multiplication $\epsilon (e_ a)$ by $e_ a$ and its adjoint $\epsilon (e_ a)^\dagger $, which maps $e_ a\wedge e_ K$ to $e_ K$ for $a
otin K$ and kills the basis forms $e_ J$ with $a
otin J$, satisfy $\epsilon (e_ a)\epsilon (e_ b)^\dagger +\epsilon (e_ b)^\dagger \epsilon (e_ a)=\delta _{ab}$. Indeed, for $a=b$, exactly one of the two terms maps a given basis form $e_ J$ to itself, namely the first if $a\in J$ and the second if $a
otin J$, and the other term kills it. For $a
eq b$, both terms kill $e_ J$ unless $b\in J$ and $a
otin J$; in that case, writing $e_ J=\pm e_ b\wedge e_ K$, they map $e_ b\wedge e_ K$ to $e_ a\wedge e_ K$ and to $\epsilon (e_ b)^\dagger (e_ a\wedge e_ b\wedge e_ K)=-e_ a\wedge e_ K$, respectively. Writing $\mathrm dx_ i=\sum _ aM_{ia}e_ a$, so that $\sum _ aM_{ia}M_{ja}=g^{ij}$, we obtain by bilinearity 14.9  egin{equation} \label{eq:exterior-contraction-anticommutator} \epsilon _ i\epsilon _ j^\dagger +\epsilon _ j^\dagger \epsilon _ i=g^{ij}. \end{equation} In the coordinate frame $\mathrm du=\sum _ i\epsilon _ i\partial _ iu$, where $\partial _ i$ acts on the coefficients. Integrating by parts in $\int \sum _{I,J}G_{IJ}(\epsilon _ i\partial _ iu)_ I\overline{v_ J}\, ho \, \mathrm dx$, we find $\mathrm d^*v=-\sum _ i\epsilon _ i^\dagger \partial _ iv+B_0v$, where $B_0$ is a matrix whose entries are linear combinations, with smooth coefficients, of first derivatives of the $G_{IJ}$ and of $ho $. Since the $\epsilon _ i$ have constant coefficients in the coordinate frame, ( 14.9 ) gives \[  \mathcal L=\mathrm d\mathrm d^*+\mathrm d^*\mathrm d=-\sum _{i,j}g^{ij}\partial _ i\partial _ j+B_1  \] on each coefficient, where $B_1$ is a differential operator of order at most one with smooth coefficients. On functions $\mathrm d^*$ vanishes, so that 14.10  egin{equation} \label{eq:laplace-beltrami-local} Lf=\mathrm d^*\mathrm df=-\sum _{i,j}g^{ij}\partial _ i\partial _ jf+B_0\Bigl (\sum _ i\partial _ if\, \mathrm dx_ i\Bigr ); \end{equation} at a point where the first derivatives of the metric coefficients vanish, $Lf=-\sum _{i,j}g^{ij}\partial _ i\partial _ jf$ there. Now let $u$ be smooth with compact support in the chart. Since $\langle \mathcal Lu,uangle =\| \mathrm du\| ^2+\| \mathrm d^*u\| ^2$, integrating the second-order term by parts once gives \[  \| \mathrm du\| ^2+\| \mathrm d^*u\| ^2 =\int \sum _{i,j,I,J}g^{ij}G_{IJ}\, \partial _ ju_ I\, \overline{\partial _ iu_ J}\, ho \, \mathrm dx+E(u),  \] where $|E(u)|\leq C\| u\| _{L^2}\| u\| _{H^1}$, with $C$ depending on a compact set containing the support of $u$. For $\zeta =(\zeta _{jI})\in \mathbb C^{2n	imes N}$, where $N$ is the number of multi-indices $I$, write $\zeta _ j=(\zeta _{jI})_ I$ and $G(\zeta _ j,\zeta _ i)=\sum _{I,J}G_{IJ}\zeta _{jI}\overline{\zeta _{iJ}}$. Diagonalizing the positive definite real symmetric matrix $(g^{ij})$ by an orthogonal matrix $O$, we get $\sum _{i,j}g^{ij}G(\zeta _ j,\zeta _ i)=\sum _ ad_ aG(\eta _ a,\eta _ a)$ with eigenvalues $d_ a>0$ and $\eta _ a=\sum _ jO_{aj}\zeta _ j$; hence this Hermitian form is positive definite, uniformly on compact subsets of the chart, and the integral is at least $\lambda \| 
abla u\| _{L^2}^2$ for some $\lambda >0$. Applying this to the $\chi _ ku$, whose images under $\mathrm d$ and $\mathrm d^*$ differ from $\chi _ k\, \mathrm du$ and $\chi _ k\, \mathrm d^*u$ by terms bounded by $C|u|$, summing over $k$, using $\sum _ k\chi _ k^2\leq 1$ and absorbing the error terms by $ab\leq 	au a^2+b^2/(4	au )$ with small $	au >0$, we obtain 14.11  egin{equation} \label{eq:compact-garding} \| u\| _{H^1}^2\leq C igl (\| \mathrm du\| _{L^2}^2+ \| \mathrm d^*u\| _{L^2}^2+\| u\| _{L^2}^2 igr ) \end{equation} for smooth forms $u$ on $X$, and hence for all $u\in H^1$, since both sides are continuous for the norm of $H^1$. Step 3: weak solutions. Fix $c>0$ and put $P=\mathcal L+c$, with the quadratic form $Q(v,w)=\langle \mathrm dv,\mathrm dwangle +\langle \mathrm d^*v,\mathrm d^*wangle +c\langle v,wangle $. Since $\mathrm d$ and $\mathrm d^*$ are first-order operators with smooth coefficients, $|Q(v,w)|\leq C\| v\| _{H^1}\| w\| _{H^1}$ for smooth forms, so $Q$ extends to a bounded sesquilinear form on $H^1$, and by ( 14.11 ) the norm $Q(u,u)^{1/2}$ is equivalent to the norm of $H^1$. For $b\in H^{-1}$, the map $w\mapsto \langle b,wangle $ is a bounded conjugate-linear functional on $H^1$, so the Riesz representation theorem (proposition 11.1.1 ) gives a unique $v\in H^1$ with $Q(v,w)=\langle b,wangle $ for all $w\in H^1$, and $\| v\| _{H^1}\leq C\| b\| _{H^{-1}}$. For smooth $\phi $ we have $Q(v,\phi )=\langle v,P\phi angle $, first for smooth $v$ and then for all $v\in H^1$, since both sides are continuous in $v$ for the norm of $H^1$; hence $Pv=b$ as distributional forms. We write $v=P^{-1}b$. Step 4: interior regularity. We apply lemma 14.1.2 to $P$. In a chart, with the notation of Step 2, one integration by parts in the expression of $\mathcal L$ shows that $\langle Pv,wangle =\mathcal A(v,w)$ for smooth $v$ and $w$, the latter with compact support in the chart, where $\mathcal A$ is a form as in lemma 14.1.2 with principal coefficients $a^{ij}_{IJ}=g^{ij}G_{IJ}ho $ and smooth lower-order coefficients. These principal coefficients satisfy the ellipticity condition on compact subsets of the chart, as shown in Step 2. Both sides are continuous in $v\in H^1$, so the equation $Q(v,w)=\langle b,wangle $ of Step 3 reads $\mathcal A(v,w)=\int \sum _ JF_ J\overline{w_ J}\, \mathrm dx$ with $F_ J=ho \sum _ IG_{IJ}b_ I$. Let $b\in H^ r$, $r\geq 0$, and $v=P^{-1}b$. Applying lemma 14.1.2 with $\chi =\chi _ k$ on relatively compact open subsets of the finitely many charts, and using lemma 14.1.1 (2), we obtain $\| v\| _{H^{r+2}}\leq C(\| b\| _{H^ r}+\| v\| _{H^1})$, and since $\| v\| _{H^1}\leq C\| b\| _{H^{-1}}\leq C\| b\| _{L^2}$, \[  \| P^{-1}b\| _{H^{r+2}}\leq C_ r\| b\| _{H^ r},\qquad r\geq 0.  \] In particular, if $b$ is smooth, then $P^{-1}b$ lies in every $H^ r$ and is therefore smooth by lemma 14.1.1 (3), and $PP^{-1}b=b$; and if $u$ is smooth, then $P^{-1}Pu=u$, because $Q(u,w)=\langle Pu,wangle $ for $w\in H^1$ and the solution in Step 3 is unique. For smooth $b$ and $\phi $, with $\psi =P^{-1}\phi $, we get $\langle P^{-1}b,\phi angle =\langle P^{-1}b,P\psi angle =Q(P^{-1}b,\psi )=\langle b,P^{-1}\phi angle $. We therefore extend $P^{-1}$ to all distributional forms by $\langle P^{-1}u,\phi angle =\langle u,P^{-1}\phi angle $ for smooth $\phi $. If $u\in H^{-s}$ with $s\geq 2$, then $|\langle u,P^{-1}\phi angle |\leq \| u\| _{H^{-s}}\| P^{-1}\phi \| _{H^ s}\leq C\| u\| _{H^{-s}}\| \phi \| _{H^{s-2}}$, so $P^{-1}u\in H^{-s+2}$ and $P^{-1}$ is bounded from $H^ r$ to $H^{r+2}$ for $r\leq -2$; for $u\in H^{-1}$ the new definition agrees with that of Step 3, by the same computation with $b=u$. Since $P$ is formally self-adjoint, $\langle PP^{-1}u,\phi angle =\langle u,P^{-1}P\phi angle =\langle u,\phi angle $ and $\langle P^{-1}Pu,\phi angle =\langle u,PP^{-1}\phi angle =\langle u,\phi angle $ for every distributional form $u$, so $P$ is a bijection of the space of distributional forms onto itself with inverse $P^{-1}$. Conversely, $P$ is bounded from $H^{r+2}$ to $H^ r$ for every integer $r$: for $r\geq 0$ because it is a differential operator of order two with smooth coefficients, for $r=-1$ because $|\langle Pv,\phi angle |=|Q(v,\phi )|\leq C\| v\| _{H^1}\| \phi \| _{H^1}$, and for $r\leq -2$ by transposition, since $|\langle Pu,\phi angle |=|\langle u,P\phi angle |\leq C\| u\| _{H^{r+2}}\| \phi \| _{H^{-r}}$. Hence $P$ maps $H^{r+2}$ isomorphically onto $H^ r$. As $c>0$ was arbitrary, this proves (3). Step 5: harmonic forms. If $\mathcal Lu=0$ distributionally, then $Pu=cu$, so $u=cP^{-1}u$. By lemma 14.1.1 (5), $u\in H^{-r}$ for some $r$; iterating this identity raises the Sobolev order by two at each step, so $u$ lies in every $H^ r$ and is smooth by lemma 14.1.1 (3). For smooth harmonic $u$, ( 14.11 ) gives $\| u\| _{H^1}\leq C\| u\| _{L^2}$. An $L^2$ limit of harmonic forms is distributionally harmonic, hence smooth and harmonic, so the closed unit ball of the space of harmonic forms in $L^2$ is bounded in $H^1$ and therefore compact by Step 1. A normed space with compact closed unit ball is finite dimensional: an infinite orthonormal sequence would have no convergent subsequence. This proves (1). Step 6: the scalar equation. We first prove (4). If it fails, there are scalar functions $v_ j\in H^1$ of mean zero with $\| v_ j\| _{L^2}=1$ and $\mathrm dv_ j	o 0$ in $L^2$. Since $\mathrm d^*$ vanishes on functions, ( 14.11 ) shows that $(v_ j)$ is bounded in $H^1$, so by Step 1 a subsequence converges in $L^2$ to some $v$ of norm one and mean zero, and $\mathrm dv=\lim _ j\mathrm dv_ j=0$ in the sense of distributions. In every chart $v$ is locally constant by corollary 1.4.4 , so $v$ is constant on the connected manifold $X$, which contradicts $\| v\| _{L^2}=1$ and mean zero. This proves (4). Consequently $\| \mathrm dv\| _{L^2}$ is an equivalent Hilbert norm on the closed subspace of $H^1$ of functions of mean zero. Let $a$ be smooth of mean zero. The Riesz representation theorem (proposition 11.1.1 ) gives $f$ in this subspace with $\langle \mathrm df,\mathrm dwangle =\langle a,wangle $ for all $w$ of mean zero, hence for all $w\in H^1$, since both sides vanish for constant $w$. Testing with $w=f$ gives $\| \mathrm df\| ^2=\langle a,fangle \leq \| a\| \, \| f\| \leq C\| a\| \, \| \mathrm df\| $, hence $\| f\| _{H^1}\leq C\| a\| _{L^2}$. With $c=1$ the function $f$ satisfies $Q(f,w)=\langle a+f,wangle $ for all $w\in H^1$, so $f=P^{-1}(a+f)$ by the uniqueness in Step 3; if $f\in H^ r$, $r\geq 0$, then Step 4 gives $f\in H^{r+2}$ with $\| f\| _{H^{r+2}}\leq C(\| a\| _{H^ r}+\| f\| _{H^ r})$. By induction $f$ lies in every $H^ r$, so it is smooth, and $\| f\| _{H^{r+2}}\leq C_ r\| a\| _{H^ r}$ for every $r\geq 0$. Let $\Pi a=\langle a,1angle /\int _ X\mathrm dV$ be the average of $a$, and let $\mathcal G$ be the operator $a\mapsto f$ applied to $a-\Pi a$, for smooth $a$. Then $\| \mathcal Ga\| _{H^{r+2}}\leq C_ r\| a\| _{H^ r}$ for $r\geq 0$, and $L\mathcal G=1-\Pi $ by construction. If $a$ is smooth, then $La$ has mean zero, because $\langle La,1angle =\langle a,L1angle =0$, and both $\mathcal GLa$ and $a-\Pi a$ are smooth solutions $f$ of mean zero of $Lf=La$. The difference $f_0$ of two such solutions satisfies $\int _ X|\mathrm df_0|^2\, \mathrm dV=\langle Lf_0,f_0angle =0$, so it is constant, and it vanishes since it has mean zero; hence $\mathcal GL=1-\Pi $. For smooth $a$ and $b$, since $\mathcal Ga$ has mean zero and $L$ is formally self-adjoint, \[  \langle \mathcal Ga,bangle =\langle \mathcal Ga,L\mathcal Gb+\Pi bangle =\langle L\mathcal Ga,\mathcal Gbangle =\langle a-\Pi a,\mathcal Gbangle =\langle a,\mathcal Gbangle ,  \] so $\mathcal G$ is formally self-adjoint, and so is $\Pi $. Extend $\mathcal G$ to distributions by transposition, $\langle \mathcal Ga,\chi angle =\langle a,\mathcal G\chi angle $. This defines a distribution: if $a\in H^{-s}$ with $s\geq 2$, then $|\langle a,\mathcal G\chi angle |\leq C\| a\| _{H^{-s}}\| \chi \| _{H^{s-2}}$. The two identities $L\mathcal G=\mathcal GL=1-\Pi $ remain valid, by transposition of the same identities for smooth functions. Hence $f=\mathcal Ga$ solves $Lf=a$ for every distribution $a$ of mean zero, and $\langle \mathcal Ga,1angle =\langle a,\mathcal G1angle =0$. If $Lf=0$ for a distribution $f$, then $\mathcal Lf=0$, so $f$ is smooth by Step 5, and $\int _ X|\mathrm df|^2\, \mathrm dV=\langle Lf,fangle =0$ shows that $f$ is constant; this proves uniqueness. If $a$ is real, then $\overline f$ is another solution of mean zero, since $L$ has real coefficients, so $f$ is real. $\square$

title: Mixed scalar poisson
topic: Global potentials and positive cohomology classes
text: Lemma 14.1.4 . Let $\omega _1,\ldots ,\omega _{n-1}$ be Kähler forms on $X$ and put $A=\omega _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \omega _{n-1}$, with $A=1$ when $n=1$. For every smooth real $(n,n)$-form $\eta $ with $\int _ X\eta =0$, there is a unique smooth real function $f$ of mean zero such that \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f\wedge A=\eta .  \] Proof. For smooth real functions $f,g$ put $B(f,g)=\int _ X\mathrm{d}f\wedge \mathrm{d}^{\mathrm c}g\wedge A$. Only the $(1,1)$-part of $\mathrm df\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}g$ contributes, and this part equals $\frac{\mathrm i}{4\pi }(\partial f\wedge \bar\partial g+\partial g\wedge \bar\partial f)$, which is symmetric in $f$ and $g$; in particular $\mathrm{d}f\wedge \mathrm{d}^{\mathrm c}f$ has $(1,1)$-part $\frac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }\partial f\wedge \bar\partial f$. Thus $B$ is symmetric. Since $A$ is closed, Stokes' formula (proposition 7.1.3 ) applied to $\mathrm d(g\, \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}f\wedge A)$ gives \[  B(f,g)=B(g,f)=-\int _ Xg\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f\wedge A.  \] On the compact manifold there are constants $0<c\leq C$ with $c\, \omega \leq \omega _ j\leq C\omega $ for all $j$, by lemma 13.1.1 . For $(1,1)$-forms $\gamma _ j,\gamma '_ j$ we have the telescoping identity 14.12 \begin{equation} \label{eq:wedge-product-telescoping} \gamma _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \gamma _{n-1}-\gamma '_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \gamma '_{n-1}=\sum _{m=1}^{n-1}\gamma _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \gamma _{m-1}\wedge (\gamma _ m-\gamma '_ m)\wedge \gamma '_{m+1}\wedge \cdots \wedge \gamma '_{n-1}. \end{equation} Applying it with $\gamma _ j=\omega _ j$, $\gamma '_ j=c\, \omega $ and with $\gamma _ j=C\omega $, $\gamma '_ j=\omega _ j$, we see that the forms $A-c^{n-1}\omega ^{n-1}$ and $C^{n-1}\omega ^{n-1}-A$ are sums of products of semipositive $(1,1)$-forms. Such products, and their products with the semipositive form $\mathrm i\partial f\wedge \bar\partial f$, are strongly positive (proposition 7.2.1 ). Hence $B(f,f)$ lies between $c^{n-1}$ and $C^{n-1}$ times $\int _ X\frac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }\partial f\wedge \bar\partial f\wedge \omega ^{n-1}$. At a point, if $\theta _1,\ldots ,\theta _ n$ is a unitary coframe, that is, $\omega =\mathrm i\sum _ j\theta _ j\wedge \bar\theta _ j$, and $\partial f=\sum _ ja_ j\theta _ j$, then $\mathrm i\partial f\wedge \bar\partial f\wedge \omega ^{n-1}/(n-1)!=\sum _ j|a_ j|^2\omega ^ n/n!$ and $|\mathrm df|^2=2\sum _ j|a_ j|^2$; so the last integral is $\frac{(n-1)!}{4\pi }\| \mathrm df\| _{L^2}^2$. By lemma 14.1.3 (4), $B$ is therefore an equivalent inner product on the closed subspace of real functions of mean zero in $H^1$. The sesquilinear extension $B_{\mathbb C}(f_1+\mathrm if_2,g_1+\mathrm ig_2)=B(f_1,g_1)+B(f_2,g_2)+\mathrm i\bigl (B(f_2,g_1)-B(f_1,g_2)\bigr )$ to complex-valued functions is, by the symmetry of $B$, a Hermitian form with $B_{\mathbb C}(f,f)=B(f_1,f_1)+B(f_2,f_2)$, hence an equivalent inner product on the complex Hilbert space of functions of mean zero in $H^1$. The Riesz representation theorem (proposition 11.1.1 ), applied to the bounded conjugate-linear functional $g\mapsto -\int _ X\overline g\, \eta $, gives $F$ in this space with $B_{\mathbb C}(F,g)=-\int _ X\overline g\, \eta $ for all $g$. For real $g$ the right side is real and $B_{\mathbb C}(F,g)=B(\operatorname{Re}F,g)+\mathrm iB(\operatorname{Im}F,g)$, so $f=\operatorname{Re}F$ is a real function of mean zero in $H^1$ with $B(f,g)=-\int _ Xg\eta $ for every real mean-zero $g\in H^1$. Since $\int _ X\eta =0$ and $B(f,1)=0$, the identity holds for all $g\in H^1$; this is the equation $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f\wedge A=\eta $ in the weak sense. It remains to prove that $f$ is smooth. In a chart, with $\eta =\tilde\eta \, \mathrm dx$, the weak equation reads $\mathcal A(f,w)=-\int \tilde\eta \, \overline w\, \mathrm dx$ for $w\in C^\infty _ c$, where $\mathcal A(f,w)=B(f,\overline w)=\int \sum _{i,j}a^{ij}\partial _ jf\, \overline{\partial _ iw}\, \mathrm dx$ and the real symmetric matrix $(a^{ij})$ is the density of the quadratic form $\mathrm df\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}f\wedge A$. By the bounds just proved, $(a^{ij})$ is uniformly positive definite on compact subsets of the chart. This is a form of the kind considered in lemma 14.1.2 , with $N=1$, and since $\tilde\eta $ is smooth, that lemma, applied with the cutoffs $\chi _ k$ on relatively compact open subsets of the charts, shows that every $\chi _ kf$ has square integrable distributional derivatives of all orders. Hence $f$ lies in every $H^ r$ by lemma 14.1.1 (2), and it is smooth by lemma 14.1.1 (3). If $f$ and $f'$ are two solutions, then $B(f-f',f-f')=0$, so $f-f'$ is constant on the connected manifold $X$, and it vanishes since it has mean zero. $\square$

title: Kahler normal coordinates
topic: Global potentials and positive cohomology classes
text: Lemma 14.1.5 . Let $\sigma $ be a Kähler form on a complex manifold $M$ of dimension $n\geq 1$, and let $x\in M$. There are holomorphic coordinates $w$ centered at $x$ in which $\sigma =\frac{\mathrm i}{2}\sum _{k,l}\tilde g_{k\bar l}\, \mathrm dw_ k\wedge \mathrm d\bar w_ l$ with $\tilde g_{k\bar l}(0)=\delta _{kl}$ and with all first derivatives of the functions $\tilde g_{k\bar l}$ vanishing at $0$. Proof. Choose holomorphic coordinates $z$ centered at $x$. Since the matrix of $\sigma $ at $x$ is positive definite Hermitian, after a linear change of coordinates $\sigma =\frac{\mathrm i}{2}\sum _{k,l}g_{k\bar l}\, \mathrm dz_ k\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ l$ with $g_{k\bar l}(0)=\delta _{kl}$; moreover $\overline{g_{l\bar k}}=g_{k\bar l}$, since $\sigma $ is real. The $(2,1)$-part of $\mathrm d\sigma =0$ is $\partial \sigma =\frac{\mathrm i}{2}\sum _{k,l,m}\partial _ mg_{k\bar l}\, \mathrm dz_ m\wedge \mathrm dz_ k\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ l=0$, which gives $\partial _ mg_{k\bar l}=\partial _ kg_{m\bar l}$. By the holomorphic inverse function theorem (proposition 7.1.2 (1)), the equations $z_ l=w_ l-\frac12\sum _{k,m}\partial _ mg_{k\bar l}(0)w_ kw_ m$ define holomorphic coordinates $w$ near $0$, since the Jacobian matrix of this map at $0$ is the identity. Substituting $\mathrm dz_ l=\mathrm dw_ l-\sum _{k,m}\partial _ mg_{k\bar l}(0)w_ m\, \mathrm dw_ k$, which uses the symmetry in $k$ and $m$, and $g_{k\bar l}(z)=\delta _{kl}+\sum _ m\partial _ mg_{k\bar l}(0)w_ m+\sum _ m\partial _{\bar m}g_{k\bar l}(0)\bar w_ m+O(|w|^2)$, we find that the coefficient of $\frac{\mathrm i}{2}\mathrm dw_ k\wedge \mathrm d\bar w_ l$ in $\sigma $ is $\delta _{kl}$ plus terms of order two in $w$: the terms $\sum _ m\partial _ mg_{k\bar l}(0)w_ m$ of $g_{k\bar l}$ cancel against the correction in $\mathrm dz_ k$, and their conjugates $\sum _ m\partial _{\bar m}g_{k\bar l}(0)\bar w_ m=\sum _ m\overline{\partial _ mg_{l\bar k}(0)}\, \bar w_ m$ cancel against the correction in $\mathrm d\bar z_ l$. Hence the first derivatives of the new coefficients vanish at $0$. $\square$

title: Kahler trace star
topic: Global potentials and positive cohomology classes
text: Lemma 14.1.6 . For a scalar distribution $f$ and a real $(1,1)$-current $T$ on $X$, 14.13 \begin{equation} \label{eq:kahler-trace-star} \Lambda \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f=-\frac{Lf}{4\pi },\qquad *T=(\Lambda T)\frac{\omega ^{n-1}}{(n-1)!} -T\wedge \frac{\omega ^{n-2}}{(n-2)!}\quad (n\geq 2). \end{equation} If $\mathrm dT=0$ and $\Lambda T$ is constant, then $\mathcal LT=0$. Proof. Both sides of each identity are differential operators, or bundle maps, with smooth coefficients, acting on distributions and currents as explained at the beginning of this section. Hence it suffices to verify the identities for smooth $f$ and $T$, at an arbitrary point. By lemma 14.1.5 , there are holomorphic coordinates centered at the point in which $\omega =\frac{\mathrm i}{2}\sum _ j\mathrm dz_ j\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ j$ at the point and the first derivatives of the coefficients of $\omega $, hence of the metric coefficients, vanish there. Thus ( 14.10 ) gives $Lf=-\sum _ j(\partial _{x_ j}^2+\partial _{y_ j}^2)f=-4\sum _ j\partial _ j\partial _{\bar j}f$ there, while $\theta _ j=\mathrm dz_ j/\sqrt2$ is a unitary coframe and \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f=\frac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }\sum _{j,k}f_{j\bar k}\, \mathrm dz_ j\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ k =\mathrm i\sum _{j,k}\frac{f_{j\bar k}}{\pi }\, \theta _ j\wedge \bar\theta _ k .  \] Hence $\Lambda \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f=\pi ^{-1}\sum _ jf_{j\bar j}=-Lf/(4\pi )$. For the second identity, diagonalize the Hermitian matrix of $T$ by a unitary change of coframe; by linearity it suffices to treat $T=\mathrm i\theta _1\wedge \bar\theta _1$. Write $\sqrt2\theta _ j=e_{2j-1}+\mathrm ie_{2j}$ with real covectors $e_ a$; they form an orthonormal basis, positively oriented since $\omega ^ n/n!=e_1\wedge \cdots \wedge e_{2n}$, and $\omega _ j=\mathrm i\theta _ j\wedge \bar\theta _ j=e_{2j-1}\wedge e_{2j}$. By the explicit formula for $*$, the star of $\omega _1$ is $\omega _2\wedge \cdots \wedge \omega _ n$. On the other hand $\omega ^{n-1}/(n-1)!$ is the sum of all products of $n-1$ distinct $\omega _ j$, while $\omega _1\wedge \omega ^{n-2}/(n-2)!$ is the sum of those products that contain $\omega _1$; their difference is exactly $\omega _2\wedge \cdots \wedge \omega _ n$, and $\Lambda \omega _1=1$. If $\mathrm dT=0$ and $\Lambda T$ is constant, the second identity and $\mathrm d\omega =0$ give $\mathrm d*T=0$, hence $\mathrm d^*T=-*\mathrm d*T=0$, and $\mathcal LT=\mathrm d\mathrm d^*T+\mathrm d^*\mathrm dT=0$. In dimension one a $(1,1)$-current is $T=(\Lambda T)\omega $, so $*T=\Lambda T$ is constant and the same conclusion holds. $\square$

title: The ddc-lemma
topic: Global potentials and positive cohomology classes
text: Theorem 14.1.7 (The $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-lemma) . Every closed real $(1,1)$-current $T$ on $X$ has a unique decomposition 14.15 \begin{equation} \label{eq:global-current-decomposition} T=H+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f, \end{equation} where $H$ is a smooth harmonic real $(1,1)$-form and $f$ is a real distribution of mean zero. If $T$ is smooth, then $f$ is smooth. If $T$ is positive, then $f$ has a canonical quasi-plurisubharmonic representative. Moreover, $T$ is exact as a current if and only if $H=0$. Proof. Put $a=\int _ XT\wedge \omega ^{n-1}/\int _ X\omega ^ n$. Since $T\wedge \omega ^{n-1}=(\Lambda T)\omega ^ n/n$, the distribution $\Lambda T-na$ has mean zero, and lemma 14.1.3 gives a real distribution $f$ of mean zero with $Lf=-4\pi (\Lambda T-na)$. By lemma 14.1.6 , $\Lambda \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f=\Lambda T-na$, so the closed current $U=T-a\omega -\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$ has $\Lambda U=0$. By lemma 14.1.6 again, $U$ is harmonic, and by lemma 14.1.3 it is smooth. The Kähler form is harmonic as well, since $\mathrm d\omega =0$ and $*\omega =\omega ^{n-1}/(n-1)!$ is closed. Hence $H=a\omega +U$ and $f$ give the decomposition ( 14.15 ). If $T$ is smooth, then $\Lambda T$ is smooth, and so is $f$ by lemma 14.1.3 . An exact harmonic form $B$ vanishes: if $B=\mathrm dS$ for a current $S$, then \[  \| B\| _{L^2}^2=\int _ X\mathrm dS\wedge *B=\pm \,  S(\mathrm d*B)=0,  \] since $\mathrm d*B=0$. If $T=H'+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f'$ is a second decomposition, then $H-H'=\mathrm d\, \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}(f'-f)$ is exact and harmonic, hence zero. Then $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(f-f')=0$, so $L(f-f')=0$ by lemma 14.1.6 ; thus $f-f'$ is constant by lemma 14.1.3 , and it vanishes because both have mean zero. The same argument proves the exactness criterion: if $T$ is exact, so is $H=T-\mathrm d\, \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}f$, whence $H=0$; conversely, if $H=0$, then $T=\mathrm d\, \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}f$. Suppose now that $T\geq 0$. By theorem 7.3.2 , theorem 8.2.1 , lemma 13.1.2 , every point of $X$ has a coordinate ball on which $T=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ with $u$ plurisubharmonic and $H=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h$ with $h$ smooth. Then $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(f+h-u)=0$, so the scalar Laplacian of the distribution $f+h-u$ vanishes, and Weyl's lemma (theorem 2.1.4 ) shows that it is a smooth pluriharmonic function $p$. Thus $f=u-h+p$ is, on the ball, the class of a plurisubharmonic function minus a smooth function. On the overlap of two balls, the two local representatives $u_1-h_1+p_1$ and $u_2-h_2+p_2$ agree almost everywhere; after adding $h_1-p_1$ to both, both become plurisubharmonic, because $h_1-p_1-h_2+p_2$ is smooth with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(h_1-p_1-h_2+p_2)=H-H=0$, and plurisubharmonic functions that agree almost everywhere agree everywhere (theorem 8.2.1 ). Hence the local representatives define a global quasi-plurisubharmonic representative of $f$. It is the only one, since two quasi-plurisubharmonic functions that agree almost everywhere agree everywhere (lemma 13.1.4 (1)). $\square$

text: Corollary 14.1.9 . Let $\theta $ be a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form on $X$. A closed positive $(1,1)$-current $T$ on $X$ satisfies $\{ T\} =\{ \theta \} $ if and only if $T=\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $ for some $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, and then $\varphi $ is unique up to an additive constant. In particular, the class $\{ \theta \} $ contains a closed positive current if and only if $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )\neq \varnothing $. Proof. Let $T\geq 0$ be closed with $\{ T\} =\{ \theta \} $. Write $T=H+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$ as in ( 14.15 ); since $\{ T\} =\{ \theta \} $, also $\theta =H+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g$ with $g$ smooth. By theorem 14.1.7 , $f$ has a canonical quasi-plurisubharmonic representative, and the difference $\varphi $ of this representative and $g$ satisfies $T=\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $; thus $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Conversely, if $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, then $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $ is a closed positive current, and it lies in $\{ \theta \} $ because adding $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ of a distribution does not change the class. If $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi =\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi '$ with $\varphi ,\varphi '\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, then $\varphi -\varphi '$ is constant almost everywhere by the uniqueness part of theorem 14.1.7 , say equal to $c$, and the quasi-plurisubharmonic functions $\varphi $ and $\varphi '+c$, which agree almost everywhere, agree everywhere by lemma 13.1.4 (1). $\square$

14.2 Normalized potentials and minimal singularities Fix a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form $	heta $ on $X$. A function $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ is determined by its current $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $ up to an additive constant, which we fix by normalizing the supremum. The local compactness and integrability theorems then become uniform statements for normalized potentials, and the upper envelope of the nonpositive potentials has minimal singularities. We also compare potentials on $X$ and on a modification of $X$. Integrals over $X$ are taken with respect to $\mathrm dV$, or equivalently $\omega ^ n$, unless stated otherwise. A $	heta $-plurisubharmonic function is integrable on the compact manifold $X$, being locally integrable. If $\varphi $ is quasi-plurisubharmonic and $\psi $ is quasi-plurisubharmonic or continuous, an inequality between $\varphi $ and $\psi $ that holds almost everywhere holds everywhere. Indeed, by lemma 13.1.4 (1) the value of a quasi-plurisubharmonic function at a point is the limit of its averages over small coordinate balls centered at that point, a continuous function has the same property, and the inequality holds between these averages. In particular, a $	heta $-plurisubharmonic function is determined by its class in $L^1(X)$, and we regard $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ as a subset of $L^1(X)$. Proposition 14.2.1 . Let $a\leq b$ be real numbers. The set of $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ with $a\leq \sup _ X\varphi \leq b$ is compact in $L^1(X)$, and the map $\varphi \mapsto \sup _ X\varphi $ is continuous on $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ for the $L^1$ topology. In particular, the functions $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ with $\sup _ X\varphi =0$ are uniformly bounded in $L^1(X)$. The same statements hold for a sequence of backgrounds: if smooth closed real $(1,1)$-forms $	heta _ j$ converge smoothly to $	heta $ and $\varphi _ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta _ j)$ satisfy $a\leq \sup _ X\varphi _ j\leq b$, then a subsequence converges in $L^1(X)$ to some $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ with $a\leq \sup _ X\varphi \leq b$, and $\sup _ X\varphi _ j	o \sup _ X\varphi $ whenever $\varphi _ j	o \varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ in $L^1(X)$. The assertions for a fixed background hold more generally on every connected compact complex manifold $X'$ of positive dimension, for every smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form $	heta '$ on $X'$, with $L^1(X')$ taken with respect to any smooth positive volume form. Proof. Choose finitely many coordinate balls $B_ k$ covering $X$, smaller concentric balls $B'_ k$ still covering $X$, and smooth functions $h_ k$ near $\overline{B_ k}$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h_ k=	heta $ (lemma 13.1.2 , applied on slightly larger concentric balls). For $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ the functions $\varphi +h_ k$ are plurisubharmonic on $B_ k$. Let $(\varphi _ j)$ be a sequence with $a\leq \sup _ X\varphi _ j\leq b$. The plurisubharmonic functions $\varphi _ j+h_ k$ are uniformly bounded above on each $B_ k$. Since $\varphi _ j$ is upper semicontinuous on the compact manifold $X$, it attains its supremum at a point $x_ j$, and after passing to a subsequence $x_ j	o x$, since $X$ is compact and metrizable. Choose $k$ with $x\in B'_ k$. On $B_ k$ the functions $\varphi _ j+h_ k$ cannot converge locally uniformly to $-\infty $, because their values at $x_ j$ are bounded below by $a+\inf _{B'_ k}h_ k$ for large $j$. By theorem 8.3.4 , a further subsequence converges in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(B_ k)$. If $B_ l$ meets $B_ k$, the functions $\varphi _ j+h_ l$ cannot tend to $-\infty $ locally uniformly on $B_ l$, since on the nonempty open set $B_ k\cap B_ l$ they differ by the smooth function $h_ l-h_ k$ from a sequence that converges in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$; so again a subsequence converges in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(B_ l)$. Since $X$ is connected, every ball is joined to $B_ k$ by a finite chain of overlapping balls, and after finitely many extractions the sequence converges in $L^1(B'_ l)$ for every $l$, hence in $L^1(X)$, to some $\varphi $. The limit satisfies $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi \geq 0$ as a distributional limit of positive currents, and its canonical representative belongs to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$. Now let $\varphi _ j	o \varphi $ in $L^1(X)$, all in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$; we show that $\sup _ X\varphi _ j	o \sup _ X\varphi $. The submean inequality for $\varphi _ j+h_ k$ on small balls shows that the $\varphi _ j$ are uniformly bounded above. Let $x_ j	o x$; we claim that $\varlimsup _ j\varphi _ j(x_ j)\leq \varphi (x)$. Indeed, choose $k$ with $x\in B_ k$, let $c>\varphi (x)$ be real, and use upper semicontinuity to choose a closed ball $K\subset B_ k$ around $x$ on which $\varphi <c$. The function $c+h_ k$ is continuous near $K$ and $\varphi +h_ k<c+h_ k$ on $K$, so the second part of theorem 8.3.4 gives $\varphi _ j+h_ k<c+h_ k$ on $K$ for large $j$; hence $\varphi _ j(x_ j)<c$ for large $j$. Choose a subsequence along which $\sup _ X\varphi _ j$ tends to $\varlimsup _ j\sup _ X\varphi _ j$ and points $x_ j$ with $\varphi _ j(x_ j)=\sup _ X\varphi _ j$ converge to some $x$; the claim gives $\varlimsup _ j\sup _ X\varphi _ j\leq \varphi (x)\leq \sup _ X\varphi $. Conversely, choose a subsequence along which $\sup _ X\varphi _ j$ tends to $\varliminf _ j\sup _ X\varphi _ j$ and $\sum _ j\| \varphi _ j-\varphi \| _{L^1}<\infty $; by monotone convergence $\sum _ j|\varphi _ j-\varphi |$ is integrable, hence finite almost everywhere, so $\varphi _ j	o \varphi $ almost everywhere along it. We get $\varphi \leq \varliminf _ j\sup _ X\varphi _ j$ almost everywhere, hence everywhere, as noted at the beginning of this section. The two inequalities prove that the supremum is continuous; in particular, the limit in the previous paragraph satisfies $a\leq \sup _ X\varphi \leq b$. Thus the set in question is sequentially compact, hence compact, in the metric space $L^1(X)$. The continuous function $\| \cdot \| _{L^1}$ is bounded on the compact set of normalized functions. The arguments so far use only that $X$ is a connected compact complex manifold of positive dimension and that the volume form defining $L^1(X)$ is smooth and positive; hence they also prove the last assertion of the proposition. For smoothly convergent backgrounds, choose $C\geq 0$ with $	heta _ j\leq C\omega $ for all $j$. Then $C\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ j\geq 0$, so all $\varphi _ j$ lie in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,C\omega )$, and the first part, applied to the closed form $C\omega $, gives an $L^1$-convergent subsequence and the convergence of the suprema. Since $	heta _ j+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ j	o 	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $ as distributions, the limit belongs to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$. $\square$ Corollary 14.2.2 . For every $1\leq p<\infty $ there is a constant $M_ p$, depending only on $X$, $	heta $, $\omega $ and $p$, such that \[  \| u\| _{L^ p(X,\omega ^ n)}\leq M_ p \quad 	ext{for all }u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )	ext{ with }\sup _ Xu=0.  \] Proof. (If $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ is empty, there is nothing to prove.) Choose finitely many coordinate polydiscs $D_ k$ such that the polydiscs $ rac14D_ k$ with the same centers and a quarter of the radii cover $X$, and smooth functions $h_ k$ near $\overline{D_ k}$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h_ k=	heta $. For $u$ as in the statement, $v_ k=u+h_ k-\sup _{D_ k}h_ k$ is a nonpositive plurisubharmonic function on $D_ k$. By proposition 14.2.1 and the boundedness of the $h_ k$ and of the coordinate volume densities, the norms $\| v_ k\| _{L^1(D_ k)}$ are bounded independently of $u$. After rescaling $D_ k$ to the unit polydisc, ( 8.6 ) bounds $\| v_ k\| _{L^ p( rac14D_ k)}$ independently of $u$. Since $u=v_ k-h_ k+\sup _{D_ k}h_ k$ on $D_ k$, the bounded functions $h_ k$ and the bounded volume densities give the assertion. $\square$ Corollary 14.2.3 . There are $\alpha ,C>0$, depending only on $X$, $	heta $ and $\omega $, such that 14.17  egin{equation} \label{eq:normalized-global-psh-exponential-bound} \int _ X\mathrm e^{-\alpha u}\omega ^ n\leq C \quad 	ext{for all }u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )	ext{ with }\sup _ Xu=0. \end{equation} Proof. (If $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ is empty, any $\alpha ,C>0$ will do.) Choose finitely many coordinate unit balls $B_ j$ such that the balls $ rac14B_ j$ with the same centers and a quarter of the radii cover $X$, and smooth functions $ho _ j$ near $\overline{B_ j}$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}ho _ j=	heta $. For $u$ as in the statement put $v_ j=u+ho _ j-\sup _{B_ j}ho _ j$ on $B_ j$; then $v_ j$ is plurisubharmonic and $v_ j\leq u\leq 0$. By proposition 14.2.1 and comparison of the coordinate volume densities, $\| v_ j\| _{L^1(B_ j)}\leq M_ j$ for a constant $M_ j\geq 1$ independent of $u$. Applying proposition 8.3.9 to $v_ j/M_ j$, we see that $\int _{ rac14B_ j}\mathrm e^{-\alpha _ jv_ j}$ is bounded independently of $u$, where $\alpha _ j=\alpha _ n/M_ j$. Put $\alpha =\min _ j\alpha _ j>0$. Since $v_ j\leq u\leq 0$ and $\alpha \leq \alpha _ j$, we have $\mathrm e^{-\alpha u}\leq \mathrm e^{-\alpha _ ju}\leq \mathrm e^{-\alpha _ jv_ j}$ on $B_ j$. Summing over $j$ and comparing the coordinate volume densities with $\omega ^ n$ gives ( 14.17 ). $\square$ Recall from definition 10.1.1 that a subset of $X$ is pluripolar if it is locally contained in the pole set of a plurisubharmonic function. Corollary 14.2.4 . Let $K\subset X$ be a compact set that is not pluripolar. Then there is a constant $C$ such that \[  \sup _ X\varphi \leq \sup _ K\varphi +C\qquad 	ext{for all }\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta ).  \] Consequently, every subset of $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ on which $\sup _ K\varphi $ is bounded above and below is relatively compact in $L^1(X)$. Proof. Suppose that no such constant exists. Since $\sup _ X\varphi -\sup _ K\varphi $ does not change when a constant is added to $\varphi $, there are $\varphi _ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ with $\sup _ X\varphi _ j=0$ and $\sup _ K\varphi _ j\leq -2^ j$. Choose $C\geq 0$ with $	heta \leq C\omega $ (lemma 13.1.1 ) and put $\psi _ N=\sum _{j=1}^ N2^{-j}\varphi _ j$. Since $\sum _{j\leq N}2^{-j}\leq 1$, we have \[  C\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi _ N=\Bigl (1-\sum _{j\leq N}2^{-j}\Bigr )C\omega +\sum _{j\leq N}2^{-j}(C\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ j)\geq \sum _{j\leq N}2^{-j}(	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ j)\geq 0.  \] The sequence $(\psi _ N)$ is decreasing because $\varphi _ j\leq 0$, and $\| \psi _ N\| _{L^1}\leq \sup _ j\| \varphi _ j\| _{L^1}<\infty $ by proposition 14.2.1 . By monotone convergence the limit $\psi $ is integrable, so it is not identically $-\infty $, and theorem 8.3.1 , applied on coordinate balls after adding local potentials of $C\omega $, shows that $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,C\omega )$. On $K$ every term $2^{-j}\varphi _ j$ is at most $-1$, so $\psi =-\infty $ on $K$. On every coordinate ball $U$ with a smooth function $h$ such that $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h=C\omega $, the function $\psi +h$ is plurisubharmonic and equals $-\infty $ on $K\cap U$. Hence $K$ is pluripolar, a contradiction. The last assertion follows: bounds for $\sup _ K\varphi $ give bounds for $\sup _ X\varphi $, and proposition 14.2.1 applies. $\square$ Corollary 14.2.5 . Let $(\varphi _ i)$ be a decreasing net in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ whose suprema $\sup _ X\varphi _ i$ are bounded below. Then its pointwise infimum $\varphi $ belongs to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$, $\varphi _ i	o \varphi $ in $L^1(X)$, and $\sup _ X\varphi _ i	o \sup _ X\varphi $. Proof. Fix an index $i_0$. For $i\geq i_0$ the suprema are bounded above by $\sup _ X\varphi _{i_0}$, so the tail of the net lies in a compact subset of $L^1(X)$ by proposition 14.2.1 , and a subnet converges in $L^1$ to some $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$. For each fixed $i$, the members of the subnet are eventually below $\varphi _ i$, so $\psi \leq \varphi _ i$ almost everywhere, and therefore everywhere, as noted at the beginning of this section. Hence the pointwise infimum $\varphi $ is at least $\psi $ and is not identically $-\infty $. Applying theorem 8.3.1 on the coordinate balls of a finite cover, after adding local potentials of $	heta $, we find that $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ and $\varphi _ i	o \varphi $ in $L^1(X)$. The continuity of the supremum in proposition 14.2.1 gives the last assertion. $\square$ Definition 14.2.6 . Let $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$. Recall from section 13.5 that $\varphi $ is more singular than $\psi $, written $\varphi \preceq \psi $, if $\varphi \leq \psi +C$ on $X$ for some constant $C$; we then also say that $\psi $ is less singular than $\varphi $. The family whose upper envelope defines $V_	heta $ in definition 14.2.6 is nonempty, because $\varphi -\sup _ X\varphi $ belongs to it for every $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$, and it is bounded above by $0$. Then $Y$ is compact and connected, and $\varphi \mapsto \varphi \circ \pi $ is a bijection from $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ onto $\mathrm{PSH}(Y,\pi ^*	heta )$, which is continuous for convergence in $L^1(X)$ and $L^1(Y)$, the latter taken with respect to any smooth positive volume form. For every prime divisor $E$ on $Y$, the generic Lelong numbers $
u (\varphi ,E)=
u (\varphi \circ \pi ,E)$ are bounded above uniformly for $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$. Proof. The manifold $Y=\pi ^{-1}(X)$ is compact, because $\pi $ is proper. By the definition of bimeromorphic maps (section A.3 ), there is a nowhere dense analytic subset $E_0\subset X$ such that $\pi ^{-1}(E_0)$ is nowhere dense and $\pi $ restricts to an isomorphism of $Y\setminus \pi ^{-1}(E_0)$ onto $X\setminus E_0$. The set $X\setminus E_0$ is connected by lemma A.1.7 , hence so is its dense preimage, and therefore $Y$ is connected. The image $\pi (Y)$ is closed, since proper maps are closed, and it contains the dense set $X\setminus E_0$; so $\pi $ is surjective. By proposition A.7.3 there is an analytic subset $A\subset X$ of codimension at least two such that $\pi $ is an isomorphism over $X\setminus A$. Then $\pi ^{-1}(A)$ is an analytic subset of $Y$ different from $Y$, because $\pi $ is surjective. Since $Y$ is connected, $\pi ^{-1}(A)$ is locally contained in the zero set of a holomorphic function that does not vanish identically on a connected neighborhood (section A.1 ), so it is nowhere dense and a null set (lemma 7.4.1 ). The same holds for $A$ in $X$. If $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$, let $B$ be a coordinate ball and $h$ a smooth function on $B$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h=	heta $ (lemma 13.1.2 ). On every connected coordinate neighborhood $W\subset \pi ^{-1}(B)$ the function $(\varphi +h)\circ \pi $ is plurisubharmonic or identically $-\infty $, by proposition 8.2.3 , and the second case is excluded because $\varphi +h$ is finite almost everywhere on the image under the biholomorphism $\pi $ of the nonempty open set $W\setminus \pi ^{-1}(A)$. Thus $\varphi \circ \pi \in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\pi ^*	heta )$. If $\varphi \circ \pi =\varphi '\circ \pi $, then $\varphi =\varphi '$ on $X\setminus A$, hence almost everywhere, and therefore everywhere, as noted at the beginning of this section; this proves injectivity. The pullback $\varphi \circ \pi $ equals $\psi $ outside the null set $\pi ^{-1}(A)$, hence everywhere. This proves surjectivity. By the continuity of the supremum, it suffices to treat normalized functions, $\sup _ X\varphi _ j=\sup _ X\varphi =0$, since subtracting the suprema preserves $L^1$ convergence. The pullbacks have the same suprema, because $\pi $ is surjective, so they are relatively compact in $L^1(Y)$, and every cluster value lies in $\mathrm{PSH}(Y,\pi ^*	heta )$. u (\varphi \circ \pi ,E)$ is the infimum over $y\in E$ of the point Lelong numbers $
u (\varphi \circ \pi ,y)$. Near $y$ choose a smooth $g$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g=\pi ^*	heta $, so that the functions $\varphi \circ \pi +g$ are plurisubharmonic. By ( 12.8 ), applied to them, each $
u (\varphi \circ \pi ,y)$ is upper semicontinuous for $L^1$ convergence of $\varphi \circ \pi $, hence, by the continuity just proved, for $L^1$ convergence of $\varphi $; and an infimum of upper semicontinuous functions is upper semicontinuous. Since Lelong numbers do not change when a constant is added, we may restrict to the normalized functions, which form a compact set by proposition 14.2.1 . An upper semicontinuous function with finite values attains its maximum on a compact set, which gives the uniform bound. $\square$ Corollary 14.2.9 . Let $B'$ be a coordinate ball in $X$ and $B\Subset B'$ a ball in the same coordinates, and let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ be bounded near $\overline{B'}$. There is $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ with $\psi \geq \varphi $, $\psi =\varphi $ on $X\setminus B$, $\psi $ bounded near $\overline B$, and $(	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi )^ n=0$ on $B$. It is the largest function in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ with these properties, and any two functions with these properties that are continuous on $\overline B$ coincide. Proof. Choose a ball $B''$ in the same coordinates with $\overline B\subset B''$ and $\overline{B''}\subset B'$. Write $	heta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h$ on $B''$, with $h$ smooth (lemma 13.1.2 ), and apply corollary 9.6.4 to the locally bounded plurisubharmonic function $\varphi +h$ on $B''$. Subtracting $h$ from the result on $B''$ and keeping $\varphi $ outside $B''$ gives $\psi $, since the result equals $\varphi +h$ on $B''\setminus B$; here $(	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi )^ n=(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\psi +h))^ n$ is the Bedford–Taylor product of the bounded plurisubharmonic function $\psi +h$. If $\psi '$ is another function with the stated properties, then by upper semicontinuity $\varlimsup _{z	o \zeta ,\, z\in B}\psi '(z)\leq \psi '(\zeta )=\varphi (\zeta )$ for every $\zeta \in \partial B$. Hence $\psi '+h$ belongs to the family whose upper envelope is $\psi +h$ in corollary 9.6.4 , and $\psi '\leq \psi $ on $B$. If $\psi '$ is continuous on $\overline B$, then its boundary values $\varphi |_{\partial B}$ are continuous, and $\psi '+h$ is the solution of the homogeneous Dirichlet problem with the continuous boundary values $(\varphi +h)|_{\partial B}$; by the uniqueness in theorem 9.6.3 , any two such continuous functions coincide. $\square$

title: Normalized global psh compactness
topic: Global potentials and positive cohomology classes
text: Proposition 14.2.1 . Let $a\leq b$ be real numbers. The set of $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $a\leq \sup _ X\varphi \leq b$ is compact in $L^1(X)$, and the map $\varphi \mapsto \sup _ X\varphi $ is continuous on $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ for the $L^1$ topology. In particular, the functions $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $\sup _ X\varphi =0$ are uniformly bounded in $L^1(X)$. The same statements hold for a sequence of backgrounds: if smooth closed real $(1,1)$-forms $\theta _ j$ converge smoothly to $\theta $ and $\varphi _ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta _ j)$ satisfy $a\leq \sup _ X\varphi _ j\leq b$, then a subsequence converges in $L^1(X)$ to some $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $a\leq \sup _ X\varphi \leq b$, and $\sup _ X\varphi _ j\to \sup _ X\varphi $ whenever $\varphi _ j\to \varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ in $L^1(X)$. The assertions for a fixed background hold more generally on every connected compact complex manifold $X'$ of positive dimension, for every smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form $\theta '$ on $X'$, with $L^1(X')$ taken with respect to any smooth positive volume form. Proof. Choose finitely many coordinate balls $B_ k$ covering $X$, smaller concentric balls $B'_ k$ still covering $X$, and smooth functions $h_ k$ near $\overline{B_ k}$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h_ k=\theta $ (lemma 13.1.2 , applied on slightly larger concentric balls). For $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ the functions $\varphi +h_ k$ are plurisubharmonic on $B_ k$. Let $(\varphi _ j)$ be a sequence with $a\leq \sup _ X\varphi _ j\leq b$. The plurisubharmonic functions $\varphi _ j+h_ k$ are uniformly bounded above on each $B_ k$. Since $\varphi _ j$ is upper semicontinuous on the compact manifold $X$, it attains its supremum at a point $x_ j$, and after passing to a subsequence $x_ j\to x$, since $X$ is compact and metrizable. Choose $k$ with $x\in B'_ k$. On $B_ k$ the functions $\varphi _ j+h_ k$ cannot converge locally uniformly to $-\infty $, because their values at $x_ j$ are bounded below by $a+\inf _{B'_ k}h_ k$ for large $j$. By theorem 8.3.4 , a further subsequence converges in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(B_ k)$. If $B_ l$ meets $B_ k$, the functions $\varphi _ j+h_ l$ cannot tend to $-\infty $ locally uniformly on $B_ l$, since on the nonempty open set $B_ k\cap B_ l$ they differ by the smooth function $h_ l-h_ k$ from a sequence that converges in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$; so again a subsequence converges in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(B_ l)$. Since $X$ is connected, every ball is joined to $B_ k$ by a finite chain of overlapping balls, and after finitely many extractions the sequence converges in $L^1(B'_ l)$ for every $l$, hence in $L^1(X)$, to some $\varphi $. The limit satisfies $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi \geq 0$ as a distributional limit of positive currents, and its canonical representative belongs to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Now let $\varphi _ j\to \varphi $ in $L^1(X)$, all in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$; we show that $\sup _ X\varphi _ j\to \sup _ X\varphi $. The submean inequality for $\varphi _ j+h_ k$ on small balls shows that the $\varphi _ j$ are uniformly bounded above. Let $x_ j\to x$; we claim that $\varlimsup _ j\varphi _ j(x_ j)\leq \varphi (x)$. Indeed, choose $k$ with $x\in B_ k$, let $c>\varphi (x)$ be real, and use upper semicontinuity to choose a closed ball $K\subset B_ k$ around $x$ on which $\varphi <c$. The function $c+h_ k$ is continuous near $K$ and $\varphi +h_ k<c+h_ k$ on $K$, so the second part of theorem 8.3.4 gives $\varphi _ j+h_ k<c+h_ k$ on $K$ for large $j$; hence $\varphi _ j(x_ j)<c$ for large $j$. Choose a subsequence along which $\sup _ X\varphi _ j$ tends to $\varlimsup _ j\sup _ X\varphi _ j$ and points $x_ j$ with $\varphi _ j(x_ j)=\sup _ X\varphi _ j$ converge to some $x$; the claim gives $\varlimsup _ j\sup _ X\varphi _ j\leq \varphi (x)\leq \sup _ X\varphi $. Conversely, choose a subsequence along which $\sup _ X\varphi _ j$ tends to $\varliminf _ j\sup _ X\varphi _ j$ and $\sum _ j\| \varphi _ j-\varphi \| _{L^1}<\infty $; by monotone convergence $\sum _ j|\varphi _ j-\varphi |$ is integrable, hence finite almost everywhere, so $\varphi _ j\to \varphi $ almost everywhere along it. We get $\varphi \leq \varliminf _ j\sup _ X\varphi _ j$ almost everywhere, hence everywhere, as noted at the beginning of this section. The two inequalities prove that the supremum is continuous; in particular, the limit in the previous paragraph satisfies $a\leq \sup _ X\varphi \leq b$. Thus the set in question is sequentially compact, hence compact, in the metric space $L^1(X)$. The continuous function $\| \cdot \| _{L^1}$ is bounded on the compact set of normalized functions. The arguments so far use only that $X$ is a connected compact complex manifold of positive dimension and that the volume form defining $L^1(X)$ is smooth and positive; hence they also prove the last assertion of the proposition. For smoothly convergent backgrounds, choose $C\geq 0$ with $\theta _ j\leq C\omega $ for all $j$. Then $C\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ j\geq 0$, so all $\varphi _ j$ lie in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,C\omega )$, and the first part, applied to the closed form $C\omega $, gives an $L^1$-convergent subsequence and the convergence of the suprema. Since $\theta _ j+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ j\to \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $ as distributions, the limit belongs to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. $\square$

title: Normalized global psh lp bound
topic: Global potentials and positive cohomology classes
text: Corollary 14.2.2 . For every $1\leq p<\infty $ there is a constant $M_ p$, depending only on $X$, $\theta $, $\omega $ and $p$, such that \[  \| u\| _{L^ p(X,\omega ^ n)}\leq M_ p \quad \text{for all }u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )\text{ with }\sup _ Xu=0.  \] Proof. (If $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ is empty, there is nothing to prove.) Choose finitely many coordinate polydiscs $D_ k$ such that the polydiscs $\frac14D_ k$ with the same centers and a quarter of the radii cover $X$, and smooth functions $h_ k$ near $\overline{D_ k}$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h_ k=\theta $. For $u$ as in the statement, $v_ k=u+h_ k-\sup _{D_ k}h_ k$ is a nonpositive plurisubharmonic function on $D_ k$. By proposition 14.2.1 and the boundedness of the $h_ k$ and of the coordinate volume densities, the norms $\| v_ k\| _{L^1(D_ k)}$ are bounded independently of $u$. After rescaling $D_ k$ to the unit polydisc, ( 8.6 ) bounds $\| v_ k\| _{L^ p(\frac14D_ k)}$ independently of $u$. Since $u=v_ k-h_ k+\sup _{D_ k}h_ k$ on $D_ k$, the bounded functions $h_ k$ and the bounded volume densities give the assertion. $\square$

title: Normalized global psh exponential bound
topic: Global potentials and positive cohomology classes
text: Corollary 14.2.3 . There are $\alpha ,C>0$, depending only on $X$, $\theta $ and $\omega $, such that 14.17 \begin{equation} \label{eq:normalized-global-psh-exponential-bound} \int _ X\mathrm e^{-\alpha u}\omega ^ n\leq C \quad \text{for all }u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )\text{ with }\sup _ Xu=0. \end{equation} Proof. (If $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ is empty, any $\alpha ,C>0$ will do.) Choose finitely many coordinate unit balls $B_ j$ such that the balls $\frac14B_ j$ with the same centers and a quarter of the radii cover $X$, and smooth functions $\rho _ j$ near $\overline{B_ j}$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho _ j=\theta $. For $u$ as in the statement put $v_ j=u+\rho _ j-\sup _{B_ j}\rho _ j$ on $B_ j$; then $v_ j$ is plurisubharmonic and $v_ j\leq u\leq 0$. By proposition 14.2.1 and comparison of the coordinate volume densities, $\| v_ j\| _{L^1(B_ j)}\leq M_ j$ for a constant $M_ j\geq 1$ independent of $u$. Applying proposition 8.3.9 to $v_ j/M_ j$, we see that $\int _{\frac14B_ j}\mathrm e^{-\alpha _ jv_ j}$ is bounded independently of $u$, where $\alpha _ j=\alpha _ n/M_ j$. Put $\alpha =\min _ j\alpha _ j>0$. Since $v_ j\leq u\leq 0$ and $\alpha \leq \alpha _ j$, we have $\mathrm e^{-\alpha u}\leq \mathrm e^{-\alpha _ ju}\leq \mathrm e^{-\alpha _ jv_ j}$ on $B_ j$. Summing over $j$ and comparing the coordinate volume densities with $\omega ^ n$ gives ( 14.17 ). $\square$

title: Nonpluripolar normalization
topic: Global potentials and positive cohomology classes
text: Corollary 14.2.4 . Let $K\subset X$ be a compact set that is not pluripolar. Then there is a constant $C$ such that \[  \sup _ X\varphi \leq \sup _ K\varphi +C\qquad \text{for all }\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ).  \] Consequently, every subset of $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ on which $\sup _ K\varphi $ is bounded above and below is relatively compact in $L^1(X)$. Proof. Suppose that no such constant exists. Since $\sup _ X\varphi -\sup _ K\varphi $ does not change when a constant is added to $\varphi $, there are $\varphi _ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $\sup _ X\varphi _ j=0$ and $\sup _ K\varphi _ j\leq -2^ j$. Choose $C\geq 0$ with $\theta \leq C\omega $ (lemma 13.1.1 ) and put $\psi _ N=\sum _{j=1}^ N2^{-j}\varphi _ j$. Since $\sum _{j\leq N}2^{-j}\leq 1$, we have \[  C\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi _ N=\Bigl (1-\sum _{j\leq N}2^{-j}\Bigr )C\omega +\sum _{j\leq N}2^{-j}(C\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ j)\geq \sum _{j\leq N}2^{-j}(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ j)\geq 0.  \] The sequence $(\psi _ N)$ is decreasing because $\varphi _ j\leq 0$, and $\| \psi _ N\| _{L^1}\leq \sup _ j\| \varphi _ j\| _{L^1}<\infty $ by proposition 14.2.1 . By monotone convergence the limit $\psi $ is integrable, so it is not identically $-\infty $, and theorem 8.3.1 , applied on coordinate balls after adding local potentials of $C\omega $, shows that $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,C\omega )$. On $K$ every term $2^{-j}\varphi _ j$ is at most $-1$, so $\psi =-\infty $ on $K$. On every coordinate ball $U$ with a smooth function $h$ such that $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h=C\omega $, the function $\psi +h$ is plurisubharmonic and equals $-\infty $ on $K\cap U$. Hence $K$ is pluripolar, a contradiction. The last assertion follows: bounds for $\sup _ K\varphi $ give bounds for $\sup _ X\varphi $, and proposition 14.2.1 applies. $\square$

title: Global decreasing nets
topic: Global potentials and positive cohomology classes
text: Corollary 14.2.5 . Let $(\varphi _ i)$ be a decreasing net in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ whose suprema $\sup _ X\varphi _ i$ are bounded below. Then its pointwise infimum $\varphi $ belongs to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, $\varphi _ i\to \varphi $ in $L^1(X)$, and $\sup _ X\varphi _ i\to \sup _ X\varphi $. Proof. Fix an index $i_0$. For $i\geq i_0$ the suprema are bounded above by $\sup _ X\varphi _{i_0}$, so the tail of the net lies in a compact subset of $L^1(X)$ by proposition 14.2.1 , and a subnet converges in $L^1$ to some $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. For each fixed $i$, the members of the subnet are eventually below $\varphi _ i$, so $\psi \leq \varphi _ i$ almost everywhere, and therefore everywhere, as noted at the beginning of this section. Hence the pointwise infimum $\varphi $ is at least $\psi $ and is not identically $-\infty $. Applying theorem 8.3.1 on the coordinate balls of a finite cover, after adding local potentials of $\theta $, we find that $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and $\varphi _ i\to \varphi $ in $L^1(X)$. The continuity of the supremum in proposition 14.2.1 gives the last assertion. $\square$

title: Global minimal potential
topic: Global potentials and positive cohomology classes
text: Definition 14.2.6 . Let $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Recall from section 13.5 that $\varphi $ is more singular than $\psi $, written $\varphi \preceq \psi $, if $\varphi \leq \psi +C$ on $X$ for some constant $C$; we then also say that $\psi $ is less singular than $\varphi $. A potential $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ has minimal singularities if every $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ is more singular than $\psi $. If $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )\ne \varnothing $, put \[  V_\theta =\bigl (\sup \{ \varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ):\varphi \leq 0\} \bigr )^*,  \] where ${}^*$ denotes the upper semicontinuous regularization.

title: Global minimal envelope
topic: Global potentials and positive cohomology classes
text: Lemma 14.2.7 . Suppose that $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )\neq \varnothing $. Then $V_\theta \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, $\sup _ XV_\theta =0$, and $\varphi \leq V_\theta +\sup _ X\varphi $ for every $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$; in particular, $V_\theta $ has minimal singularities. Any two potentials with minimal singularities differ by a bounded function on the set where both are finite, and the notion of minimal singularities depends only on the class $\{ \theta \} $. Proof. The family whose upper envelope defines $V_\theta $ in definition 14.2.6 is nonempty, because $\varphi -\sup _ X\varphi $ belongs to it for every $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, and it is bounded above by $0$. Theorem 8.3.2 , applied on coordinate balls after adding smooth local potentials of $\theta $, therefore gives $V_\theta \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and $V_\theta \leq 0$; and $\sup _ XV_\theta =0$, because $V_\theta \geq \varphi -\sup _ X\varphi $ for every $\varphi $. The same inequality reads $\varphi \leq V_\theta +\sup _ X\varphi $, so $V_\theta $ has minimal singularities. Any two potentials with minimal singularities are each more singular than the other, so their difference is bounded on the set where both are finite. Replacing $\theta $ by $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h$ with $h$ smooth replaces $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ by $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )-h$; since $h$ is bounded, the notion of minimal singularities depends only on the class $\{ \theta \} $. $\square$

u (\varphi \circ \pi ,y)$ is upper semicontinuous for $L^1$ convergence of $\varphi \circ \pi $, hence, by the continuity just proved, for $L^1$ convergence of $\varphi $; and an infimum of upper semicontinuous functions is upper semicontinuous. An upper semicontinuous function with finite values attains its maximum on a compact set, which gives the uniform bound. $\square$

title: Global psh balayage
topic: Global potentials and positive cohomology classes
text: Corollary 14.2.9 . Let $B'$ be a coordinate ball in $X$ and $B\Subset B'$ a ball in the same coordinates, and let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ be bounded near $\overline{B'}$. There is $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $\psi \geq \varphi $, $\psi =\varphi $ on $X\setminus B$, $\psi $ bounded near $\overline B$, and $(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi )^ n=0$ on $B$. It is the largest function in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with these properties, and any two functions with these properties that are continuous on $\overline B$ coincide. Proof. Choose a ball $B''$ in the same coordinates with $\overline B\subset B''$ and $\overline{B''}\subset B'$. Write $\theta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h$ on $B''$, with $h$ smooth (lemma 13.1.2 ), and apply corollary 9.6.4 to the locally bounded plurisubharmonic function $\varphi +h$ on $B''$. Subtracting $h$ from the result on $B''$ and keeping $\varphi $ outside $B''$ gives $\psi $, since the result equals $\varphi +h$ on $B''\setminus B$; here $(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi )^ n=(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\psi +h))^ n$ is the Bedford–Taylor product of the bounded plurisubharmonic function $\psi +h$. If $\psi '$ is another function with the stated properties, then by upper semicontinuity $\varlimsup _{z\to \zeta ,\, z\in B}\psi '(z)\leq \psi '(\zeta )=\varphi (\zeta )$ for every $\zeta \in \partial B$. Hence $\psi '+h$ belongs to the family whose upper envelope is $\psi +h$ in corollary 9.6.4 , and $\psi '\leq \psi $ on $B$. If $\psi '$ is continuous on $\overline B$, then its boundary values $\varphi |_{\partial B}$ are continuous, and $\psi '+h$ is the solution of the homogeneous Dirichlet problem with the continuous boundary values $(\varphi +h)|_{\partial B}$; by the uniqueness in theorem 9.6.3 , any two such continuous functions coincide. $\square$

title: Positivity cones and divisorial decomposition
topic: Global potentials and positive cohomology classes
