Hence a current $S\geq \delta \omega _ Y$ on $Y$ has $\pi _*S\geq \delta C^{-1}\omega $, which proves the assertion for $\pi _*$. Let $\alpha $ be big on $X$ and $T\in \alpha $ with $T\geq \delta \omega $. Choose a smooth closed representative $\eta $ of the class $\{ \pi _*\omega _ Y\} $, a constant $B>0$ with $\eta \leq B\omega $ (lemma 13.1.1 ), and $t>0$ with $tB\leq \delta $, so that $T-t\eta \geq 0$. The positive current $T-t\eta +t\pi _*\omega _ Y$ lies in $\alpha $. By lemma 14.4.6 , applied to the smooth, hence non-divisorial, current $\omega _ Y$, its pullback is \[  \pi ^*(T-t\eta )+t\omega _ Y+t\sum _ E c_ E[E]\geq t\omega _ Y.  \] This is a Kähler current in $\pi ^*\alpha $, so $\pi ^*\alpha $ is big. $\square$

title: Nef boundary minimal current
topic: Global potentials and positive cohomology classes
text: Example 14.4.8 . The zero class $\alpha =0$ is nef, so $E_{\mathrm{nn}}(0)=\varnothing $ by theorem 14.4.4 . It is not big: a Kähler current $T\geq \delta \omega $ would have $\int _ XT\wedge \omega ^{n-1}\geq \delta \int _ X\omega ^ n>0$, whereas this integral vanishes for every closed current in the zero class. Hence $E_{\mathrm{nK}}(0)=X$. More generally, $E_{\mathrm{nK}}(\alpha )=X$ for every class that is not big, while $E_{\mathrm{nn}}(\alpha )=\varnothing $ for every nef class; on the boundary of the pseudo-effective cone the two loci therefore detect different failures of positivity. This is also why the minimal multiplicities are defined with the allowances $\varepsilon \omega $ rather than through $V_\theta $: for a class that is not big, proposition 14.4.2 gives only the inequality $\nu (\alpha ,x)\leq \nu (V_\theta ,x)$, since the proof of equality uses a Kähler current in $\alpha $.

title: Curvature and metrics defined by sections
topic: Global potentials and positive cohomology classes
text:
14.5 Curvature and metrics defined by sections This section collects the notions for line bundles on $X$ used in the rest of the chapter, from the curvature class to the Fubini–Study metrics defined by holomorphic sections, and shows that spaces of global holomorphic sections are finite dimensional. Let $L	o X$ be a holomorphic line bundle, given as in definition 13.1.8 by frames $e_ i$ over an open cover $(V_ i)$ of $X$, and let $h_0$ be a smooth quadratic Hermitian metric on $L$. Its curvature form, which we denote by $c_1(L,h_0)$, equals $-\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |e_ i|_{h_0}^2$ on $V_ i$. It also equals $-\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |e|_{h_0}^2$ for every local holomorphic frame $e$ of $L$: on $V_ i$ we have $e=ge_ i$ with $g$ holomorphic and nowhere zero, so $\log |e|_{h_0}^2=\log |g|^2+\log |e_ i|_{h_0}^2$, and $\log |g|^2$ is pluriharmonic (section 7.3 ). Any other smooth metric is $h_1=h_0\mathrm e^{-f}$ with $f$ smooth and real, and then $c_1(L,h_1)=c_1(L,h_0)+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$ (lemma 13.1.9 (3)). Hence the class $c_1(L)=\{ c_1(L,h_0)\} \in H^{1,1}(X,\mathbb R)$ does not depend on the metric. A holomorphic section of $L$ is given by holomorphic functions $f_ i$ on $V_ i$ with $f_ ie_ i=f_ je_ j$ on $V_ i\cap V_ j$. If $L$ and $L'$ are given by frames $e_ i$ and $e'_ i$ over a common cover, with transition functions $g_{ij}$ and $g'_{ij}$, their tensor product $L\otimes L'$ is given by the frames $e_ i\otimes e'_ i$ with the transition functions $g_{ij}g'_{ij}$, and the dual $L^{-1}$ of $L$ by the dual frames $e_ i^*$ with the transition functions $g_{ij}^{-1}$. Metrics on $L$ and $L'$ induce metrics with $|e_ i\otimes e'_ i|^2=|e_ i|^2|e'_ i|^2$ and $|e_ i^*|^2=|e_ i|^{-2}$. The curvature of a tensor product of metrics is the sum of the curvatures, and the curvature of a pullback metric is the pullback of the curvature, because the logarithms of the squared norms of local frames add, respectively compose. Line bundles are trivial over coordinate balls; we use this to work in a single frame on balls of a fixed size. Lemma 14.5.1 . Let $L$ be a holomorphic line bundle on a complex manifold $M$, and let $B$ be a coordinate ball whose closure is contained in the domain of its chart. Then $L$ has a holomorphic frame over $B$, that is, a nowhere vanishing holomorphic section of $L$ on $B$. Proof. We make the metric flat on $B$ and obtain the frame by parallel transport along the segments issuing from the center of $B$. Choose a smooth metric $h_0$ on $L$ (lemma 13.1.9 (1)). By lemma 13.1.2 there is a smooth real function $p$ on $B$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}p=c_1(L,h_0)$, and the metric $h_1=h_0\mathrm e^{p}$ on $L|_ B$ has curvature $c_1(L,h_0)-\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}p=0$, by lemma 13.1.9 (3). We call a holomorphic frame of $h_1$-length one over an open subset of $B$ a unit frame . Unit frames exist near every point of $B$. Indeed, every point of $B$ has a ball neighborhood $V\subset B$ over which $L$ has a holomorphic frame $e$, and $\log |e|_{h_1}^2$ is smooth and pluriharmonic, since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |e|_{h_1}^2=-c_1(L,h_1)=0$, so by lemma 13.1.2 it equals $\operatorname{Re}F$ for a holomorphic function $F$ on $V$, and $\mathrm e^{-F/2}e$ is a unit frame. Two unit frames on a connected open set differ by a holomorphic factor $g$ with $|g|=1$; then $ ar g=1/g$ is both holomorphic and antiholomorphic, so $\mathrm d ar g=0$ and $g$ is constant. Let $c$ be the center of $B$ and fix a unit vector $e_ c\in L_ c$. For $z\in B$, a flat lift along the segment from $c$ to $z$ is a continuous map $t\mapsto \varepsilon (t)\in L_{c+t(z-c)}$, $t\in [0,1]$, with $\varepsilon (0)=e_ c$, which near every $t$ is a constant multiple of a unit frame. There is at most one flat lift: if $\varepsilon '$ is another one, then $\varepsilon '=g\varepsilon $ for a continuous function $g$ on $[0,1]$ which is locally constant, by the preceding paragraph, and equals $1$ at $t=0$, so $g=1$. It remains to show that flat lifts exist and that their values at $t=1$ depend holomorphically on $z$. Let $z_0\in B$, and choose $\delta _0>0$ with $\overline{B(z_0,\delta _0)}\subset B$. The set $\Gamma _0=\{ c+t(z-c):t\in [0,1],\  |z-z_0|\leq \delta _0\} $ is a compact subset of the convex set $B$. Cover it by finitely many balls $V_ i\subset B$ carrying unit frames $e_ i$, let $\lambda >0$ be a Lebesgue number of this cover, choose $\delta \leq \delta _0$ with $2\delta <\lambda /2$, and choose $0=t_0<t_1<\cdots <t_ N=1$ with $(t_ k-t_{k-1})(|z_0-c|+\delta _0)<\lambda /2$. For $W=B(z_0,\delta )$, each set $\Gamma _ k=\{ c+t(z-c):t\in [t_{k-1},t_ k],\  z\in W\} $ has diameter less than $\lambda $, because $|(c+t(z-c))-(c+t'(z'-c))|\leq |t-t'|\, |z-c|+|z-z'|$; so $\Gamma _ k$ lies in some $V_{i_ k}$. The convex set $V_{i_ k}\cap V_{i_{k+1}}$ is connected and contains $c+t_ k(z_0-c)$, so $e_{i_ k}=\gamma _ ke_{i_{k+1}}$ there for a constant $\gamma _ k$. Let $a$ be the number with $e_ c=a\, e_{i_1}(c)$. For $z\in W$, the map equal to $a\gamma _1\cdots \gamma _{k-1}e_{i_ k}(c+t(z-c))$ for $t\in [t_{k-1},t_ k]$ is well defined at the points $t_ k$ and is a flat lift along the segment from $c$ to $z$. Hence, on $W$, the value $E(z)$ of the unique flat lift at $t=1$ is $a\gamma _1\cdots \gamma _{N-1}e_{i_ N}(z)$, a constant multiple of the unit frame $e_{i_ N}$. Since $z_0$ was arbitrary, $E$ is a nowhere vanishing holomorphic section of $L$ on $B$. $\square$ Families of holomorphic sections that are bounded in $L^2$ are relatively compact for uniform convergence. Lemma 14.5.2 . Let $U\subset \mathbb C^ n$ be open, $n\geq 1$, and let $(f_ j)$ be a sequence of holomorphic functions on $U$ with $\sup _ j\int _ U|f_ j|^2\, \mathrm dV<\infty $. Then a subsequence converges locally uniformly on $U$ to a holomorphic function. Let $E$ be a holomorphic line bundle on $X$ with a smooth quadratic metric $h_ E$, and let $(s_ j)$ be a sequence of holomorphic sections of $E$ over $X$ with $\sup _ j\int _ X|s_ j|_{h_ E}^2\, \mathrm dV<\infty $. Then a subsequence converges uniformly on $X$ to a holomorphic section $s$ of $E$, that is, $\sup _ X|s_ j-s|_{h_ E}	o 0$ along the subsequence. For every holomorphic line bundle $E$ on $X$, the space $H^0(X,E)$ of holomorphic sections of $E$ over $X$ is finite dimensional. Assertions (2) and (3) hold more generally on every compact complex manifold $X'$ of positive dimension in place of $X$, with $\mathrm dV$ in (2) replaced by any smooth positive volume form on $X'$. Proof. (1) Let $M$ be the supremum in the statement. If $\overline{B(z,\delta )}\subset U$, then $|f_ j(z)|^2\leq |B(z,\delta )|^{-1}M$ by ( 12.9 ). Hence the $f_ j$ are uniformly bounded on every compact subset of $U$: if $K\subset U$ is compact and $\delta >0$ is smaller than the distance from $K$ to $\mathbb C^ n\setminus U$ (any $\delta >0$ if $U=\mathbb C^ n$), then $|f_ j|^2\leq |B(0,\delta )|^{-1}M$ on $K$. We next show that the sequence is equicontinuous on compact sets. Let $K\subset U$ be compact, and choose $r>0$ such that the compact set $K'$ of points at distance at most $2\sqrt n\, r$ from $K$ lies in $U$; let $M'$ be a bound for all $|f_ j|$ on $K'$. For $z$ at distance at most $\sqrt n\, r$ from $K$, the closed polydisc of radius $r$ centered at $z$ lies in $K'$, and the coefficient bound in ( 7.1 ) gives $|\partial _{z_ l}f_ j(z)|\leq M'/r$ for $1\leq l\leq n$. Since $\mathrm df_ j=\sum _ l\partial _{z_ l}f_ j\, \mathrm dz_ l$, the $f_ j$ are Lipschitz with a common constant on every ball of radius $\sqrt n\, r$ centered at a point of $K$, so the sequence is equicontinuous on $K$. By proposition 1.6.4 , applied on the compact sets $K_ m=\{ z\in U:|z|\leq m,\  \operatorname {dist}(z,\mathbb C^ n\setminus U)\geq 1/m\} $, which exhaust $U$, and a diagonal argument, a subsequence converges locally uniformly on $U$ to a continuous function $f$. Then $ ar\partial f=0$ in the sense of distributions, as a limit of $ ar\partial f_ j=0$, so $f$ agrees almost everywhere with a holomorphic function by lemma 11.3.5 (1); both being continuous, $f$ is holomorphic. (2) Choose finitely many coordinate balls $B_ k$, with closures in the domains of their charts, such that the concentric balls $B'_ k$ of half the radius cover $X$, and let $B''_ k$ be the concentric balls of three quarters of the radius. By lemma 14.5.1 , $E$ has a holomorphic frame $e_ k$ over $B_ k$; write $s_ j=f_{j,k}e_ k$ on $B_ k$. On the compact set $\overline{B''_ k}$ the function $|e_ k|_{h_ E}^2$ is bounded below by a positive constant and $\mathrm dV$ is bounded below by a positive multiple of Lebesgue measure in the chart, so the integrals of $|f_{j,k}|^2$ over $B''_ k$ with respect to Lebesgue measure in the chart are bounded independently of $j$. Applying (1) successively for the finitely many $k$, we obtain a subsequence along which $f_{j,k}$ converges locally uniformly on $B''_ k$, hence uniformly on $\overline{B'_ k}$, to a holomorphic function $f_ k$, for every $k$. On $B''_ k\cap B''_ l$ the sections $f_ ke_ k$ and $f_ le_ l$ are both the pointwise limit of $s_ j$, so they define a holomorphic section $s$ of $E$ over $X$, and $\sup _{B'_ k}|s_ j-s|_{h_ E}\leq \sup _{\overline{B'_ k}}|e_ k|_{h_ E}\cdot \sup _{\overline{B'_ k}}|f_{j,k}-f_ k|	o 0$ for every $k$. (3) Fix a smooth quadratic metric $h_ E$ on $E$ (lemma 13.1.9 (1)). The integral $\| s\| ^2=\int _ X|s|_{h_ E}^2\, \mathrm dV$ defines an inner product on $H^0(X,E)$: if $\| s\| =0$, then the continuous function $|s|_{h_ E}$ vanishes almost everywhere, hence everywhere. If $H^0(X,E)$ were infinite dimensional, the Gram–Schmidt process would give an orthonormal sequence $(s_ j)$. By (2), a subsequence converges uniformly on $X$, hence in $L^2$, since $X$ has finite volume; but $\| s_ i-s_ j\| ^2=2$ for $i
eq j$. This contradiction proves (3). The proofs of (2) and (3) use only that $X$ is a compact complex manifold of positive dimension and that $\mathrm dV$ is a smooth positive volume form; hence they also prove the last assertion of the lemma. $\square$ A line bundle is positive if it admits a smooth metric with positive definite curvature form. It is very ample if its full space of global holomorphic sections defines a holomorphic embedding into a projective space: this space is finite dimensional by lemma 14.5.2 (3), and for a basis $s_0,\ldots ,s_ N$ we require that the sections have no common zero and that $x\mapsto [s_0(x):\cdots :s_ N(x)]$ is a holomorphic embedding of $X$ into $\mathbb P^ N$. A compact complex manifold is projective if it admits a holomorphic embedding into a projective space. Definition 14.5.3 . A plurisubharmonic metric on $L$ is a quadratic metric of the form $h=h_0\mathrm e^{-\varphi }$ with $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,c_1(L,h_0))$. It assigns the value zero to the zero vector, also over the pole set of $\varphi $, and the value $+\infty $ to a nonzero vector over a pole of $\varphi $. Its Chern current is \[  c_1(L,h)=c_1(L,h_0)+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi .  \] This definition uses the pointwise function $\varphi $, that is, the canonical quasi-plurisubharmonic representative; for an arbitrary measurable weight, the distributional curvature inequality would determine the metric only almost everywhere. If $h_0$ is replaced by $h_0\mathrm e^{-f}$, then $\varphi $ is replaced by $\varphi -f$, so the class of plurisubharmonic metrics and the pointwise metric $h$ do not depend on $h_0$. In particular, $L$ admits a plurisubharmonic metric if and only if $c_1(L)$ is pseudo-effective. The tensor product of two plurisubharmonic metrics is defined by adding their local weights; the norm of a nonzero vector is infinite over a pole of either factor. The pullback of a plurisubharmonic metric by a holomorphic map is a plurisubharmonic metric provided the pulled-back weights are not identically $-\infty $ on any connected component; the restriction to a submanifold is defined under the same condition. Proposition 14.5.4 . For a nonzero holomorphic section $s$ of $L$ and a smooth metric $h_0$, 14.22  egin{equation} \label{eq:line-bundle-poincare-lelong} c_1(L,h_0)+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |s|_{h_0}^2=[Z(s)], \end{equation} where $[Z(s)]$ is the current of integration along the zero divisor of $s$, counted with multiplicities. In particular $[Z(s)]$ represents $c_1(L)$. Proof. In a local frame write $s=fe$. Since $\log |s|_{h_0}^2=\log |f|^2+\log |e|_{h_0}^2$, the left side equals $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |f|^2$, which is the current of integration along the zero divisor of $f$ by theorem 7.4.5 . These local divisors agree on overlaps, because the transition functions have no zeros. $\square$ Example 14.5.5 . Let $N\geq 0$. The projective space $\mathbb P^ N$ is the quotient of $\mathbb C^{N+1}\setminus \{ 0\} $ by the action of $\mathbb C^*$ by multiplication, with the quotient topology; we write $q$ for the quotient map and $[Z]=[Z_0:\cdots :Z_ N]$ for the class of $Z$. For $0\leq i\leq N$ the sets $U_ i=\{ [Z]:Z_ i
eq 0\} $ are open and cover $\mathbb P^ N$, and the map $\phi _ i\colon U_ i	o \mathbb C^ N$, $[Z]\mapsto (Z_ k/Z_ i)_{k
eq i}$, is a homeomorphism: it is continuous because $\phi _ i\circ q$ is, and its inverse is $q$ composed with the map inserting the coordinate $1$ in the $i$th place. On $\phi _ i(U_ i\cap U_ j)=\{ w_ j
eq 0\} $, where we put $w_ i=1$, the transition map $\phi _ j\circ \phi _ i^{-1}$ is $w\mapsto (w_ k/w_ j)_{k
eq j}$, which is holomorphic, and so is its inverse $\phi _ i\circ \phi _ j^{-1}$. The space $\mathbb P^ N$ is compact and connected, as the image under $q$ of the unit sphere of $\mathbb C^{N+1}$. It is Hausdorff, because the continuous map $[Z]\mapsto Z\overline Z^{\mathsf T}/|Z|^2$ to the space of complex matrices is injective, the matrix being the orthogonal projection onto the line $\mathbb CZ$; and being compact, it is paracompact. Thus $\mathbb P^ N$ is a connected compact complex manifold of dimension $N$ (definition 7.1.1 ). The tautological line bundle $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^ N}(-1)$ has the fiber $\mathbb CZ$ over $[Z]$. In the sense of definition 13.1.8 it is given by the frames $e_ i([Z])=Z/Z_ i$ over $U_ i$, the points of the line with $i$th coordinate one. Since $e_ i=(Z_ j/Z_ i)e_ j$ on $U_ i\cap U_ j$, its transition functions are $g_{ij}=Z_ j/Z_ i$, which are holomorphic and nowhere zero on $U_ i\cap U_ j$ and satisfy $g_{ij}g_{jk}=g_{ik}$. The Euclidean norm of $\mathbb C^{N+1}$ gives the smooth metric $|e_ i|^2=|Z|^2/|Z_ i|^2$, which satisfies $|e_ i|^2=|g_{ij}|^2|e_ j|^2$. The dual line bundle $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^ N}(1)$ has the dual frames $e_ i^*$, with $e_ i^*(e_ i)=1$ and transition functions $g_{ij}^{-1}$, and the dual metric $|e_ i^*|^2=|e_ i|^{-2}=|Z_ i|^2/|Z|^2$, the Fubini–Study metric $h_{\mathrm{FS}}$. A linear form $\ell $ on $\mathbb C^{N+1}$ defines a holomorphic section $s_\ell $ of $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^ N}(1)$, the restriction of $\ell $ to the fibers of $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^ N}(-1)$: on $U_ i$ it is $s_\ell =\ell (e_ i)e_ i^*=(\ell (Z)/Z_ i)\, e_ i^*$, and these expressions agree on overlaps, because $\ell (e_ i)e_ i^*=\ell (g_{ij}e_ j)\, g_{ij}^{-1}e_ j^*$. For the coordinate forms we write $X_ k=s_{Z_ k}$. Thus $X_ i=e_ i^*$ on $U_ i$, and \[  |X_ k|_{\mathrm{FS}}^2([Z])= rac{|Z_ k|^2}{|Z|^2}.  \] The tensor power $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^ N}(k)=\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^ N}(1)^{\otimes k}$, $k\geq 1$, has the frames $(e_ i^*)^{\otimes k}$, the transition functions $g_{ij}^{-k}$ and the metric $h_{\mathrm{FS}}^ k$; products of $k$ sections of $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^ N}(1)$, such as the monomials $X_0^{a_0}\cdots X_ N^{a_ N}$ with $a_0+\cdots +a_ N=k$, are holomorphic sections of $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^ N}(k)$. Example 14.5.6 . Let $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^ N}(1)$ carry the Fubini–Study metric $h_{\mathrm{FS}}$ of example 14.5.5 , dual to the Euclidean norm on the tautological line. On the chart $U_0=\{ [1:z_1:\cdots :z_ N]\} $ the tautological line is spanned by $(1,z)$, so the frame $X_0=e_0^*$ has squared norm $|X_0(1,z)|^2/|(1,z)|^2=(1+|z|^2)^{-1}$, and the curvature is \[  \omega _{\mathrm{FS}}=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log (1+|z|^2).  \] The matrix of $\partial _ j\partial _{ ar k}\log (1+|z|^2)$ is $ igl ((1+|z|^2)\delta _{jk}- ar z_ jz_ k igr )/(1+|z|^2)^2$, which is positive definite by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality $|\sum _ j ar z_ j\xi _ j|^2\leq |z|^2|\xi |^2$. The same computation in the chart $U_ i$, with the frame $X_ i$, shows that $\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$ is a Kähler form on $\mathbb P^ N$; thus $\mathbb P^ N$ is a compact Kähler manifold. On $\mathbb P^1$, integration in polar coordinates gives $\int _{\mathbb P^1}\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}= rac1\pi \int _{\mathbb C}(1+|z|^2)^{-2}\, \mathrm dV=1$. The function $\log |X_1|_{\mathrm{FS}}^2=\log  igl (|z|^2/(1+|z|^2) igr )$, which vanishes at the point at infinity, is the weight of a singular plurisubharmonic metric whose Chern current is the Dirac current $[0]$ at the point $[1:0]$, by ( 14.22 ). Definition 14.5.7 . A Fubini–Study metric on $L$ is a metric $h_0\mathrm e^{-\varphi }$ with \[  \varphi = rac1m\max _{1\leq i\leq N}  igl (\log |s_ i|_{h_0^ m}^2+\lambda _ i igr ), \qquad m,N\in \mathbb Z_{\geq 1},\quad \lambda _ i\in \mathbb Q,  \] where $s_1,\ldots ,s_ N$ are holomorphic sections of $L^ m$, not all zero. We denote the set of these metrics by $\mathrm{FS}(L)$. The set of generalized Fubini–Study metrics is the smallest set of plurisubharmonic metrics that contains $\mathrm{FS}(L)$ and is closed under minima of metrics and under convex combinations of weights with rational coefficients. A convex combination of weights corresponds to the weighted geometric mean of the quadratic metrics, with value zero on the zero vector and the value $+\infty $ on a nonzero vector over a pole of a factor with positive coefficient. The classical Fubini–Study metric of example 14.5.6 , whose weight is the logarithm of a sum of squares rather than a maximum, does not belong to $\mathrm{FS}(\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^ N}(1))$ when $N\geq 1$, since its curvature form $\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$ is positive definite, whereas the curvature current of a metric in $\mathrm{FS}(L)$ vanishes on a nonempty open set. Indeed, one of the finitely many closed sets on which a single term attains the maximum has interior points. There, away from the zeros of the corresponding section $s_ i$, the induced metric on $L^ m$ gives $s_ i$ the constant norm $\mathrm e^{-\lambda _ i/2}$, so the curvature vanishes by proposition 14.5.4 . The classical metric differs, however, only by a bounded factor from a metric in $\mathrm{FS}(\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^ N}(1))$: with $h_0=h_{\mathrm{FS}}$, the coordinate sections $X_0,\ldots ,X_ N$, $m=1$ and $\lambda _ i=0$ give the metric $h_{\mathrm{FS}}\mathrm e^{-\varphi }$ with $\varphi =\max _ i\log |X_ i|_{\mathrm{FS}}^2$, and $1\leq \mathrm e^{-\varphi }\leq N+1$ because $|X_ i|_{\mathrm{FS}}^2([Z])=|Z_ i|^2/|Z|^2$. Proposition 14.5.8 . Fubini–Study metrics do not depend on the choice of $h_0$, they have analytic singularities, and $\mathrm{FS}(L)$ is closed under minima and rational convex combinations of weights. Consequently the generalized Fubini–Study metrics are exactly the metrics in $\mathrm{FS}(L)$. The set $\mathrm{FS}(L)$ is empty if no positive tensor power of $L$ has a nonzero holomorphic section, even when $L$ admits plurisubharmonic metrics. Proof. In a local frame $e$ write $s_ i=f_ ie^ m$. The local weight $-\log |e|_ h^2=\varphi -\log |e|_{h_0}^2$ of the metric equals $m^{-1}\max _ i(\log |f_ i|^2+\lambda _ i)$, which does not involve $h_0$; it is plurisubharmonic and not identically $-\infty $, since $X$ is connected and some $s_ i
e 0$. It differs by a bounded function from $m^{-1}\log \sum _ i\mathrm e^{\lambda _ i}|f_ i|^2$, so it has analytic singularities with the rational coefficient $1/m$; the pole set is the common zero set of the $s_ i$. Consider two such metrics, given by sections $s_ i$ of $L^ m$ with constants $\lambda _ i$ and sections $r_ j$ of $L^ l$ with constants $\mu _ j$. Replacing $s_ i$ by $s_ i^{M/m}$ and $\lambda _ i$ by $(M/m)\lambda _ i$, and similarly for the $r_ j$, where $M$ is a common multiple of $m$ and $l$, does not change the potentials, so we may assume that both are given in degree $M$. The maximum of the two potentials, which corresponds to the minimum of the metrics, is then given by the union of the two lists. For a rational $t=a/b\in (0,1)$, the combination $t\varphi +(1-t)\psi $ of the two maxima is the maximum over all pairs $(i,j)$ of the corresponding combinations, that is, \[  t\varphi +(1-t)\psi = rac1{Mb}\max _{i,j}\Bigl (\log  igl |s_ i^ ar_ j^{b-a} igr |_{h_0^{Mb}}^2+a\lambda _ i+(b-a)\mu _ j\Bigr ),  \] where the sections $s_ i^ ar_ j^{b-a}$ of $L^{Mb}$ are not all zero and the constants are rational. Thus $\mathrm{FS}(L)$ is closed under both operations, and by induction under every finite sequence of them, so the generated set is $\mathrm{FS}(L)$ itself. If no positive tensor power of $L$ has a nonzero section, no presentation as in definition 14.5.7 exists. $\square$

title: Line bundle ball frame
topic: Global potentials and positive cohomology classes
text: Lemma 14.5.1 . Let $L$ be a holomorphic line bundle on a complex manifold $M$, and let $B$ be a coordinate ball whose closure is contained in the domain of its chart. Then $L$ has a holomorphic frame over $B$, that is, a nowhere vanishing holomorphic section of $L$ on $B$. Proof. We make the metric flat on $B$ and obtain the frame by parallel transport along the segments issuing from the center of $B$. Choose a smooth metric $h_0$ on $L$ (lemma 13.1.9 (1)). By lemma 13.1.2 there is a smooth real function $p$ on $B$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}p=c_1(L,h_0)$, and the metric $h_1=h_0\mathrm e^{p}$ on $L|_ B$ has curvature $c_1(L,h_0)-\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}p=0$, by lemma 13.1.9 (3). We call a holomorphic frame of $h_1$-length one over an open subset of $B$ a unit frame . Unit frames exist near every point of $B$. Indeed, every point of $B$ has a ball neighborhood $V\subset B$ over which $L$ has a holomorphic frame $e$, and $\log |e|_{h_1}^2$ is smooth and pluriharmonic, since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |e|_{h_1}^2=-c_1(L,h_1)=0$, so by lemma 13.1.2 it equals $\operatorname{Re}F$ for a holomorphic function $F$ on $V$, and $\mathrm e^{-F/2}e$ is a unit frame. Two unit frames on a connected open set differ by a holomorphic factor $g$ with $|g|=1$; then $\bar g=1/g$ is both holomorphic and antiholomorphic, so $\mathrm d\bar g=0$ and $g$ is constant. Let $c$ be the center of $B$ and fix a unit vector $e_ c\in L_ c$. For $z\in B$, a flat lift along the segment from $c$ to $z$ is a continuous map $t\mapsto \varepsilon (t)\in L_{c+t(z-c)}$, $t\in [0,1]$, with $\varepsilon (0)=e_ c$, which near every $t$ is a constant multiple of a unit frame. There is at most one flat lift: if $\varepsilon '$ is another one, then $\varepsilon '=g\varepsilon $ for a continuous function $g$ on $[0,1]$ which is locally constant, by the preceding paragraph, and equals $1$ at $t=0$, so $g=1$. It remains to show that flat lifts exist and that their values at $t=1$ depend holomorphically on $z$. Let $z_0\in B$, and choose $\delta _0>0$ with $\overline{B(z_0,\delta _0)}\subset B$. The set $\Gamma _0=\{ c+t(z-c):t\in [0,1],\  |z-z_0|\leq \delta _0\} $ is a compact subset of the convex set $B$. Cover it by finitely many balls $V_ i\subset B$ carrying unit frames $e_ i$, let $\lambda >0$ be a Lebesgue number of this cover, choose $\delta \leq \delta _0$ with $2\delta <\lambda /2$, and choose $0=t_0<t_1<\cdots <t_ N=1$ with $(t_ k-t_{k-1})(|z_0-c|+\delta _0)<\lambda /2$. For $W=B(z_0,\delta )$, each set $\Gamma _ k=\{ c+t(z-c):t\in [t_{k-1},t_ k],\  z\in W\} $ has diameter less than $\lambda $, because $|(c+t(z-c))-(c+t'(z'-c))|\leq |t-t'|\, |z-c|+|z-z'|$; so $\Gamma _ k$ lies in some $V_{i_ k}$. The convex set $V_{i_ k}\cap V_{i_{k+1}}$ is connected and contains $c+t_ k(z_0-c)$, so $e_{i_ k}=\gamma _ ke_{i_{k+1}}$ there for a constant $\gamma _ k$. Let $a$ be the number with $e_ c=a\, e_{i_1}(c)$. For $z\in W$, the map equal to $a\gamma _1\cdots \gamma _{k-1}e_{i_ k}(c+t(z-c))$ for $t\in [t_{k-1},t_ k]$ is well defined at the points $t_ k$ and is a flat lift along the segment from $c$ to $z$. Hence, on $W$, the value $E(z)$ of the unique flat lift at $t=1$ is $a\gamma _1\cdots \gamma _{N-1}e_{i_ N}(z)$, a constant multiple of the unit frame $e_{i_ N}$. Since $z_0$ was arbitrary, $E$ is a nowhere vanishing holomorphic section of $L$ on $B$. $\square$

title: L2 bounded holomorphic compactness
topic: Global potentials and positive cohomology classes
text: Lemma 14.5.2 . Let $U\subset \mathbb C^ n$ be open, $n\geq 1$, and let $(f_ j)$ be a sequence of holomorphic functions on $U$ with $\sup _ j\int _ U|f_ j|^2\, \mathrm dV<\infty $. Then a subsequence converges locally uniformly on $U$ to a holomorphic function. Let $E$ be a holomorphic line bundle on $X$ with a smooth quadratic metric $h_ E$, and let $(s_ j)$ be a sequence of holomorphic sections of $E$ over $X$ with $\sup _ j\int _ X|s_ j|_{h_ E}^2\, \mathrm dV<\infty $. Then a subsequence converges uniformly on $X$ to a holomorphic section $s$ of $E$, that is, $\sup _ X|s_ j-s|_{h_ E}\to 0$ along the subsequence. For every holomorphic line bundle $E$ on $X$, the space $H^0(X,E)$ of holomorphic sections of $E$ over $X$ is finite dimensional. Assertions (2) and (3) hold more generally on every compact complex manifold $X'$ of positive dimension in place of $X$, with $\mathrm dV$ in (2) replaced by any smooth positive volume form on $X'$. Proof. (1) Let $M$ be the supremum in the statement. If $\overline{B(z,\delta )}\subset U$, then $|f_ j(z)|^2\leq |B(z,\delta )|^{-1}M$ by ( 12.9 ). Hence the $f_ j$ are uniformly bounded on every compact subset of $U$: if $K\subset U$ is compact and $\delta >0$ is smaller than the distance from $K$ to $\mathbb C^ n\setminus U$ (any $\delta >0$ if $U=\mathbb C^ n$), then $|f_ j|^2\leq |B(0,\delta )|^{-1}M$ on $K$. We next show that the sequence is equicontinuous on compact sets. Let $K\subset U$ be compact, and choose $r>0$ such that the compact set $K'$ of points at distance at most $2\sqrt n\, r$ from $K$ lies in $U$; let $M'$ be a bound for all $|f_ j|$ on $K'$. For $z$ at distance at most $\sqrt n\, r$ from $K$, the closed polydisc of radius $r$ centered at $z$ lies in $K'$, and the coefficient bound in ( 7.1 ) gives $|\partial _{z_ l}f_ j(z)|\leq M'/r$ for $1\leq l\leq n$. Since $\mathrm df_ j=\sum _ l\partial _{z_ l}f_ j\, \mathrm dz_ l$, the $f_ j$ are Lipschitz with a common constant on every ball of radius $\sqrt n\, r$ centered at a point of $K$, so the sequence is equicontinuous on $K$. By proposition 1.6.4 , applied on the compact sets $K_ m=\{ z\in U:|z|\leq m,\  \operatorname {dist}(z,\mathbb C^ n\setminus U)\geq 1/m\} $, which exhaust $U$, and a diagonal argument, a subsequence converges locally uniformly on $U$ to a continuous function $f$. Then $\bar\partial f=0$ in the sense of distributions, as a limit of $\bar\partial f_ j=0$, so $f$ agrees almost everywhere with a holomorphic function by lemma 11.3.5 (1); both being continuous, $f$ is holomorphic. (2) Choose finitely many coordinate balls $B_ k$, with closures in the domains of their charts, such that the concentric balls $B'_ k$ of half the radius cover $X$, and let $B''_ k$ be the concentric balls of three quarters of the radius. By lemma 14.5.1 , $E$ has a holomorphic frame $e_ k$ over $B_ k$; write $s_ j=f_{j,k}e_ k$ on $B_ k$. On the compact set $\overline{B''_ k}$ the function $|e_ k|_{h_ E}^2$ is bounded below by a positive constant and $\mathrm dV$ is bounded below by a positive multiple of Lebesgue measure in the chart, so the integrals of $|f_{j,k}|^2$ over $B''_ k$ with respect to Lebesgue measure in the chart are bounded independently of $j$. Applying (1) successively for the finitely many $k$, we obtain a subsequence along which $f_{j,k}$ converges locally uniformly on $B''_ k$, hence uniformly on $\overline{B'_ k}$, to a holomorphic function $f_ k$, for every $k$. On $B''_ k\cap B''_ l$ the sections $f_ ke_ k$ and $f_ le_ l$ are both the pointwise limit of $s_ j$, so they define a holomorphic section $s$ of $E$ over $X$, and $\sup _{B'_ k}|s_ j-s|_{h_ E}\leq \sup _{\overline{B'_ k}}|e_ k|_{h_ E}\cdot \sup _{\overline{B'_ k}}|f_{j,k}-f_ k|\to 0$ for every $k$. (3) Fix a smooth quadratic metric $h_ E$ on $E$ (lemma 13.1.9 (1)). The integral $\| s\| ^2=\int _ X|s|_{h_ E}^2\, \mathrm dV$ defines an inner product on $H^0(X,E)$: if $\| s\| =0$, then the continuous function $|s|_{h_ E}$ vanishes almost everywhere, hence everywhere. If $H^0(X,E)$ were infinite dimensional, the Gram–Schmidt process would give an orthonormal sequence $(s_ j)$. By (2), a subsequence converges uniformly on $X$, hence in $L^2$, since $X$ has finite volume; but $\| s_ i-s_ j\| ^2=2$ for $i\neq j$. This contradiction proves (3). The proofs of (2) and (3) use only that $X$ is a compact complex manifold of positive dimension and that $\mathrm dV$ is a smooth positive volume form; hence they also prove the last assertion of the lemma. $\square$

title: Psh quadratic line metric
topic: Global potentials and positive cohomology classes
text: Definition 14.5.3 . A plurisubharmonic metric on $L$ is a quadratic metric of the form $h=h_0\mathrm e^{-\varphi }$ with $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,c_1(L,h_0))$. It assigns the value zero to the zero vector, also over the pole set of $\varphi $, and the value $+\infty $ to a nonzero vector over a pole of $\varphi $. Its Chern current is \[  c_1(L,h)=c_1(L,h_0)+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi .  \]

title: Line bundle poincare lelong
topic: Global potentials and positive cohomology classes
text: Proposition 14.5.4 . For a nonzero holomorphic section $s$ of $L$ and a smooth metric $h_0$, 14.22 \begin{equation} \label{eq:line-bundle-poincare-lelong} c_1(L,h_0)+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |s|_{h_0}^2=[Z(s)], \end{equation} where $[Z(s)]$ is the current of integration along the zero divisor of $s$, counted with multiplicities. In particular $[Z(s)]$ represents $c_1(L)$. Proof. In a local frame write $s=fe$. Since $\log |s|_{h_0}^2=\log |f|^2+\log |e|_{h_0}^2$, the left side equals $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |f|^2$, which is the current of integration along the zero divisor of $f$ by theorem 7.4.5 . These local divisors agree on overlaps, because the transition functions have no zeros. $\square$

title: Projective space line bundles
topic: Global potentials and positive cohomology classes
text:
Example 14.5.5 . Let $N\geq 0$. The projective space $\mathbb P^ N$ is the quotient of $\mathbb C^{N+1}\setminus \{ 0\} $ by the action of $\mathbb C^*$ by multiplication, with the quotient topology; we write $q$ for the quotient map and $[Z]=[Z_0:\cdots :Z_ N]$ for the class of $Z$. For $0\leq i\leq N$ the sets $U_ i=\{ [Z]:Z_ i
eq 0\} $ are open and cover $\mathbb P^ N$, and the map $\phi _ i\colon U_ i	o \mathbb C^ N$, $[Z]\mapsto (Z_ k/Z_ i)_{k
eq i}$, is a homeomorphism: it is continuous because $\phi _ i\circ q$ is, and its inverse is $q$ composed with the map inserting the coordinate $1$ in the $i$th place. On $\phi _ i(U_ i\cap U_ j)=\{ w_ j
eq 0\} $, where we put $w_ i=1$, the transition map $\phi _ j\circ \phi _ i^{-1}$ is $w\mapsto (w_ k/w_ j)_{k
eq j}$, which is holomorphic, and so is its inverse $\phi _ i\circ \phi _ j^{-1}$. The space $\mathbb P^ N$ is compact and connected, as the image under $q$ of the unit sphere of $\mathbb C^{N+1}$. It is Hausdorff, because the continuous map $[Z]\mapsto Z\overline Z^{\mathsf T}/|Z|^2$ to the space of complex matrices is injective, the matrix being the orthogonal projection onto the line $\mathbb CZ$; and being compact, it is paracompact. Thus $\mathbb P^ N$ is a connected compact complex manifold of dimension $N$ (definition 7.1.1 ). The tautological line bundle $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^ N}(-1)$ has the fiber $\mathbb CZ$ over $[Z]$. In the sense of definition 13.1.8 it is given by the frames $e_ i([Z])=Z/Z_ i$ over $U_ i$, the points of the line with $i$th coordinate one. Since $e_ i=(Z_ j/Z_ i)e_ j$ on $U_ i\cap U_ j$, its transition functions are $g_{ij}=Z_ j/Z_ i$, which are holomorphic and nowhere zero on $U_ i\cap U_ j$ and satisfy $g_{ij}g_{jk}=g_{ik}$. The Euclidean norm of $\mathbb C^{N+1}$ gives the smooth metric $|e_ i|^2=|Z|^2/|Z_ i|^2$, which satisfies $|e_ i|^2=|g_{ij}|^2|e_ j|^2$. The dual line bundle $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^ N}(1)$ has the dual frames $e_ i^*$, with $e_ i^*(e_ i)=1$ and transition functions $g_{ij}^{-1}$, and the dual metric $|e_ i^*|^2=|e_ i|^{-2}=|Z_ i|^2/|Z|^2$, the Fubini–Study metric $h_{\mathrm{FS}}$. A linear form $\ell $ on $\mathbb C^{N+1}$ defines a holomorphic section $s_\ell $ of $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^ N}(1)$, the restriction of $\ell $ to the fibers of $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^ N}(-1)$: on $U_ i$ it is $s_\ell =\ell (e_ i)e_ i^*=(\ell (Z)/Z_ i)\, e_ i^*$, and these expressions agree on overlaps, because $\ell (e_ i)e_ i^*=\ell (g_{ij}e_ j)\, g_{ij}^{-1}e_ j^*$. For the coordinate forms we write $X_ k=s_{Z_ k}$. Thus $X_ i=e_ i^*$ on $U_ i$, and \[  |X_ k|_{\mathrm{FS}}^2([Z])= rac{|Z_ k|^2}{|Z|^2}.  \] The tensor power $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^ N}(k)=\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^ N}(1)^{\otimes k}$, $k\geq 1$, has the frames $(e_ i^*)^{\otimes k}$, the transition functions $g_{ij}^{-k}$ and the metric $h_{\mathrm{FS}}^ k$; products of $k$ sections of $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^ N}(1)$, such as the monomials $X_0^{a_0}\cdots X_ N^{a_ N}$ with $a_0+\cdots +a_ N=k$, are holomorphic sections of $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^ N}(k)$.

title: Projective fubini study curvature
topic: Global potentials and positive cohomology classes
text: Example 14.5.6 . Let $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^ N}(1)$ carry the Fubini–Study metric $h_{\mathrm{FS}}$ of example 14.5.5 , dual to the Euclidean norm on the tautological line. On the chart $U_0=\{ [1:z_1:\cdots :z_ N]\} $ the tautological line is spanned by $(1,z)$, so the frame $X_0=e_0^*$ has squared norm $|X_0(1,z)|^2/|(1,z)|^2=(1+|z|^2)^{-1}$, and the curvature is \[  \omega _{\mathrm{FS}}=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log (1+|z|^2).  \] The matrix of $\partial _ j\partial _{\bar k}\log (1+|z|^2)$ is $\bigl ((1+|z|^2)\delta _{jk}-\bar z_ jz_ k\bigr )/(1+|z|^2)^2$, which is positive definite by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality $|\sum _ j\bar z_ j\xi _ j|^2\leq |z|^2|\xi |^2$. The same computation in the chart $U_ i$, with the frame $X_ i$, shows that $\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$ is a Kähler form on $\mathbb P^ N$; thus $\mathbb P^ N$ is a compact Kähler manifold. On $\mathbb P^1$, integration in polar coordinates gives $\int _{\mathbb P^1}\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}=\frac1\pi \int _{\mathbb C}(1+|z|^2)^{-2}\, \mathrm dV=1$. The function $\log |X_1|_{\mathrm{FS}}^2=\log \bigl (|z|^2/(1+|z|^2)\bigr )$, which vanishes at the point at infinity, is the weight of a singular plurisubharmonic metric whose Chern current is the Dirac current $[0]$ at the point $[1:0]$, by ( 14.22 ).

title: Section fubini study metrics
topic: Global potentials and positive cohomology classes
text: Definition 14.5.7 . A Fubini–Study metric on $L$ is a metric $h_0\mathrm e^{-\varphi }$ with \[  \varphi =\frac1m\max _{1\leq i\leq N} \bigl (\log |s_ i|_{h_0^ m}^2+\lambda _ i\bigr ), \qquad m,N\in \mathbb Z_{\geq 1},\quad \lambda _ i\in \mathbb Q,  \] where $s_1,\ldots ,s_ N$ are holomorphic sections of $L^ m$, not all zero. We denote the set of these metrics by $\mathrm{FS}(L)$. The set of generalized Fubini–Study metrics is the smallest set of plurisubharmonic metrics that contains $\mathrm{FS}(L)$ and is closed under minima of metrics and under convex combinations of weights with rational coefficients. A convex combination of weights corresponds to the weighted geometric mean of the quadratic metrics, with value zero on the zero vector and the value $+\infty $ on a nonzero vector over a pole of a factor with positive coefficient.

title: Fubini study finite operations
topic: Global potentials and positive cohomology classes
text: Proposition 14.5.8 . Fubini–Study metrics do not depend on the choice of $h_0$, they have analytic singularities, and $\mathrm{FS}(L)$ is closed under minima and rational convex combinations of weights. Consequently the generalized Fubini–Study metrics are exactly the metrics in $\mathrm{FS}(L)$. The set $\mathrm{FS}(L)$ is empty if no positive tensor power of $L$ has a nonzero holomorphic section, even when $L$ admits plurisubharmonic metrics. Proof. In a local frame $e$ write $s_ i=f_ ie^ m$. The local weight $-\log |e|_ h^2=\varphi -\log |e|_{h_0}^2$ of the metric equals $m^{-1}\max _ i(\log |f_ i|^2+\lambda _ i)$, which does not involve $h_0$; it is plurisubharmonic and not identically $-\infty $, since $X$ is connected and some $s_ i\ne 0$. It differs by a bounded function from $m^{-1}\log \sum _ i\mathrm e^{\lambda _ i}|f_ i|^2$, so it has analytic singularities with the rational coefficient $1/m$; the pole set is the common zero set of the $s_ i$. Consider two such metrics, given by sections $s_ i$ of $L^ m$ with constants $\lambda _ i$ and sections $r_ j$ of $L^ l$ with constants $\mu _ j$. Replacing $s_ i$ by $s_ i^{M/m}$ and $\lambda _ i$ by $(M/m)\lambda _ i$, and similarly for the $r_ j$, where $M$ is a common multiple of $m$ and $l$, does not change the potentials, so we may assume that both are given in degree $M$. The maximum of the two potentials, which corresponds to the minimum of the metrics, is then given by the union of the two lists. For a rational $t=a/b\in (0,1)$, the combination $t\varphi +(1-t)\psi $ of the two maxima is the maximum over all pairs $(i,j)$ of the corresponding combinations, that is, \[  t\varphi +(1-t)\psi =\frac1{Mb}\max _{i,j}\Bigl (\log \bigl |s_ i^ ar_ j^{b-a}\bigr |_{h_0^{Mb}}^2+a\lambda _ i+(b-a)\mu _ j\Bigr ),  \] where the sections $s_ i^ ar_ j^{b-a}$ of $L^{Mb}$ are not all zero and the constants are rational. Thus $\mathrm{FS}(L)$ is closed under both operations, and by induction under every finite sequence of them, so the generated set is $\mathrm{FS}(L)$ itself. If no positive tensor power of $L$ has a nonzero section, no presentation as in definition 14.5.7 exists. $\square$

title: Compact interpolation and global Bergman kernels
topic: Global potentials and positive cohomology classes
text:
14.6 Compact interpolation and global Bergman kernels The local extension theorems of chapter 11 produce holomorphic functions with prescribed values on pseudoconvex domains. On the compact manifold $X$ we obtain global holomorphic sections in the same way, by cutting off a local solution and correcting it with an $L^2$ estimate for $ ar\partial $ on line bundles; the curvature must dominate the cost of a logarithmic pole at the interpolation point. Since the weights are singular, we prove the $L^2$ estimate (lemma 14.6.5 ) on complements of analytic subsets of $X$, starting from the Bochner–Kodaira identity. After the interpolation theorem at a point (theorem 14.6.7 ) we describe the weighted spaces of global sections and their Bergman kernels. All norms use the volume $\mathrm dV=\omega ^ n/n!$. The canonical bundle $K_ X=\Lambda ^{n,0}T^*X$ is the holomorphic line bundle of $(n,0)$-forms; we give it the metric induced by $\omega $, and its dual $K_ X^{-1}$ the dual metric $h_{K^{-1},\omega }$. Recall that $H^0(X,L)$ denotes the vector space of global holomorphic sections of $L$ (lemma 14.5.2 ). We begin with the pointwise linear algebra behind the $L^2$ estimates of this chapter. Let $\sigma $ be a Hermitian form on a complex manifold $M$ of dimension $n\geq 1$. Forms on $M$ carry the pointwise inner product defined by the Riemannian metric $\sigma (\cdot ,J\cdot )$ as in section 14.1 ; for a holomorphic line bundle $F$ with a smooth quadratic metric $h$, $F$-valued forms carry the product of this inner product with $h$, written $\langle \cdot ,\cdot angle _{\sigma ,h}$ or $\langle \cdot ,\cdot angle _\sigma $, and $\mathrm dV_\sigma =\sigma ^ n/n!$. Let $\Lambda _\sigma $ be the pointwise adjoint of the Lefschetz operator $u\mapsto \sigma \wedge u$, and for a real $(1,1)$-form $\gamma $ put $[\gamma ,\Lambda _\sigma ]u=\gamma \wedge \Lambda _\sigma u-\Lambda _\sigma (\gamma \wedge u)$. A basis $	heta _1,\ldots ,	heta _ n$ of the $(1,0)$-covectors at a point $x$ is a $\sigma $-unitary coframe if $\sigma =\mathrm i\sum _ j	heta _ j\wedge  ar	heta _ j$ at $x$. By the spectral theorem for Hermitian matrices, for every real $(1,1)$-form $\gamma $ there is a $\sigma $-unitary coframe at $x$ in which $\gamma =\mathrm i\sum _ j\lambda _ j	heta _ j\wedge  ar	heta _ j$ at $x$, with real numbers $\lambda _ j$, the eigenvalues of $\gamma $ with respect to $\sigma $ at $x$. Lemma 14.6.1 . Let $\sigma $, $F$ and $h$ be as above, let $\gamma $ be a real $(1,1)$-form on $M$, let $x\in M$, and let $	heta _1,\ldots ,	heta _ n$ be a $\sigma $-unitary coframe at $x$ in which $\gamma =\mathrm i\sum _ j\lambda _ j	heta _ j\wedge  ar	heta _ j$. Put $e=	heta _1\wedge \cdots \wedge 	heta _ n$. For an $F$-valued $(n,1)$-covector $v=\sum _ jv_ j\, e\wedge  ar	heta _ j$ at $x$ we have $[\gamma ,\Lambda _\sigma ]v=\sum _ j\lambda _ jv_ j\, e\wedge  ar	heta _ j$ and $\langle [\gamma ,\Lambda _\sigma ]v,vangle _{\sigma ,h}=\sum _ j\lambda _ j|v_ j|_ h^2$. In particular, $[\gamma ,\Lambda _\sigma ]$ is positive semidefinite on $(n,1)$-covectors at $x$ if $\gamma \geq 0$ at $x$, and positive definite if $\gamma $ is positive definite at $x$. If $\alpha $ is a $(1,0)$-covector and $u$ an $F$-valued $(n,0)$-covector at $x$, then $|\langle  ar\alpha \wedge u,vangle _{\sigma ,h}|^2\leq |u|_{\sigma ,h}^2\, \langle [\mathrm i\alpha \wedge  ar\alpha ,\Lambda _\sigma ]v,vangle _{\sigma ,h}$ for every $F$-valued $(n,1)$-covector $v$ at $x$. Let $\gamma $ be positive definite at $x$, and let $g$ be an $F$-valued $(n,1)$-covector at $x$. Then the $(n,n)$-covector $\langle [\gamma ,\Lambda _\sigma ]^{-1}g,gangle _{\sigma ,h}\, \mathrm dV_\sigma $ does not depend on the Hermitian form $\sigma $, and neither does $|u|_{\sigma ,h}^2\, \mathrm dV_\sigma $ for an $F$-valued $(n,0)$-covector $u$ at $x$. If $\gamma \geq a\sigma $ at $x$ for a constant $a>0$, then $\langle [\gamma ,\Lambda _\sigma ]^{-1}g,gangle _{\sigma ,h}\leq a^{-1}|g|_{\sigma ,h}^2$. If $\sigma '$ is a second Hermitian form with $\sigma '\geq c\sigma $ at $x$ for a constant $c>0$, then $|g|_{\sigma ',h}^2\, \mathrm dV_{\sigma '}\leq c^{-1}|g|_{\sigma ,h}^2\, \mathrm dV_\sigma $. Proof. In linear coordinates at $x$ with $\mathrm dz_ j=\sqrt2\, 	heta _ j$ we have $\sigma = rac{\mathrm i}{2}\sum _ j\mathrm dz_ j\wedge \mathrm d ar z_ j=\sum _ j\mathrm dx_ j\wedge \mathrm dy_ j$ at $x$, so the Riemannian metric of $\sigma $ at $x$ is Euclidean in the real coordinates, and $\langle \mathrm dx_ j+\mathrm i\, \mathrm dy_ j,\mathrm dx_ k\pm \mathrm i\, \mathrm dy_ kangle =(1\pm 1)\delta _{jk}$ shows that the covectors $	heta _ j, ar	heta _ k$ form an orthonormal basis of the complexified cotangent space at $x$. Hence the products $	heta _ I\wedge  ar	heta _ J$ form an orthonormal basis of the complex covectors at $x$. Let $\iota _ j$ and $ ar\iota _ j$ be the adjoints of the exterior products with $	heta _ j$ and $ ar	heta _ j$; thus $\iota _ j$ maps $	heta _ j\wedge 	heta _ K\wedge  ar	heta _ L$ to $	heta _ K\wedge  ar	heta _ L$ for $j
otin K$ and annihilates the basis covectors that do not contain $	heta _ j$, and similarly for $ ar\iota _ j$. Since $\sigma \wedge {}$ is $\mathrm i\sum _ j(	heta _ j\wedge )( ar	heta _ j\wedge )$, its adjoint is $\Lambda _\sigma =-\mathrm i\sum _ j ar\iota _ j\iota _ j$. (1) The covector $\gamma \wedge v$ has bidegree $(n+1,2)$ and vanishes, so $[\gamma ,\Lambda _\sigma ]v=\gamma \wedge \Lambda _\sigma v$. We have $\iota _ j(e\wedge  ar	heta _ k)=(-1)^{j-1}	heta _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \widehat{	heta _ j}\wedge \cdots \wedge 	heta _ n\wedge  ar	heta _ k$, and $ ar\iota _ j$ maps this to $(-1)^{j+n}\delta _{jk}\, 	heta _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \widehat{	heta _ j}\wedge \cdots \wedge 	heta _ n$, the factor $ ar	heta _ k$ standing in the $n$th place. Hence $\Lambda _\sigma v=-\mathrm i\sum _ j(-1)^{j+n}v_ j\, 	heta _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \widehat{	heta _ j}\wedge \cdots \wedge 	heta _ n$. In the product of the $j$th term with $\gamma $ only $\mathrm i\lambda _ j	heta _ j\wedge  ar	heta _ j$ contributes, and $	heta _ j\wedge  ar	heta _ j\wedge 	heta _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \widehat{	heta _ j}\wedge \cdots \wedge 	heta _ n=(-1)^{n-j}e\wedge  ar	heta _ j$; so $\gamma \wedge \Lambda _\sigma v=\sum _ j\lambda _ jv_ j\, e\wedge  ar	heta _ j$. Since the covectors $e\wedge  ar	heta _ j$ are orthonormal, this gives the formula for $\langle [\gamma ,\Lambda _\sigma ]v,vangle _{\sigma ,h}$, and the last assertion follows because the $\lambda _ j$ are nonnegative if $\gamma \geq 0$ and positive if $\gamma $ is positive definite. (2) We may assume that $\alpha 
eq 0$. Since the assertion does not involve $\gamma $, we may choose the $\sigma $-unitary coframe with $	heta _1=\alpha /|\alpha |_\sigma $, by completing this unit covector to an orthonormal basis of the $(1,0)$-covectors. Then $\mathrm i\alpha \wedge  ar\alpha =\mathrm i|\alpha |_\sigma ^2	heta _1\wedge  ar	heta _1$, so (1) gives $\langle [\mathrm i\alpha \wedge  ar\alpha ,\Lambda _\sigma ]v,vangle _{\sigma ,h}=|\alpha |_\sigma ^2|v_1|_ h^2$. Writing $u=fe$, we have $ ar\alpha \wedge u=(-1)^ n|\alpha |_\sigma f\, e\wedge  ar	heta _1$, hence $|\langle  ar\alpha \wedge u,vangle _{\sigma ,h}|\leq |\alpha |_\sigma |f|_ h|v_1|_ h$, and $|f|_ h=|u|_{\sigma ,h}$. (3) Write $g=e\wedge 	au =\sum _ j	au _ j\, e\wedge  ar	heta _ j$ with an $F$-valued $(0,1)$-covector $	au =\sum _ j	au _ j ar	heta _ j$. By (1), $\langle [\gamma ,\Lambda _\sigma ]^{-1}g,gangle _{\sigma ,h}=\sum _ j|	au _ j|_ h^2/\lambda _ j=|	au |_\gamma ^2$, the squared norm of $	au $ in the metric induced by $\gamma $ on $(0,1)$-covectors, which does not involve $\sigma $. Moreover $\mathrm dV_\sigma =\sigma ^ n/n!=c_ n\, e\wedge  ar e$ with $c_ n=\mathrm i^ n(-1)^{n(n-1)/2}$. Hence $\langle [\gamma ,\Lambda _\sigma ]^{-1}g,gangle _{\sigma ,h}\, \mathrm dV_\sigma =c_ n|	au |_\gamma ^2\, e\wedge  ar e$. If $\kappa =\mu ^{-1}e$, $\mu

By corollary 11.4.5 , applied in this frame on the ball of radius $r_0$ around $x$, whose diameter $2r_0$ is fixed, there is a holomorphic section $f$ of $L$ over this ball with $f(x)=v$ and \[  \int _{|z-z(x)|<r_0}|f|_ h^2\, \mathrm dV\leq C_0|v|_ h^2;  \] here $C_0$ does not depend on $x$, because the volume densities are uniformly comparable on the finite cover. Let $\chi $ be a cutoff equal to one for $|z-z(x)|<r_0/2$ and zero for $|z-z(x)|>3r_0/4$, obtained by translating a fixed one. Put $G=\chi f$, extended by zero, and $g= ar\partial G=f\,  ar\partial \chi $. The form $g$ is supported in the annulus $r_0/2\leq |z-z(x)|\leq 3r_0/4$, on which $\psi _ x$ and $ ar\partial \chi $ are bounded independently of $x$. Step 3: global sections for the approximations of $\varphi $. Apply theorem 13.4.5 to $\varphi $ with the background $c_1(L,h_0)-N\omega $. It gives functions $\varphi _ j\downarrow \varphi $ with gentle analytic singularities, analytic pole sets $A_ j$, and $c_1(L,h_0)+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ j\geq (N-\varepsilon _ j)\omega $ with $\varepsilon _ j	o 0$. Since $\varphi _ j(x)\geq \varphi (x)>-\infty $, no $A_ j$ contains $x$. Put \[  F=L\otimes K_ X^{-1},\qquad h_{F,j}=h_0\mathrm e^{-\varphi _ j-\psi _ x}\otimes h_{K^{-1},\omega }.  \] For $j$ so large that $\varepsilon _ j\leq 1$, this metric is smooth on $M_ j=X\setminus (A_ j\cup \{ x\} )$ and its curvature is at least $(N-\varepsilon _ j-b_0-b_1)\omega \geq \omega $. By lemma 14.6.4 , applied to $\varphi _ j+\psi _ x$, the manifold $M_ j$ carries a Kähler form $\sigma \geq \omega /2$ and cutoffs as required in lemma 14.6.5 . The canonical identification of $L$-valued $(0,q)$-forms with $F$-valued $(n,q)$-forms preserves the pointwise norms for $\omega $, because the $(n,0)$-covector and its dual cancel. Under this identification $g$ is $ ar\partial $-closed, and since $\varphi _ j\geq \varphi $, \[  \int _{M_ j}|g|_{h_0}^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi _ j-\psi _ x}\, \mathrm dV \leq C_1\int _{|z-z(x)|<r_0}|f|_ h^2\, \mathrm dV \leq C_1C_0|v|_ h^2,  \] with $C_1$ depending only on the fixed cutoffs and the bounds for $\psi _ x$ on the annulus. Lemma 14.6.5 , with $a=1$, gives $u_ j$ on $M_ j$ with $ ar\partial u_ j=g$ and \[  \int _{M_ j}|u_ j|_{h_0}^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi _ j-\psi _ x}\, \mathrm dV\leq  rac{C_1C_0}{2\pi }|v|_ h^2.  \] The section $s_ j=G-u_ j$ is holomorphic on $M_ j$. The weights $\mathrm e^{-\varphi _ j-\psi _ x}$ are bounded below by a positive constant, since $\varphi _ j\leq \varphi _1$ is bounded above and $\psi _ x\leq 0$; hence $s_ j$ is square integrable for $h_0$ near $A_ j\cup \{ x\} $, and lemma 14.6.6 extends it to a global holomorphic section. Near $x$ we have $g=0$ and no point of $A_ j$, so $u_ j=G-s_ j$ is holomorphic near $x$. Moreover $|u_ j|_{h_0}^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi _ j-\psi _ x}\geq c\, |u_ j|_{h_0}^2|z-z(x)|^{-2n}$ near $x$ for a constant $c>0$, by the upper bound for $\varphi _ j$ and since $\psi _ x=n\log |z-z(x)|^2+O(1)$. Since $\int _{|z-z(x)|<r}|z-z(x)|^{-2n}\, \mathrm dV=\infty $ for every $r>0$, by polar coordinates in $\mathbb R^{2n}$, the finiteness of the weighted integral of the continuous function $u_ j$ forces $u_ j(x)=0$. Hence $s_ j(x)=G(x)=v$. Since $\psi _ x\leq 0$, dropping the factor $\mathrm e^{-\psi _ x}$ only decreases the integrals, and with $|G|_{h_0}^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi _ j}\leq |f|_ h^2$ on the ball we obtain \[  \int _ X|s_ j|_{h_0}^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi _ j}\, \mathrm dV \leq C_2|v|_ h^2,  \] where $C_2$ depends only on the fixed geometric cutoffs and on the constant of the local point estimate. Step 4: the limit. Since $\varphi _ j\leq \varphi _1\leq \sup _ X\varphi _1$, the sections $s_ j$ are bounded in $L^2$ for $h_0$, and by lemma 14.5.2 (2) a subsequence converges uniformly to a holomorphic section $s$ of $L$, which satisfies $s(x)=v$. Since $\varphi _ j\downarrow \varphi $, Fatou's lemma gives ( 14.29 ) with $C=C_2$. $\square$ Lemma 14.6.8 . Let $L$ and $T$ be holomorphic line bundles on $X$ with smooth quadratic metrics $h_0$ and $h_ T$, and let $\mathrm dV$ be a smooth positive volume form on $X$. For an integer $k\geq 1$ and a quasi-plurisubharmonic function $\varphi $ on $X$, the space \[  \mathcal H_ k=\left\{ s\in H^0(X,L^ k\otimes T): \int _ X|s|_{h_0^ k\otimes h_ T}^2\mathrm e^{-k\varphi }\, \mathrm dV<\infty ight\}   \] is a finite-dimensional Hilbert space for the displayed squared norm $\| s\| _ k^2$. If $\mathcal H_ k
e \{ 0\} $ and $s_1,\ldots ,s_{d_ k}$ is an orthonormal basis, then 14.30  egin{equation} \label{eq:compact-bergman-potential} \varphi _ k= rac1k\log \sup _{\| s\| _ k\leq 1}|s|_{h_0^ k\otimes h_ T}^2 = rac1k\log \sum _{i=1}^{d_ k}|s_ i|_{h_0^ k\otimes h_ T}^2. \end{equation} Writing $	heta =c_1(L,h_0)$ and $	heta _ T=c_1(T,h_ T)$, the function $\varphi _ k$ belongs to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta +k^{-1}	heta _ T)$ and has gentle analytic singularities with coefficient $1/k$. Except for the gentle analytic singularities, which are defined only on compact Kähler manifolds (definition 13.1.11 ), these assertions hold more generally on every compact complex manifold $X'$ of positive dimension in place of $X$. Proof. By lemma 14.5.2 (3), $H^0(X,L^ k\otimes T)$ and its linear subspace $\mathcal H_ k$ are finite dimensional. The weighted integral defines an inner product on $\mathcal H_ k$: the function $\varphi $ is finite almost everywhere, so the weight is positive almost everywhere, and a section of norm zero vanishes almost everywhere and hence identically. A finite-dimensional inner product space is complete. At a point $y$, with the coefficients $c_ i$ of $s=\sum _ ic_ is_ i$, the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality gives $|s(y)|^2\leq \sum _ i|c_ i|^2\sum _ i|s_ i(y)|^2$, with equality when the $c_ i$ are proportional to the complex conjugates of the values of the $s_ i$ at $y$ in a local frame. This proves the equality in ( 14.30 ). In local frames with $|e|_{h_0}^2=\mathrm e^{-p_0}$ and $|e_ T|_{h_ T}^2=\mathrm e^{-p_ T}$, write $s_ i=f_ ie^ k\otimes e_ T$. Then \[  \varphi _ k= rac1k\log \sum _ i|f_ i|^2-p_0- rac{p_ T}k,  \] and $	heta +k^{-1}	heta _ T+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ k=k^{-1}\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log \sum _ i|f_ i|^2\geq 0$ by proposition 8.3.3 . Hence $\varphi _ k\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta +k^{-1}	heta _ T)$, with analytic singularities of type $(1/k,\mathfrak b)$, where $\mathfrak b$ is the ideal sheaf generated locally by the $f_ i$. This ideal sheaf does not depend on the frames, because a change of frames multiplies all $f_ i$ by the same nowhere vanishing holomorphic function, and it is coherent by lemma 12.2.4 . Moreover $\mathrm e^{k\varphi _ k}=\sum _ i|s_ i|^2$ is smooth on $X$. The local expressions for $\varphi _ k$ above are presentations with the smooth remainders $-p_0-p_ T/k$, so proposition 13.1.7 shows that on every log resolution $\pi $ of $\mathfrak b$, with $\pi ^*\mathfrak b=\mathcal O(-D)$, locally $\varphi _ k\circ \pi $ is $k^{-1}\log |s_ D|^2$ plus a smooth function. These are the conditions of definition 13.1.11 . Apart from this appeal to definition 13.1.11 , the proof uses only that $X$ is a compact complex manifold of positive dimension, since the last assertion of lemma 14.5.2 gives its part (3) in this generality; hence it also proves the last assertion of the lemma. $\square$ Example 14.6.9 . On $\mathbb P^1$ take $L=\mathcal O(1)$ with its Fubini–Study metric, $T$ trivial, $\varphi =0$ and $\mathrm dV=\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$. A section of $L^ k$ is $f(z)X_0^ k$ on the chart $[1:z]$ with $f$ entire, and in the chart at infinity, with $\zeta =1/z$, it equals $\zeta ^ kf(1/\zeta )X_1^ k$; holomorphicity at $\zeta =0$ and Cauchy's estimates show that $f$ is a polynomial of degree at most $k$. Integration over circles makes the monomials orthogonal, and with $t=|z|^2$, \[  \| z^ j\| _ k^2=\int _0^\infty  rac{t^ j}{(1+t)^{k+2}}\, \mathrm dt = rac{j!(k-j)!}{(k+1)!},\qquad 0\leq j\leq k;  \] the last equality follows from the substitution $u=t/(1+t)$ and repeated integration by parts. Thus the sections $\sqrt{(k+1) inom {k}{j}}X_0^{k-j}X_1^ j$, $0\leq j\leq k$, form an orthonormal basis, and the sum of their squared norms is \[   rac{k+1}{(1+|z|^2)^ k}\sum _{j=0}^ k inom {k}{j}|z|^{2j}=k+1.  \] Consequently $\varphi _ k=k^{-1}\log (k+1)$, which tends to zero uniformly.

Lemma 14.6.1 . Let $\sigma $, $F$ and $h$ be as above, let $\gamma $ be a real $(1,1)$-form on $M$, let $x\in M$, and let $	heta _1,\ldots ,	heta _ n$ be a $\sigma $-unitary coframe at $x$ in which $\gamma =\mathrm i\sum _ j\lambda _ j	heta _ j\wedge  ar	heta _ j$. Put $e=	heta _1\wedge \cdots \wedge 	heta _ n$. For an $F$-valued $(n,1)$-covector $v=\sum _ jv_ j\, e\wedge  ar	heta _ j$ at $x$ we have $[\gamma ,\Lambda _\sigma ]v=\sum _ j\lambda _ jv_ j\, e\wedge  ar	heta _ j$ and $\langle [\gamma ,\Lambda _\sigma ]v,vangle _{\sigma ,h}=\sum _ j\lambda _ j|v_ j|_ h^2$. In particular, $[\gamma ,\Lambda _\sigma ]$ is positive semidefinite on $(n,1)$-covectors at $x$ if $\gamma \geq 0$ at $x$, and positive definite if $\gamma $ is positive definite at $x$. If $\alpha $ is a $(1,0)$-covector and $u$ an $F$-valued $(n,0)$-covector at $x$, then $|\langle  ar\alpha \wedge u,vangle _{\sigma ,h}|^2\leq |u|_{\sigma ,h}^2\, \langle [\mathrm i\alpha \wedge  ar\alpha ,\Lambda _\sigma ]v,vangle _{\sigma ,h}$ for every $F$-valued $(n,1)$-covector $v$ at $x$. Let $\gamma $ be positive definite at $x$, and let $g$ be an $F$-valued $(n,1)$-covector at $x$. Then the $(n,n)$-covector $\langle [\gamma ,\Lambda _\sigma ]^{-1}g,gangle _{\sigma ,h}\, \mathrm dV_\sigma $ does not depend on the Hermitian form $\sigma $, and neither does $|u|_{\sigma ,h}^2\, \mathrm dV_\sigma $ for an $F$-valued $(n,0)$-covector $u$ at $x$. If $\gamma \geq a\sigma $ at $x$ for a constant $a>0$, then $\langle [\gamma ,\Lambda _\sigma ]^{-1}g,gangle _{\sigma ,h}\leq a^{-1}|g|_{\sigma ,h}^2$. If $\sigma '$ is a second Hermitian form with $\sigma '\geq c\sigma $ at $x$ for a constant $c>0$, then $|g|_{\sigma ',h}^2\, \mathrm dV_{\sigma '}\leq c^{-1}|g|_{\sigma ,h}^2\, \mathrm dV_\sigma $. Proof. In linear coordinates at $x$ with $\mathrm dz_ j=\sqrt2\, 	heta _ j$ we have $\sigma = rac{\mathrm i}{2}\sum _ j\mathrm dz_ j\wedge \mathrm d ar z_ j=\sum _ j\mathrm dx_ j\wedge \mathrm dy_ j$ at $x$, so the Riemannian metric of $\sigma $ at $x$ is Euclidean in the real coordinates, and $\langle \mathrm dx_ j+\mathrm i\, \mathrm dy_ j,\mathrm dx_ k\pm \mathrm i\, \mathrm dy_ kangle =(1\pm 1)\delta _{jk}$ shows that the covectors $	heta _ j, ar	heta _ k$ form an orthonormal basis of the complexified cotangent space at $x$. Hence the products $	heta _ I\wedge  ar	heta _ J$ form an orthonormal basis of the complex covectors at $x$. Let $\iota _ j$ and $ ar\iota _ j$ be the adjoints of the exterior products with $	heta _ j$ and $ ar	heta _ j$; thus $\iota _ j$ maps $	heta _ j\wedge 	heta _ K\wedge  ar	heta _ L$ to $	heta _ K\wedge  ar	heta _ L$ for $j
otin K$ and annihilates the basis covectors that do not contain $	heta _ j$, and similarly for $ ar\iota _ j$. Since $\sigma \wedge {}$ is $\mathrm i\sum _ j(	heta _ j\wedge )( ar	heta _ j\wedge )$, its adjoint is $\Lambda _\sigma =-\mathrm i\sum _ j ar\iota _ j\iota _ j$. (1) The covector $\gamma \wedge v$ has bidegree $(n+1,2)$ and vanishes, so $[\gamma ,\Lambda _\sigma ]v=\gamma \wedge \Lambda _\sigma v$. We have $\iota _ j(e\wedge  ar	heta _ k)=(-1)^{j-1}	heta _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \widehat{	heta _ j}\wedge \cdots \wedge 	heta _ n\wedge  ar	heta _ k$, and $ ar\iota _ j$ maps this to $(-1)^{j+n}\delta _{jk}\, 	heta _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \widehat{	heta _ j}\wedge \cdots \wedge 	heta _ n$, the factor $ ar	heta _ k$ standing in the $n$th place. Hence $\Lambda _\sigma v=-\mathrm i\sum _ j(-1)^{j+n}v_ j\, 	heta _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \widehat{	heta _ j}\wedge \cdots \wedge 	heta _ n$. In the product of the $j$th term with $\gamma $ only $\mathrm i\lambda _ j	heta _ j\wedge  ar	heta _ j$ contributes, and $	heta _ j\wedge  ar	heta _ j\wedge 	heta _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \widehat{	heta _ j}\wedge \cdots \wedge 	heta _ n=(-1)^{n-j}e\wedge  ar	heta _ j$; so $\gamma \wedge \Lambda _\sigma v=\sum _ j\lambda _ jv_ j\, e\wedge  ar	heta _ j$. Since the covectors $e\wedge  ar	heta _ j$ are orthonormal, this gives the formula for $\langle [\gamma ,\Lambda _\sigma ]v,vangle _{\sigma ,h}$, and the last assertion follows because the $\lambda _ j$ are nonnegative if $\gamma \geq 0$ and positive if $\gamma $ is positive definite. (2) We may assume that $\alpha 
eq 0$. Since the assertion does not involve $\gamma $, we may choose the $\sigma $-unitary coframe with $	heta _1=\alpha /|\alpha |_\sigma $, by completing this unit covector to an orthonormal basis of the $(1,0)$-covectors. Then $\mathrm i\alpha \wedge  ar\alpha =\mathrm i|\alpha |_\sigma ^2	heta _1\wedge  ar	heta _1$, so (1) gives $\langle [\mathrm i\alpha \wedge  ar\alpha ,\Lambda _\sigma ]v,vangle _{\sigma ,h}=|\alpha |_\sigma ^2|v_1|_ h^2$. Writing $u=fe$, we have $ ar\alpha \wedge u=(-1)^ n|\alpha |_\sigma f\, e\wedge  ar	heta _1$, hence $|\langle  ar\alpha \wedge u,vangle _{\sigma ,h}|\leq |\alpha |_\sigma |f|_ h|v_1|_ h$, and $|f|_ h=|u|_{\sigma ,h}$. (3) Write $g=e\wedge 	au =\sum _ j	au _ j\, e\wedge  ar	heta _ j$ with an $F$-valued $(0,1)$-covector $	au =\sum _ j	au _ j ar	heta _ j$. By (1), $\langle [\gamma ,\Lambda _\sigma ]^{-1}g,gangle _{\sigma ,h}=\sum _ j|	au _ j|_ h^2/\lambda _ j=|	au |_\gamma ^2$, the squared norm of $	au $ in the metric induced by $\gamma $ on $(0,1)$-covectors, which does not involve $\sigma $. Moreover $\mathrm dV_\sigma =\sigma ^ n/n!=c_ n\, e\wedge  ar e$ with $c_ n=\mathrm i^ n(-1)^{n(n-1)/2}$. Hence $\langle [\gamma ,\Lambda _\sigma ]^{-1}g,gangle _{\sigma ,h}\, \mathrm dV_\sigma =c_ n|	au |_\gamma ^2\, e\wedge  ar e$. If $\kappa =\mu ^{-1}e$, $\mu 
eq 0$, is another nonzero $(n,0)$-covector, then $g=\kappa \wedge \mu 	au $ and $c_ n|\mu 	au |_\gamma ^2\, \kappa \wedge  ar\kappa =c_ n|	au |_\gamma ^2\, e\wedge  ar e$. Thus the density equals $c_ n|	au '|_\gamma ^2\, \kappa \wedge  ar\kappa $ whenever $g=\kappa \wedge 	au '$, an expression that does not involve $\sigma $. In the same way, $|u|_{\sigma ,h}^2\, \mathrm dV_\sigma =c_ n|f|_ h^2\, \kappa \wedge  ar\kappa $ for $u=f\kappa $. If $\gamma \geq a\sigma $, all $\lambda _ j$ are at least $a$, and $\sum _ j|	au _ j|_ h^2/\lambda _ j\leq a^{-1}\sum _ j|	au _ j|_ h^2=a^{-1}|g|_{\sigma ,h}^2$. Finally, the eigenvalues of $\sigma '$ with respect to $\sigma '$ itself are all equal to one, so $[\sigma ',\Lambda _{\sigma '}]$ is the identity on $(n,1)$-covectors by (1), and the independence just proved gives \[   egin{aligned}  |g|_{\sigma ',h}^2\, \mathrm dV_{\sigma '}& =\langle [\sigma ',\Lambda _{\sigma '}]^{-1}g,gangle _{\sigma ',h}\, \mathrm dV_{\sigma '}\ & =\langle [\sigma ',\Lambda _\sigma ]^{-1}g,gangle _{\sigma ,h}\, \mathrm dV_\sigma \leq c^{-1}|g|_{\sigma ,h}^2\, \mathrm dV_\sigma \end{aligned}  \] if $\sigma '\geq c\sigma $. $\square$

title: Kahler bochner kodaira
topic: Global potentials and positive cohomology classes
text: Lemma 14.6.2 . Let $M$ be a complex manifold of dimension $n\geq 1$ with a Kähler form $\sigma $, and let $F\to M$ be a holomorphic line bundle with a smooth quadratic metric $h$. In a holomorphic frame of $F$ with squared norm $\mathrm e^{-p}$, let $D'=\partial -\partial p\wedge $ and $D''=\bar\partial $, acting on the coefficients of $F$-valued forms; these are the components of the Chern connection, and they do not depend on the frame. Let $D'{}^*,D''{}^*$ be their formal adjoints for $\sigma $ and $h$, and put $B_\sigma =[2\pi c_1(F,h),\Lambda _\sigma ]$. Then, for every compactly supported smooth $F$-valued $(n,1)$-form $v$, 14.25 \begin{equation} \label{eq:kahler-bundle-bochner} \| D''{}^*v\| _\sigma ^2+\| D''v\| _\sigma ^2 =\| D'{}^*v\| _\sigma ^2+ \int _ M\langle B_\sigma v,v\rangle _\sigma \, \mathrm dV_\sigma . \end{equation} Proof. If $e'=ge$ is a second holomorphic frame, with $g$ holomorphic and nowhere zero, then its weight is $p'=p-\log |g|^2$, and for a form $u'$ we have $\partial (gu')-\partial p\wedge gu'=g(\partial u'-\partial p'\wedge u')$, since $\partial \log |g|^2=g^{-1}\partial g$; so $D'$ does not depend on the frame. In a frame we have $D'D''+D''D'=\partial \bar\partial p\wedge $, and $\mathrm i\partial \bar\partial p=2\pi c_1(F,h)$. We prove the Kähler identities at a point, in coordinates and a frame adapted to $\sigma $ and $h$, and deduce the Bochner–Kodaira formula from them. Fix a point, choose holomorphic coordinates centered at it in which $\sigma =\mathrm i\sum _ j\mathrm dz_ j\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ j$ at the point and the first derivatives of the coefficients of $\sigma $ vanish there (lemma 14.1.5 , after replacing the coordinates $z$ by $z/\sqrt2$), and a frame with $\partial p=0$ at the point: replacing a frame $e$ by $e\exp (\sum _ j\partial _ jp(0)z_ j)$ replaces $p$ by $p-2\operatorname{Re}\sum _ j\partial _ jp(0)z_ j$. Let $\epsilon _ k,\bar\epsilon _ k$ denote exterior multiplication by $\mathrm dz_ k,\mathrm d\bar z_ k$, and $\iota _ k,\bar\iota _ k$ their pointwise adjoints, the contractions. At the point they satisfy $\iota _ j\epsilon _ k+\epsilon _ k\iota _ j=\delta _{jk}$ and $\bar\iota _ j\bar\epsilon _ k+\bar\epsilon _ k\bar\iota _ j=\delta _{jk}$, while operators of different types anticommute; moreover $\Lambda _\sigma =-\mathrm i\sum _ j\bar\iota _ j\iota _ j$, as the adjoint of $\mathrm i\sum _ j\epsilon _ j\bar\epsilon _ j$. The formal adjoints of $\sum _ k\epsilon _ k\partial _ k$ and $\sum _ k\bar\epsilon _ k\partial _{\bar k}$ are $-\sum _ k\iota _ k\partial _{\bar k}$ and $-\sum _ k\bar\iota _ k\partial _ k$, with $\iota _ k,\bar\iota _ k$ computed for the metric at each point, plus zero-order terms whose coefficients are linear in the first derivatives of the coefficients of $\sigma $ and of $\mathrm e^{-p}$. Indeed, in the frame $\mathrm dz_ I\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ J$ the operators $\epsilon _ k$ have constant matrices, and the pointwise inner product of $F$-valued forms times the density of $\mathrm dV_\sigma $ is $\overline w^{\mathsf T}Hu$ for a smooth positive definite Hermitian matrix $H$ whose entries are smooth functions of the coefficients of $\sigma $ times $\mathrm e^{-p}$. For a constant matrix $A$ and compactly supported smooth $u,w$, integration by parts and $\partial _ k\overline w=\overline{\partial _{\bar k}w}$ give $\int \overline w^{\mathsf T}HA\, \partial _ ku=-\int \overline{(\partial _{\bar k}w)}^{\mathsf T}HAu-\int \overline w^{\mathsf T}(\partial _ kH)Au$, so the formal adjoint of $A\partial _ k$ is $-A^\dagger \partial _{\bar k}-H^{-1}A^*(\partial _{\bar k}H)$, where $A^\dagger =H^{-1}A^*H$ is the pointwise adjoint of $A$ and $A^*$ the conjugate transpose; the same computation applies with $\partial _ k$ and $\partial _{\bar k}$ exchanged. Since these first derivatives, and $\partial p$, vanish at the point, there \[  D'=\sum _ k\epsilon _ k\partial _ k,\quad D''=\sum _ k\bar\epsilon _ k\partial _{\bar k},\quad D'{}^*=-\sum _ k\iota _ k\partial _{\bar k},\quad D''{}^*=-\sum _ k\bar\iota _ k\partial _ k,  \] where $\partial _ k,\partial _{\bar k}$ act on the coefficients. The anticommutation rules give $\bar\iota _ j\iota _ j\epsilon _ k-\epsilon _ k\bar\iota _ j\iota _ j=\delta _{jk}\bar\iota _ j$ and $\bar\iota _ j\iota _ j\bar\epsilon _ k-\bar\epsilon _ k\bar\iota _ j\iota _ j=-\delta _{jk}\iota _ j$, hence $[\Lambda _\sigma ,D']=-\mathrm i\sum _ k\bar\iota _ k\partial _ k$ and $[\Lambda _\sigma ,D'']=\mathrm i\sum _ k\iota _ k\partial _{\bar k}$ at the point, since the coefficients of $\Lambda _\sigma $ in the frame $\mathrm dz_ I\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ J$ have vanishing first derivatives there. These are the Kähler identities \[  D''{}^*=-\mathrm i[\Lambda _\sigma ,D'],\qquad D'{}^*=\mathrm i[\Lambda _\sigma ,D''],  \] which therefore hold everywhere, the point being arbitrary. Substituting them into $\Delta ''=D''D''{}^*+D''{}^*D''$ and $\Delta '=D'D'{}^*+D'{}^*D'$, the mixed compositions $D''\Lambda _\sigma D'$ and $D'\Lambda _\sigma D''$ cancel in the difference, and the curvature identity gives the Bochner–Kodaira formula \[  \Delta ''-\Delta '=\mathrm i\bigl [D'D''+D''D',\Lambda _\sigma \bigr ]=[2\pi c_1(F,h),\Lambda _\sigma ],  \] that is, $\Delta ''-\Delta '=B_\sigma $. For a compactly supported smooth $(n,1)$-form $v$, the form $D'v$ vanishes for degree reasons, and integrating $\langle (\Delta ''-\Delta ')v,v\rangle _\sigma $ over $M$, using the definition of the formal adjoints, gives ( 14.25 ). $\square$
