title: Metric laplacian unbounded hessian
text:
Example 16.2.7 . Let $n\geq 2$ and $x_0\in X$. Choose holomorphic coordinates $z$ centered at $x_0$ in which $h_{i ar j}(0)=\delta _{ij}$, which is possible after a complex-linear change of coordinates, and choose $0<r_0<\mathrm e^{-1}$ such that the coordinates are defined on a neighborhood of $\{ |z|\leq r_0\} $. On $0<|z|<1$ put \[  \ell (z)=\log (-\log |z|),\qquad P(z)=|z_1|^2-|z_2|^2,\qquad \phi =P\ell ,  \] and $\phi (0)=0$. Write $r=|z|$. Since $\partial _{z_ i}\log r= ar z_ i/(2r^2)$ and $\partial _{ ar z_ j}(r^2\log r)=z_ j(\log r+ rac12)$, we have \[  \partial _{z_ i}\ell = rac{ ar z_ i}{2r^2\log r},\qquad \partial _{z_ i}\partial _{z_ j}\ell =- rac{(\log r+ rac12) ar z_ i ar z_ j}{2r^4(\log r)^2},  \] \[  \ell _{i ar j}= rac{\delta _{ij}}{2r^2\log r}- rac{(\log r+ rac12) ar z_ iz_ j}{2r^4(\log r)^2}.  \] For $0<r<r_0$ we have $\log r<-1$, hence $|\log r+ rac12|\leq |\log r|$, and these formulas give $|
abla \ell |\leq C/(r|\log r|)$ and $|D^2\ell |\leq C/(r^2|\log r|)$ for the real gradient and Hessian, with a constant $C$ depending only on $n$. Moreover $|P|\leq r^2$, $|
abla P|\leq 2r$, the real Hessian of $P$ is constant, $P_{1 ar1}=1$, $P_{2 ar2}=-1$, and all other $P_{i ar j}$ vanish. By the Leibniz rule, on $0<r<r_0$, \[  |
abla \phi |\leq 2r\ell + rac{Cr}{|\log r|},\qquad |D^2\phi -\ell D^2P|\leq  rac{C}{|\log r|},\qquad \Bigl |\phi _{i ar j}-\ell P_{i ar j}\Bigr |\leq  rac{C}{|\log r|}.  \] In particular $\phi $ is continuously differentiable on $\{ |z|<r_0\} $, with $
abla \phi (0)=0$, since $|\phi |\leq r^2\ell $ and $
abla \phi 	o 0$ as $z	o 0$; and its pointwise second derivatives off the origin are bounded by $C(1+\ell )\leq C(1-\log |z|)$, hence locally integrable. These pointwise derivatives are the distributional second derivatives of $\phi $. Indeed, let $\eta $ be a smooth function on $\mathbb R$ with $\eta =0$ on $(-\infty ,1]$ and $\eta =1$ on $[2,\infty )$, put $\eta _\varepsilon (z)=\eta (|z|/\varepsilon )$, and let $\psi $ be a test function on $\{ |z|<r_0\} $. Since $\phi $ is $C^1$, we have $\int \phi \, \partial _ a\partial _ b\psi =-\int \partial _ a\phi \, \partial _ b\psi $ for real coordinate derivatives $\partial _ a,\partial _ b$. Splitting $\psi =\eta _\varepsilon \psi +(1-\eta _\varepsilon )\psi $ and integrating by parts once more in the first term, where $\phi $ is smooth, we get \[  \int \phi \, \partial _ a\partial _ b\psi =\int \partial _ b\partial _ a\phi \, \eta _\varepsilon \psi -\int \partial _ a\phi \, \partial _ b igl ((1-\eta _\varepsilon )\psi  igr ).  \] The last integral is bounded by $\sup _{|z|\leq 2\varepsilon }|
abla \phi |\cdot C_\psi (\varepsilon ^{-1}+1)\varepsilon ^{2n}$, which tends to zero, and the first tends to $\int \partial _ b\partial _ a\phi \, \psi $ by dominated convergence. Choose a smooth function $\chi $ on $X$ with support in $\{ |z|<r_0\} $ that equals $1$ on $\{ |z|\leq r_0/2\} $, and put $f=\chi \phi $, extended by zero. Then $f$ is continuous. On $\{ |z|<r_0/2\} $, ( 16.1 ) and the estimates above give \[  \Bigl | rac{Lf}{4\pi }\Bigr |\leq \ell \, |h^{1 ar1}-h^{2 ar2}|+ rac{C'}{|\log r|}\leq C'' igl (r\ell +1 igr ),  \] because $h^{1 ar1}-h^{2 ar2}$ is smooth and vanishes at the origin; the right side is bounded, since $r\ell 	o 0$ as $r	o 0$, and elsewhere $f$ is smooth. Hence $f$ has bounded metric Laplacian. On the other hand $f_{1 ar1}=\phi _{1 ar1}\geq \ell -C/|\log r|$ near $x_0$, which is unbounded. Thus the complex Hessian of $f$ is not locally bounded.

title: Sobolev chart restriction
text: 16.2 \begin{equation} \label{eq:sobolev-chart-restriction} \| v\circ \psi ^{-1}\| _{W^{k,p}(\psi (U'))}\leq C\| v\| _{W^{k,p}(X)}, \end{equation}

title: Metric laplacian local weak hessian
text: Lemma 16.2.8 . Let $U\subset X$ be open, and let $f\in L^2_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$ be such that its distributional metric Laplacian $Lf$ belongs to $L^2_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$. Then $f\in W^{2,2}_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$. More precisely, for open sets $U'\Subset V\Subset U$ there is a constant $C$, depending only on $U'$, $V$ and $\omega $ (and on the fixed charts defining the norms), such that \[  \| f\| _{W^{2,2}(U')}\leq C\bigl (\| f\| _{L^2(V)}+\| Lf\| _{L^2(V)}\bigr ).  \] In particular, every continuous function on $U$ with locally bounded metric Laplacian belongs to $W^{2,2}_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$. Proof. Fix $c>0$. By lemma 14.1.3 (3), applied to functions, on which $\mathcal L=L$, the operator $P=L+c$ is a bijection of the space of distributions on $X$ onto itself, and its inverse maps $H^{-1}$ boundedly into $H^1$ and $H^0=L^2$ (lemma 14.1.1 (2)) boundedly into $H^2$. Since no derivative of $f$ is known in advance, we gain regularity in two steps, using two cutoff functions. For a smooth function $\chi $ on $X$, the Leibniz rules $\mathrm d(\chi u)=\chi \, \mathrm du+u\, \mathrm d\chi $ and $\mathrm d^*(\chi \alpha )=\chi \, \mathrm d^*\alpha -\langle \alpha ,\mathrm d\chi \rangle $, for smooth functions $u$ and real $1$-forms $\alpha $, give 16.3 \begin{equation} \label{eq:metric-laplacian-commutator} L(\chi u)=\chi Lu+[L,\chi ]u,\qquad [L,\chi ]u=-2\langle \mathrm d\chi ,\mathrm du\rangle +(L\chi )u, \end{equation} where $\langle \cdot ,\cdot \rangle $ is the pointwise inner product of real $1$-forms, extended bilinearly. Since $L$ and multiplication by $\chi $ are formally self-adjoint, the transpose of $[L,\chi ]$ is $-[L,\chi ]$, and ( 16.3 ) extends to distributions $u$, with $\langle [L,\chi ]u,\phi \rangle =-\langle u,[L,\chi ]\phi \rangle $ for smooth $\phi $. By proposition 7.1.3 , choose smooth functions $\chi _0,\chi _1$ on $X$ with compact supports in $V$ such that $\chi _1=1$ on a neighborhood of $\overline{U'}$ and $\chi _0=1$ on a neighborhood of $\operatorname{Supp}\chi _1$. Extend $\chi _0f$ by zero to a function on $X$. By ( 16.3 ), \[  P(\chi _0f)=\chi _0(Lf+cf)+[L,\chi _0]f.  \] The first term lies in $L^2$, with norm at most $\| Lf\| _{L^2(V)}+c\| f\| _{L^2(V)}$, hence in $H^{-1}$ with a comparable norm. For smooth $\phi $, the function $[L,\chi _0]\phi $ is a first-order expression in $\phi $ with smooth coefficients supported in $V$, so \[  |\langle [L,\chi _0]f,\phi \rangle |=|\langle f,[L,\chi _0]\phi \rangle |\leq C\| f\| _{L^2(V)}\| \phi \| _{H^1},  \] because the norm of $H^1$ dominates the $L^2$ norms of the first derivatives on compact subsets of the charts (lemma 14.1.1 (2)). Hence $[L,\chi _0]f\in H^{-1}$, and the right side of the last identity has $H^{-1}$ norm at most $C(\| Lf\| _{L^2(V)}+\| f\| _{L^2(V)})$. Applying $P^{-1}$, we obtain $\chi _0f\in H^1$ with the same bound. In particular $f$ has square-integrable first derivatives on the interior of $\{ \chi _0=1\} $, which contains $\operatorname{Supp}\chi _1$, with $L^2$ norm bounded in the same way. Therefore the distribution $[L,\chi _1]f=-2\langle \mathrm d\chi _1,\mathrm df\rangle +(L\chi _1)f$ is a square-integrable function, and in the identity \[  P(\chi _1f)=\chi _1(Lf+cf)+[L,\chi _1]f  \] the right side lies in $L^2$, with norm at most $C(\| Lf\| _{L^2(V)}+\| f\| _{L^2(V)})$. Since $P^{-1}$ is bounded from $L^2$ to $H^2$, it follows that $\chi _1f\in H^2\subset W^{2,2}(X)$, with this bound for its norm in $W^{2,2}(X)$. Since $\chi _1=1$ on $U'$, this proves the estimate. Finally, let $\psi \colon U_0\to \mathbb C^ n$ be a holomorphic chart with $U_0\subset U$, and let $U''\Subset U_0$ be open. Applying the preceding argument with $U'=U''$ and some open $V$ with $U''\Subset V\Subset U$, we find $\chi _1f\in W^{2,2}(X)$ with $\chi _1=1$ on $U''$, so $f\circ \psi ^{-1}\in W^{2,2}(\psi (U''))$ by ( 16.2 ). Hence $f\in W^{2,2}_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$. The last assertion holds because continuous functions and locally bounded measurable functions are locally square-integrable. $\square$

title: Metric laplacian commutator
text: 16.3 \begin{equation} \label{eq:metric-laplacian-commutator} L(\chi u)=\chi Lu+[L,\chi ]u,\qquad [L,\chi ]u=-2\langle \mathrm d\chi ,\mathrm du\rangle +(L\chi )u, \end{equation}

title: Metric laplacian regular contact density
text: Proposition 16.2.9 . Let $U\subset X$ be open. For $1\leq j\leq n$, let $\theta _ j$ be a closed smooth real $(1,1)$-form on $U$, let $u_ j$ be a continuous $\theta _ j$-psh function on $U$ with locally bounded metric Laplacian, and let $f_ j$ be a real Borel function on $U$ that belongs to $W^{2,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$. By lemma 16.2.8 , this holds, for instance, if $f_ j$ is continuous and has locally bounded metric Laplacian. Put \[  E=\bigcap _{j=1}^ n\{ u_ j=f_ j\} .  \] Let $W\Subset U$ be a coordinate ball, choose smooth real functions $\rho _ j$ on $W$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho _ j=\theta _ j$, and let \[  A_ j=\bigl ((\rho _ j+u_ j)_{a\bar b}\bigr )_{a,b}, \qquad B_ j=\bigl ((\rho _ j+f_ j)_{a\bar b}\bigr )_{a,b}  \] be the weak complex Hessian matrices, defined almost everywhere on $W$. Then each $A_ j$ is positive semidefinite almost everywhere and locally bounded, and on $W$ \[  \begin{aligned}  \bigwedge _{j=1}^ n(\theta _ j+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j) & =\frac{n!}{\pi ^ n}D(A_1,\ldots ,A_ n)\, \mathrm dV_{2n},\\  \mathbf1_ E\bigwedge _{j=1}^ n(\theta _ j+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j) & =\frac{n!}{\pi ^ n}\mathbf1_ E D(B_1,\ldots ,B_ n)\, \mathrm dV_{2n}. \end{aligned}  \] In particular the density $\mathbf1_ ED(B_1,\ldots ,B_ n)$ is nonnegative and locally bounded, although the $f_ j$ need not be $\theta _ j$-psh. Proof. The potentials $\rho _ j$ exist by lemma 13.1.2 . By lemma 16.2.8 , all $u_ j$ belong to $W^{2,2}_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)\subset W^{2,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$, so the matrices $A_ j$ and $B_ j$ are defined almost everywhere, and the positive current $T_ j=\theta _ j+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\rho _ j+u_ j)$ has coefficients in $L^2_{\mathrm{loc}}$. We first show that $A_ j$ is positive semidefinite almost everywhere. For each $\xi \in \mathbb C^ n$ the distribution $\sum _{a,b}(\rho _ j+u_ j)_{a\bar b}\xi _ a\bar\xi _ b$ is positive, because $T_ j$ is a positive current; since it is a locally integrable function, it is nonnegative almost everywhere, by proposition 1.4.3 (3),(4) and lemma 1.4.1 (2) (its mollifications are nonnegative and converge to it in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$). We apply this to the countably many $\xi $ with rational real and imaginary parts. Outside the union of the corresponding null sets, $\sum _{a,b}(A_ j)_{ab}\xi _ a\bar\xi _ b\geq 0$ for all such $\xi $, hence for all $\xi \in \mathbb C^ n$, because these $\xi $ are dense and a quadratic form on $\mathbb C^ n$ is continuous. Next we bound the coefficients. By the trace identity ( 14.13 ), \[  \Lambda T_ j=\Lambda \theta _ j-\frac{Lu_ j}{4\pi },  \] which is bounded on $W$, since $Lu_ j$ is locally bounded and $\overline W$ is compact. Since $T_ j=\frac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }\sum _{a,b}(A_ j)_{ab}\, \mathrm dz_ a\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ b$, the function $\Lambda T_ j$ is the trace $\sum _{a,b}h^{a\bar b}(A_ j)_{ab}=\operatorname {tr}(H^{-1}A_ j)$ of $A_ j$ relative to $h$, as in ( 14.14 ), where $H=(h_{a\bar b})$. As $\overline W$ is compact, $H\leq CI$ on $W$ for a constant $C$, so $H^{-1}\geq C^{-1}I$; since $A_ j$ is positive semidefinite, $\operatorname {tr}(H^{-1}A_ j)=\operatorname {tr}(A_ j^{1/2}H^{-1}A_ j^{1/2})\geq C^{-1}\operatorname {tr}A_ j$ almost everywhere on $W$. For a positive semidefinite Hermitian matrix every diagonal entry is at most the trace, and every entry satisfies $|a_{ab}|^2\leq a_{aa}a_{bb}$, by the positivity of the principal $2\times 2$ minors. Therefore $A_ j$ is bounded on $W$. The functions $\rho _ j+u_ j$ are continuous and plurisubharmonic on $W$, and they have bounded complex Hessian in the sense of section 9.12 . The first identity is therefore the first part of proposition 9.12.4 . The functions $\rho _ j+f_ j$ are real Borel functions in $W^{2,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(W)$, and adding $\rho _ j$ to both $u_ j$ and $f_ j$ does not change the contact set $\{ u_ j=f_ j\} $. Hence the second part of proposition 9.12.4 gives the second identity. Moreover proposition 9.12.3 , applied to $\rho _ j+u_ j$ and $\rho _ j+f_ j$, shows that $A_ j=B_ j$ almost everywhere on $\{ u_ j=f_ j\} $, hence on $E$. Consequently $\mathbf1_ ED(B_1,\ldots ,B_ n)=\mathbf1_ ED(A_1,\ldots ,A_ n)$ almost everywhere. This density is nonnegative, since the mixed discriminant of positive semidefinite matrices is nonnegative (lemma 7.2.2 (3)), and it is bounded, since $D$ is a polynomial in the entries of the bounded matrices $A_ j$. $\square$

title: Frozen coefficient lp
text: Lemma 16.2.10 . Let $d\geq 1$, $1<p<\infty $ and $\lambda >0$. There are constants $\delta _0>0$ and $C$, depending only on $d$, $p$ and $\lambda $, with the following property. Let $B\subset \mathbb R^ d$ be a ball with center $x_ B$, and let $A$ be a measurable function on $B$ with values in the real symmetric $d\times d$ matrices such that \[  A(x_ B)\geq \lambda I,\qquad |A(x)-A(x_ B)|\leq \delta _0\quad \text{for }x\in B.  \] Then every $w\in W^{2,p}(\mathbb R^ d)$ that vanishes almost everywhere outside a compact subset of $B$ satisfies \[  \| D^2w\| _ p\leq C\| A:D^2w\| _{L^ p(B)}.  \] Proof. First let $A_0$ be a constant real symmetric matrix with $A_0\geq \lambda I$, and put $M=A_0^{-1/2}$, a symmetric matrix of operator norm at most $\lambda ^{-1/2}$. For $v\in C_ c^\infty (\mathbb R^ d)$ let $\tilde v(y)=v(M^{-1}y)$, so that $v(x)=\tilde v(Mx)$. Then $D^2v(x)=M\, D^2\tilde v(Mx)\, M$ and $A_0:D^2v(x)=\operatorname {tr}(MA_0M\, D^2\tilde v(Mx))=\Delta \tilde v(Mx)$. Since $|MNM|\leq \lambda ^{-1}|N|$ for every matrix $N$, the change of variables $y=Mx$ and ( 6.7 ) give \[  \begin{aligned}  \| D^2v\| _ p& \leq \lambda ^{-1}|\det M|^{-1/p}\| D^2\tilde v\| _ p\\ & \leq \lambda ^{-1}C_{d,p}|\det M|^{-1/p}\| \Delta \tilde v\| _ p =\lambda ^{-1}C_{d,p}\| A_0:D^2v\| _ p. \end{aligned}  \] This estimate extends to every $w\in W^{2,p}(\mathbb R^ d)$ that vanishes almost everywhere outside a compact set $K$. Indeed, for $0<\varepsilon \leq 1$ the mollifications $w*\rho _\varepsilon $ are test functions supported in the compact set $K'=\{ x:\operatorname {dist}(x,K)\leq 1\} $, their second derivatives are $(\partial _\mu \partial _\sigma w)*\rho _\varepsilon $, by proposition 1.4.3 (1), and these converge to $\partial _\mu \partial _\sigma w$ in $L^ p(K')$, by lemma 1.4.1 (2), hence in $L^ p(\mathbb R^ d)$, since all these functions vanish almost everywhere outside $K'$. Applying the estimate to $v=w*\rho _\varepsilon $ and letting $\varepsilon \to 0$, we obtain it for $w$. Now let $A$ and $w$ be as in the statement, put $C_1=\lambda ^{-1}C_{d,p}$, $\delta _0=1/(2C_1)$, and $A_0=A(x_ B)$. Since $|\sum _{\mu ,\sigma }m_{\mu \sigma }m'_{\mu \sigma }|\leq |m|\, |m'|$ for matrices $m$ and $m'$, we have $|A_0:D^2w-A:D^2w|\leq \delta _0|D^2w|$ almost everywhere on $B$, and both sides vanish outside $B$. Hence \[  \| D^2w\| _ p\leq C_1\| A_0:D^2w\| _ p\leq C_1\| A:D^2w\| _{L^ p(B)}+\tfrac 12\| D^2w\| _ p,  \] and since $\| D^2w\| _ p<\infty $ we obtain the lemma with $C=2C_1$. $\square$

title: Compact metric laplacian lp
text:
Proposition 16.2.11 . Let $1<p<\infty $, and let $f\in L^ p(X)$ be such that its distributional metric Laplacian $Lf$ belongs to $L^ p(X)$. Then $f\in W^{2,p}(X)$, and 16.9  egin{equation} \label{eq:compact-metric-laplacian-lp} \| f\| _{W^{2,p}(X)}\leq C_{X,\omega ,p}  igl (\| Lf\| _{L^ p(X)}+\| f\| _{L^ p(X)} igr ), \end{equation} where the constant $C_{X,\omega ,p}$ depends only on $X$, $\omega $ and $p$ (and on the fixed charts defining the norm). In particular, a continuous function on $X$ with bounded metric Laplacian belongs to $W^{2,p}(X)$ for every finite $p\geq 1$ and to $C^{1,\alpha }(X)$ for every $0<\alpha <1$. Proof. We first treat smooth functions and then pass to the general case through the inverse of $L+c$. Step 1: the estimate for smooth real functions. Let $d=2n$. Fix finitely many holomorphic charts and compact subsets $K_\iota $ of their domains whose interiors cover $X$. By ( 16.8 ), in these charts $L=-4\pi \, A:D^2$ on real functions, with smooth real symmetric matrices $A$; by compactness there is $\lambda >0$ with $A\geq \lambda I$ on every $K_\iota $. Let $\delta _0$ and $C$ be the constants of lemma 16.2.10 for $d$, $p$ and $\lambda $. Since $A$ is uniformly continuous on a compact neighborhood of each $K_\iota $, there is $r>0$ such that, for every $x\in K_\iota $, the ball $B(x,r)$ lies in that neighborhood and $|A(y)-A(x)|\leq \delta _0$ for $y\in B(x,r)$. For a smooth real function $\psi $, lemma 14.1.3 (3) gives a unique distributional solution $u=P^{-1}\psi $, which lies in every $H^ r$ and is therefore smooth, by lemma 14.1.1 (3); it is real since $P$ is a real operator. Since $\mathrm d^*$ is the formal adjoint of $\mathrm d$, we have $\int _ X(Lu)\phi _\eta (u)\, \mathrm dV=\int _ X\phi _\eta '(u)|\mathrm du|^2\, \mathrm dV\geq 0$, and therefore \[  c\int _ Xu\phi _\eta (u)\, \mathrm dV\leq \int _ X\psi \phi _\eta (u)\, \mathrm dV.  \] As $\eta \downarrow 0$, $u\phi _\eta (u)	o |u|^ p$ and $\phi _\eta (u)	o u|u|^{p-2}$ pointwise, the latter being $0$ where $u=0$. For $p\geq 2$ and $\eta \leq 1$ both functions are bounded by $(1+u^2)^{p/2}$, which is bounded since $u$ is continuous on the compact manifold $X$; for $1<p<2$ we have $(u^2+\eta )^{(p-2)/2}\leq |u|^{p-2}$ where $u
eq 0$, so they are bounded by $|u|^ p$ and $|u|^{p-1}$. Dominated convergence and Hölder's inequality therefore give $c\| u\| _ p^ p\leq \| \psi \| _ p\| u\| _ p^{p-1}$, that is (if $u
eq 0$; otherwise there is nothing to prove), \[  \| P^{-1}\psi \| _ p\leq c^{-1}\| \psi \| _ p.  \] Applying Step 1 to $u$, for which $Lu=\psi -cu$, we conclude that $\| P^{-1}\psi \| _{W^{2,p}}\leq C\| \psi \| _ p$. Step 3: the general case. Let $f$ be real, put $\psi =Lf+cf\in L^ p(X)$, and choose smooth real functions $\psi _ j	o \psi $ in $L^ p(X)$, using chart cutoffs and mollification (lemma 1.4.1 ). By Step 2 the solutions $u_ j=P^{-1}\psi _ j$ form a Cauchy sequence in $W^{2,p}(X)$. This space is complete: in each chart the derivatives of order at most two converge in $L^ p$, and testing against smooth functions identifies the limits with the weak derivatives of the limit function. Let $u$ be the limit. Then $Pu_ j	o Pu$ in the sense of distributions, so $Pu=\psi $. Thus $P(u-f)=0$, and since $P$ is injective on distributions (lemma 14.1.3 (3)), $u=f$. Passing to the limit in the estimate of Step 2 gives $\| f\| _{W^{2,p}}\leq C\| \psi \| _ p\leq C(\| Lf\| _ p+\| f\| _ p)$. For complex $f$ we apply this to the real and imaginary parts, since $L$ is a real operator. Step 4: continuous functions with bounded Laplacian. If $f$ is continuous and $Lf$ is bounded, then $f$ and $Lf$ lie in every $L^ p(X)$ with $p<\infty $, which proves the assertion for $1<p<\infty $; the case $p=1$ follows from the case $p=2$, since $X$ has finite volume. Given $0<\alpha <1$, choose $p>d/(1-\alpha )$. In every chart, $f$ belongs to $W^{2,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}$ by ( 16.2 ), so Morrey's inequality (lemma 6.2.6 ) gives a representative of $f$ in $C^{1,1-d/p}_{\mathrm{loc}}$, hence in $C^{1,\alpha }_{\mathrm{loc}}$. This representative agrees with the continuous function $f$ almost everywhere, hence everywhere. $\square$

title: Compact metric laplacian lp
text: 16.9 \begin{equation} \label{eq:compact-metric-laplacian-lp} \| f\| _{W^{2,p}(X)}\leq C_{X,\omega ,p} \bigl (\| Lf\| _{L^ p(X)}+\| f\| _{L^ p(X)}\bigr ), \end{equation}

title: Metric laplacian barrier determinants
text: Corollary 16.2.12 . Let $\theta _1,\ldots ,\theta _ n$ be closed smooth real $(1,1)$-forms on $X$, and let $f_1,\ldots ,f_ n$ be continuous real functions on $X$ with bounded metric Laplacian. Then each $\theta _ j+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f_ j$ is a real $(1,1)$-form whose coefficients, computed from the weak second derivatives of $f_ j$, lie in $L^ p$ for every $p<\infty $. Their pointwise wedge product is defined almost everywhere and satisfies \[  \bigwedge _{j=1}^ n(\theta _ j+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f_ j) =F\, \mathrm dV,\qquad F\in L^ q(X)\quad \text{for every }1\leq q<\infty ;  \] in particular it is a finite signed Radon measure. On a coordinate ball, with smooth real $\rho _ j$ such that $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho _ j=\theta _ j$, it equals $n!\pi ^{-n}D(B_1,\ldots ,B_ n)\, \mathrm dV_{2n}$, where $B_ j=((\rho _ j+f_ j)_{a\bar b})_{a,b}$. If moreover $u_ j$ are continuous $\theta _ j$-psh functions on $X$ with bounded metric Laplacian, then on $E=\bigcap _ j\{ u_ j=f_ j\} $ this signed measure agrees with the positive measure $\mathbf1_ E\bigwedge _ j(\theta _ j+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j)$ of proposition 16.2.9 . Proof. By proposition 16.2.11 and ( 16.2 ), every $f_ j$ belongs to $W^{2,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}$ in every chart, for every finite $p$. In a chart, the current $\theta _ j+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f_ j$ is therefore given by integration against the form $\theta _ j+\frac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }\sum _{a,b}(f_ j)_{a\bar b}\, \mathrm dz_ a\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ b$, where the $(f_ j)_{a\bar b}$ are the weak derivatives, as in ( 7.5 ); its coefficients lie in $L^ p_{\mathrm{loc}}$. On the overlap of two charts, the forms obtained in the two charts represent the same current. For a current with locally integrable coefficients, ( 7.8 ), in which $\delta $ is the Jacobian determinant relating the two Lebesgue measures, says that the coefficients in the two charts are related, as distributions and hence almost everywhere (proposition 1.4.3 (4)), by the pointwise change of variables of forms. Thus the two forms agree almost everywhere as pointwise forms. Hence the pointwise wedge product of the forms $\theta _ j+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f_ j$ is a well-defined $(n,n)$-form, almost everywhere on $X$, and we write it as $F\, \mathrm dV$. A coefficient of the wedge product in a chart is a sum of products of $n$ coefficients of the factors and of smooth functions; by Hölder's inequality, with each factor in $L^{nq}$ on compact subsets of the chart, these products lie in $L^ q$ there, for every $1\leq q<\infty $. Covering $X$ by finitely many compact subsets of charts, we obtain $F\in L^ q(X)$. A real function in $L^1(X)$ defines a finite signed Radon measure through its positive and negative parts. On a coordinate ball, $\theta _ j+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f_ j=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\rho _ j+f_ j)=\frac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }\sum _{a,b}(B_ j)_{ab}\, \mathrm dz_ a\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ b$ almost everywhere, and the identity $\omega _{A_1}\wedge \cdots \wedge \omega _{A_ n}=D(A_1,\ldots ,A_ n)\, \omega _ I^ n$ of lemma 7.2.2 (2), applied pointwise with $A_ j=B_ j/(2\pi )$, together with $\omega _ I^ n=n!\, 2^ n\, \mathrm dV_{2n}$, gives $\bigwedge _ j(\theta _ j+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f_ j)=n!\pi ^{-n}D(B_1,\ldots ,B_ n)\, \mathrm dV_{2n}$. Finally, on every coordinate ball $W$ the second identity of proposition 16.2.9 , applied with $U=X$, shows that $\mathbf1_ E\bigwedge _ j(\theta _ j+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j)=\mathbf1_ EF\, \mathrm dV$ on $W$. Since coordinate balls cover $X$, the two measures agree on $X$. $\square$

title: Penalized equations and metric-Laplacian envelopes
text: 16.2.3 Penalized equations and metric-Laplacian envelopes We now show that, for a Kähler background, the envelope of the minimum of finitely many obstacles with bounded metric Laplacian again has bounded metric Laplacian (theorem 16.2.24 ). Throughout this subsection $\kappa $ is a fixed Kähler form on $X$. It is the background of the envelopes, while $\omega $ remains the metric with respect to which the Laplacians of obstacles are measured. Constants are $\kappa $-psh, so for a continuous obstacle $f$ the envelope $P_\kappa (f)$ is a bounded $\kappa $-psh function with $\min _ Xf\leq P_\kappa (f)\leq f$ everywhere, by proposition 16.1.4 (1),(2). For smooth $f$ we approximate $P_\kappa (f)$ by the smooth solutions $a_\beta $ of the Monge–Ampère equation with exponential penalty \[  (\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a)^ n=\mathrm e^{\beta (a-f)}\kappa ^ n,  \] where $\beta >0$ is a large parameter. On the set where $a>f$ the right side is very large, which forces the solution to lie essentially below $f$; on the set where $a<f$ it is very small, just as the Monge–Ampère measure of the envelope vanishes off the contact set. As $\beta \to \infty $ the solutions converge uniformly to $P_\kappa (f)$, with an explicit rate (proposition 16.2.22 ). The main estimate is a bound for the Laplacian of $a_\beta $ that is uniform in $\beta $ and depends on the obstacle $f$ only through its supremum norm and an upper bound for the trace $\Lambda \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f=-Lf/(4\pi )$ of its complex Hessian, that is, a lower bound for its metric Laplacian (lemma 16.2.15 ). This one-sided dependence is what makes finite minima accessible. The complex Hessian of $\min _ jf_ j$ can have a negative singular part on the set where two of the $f_ j$ cross. For instance, in a chart, with $x_1=\operatorname{Re}z_1$, the function $\min \{ x_1,-x_1\} =-|x_1|$ satisfies $\partial _{z_1}\partial _{\bar z_1}(-|x_1|)=-\frac14\partial _{x_1}^2|x_1|=-\frac12\sigma $, where $\sigma $ is Lebesgue measure on the hyperplane $\{ x_1=0\} $. However, the smooth approximations $-\delta \log \sum _ j\mathrm e^{-f_ j/\delta }$ of the minimum have complex Hessians whose traces are bounded above independently of $\delta $ (lemma 16.2.23 ). We solve the penalized equation by the continuity method (theorem 16.2.21 ). Besides the trace bound, the a priori estimates require control of the third derivatives of the solutions. We obtain it from Calabi's maximum principle for the squared norm of the difference of two Chern connections (lemma 16.2.17 ). The higher derivatives, and the smoothness of the solutions produced by perturbation, are then controlled by the elliptic $L^ p$ estimates of section 16.2.2 (lemma 16.2.19 ). In local holomorphic coordinates we put $\partial _ i=\partial _{z_ i}$ and $\partial _{\bar j}=\partial _{\bar z_ j}$, sum over repeated indices, and write \[  \omega =\frac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }h_{i\bar j}\,  \mathrm dz_ i\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ j, \qquad \kappa =\frac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }k_{i\bar j}\,  \mathrm dz_ i\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ j,  \] so that $h=(h_{i\bar j})$ and $k=(k_{i\bar j})$ are the coefficient matrices of $2\pi \omega $ and $2\pi \kappa $. As in ( 14.14 ), let $(h^{i\bar j})$ be the inverse matrix of $h$, normalized by $h^{i\bar j}h_{l\bar j}=\delta _{il}$ (then also $h^{j\bar i}h_{j\bar l}=\delta _{il}$), and for a Hermitian matrix $m=(m_{i\bar j})$ put $\operatorname {tr}_ hm=h^{i\bar j}m_{i\bar j}$. For a real function $a$ write $a_{i\bar j}=\partial _ i\partial _{\bar j}a$. The operator $D_ h=h^{i\bar j}\partial _ i\partial _{\bar j}$ is the operator $D_ g$ of ( 14.14 ) for the Kähler form $\omega '=\omega $, so that \[  D_ ha=h^{i\bar j}a_{i\bar j}=\Lambda \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a=-\frac{La}{4\pi }.  \] Hence $D_ h$ is the metric Laplacian up to the factor $-1/(4\pi )$; in particular, an upper bound for $D_ hf$ is a lower bound for $Lf$. Since $\omega $ is an arbitrary Kähler form on $X$, everything in this subsection holds with $\omega $ replaced by any Kähler form, for instance by $\kappa $. As $X$ is compact, there is $\gamma >0$ with $k\geq \gamma h$. For a smooth real function $a$ put $g_{i\bar j}=k_{i\bar j}+a_{i\bar j}$, so that $\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a=\frac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }g_{i\bar j}\, \mathrm dz_ i\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ j$. When $g>0$, that is, when $\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a$ is a Kähler form, we define $D_ g=g^{i\bar j}\partial _ i\partial _{\bar j}$ and $\operatorname {tr}_ gm=g^{i\bar j}m_{i\bar j}$ in the same way; by ( 14.14 ), $D_ g=-L_{\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a}/(4\pi )$. For a $(1,0)$-form $\xi =\xi _ i\, \mathrm dz_ i$ we write $|\xi |_ g^2=g^{i\bar j}\xi _ i\bar\xi _ j$ and $|\xi |_ h^2=h^{i\bar j}\xi _ i\bar\xi _ j$, and we set \[  H=\operatorname {tr}_ hg=\operatorname {tr}_ hk+D_ ha.  \] The eigenvalues of $g$ relative to $h$ are the eigenvalues of the matrix $h^{-1}g$; they are positive, their sum is $H$, the sum of their inverses is $\operatorname {tr}_ gh$, and their product is $\det g/\det h$. Under a holomorphic change of coordinates $z=z(w)$ with Jacobian matrix $J=(\partial z_ a/\partial w_ b)$, the coefficient matrices change by $k\mapsto J^{\mathrm T}k\bar J$, so $\det k$ is multiplied by $|\det J|^2$, and $\log \det k$ changes by the function $\log |\det J|^2$. This function is pluriharmonic: for a nonvanishing holomorphic function $F$, $\partial _{\bar j}\log |F|^2=\overline{\partial _ jF}/\bar F$ is antiholomorphic, so $\partial _ i\partial _{\bar j}\log |F|^2=0$. Consequently the ratios $\det k/\det h$ and $\det g/\det k$ are smooth positive functions on $X$, the functions $D_ h\log \det k$ and $D_ h\log \det g$ do not depend on the coordinates, and the functions $\operatorname {Ric}(k)_{i\bar j}=-\partial _ i\partial _{\bar j}\log \det k$ are the coefficients of a well-defined smooth real $(1,1)$-form $\frac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }\operatorname {Ric}(k)_{i\bar j}\, \mathrm dz_ i\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ j$ on $X$. By lemma 7.2.2 (2), $\omega _ A^ n=\det A\, \omega _ I^ n$ for every Hermitian $n\times n$ matrix $A$, where $\omega _ A=\mathrm i\sum _{i,j}A_{i\bar j}\, \mathrm dz_ i\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ j$; since $\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a=\omega _{g/2\pi }$ and $\kappa =\omega _{k/2\pi }$, it follows that $(\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a)^ n/\kappa ^ n=\det g/\det k$. We also use Jacobi's formula $\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm d\tau }\log \det M(\tau )=\operatorname {tr}(M^{-1}M')$ for a differentiable family of matrices with positive determinant. It follows from the identities $\det (M+\varepsilon N)=\det M\det (I+\varepsilon M^{-1}N)$ and $\det (I+\varepsilon N')=1+\varepsilon \operatorname {tr}N'+O(\varepsilon ^2)$. With our normalization of the inverse matrix, it reads $\partial \log \det g=g^{i\bar j}\partial g_{i\bar j}$ for every first-order derivative $\partial $. The maximum principle enters through the following observation. If a smooth real function $b$ has a local maximum at a point $x$, then its complex Hessian is negative semidefinite at $x$: for $\xi \in \mathbb C^ n$ the function $s\mapsto b(x+s\xi )$ of one complex variable has a local maximum at $s=0$, so its Laplacian $4b_{i\bar j}\xi _ i\bar\xi _ j$ is nonpositive there. Consequently $D_ gb\leq 0$ at $x$, since the trace of the product of a positive definite and a negative semidefinite Hermitian matrix is nonpositive. Finally $\operatorname {osc}_ Xf=\max _ Xf-\min _ Xf$ denotes the oscillation of a continuous function $f$. For smooth $f$, Stokes' formula gives $\int _ XD_ hf\, \mathrm dV=-(4\pi )^{-1}\int _ XLf\, \mathrm dV=-(4\pi )^{-1}\int _ X\langle \mathrm df,\mathrm d1\rangle \, \mathrm dV=0$, so that 16.10 \begin{equation} \label{eq:penalized-upper-laplacian-nonnegative} \sup _ XD_ hf\geq 0. \end{equation} Moreover, two-sided bounds for $D_ hv$ in the sense of distributions are pointwise bounds. Let $v$ be a real function in $L^1(X)$; since $D_ h=-L/(4\pi )$ is formally self-adjoint, $\langle D_ hv,\chi \rangle =\int _ Xv\, D_ h\chi \, \mathrm dV$ for smooth $\chi $. Suppose that there are constants $c_1,c_2\geq 0$ such that 16.11 \begin{equation} \label{eq:penalized-distributional-trace-bound} -c_1\int _ X\chi \, \mathrm dV\leq \langle D_ hv,\chi \rangle \leq c_2\int _ X\chi \, \mathrm dV \qquad \text{for every smooth function }\chi \geq 0. \end{equation} Then $D_ hv$, and hence $Lv=-4\pi D_ hv$, is a bounded function, with $|D_ hv|\leq c=\max \{ c_1,c_2\} $. Indeed, let $\mathrm dV=\varrho \, \mathrm dV_{2n}$ in a chart, with $\varrho $ smooth and positive. Pairing the real distribution $D_ hv$ with a test function $\chi $ through Lebesgue measure amounts to pairing it with $\chi /\varrho $ through $\mathrm dV$, so $|\langle D_ hv,\chi \rangle |\leq c\int \chi \, \mathrm dV_{2n}$ for nonnegative test functions $\chi $, and corollary 1.7.2 (1) applies. The maximum principle arguments below are carried out at a point, in holomorphic coordinates centered there in which the coefficient matrix of a Kähler form equals the identity matrix at the point and has vanishing first derivatives there. Such coordinates exist by lemma 14.1.5 , after a linear rescaling that adapts its normalization to ours. Since our estimates must be uniform in the point, we use the following explicit choice, for which all derivatives of the coefficients at the center are bounded uniformly. Lemma 16.2.13 . Let $U\subset \mathbb C^ n$ be open, and let $e=(e_{i\bar j})$ be a smooth function on $U$ with values in the positive definite Hermitian matrices such that the form $\frac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }e_{i\bar j}\, \mathrm dz_ i\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ j$ is closed. For every $z_0\in U$ there is a polynomial map $\Phi _{z_0}\colon \mathbb C^ n\to \mathbb C^ n$ of degree at most two, with $\Phi _{z_0}(0)=z_0$, which is a biholomorphism from a neighborhood of $0$ onto a neighborhood of $z_0$, such that the coefficient matrix $\tilde e$ of the form in the coordinates $w$ given by $z=\Phi _{z_0}(w)$ satisfies $\tilde e(0)=I$ and $\mathrm d\tilde e(0)=0$. For every compact set $K\subset U$ and every integer $q\geq 0$, the derivatives of order at most $q$ of $\tilde e$ at $0$ are bounded independently of $z_0\in K$. These properties persist if $\Phi _{z_0}$ is composed with a unitary linear map. Proof. The form is closed if and only if its $(2,1)$-part $\frac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }\partial _ le_{i\bar j}\, \mathrm dz_ l\wedge \mathrm dz_ i\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ j$ and the conjugate $(1,2)$-part vanish, that is, if and only if $\partial _ le_{i\bar j}=\partial _ ie_{l\bar j}$; this holds in all holomorphic coordinates. If $z=\Phi (w)$ with $\Phi $ holomorphic and $J=D\Phi $ its complex Jacobian matrix, then $\mathrm dz_ i=J_{ia}\, \mathrm dw_ a$, so the new coefficients are $\tilde e(w)=J(w)^{\mathrm T}e(\Phi (w))\overline{J(w)}$. Let $A=\overline{e(z_0)^{-1/2}}$, where $e(z_0)^{-1/2}$ is the positive square root of the inverse matrix; its operator norm is $\lambda (z_0)^{-1/2}$, where $\lambda (z)=\min _{|\xi |=1}\sum _{i,j}e_{i\bar j}(z)\xi _ i\bar\xi _ j$ is the smallest eigenvalue of $e(z)$, and $A^{\mathrm T}e(z_0)\bar A=e(z_0)^{-1/2}e(z_0)e(z_0)^{-1/2}=I$. In the coordinates $v$ with $z=z_0+Av$ the coefficient matrix $e'$ satisfies $e'(0)=I$. Put $c^ m_{ij}=\partial _{v_ i}e'_{j\bar m}(0)$, which is symmetric in $i$ and $j$ by the closedness, and define $v=w-\frac12c(w,w)$, that is, $v_ m=w_ m-\frac12c^ m_{ij}w_ iw_ j$. Then $J_{ia}=\partial v_ i/\partial w_ a=\delta _{ia}-c^ i_{aj}w_ j$, so $J(0)=I$ and $\partial _{w_ p}J_{ia}(0)=-c^ i_{ap}$. Differentiating $\tilde e_{a\bar b}=J_{ia}e'_{i\bar j}(v(w))\overline{J_{jb}}$ at $w=0$, and using that $\overline{J_{jb}}$ and $\bar v$ are antiholomorphic in $w$, we find \[  \partial _{w_ p}\tilde e_{a\bar b}(0)=-c^ b_{ap}+\partial _{v_ p}e'_{a\bar b}(0)=-\partial _{v_ a}e'_{p\bar b}(0)+\partial _{v_ p}e'_{a\bar b}(0)=0,  \] by the closedness, and $\partial _{\bar w_ p}\tilde e_{a\bar b}(0)=\overline{\partial _{w_ p}\tilde e_{b\bar a}(0)}=0$. Put $\Phi _{z_0}(w)=z_0+A(w-\frac12c(w,w))$. Its derivative at $0$ is the invertible matrix $A$, so it is a biholomorphism near $0$ by the holomorphic inverse function theorem (proposition 7.1.2 (1)). By the chain rule, the derivatives of $\tilde e$ at $0$ are polynomials in the derivatives of $e$ at $z_0$ and in the entries of $A$, $\bar A$ and $c$, and the entries of $c$ are polynomials in the first derivatives of $e$ at $z_0$ and in the entries of $A$ and $\bar A$. The derivatives of $e$ are bounded on compact sets, and so are the entries of $A$, because the function $\lambda $ is continuous and positive, as a minimum over the unit sphere of a function that is continuous in $(z,\xi )$; hence these polynomials are bounded for $z_0\in K$. Finally, if $Q$ is unitary, replacing $\Phi _{z_0}(w)$ by $\Phi _{z_0}(Qw)$ replaces $\tilde e(w)$ by $Q^{\mathrm T}\tilde e(Qw)\bar Q$, which equals $Q^{\mathrm T}\bar Q=\overline{Q^*Q}=I$ at $0$, still has vanishing differential at $0$, and has derivatives at $0$ bounded by a constant depending only on $n$ times those of $\tilde e$. $\square$ We first compute the Laplacian of the trace $H=\operatorname {tr}_ hg$ with respect to $g$, for an arbitrary Kähler form $\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a$. Lemma 16.2.14 . There is a constant $C_ E$, depending only on $X$ and $\omega $, with the following property. Let $a$ be a smooth real function on $X$ with $\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a>0$, let $g=(k_{i\bar j}+a_{i\bar j})$ be the coefficient matrix of $2\pi (\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a)$, and put $H=\operatorname {tr}_ hg$. Then $H\operatorname {tr}_ gh\geq n^2$ on $X$. Moreover, every $x\in X$ is the center of holomorphic coordinates in which $h_{i\bar j}=\delta _{ij}$ and all first derivatives of $h$ vanish at $x$, and $g$ is diagonal at $x$, with eigenvalues $\lambda _1,\ldots ,\lambda _ n>0$, such that at $x$ 16.12 \begin{equation} \label{eq:penalized-trace-laplacian} D_ gH=D_ h\log \det g +\sum _{i,p,q}\frac{|\partial _ pg_{i\bar q}|^2}{\lambda _ i\lambda _ q}+E, \qquad |E|\leq C_ EH\operatorname {tr}_ gh, \end{equation} and 16.13 \begin{equation} \label{eq:kahler-log-trace-inequality} D_ g\log H\geq \frac1H\bigl (D_ h\log \det g+E\bigr ). \end{equation} Proof. At every point the eigenvalues of $g$ relative to $h$ are positive, their sum is $H$ and the sum of their inverses is $\operatorname {tr}_ gh$, so the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality gives $H\operatorname {tr}_ gh\geq n^2$. Fix finitely many charts and compact subsets of their domains whose union is $X$, and let $x\in X$. By lemma 16.2.13 , applied to $h$ in one of these charts, followed by a unitary change of coordinates that diagonalizes $g$ at $x$, there are coordinates as in the statement. In them, the derivatives of order at most two of $h$ at $x$ are bounded by a constant depending only on $X$ and $\omega $. All the following computations are at $x$, in these coordinates. Locally $\kappa $ and $\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a$ have Kähler potentials (lemma 13.1.2 ): $g_{i\bar j}=\partial _ i\partial _{\bar j}\varphi $ with $\varphi $ smooth. Hence the derivatives $\partial _ pg_{i\bar q}$ are symmetric in $p$ and $i$, and the second derivatives $\partial _ p\partial _{\bar l}g_{i\bar q}$ are symmetric in $p,i$ and in $\bar l,\bar q$. Differentiating $H=h^{i\bar q}g_{i\bar q}$ twice, and using that the first derivatives of $h$, hence of $h^{-1}$, vanish at $x$, we get \[  D_ gH=\sum _ p\lambda _ p^{-1}\sum _ i\partial _ p\partial _{\bar p}g_{i\bar i}+E, \qquad E=\sum _ p\lambda _ p^{-1}\bigl (\partial _ p\partial _{\bar p}h^{i\bar q}\bigr )g_{i\bar q}.  \] Since $g$ is diagonal with positive eigenvalues, $|E|\leq C_ EH\operatorname {tr}_ gh$, where $C_ E$ bounds the second derivatives of $h^{-1}$ at $x$. As $h=I$ and $\mathrm dh=0$ at $x$, the formula $\partial (h^{-1})=-h^{-1}(\partial h)h^{-1}$ shows that these are the second derivatives of $-h$, up to transposition; so $C_ E$ depends only on $X$ and $\omega $. On the other hand, differentiating the identity $\partial _ p\log \det g=g^{i\bar q}\partial _ pg_{i\bar q}$ and using $\partial (g^{-1})=-g^{-1}(\partial g)g^{-1}$ gives \[  \partial _ p\partial _{\bar p}\log \det g =\sum _ i\lambda _ i^{-1}\partial _ p\partial _{\bar p}g_{i\bar i} -\sum _{i,q}\frac{|\partial _ pg_{i\bar q}|^2}{\lambda _ i\lambda _ q}.  \] By the symmetry of the second derivatives, $\partial _ p\partial _{\bar p}g_{i\bar i}=\partial _ i\partial _{\bar i}g_{p\bar p}$. Summing over $p$, comparing with the formula for $D_ gH$, and noting that $\sum _ p\partial _ p\partial _{\bar p}=D_ h$ at $x$, we obtain the identity ( 16.12 ), with the bound for $E$ just proved. For the inequality for $\log H$, note that $\partial _ pH=\sum _ i\partial _ pg_{i\bar i}=\sum _ i\partial _ ig_{p\bar i}$ by the symmetry of the first derivatives. The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality with weights $\lambda _ i$ therefore gives \[  |\partial H|_ g^2 =\sum _ p\frac1{\lambda _ p}\Bigl |\sum _ i\partial _ ig_{p\bar i}\Bigr |^2 \leq H\sum _{p,i}\frac{|\partial _ ig_{p\bar i}|^2}{\lambda _ p\lambda _ i} \leq H\sum _{i,p,q}\frac{|\partial _ pg_{i\bar q}|^2}{\lambda _ i\lambda _ q},  \] the last sum containing the previous one (take $p=q$ in the term of index $(i,p,q)$ and rename). Since $D_ g\log H=H^{-1}D_ gH-H^{-2}|\partial H|_ g^2$, the quadratic term in $D_ gH$ absorbs the negative term, and ( 16.13 ) follows. $\square$ For a solution of the penalized equation, the identity $\log \det g=\log \det k+\beta (a-f)$ controls the term $D_ h\log \det g$, and the maximum principle then bounds $H$. Lemma 16.2.15 . Let $f$ be a smooth real function on $X$ and $\beta >0$, and let $a$ be a smooth real function satisfying 16.14 \begin{equation} \label{eq:penalized-kahler-equation} (\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a)^ n=\mathrm e^{\beta (a-f)}\kappa ^ n, \qquad \kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a>0. \end{equation} Then $\min _ Xf\leq a\leq \max _ Xf$, and the metrics $g$ and $h$ are uniformly equivalent: $C^{-1}h\leq g\leq Ch$ on $X$, with $C$ depending only on $X$, $\omega $, $\kappa $, $\beta $ and upper bounds for $\| f\| _\infty $ and $\sup _ XD_ hf$. Moreover, there is $\beta _0>0$, depending only on $X$, $\omega $ and $\kappa $, such that for $\beta >\beta _0$ \[  H\leq 2B\, \mathrm e^{A\operatorname {osc}_ Xf}\quad \text{on }X, \qquad B=\sup _ X\operatorname {tr}_ hk+\sup _ XD_ hf,  \] where $A>0$ depends only on $X$, $\omega $ and $\kappa $. In particular, for $\beta >\beta _0$ the trace $H$ is bounded by a constant depending only on $X$, $\omega $, $\kappa $ and upper bounds for $\| f\| _\infty $ and $\sup _ XD_ hf$. Proof. In general, let $K\subset D'$ be compact; the set $K'=\{ x+tse:x\in K,\  0\leq t\leq 1\} $ is a compact subset of $D$. The mollifications $Z_\varepsilon =Z*\rho _\varepsilon $ are smooth near $K'$ for small $\varepsilon $, they converge to $Z$ in $L^1(K')$, and $\partial _ eZ_\varepsilon =(\partial _ eZ)*\rho _\varepsilon \to \partial _ eZ$ in $L^1(K')$, by proposition 1.4.3 (1) and lemma 1.4.1 (2). Hence the identity for $Z_\varepsilon $ passes to the limit in $L^1(K)$; for the right side we use $\int _ K\int _0^1|F(x+tse)|\, \mathrm dt\, \mathrm dx\leq \int _{K'}|F|$, by Tonelli's theorem. This proves the claim. By Hölder's inequality on $[0,1]$ and Tonelli's theorem, \[  \int _{D'}|\delta _ sZ|^ p\leq \int _0^1\int _{D'}|\partial _ eZ(x+tse)|^ p\, \mathrm dx\, \mathrm dt\leq \| \partial _ eZ\| _{L^ p(D)}^ p.  \] Similarly, since $\delta _ sZ(x)-\partial _ eZ(x)=\int _0^1\bigl (\partial _ eZ(x+tse)-\partial _ eZ(x)\bigr )\, \mathrm dt$ for almost every $x\in D'$, Hölder's inequality and Tonelli's theorem give, with $F$ the extension of $\partial _ eZ$ by zero to $\mathbb R^ d$, \[  \| \delta _ sZ-\partial _ eZ\| _{L^ p(D')}\leq \sup _{|r|\leq |s|}\| F(\cdot +re)-F\| _{L^ p(\mathbb R^ d)},  \] which tends to zero as $s\to 0$ by the continuity of translation in $L^ p(\mathbb R^ d)$ (lemma 1.4.1 (2)). (2) Let $\chi \in C_ c^\infty (D')$ with $0\leq \chi \leq 1$, extend $\chi Z$ by zero, and let $0<|s|<\min \{ s_1,\operatorname {dist}(\operatorname{Supp}\chi ,\mathbb R^ d\setminus D')\} $. Fatou's lemma gives $\| \partial _ eZ\| _{L^ p(D'')}\leq \varliminf _ j\| \delta _{s_ j}Z\| _{L^ p(D'')}\leq M$. Exhausting $D'$ by such sets $D''$ and using monotone convergence, we obtain $\| \partial _ eZ\| _{L^ p(D')}\leq M$. $\square$ We now prove this regularity in a chart, with estimates for the higher derivatives. For a function $G=(G_{i\bar j})$ with values in the positive definite Hermitian matrices we write $(g^{i\bar j})$ for its inverse in the normalization above and $D_ Gw=g^{i\bar j}\partial _ i\partial _{\bar j}w$; by Jacobi's formula, $\partial \log \det G=g^{i\bar j}\partial G_{i\bar j}=\operatorname {tr}(G^{-1}\partial G)$ for every first-order derivative $\partial $. Lemma 16.2.19 . Let $U\subset \mathbb C^ n$ be open, let $k=(k_{i\bar j})$ be a smooth function on $U$ with values in the Hermitian matrices, let $\phi _0$ be a smooth real function on $U$, and let $\beta \in \mathbb R$. Moreover, let $V\Subset U$ be open, let $\ell \geq 3$ be an integer and $2\leq p<\infty $, and suppose that $\lambda I\leq G\leq \Lambda I$ on $U$ for constants $0<\lambda \leq \Lambda $, that $|G(x)-G(y)|\leq \varpi (|x-y|)$ for $x,y\in U$, where $\varpi (r)\to 0$ as $r\to 0$, and that $\| u\| _{C^1(U)}+\| D^2u\| _{L^ q(U)}\leq M$, where $q=2^\ell (p+2n)$. Proof. For the quantitative assertion, $C$ denotes constants depending only on the quantities listed there; $O'\Subset O\Subset O_1\Subset U$ denote open sets, and the constants may also depend on them. The qualitative assertion follows from the quantitative one. Indeed, if $V\Subset U'\Subset U$ with $U'$ open, then on $U'$ the matrix $G$ is bounded above and below and uniformly continuous, and $u$ has finite $C^1$ norm and bounded second derivatives. The quantitative assertion, applied on $U'$, therefore gives $u\in W^{\ell ,p}(V)$ for all $\ell $ and $p$, and Morrey's inequality (lemma 6.2.6 ), applied to the derivatives of $u$, shows that all derivatives of $u$ are continuous on $V$. We prove the estimate by bootstrapping: an interior $L^ p$ estimate (Step 1), applied to difference quotients, raises the order of differentiability by one at a time (Steps 2 and 3), on smaller domains and with smaller exponents, and Step 4 chains these steps. Step 1: an interior estimate. Let $(a^{i\bar j})$ be a function on $O$ with $\overline{a^{i\bar j}}=a^{j\bar i}$, $\Lambda ^{-1}|\zeta |^2\leq a^{i\bar j}\zeta _ i\bar\zeta _ j\leq \lambda ^{-1}|\zeta |^2$ and $|a(x)-a(y)|\leq \varpi '(|x-y|)$, where $\varpi '(r)\to 0$ as $r\to 0$. Indeed, by ( 16.8 ), $a^{i\bar j}\partial _ i\partial _{\bar j}w=A:D^2w$ with a real symmetric $A\geq (4\Lambda )^{-1}I$, $|A|\leq C\lambda ^{-1}$ and $|A(x)-A(y)|\leq \varpi '(|x-y|)$. By lemma 6.2.4 (1) and lemma 16.2.10 , \[  \| D^2(\chi _\nu w)\| _ p\leq C_1\| A:D^2(\chi _\nu w)\| _{L^ p(B(x_\nu ,r))},  \] and $A:D^2(\chi _\nu w)=\chi _\nu \, A:D^2w+2\sum _{\mu ,\sigma }A^{\mu \sigma }\partial _\mu \chi _\nu \, \partial _\sigma w+w\, A:D^2\chi _\nu $. Let $e$ be a real coordinate unit vector, and let $0<|s|<\operatorname {dist}(O,\mathbb R^{2n}\setminus O_1)$, with the notation $\tau _ s$, $\delta _ s$ of lemma 16.2.18 . For $x\in O$ and $0\leq t\leq 1$ the matrix $G_ t(x)=(1-t)G(x)+tG(x+se)$ satisfies $\lambda I\leq G_ t\leq \Lambda I$; let $(g_ t^{i\bar j})$ be its inverse and $a_ s^{i\bar j}=\int _0^1g_ t^{i\bar j}\, \mathrm dt$. Since $\delta _ s\partial _\mu \partial _\sigma u=\partial _\mu \partial _\sigma \delta _ su$, lemma 16.2.18 (2), applied to $Z=\partial _\mu \partial _\sigma u$, shows that $\partial _ e\partial _\mu \partial _\sigma u\in L^ p(O')$, with norm at most $C$. Let $\ell \geq 3$ and suppose that $u\in W^{\ell ,q'}(O_1)$ for some $q'\geq 2p+2n$. By Morrey's inequality (lemma 6.2.6 ), applied to the derivatives of $u$ of order at most $\ell -2$, which lie in $W^{2,q'}(O_1)$, the function $u$ is of class $C^{\ell -1}$ on $O_1$, and on a slightly smaller set, which we again call $O_1$, its derivatives of order at most $\ell -1$ are bounded by $C\| u\| _{W^{\ell ,q'}}$. Thus $G\in C^{\ell -3}(O_1)$, its derivatives of order at most $\ell -3$ lie in $W^{1,2p}(O_1)$, and those of order $\ell -2$ lie in $L^{2p}(O_1)$. We first record a formula for the derivatives of $\log \det G$. For a smooth function $G$ with values in the positive definite Hermitian matrices and a multi-index $\gamma $ with $|\gamma |\geq 1$, \[  \partial ^\gamma \log \det G=\operatorname {tr}(G^{-1}\partial ^\gamma G)+P_\gamma (G),  \] where $P_\gamma (G)$ is a linear combination, with coefficients depending only on $\gamma $, of functions $\operatorname {tr}(G^{-1}\partial ^{\beta _1}G\, G^{-1}\partial ^{\beta _2}G\cdots G^{-1}\partial ^{\beta _ r}G)$ with $r\geq 2$, $|\beta _ i|\geq 1$ and $\beta _1+\cdots +\beta _ r=\gamma $; in particular $|\beta _ i|\leq |\gamma |-1$. For $|\gamma |=1$ this is Jacobi's formula, with $P_\gamma =0$. If it holds for $\gamma $, differentiate once more: by the Leibniz rule and $\partial _\mu (G^{-1})=-G^{-1}(\partial _\mu G)G^{-1}$, the derivative of each term $\operatorname {tr}(G^{-1}\partial ^{\beta _1}G\cdots )$ is a sum of terms of the same form, with $r$ or $r+1$ factors and total multi-index $\gamma +e_\mu $, and the derivative of $\operatorname {tr}(G^{-1}\partial ^\gamma G)$ is $\operatorname {tr}(G^{-1}\partial ^{\gamma +e_\mu }G)-\operatorname {tr}(G^{-1}\partial _\mu G\, G^{-1}\partial ^\gamma G)$. Note that $\operatorname {tr}(G^{-1}\partial ^\gamma G)=g^{i\bar j}\partial ^\gamma G_{i\bar j}$. Now fix $\gamma $ with $|\gamma |=\ell -2\geq 1$. We claim that, almost everywhere on $O_1$, \[  \operatorname {tr}(G^{-1}\partial ^\gamma G)+P_\gamma (G)=\partial ^\gamma \phi _0+\beta \, \partial ^\gamma u,  \] where $\partial ^\gamma G$ is formed with weak derivatives. Let $K\subset O_1$ be compact, and let $u_\varepsilon =u*\rho _\varepsilon $ and $G_\varepsilon =k+(\partial _ i\partial _{\bar j}u_\varepsilon )$. By proposition 1.4.3 (1) and lemma 1.4.1 (1),(2), as $\varepsilon \to 0$ the derivatives of $u_\varepsilon $ of order at most $\ell -1$ converge uniformly on $K$ to those of $u$, and those of order $\ell $ converge in $L^{2p}(K)$. Hence $G_\varepsilon $ is positive definite on $K$ for small $\varepsilon $, its derivatives of order at most $\ell -3$ converge uniformly on $K$ to those of $G$, and $\partial ^\gamma G_\varepsilon \to \partial ^\gamma G$ in $L^{2p}(K)$. The formula above holds for the smooth functions $G_\varepsilon $ on the interior of $K$. Its left side converges to $\partial ^\gamma \log \det G=\partial ^\gamma \phi _0+\beta \partial ^\gamma u$ in the sense of distributions, since $\log \det G_\varepsilon \to \log \det G$ uniformly on $K$ and $\log \det G=\phi _0+\beta u$, and its right side converges in $L^1(K)$, since every factor of $P_\gamma (G_\varepsilon )$ involves derivatives of $G_\varepsilon $ of order at most $\ell -3$. Hence the identity holds in the sense of distributions on the interior of $K$, and therefore almost everywhere (proposition 1.4.3 (4)). This proves the claim. Put $v=\partial ^\gamma u\in W^{2,2p}(O_1)$. Since $\operatorname {tr}(G^{-1}\partial ^\gamma G)=D_ Gv+g^{i\bar j}\partial ^\gamma k_{i\bar j}$, the claim says that \[  D_ Gv=R:=\partial ^\gamma \phi _0+\beta v-g^{i\bar j}\partial ^\gamma k_{i\bar j}-P_\gamma (G)\qquad \text{almost everywhere on }O_1.  \] For $x\in O$ and small $s$, as in Step 2, the discrete product rule $\delta _ s(FF')=(\tau _ sF)\delta _ sF'+(\delta _ sF)F'$ gives \[  (\tau _ sg^{i\bar j})\, \partial _ i\partial _{\bar j}(\delta _ sv)=\delta _ sR-(\delta _ sg^{i\bar j})\, \partial _ i\partial _{\bar j}v\qquad \text{almost everywhere on }O.  \] We bound the right side in $L^ p(O)$ uniformly in $s$, using lemma 16.2.18 (1) on $O\Subset O_1$. Next, $\| \delta _ s\partial ^\gamma \phi _0\| _\infty \leq C$ and $\| \delta _ sv\| _{L^ p(O)}\leq \| \partial _ ev\| _{L^ p(O_1)}\leq C$. Thus the right side is bounded in $L^ p(O)$, and $\| \delta _ sv\| _{W^{1,p}(O)}\leq \| \partial _ ev\| _{W^{1,p}(O_1)}\leq C$. Choose open sets $V=O_{3\ell }\Subset O_{3\ell -1}\Subset \cdots \Subset O_0=U$, depending only on $V$, $U$ and $\ell $, and put $p_ m=2^{\ell -m}(p+2n)-2n$ for $3\leq m\leq \ell $. For $m=\ell -1$ we obtain the bound for $\| u\| _{W^{\ell ,p}(V)}$. $\square$ The openness part of the continuity method is a perturbation argument in Sobolev spaces that are algebras.
