Therefore $D_ hP_\kappa (F_ m)	o D_ hu$ in the sense of distributions, and $u$ satisfies ( 16.11 ) with $c_1=\sup _ X\operatorname {tr}_ hk$ and $c_2=\sup _ m2B_ m\mathrm e^{2A\| F_ m\| _\infty }$. By the remark following ( 16.11 ), $D_ hu$, and hence $Lu=-4\pi D_ hu$, is a bounded function with the asserted bound. The function $u$ is continuous, as a uniform limit of the functions $P_\kappa (F_ m)$, which are continuous by proposition 16.2.22 ; so proposition 16.2.11 shows that $u\in C^{1,\alpha }(X)$ for every $0<\alpha <1$. Finally, $u$ is a continuous $\kappa $-psh function with bounded metric Laplacian, so by proposition 16.2.9 , applied with $U=X$, $	heta _ j=\kappa $, and $u$ in place of both $u_ j$ and $f_ j$ for every $j$, the coefficients of $\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ are bounded on every coordinate ball $W\Subset X$, hence on $X$. $\square$

title: Real Hessian bounds for Kähler envelopes
text:
16.2.4 Real Hessian bounds for Kähler envelopes A bounded metric Laplacian bounds the complex Hessian of a potential, by positivity, but the full real Hessian also contains the $(2,0)$ and $(0,2)$ parts, and bounding these requires a different argument. We now show that, for a Kähler background, the envelope of a finite minimum of $C^{1,1}$ obstacles is again $C^{1,1}$ (theorem 16.2.26 ). The main step is an a priori bound for the full real Hessian of the solutions of the penalized equation (lemma 16.2.25 ), obtained from the maximum principle applied to the largest eigenvalue of the real Hessian. Differentiating this eigenvalue twice produces positive third-derivative terms, and we keep them: they absorb the negative term that comes from differentiating its logarithm. We first recall the covariant Hessian of a Riemannian metric. Let $g$ be a smooth Riemannian metric on $X$. For smooth vector fields $Y,Z,W$ on an open set $U\subset X$ let $\mathcal K_{Y,Z}(W)$ be the right side of the Koszul formula  egin{align*}  2g(
abla _ YZ,W)={}& Y\, g(Z,W)+Z\, g(Y,W)-W\, g(Y,Z)\ & +g([Y,Z],W)-g([Y,W],Z)-g([Z,W],Y). \end{align*} If $W$ is replaced by $\phi W$ for a smooth function $\phi $, the terms of $\mathcal K_{Y,Z}(\phi W)$ containing derivatives of $\phi $ cancel in pairs, so $\mathcal K_{Y,Z}(\phi W)=\phi \, \mathcal K_{Y,Z}(W)$. In a chart, therefore, $\mathcal K_{Y,Z}(W)=\sum _ sW^ s\mathcal K_{Y,Z}(\partial _ s)$, and since $g$ is nondegenerate there is a unique smooth vector field $
abla _ YZ$ satisfying the Koszul formula for all $W$; by uniqueness, the vector fields obtained in different charts agree on overlaps. This is the Levi-Civita connection of $g$. Replacing $Y$ or $Z$ by $\phi Y$ or $\phi Z$ in the formula, the terms containing derivatives of $\phi $ cancel, respectively add up to $2(Y\phi )g(Z,W)$, so $
abla _{\phi Y}Z=\phi 
abla _ YZ$ and $
abla _ Y(\phi Z)=(Y\phi )Z+\phi 
abla _ YZ$; and interchanging $Y$ and $Z$ changes the right side by $-2g([Y,Z],W)$, so $
abla _ YZ-
abla _ ZY=[Y,Z]$. In coordinates, with $g_{uv}=g(\partial _ u,\partial _ v)$, the Koszul formula for coordinate vector fields gives $
abla _{\partial _ u}\partial _ v=\sum _ t\Gamma ^ t_{uv}\partial _ t$, where the Christoffel symbols are determined by $\sum _ tg_{st}\Gamma ^ t_{uv}= rac12(\partial _ ug_{vs}+\partial _ vg_{us}-\partial _ sg_{uv})$; they are symmetric in $u$ and $v$ and vanish at a point where the first derivatives of the $g_{uv}$ vanish. For a smooth function $b$, the covariant Hessian $
abla ^2b(Y,Z)=Y(Zb)-(
abla _ YZ)b$ is, by these rules, given in coordinates by \[  
abla ^2b(Y,Z)=\sum _{u,v}Y^ uZ^ v\Bigl (\partial _ u\partial _ vb-\sum _ t\Gamma ^ t_{uv}\partial _ tb\Bigr ).  \] Hence $
abla ^2b$ is a symmetric bilinear form on each tangent space, and at a point where the first derivatives of the metric vanish it is the matrix of second derivatives of $b$. If $g'$ is another smooth Riemannian metric, the difference $
abla '_ YZ-
abla _ YZ$ is linear over smooth functions in $Y$ and in $Z$, by the rules above, so the two covariant Hessians of $b$ differ by a smooth tensor applied to $\mathrm db$. For a $C^1$ function $b$ the same coordinate formula, with distributional second derivatives, defines the weak covariant Hessian . Recall that a function is of class $C^{1,1}$ if it is $C^1$ and its first derivatives are locally Lipschitz in smooth real coordinates (proposition 1.7.5 ). On the compact manifold $X$ we measure such a function by the supremum norms of its value, its gradient and its weak covariant Hessian with respect to a fixed smooth Riemannian metric; the sum of these three norms is its $C^{1,1}$ norm . The two descriptions agree: the first derivatives of a $C^1$ function are locally Lipschitz exactly when its weak second derivatives are locally bounded. Indeed, if a first derivative $\partial _ af$ is Lipschitz with constant $M$ on a coordinate ball, its difference quotients in a direction $e_ b$ are bounded by $M$; pairing them with a test function $\varphi $ and passing to the limit gives $|\langle \partial _ b\partial _ af,\varphi angle |\leq M\int |\varphi |\, \mathrm dx$. By corollary 1.7.2 (1), $\partial _ b\partial _ af$ is therefore a bounded function, with $|\partial _ b\partial _ af|\leq M$. Conversely, by proposition 1.7.5 , a continuous function whose weak second derivatives are bounded by $M$ on a ball has a gradient that is Lipschitz on this ball with constant $2nM$, the real dimension being $2n$. The Christoffel symbols of a metric and the derivatives of coordinate changes are bounded on compact subsets of the charts, and they multiply only first derivatives, so different smooth metrics give equivalent $C^{1,1}$ norms. In the applications below, the $C^1$ property of the envelope will be known in advance from proposition 16.2.11 . Lemma 16.2.25 . Let $\kappa $ be a Kähler form on $X$, and let $g_0$ be a smooth Riemannian metric on $X$ with Levi-Civita connection $
abla $. Let $B>0$, and let $f$ be a smooth real function such that \[  \| f\| _\infty +\| 
abla f\| _\infty \leq B, \qquad 
abla ^2f\leq Bg_0  \] as real quadratic forms, and for $ eta >0$ let $a_ eta $ be the solution of ( 16.14 ) given by theorem 16.2.21 . Then there are constants $ eta _0$ and $C$, depending only on $B$ and on the fixed geometry ($X$, $\kappa $ and $g_0$), such that \[  \| a_ eta \| _\infty +\| 
abla a_ eta \| _\infty +\| 
abla ^2a_ eta \| _\infty \leq C \qquad ( eta \geq  eta _0).  \] Proof. Step 1 reduces to a metric defined by $\kappa $ and collects the bounds for $a_ eta $ and its gradient. Steps 2 and 3 apply the maximum principle to the logarithm of the largest eigenvalue of $
abla ^2a_ eta $, corrected by functions of the gradient and of $a_ eta $, and Step 4 absorbs the negative term with third derivatives. Step 1: reductions and first bounds. Any two smooth Riemannian metrics on $X$ are uniformly equivalent, and, as observed before the lemma, the Hessians of a function for the two metrics differ by a bounded tensor applied to its gradient. Changing $g_0$ therefore changes $B$ and the constants only by factors depending on the two metrics, and we may assume that $g_0$ is the following Riemannian metric defined by $\kappa $. In local holomorphic coordinates write $\kappa = rac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }k_{i ar j}\, \mathrm dz_ i\wedge \mathrm d ar z_ j$, so that $k$ is the coefficient matrix of $2\pi \kappa $ as in section 16.2.3 , and let $g_0=2\operatorname{Re}(k_{i ar j}\, \mathrm dz_ i\otimes \mathrm d ar z_ j)$; this is $2\pi $ times the Riemannian metric $\kappa (\cdot ,J\cdot )$, where $J$ is the complex structure. At the center of normal coordinates for $\kappa $, given by lemma 16.2.13 , we have $k_{i ar j}=\delta _{ij}$ and $\mathrm dk=0$; hence the Christoffel symbols of $g_0$ vanish and $g_0=2\sum _ i(\mathrm dx_ i^2+\mathrm dy_ i^2)$. Comparing coordinate derivatives at such a point, we obtain for every smooth function $b$ 16.26  egin{equation} \label{eq:real-hessian-trace-identity} \operatorname {tr}_{g_0}
abla ^2b=2D_ kb, \qquad D_ kb=k^{i ar j}b_{i ar j}. \end{equation} In particular the upper bound for $
abla ^2f$ gives $D_ kf\leq nB$. Write $a=a_ eta $, $G=(k_{i ar j}+a_{i ar j})$ and $D_ G=G^{i ar j}\partial _ i\partial _{ ar j}$; thus $G$ is the matrix denoted $g$ in section 16.2.3 . We apply lemma 16.2.15 with $\kappa $ also as the measuring metric. It bounds $|a|$ by $\| f\| _\infty $ and, for all sufficiently large $ eta $, bounds $\operatorname {tr}_ kG$ in terms of $B$ and the fixed geometry. Since $G>0$ and $\operatorname {tr}_ kG$ is bounded, all coefficients of $G$, and hence of the complex Hessian of $a$, are bounded; in particular the metric Laplacian $La$ for the fixed Kähler form $\omega $, which is a constant multiple of the trace of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a$ with respect to $\omega $ (lemma 14.1.6 ), is uniformly bounded. Fix $p>2n$. By proposition 16.2.11 , $\| a\| _{W^{2,p}(X)}\leq C(\| La\| _{L^ p}+\| a\| _{L^ p})$ is uniformly bounded, and Morrey's inequality (lemma 6.2.6 ), applied in the charts defining the norm to the first derivatives of the products of $a$ with the cutoff functions, bounds $
abla a$ uniformly. From now on $C$ denotes a constant depending only on these bounds, on $B$ and on the fixed geometry; it may increase from line to line, but it never depends on $ eta $. Step 2: the auxiliary function. Let $\ell $ be the largest eigenvalue of the real covariant Hessian $
abla ^2a$ with respect to $g_0$. By ( 16.26 ), the sum of all eigenvalues is $2D_ ka=2\operatorname {tr}_ kG-2n\geq -2n$. Since each eigenvalue is at most $\ell $, it is at least $-2n-(2n-1)\ell $; hence every eigenvalue of $
abla ^2a$ has absolute value at most $2n(\max \{ \ell ,0\} +1)$. It therefore suffices to bound $\ell $ from above, and we do so by the maximum principle. Put \[  s=|\partial a|_ k^2,\quad S=\sup _ Xs,\quad 	au =(1+2\sup _ X|\partial f|_ k^2)^{-1},\quad \eta (s)=- rac	au 2\log (1+S-s).  \] Then $S\leq C$, the number $	au \in (0,1]$ has a uniform positive lower bound, and since $0\leq s\leq S$, 16.27  egin{equation} \label{eq:real-hessian-gradient-weight}  rac{	au }{2(1+S)}\leq \eta '\leq  rac	au 2, \qquad \eta ''= rac{2(\eta ')^2}{	au }\geq 2(\eta ')^2. \end{equation} For a constant $A>0$ to be chosen later, consider the function $Q=\log \ell +\eta (s)-Aa$ on the open set $\{ \ell >0\} $. If this set is empty, then $\ell \leq 0$ and there is nothing to prove. Otherwise, since $a$ and $\eta (s)$ are bounded, $Q$ tends to $-\infty $ where $\ell $ tends to zero, so by compactness of $X$ it attains its maximum at some point $x_0$ with $\ell (x_0)>0$. For the same reason a uniform bound for $\ell (x_0)$ bounds $\ell $ on all of $X$. We may therefore assume that $\ell (x_0)\geq 1$, and that $\ell (x_0)$ exceeds any uniform threshold used below. Choose normal coordinates for $\kappa $ at $x_0$ in which $G(x_0)$ is diagonal, with diagonal entries $r_ i>0$: by lemma 16.2.13 , applied to $k$ in one of finitely many fixed charts that contains $x_0$ in a fixed compact subset, and followed by a unitary change of coordinates that diagonalizes $G(x_0)$, there are such coordinates in which the derivatives of $k$ of every fixed order at $x_0$ are bounded independently of $x_0$. Since $\sum _ ir_ i=\operatorname {tr}_ kG\leq C$, we have $r_ i\leq C$, hence $r_ i^{-1}\geq c$ for a uniform $c>0$. Write $T=\sum _ ir_ i^{-1}$; thus $T\geq c$. Take a $g_0$-orthonormal basis $V_1,\ldots ,V_{2n}$ of the real tangent space at $x_0$ consisting of eigenvectors of $
abla ^2a(x_0)$, with $V_1$ belonging to the eigenvalue $\ell (x_0)$, and extend these vectors to the chart as vector fields with constant real coordinate coefficients. The largest eigenvalue $\ell $ may be multiple and need not be smooth, so we perturb the Hessian. Let $B_0$ be the symmetric bilinear form with constant coefficients in this chart which at $x_0$ is the $g_0$-orthogonal projection onto $V_1^\perp $, that is, $B_0(Y,Z)=g_0(PY,PZ)$ at $x_0$ for this projection $P$, and set \[  \Phi =g_0^{-1}(
abla ^2a-B_0).  \] The form $B_0$ is positive semidefinite everywhere in the chart. Hence the largest eigenvalue $\lambda _1(\Phi )$ of $\Phi $ is at most $\ell $, and it equals $\ell $ at $x_0$. Denote the eigenvalues of $\Phi $ at $x_0$ by $\lambda =\ell (x_0),\lambda _2,\ldots ,\lambda _{2n}$, with eigenvectors $V_1,\ldots ,V_{2n}$. For $\alpha >1$, $\lambda _\alpha $ is the Hessian eigenvalue belonging to $V_\alpha $ minus one, so $\lambda -\lambda _\alpha \geq 1$. In particular $\lambda _1(\Phi )$ is a smooth function near $x_0$. Indeed, $\lambda $ is a simple root of the characteristic polynomial of $\Phi (x_0)$, so by the implicit function theorem the characteristic polynomial of $\Phi $ has, near $x_0$, exactly one root close to $\lambda $, and this root depends smoothly on the point; it equals $\lambda _1(\Phi )$, which is continuous as the maximum of $(
abla ^2a-B_0)(Y,Y)$ over $g_0$-unit vectors $Y$, and it is a simple eigenvalue. The smooth function $\widehat Q=\log \lambda _1(\Phi )+\eta (s)-Aa$ satisfies $\widehat Q\leq Q\leq Q(x_0)=\widehat Q(x_0)$, so it has a local maximum at $x_0$. Step 3: the inequality at the maximum point. From now on all quantities are evaluated at $x_0$. Write $a_{V_\alpha V_\gamma }=
abla ^2a(V_\alpha ,V_\gamma )$, a smooth function near $x_0$, and define the nonnegative quantities  egin{align*}  U& =2\sum _{i,\alpha >1}  rac{|\partial _ i a_{V_\alpha V_1}|^2}{r_ i\lambda (\lambda -\lambda _\alpha )},&  R& =\sum _{p,q} rac{|V_1G_{p ar q}|^2}{r_ pr_ q\lambda },\  N& =\sum _ i rac{|\partial _ i a_{V_1V_1}|^2}{r_ i\lambda ^2},&  K& =\sum _{i,p} rac{|a_{ip}|^2+|a_{i ar p}|^2}{r_ i}. \end{align*} We first compute $D_ G\log \lambda _1(\Phi )$, keeping the third-derivative terms. Let $M(t)$ be a smooth family of real symmetric matrices, and let $\lambda (t)$ be a simple eigenvalue with unit eigenvector $V_1$ at $t=0$, the other eigenvalues being $\lambda _\alpha $ with orthonormal eigenvectors $V_\alpha $. Then \[  \lambda '=\langle M'V_1,V_1angle ,\qquad \lambda ''=\langle M''V_1,V_1angle +2\sum _{\alpha >1}  rac{|\langle M'V_1,V_\alpha angle |^2}{\lambda -\lambda _\alpha }.  \] Indeed, near $t=0$ the simple eigenvalue $\lambda (t)$ is a smooth function of $t$, by the implicit function theorem applied to the characteristic polynomial, and the columns of the adjugate matrix of $\lambda (t)I-M(t)$, which has rank one, span the eigenspace; normalizing a column that does not vanish at $t=0$ gives a smooth unit eigenvector $y(t)$ with $y(0)=\pm V_1$, and we may take the sign $+$. Differentiate the eigenvector equation $M(t)y(t)=\lambda (t)y(t)$. Pairing with $V_1$ gives the first formula, and pairing with $V_\alpha $ shows that the derivative of the eigenvector has component $\langle M'V_1,V_\alpha angle /(\lambda -\lambda _\alpha )$ along $V_\alpha $, and it has no component along $V_1$, because $|y(t)|=1$. Differentiating the identity $\lambda '(t)=\langle M'(t)y(t),y(t)angle $, where $y(t)$ is the normalized eigenvector with $y(0)=V_1$, and substituting these components gives the second formula. We apply these formulas to the symmetric matrix $M$ with entries $(
abla ^2a-B_0)(e_\alpha ,e_\gamma )$, where $e_1,\ldots ,e_{2n}$ is the $g_0$-orthonormal frame obtained from the constant vector fields $V_1,\ldots ,V_{2n}$ by the Gram–Schmidt process; $M$ has the same eigenvalues as $\Phi $. The frame depends smoothly on the point, equals $V_1,\ldots ,V_{2n}$ at $x_0$, and its first derivatives vanish at $x_0$, because those of $g_0$ do. We differentiate along the real coordinate directions and use $\partial _ i\partial _{ ar i}= rac14(\partial _{x_ i}^2+\partial _{y_ i}^2)$. Since $B_0$ is constant, the first derivatives of $M$ at $x_0$ are those of the functions $
abla ^2a(V_\alpha ,V_\gamma )$. In the second derivatives, the second derivatives of the frame multiply $
abla ^2a-B_0$, which is bounded by $C(\lambda +1)$; after weighting with $r_ i^{-1}$ and summing they contribute at most $C\lambda T$. Since $|\partial _ ib|^2= rac14(|\partial _{x_ i}b|^2+|\partial _{y_ i}b|^2)$ for a real function $b$, we obtain \[  D_ G\lambda _1(\Phi )\geq 2\sum _{i,\alpha >1}  rac{|\partial _ i a_{V_\alpha V_1}|^2}{r_ i(\lambda -\lambda _\alpha )} +\sum _ i r_ i^{-1}V_1V_1G_{i ar i}-C\lambda T.  \] Here the middle term comes from $\sum _ ir_ i^{-1}\partial _ i\partial _{ ar i}a_{V_1V_1}$ after commuting derivatives, and we check that this commutation costs at most $C\lambda T$. In real coordinates $a_{V_1V_1}=V_1V_1a-\Gamma ^ t_{uv}V_1^ uV_1^ v\partial _ ta$, where the Christoffel symbols $\Gamma $ of $g_0$ vanish at $x_0$. When we apply $\partial _ i\partial _{ ar i}$, the term containing third derivatives of $a$ is multiplied by $\Gamma (x_0)=0$; the remaining terms are a first derivative of $\Gamma $ times a second derivative of $a$, or a second derivative of $\Gamma $ times a first derivative of $a$. By the Hessian and gradient bounds above they are at most $C(\lambda +1)$. Moreover $\partial _ i\partial _{ ar i}V_1V_1a=V_1V_1a_{i ar i}=V_1V_1G_{i ar i}-V_1V_1k_{i ar i}$, and the derivatives of the fixed matrix $k$ are bounded. Summing with the weights $r_ i^{-1}$ gives an error at most $C\lambda T$, and no third derivative of $a$ enters it. Next we use the equation. Taking logarithms in ( 16.14 ) gives $\log \det G=\log \det k+ eta (a-f)$. Differentiating twice along $V_1$ and using $\partial (G^{-1})=-G^{-1}(\partial G)G^{-1}$, we obtain at $x_0$ \[  \sum _ i r_ i^{-1}V_1V_1G_{i ar i} =\sum _{p,q} rac{|V_1G_{p ar q}|^2}{r_ pr_ q} +V_1V_1\log \det k+ eta (\lambda -f_{V_1V_1}).  \] Here we used that at the center of normal coordinates directional and covariant second derivatives agree, so that $V_1V_1a=\lambda $ and $V_1V_1f=f_{V_1V_1}$. If $\lambda \geq 2\max \{ 1,\sup _{X,|Y|_{g_0}=1}f_{YY}\} $, which is a uniform threshold because $
abla ^2f\leq Bg_0$, the last term is at least $ eta \lambda /2$. The term $V_1V_1\log \det k$ is bounded, hence at least $-CT$ because $T\geq c$. By the first variation formula, $\partial _ i\lambda _1(\Phi )=\partial _ i a_{V_1V_1}$ at $x_0$. Since $D_ G\log \lambda _1=\lambda ^{-1}D_ G\lambda _1-\sum _ ir_ i^{-1}|\partial _ i\lambda _1|^2/\lambda ^2$, we conclude that \[  D_ G\log \lambda _1(\Phi )\geq U+R-N-CT+ eta /2.  \] Next we differentiate the logarithmic equation once and apply the product rule to $s=k^{p ar q}a_ pa_{ ar q}$. At $x_0$, \[  \partial _ i\partial _{ ar i}s=\sum _ p igl (|a_{pi}|^2+|a_{p ar i}|^2 igr ) +2\operatorname{Re}\sum _ pa_{ ar p}\, \partial _ pa_{i ar i} +(\partial _ i\partial _{ ar i}k^{p ar q})a_ pa_{ ar q}.  \] The last term involves only the bounded gradient. In the middle term the third derivatives occur only in the contraction $\sum _ ir_ i^{-1}\partial _ pa_{i ar i}=\partial _ p\log \det G= eta (a_ p-f_ p)$, because $\mathrm dk(x_0)=0$; so we need no estimate for third derivatives. Weighting with $r_ i^{-1}$ and summing, we get \[  D_ Gs\geq K-CT +2 eta \operatorname{Re}\sum _ p a_{ ar p}(a_ p-f_ p) \geq K-CT+ eta s- eta |\partial f|_ k^2.  \] Also $D_ Ga=\sum _ ir_ i^{-1}(r_ i-1)=n-T$. At the local maximum $x_0$ we have $D_ G\widehat Q\leq 0$, where \[  D_ G\widehat Q=D_ G\log \lambda _1(\Phi )+\eta 'D_ Gs +\eta ''\sum _ i rac{|s_ i|^2}{r_ i}-AD_ Ga.  \] Since $0<\eta '\leq  rac12$ and $\eta '|\partial f|_ k^2\leq  rac	au 2\sup _ X|\partial f|_ k^2\leq  rac14$, the three preceding estimates yield 16.28  egin{equation} \label{eq:real-hessian-maximum} 0\geq U+R-N+\eta 'K +\eta ''\sum _ i rac{|s_ i|^2}{r_ i} +(A-C_0)T-An+ eta \eta 's+ eta /4, \end{equation} where $C_0$ is a uniform constant that does not depend on $A$. Step 4: absorption of the third-order term. It remains to absorb the negative term $-N$ completely. Fix $0<\varepsilon <1/2$, to be chosen below, and assume that $\lambda \geq C/\varepsilon ^2$. Let $J$ be the complex structure of $X$, and define a $(1,0)$-vector $W$ and real numbers $\mu _\alpha $ by \[  W=(V_1-\mathrm iJV_1)/\sqrt2 =\sum _ q
u _ q\partial _ q,\qquad JV_1=\sum _{\alpha >1}\mu _\alpha V_\alpha .  \] Since $k(x_0)$ is the identity, $\sum _ q|
u _ q|^2=g_0(V_1,V_1)=1$; since $JV_1$ is a $g_0$-unit vector orthogonal to $V_1$, also $\sum _{\alpha >1}\mu _\alpha ^2=1$. The coefficients $
u _ q,\mu _\alpha $, and $J$ itself, are constant in our coordinate system. Writing $V_1=\sqrt2\, \overline W-\mathrm iJV_1$ in the outer derivative of $\partial _ ia_{V_1V_1}$, we obtain 16.29  egin{equation} \label{eq:real-hessian-third-splitting} \partial _ i a_{V_1V_1} =\sqrt2\sum _ q\overline
u _ q V_1G_{i ar q} -\mathrm i\sum _{\alpha >1}\mu _\alpha \partial _ i a_{V_1V_\alpha }+E_ i, \qquad |E_ i|\leq C. \end{equation} Indeed, the third coordinate derivatives of the scalar function $a$ commute, and $\partial _ i\overline W=\sum _ q\overline
u _ q\partial _ i\partial _{ ar q}$. Replacing coordinate second derivatives by covariant ones before the last differentiation introduces only first derivatives of $\Gamma $ times the bounded gradient of $a$, since $\Gamma (x_0)=0$; and the derivatives of the fixed matrix $k$ are bounded. Thus the error $E_ i$ involves only the gradient bound. We use twice the inequality $|b+c|^2\leq (1+t)|b|^2+(1+t^{-1})|c|^2$, $t>0$. First take $t=\varepsilon /(1-2\varepsilon )$ to separate $E_ i$; then $(1-2\varepsilon )(1+t)=1-\varepsilon $ and $(1-2\varepsilon )(1+t^{-1})\leq \varepsilon ^{-1}$, so the contribution of $E_ i$ to $(1-2\varepsilon )N$ is at most $CT/(\varepsilon \lambda ^2)\leq T$. Then take $t=\varepsilon $ for the two principal terms (with the factor $1+\varepsilon $ on the second one). This gives  egin{align*}  (1-2\varepsilon )N\leq {}&  (1-\varepsilon )(1+\varepsilon ^{-1}) \sum _ i rac{2|\sum _ q\overline
u _ q V_1G_{i ar q}|^2}{r_ i\lambda ^2}\ & +(1-\varepsilon ^2) \sum _ i rac{|\sum _{\alpha >1}\mu _\alpha \partial _ i a_{V_1V_\alpha }|^2}{r_ i\lambda ^2}+T. \end{align*} By the weighted Cauchy–Schwarz inequality and $\sum _ qr_ q|
u _ q|^2\leq C$, the first line is at most $CR/(\varepsilon \lambda )\leq R$. For the second line the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality and $\sum _{\alpha >1}\mu _\alpha ^2=1$ give \[  \left|\sum _{\alpha >1}\mu _\alpha \partial _ i a_{V_1V_\alpha }ight|^2 \leq \left(\lambda -\sum _{\alpha >1}\lambda _\alpha \mu _\alpha ^2ight) \sum _{\alpha >1}  rac{|\partial _ i a_{V_1V_\alpha }|^2}{\lambda -\lambda _\alpha }.  \] To bound the first factor we use the positivity of $G$. Since the Hessian eigenvalue of $V_\alpha $ is $\lambda _\alpha +1$ (this is where the perturbation by $B_0$ enters) and $\partial  ar\partial a(W,\overline W)= rac12 igl (a_{V_1V_1}+a_{JV_1JV_1} igr )$ at $x_0$, we have \[  0<G(W,\overline W) =1+	frac 12\left(\lambda + \sum _{\alpha >1}(\lambda _\alpha +1)\mu _\alpha ^2ight).  \] Thus $\lambda -\sum _{\alpha >1}\lambda _\alpha \mu _\alpha ^2\leq 2\lambda +3$. If $\lambda \geq 3/(2\varepsilon ^2)$, then $(1-\varepsilon ^2)(2\lambda +3)\leq 2\lambda $, so the second line is at most $U$. Finally, the critical point equation for $\widehat Q$ at $x_0$ reads \[   rac{\partial _ i a_{V_1V_1}}\lambda =Aa_ i-\eta 's_ i.  \] Together with $|b+c|^2\leq 2|b|^2+2|c|^2$ and $4\varepsilon <2$, it bounds the remaining part of $N$: \[  2\varepsilon N\leq 4\varepsilon A^2\sum _ i rac{|a_ i|^2}{r_ i}+2(\eta ')^2\sum _ i rac{|s_ i|^2}{r_ i}.  \] Combining the three bounds, we obtain 16.30  egin{equation} \label{eq:real-hessian-third-absorption} N\leq U+R+T+4\varepsilon A^2\sum _ i rac{|a_ i|^2}{r_ i} +2(\eta ')^2\sum _ i rac{|s_ i|^2}{r_ i}. \end{equation} Now choose $A=C_0+3$, after enlarging $C_0$ so that it is positive, and $\varepsilon =[4A^2(S+1)]^{-1}<1/2$. Both choices are uniform, and so are the thresholds for $\lambda $ used above. By ( 16.27 ), the $\eta ''$ term of ( 16.28 ) absorbs the last term of ( 16.30 ), and $4\varepsilon A^2\sum _ i|a_ i|^2/r_ i\leq sT/(S+1)\leq T$. Substituting ( 16.30 ) into ( 16.28 ) and dropping its nonnegative $ eta $ terms, we get \[  0\geq \eta 'K+T-An.  \] By the lower bound for $\eta '$ in ( 16.27 ) and $r_ i^{-1}\geq c$, this bounds every $a_{ip}$ and $a_{i ar p}$ at $x_0$, and hence every real second derivative of $a$ there; at $x_0$ these coincide with the covariant ones. Thus $\lambda =\ell (x_0)$ is uniformly bounded, either by the thresholds assumed above or by this estimate. As observed at the beginning, the maximum property of $Q$ then bounds $\ell $ everywhere, and the lower bound for the trace bounds the remaining eigenvalues of $
abla ^2a$. This proves the lemma. $\square$ Theorem 16.2.26 . Let $\kappa $ be a Kähler form on $X$, let $r\geq 1$ be an integer, and let $f_1,\ldots ,f_ r$ be real $C^{1,1}$ functions on $X$. Then the envelope \[  P_\kappa  igl (\min _{1\leq j\leq r}f_ j igr )  \] is $C^{1,1}$. Its $C^{1,1}$ norm is bounded by a constant depending only on the fixed geometry and on a common bound for the $C^{1,1}$ norms of the obstacles. Proof. First let $r=1$, and suppose that $f=f_1$ is smooth. By lemma 16.2.25 , the solutions $a_ eta $ have uniformly bounded values, gradients and full real Hessians for $ eta \geq  eta _0$, and by proposition 16.2.22 they converge uniformly to $P_\kappa (f)$. The limit $P_\kappa (f)$ is therefore continuous, and by the same proposition it has bounded metric Laplacian; hence it belongs to $C^{1,\alpha }(X)$ by proposition 16.2.11 , and in particular it is $C^1$. We now pass to the limit in the Hessian bounds. For a smooth vector field $Y$, the function $
abla ^2a_ eta (Y,Y)=YYa_ eta -(
abla _ YY)a_ eta $ is obtained from $a_ eta $ by a second-order differential operator. Since $a_ eta 	o P_\kappa (f)$ uniformly, $
abla ^2a_ eta (Y,Y)	o 
abla ^2P_\kappa (f)(Y,Y)$ in the sense of distributions, where the right side is the weak covariant Hessian, and for every nonnegative test function $\varphi $ we obtain $|\langle 
abla ^2P_\kappa (f)(Y,Y),\varphi angle |\leq C\int |Y|_{g_0}^2\varphi $. By corollary 1.7.2 (1), the weak quadratic components $
abla ^2P_\kappa (f)(Y,Y)$ are bounded functions, with $|
abla ^2P_\kappa (f)(Y,Y)|\leq C|Y|_{g_0}^2$ almost everywhere; by polarization, so are all components of the weak covariant Hessian. The gradient is treated in the same way: $Ya_ eta 	o YP_\kappa (f)$ in the sense of distributions, and $|Ya_ eta |\leq C|Y|_{g_0}$; since $YP_\kappa (f)$ is continuous, pairing with nonnegative test functions of integral one supported in small balls about a point shows that $|YP_\kappa (f)|\leq C|Y|_{g_0}$ everywhere, so $|
abla P_\kappa (f)|_{g_0}\leq C$. In a chart, the weak second derivatives of $P_\kappa (f)$ differ from the components of its weak covariant Hessian by the Christoffel symbols times its first derivatives, so they are bounded on compact subsets of the chart. Hence $P_\kappa (f)$ is $C^{1,1}$, by proposition 1.7.5 , and the bounds just proved show that its $C^{1,1}$ norm is bounded by a constant depending only on the fixed geometry and on the constant $B$ of lemma 16.2.25 for $f$. Now let the $f_ j$ be arbitrary $C^{1,1}$ functions. Using convolution in finitely many charts and a smooth partition of unity, we obtain smooth functions $f_{j,ho }$ that converge to $f_ j$ in $C^1$ as $ho 	o 0$ and have uniformly bounded covariant Hessians. Indeed, the second derivatives of such a partitioned convolution are the cutoffs times the convolutions of the bounded weak second derivatives of $f_ j$, plus terms that involve only the values and first derivatives of the local convolutions; all of these are uniformly bounded. For $\delta >0$ put \[  F_{ho ,\delta }=-\delta \log \sum _ j \mathrm e^{-f_{j,ho }/\delta }, \qquad p_ j= rac{\mathrm e^{-f_{j,ho }/\delta }}{\sum _ k\mathrm e^{-f_{k,ho }/\delta }}.  \] The weights $p_ j$ are positive with sum one, $\min _ jf_{j,ho }-\delta \log r\leq F_{ho ,\delta }\leq \min _ jf_{j,ho }$, and the gradient of $F_{ho ,\delta }$ is the convex combination $\sum _ jp_ j
abla f_{j,ho }$. For every real tangent vector $Y$ the chain rule gives  egin{align*}  
abla ^2F_{ho ,\delta }(Y,Y) &  =\sum _ jp_ j
abla ^2f_{j,ho }(Y,Y)\ & \quad - rac1\delta \left(\sum _ jp_ j(\mathrm df_{j,ho }(Y))^2 -\left(\sum _ jp_ j\mathrm df_{j,ho }(Y)ight)^2ight)\ & \leq C|Y|_{g_0}^2, \end{align*} because the term in parentheses is a variance and hence nonnegative. Let $ho ,\delta 	o 0$ with $\delta \log r\leq 1$. Then the smooth obstacles $F_{ho ,\delta }$ have uniformly bounded values and gradients and a uniform upper bound for their Hessians, although their Hessians have no uniform lower bound as $\delta 	o 0$; this is why lemma 16.2.25 uses only an upper bound. Since the smooth case bounds the $C^{1,1}$ norm of the envelope in terms of the fixed geometry and the constant $B$ of that lemma, the envelopes $P_\kappa (F_{ho ,\delta })$ have uniformly bounded $C^{1,1}$ norms. The obstacles converge uniformly to $\min _ jf_ j$, so the envelopes converge uniformly to $P_\kappa (\min _ jf_ j)$ by the stability estimate of proposition 16.1.4 (4). The limit is $C^1$ by theorem 16.2.24 , since $C^{1,1}$ functions have bounded metric Laplacian. The same passage to the limit as in the smooth case, with the smooth functions $a_ eta $ replaced by the $C^{1,1}$ functions $P_\kappa (F_{ho ,\delta })$, whose gradients and weak covariant Hessians are bounded by a uniform constant, now proves the theorem, together with the bound for the norm. $\square$

title: Penalized real hessian
text:
Lemma 16.2.25 . Let $\kappa $ be a Kähler form on $X$, and let $g_0$ be a smooth Riemannian metric on $X$ with Levi-Civita connection $
abla $. Let $B>0$, and let $f$ be a smooth real function such that \[  \| f\| _\infty +\| 
abla f\| _\infty \leq B, \qquad 
abla ^2f\leq Bg_0  \] as real quadratic forms, and for $ eta >0$ let $a_ eta $ be the solution of ( 16.14 ) given by theorem 16.2.21 . Then there are constants $ eta _0$ and $C$, depending only on $B$ and on the fixed geometry ($X$, $\kappa $ and $g_0$), such that \[  \| a_ eta \| _\infty +\| 
abla a_ eta \| _\infty +\| 
abla ^2a_ eta \| _\infty \leq C \qquad ( eta \geq  eta _0).  \] Proof. Step 1 reduces to a metric defined by $\kappa $ and collects the bounds for $a_ eta $ and its gradient. Steps 2 and 3 apply the maximum principle to the logarithm of the largest eigenvalue of $
abla ^2a_ eta $, corrected by functions of the gradient and of $a_ eta $, and Step 4 absorbs the negative term with third derivatives. Step 1: reductions and first bounds. Any two smooth Riemannian metrics on $X$ are uniformly equivalent, and, as observed before the lemma, the Hessians of a function for the two metrics differ by a bounded tensor applied to its gradient. Changing $g_0$ therefore changes $B$ and the constants only by factors depending on the two metrics, and we may assume that $g_0$ is the following Riemannian metric defined by $\kappa $. In local holomorphic coordinates write $\kappa = rac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }k_{i ar j}\, \mathrm dz_ i\wedge \mathrm d ar z_ j$, so that $k$ is the coefficient matrix of $2\pi \kappa $ as in section 16.2.3 , and let $g_0=2\operatorname{Re}(k_{i ar j}\, \mathrm dz_ i\otimes \mathrm d ar z_ j)$; this is $2\pi $ times the Riemannian metric $\kappa (\cdot ,J\cdot )$, where $J$ is the complex structure. At the center of normal coordinates for $\kappa $, given by lemma 16.2.13 , we have $k_{i ar j}=\delta _{ij}$ and $\mathrm dk=0$; hence the Christoffel symbols of $g_0$ vanish and $g_0=2\sum _ i(\mathrm dx_ i^2+\mathrm dy_ i^2)$. Comparing coordinate derivatives at such a point, we obtain for every smooth function $b$ 16.26  egin{equation} \label{eq:real-hessian-trace-identity} \operatorname {tr}_{g_0}
abla ^2b=2D_ kb, \qquad D_ kb=k^{i ar j}b_{i ar j}. \end{equation} In particular the upper bound for $
abla ^2f$ gives $D_ kf\leq nB$. Write $a=a_ eta $, $G=(k_{i ar j}+a_{i ar j})$ and $D_ G=G^{i ar j}\partial _ i\partial _{ ar j}$; thus $G$ is the matrix denoted $g$ in section 16.2.3 . We apply lemma 16.2.15 with $\kappa $ also as the measuring metric. It bounds $|a|$ by $\| f\| _\infty $ and, for all sufficiently large $ eta $, bounds $\operatorname {tr}_ kG$ in terms of $B$ and the fixed geometry. Since $G>0$ and $\operatorname {tr}_ kG$ is bounded, all coefficients of $G$, and hence of the complex Hessian of $a$, are bounded; in particular the metric Laplacian $La$ for the fixed Kähler form $\omega $, which is a constant multiple of the trace of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a$ with respect to $\omega $ (lemma 14.1.6 ), is uniformly bounded. Fix $p>2n$. By proposition 16.2.11 , $\| a\| _{W^{2,p}(X)}\leq C(\| La\| _{L^ p}+\| a\| _{L^ p})$ is uniformly bounded, and Morrey's inequality (lemma 6.2.6 ), applied in the charts defining the norm to the first derivatives of the products of $a$ with the cutoff functions, bounds $
abla a$ uniformly. From now on $C$ denotes a constant depending only on these bounds, on $B$ and on the fixed geometry; it may increase from line to line, but it never depends on $ eta $. Step 2: the auxiliary function. Let $\ell $ be the largest eigenvalue of the real covariant Hessian $
abla ^2a$ with respect to $g_0$. By ( 16.26 ), the sum of all eigenvalues is $2D_ ka=2\operatorname {tr}_ kG-2n\geq -2n$. Since each eigenvalue is at most $\ell $, it is at least $-2n-(2n-1)\ell $; hence every eigenvalue of $
abla ^2a$ has absolute value at most $2n(\max \{ \ell ,0\} +1)$. It therefore suffices to bound $\ell $ from above, and we do so by the maximum principle. Put \[  s=|\partial a|_ k^2,\quad S=\sup _ Xs,\quad 	au =(1+2\sup _ X|\partial f|_ k^2)^{-1},\quad \eta (s)=- rac	au 2\log (1+S-s).  \] Then $S\leq C$, the number $	au \in (0,1]$ has a uniform positive lower bound, and since $0\leq s\leq S$, 16.27  egin{equation} \label{eq:real-hessian-gradient-weight}  rac{	au }{2(1+S)}\leq \eta '\leq  rac	au 2, \qquad \eta ''= rac{2(\eta ')^2}{	au }\geq 2(\eta ')^2. \end{equation} For a constant $A>0$ to be chosen later, consider the function $Q=\log \ell +\eta (s)-Aa$ on the open set $\{ \ell >0\} $. If this set is empty, then $\ell \leq 0$ and there is nothing to prove. Otherwise, since $a$ and $\eta (s)$ are bounded, $Q$ tends to $-\infty $ where $\ell $ tends to zero, so by compactness of $X$ it attains its maximum at some point $x_0$ with $\ell (x_0)>0$. For the same reason a uniform bound for $\ell (x_0)$ bounds $\ell $ on all of $X$. We may therefore assume that $\ell (x_0)\geq 1$, and that $\ell (x_0)$ exceeds any uniform threshold used below. Choose normal coordinates for $\kappa $ at $x_0$ in which $G(x_0)$ is diagonal, with diagonal entries $r_ i>0$: by lemma 16.2.13 , applied to $k$ in one of finitely many fixed charts that contains $x_0$ in a fixed compact subset, and followed by a unitary change of coordinates that diagonalizes $G(x_0)$, there are such coordinates in which the derivatives of $k$ of every fixed order at $x_0$ are bounded independently of $x_0$. Since $\sum _ ir_ i=\operatorname {tr}_ kG\leq C$, we have $r_ i\leq C$, hence $r_ i^{-1}\geq c$ for a uniform $c>0$. Write $T=\sum _ ir_ i^{-1}$; thus $T\geq c$. Take a $g_0$-orthonormal basis $V_1,\ldots ,V_{2n}$ of the real tangent space at $x_0$ consisting of eigenvectors of $
abla ^2a(x_0)$, with $V_1$ belonging to the eigenvalue $\ell (x_0)$, and extend these vectors to the chart as vector fields with constant real coordinate coefficients. The largest eigenvalue $\ell $ may be multiple and need not be smooth, so we perturb the Hessian. Let $B_0$ be the symmetric bilinear form with constant coefficients in this chart which at $x_0$ is the $g_0$-orthogonal projection onto $V_1^\perp $, that is, $B_0(Y,Z)=g_0(PY,PZ)$ at $x_0$ for this projection $P$, and set \[  \Phi =g_0^{-1}(
abla ^2a-B_0).  \] The form $B_0$ is positive semidefinite everywhere in the chart. Hence the largest eigenvalue $\lambda _1(\Phi )$ of $\Phi $ is at most $\ell $, and it equals $\ell $ at $x_0$. Denote the eigenvalues of $\Phi $ at $x_0$ by $\lambda =\ell (x_0),\lambda _2,\ldots ,\lambda _{2n}$, with eigenvectors $V_1,\ldots ,V_{2n}$. For $\alpha >1$, $\lambda _\alpha $ is the Hessian eigenvalue belonging to $V_\alpha $ minus one, so $\lambda -\lambda _\alpha \geq 1$. In particular $\lambda _1(\Phi )$ is a smooth function near $x_0$. Indeed, $\lambda $ is a simple root of the characteristic polynomial of $\Phi (x_0)$, so by the implicit function theorem the characteristic polynomial of $\Phi $ has, near $x_0$, exactly one root close to $\lambda $, and this root depends smoothly on the point; it equals $\lambda _1(\Phi )$, which is continuous as the maximum of $(
abla ^2a-B_0)(Y,Y)$ over $g_0$-unit vectors $Y$, and it is a simple eigenvalue. The smooth function $\widehat Q=\log \lambda _1(\Phi )+\eta (s)-Aa$ satisfies $\widehat Q\leq Q\leq Q(x_0)=\widehat Q(x_0)$, so it has a local maximum at $x_0$. Step 3: the inequality at the maximum point. From now on all quantities are evaluated at $x_0$. Write $a_{V_\alpha V_\gamma }=
abla ^2a(V_\alpha ,V_\gamma )$, a smooth function near $x_0$, and define the nonnegative quantities  egin{align*}  U& =2\sum _{i,\alpha >1}  rac{|\partial _ i a_{V_\alpha V_1}|^2}{r_ i\lambda (\lambda -\lambda _\alpha )},&  R& =\sum _{p,q} rac{|V_1G_{p ar q}|^2}{r_ pr_ q\lambda },\  N& =\sum _ i rac{|\partial _ i a_{V_1V_1}|^2}{r_ i\lambda ^2},&  K& =\sum _{i,p} rac{|a_{ip}|^2+|a_{i ar p}|^2}{r_ i}. \end{align*} We first compute $D_ G\log \lambda _1(\Phi )$, keeping the third-derivative terms. Let $M(t)$ be a smooth family of real symmetric matrices, and let $\lambda (t)$ be a simple eigenvalue with unit eigenvector $V_1$ at $t=0$, the other eigenvalues being $\lambda _\alpha $ with orthonormal eigenvectors $V_\alpha $. Then \[  \lambda '=\langle M'V_1,V_1angle ,\qquad \lambda ''=\langle M''V_1,V_1angle +2\sum _{\alpha >1}  rac{|\langle M'V_1,V_\alpha angle |^2}{\lambda -\lambda _\alpha }.  \] Indeed, near $t=0$ the simple eigenvalue $\lambda (t)$ is a smooth function of $t$, by the implicit function theorem applied to the characteristic polynomial, and the columns of the adjugate matrix of $\lambda (t)I-M(t)$, which has rank one, span the eigenspace; normalizing a column that does not vanish at $t=0$ gives a smooth unit eigenvector $y(t)$ with $y(0)=\pm V_1$, and we may take the sign $+$. Differentiate the eigenvector equation $M(t)y(t)=\lambda (t)y(t)$. Pairing with $V_1$ gives the first formula, and pairing with $V_\alpha $ shows that the derivative of the eigenvector has component $\langle M'V_1,V_\alpha angle /(\lambda -\lambda _\alpha )$ along $V_\alpha $, and it has no component along $V_1$, because $|y(t)|=1$. Differentiating the identity $\lambda '(t)=\langle M'(t)y(t),y(t)angle $, where $y(t)$ is the normalized eigenvector with $y(0)=V_1$, and substituting these components gives the second formula. We apply these formulas to the symmetric matrix $M$ with entries $(
abla ^2a-B_0)(e_\alpha ,e_\gamma )$, where $e_1,\ldots ,e_{2n}$ is the $g_0$-orthonormal frame obtained from the constant vector fields $V_1,\ldots ,V_{2n}$ by the Gram–Schmidt process; $M$ has the same eigenvalues as $\Phi $. The frame depends smoothly on the point, equals $V_1,\ldots ,V_{2n}$ at $x_0$, and its first derivatives vanish at $x_0$, because those of $g_0$ do. We differentiate along the real coordinate directions and use $\partial _ i\partial _{ ar i}= rac14(\partial _{x_ i}^2+\partial _{y_ i}^2)$. Since $B_0$ is constant, the first derivatives of $M$ at $x_0$ are those of the functions $
abla ^2a(V_\alpha ,V_\gamma )$. In the second derivatives, the second derivatives of the frame multiply $
abla ^2a-B_0$, which is bounded by $C(\lambda +1)$; after weighting with $r_ i^{-1}$ and summing they contribute at most $C\lambda T$. Since $|\partial _ ib|^2= rac14(|\partial _{x_ i}b|^2+|\partial _{y_ i}b|^2)$ for a real function $b$, we obtain \[  D_ G\lambda _1(\Phi )\geq 2\sum _{i,\alpha >1}  rac{|\partial _ i a_{V_\alpha V_1}|^2}{r_ i(\lambda -\lambda _\alpha )} +\sum _ i r_ i^{-1}V_1V_1G_{i ar i}-C\lambda T.  \] Here the middle term comes from $\sum _ ir_ i^{-1}\partial _ i\partial _{ ar i}a_{V_1V_1}$ after commuting derivatives, and we check that this commutation costs at most $C\lambda T$. In real coordinates $a_{V_1V_1}=V_1V_1a-\Gamma ^ t_{uv}V_1^ uV_1^ v\partial _ ta$, where the Christoffel symbols $\Gamma $ of $g_0$ vanish at $x_0$. When we apply $\partial _ i\partial _{ ar i}$, the term containing third derivatives of $a$ is multiplied by $\Gamma (x_0)=0$; the remaining terms are a first derivative of $\Gamma $ times a second derivative of $a$, or a second derivative of $\Gamma $ times a first derivative of $a$. By the Hessian and gradient bounds above they are at most $C(\lambda +1)$. Moreover $\partial _ i\partial _{ ar i}V_1V_1a=V_1V_1a_{i ar i}=V_1V_1G_{i ar i}-V_1V_1k_{i ar i}$, and the derivatives of the fixed matrix $k$ are bounded. Summing with the weights $r_ i^{-1}$ gives an error at most $C\lambda T$, and no third derivative of $a$ enters it. Next we use the equation. Taking logarithms in ( 16.14 ) gives $\log \det G=\log \det k+ eta (a-f)$. Differentiating twice along $V_1$ and using $\partial (G^{-1})=-G^{-1}(\partial G)G^{-1}$, we obtain at $x_0$ \[  \sum _ i r_ i^{-1}V_1V_1G_{i ar i} =\sum _{p,q} rac{|V_1G_{p ar q}|^2}{r_ pr_ q} +V_1V_1\log \det k+ eta (\lambda -f_{V_1V_1}).  \] Here we used that at the center of normal coordinates directional and covariant second derivatives agree, so that $V_1V_1a=\lambda $ and $V_1V_1f=f_{V_1V_1}$. If $\lambda \geq 2\max \{ 1,\sup _{X,|Y|_{g_0}=1}f_{YY}\} $, which is a uniform threshold because $
abla ^2f\leq Bg_0$, the last term is at least $ eta \lambda /2$. The term $V_1V_1\log \det k$ is bounded, hence at least $-CT$ because $T\geq c$. By the first variation formula, $\partial _ i\lambda _1(\Phi )=\partial _ i a_{V_1V_1}$ at $x_0$. Since $D_ G\log \lambda _1=\lambda ^{-1}D_ G\lambda _1-\sum _ ir_ i^{-1}|\partial _ i\lambda _1|^2/\lambda ^2$, we conclude that \[  D_ G\log \lambda _1(\Phi )\geq U+R-N-CT+ eta /2.  \] Next we differentiate the logarithmic equation once and apply the product rule to $s=k^{p ar q}a_ pa_{ ar q}$. At $x_0$, \[  \partial _ i\partial _{ ar i}s=\sum _ p igl (|a_{pi}|^2+|a_{p ar i}|^2 igr ) +2\operatorname{Re}\sum _ pa_{ ar p}\, \partial _ pa_{i ar i} +(\partial _ i\partial _{ ar i}k^{p ar q})a_ pa_{ ar q}.  \] The last term involves only the bounded gradient. In the middle term the third derivatives occur only in the contraction $\sum _ ir_ i^{-1}\partial _ pa_{i ar i}=\partial _ p\log \det G= eta (a_ p-f_ p)$, because $\mathrm dk(x_0)=0$; so we need no estimate for third derivatives. Weighting with $r_ i^{-1}$ and summing, we get \[  D_ Gs\geq K-CT +2 eta \operatorname{Re}\sum _ p a_{ ar p}(a_ p-f_ p) \geq K-CT+ eta s- eta |\partial f|_ k^2.  \] Also $D_ Ga=\sum _ ir_ i^{-1}(r_ i-1)=n-T$. At the local maximum $x_0$ we have $D_ G\widehat Q\leq 0$, where \[  D_ G\widehat Q=D_ G\log \lambda _1(\Phi )+\eta 'D_ Gs +\eta ''\sum _ i rac{|s_ i|^2}{r_ i}-AD_ Ga.  \] Since $0<\eta '\leq  rac12$ and $\eta '|\partial f|_ k^2\leq  rac	au 2\sup _ X|\partial f|_ k^2\leq  rac14$, the three preceding estimates yield 16.28  egin{equation} \label{eq:real-hessian-maximum} 0\geq U+R-N+\eta 'K +\eta ''\sum _ i rac{|s_ i|^2}{r_ i} +(A-C_0)T-An+ eta \eta 's+ eta /4, \end{equation} where $C_0$ is a uniform constant that does not depend on $A$. Step 4: absorption of the third-order term. It remains to absorb the negative term $-N$ completely. Fix $0<\varepsilon <1/2$, to be chosen below, and assume that $\lambda \geq C/\varepsilon ^2$. Let $J$ be the complex structure of $X$, and define a $(1,0)$-vector $W$ and real numbers $\mu _\alpha $ by \[  W=(V_1-\mathrm iJV_1)/\sqrt2 =\sum _ q
u _ q\partial _ q,\qquad JV_1=\sum _{\alpha >1}\mu _\alpha V_\alpha .  \] Since $k(x_0)$ is the identity, $\sum _ q|
u _ q|^2=g_0(V_1,V_1)=1$; since $JV_1$ is a $g_0$-unit vector orthogonal to $V_1$, also $\sum _{\alpha >1}\mu _\alpha ^2=1$. The coefficients $
u _ q,\mu _\alpha $, and $J$ itself, are constant in our coordinate system. Writing $V_1=\sqrt2\, \overline W-\mathrm iJV_1$ in the outer derivative of $\partial _ ia_{V_1V_1}$, we obtain 16.29  egin{equation} \label{eq:real-hessian-third-splitting} \partial _ i a_{V_1V_1} =\sqrt2\sum _ q\overline

u _ q\partial _ i\partial _{ ar q}$. Replacing coordinate second derivatives by covariant ones before the last differentiation introduces only first derivatives of $\Gamma $ times the bounded gradient of $a$, since $\Gamma (x_0)=0$; and the derivatives of the fixed matrix $k$ are bounded. Thus the error $E_ i$ involves only the gradient bound. We use twice the inequality $|b+c|^2\leq (1+t)|b|^2+(1+t^{-1})|c|^2$, $t>0$. First take $t=\varepsilon /(1-2\varepsilon )$ to separate $E_ i$; then $(1-2\varepsilon )(1+t)=1-\varepsilon $ and $(1-2\varepsilon )(1+t^{-1})\leq \varepsilon ^{-1}$, so the contribution of $E_ i$ to $(1-2\varepsilon )N$ is at most $CT/(\varepsilon \lambda ^2)\leq T$. Then take $t=\varepsilon $ for the two principal terms (with the factor $1+\varepsilon $ on the second one). This gives  egin{align*}  (1-2\varepsilon )N\leq {}&  (1-\varepsilon )(1+\varepsilon ^{-1}) \sum _ i rac{2|\sum _ q\overline
u _ q V_1G_{i ar q}|^2}{r_ i\lambda ^2}\ & +(1-\varepsilon ^2) \sum _ i rac{|\sum _{\alpha >1}\mu _\alpha \partial _ i a_{V_1V_\alpha }|^2}{r_ i\lambda ^2}+T. \end{align*} By the weighted Cauchy–Schwarz inequality and $\sum _ qr_ q|
u _ q|^2\leq C$, the first line is at most $CR/(\varepsilon \lambda )\leq R$. For the second line the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality and $\sum _{\alpha >1}\mu _\alpha ^2=1$ give \[  \left|\sum _{\alpha >1}\mu _\alpha \partial _ i a_{V_1V_\alpha }ight|^2 \leq \left(\lambda -\sum _{\alpha >1}\lambda _\alpha \mu _\alpha ^2ight) \sum _{\alpha >1}  rac{|\partial _ i a_{V_1V_\alpha }|^2}{\lambda -\lambda _\alpha }.  \] To bound the first factor we use the positivity of $G$. Since the Hessian eigenvalue of $V_\alpha $ is $\lambda _\alpha +1$ (this is where the perturbation by $B_0$ enters) and $\partial  ar\partial a(W,\overline W)= rac12 igl (a_{V_1V_1}+a_{JV_1JV_1} igr )$ at $x_0$, we have \[  0<G(W,\overline W) =1+	frac 12\left(\lambda + \sum _{\alpha >1}(\lambda _\alpha +1)\mu _\alpha ^2ight).  \] Thus $\lambda -\sum _{\alpha >1}\lambda _\alpha \mu _\alpha ^2\leq 2\lambda +3$. If $\lambda \geq 3/(2\varepsilon ^2)$, then $(1-\varepsilon ^2)(2\lambda +3)\leq 2\lambda $, so the second line is at most $U$. Finally, the critical point equation for $\widehat Q$ at $x_0$ reads \[   rac{\partial _ i a_{V_1V_1}}\lambda =Aa_ i-\eta 's_ i.  \] Together with $|b+c|^2\leq 2|b|^2+2|c|^2$ and $4\varepsilon <2$, it bounds the remaining part of $N$: \[  2\varepsilon N\leq 4\varepsilon A^2\sum _ i rac{|a_ i|^2}{r_ i}+2(\eta ')^2\sum _ i rac{|s_ i|^2}{r_ i}.  \] Combining the three bounds, we obtain 16.30  egin{equation} \label{eq:real-hessian-third-absorption} N\leq U+R+T+4\varepsilon A^2\sum _ i rac{|a_ i|^2}{r_ i} +2(\eta ')^2\sum _ i rac{|s_ i|^2}{r_ i}. \end{equation} Now choose $A=C_0+3$, after enlarging $C_0$ so that it is positive, and $\varepsilon =[4A^2(S+1)]^{-1}<1/2$. Both choices are uniform, and so are the thresholds for $\lambda $ used above. By ( 16.27 ), the $\eta ''$ term of ( 16.28 ) absorbs the last term of ( 16.30 ), and $4\varepsilon A^2\sum _ i|a_ i|^2/r_ i\leq sT/(S+1)\leq T$. Substituting ( 16.30 ) into ( 16.28 ) and dropping its nonnegative $ eta $ terms, we get \[  0\geq \eta 'K+T-An.  \] By the lower bound for $\eta '$ in ( 16.27 ) and $r_ i^{-1}\geq c$, this bounds every $a_{ip}$ and $a_{i ar p}$ at $x_0$, and hence every real second derivative of $a$ there; at $x_0$ these coincide with the covariant ones. Thus $\lambda =\ell (x_0)$ is uniformly bounded, either by the thresholds assumed above or by this estimate. As observed at the beginning, the maximum property of $Q$ then bounds $\ell $ everywhere, and the lower bound for the trace bounds the remaining eigenvalues of $
abla ^2a$. This proves the lemma. $\square$

Theorem 16.2.26 . Let $\kappa $ be a Kähler form on $X$, let $r\geq 1$ be an integer, and let $f_1,\ldots ,f_ r$ be real $C^{1,1}$ functions on $X$. Then the envelope \[  P_\kappa  igl (\min _{1\leq j\leq r}f_ j igr )  \] is $C^{1,1}$. Its $C^{1,1}$ norm is bounded by a constant depending only on the fixed geometry and on a common bound for the $C^{1,1}$ norms of the obstacles. Proof. First let $r=1$, and suppose that $f=f_1$ is smooth. By lemma 16.2.25 , the solutions $a_ eta $ have uniformly bounded values, gradients and full real Hessians for $ eta \geq  eta _0$, and by proposition 16.2.22 they converge uniformly to $P_\kappa (f)$. The limit $P_\kappa (f)$ is therefore continuous, and by the same proposition it has bounded metric Laplacian; hence it belongs to $C^{1,\alpha }(X)$ by proposition 16.2.11 , and in particular it is $C^1$. We now pass to the limit in the Hessian bounds. For a smooth vector field $Y$, the function $
abla ^2a_ eta (Y,Y)=YYa_ eta -(
abla _ YY)a_ eta $ is obtained from $a_ eta $ by a second-order differential operator. Since $a_ eta 	o P_\kappa (f)$ uniformly, $
abla ^2a_ eta (Y,Y)	o 
abla ^2P_\kappa (f)(Y,Y)$ in the sense of distributions, where the right side is the weak covariant Hessian, and for every nonnegative test function $\varphi $ we obtain $|\langle 
abla ^2P_\kappa (f)(Y,Y),\varphi angle |\leq C\int |Y|_{g_0}^2\varphi $. By corollary 1.7.2 (1), the weak quadratic components $
abla ^2P_\kappa (f)(Y,Y)$ are bounded functions, with $|
abla ^2P_\kappa (f)(Y,Y)|\leq C|Y|_{g_0}^2$ almost everywhere; by polarization, so are all components of the weak covariant Hessian. The gradient is treated in the same way: $Ya_ eta 	o YP_\kappa (f)$ in the sense of distributions, and $|Ya_ eta |\leq C|Y|_{g_0}$; since $YP_\kappa (f)$ is continuous, pairing with nonnegative test functions of integral one supported in small balls about a point shows that $|YP_\kappa (f)|\leq C|Y|_{g_0}$ everywhere, so $|
abla P_\kappa (f)|_{g_0}\leq C$. In a chart, the weak second derivatives of $P_\kappa (f)$ differ from the components of its weak covariant Hessian by the Christoffel symbols times its first derivatives, so they are bounded on compact subsets of the chart. Hence $P_\kappa (f)$ is $C^{1,1}$, by proposition 1.7.5 , and the bounds just proved show that its $C^{1,1}$ norm is bounded by a constant depending only on the fixed geometry and on the constant $B$ of lemma 16.2.25 for $f$. Now let the $f_ j$ be arbitrary $C^{1,1}$ functions. Using convolution in finitely many charts and a smooth partition of unity, we obtain smooth functions $f_{j,ho }$ that converge to $f_ j$ in $C^1$ as $ho 	o 0$ and have uniformly bounded covariant Hessians. Indeed, the second derivatives of such a partitioned convolution are the cutoffs times the convolutions of the bounded weak second derivatives of $f_ j$, plus terms that involve only the values and first derivatives of the local convolutions; all of these are uniformly bounded. For $\delta >0$ put \[  F_{ho ,\delta }=-\delta \log \sum _ j \mathrm e^{-f_{j,ho }/\delta }, \qquad p_ j= rac{\mathrm e^{-f_{j,ho }/\delta }}{\sum _ k\mathrm e^{-f_{k,ho }/\delta }}.  \] The weights $p_ j$ are positive with sum one, $\min _ jf_{j,ho }-\delta \log r\leq F_{ho ,\delta }\leq \min _ jf_{j,ho }$, and the gradient of $F_{ho ,\delta }$ is the convex combination $\sum _ jp_ j
abla f_{j,ho }$. For every real tangent vector $Y$ the chain rule gives  egin{align*}  
abla ^2F_{ho ,\delta }(Y,Y) &  =\sum _ jp_ j
abla ^2f_{j,ho }(Y,Y)\ & \quad - rac1\delta \left(\sum _ jp_ j(\mathrm df_{j,ho }(Y))^2 -\left(\sum _ jp_ j\mathrm df_{j,ho }(Y)ight)^2ight)\ & \leq C|Y|_{g_0}^2, \end{align*} because the term in parentheses is a variance and hence nonnegative. Let $ho ,\delta 	o 0$ with $\delta \log r\leq 1$. Then the smooth obstacles $F_{ho ,\delta }$ have uniformly bounded values and gradients and a uniform upper bound for their Hessians, although their Hessians have no uniform lower bound as $\delta 	o 0$; this is why lemma 16.2.25 uses only an upper bound. Since the smooth case bounds the $C^{1,1}$ norm of the envelope in terms of the fixed geometry and the constant $B$ of that lemma, the envelopes $P_\kappa (F_{ho ,\delta })$ have uniformly bounded $C^{1,1}$ norms. The obstacles converge uniformly to $\min _ jf_ j$, so the envelopes converge uniformly to $P_\kappa (\min _ jf_ j)$ by the stability estimate of proposition 16.1.4 (4). The limit is $C^1$ by theorem 16.2.24 , since $C^{1,1}$ functions have bounded metric Laplacian. The same passage to the limit as in the smooth case, with the smooth functions $a_ eta $ replaced by the $C^{1,1}$ functions $P_\kappa (F_{ho ,\delta })$, whose gradients and weak covariant Hessians are bounded by a uniform constant, now proves the theorem, together with the bound for the norm. $\square$

title: Smoothing and its joint complex Hessian
text:
16.2.5 Smoothing and its joint complex Hessian We now turn to envelopes in a big class $\{ 	heta \} $. The background $	heta $ is no longer positive, so the penalized equations of section 16.2.3 are not available. Instead we compare the envelope $u$ with a smoothing $\Psi _ u(x,r)$, an average of $u$ over a neighborhood of $x$ of size $r$, and the metric-Laplacian bound will follow from an estimate $\Psi _ u(x,r)-u(x)=O(r^2)$. Convolution in coordinates does not define a global family on $X$, so we build the smoothing kernel from finite holomorphic jets of the exponential map of $\omega $. Smoothing loses a small amount of positivity. This loss will be corrected by minimizing over the radius, as in Kiselman's minimum principle, and for that we need the complex Hessian of the smoothing jointly in the base point and the radius. This joint estimate is lemma 16.2.27 . For the calculations in this and the next two subsections we put \[  \mathcal D=\mathrm i\partial  ar\partial =2\pi \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}, \qquad \alpha =2\pi 	heta ,\qquad \widehat\omega =2\pi \omega .  \] Thus $\alpha +\mathcal Du\geq 0$ is precisely the condition that $u$ is $	heta $-psh, and multiplying forms by $2\pi $ only changes the constants in the estimates. Let $h$ be the coefficient matrix of $\widehat\omega $ in local holomorphic coordinates, as in section 16.2.3 , and write $|v|_ h$ for the corresponding norm of a tangent vector $v$. For a real $(1,1)$-form $T=\mathrm i\sum _{l,m}t_{l ar m}\, \mathrm dz_ l\wedge \mathrm d ar z_ m$ we write $T[y]^2=\sum _{l,m}t_{l ar m}y_ l ar y_ m$ for the value of the associated Hermitian quadratic form on a vector $y$; thus $\widehat\omega [v]^2=|v|_ h^2$. For a real $(1,1)$-form on a product of an open subset of $X$ with an open subset of $\mathbb C$, we write $T[v,\eta ]^2$ for its value on the product tangent vector $(v,\eta )$. If $P=(p_{l ar m})$ and $M=(M_{lm})$ are Hermitian matrices, we write $P[M]=\sum _{l,m}p_{l ar m}M_{lm}$ for their contraction, so that $P[y]^2=P[yy^*]$. Lemma 16.2.27 . There are $r_0>0$ and, for every integrable function $u$ on $X$, a function $\Psi _ u(x,w)$ of $x\in X$ and $w\in \mathbb C$ with $0<|w|<r_0$, obtained by integrating $u$ against a positive kernel of total mass one, such that $\Psi _ u$ is smooth, invariant under rotations of $w$ and linear in $u$, and has the following properties. The kernel is built from the radial weight $\chi (t)=C_ n(1-t)^{-2}\mathrm e^{-1/(1-t)}$ for $t<1$, $\chi (t)=0$ for $t\geq 1$, where the constant $C_ n>0$ is chosen so that $\int _{\mathbb C^ n}\chi (|\zeta |^2)\, \mathrm d\zeta =1$. We write $\Psi _ u(x,r)$ for the value of $\Psi _ u$ at $|w|=r$. In the assertions about $H_ u$ and its joint Levi form we assume that $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$; constants denoted by $C$ may then depend on the fixed geometry, $\sup _ Xu$ and $\| u\| _{L^1}$, but not on the radius, and the constant $A$ depends only on the fixed geometry. For a sufficiently large constant $K$ of the same kind as $C$, put \[  H_ u(x,r)=\Psi _ u(x,r)+Kr^2,\qquad \lambda _ u(x,r)=r\partial _ rH_ u(x,r).  \] Then $H_ u(x,\mathrm e^ s)$ is a strictly convex nondecreasing function of $s$ which tends to $u(x)$ as $s	o -\infty $; in particular $\lambda _ u\geq 0$. If $u$ is bounded near $x$, then $\lambda _ u(x,r)	o 0$ as $r	o 0$. At each point $x$ we use holomorphic normal coordinates for $\omega $ centered at $x$ (lemma 16.2.13 ), defined on a ball of a fixed size (Step 1 of the proof). Let $q$ be a smooth function there with $\mathcal Dq=\alpha $, so that $p=u+q$ is plurisubharmonic, and let $\mu _ p$ be the trace of the complex Hessian of $p$ in these coordinates, a positive measure. Put $d=2n$ and \[  m_ u(x,r)=1+r^{-d}\mu _ p(B(x,4r)).  \] All estimates below hold uniformly over these fixed normal charts. For a tangent vector $v$ at $x$ and a tangent vector $\eta \in \mathbb C$ in the radius variable, the joint Levi form of $H_ u$ in $(x,w)$ satisfies 16.31  egin{align} \label{eq:chern-joint-mass-estimate} (\alpha +\mathcal D_{x,w}H_ u)[v,\eta ]^2 \geq {}& - igl (A\lambda _ u+C(r^2+r^3m_ u) igr )|v|_ h^2
otag \ & -C(r+r^2m_ u)|v|_ h|\eta |-Cr^2|\eta |^2, \qquad r=|w|. \end{align} Since $m_ u\leq Cr^{-2}$, as we show in the proof, this gives 16.32  egin{equation} \label{eq:chern-initial-joint-bound} (\alpha +\mathcal D_{x,w}H_ u)[v,\eta ]^2 \geq -(A\lambda _ u+Cr)|v|_ h^2-C|v|_ h|\eta |-C|\eta |^2. \end{equation} If $m_ u(x,r)\leq M(x)/r$ with $M(x)\geq 1$, then the stronger estimate 16.33  egin{equation} \label{eq:chern-improved-joint-bound} (\alpha +\mathcal D_{x,w}H_ u)[v,\eta ]^2 \geq -(A\lambda _ u+CM(x)r^2)|v|_ h^2 -CM(x)r|v|_ h|\eta |-CM(x)r|\eta |^2 \end{equation} holds. Moreover, if $u$ is bounded on the ball $B(x,2r)$ of the normal coordinates at $x$, then $\Psi _ u(x,r)$ differs from the ordinary radial convolution $\int u(x+r\zeta )\chi (|\zeta |^2)\, \mathrm d\zeta $ in these coordinates by at most $Cr^2\sup _{B(x,2r)}|u|$, where $C$ depends only on the fixed geometry. For a $C^1$ function $f$ with bounded weak complex Hessian, 16.34  egin{equation} \label{eq:chern-regular-obstacle-error} |\Psi _ f(x,r)-f(x)|\leq C_ f r^2 \end{equation} uniformly on $X$, where $C_ f$ is controlled by the bounds for the value, the gradient and the complex Hessian of $f$. Finally, for every integrable function $u$ on $X$, 16.35  egin{equation} \label{eq:chern-smoothing-generator}  rac{\Psi _ u(\cdot ,r)-u}{r^2}\longrightarrow a_\chi D_ hu \quad 	ext{in the sense of distributions as }r	o 0, \end{equation} where $D_ hu=\sum _{i,j}h^{i ar j}u_{i ar j}$ is the trace of the complex Hessian, as in section 16.2.3 , and $a_\chi = rac1n\int |\zeta |^2\chi (|\zeta |^2)\, \mathrm d\zeta >0$. Proof. We construct the smoothing in Step 1. In Steps 2–4 we compute, for a smooth plurisubharmonic local potential $p$, the joint complex Hessian of $\Psi _ p$ up to a remainder of high order in the radius; the result is the identity ( 16.50 ). From this identity we derive the joint estimates, first for smooth potentials (Step 5) and then in general (Step 6), and Step 7 proves the remaining assertions. All bounds are uniform over the centers, because the constructions are made in the charts of a fixed finite atlas, with coefficients bounded uniformly in the center. Step 1: construction of the smoothing. We construct a smooth map $F(x,\zeta )\in X$, defined for small tangent vectors $\zeta \in T_ xX$, from the holomorphic parts of the jets of geodesics, first in coordinates and then globally; $\Psi _ u$ is then an average of $u\circ F$. We begin with uniform normal coordinates. Fix the jet order $N=8$. For $x\in X$ we use the normal coordinates for $\omega $ at $x$ of lemma 16.2.13 , applied in a chart of a fixed finite atlas that contains $x$ in a fixed compact subset; in them $h(0)=I$ and $\mathrm dh(0)=0$. The coordinate change there is a polynomial map of degree at most two. Its linear part $L_ x$ satisfies $L_ x^{\mathrm T}h(x)\overline{L_ x}=I$, where $h(x)$ is the coefficient matrix in the chart of the atlas, so $L_ x$ and $L_ x^{-1}$ are bounded uniformly in $x$. The condition $\mathrm dh(0)=0$ is a linear equation for the quadratic part, whose coefficient matrix $h(x)\overline{L_ x}$ is invertible and whose right side is built from $L_ x$ and the first derivatives of $h$ at $x$; so the quadratic part is bounded uniformly in $x$ as well. Hence these coordinates are defined on balls of a fixed size, and all finite jets of $h$ in them are bounded uniformly in $x$. Next we define the jet map, in arbitrary holomorphic coordinates. Let $\Gamma ^ m_{jl}$ be given by $\sum _ m\Gamma ^ m_{jl}h_{m ar k}=\partial _ jh_{l ar k}$. Thus $\Gamma (z)$ is a bilinear map $\mathbb C^ n	imes \mathbb C^ n	o \mathbb C^ n$, symmetric because $\widehat\omega $ is closed, depending smoothly on $z$, and $\Gamma (0)=0$ in normal coordinates. Consider the geodesic equation \[  \ddot\gamma +\Gamma (\gamma )(\dot\gamma ,\dot\gamma )=0  \] for formal power series $\gamma (t)=z+\sum _{k\geq 1}c_ kt^ k/k!$ in a real variable $t$, with $c_ k\in \mathbb C^ n$; here $\Gamma (\gamma (t))$ is the composition of the Taylor series of $\Gamma $ at $z$ with the series $\gamma (t)-z$, which has no constant term. Prescribe $c_1=\zeta $. Comparing the coefficients of $t^ k$ in the equation determines $c_{k+2}$ as a polynomial in $c_1,\ldots ,c_{k+1}$ whose coefficients are derivatives of $\Gamma $ at $z$ of order at most $k$. By induction, $c_ k$ is a polynomial in $\zeta $ and $ ar\zeta $ with coefficients depending smoothly on $z$, and it is homogeneous of degree $k$: for real $\lambda $ the series $\gamma (\lambda t)$ is the formal solution with initial velocity $\lambda \zeta $, so that $c_ k(\lambda \zeta )=\lambda ^ kc_ k(\zeta )$. Let $c_ k^{\mathrm h}(z,\zeta )$ be the sum of the monomials of $c_ k$ that contain no $ ar\zeta $, and define \[  J_ z(\zeta )=z+\zeta +\sum _{k=2}^ N rac{c_ k^{\mathrm h}(z,\zeta )}{k!},  \] a holomorphic polynomial in $\zeta $ with coefficients depending smoothly on $z$. Since $c_2=-\Gamma (z)(\zeta ,\zeta )$, in normal coordinates at $x$ we have $J_0(\zeta )=\zeta +O(|\zeta |^3)$. These jets do not depend on the coordinates. Let $y=\phi (z)$ be a holomorphic change of coordinates, with derivative $\Phi =D\phi $, and let $\widetilde h$, $\widetilde\Gamma $ and $\widetilde J$ be the corresponding objects in the coordinates $y$. Then $h_{j ar k}=\sum _{a,b}\Phi ^ a_ j\, \widetilde h_{a ar b}(\phi )\, \overline{\Phi ^ b_ k}$, and since $\Phi $ is holomorphic, \[  \partial _ jh_{l ar k}=\sum _{a,b}\Bigl (\partial _ j\Phi ^ a_ l+\sum _{c,e}\Phi ^ c_ j\Phi ^ e_ l\, \widetilde\Gamma ^ a_{ce}(\phi )\Bigr )\widetilde h_{a ar b}(\phi )\, \overline{\Phi ^ b_ k}.  \] Comparing with the definition of $\Gamma $, and using that the matrix $(\sum _ b\widetilde h_{a ar b}\overline{\Phi ^ b_ k})_{a,k}$ is invertible, we obtain $\Phi \, \Gamma (\zeta ,\zeta ')=D^2\phi (\zeta ,\zeta ')+\widetilde\Gamma (\phi )(\Phi \zeta ,\Phi \zeta ')$ for all $\zeta ,\zeta '\in \mathbb C^ n$. Let $\gamma $ be a formal solution in the coordinates $z$. The second derivative of $\phi \circ \gamma $ is $\Phi (\gamma )\ddot\gamma +D^2\phi (\gamma )(\dot\gamma ,\dot\gamma )$, because $\Phi $ is holomorphic, and therefore \[   rac{\mathrm d^2(\phi \circ \gamma )}{\mathrm dt^2}+\widetilde\Gamma (\phi \circ \gamma )\Bigl ( rac{\mathrm d(\phi \circ \gamma )}{\mathrm dt}, rac{\mathrm d(\phi \circ \gamma )}{\mathrm dt}\Bigr )=\Phi (\gamma ) igl (\ddot\gamma +\Gamma (\gamma )(\dot\gamma ,\dot\gamma ) igr )=0.  \] By uniqueness, $\phi \circ \gamma $ is the formal solution with initial point $\phi (z)$ and initial velocity $\Phi (z)\zeta $. By homogeneity we may put $t=1$ degree by degree, and we obtain an identity between formal power series in $\zeta $ and $ ar\zeta $. Call a monomial in $\zeta $ and $ ar\zeta $ discardable if it contains a factor $ ar\zeta _ m$ or has degree at least $N+1$; the product of a discardable monomial with any monomial is discardable. The two sides of this identity, the formal solution in the coordinates $y$ and the series $\phi \circ \gamma $, differ from $\widetilde J_{\phi (z)}(\Phi (z)\zeta )$ and from $\phi (J_ z(\zeta ))$, respectively, by series of discardable monomials; for $\phi \circ \gamma $ we use the Taylor expansion of the holomorphic map $\phi $ at $J_ z(\zeta )$, each of whose terms beyond the first contains the discardable difference as a factor. The two holomorphic functions of $\zeta $ just named therefore have the same Taylor coefficients of degree at most $N$ at $\zeta =0$, and Taylor's formula gives 16.36  egin{equation} \label{eq:chern-jet-compatibility} \widetilde J_{\phi (z)} igl (\Phi (z)\zeta  igr )=\phi  igl (J_ z(\zeta ) igr )+O(|\zeta |^{N+1}), \end{equation} where the remainder is a smooth function vanishing to order $N+1$ at $\zeta =0$, with bounds for its derivatives that are locally uniform in $z$.
