Integrating by parts in $ ar s_ l$ and using ( 16.44 ) and $\partial _{s_ m}\chi _1(|s|^2)=\chi  ar s_ m$, we get  egin{align*}  -\int \mathcal LG\, \partial _{s_ m} igl (\chi  eta ^ k_ m igr )\, \mathrm ds & =\sum _ l\int \partial _{ ar s_ l}(\mathcal LG)\, \partial _{s_ m} igl (\chi _1\sigma ^ k_{ml} igr )\, \mathrm ds\ & = ar w\sum _ l\int P igl (Y,\overline{\partial _{ho _ l}a} igr ) igl (\chi  ar s_ m\sigma ^ k_{ml}+\chi _1\partial _{s_ m}\sigma ^ k_{ml} igr )\, \mathrm ds. \end{align*} We multiply by $ ar v_ k$ and sum over $k$ and $m$. To write the result, we define vectors $\Xi $ and $\Theta $ by  egin{align*}  \Xi ^ m={}& \sum _{I,j,l} rac{I_ m}{|I|}\overline d_{Ijl}  ar w^{|I|-2}s_ l ar s^{I-1_ m}v_ j,\  \Theta ^ m={}& \sum _{I,j,l} rac{I_ m}{|I|}(I-1_ m)_ l\, \overline d_{Ijl}  ar w^{|I|-2} ar s^{I-1_ m-1_ l}v_ j, \end{align*} where the factor $(I-1_ m)_ l ar s^{I-1_ m-1_ l}$ is zero when $(I-1_ m)_ l=0$. Then $ ar w\sum _{k,m} ar v_ k ar s_ m\sigma ^ k_{ml}=r^2\, \overline{\Xi ^ l}$ and $ ar w\sum _{k,m} ar v_ k\partial _{s_ m}\sigma ^ k_{ml}=r^2\, \overline{\Theta ^ l}$, and $P$ is antilinear in its second argument. Therefore \[  T_2=2r^2\operatorname{Re}\int P igl (Y,\overline{D_ho a\, \Xi } igr )\chi \, \mathrm ds+2r^2\operatorname{Re}\int P igl (Y,\overline{D_ho a\, \Theta } igr )\chi _1\, \mathrm ds.  \] Next we compute $T_3$. By ( 16.47 ), each explicit term of $\mathcal L ar{\mathcal L}W$ is a sum of second derivatives $\partial _{s_ m}\partial _{ ar s_ l}$ of weights, and two integrations by parts move these derivatives onto $G$. For the curvature term we use $\partial _{s_ m}(\chi s_ l)=\partial _{s_ m}\partial _{ ar s_ l}\chi _1$ and ( 16.44 ), and we let $C^ v$ be the matrix with entries $C^ v_{ml}=\sum _{j,k}c_{jklm}v_ j ar v_ k$: \[  -\sum _{j,k,l,m}v_ j ar v_ kc_{jklm}\int G\, \partial _{s_ m}(\chi s_ l)\, \mathrm ds=-r^2\sum _{l,m}\int P igl (\partial _{ho _ m}a,\overline{\partial _{ho _ l}a} igr )\chi _1C^ v_{ml}\, \mathrm ds.  \] Since $h$ is Hermitian, $\overline{c_{jklm}}=c_{kjml}$; hence $C^ v$ is Hermitian, and $\| C^ v\| \leq C|v|^2$ for its operator norm. For the terms containing $\gamma ^{jk}$ and $\partial _ w eta ^ k$, ( 16.47 ) writes $\chi \gamma ^{jk}_ m=\sum _ l\partial _{ ar s_ l}(\chi _1	au ^{jk}_{ml})$ and $\chi \partial _ w eta ^ k_ m=\sum _ l\partial _{ ar s_ l}(\chi _1\partial _ w\sigma ^ k_{ml})$, with $\sigma ^ k_{ml}$ as above and \[  	au ^{jk}_{ml}=\sum _ Ie_{Ijkm}w^{|I|-1} rac{I_ l}{|I|}s^{I-1_ l},\qquad \partial _ w\sigma ^ k_{ml}=\sum _ Id_{Ikm}(|I|-1)w^{|I|-2} rac{I_ l}{|I|}s^{I-1_ l}.  \] Two integrations by parts give the contribution \[  -r^2\sum _{l,m}\int P igl (\partial _{ho _ m}a,\overline{\partial _{ho _ l}a} igr )\chi _1B_{ml}\, \mathrm ds,\qquad B_{ml}=\sum _{j,k}v_ j ar v_ k	au ^{jk}_{ml}+\eta \sum _ k ar v_ k\partial _ w\sigma ^ k_{ml}.  \] The terms containing $\overline{\gamma ^{kj}}$ and $\overline{\partial _ w eta ^ j}$ are treated with the conjugate formula in ( 16.47 ), and after renaming $j\leftrightarrow k$ they give the same expression with the matrix $B$ replaced by its conjugate transpose $B^*$. Finally, with $ eta =\sum _ k ar v_ k eta ^ k$, two integrations by parts turn the last term of ( 16.40 ) into \[  \sum _{j,k}v_ j ar v_ k\sum _{l,m}\int G\, \partial _{s_ m}\partial _{ ar s_ l} igl (\chi  eta ^ k_ m\overline{ eta ^ j_ l} igr )\mathrm ds =r^2\int P igl [D_ho a\,  eta  igr ]^2\chi \, \mathrm ds.  \] For a matrix $M$ in the fiber variables write \[  P[Da(M)]=\sum _{l,m}M_{ml}P igl (\partial _{ho _ m}a,\overline{\partial _{ho _ l}a} igr ),  \] so that $P[Da(yy'^*)]=P(D_ho a\, y,\overline{D_ho a\, y'})$ for vectors $y$ and $y'$. Since $\chi $ and $\chi _1$ vanish outside the unit ball, on which $\chi >0$, we have shown that $T_3=r^2\int P[Da(U)]\chi \, \mathrm ds$, where, on the unit ball, $U=- rac{\chi _1}{\chi }(C^ v+B+B^*)+ eta  eta ^*$, with the quotient $\chi _1/\chi $ evaluated at $|s|^2$. Explicitly, $U$ is the Hermitian part of the matrix $U'=- rac{\chi _1}{\chi }(C^ v+2B)+ eta  eta ^*$, whose entries are  egin{align*}  U'_{ml}={}& - rac{\chi _1}{\chi }\left( \sum _{j,k}c_{jklm}v_ j ar v_ k +2\sum _{I,j,k}e_{Ijkm}w^{|I|-1}  rac{I_ l}{|I|}s^{I-1_ l}v_ j ar v_ kight.\ & \hspace{29mm}\left. +2\sum _{I,k}d_{Ikm}(|I|-1)w^{|I|-2}  rac{I_ l}{|I|}s^{I-1_ l}\eta  ar v_ kight)\ & +\sum _{I,J,j,k}d_{Ikm}\overline d_{Jjl} w^{|I|-1} ar w^{|J|-1}s^ I ar s^ Jv_ j ar v_ k. \end{align*} Finally we add $T_1$, $T_2$ and $T_3$. Completing the square, $P[Y]^2+2r^2\operatorname{Re}P(Y,\overline{D_ho a\, \Xi })=P[Y+r^2D_ho a\, \Xi ]^2-r^4P[D_ho a\, \Xi ]^2$, where $Y+r^2D_ho a\, \Xi =Da(v,\eta s+r^2\Xi )$. Moreover, the real part of $P(Y,\overline{D_ho a\, \Theta })$ equals that of $P(D_ho a\, \Theta ,\overline Y)$, because $P$ is Hermitian. We have therefore proved the identity 16.50  egin{equation} \label{eq:chern-kernel-square-identity}  egin{aligned}  \mathcal D\Psi _ p[v,\eta ]^2 ={}& \int P igl [Da(v,\eta s+r^2\Xi ) igr ]^2\chi \, \mathrm ds +r^2\int P igl [Da(U-r^2\Xi \Xi ^*) igr ]\chi \, \mathrm ds\ & +2r^2\operatorname{Re}\int P igl (Da(0,\Theta ),\overline{Da(v,\eta s)} igr )\chi _1\, \mathrm ds+E. \end{aligned} \end{equation} Here $Da$ is the differential of $a$ at $(0,ws)$, $P[Da(\cdot )]$ is the contraction defined above, and the remainder $E$ is given by ( 16.46 ). Step 5: the joint estimate for smooth potentials. In this step we assume that $p=u+q$ is smooth near $\overline{B(0,3r)}$. We derive ( 16.31 ) from ( 16.50 ) and prove that $H_ u$ is a strictly convex function of $\log r$. We choose $q$ as a fixed local potential of $\alpha $ on one of finitely many coordinate balls covering $X$ (lemma 7.3.1 ); by a Lebesgue number argument, the normal ball of a fixed radius about each center lies in one of them. This choice is harmless, because $\mu _ p$, and hence $m_ u$, is the trace measure of $\alpha +\mathcal Du$ and does not depend on $q$. We also use two elementary facts. For a nonnegative Hermitian matrix $P$ and any matrix $M$ we have $|\sum _{l,m}p_{l ar m}M_{lm}|\leq \| M\| \operatorname {tr}P$, by diagonalizing $P$; in particular $|P(y, ar y')|\leq |y||y'|\operatorname {tr}P$. Moreover, since $a(0,ho )$ is the Taylor polynomial of degree $N$ of $F(0,\cdot )$, which is that of $J_0$, we have $D_ho a=I+O(r^2)$ and $\partial _ za(0,ws)=I+O(r)$, and $a(0,ws)=ws+O(r^3)$, for $|s|\leq 2$. Hence the map $s\mapsto a(0,ws)$ is injective on $\{ |s|\leq 2\} $, has real Jacobian determinant at least $r^ d/2$, and takes values in $B(0,3r)$. We first bound the masses of $p$ on small balls about the center; this part does not use the smoothness of $p$. By the Jensen–Lelong formula (theorem 12.1.3 ), the normalized trace mass $D_ p(x,t)$ of ( 12.3 ) is nondecreasing in $t$, and $\mu _ p(B(x,t))$ is a fixed multiple of $t^{d-2}D_ p(x,t)$. On a fixed larger ball the trace mass of $p$ is bounded by $C\| p\| _{L^1}$ of a still larger ball: pair $\Delta p\geq 0$ with a cutoff function. Hence \[  \mu _ p(B(x,t))\leq Ct^{d-2},\qquad t^{-d}\int _{B(x,t)}|u|\leq C(1+|\log t|).  \] For the second estimate, ( 12.4 ) and the bound for $D_ p$ give $M_ p(x,\varrho )\geq M_ p(x,R)-2C\log (R/\varrho )$ for $\varrho <R$, where $M_ p$ denotes spherical means. Averaging over $R$ in a fixed interval bounds the right side below by $-C(1+|\log \varrho |)$, since the average of $|p|$ over a fixed annulus is bounded in terms of $\| u\| _{L^1}$. As $|p|=2p^+-p$ and $p^+$ is bounded in terms of $\sup _ Xu$, integration over spheres gives $\int _{B(x,t)}|p|\leq Ct^ d(1+|\log t|)$, and $|u|\leq |p|+|q|$. In particular $m_ u\leq Cr^{-2}$. To bound $E$, note that $|Y|\leq C(|v|+|\eta |)$ and $P[Y]^2\leq |Y|^2\operatorname {tr}P$ for $|s|\leq 2$. Moreover $\mathcal LG=\sum _ mb_ m\partial _{s_ m}G$ with $b=w^{-1}(D_ho a)^{-1}Y$, by ( 16.44 ) and its proof, and $|b|+|
abla _ sb|\leq Cr^{-1}(|v|+|\eta |)$; an integration by parts gives $\int \mathcal LG\, \delta _1\, \mathrm ds=-\int G\sum _ m\partial _{s_ m}(b_ m\delta _1)\, \mathrm ds$. By ( 16.45 ), \[  |E|\leq Cr^{N-2}(|v|+|\eta |)^2\int _{|s|\leq 2} igl (r^2\operatorname {tr}P+|G| igr )\mathrm ds.  \] Changing variables by the map $s\mapsto a(0,ws)$ and using the two mass bounds, we obtain $|E|\leq Cr^{N-2}(1+|\log r|)(|v|^2+|\eta |^2)\leq Cr^2(|v|^2+|\eta |^2)$, since $N=8$. Now we bound the right side of ( 16.50 ) from below. Its first integral is nonnegative. The formulas for the coefficients give $|\Xi |\leq C|v|$ and $|\Theta |\leq (C_ d+Cr)|v|$, where $C_ d$ is the norm of the linear map $v\mapsto \Theta $ formed by the terms with $|I|=2$, which do not depend on $s$ and $w$; the terms with $|I|\geq 3$ carry a factor $ ar w$. Every term of $U$ except the last carries the factor $-\chi _1/\chi =(1-|s|^2)^2\in [0,1]$; after this factor is removed, the curvature term has norm $\| C^ v\| \leq C_ c|v|^2$, where $C_ c$ depends only on the $c_{jklm}$, the $e$ term at most $Cr|v|^2$ and the mixed $d$ term at most $C|v||\eta |$, while the last term $ eta  eta ^*$ of $U$ gives the nonnegative contribution $r^2\int P[D_ho a\,  eta ]^2\chi \, \mathrm ds$. Put \[  \lambda _0(x,r)=2r^2\int (-\chi _1(|s|^2)) \operatorname {tr}P(x+rs)\, \mathrm ds, \qquad m_0=1+r^{-d}\mu _ p(B(x,3r)).  \] The substitution $s\mapsto w^{-1}a(0,ws)=s+O(r^2)$, whose derivative is $I+O(r^2)$, changes the kernel $-\chi _1(|s|^2)$ by $O(r^2)$ on $\{ |s|\leq 2\} $, and the unitary substitution $s\mapsto (w/r)s$ does not change it. Hence $r^2\int (-\chi _1)|D_ho a|^2\operatorname {tr}P\, \mathrm ds\leq  rac12\lambda _0+Cr^4m_0$, and similarly $r^2\int _{|s|\leq 1}\operatorname {tr}P\, \mathrm ds\leq Cr^2m_0$. Consequently the second and third integrals of ( 16.50 ), the second including the term $-r^2\Xi \Xi ^*$ from the square, are bounded below by \[  -A\lambda _0(x,r)|v|^2 -C(r^3m_0+r^2)|v|^2-Cr^2m_0|v||\eta |, \qquad A=	frac 12C_ c+C_ d .  \] Thus $A$ depends only on the fixed geometry, and since also $|E|\leq Cr^2(|v|^2+|\eta |^2)$, we obtain 16.53  egin{equation} \label{eq:chern-potential-joint-bound} \mathcal D\Psi _ p[v,\eta ]^2\geq - igl (A\lambda _0+C(r^2+r^3m_0) igr )|v|^2-Cr^2m_0|v||\eta |-Cr^2|\eta |^2. \end{equation} For $v=0$ the coefficients $\Xi $, $\Theta $ and $U$ vanish, and ( 16.50 ) reads $\partial _ w\partial _{ ar w}\Psi _ p=\int P[D_ho a\, s]^2\chi \, \mathrm ds+E$. It remains to subtract the smoothing of the smooth function $q$. Since $q$ is smooth, $\Psi _ q(z,w)$ is smooth also at $w=0$, where it equals $q(z)$. By rotation invariance, the terms of degree one and the terms in $w^2$ and $ ar w^2$ of its Taylor expansion in $w$ vanish, so $\Psi _ q(z,w)-q(z)$ is $|w|^2$ times a smooth function of $z$, up to an error $O(|w|^3)$ whose derivatives lose one power of $|w|$ for each derivative in $w$. Hence, with $\mathcal Dq=\alpha $, \[  \alpha [v]^2-\mathcal D\Psi _ q[v,\eta ]^2\geq -Cr^2|v|^2-Cr|v||\eta |-C_ q|\eta |^2.  \] Since $\Psi _ u=\Psi _ p-\Psi _ q$ and $\partial _ w\partial _{ ar w}(K|w|^2)=K$, we choose $K\geq C_ q+1$. Adding these estimates proves ( 16.31 ) with $\lambda _0$ in place of $\lambda _ u$ and $m_0$ in place of $m_ u$. Moreover, for $v=0$ it gives $\partial _ w\partial _{ ar w}H_ u\geq K-C_ q-Cr^2>0$. Since $\partial _ w\partial _{ ar w}g= rac1{4r}\partial _ r(r\partial _ rg)$ for a function $g$ of $r=|w|$, the second derivative of $H_ u$ with respect to $\log r$ is $(r\partial _ r)^2H_ u=4r^2\partial _ w\partial _{ ar w}H_ u>0$, so $H_ u$ is a strictly convex function of $\log r$. Finally we compare $\lambda _0$ with $\lambda _ u$. Let $\Psi ^{\mathrm e}_ g(r)=\int g(x+rs)\chi (|s|^2)\, \mathrm ds$ denote the Euclidean radial convolution in the normal coordinates. For a smooth function $g$, the radial derivative is 16.54  egin{equation} \label{eq:chern-radial-derivative} r\partial _ r\Psi ^{\mathrm e}_ g(r)=-2r^2\int \chi _1(|s|^2)\sum _ mg_{m ar m}(x+rs)\, \mathrm ds. \end{equation} Indeed, $r\partial _ r[g(x+rs)]=\sum _ m igl (s_ m\partial _{s_ m}+ ar s_ m\partial _{ ar s_ m} igr )[g(x+rs)]$, and by $s_ m\chi =\partial _{ ar s_ m}\chi _1$ and an integration by parts, $\int s_ m\partial _{s_ m}[g(x+rs)]\chi \, \mathrm ds=-\int \partial _{s_ m}\partial _{ ar s_ m}[g(x+rs)]\chi _1\, \mathrm ds=-r^2\int g_{m ar m}(x+rs)\chi _1\, \mathrm ds$; the terms with $ ar s_ m$ are the complex conjugates. In particular $r\partial _ r\Psi ^{\mathrm e}_ p=\lambda _0$, and $|r\partial _ r\Psi ^{\mathrm e}_ q|\leq Cr^2$. By ( 16.37 ), the substitution $s\mapsto r^{-1}F(x,rs)=s+O(r^2)$, with derivative $I+O(r^2)$, shows that the kernel of $\Psi _ u(x,r)$ differs from that of $\Psi ^{\mathrm e}_ u(r)$ by at most $Cr^{2-d}$ on $B(x,2r)$, where $\Psi ^{\mathrm e}_ u=\Psi ^{\mathrm e}_ p-\Psi ^{\mathrm e}_ q$. Hence the radial function $\psi (r)=\Psi _ u(x,r)-\Psi ^{\mathrm e}_ u(r)$ satisfies $|\psi (r)|\leq Cr^{2-d}\int _{B(x,2r)}|u|\leq Cr^2(1+|\log r|)$, so $\psi (r)	o 0$ as $r	o 0$; like the mass bounds, this holds for every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$. In the same way, by the case $v=0$ of ( 16.50 ), the matrix-valued kernels against which $P$ is integrated in $\partial _ w\partial _{ ar w}\Psi _ p$ and in $\partial _ w\partial _{ ar w}\Psi ^{\mathrm e}_ p=\int P(x+ws)[s]^2\chi \, \mathrm ds$ differ in norm by at most $Cr^{2-d}$ on $B(x,3r)$; since $|P[M]|\leq \| M\| \operatorname {tr}P$, these vertical derivatives differ by at most $Cr^2m_0+|E|\leq C$. The smooth function $q$ contributes bounded vertical derivatives as well. Thus $|\partial _ r(r\partial _ r\psi )|=4r|\partial _ w\partial _{ ar w}\psi |\leq Cr$ for all small $r$. Integrating from $r'$ to $r$ shows that $\ell =\lim _{r'	o 0}r'\psi '(r')$ exists and $|r\psi '(r)-\ell |\leq Cr^2$. If $\ell 
eq 0$, then $\psi '(r)=\ell /r+O(r)$, and $\psi (r)-\psi (r')=\ell \log (r/r')+O(r^2)$ would be unbounded as $r'	o 0$, contradicting $\psi 	o 0$. Hence $\ell =0$ and $|r\partial _ r\psi |\leq Cr^2$. Since $\lambda _ u=r\partial _ r\Psi ^{\mathrm e}_ p-r\partial _ r\Psi ^{\mathrm e}_ q+r\partial _ r\psi +2Kr^2$, we obtain $|\lambda _ u-\lambda _0|\leq Cr^2$. Since $m_0\leq m_ u$, this proves ( 16.31 ) for smooth $p$; we record that it holds with $m_0$ in place of $m_ u$. Step 6: nonsmooth potentials. Let $p$ be plurisubharmonic near $\overline{B(0,4r)}$. We approximate $p$ by its mollifications $p_\varepsilon $, $0<\varepsilon <r$ (section 1.4 ), and pass to the limit in the estimates of Step 5. By ( 3.3 ), applied to the subharmonic function $p$, we have $p\leq p_\varepsilon \leq \sup _{B(0,4r)}p$, so $|p_\varepsilon |\leq |p|+C$ on $B(0,3r)$. The functions $p_\varepsilon $ are smooth and plurisubharmonic on $B(0,3r)$, by proposition 8.2.2 (2). Since derivatives commute with mollification (proposition 1.4.3 (1)), the trace measure of $p_\varepsilon $ is the mollification of $\mu _ p$, so $\mu _{p_\varepsilon }(B(0,3r))\leq \mu _ p(B(0,4r))$, and the monotonicity of the normalized trace mass of $p_\varepsilon $ gives $\mu _{p_\varepsilon }(B(0,t))\leq Ct^{d-2}$ for $t\leq 3r$. Thus the mass bounds used above hold for $p_\varepsilon $ on these balls, with constants independent of $\varepsilon $, and ( 16.31 ) holds for $u_\varepsilon =p_\varepsilon -q$ at the center, with $1+r^{-d}\mu _{p_\varepsilon }(B(0,3r))\leq m_ u$ in place of $m_ u$; so do the inequalities $|\lambda _{u_\varepsilon }-\lambda _0(p_\varepsilon )|\leq Cr^2$ and $\partial _ w\partial _{ ar w}H_{u_\varepsilon }\geq K-C_ q-Cr^2$. Since $p_\varepsilon 	o p$ in $L^1(B(0,3r))$ (lemma 1.4.1 (2)), and $\Psi $, its derivatives in $(z,w)$ for $w
eq 0$ and $\Psi ^{\mathrm e}$ are given by integration against smooth kernels, the joint Levi form of $H_{u_\varepsilon }$ at $(0,w)$, $\lambda _{u_\varepsilon }$ and $\lambda _0(p_\varepsilon )=r\partial _ r\Psi ^{\mathrm e}_{p_\varepsilon }$ converge to the corresponding quantities for $u$. Letting $\varepsilon 	o 0$ proves ( 16.31 ) and the strict convexity of $H_ u$ in $\log r$ for every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$. Finally, inserting $m_ u\leq Cr^{-2}$, or the hypothesis $m_ u\leq M(x)/r$, and using $r<1$, we obtain ( 16.32 ) and ( 16.33 ). Step 7: the remaining assertions. We first study $H_ u(x,r)$ as $r	o 0$; by Steps 5 and 6 it is a convex function of $\log r$. The kernel of $\Psi _ u$ is positive with mass one, so the upper bound for $u$ bounds $H_ u(x,r)$ from above as $r	o 0$. A convex function of $\log r$ that is bounded above as $r	o 0$ is nondecreasing: if its slope were negative at some point, the tangent line there, which lies below the function, would tend to $+\infty $ as $r	o 0$. Hence its slope $\lambda _ u=r\partial _ rH_ u$ is nonnegative. To identify the limit, recall from theorem 3.1.3 (2), applied to the subharmonic function $p$ (theorem 8.2.1 ), that the spherical means of $p$ about $x$ decrease to $p(x)$ as the radius decreases to zero; since $\Psi ^{\mathrm e}_ p(r)$ is an average of these spherical means at radii at most $r$, monotone convergence gives $\Psi ^{\mathrm e}_ p(r)	o p(x)$, and $\Psi ^{\mathrm e}_ q(r)	o q(x)$. Since $\psi (r)	o 0$, we get $H_ u(x,r)	o u(x)$ as $r	o 0$. If $u$ is bounded near $x$, this limit is finite. The slope of a convex function is nondecreasing, so it has a limit as $r	o 0$; a positive limit would force $H_ u(x,r)	o -\infty $. Therefore $\lambda _ u(x,r)	o 0$. Next we prove the two comparison statements. If $u$ is bounded on $B(x,2r)$, the comparison of the kernels in Step 5 gives $|\Psi _ u(x,r)-\Psi ^{\mathrm e}_ u(r)|\leq Cr^2\sup _{B(x,2r)}|u|$, which is the asserted comparison with radial convolution. Now let $f$ be a $C^1$ function whose weak complex Hessian is bounded by $M_ f$. In normal coordinates its Euclidean Laplacian $4\sum _ mf_{m ar m}$ is bounded by $CM_ f$, and so is the Laplacian of its mollifications $f_\varepsilon $. By ( 16.54 ), $|\partial _ r\Psi ^{\mathrm e}_{f_\varepsilon }(r)|\leq CM_ fr$, and since $\Psi ^{\mathrm e}_{f_\varepsilon }(r)	o f_\varepsilon (x)$ as $r	o 0$, we get $|\Psi ^{\mathrm e}_{f_\varepsilon }(r)-f_\varepsilon (x)|\leq CM_ fr^2$. Letting $\varepsilon 	o 0$, the same bound holds for $f$, by uniform convergence. Finally, by ( 16.37 ), $|f(F(x,r\zeta ))-f(x+r\zeta )|\leq Cr^3\| 
abla f\| _\infty $ for $|\zeta |\leq 1$, and $h(0)=I$, so $|\Psi _ f(x,r)-\Psi ^{\mathrm e}_ f(r)|\leq Cr^3\| 
abla f\| _\infty $. This proves ( 16.34 ). Finally we prove ( 16.35 ). We work in a fixed coordinate chart with a smooth frame of $T X$ that is unitary for $h$, obtained by the Gram–Schmidt process, and we describe a tangent vector by its vector $\zeta \in \mathbb C^ n$ of coefficients in this frame. Then $\mathrm d\zeta _ h=\mathrm d\zeta $, and the frame matrix $S(x)$, which satisfies $SS^*=(h^{i ar j})$, gives the vector $S(x)\zeta $ of coordinate components. In the chart, ( 16.36 ) shows that $F(x,\zeta )$ differs by $O(|\zeta |^{N+1})$ from $J_ z(S(x)\zeta )$, where $z$ is the coordinate of $x$ and $J_ z(\xi )=z+\xi - rac12\Gamma (z)(\xi ,\xi )+O(|\xi |^3)$ is the jet map of the chart. Hence $F(x,\zeta )=x+S(x)\zeta +Q_ x(S(x)\zeta ,S(x)\zeta )+O(|\zeta |^3)$ with the holomorphic quadratic map $Q_ x=- rac12\Gamma (z)$. The first moments of the radial weight vanish, and so do the moments $\int \zeta _ i\zeta _ j\chi (|\zeta |^2)\, \mathrm d\zeta $, by the substitution $\zeta \mapsto \mathrm e^{\mathrm it}\zeta $; by symmetry, $\int \zeta _ i ar\zeta _ j\chi (|\zeta |^2)\, \mathrm d\zeta =a_\chi \delta _{ij}$. For smooth $g$, the second-order Taylor expansion of $g(F(x,r\zeta ))$ in $r\zeta $, integrated against $\chi (|\zeta |^2)\, \mathrm d\zeta $, therefore gives \[  \Psi _ g(x,r)=g(x)+a_\chi r^2\sum _{i,j}h^{i ar j}g_{i ar j}(x)+O(r^3),  \] uniformly on compact subsets of the chart. For the distributional statement let $\varphi $ be a test function in the chart. For fixed $\zeta $ near $0$ the map $\Phi _\zeta (x)=F(x,\zeta )$ is a diffeomorphism near $\operatorname{Supp}\varphi $, with $\Phi _0$ the identity, and its inverse depends smoothly on $(\zeta ,y)$, by the inverse function theorem. By Fubini's theorem and the change of variables $y=\Phi _{r\zeta }(x)$, the adjoint kernel is  egin{gather*}  \int \Psi _ g(x,r)\varphi (x)\, \mathrm dx=\int g(y)\, \Psi _ r^*\varphi (y)\, \mathrm dy,\  \Psi _ r^*\varphi (y)=\int \varphi  igl (\Phi _{r\zeta }^{-1}(y) igr ) igl |\det D\Phi _{r\zeta }^{-1}(y) igr |\chi (|\zeta |^2)\, \mathrm d\zeta . \end{gather*} The integrand is a smooth function of $(r\zeta ,y)$, equal to $\varphi (y)$ at $r=0$, so Taylor's formula in $r\zeta $ gives $\Psi _ r^*\varphi =\varphi +r\varphi _1+r^2\varphi _2+O(r^3)$, with continuous functions $\varphi _1,\varphi _2$ supported in a fixed compact set and a remainder bounded uniformly in $y$. Pairing this with an arbitrary smooth $g$ and comparing with the expansion of $\Psi _ g$, we find $\int g\varphi _1=0$ and $\int g\varphi _2=a_\chi \int \varphi \sum h^{i ar j}g_{i ar j}$ for every smooth $g$; hence $\varphi _1=0$ and $\varphi _2=a_\chi \sum _{i,j}\partial _ i\partial _{ ar j}(h^{i ar j}\varphi )$. Pairing the expansion of $\Psi _ r^*\varphi $ with a locally integrable $u$ gives \[  \int  rac{\Psi _ u(\cdot ,r)-u}{r^2}\varphi \, \mathrm dx=\int u\,  rac{\Psi _ r^*\varphi -\varphi }{r^2}\, \mathrm dx\longrightarrow a_\chi \int u\sum _{i,j}\partial _ i\partial _{ ar j}(h^{i ar j}\varphi )\, \mathrm dx,  \] which is ( 16.35 ), because the right side is $a_\chi \langle D_ hu,\varphi angle $ by the definition of distributional derivatives. $\square$

title: Chern joint smoothing
text:
Lemma 16.2.27 . There are $r_0>0$ and, for every integrable function $u$ on $X$, a function $\Psi _ u(x,w)$ of $x\in X$ and $w\in \mathbb C$ with $0<|w|<r_0$, obtained by integrating $u$ against a positive kernel of total mass one, such that $\Psi _ u$ is smooth, invariant under rotations of $w$ and linear in $u$, and has the following properties. The kernel is built from the radial weight $\chi (t)=C_ n(1-t)^{-2}\mathrm e^{-1/(1-t)}$ for $t<1$, $\chi (t)=0$ for $t\geq 1$, where the constant $C_ n>0$ is chosen so that $\int _{\mathbb C^ n}\chi (|\zeta |^2)\, \mathrm d\zeta =1$. We write $\Psi _ u(x,r)$ for the value of $\Psi _ u$ at $|w|=r$. In the assertions about $H_ u$ and its joint Levi form we assume that $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$; constants denoted by $C$ may then depend on the fixed geometry, $\sup _ Xu$ and $\| u\| _{L^1}$, but not on the radius, and the constant $A$ depends only on the fixed geometry. For a sufficiently large constant $K$ of the same kind as $C$, put \[  H_ u(x,r)=\Psi _ u(x,r)+Kr^2,\qquad \lambda _ u(x,r)=r\partial _ rH_ u(x,r).  \] Then $H_ u(x,\mathrm e^ s)$ is a strictly convex nondecreasing function of $s$ which tends to $u(x)$ as $s	o -\infty $; in particular $\lambda _ u\geq 0$. If $u$ is bounded near $x$, then $\lambda _ u(x,r)	o 0$ as $r	o 0$. At each point $x$ we use holomorphic normal coordinates for $\omega $ centered at $x$ (lemma 16.2.13 ), defined on a ball of a fixed size (Step 1 of the proof). Let $q$ be a smooth function there with $\mathcal Dq=\alpha $, so that $p=u+q$ is plurisubharmonic, and let $\mu _ p$ be the trace of the complex Hessian of $p$ in these coordinates, a positive measure. Put $d=2n$ and \[  m_ u(x,r)=1+r^{-d}\mu _ p(B(x,4r)).  \] All estimates below hold uniformly over these fixed normal charts. For a tangent vector $v$ at $x$ and a tangent vector $\eta \in \mathbb C$ in the radius variable, the joint Levi form of $H_ u$ in $(x,w)$ satisfies 16.31  egin{align} \label{eq:chern-joint-mass-estimate} (\alpha +\mathcal D_{x,w}H_ u)[v,\eta ]^2 \geq {}& - igl (A\lambda _ u+C(r^2+r^3m_ u) igr )|v|_ h^2
otag \ & -C(r+r^2m_ u)|v|_ h|\eta |-Cr^2|\eta |^2, \qquad r=|w|. \end{align} Since $m_ u\leq Cr^{-2}$, as we show in the proof, this gives 16.32  egin{equation} \label{eq:chern-initial-joint-bound} (\alpha +\mathcal D_{x,w}H_ u)[v,\eta ]^2 \geq -(A\lambda _ u+Cr)|v|_ h^2-C|v|_ h|\eta |-C|\eta |^2. \end{equation} If $m_ u(x,r)\leq M(x)/r$ with $M(x)\geq 1$, then the stronger estimate 16.33  egin{equation} \label{eq:chern-improved-joint-bound} (\alpha +\mathcal D_{x,w}H_ u)[v,\eta ]^2 \geq -(A\lambda _ u+CM(x)r^2)|v|_ h^2 -CM(x)r|v|_ h|\eta |-CM(x)r|\eta |^2 \end{equation} holds. Moreover, if $u$ is bounded on the ball $B(x,2r)$ of the normal coordinates at $x$, then $\Psi _ u(x,r)$ differs from the ordinary radial convolution $\int u(x+r\zeta )\chi (|\zeta |^2)\, \mathrm d\zeta $ in these coordinates by at most $Cr^2\sup _{B(x,2r)}|u|$, where $C$ depends only on the fixed geometry. For a $C^1$ function $f$ with bounded weak complex Hessian, 16.34  egin{equation} \label{eq:chern-regular-obstacle-error} |\Psi _ f(x,r)-f(x)|\leq C_ f r^2 \end{equation} uniformly on $X$, where $C_ f$ is controlled by the bounds for the value, the gradient and the complex Hessian of $f$. Finally, for every integrable function $u$ on $X$, 16.35  egin{equation} \label{eq:chern-smoothing-generator}  rac{\Psi _ u(\cdot ,r)-u}{r^2}\longrightarrow a_\chi D_ hu \quad 	ext{in the sense of distributions as }r	o 0, \end{equation} where $D_ hu=\sum _{i,j}h^{i ar j}u_{i ar j}$ is the trace of the complex Hessian, as in section 16.2.3 , and $a_\chi = rac1n\int |\zeta |^2\chi (|\zeta |^2)\, \mathrm d\zeta >0$. Proof. We construct the smoothing in Step 1. In Steps 2–4 we compute, for a smooth plurisubharmonic local potential $p$, the joint complex Hessian of $\Psi _ p$ up to a remainder of high order in the radius; the result is the identity ( 16.50 ). From this identity we derive the joint estimates, first for smooth potentials (Step 5) and then in general (Step 6), and Step 7 proves the remaining assertions. All bounds are uniform over the centers, because the constructions are made in the charts of a fixed finite atlas, with coefficients bounded uniformly in the center. Step 1: construction of the smoothing. We construct a smooth map $F(x,\zeta )\in X$, defined for small tangent vectors $\zeta \in T_ xX$, from the holomorphic parts of the jets of geodesics, first in coordinates and then globally; $\Psi _ u$ is then an average of $u\circ F$. We begin with uniform normal coordinates. Fix the jet order $N=8$. For $x\in X$ we use the normal coordinates for $\omega $ at $x$ of lemma 16.2.13 , applied in a chart of a fixed finite atlas that contains $x$ in a fixed compact subset; in them $h(0)=I$ and $\mathrm dh(0)=0$. The coordinate change there is a polynomial map of degree at most two. Its linear part $L_ x$ satisfies $L_ x^{\mathrm T}h(x)\overline{L_ x}=I$, where $h(x)$ is the coefficient matrix in the chart of the atlas, so $L_ x$ and $L_ x^{-1}$ are bounded uniformly in $x$. The condition $\mathrm dh(0)=0$ is a linear equation for the quadratic part, whose coefficient matrix $h(x)\overline{L_ x}$ is invertible and whose right side is built from $L_ x$ and the first derivatives of $h$ at $x$; so the quadratic part is bounded uniformly in $x$ as well. Hence these coordinates are defined on balls of a fixed size, and all finite jets of $h$ in them are bounded uniformly in $x$. Next we define the jet map, in arbitrary holomorphic coordinates. Let $\Gamma ^ m_{jl}$ be given by $\sum _ m\Gamma ^ m_{jl}h_{m ar k}=\partial _ jh_{l ar k}$. Thus $\Gamma (z)$ is a bilinear map $\mathbb C^ n	imes \mathbb C^ n	o \mathbb C^ n$, symmetric because $\widehat\omega $ is closed, depending smoothly on $z$, and $\Gamma (0)=0$ in normal coordinates. Consider the geodesic equation \[  \ddot\gamma +\Gamma (\gamma )(\dot\gamma ,\dot\gamma )=0  \] for formal power series $\gamma (t)=z+\sum _{k\geq 1}c_ kt^ k/k!$ in a real variable $t$, with $c_ k\in \mathbb C^ n$; here $\Gamma (\gamma (t))$ is the composition of the Taylor series of $\Gamma $ at $z$ with the series $\gamma (t)-z$, which has no constant term. Prescribe $c_1=\zeta $. Comparing the coefficients of $t^ k$ in the equation determines $c_{k+2}$ as a polynomial in $c_1,\ldots ,c_{k+1}$ whose coefficients are derivatives of $\Gamma $ at $z$ of order at most $k$. By induction, $c_ k$ is a polynomial in $\zeta $ and $ ar\zeta $ with coefficients depending smoothly on $z$, and it is homogeneous of degree $k$: for real $\lambda $ the series $\gamma (\lambda t)$ is the formal solution with initial velocity $\lambda \zeta $, so that $c_ k(\lambda \zeta )=\lambda ^ kc_ k(\zeta )$. Let $c_ k^{\mathrm h}(z,\zeta )$ be the sum of the monomials of $c_ k$ that contain no $ ar\zeta $, and define \[  J_ z(\zeta )=z+\zeta +\sum _{k=2}^ N rac{c_ k^{\mathrm h}(z,\zeta )}{k!},  \] a holomorphic polynomial in $\zeta $ with coefficients depending smoothly on $z$. Since $c_2=-\Gamma (z)(\zeta ,\zeta )$, in normal coordinates at $x$ we have $J_0(\zeta )=\zeta +O(|\zeta |^3)$. These jets do not depend on the coordinates. Let $y=\phi (z)$ be a holomorphic change of coordinates, with derivative $\Phi =D\phi $, and let $\widetilde h$, $\widetilde\Gamma $ and $\widetilde J$ be the corresponding objects in the coordinates $y$. Then $h_{j ar k}=\sum _{a,b}\Phi ^ a_ j\, \widetilde h_{a ar b}(\phi )\, \overline{\Phi ^ b_ k}$, and since $\Phi $ is holomorphic, \[  \partial _ jh_{l ar k}=\sum _{a,b}\Bigl (\partial _ j\Phi ^ a_ l+\sum _{c,e}\Phi ^ c_ j\Phi ^ e_ l\, \widetilde\Gamma ^ a_{ce}(\phi )\Bigr )\widetilde h_{a ar b}(\phi )\, \overline{\Phi ^ b_ k}.  \] Comparing with the definition of $\Gamma $, and using that the matrix $(\sum _ b\widetilde h_{a ar b}\overline{\Phi ^ b_ k})_{a,k}$ is invertible, we obtain $\Phi \, \Gamma (\zeta ,\zeta ')=D^2\phi (\zeta ,\zeta ')+\widetilde\Gamma (\phi )(\Phi \zeta ,\Phi \zeta ')$ for all $\zeta ,\zeta '\in \mathbb C^ n$. Let $\gamma $ be a formal solution in the coordinates $z$. The second derivative of $\phi \circ \gamma $ is $\Phi (\gamma )\ddot\gamma +D^2\phi (\gamma )(\dot\gamma ,\dot\gamma )$, because $\Phi $ is holomorphic, and therefore \[   rac{\mathrm d^2(\phi \circ \gamma )}{\mathrm dt^2}+\widetilde\Gamma (\phi \circ \gamma )\Bigl ( rac{\mathrm d(\phi \circ \gamma )}{\mathrm dt}, rac{\mathrm d(\phi \circ \gamma )}{\mathrm dt}\Bigr )=\Phi (\gamma ) igl (\ddot\gamma +\Gamma (\gamma )(\dot\gamma ,\dot\gamma ) igr )=0.  \] By uniqueness, $\phi \circ \gamma $ is the formal solution with initial point $\phi (z)$ and initial velocity $\Phi (z)\zeta $. By homogeneity we may put $t=1$ degree by degree, and we obtain an identity between formal power series in $\zeta $ and $ ar\zeta $. Call a monomial in $\zeta $ and $ ar\zeta $ discardable if it contains a factor $ ar\zeta _ m$ or has degree at least $N+1$; the product of a discardable monomial with any monomial is discardable. The two sides of this identity, the formal solution in the coordinates $y$ and the series $\phi \circ \gamma $, differ from $\widetilde J_{\phi (z)}(\Phi (z)\zeta )$ and from $\phi (J_ z(\zeta ))$, respectively, by series of discardable monomials; for $\phi \circ \gamma $ we use the Taylor expansion of the holomorphic map $\phi $ at $J_ z(\zeta )$, each of whose terms beyond the first contains the discardable difference as a factor. The two holomorphic functions of $\zeta $ just named therefore have the same Taylor coefficients of degree at most $N$ at $\zeta =0$, and Taylor's formula gives 16.36  egin{equation} \label{eq:chern-jet-compatibility} \widetilde J_{\phi (z)} igl (\Phi (z)\zeta  igr )=\phi  igl (J_ z(\zeta ) igr )+O(|\zeta |^{N+1}), \end{equation} where the remainder is a smooth function vanishing to order $N+1$ at $\zeta =0$, with bounds for its derivatives that are locally uniform in $z$. We now glue the local jet maps. Choose finitely many holomorphic charts $\kappa _

Given $\widehat F_{k-1}$, choose an open set $O'$ with $\overline{V_1\cup \cdots \cup V_{k-1}}\subset O'\Subset O_{k-1}$, a function $\vartheta \in C^\infty _ c(\Omega _ k)$ with $0\leq \vartheta \leq 1$ that equals one on a relatively compact open neighborhood $O''\subset \Omega _ k$ of the compact set $\overline{V_ k}\setminus O'$ (lemma 1.4.1 (4)), and an open set $\Omega '$ with $\operatorname{Supp}\vartheta \subset \Omega '\Subset \Omega _ k$. Put $O_ k=O'\cup O''$, and define $\widehat F_ k=\widehat F_{k-1}$ on $O'\setminus \operatorname{Supp}\vartheta $, $\widehat F_ k=F_ k$ on $O''$, and \[  \widehat F_ k=\kappa _ k^{-1} igl ((1-\vartheta )\, \kappa _ k\circ \widehat F_{k-1}+\vartheta \, \kappa _ k\circ F_ k igr )\qquad 	ext{on }O'\cap \Omega '.  \] For $x$ in the compact set $\overline{O'}\cap \overline{\Omega '}$ and small $\zeta $, the points $\widehat F_{k-1}(x,\zeta )$ and $F_ k(x,\zeta )$ lie in a small ball about $\kappa _ k(x)$ in the chart $\kappa _ k$, so the last formula is defined. The three sets cover $O_ k$, and the three definitions agree on the overlaps, because $\vartheta =0$ outside $\operatorname{Supp}\vartheta $ and $\vartheta =1$ on $O''$. In the chart $\kappa _ k$ the last formula gives $\widehat F_ k-F_ k=(1-\vartheta )(\widehat F_{k-1}-F_ k)=O(|\zeta |^{N+1})$, so $\widehat F_ k$ has the geodesic jets of order $N$. The resulting map $F=\widehat F_{
u _0}$ is defined on $X$ for $|\zeta |<r_1$, with a fixed $r_1>0$. Since $F(x,0)=x$ and $D_\zeta F(x,0)$ is the identity, we may decrease $r_1$ so that, in each chart, $\| D_\zeta F-I\| \leq  rac12$ for $|\zeta |<r_1$; then each fiber map $\zeta \mapsto F(x,\zeta )$ is injective, because $|F(x,\zeta )-F(x,\zeta ')-(\zeta -\zeta ')|\leq  rac12|\zeta -\zeta '|$, and by the inverse function theorem it is a diffeomorphism onto its image. In the normal coordinates at a center $x$, ( 16.36 ) shows that $F(x',\zeta )$ differs from the jet map $J_{z'}(\zeta )$ of these coordinates by $O(|\zeta |^{N+1})$, where $z'$ is the coordinate of $x'$. Since $J_0(\zeta )=\zeta +O(|\zeta |^3)$, we obtain at the center 16.37  egin{equation} \label{eq:chern-normal-kernel-map} F(x,\zeta )=x+\zeta +O(|\zeta |^3), \qquad D_\zeta F=I+O(|\zeta |^2). \end{equation} Now we define the smoothing. Let $\chi $ be the weight of the statement, and let $\chi _1(t)=-C_ n\mathrm e^{-1/(1-t)}$ for $t<1$ and $\chi _1(t)=0$ otherwise. Both functions are smooth on $\mathbb R$, $\chi _1'=\chi $, and $-\chi _1/\chi =(1-t)^2$ for $t<1$. Define \[  \Psi _ u(x,w)=\int _{T_ xX}u(F(x,w\zeta )) \chi (|\zeta |_ h^2)\, \mathrm d\zeta _ h,  \] where $\mathrm d\zeta _ h$ is the Lebesgue measure of the Hermitian space $(T_ xX,h)$; in coordinates it is $\det h$ times the Lebesgue measure of the components of $\zeta $, and in unitary coordinates of $T_ xX$ the kernel has total mass $\int \chi (|\zeta |^2)\, \mathrm d\zeta =1$. The substitution $\zeta \mapsto \mathrm e^{\mathrm it}\zeta $ shows that $\Psi _ u$ is invariant under rotations of $w$. For $w
eq 0$, the change of variables $y=F(x,w\zeta )$ in the fiber, whose inverse depends smoothly on $(x,w,y)$ by the inverse function theorem, writes $\Psi _ u(x,w)$, in a chart around $x$, as the integral of $u$ against a smooth nonnegative kernel supported in a ball of radius $C|w|$ about $x$. Differentiation under the integral sign shows that $\Psi _ u$ is smooth for $w
eq 0$ even when $u$ has poles. Step 2: a holomorphic parametrization of the fiber. Throughout Steps 2–4 we fix a center, the origin of its normal coordinates $z$, and a smooth plurisubharmonic function $p$ on a neighborhood of $\overline{B(0,3r)}$, where $r=|w|$ and $0<|w|<r_0$; Step 6 removes the smoothness. In this step we rewrite $\Psi _ p$ so that $p$ is composed with a map that is holomorphic in all variables. We write $F(z,\xi )$ for $F(x',\zeta )$ when $x'$ has coordinate $z$ and $\zeta =\sum _ m\xi _ m\partial /\partial z_ m$. We use multi-indices $I,J$ with $2\leq |I|,|J|\leq N$ and write $1_ l$ for the $l$th coordinate multi-index; a product such as $I_ ls^{I-1_ l}$ is zero when $I_ l=0$, and the same convention applies to conjugates and to $J$. We first separate the holomorphic part of $F$. Let $a(z,ho )$ be the polynomial formed by the holomorphic monomials of the Taylor expansion of $F$ at $(0,0)$ that have degree at most two in $z$ and at most $N$ in $\xi $, with $\xi $ renamed $ho $. Since $F(z,0)=z$ and $D_\xi F(z,0)$ is the identity, $a(z,0)=z$ and $\partial _ho a(z,0)=I$. Hence, for small $z$, the holomorphic map $a(z,\cdot )$ has a holomorphic inverse near $0$, and we define \[  ho (z,\xi )=a(z,\cdot )^{-1} igl (F(z,\xi ) igr ),\qquad 	ext{so that}\qquad F(z,\xi )=a igl (z,ho (z,\xi ) igr ).  \] We extend the notion of a discardable monomial to the variables $(z,\xi )$: a monomial in $z, ar z,\xi , ar\xi $ is discardable if it contains a factor $ ar z_ j$ or $ ar\xi _ m$, has degree at least three in $z$, or has degree at least $N+1$ in $(\xi , ar\xi )$. Again the product of a discardable monomial with any monomial is discardable. By construction, the Taylor expansion of $F(z,\xi )-a(z,\xi )$ at $(0,0)$ consists of discardable monomials. Since $ho (z,\xi )-\xi $ is the integral over $t\in [0,1]$ of the derivative of $a(z,\cdot )^{-1}$ at $a(z,\xi )+t(F(z,\xi )-a(z,\xi ))$, applied to $F(z,\xi )-a(z,\xi )$, the same holds for $ho (z,\xi )-\xi $. Moreover, for each fixed $z$, the Taylor polynomial of degree $N$ of $F(z,\cdot )$ at $0$ is holomorphic, because it is that of $J_ z$; since $a(z,\cdot )^{-1}$ is holomorphic, the same holds for $ho (z,\cdot )$. Together with $ho (z,0)=0$ and $\partial _\xi ho (z,0)=I$, Taylor's formula in $\xi $ therefore gives 16.38  egin{equation} \label{eq:chern-fiber-factorization} ho (z,\xi )=\xi +\sum _ Iho _ I(z)\xi ^ I+R(z,\xi ), \end{equation} with smooth vector-valued coefficients $ho _ I$ and a smooth remainder $R$ whose derivatives of order at most seven, with $k$ of them in $\xi $ or $ ar\xi $, are bounded by $C|\xi |^{N+1-k}$. The monomials $\xi ^ I$ and $z_ j\xi ^ I$ are not discardable, so $ho _ I(0)=0$ and $\partial _{z_ j}ho _ I(0)=0$. We put \[  d_{Ik}=\partial _{ ar z_ k}ho _ I(0),\qquad e_{Ijk}=\partial _{z_ j}\partial _{ ar z_ k}ho _ I(0),  \] vectors with components $d_{Ikm}$ and $e_{Ijkm}$. Put $	ildeho (z,w,\xi )=w^{-1}ho (z,w\xi )$, so that \[  	ildeho (z,w,\xi )=\xi +\sum _ Iho _ I(z)w^{|I|-1}\xi ^ I+	ilde R(z,w,\xi ),\qquad 	ilde R(z,w,\xi )=w^{-1}R(z,w\xi ).  \] By the chain rule and the bounds for $R$, for $|\xi |\leq 3$ every derivative of $	ilde R$ of order at most two in $(z, ar z)$, at most three in $(\xi , ar\xi )$ and $k\leq 2$ in $(w, ar w)$ is bounded by $Cr^{N-k}$. Since also $ho _ I(z)=O(|z|)$, we have $\| \partial _\xi 	ildeho -I\| +\| \partial _{ ar\xi }	ildeho \| \leq  rac14$ for $|\xi |\leq 3$ when $|z|$ and $r$ are small. As above, $\xi \mapsto 	ildeho (z,w,\xi )$ is then a diffeomorphism of $\{ |\xi |<3\} $ onto an open set, which contains $\{ |s|\leq 2\} $ by the contraction mapping principle, applied to $\xi \mapsto s+\xi -	ildeho (z,w,\xi )$ on $\{ |\xi |\leq 8/3\} $ (note that $	ildeho (z,w,0)=0$); we denote its inverse by $s\mapsto \xi (z,w,s)$. Since $a(z,w	ildeho (z,w,\xi ))=F(z,w\xi )$, the substitution $s=	ildeho (z,w,\xi )$ gives \[  \Psi _ u(z,w)=\int u igl (a(z,ws) igr )W(z,w,s)\, \mathrm ds,\qquad W=\chi (\mathcal Q)\mathcal J,  \] where $\mathcal Q=|\xi (z,w,s)|^2_{h(z)}$, $\mathcal J$ is $\det h(z)$ times the real Jacobian determinant of $s\mapsto \xi (z,w,s)$, and $W$ is extended by zero outside the image. On the support of $\chi (|\xi |_ h^2)$ we have $|\xi |<2$ and hence $|s|<2$ for small $|z|$ and $r$, so $W$ is smooth and vanishes for $|s|\geq 2$. Thus the argument $a(z,ws)$ of $u$ is holomorphic in $(z,w,s)$, and the weight $W$ carries the nonholomorphic dependence on the base point. Step 3: the weight at the center. We compute the first and the mixed second derivatives of $W$ in $z$ at $z=0$, up to errors of order $r^ N$, and write them as divergences in $s$; the result is ( 16.40 ). For functions of $(w,s)$ with $0<|w|<r_0$ and $|s|\leq 2$, we write $O_ N$ for any function whose derivatives of order at most two in $(s, ar s)$ and $k\leq 2$ in $(w, ar w)$ are bounded by $Cr^{N-k}$, where $r=|w|$. Put \[   eta ^ k(w,s)=\sum _ Id_{Ik}w^{|I|-1}s^ I,\qquad \gamma ^{jk}(w,s)=\sum _ Ie_{Ijk}w^{|I|-1}s^ I,  \] vectors that are holomorphic in $s$; for a holomorphic vector field $b(s)$ write $\operatorname {div}b=\sum _ m\partial _{s_ m}b_ m$, $b\cdot  ar s=\sum _ mb_ m ar s_ m$, and $b\cdot  ar b'=\sum _ mb_ m\overline{b'_ m}$. We begin with the derivatives of $\xi $. We differentiate the identity $	ildeho (z,w,\xi (z,w,s))=s$ in $ ar z_ k$, in $z_ j$, and then in $z_ j$ and $ ar z_ k$, and evaluate at $z=0$, where $ho _ I=0$ and $\partial _{z_ j}ho _ I=0$. In each case the derivative of $\xi $ to be determined appears multiplied by $\partial _\xi 	ildeho =I+\partial _\xi 	ilde R$, and the remaining terms are the explicit terms $\partial _{ ar z_ k}ho _ Iw^{|I|-1}\xi ^ I$ and $\partial _{z_ j}\partial _{ ar z_ k}ho _ Iw^{|I|-1}\xi ^ I$, terms containing a derivative of $	ilde R$, and terms containing the factor $\partial _{z_ j}\xi $. The conjugates of these derivatives of $\xi $ also occur, multiplied by $\partial _{ ar\xi }	ilde R$; since $\partial _\xi 	ilde R$ and $\partial _{ ar\xi }	ilde R$ are bounded by $Cr^ N$, each of these linear systems is a small perturbation of the identity, and its solutions are bounded uniformly. Using this, the bounds for $	ilde R$, and the fact that $ eta ^ k$ and $\gamma ^{jk}$ have bounded derivatives, we find successively that at $z=0$ 16.39  egin{equation} \label{eq:chern-inverse-jet} \xi =s+O_ N,\qquad \partial _{z_ j}\xi =O_ N,\qquad \partial _{ ar z_ k}\xi =- eta ^ k+O_ N,\qquad \partial _{z_ j}\partial _{ ar z_ k}\xi =-\gamma ^{jk}+O_ N; \end{equation} the bounds for one further derivative in $s$ follow in the same way, because $	ilde R$ has bounded derivatives of order three in $\xi $. Differentiating the identity in $ ar s$ instead, we find $\partial _{ ar s}\xi =-(\partial _\xi 	ildeho )^{-1}\partial _{ ar\xi }	ilde R\; \overline{\partial _ s\xi }$, because the coefficients of ( 16.38 ) do not involve $ ar\xi $; hence $\partial _{ ar s}\xi $ and its derivatives $\partial _{z_ j}$, $\partial _{ ar z_ k}$ and $\partial _{z_ j}\partial _{ ar z_ k}$ are $O_ N$ at $z=0$. Next, $\mathcal Q=\sum _{l,m}h_{l ar m}(z)\xi _ l ar\xi _ m$, where $h(0)=I$ and $\mathrm dh(0)=0$; we put $c_{jklm}=-\partial _{z_ j}\partial _{ ar z_ k}h_{l ar m}(0)$. By the product rule, ( 16.39 ) and $\partial _{z_ j} ar\xi =\overline{\partial _{ ar z_ j}\xi }$, at $z=0$  egin{align*}  \mathcal Q& =|s|^2+O_ N,\qquad \partial _{ ar z_ k}\mathcal Q=- eta ^ k\cdot  ar s+O_ N,\  \partial _{z_ j}\partial _{ ar z_ k}\mathcal Q& =-\sum _{l,m}c_{jklm}s_ l ar s_ m-\gamma ^{jk}\cdot  ar s-\overline{\gamma ^{kj}\cdot  ar s}+ eta ^ k\cdot \overline{ eta ^ j}+O_ N, \end{align*} and $\partial _{z_ j}\mathcal Q=\overline{\partial _{ ar z_ j}\mathcal Q}$, since $\mathcal Q$ is real. For the Jacobian factor $\mathcal J$, let $M=\partial _ s\xi $. The real Jacobian determinant of $s\mapsto \xi $ is the determinant of the matrix $ igl ( egin{smallmatrix}M& \partial _{ ar s}\xi \ \overline{\partial _{ ar s}\xi }& \overline M\end{smallmatrix} igr )$, that is, $|\det M|^2$ plus a polynomial in the entries of these blocks each of whose terms contains an entry of $\partial _{ ar s}\xi $ or of its conjugate; as shown above, these entries and their relevant derivatives are $O_ N$ at $z=0$. Differentiating ( 16.39 ) in $s$, we have at $z=0$: $M=I+O_ N$, $\partial _{z_ j}M=O_ N$, $\partial _{ ar z_ k}M=-\partial _ s eta ^ k+O_ N$ and $\partial _{z_ j}\partial _{ ar z_ k}M=-\partial _ s\gamma ^{jk}+O_ N$. eq 0$, then $\psi '(r)=\ell /r+O(r)$, and $\psi (r)-\psi (r')=\ell \log (r/r')+O(r^2)$ would be unbounded as $r'	o 0$, contradicting $\psi 	o 0$. Hence $\ell =0$ and $|r\partial _ r\psi |\leq Cr^2$. By ( 3.3 ), applied to the subharmonic function $p$, we have $p\leq p_\varepsilon \leq \sup _{B(0,4r)}p$, so $|p_\varepsilon |\leq |p|+C$ on $B(0,3r)$. Since derivatives commute with mollification (proposition 1.4.3 (1)), the trace measure of $p_\varepsilon $ is the mollification of $\mu _ p$, so $\mu _{p_\varepsilon }(B(0,3r))\leq \mu _ p(B(0,4r))$, and the monotonicity of the normalized trace mass of $p_\varepsilon $ gives $\mu _{p_\varepsilon }(B(0,t))\leq Ct^{d-2}$ for $t\leq 3r$. Since $p_\varepsilon 	o p$ in $L^1(B(0,3r))$ (lemma 1.4.1 (2)), and $\Psi $, its derivatives in $(z,w)$ for $w
eq 0$ and $\Psi ^{\mathrm e}$ are given by integration against smooth kernels, the joint Levi form of $H_{u_\varepsilon }$ at $(0,w)$, $\lambda _{u_\varepsilon }$ and $\lambda _0(p_\varepsilon )=r\partial _ r\Psi ^{\mathrm e}_{p_\varepsilon }$ converge to the corresponding quantities for $u$. title: A minimum with a varying upper radius
text: 16.2.6 A minimum with a varying upper radius Near the pole set of the potential of a Kähler current with analytic singularities the smoothing radius must be taken smaller, so the minimum over radii will be taken over an interval whose upper end depends on the base point. Kiselman's minimum principle (theorem 8.5.1 ) concerns functions that are plurisubharmonic on a domain with open fibers. Here the minimum is taken over a closed interval and may be attained at its end point, and the joint Levi form is controlled only where the slope in the radius is small; the curvature of the end point function then enters. The following lemma records this curvature error explicitly. Lemma 16.2.28 . Let $D\subset \mathbb C^ n$ be a domain, let $\widehat\omega $ be a Hermitian form on $D$, and let $b$ be a smooth real function on $D$ with $\mathrm i\partial \bar\partial b\leq C_ b\widehat\omega $ for a constant $C_ b\geq 0$. Let $H(z,s)$ be a smooth function, defined for $z\in D$ and $s$ in a neighborhood of $(-\infty ,b(z)]$, such that $H_ s\geq 0$ and $H_{ss}>0$, and such that $H$ is bounded below, locally uniformly in $z$, as $s\to -\infty $. Regard $H$ as a function of $(z,\zeta )\in D\times \mathbb C$ with $s=\operatorname{Re}\zeta $. Fix $c>0$ and a smooth real $(1,1)$-form $\Lambda $ on $D$, and let $\pi _ D$ denote the projection to $D$. Suppose that at every point with $s\leq b(z)$ and $H_ s\leq c$ the joint Levi form satisfies \[  \mathrm i\partial \bar\partial _{z,\zeta }H\geq -\pi _ D^*\Lambda .  \] Then the constrained minimum \[  v(z)=\inf _{s\leq b(z)}\bigl (H(z,s)-cs\bigr )  \] is finite and continuous, and it satisfies, in the sense of distributions, \[  \mathrm i\partial \bar\partial v\geq -\Lambda -cC_ b\widehat\omega .  \] In particular, if $b$ is constant, or more generally plurisuperharmonic, we may take $C_ b=0$, and the upper end point produces no additional curvature error. Proof. For $\varepsilon >0$ we minimize instead the penalized function \[  H_\varepsilon (z,s)=H(z,s)-cs-\varepsilon \log (b(z)-s),\qquad s<b(z).  \] For fixed $z$ it tends to $+\infty $ at both ends of the interval: as $s\to -\infty $ the linear term $-cs$ dominates the logarithm, because $H$ is bounded below. Its second derivative in $s$ is $H_{ss}+\varepsilon /(b-s)^2>0$, so it has a unique minimizer $s_\varepsilon (z)$, a nondegenerate critical point. By the implicit function theorem, $s_\varepsilon $ and the minimum value $v_\varepsilon (z)=H_\varepsilon (z,s_\varepsilon (z))$ are smooth. The critical equation is \[  H_ s-c+\frac\varepsilon {b-s}=0,  \] so at the minimizer $0\leq H_ s\leq c$ and $0\leq \sigma :=\varepsilon /(b-s)\leq c$. Since $\operatorname{Re}\zeta $ is pluriharmonic, the joint Levi form of the barrier $-\varepsilon \log (b(z)-\operatorname{Re}\zeta )$ is $\varepsilon \, \mathrm i\partial \phi \wedge \bar\partial \phi /\phi ^2-\sigma \, \mathrm i\partial \bar\partial b$, where $\phi =b(z)-\operatorname{Re}\zeta $; the first term is nonnegative, and the second is at least $-\sigma C_ b\widehat\omega \geq -cC_ b\widehat\omega $. Hence, at the minimizer, the joint Levi form of $H_\varepsilon $ is bounded below by $-\pi _ D^*(\Lambda +cC_ b\widehat\omega )$. We now use the Schur complement argument of Kiselman's minimum principle (theorem 8.5.1 ); it needs the Levi bound only at the minimizer, not elsewhere in the fiber. At the minimizer write the joint complex Hessian of $H_\varepsilon $ in block form $\bigl (\begin{smallmatrix}P& y/2\\ y^*/2& a/4\end{smallmatrix}\bigr )$, where $P=(\partial ^2H_\varepsilon /\partial z_ j\partial \bar z_ k)$, $y=(\partial ^2H_\varepsilon /\partial z_ j\partial s)$ and $a=\partial ^2H_\varepsilon /\partial s^2>0$; here we used that $\partial _\zeta =\partial _{\bar\zeta }=\frac12\partial _ s$ on functions of $z$ and $s=\operatorname{Re}\zeta $. Since $\partial _ sH_\varepsilon (z,s_\varepsilon (z))=0$, the chain rule gives $\partial _{z_ j}v_\varepsilon (z)=(\partial _{z_ j}H_\varepsilon )(z,s_\varepsilon (z))$, and differentiating the critical equation in $\bar z_ k$ gives $\bar y_ k+a\, \partial _{\bar z_ k}s_\varepsilon =0$, because $H_\varepsilon $ is real. Hence $\partial _{z_ j}\partial _{\bar z_ k}v_\varepsilon =P_{jk}+y_ j\partial _{\bar z_ k}s_\varepsilon $, that is, the complex Hessian of $v_\varepsilon $ is $P-a^{-1}yy^*$. To bound it from below, let $M$ be the coefficient matrix of $\Lambda +cC_ b\widehat\omega =\mathrm i\sum _{j,k}M_{jk}\, \mathrm dz_ j\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ k$. By the Levi bound at the minimizer, the block matrix $\bigl (\begin{smallmatrix}P+M& y/2\\ y^*/2& a/4\end{smallmatrix}\bigr )$ is positive semidefinite, and evaluating its Hermitian form at the vector $(\xi ,-2a^{-1}y^*\xi )$, $\xi \in \mathbb C^ n$, gives $\xi ^*(P+M-a^{-1}yy^*)\xi \geq 0$. Thus \[  \mathrm i\partial \bar\partial v_\varepsilon \geq -\Lambda -cC_ b\widehat\omega .  \] It remains to pass to the limit $\varepsilon \to 0$. On a compact neighborhood in the base, $b$ is bounded, and evaluating at $s=b-1$ gives a uniform upper bound for $v_\varepsilon $ when $0<\varepsilon \leq 1$. Since $H$ is bounded below and $-cs-\log (b-s)$ grows linearly as $s\to -\infty $, the minimizers $s_\varepsilon $ are bounded below uniformly; the minimizers of the unpenalized problem have the same lower bound. Both problems may therefore be restricted to a common compact interval below their varying upper end point. The unpenalized minimum $v$ is finite, and it is continuous: after the substitution $s=b(z)-t$ the upper end point becomes fixed, the range of $t$ is a fixed compact interval, and a minimum of a continuous function over a fixed compact interval depends continuously on the parameter. On this range the penalty is bounded below by a quantity that tends uniformly to zero, so $v_\varepsilon \geq v-o(1)$. For an upper bound, evaluate $H_\varepsilon $ at an unpenalized minimizer if it lies at least $\sqrt\varepsilon $ below $b$, and otherwise at $s=b-\sqrt\varepsilon $. In the first case the penalty is at most $\varepsilon |\log \sqrt\varepsilon |$; in the second, the unpenalized function changes by $o(1)$, uniformly, by its uniform continuity on the compact range. Consequently $v_\varepsilon \to v$ locally uniformly, and the inequalities for $\mathrm i\partial \bar\partial v_\varepsilon $ pass to the distributional limit. $\square$
