By the implicit function theorem, $s_\varepsilon $ and the minimum value $v_\varepsilon (z)=H_\varepsilon (z,s_\varepsilon (z))$ are smooth. The critical equation is \[  H_ s-c+\frac\varepsilon {b-s}=0,  \] so at the minimizer $0\leq H_ s\leq c$ and $0\leq \sigma :=\varepsilon /(b-s)\leq c$. Since $\operatorname{Re}\zeta $ is pluriharmonic, the joint Levi form of the barrier $-\varepsilon \log (b(z)-\operatorname{Re}\zeta )$ is $\varepsilon \, \mathrm i\partial \phi \wedge \bar\partial \phi /\phi ^2-\sigma \, \mathrm i\partial \bar\partial b$, where $\phi =b(z)-\operatorname{Re}\zeta $; the first term is nonnegative, and the second is at least $-\sigma C_ b\widehat\omega \geq -cC_ b\widehat\omega $. Hence, at the minimizer, the joint Levi form of $H_\varepsilon $ is bounded below by $-\pi _ D^*(\Lambda +cC_ b\widehat\omega )$. We now use the Schur complement argument of Kiselman's minimum principle (theorem 8.5.1 ); it needs the Levi bound only at the minimizer, not elsewhere in the fiber. At the minimizer write the joint complex Hessian of $H_\varepsilon $ in block form $\bigl (\begin{smallmatrix}P& y/2\\ y^*/2& a/4\end{smallmatrix}\bigr )$, where $P=(\partial ^2H_\varepsilon /\partial z_ j\partial \bar z_ k)$, $y=(\partial ^2H_\varepsilon /\partial z_ j\partial s)$ and $a=\partial ^2H_\varepsilon /\partial s^2>0$; here we used that $\partial _\zeta =\partial _{\bar\zeta }=\frac12\partial _ s$ on functions of $z$ and $s=\operatorname{Re}\zeta $. Since $\partial _ sH_\varepsilon (z,s_\varepsilon (z))=0$, the chain rule gives $\partial _{z_ j}v_\varepsilon (z)=(\partial _{z_ j}H_\varepsilon )(z,s_\varepsilon (z))$, and differentiating the critical equation in $\bar z_ k$ gives $\bar y_ k+a\, \partial _{\bar z_ k}s_\varepsilon =0$, because $H_\varepsilon $ is real. Hence $\partial _{z_ j}\partial _{\bar z_ k}v_\varepsilon =P_{jk}+y_ j\partial _{\bar z_ k}s_\varepsilon $, that is, the complex Hessian of $v_\varepsilon $ is $P-a^{-1}yy^*$. To bound it from below, let $M$ be the coefficient matrix of $\Lambda +cC_ b\widehat\omega =\mathrm i\sum _{j,k}M_{jk}\, \mathrm dz_ j\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ k$. By the Levi bound at the minimizer, the block matrix $\bigl (\begin{smallmatrix}P+M& y/2\\ y^*/2& a/4\end{smallmatrix}\bigr )$ is positive semidefinite, and evaluating its Hermitian form at the vector $(\xi ,-2a^{-1}y^*\xi )$, $\xi \in \mathbb C^ n$, gives $\xi ^*(P+M-a^{-1}yy^*)\xi \geq 0$. Thus \[  \mathrm i\partial \bar\partial v_\varepsilon \geq -\Lambda -cC_ b\widehat\omega .  \] It remains to pass to the limit $\varepsilon \to 0$. On a compact neighborhood in the base, $b$ is bounded, and evaluating at $s=b-1$ gives a uniform upper bound for $v_\varepsilon $ when $0<\varepsilon \leq 1$. Since $H$ is bounded below and $-cs-\log (b-s)$ grows linearly as $s\to -\infty $, the minimizers $s_\varepsilon $ are bounded below uniformly; the minimizers of the unpenalized problem have the same lower bound. Both problems may therefore be restricted to a common compact interval below their varying upper end point. The unpenalized minimum $v$ is finite, and it is continuous: after the substitution $s=b(z)-t$ the upper end point becomes fixed, the range of $t$ is a fixed compact interval, and a minimum of a continuous function over a fixed compact interval depends continuously on the parameter. On this range the penalty is bounded below by a quantity that tends uniformly to zero, so $v_\varepsilon \geq v-o(1)$. For an upper bound, evaluate $H_\varepsilon $ at an unpenalized minimizer if it lies at least $\sqrt\varepsilon $ below $b$, and otherwise at $s=b-\sqrt\varepsilon $. In the first case the penalty is at most $\varepsilon |\log \sqrt\varepsilon |$; in the second, the unpenalized function changes by $o(1)$, uniformly, by its uniform continuity on the compact range. Consequently $v_\varepsilon \to v$ locally uniformly, and the inequalities for $\mathrm i\partial \bar\partial v_\varepsilon $ pass to the distributional limit. $\square$

title: Big-class envelopes on the ample locus
text:
16.2.7 Big-class envelopes on the ample locus We now prove that envelopes in a big class have locally bounded metric Laplacian away from the non-Kähler locus. The positivity that $	heta $ lacks is supplied by a Kähler current in $\{ 	heta \} $ with analytic singularities, whose pole set becomes a divisor after a modification. Near that divisor we shrink the smoothing radius of lemma 16.2.27 . A first bound for the admissible radius comes from the maximality of the envelope. High powers of the local equations of the divisor then turn the variable coefficients in the joint Hessian estimate into uniform ones, and a second application of maximality gives a quadratic bound for the smoothing error. Theorem 16.2.29 . Suppose that $\{ 	heta \} $ is big, let $r\geq 1$ be an integer, and let $f_1,\ldots ,f_ r$ be continuous real functions on $X$ with bounded metric Laplacian. Let \[  \operatorname {Amp}(\{ 	heta \} )=X\setminus E_{\mathrm{nK}}(\{ 	heta \} )  \] be the ample locus of $\{ 	heta \} $, the complement of its non-Kähler locus (definition 14.4.1 ). Then \[  u=P_	heta  igl (\min _ j f_ j igr )  \] has bounded metric Laplacian on every compact subset of $\operatorname {Amp}(\{ 	heta \} )$. On $\operatorname {Amp}(\{ 	heta \} )$ its complex Hessian has locally bounded coefficients, $u\in W^{2,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}$ for every $1\leq p<\infty $, and hence $u\in C^{1,\gamma }_{\mathrm{loc}}$ for every $0<\gamma <1$. Proof. After reducing to one obstacle and passing to a modification, we bound the smoothing error $H_ u(x,r)-u(x)$ off the divisor, first linearly and then quadratically in $r$, as outlined above; the quadratic bound and ( 16.35 ) then bound $D_ hu$, and the Sobolev regularity follows. Reduction to one obstacle with bounded complex Hessian. Choose a Kähler form $\kappa \geq 	heta $, for instance a large multiple of $\omega $, and put $f=P_\kappa (\min _ jf_ j)$. By theorem 16.2.24 , $f$ is $C^1$ and has bounded complex Hessian. Every $	heta $-psh function below $\min _ jf_ j$ is $\kappa $-psh, and hence lies below $f$. Conversely $f\leq \min _ jf_ j$. These two inclusions of competitor families give $P_	heta (f)=u$. Passage to a modification. Put $Z=E_{\mathrm{nK}}(\{ 	heta \} )$. By theorem 14.4.4 , $Z$ is the pole set of a function $\phi _1\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ with analytic singularities such that $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\phi _1\geq 2\delta _1\omega $ for some $\delta _1>0$. We apply lemma 13.4.1 to $\phi _1$, regarded as an element of $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta -2\delta _1\omega )$, with an integer $m_0$ so large that the constant $c'$ of that lemma satisfies $c'/m_0\leq \delta _1$, and we let $\phi _0$ be the resulting function. Then $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\phi _0\geq \delta _1\omega $, and $\phi _0$ has gentle analytic singularities (definition 13.1.11 ) of type $(m_0^{-1},\mathfrak a)$, where $\mathfrak a=\mathcal I(m_0\phi _1)$. The pole set of $\phi _0$ is the zero set of $\mathfrak a$, and it equals $Z$. Indeed, near a point where $\phi _1$ is finite, $\phi _1$ is bounded, because it has analytic singularities, so $\mathfrak a$ is the unit ideal there; thus the pole set of $\phi _0$ is contained in $Z$. Conversely, $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\phi _0$ is a Kähler current whose potential has analytic singularities, so its pole set contains $Z$ by the definition of the non-Kähler locus (definition 14.4.1 ). Let $\pi \colon Y	o X$ be a log resolution of $\mathfrak a$, that is, a principalization of $\mathfrak a$ by finitely many blowups with smooth centers (theorem A.5.5 ), and write $\pi ^*\mathfrak a=\mathcal O_ Y(-D_0)$; the support of the effective divisor $D_0$ is $\pi ^{-1}(Z)$. By definition 13.1.11 , locally on $Y$ the function $\phi _0\circ \pi $ is $m_0^{-1}\log |s_{D_0}|^2$ plus a smooth function. By theorem A.5.5 , $\pi $ is an isomorphism over $X\setminus Z$, and all its centers lie over $Z$. If $\sigma $ blows up a compact Kähler manifold with Kähler form $\omega '$ along a closed submanifold of positive codimension, with exceptional divisor $E$, then $\sigma ^*\omega '+\varepsilon \eta $ is Kähler for every sufficiently small $\varepsilon >0$, where $\eta $ is the curvature of a suitable smooth quadratic Hermitian metric on $\mathcal O(-E)$ (proposition 13.1.10 ). Applying this to the successive blowups of $\pi $, with rational $\varepsilon $, and pulling the forms back to $Y$, we obtain a Kähler form \[  \omega _ Y=\pi ^*\omega +\sum _\ell \varepsilon _\ell \eta _\ell >0,  \] where $\eta _\ell $ is the curvature of a smooth metric on $\mathcal O(-E_\ell )$ for effective exceptional divisors $E_\ell $, and the coefficients $\varepsilon _\ell >0$ can be taken rational. The pulled-back current $\pi ^*(	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\phi _0)$ is at least $\delta _1\pi ^*\omega $. Let $s_{E_\ell }$ be the canonical section of $\mathcal O(E_\ell )$, with norm $|s_{E_\ell }|$ computed in the dual metric. Choose a rational number $0<\delta _2\leq \delta _1$ and add $\delta _2\sum _\ell \varepsilon _\ell \log |s_{E_\ell }|^2$ to the pulled-back potential $\phi _0\circ \pi $. Since, by the Poincaré–Lelong formula (theorem 7.4.5 ), \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |s_{E_\ell }|^2=[E_\ell ]+\eta _\ell ,  \] the resulting current is at least $\delta _2\omega _ Y$. Locally its potential is still of the form $\sum _ j eta _ j\log |g_ j|^2$ plus a smooth function, where the $g_ j$ are local equations of the components of an effective divisor with support $\pi ^{-1}(Z)$ (the exceptional divisors lie over $Z$) and the $ eta _ j$ are positive rational numbers. Replacing $\omega _ Y$ by $\delta _2\omega _ Y$, we may assume that the lower bound is $\omega _ Y$ itself. By proposition 14.2.8 , pullback is a bijection from $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ onto $\mathrm{PSH}(Y,\pi ^*	heta )$. Since $f$ is continuous, a potential lies below $f$ if and only if its pullback lies below $f\circ \pi $, so $u\circ \pi =P_{\pi ^*	heta }(f\circ \pi )$. The pullback $f\circ \pi $ is $C^1$ and has bounded complex Hessian. Indeed, off $\pi ^{-1}(Z)$ the map $\pi $ is a local biholomorphism, and since its differential is bounded, the chain rule bounds the coefficients of $\pi ^*(\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f)$ there. Locally, $f\circ \pi $ plus a smooth local potential of $\pi ^*\kappa $ is a bounded plurisubharmonic function. Applying theorem 9.3.1 to it and to $\log |g|$, where $g$ is a local equation of the hypersurface $\pi ^{-1}(Z)$, shows that this logarithm is integrable for the trace measure of its complex Hessian, so the trace measure gives $\pi ^{-1}(Z)$ zero mass. Hence the positive current $\pi ^*\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(f\circ \pi )$, whose coefficients are bounded off $\pi ^{-1}(Z)$, has bounded coefficients everywhere. We may therefore work on $Y$ with the pulled-back form and obstacle, and return through the isomorphism over $X\setminus Z$ at the end. From now on we write $X$, $	heta $, $\omega $, $f$ and $u$ for $Y$, $\pi ^*	heta $, the Kähler form just constructed, $f\circ \pi $ and $u\circ \pi $, and again put $\alpha =2\pi 	heta $ and $\widehat\omega =2\pi \omega $. Adding a constant to the obstacle, we may assume that $0\leq f\leq B$ with $B\geq 1$. Let $\phi $ be the potential $\phi _0\circ \pi +\delta _2\sum _\ell \varepsilon _\ell \log |s_{E_\ell }|^2$ constructed above, minus a constant chosen so that 16.55  egin{equation} \label{eq:big-envelope-reference-bounds} \alpha +\mathcal D\phi \geq \widehat\omega ,\qquad \phi \leq -B-1,\qquad \phi \leq u\leq f\leq B; \end{equation} here $\phi \leq u$ holds because $\phi $ is a competitor for the envelope. Cover $X$ by finitely many coordinate charts, with smaller charts still covering $X$, on each of which \[  \phi =\sum _ j  eta _ j\log |g_ j|^2+\sigma , \qquad  eta _ j>0,\quad |g_ j|<	frac 12,  \] where the $g_ j$ are local equations of the components of the divisor meeting the chart (there are none if the chart does not meet the divisor) and $\sigma $ is smooth. Write $D$ for the divisor and $U=X\setminus D$. In particular $\mathcal D\phi $ is uniformly bounded on $U$, although $\phi $ tends to $-\infty $ near $D$. All bounds below are uniform on this finite atlas; only the explicitly displayed functions of $\phi $ are allowed to grow. A first-order smoothing bound. Let $H=H_ u$ and $\lambda =\lambda _ u$ be as in lemma 16.2.27 . The initial joint estimate ( 16.32 ) improves after adding $K_1r$. Indeed, the vertical Levi form of $K_1|w|$ is $K_1/(4r)$, and Young's inequality absorbs the bounded mixed term at a horizontal cost $Cr$. Hence, for a fixed sufficiently large $K_1$ and small $r$, 16.56  egin{equation} \label{eq:big-first-corrected-joint} \alpha +\mathcal D(H+K_1r)\geq -(A\lambda +Cr)\widehat\omega \end{equation} as joint forms; the right side is pulled back from $X$. Fix a small $\delta _0>0$; it will be decreased finitely many times, each time depending only on the fixed data. For $0<\delta <\delta _0$ and $c>0$ define on $U$ \[  \psi _{c,\delta }(x)=\inf _{0<t\leq \delta } \{ H(x,t)+K_1t-K_1\delta -c\log (t/\delta )\} .  \] The infimum over $t$ is finite and attained, because $H\geq u$, $u$ is locally bounded on $U$, and $-c\log (t/\delta )	o +\infty $ as $t	o 0$. At a minimizing radius, including the upper end point, the logarithmic slope $\lambda +K_1t$ of the nondecreasing part $H+K_1t$ is at most $c$, so $\lambda \leq c$. We apply lemma 16.2.28 in the variable $s=\log t$, with the constant upper end point $\log \delta $, to $H(x,\mathrm e^ s)+K_1\mathrm e^ s$ plus a smooth local potential of $\alpha $; by ( 16.56 ), the Levi bound required in the lemma holds with $\Lambda =(Ac+C\delta )\widehat\omega $. Moreover, since $u\leq f$ and the kernel of $\Psi $ is positive, evaluation at $t=\delta $ gives $\psi _{c,\delta }\leq \Psi _ u(x,\delta )+K\delta ^2\leq \Psi _ f(x,\delta )+K\delta ^2$, and ( 16.34 ) bounds the right side by $f+C\delta ^2$. Thus \[  \alpha +\mathcal D\psi _{c,\delta }\geq -(Ac+C\delta )\widehat\omega , \qquad \psi _{c,\delta }\leq f+C\delta ^2.  \] Put $e=Ac+C\delta $ and $	au =e/(1+e)$. Then $(1-	au )(\psi _{c,\delta }-C\delta ^2)+	au \phi $ is $	heta $-psh on $U$, by ( 16.55 ), since $-(1-	au )e+	au =0$; and it lies below $(1-	au )f\leq f$, because $\phi \leq 0\leq f$. It is bounded above near $D$, so by theorem 8.4.1 , applied after adding smooth local potentials of $\alpha $, it extends across $D$; the extension is given by upper limits and therefore still lies below the continuous obstacle. By the maximality of the envelope, this extension lies below $u$. Rearranging, and using $\psi _{c,\delta }\leq B+C\delta ^2$ so that no unbounded factor is divided by $1-	au $, we obtain 16.57  egin{equation} \label{eq:big-first-envelope-comparison} \psi _{c,\delta }\leq u+C\delta ^2 +	au (B-\phi +C\delta ^2). \end{equation} Now take $c=\delta $, so that $e$ and $	au $ are $O(\delta )$, and let $t_0$ be a minimizing radius for $\psi _{\delta ,\delta }(x)$. The two nonnegative quantities $H(x,t_0)+K_1t_0-u(x)$ and $\delta \log (\delta /t_0)$ add up to $\psi _{\delta ,\delta }(x)-u(x)+K_1\delta $, so ( 16.57 ) gives, with $R=C(1+B+|\phi |)$ for a suitable uniform $C$, \[  t_0\geq \delta \mathrm e^{-R(x)},\qquad H(x,t_0)+K_1t_0-u(x)\leq R(x)\delta .  \] Since $H$ is nondecreasing in the radius, the choice $\delta =r\mathrm e^{R(x)}$ yields 16.58  egin{equation} \label{eq:big-first-smoothing-error} 0\leq H(x,r)-u(x)\leq R(x)\mathrm e^{R(x)}r \quad 	ext{if }0<r<\delta _0\mathrm e^{-R(x)}. \end{equation} Since $\phi \leq -B-1$, we have $1+B\leq |\phi |$, so we may take $R(x)=B_0|\phi (x)|$ with a fixed large $B_0$. This estimate also improves the bound for the trace mass. Enlarging $B_0$ if necessary, we may assume $B_0 eta _ j\geq 1$ for all $j$; since $|g_ j|<1/2$, the formula for $\phi $ then gives $\mathrm e^{-R(x)}\leq C|g_ j(x)|^2$ for each local equation $g_ j$. As the first derivatives of the $g_ j$ are bounded, there is a fixed small $S>0$ such that, for $|y-x|\leq S\mathrm e^{-R(x)}$, the ratios $|g_ j(y)|/|g_ j(x)|$ lie between $1/2$ and $3/2$. Hence $|\phi (y)-\phi (x)|\leq C$ there. On a chart that does not meet the divisor, $\phi $ is smooth, and the same oscillation bound holds after decreasing $S$. By ( 16.55 ), $|u(y)|\leq C(1+|\phi (x)|)$ on that ball. The comparison with radial convolution in lemma 16.2.27 therefore transfers ( 16.58 ) to the Euclidean radial mean of the local plurisubharmonic potential $p=u+q$, with an additional error $Cr^2(1+|\phi (x)|)$. We also need the following consequence of the Jensen–Lelong formula, with positive constants $c_0$ and $0<c_1<1$ independent of $x$ and $r$: \[  \int p(x+r\zeta )\chi (|\zeta |^2)\, \mathrm d\zeta -p(x) \geq c_0 r^{2-d}\mu _ p(B(x,c_1r)), \qquad d=2n.  \] Indeed, the spherical means of $p$ about $x$ are nondecreasing in the radius and tend to $p(x)$. Letting $r_1	o 0$ in ( 12.4 ) and using that $D_ p(x,\cdot )$ is nondecreasing, we see that the spherical mean of radius $\varrho $ exceeds $p(x)$ by at least $2\log (1/c_1)D_ p(x,c_1\varrho )$, which by ( 12.3 ) is a fixed positive multiple of $\varrho ^{2-d}\mu _ p(B(x,c_1\varrho ))$. It remains to integrate over the radii $\varrho =r\varrho '$ with $\varrho '$ in a fixed subinterval of $(0,1)$ on which $\chi (\varrho '^2)>0$, and to decrease $c_1$. We apply this inequality at a fixed multiple of $r$, decrease $S$, and use ( 16.58 ). This gives 16.59  egin{equation} \label{eq:big-improved-trace-mass} m_ u(x,r)\leq  rac{M(x)}r\quad (0<r<S\mathrm e^{-R(x)}), \qquad 1\leq M(x)\leq C R(x)\mathrm e^{CR(x)}. \end{equation} Thus the improved joint estimate ( 16.33 ) is available for these radii. Uniform joint estimates in divisor coordinates. On each chart put $G=(\prod _ jg_ j)^ m$, where an empty product equals one. By the formula for $R$ and ( 16.59 ), $M$ is bounded by a fixed product of negative powers of the $|g_ j|$, and differentiating $G$ loses only one power of one factor. Hence we can choose the integer $m$ so large that $M|G|$ and $M|\mathrm dG|$ are uniformly bounded. Next, by the same formula for $R$, we can choose an integer $k\geq 1$ so large that \[   rac{\mathrm e^{-kR(x)}}{|G(x)|}\leq T  \] with $T$ uniform on the finite cover. Put $ho _\delta (x)=\delta \mathrm e^{-kR(x)}$, and take $\delta _0<S$, so that these radii lie in the range of ( 16.59 ). In the holomorphic coordinate $\xi $ defined by $w=G(x)\xi $, the range $0<|w|\leq ho _\delta (x)$ corresponds to $|\xi |\leq T\delta $. The differential of the change of variables $(x,\xi )\mapsto (x,G(x)\xi )$ sends $(v,\eta )$ to $(v,G\eta +\xi \, \mathrm dG(v))$. Substituting this in ( 16.33 ) and using the bounds just obtained, $|G|\leq 1$ and a uniform bound for $|\mathrm dG|$, we get 16.60  egin{align} \label{eq:big-divisor-transformed-joint} (\alpha +\mathcal D H(x,|G\xi |))[v,\eta ]^2 \geq {}& -(A\lambda +C_1|\xi |^2)|v|^2
otag \ & -C_1|G||\xi ||v||\eta | -C_1|G|^2|\xi ||\eta |^2. \end{align} For example, the purely horizontal error is bounded by a constant times $M(|G|^2+|G||\mathrm dG|+|G||\mathrm dG|^2)|\xi |^2$, the mixed coefficient by $C|G||\xi |$, and the vertical coefficient by $C|G|^2|\xi |$. These estimates use only the boundedness of $M|G|$ and $M|\mathrm dG|$. Now add $K_2|G\xi |^2$. Its Levi form is the square $K_2|G\eta +\xi \, \mathrm dG(v)|^2$, and the inequality $|a+b|^2\geq 	frac 12|a|^2-|b|^2$ shows that it is at least $ rac{K_2}2|G|^2|\eta |^2$ minus a horizontal term $K_2|\mathrm dG|^2|\xi |^2|v|^2$. For $\delta _0$ small and $K_2$ fixed and large, this absorbs the last term of ( 16.60 ), and Young's inequality absorbs its mixed term at a cost $C|\xi |^2|v|^2$. Since $|\xi |\leq T\delta $, we have proved the uniform joint bound 16.61  egin{equation} \label{eq:big-second-corrected-joint} \alpha +\mathcal D(H(x,|G\xi |)+K_2|G\xi |^2) \geq -(A\lambda +C_2\delta ^2)\widehat\omega . \end{equation} All constants here are independent of the chart and of the point of $U$. A second-order smoothing bound. For $c>0$ set \[  \psi (x)=\inf _{0<t\leq ho _\delta (x)} \{ H(x,t)+K_2t^2-c\log t\} .  \] In the variable $s=\log |\xi |$, so that $t=|G|\mathrm e^ s$, the upper end point of the interval is $b(x)=\log \delta -kR(x)-\log |G(x)|$. The last summand is pluriharmonic on $U$, and $\mathcal D R=-B_0\mathcal D\phi $ is uniformly bounded there. Thus $|\mathcal D b|\leq C_ b\widehat\omega $ with a uniform constant $C_ b$. The logarithmic slope of the nondecreasing part $H+K_2t^2$ is $\lambda +2K_2t^2$, so at a minimizing radius it is at most $c$. Since $-c\log t=-cs-c\log |G|$ and $\log |G|$ is pluriharmonic on $U$, lemma 16.2.28 , applied to ( 16.61 ) (again after adding a smooth local potential of $\alpha $), proves 16.62  egin{equation} \label{eq:big-second-minimum-curvature} \alpha +\mathcal D\psi \geq -C_0\widehat\omega , \qquad C_0=A'c+C_2\delta ^2,\quad A'=A+C_ b. \end{equation} Let $a=ckB_0$ and $C_3=C_ f+K+K_2$, with $C_ f$ from ( 16.34 ). Since $-c\log ho _\delta =-c\log \delta -a\phi $, evaluation at $t=ho _\delta (x)\leq \delta $, together with $\Psi _ u\leq \Psi _ f$ and ( 16.34 ), gives \[  Q:=\psi +c\log \delta +a\phi -C_3\delta ^2\leq f, \qquad (1+a)\alpha +\mathcal DQ\geq -C_0\widehat\omega ;  \] the second inequality follows from ( 16.62 ) and $a(\alpha +\mathcal D\phi )\geq 0$, a consequence of ( 16.55 ). Put \[  
u = rac{C_0}{1+a+C_0},\qquad W=(1-
u )Q+
u (1+a)\phi .  \] Since $
u (1+a)=(1-
u )C_0$, we have $(1+a)\alpha +\mathcal DW\geq 0$, that is, $W$ is $(1+a)	heta $-psh. It lies below $f$, because $Q\leq f$, $\phi \leq 0$ and $f\geq 0$. As before, $W$ is bounded above near $D$, so it extends across $D$ by theorem 8.4.1 , applied after adding smooth local potentials of $(1+a)\alpha $, and the extension, given by upper limits, still lies below the continuous function $f$. Consequently $W/(1+a)$, which lies below $f/(1+a)\leq f$, is a competitor for $u$, and $(1+a)u\geq W$. Since $u\leq B$ and $Q\leq B$, we can rearrange this without losing an unbounded positive term: 16.63  egin{equation} \label{eq:big-second-envelope-comparison} u\geq Q+
u (1+a)\phi -(
u +a)B. \end{equation} Now take $c=\delta ^2$, so that $a$ and $
u $ are $O(\delta ^2)$, and let $t_0$ be a minimizing radius for $\psi (x)$. Writing $\psi (x)$ as the value at $t_0$ of the minimized expression and substituting it into ( 16.63 ), we obtain 16.64  egin{equation} \label{eq:big-second-radius-and-value} t_0\geq \delta \mathrm e^{-R_2(x)},\qquad 0\leq H(x,t_0)+K_2t_0^2-u(x)\leq R_2(x)\delta ^2, \qquad R_2=C(1+B+|\phi |). \end{equation} Indeed, after rearrangement the left side consists of the two nonnegative terms $H(x,t_0)+K_2t_0^2-u(x)$ and $-\delta ^2\log (t_0/\delta )$ (recall $H\geq u$ and $t_0\leq \delta $), while every term on the right is bounded by $C\delta ^2(1+B+|\phi |)$. Fix a compact set $F\Subset U$ and a number $M_2\geq \sup _ FR_2$. For every sufficiently small $r$, choose $\delta =r\mathrm e^{M_2}$. Then $r\leq t_0$ at every $x\in F$, and since $H$ is nondecreasing in the radius we obtain the uniform quadratic estimate 16.65  egin{equation} \label{eq:big-quadratic-smoothing-error} 0\leq H(x,r)-u(x)\leq M_2\mathrm e^{2M_2}r^2, \qquad x\in F. \end{equation} Regularity. Divide ( 16.65 ) by $r^2$: on $F$ we have $0\leq (\Psi _ u(x,r)-u(x))/r^2+K\leq M_2\mathrm e^{2M_2}$. Pairing with nonnegative test functions supported in the interior of $F$ and letting $r	o 0$, ( 16.35 ) shows that, in the sense of distributions on the interior of $F$, $a_\chi D_ hu+K$ lies between zero and the constant $M_2\mathrm e^{2M_2}$. In particular $|\langle a_\chi D_ hu,\varphi angle |\leq (K+M_2\mathrm e^{2M_2})\int \varphi \, \mathrm dx$ for these test functions $\varphi \geq 0$. Since every point of $U$ lies in the interior of such a set $F$, corollary 1.7.2 (2), applied in the charts with Lebesgue measure, shows that $D_ hu$ is an $L^\infty _{\mathrm{loc}}$ function on $U$. The positive current $\alpha +\mathcal Du$ therefore has locally bounded $h$-trace, so in a fixed chart each of its diagonal coefficient measures is bounded by a constant times Lebesgue measure. The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality for positive Hermitian matrices bounds the off-diagonal coefficient measures as well. Thus all complex coefficients of $\alpha +\mathcal Du$, and hence those of $\mathcal Du$, are locally bounded on $U$. It remains to obtain the real Sobolev regularity; note that no weak first derivatives of $u$ are known in advance. Let $V\Subset U$ be a coordinate ball. The complex second derivatives $u_{i ar j}$ are bounded on $V$, so the Euclidean Laplacian $\Delta u=4\sum _ iu_{i ar i}$ is a bounded function there. Let $V'$ be a smaller concentric ball with $\overline{V'}\subset V$, choose $\vartheta \in C^\infty _ c(V)$ equal to one near $\overline{V'}$, and let $N=E_{2n}*g$ be the fundamental potential of the bounded compactly supported function $g=\vartheta \Delta u$, where $E_{2n}$ is the fundamental solution of proposition 2.2.1 . By proposition 3.2.1 , applied to the positive and negative parts of $g\, \mathrm dx$, we have $\Delta N=g$ in the sense of distributions. Hence $u-N$ is distributionally harmonic near $\overline{V'}$, and by Weyl's lemma (theorem 2.1.4 ) it is smooth there. It therefore suffices to show that $N\in W^{2,p}(V')$ for $1<p<\infty $. The Hessian estimate of theorem 6.2.3 concerns compactly supported smooth functions, so we mollify. Let $g_\varepsilon $ be the mollifications of $g$, and put $N_\varepsilon =E_{2n}*g_\varepsilon $. For small $\varepsilon $ the $g_\varepsilon $ are smooth and supported in a fixed compact set, and $g_\varepsilon 	o g$ in $L^ s$ for every $1\leq s<\infty $, by lemma 1.4.1 . By proposition 2.2.1 , $N_\varepsilon $ is smooth and $\Delta N_\varepsilon =g_\varepsilon $. Moreover $\partial _ a N_\varepsilon =E_{2n}*\partial _ ag_\varepsilon =(\partial _ aE_{2n})*g_\varepsilon $, where the second identity follows by integration by parts outside a small ball about the singularity of $E_{2n}$, whose boundary term tends to zero. Fix $q_0$ with $1<q_0<2n/(2n-1)$, and let $q_0'=q_0/(q_0-1)$. The functions $E_{2n}$ and $\partial _ aE_{2n}$, the latter bounded by $C|y|^{1-2n}$, belong to $L^{q_0}$ on bounded sets, so Hölder's inequality gives \[  \sup _ V|N_\varepsilon -N|+\sup _ V igl |\partial _ aN_\varepsilon -(\partial _ aE_{2n})*g igr | \leq C\| g_\varepsilon -g\| _{L^{q_0'}}\longrightarrow 0.  \] Thus $N_\varepsilon 	o N$ and $\partial _ aN_\varepsilon 	o (\partial _ aE_{2n})*g$ uniformly on $V$. Passing to the limit in the sense of distributions, we see that $N$ is bounded on $V$ and that its first distributional derivatives there are the bounded functions $(\partial _ aE_{2n})*g$. Choose $\vartheta _1\in C^\infty _ c(V)$ equal to one on $V'$. For small $\varepsilon ,\varepsilon '$, the function $\vartheta _1(N_\varepsilon -N_{\varepsilon '})$ is smooth with compact support, and ( 6.7 ) gives \[   igl \| D^2 igl (\vartheta _1(N_\varepsilon -N_{\varepsilon '}) igr ) igr \| _ p \leq C_{2n,p} igl \| \vartheta _1(g_\varepsilon -g_{\varepsilon '}) +2
abla \vartheta _1\cdot 
abla (N_\varepsilon -N_{\varepsilon '}) +(N_\varepsilon -N_{\varepsilon '})\Delta \vartheta _1 igr \| _ p.  \] By the convergences just proved, the right side tends to zero as $\varepsilon ,\varepsilon '	o 0$. Hence, along a sequence $\varepsilon _ k	o 0$, the second derivatives $\partial _ a\partial _ b(\vartheta _1N_{\varepsilon _ k})$ form a Cauchy sequence in $L^ p(\mathbb R^{2n})$ and converge in $L^ p$. The limits are supported in the fixed compact set $\operatorname{Supp}\vartheta _1$, so by Hölder's inequality the convergence also holds in the sense of distributions. On the other hand $\vartheta _1N_{\varepsilon _ k}	o \vartheta _1N$ uniformly, so $\partial _ a\partial _ b(\vartheta _1N_{\varepsilon _ k})	o \partial _ a\partial _ b(\vartheta _1N)$ in the sense of distributions. Therefore $\partial _ a\partial _ b(\vartheta _1N)$ is the $L^ p$ limit and belongs to $L^ p$, and since $\vartheta _1=1$ on $V'$, the second distributional derivatives of $N$ belong to $L^ p(V')$. Hence $N\in W^{2,p}(V')$, and therefore $u\in W^{2,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$ for every $1<p<\infty $; the case $p=1$ follows on relatively compact sets because their volume is finite. Morrey's inequality (lemma 6.2.6 ), with $p>2n/(1-\gamma )$, gives a representative in $C^{1,\gamma }_{\mathrm{loc}}$ for every $\gamma <1$. This continuous representative coincides with $u$: by lemma 13.1.4 (1), the quasi-plurisubharmonic function $u$ is at every point the limit of its averages over small coordinate balls centered there, and these averages converge to the continuous representative. Transferring these statements through the biholomorphism $Y\setminus \pi ^{-1}(Z)	o X\setminus Z$, under which all smooth metrics are locally equivalent and local Sobolev spaces are preserved (lemma 6.2.4 (2)), proves the theorem. $\square$

title: Big metric laplacian rooftop
text:
Theorem 16.2.29 . Suppose that $\{ 	heta \} $ is big, let $r\geq 1$ be an integer, and let $f_1,\ldots ,f_ r$ be continuous real functions on $X$ with bounded metric Laplacian. Let \[  \operatorname {Amp}(\{ 	heta \} )=X\setminus E_{\mathrm{nK}}(\{ 	heta \} )  \] be the ample locus of $\{ 	heta \} $, the complement of its non-Kähler locus (definition 14.4.1 ). Then \[  u=P_	heta  igl (\min _ j f_ j igr )  \] has bounded metric Laplacian on every compact subset of $\operatorname {Amp}(\{ 	heta \} )$. On $\operatorname {Amp}(\{ 	heta \} )$ its complex Hessian has locally bounded coefficients, $u\in W^{2,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}$ for every $1\leq p<\infty $, and hence $u\in C^{1,\gamma }_{\mathrm{loc}}$ for every $0<\gamma <1$. Proof. After reducing to one obstacle and passing to a modification, we bound the smoothing error $H_ u(x,r)-u(x)$ off the divisor, first linearly and then quadratically in $r$, as outlined above; the quadratic bound and ( 16.35 ) then bound $D_ hu$, and the Sobolev regularity follows. Reduction to one obstacle with bounded complex Hessian. Choose a Kähler form $\kappa \geq 	heta $, for instance a large multiple of $\omega $, and put $f=P_\kappa (\min _ jf_ j)$. By theorem 16.2.24 , $f$ is $C^1$ and has bounded complex Hessian. Every $	heta $-psh function below $\min _ jf_ j$ is $\kappa $-psh, and hence lies below $f$. Conversely $f\leq \min _ jf_ j$. These two inclusions of competitor families give $P_	heta (f)=u$. Passage to a modification. Put $Z=E_{\mathrm{nK}}(\{ 	heta \} )$. By theorem 14.4.4 , $Z$ is the pole set of a function $\phi _1\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ with analytic singularities such that $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\phi _1\geq 2\delta _1\omega $ for some $\delta _1>0$. We apply lemma 13.4.1 to $\phi _1$, regarded as an element of $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta -2\delta _1\omega )$, with an integer $m_0$ so large that the constant $c'$ of that lemma satisfies $c'/m_0\leq \delta _1$, and we let $\phi _0$ be the resulting function. Then $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\phi _0\geq \delta _1\omega $, and $\phi _0$ has gentle analytic singularities (definition 13.1.11 ) of type $(m_0^{-1},\mathfrak a)$, where $\mathfrak a=\mathcal I(m_0\phi _1)$. The pole set of $\phi _0$ is the zero set of $\mathfrak a$, and it equals $Z$. Indeed, near a point where $\phi _1$ is finite, $\phi _1$ is bounded, because it has analytic singularities, so $\mathfrak a$ is the unit ideal there; thus the pole set of $\phi _0$ is contained in $Z$. Conversely, $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\phi _0$ is a Kähler current whose potential has analytic singularities, so its pole set contains $Z$ by the definition of the non-Kähler locus (definition 14.4.1 ). Let $\pi \colon Y	o X$ be a log resolution of $\mathfrak a$, that is, a principalization of $\mathfrak a$ by finitely many blowups with smooth centers (theorem A.5.5 ), and write $\pi ^*\mathfrak a=\mathcal O_ Y(-D_0)$; the support of the effective divisor $D_0$ is $\pi ^{-1}(Z)$. By definition 13.1.11 , locally on $Y$ the function $\phi _0\circ \pi $ is $m_0^{-1}\log |s_{D_0}|^2$ plus a smooth function. By theorem A.5.5 , $\pi $ is an isomorphism over $X\setminus Z$, and all its centers lie over $Z$. If $\sigma $ blows up a compact Kähler manifold with Kähler form $\omega '$ along a closed submanifold of positive codimension, with exceptional divisor $E$, then $\sigma ^*\omega '+\varepsilon \eta $ is Kähler for every sufficiently small $\varepsilon >0$, where $\eta $ is the curvature of a suitable smooth quadratic Hermitian metric on $\mathcal O(-E)$ (proposition 13.1.10 ). Applying this to the successive blowups of $\pi $, with rational $\varepsilon $, and pulling the forms back to $Y$, we obtain a Kähler form \[  \omega _ Y=\pi ^*\omega +\sum _\ell \varepsilon _\ell \eta _\ell >0,  \] where $\eta _\ell $ is the curvature of a smooth metric on $\mathcal O(-E_\ell )$ for effective exceptional divisors $E_\ell $, and the coefficients $\varepsilon _\ell >0$ can be taken rational. The pulled-back current $\pi ^*(	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\phi _0)$ is at least $\delta _1\pi ^*\omega $. Let $s_{E_\ell }$ be the canonical section of $\mathcal O(E_\ell )$, with norm $|s_{E_\ell }|$ computed in the dual metric. Choose a rational number $0<\delta _2\leq \delta _1$ and add $\delta _2\sum _\ell \varepsilon _\ell \log |s_{E_\ell }|^2$ to the pulled-back potential $\phi _0\circ \pi $. Since, by the Poincaré–Lelong formula (theorem 7.4.5 ), \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |s_{E_\ell }|^2=[E_\ell ]+\eta _\ell ,  \] the resulting current is at least $\delta _2\omega _ Y$. Locally its potential is still of the form $\sum _ j eta _ j\log |g_ j|^2$ plus a smooth function, where the $g_ j$ are local equations of the components of an effective divisor with support $\pi ^{-1}(Z)$ (the exceptional divisors lie over $Z$) and the $ eta _ j$ are positive rational numbers. Replacing $\omega _ Y$ by $\delta _2\omega _ Y$, we may assume that the lower bound is $\omega _ Y$ itself. By proposition 14.2.8 , pullback is a bijection from $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ onto $\mathrm{PSH}(Y,\pi ^*	heta )$. Since $f$ is continuous, a potential lies below $f$ if and only if its pullback lies below $f\circ \pi $, so $u\circ \pi =P_{\pi ^*	heta }(f\circ \pi )$. The pullback $f\circ \pi $ is $C^1$ and has bounded complex Hessian. Indeed, off $\pi ^{-1}(Z)$ the map $\pi $ is a local biholomorphism, and since its differential is bounded, the chain rule bounds the coefficients of $\pi ^*(\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f)$ there. Locally, $f\circ \pi $ plus a smooth local potential of $\pi ^*\kappa $ is a bounded plurisubharmonic function. Applying theorem 9.3.1 to it and to $\log |g|$, where $g$ is a local equation of the hypersurface $\pi ^{-1}(Z)$, shows that this logarithm is integrable for the trace measure of its complex Hessian, so the trace measure gives $\pi ^{-1}(Z)$ zero mass. Hence the positive current $\pi ^*\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(f\circ \pi )$, whose coefficients are bounded off $\pi ^{-1}(Z)$, has bounded coefficients everywhere. We may therefore work on $Y$ with the pulled-back form and obstacle, and return through the isomorphism over $X\setminus Z$ at the end. From now on we write $X$, $	heta $, $\omega $, $f$ and $u$ for $Y$, $\pi ^*	heta $, the Kähler form just constructed, $f\circ \pi $ and $u\circ \pi $, and again put $\alpha =2\pi 	heta $ and $\widehat\omega =2\pi \omega $. Adding a constant to the obstacle, we may assume that $0\leq f\leq B$ with $B\geq 1$. Let $\phi $ be the potential $\phi _0\circ \pi +\delta _2\sum _\ell \varepsilon _\ell \log |s_{E_\ell }|^2$ constructed above, minus a constant chosen so that 16.55  egin{equation} \label{eq:big-envelope-reference-bounds} \alpha +\mathcal D\phi \geq \widehat\omega ,\qquad \phi \leq -B-1,\qquad \phi \leq u\leq f\leq B; \end{equation} here $\phi \leq u$ holds because $\phi $ is a competitor for the envelope. Cover $X$ by finitely many coordinate charts, with smaller charts still covering $X$, on each of which \[  \phi =\sum _ j  eta _ j\log |g_ j|^2+\sigma , \qquad  eta _ j>0,\quad |g_ j|<	frac 12,  \] where the $g_ j$ are local equations of the components of the divisor meeting the chart (there are none if the chart does not meet the divisor) and $\sigma $ is smooth. Write $D$ for the divisor and $U=X\setminus D$. In particular $\mathcal D\phi $ is uniformly bounded on $U$, although $\phi $ tends to $-\infty $ near $D$. All bounds below are uniform on this finite atlas; only the explicitly displayed functions of $\phi $ are allowed to grow. A first-order smoothing bound. Let $H=H_ u$ and $\lambda =\lambda _ u$ be as in lemma 16.2.27 . The initial joint estimate ( 16.32 ) improves after adding $K_1r$. Indeed, the vertical Levi form of $K_1|w|$ is $K_1/(4r)$, and Young's inequality absorbs the bounded mixed term at a horizontal cost $Cr$. Hence, for a fixed sufficiently large $K_1$ and small $r$, 16.56  egin{equation} \label{eq:big-first-corrected-joint} \alpha +\mathcal D(H+K_1r)\geq -(A\lambda +Cr)\widehat\omega \end{equation} as joint forms; the right side is pulled back from $X$. Fix a small $\delta _0>0$; it will be decreased finitely many times, each time depending only on the fixed data. For $0<\delta <\delta _0$ and $c>0$ define on $U$ \[  \psi _{c,\delta }(x)=\inf _{0<t\leq \delta } \{ H(x,t)+K_1t-K_1\delta -c\log (t/\delta )\} .  \] The infimum over $t$ is finite and attained, because $H\geq u$, $u$ is locally bounded on $U$, and $-c\log (t/\delta )	o +\infty $ as $t	o 0$. At a minimizing radius, including the upper end point, the logarithmic slope $\lambda +K_1t$ of the nondecreasing part $H+K_1t$ is at most $c$, so $\lambda \leq c$. We apply lemma 16.2.28 in the variable $s=\log t$, with the constant upper end point $\log \delta $, to $H(x,\mathrm e^ s)+K_1\mathrm e^ s$ plus a smooth local potential of $\alpha $; by ( 16.56 ), the Levi bound required in the lemma holds with $\Lambda =(Ac+C\delta )\widehat\omega $. Moreover, since $u\leq f$ and the kernel of $\Psi $ is positive, evaluation at $t=\delta $ gives $\psi _{c,\delta }\leq \Psi _ u(x,\delta )+K\delta ^2\leq \Psi _ f(x,\delta )+K\delta ^2$, and ( 16.34 ) bounds the right side by $f+C\delta ^2$. Thus \[  \alpha +\mathcal D\psi _{c,\delta }\geq -(Ac+C\delta )\widehat\omega , \qquad \psi _{c,\delta }\leq f+C\delta ^2.  \] Put $e=Ac+C\delta $ and $	au =e/(1+e)$. Then $(1-	au )(\psi _{c,\delta }-C\delta ^2)+	au \phi $ is $	heta $-psh on $U$, by ( 16.55 ), since $-(1-	au )e+	au =0$; and it lies below $(1-	au )f\leq f$, because $\phi \leq 0\leq f$. It is bounded above near $D$, so by theorem 8.4.1 , applied after adding smooth local potentials of $\alpha $, it extends across $D$; the extension is given by upper limits and therefore still lies below the continuous obstacle. By the maximality of the envelope, this extension lies below $u$. Rearranging, and using $\psi _{c,\delta }\leq B+C\delta ^2$ so that no unbounded factor is divided by $1-	au $, we obtain 16.57  egin{equation} \label{eq:big-first-envelope-comparison} \psi _{c,\delta }\leq u+C\delta ^2 +	au (B-\phi +C\delta ^2). \end{equation} Now take $c=\delta $, so that $e$ and $	au $ are $O(\delta )$, and let $t_0$ be a minimizing radius for $\psi _{\delta ,\delta }(x)$. The two nonnegative quantities $H(x,t_0)+K_1t_0-u(x)$ and $\delta \log (\delta /t_0)$ add up to $\psi _{\delta ,\delta }(x)-u(x)+K_1\delta $, so ( 16.57 ) gives, with $R=C(1+B+|\phi |)$ for a suitable uniform $C$, \[  t_0\geq \delta \mathrm e^{-R(x)},\qquad H(x,t_0)+K_1t_0-u(x)\leq R(x)\delta .  \] Since $H$ is nondecreasing in the radius, the choice $\delta =r\mathrm e^{R(x)}$ yields 16.58  egin{equation} \label{eq:big-first-smoothing-error} 0\leq H(x,r)-u(x)\leq R(x)\mathrm e^{R(x)}r \quad 	ext{if }0<r<\delta _0\mathrm e^{-R(x)}. \end{equation} Since $\phi \leq -B-1$, we have $1+B\leq |\phi |$, so we may take $R(x)=B_0|\phi (x)|$ with a fixed large $B_0$. This estimate also improves the bound for the trace mass. Enlarging $B_0$ if necessary, we may assume $B_0 eta _ j\geq 1$ for all $j$; since $|g_ j|<1/2$, the formula for $\phi $ then gives $\mathrm e^{-R(x)}\leq C|g_ j(x)|^2$ for each local equation $g_ j$. As the first derivatives of the $g_ j$ are bounded, there is a fixed small $S>0$ such that, for $|y-x|\leq S\mathrm e^{-R(x)}$, the ratios $|g_ j(y)|/|g_ j(x)|$ lie between $1/2$ and $3/2$. Hence $|\phi (y)-\phi (x)|\leq C$ there. On a chart that does not meet the divisor, $\phi $ is smooth, and the same oscillation bound holds after decreasing $S$. By ( 16.55 ), $|u(y)|\leq C(1+|\phi (x)|)$ on that ball. The comparison with radial convolution in lemma 16.2.27 therefore transfers ( 16.58 ) to the Euclidean radial mean of the local plurisubharmonic potential $p=u+q$, with an additional error $Cr^2(1+|\phi (x)|)$. We also need the following consequence of the Jensen–Lelong formula, with positive constants $c_0$ and $0<c_1<1$ independent of $x$ and $r$: \[  \int p(x+r\zeta )\chi (|\zeta |^2)\, \mathrm d\zeta -p(x) \geq c_0 r^{2-d}\mu _ p(B(x,c_1r)), \qquad d=2n.  \] Indeed, the spherical means of $p$ about $x$ are nondecreasing in the radius and tend to $p(x)$. Letting $r_1	o 0$ in ( 12.4 ) and using that $D_ p(x,\cdot )$ is nondecreasing, we see that the spherical mean of radius $\varrho $ exceeds $p(x)$ by at least $2\log (1/c_1)D_ p(x,c_1\varrho )$, which by ( 12.3 ) is a fixed positive multiple of $\varrho ^{2-d}\mu _ p(B(x,c_1\varrho ))$. It remains to integrate over the radii $\varrho =r\varrho '$ with $\varrho '$ in a fixed subinterval of $(0,1)$ on which $\chi (\varrho '^2)>0$, and to decrease $c_1$. We apply this inequality at a fixed multiple of $r$, decrease $S$, and use ( 16.58 ). This gives 16.59  egin{equation} \label{eq:big-improved-trace-mass} m_ u(x,r)\leq  rac{M(x)}r\quad (0<r<S\mathrm e^{-R(x)}), \qquad 1\leq M(x)\leq C R(x)\mathrm e^{CR(x)}. \end{equation} Thus the improved joint estimate ( 16.33 ) is available for these radii. Uniform joint estimates in divisor coordinates. On each chart put $G=(\prod _ jg_ j)^ m$, where an empty product equals one. By the formula for $R$ and ( 16.59 ), $M$ is bounded by a fixed product of negative powers of the $|g_ j|$, and differentiating $G$ loses only one power of one factor. Hence we can choose the integer $m$ so large that $M|G|$ and $M|\mathrm dG|$ are uniformly bounded. Next, by the same formula for $R$, we can choose an integer $k\geq 1$ so large that \[   rac{\mathrm e^{-kR(x)}}{|G(x)|}\leq T  \] with $T$ uniform on the finite cover. Put $ho _\delta (x)=\delta \mathrm e^{-kR(x)}$, and take $\delta _0<S$, so that these radii lie in the range of ( 16.59 ). In the holomorphic coordinate $\xi $ defined by $w=G(x)\xi $, the range $0<|w|\leq ho _\delta (x)$ corresponds to $|\xi |\leq T\delta $. The differential of the change of variables $(x,\xi )\mapsto (x,G(x)\xi )$ sends $(v,\eta )$ to $(v,G\eta +\xi \, \mathrm dG(v))$. Substituting this in ( 16.33 ) and using the bounds just obtained, $|G|\leq 1$ and a uniform bound for $|\mathrm dG|$, we get 16.60  egin{align} \label{eq:big-divisor-transformed-joint} (\alpha +\mathcal D H(x,|G\xi |))[v,\eta ]^2 \geq {}& -(A\lambda +C_1|\xi |^2)|v|^2
otag \ & -C_1|G||\xi ||v||\eta | -C_1|G|^2|\xi ||\eta |^2. \end{align} For example, the purely horizontal error is bounded by a constant times $M(|G|^2+|G||\mathrm dG|+|G||\mathrm dG|^2)|\xi |^2$, the mixed coefficient by $C|G||\xi |$, and the vertical coefficient by $C|G|^2|\xi |$. These estimates use only the boundedness of $M|G|$ and $M|\mathrm dG|$. Now add $K_2|G\xi |^2$. Its Levi form is the square $K_2|G\eta +\xi \, \mathrm dG(v)|^2$, and the inequality $|a+b|^2\geq 	frac 12|a|^2-|b|^2$ shows that it is at least $ rac{K_2}2|G|^2|\eta |^2$ minus a horizontal term $K_2|\mathrm dG|^2|\xi |^2|v|^2$. For $\delta _0$ small and $K_2$ fixed and large, this absorbs the last term of ( 16.60 ), and Young's inequality absorbs its mixed term at a cost $C|\xi |^2|v|^2$. Since $|\xi |\leq T\delta $, we have proved the uniform joint bound 16.61  egin{equation} \label{eq:big-second-corrected-joint} \alpha +\mathcal D(H(x,|G\xi |)+K_2|G\xi |^2) \geq -(A\lambda +C_2\delta ^2)\widehat\omega . \end{equation} All constants here are independent of the chart and of the point of $U$. A second-order smoothing bound. For $c>0$ set \[  \psi (x)=\inf _{0<t\leq ho _\delta (x)} \{ H(x,t)+K_2t^2-c\log t\} .  \] In the variable $s=\log |\xi |$, so that $t=|G|\mathrm e^ s$, the upper end point of the interval is $b(x)=\log \delta -kR(x)-\log |G(x)|$. The last summand is pluriharmonic on $U$, and $\mathcal D R=-B_0\mathcal D\phi $ is uniformly bounded there. Thus $|\mathcal D b|\leq C_ b\widehat\omega $ with a uniform constant $C_ b$. The logarithmic slope of the nondecreasing part $H+K_2t^2$ is $\lambda +2K_2t^2$, so at a minimizing radius it is at most $c$. Since $-c\log t=-cs-c\log |G|$ and $\log |G|$ is pluriharmonic on $U$, lemma 16.2.28 , applied to ( 16.61 ) (again after adding a smooth local potential of $\alpha $), proves 16.62  egin{equation} \label{eq:big-second-minimum-curvature} \alpha +\mathcal D\psi \geq -C_0\widehat\omega , \qquad C_0=A'c+C_2\delta ^2,\quad A'=A+C_ b. \end{equation} Let $a=ckB_0$ and $C_3=C_ f+K+K_2$, with $C_ f$ from ( 16.34 ). Since $-c\log ho _\delta =-c\log \delta -a\phi $, evaluation at $t=ho _\delta (x)\leq \delta $, together with $\Psi _ u\leq \Psi _ f$ and ( 16.34 ), gives \[  Q:=\psi +c\log \delta +a\phi -C_3\delta ^2\leq f, \qquad (1+a)\alpha +\mathcal DQ\geq -C_0\widehat\omega ;  \] the second inequality follows from ( 16.62 ) and $a(\alpha +\mathcal D\phi )\geq 0$, a consequence of ( 16.55 ). Put \[

As before, $W$ is bounded above near $D$, so it extends across $D$ by theorem 8.4.1 , applied after adding smooth local potentials of $(1+a)\alpha $, and the extension, given by upper limits, still lies below the continuous function $f$. Consequently $W/(1+a)$, which lies below $f/(1+a)\leq f$, is a competitor for $u$, and $(1+a)u\geq W$. Since $u\leq B$ and $Q\leq B$, we can rearrange this without losing an unbounded positive term: 16.63  egin{equation} \label{eq:big-second-envelope-comparison} u\geq Q+

u $ are $O(\delta ^2)$, and let $t_0$ be a minimizing radius for $\psi (x)$. Writing $\psi (x)$ as the value at $t_0$ of the minimized expression and substituting it into ( 16.63 ), we obtain 16.64  egin{equation} \label{eq:big-second-radius-and-value} t_0\geq \delta \mathrm e^{-R_2(x)},\qquad 0\leq H(x,t_0)+K_2t_0^2-u(x)\leq R_2(x)\delta ^2, \qquad R_2=C(1+B+|\phi |). \end{equation} Indeed, after rearrangement the left side consists of the two nonnegative terms $H(x,t_0)+K_2t_0^2-u(x)$ and $-\delta ^2\log (t_0/\delta )$ (recall $H\geq u$ and $t_0\leq \delta $), while every term on the right is bounded by $C\delta ^2(1+B+|\phi |)$. Fix a compact set $F\Subset U$ and a number $M_2\geq \sup _ FR_2$. For every sufficiently small $r$, choose $\delta =r\mathrm e^{M_2}$. Then $r\leq t_0$ at every $x\in F$, and since $H$ is nondecreasing in the radius we obtain the uniform quadratic estimate 16.65  egin{equation} \label{eq:big-quadratic-smoothing-error} 0\leq H(x,r)-u(x)\leq M_2\mathrm e^{2M_2}r^2, \qquad x\in F. \end{equation} Regularity. Divide ( 16.65 ) by $r^2$: on $F$ we have $0\leq (\Psi _ u(x,r)-u(x))/r^2+K\leq M_2\mathrm e^{2M_2}$. Pairing with nonnegative test functions supported in the interior of $F$ and letting $r	o 0$, ( 16.35 ) shows that, in the sense of distributions on the interior of $F$, $a_\chi D_ hu+K$ lies between zero and the constant $M_2\mathrm e^{2M_2}$. In particular $|\langle a_\chi D_ hu,\varphi angle |\leq (K+M_2\mathrm e^{2M_2})\int \varphi \, \mathrm dx$ for these test functions $\varphi \geq 0$. Since every point of $U$ lies in the interior of such a set $F$, corollary 1.7.2 (2), applied in the charts with Lebesgue measure, shows that $D_ hu$ is an $L^\infty _{\mathrm{loc}}$ function on $U$. The positive current $\alpha +\mathcal Du$ therefore has locally bounded $h$-trace, so in a fixed chart each of its diagonal coefficient measures is bounded by a constant times Lebesgue measure. The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality for positive Hermitian matrices bounds the off-diagonal coefficient measures as well. Thus all complex coefficients of $\alpha +\mathcal Du$, and hence those of $\mathcal Du$, are locally bounded on $U$. It remains to obtain the real Sobolev regularity; note that no weak first derivatives of $u$ are known in advance. Let $V\Subset U$ be a coordinate ball. The complex second derivatives $u_{i ar j}$ are bounded on $V$, so the Euclidean Laplacian $\Delta u=4\sum _ iu_{i ar i}$ is a bounded function there. Let $V'$ be a smaller concentric ball with $\overline{V'}\subset V$, choose $\vartheta \in C^\infty _ c(V)$ equal to one near $\overline{V'}$, and let $N=E_{2n}*g$ be the fundamental potential of the bounded compactly supported function $g=\vartheta \Delta u$, where $E_{2n}$ is the fundamental solution of proposition 2.2.1 . By proposition 3.2.1 , applied to the positive and negative parts of $g\, \mathrm dx$, we have $\Delta N=g$ in the sense of distributions. Hence $u-N$ is distributionally harmonic near $\overline{V'}$, and by Weyl's lemma (theorem 2.1.4 ) it is smooth there. It therefore suffices to show that $N\in W^{2,p}(V')$ for $1<p<\infty $. The Hessian estimate of theorem 6.2.3 concerns compactly supported smooth functions, so we mollify. Let $g_\varepsilon $ be the mollifications of $g$, and put $N_\varepsilon =E_{2n}*g_\varepsilon $. For small $\varepsilon $ the $g_\varepsilon $ are smooth and supported in a fixed compact set, and $g_\varepsilon 	o g$ in $L^ s$ for every $1\leq s<\infty $, by lemma 1.4.1 . By proposition 2.2.1 , $N_\varepsilon $ is smooth and $\Delta N_\varepsilon =g_\varepsilon $. Moreover $\partial _ a N_\varepsilon =E_{2n}*\partial _ ag_\varepsilon =(\partial _ aE_{2n})*g_\varepsilon $, where the second identity follows by integration by parts outside a small ball about the singularity of $E_{2n}$, whose boundary term tends to zero. Fix $q_0$ with $1<q_0<2n/(2n-1)$, and let $q_0'=q_0/(q_0-1)$. The functions $E_{2n}$ and $\partial _ aE_{2n}$, the latter bounded by $C|y|^{1-2n}$, belong to $L^{q_0}$ on bounded sets, so Hölder's inequality gives \[  \sup _ V|N_\varepsilon -N|+\sup _ V igl |\partial _ aN_\varepsilon -(\partial _ aE_{2n})*g igr | \leq C\| g_\varepsilon -g\| _{L^{q_0'}}\longrightarrow 0.  \] Thus $N_\varepsilon 	o N$ and $\partial _ aN_\varepsilon 	o (\partial _ aE_{2n})*g$ uniformly on $V$. Passing to the limit in the sense of distributions, we see that $N$ is bounded on $V$ and that its first distributional derivatives there are the bounded functions $(\partial _ aE_{2n})*g$. Choose $\vartheta _1\in C^\infty _ c(V)$ equal to one on $V'$. For small $\varepsilon ,\varepsilon '$, the function $\vartheta _1(N_\varepsilon -N_{\varepsilon '})$ is smooth with compact support, and ( 6.7 ) gives \[   igl \| D^2 igl (\vartheta _1(N_\varepsilon -N_{\varepsilon '}) igr ) igr \| _ p \leq C_{2n,p} igl \| \vartheta _1(g_\varepsilon -g_{\varepsilon '}) +2
abla \vartheta _1\cdot 
abla (N_\varepsilon -N_{\varepsilon '}) +(N_\varepsilon -N_{\varepsilon '})\Delta \vartheta _1 igr \| _ p.  \] By the convergences just proved, the right side tends to zero as $\varepsilon ,\varepsilon '	o 0$. Hence, along a sequence $\varepsilon _ k	o 0$, the second derivatives $\partial _ a\partial _ b(\vartheta _1N_{\varepsilon _ k})$ form a Cauchy sequence in $L^ p(\mathbb R^{2n})$ and converge in $L^ p$. The limits are supported in the fixed compact set $\operatorname{Supp}\vartheta _1$, so by Hölder's inequality the convergence also holds in the sense of distributions. On the other hand $\vartheta _1N_{\varepsilon _ k}	o \vartheta _1N$ uniformly, so $\partial _ a\partial _ b(\vartheta _1N_{\varepsilon _ k})	o \partial _ a\partial _ b(\vartheta _1N)$ in the sense of distributions. Therefore $\partial _ a\partial _ b(\vartheta _1N)$ is the $L^ p$ limit and belongs to $L^ p$, and since $\vartheta _1=1$ on $V'$, the second distributional derivatives of $N$ belong to $L^ p(V')$. Hence $N\in W^{2,p}(V')$, and therefore $u\in W^{2,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$ for every $1<p<\infty $; the case $p=1$ follows on relatively compact sets because their volume is finite. Morrey's inequality (lemma 6.2.6 ), with $p>2n/(1-\gamma )$, gives a representative in $C^{1,\gamma }_{\mathrm{loc}}$ for every $\gamma <1$. This continuous representative coincides with $u$: by lemma 13.1.4 (1), the quasi-plurisubharmonic function $u$ is at every point the limit of its averages over small coordinate balls centered there, and these averages converge to the continuous representative. Transferring these statements through the biholomorphism $Y\setminus \pi ^{-1}(Z)	o X\setminus Z$, under which all smooth metrics are locally equivalent and local Sobolev spaces are preserved (lemma 6.2.4 (2)), proves the theorem. $\square$

title: Contact with an arbitrary singular potential
text:
16.2.8 Contact with an arbitrary singular potential Proposition 16.2.9 computes the contact density of a potential with bounded metric Laplacian. We now remove this regularity assumption on the potential and keep it only for the obstacle. Let $u$ be an arbitrary quasi-plurisubharmonic potential below an obstacle $f$ with bounded metric Laplacian. Between $u$ and $f$ we insert the envelopes of smooth functions decreasing to $u$; by theorem 16.2.24 they have bounded metric Laplacian, so the regular theory applies to their contact with $f$. We then pass to the limit. The non-pluripolar measures of a decreasing sequence of unbounded potentials need not converge, so before passing to the limit we truncate at a fixed level and multiply by a bounded weight that vanishes below this level. The smooth functions decreasing to $u$ are provided by the following lemma. Lemma 16.2.30 . Let $u\colon X	o [-\infty ,\infty )$ be upper semicontinuous. Then $u$ is the pointwise limit of a decreasing sequence of smooth real functions $\phi _ j$ on $X$. Proof. If $u$ is identically $-\infty $, the constants $\phi _ j=-j$ will do, so we assume that $u$ takes a finite value somewhere. Fix a distance $d$ defining the topology of the compact manifold $X$, and put $M=\max _ Xu<\infty $. For each positive integer $j$ define \[  v_ j(x)=\max _{y\in X}\{ u(y)-j d(x,y)\} ;  \] the maximum is attained because the function in braces is upper semicontinuous in $y$. The $v_ j$ are finite and $j$-Lipschitz: a point where $u$ is finite bounds the maximum from below, and the triangle inequality bounds their differences. They decrease in $j$ and dominate $u$ (take $y=x$). If $u(x)$ is finite, a maximizing point $y_ j$ satisfies $jd(x,y_ j)\leq M-u(x)$, so $y_ j	o x$, and since $v_ j(x)\leq u(y_ j)$, upper semicontinuity gives $v_ j(x)\downarrow u(x)$. If $u(x)=-\infty $, then for every $N$ there is a small ball about $x$ on which $u<-N$, while outside this ball $u(y)-jd(x,y)\leq M-jd(x,y)<-N$ for large $j$. Thus $v_ j(x)\downarrow u(x)$ in this case as well. The $v_ j$ are only Lipschitz, so we smooth them while keeping monotonicity. Set $\phi _0=M+1$ and $\eta _ j=4^{-j}$, and suppose inductively that $\phi _{j-1}\geq u+\eta _{j-1}$. The continuous function \[  q_ j=\min \{ \phi _{j-1}-2\eta _ j,\  v_ j+2\eta _ j\}   \] is at least $u+2\eta _ j$, since $\eta _{j-1}=4\eta _ j$. A continuous function on $X$ can be approximated uniformly by smooth functions: convolution in a chart converges uniformly on compact subsets of the chart (lemma 1.4.1 (1)), and a finite smooth partition of unity subordinate to charts (proposition 7.1.3 ) sums these errors with total weight one. Choose a smooth real $\phi _ j$ with $\| \phi _ j-q_ j\| _\infty <\eta _ j$. Then \[  u+\eta _ j\leq \phi _ j\leq \phi _{j-1}-\eta _ j, \qquad \phi _ j\leq v_ j+3\eta _ j.  \] These bounds continue the induction, show that the sequence $\phi _ j$ decreases, and, since $v_ j+3\eta _ j\downarrow u$, show that $\phi _ j\downarrow u$, also at the points where $u=-\infty $. $\square$ Theorem 16.2.31 . Let $	heta _1,\ldots ,	heta _ n$ be closed smooth real $(1,1)$-forms. For each $j$ let $u_ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta _ j)$, and let $f_ j$ be a continuous real function on $X$ with bounded metric Laplacian. Suppose that $u_ j\leq f_ j$ everywhere, and put $E= igcap _ j\{ u_ j=f_ j\} $. Then 16.66  egin{equation} \label{eq:irregular-mixed-contact-density} \mathbf1_ E\left\langle  igwedge _{j=1}^ n (	heta _ j+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j)ightangle =\mathbf1_ E igwedge _{j=1}^ n(	heta _ j+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f_ j). \end{equation} Here the right side is the restriction to $E$ of the finite signed measure of corollary 16.2.12 , defined by the weak second derivatives of the $f_ j$; on $E$ its density is nonnegative and bounded. Proof. We first prove the scalar case, in which all $	heta _ j$, $u_ j$ and $f_ j$ coincide, in three steps of increasing generality (Steps 1–3). The mixed case then follows by polarization (Step 4), and Step 5 proves the assertion about the density. Step 1: a Kähler background and a plurisubharmonic obstacle. Let $\kappa $ be a Kähler form, let $u$ be $\kappa $-psh, and let $f\geq u$ be a continuous $\kappa $-psh function with bounded metric Laplacian. Write $F=\{ u=f\} $ and $\mu _ a=\langle (\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a)^ nangle $ for $\kappa $-psh $a$. Since $f$ is bounded, $\mu _ f$ is the Bedford–Taylor product $(\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f)^ n$ (proposition 15.3.3 , applied with smooth local potentials of $\kappa $). By proposition 16.2.9 , applied with $u_ j=f_ j=f$, this measure is given by the weak second derivatives of $f$, so it is the measure $(\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f)^ n$ of corollary 16.2.12 ; we must show that $\mathbf1_ F\mu _ u=\mathbf1_ F\mu _ f$. Take smooth functions $\phi _ j\downarrow u$ as in lemma 16.2.30 , and set \[  \psi _ j=P_\kappa (\min \{ \phi _ j,f\} ).  \] Each $\psi _ j$ has bounded metric Laplacian by theorem 16.2.24 . Since $u\leq \phi _ j$ and $u\leq f$, the function $u$ is a competitor for $\min \{ \phi _ j,f\} $, and since this obstacle is continuous, proposition 16.1.4 (1),(2) give $u\leq \psi _ j\leq f$. The obstacles $\min \{ \phi _ j,f\} $ decrease to $\min \{ u,f\} =u$, so $\psi _ j$ decreases to $P_\kappa (u)$ by proposition 16.1.4 (5), and $P_\kappa (u)=u$, because $u$ is itself a competitor and every competitor lies below the upper semicontinuous obstacle $u$ by proposition 16.1.4 (2). Moreover $\psi _ j=f$ on $F$, because $u\leq \psi _ j\leq f$. The regular contact identity, proposition 16.2.9 , applied on the contact set $\{ \psi _ j=f\} \supset F$, therefore gives \[  \mu _{\psi _ j}\geq 
u , \qquad 
u =\mathbf1_ F\mu _ f.  \] To pass to the limit, choose $C>0$ with $\min _ Xf>-C$, fix $\varepsilon >0$, and put \[   egin{aligned}  \psi _ j^ C& =\max \{ \psi _ j,-C\} ,&  u^ C& =\max \{ u,-C\} ,\  b_ j& = rac{\psi _ j^ C+C}{\psi _ j^ C+C+\varepsilon },&  b& = rac{u^ C+C}{u^ C+C+\varepsilon }. \end{aligned}  \] The bounded $\kappa $-psh functions $\psi _ j^ C$ decrease to $u^ C$, so they converge locally in capacity by proposition 9.4.6 . The weights $b_ j$ and $b$ are bounded by one, and they are quasi-continuous, since $\psi _ j^ C$ and $u^ C$ are, by theorem 9.4.2 applied to their sums with smooth local potentials of $\kappa $; moreover $b_ j	o b$ in capacity, because the map $t\mapsto t/(t+\varepsilon )$ on $[0,\infty )$ has Lipschitz constant at most $1/\varepsilon $. The weighted form of theorem 9.4.8 , applied with smooth local potentials of $\kappa $ and a finite partition of unity, gives \[  b_ j\mu _{\psi _ j^ C}\longrightarrow b\mu _{u^ C} \quad 	ext{weakly on }X.  \] The measures $\mu _{\psi _ j^ C}$ and $\mu _{\psi _ j}$ agree on the plurifine open set $\{ \psi _ j>-C\} $, by plurifine locality (proposition 15.1.5 ), and $b_ j$ vanishes on $\{ \psi _ j\leq -C\} $; hence $b_ j\mu _{\psi _ j^ C}=b_ j\mu _{\psi _ j}$. In the same way $b\mu _{u^ C}=b\mu _ u$. On $F$ all the weights take the same continuous value $b_ f=(f+C)/(f+C+\varepsilon )$, which is strictly positive on $X$. Since $
u $ is carried by $F$, we get $b_ j\mu _{\psi _ j}\geq b_ j
u =b_ f
u $ for every $j$, and in the weak limit $b\mu _ u\geq b_ f
u $. Restricting to $F$, where $b=b_ f$, and dividing by $b_ f$, whose reciprocal is bounded on $X$, we obtain $\mathbf1_ F\mu _ u\geq 
u $. The reverse inequality is the ordered contact inequality of lemma 16.2.2 . This proves the scalar identity for a Kähler background and a plurisubharmonic obstacle. Step 2: obstacles that are psh for a larger background. Let $	heta $ be any closed smooth real $(1,1)$-form, let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$, and suppose that $u\leq f$ and that $f$ is $(	heta +A\omega )$-psh for some $A>0$. Increasing $A$, we may assume that $	heta +A\omega $ is Kähler. For every $t>A$, Step 1 applies to the Kähler background $	heta +t\omega $, with the same measuring metric $\omega $. For a continuous real function $g$ on $X$ consider \[  Q_ g(t)=\int _{\{ u=f\} }g\,  \langle (	heta +t\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ nangle -\int _{\{ u=f\} }g\, (	heta +t\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f)^ n.  \] This is a polynomial in $t$. Indeed, the first integrand expands by the multilinearity of the non-pluripolar product and its compatibility with smooth bounded factors (proposition 15.1.5 , proposition 15.3.3 ), and the second by expanding the wedge products of the weak forms. Every coefficient is a finite measure, by theorem 15.4.3 and corollary 16.2.12 . Step 1 gives $Q_ g(t)=0$ for all $t>A$, so every coefficient vanishes, and in particular $Q_ g(0)=0$. Now a finite signed Borel measure $\sigma $ on $X$ with $\int g\, \mathrm d\sigma =0$ for every continuous $g$ vanishes. Indeed, write $\sigma =\sigma ^+-\sigma ^-$ with finite positive Borel measures $\sigma ^\pm $; then $\int g\, \mathrm d\sigma ^+=\int g\, \mathrm d\sigma ^-$ for every continuous $g\geq 0$, so $\sigma ^+\leq \sigma ^-$ and $\sigma ^-\leq \sigma ^+$ on Borel sets by lemma 16.2.1 (2), applied with $W=X$. Applied to the difference of the two measures in $Q_ g(0)$, this proves the scalar identity whenever $f$ is $(	heta +A\omega )$-psh for some $A$. Step 3: general obstacles. Let $f$ be any continuous real function with bounded metric Laplacian, and $u\leq f$. Choose $A>0$ such that $\kappa =	heta +A\omega $ is Kähler, and insert the envelope $v=P_\kappa (f)$: \[  u\leq v\leq f.  \] Here $u\leq v$ because $u$ is $\kappa $-psh and lies below $f$. By theorem 16.2.24 , $v$ is a continuous $\kappa $-psh function with bounded metric Laplacian. Step 2, with $v$ as the obstacle, gives \[  \mathbf1_{\{ u=v\} }\langle (	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ nangle =\mathbf1_{\{ u=v\} }(	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n.  \] Both $v$ and $f$ belong to $W^{2,p}$ for every finite $p$, by proposition 16.2.11 , and the locality of weak Hessians (proposition 9.12.3 ) shows that their weak second derivatives agree almost everywhere on $\{ v=f\} $. Since $\{ u=f\} =\{ u=v\} \cap \{ v=f\} $, restricting the last identity to $\{ u=f\} $ proves the scalar identity for $f$. Step 4: the mixed identity. For $\lambda _1,\ldots ,\lambda _ n>0$ put $	heta _\lambda =\sum _ j\lambda _ j	heta _ j$, $u_\lambda =\sum _ j\lambda _ ju_ j$ and $f_\lambda =\sum _ j\lambda _ jf_ j$. Then $u_\lambda $ is $	heta _\lambda $-psh, $f_\lambda $ is continuous with bounded metric Laplacian, $u_\lambda \leq f_\lambda $, and $E\subset \{ u_\lambda =f_\lambda \} $. (Since the $f_ j$ are finite, $E$ contains no pole of any $u_ j$.) We restrict the scalar identity for $u_\lambda $ and $f_\lambda $ to $E$ and expand both sides as measure-valued polynomials in $\lambda $, using, as in Step 2, the multilinearity of the non-pluripolar product (proposition 15.1.5 ) and of the wedge product of the weak forms. Testing against a continuous function and comparing the coefficients of $\lambda _1\cdots \lambda _ n$, which are $n!$ times the integrals of this function against the two sides of ( 16.66 ), we see that these integrals agree; by the uniqueness proved in Step 2, we obtain ( 16.66 ). Step 5: the density on $E$. For each $j$ choose $A_ j>0$ such that $	heta _ j+A_ j\omega $ is Kähler, and insert the envelope $v_ j=P_{	heta _ j+A_ j\omega }(f_ j)$. Since $u_ j$ is $(	heta _ j+A_ j\omega )$-psh and lies below the continuous function $f_ j$, we have $u_ j\leq v_ j\leq f_ j$ by proposition 16.1.4 (1),(2), so $v_ j=f_ j$ on $\{ u_ j=f_ j\} $; as in Step 3, proposition 16.2.11 , proposition 9.12.3 show that the weak Hessians of $v_ j$ and $f_ j$ agree almost everywhere there. The positive form $	heta _ j+A_ j\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ j$ has bounded coefficients by theorem 16.2.24 , so $	heta _ j+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f_ j$ has bounded coefficients almost everywhere on $\{ u_ j=f_ j\} $. Hence the density of the mixed product of the weak forms is bounded on $E$. It is nonnegative there, because by ( 16.66 ) its restriction to $E$ equals the restriction of a positive non-pluripolar product. $\square$ Corollary 16.2.32 . Suppose that $\{ 	heta \} $ is big, and let $f$ be a continuous real function with bounded metric Laplacian. Then \[  \langle (	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}P_	heta (f))^ nangle =\mathbf1_{\{ P_	heta (f)=f\} }(	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f)^ n.  \] In particular $\langle (	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V_	heta )^ nangle =\mathbf1_{\{ V_	heta =0\} }	heta ^ n$. The same identities hold in every pseudo-effective class; this is corollary 17.4.22 in the next chapter, which adds a zero-mass argument for classes that are not big. Proof. A constant shift of $V_	heta $ lies below the bounded function $f$, so the competitor family of $P_	heta (f)$ is nonempty, and it is bounded above by $\max _ Xf$. Since $f$ is continuous, $u=P_	heta (f)$ satisfies $u\leq f$ everywhere, by proposition 16.1.4 . Theorem 16.2.31 , with all $	heta _ j=	heta $, $u_ j=u$ and $f_ j=f$, identifies the restriction of $\langle (	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ nangle $ to $\{ u=f\} $ with that of $(	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f)^ n$. By theorem 16.2.5 , applied to the continuous and hence quasi-continuous obstacle $f$, the measure $\langle (	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ nangle $ is carried by $\{ u=f\} $. This proves the first identity. For $f=0$ the envelope is $V_	heta $ by definition, which gives the second. $\square$

Theorem 16.2.31 . Let $	heta _1,\ldots ,	heta _ n$ be closed smooth real $(1,1)$-forms.
