title: Penalized compact envelope
text: Lemma 16.9.3 . Suppose that $\{ \theta \} $ is big, let $\phi $ be a model potential of mass $m>0$, and let $K\subset X$ be a compact non-pluripolar set. There is a smooth function $g\geq 0$ on $X$ whose zero set is $K$. For every such $g$, the envelopes $q_ j=P_\theta (\phi +jg)$, $j\geq 1$, are potentials that increase with $j$, and their regularized limit $S=(\sup _ jq_ j)^*$ is a potential such that $L=\sup _ XS\geq 0$ and \[  \begin{gathered} \phi \leq S\leq \phi +L,\qquad S=\phi \text{ quasi-everywhere on }K,\\ \int _ X\langle \theta _ S^ n\rangle =m,\qquad \mu _ S(X\setminus K)=0. \end{gathered}  \] In particular, 16.81 \begin{equation} \label{eq:penalized-capacity-lower-bound} \operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }(K) \geq \frac{m}{\max \{ 1,L\} ^{n}}. \end{equation} If $\theta =\kappa $ is a Kähler form, then also 16.82 \begin{equation} \label{eq:penalized-capacity-upper-bound} \operatorname {Cap}_{\kappa ,\phi }(K) \leq \frac{C}{\max \{ 1,L\} }, \end{equation} where $C$ depends only on $X$ and $\kappa $. Proof. We first construct $g$. If $K=X$, take $g=0$. Otherwise fix finitely many coordinate charts $D_ i$ and compact sets $K_ i\subset D_ i$ whose interiors cover $X$, and measure derivatives on $K_ i$ in the coordinates of $D_ i$. Each point of $X\setminus K$ is the center of a coordinate ball whose closure lies in $X\setminus K$; since $X\setminus K$ has a countable basis, countably many of the concentric balls of half the radius, say $B_1',B_2',\ldots $, cover $X\setminus K$. Let $B_ l$ be the corresponding ball of full radius, and choose a smooth function $g_ l\geq 0$ with compact support in $B_ l$ that is positive on $\overline{B_ l'}$ (a smooth cutoff function, lemma 1.4.1 ). Multiplying $g_ l$ by a small positive constant, we may assume that all its derivatives of order at most $l$ are bounded by $2^{-l}$ on every $K_ i$. Then the series $g=\sum _ lg_ l$ converges uniformly on every $K_ i$ together with all its derivatives, so $g$ is smooth on the interior of every $K_ i$, hence on $X$; it vanishes on $K$, and it is positive on $X\setminus K$, because every point there lies in some $B_ l'$. Now let $g$ be any smooth nonnegative function with zero set $K$, and put $q_ j=P_\theta (\phi +jg)$. Since $\phi $ is a competitor and every competitor is at most $\phi +j\sup _ Xg$, we have $\phi \leq q_ j\leq \phi +j\sup _ Xg$, so $q_ j\sim \phi $. The obstacle $\phi +jg$ is upper semicontinuous, so $q_ j\leq \phi +jg$ everywhere by proposition 16.1.4 , and therefore $q_ j=\phi $ on $K$. In particular $\sup _ Kq_ j\leq 0$, and corollary 14.2.4 bounds $\sup _ Xq_ j$ uniformly in $j$. The envelopes $q_ j$ increase with $j$, since $g\geq 0$, so $S=(\sup _ jq_ j)^*$ is a potential; put $L=\sup _ XS$. Then $L\geq 0$, because $S\geq \phi $ and $\sup _ X\phi =0$. Since $q_ j\preceq \phi $ and $\sup _ Xq_ j\leq \sup _ XS=L$, lemma 16.4.2 gives $q_ j\leq \phi +L$, hence $\phi \leq S\leq \phi +L$. By corollary 10.2.2 , applied after adding smooth local potentials of $\theta $, the regularization changes $\sup _ jq_ j$ only on a pluripolar set, so $S=\phi $ quasi-everywhere on $K$. Since $S\sim \phi $, $\int _ X\langle \theta _ S^ n\rangle =m$. The obstacle $\phi +jg$ is quasi-continuous, and its family of competitors is nonempty and bounded above by $j\sup _ Xg$, so theorem 16.2.5 shows that $\mu _{q_ j}$ is carried by the contact set $\{ q_ j=\phi +jg\} $. At a point of this set where $\phi $ is finite, the bound $q_ j\leq \phi +L$ gives $jg\leq L$. Thus $\mu _{q_ j}$ is carried by $\{ g\leq L/j\} $. By corollary 15.7.6 , $\mu _{q_ j}\to \mu _ S$ weakly. If $\chi \geq 0$ is continuous with compact support in $X\setminus K$, then $g$ has a positive lower bound $c$ on the support of $\chi $, so $\int _ X\chi \, \mu _{q_ j}=0$ for $j>L/c$, and in the limit $\int _ X\chi \, \mu _ S=0$. By lemma 16.2.1 (2), applied on $W=X\setminus K$ with the zero measure, $\mu _ S(X\setminus K)=0$. Set $t=1/\max \{ 1,L\} $ and $h=(1-t)\phi +tS-tL$. Then $\phi -1\leq \phi -tL\leq h\leq \phi $, so $h$ is a competitor for $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }$, and $\mu _ h\geq t^ n\mu _ S$. Hence $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }(K)\geq t^ n\mu _ S(K)=t^ nm$, which is ( 16.81 ). In the Kähler case apply ( 16.78 ) to the potential $p=S-L$, which has supremum zero. Quasi-everywhere on $K$ we have $-p=L-\phi \geq L$, so $L\mu _ v(K)\leq C_\kappa $ for every competitor $v$ for $\operatorname {Cap}_{\kappa ,\phi }$. If $L\geq 1$, this gives ( 16.82 ) with $C=C_\kappa $. If $L<1$, use $\operatorname {Cap}_{\kappa ,\phi }(K)\leq \operatorname {Cap}_{\kappa ,\phi }(X)=m\leq \Omega $; the last inequality is the monotonicity of mass, because $\phi \preceq V_\kappa =0$ and the mass of $0$ is $\int _ X\kappa ^ n=\Omega $. Thus $C=\max \{ C_\kappa ,\Omega \} $ works. $\square$

title: Relative volume capacity exponential
text: Proposition 16.9.4 . Suppose that $\{ \theta \} $ is big, and let $\phi $ be a model potential of mass $m>0$. There are $\alpha ,C>0$, depending only on $X$, $\theta $ and $\omega $, such that every Borel set $E\subset X$ satisfies 16.83 \begin{equation} \label{eq:relative-volume-capacity-exponential} \int _ E\omega ^ n\leq C\exp \left[-\alpha \left(\frac{m}{\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }(E)}\right)^{1/n}\right], \end{equation} where the right side is interpreted as zero when the capacity is zero. Proof. Let $\alpha $ and $C_0$ be the constants of corollary 14.2.3 . First let $K$ be compact and non-pluripolar, and let $S,L$ be as in lemma 16.9.3 . The potential $p=S-L$ has supremum zero and satisfies $p\leq -L$ quasi-everywhere on $K$, because $S=\phi \leq 0$ there. Since pluripolar sets have zero volume, ( 14.17 ) gives \[  \int _ K\omega ^ n\leq \int _ K\mathrm e^{-\alpha p-\alpha L}\, \omega ^ n\leq C_0\mathrm e^{-\alpha L}.  \] Write $c=\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }(K)$, which is positive by ( 16.81 ). By the same inequality, \[  \left(\frac mc\right)^{1/n}\leq \max \{ 1,L\} \leq 1+L,  \] so ( 16.83 ) holds for $K$ with $C=C_0\mathrm e^\alpha $. If $K$ is pluripolar, its volume and its capacity both vanish. Now let $E$ be a Borel set. If $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }(E)>0$, the estimate for compact subsets $K\subset E$, together with the monotonicity of capacity and the inner regularity of the smooth volume, gives ( 16.83 ). If $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }(E)=0$, every compact subset of $E$ has zero capacity, hence is pluripolar by ( 16.81 ) and has zero volume; by inner regularity, $E$ has zero volume. $\square$

title: Relative volume capacity exponential
text: 16.83 \begin{equation} \label{eq:relative-volume-capacity-exponential} \int _ E\omega ^ n\leq C\exp \left[-\alpha \left(\frac{m}{\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }(E)}\right)^{1/n}\right], \end{equation}

title: Relative lp capacity domination
text: Corollary 16.9.5 . Under the hypotheses of proposition 16.9.4 , let $p>1$, $0\leq f\in L^ p(X,\omega ^ n)$ and $r>0$. There is $B_ r>0$, depending only on $X$, $\theta $, $\omega $, $p$ and $r$, such that every Borel set $E$ satisfies 16.84 \begin{equation} \label{eq:relative-lp-capacity-domination} \int _ E f\omega ^ n\leq B_ r\| f\| _{L^ p} \left(\frac{\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }(E)}m\right)^ r. \end{equation} In particular, for every $r>1$ the measure $f\omega ^ n$ is dominated by a constant multiple of $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }^ r$. Proof. If $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }(E)=0$, then $E$ has zero volume by proposition 16.9.4 , and both sides vanish. Otherwise let $q=p/(p-1)$. By Hölder's inequality and ( 16.83 ), the integral is at most \[  \| f\| _{L^ p}C^{1/q}\exp \left[-\frac\alpha q \left(\frac{m}{\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }(E)}\right)^{1/n}\right].  \] Put $t=(m/\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }(E))^{1/n}$; then $t\geq 1$, since the capacity is at most $\int _ X\langle \theta _\phi ^ n\rangle =m$. The function $t^{nr}\mathrm e^{-\alpha t/q}$ is bounded on $[1,\infty )$: its logarithmic derivative is $nr/t-\alpha /q$, so its maximum is attained at $1$ or at $nrq/\alpha $. Hence $\mathrm e^{-\alpha t/q}\leq A\, t^{-nr}$ for a constant $A$ depending only on $n,r,q,\alpha $, and this proves ( 16.84 ). $\square$

title: Relative lp capacity domination
text: 16.84 \begin{equation} \label{eq:relative-lp-capacity-domination} \int _ E f\omega ^ n\leq B_ r\| f\| _{L^ p} \left(\frac{\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }(E)}m\right)^ r. \end{equation}

title: Kahler model capacity powers
text: Proposition 16.9.6 . Let $\kappa $ be a Kähler form and $\phi $ a model potential for $\kappa $ of mass $m>0$. There is $A\geq 1$ such that every Borel set $E\subset X$ satisfies 16.85 \begin{equation} \label{eq:kahler-model-capacity-powers} A^{-1}\operatorname {Cap}_\kappa (E)^ n \leq \operatorname {Cap}_{\kappa ,\phi }(E) \leq A\operatorname {Cap}_\kappa (E)^{1/n}. \end{equation} More generally, if $\theta \leq \kappa $, $\{ \theta \} $ is big and $\phi $ is a model potential for $\theta $ of mass $m>0$, then 16.86 \begin{equation} \label{eq:big-model-capacity-lower-power} \operatorname {Cap}_\kappa (E)^ n \leq \frac{C^ n}{m}\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }(E), \end{equation} where $C$ depends only on $X$ and $\kappa $. Proof. All capacities involved are inner regular (proposition 16.7.6 ), so it suffices to treat compact sets $K$: the inequalities for a Borel set $E$ follow by applying them to the compact subsets of $E$ and taking suprema. If $K$ is pluripolar, all capacities of $K$ vanish. Otherwise fix a smooth function $g\geq 0$ with zero set $K$, and apply lemma 16.9.3 with this $g$ to $(\theta ,\phi )$ and to $(\kappa ,0)$; here $0=V_\kappa $ is a model potential for $\kappa $ of mass $\Omega $, by proposition 16.3.2 (4). Denote the resulting envelopes by $S_\phi $ and $S_0$ and their suprema by $L_\phi $ and $L_0$. Every competitor for $P_\theta (\phi +jg)$ is $\kappa $-plurisubharmonic, because $\theta \leq \kappa $, and it is at most $\phi +jg\leq jg$ quasi-everywhere, so $P_\theta (\phi +jg)\leq P_\kappa (jg)$ for every $j$; hence $S_\phi \leq S_0$ and $L_\phi \leq L_0$. The two estimates of lemma 16.9.3 give \[  \operatorname {Cap}_\kappa (K)^ n \leq \frac{C^ n}{\max \{ 1,L_0\} ^ n} \leq \frac{C^ n}{\max \{ 1,L_\phi \} ^ n} \leq \frac{C^ n}{m}\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }(K).  \] This proves ( 16.86 ) and, for $\theta =\kappa $, the first inequality in ( 16.85 ). For the upper bound let $\theta =\kappa $, and choose $b>1$ with $b^ n(\Omega -m)<\Omega $. By theorem 16.4.4 , applied to $\phi \preceq 0$, where the mass of $0$ is $\int _ X\kappa ^ n=\Omega $, the envelope $\eta =E_ b(\phi ,0)=P_\kappa (b\phi )$ is a potential, and it satisfies $b^{-1}\eta \leq \phi $; in particular $\eta =-\infty $ at the poles of $\phi $. Write $c=1-b^{-1}>0$. For fixed $j$ and $\delta >0$ consider \[  v_ j=c\, P_\kappa (jg)+b^{-1}\eta -\delta ,  \] a convex combination of $\kappa $-plurisubharmonic functions minus a constant. The function $P_\kappa (jg)$ is upper semicontinuous and vanishes on $K$, because $0\leq P_\kappa (jg)\leq jg$. Hence $P_\kappa (jg)<\delta /c$ on a neighborhood $U$ of $K$, and there $v_ j<b^{-1}\eta \leq \phi $. Outside the poles of $\phi $, the difference $v_ j-\phi $ is bounded above by $cj\sup _ Xg$, and $g$ has a positive minimum on $X\setminus U$. Therefore $v_ j\leq \phi +lg$ for a sufficiently large integer $l$, so $v_ j\leq P_\kappa (\phi +lg)\leq S_\phi $. Letting $\delta \downarrow 0$ and then $j\to \infty $, and using that the increasing limit of $P_\kappa (jg)$ equals $S_0$ almost everywhere, we obtain \[  cS_0+b^{-1}\eta \leq S_\phi  \] almost everywhere, hence everywhere. Choose a Borel set $G$ of positive volume on which $b^{-1}\eta \geq -D$ for a constant $D$; such a set exists because $\eta $ is finite almost everywhere. By proposition 14.2.1 , there is a constant $B$, independent of $K$, with $\int _ X|S_0-L_0|\, \kappa ^ n\leq B$. Hence $S_0\geq L_0-B/\int _ G\kappa ^ n$ at some point $x\in G$, for otherwise $\int _ G(L_0-S_0)\, \kappa ^ n>B$. At this point the last display gives $L_\phi \geq S_\phi (x)\geq cL_0-D'$ with $D'=cB/\int _ G\kappa ^ n+D$, which does not depend on $K$. If $L_0\geq \max \{ 1,2D'/c\} $, then $L_\phi \geq cL_0/2$, and lemma 16.9.3 gives \[  \operatorname {Cap}_{\kappa ,\phi }(K)\leq \frac{2C}{cL_0} \leq \frac{2C}{c\, \Omega ^{1/n}}\operatorname {Cap}_\kappa (K)^{1/n};  \] the last inequality is the lower bound ( 16.81 ) for the construction with reference potential $0$, which gives $\Omega /L_0^ n\leq \operatorname {Cap}_\kappa (K)$. In the remaining range $L_0<\max \{ 1,2D'/c\} $, the same lower bound shows that $\operatorname {Cap}_\kappa (K)$ is bounded below by a positive constant independent of $K$, and we use $\operatorname {Cap}_{\kappa ,\phi }(K)\leq m$, enlarging $A$ if necessary. The constant $A$ in the upper bound depends on $\phi $. $\square$

title: Full mass capacity downward comparison
text: Lemma 16.9.7 . Suppose that $\{ \theta \} $ is big, let $\phi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ have positive mass, and let $\psi \in \mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi )$. There is a continuous nondecreasing function $F\colon [0,\infty )\to [0,\infty )$ with $F(0)=0$, which may depend on $\psi $ and $\phi $, such that \[  \operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\psi }(E) \leq F(\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }(E))  \] for every Borel set $E\subset X$. Proof. Since $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }$ does not change when a constant is added to $\phi $ (proposition 16.7.6 ), we may assume that $\psi \leq \phi $. Let $u$ be a competitor for $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\psi }$, so that $\psi -1\leq u\leq \psi $, and let $t\geq 1$. We estimate $\mu _ u(E)$ separately on $\{ u>\phi -2t\} $ and on $\{ u\leq \phi -2t\} $. Put $u_ t=\max \{ u,\phi -2t\} $, so that $\phi -2t\leq u_ t\leq \phi $. The potential $(1-(2t)^{-1})\phi +(2t)^{-1}u_ t$ is a competitor for $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }$, and its measure is at least $(2t)^{-n}\mu _{u_ t}$. Since $u_ t=u$ on the plurifine open set $\{ u>\phi -2t\} $, it follows that \[  \mu _ u(E\cap \{ u>\phi -2t\} ) \leq (2t)^ n\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }(E).  \] The potentials $\psi $, $u$ and $\psi -1$ belong to $\mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi )$. So does the midpoint $q=(u+\phi )/2$: by proposition 16.4.10 , $P_\theta [u]=P_\theta [\phi ]$, so by proposition 16.3.2 each mixed mass $\int _ X\langle \theta _ u^ k\wedge \theta _\phi ^{n-k}\rangle $ equals the mass of $\phi $. Expanding $\mu _ q$ by multilinearity, we see that $q$ also has the mass of $\phi $. On the set $\{ u\leq \phi -2t\} $ we have $q-t\geq u\geq \psi -1$, and on $\{ \psi -1\leq q-t\} $ we have $\psi -1\leq (\psi +\phi )/2-t$, that is, $\psi \leq \phi -2t+2\leq \phi -t+1$. Thus \[  \{ u\leq \phi -2t\} \subset \{ \psi -1\leq q-t\}  \subset \{ \psi \leq \phi -t+1\} .  \] The non-strict comparison in proposition 16.7.4 , applied with $p=n$ to $\psi -1$ and $q-t$, together with $\mu _ q\geq 2^{-n}\mu _ u$, gives \[  \begin{split}  \mu _ u(\{ u\leq \phi -2t\} )& \leq 2^ n\mu _ q(\{ \psi -1\leq q-t\} ) \leq 2^ n\mu _\psi (\{ \psi -1\leq q-t\} )\\ & \leq 2^ n\mu _\psi (\{ \psi \leq \phi -t+1\} ). \end{split}  \] Adding the two estimates and taking the supremum over $u$, we obtain 16.89 \begin{equation} \label{eq:full-mass-capacity-tail-bound} \operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\psi }(E) \leq (2t)^ n\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }(E) +2^ n\mu _\psi (\{ \psi \leq \phi -t+1\} ) \qquad (t\geq 1). \end{equation} The last term tends to zero as $t\to \infty $, since $\psi $ and $\phi $ are finite outside a $\mu _\psi $-null set. It remains to replace the right side by a continuous function of the capacity. Put $m=\int _ X\langle \theta _\psi ^ n\rangle $, and let $H(s)$ be the minimum of $m$ and of the infimum over $t\geq 1$ of the right side of ( 16.89 ) with $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }(E)$ replaced by $s$. Since $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\psi }\leq \int _ X\langle \theta _\psi ^ n\rangle =m$, we have $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\psi }(E)\leq H(\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }(E))$. The function $H$ is nondecreasing, and $H(s)\to 0$ as $s\downarrow 0$. Choose a strictly decreasing sequence $s_ k\downarrow 0$ with $H(s_ k)\leq m2^{-k}$. Define $F(0)=0$, $F(s_ k)=m2^{1-k}$, $F$ linear on each interval $[s_{k+1},s_ k]$, and $F=m$ on $[s_1,\infty )$. On $[s_{k+1},s_ k]$ we have $H(s)\leq H(s_ k)\leq m2^{-k}=F(s_{k+1})\leq F(s)$, and $H\leq m=F$ on $[s_1,\infty )$. Thus $F$ is a continuous nondecreasing majorant of $H$ with $F(0)=0$. $\square$

title: Full mass capacity tail bound
text: 16.89 \begin{equation} \label{eq:full-mass-capacity-tail-bound} \operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\psi }(E) \leq (2t)^ n\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }(E) +2^ n\mu _\psi (\{ \psi \leq \phi -t+1\} ) \qquad (t\geq 1). \end{equation}

title: Global relative capacity comparison
text: Theorem 16.9.8 . Suppose that $\{ \theta \} $ is big and that $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ has positive mass. There are continuous nondecreasing functions $F,G\colon [0,\infty )\to [0,\infty )$, vanishing at zero, such that every Borel set $E\subset X$ satisfies \[  \operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\psi }(E)\leq F(\operatorname {Cap}_\omega (E)), \qquad \operatorname {Cap}_\omega (E)\leq G(\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\psi }(E)).  \] Consequently, any two capacities of this kind, for possibly different big backgrounds and potentials of positive mass, are bounded by such functions of each other. In particular, they define the same notion of convergence in capacity , in which Borel functions $f_ j$ converge to $f$ if the capacities of the sets $\{ |f_ j-f|>\varepsilon \} $ tend to zero for every $\varepsilon >0$. They also define the same notion of uniform absolute continuity of a family of positive Borel measures: $\lambda (A)$ is small, uniformly over the members $\lambda $ of the family, whenever the Borel set $A$ has small capacity. Proof. Choose $A\geq 1$ with $\theta \leq \kappa =A\omega $. Every competitor $v$ for $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\psi }$ is a competitor for $\operatorname {Cap}_{\kappa ,\psi }$, and its measure for $\kappa $ dominates its measure for $\theta $: since $\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v=(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)+(\kappa -\theta )$ with a smooth closed semipositive form $\kappa -\theta $, multilinearity and positivity of non-pluripolar products give $\langle (\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n\rangle \geq \langle (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n\rangle $; hence $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\psi }\leq \operatorname {Cap}_{\kappa ,\psi }$, and the mass of $\psi $ for $\kappa $ is at least its mass for $\theta $, hence positive. Adding a constant to $\psi $ does not change the capacities, so we may assume $\psi \leq 0$. Let $\Phi =P_\kappa [\psi ]$. By theorem 16.4.7 , $\Phi $ is a model potential for $\kappa $ with $\psi \leq \Phi $ and with the same mass for $\kappa $ as $\psi $. Thus $\psi \in \mathcal E(X,\kappa ,\Phi )$, and lemma 16.9.7 and proposition 16.9.6 bound $\operatorname {Cap}_{\kappa ,\psi }$ by a continuous nondecreasing function, vanishing at zero, of $\operatorname {Cap}_\kappa $. Finally, rescaling the competitors gives \[  \operatorname {Cap}_\omega \leq \operatorname {Cap}_\kappa \leq A^ n\operatorname {Cap}_\omega :  \] every competitor for $\operatorname {Cap}_\omega $ is one for $\operatorname {Cap}_\kappa $, with a larger measure by the same argument, and if $v$ is a competitor for $\operatorname {Cap}_\kappa $, then $v/A$ is a competitor for $\operatorname {Cap}_\omega $ with measure $A^{-n}(\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n$. This proves the first inequality. For the second inequality use the model potential $\phi =P_\theta [\psi ]$ for $\theta $, which has the same positive mass $m=\int _ X\langle \theta _\psi ^ n\rangle $ as $\psi $. By ( 16.86 ), $\operatorname {Cap}_\kappa ^ n\leq (C^ n/m)\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }$. By theorem 16.8.1 with $a=2$, applied to $\psi $ and $\phi $, whose singularity envelopes agree, the potential $\eta =P_\theta (2\psi -\phi )$ has mass $m$ and satisfies $P_\theta [\eta ]=\phi $ and $(\eta +\phi )/2\leq \psi $. It remains to bound $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }$ by a function of $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\psi }$. Put $u=(\eta +\phi )/2$. Since $P_\theta [\eta ]=P_\theta [\phi ]$, the preservation of mixed masses in proposition 16.3.2 shows that $u$ also has mass $m$. Since $u\leq \psi $, this means that $u\in \mathcal E(X,\theta ,\psi )$, and lemma 16.9.7 bounds $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,u}$ by a continuous nondecreasing function, vanishing at zero, of $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\psi }$. If $v$ is a competitor for $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }$, then $h=(v+\eta )/2$ satisfies $u-1/2\leq h\leq u$, so it is a competitor for $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,u}$, and $\mu _ h\geq 2^{-n}\mu _ v$. Thus \[  \operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }\leq 2^ n\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,u}.  \] Combining these inequalities with $\operatorname {Cap}_\omega \leq \operatorname {Cap}_\kappa $ gives $G$; compositions, positive multiples and $n$th roots preserve continuity, monotonicity and the value zero at the origin. The remaining assertions follow by comparing both capacities with $\operatorname {Cap}_\omega $. $\square$

title: Global local capacity equivalence
text: Proposition 16.9.9 . Let $B_\alpha \Subset B'_\alpha $ be finitely many pairs of concentric coordinate balls such that each $\overline{B'_\alpha }$ lies in a coordinate chart and the balls $B_\alpha $ cover $X$, and let $\operatorname {Cap}_{B'_\alpha }$ be the capacities of definition 9.3.2 in these coordinates. Then there is a constant $c\geq 1$ such that every Borel set $E\subset X$ satisfies \[  c^{-1}\sum _\alpha \operatorname {Cap}_{B'_\alpha }(E\cap B_\alpha ) \leq \operatorname {Cap}_\omega (E) \leq c\sum _\alpha \operatorname {Cap}_{B'_\alpha }(E\cap B_\alpha ),  \] and moreover $\operatorname {Cap}_\omega (E)\leq c\operatorname {Cap}_{B'_\alpha }(E)$ for every $\alpha $ and every Borel set $E\subset B'_\alpha $. Consequently, every relative capacity $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\psi }$ as in theorem 16.9.8 has the following properties. A compact set has capacity zero if and only if it is pluripolar. Hence a Borel set has capacity zero if and only if all its compact subsets are pluripolar. If real Borel functions $f_ j$ converge to a real Borel function $f$ locally in capacity on every ball $B'_\alpha $ (definition 9.4.5 ), then $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\psi }(\{ |f_ j-f|>\delta \} )\to 0$ for every $\delta >0$. Every quasi-continuous function on $X$ is continuous outside open sets of arbitrarily small capacity. Moreover, let $\theta '$ be any smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form on $X$. For every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ')$ and every $\varepsilon >0$ there is an open set $G$ with $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\psi }(G)<\varepsilon $ which contains the pole set of $u$ and such that $u$ is finite and continuous on $X\setminus G$. Proof. Let $v$ be a competitor for $\operatorname {Cap}_\omega $, so that $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ and $-1\leq v\leq 0$. Fix $\alpha $ and write $B'_\alpha =B(0,R_\alpha )$ in its coordinates. Since $\overline{B'_\alpha }$ is a compact subset of a chart, there is $A_\alpha >0$ with $\omega \leq A_\alpha \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|z|^2$ on $B'_\alpha $ (lemma 13.1.1 ). Then $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v+A_\alpha |z|^2)=(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)+(A_\alpha \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|z|^2-\omega )\geq 0$, so $v+A_\alpha |z|^2$ is plurisubharmonic on $B'_\alpha $, by lemma 13.1.4 (2), applied on $B'_\alpha $ to the form $A_\alpha \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|z|^2=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(A_\alpha |z|^2)$, and the multilinearity and positivity of Bedford–Taylor products give $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v+A_\alpha |z|^2))^ n\geq (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n$ on $B'_\alpha $. Put $c_\alpha =1+A_\alpha R_\alpha ^2$. The function $w=(v+A_\alpha |z|^2+1)/c_\alpha $ is plurisubharmonic on $B'_\alpha $ with values in $[0,1]$, and $(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n\leq c_\alpha ^ n(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w)^ n$ there. Hence $\mu _ v(E)\leq c_\alpha ^ n\operatorname {Cap}_{B'_\alpha }(E)$ for every Borel set $E\subset B'_\alpha $, and taking the supremum over $v$ gives $\operatorname {Cap}_\omega (E)\leq c_\alpha ^ n\operatorname {Cap}_{B'_\alpha }(E)$. Applying this to the sets $E\cap B_\alpha $ and using the subadditivity of $\operatorname {Cap}_\omega $ (proposition 16.7.6 ), we obtain the upper bound. For the lower bound fix $\alpha $ and write $B_\alpha =B(0,r)$ and $B'_\alpha =B(0,R)$ in the coordinates, with $r<R$. Choose $L>0$ with $L(R^2-r^2)>1$, and then $b>0$ so small that $\omega \geq bL\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|z|^2$ on $B(0,R)$ (lemma 13.1.1 ) and that we can choose a number $a$ with \[  b(1+Lr^2)<a<bLR^2,\qquad a\leq 1.  \] Let $w$ be plurisubharmonic on $B(0,R)$ with $-1\leq w\leq 0$, and put $q=bw-bL|z|^2$. Then $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q\geq b\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w\geq 0$ on $B(0,R)$. At the points of $B(0,R)$ where $|z|^2>a/(bL)$, which include a neighborhood of the boundary sphere because $a<bLR^2$, we have $q\leq -bL|z|^2<-a$. Define $v$ to be $\max \{ q,-a\} $ on $B(0,R)$ and $-a$ elsewhere. Then $v=-a$ on the open set $U$ formed by $X\setminus \overline{B(0,R)}$ and the points of the chart where $|z|^2>a/(bL)$. Since $U$ and $B(0,R)$ cover $X$, and $v$ is $\omega $-plurisubharmonic on each of them, $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$. It takes values in $[-1,0]$, and on $B(0,r)$ we have $q\geq -b(1+Lr^2)>-a$, so $v=q$ there. Since $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q$ is the sum of the semipositive form $\omega -bL\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|z|^2$ and $b\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w$, positivity of the mixed terms gives $(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n\geq b^ n(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w)^ n$ on $B(0,r)$. The capacity $\operatorname {Cap}_{B(0,R)}$ may equally be computed with competitors taking values in $[-1,0]$, so it follows that \[  \operatorname {Cap}_\omega (E)\geq b^ n \operatorname {Cap}_{B(0,R)}(E) \qquad (E\subset B(0,r)\text{ Borel}).  \] Summing over the finitely many balls gives the lower bound. It remains to prove (1)–(3). Let $F$ and $G$ be the functions of theorem 16.9.8 for $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\psi }$; since they are continuous and vanish at zero, a sequence of Borel sets has capacities $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\psi }$ tending to zero if and only if their capacities $\operatorname {Cap}_\omega $ tend to zero. (1) Pluripolar Borel sets have capacity zero by proposition 16.7.6 . Conversely, let $K$ be a compact set that is not pluripolar. Since $\omega $ is Kähler, $0=V_\omega $ is a model potential for $\omega $ of mass $\int _ X\omega ^ n>0$, by proposition 16.3.2 , and ( 16.81 ) for this model potential gives $\operatorname {Cap}_\omega (K)>0$. Since $\operatorname {Cap}_\omega (K)\leq G(\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\psi }(K))$ and $G(0)=0$, it follows that $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\psi }(K)>0$. The assertion about Borel sets follows from the inner regularity in proposition 16.7.6 . (2) Let $\delta >0$ and $A_ j=\{ |f_ j-f|>\delta \} $. By the upper bound, $\operatorname {Cap}_\omega (A_ j)\leq c\sum _\alpha \operatorname {Cap}_{B'_\alpha }(A_ j\cap B_\alpha )$. Each term is at most the outer capacity $\operatorname {Cap}^*_{B'_\alpha }(\overline{B_\alpha }\cap A_ j)$, which tends to zero because $\overline{B_\alpha }$ is a compact subset of $B'_\alpha $. Hence $\operatorname {Cap}_\omega (A_ j)\to 0$, and therefore $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\psi }(A_ j)\to 0$. (3) Let $f$ be quasi-continuous on $X$ and $\eta >0$. For each $\alpha $ there is an open set $W_\alpha \subset B'_\alpha $ with $\operatorname {Cap}_{B'_\alpha }(W_\alpha )<\eta $ such that $f$ is continuous on the compact set $\overline{B_\alpha }\setminus W_\alpha $. Put $W=\bigcup _\alpha W_\alpha $. Then $X\setminus W$ is the union of the finitely many closed sets $\overline{B_\alpha }\setminus W$, on each of which $f$ is continuous, so $f$ is continuous on $X\setminus W$; and $\operatorname {Cap}_\omega (W)\leq \sum _\alpha c\operatorname {Cap}_{B'_\alpha }(W_\alpha )<Nc\eta $, where $N$ is the number of balls. Now let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ')$. By lemma 16.1.2 (1), $u$ is quasi-continuous. Its pole set $P$ is pluripolar, because near each point $u$ is a plurisubharmonic function plus a smooth one (definition 13.1.3 ). Hence, by lemma 16.1.1 (2) there are open sets $W'_\alpha \subset B'_\alpha $ with $P\cap B'_\alpha \subset W'_\alpha $ and $\operatorname {Cap}_{B'_\alpha }(W'_\alpha )<\eta $. Replacing $W_\alpha $, chosen as above for $f=u$, by $W_\alpha \cup W'_\alpha $, we obtain an open set $W$ with $\operatorname {Cap}_\omega (W)<2Nc\eta $ which contains $P$, such that $u$ is continuous on $X\setminus W$ and finite there. In both cases $\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\psi }(W)\leq F(\operatorname {Cap}_\omega (W))\leq F(2Nc\eta )$, which is arbitrarily small when $\eta $ is small. $\square$

title: Relative energy and Perron segments
text:
17 Relative energy and Perron segments Let $(X,\omega )$ be a connected compact Kähler manifold of dimension $n\geq 1$, and let $	heta $ be a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form on $X$. In this chapter we study the Monge–Ampère energy of $	heta $-plurisubharmonic potentials relative to a model potential $\phi $ (definition 16.3.1 ); recall that model potentials have positive mass. The energy is a concave functional whose derivative is the non-pluripolar Monge–Ampère measure. We use it for two purposes: to solve Monge–Ampère equations with prescribed non-pluripolar measures by maximizing suitable functionals, and to show that the energy is affine along weak geodesics, which we construct as Perron envelopes of subgeodesics. Everything rests on integration by parts for non-pluripolar products of potentials with bounded difference. Such potentials may be unbounded, so Stokes' formula for bounded potentials (lemma 15.4.2 ) does not apply to them directly. In section 17.1 we truncate them and control the truncation errors with the relative capacities of chapter 16 . This control requires a strictly positive background, a restriction that a polynomial expansion in an auxiliary Kähler form removes at the end. The resulting formula (theorem 17.1.3 ) makes no assumption on the masses of the potentials. The energy $E_	heta ^\phi $ is first defined for potentials with bounded difference from $\phi $, where integration by parts computes its first and second variations, and is then extended by decreasing truncation to all potentials $u$ with $u\leq \phi +O(1)$. It is finite exactly on the relative finite-energy class $\mathcal E^1(X,	heta ,\phi )$ (theorem 17.2.8 ), continuous along monotone sequences, and upper semicontinuous for $L^1$ convergence, so that sets of normalized potentials with energy bounded below are compact. In section 17.4 these properties turn maximizers of suitable functionals into solutions of Monge–Ampère equations, first for bounded densities and for the exponential equations $\mu _ u=\mathrm e^{\lambda u}
u $, and then, letting $\lambda 	o 0$, for $\mu _ u=
u $ with an arbitrary non-pluripolar measure $
u $ of the same mass as $\phi $ (theorem 17.4.13 ). The solution is unique up to an additive constant (theorem 17.4.14 ), and it has bounded difference from $\phi $ when $
u $ has an $L^ p$ density with $p>1$ (corollary 17.4.17 ). Two further consequences are that a pseudo-effective class of positive volume is big (theorem 17.4.20 ) and that mixed non-pluripolar masses dominate the geometric mean of the individual masses (theorem 17.4.23 ). With these equations we show in section 17.5 that, in a big class, the singularity ceiling of a potential $u$ (definition 17.5.2 ) coincides with its singularity envelope $P_	heta [u]$, and that $P_	heta [P_	heta [u]]=P_	heta [u]$ (theorem 17.5.3 ). This is [ Theorem 1.2 , PSWZ26 ] ; it includes the case of zero mass, $\int _ X\langle 	heta _ u^ nangle =0$, to which the characterization of $P_	heta [u]$ in theorem 16.4.7 does not apply. In the last three sections we return to a fixed model potential $\phi $ and join two potentials of full mass relative to $\phi $ by a Perron segment, the upper envelope of all subgeodesics lying below them at the endpoints. Rooftop envelopes show that the segment attains the prescribed endpoints. Its complexification is locally maximal on the product of $X$ with a strip, so its top-degree non-pluripolar measure vanishes, and integration by parts on $X	imes \mathbb P^1$ then shows that the energy is affine along the segment (theorem 17.7.3 ). We conclude with estimates for the extremal slopes of a segment and for long segments; the latter produce profiles that depend only on the singularity type of the endpoint (proposition 17.8.2 ). Historical remarks and references for this chapter are collected in section B.17 , section B.18 , section B.19 .

title: Integration by parts for bounded differences
text:
17.1 Integration by parts for bounded differences As in chapter 16 , for a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form $	heta $ on $X$ and $q\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ we write \[  	heta _ q=	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q,\qquad \mu _ q=\langle 	heta _ q^ nangle ,  \] so that $\mu _ q(X)=\int _ X\langle 	heta _ q^ nangle $ is the total mass of $q$, and we indicate the background when several occur. Recall from definition 14.2.6 that $v$ is more singular than $u$, written $v\preceq u$, if $v\leq u+C$ on $X$ for some constant $C$, and that $u$ and $v$ have the same singularity type, written $u\sim v$, if $u\preceq v$ and $v\preceq u$. A difference $u-v$ of two quasi-psh functions is evaluated on their common finite locus $\{ u>-\infty \} \cap \{ v>-\infty \} $, whose complement is pluripolar. Non-pluripolar products do not charge pluripolar sets (lemma 15.1.2 ), so the values assigned to such a difference on the pole sets never affect the integrals below. A bounded quasi-psh difference is a bounded Borel function $a$ on $X$ such that $a=\varphi _1-\varphi _2$ quasi-everywhere, that is, outside a pluripolar set, for two quasi-psh functions $\varphi _1,\varphi _2$ on $X$; we call $(\varphi _1,\varphi _2)$ a presentation of $a$. The two functions then have the same singularity type. Indeed, if $|a|\leq C$, then $\varphi _1\leq \varphi _2+C$ quasi-everywhere, hence everywhere, because an inequality between quasi-psh functions that holds quasi-everywhere holds everywhere (section 16.1 ); by symmetry, $\varphi _1\sim \varphi _2$. Let $T_1,\ldots ,T_{n-1}$ be closed positive $(1,1)$-currents on $X$ and put $R=\langle T_1\wedge \cdots \wedge T_{n-1}angle $, with $R=1$ if $n=1$. For a bounded quasi-psh difference $a$ with presentation $(\varphi _1,\varphi _2)$ we define the signed measure 17.1  egin{equation} \label{eq:bounded-difference-hessian-product}  egin{aligned}  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a\wedge R & =\left\langle (\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _1)\wedge T_1\wedge \cdots \wedge T_{n-1}ightangle \ & \quad -\left\langle (\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _2)\wedge T_1\wedge \cdots \wedge T_{n-1}ightangle , \end{aligned} \end{equation} where $\kappa $ is a multiple of $\omega $ so large that $\varphi _1,\varphi _2\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\kappa )$. Both terms are non-pluripolar products of $n$ closed positive $(1,1)$-currents, hence finite measures by theorem 15.4.3 ; for $n=1$ they are first-degree non-pluripolar products. The measure $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a\wedge R$ does not depend on the choices made. First, let $	heta $ be any smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form with $\varphi _1,\varphi _2\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$, and let $\kappa \geq 	heta $ be a multiple of $\omega $, so that $\varphi _1,\varphi _2\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\kappa )$. Multilinearity of non-pluripolar products (proposition 15.1.5 ) gives \[   egin{aligned}  \left\langle (\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ j)\wedge T_1\wedge \cdots \wedge T_{n-1}ightangle & =\left\langle (	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ j)\wedge T_1\wedge \cdots \wedge T_{n-1}ightangle \ & \quad +\left\langle (\kappa -	heta )\wedge T_1\wedge \cdots \wedge T_{n-1}ightangle \end{aligned}  \] for $j=1,2$. The last term cancels in the difference, so the right side of ( 17.1 ) does not change when $\kappa $ is replaced by $	heta $. Taking for $	heta $ a smaller multiple of $\omega $ with respect to which $\varphi _1,\varphi _2$ are psh, we see that the measure does not depend on $\kappa $; hence it may be computed with any form $	heta $ as above in place of $\kappa $. Finally, the measure does not depend on the presentation of $a$. Let $(\psi _1,\psi _2)$ be another presentation and choose $\kappa $ so that all four functions are $\kappa $-psh. Then $\varphi _1+\psi _2=\varphi _2+\psi _1$ quasi-everywhere, hence everywhere, since both sides are $2\kappa $-psh. Therefore the currents $2\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\varphi _1+\psi _2)$ and $2\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\varphi _2+\psi _1)$ coincide. By multilinearity, \[   egin{aligned} & \left\langle (\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _1)\wedge T_1\wedge \cdots \wedge T_{n-1}ightangle +\left\langle (\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi _2)\wedge T_1\wedge \cdots \wedge T_{n-1}ightangle \ & \qquad =\left\langle (\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _2)\wedge T_1\wedge \cdots \wedge T_{n-1}ightangle +\left\langle (\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi _1)\wedge T_1\wedge \cdots \wedge T_{n-1}ightangle . \end{aligned}  \] All four measures are finite, so the two presentations give the same measure ( 17.1 ). We extend the notation linearly to finite sums of such products. The truncation argument below passes to the limit in integrals whose weights converge only in capacity. We use the capacity $\operatorname {Cap}_\omega =\operatorname {Cap}_{\omega ,0}$ of definition 16.7.5 , relative to $V_\omega =0$. Quasi-continuity of functions on $X$ is understood as in section 16.1 ; by proposition 16.9.9 , the exceptional open sets may be taken of arbitrarily small $\operatorname {Cap}_\omega $. Recall from theorem 16.9.8 that Borel functions $f_ j$ converge in capacity to $f$ if $\operatorname {Cap}_\omega (\{ |f_ j-f|>\varepsilon \} )	o 0$ for every $\varepsilon >0$, and that a family of positive Borel measures on $X$ is uniformly absolutely continuous with respect to $\operatorname {Cap}_\omega $ if the supremum of $\lambda (A)$, over all members $\lambda $ of the family and all Borel sets $A$ with $\operatorname {Cap}_\omega (A)\leq \delta $, tends to zero as $\delta \downarrow 0$. Lemma 17.1.1 . Let $

Let $f_ j$ and $f$ be Borel functions on $X$ with $|f_ j|,|f|\leq B$ for a constant $B$, and suppose that $f_ j	o f$ in capacity and that $f$ is continuous outside open sets of arbitrarily small capacity: for every $\eta >0$ there is an open set $G\subset X$ with $\operatorname {Cap}_\omega (G)<\eta $ such that the restriction of $f$ to $X\setminus G$ is continuous. (By proposition 16.9.9 (3), the last condition holds if $f$ is quasi-continuous.) Then \[  \int _ Xf_ j\,

u _ jight|\leq 2B

u _ k(X)$, and $\varepsilon $ is arbitrary. For the second term let $\eta >0$, and choose an open set $G$ with $\operatorname {Cap}_\omega (G)<\eta $ such that the restriction of $f$ to the compact set $X\setminus G$ is continuous. By lemma 7.1.4 , there is a metric $d$ on $X$ which induces its topology, and by lemma 9.4.3 , applied in the metric space $(X,d)$, the restriction of $f$ to $X\setminus G$ extends to a continuous function $g$ on $X$ with $|g|\leq B$. Since $X$ is compact, $g$ has compact support, so weak convergence of measures (see the discussion following definition 7.2.4 ) gives $\int _ Xg\, 
u _ j	o \int _ Xg\, 
u $. Since $f=g$ outside $G$, we have $|\int _ Xf\, \lambda -\int _ Xg\, \lambda |\leq 2B\lambda (G)$ for each $\lambda \in \{ 
u ,

u _2,\ldots \} $. The upper limit of the second term is therefore at most $4B$ times the supremum of $\lambda (G)$ over the family, which tends to zero as $\eta \downarrow 0$ by uniform absolute continuity. $\square$ Lemma 17.1.2 . Let $	heta $ be a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form on $X$, and let $\varphi _1,\varphi _2,\psi _1,\psi _2\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ satisfy $\varphi _1\sim \varphi _2$ and $\psi _1\sim \psi _2$. Put $a=\varphi _1-\varphi _2$, $b=\psi _1-\psi _2$, and \[  S_ j=\sum _{k=0}^{n-1} \left\langle 	heta _{\varphi _ j}\wedge 	heta _{\psi _1}^{k} \wedge 	heta _{\psi _2}^{n-1-k}ightangle , \qquad j=1,2.  \] Then 17.8  egin{equation} \label{eq:singular-monge-ampere-difference-identity} \int _ Xa(\mu _{\psi _1}-\mu _{\psi _2}) =\int _ Xb(S_1-S_2). \end{equation} Proof. If the potentials were bounded, ( 17.8 ) would follow from Stokes' formula. We reduce to that case by truncation in three steps, assuming first that $	heta $ is a Kähler form, and remove this assumption in a fourth step. Step 1: agreement on deep sublevel sets. Let $	heta =\kappa $ be a Kähler form, and assume that $\varphi _1\leq \varphi _2$, $\psi _1\leq \psi _2$, and that there is $L>0$ such that $\varphi _1=\varphi _2$ on $U=\{ \varphi _1<-L\} $ and $\psi _1=\psi _2$ on $V=\{ \psi _1<-L\} $. These sets are open, because $\varphi _1$ and $\psi _1$ are upper semicontinuous. For an integer $l>L$ put $\varphi _ j^ l=\max \{ \varphi _ j,-l\} $ and $\psi _ j^ l=\max \{ \psi _ j,-l\} $. These are bounded $\kappa $-psh functions; let $a^ l=\varphi _1^ l-\varphi _2^ l$, $b^ l=\psi _1^ l-\psi _2^ l$, and let $S_ j^ l$ be defined as $S_ j$ with the truncated functions. The algebraic identity $x^ n-y^ n=(x-y)\sum _ kx^ ky^{n-1-k}$ for the commuting Bedford–Taylor products gives \[  \mu _{\psi _1^ l}-\mu _{\psi _2^ l}=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b^ l\wedge \Sigma ^ l,\qquad S_1^ l-S_2^ l=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a^ l\wedge \Sigma ^ l,\qquad \Sigma ^ l=\sum _{k=0}^{n-1}\kappa _{\psi _1^ l}^ k\wedge \kappa _{\psi _2^ l}^{n-1-k}.  \] Since $\Sigma ^ l$ is a closed positive current, Stokes' formula for bounded potentials (lemma 15.4.2 ) yields $\int _ Xa^ l\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b^ l\wedge \Sigma ^ l=\int _ Xb^ l\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a^ l\wedge \Sigma ^ l$, which is ( 17.8 ) for the truncated functions. We show that both sides of this identity coincide with the corresponding sides of ( 17.8 ). On $U$ we have $a^ l=a=0$. On the open set $V$ we have $\psi _1^ l=\psi _2^ l$ and $\psi _1=\psi _2$, so $\mu _{\psi _1^ l}=\mu _{\psi _2^ l}$ and $\mu _{\psi _1}=\mu _{\psi _2}$ there, by locality of Bedford–Taylor and non-pluripolar products. Hence both left sides are integrals over the closed set $F=X\setminus (U\cup V)$. On $F$ we have $\varphi _2\geq \varphi _1\geq -L$ and $\psi _2\geq \psi _1\geq -L$. Thus $F$ is contained in the plurifine open set where all four potentials exceed $-l$; there every truncation coincides with its potential, so the bounded products of the truncations coincide with the corresponding non-pluripolar products, by plurifine locality (proposition 15.1.5 ). Consequently the two left sides are equal. The right sides are treated in the same way with the roles of $U$ and $V$ exchanged: $b^ l=b=0$ on $V$, while $S_1^ l=S_2^ l$ and $S_1=S_2$ on $U$. This proves ( 17.8 ) under the assumptions of this step. Step 2: a Kähler background with a margin. Let $	heta =\kappa $ be Kähler, and suppose that all four potentials are $\lambda \kappa $-psh for some $0<\lambda <1$. Adding a constant to one of the four potentials changes neither side of ( 17.8 ). Indeed, the measures are unchanged, and a constant added to $a$ or $b$ contributes nothing, since $\int _ X(\mu _{\psi _1}-\mu _{\psi _2})=0$ and $\int _ X(S_1-S_2)=0$ by corollary 15.7.5 . Subtracting suitable constants from $\varphi _1$ and $\psi _1$, and then a common constant from each pair, we may therefore assume that all four potentials are nonpositive and that \[  \varphi _1\leq \varphi _2\leq \varphi _1+B, \qquad \psi _1\leq \psi _2\leq \psi _1+B  \] for a constant $B\geq 1$. Take a sequence $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ with $\lambda (1+\varepsilon )<1$ and put \[  \varphi _{2,\varepsilon }=\max \{ \varphi _1,(1+\varepsilon )\varphi _2\} , \qquad \psi _{2,\varepsilon }=\max \{ \psi _1,(1+\varepsilon )\psi _2\} .  \] Since $(1+\varepsilon )\varphi _2$ is $(1+\varepsilon )\lambda \kappa $-psh, the function $\varphi _{2,\varepsilon }$ is $\kappa $-psh, and $\varphi _1\leq \varphi _{2,\varepsilon }\leq \varphi _2\leq \varphi _1+B$ because $\varphi _2\leq 0$. Where $\varphi _1<-B-B/\varepsilon $, \[  (1+\varepsilon )\varphi _2\leq (1+\varepsilon )(\varphi _1+B)=\varphi _1+B+\varepsilon (\varphi _1+B)<\varphi _1,  \] so $\varphi _{2,\varepsilon }=\varphi _1$ there. The same holds for the $\psi $'s. Step 1 therefore applies to the pairs $(\varphi _1,\varphi _{2,\varepsilon })$ and $(\psi _1,\psi _{2,\varepsilon })$ and gives ( 17.8 ) with $a_\varepsilon =\varphi _1-\varphi _{2,\varepsilon }$ and $b_\varepsilon =\psi _1-\psi _{2,\varepsilon }$ in place of $a,b$, and with the corresponding measures. Step 3: the limit $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. As $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, the functions $(1+\varepsilon )\varphi _2$ increase to $\varphi _2$, so $\varphi _{2,\varepsilon }$ increases to $\varphi _{2,0}=\max \{ \varphi _1,\varphi _2\} =\varphi _2$; likewise $\psi _{2,\varepsilon }\uparrow \psi _{2,0}=\psi _2$. By corollary 15.7.6 , every measure in the identity of Step 2 converges weakly to the corresponding measure in ( 17.8 ). To pass to the limit in the integrals we apply lemma 17.1.1 to each of the finitely many terms, each of which is the integral of a bounded weight against a positive measure. We first check uniform absolute continuity. For $\varepsilon \geq 0$ put \[  \zeta _\varepsilon =	frac 15 (\varphi _1+\varphi _{2,\varepsilon }+\psi _1+\psi _{2,\varepsilon }), \qquad \chi =\zeta _0-B.  \] Since $-B\leq \varphi _{2,\varepsilon }-\varphi _2\leq 0$ and $-B\leq \psi _{2,\varepsilon }-\psi _2\leq 0$, we have $\chi \leq \zeta _\varepsilon \leq \chi +B$ for all $\varepsilon \geq 0$. Each of the four potentials is $\lambda \kappa $-psh, so $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi \geq - rac45\lambda \kappa $, and $\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi $ is the sum of $(1-4\lambda /5)\kappa $ and the closed positive current $ rac45\lambda \kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi $. In particular $\chi $ is $\kappa $-psh, and expanding $\langle (\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi )^ nangle $ by multilinearity and compatibility with smooth factors (proposition 15.1.5 , proposition 15.3.3 ) gives $\int _ X\langle (\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi )^ nangle \geq (1-4\lambda /5)^ n\int _ X\kappa ^ n>0$. Now let $\mu $ refer to the background $\kappa $. By the identity \[  5\kappa _{\zeta _\varepsilon } =\kappa _{\varphi _1}+\kappa _{\varphi _{2,\varepsilon }} +\kappa _{\psi _1}+\kappa _{\psi _{2,\varepsilon }}+\kappa  \] and multilinearity, each measure occurring in the identity of Step 2 (for $\varepsilon >0$) or in ( 17.8 ) (for $\varepsilon =0$) is a non-pluripolar product of $n$ of the currents on the right, and hence is at most $5^ n\mu _{\zeta _\varepsilon }$. The potential $q=B^{-1}\zeta _\varepsilon +(1-B^{-1})\chi $ satisfies $\chi \leq q\leq \chi +1$, so $q-1$ is a competitor for $\operatorname {Cap}_{\kappa ,\chi }$, and $\mu _ q\geq B^{-n}\mu _{\zeta _\varepsilon }$ by multilinearity, since $B\geq 1$. Hence $\mu _{\zeta _\varepsilon }(A)\leq B^ n\operatorname {Cap}_{\kappa ,\chi }(A)$ for every Borel set $A$, and every measure in question, for every $\varepsilon \geq 0$, is bounded by $5^ nB^ n\operatorname {Cap}_{\kappa ,\chi }$; in particular its total mass is at most $5^ nB^ n\operatorname {Cap}_{\kappa ,\chi }(X)=5^ nB^ n\int _ X\langle (\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi )^ nangle \leq 5^ nB^ n\int _ X\kappa ^ n$, by proposition 16.7.6 , theorem 15.4.3 . Since $\chi $ has positive mass, theorem 16.9.8 bounds $\operatorname {Cap}_{\kappa ,\chi }(A)$ by a continuous nondecreasing function of $\operatorname {Cap}_\omega (A)$ vanishing at zero. Uniform absolute continuity follows. Next we check the weights. Assign the value zero to $a_\varepsilon ,b_\varepsilon ,a,b$ on the pole sets; these are Borel functions with values in $[-B,0]$. Given $\eta >0$, proposition 16.9.9 (3), applied to each of the four potentials with the bound $\eta /4$, and the countable subadditivity of $\operatorname {Cap}_\omega $ (proposition 16.7.6 ) give an open set $G$ with $\operatorname {Cap}_\omega (G)<\eta $ which contains the pole sets of the four potentials and such that the four potentials are finite and continuous on the compact set $X\setminus G$. Then $a$ and $b$ are continuous on $X\setminus G$, so they satisfy the continuity hypothesis of lemma 17.1.1 . Moreover the four potentials are bounded in absolute value on $X\setminus G$ by a constant $C_\eta >0$. Since $(1+\varepsilon )\varphi _2\leq \varphi _{2,\varepsilon }\leq \varphi _2$, we have on $X\setminus G$ \[  |a_\varepsilon -a|=|\varphi _{2,\varepsilon }-\varphi _2|\leq |(1+\varepsilon )\varphi _2-\varphi _2|\leq \varepsilon C_\eta ,  \] and likewise $|b_\varepsilon -b|\leq \varepsilon C_\eta $. Hence, for every $\delta >0$ and $\varepsilon <\delta /C_\eta $, the sets $\{ |a_\varepsilon -a|>\delta \} $ and $\{ |b_\varepsilon -b|>\delta \} $ lie in $G$ and have capacity less than $\eta $. Since $\eta $ is arbitrary, $a_\varepsilon 	o a$ and $b_\varepsilon 	o b$ in capacity. Lemma 17.1.1 now passes the identity of Step 2 to the limit, which is ( 17.8 ). Step 4: an arbitrary background. For all sufficiently large $s>0$ we have $s\omega \geq 	heta $ and the form $\kappa _ s=	heta +s\omega $ is Kähler. Each $q\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ is then $	frac 12\kappa _ s$-psh, because $	frac 12\kappa _ s+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q=	heta _ q+	frac 12(s\omega -	heta )\geq 0$. By Steps 2 and 3 with $\lambda = rac12$, ( 17.8 ) holds in the background $\kappa _ s$ for all large $s$. Since $\kappa _ s+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q=	heta _ q+s\omega $, multilinearity and compatibility with smooth factors (proposition 15.1.5 , proposition 15.3.3 ) show that every measure in the identity is a polynomial in $s$ whose coefficients are finite measures of the form $\langle 	heta _{q_1}\wedge \cdots \wedge 	heta _{q_ k}angle \wedge \omega ^{n-k}$; the weights $a,b$ do not depend on $s$. Both sides of the identity are therefore polynomials in $s$, and since they agree for all large $s$, their coefficients agree. The constant coefficients are the two sides of ( 17.8 ) in the background $	heta $. $\square$ Theorem 17.1.3 . Let $a,b$ be bounded quasi-psh differences on $X$, and let $T_1,\ldots ,T_{n-1}$ be closed positive $(1,1)$-currents on $X$. Then 17.9  egin{equation} \label{eq:nonpluripolar-bounded-difference-integration-by-parts} \int _ Xa\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b\wedge \langle T_1\wedge \cdots \wedge T_{n-1}angle =\int _ Xb\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a\wedge \langle T_1\wedge \cdots \wedge T_{n-1}angle , \end{equation} where the Hessian factors are the signed measures defined in ( 17.1 ). Proof. Step 1: a repeated factor and a common background. Let $(\varphi _1,\varphi _2)$ and $(\psi _1,\psi _2)$ be presentations of $a$ and $b$, and suppose that these four functions and a further potential $\eta $ all belong to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ for one smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form $	heta $. For $0\leq t\leq 1$ the functions $\psi _ j^ t=(1-t)\eta +t\psi _ j$ are $	heta $-psh, and $\psi _1^ t-\psi _2^ t=tb$ is bounded. Lemma 17.1.2 , applied to $\varphi _1,\varphi _2,\psi _1^ t,\psi _2^ t$, gives \[  \int _ Xa(\mu _{\psi _1^ t}-\mu _{\psi _2^ t})=t\int _ Xb(S_1^ t-S_2^ t), \qquad S_ j^ t=\sum _{k=0}^{n-1}\left\langle 	heta _{\varphi _ j}\wedge 	heta _{\psi _1^ t}^ k\wedge 	heta _{\psi _2^ t}^{n-1-k}ightangle .  \] Since $	heta _{\psi _ j^ t}=(1-t)	heta _\eta +t	heta _{\psi _ j}$, multilinearity expands every measure here as a polynomial in $t$ with finite measures as coefficients, so both sides are polynomials in $t$. We compare their coefficients of $t$. On the left this coefficient is \[  n\int _ Xa\left(\langle 	heta _{\psi _1}\wedge 	heta _\eta ^{n-1}angle -\langle 	heta _{\psi _2}\wedge 	heta _\eta ^{n-1}angle ight) =n\int _ Xa\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b\wedge \langle 	heta _\eta ^{n-1}angle ,  \] where we used that ( 17.1 ) may be computed in any smooth background with respect to which the presentation is psh. On the right it is $\int _ Xb(S_1^0-S_2^0)$, and $S_ j^0=n\langle 	heta _{\varphi _ j}\wedge 	heta _\eta ^{n-1}angle $, so it equals $n\int _ Xb\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a\wedge \langle 	heta _\eta ^{n-1}angle $. This proves ( 17.9 ) when $T_1=\cdots =T_{n-1}=	heta _\eta $ and all potentials share the background $	heta $. For $n=1$ there are no currents $T_ j$, and ( 17.9 ) is ( 17.8 ) for a Kähler background with respect to which the four functions are psh. Step 2: arbitrary currents. Let $n>1$. By theorem 14.1.7 , write $T_ j=	heta _ j+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\eta _ j$ with $	heta _ j$ smooth closed and $\eta _ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta _ j)$. For positive numbers $r_1,\ldots ,r_{n-1}$ with $\sum _ jr_ j=1$ put $	heta _ r=\sum _ jr_ j	heta _ j$ and $\eta _ r=\sum _ jr_ j\eta _ j$, so that $\sum _ jr_ jT_ j=	heta _ r+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\eta _ r$. The potential $\eta _ r$ is $(	heta _ r+s\omega )$-psh for every $s\geq 0$, since $	heta _ r+s\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\eta _ r=\sum _ jr_ jT_ j+s\omega \geq 0$. Let $\kappa $ be a multiple of $\omega $ such that the presentations of $a$ and $b$ are $\kappa $-psh. Since the forms $	heta _ r$ are convex combinations of the finitely many smooth forms $	heta _ j$, there is $s_0$ with $	heta _ r+s\omega \geq \kappa $ for all $r$ and all $s\geq s_0$, and then the presentations are $(	heta _ r+s\omega )$-psh as well. Step 1 applied to the current $\sum _ jr_ jT_ j+s\omega =(	heta _ r+s\omega )+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\eta _ r$ gives \[  \int _ Xa\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b\wedge \Bigl \langle \Bigl (\sum _ jr_ jT_ j+s\omega \Bigr )^{n-1}\Bigr angle =\int _ Xb\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a\wedge \Bigl \langle \Bigl (\sum _ jr_ jT_ j+s\omega \Bigr )^{n-1}\Bigr angle ,  \] where, by the independence of ( 17.1 ) from the background, the Hessian factors may be computed in one fixed Kähler background. Expanding the repeated current by multilinearity, both sides become polynomials in $s$, and comparing constant coefficients gives \[  \int _ Xa\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b\wedge \Bigl \langle \Bigl (\sum _ jr_ jT_ j\Bigr )^{n-1}\Bigr angle =\int _ Xb\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a\wedge \Bigl \langle \Bigl (\sum _ jr_ jT_ j\Bigr )^{n-1}\Bigr angle .  \] Both sides are homogeneous polynomials of degree $n-1$ in $(r_1,\ldots ,r_{n-1})$. Since they agree on the open simplex, homogeneity makes them agree on the open positive cone of $\mathbb R^{n-1}$. Hence their coefficients agree: a polynomial that vanishes on a nonempty open set is zero, because all its partial derivatives vanish at a point $r_0$ of that set and it equals its finite Taylor expansion at $r_0$. The coefficient of $r_1\cdots r_{n-1}$ is $(n-1)!$ times the corresponding side of ( 17.9 ). $\square$ Lemma 17.1.4 . Let $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ satisfy $u\sim v$, let $T_1,\ldots ,T_{n-1}$ be closed positive $(1,1)$-currents on $X$, and put $R=\langle T_1\wedge \cdots \wedge T_{n-1}angle $. Then \[  \int _ X(u-v)\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u-v)\wedge R\leq 0.  \] Proof. Put $\lambda _ u=\langle 	heta _ u\wedge T_1\wedge \cdots \wedge T_{n-1}angle $ and define $\lambda _ v$ in the same way, so that $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u-v)\wedge R=\lambda _ u-\lambda _ v$ by ( 17.1 ). Since $u-v$ is bounded, corollary 15.7.5 , applied after writing $T_ i=	heta _ i+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\eta _ i$ with smooth $	heta _ i$ and $\eta _ i\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta _ i)$ (theorem 14.1.7 ), gives $\lambda _ u(X)=\lambda _ v(X)$. Hence the integral does not change if a constant is added to $u$, and we may assume $u\leq v$. We must show that $\int _ X(v-u)\lambda _ v\leq \int _ X(v-u)\lambda _ u$. Let $t\geq 0$ and $\varepsilon >0$, and put $q=\max \{ u,v-t-\varepsilon \} $. Then $v-t-\varepsilon \leq q\leq v$, so $\lambda _ q(X)=\lambda _ v(X)=\lambda _ u(X)$ by the same corollary. The sets $O_1=\{ u<v-t-\varepsilon \} $ and $O_2=\{ u>v-t-\varepsilon \} $ are disjoint and plurifine open, by proposition 10.5.1 applied in charts after adding the same smooth local potential of $	heta $ to $u$ and $v$; neither of them meets the common pole set of $u$ and $v$. Moreover $q=v-t-\varepsilon $ on $O_1$ and $q=u$ on $O_2$, so plurifine locality (proposition 15.1.5 ) gives $\lambda _ q=\lambda _ v$ on $O_1$ and $\lambda _ q=\lambda _ u$ on $O_2$, and hence \[  \lambda _ v(O_1)+\lambda _ u(O_2)\leq \lambda _ q(X)=\lambda _ u(X).  \] Since pole sets carry no mass, it follows that \[  \lambda _ v(\{ u<v-t-\varepsilon \} ) \leq \lambda _ u(\{ u\leq v-t-\varepsilon \} ) \leq \lambda _ u(\{ u<v-t\} ).  \] As $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ the sets $\{ u<v-t-\varepsilon \} $ increase to $\{ u<v-t\} $, and therefore \[  \lambda _ v(\{ u<v-t\} )\leq \lambda _ u(\{ u<v-t\} )\qquad 	ext{for every }t\geq 0.  \] On the common finite locus the bounded function $v-u\geq 0$ equals $\int _0^\infty \mathbf1_{\{ u<v-t\} }\, \mathrm dt$. Integrating the last inequality in $t$ and using Tonelli's theorem, we obtain $\int _ X(v-u)\lambda _ v\leq \int _ X(v-u)\lambda _ u$, as required. $\square$

text: 17.1 \begin{equation} \label{eq:bounded-difference-hessian-product} \begin{aligned}  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a\wedge R & =\left\langle (\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _1)\wedge T_1\wedge \cdots \wedge T_{n-1}\right\rangle \\ & \quad -\left\langle (\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _2)\wedge T_1\wedge \cdots \wedge T_{n-1}\right\rangle , \end{aligned} \end{equation}
