title: Singular monge ampere difference identity
text: Lemma 17.1.2 . Let $\theta $ be a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form on $X$, and let $\varphi _1,\varphi _2,\psi _1,\psi _2\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ satisfy $\varphi _1\sim \varphi _2$ and $\psi _1\sim \psi _2$. Put $a=\varphi _1-\varphi _2$, $b=\psi _1-\psi _2$, and \[  S_ j=\sum _{k=0}^{n-1} \left\langle \theta _{\varphi _ j}\wedge \theta _{\psi _1}^{k} \wedge \theta _{\psi _2}^{n-1-k}\right\rangle , \qquad j=1,2.  \] Then 17.8 \begin{equation} \label{eq:singular-monge-ampere-difference-identity} \int _ Xa(\mu _{\psi _1}-\mu _{\psi _2}) =\int _ Xb(S_1-S_2). \end{equation} Proof. If the potentials were bounded, ( 17.8 ) would follow from Stokes' formula. We reduce to that case by truncation in three steps, assuming first that $\theta $ is a Kähler form, and remove this assumption in a fourth step. Step 1: agreement on deep sublevel sets. Let $\theta =\kappa $ be a Kähler form, and assume that $\varphi _1\leq \varphi _2$, $\psi _1\leq \psi _2$, and that there is $L>0$ such that $\varphi _1=\varphi _2$ on $U=\{ \varphi _1<-L\} $ and $\psi _1=\psi _2$ on $V=\{ \psi _1<-L\} $. These sets are open, because $\varphi _1$ and $\psi _1$ are upper semicontinuous. For an integer $l>L$ put $\varphi _ j^ l=\max \{ \varphi _ j,-l\} $ and $\psi _ j^ l=\max \{ \psi _ j,-l\} $. These are bounded $\kappa $-psh functions; let $a^ l=\varphi _1^ l-\varphi _2^ l$, $b^ l=\psi _1^ l-\psi _2^ l$, and let $S_ j^ l$ be defined as $S_ j$ with the truncated functions. The algebraic identity $x^ n-y^ n=(x-y)\sum _ kx^ ky^{n-1-k}$ for the commuting Bedford–Taylor products gives \[  \mu _{\psi _1^ l}-\mu _{\psi _2^ l}=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b^ l\wedge \Sigma ^ l,\qquad S_1^ l-S_2^ l=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a^ l\wedge \Sigma ^ l,\qquad \Sigma ^ l=\sum _{k=0}^{n-1}\kappa _{\psi _1^ l}^ k\wedge \kappa _{\psi _2^ l}^{n-1-k}.  \] Since $\Sigma ^ l$ is a closed positive current, Stokes' formula for bounded potentials (lemma 15.4.2 ) yields $\int _ Xa^ l\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b^ l\wedge \Sigma ^ l=\int _ Xb^ l\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a^ l\wedge \Sigma ^ l$, which is ( 17.8 ) for the truncated functions. We show that both sides of this identity coincide with the corresponding sides of ( 17.8 ). On $U$ we have $a^ l=a=0$. On the open set $V$ we have $\psi _1^ l=\psi _2^ l$ and $\psi _1=\psi _2$, so $\mu _{\psi _1^ l}=\mu _{\psi _2^ l}$ and $\mu _{\psi _1}=\mu _{\psi _2}$ there, by locality of Bedford–Taylor and non-pluripolar products. Hence both left sides are integrals over the closed set $F=X\setminus (U\cup V)$. On $F$ we have $\varphi _2\geq \varphi _1\geq -L$ and $\psi _2\geq \psi _1\geq -L$. Thus $F$ is contained in the plurifine open set where all four potentials exceed $-l$; there every truncation coincides with its potential, so the bounded products of the truncations coincide with the corresponding non-pluripolar products, by plurifine locality (proposition 15.1.5 ). Consequently the two left sides are equal. The right sides are treated in the same way with the roles of $U$ and $V$ exchanged: $b^ l=b=0$ on $V$, while $S_1^ l=S_2^ l$ and $S_1=S_2$ on $U$. This proves ( 17.8 ) under the assumptions of this step. Step 2: a Kähler background with a margin. Let $\theta =\kappa $ be Kähler, and suppose that all four potentials are $\lambda \kappa $-psh for some $0<\lambda <1$. Adding a constant to one of the four potentials changes neither side of ( 17.8 ). Indeed, the measures are unchanged, and a constant added to $a$ or $b$ contributes nothing, since $\int _ X(\mu _{\psi _1}-\mu _{\psi _2})=0$ and $\int _ X(S_1-S_2)=0$ by corollary 15.7.5 . Subtracting suitable constants from $\varphi _1$ and $\psi _1$, and then a common constant from each pair, we may therefore assume that all four potentials are nonpositive and that \[  \varphi _1\leq \varphi _2\leq \varphi _1+B, \qquad \psi _1\leq \psi _2\leq \psi _1+B  \] for a constant $B\geq 1$. Take a sequence $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ with $\lambda (1+\varepsilon )<1$ and put \[  \varphi _{2,\varepsilon }=\max \{ \varphi _1,(1+\varepsilon )\varphi _2\} , \qquad \psi _{2,\varepsilon }=\max \{ \psi _1,(1+\varepsilon )\psi _2\} .  \] Since $(1+\varepsilon )\varphi _2$ is $(1+\varepsilon )\lambda \kappa $-psh, the function $\varphi _{2,\varepsilon }$ is $\kappa $-psh, and $\varphi _1\leq \varphi _{2,\varepsilon }\leq \varphi _2\leq \varphi _1+B$ because $\varphi _2\leq 0$. Where $\varphi _1<-B-B/\varepsilon $, \[  (1+\varepsilon )\varphi _2\leq (1+\varepsilon )(\varphi _1+B)=\varphi _1+B+\varepsilon (\varphi _1+B)<\varphi _1,  \] so $\varphi _{2,\varepsilon }=\varphi _1$ there. The same holds for the $\psi $'s. Step 1 therefore applies to the pairs $(\varphi _1,\varphi _{2,\varepsilon })$ and $(\psi _1,\psi _{2,\varepsilon })$ and gives ( 17.8 ) with $a_\varepsilon =\varphi _1-\varphi _{2,\varepsilon }$ and $b_\varepsilon =\psi _1-\psi _{2,\varepsilon }$ in place of $a,b$, and with the corresponding measures. Step 3: the limit $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. As $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, the functions $(1+\varepsilon )\varphi _2$ increase to $\varphi _2$, so $\varphi _{2,\varepsilon }$ increases to $\varphi _{2,0}=\max \{ \varphi _1,\varphi _2\} =\varphi _2$; likewise $\psi _{2,\varepsilon }\uparrow \psi _{2,0}=\psi _2$. By corollary 15.7.6 , every measure in the identity of Step 2 converges weakly to the corresponding measure in ( 17.8 ). To pass to the limit in the integrals we apply lemma 17.1.1 to each of the finitely many terms, each of which is the integral of a bounded weight against a positive measure. We first check uniform absolute continuity. For $\varepsilon \geq 0$ put \[  \zeta _\varepsilon =\tfrac 15 (\varphi _1+\varphi _{2,\varepsilon }+\psi _1+\psi _{2,\varepsilon }), \qquad \chi =\zeta _0-B.  \] Since $-B\leq \varphi _{2,\varepsilon }-\varphi _2\leq 0$ and $-B\leq \psi _{2,\varepsilon }-\psi _2\leq 0$, we have $\chi \leq \zeta _\varepsilon \leq \chi +B$ for all $\varepsilon \geq 0$. Each of the four potentials is $\lambda \kappa $-psh, so $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi \geq -\frac45\lambda \kappa $, and $\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi $ is the sum of $(1-4\lambda /5)\kappa $ and the closed positive current $\frac45\lambda \kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi $. In particular $\chi $ is $\kappa $-psh, and expanding $\langle (\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi )^ n\rangle $ by multilinearity and compatibility with smooth factors (proposition 15.1.5 , proposition 15.3.3 ) gives $\int _ X\langle (\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi )^ n\rangle \geq (1-4\lambda /5)^ n\int _ X\kappa ^ n>0$. Now let $\mu $ refer to the background $\kappa $. By the identity \[  5\kappa _{\zeta _\varepsilon } =\kappa _{\varphi _1}+\kappa _{\varphi _{2,\varepsilon }} +\kappa _{\psi _1}+\kappa _{\psi _{2,\varepsilon }}+\kappa  \] and multilinearity, each measure occurring in the identity of Step 2 (for $\varepsilon >0$) or in ( 17.8 ) (for $\varepsilon =0$) is a non-pluripolar product of $n$ of the currents on the right, and hence is at most $5^ n\mu _{\zeta _\varepsilon }$. The potential $q=B^{-1}\zeta _\varepsilon +(1-B^{-1})\chi $ satisfies $\chi \leq q\leq \chi +1$, so $q-1$ is a competitor for $\operatorname {Cap}_{\kappa ,\chi }$, and $\mu _ q\geq B^{-n}\mu _{\zeta _\varepsilon }$ by multilinearity, since $B\geq 1$. Hence $\mu _{\zeta _\varepsilon }(A)\leq B^ n\operatorname {Cap}_{\kappa ,\chi }(A)$ for every Borel set $A$, and every measure in question, for every $\varepsilon \geq 0$, is bounded by $5^ nB^ n\operatorname {Cap}_{\kappa ,\chi }$; in particular its total mass is at most $5^ nB^ n\operatorname {Cap}_{\kappa ,\chi }(X)=5^ nB^ n\int _ X\langle (\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi )^ n\rangle \leq 5^ nB^ n\int _ X\kappa ^ n$, by proposition 16.7.6 , theorem 15.4.3 . Since $\chi $ has positive mass, theorem 16.9.8 bounds $\operatorname {Cap}_{\kappa ,\chi }(A)$ by a continuous nondecreasing function of $\operatorname {Cap}_\omega (A)$ vanishing at zero. Uniform absolute continuity follows. Next we check the weights. Assign the value zero to $a_\varepsilon ,b_\varepsilon ,a,b$ on the pole sets; these are Borel functions with values in $[-B,0]$. Given $\eta >0$, proposition 16.9.9 (3), applied to each of the four potentials with the bound $\eta /4$, and the countable subadditivity of $\operatorname {Cap}_\omega $ (proposition 16.7.6 ) give an open set $G$ with $\operatorname {Cap}_\omega (G)<\eta $ which contains the pole sets of the four potentials and such that the four potentials are finite and continuous on the compact set $X\setminus G$. Then $a$ and $b$ are continuous on $X\setminus G$, so they satisfy the continuity hypothesis of lemma 17.1.1 . Moreover the four potentials are bounded in absolute value on $X\setminus G$ by a constant $C_\eta >0$. Since $(1+\varepsilon )\varphi _2\leq \varphi _{2,\varepsilon }\leq \varphi _2$, we have on $X\setminus G$ \[  |a_\varepsilon -a|=|\varphi _{2,\varepsilon }-\varphi _2|\leq |(1+\varepsilon )\varphi _2-\varphi _2|\leq \varepsilon C_\eta ,  \] and likewise $|b_\varepsilon -b|\leq \varepsilon C_\eta $. Hence, for every $\delta >0$ and $\varepsilon <\delta /C_\eta $, the sets $\{ |a_\varepsilon -a|>\delta \} $ and $\{ |b_\varepsilon -b|>\delta \} $ lie in $G$ and have capacity less than $\eta $. Since $\eta $ is arbitrary, $a_\varepsilon \to a$ and $b_\varepsilon \to b$ in capacity. Lemma 17.1.1 now passes the identity of Step 2 to the limit, which is ( 17.8 ). Step 4: an arbitrary background. For all sufficiently large $s>0$ we have $s\omega \geq \theta $ and the form $\kappa _ s=\theta +s\omega $ is Kähler. Each $q\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ is then $\tfrac 12\kappa _ s$-psh, because $\tfrac 12\kappa _ s+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q=\theta _ q+\tfrac 12(s\omega -\theta )\geq 0$. By Steps 2 and 3 with $\lambda =\frac12$, ( 17.8 ) holds in the background $\kappa _ s$ for all large $s$. Since $\kappa _ s+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q=\theta _ q+s\omega $, multilinearity and compatibility with smooth factors (proposition 15.1.5 , proposition 15.3.3 ) show that every measure in the identity is a polynomial in $s$ whose coefficients are finite measures of the form $\langle \theta _{q_1}\wedge \cdots \wedge \theta _{q_ k}\rangle \wedge \omega ^{n-k}$; the weights $a,b$ do not depend on $s$. Both sides of the identity are therefore polynomials in $s$, and since they agree for all large $s$, their coefficients agree. The constant coefficients are the two sides of ( 17.8 ) in the background $\theta $. $\square$

title: Singular monge ampere difference identity
text: 17.8 \begin{equation} \label{eq:singular-monge-ampere-difference-identity} \int _ Xa(\mu _{\psi _1}-\mu _{\psi _2}) =\int _ Xb(S_1-S_2). \end{equation}

title: Nonpluripolar bounded difference integration by parts
text: Theorem 17.1.3 . Let $a,b$ be bounded quasi-psh differences on $X$, and let $T_1,\ldots ,T_{n-1}$ be closed positive $(1,1)$-currents on $X$. Then 17.9 \begin{equation} \label{eq:nonpluripolar-bounded-difference-integration-by-parts} \int _ Xa\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b\wedge \langle T_1\wedge \cdots \wedge T_{n-1}\rangle =\int _ Xb\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a\wedge \langle T_1\wedge \cdots \wedge T_{n-1}\rangle , \end{equation} where the Hessian factors are the signed measures defined in ( 17.1 ). Proof. Step 1: a repeated factor and a common background. Let $(\varphi _1,\varphi _2)$ and $(\psi _1,\psi _2)$ be presentations of $a$ and $b$, and suppose that these four functions and a further potential $\eta $ all belong to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ for one smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form $\theta $. For $0\leq t\leq 1$ the functions $\psi _ j^ t=(1-t)\eta +t\psi _ j$ are $\theta $-psh, and $\psi _1^ t-\psi _2^ t=tb$ is bounded. Lemma 17.1.2 , applied to $\varphi _1,\varphi _2,\psi _1^ t,\psi _2^ t$, gives \[  \int _ Xa(\mu _{\psi _1^ t}-\mu _{\psi _2^ t})=t\int _ Xb(S_1^ t-S_2^ t), \qquad S_ j^ t=\sum _{k=0}^{n-1}\left\langle \theta _{\varphi _ j}\wedge \theta _{\psi _1^ t}^ k\wedge \theta _{\psi _2^ t}^{n-1-k}\right\rangle .  \] Since $\theta _{\psi _ j^ t}=(1-t)\theta _\eta +t\theta _{\psi _ j}$, multilinearity expands every measure here as a polynomial in $t$ with finite measures as coefficients, so both sides are polynomials in $t$. We compare their coefficients of $t$. On the left this coefficient is \[  n\int _ Xa\left(\langle \theta _{\psi _1}\wedge \theta _\eta ^{n-1}\rangle -\langle \theta _{\psi _2}\wedge \theta _\eta ^{n-1}\rangle \right) =n\int _ Xa\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b\wedge \langle \theta _\eta ^{n-1}\rangle ,  \] where we used that ( 17.1 ) may be computed in any smooth background with respect to which the presentation is psh. On the right it is $\int _ Xb(S_1^0-S_2^0)$, and $S_ j^0=n\langle \theta _{\varphi _ j}\wedge \theta _\eta ^{n-1}\rangle $, so it equals $n\int _ Xb\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a\wedge \langle \theta _\eta ^{n-1}\rangle $. This proves ( 17.9 ) when $T_1=\cdots =T_{n-1}=\theta _\eta $ and all potentials share the background $\theta $. For $n=1$ there are no currents $T_ j$, and ( 17.9 ) is ( 17.8 ) for a Kähler background with respect to which the four functions are psh. Step 2: arbitrary currents. Let $n>1$. By theorem 14.1.7 , write $T_ j=\theta _ j+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\eta _ j$ with $\theta _ j$ smooth closed and $\eta _ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta _ j)$. For positive numbers $r_1,\ldots ,r_{n-1}$ with $\sum _ jr_ j=1$ put $\theta _ r=\sum _ jr_ j\theta _ j$ and $\eta _ r=\sum _ jr_ j\eta _ j$, so that $\sum _ jr_ jT_ j=\theta _ r+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\eta _ r$. The potential $\eta _ r$ is $(\theta _ r+s\omega )$-psh for every $s\geq 0$, since $\theta _ r+s\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\eta _ r=\sum _ jr_ jT_ j+s\omega \geq 0$. Let $\kappa $ be a multiple of $\omega $ such that the presentations of $a$ and $b$ are $\kappa $-psh. Since the forms $\theta _ r$ are convex combinations of the finitely many smooth forms $\theta _ j$, there is $s_0$ with $\theta _ r+s\omega \geq \kappa $ for all $r$ and all $s\geq s_0$, and then the presentations are $(\theta _ r+s\omega )$-psh as well. Step 1 applied to the current $\sum _ jr_ jT_ j+s\omega =(\theta _ r+s\omega )+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\eta _ r$ gives \[  \int _ Xa\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b\wedge \Bigl \langle \Bigl (\sum _ jr_ jT_ j+s\omega \Bigr )^{n-1}\Bigr \rangle =\int _ Xb\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a\wedge \Bigl \langle \Bigl (\sum _ jr_ jT_ j+s\omega \Bigr )^{n-1}\Bigr \rangle ,  \] where, by the independence of ( 17.1 ) from the background, the Hessian factors may be computed in one fixed Kähler background. Expanding the repeated current by multilinearity, both sides become polynomials in $s$, and comparing constant coefficients gives \[  \int _ Xa\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b\wedge \Bigl \langle \Bigl (\sum _ jr_ jT_ j\Bigr )^{n-1}\Bigr \rangle =\int _ Xb\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a\wedge \Bigl \langle \Bigl (\sum _ jr_ jT_ j\Bigr )^{n-1}\Bigr \rangle .  \] Both sides are homogeneous polynomials of degree $n-1$ in $(r_1,\ldots ,r_{n-1})$. Since they agree on the open simplex, homogeneity makes them agree on the open positive cone of $\mathbb R^{n-1}$. Hence their coefficients agree: a polynomial that vanishes on a nonempty open set is zero, because all its partial derivatives vanish at a point $r_0$ of that set and it equals its finite Taylor expansion at $r_0$. The coefficient of $r_1\cdots r_{n-1}$ is $(n-1)!$ times the corresponding side of ( 17.9 ). $\square$

title: Nonpluripolar bounded difference integration by parts
text: 17.9 \begin{equation} \label{eq:nonpluripolar-bounded-difference-integration-by-parts} \int _ Xa\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b\wedge \langle T_1\wedge \cdots \wedge T_{n-1}\rangle =\int _ Xb\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a\wedge \langle T_1\wedge \cdots \wedge T_{n-1}\rangle , \end{equation}

title: Bounded difference negative hessian energy
text: Lemma 17.1.4 . Let $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ satisfy $u\sim v$, let $T_1,\ldots ,T_{n-1}$ be closed positive $(1,1)$-currents on $X$, and put $R=\langle T_1\wedge \cdots \wedge T_{n-1}\rangle $. Then \[  \int _ X(u-v)\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u-v)\wedge R\leq 0.  \] Proof. Put $\lambda _ u=\langle \theta _ u\wedge T_1\wedge \cdots \wedge T_{n-1}\rangle $ and define $\lambda _ v$ in the same way, so that $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u-v)\wedge R=\lambda _ u-\lambda _ v$ by ( 17.1 ). Since $u-v$ is bounded, corollary 15.7.5 , applied after writing $T_ i=\theta _ i+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\eta _ i$ with smooth $\theta _ i$ and $\eta _ i\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta _ i)$ (theorem 14.1.7 ), gives $\lambda _ u(X)=\lambda _ v(X)$. Hence the integral does not change if a constant is added to $u$, and we may assume $u\leq v$. We must show that $\int _ X(v-u)\lambda _ v\leq \int _ X(v-u)\lambda _ u$. Let $t\geq 0$ and $\varepsilon >0$, and put $q=\max \{ u,v-t-\varepsilon \} $. Then $v-t-\varepsilon \leq q\leq v$, so $\lambda _ q(X)=\lambda _ v(X)=\lambda _ u(X)$ by the same corollary. The sets $O_1=\{ u<v-t-\varepsilon \} $ and $O_2=\{ u>v-t-\varepsilon \} $ are disjoint and plurifine open, by proposition 10.5.1 applied in charts after adding the same smooth local potential of $\theta $ to $u$ and $v$; neither of them meets the common pole set of $u$ and $v$. Moreover $q=v-t-\varepsilon $ on $O_1$ and $q=u$ on $O_2$, so plurifine locality (proposition 15.1.5 ) gives $\lambda _ q=\lambda _ v$ on $O_1$ and $\lambda _ q=\lambda _ u$ on $O_2$, and hence \[  \lambda _ v(O_1)+\lambda _ u(O_2)\leq \lambda _ q(X)=\lambda _ u(X).  \] Since pole sets carry no mass, it follows that \[  \lambda _ v(\{ u<v-t-\varepsilon \} ) \leq \lambda _ u(\{ u\leq v-t-\varepsilon \} ) \leq \lambda _ u(\{ u<v-t\} ).  \] As $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ the sets $\{ u<v-t-\varepsilon \} $ increase to $\{ u<v-t\} $, and therefore \[  \lambda _ v(\{ u<v-t\} )\leq \lambda _ u(\{ u<v-t\} )\qquad \text{for every }t\geq 0.  \] On the common finite locus the bounded function $v-u\geq 0$ equals $\int _0^\infty \mathbf1_{\{ u<v-t\} }\, \mathrm dt$. Integrating the last inequality in $t$ and using Tonelli's theorem, we obtain $\int _ X(v-u)\lambda _ v\leq \int _ X(v-u)\lambda _ u$, as required. $\square$

title: Relative Monge–Ampère energy
text: 17.2 Relative Monge–Ampère energy Fix a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form $\theta $ whose class is big, and a model potential $\phi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, that is, $P_\theta [\phi ]=\phi $ and $m=\int _ X\langle \theta _\phi ^ n\rangle >0$ (definition 16.3.1 ). In particular $\phi \leq 0$ and $\sup _ X\phi =0$. Recall from definition 15.8.3 that $\mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi )$ consists of the potentials $u\preceq \phi $ with $\int _ X\langle \theta _ u^ n\rangle =m$. If $u_1,\ldots ,u_ n\in \mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi )$, then \[  \int _ X\langle \theta _{u_1}\wedge \cdots \wedge \theta _{u_ n}\rangle =m.  \] Indeed $P_\theta [u_ j]=P_\theta [\phi ]=\phi $ by proposition 16.4.10 , and the singularity envelope preserves mixed masses by proposition 16.3.2 . Definition 17.2.1 . Put \[  \begin{aligned}  \mathcal E^\infty (X,\theta ,\phi ) & =\{ u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ):u\sim \phi \} ,\\  \mathcal E^1(X,\theta ,\phi ) & =\left\{ u\in \mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi ): \int _ X|u-\phi |\, \mu _ u<\infty \right\} . \end{aligned}  \] The potentials in $\mathcal E^\infty (X,\theta ,\phi )$ have bounded difference from $\phi $, but they need not be bounded functions. The class $\mathcal E^1(X,\theta ,\phi )$ is the relative finite-energy class . For the potential $\phi =V_\theta $ with minimal singularities (definition 14.2.6 ) we omit the reference from these notations. If $u\sim \phi $, then $\int _ X\langle \theta _ u^ n\rangle =m$ by corollary 15.7.5 , and $|u-\phi |$ is bounded. Hence \[  \mathcal E^\infty (X,\theta ,\phi )\subset \mathcal E^1(X,\theta ,\phi )\subset \mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi ).  \] The potential $V_\theta $ is indeed a model potential: $P_\theta [V_\theta ]=V_\theta $ by proposition 16.3.2 (4), and $\int _ X\langle \theta _{V_\theta }^ n\rangle =\operatorname {vol}(\{ \theta \} )>0$ by definition 15.8.1 , proposition 15.8.2 . For $\phi =V_\theta $, the class $\mathcal E^\infty (X,\theta )$ consists of the potentials with minimal singularities, and $\mathcal E(X,\theta )=\mathcal E(X,\theta ,V_\theta )$ is the class of potentials of full Monge–Ampère mass of definition 15.8.3 . These classes of global potentials are not related to the local class $\mathcal E_0(B)$ of bounded functions on a ball in definition 9.10.1 . Definition 17.2.2 . For $u\in \mathcal E^\infty (X,\theta ,\phi )$ define 17.12 \begin{equation} \label{eq:relative-energy-bounded-type} E_\theta ^\phi (u)=\frac1{n+1}\sum _{j=0}^ n \int _ X(u-\phi )\,  \langle \theta _ u^ j\wedge \theta _\phi ^{n-j}\rangle . \end{equation} All these integrals are finite, since the weight is bounded and every mixed measure has total mass $m$. For $\phi =V_\theta $ we write $E_\theta $. Proposition 17.2.3 . Let $u,v\in \mathcal E^\infty (X,\theta ,\phi )$ and put $u_ t=(1-t)u+tv$ for $0\leq t\leq 1$. Then 17.13 \begin{equation} \label{eq:bounded-type-energy-first-variation} \frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}E_\theta ^\phi (u_ t) =\int _ X(v-u)\, \mu _{u_ t}, \end{equation} with one-sided derivatives at the endpoints, and 17.14 \begin{equation} \label{eq:bounded-type-energy-cocycle} E_\theta ^\phi (v)-E_\theta ^\phi (u) =\frac1{n+1}\sum _{j=0}^ n\int _ X(v-u) \langle \theta _ v^ j\wedge \theta _ u^{n-j}\rangle . \end{equation} In particular, the energy is increasing, and $E_\theta ^\phi (u+C)=E_\theta ^\phi (u)+Cm$ for every constant $C$. Proof. Let $w\in \mathcal E^\infty (X,\theta ,\phi )$. For $0\leq r\leq 1$ the potential $\phi +r(w-\phi )=(1-r)\phi +rw$ again belongs to $\mathcal E^\infty (X,\theta ,\phi )$, and multilinearity gives \[  \mu _{\phi +r(w-\phi )}=\sum _{j=0}^ n\binom nj r^ j(1-r)^{n-j}\langle \theta _ w^ j\wedge \theta _\phi ^{n-j}\rangle .  \] Since $\binom nj\int _0^1r^ j(1-r)^{n-j}\, \mathrm dr=1/(n+1)$, as one sees by integrating by parts $j$ times, we obtain 17.15 \begin{equation} \label{eq:relative-energy-segment-integral} E_\theta ^\phi (w)=\int _0^1\int _ X(w-\phi )\,  \mu _{\phi +r(w-\phi )}\, \mathrm dr. \end{equation} Now put $h=v-u$ and $q_{r,t}=\phi +r(u_ t-\phi )$. Since $\theta _{q_{r,t}}=(1-r)\theta _\phi +r(1-t)\theta _ u+rt\theta _ v$, the measures $\mu _{q_{r,t}}$ are polynomials in $(r,t)$ whose coefficients are mixed measures of total mass $m$, and the weights $u_ t-\phi =(u-\phi )+th$ are bounded. All expressions below are therefore polynomials in $(r,t)$ with finite coefficients, and the derivatives are derivatives of polynomials. Identities between such polynomials of measures follow from the corresponding identities between polynomials in commuting variables $x,y,z$, by substituting the mixed measure $\langle \theta _\phi ^ a\wedge \theta _ u^ b\wedge \theta _ v^ c\rangle $ for the monomial $x^ ay^ bz^ c$; multilinearity shows that this substitution is compatible with the products occurring here. For instance, the identities $\partial _ t\ell ^ n=nr(z-y)\ell ^{n-1}$ and $\partial _ r\ell ^ n=n\bigl ((1-t)y+tz-x\bigr )\ell ^{n-1}$ for $\ell =(1-r)x+r(1-t)y+rtz$ give 17.16 \begin{equation} \label{eq:bounded-type-measure-derivatives} \partial _ t\mu _{q_{r,t}}=nr\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h\wedge \langle \theta _{q_{r,t}}^{n-1}\rangle ,\qquad \partial _ r\mu _{q_{r,t}}=n\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u_ t-\phi )\wedge \langle \theta _{q_{r,t}}^{n-1}\rangle , \end{equation} in the sense of ( 17.1 ). Differentiating ( 17.15 ) with $w=u_ t$ and using the first of these identities, we obtain \[  \frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}E_\theta ^\phi (u_ t) =\int _0^1\left[\int _ Xh\, \mu _{q_{r,t}} +nr\int _ X(u_ t-\phi )\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h\wedge \langle \theta _{q_{r,t}}^{n-1}\rangle \right]\mathrm dr.  \] By theorem 17.1.3 , applied to the bounded quasi-psh differences $u_ t-\phi $ and $h$, the second integral equals $\int _ Xh\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u_ t-\phi )\wedge \langle \theta _{q_{r,t}}^{n-1}\rangle $, which is $\frac1n\partial _ r\int _ Xh\, \mu _{q_{r,t}}$ by the second identity. The integrand in $r$ is therefore $\partial _ r\bigl [r\int _ Xh\, \mu _{q_{r,t}}\bigr ]$, and since $q_{1,t}=u_ t$, \[  \frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}E_\theta ^\phi (u_ t)=\int _ Xh\, \mu _{u_ t}.  \] This is ( 17.13 ). Integrating it from $t=0$ to $t=1$, and expanding $\mu _{u_ t}=\sum _ j\binom nj t^ j(1-t)^{n-j}\langle \theta _ v^ j\wedge \theta _ u^{n-j}\rangle $ with the same beta integrals, gives ( 17.14 ). If $u\leq v$, every term of the cocycle formula is nonnegative, so the energy is increasing. Every mixed measure has total mass $m$, so taking $v=u+C$ in the cocycle formula gives the last assertion. $\square$ Proposition 17.2.4 . The energy is concave on $\mathcal E^\infty (X,\theta ,\phi )$, and for $u,v\in \mathcal E^\infty (X,\theta ,\phi )$, 17.17 \begin{equation} \label{eq:bounded-type-energy-tangent-bounds} \int _ X(v-u)\, \mu _ v \leq E_\theta ^\phi (v)-E_\theta ^\phi (u) \leq \int _ X(v-u)\, \mu _ u. \end{equation} Moreover $|E_\theta ^\phi (v)-E_\theta ^\phi (u)|\leq m\sup |v-u|$, the supremum being taken over the common finite locus. If $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and $\psi \sim \phi $, then the functional $E_\theta ^\psi $ defined by ( 17.12 ) with $\psi $ in place of $\phi $ satisfies \[  E_\theta ^\psi (u)=E_\theta ^\phi (u)-E_\theta ^\phi (\psi ).  \] Proof. Let $u_ t=(1-t)u+tv$ and $h=v-u$. Then $\partial _ t\mu _{u_ t}=n\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h\wedge \langle \theta _{u_ t}^{n-1}\rangle $. Indeed, by multilinearity and ( 17.1 ), both sides expand into combinations of the mixed measures $\langle \theta _ u^ a\wedge \theta _ v^{n-a}\rangle $, obtained by substituting $\langle \theta _ u^ a\wedge \theta _ v^{n-a}\rangle $ for $y^ az^{n-a}$ in the two sides of the identity $\partial _ t((1-t)y+tz)^ n=n(z-y)((1-t)y+tz)^{n-1}$ in commuting variables $y,z$. Differentiating ( 17.13 ) once more, again as a polynomial in $t$, and using this identity, we obtain \[  \frac{\mathrm d^2}{\mathrm dt^2}E_\theta ^\phi (u_ t) =n\int _ Xh\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h\wedge \langle \theta _{u_ t}^{n-1}\rangle \leq 0  \] by lemma 17.1.4 . Thus $t\mapsto E_\theta ^\phi (u_ t)$ is concave, and its derivative decreases from $\int _ Xh\, \mu _ u$ at $t=0$ to $\int _ Xh\, \mu _ v$ at $t=1$. Integrating the derivative over $[0,1]$ gives the tangent bounds ( 17.17 ). Since $\int _ X\langle \theta _{u_ t}^ n\rangle =m$, the first variation formula also gives $|E_\theta ^\phi (v)-E_\theta ^\phi (u)|\leq m\sup |v-u|$. Finally, the cocycle formula ( 17.14 ) applied to the pair $\psi ,u$ reads $E_\theta ^\phi (u)-E_\theta ^\phi (\psi )=E_\theta ^\psi (u)$. $\square$ We now extend the energy to all potentials that are at least as singular as $\phi $. Definition 17.2.5 . For $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $u\preceq \phi $ put \[  E_\theta ^\phi (u)=\inf \{ E_\theta ^\phi (w):w\in \mathcal E^\infty (X,\theta ,\phi ),\  u\leq w\} .  \] The family on the right is nonempty, since $\phi +C$ belongs to it for large $C$; hence $E_\theta ^\phi (u)\in [-\infty ,\infty )$. Because the energy is increasing on $\mathcal E^\infty (X,\theta ,\phi )$, the new definition agrees with ( 17.12 ) there. Proposition 17.2.6 . The extended energy is increasing, satisfies $E_\theta ^\phi (u+C)=E_\theta ^\phi (u)+Cm$, and \[  E_\theta ^\phi (u)=\lim _{k\to \infty } E_\theta ^\phi (\max \{ u,\phi -k\} ),  \] where the limit exists in $[-\infty ,\infty )$. Proof. If $u\leq u'$, every majorant of $u'$ in the definition is a majorant of $u$, so $E_\theta ^\phi (u)\leq E_\theta ^\phi (u')$. Translating majorants by a constant and using the shift formula on $\mathcal E^\infty (X,\theta ,\phi )$ gives the shift formula. The potentials $u_ k=\max \{ u,\phi -k\} $ belong to $\mathcal E^\infty (X,\theta ,\phi )$, decrease with $k$ and dominate $u$; hence $E_\theta ^\phi (u_ k)$ decreases and is bounded below by $E_\theta ^\phi (u)$. Conversely, let $w$ be any majorant in the definition, and choose $C$ with $w\geq \phi -C$. For $k\geq C$ both $u$ and $\phi -k$ lie below $w$, so $u_ k\leq w$ and $E_\theta ^\phi (u_ k)\leq E_\theta ^\phi (w)$. Letting $k\to \infty $ and taking the infimum over $w$ gives $\lim _ kE_\theta ^\phi (u_ k)\leq E_\theta ^\phi (u)$. $\square$ Proposition 17.2.7 . Let $(u_ i)_{i\in I}$ be a decreasing net in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $u_ i\preceq \phi $, and suppose that $u=\inf _ iu_ i$ belongs to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Then \[  E_\theta ^\phi (u_ i)\downarrow E_\theta ^\phi (u).  \] Consequently the extended energy is concave on $\{ u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ):u\preceq \phi \} $, and the set where it is finite is convex. Proof. First let the net be a sequence $(u_ j)$. By monotonicity $E_\theta ^\phi (u_ j)$ decreases to a limit $L\geq E_\theta ^\phi (u)$. Let $w\in \mathcal E^\infty (X,\theta ,\phi )$ with $w\geq u$, and put $v_ j=\max \{ u_ j,w\} $. Then $v_ j$ decreases pointwise to $\max \{ u,w\} =w$. Since $u_ j\leq u_1\leq \phi +C$ and $w\geq \phi -C$ for some constant $C$, the differences $v_ j-w$ are uniformly bounded. The tangent bound ( 17.17 ) gives \[  0\leq E_\theta ^\phi (v_ j)-E_\theta ^\phi (w) \leq \int _ X(v_ j-w)\, \mu _ w\longrightarrow 0  \] by bounded convergence. Since $E_\theta ^\phi (u_ j)\leq E_\theta ^\phi (v_ j)$, we get $L\leq E_\theta ^\phi (w)$, and taking the infimum over $w$ gives $L\leq E_\theta ^\phi (u)$. For a general net, corollary 14.2.5 shows that $u_ i\to u$ in $L^1(X)$; its hypothesis holds because $\sup _ Xu_ i\geq \sup _ Xu>-\infty $. Choose indices $i_1\leq i_2\leq \cdots $ with $\| u_{i_ k}-u\| _{L^1}<1/k$. The decreasing pointwise limit $\tilde u$ of $(u_{i_ k})$ is a $\theta $-psh function by theorem 8.3.1 , applied in charts after adding smooth local potentials of $\theta $, since it dominates $u$ and so is not identically $-\infty $. By monotone convergence, $\int _ X(\tilde u-u)\, \omega ^ n=\lim _ k\int _ X(u_{i_ k}-u)\, \omega ^ n=0$, so $\tilde u=u$ almost everywhere, hence everywhere. The sequence case gives $E_\theta ^\phi (u_{i_ k})\to E_\theta ^\phi (u)$. The net $E_\theta ^\phi (u_ i)$ is decreasing, so its limit is its infimum, which is at most $\lim _ kE_\theta ^\phi (u_{i_ k})=E_\theta ^\phi (u)$; the reverse inequality is monotonicity. (The selected indices need not be cofinal in $I$; this is why we compare infima.) For concavity let $u,v\preceq \phi $ and $0<t<1$; we may assume that $E_\theta ^\phi (u)$ and $E_\theta ^\phi (v)$ are finite, since otherwise there is nothing to prove. The potentials $(1-t)\max \{ u,\phi -k\} +t\max \{ v,\phi -k\} $ belong to $\mathcal E^\infty (X,\theta ,\phi )$ and decrease to $(1-t)u+tv$ as $k\to \infty $. Concavity on $\mathcal E^\infty (X,\theta ,\phi )$ and decreasing continuity give \[  E_\theta ^\phi ((1-t)u+tv) \geq (1-t)E_\theta ^\phi (u)+tE_\theta ^\phi (v).  \] In particular the finite locus of the energy is convex. $\square$ Theorem 17.2.8 . For $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $u\preceq \phi $, \[  E_\theta ^\phi (u)>-\infty \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad u\in \mathcal E^1(X,\theta ,\phi ).  \] In particular, finite extended energy forces full mass relative to $\phi $. If $u\in \mathcal E^1(X,\theta ,\phi )$ and $u\leq \phi $, then 17.18 \begin{equation} \label{eq:relative-energy-integrability-bounds} \frac1{n+1}\int _ X(\phi -u)\, \mu _ u \leq -E_\theta ^\phi (u) \leq \int _ X(\phi -u)\, \mu _ u. \end{equation} Proof. Both conditions are invariant under adding a constant to $u$, so we may assume $u\leq \phi $. Put $u_ k=\max \{ u,\phi -k\} $ and $A_ k=\{ u>\phi -k\} $. The potentials $u_ k$ belong to $\mathcal E^\infty (X,\theta ,\phi )$ and have mass $m$. Since $u_ k\leq \phi $, all terms in ( 17.12 ) are nonpositive, and keeping only the term $j=n$ gives \[  \int _ X(\phi -u_ k)\mu _{u_ k}\leq (n+1)\bigl (-E_\theta ^\phi (u_ k)\bigr ).  \] Suppose that $E_\theta ^\phi (u)>-\infty $. Since $E_\theta ^\phi (u)\leq E_\theta ^\phi (u_ k)\leq E_\theta ^\phi (\phi )=0$, the right side is bounded by $C=-(n+1)E_\theta ^\phi (u)$. On $X\setminus A_ k$ the weight $\phi -u_ k$ equals $k$ outside a pluripolar set; on the plurifine open set $A_ k$ we have $u_ k=u$, so $\mu _{u_ k}=\mu _ u$ there by locality. Hence \[  m-\mu _ u(A_ k)=\mu _{u_ k}(X\setminus A_ k)\leq C/k.  \] The sets $A_ k$ increase to the set where $u$ is finite, which carries $\mu _ u$, so $\int _ X\langle \theta _ u^ n\rangle \geq m$; since $u\leq \phi $, mass monotonicity (theorem 15.7.4 ) gives the reverse inequality, and therefore $u\in \mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi )$. Locality also gives $\int _{A_ k}(\phi -u)\mu _ u\leq C$, and monotone convergence yields $\int _ X(\phi -u)\mu _ u\leq C$. This proves that $u\in \mathcal E^1(X,\theta ,\phi )$ and the first inequality in ( 17.18 ). Conversely, suppose $u\in \mathcal E^1(X,\theta ,\phi )$, and let $I=\int _ X(\phi -u)\mu _ u<\infty $. The measures $\mu _{u_ k}$ and $\mu _ u$ have the same total mass $m$ and agree on $A_ k$, so $\mu _{u_ k}(X\setminus A_ k)=\mu _ u(X\setminus A_ k)$. Thus \[  \int _ X(\phi -u_ k)\mu _{u_ k} =\int _ X\min \{ \phi -u,k\} \, \mu _ u\leq I.  \] The lower tangent bound in ( 17.17 ), applied to $u_ k$ and $\phi $, gives $E_\theta ^\phi (u_ k)\geq -I$. Letting $k\to \infty $ and using proposition 17.2.6 , we obtain $E_\theta ^\phi (u)\geq -I>-\infty $, which is the second inequality in ( 17.18 ). The first inequality was proved above. $\square$ Example 17.2.9 . Let $X$ be a compact Kähler curve, so $n=1$, and take $\theta =\omega $ and the reference $V_\omega =0$. For a smooth $\omega $-psh function $u$, \[  E_\omega (u)=\int _ Xu\, \omega -\tfrac 12 \int _ X\mathrm du\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}u,  \] where $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}$ is the real operator of ( 7.6 ), so that $\mathrm d\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$. Indeed, by definition $E_\omega (u)=\frac12\bigl (\int _ Xu\, \omega +\int _ Xu(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)\bigr )$, and Stokes' formula (lemma 15.4.2 ) gives $\int _ Xu\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=-\int _ X\mathrm du\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}u$. Since $\mathrm du\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}u=\frac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }\partial u\wedge \bar\partial u$, the second term is a multiple of the classical Dirichlet energy of $u$. The unbounded potential $u$ on $\mathbb P^1$ of example 16.4.8 , which has full mass, also lies in $\mathcal E^1(\mathbb P^1,\omega )$. Away from its only pole $z=0$ the function $u$ is bounded, and $\mu _ u$ is a finite measure. Near the pole write $r=\log |z|^2$. If $G$ is a smooth function of one real variable, then $\bar\partial G(\log |z|^2)=G'(r)\, \mathrm d\bar z/\bar z$ and $\partial \bar\partial G(\log |z|^2)=G''(r)\, \mathrm dz\wedge \mathrm d\bar z/|z|^2$ on $\mathbb C\setminus \{ 0\} $; since $\mathrm i\, \mathrm dz\wedge \mathrm d\bar z=2\, \mathrm dA$, where $\mathrm dA$ is Lebesgue measure, we get $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}G(\log |z|^2)=\pi ^{-1}G''(r)|z|^{-2}\, \mathrm dA$, which in polar coordinates $z=\rho \mathrm e^{\mathrm i\vartheta }$, with $r=2\log \rho $, is $(2\pi )^{-1}G''(r)\, \mathrm dr\, \mathrm d\vartheta $. The function $F$ of example 16.4.8 satisfies $F(r)=-\log (-r)$ for $r\leq r_0$, with $r_0$ sufficiently negative, and is therefore smooth there, with $F''(r)=r^{-2}$. On the punctured disc $\{ 0<|z|^2<\mathrm e^{r_0}\} $ the measure $\mu _ u$ is $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F(\log |z|^2)$, and it does not charge the pole; hence the image of its restriction to $\{ |z|^2<\mathrm e^{r_0}\} $ under $z\mapsto \log |z|^2$ is $F''(r)\, \mathrm dr=r^{-2}\, \mathrm dr$ on $(-\infty ,r_0)$. Since $u-F(\log |z|^2)=-\log (1+|z|^2)$ is bounded near the pole, the finiteness of $\int |u|\, \mu _ u$ near the pole reduces, after the substitution $t=-r$, to \[  \int _ a^\infty \frac{\log t}{t^2}\, \mathrm dt =\frac{\log a+1}{a}<\infty \qquad (a>1).  \] Hence $u$ is a potential of finite energy whose difference from the reference $V_\omega =0$ is unbounded. Corollary 17.2.10 . The classes $\mathcal E^\infty (X,\theta ,\phi )$, $\mathcal E^1(X,\theta ,\phi )$ and $\mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi )$ are convex. If $u\in \mathcal E^1(X,\theta ,\phi )$, $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and $u\leq v\preceq \phi $, then $v\in \mathcal E^1(X,\theta ,\phi )$. Proof. Convex combinations of potentials with the same singularity type as $\phi $ have that singularity type. For $\mathcal E^1(X,\theta ,\phi )$, convexity follows from the concavity of the extended energy (proposition 17.2.7 ) and theorem 17.2.8 . If $u,v\in \mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi )$ and $0<t<1$, then $(1-t)u+tv\preceq \phi $, and by multilinearity $\mu _{(1-t)u+tv}$ is a combination of the mixed measures $\langle \theta _ u^ j\wedge \theta _ v^{n-j}\rangle $ with coefficients $\binom nj(1-t)^ jt^{n-j}$. Each of these measures has total mass $m$, as noted at the beginning of this section, so $\int _ X\langle \theta _{(1-t)u+tv}^ n\rangle =m$. The last assertion follows from the monotonicity of the extended energy and theorem 17.2.8 . $\square$ Lemma 17.2.11 . Let $u\in \mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi )$, let $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ satisfy $v\preceq \phi $, and let $\gamma \colon X\to [-\infty ,\infty ]$ be a Borel function, for instance a $\theta $-psh function, with $\gamma \geq \max \{ u,v\} $. Then, allowing infinite values, \[  \int _ X(\gamma -u)\mu _ v \leq 2\int _ X(\gamma -u)\mu _ u +2\int _ X(\gamma -v)\mu _ v.  \] Consequently, if $u,v,w_1,\ldots ,w_ n\in \mathcal E^1(X,\theta ,\phi )$, then \[  \int _ X|u-v|\, \langle \theta _{w_1}\wedge \cdots \wedge \theta _{w_ n}\rangle <\infty .  \] Proof. For $t\geq 0$ we have \[  \{ \gamma >u+2t\} \subset \{ \gamma >v+t\} \cup \{ v>u+t\} ,  \] because $\gamma \leq v+t$ and $v\leq u+t$ imply $\gamma \leq u+2t$. The weights $\gamma -u$ and $\gamma -v$ are Borel functions with values in $[0,\infty ]$ on the complements of the pole sets of $u$ and $v$, respectively, and these pole sets carry no mass; the level sets above are taken on these complements. Since $u\in \mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi )$ and $v-t\preceq \phi $, the comparison principle of proposition 16.7.4 , applied with $p=n$ to $u$ and $v-t$, gives \[  \mu _ v(\{ v>u+t\} )\leq \mu _ u(\{ v>u+t\} )+\int _ X\langle \theta _\phi ^ n\rangle -\int _ X\langle \theta _ u^ n\rangle =\mu _ u(\{ v>u+t\} ).  \] Integrating over level sets, we obtain \[  \begin{split}  \int _ X(\gamma -u)\mu _ v & \leq 2\int _0^\infty \mu _ v(\{ \gamma >v+t\} )\, \mathrm dt +2\int _0^\infty \mu _ u(\{ v>u+t\} )\, \mathrm dt\\ & \leq 2\int _ X(\gamma -v)\mu _ v+2\int _ X(\gamma -u)\mu _ u, \end{split}  \] where in the last step we used $(v-u)_+\leq \gamma -u$, which holds because $\gamma \geq \max \{ u,v\} $. All functions involved are nonnegative, so Tonelli's theorem applies without any integrability assumption. For the second assertion, add constants to $u$ and $v$ so that $u,v\leq \phi $; this changes $|u-v|$ by at most a constant, and the mixed measure has finite mass $m$. Put $w=\frac1n\sum _ jw_ j$, which lies in $\mathcal E^1(X,\theta ,\phi )$ by corollary 17.2.10 . By multilinearity, $\langle \theta _{w_1}\wedge \cdots \wedge \theta _{w_ n}\rangle \leq n^ n\mu _ w$. Choose $C$ with $w\leq \phi +C$ and apply the first assertion to $u$, $w$ and $\gamma =\phi +C$: its right side is finite because $u,w\in \mathcal E^1(X,\theta ,\phi )$. Hence $\phi -u$ is integrable for $\mu _ w$, and so for the mixed measure. The same holds for $\phi -v$, and $|u-v|\leq (\phi -u)+(\phi -v)$. $\square$ Proposition 17.2.12 . For $u,v\in \mathcal E^1(X,\theta ,\phi )$, the cocycle formula ( 17.14 ) and the tangent bounds ( 17.17 ) remain valid. In particular, ( 17.12 ) computes the extended energy on $\mathcal E^1(X,\theta ,\phi )$. Proof. All mixed measures involved have total mass $m$, so both assertions are unchanged if constants are added to $u$ and $v$; we may therefore assume $u,v\leq \phi $. Put $u_ k=\max \{ u,\phi -k\} $ and $v_ k=\max \{ v,\phi -k\} $. Fix $0\leq j\leq n$ and write $\lambda _ k=\langle \theta _{u_ k}^ j\wedge \theta _{v_ k}^{n-j}\rangle $ and $\lambda =\langle \theta _ u^ j\wedge \theta _ v^{n-j}\rangle $. We show that 17.21 \begin{equation} \label{eq:finite-energy-cocycle-term-limit} \int _ X(u_ k-v_ k)\lambda _ k\longrightarrow \int _ X(u-v)\lambda . \end{equation} On the plurifine open set $A_ k=\{ u>\phi -k\} \cap \{ v>\phi -k\} $ the measures $\lambda _ k$ and $\lambda $ agree by locality, and $u_ k-v_ k=u-v$. By lemma 17.2.11 , $|u-v|$ is $\lambda $-integrable. The sets $X\setminus A_ k$ decrease to the union of the pole sets of $u$, $v$ and $\phi $, which is pluripolar and therefore $\lambda $-null, so dominated convergence gives $\int _{X\setminus A_ k}|u-v|\lambda \to 0$. It remains to show that the integral of $|u_ k-v_ k|$ against $\lambda _ k$ over $X\setminus A_ k$ tends to zero. For $z\in \{ u,v\} $ put $D_ k(z)=\{ z\leq \phi -k\} $, so that $X\setminus A_ k=D_ k(u)\cup D_ k(v)$. We claim that 17.22 \begin{equation} \label{eq:finite-energy-mixed-truncation-tail} k\lambda _ k(D_ k(z))\leq 2^ n k\mu _ z(\{ z\leq \phi -k/2\} )\longrightarrow 0. \end{equation} Consider $z=u$ and $j<n$, and put $q=(v_ k+\phi -k)/2$. Since $\phi -k\leq v_ k\leq \phi $, we have $q\leq \phi -k/2$ on $X$, and $u_ k=\phi -k\leq q$ on $D_ k(u)$. Moreover $\theta _{v_ k}\leq 2\theta _ q$, since $2\theta _ q-\theta _{v_ k}=\theta _\phi \geq 0$, so multilinearity gives $\lambda _ k\leq 2^{n-j}\langle \theta _{u_ k}^ j\wedge \theta _ q^{n-j}\rangle $. The potentials $q$ and $u_ k$ belong to $\mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi )$, and the non-strict comparison principle of proposition 16.7.4 , with $n-j$ factors $\theta _ q$ and the $j$ fixed factors $\theta _{u_ k}$, gives \[  \lambda _ k(D_ k(u)) \leq 2^{n-j}\mu _{u_ k}(\{ u_ k\leq q\} ) \leq 2^{n-j}\mu _{u_ k}(\{ u\leq \phi -k/2\} ).  \] For $j=n$ the same bound holds directly, since then $\lambda _ k=\mu _{u_ k}$ and $D_ k(u)\subset \{ u\leq \phi -k/2\} $. The measures $\mu _{u_ k}$ and $\mu _ u$ have the same total mass and agree on $\{ u>\phi -k/2\} $ by locality, so the last mass equals $\mu _ u(\{ u\leq \phi -k/2\} )$. Since exchanging $u$ and $v$ and replacing $j$ by $n-j$ does not change $\lambda _ k$, the case $z=v$ follows from the case $z=u$. Finally, \[  k\mu _ z(\{ z\leq \phi -k/2\} )\leq 2\int _{\{ z\leq \phi -k/2\} }(\phi -z)\mu _ z\longrightarrow 0  \] because $\phi -z$ is $\mu _ z$-integrable. This proves ( 17.22 ). Since $u_ k-\phi $ and $v_ k-\phi $ take values in $[-k,0]$, we have $|u_ k-v_ k|\leq k$, and ( 17.22 ) shows that the integral of $|u_ k-v_ k|$ against $\lambda _ k$ over $X\setminus A_ k$ tends to zero. This proves ( 17.21 ). Now pass to the limit in the cocycle formula for $u_ k,v_ k$: its left side converges to $E_\theta ^\phi (v)-E_\theta ^\phi (u)$ by proposition 17.2.6 , and each term on the right converges by ( 17.21 ). The tangent bounds pass to the limit in the same way, using the terms $j=n$ and $j=0$. Taking $v=\phi $ in the cocycle formula gives the last assertion. $\square$

title: Relative bounded and finite energy classes
text: Definition 17.2.1 . Put \[  \begin{aligned}  \mathcal E^\infty (X,\theta ,\phi ) & =\{ u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ):u\sim \phi \} ,\\  \mathcal E^1(X,\theta ,\phi ) & =\left\{ u\in \mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi ): \int _ X|u-\phi |\, \mu _ u<\infty \right\} . \end{aligned}  \] The potentials in $\mathcal E^\infty (X,\theta ,\phi )$ have bounded difference from $\phi $, but they need not be bounded functions. The class $\mathcal E^1(X,\theta ,\phi )$ is the relative finite-energy class . For the potential $\phi =V_\theta $ with minimal singularities (definition 14.2.6 ) we omit the reference from these notations.

title: Relative monge ampere energy
text: Definition 17.2.2 . For $u\in \mathcal E^\infty (X,\theta ,\phi )$ define 17.12 \begin{equation} \label{eq:relative-energy-bounded-type} E_\theta ^\phi (u)=\frac1{n+1}\sum _{j=0}^ n \int _ X(u-\phi )\,  \langle \theta _ u^ j\wedge \theta _\phi ^{n-j}\rangle . \end{equation} All these integrals are finite, since the weight is bounded and every mixed measure has total mass $m$. For $\phi =V_\theta $ we write $E_\theta $.

title: Relative energy bounded type
text: 17.12 \begin{equation} \label{eq:relative-energy-bounded-type} E_\theta ^\phi (u)=\frac1{n+1}\sum _{j=0}^ n \int _ X(u-\phi )\,  \langle \theta _ u^ j\wedge \theta _\phi ^{n-j}\rangle . \end{equation}

title: Bounded type energy variation and cocycle
text: Proposition 17.2.3 . Let $u,v\in \mathcal E^\infty (X,\theta ,\phi )$ and put $u_ t=(1-t)u+tv$ for $0\leq t\leq 1$. Then 17.13 \begin{equation} \label{eq:bounded-type-energy-first-variation} \frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}E_\theta ^\phi (u_ t) =\int _ X(v-u)\, \mu _{u_ t}, \end{equation} with one-sided derivatives at the endpoints, and 17.14 \begin{equation} \label{eq:bounded-type-energy-cocycle} E_\theta ^\phi (v)-E_\theta ^\phi (u) =\frac1{n+1}\sum _{j=0}^ n\int _ X(v-u) \langle \theta _ v^ j\wedge \theta _ u^{n-j}\rangle . \end{equation} In particular, the energy is increasing, and $E_\theta ^\phi (u+C)=E_\theta ^\phi (u)+Cm$ for every constant $C$. Proof. Let $w\in \mathcal E^\infty (X,\theta ,\phi )$. For $0\leq r\leq 1$ the potential $\phi +r(w-\phi )=(1-r)\phi +rw$ again belongs to $\mathcal E^\infty (X,\theta ,\phi )$, and multilinearity gives \[  \mu _{\phi +r(w-\phi )}=\sum _{j=0}^ n\binom nj r^ j(1-r)^{n-j}\langle \theta _ w^ j\wedge \theta _\phi ^{n-j}\rangle .  \] Since $\binom nj\int _0^1r^ j(1-r)^{n-j}\, \mathrm dr=1/(n+1)$, as one sees by integrating by parts $j$ times, we obtain 17.15 \begin{equation} \label{eq:relative-energy-segment-integral} E_\theta ^\phi (w)=\int _0^1\int _ X(w-\phi )\,  \mu _{\phi +r(w-\phi )}\, \mathrm dr. \end{equation} Now put $h=v-u$ and $q_{r,t}=\phi +r(u_ t-\phi )$. Since $\theta _{q_{r,t}}=(1-r)\theta _\phi +r(1-t)\theta _ u+rt\theta _ v$, the measures $\mu _{q_{r,t}}$ are polynomials in $(r,t)$ whose coefficients are mixed measures of total mass $m$, and the weights $u_ t-\phi =(u-\phi )+th$ are bounded. All expressions below are therefore polynomials in $(r,t)$ with finite coefficients, and the derivatives are derivatives of polynomials. Identities between such polynomials of measures follow from the corresponding identities between polynomials in commuting variables $x,y,z$, by substituting the mixed measure $\langle \theta _\phi ^ a\wedge \theta _ u^ b\wedge \theta _ v^ c\rangle $ for the monomial $x^ ay^ bz^ c$; multilinearity shows that this substitution is compatible with the products occurring here. For instance, the identities $\partial _ t\ell ^ n=nr(z-y)\ell ^{n-1}$ and $\partial _ r\ell ^ n=n\bigl ((1-t)y+tz-x\bigr )\ell ^{n-1}$ for $\ell =(1-r)x+r(1-t)y+rtz$ give 17.16 \begin{equation} \label{eq:bounded-type-measure-derivatives} \partial _ t\mu _{q_{r,t}}=nr\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h\wedge \langle \theta _{q_{r,t}}^{n-1}\rangle ,\qquad \partial _ r\mu _{q_{r,t}}=n\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u_ t-\phi )\wedge \langle \theta _{q_{r,t}}^{n-1}\rangle , \end{equation} in the sense of ( 17.1 ). Differentiating ( 17.15 ) with $w=u_ t$ and using the first of these identities, we obtain \[  \frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}E_\theta ^\phi (u_ t) =\int _0^1\left[\int _ Xh\, \mu _{q_{r,t}} +nr\int _ X(u_ t-\phi )\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h\wedge \langle \theta _{q_{r,t}}^{n-1}\rangle \right]\mathrm dr.  \] By theorem 17.1.3 , applied to the bounded quasi-psh differences $u_ t-\phi $ and $h$, the second integral equals $\int _ Xh\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u_ t-\phi )\wedge \langle \theta _{q_{r,t}}^{n-1}\rangle $, which is $\frac1n\partial _ r\int _ Xh\, \mu _{q_{r,t}}$ by the second identity. The integrand in $r$ is therefore $\partial _ r\bigl [r\int _ Xh\, \mu _{q_{r,t}}\bigr ]$, and since $q_{1,t}=u_ t$, \[  \frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}E_\theta ^\phi (u_ t)=\int _ Xh\, \mu _{u_ t}.  \] This is ( 17.13 ). Integrating it from $t=0$ to $t=1$, and expanding $\mu _{u_ t}=\sum _ j\binom nj t^ j(1-t)^{n-j}\langle \theta _ v^ j\wedge \theta _ u^{n-j}\rangle $ with the same beta integrals, gives ( 17.14 ). If $u\leq v$, every term of the cocycle formula is nonnegative, so the energy is increasing. Every mixed measure has total mass $m$, so taking $v=u+C$ in the cocycle formula gives the last assertion. $\square$

title: Bounded type energy first variation
text: 17.13 \begin{equation} \label{eq:bounded-type-energy-first-variation} \frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}E_\theta ^\phi (u_ t) =\int _ X(v-u)\, \mu _{u_ t}, \end{equation}

title: Bounded type energy cocycle
text: 17.14 \begin{equation} \label{eq:bounded-type-energy-cocycle} E_\theta ^\phi (v)-E_\theta ^\phi (u) =\frac1{n+1}\sum _{j=0}^ n\int _ X(v-u) \langle \theta _ v^ j\wedge \theta _ u^{n-j}\rangle . \end{equation}

title: Relative energy segment integral
text: 17.15 \begin{equation} \label{eq:relative-energy-segment-integral} E_\theta ^\phi (w)=\int _0^1\int _ X(w-\phi )\,  \mu _{\phi +r(w-\phi )}\, \mathrm dr. \end{equation}

title: Bounded type measure derivatives
text: 17.16 \begin{equation} \label{eq:bounded-type-measure-derivatives} \partial _ t\mu _{q_{r,t}}=nr\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h\wedge \langle \theta _{q_{r,t}}^{n-1}\rangle ,\qquad \partial _ r\mu _{q_{r,t}}=n\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u_ t-\phi )\wedge \langle \theta _{q_{r,t}}^{n-1}\rangle , \end{equation}

title: Bounded type energy concavity
text: Proposition 17.2.4 . The energy is concave on $\mathcal E^\infty (X,\theta ,\phi )$, and for $u,v\in \mathcal E^\infty (X,\theta ,\phi )$, 17.17 \begin{equation} \label{eq:bounded-type-energy-tangent-bounds} \int _ X(v-u)\, \mu _ v \leq E_\theta ^\phi (v)-E_\theta ^\phi (u) \leq \int _ X(v-u)\, \mu _ u. \end{equation} Moreover $|E_\theta ^\phi (v)-E_\theta ^\phi (u)|\leq m\sup |v-u|$, the supremum being taken over the common finite locus. If $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and $\psi \sim \phi $, then the functional $E_\theta ^\psi $ defined by ( 17.12 ) with $\psi $ in place of $\phi $ satisfies \[  E_\theta ^\psi (u)=E_\theta ^\phi (u)-E_\theta ^\phi (\psi ).  \] Proof. Let $u_ t=(1-t)u+tv$ and $h=v-u$. Then $\partial _ t\mu _{u_ t}=n\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h\wedge \langle \theta _{u_ t}^{n-1}\rangle $. Indeed, by multilinearity and ( 17.1 ), both sides expand into combinations of the mixed measures $\langle \theta _ u^ a\wedge \theta _ v^{n-a}\rangle $, obtained by substituting $\langle \theta _ u^ a\wedge \theta _ v^{n-a}\rangle $ for $y^ az^{n-a}$ in the two sides of the identity $\partial _ t((1-t)y+tz)^ n=n(z-y)((1-t)y+tz)^{n-1}$ in commuting variables $y,z$. Differentiating ( 17.13 ) once more, again as a polynomial in $t$, and using this identity, we obtain \[  \frac{\mathrm d^2}{\mathrm dt^2}E_\theta ^\phi (u_ t) =n\int _ Xh\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h\wedge \langle \theta _{u_ t}^{n-1}\rangle \leq 0  \] by lemma 17.1.4 . Thus $t\mapsto E_\theta ^\phi (u_ t)$ is concave, and its derivative decreases from $\int _ Xh\, \mu _ u$ at $t=0$ to $\int _ Xh\, \mu _ v$ at $t=1$. Integrating the derivative over $[0,1]$ gives the tangent bounds ( 17.17 ). Since $\int _ X\langle \theta _{u_ t}^ n\rangle =m$, the first variation formula also gives $|E_\theta ^\phi (v)-E_\theta ^\phi (u)|\leq m\sup |v-u|$. Finally, the cocycle formula ( 17.14 ) applied to the pair $\psi ,u$ reads $E_\theta ^\phi (u)-E_\theta ^\phi (\psi )=E_\theta ^\psi (u)$. $\square$

title: Bounded type energy tangent bounds
text: 17.17 \begin{equation} \label{eq:bounded-type-energy-tangent-bounds} \int _ X(v-u)\, \mu _ v \leq E_\theta ^\phi (v)-E_\theta ^\phi (u) \leq \int _ X(v-u)\, \mu _ u. \end{equation}

title: Extended relative energy
text: Definition 17.2.5 . For $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $u\preceq \phi $ put \[  E_\theta ^\phi (u)=\inf \{ E_\theta ^\phi (w):w\in \mathcal E^\infty (X,\theta ,\phi ),\  u\leq w\} .  \]

title: Relative energy canonical truncations
text: Proposition 17.2.6 . The extended energy is increasing, satisfies $E_\theta ^\phi (u+C)=E_\theta ^\phi (u)+Cm$, and \[  E_\theta ^\phi (u)=\lim _{k\to \infty } E_\theta ^\phi (\max \{ u,\phi -k\} ),  \] where the limit exists in $[-\infty ,\infty )$. Proof. If $u\leq u'$, every majorant of $u'$ in the definition is a majorant of $u$, so $E_\theta ^\phi (u)\leq E_\theta ^\phi (u')$. Translating majorants by a constant and using the shift formula on $\mathcal E^\infty (X,\theta ,\phi )$ gives the shift formula. The potentials $u_ k=\max \{ u,\phi -k\} $ belong to $\mathcal E^\infty (X,\theta ,\phi )$, decrease with $k$ and dominate $u$; hence $E_\theta ^\phi (u_ k)$ decreases and is bounded below by $E_\theta ^\phi (u)$. Conversely, let $w$ be any majorant in the definition, and choose $C$ with $w\geq \phi -C$. For $k\geq C$ both $u$ and $\phi -k$ lie below $w$, so $u_ k\leq w$ and $E_\theta ^\phi (u_ k)\leq E_\theta ^\phi (w)$. Letting $k\to \infty $ and taking the infimum over $w$ gives $\lim _ kE_\theta ^\phi (u_ k)\leq E_\theta ^\phi (u)$. $\square$

title: Relative energy decreasing continuity
text: Proposition 17.2.7 . Let $(u_ i)_{i\in I}$ be a decreasing net in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $u_ i\preceq \phi $, and suppose that $u=\inf _ iu_ i$ belongs to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Then \[  E_\theta ^\phi (u_ i)\downarrow E_\theta ^\phi (u).  \] Consequently the extended energy is concave on $\{ u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ):u\preceq \phi \} $, and the set where it is finite is convex. Proof. First let the net be a sequence $(u_ j)$. By monotonicity $E_\theta ^\phi (u_ j)$ decreases to a limit $L\geq E_\theta ^\phi (u)$. Let $w\in \mathcal E^\infty (X,\theta ,\phi )$ with $w\geq u$, and put $v_ j=\max \{ u_ j,w\} $. Then $v_ j$ decreases pointwise to $\max \{ u,w\} =w$. Since $u_ j\leq u_1\leq \phi +C$ and $w\geq \phi -C$ for some constant $C$, the differences $v_ j-w$ are uniformly bounded. The tangent bound ( 17.17 ) gives \[  0\leq E_\theta ^\phi (v_ j)-E_\theta ^\phi (w) \leq \int _ X(v_ j-w)\, \mu _ w\longrightarrow 0  \] by bounded convergence. Since $E_\theta ^\phi (u_ j)\leq E_\theta ^\phi (v_ j)$, we get $L\leq E_\theta ^\phi (w)$, and taking the infimum over $w$ gives $L\leq E_\theta ^\phi (u)$. For a general net, corollary 14.2.5 shows that $u_ i\to u$ in $L^1(X)$; its hypothesis holds because $\sup _ Xu_ i\geq \sup _ Xu>-\infty $. Choose indices $i_1\leq i_2\leq \cdots $ with $\| u_{i_ k}-u\| _{L^1}<1/k$. The decreasing pointwise limit $\tilde u$ of $(u_{i_ k})$ is a $\theta $-psh function by theorem 8.3.1 , applied in charts after adding smooth local potentials of $\theta $, since it dominates $u$ and so is not identically $-\infty $. By monotone convergence, $\int _ X(\tilde u-u)\, \omega ^ n=\lim _ k\int _ X(u_{i_ k}-u)\, \omega ^ n=0$, so $\tilde u=u$ almost everywhere, hence everywhere. The sequence case gives $E_\theta ^\phi (u_{i_ k})\to E_\theta ^\phi (u)$. The net $E_\theta ^\phi (u_ i)$ is decreasing, so its limit is its infimum, which is at most $\lim _ kE_\theta ^\phi (u_{i_ k})=E_\theta ^\phi (u)$; the reverse inequality is monotonicity. (The selected indices need not be cofinal in $I$; this is why we compare infima.) For concavity let $u,v\preceq \phi $ and $0<t<1$; we may assume that $E_\theta ^\phi (u)$ and $E_\theta ^\phi (v)$ are finite, since otherwise there is nothing to prove. The potentials $(1-t)\max \{ u,\phi -k\} +t\max \{ v,\phi -k\} $ belong to $\mathcal E^\infty (X,\theta ,\phi )$ and decrease to $(1-t)u+tv$ as $k\to \infty $. Concavity on $\mathcal E^\infty (X,\theta ,\phi )$ and decreasing continuity give \[  E_\theta ^\phi ((1-t)u+tv) \geq (1-t)E_\theta ^\phi (u)+tE_\theta ^\phi (v).  \] In particular the finite locus of the energy is convex. $\square$

title: Relative finite energy characterization
text: Theorem 17.2.8 . For $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $u\preceq \phi $, \[  E_\theta ^\phi (u)>-\infty \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad u\in \mathcal E^1(X,\theta ,\phi ).  \] In particular, finite extended energy forces full mass relative to $\phi $. If $u\in \mathcal E^1(X,\theta ,\phi )$ and $u\leq \phi $, then 17.18 \begin{equation} \label{eq:relative-energy-integrability-bounds} \frac1{n+1}\int _ X(\phi -u)\, \mu _ u \leq -E_\theta ^\phi (u) \leq \int _ X(\phi -u)\, \mu _ u. \end{equation} Proof. Both conditions are invariant under adding a constant to $u$, so we may assume $u\leq \phi $. Put $u_ k=\max \{ u,\phi -k\} $ and $A_ k=\{ u>\phi -k\} $. The potentials $u_ k$ belong to $\mathcal E^\infty (X,\theta ,\phi )$ and have mass $m$. Since $u_ k\leq \phi $, all terms in ( 17.12 ) are nonpositive, and keeping only the term $j=n$ gives \[  \int _ X(\phi -u_ k)\mu _{u_ k}\leq (n+1)\bigl (-E_\theta ^\phi (u_ k)\bigr ).  \] Suppose that $E_\theta ^\phi (u)>-\infty $. Since $E_\theta ^\phi (u)\leq E_\theta ^\phi (u_ k)\leq E_\theta ^\phi (\phi )=0$, the right side is bounded by $C=-(n+1)E_\theta ^\phi (u)$. On $X\setminus A_ k$ the weight $\phi -u_ k$ equals $k$ outside a pluripolar set; on the plurifine open set $A_ k$ we have $u_ k=u$, so $\mu _{u_ k}=\mu _ u$ there by locality. Hence \[  m-\mu _ u(A_ k)=\mu _{u_ k}(X\setminus A_ k)\leq C/k.  \] The sets $A_ k$ increase to the set where $u$ is finite, which carries $\mu _ u$, so $\int _ X\langle \theta _ u^ n\rangle \geq m$; since $u\leq \phi $, mass monotonicity (theorem 15.7.4 ) gives the reverse inequality, and therefore $u\in \mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi )$. Locality also gives $\int _{A_ k}(\phi -u)\mu _ u\leq C$, and monotone convergence yields $\int _ X(\phi -u)\mu _ u\leq C$. This proves that $u\in \mathcal E^1(X,\theta ,\phi )$ and the first inequality in ( 17.18 ). Conversely, suppose $u\in \mathcal E^1(X,\theta ,\phi )$, and let $I=\int _ X(\phi -u)\mu _ u<\infty $. The measures $\mu _{u_ k}$ and $\mu _ u$ have the same total mass $m$ and agree on $A_ k$, so $\mu _{u_ k}(X\setminus A_ k)=\mu _ u(X\setminus A_ k)$. Thus \[  \int _ X(\phi -u_ k)\mu _{u_ k} =\int _ X\min \{ \phi -u,k\} \, \mu _ u\leq I.  \] The lower tangent bound in ( 17.17 ), applied to $u_ k$ and $\phi $, gives $E_\theta ^\phi (u_ k)\geq -I$. Letting $k\to \infty $ and using proposition 17.2.6 , we obtain $E_\theta ^\phi (u)\geq -I>-\infty $, which is the second inequality in ( 17.18 ). The first inequality was proved above. $\square$

title: Relative energy integrability bounds
text: 17.18 \begin{equation} \label{eq:relative-energy-integrability-bounds} \frac1{n+1}\int _ X(\phi -u)\, \mu _ u \leq -E_\theta ^\phi (u) \leq \int _ X(\phi -u)\, \mu _ u. \end{equation}

title: Curve dirichlet and loglog energy
text: Example 17.2.9 . Let $X$ be a compact Kähler curve, so $n=1$, and take $\theta =\omega $ and the reference $V_\omega =0$. For a smooth $\omega $-psh function $u$, \[  E_\omega (u)=\int _ Xu\, \omega -\tfrac 12 \int _ X\mathrm du\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}u,  \] where $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}$ is the real operator of ( 7.6 ), so that $\mathrm d\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$. Indeed, by definition $E_\omega (u)=\frac12\bigl (\int _ Xu\, \omega +\int _ Xu(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)\bigr )$, and Stokes' formula (lemma 15.4.2 ) gives $\int _ Xu\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=-\int _ X\mathrm du\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}u$. Since $\mathrm du\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}u=\frac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }\partial u\wedge \bar\partial u$, the second term is a multiple of the classical Dirichlet energy of $u$. The unbounded potential $u$ on $\mathbb P^1$ of example 16.4.8 , which has full mass, also lies in $\mathcal E^1(\mathbb P^1,\omega )$. Away from its only pole $z=0$ the function $u$ is bounded, and $\mu _ u$ is a finite measure. Near the pole write $r=\log |z|^2$. If $G$ is a smooth function of one real variable, then $\bar\partial G(\log |z|^2)=G'(r)\, \mathrm d\bar z/\bar z$ and $\partial \bar\partial G(\log |z|^2)=G''(r)\, \mathrm dz\wedge \mathrm d\bar z/|z|^2$ on $\mathbb C\setminus \{ 0\} $; since $\mathrm i\, \mathrm dz\wedge \mathrm d\bar z=2\, \mathrm dA$, where $\mathrm dA$ is Lebesgue measure, we get $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}G(\log |z|^2)=\pi ^{-1}G''(r)|z|^{-2}\, \mathrm dA$, which in polar coordinates $z=\rho \mathrm e^{\mathrm i\vartheta }$, with $r=2\log \rho $, is $(2\pi )^{-1}G''(r)\, \mathrm dr\, \mathrm d\vartheta $. The function $F$ of example 16.4.8 satisfies $F(r)=-\log (-r)$ for $r\leq r_0$, with $r_0$ sufficiently negative, and is therefore smooth there, with $F''(r)=r^{-2}$. On the punctured disc $\{ 0<|z|^2<\mathrm e^{r_0}\} $ the measure $\mu _ u$ is $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F(\log |z|^2)$, and it does not charge the pole; hence the image of its restriction to $\{ |z|^2<\mathrm e^{r_0}\} $ under $z\mapsto \log |z|^2$ is $F''(r)\, \mathrm dr=r^{-2}\, \mathrm dr$ on $(-\infty ,r_0)$. Since $u-F(\log |z|^2)=-\log (1+|z|^2)$ is bounded near the pole, the finiteness of $\int |u|\, \mu _ u$ near the pole reduces, after the substitution $t=-r$, to \[  \int _ a^\infty \frac{\log t}{t^2}\, \mathrm dt =\frac{\log a+1}{a}<\infty \qquad (a>1).  \] Hence $u$ is a potential of finite energy whose difference from the reference $V_\omega =0$ is unbounded.

title: Relative energy classes convex
text: Corollary 17.2.10 . The classes $\mathcal E^\infty (X,\theta ,\phi )$, $\mathcal E^1(X,\theta ,\phi )$ and $\mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi )$ are convex. If $u\in \mathcal E^1(X,\theta ,\phi )$, $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and $u\leq v\preceq \phi $, then $v\in \mathcal E^1(X,\theta ,\phi )$. Proof. Convex combinations of potentials with the same singularity type as $\phi $ have that singularity type. For $\mathcal E^1(X,\theta ,\phi )$, convexity follows from the concavity of the extended energy (proposition 17.2.7 ) and theorem 17.2.8 . If $u,v\in \mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi )$ and $0<t<1$, then $(1-t)u+tv\preceq \phi $, and by multilinearity $\mu _{(1-t)u+tv}$ is a combination of the mixed measures $\langle \theta _ u^ j\wedge \theta _ v^{n-j}\rangle $ with coefficients $\binom nj(1-t)^ jt^{n-j}$. Each of these measures has total mass $m$, as noted at the beginning of this section, so $\int _ X\langle \theta _{(1-t)u+tv}^ n\rangle =m$. The last assertion follows from the monotonicity of the extended energy and theorem 17.2.8 . $\square$

title: Relative cross energy estimate
text: Lemma 17.2.11 . Let $u\in \mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi )$, let $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ satisfy $v\preceq \phi $, and let $\gamma \colon X\to [-\infty ,\infty ]$ be a Borel function, for instance a $\theta $-psh function, with $\gamma \geq \max \{ u,v\} $. Then, allowing infinite values, \[  \int _ X(\gamma -u)\mu _ v \leq 2\int _ X(\gamma -u)\mu _ u +2\int _ X(\gamma -v)\mu _ v.  \] Consequently, if $u,v,w_1,\ldots ,w_ n\in \mathcal E^1(X,\theta ,\phi )$, then \[  \int _ X|u-v|\, \langle \theta _{w_1}\wedge \cdots \wedge \theta _{w_ n}\rangle <\infty .  \] Proof. For $t\geq 0$ we have \[  \{ \gamma >u+2t\} \subset \{ \gamma >v+t\} \cup \{ v>u+t\} ,  \] because $\gamma \leq v+t$ and $v\leq u+t$ imply $\gamma \leq u+2t$. The weights $\gamma -u$ and $\gamma -v$ are Borel functions with values in $[0,\infty ]$ on the complements of the pole sets of $u$ and $v$, respectively, and these pole sets carry no mass; the level sets above are taken on these complements. Since $u\in \mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi )$ and $v-t\preceq \phi $, the comparison principle of proposition 16.7.4 , applied with $p=n$ to $u$ and $v-t$, gives \[  \mu _ v(\{ v>u+t\} )\leq \mu _ u(\{ v>u+t\} )+\int _ X\langle \theta _\phi ^ n\rangle -\int _ X\langle \theta _ u^ n\rangle =\mu _ u(\{ v>u+t\} ).  \] Integrating over level sets, we obtain \[  \begin{split}  \int _ X(\gamma -u)\mu _ v & \leq 2\int _0^\infty \mu _ v(\{ \gamma >v+t\} )\, \mathrm dt +2\int _0^\infty \mu _ u(\{ v>u+t\} )\, \mathrm dt\\ & \leq 2\int _ X(\gamma -v)\mu _ v+2\int _ X(\gamma -u)\mu _ u, \end{split}  \] where in the last step we used $(v-u)_+\leq \gamma -u$, which holds because $\gamma \geq \max \{ u,v\} $. All functions involved are nonnegative, so Tonelli's theorem applies without any integrability assumption. For the second assertion, add constants to $u$ and $v$ so that $u,v\leq \phi $; this changes $|u-v|$ by at most a constant, and the mixed measure has finite mass $m$. Put $w=\frac1n\sum _ jw_ j$, which lies in $\mathcal E^1(X,\theta ,\phi )$ by corollary 17.2.10 . By multilinearity, $\langle \theta _{w_1}\wedge \cdots \wedge \theta _{w_ n}\rangle \leq n^ n\mu _ w$. Choose $C$ with $w\leq \phi +C$ and apply the first assertion to $u$, $w$ and $\gamma =\phi +C$: its right side is finite because $u,w\in \mathcal E^1(X,\theta ,\phi )$. Hence $\phi -u$ is integrable for $\mu _ w$, and so for the mixed measure. The same holds for $\phi -v$, and $|u-v|\leq (\phi -u)+(\phi -v)$. $\square$

title: Relative finite energy cocycle
text: Proposition 17.2.12 . For $u,v\in \mathcal E^1(X,\theta ,\phi )$, the cocycle formula ( 17.14 ) and the tangent bounds ( 17.17 ) remain valid. In particular, ( 17.12 ) computes the extended energy on $\mathcal E^1(X,\theta ,\phi )$. Proof. All mixed measures involved have total mass $m$, so both assertions are unchanged if constants are added to $u$ and $v$; we may therefore assume $u,v\leq \phi $. Put $u_ k=\max \{ u,\phi -k\} $ and $v_ k=\max \{ v,\phi -k\} $. Fix $0\leq j\leq n$ and write $\lambda _ k=\langle \theta _{u_ k}^ j\wedge \theta _{v_ k}^{n-j}\rangle $ and $\lambda =\langle \theta _ u^ j\wedge \theta _ v^{n-j}\rangle $. We show that 17.21 \begin{equation} \label{eq:finite-energy-cocycle-term-limit} \int _ X(u_ k-v_ k)\lambda _ k\longrightarrow \int _ X(u-v)\lambda . \end{equation} On the plurifine open set $A_ k=\{ u>\phi -k\} \cap \{ v>\phi -k\} $ the measures $\lambda _ k$ and $\lambda $ agree by locality, and $u_ k-v_ k=u-v$. By lemma 17.2.11 , $|u-v|$ is $\lambda $-integrable. The sets $X\setminus A_ k$ decrease to the union of the pole sets of $u$, $v$ and $\phi $, which is pluripolar and therefore $\lambda $-null, so dominated convergence gives $\int _{X\setminus A_ k}|u-v|\lambda \to 0$. It remains to show that the integral of $|u_ k-v_ k|$ against $\lambda _ k$ over $X\setminus A_ k$ tends to zero. For $z\in \{ u,v\} $ put $D_ k(z)=\{ z\leq \phi -k\} $, so that $X\setminus A_ k=D_ k(u)\cup D_ k(v)$. We claim that 17.22 \begin{equation} \label{eq:finite-energy-mixed-truncation-tail} k\lambda _ k(D_ k(z))\leq 2^ n k\mu _ z(\{ z\leq \phi -k/2\} )\longrightarrow 0. \end{equation} Consider $z=u$ and $j<n$, and put $q=(v_ k+\phi -k)/2$. Since $\phi -k\leq v_ k\leq \phi $, we have $q\leq \phi -k/2$ on $X$, and $u_ k=\phi -k\leq q$ on $D_ k(u)$. Moreover $\theta _{v_ k}\leq 2\theta _ q$, since $2\theta _ q-\theta _{v_ k}=\theta _\phi \geq 0$, so multilinearity gives $\lambda _ k\leq 2^{n-j}\langle \theta _{u_ k}^ j\wedge \theta _ q^{n-j}\rangle $. The potentials $q$ and $u_ k$ belong to $\mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi )$, and the non-strict comparison principle of proposition 16.7.4 , with $n-j$ factors $\theta _ q$ and the $j$ fixed factors $\theta _{u_ k}$, gives \[  \lambda _ k(D_ k(u)) \leq 2^{n-j}\mu _{u_ k}(\{ u_ k\leq q\} ) \leq 2^{n-j}\mu _{u_ k}(\{ u\leq \phi -k/2\} ).  \] For $j=n$ the same bound holds directly, since then $\lambda _ k=\mu _{u_ k}$ and $D_ k(u)\subset \{ u\leq \phi -k/2\} $. The measures $\mu _{u_ k}$ and $\mu _ u$ have the same total mass and agree on $\{ u>\phi -k/2\} $ by locality, so the last mass equals $\mu _ u(\{ u\leq \phi -k/2\} )$. Since exchanging $u$ and $v$ and replacing $j$ by $n-j$ does not change $\lambda _ k$, the case $z=v$ follows from the case $z=u$. Finally, \[  k\mu _ z(\{ z\leq \phi -k/2\} )\leq 2\int _{\{ z\leq \phi -k/2\} }(\phi -z)\mu _ z\longrightarrow 0  \] because $\phi -z$ is $\mu _ z$-integrable. This proves ( 17.22 ). Since $u_ k-\phi $ and $v_ k-\phi $ take values in $[-k,0]$, we have $|u_ k-v_ k|\leq k$, and ( 17.22 ) shows that the integral of $|u_ k-v_ k|$ against $\lambda _ k$ over $X\setminus A_ k$ tends to zero. This proves ( 17.21 ). Now pass to the limit in the cocycle formula for $u_ k,v_ k$: its left side converges to $E_\theta ^\phi (v)-E_\theta ^\phi (u)$ by proposition 17.2.6 , and each term on the right converges by ( 17.21 ). The tangent bounds pass to the limit in the same way, using the terms $j=n$ and $j=0$. Taking $v=\phi $ in the cocycle formula gives the last assertion. $\square$

title: Finite energy cocycle term limit
text: 17.21 \begin{equation} \label{eq:finite-energy-cocycle-term-limit} \int _ X(u_ k-v_ k)\lambda _ k\longrightarrow \int _ X(u-v)\lambda . \end{equation}
