text: 17.22 \begin{equation} \label{eq:finite-energy-mixed-truncation-tail} k\lambda _ k(D_ k(z))\leq 2^ n k\mu _ z(\{ z\leq \phi -k/2\} )\longrightarrow 0. \end{equation}

title: Continuity and compactness
text:
17.3 Continuity and compactness We keep $	heta $ and the model potential $\phi $ of mass $m$. Convergence in $L^1(X)$ refers to the volume form $\omega ^ n$, and a $	heta $-psh potential is determined by its class in $L^1(X)$. The energy is continuous along increasing nets and upper semicontinuous for $L^1$ convergence, so that normalized potentials with energy bounded below form compact sets (corollary 17.3.4 ), as the variational method of section 17.4 requires. The finite-energy class is also stable under rooftop envelopes, which gives finite energy along the Perron segments of section 17.6 . Proposition 17.3.1 . Let $(u_ i)_{i\in I}$ be an increasing net in $\mathcal E^1(X,	heta ,\phi )$ which is uniformly bounded above on $X$. Then its regularized upper envelope $u=(\sup _ i u_ i)^*$ belongs to $\mathcal E^1(X,	heta ,\phi )$ and \[  E_	heta ^\phi (u_ i)\uparrow E_	heta ^\phi (u).  \] Proof. By lemma 16.4.2 , $u_ i\leq \phi +\sup _ Xu_ i$, and the suprema $\sup _ Xu_ i$ are bounded above by hypothesis; hence $u\preceq \phi $. Since $u$ dominates every $u_ i$, monotonicity of the energy and theorem 17.2.8 show that $u\in \mathcal E^1(X,	heta ,\phi )$. Bounded differences. Consider first an increasing sequence $(u_ j)$ and a constant $C\geq 1$ such that $\phi -C\leq u_ j\leq u\leq \phi $ for all $j$. The pole sets of $u_ j$ and $u$ coincide with that of $\phi $. Let $f_ j$ be the function equal to $u-u_ j$ outside this pole set and to $0$ on it; it is a Borel function with values in $[0,C]$. By the tangent bound ( 17.17 ), \[  0\leq E_	heta ^\phi (u)-E_	heta ^\phi (u_ j) \leq \int _ X(u-u_ j)\, \mu _{u_ j}=\int _ Xf_ j\, \mu _{u_ j},  \] and we show that the right side tends to zero by applying lemma 17.1.1 with $
u _ j=\mu _{u_ j}$, $
u =\mu _ u$, the weights $f_ j$ and the limit weight $0$. For each $j$ the potential $C^{-1}u_ j+(1-C^{-1})\phi $ lies between $\phi -1$ and $\phi $ and its measure is at least $C^{-n}\mu _{u_ j}$; hence $\mu _{u_ j}\leq C^ n\operatorname {Cap}_{	heta ,\phi }$ on Borel sets, and likewise $\mu _ u\leq C^ n\operatorname {Cap}_{	heta ,\phi }$. By theorem 16.9.8 , the measures $\mu _{u_ j}$ and $\mu _ u$ are therefore uniformly absolutely continuous with respect to $\operatorname {Cap}_\omega $. They converge weakly by corollary 15.7.6 , since $u_ j$ increases to $u$ quasi-everywhere (corollary 10.2.2 ). It remains to show that $f_ j	o 0$ in capacity. Fix finitely many pairs of concentric coordinate balls $B_\alpha \Subset B'_\alpha $ as in proposition 16.9.9 , chosen so that $	heta $ has a smooth potential $h_\alpha $ on a neighborhood of $\overline{B'_\alpha }$ (this is possible by lemma 13.1.2 , applied on slightly larger concentric balls), and let $c$ be the constant of that proposition. Let $\delta ,\eta >0$. By proposition 16.9.9 (3) there is an open set $G$ with $\operatorname {Cap}_\omega (G)<\eta $ which contains the pole set of $\phi $ and such that $\phi $ is finite and continuous on the compact set $X\setminus G$. Let $L$ be a common bound for $|\phi |$ on $X\setminus G$ and for the functions $|h_\alpha |$ on $B'_\alpha $. The functions \[  w_{\alpha ,j}=\max \{ u_ j+h_\alpha ,-2L-C\} ,\qquad w_\alpha =\max \{ u+h_\alpha ,-2L-C\}   \] are bounded plurisubharmonic functions on $B'_\alpha $, and $w_{\alpha ,j}$ increases to $w_\alpha $ almost everywhere, because $u_ j$ increases to $u$ quasi-everywhere and pluripolar sets have Lebesgue measure zero. By theorem 9.5.1 , $w_{\alpha ,j}	o w_\alpha $ locally in capacity on $B'_\alpha $. On $B_\alpha \setminus G$ we have $u_ j+h_\alpha \geq \phi -C-L\geq -2L-C$, so the truncations are inactive there and $w_\alpha -w_{\alpha ,j}=u-u_ j$. Since the balls $B_\alpha $ cover $X$, \[  \{ f_ j>\delta \} \subset G\cup  igcup _\alpha  igl (B_\alpha \cap \{ w_{\alpha ,j}<w_\alpha -\delta \}  igr ).  \] By the countable subadditivity of $\operatorname {Cap}_\omega $ (proposition 16.7.6 ) and the bound $\operatorname {Cap}_\omega (E)\leq c\operatorname {Cap}_{B'_\alpha }(E)$ for Borel sets $E\subset B'_\alpha $ in proposition 16.9.9 , \[  \operatorname {Cap}_\omega (\{ f_ j>\delta \} )\leq \eta +c\sum _\alpha \operatorname {Cap}^*_{B'_\alpha } igl (\overline{B_\alpha }\cap \{ w_{\alpha ,j}<w_\alpha -\delta \}  igr ),  \] where we also used that the capacity of a Borel set is at most its outer capacity. By definition 9.4.5 , the sum tends to zero as $j	o \infty $. Hence $\varlimsup _ j\operatorname {Cap}_\omega (\{ f_ j>\delta \} )\leq \eta $, and since $\eta $ is arbitrary, $f_ j	o 0$ in capacity. Lemma 17.1.1 now gives $\int _ Xf_ j\, \mu _{u_ j}	o 0$, and hence $E_	heta ^\phi (u_ j)	o E_	heta ^\phi (u)$. Sequences. Now let $(u_ j)$ be an arbitrary increasing sequence; subtracting a common constant, we may assume $u_ j\leq u\leq \phi $. Put $u_{j,k}=\max \{ u_ j,\phi -k\} $ and $u_ k=\max \{ u,\phi -k\} $. For fixed $k$, the sequence $u_{j,k}$ increases to $\max \{ \sup _ ju_ j,\phi -k\} $, whose upper semicontinuous regularization is $\max \{ (\sup _ ju_ j)^*,\phi -k\} =u_ k$, because $\phi -k$ is upper semicontinuous; moreover $\phi -k\leq u_{j,k}\leq u_ k\leq \phi $. The preceding case, with $\max \{ k,1\} $ in place of $C$, gives $E_	heta ^\phi (u_{j,k})	o E_	heta ^\phi (u_ k)$ as $j	o \infty $. We bound the truncation error uniformly in $j$. The tangent bound of proposition 17.2.12 gives \[  0\leq E_	heta ^\phi (u_{j,k})-E_	heta ^\phi (u_ j) \leq \int _ X(u_{j,k}-u_ j)\, \mu _{u_ j} =\int _ k^\infty \mu _{u_ j}(\{ u_ j<\phi -t\} )\, \mathrm dt.  \] For $t\geq k$ put $q_ t=(u_ j+\phi -t)/2$. On $\{ u_ j<\phi -t\} $ we have $u_1\leq u_ j<q_ t$, and $q_ t\leq \phi -t/2$ on $X$. Since $\mu _{q_ t}\geq 2^{-n}\mu _{u_ j}$ by multilinearity, and $q_ t,u_1\in \mathcal E(X,	heta ,\phi )$, the comparison principle of proposition 16.7.4 gives \[   egin{aligned}  \mu _{u_ j}(\{ u_ j<\phi -t\} ) & \leq 2^ n\mu _{q_ t}(\{ u_1<q_ t\} )\ & \leq 2^ n\mu _{u_1}(\{ u_1<q_ t\} ) \leq 2^ n\mu _{u_1}(\{ u_1<\phi -t/2\} ). \end{aligned}  \] Consequently 17.25  egin{equation} \label{eq:relative-energy-uniform-truncation-error}  egin{aligned}  0& \leq E_	heta ^\phi (u_{j,k})-E_	heta ^\phi (u_ j)\ & \leq 2^{n+1}\int _ X(\phi -u_1-k/2)_+\, \mu _{u_1}\longrightarrow 0 \end{aligned} \end{equation} as $k	o \infty $, uniformly in $j$; the limit is zero by dominated convergence, since $\phi -u_1$ is $\mu _{u_1}$-integrable. Since $E_	heta ^\phi (u_ k)\geq E_	heta ^\phi (u)$, letting first $j	o \infty $ and then $k	o \infty $ gives $\lim _ jE_	heta ^\phi (u_ j)\geq E_	heta ^\phi (u)$, and monotonicity gives the reverse inequality. Nets. Let $(u_ i)_{i\in I}$ be a net as in the statement. Cover $X$ by finitely many coordinate charts $D_ eta $ on which $	heta $ has smooth potentials $h_ eta $. By theorem 8.3.2 , applied to the functions $u_ i+h_ eta $ on $D_ eta $, there are countable sets $J_ eta \subset I$ such that $(\sup _{i\in J_ eta }u_ i)^*=u$ on $D_ eta $. The countable set $J= igcup _ eta J_ eta $ then satisfies $(\sup _{i\in J}u_ i)^*=u$ on $X$, since on each $D_ eta $ this envelope lies between the envelopes over $J_ eta $ and over $I$. Since the index set is directed, we can choose indices $i_1\leq i_2\leq \cdots $ such that $i_ k$ dominates the first $k$ elements of an enumeration of $J$. Since the net is increasing, $\sup _ ku_{i_ k}\geq \sup _{i\in J}u_ i$, so the increasing sequence $(u_{i_ k})$ has regularized upper envelope $u$, and the sequence case gives $E_	heta ^\phi (u_{i_ k})	o E_	heta ^\phi (u)$. Each of these energies is at most $\sup _ iE_	heta ^\phi (u_ i)$, which in turn is at most $E_	heta ^\phi (u)$ by monotonicity. Hence $\sup _ iE_	heta ^\phi (u_ i)=E_	heta ^\phi (u)$, and since the net of energies is increasing, its limit is this supremum. (The selected indices need not be cofinal in $I$, which is why we compare suprema.) $\square$ Upper semicontinuity of the energy for $L^1$ convergence rests on the following description of $L^1$ limits of potentials by decreasing sequences. Lemma 17.3.2 . Let $	heta $ be a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form on $X$, and let $q_ k,q\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ satisfy $q_ k	o q$ in $L^1(X)$. Then the functions $q_ k$ are uniformly bounded above on $X$, the tail envelopes $a_ j=(\sup _{k\geq j}q_ k)^*$ belong to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$, and $a_ j$ decreases pointwise to $q$ as $j	o \infty $. In particular, if $\psi \colon X	o [-\infty ,\infty )$ is upper semicontinuous and $q_ k\leq \psi $ for every $k$, then $q\leq \psi $. Proof. By proposition 14.2.1 the suprema $\sup _ Xq_ k$ converge to $\sup _ Xq$, so they are bounded. Hence the tail envelopes $a_ j$ are $	heta $-psh, by theorem 8.3.2 applied in charts after adding smooth local potentials of $	heta $, and they decrease as $j$ increases. A subsequence of $(q_ k)$ converges to $q$ almost everywhere, so $a_ j\geq q$ almost everywhere, hence everywhere, since both functions are $	heta $-psh (section 16.1 ). Conversely, let $x\in X$ and $\varepsilon >0$, let $h$ be a smooth local potential of $	heta $ on a coordinate ball $\Omega $ around $x$, and let $M>q(x)+h(x)$ be a real number. By upper semicontinuity there is a closed coordinate ball $K\subset \Omega $ around $x$ on which $q+h<M$ and $|h-h(x)|<\varepsilon $. The plurisubharmonic functions $q_ k+h$ converge to $q+h$ in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$, so Hartogs' lemma in the form of theorem 8.3.4 , applied with the constant function $M$ on $K$, gives $q_ k+h<M$ on $K$ for all large $k$. For such $k$ we have $q_ k<M-h(x)+\varepsilon $ on $K$. Since $K$ is a neighborhood of $x$, it follows that $a_ j(x)\leq M-h(x)+\varepsilon $ for all large $j$. Letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ and $M\downarrow q(x)+h(x)$, or $M	o -\infty $ if $q(x)=-\infty $, we obtain $\lim _ ja_ j(x)\leq q(x)$. Thus $a_ j\downarrow q$. Finally, if $q_ k\leq \psi $ for all $k$ with $\psi $ upper semicontinuous, then $\sup _{k\geq j}q_ k\leq \psi $, so $a_ j\leq \psi $ for every $j$, and therefore $q=\lim _ ja_ j\leq \psi $. $\square$ Proposition 17.3.3 . The set $\{ u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta ):u\preceq \phi \} $ is closed in $L^1(X)$, and $E_	heta ^\phi $ is upper semicontinuous on it, with values in $[-\infty ,\infty )$: if $u_ j	o u$ in $L^1(X)$, then \[  E_	heta ^\phi (u)\geq \varlimsup _ j E_	heta ^\phi (u_ j).  \] Proof. Let $u_ j\preceq \phi $ converge to $u$ in $L^1(X)$. By lemma 17.3.2 , the $u_ j$ are uniformly bounded above, so lemma 16.4.2 gives a constant $C$ with $u_ j\leq \phi +C$ for all $j$. Since $\phi +C$ is upper semicontinuous, the same lemma gives $u\leq \phi +C$, which proves closedness. The lemma also shows that the tail envelopes $v_ j=(\sup _{k\geq j}u_ k)^*$ are $	heta $-psh potentials which decrease pointwise to $u$; moreover $v_ j\leq \phi +C$, because $\phi +C$ is upper semicontinuous and dominates every $u_ k$. Since $u_ j\leq v_ j$, monotonicity and proposition 17.2.7 give \[  \varlimsup _ j E_	heta ^\phi (u_ j) \leq \lim _ jE_	heta ^\phi (v_ j)=E_	heta ^\phi (u).  \] Since $L^1(X)$ is a metric space, sequential upper semicontinuity is upper semicontinuity. $\square$ Corollary 17.3.4 . For $B\geq 0$, the set \[  \{ u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta ):u\leq \phi ,\quad E_	heta ^\phi (u)\geq -B\}   \] is compact in $L^1(X)$ and is contained in $\mathcal E^1(X,	heta ,\phi )$. The set \[  K_\phi =\{ u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta ):u\leq \phi ,\quad \sup _ Xu=0\}   \] is also compact in $L^1(X)$. Proof. For $u$ in the first set, lemma 16.4.2 gives $u\leq \phi +\sup _ Xu$, so monotonicity and the shift formula give $-B\leq E_	heta ^\phi (u)\leq m\sup _ Xu$. Also $\sup _ Xu\leq \sup _ X\phi =0$. Hence the set lies in $\{ u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta ):-B/m\leq \sup _ Xu\leq 0\} $, which is compact in $L^1(X)$ by proposition 14.2.1 . The set is closed in $L^1(X)$: the inequality $u\leq \phi $ passes to $L^1$ limits by lemma 17.3.2 , since $\phi $ is upper semicontinuous, and the energy bound passes to limits by upper semicontinuity (proposition 17.3.3 ). It is therefore compact. Its members have finite energy, so they lie in $\mathcal E^1(X,	heta ,\phi )$ by theorem 17.2.8 . The set $K_\phi $ is contained in $\{ u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta ):\sup _ Xu=0\} $, which is compact in $L^1(X)$ by proposition 14.2.1 , and it is closed in $L^1(X)$, because the supremum is continuous for $L^1$ convergence of potentials (by the same proposition) and the inequality $u\leq \phi $ passes to $L^1$ limits by lemma 17.3.2 . Hence $K_\phi $ is compact. $\square$ Proposition 17.3.5 . Let $\mathcal F$ be one of the three classes $\mathcal E(X,	heta ,\phi )$, $\mathcal E^1(X,	heta ,\phi )$ and $\mathcal E^\infty (X,	heta ,\phi )$. The regularized upper envelope of a nonempty family in $\mathcal F$ which is uniformly bounded above on $X$ belongs to $\mathcal F$. Proof. By lemma 16.4.2 , every member of the family is bounded above by $\phi +C$ for a common constant $C$, and so is the regularized upper envelope $U$. Fix a member $u_0$ of the family; then $u_0\leq U\preceq \phi $. For $\mathcal F=\mathcal E(X,	heta ,\phi )$, mass monotonicity gives $m=\int _ X\langle 	heta _{u_0}^ nangle \leq \int _ X\langle 	heta _ U^ nangle \leq m$. For $\mathcal F=\mathcal E^1(X,	heta ,\phi )$, the last assertion of corollary 17.2.10 , applied to $u_0\leq U$, gives $U\in \mathcal F$. For $\mathcal F=\mathcal E^\infty (X,	heta ,\phi )$, the member $u_0$ supplies a lower bound $U\geq u_0\geq \phi -C'$. $\square$ Proposition 17.3.6 . Let $u,v\in \mathcal E(X,	heta ,\phi )$. Then the rooftop envelope $w=P_	heta (u,v)$ of definition 16.1.5 is not identically $-\infty $, and it belongs to $\mathcal E(X,	heta ,\phi )$. If moreover $u,v\in \mathcal E^1(X,	heta ,\phi )$, then $w\in \mathcal E^1(X,	heta ,\phi )$, and if in addition $u,v\leq \phi $, then \[  \int _ X(\phi -w)\, \mu _ w \leq \int _ X(\phi -u)\, \mu _ u+\int _ X(\phi -v)\, \mu _ v.  \] Proof. Since $u\leq \max \{ u,v\} \preceq \phi $, mass monotonicity gives $\int _ X\langle 	heta _{\max \{ u,v\} }^ nangle =m$. Thus $\int _ X\langle 	heta _ u^ nangle +\int _ X\langle 	heta _ v^ nangle =2m>\int _ X\langle 	heta _{\max \{ u,v\} }^ nangle $, and proposition 16.5.1 shows that $w
eq -\infty $. Theorem 16.5.5 gives $2m\leq m+\int _ X\langle 	heta _ w^ nangle $, while $\int _ X\langle 	heta _ w^ nangle \leq m$ by mass monotonicity, since $w\leq u$. Hence $w\in \mathcal E(X,	heta ,\phi )$. Now let $u,v\in \mathcal E^1(X,	heta ,\phi )$. The rooftop commutes with adding a common constant to $u$ and $v$ (proposition 16.1.4 (3)), so we may assume $u,v\leq \phi $; then $w\leq \phi $. The contact inequality of corollary 16.2.6 gives \[  \mu _ w\leq \mathbf1_{\{ w=u\} }\mu _ u +\mathbf1_{\{ w=v\} }\mu _ v.  \] Integrate the nonnegative weight $\min \{ \phi -w,N\} $ against both sides. On the first contact set the weight equals $\min \{ \phi -u,N\} $, and on the second it equals $\min \{ \phi -v,N\} $; pole sets carry no mass. Letting $N	o \infty $ gives the displayed bound. Both terms on the right are finite, so $w\in \mathcal E^1(X,	heta ,\phi )$. $\square$ Corollary 17.3.7 . For $u,v\in \mathcal E(X,	heta ,\phi )$, the singularity-constrained envelope of definition 16.7.1 satisfies $P_	heta [u](v)=v$. Proof. By proposition 17.3.6 , the rooftop $w=P_	heta (u,v)$ belongs to $\mathcal E(X,	heta ,\phi )$. Since $w\preceq v$ and $\int _ X\langle 	heta _ w^ nangle =\int _ X\langle 	heta _ v^ nangle >0$, proposition 16.4.10 gives $P_	heta [w](v)=v$. Every competitor for $P_	heta [w](v)$ is more singular than $w$, hence than $u$, so it is a competitor for $P_	heta [u](v)$; and $P_	heta [u](v)\leq v$ quasi-everywhere by proposition 16.7.2 (1), hence everywhere. Therefore $v=P_	heta [w](v)\leq P_	heta [u](v)\leq v$. $\square$ Proposition 17.3.8 . For $u,v\in \mathcal E^1(X,	heta ,\phi )$ and $u_ t=(1-t)u+tv$, the function $t\mapsto E_	heta ^\phi (u_ t)$ is continuously differentiable on $[0,1]$, with one-sided derivatives at the endpoints, and \[   rac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}E_	heta ^\phi (u_ t) =\int _ X(v-u)\, \mu _{u_ t}.  \] The derivative is a polynomial in $t$. Proof. By lemma 17.2.11 every integral $\int _ X(v-u)\langle 	heta _ v^ a\wedge 	heta _ u^{n-a}angle $ is finite. Expanding $\mu _{u_ t}$ by multilinearity shows that the right side is a polynomial in $t$ with these integrals as coefficients. The potentials $u_ t$ lie in $\mathcal E^1(X,	heta ,\phi )$ by corollary 17.2.10 . Apply the cocycle formula of proposition 17.2.12 to $u_{t+s}$ and $u_ t$, with $s
eq 0$ and $t,t+s\in [0,1]$, and use $u_{t+s}-u_ t=s(v-u)$: \[   rac{E_	heta ^\phi (u_{t+s})-E_	heta ^\phi (u_ t)}s = rac1{n+1}\sum _{j=0}^ n\int _ X(v-u)\langle 	heta _{u_{t+s}}^ j\wedge 	heta _{u_ t}^{n-j}angle .  \] Each mixed integral on the right is a polynomial in $s$ with the finite coefficients above, and at $s=0$ each of the $n+1$ terms equals $\int _ X(v-u)\mu _{u_ t}$. Letting $s	o 0$ proves the formula for the derivative, including the one-sided derivatives at the endpoints, and its continuity. $\square$ Lemma 17.3.9 . For $u,v\in \mathcal E^1(X,	heta ,\phi )$, \[  \int _ X(v-u)\, \mu _ v\leq E_	heta ^\phi (v)-E_	heta ^\phi (u) \leq \int _ X(v-u)\, \mu _ u.  \] If moreover $u\leq v$, then \[   rac1{n+1}\int _ X(v-u)\, \mu _ u\leq E_	heta ^\phi (v)-E_	heta ^\phi (u).  \] Proof. The first display is the tangent bound ( 17.17 ), which holds on $\mathcal E^1(X,	heta ,\phi )$ by proposition 17.2.12 . By the same proposition, the cocycle formula ( 17.14 ) holds for $u$ and $v$. If $u\leq v$, all its terms are nonnegative, and retaining the term $j=0$, whose measure is $\mu _ u$, gives the second display. $\square$ Example 17.3.10 . The energy is not continuous for $L^1$ convergence, even for smooth potentials on $\mathbb P^1$. Let $\omega =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log (1+|z|^2)$, which has mass one. For $0<a<1$ put $\varepsilon _ a=\exp (-a^{-2})$ and \[  u_ a(z)=a\log  rac{|z|^2+\varepsilon _ a}{1+|z|^2}.  \] These functions extend smoothly across infinity, and $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ a=(1-a)\omega +a\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log (|z|^2+\varepsilon _ a)>0$. They tend to zero in $L^1$ as $a\downarrow 0$, since $a\log (|z|^2/(1+|z|^2))\leq u_ a\leq 0$ and the left side is $a$ times a fixed integrable function. We compute their Dirichlet energies. Write $r=\log |z|^2$ and $F(r)=\log (\mathrm e^ r+\varepsilon )-\log (1+\mathrm e^ r)$ with $\varepsilon =\varepsilon _ a$, so that $u_ a=aF(\log |z|^2)$. For a smooth function $g=G(\log |z|^2)$ we have $\partial g=G'(r)\, \mathrm dz/z$, hence $\mathrm dg\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}g= rac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }\partial g\wedge  ar\partial g=\pi ^{-1}G'(r)^2|z|^{-2}\, \mathrm dA$, where $\mathrm dA$ is Lebesgue measure; integration in polar coordinates gives $\int \mathrm dg\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}g=\int _{-\infty }^\infty G'(r)^2\, \mathrm dr$. Therefore \[  \int _ X\mathrm du_ a\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}u_ a =a^2\int _{-\infty }^\infty F'(r)^2\, \mathrm dr =a^2(-\log \varepsilon _ a+O(1))\longrightarrow 1.  \] The bound $O(1)$ is uniform in $a$. Indeed, we have \[  F'(r)= rac{\mathrm e^ r}{\mathrm e^ r+\varepsilon }- rac{\mathrm e^ r}{1+\mathrm e^ r}\in [0,1],\qquad 1-F'(r)= rac{\varepsilon }{\mathrm e^ r+\varepsilon }+ rac{\mathrm e^ r}{1+\mathrm e^ r}\leq \varepsilon \mathrm e^{-r}+\mathrm e^ r.  \] On $[\log \varepsilon ,0]$ the integral of $\varepsilon \mathrm e^{-r}+\mathrm e^ r$ is at most $2$, and $1\geq F'^2\geq 1-2(1-F')$, so $\int _{\log \varepsilon }^0F'^2\, \mathrm dr=-\log \varepsilon +O(1)$. On the left tail $F'(r)\leq \mathrm e^ r/\varepsilon $, and on the right tail $F'(r)\leq \mathrm e^{-r}$; the corresponding integrals of $F'^2$ are at most $ rac12$. Since $\int _ Xu_ a\, \omega 	o 0$, the formula of example 17.2.9 gives $E_\omega (u_ a)	o - rac12$, whereas $E_\omega (0)=0$.

title: Relative energy increasing continuity
text: Proposition 17.3.1 . Let $(u_ i)_{i\in I}$ be an increasing net in $\mathcal E^1(X,\theta ,\phi )$ which is uniformly bounded above on $X$. Then its regularized upper envelope $u=(\sup _ i u_ i)^*$ belongs to $\mathcal E^1(X,\theta ,\phi )$ and \[  E_\theta ^\phi (u_ i)\uparrow E_\theta ^\phi (u).  \] Proof. By lemma 16.4.2 , $u_ i\leq \phi +\sup _ Xu_ i$, and the suprema $\sup _ Xu_ i$ are bounded above by hypothesis; hence $u\preceq \phi $. Since $u$ dominates every $u_ i$, monotonicity of the energy and theorem 17.2.8 show that $u\in \mathcal E^1(X,\theta ,\phi )$. Bounded differences. Consider first an increasing sequence $(u_ j)$ and a constant $C\geq 1$ such that $\phi -C\leq u_ j\leq u\leq \phi $ for all $j$. The pole sets of $u_ j$ and $u$ coincide with that of $\phi $. Let $f_ j$ be the function equal to $u-u_ j$ outside this pole set and to $0$ on it; it is a Borel function with values in $[0,C]$. By the tangent bound ( 17.17 ), \[  0\leq E_\theta ^\phi (u)-E_\theta ^\phi (u_ j) \leq \int _ X(u-u_ j)\, \mu _{u_ j}=\int _ Xf_ j\, \mu _{u_ j},  \] and we show that the right side tends to zero by applying lemma 17.1.1 with $\nu _ j=\mu _{u_ j}$, $\nu =\mu _ u$, the weights $f_ j$ and the limit weight $0$. For each $j$ the potential $C^{-1}u_ j+(1-C^{-1})\phi $ lies between $\phi -1$ and $\phi $ and its measure is at least $C^{-n}\mu _{u_ j}$; hence $\mu _{u_ j}\leq C^ n\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }$ on Borel sets, and likewise $\mu _ u\leq C^ n\operatorname {Cap}_{\theta ,\phi }$. By theorem 16.9.8 , the measures $\mu _{u_ j}$ and $\mu _ u$ are therefore uniformly absolutely continuous with respect to $\operatorname {Cap}_\omega $. They converge weakly by corollary 15.7.6 , since $u_ j$ increases to $u$ quasi-everywhere (corollary 10.2.2 ). It remains to show that $f_ j\to 0$ in capacity. Fix finitely many pairs of concentric coordinate balls $B_\alpha \Subset B'_\alpha $ as in proposition 16.9.9 , chosen so that $\theta $ has a smooth potential $h_\alpha $ on a neighborhood of $\overline{B'_\alpha }$ (this is possible by lemma 13.1.2 , applied on slightly larger concentric balls), and let $c$ be the constant of that proposition. Let $\delta ,\eta >0$. By proposition 16.9.9 (3) there is an open set $G$ with $\operatorname {Cap}_\omega (G)<\eta $ which contains the pole set of $\phi $ and such that $\phi $ is finite and continuous on the compact set $X\setminus G$. Let $L$ be a common bound for $|\phi |$ on $X\setminus G$ and for the functions $|h_\alpha |$ on $B'_\alpha $. The functions \[  w_{\alpha ,j}=\max \{ u_ j+h_\alpha ,-2L-C\} ,\qquad w_\alpha =\max \{ u+h_\alpha ,-2L-C\}   \] are bounded plurisubharmonic functions on $B'_\alpha $, and $w_{\alpha ,j}$ increases to $w_\alpha $ almost everywhere, because $u_ j$ increases to $u$ quasi-everywhere and pluripolar sets have Lebesgue measure zero. By theorem 9.5.1 , $w_{\alpha ,j}\to w_\alpha $ locally in capacity on $B'_\alpha $. On $B_\alpha \setminus G$ we have $u_ j+h_\alpha \geq \phi -C-L\geq -2L-C$, so the truncations are inactive there and $w_\alpha -w_{\alpha ,j}=u-u_ j$. Since the balls $B_\alpha $ cover $X$, \[  \{ f_ j>\delta \} \subset G\cup \bigcup _\alpha \bigl (B_\alpha \cap \{ w_{\alpha ,j}<w_\alpha -\delta \} \bigr ).  \] By the countable subadditivity of $\operatorname {Cap}_\omega $ (proposition 16.7.6 ) and the bound $\operatorname {Cap}_\omega (E)\leq c\operatorname {Cap}_{B'_\alpha }(E)$ for Borel sets $E\subset B'_\alpha $ in proposition 16.9.9 , \[  \operatorname {Cap}_\omega (\{ f_ j>\delta \} )\leq \eta +c\sum _\alpha \operatorname {Cap}^*_{B'_\alpha }\bigl (\overline{B_\alpha }\cap \{ w_{\alpha ,j}<w_\alpha -\delta \} \bigr ),  \] where we also used that the capacity of a Borel set is at most its outer capacity. By definition 9.4.5 , the sum tends to zero as $j\to \infty $. Hence $\varlimsup _ j\operatorname {Cap}_\omega (\{ f_ j>\delta \} )\leq \eta $, and since $\eta $ is arbitrary, $f_ j\to 0$ in capacity. Lemma 17.1.1 now gives $\int _ Xf_ j\, \mu _{u_ j}\to 0$, and hence $E_\theta ^\phi (u_ j)\to E_\theta ^\phi (u)$. Sequences. Now let $(u_ j)$ be an arbitrary increasing sequence; subtracting a common constant, we may assume $u_ j\leq u\leq \phi $. Put $u_{j,k}=\max \{ u_ j,\phi -k\} $ and $u_ k=\max \{ u,\phi -k\} $. For fixed $k$, the sequence $u_{j,k}$ increases to $\max \{ \sup _ ju_ j,\phi -k\} $, whose upper semicontinuous regularization is $\max \{ (\sup _ ju_ j)^*,\phi -k\} =u_ k$, because $\phi -k$ is upper semicontinuous; moreover $\phi -k\leq u_{j,k}\leq u_ k\leq \phi $. The preceding case, with $\max \{ k,1\} $ in place of $C$, gives $E_\theta ^\phi (u_{j,k})\to E_\theta ^\phi (u_ k)$ as $j\to \infty $. We bound the truncation error uniformly in $j$. The tangent bound of proposition 17.2.12 gives \[  0\leq E_\theta ^\phi (u_{j,k})-E_\theta ^\phi (u_ j) \leq \int _ X(u_{j,k}-u_ j)\, \mu _{u_ j} =\int _ k^\infty \mu _{u_ j}(\{ u_ j<\phi -t\} )\, \mathrm dt.  \] For $t\geq k$ put $q_ t=(u_ j+\phi -t)/2$. On $\{ u_ j<\phi -t\} $ we have $u_1\leq u_ j<q_ t$, and $q_ t\leq \phi -t/2$ on $X$. Since $\mu _{q_ t}\geq 2^{-n}\mu _{u_ j}$ by multilinearity, and $q_ t,u_1\in \mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi )$, the comparison principle of proposition 16.7.4 gives \[  \begin{aligned}  \mu _{u_ j}(\{ u_ j<\phi -t\} ) & \leq 2^ n\mu _{q_ t}(\{ u_1<q_ t\} )\\ & \leq 2^ n\mu _{u_1}(\{ u_1<q_ t\} ) \leq 2^ n\mu _{u_1}(\{ u_1<\phi -t/2\} ). \end{aligned}  \] Consequently 17.25 \begin{equation} \label{eq:relative-energy-uniform-truncation-error} \begin{aligned}  0& \leq E_\theta ^\phi (u_{j,k})-E_\theta ^\phi (u_ j)\\ & \leq 2^{n+1}\int _ X(\phi -u_1-k/2)_+\, \mu _{u_1}\longrightarrow 0 \end{aligned} \end{equation} as $k\to \infty $, uniformly in $j$; the limit is zero by dominated convergence, since $\phi -u_1$ is $\mu _{u_1}$-integrable. Since $E_\theta ^\phi (u_ k)\geq E_\theta ^\phi (u)$, letting first $j\to \infty $ and then $k\to \infty $ gives $\lim _ jE_\theta ^\phi (u_ j)\geq E_\theta ^\phi (u)$, and monotonicity gives the reverse inequality. Nets. Let $(u_ i)_{i\in I}$ be a net as in the statement. Cover $X$ by finitely many coordinate charts $D_\beta $ on which $\theta $ has smooth potentials $h_\beta $. By theorem 8.3.2 , applied to the functions $u_ i+h_\beta $ on $D_\beta $, there are countable sets $J_\beta \subset I$ such that $(\sup _{i\in J_\beta }u_ i)^*=u$ on $D_\beta $. The countable set $J=\bigcup _\beta J_\beta $ then satisfies $(\sup _{i\in J}u_ i)^*=u$ on $X$, since on each $D_\beta $ this envelope lies between the envelopes over $J_\beta $ and over $I$. Since the index set is directed, we can choose indices $i_1\leq i_2\leq \cdots $ such that $i_ k$ dominates the first $k$ elements of an enumeration of $J$. Since the net is increasing, $\sup _ ku_{i_ k}\geq \sup _{i\in J}u_ i$, so the increasing sequence $(u_{i_ k})$ has regularized upper envelope $u$, and the sequence case gives $E_\theta ^\phi (u_{i_ k})\to E_\theta ^\phi (u)$. Each of these energies is at most $\sup _ iE_\theta ^\phi (u_ i)$, which in turn is at most $E_\theta ^\phi (u)$ by monotonicity. Hence $\sup _ iE_\theta ^\phi (u_ i)=E_\theta ^\phi (u)$, and since the net of energies is increasing, its limit is this supremum. (The selected indices need not be cofinal in $I$, which is why we compare suprema.) $\square$

title: Relative energy uniform truncation error
text: 17.25 \begin{equation} \label{eq:relative-energy-uniform-truncation-error} \begin{aligned}  0& \leq E_\theta ^\phi (u_{j,k})-E_\theta ^\phi (u_ j)\\ & \leq 2^{n+1}\int _ X(\phi -u_1-k/2)_+\, \mu _{u_1}\longrightarrow 0 \end{aligned} \end{equation}

title: Global lone tail envelopes
text: Lemma 17.3.2 . Let $\theta $ be a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form on $X$, and let $q_ k,q\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ satisfy $q_ k\to q$ in $L^1(X)$. Then the functions $q_ k$ are uniformly bounded above on $X$, the tail envelopes $a_ j=(\sup _{k\geq j}q_ k)^*$ belong to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, and $a_ j$ decreases pointwise to $q$ as $j\to \infty $. In particular, if $\psi \colon X\to [-\infty ,\infty )$ is upper semicontinuous and $q_ k\leq \psi $ for every $k$, then $q\leq \psi $. Proof. By proposition 14.2.1 the suprema $\sup _ Xq_ k$ converge to $\sup _ Xq$, so they are bounded. Hence the tail envelopes $a_ j$ are $\theta $-psh, by theorem 8.3.2 applied in charts after adding smooth local potentials of $\theta $, and they decrease as $j$ increases. A subsequence of $(q_ k)$ converges to $q$ almost everywhere, so $a_ j\geq q$ almost everywhere, hence everywhere, since both functions are $\theta $-psh (section 16.1 ). Conversely, let $x\in X$ and $\varepsilon >0$, let $h$ be a smooth local potential of $\theta $ on a coordinate ball $\Omega $ around $x$, and let $M>q(x)+h(x)$ be a real number. By upper semicontinuity there is a closed coordinate ball $K\subset \Omega $ around $x$ on which $q+h<M$ and $|h-h(x)|<\varepsilon $. The plurisubharmonic functions $q_ k+h$ converge to $q+h$ in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$, so Hartogs' lemma in the form of theorem 8.3.4 , applied with the constant function $M$ on $K$, gives $q_ k+h<M$ on $K$ for all large $k$. For such $k$ we have $q_ k<M-h(x)+\varepsilon $ on $K$. Since $K$ is a neighborhood of $x$, it follows that $a_ j(x)\leq M-h(x)+\varepsilon $ for all large $j$. Letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ and $M\downarrow q(x)+h(x)$, or $M\to -\infty $ if $q(x)=-\infty $, we obtain $\lim _ ja_ j(x)\leq q(x)$. Thus $a_ j\downarrow q$. Finally, if $q_ k\leq \psi $ for all $k$ with $\psi $ upper semicontinuous, then $\sup _{k\geq j}q_ k\leq \psi $, so $a_ j\leq \psi $ for every $j$, and therefore $q=\lim _ ja_ j\leq \psi $. $\square$

title: Relative energy lone upper semicontinuity
text: Proposition 17.3.3 . The set $\{ u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ):u\preceq \phi \} $ is closed in $L^1(X)$, and $E_\theta ^\phi $ is upper semicontinuous on it, with values in $[-\infty ,\infty )$: if $u_ j\to u$ in $L^1(X)$, then \[  E_\theta ^\phi (u)\geq \varlimsup _ j E_\theta ^\phi (u_ j).  \] Proof. Let $u_ j\preceq \phi $ converge to $u$ in $L^1(X)$. By lemma 17.3.2 , the $u_ j$ are uniformly bounded above, so lemma 16.4.2 gives a constant $C$ with $u_ j\leq \phi +C$ for all $j$. Since $\phi +C$ is upper semicontinuous, the same lemma gives $u\leq \phi +C$, which proves closedness. The lemma also shows that the tail envelopes $v_ j=(\sup _{k\geq j}u_ k)^*$ are $\theta $-psh potentials which decrease pointwise to $u$; moreover $v_ j\leq \phi +C$, because $\phi +C$ is upper semicontinuous and dominates every $u_ k$. Since $u_ j\leq v_ j$, monotonicity and proposition 17.2.7 give \[  \varlimsup _ j E_\theta ^\phi (u_ j) \leq \lim _ jE_\theta ^\phi (v_ j)=E_\theta ^\phi (u).  \] Since $L^1(X)$ is a metric space, sequential upper semicontinuity is upper semicontinuity. $\square$

title: Relative energy compact sublevels
text: Corollary 17.3.4 . For $B\geq 0$, the set \[  \{ u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ):u\leq \phi ,\quad E_\theta ^\phi (u)\geq -B\}   \] is compact in $L^1(X)$ and is contained in $\mathcal E^1(X,\theta ,\phi )$. The set \[  K_\phi =\{ u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ):u\leq \phi ,\quad \sup _ Xu=0\}   \] is also compact in $L^1(X)$. Proof. For $u$ in the first set, lemma 16.4.2 gives $u\leq \phi +\sup _ Xu$, so monotonicity and the shift formula give $-B\leq E_\theta ^\phi (u)\leq m\sup _ Xu$. Also $\sup _ Xu\leq \sup _ X\phi =0$. Hence the set lies in $\{ u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ):-B/m\leq \sup _ Xu\leq 0\} $, which is compact in $L^1(X)$ by proposition 14.2.1 . The set is closed in $L^1(X)$: the inequality $u\leq \phi $ passes to $L^1$ limits by lemma 17.3.2 , since $\phi $ is upper semicontinuous, and the energy bound passes to limits by upper semicontinuity (proposition 17.3.3 ). It is therefore compact. Its members have finite energy, so they lie in $\mathcal E^1(X,\theta ,\phi )$ by theorem 17.2.8 . The set $K_\phi $ is contained in $\{ u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ):\sup _ Xu=0\} $, which is compact in $L^1(X)$ by proposition 14.2.1 , and it is closed in $L^1(X)$, because the supremum is continuous for $L^1$ convergence of potentials (by the same proposition) and the inequality $u\leq \phi $ passes to $L^1$ limits by lemma 17.3.2 . Hence $K_\phi $ is compact. $\square$

title: Relative energy family supremum
text: Proposition 17.3.5 . Let $\mathcal F$ be one of the three classes $\mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi )$, $\mathcal E^1(X,\theta ,\phi )$ and $\mathcal E^\infty (X,\theta ,\phi )$. The regularized upper envelope of a nonempty family in $\mathcal F$ which is uniformly bounded above on $X$ belongs to $\mathcal F$. Proof. By lemma 16.4.2 , every member of the family is bounded above by $\phi +C$ for a common constant $C$, and so is the regularized upper envelope $U$. Fix a member $u_0$ of the family; then $u_0\leq U\preceq \phi $. For $\mathcal F=\mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi )$, mass monotonicity gives $m=\int _ X\langle \theta _{u_0}^ n\rangle \leq \int _ X\langle \theta _ U^ n\rangle \leq m$. For $\mathcal F=\mathcal E^1(X,\theta ,\phi )$, the last assertion of corollary 17.2.10 , applied to $u_0\leq U$, gives $U\in \mathcal F$. For $\mathcal F=\mathcal E^\infty (X,\theta ,\phi )$, the member $u_0$ supplies a lower bound $U\geq u_0\geq \phi -C'$. $\square$

title: Relative finite energy rooftop closure
text: Proposition 17.3.6 . Let $u,v\in \mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi )$. Then the rooftop envelope $w=P_\theta (u,v)$ of definition 16.1.5 is not identically $-\infty $, and it belongs to $\mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi )$. If moreover $u,v\in \mathcal E^1(X,\theta ,\phi )$, then $w\in \mathcal E^1(X,\theta ,\phi )$, and if in addition $u,v\leq \phi $, then \[  \int _ X(\phi -w)\, \mu _ w \leq \int _ X(\phi -u)\, \mu _ u+\int _ X(\phi -v)\, \mu _ v.  \] Proof. Since $u\leq \max \{ u,v\} \preceq \phi $, mass monotonicity gives $\int _ X\langle \theta _{\max \{ u,v\} }^ n\rangle =m$. Thus $\int _ X\langle \theta _ u^ n\rangle +\int _ X\langle \theta _ v^ n\rangle =2m>\int _ X\langle \theta _{\max \{ u,v\} }^ n\rangle $, and proposition 16.5.1 shows that $w\neq -\infty $. Theorem 16.5.5 gives $2m\leq m+\int _ X\langle \theta _ w^ n\rangle $, while $\int _ X\langle \theta _ w^ n\rangle \leq m$ by mass monotonicity, since $w\leq u$. Hence $w\in \mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi )$. Now let $u,v\in \mathcal E^1(X,\theta ,\phi )$. The rooftop commutes with adding a common constant to $u$ and $v$ (proposition 16.1.4 (3)), so we may assume $u,v\leq \phi $; then $w\leq \phi $. The contact inequality of corollary 16.2.6 gives \[  \mu _ w\leq \mathbf1_{\{ w=u\} }\mu _ u +\mathbf1_{\{ w=v\} }\mu _ v.  \] Integrate the nonnegative weight $\min \{ \phi -w,N\} $ against both sides. On the first contact set the weight equals $\min \{ \phi -u,N\} $, and on the second it equals $\min \{ \phi -v,N\} $; pole sets carry no mass. Letting $N\to \infty $ gives the displayed bound. Both terms on the right are finite, so $w\in \mathcal E^1(X,\theta ,\phi )$. $\square$

title: Mutual full mass singularity envelopes
text: Corollary 17.3.7 . For $u,v\in \mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi )$, the singularity-constrained envelope of definition 16.7.1 satisfies $P_\theta [u](v)=v$. Proof. By proposition 17.3.6 , the rooftop $w=P_\theta (u,v)$ belongs to $\mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi )$. Since $w\preceq v$ and $\int _ X\langle \theta _ w^ n\rangle =\int _ X\langle \theta _ v^ n\rangle >0$, proposition 16.4.10 gives $P_\theta [w](v)=v$. Every competitor for $P_\theta [w](v)$ is more singular than $w$, hence than $u$, so it is a competitor for $P_\theta [u](v)$; and $P_\theta [u](v)\leq v$ quasi-everywhere by proposition 16.7.2 (1), hence everywhere. Therefore $v=P_\theta [w](v)\leq P_\theta [u](v)\leq v$. $\square$

title: Finite energy affine first variation
text: Proposition 17.3.8 . For $u,v\in \mathcal E^1(X,\theta ,\phi )$ and $u_ t=(1-t)u+tv$, the function $t\mapsto E_\theta ^\phi (u_ t)$ is continuously differentiable on $[0,1]$, with one-sided derivatives at the endpoints, and \[  \frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}E_\theta ^\phi (u_ t) =\int _ X(v-u)\, \mu _{u_ t}.  \] The derivative is a polynomial in $t$. Proof. By lemma 17.2.11 every integral $\int _ X(v-u)\langle \theta _ v^ a\wedge \theta _ u^{n-a}\rangle $ is finite. Expanding $\mu _{u_ t}$ by multilinearity shows that the right side is a polynomial in $t$ with these integrals as coefficients. The potentials $u_ t$ lie in $\mathcal E^1(X,\theta ,\phi )$ by corollary 17.2.10 . Apply the cocycle formula of proposition 17.2.12 to $u_{t+s}$ and $u_ t$, with $s\neq 0$ and $t,t+s\in [0,1]$, and use $u_{t+s}-u_ t=s(v-u)$: \[  \frac{E_\theta ^\phi (u_{t+s})-E_\theta ^\phi (u_ t)}s =\frac1{n+1}\sum _{j=0}^ n\int _ X(v-u)\langle \theta _{u_{t+s}}^ j\wedge \theta _{u_ t}^{n-j}\rangle .  \] Each mixed integral on the right is a polynomial in $s$ with the finite coefficients above, and at $s=0$ each of the $n+1$ terms equals $\int _ X(v-u)\mu _{u_ t}$. Letting $s\to 0$ proves the formula for the derivative, including the one-sided derivatives at the endpoints, and its continuity. $\square$

title: Relative energy tangent and order bounds
text: Lemma 17.3.9 . For $u,v\in \mathcal E^1(X,\theta ,\phi )$, \[  \int _ X(v-u)\, \mu _ v\leq E_\theta ^\phi (v)-E_\theta ^\phi (u) \leq \int _ X(v-u)\, \mu _ u.  \] If moreover $u\leq v$, then \[  \frac1{n+1}\int _ X(v-u)\, \mu _ u\leq E_\theta ^\phi (v)-E_\theta ^\phi (u).  \] Proof. The first display is the tangent bound ( 17.17 ), which holds on $\mathcal E^1(X,\theta ,\phi )$ by proposition 17.2.12 . By the same proposition, the cocycle formula ( 17.14 ) holds for $u$ and $v$. If $u\leq v$, all its terms are nonnegative, and retaining the term $j=0$, whose measure is $\mu _ u$, gives the second display. $\square$

title: Lone convergence energy drop
text: Example 17.3.10 . The energy is not continuous for $L^1$ convergence, even for smooth potentials on $\mathbb P^1$. Let $\omega =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log (1+|z|^2)$, which has mass one. For $0<a<1$ put $\varepsilon _ a=\exp (-a^{-2})$ and \[  u_ a(z)=a\log \frac{|z|^2+\varepsilon _ a}{1+|z|^2}.  \] These functions extend smoothly across infinity, and $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ a=(1-a)\omega +a\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log (|z|^2+\varepsilon _ a)>0$. They tend to zero in $L^1$ as $a\downarrow 0$, since $a\log (|z|^2/(1+|z|^2))\leq u_ a\leq 0$ and the left side is $a$ times a fixed integrable function. We compute their Dirichlet energies. Write $r=\log |z|^2$ and $F(r)=\log (\mathrm e^ r+\varepsilon )-\log (1+\mathrm e^ r)$ with $\varepsilon =\varepsilon _ a$, so that $u_ a=aF(\log |z|^2)$. For a smooth function $g=G(\log |z|^2)$ we have $\partial g=G'(r)\, \mathrm dz/z$, hence $\mathrm dg\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}g=\frac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }\partial g\wedge \bar\partial g=\pi ^{-1}G'(r)^2|z|^{-2}\, \mathrm dA$, where $\mathrm dA$ is Lebesgue measure; integration in polar coordinates gives $\int \mathrm dg\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}g=\int _{-\infty }^\infty G'(r)^2\, \mathrm dr$. Therefore \[  \int _ X\mathrm du_ a\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}u_ a =a^2\int _{-\infty }^\infty F'(r)^2\, \mathrm dr =a^2(-\log \varepsilon _ a+O(1))\longrightarrow 1.  \] The bound $O(1)$ is uniform in $a$. Indeed, we have \[  F'(r)=\frac{\mathrm e^ r}{\mathrm e^ r+\varepsilon }-\frac{\mathrm e^ r}{1+\mathrm e^ r}\in [0,1],\qquad 1-F'(r)=\frac{\varepsilon }{\mathrm e^ r+\varepsilon }+\frac{\mathrm e^ r}{1+\mathrm e^ r}\leq \varepsilon \mathrm e^{-r}+\mathrm e^ r.  \] On $[\log \varepsilon ,0]$ the integral of $\varepsilon \mathrm e^{-r}+\mathrm e^ r$ is at most $2$, and $1\geq F'^2\geq 1-2(1-F')$, so $\int _{\log \varepsilon }^0F'^2\, \mathrm dr=-\log \varepsilon +O(1)$. On the left tail $F'(r)\leq \mathrm e^ r/\varepsilon $, and on the right tail $F'(r)\leq \mathrm e^{-r}$; the corresponding integrals of $F'^2$ are at most $\frac12$. Since $\int _ Xu_ a\, \omega \to 0$, the formula of example 17.2.9 gives $E_\omega (u_ a)\to -\frac12$, whereas $E_\omega (0)=0$.

title: Variational Monge–Ampère equations
text:
17.4 Variational Monge–Ampère equations We keep the big class of $	heta $, the model potential $\phi $ and its mass $m=\int _ X\langle 	heta _\phi ^ nangle >0$, and write $E=E_	heta ^\phi $. We solve the equation $\mu _ u=
u $ for non-pluripolar measures $
u $ of mass $m$ (definition 17.4.1 ) by a variational method. By the tangent bounds, a potential $u$ with $\mu _ u=
u $ maximizes $v\mapsto E(v)-\int _ X(v-\phi )\, \mathrm d
u $. For the converse we perturb a maximizer $u$ in the direction of a continuous function $f$. Since $u+tf$ need not be $	heta $-psh, we replace it by its envelope $P_	heta (u+tf)$ and compute the derivative of the energy along these envelopes (proposition 17.4.3 ). Maximizers exist by the compactness of corollary 17.3.4 when the integral term of the functional is continuous for $L^1$ convergence, as it is for measures with bounded densities. For an arbitrary non-pluripolar measure $
u $ we replace the linear term by the exponential term $\lambda ^{-1}\int _ X\mathrm e^{\lambda v}\, \mathrm d
u $, $\lambda >0$, which is continuous for $L^1$ convergence of potentials, and then let $\lambda 	o 0$. The remaining subsections prove uniqueness (section 17.4.2 ) and the boundedness of $u-\phi $ for $L^ p$ densities (section 17.4.3 ), and derive two consequences of the existence theorem (section 17.4.4 , section 17.4.5 ).

title: Existence by maximization
text:
17.4.1 Existence by maximization Definition 17.4.1 . A finite positive Radon measure $
u $ on $X$ is non-pluripolar if $
u (A)=0$ for every pluripolar Borel set $A\subset X$. Integrals against $
u $ use its completion, so subsets of pluripolar sets are also $
u $-null. For example, every measure of the form $g\, \omega ^ n$ with $0\leq g\in L^1(X,\omega ^ n)$ is non-pluripolar, since pluripolar sets have volume zero (see the remarks after definition 10.1.1 ). Every $	heta $-psh function is finite $
u $-almost everywhere, because its pole set is a pluripolar Borel set. Finite positive Borel measures on $X$ are compared through their integrals of continuous functions. Lemma 17.4.2 . Let $\lambda $ and $\sigma $ be finite positive Borel measures on $X$. If $\int _ Xg\, \mathrm d\lambda \geq \int _ Xg\, \mathrm d\sigma $ for every continuous function $g\geq 0$ on $X$, then $\lambda (E)\geq \sigma (E)$ for every Borel set $E\subset X$. In particular, two finite positive Borel measures on $X$ with the same integrals of all continuous functions coincide. If finite positive Borel measures $\lambda _ j$ converge weakly to $\lambda $ and satisfy $\lambda _ j\geq \sigma $ for every $j$, then $\lambda \geq \sigma $. Proof. (1) This is lemma 16.2.1 (2) with $W=X$; the second assertion follows by applying the first in both directions. (2) Since $X$ is compact, weak convergence of measures on $X$ is convergence of the integrals of all continuous functions (see the discussion following definition 7.2.4 ). Hence $\int _ Xg\, \mathrm d\lambda =\lim _ j\int _ Xg\, \mathrm d\lambda _ j\geq \int _ Xg\, \mathrm d\sigma $ for every continuous function $g\geq 0$ on $X$, and (1) gives $\lambda \geq \sigma $. $\square$ Proposition 17.4.3 . Let $u\in \mathcal E^1(X,	heta ,\phi )$ and $f\in C(X,\mathbb R)$, and put $u_ t=P_	heta (u+tf)$ for $t\in \mathbb R$, the envelope of definition 16.1.3 . Then $u_0=u$, and for every $t$ we have $u_ t\sim u$ and $u_ t\leq u+tf$ on $X$. Each $u_ t$ has finite energy, and \[   rac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}E(u_ t)=\int _ Xf\, \mu _{u_ t}.  \] The derivative is continuous on $\mathbb R$. Proof. Let $B=\sup _ X|f|$. The potential $u-|t|B$ is a competitor for the obstacle $u+tf$, and every competitor lies below $u+|t|B$, so $u-|t|B\leq u_ t\leq u+|t|B$. Hence $u_ t\sim u$, and $E(u_ t)\geq E(u)-|t|Bm>-\infty $, so $u_ t\in \mathcal E^1(X,	heta ,\phi )$ by theorem 17.2.8 . The obstacle $u+tf$ is upper semicontinuous, so $u_ t\leq u+tf$ everywhere, by proposition 16.1.4 (1),(2). In particular $u_0\leq u$; since $u$ is itself a competitor for the obstacle $u$, also $u\leq u_0$, so $u_0=u$. Next we show that $\mu _{u_{t+s}}	o \mu _{u_ t}$ weakly as $s	o 0$. The obstacles $u+tf$ and $u+(t+s)f$ differ by at most $|s|B$, so proposition 16.1.4 (4) gives $u_ t-|s|B\leq u_{t+s}\leq u_ t+|s|B$. In particular all $u_ t$ have the pole set of $u$, and $|u_{t+s}-u_ t|\leq |s|B$ outside it. Since $|\arctan a-\arctan b|\leq |a-b|$ for real $a,b$, and adding the same smooth local potential of $	heta $ to $u_{t+s}$ and $u_ t$ does not change their difference, the distance $d_*$ of definition 15.6.2 between the local potentials of $u_{t+s}$ and $u_ t$ is at most $|s|B$ everywhere. Hence, for every $\delta >0$, the sets where it exceeds $\delta $ are empty once $|s|B<\delta $, and $u_{t+s}	o u_ t$ in extended capacity as $s	o 0$. These potentials have full mass relative to $\phi $, so corollary 15.8.4 , applied along every sequence $s_ k	o 0$, gives the asserted weak convergence; in particular $\int _ Xf\, \mu _{u_{t+s}}	o \int _ Xf\, \mu _{u_ t}$. The obstacle $u+tf$ is bounded above, and it is quasi-continuous, because $u$ is (section 16.1 ) and $f$ is continuous. Hence theorem 16.2.5 shows that $\mu _{u_ t}$ is carried by the contact set $\{ u_ t=u+tf\} $. On the contact set of $u_{t+s}$ we have $u_{t+s}=u+(t+s)f$ and $u_ t\leq u+tf$, so $u_{t+s}-u_ t\geq sf$ there. On the contact set of $u_ t$ we have $u_ t=u+tf$ and $u_{t+s}\leq u+(t+s)f$, so $u_{t+s}-u_ t\leq sf$ there. The differences are bounded and the pole sets carry no mass, so the tangent bounds of lemma 17.3.9 give, for every real $s$, \[  s\int _ Xf\, \mu _{u_{t+s}} \leq E(u_{t+s})-E(u_ t) \leq s\int _ Xf\, \mu _{u_ t}.  \] Dividing by $s>0$, respectively $s<0$, and letting $s	o 0$, we obtain the right and left derivatives from the weak convergence just proved. Both equal $\int _ Xf\, \mu _{u_ t}$, which depends continuously on $t$ by the same weak convergence. $\square$ Theorem 17.4.4 . Let $
u $ be a non-pluripolar measure on $X$, and suppose that $\mathcal D_
u =\mathcal E^1(X,	heta ,\phi )\cap L^1(
u )$ is nonempty. Then $\phi \in L^1(

u ,  \] a potential $u\in \mathcal D_

Then there is $u\in \mathcal E^1(X,	heta ,\phi )$ with \[  \mu _ u=g\, \mathrm dV,\qquad \sup _ Xu=0.  \] It maximizes $F_{g\, \mathrm dV}$. Proof. Put $
u =g\, \mathrm dV$, a non-pluripolar measure of mass $m$. Every $	heta $-psh potential is integrable for $\mathrm dV$, hence for $
u $, so $\mathcal D_
u =\mathcal E^1(X,	heta ,\phi )$; we write $F=F_
u $. By the shift formula for the energy and $
u (X)=m$, the functional $F$ is invariant under adding constants, so we may restrict it to potentials $v$ with $\sup _ Xv=0$. For such $v$, lemma 16.4.2 gives $v\leq \phi $, hence $E(v)\leq 0$. Since $\mathrm dV\leq c_ V\, \omega ^ n$ for a constant $c_ V$, proposition 14.2.1 shows that $\int _ X|v|\, \mathrm dV$ is bounded independently of $v$, and $\phi \in L^1(\mathrm dV)$, so \[  0\leq -\int _ X(v-\phi )g\, \mathrm dV\leq C  \] with $C$ independent of $v$. Consequently $\sup F\in [0,C]$, since $F(\phi )=0$ and $F(v)\leq 0+C$. Let $(v_ j)$ be a normalized maximizing sequence with $F(v_ j)\geq -1$. Then $E(v_ j)=F(v_ j)+\int _ X(v_ j-\phi )g\, \mathrm dV\geq -C-1$. By corollary 17.3.4 a subsequence converges in $L^1(X)$ to some $u\in \mathcal E^1(X,	heta ,\phi )$, and $\sup _ Xu=0$, because the supremum is continuous for $L^1$ convergence of potentials (proposition 14.2.1 ). The linear term $v\mapsto \int _ X(v-\phi )g\, \mathrm dV$ is continuous for $L^1$ convergence because $g$ is bounded, and the energy is upper semicontinuous by proposition 17.3.3 . Hence $F(u)\geq \varlimsup _ jF(v_ j)=\sup F$, so $u$ is a maximizer, and theorem 17.4.4 gives $\mu _ u=
u $. $\square$ Proposition 17.4.6 . Let $\lambda >0$ and let $
u $ be a finite positive non-pluripolar measure on $X$. If $u,v\in \mathcal E(X,	heta ,\phi )$ satisfy \[  \mu _ u=\mathrm e^{\lambda u}
u , \qquad \mu _ v\geq \mathrm e^{\lambda v}
u ,  \] then $u\geq v$. In particular, the equation $\mu _ u=\mathrm e^{\lambda u}
u $ has at most one solution in $\mathcal E(X,	heta ,\phi )$. Proof. Let $A=\{ u<v\} $. The comparison principle of proposition 16.7.4 gives \[  \int _ A\mathrm e^{\lambda v}\, \mathrm d
u \leq \mu _ v(A)\leq \mu _ u(A) =\int _ A\mathrm e^{\lambda u}\, \mathrm d
u \leq m.  \] Both potentials are finite $
u $-almost everywhere, and on $A$ we have $\mathrm e^{\lambda v}>\mathrm e^{\lambda u}$. The difference $\mathrm e^{\lambda v}-\mathrm e^{\lambda u}$ is therefore positive on $A$ and has nonpositive integral over $A$, so $
u (A)=0$. Hence $\mu _ u(A)=0$, and the domination principle (theorem 16.4.6 ) gives $u\geq v$ everywhere. If $u$ and $v$ are two solutions, applying this in both directions gives $u=v$. $\square$ Solutions of the exponential equations are obtained as maximizers of the functionals 17.28  egin{equation} \label{eq:relative-exponential-functional} F_\lambda (v)=E(v)-\lambda ^{-1}\int _ X\mathrm e^{\lambda v}\, \mathrm d
u ,\qquad v\in \mathcal E^1(X,	heta ,\phi ), \end{equation} where $\lambda >0$ and $

These functionals are finite: the energy is finite on $\mathcal E^1(X,	heta ,\phi )$, and the Borel function $\mathrm e^{\lambda v}$ satisfies $0\leq \mathrm e^{\lambda v}\leq \mathrm e^{\lambda \sup _ Xv}$, where $\mathrm e^{\lambda v}=0$ on the pole set of $v$. Lemma 17.4.7 . Let $
u $ be a finite positive Borel measure on $X$ and $\lambda >0$. If $u\in \mathcal E^1(X,	heta ,\phi )$ maximizes the functional $F_\lambda $ of ( 17.28 ) on $\mathcal E^1(X,	heta ,\phi )$, then $\mu _ u=\mathrm e^{\lambda u}
u $. Proof. Let $f\in C(X,\mathbb R)$ and $u_ t=P_	heta (u+tf)$ for $t\in \mathbb R$. By proposition 17.4.3 , $u_ t\in \mathcal E^1(X,	heta ,\phi )$, $u_0=u$ and $u_ t\leq u+tf$ everywhere. Hence $\mathrm e^{\lambda u_ t}\leq \mathrm e^{\lambda (u+tf)}$, and $F_\lambda (u_ t)\leq F_\lambda (u)$ gives \[  E(u_ t)-E(u)-\lambda ^{-1} \int _ X\left(\mathrm e^{\lambda (u+tf)}-\mathrm e^{\lambda u}ight) \, \mathrm d
u \leq 0.  \] The left side vanishes at $t=0$. Its energy term is differentiable, with derivative $\int _ Xf\, \mu _{u_ t}$, by proposition 17.4.3 . For $|t|\leq 1$ the $t$-derivative $\lambda f\mathrm e^{\lambda (u+tf)}$ of the integrand is bounded by $\lambda \sup _ X|f|\, \mathrm e^{\lambda \sup _ Xu+\lambda \sup _ X|f|}$, which is integrable for the finite measure $
u $; by the mean value theorem and dominated convergence, the integral is differentiable as well, with derivative $\lambda \int _ Xf\mathrm e^{\lambda (u+tf)}\, \mathrm d
u $. Since the left side is maximal at $t=0$, its derivative vanishes there: $\int _ Xf\, \mu _ u=\int _ Xf\mathrm e^{\lambda u}\, \mathrm d
u $. Since $f$ is arbitrary and $\mathrm e^{\lambda u}
u $ is a finite measure, lemma 17.4.2 (1) gives $\mu _ u=\mathrm e^{\lambda u}
u $. $\square$ To find maximizers for an arbitrary non-pluripolar measure $
u $, we need the continuity of $v\mapsto \int _ X\mathrm e^{\lambda v}\, \mathrm d
u $ for $L^1$ convergence of potentials. This rests on the following two lemmas, in which $	heta $ is an arbitrary smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form. Lemma 17.4.8 . Let $	heta $ be a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form on $X$. If $q_ j,q\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ and $q_ j	o q$ in $L^1(X)$, then $\varlimsup _ jq_ j=q$ quasi-everywhere. Proof. By lemma 17.3.2 , the tail envelopes $a_ j=(\sup _{k\geq j}q_ k)^*$ are $	heta $-psh and decrease pointwise to $q$. For each $j$, corollary 10.2.2 , applied after adding smooth local potentials of $	heta $, gives $a_ j=\sup _{k\geq j}q_ k$ outside a pluripolar set. The countable union of these sets is pluripolar (theorem 10.1.4 ), and outside it $q=\lim _ ja_ j=\varlimsup _ jq_ j$. $\square$ Lemma 17.4.9 . Let $
u $ be a finite non-pluripolar measure on $X$, let $	heta $ be a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form on $X$, and let $B\geq 0$. Suppose that $q_ j,q\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ satisfy $|q_ j|,|q|\leq B$ and $q_ j	o q$ in $L^1(X)$. Then $q_ j	o q$ in $L^1(
u )$. Proof. By lemma 17.4.8 , $\varlimsup _ jq_ j=q$ outside a pluripolar set, hence $
u $-almost everywhere. Thus $(q_ j-q)_+	o 0$ $
u $-almost everywhere, and $\int _ X(q_ j-q)_+\, \mathrm d
u 	o 0$ by bounded convergence, since $0\leq (q_ j-q)_+\leq 2B$ and $
u $ is finite. Since $|q_ j-q|=2(q_ j-q)_+-(q_ j-q)$, it remains to show that $\int _ Xq_ j\, \mathrm d
u 	o \int _ Xq\, \mathrm d
u $. We have just seen that $\varlimsup _ j\int _ X(q_ j-q)\, \mathrm d
u \leq 0$, so it suffices to prove that $L=\varliminf _ j\int _ Xq_ j\, \mathrm d
u $ is at least $\int _ Xq\, \mathrm d
u $. Choose a subsequence $(q_{j_ k})$ with $\int _ Xq_{j_ k}\, \mathrm d
u 	o L$. For bounded Borel functions $y$ on $X$ put $\| y\| =(\int _ Xy^2\, \mathrm d
u )^{1/2}$. For $l\geq 1$ let $C_ l$ be the set of finite convex combinations of the functions $q_{j_ k}$ with $k\geq l$, and let $d_ l=\inf \{ \| y\| :y\in C_ l\} $. Since $C_{l+1}\subset C_ l$ and $\| y\| \leq B
u (X)^{1/2}$ for $y\in C_ l$, the numbers $d_ l$ increase to a finite limit. Choose $y_ l\in C_ l$ with $\| y_ l\| ^2\leq d_ l^2+1/l$. For $l\leq l'$ the function $ rac12(y_ l+y_{l'})$ belongs to the convex set $C_ l$, so its norm is at least $d_ l$. The parallelogram identity, obtained by integrating the pointwise identity $(a-b)^2+(a+b)^2=2a^2+2b^2$, therefore gives \[  \| y_ l-y_{l'}\| ^2=2\| y_ l\| ^2+2\| y_{l'}\| ^2-4 igl \| 	frac 12(y_ l+y_{l'}) igr \| ^2 \leq 2(d_{l'}^2-d_ l^2)+ rac2l+ rac2{l'},  \] and the right side tends to zero as $l	o \infty $, uniformly in $l'\geq l$. By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, $\int _ X|y_ l-y_{l'}|\, \mathrm d

Each $y_{l_ i}$ is a convex combination of $	heta $-psh functions, hence $	heta $-psh, and $\| y_{l_ i}-q\| _{L^1(X)}\leq \sup _{k\geq l_ i}\| q_{j_ k}-q\| _{L^1(X)}$, which tends to zero. By lemma 17.4.8 , applied to the sequence $(y_{l_ i})_ i$, the function $h=\varlimsup _ iy_{l_ i}$ equals $q$ outside a pluripolar set, hence $
u $-almost everywhere. Thus $L=\int _ Xq\, \mathrm d

u $ be a finite non-pluripolar measure on $X$. Then for every $\lambda >0$, \[  \mathrm e^{\lambda q_ j}\longrightarrow \mathrm e^{\lambda q} \quad 	ext{in }L^1(
u ).  \] Proof. By proposition 14.2.1 there is a constant $C$ with $q_ j,q\leq C$. We show that the functions $\mathrm e^{\lambda q_ j}$ and $\mathrm e^{\lambda q}$, with value zero on the pole sets, are $C_1\omega $-psh for a constant $C_1$ independent of $j$; the preceding lemma then applies to them. Choose $C_0\geq 0$ with $	heta \leq C_0\omega $, and a finite cover of $X$ by coordinate balls $W'\Subset W$ such that the smaller balls $W'$ still cover $X$, together with smooth functions $h_ W$ near $\overline W$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h_ W=	heta $. The function $q_ j+h_ W$ is plurisubharmonic on $W$, so for every $\delta >0$ smaller than the distance from $W'$ to the boundary of $W$, its regularization $g_\delta =(q_ j+h_ W)*ho _\delta $ by the radial mollifier is a smooth plurisubharmonic function on the ball $W'$, and $g_\delta $ decreases to $q_ j+h_ W$ as $\delta \downarrow 0$, by proposition 8.2.2 (2). Put $q_{j,\delta }=g_\delta -h_ W$. Then $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q_{j,\delta }\geq -	heta \geq -C_0\omega $. Moreover $g_\delta (x)$ is an average of values of $q_ j+h_ W\leq C+h_ W$ at points within distance $\delta $ of $x$, so by uniform continuity of $h_ W$ on a compact neighborhood of $\overline{W'}$ in $W$ we have $q_{j,\delta }\leq C+1$ on $W'$ for all small $\delta $, independently of $j$. For a smooth real function $s$, the chain rule $\partial  ar\partial \, \mathrm e^{\lambda s}=\lambda \mathrm e^{\lambda s}\partial  ar\partial s+\lambda ^2\mathrm e^{\lambda s}\partial s\wedge  ar\partial s$ and the identity $ rac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }\partial s\wedge  ar\partial s=\mathrm ds\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}s$, which follows from ( 7.6 ), give \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\mathrm e^{\lambda q_{j,\delta }} =\lambda \mathrm e^{\lambda q_{j,\delta }}\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q_{j,\delta } +\lambda ^2\mathrm e^{\lambda q_{j,\delta }} \mathrm dq_{j,\delta }\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}q_{j,\delta } \geq -\lambda C_0\mathrm e^{\lambda (C+1)}\omega ,  \] because $\mathrm dq_{j,\delta }\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}q_{j,\delta }$ is a semipositive $(1,1)$-form. Thus $\mathrm e^{\lambda q_{j,\delta }}$ is $C_1\omega $-psh on $W'$ with $C_1=\lambda C_0\mathrm e^{\lambda (C+1)}$, and so is its decreasing limit $\mathrm e^{\lambda q_ j}$ as $\delta \downarrow 0$, by theorem 8.3.1 applied after adding a smooth local potential of $C_1\omega $; the limit is not identically $-\infty $, since it is nonnegative. Since the balls $W'$ cover $X$, the function $\mathrm e^{\lambda q_ j}$ belongs to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,C_1\omega )$, and the same argument applies to $\mathrm e^{\lambda q}$. The exponential is Lipschitz with constant $\lambda \mathrm e^{\lambda C}$ on $(-\infty ,C]$, so $\mathrm e^{\lambda q_ j}	o \mathrm e^{\lambda q}$ in $L^1(X)$. These functions take values in $[0,\mathrm e^{\lambda C}]$, and lemma 17.4.9 , with the background $C_1\omega $, gives the assertion. $\square$ Theorem 17.4.11 . Let $
u $ be a finite positive non-pluripolar measure on $X$ with $
u (X)>0$, and let $\lambda >0$. There is a unique $u\in \mathcal E(X,	heta ,\phi )$ satisfying \[  \mu _ u=\mathrm e^{\lambda u}
u .  \] This solution belongs to $\mathcal E^1(X,	heta ,\phi )$ and maximizes $F_\lambda (v)=E(v)-\lambda ^{-1}\int _ X\mathrm e^{\lambda v}\, \mathrm d
u $ on $\mathcal E^1(X,	heta ,\phi )$. Proof. By corollary 17.3.4 , the set $K_\phi $ of potentials $w\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ with $w\leq \phi $ and $\sup _ Xw=0$ is compact in $L^1(X)$; it contains $\phi $. By corollary 17.4.10 , the function $w\mapsto \int _ X\mathrm e^{\lambda w}\, \mathrm d
u $ is continuous on $K_\phi $. Its values are positive, since the pole set of $w$ is $
u $-null and $
u (X)>0$. Hence it has a positive minimum $a$ on $K_\phi $. Any $v\in \mathcal E^1(X,	heta ,\phi )$ can be written $v=w+c$ with $c=\sup _ Xv$ and $w\in K_\phi $, by lemma 16.4.2 . Since $E(w)\leq 0$, the shift formula for the energy gives \[  F_\lambda (v)=E(w)+mc-\lambda ^{-1}\mathrm e^{\lambda c}\int _ X\mathrm e^{\lambda w}\, \mathrm d
u \leq mc-\lambda ^{-1}a\mathrm e^{\lambda c}.  \] The right side tends to $-\infty $ as $c	o \pm \infty $. Since $F_\lambda (\phi )$ is finite, a maximizing sequence $v_ j=w_ j+c_ j$ with $F_\lambda (v_ j)\geq F_\lambda (\phi )-1$ therefore has bounded constants $c_ j$. Moreover $E(v_ j)\geq F_\lambda (v_ j)$, because the exponential term is nonnegative, so $E(w_ j)=E(v_ j)-mc_ j$ is bounded below. By corollary 17.3.4 , after passing to a subsequence, $c_ j$ converges and $w_ j$ converges in $L^1(X)$; hence $v_ j	o u$ in $L^1(X)$ for some $u\in \mathcal E^1(X,	heta ,\phi )$. The energy is upper semicontinuous (proposition 17.3.3 ), and $\int _ X\mathrm e^{\lambda v_ j}\, \mathrm d
u 	o \int _ X\mathrm e^{\lambda u}\, \mathrm d

title: Nonpluripolar radon measure
text:
Definition 17.4.1 . A finite positive Radon measure $
u $ on $X$ is non-pluripolar if $

title: Global measure continuous comparison
text: Lemma 17.4.2 . Let $\lambda $ and $\sigma $ be finite positive Borel measures on $X$. If $\int _ Xg\, \mathrm d\lambda \geq \int _ Xg\, \mathrm d\sigma $ for every continuous function $g\geq 0$ on $X$, then $\lambda (E)\geq \sigma (E)$ for every Borel set $E\subset X$. In particular, two finite positive Borel measures on $X$ with the same integrals of all continuous functions coincide. If finite positive Borel measures $\lambda _ j$ converge weakly to $\lambda $ and satisfy $\lambda _ j\geq \sigma $ for every $j$, then $\lambda \geq \sigma $. Proof. (1) This is lemma 16.2.1 (2) with $W=X$; the second assertion follows by applying the first in both directions. (2) Since $X$ is compact, weak convergence of measures on $X$ is convergence of the integrals of all continuous functions (see the discussion following definition 7.2.4 ). Hence $\int _ Xg\, \mathrm d\lambda =\lim _ j\int _ Xg\, \mathrm d\lambda _ j\geq \int _ Xg\, \mathrm d\sigma $ for every continuous function $g\geq 0$ on $X$, and (1) gives $\lambda \geq \sigma $. $\square$

title: Projected energy first variation
text: Proposition 17.4.3 . Let $u\in \mathcal E^1(X,\theta ,\phi )$ and $f\in C(X,\mathbb R)$, and put $u_ t=P_\theta (u+tf)$ for $t\in \mathbb R$, the envelope of definition 16.1.3 . Then $u_0=u$, and for every $t$ we have $u_ t\sim u$ and $u_ t\leq u+tf$ on $X$. Each $u_ t$ has finite energy, and \[  \frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}E(u_ t)=\int _ Xf\, \mu _{u_ t}.  \] The derivative is continuous on $\mathbb R$. Proof. Let $B=\sup _ X|f|$. The potential $u-|t|B$ is a competitor for the obstacle $u+tf$, and every competitor lies below $u+|t|B$, so $u-|t|B\leq u_ t\leq u+|t|B$. Hence $u_ t\sim u$, and $E(u_ t)\geq E(u)-|t|Bm>-\infty $, so $u_ t\in \mathcal E^1(X,\theta ,\phi )$ by theorem 17.2.8 . The obstacle $u+tf$ is upper semicontinuous, so $u_ t\leq u+tf$ everywhere, by proposition 16.1.4 (1),(2). In particular $u_0\leq u$; since $u$ is itself a competitor for the obstacle $u$, also $u\leq u_0$, so $u_0=u$. Next we show that $\mu _{u_{t+s}}\to \mu _{u_ t}$ weakly as $s\to 0$. The obstacles $u+tf$ and $u+(t+s)f$ differ by at most $|s|B$, so proposition 16.1.4 (4) gives $u_ t-|s|B\leq u_{t+s}\leq u_ t+|s|B$. In particular all $u_ t$ have the pole set of $u$, and $|u_{t+s}-u_ t|\leq |s|B$ outside it. Since $|\arctan a-\arctan b|\leq |a-b|$ for real $a,b$, and adding the same smooth local potential of $\theta $ to $u_{t+s}$ and $u_ t$ does not change their difference, the distance $d_*$ of definition 15.6.2 between the local potentials of $u_{t+s}$ and $u_ t$ is at most $|s|B$ everywhere. Hence, for every $\delta >0$, the sets where it exceeds $\delta $ are empty once $|s|B<\delta $, and $u_{t+s}\to u_ t$ in extended capacity as $s\to 0$. These potentials have full mass relative to $\phi $, so corollary 15.8.4 , applied along every sequence $s_ k\to 0$, gives the asserted weak convergence; in particular $\int _ Xf\, \mu _{u_{t+s}}\to \int _ Xf\, \mu _{u_ t}$. The obstacle $u+tf$ is bounded above, and it is quasi-continuous, because $u$ is (section 16.1 ) and $f$ is continuous. Hence theorem 16.2.5 shows that $\mu _{u_ t}$ is carried by the contact set $\{ u_ t=u+tf\} $. On the contact set of $u_{t+s}$ we have $u_{t+s}=u+(t+s)f$ and $u_ t\leq u+tf$, so $u_{t+s}-u_ t\geq sf$ there. On the contact set of $u_ t$ we have $u_ t=u+tf$ and $u_{t+s}\leq u+(t+s)f$, so $u_{t+s}-u_ t\leq sf$ there. The differences are bounded and the pole sets carry no mass, so the tangent bounds of lemma 17.3.9 give, for every real $s$, \[  s\int _ Xf\, \mu _{u_{t+s}} \leq E(u_{t+s})-E(u_ t) \leq s\int _ Xf\, \mu _{u_ t}.  \] Dividing by $s>0$, respectively $s<0$, and letting $s\to 0$, we obtain the right and left derivatives from the weak convergence just proved. Both equal $\int _ Xf\, \mu _{u_ t}$, which depends continuously on $t$ by the same weak convergence. $\square$

Theorem 17.4.5 . Let $\mathrm dV$ be a smooth positive volume form on $X$, and let $g\in L^\infty (\mathrm dV)$ satisfy $g\geq 0$ and $\int _ Xg\, \mathrm dV=m$. Then there is $u\in \mathcal E^1(X,	heta ,\phi )$ with \[  \mu _ u=g\, \mathrm dV,\qquad \sup _ Xu=0.  \] It maximizes $F_{g\, \mathrm dV}$. Proof. Put $

Since $\mathrm dV\leq c_ V\, \omega ^ n$ for a constant $c_ V$, proposition 14.2.1 shows that $\int _ X|v|\, \mathrm dV$ is bounded independently of $v$, and $\phi \in L^1(\mathrm dV)$, so \[  0\leq -\int _ X(v-\phi )g\, \mathrm dV\leq C  \] with $C$ independent of $v$. Consequently $\sup F\in [0,C]$, since $F(\phi )=0$ and $F(v)\leq 0+C$. Let $(v_ j)$ be a normalized maximizing sequence with $F(v_ j)\geq -1$. Then $E(v_ j)=F(v_ j)+\int _ X(v_ j-\phi )g\, \mathrm dV\geq -C-1$. The linear term $v\mapsto \int _ X(v-\phi )g\, \mathrm dV$ is continuous for $L^1$ convergence because $g$ is bounded, and the energy is upper semicontinuous by proposition 17.3.3 . Hence $F(u)\geq \varlimsup _ jF(v_ j)=\sup F$, so $u$ is a maximizer, and theorem 17.4.4 gives $\mu _ u=
u $. $\square$

title: Relative exponential maximizer equation
Psh lone quasieverywhere limsup
text: Lemma 17.4.8 . Let $\theta $ be a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form on $X$. If $q_ j,q\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and $q_ j\to q$ in $L^1(X)$, then $\varlimsup _ jq_ j=q$ quasi-everywhere. Proof. By lemma 17.3.2 , the tail envelopes $a_ j=(\sup _{k\geq j}q_ k)^*$ are $\theta $-psh and decrease pointwise to $q$. For each $j$, corollary 10.2.2 , applied after adding smooth local potentials of $\theta $, gives $a_ j=\sup _{k\geq j}q_ k$ outside a pluripolar set. The countable union of these sets is pluripolar (theorem 10.1.4 ), and outside it $q=\lim _ ja_ j=\varlimsup _ jq_ j$. $\square$

title: Exponential psh measure continuity
text: Corollary 17.4.10 . Let $\theta $ be a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form on $X$, let $q_ j,q\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ satisfy $q_ j\to q$ in $L^1(X)$, and let $\nu $ be a finite non-pluripolar measure on $X$. Then for every $\lambda >0$, \[  \mathrm e^{\lambda q_ j}\longrightarrow \mathrm e^{\lambda q} \quad \text{in }L^1(\nu ).  \] Proof. By proposition 14.2.1 there is a constant $C$ with $q_ j,q\leq C$. We show that the functions $\mathrm e^{\lambda q_ j}$ and $\mathrm e^{\lambda q}$, with value zero on the pole sets, are $C_1\omega $-psh for a constant $C_1$ independent of $j$; the preceding lemma then applies to them. Choose $C_0\geq 0$ with $\theta \leq C_0\omega $, and a finite cover of $X$ by coordinate balls $W'\Subset W$ such that the smaller balls $W'$ still cover $X$, together with smooth functions $h_ W$ near $\overline W$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h_ W=\theta $. The function $q_ j+h_ W$ is plurisubharmonic on $W$, so for every $\delta >0$ smaller than the distance from $W'$ to the boundary of $W$, its regularization $g_\delta =(q_ j+h_ W)*\rho _\delta $ by the radial mollifier is a smooth plurisubharmonic function on the ball $W'$, and $g_\delta $ decreases to $q_ j+h_ W$ as $\delta \downarrow 0$, by proposition 8.2.2 (2). Put $q_{j,\delta }=g_\delta -h_ W$. Then $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q_{j,\delta }\geq -\theta \geq -C_0\omega $. Moreover $g_\delta (x)$ is an average of values of $q_ j+h_ W\leq C+h_ W$ at points within distance $\delta $ of $x$, so by uniform continuity of $h_ W$ on a compact neighborhood of $\overline{W'}$ in $W$ we have $q_{j,\delta }\leq C+1$ on $W'$ for all small $\delta $, independently of $j$. For a smooth real function $s$, the chain rule $\partial \bar\partial \, \mathrm e^{\lambda s}=\lambda \mathrm e^{\lambda s}\partial \bar\partial s+\lambda ^2\mathrm e^{\lambda s}\partial s\wedge \bar\partial s$ and the identity $\frac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }\partial s\wedge \bar\partial s=\mathrm ds\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}s$, which follows from ( 7.6 ), give \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\mathrm e^{\lambda q_{j,\delta }} =\lambda \mathrm e^{\lambda q_{j,\delta }}\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q_{j,\delta } +\lambda ^2\mathrm e^{\lambda q_{j,\delta }} \mathrm dq_{j,\delta }\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}q_{j,\delta } \geq -\lambda C_0\mathrm e^{\lambda (C+1)}\omega ,  \] because $\mathrm dq_{j,\delta }\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}q_{j,\delta }$ is a semipositive $(1,1)$-form. Thus $\mathrm e^{\lambda q_{j,\delta }}$ is $C_1\omega $-psh on $W'$ with $C_1=\lambda C_0\mathrm e^{\lambda (C+1)}$, and so is its decreasing limit $\mathrm e^{\lambda q_ j}$ as $\delta \downarrow 0$, by theorem 8.3.1 applied after adding a smooth local potential of $C_1\omega $; the limit is not identically $-\infty $, since it is nonnegative. Since the balls $W'$ cover $X$, the function $\mathrm e^{\lambda q_ j}$ belongs to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,C_1\omega )$, and the same argument applies to $\mathrm e^{\lambda q}$. The exponential is Lipschitz with constant $\lambda \mathrm e^{\lambda C}$ on $(-\infty ,C]$, so $\mathrm e^{\lambda q_ j}\to \mathrm e^{\lambda q}$ in $L^1(X)$. These functions take values in $[0,\mathrm e^{\lambda C}]$, and lemma 17.4.9 , with the background $C_1\omega $, gives the assertion. $\square$

title: Nonpluripolar relative exponential equation
text:
Theorem 17.4.11 . Let $
u $ be a finite positive non-pluripolar measure on $X$ with $
u (X)>0$, and let $\lambda >0$. There is a unique $u\in \mathcal E(X,	heta ,\phi )$ satisfying \[  \mu _ u=\mathrm e^{\lambda u}
u .  \] This solution belongs to $\mathcal E^1(X,	heta ,\phi )$ and maximizes $F_\lambda (v)=E(v)-\lambda ^{-1}\int _ X\mathrm e^{\lambda v}\, \mathrm d
u $ on $\mathcal E^1(X,	heta ,\phi )$. Proof. By corollary 17.3.4 , the set $K_\phi $ of potentials $w\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ with $w\leq \phi $ and $\sup _ Xw=0$ is compact in $L^1(X)$; it contains $\phi $. By corollary 17.4.10 , the function $w\mapsto \int _ X\mathrm e^{\lambda w}\, \mathrm d
u $ is continuous on $K_\phi $. Its values are positive, since the pole set of $w$ is $

title: Uniqueness by concentration of mass
text: 17.4.2 Uniqueness by concentration of mass We now show that the solution given by theorem 17.4.13 is unique up to an additive constant. The proof uses existence once more. If two solutions $u,v$ with $\mu _ u=\mu _ v=\mu $ do not differ by a constant $\mu $-almost everywhere, then, after a shift of $v$, the set $U=\{ u<v\} $ carries a proper fraction of the mass of $\mu $. We solve the equation whose right-hand side is $\mu $ restricted to $U$ and rescaled to total mass $m$. Mixing this auxiliary solution into $v$ raises the density of the Monge–Ampère measure on $U$ (corollary 15.4.7 ), in contradiction with the comparison principle. The domination principle then turns equality $\mu $-almost everywhere into equality everywhere. Theorem 17.4.14 . Let $u,v\in \mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi )$ satisfy $\mu _ u=\mu _ v$. Then there is a constant $C\in \mathbb R$ such that $u=v+C$ everywhere on $X$. Consequently, every non-pluripolar measure of mass $m$ is the Monge–Ampère measure $\mu _ u$ of exactly one $u\in \mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi )$ with $\sup _ Xu=0$. Proof. Put $\mu =\mu _ u=\mu _ v$. Since $u\in \mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi )$, this is a finite measure of mass $\int _ X\langle \theta _ u^ n\rangle =\int _ X\langle \theta _\phi ^ n\rangle =m$, and it is non-pluripolar, because non-pluripolar products give no mass to pluripolar sets (lemma 15.1.2 ). Hence the pole sets of $u$ and $v$ are $\mu $-null, and $u-v$ is defined and finite $\mu $-almost everywhere. We first show that $u-v$ is constant $\mu $-almost everywhere. Suppose not. Let $\lambda $ be the image of $\mu $ under $u-v$, a finite Borel measure on $\mathbb R$ of total mass $m>0$, and put \[  c_-=\sup \{ c\in \mathbb R:\lambda ((-\infty ,c))=0\} ,\qquad c_+=\inf \{ c\in \mathbb R:\lambda ((c,\infty ))=0\} ,  \] with $\sup \varnothing =-\infty $ and $\inf \varnothing =+\infty $. The sets $(-\infty ,c)$ increase to $\mathbb R$ as $c\to +\infty $, so $\lambda ((-\infty ,c))\to m>0$; hence $c_-<+\infty $, and similarly $c_+>-\infty $. If $c_->-\infty $, the $\lambda $-null sets $(-\infty ,c)$ with $c<c_-$ increase to $(-\infty ,c_-)$, so $\lambda ((-\infty ,c_-))=0$; similarly $\lambda ((c_+,\infty ))=0$ if $c_+<+\infty $. Hence $c_+<c_-$ is impossible, since $\mathbb R=(-\infty ,c_-)\cup (c_+,\infty )$ would then be $\lambda $-null. If $c_-=c_+$, then $\lambda $ is carried by the point $c_-$, that is, $u-v$ is constant $\mu $-almost everywhere, contrary to our assumption. Thus $c_-<c_+$, and every $c\in (c_-,c_+)$ satisfies $\lambda ((-\infty ,c))>0$ and $\lambda ((c,\infty ))>0$, that is, \[  \mu (\{ u-v<c\} )>0,\qquad \mu (\{ u-v>c\} )>0.  \] The singletons $\{ c\} $ with $\lambda (\{ c\} )>0$ are pairwise disjoint sets of positive measure, so there are only countably many of them by lemma 1.1.5 . Since the interval $(c_-,c_+)$ is uncountable, we may choose $c$ in it with $\mu (\{ u-v=c\} )=0$. Replacing $v$ by $v+c$ changes neither the class $\mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi )$ nor the measure $\mu _ v$, so we may assume $c=0$. Then $\mu (\{ u<v\} )$ and $\mu (\{ u>v\} )$ are positive, and the set $U=\{ u<v\} $ satisfies \[  0<\mu (U)<m,\qquad \mu (\{ u=v\} )=0.  \] Set $q=(m/\mu (U))^{1/n}>1$. The measure $q^ n\mathbf1_ U\mu $ is non-pluripolar and has mass $m$, so theorem 17.4.13 gives $h\in \mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi )$ with \[  \mu _ h=q^ n\mathbf1_ U\mu .  \] For $0<t<1$ put $w_ t=(1-t)v+th$. By corollary 17.2.10 , $w_ t\in \mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi )$. Since $\theta _{w_ t}=(1-t)\theta _ v+t\theta _ h$, corollary 15.4.7 , applied to the currents $\theta _ v,\theta _ h$, the common measure $\mu $ and the densities $1$ and $q^ n\mathbf1_ U$, gives \[  \mu _{w_ t}\geq \big ((1-t)+tq\mathbf1_ U\big )^ n\mu .  \] Let $U_ t=\{ u<w_ t\} $, and put \[  d_ t=(1-t)^ n,\qquad b_ t=(1-t+tq)^ n.  \] The comparison principle for relative full mass, proposition 16.7.4 , applied to $u$ and $w_ t$, and the preceding lower bound give \[  \mu (U_ t)=\mu _ u(U_ t)\geq \mu _{w_ t}(U_ t) \geq d_ t\mu (U_ t)+(b_ t-d_ t)\mu (U_ t\cap U).  \] Since $1-d_ t>0$, it follows that 17.29 \begin{equation} \label{eq:relative-uniqueness-concentration} \frac{b_ t-d_ t}{1-d_ t}\, \mu (U_ t\cap U)\leq \mu (U_ t). \end{equation} We let $t\downarrow 0$. At every point where $u,v,h$ are finite and $u\neq v$, we have $w_ t=v+t(h-v)$, so $\mathbf1_{U_ t}\to \mathbf1_ U$ there. These points have full $\mu $-measure, because the three pole sets and the level set $\{ u=v\} $ are $\mu $-null. By dominated convergence, \[  \mu (U_ t\cap U)\longrightarrow \mu (U),\qquad \mu (U_ t)\longrightarrow \mu (U).  \] Moreover $b_ t-d_ t=ntq+O(t^2)$ and $1-d_ t=nt+O(t^2)$, so $(b_ t-d_ t)/(1-d_ t)\to q$. Passing to the limit in ( 17.29 ) gives $q\mu (U)\leq \mu (U)$, which contradicts $q>1$ and $\mu (U)>0$. Hence, for the original pair, there is a finite constant $C$ such that $u=v+C$ $\mu $-almost everywhere. Both $u$ and $v+C$ belong to $\mathcal E(X,\theta ,\phi )$, and their common measure $\mu $ gives zero mass to $\{ u<v+C\} $ and to $\{ v+C<u\} $. The domination principle (theorem 16.4.6 ), applied in both directions, gives $u=v+C$ everywhere, including at the common poles. This proves the first assertion. For the second, theorem 17.4.13 provides a solution with supremum zero. If $u$ and $v$ are two such solutions, then $u=v+C$, and comparing suprema gives $C=0$. $\square$

title: Bounded differences from the reference
text:
17.4.3 Bounded differences from the reference The solutions constructed so far belong to $\mathcal E(X,	heta ,\phi )$, but in general their difference from $\phi $ is unbounded. We now show that the difference is bounded when the measure is dominated by a power $1+\delta >1$ of the Monge–Ampère capacity $\operatorname {Cap}_{	heta ,\phi }$ relative to $\phi $ (definition 16.7.5 ). If $\mu _ u\leq A\operatorname {Cap}_{	heta ,\phi }^{1+\delta }$, the sublevel estimate of proposition 16.7.7 bounds the capacity of the deeper sublevel set $\{ u<\phi -s-t\} $ by $At^{-n}$ times the $(1+\delta )$th power of the capacity of $\{ u<\phi -s\} $. Iterating with geometrically decreasing steps $t$, we reach a finite level beyond which the capacity vanishes. Measures with $L^ p$ densities, $p>1$, satisfy such a bound by corollary 16.9.5 . Theorem 17.4.15 . Let $u\in \mathcal E(X,	heta ,\phi )$ with $u\leq \phi $. Let $0\leq a<1$, $A>0$ and $\delta >0$, and let $
u $ be a positive Borel measure on $X$ such that 17.30  egin{equation} \label{eq:relative-capacity-measure-domination} \mu _ u\leq 
u +a\mu _\phi ,\qquad 
u (E)\leq A\operatorname {Cap}_{	heta ,\phi }(E)^{1+\delta } \quad 	ext{for every Borel set }E\subset X. \end{equation} Then there is a finite constant $C\geq 0$ such that $\phi -C\leq u\leq \phi $ on $X$. If, in addition, $I=\int _ X(\phi -u)\, \mathrm d
u <\infty $, then one can take 17.31  egin{equation} \label{eq:relative-capacity-moment-depth} C=2+ rac I{1-a}\left(2\left( rac A{1-a}ight)^{1/n}ight)^{n/\delta } + rac1{1-2^{-\delta }}. \end{equation} Here $\phi -u$ and the sublevel sets $\{ u<\phi -s\} $ are taken on the set where $\phi $ is finite; its complement is pluripolar, hence of zero capacity (proposition 16.7.6 ) and therefore $
u $-null. Proof. We derive a recursive inequality for the capacities of the sublevel sets of $u-\phi $ and iterate it along levels that converge to a finite depth. For $s>0$ put \[  E_ s=\{ u<\phi -s\} ,\qquad g(s)=\operatorname {Cap}_{	heta ,\phi }(E_ s)^{1/n},\qquad B=\left( rac A{1-a}ight)^{1/n}.  \] The sets $E_ s$ decrease as $s$ increases, so $g$ is nonincreasing. We first compare the measures on $E_ s$. Both $u$ and $\phi -s$ belong to $\mathcal E(X,	heta ,\phi )$, so the comparison principle of proposition 16.7.4 , applied to $u$ and $\phi -s$, gives $\mu _\phi (E_ s)\leq \mu _ u(E_ s)$. By ( 17.30 ), \[  \mu _ u(E_ s)\leq 
u (E_ s)+a\mu _\phi (E_ s)\leq 
u (E_ s)+a\mu _ u(E_ s),  \] and hence $(1-a)\mu _ u(E_ s)\leq 
u (E_ s)$. Since $u$ has full mass relative to $\phi $, proposition 16.7.7 gives $t^ n\operatorname {Cap}_{	heta ,\phi }(E_{s+t})\leq \mu _ u(E_ s)$ for $0<t\leq 1$. Combining this with the last inequality and the capacity bound in ( 17.30 ), we obtain $t^ ng(s+t)^ n\leq B^ ng(s)^{n(1+\delta )}$, that is, 17.32  egin{equation} \label{eq:relative-capacity-iteration} t g(s+t)\leq B g(s)^{1+\delta },\qquad s>0,\quad 0<t\leq 1. \end{equation} By the second assertion of proposition 16.7.7 , $g(s)	o 0$ as $s	o \infty $. Choose $s_0>0$ with $2Bg(s_0)^\delta \leq 1$, and put 17.33  egin{equation} \label{eq:relative-capacity-explicit-depth} C=s_0+ rac{2B}{1-2^{-\delta }}g(s_0)^\delta . \end{equation} We claim that $g(C)=0$. If $g(s_0)=0$, then $C=s_0$ and there is nothing to prove. Otherwise, as long as $g(s_ j)>0$, define inductively \[  t_ j=2B g(s_ j)^\delta ,\qquad s_{j+1}=s_ j+t_ j.  \] Since $g$ is nonincreasing, $t_ j\leq 2Bg(s_0)^\delta \leq 1$, and ( 17.32 ) with $s=s_ j$ and $t=t_ j$ gives \[  g(s_{j+1})\leq  rac{Bg(s_ j)^{1+\delta }}{t_ j}= rac{g(s_ j)}2.  \] Hence $g(s_ j)\leq 2^{-j}g(s_0)$ and $t_ j\leq 2^{-j\delta }\cdot 2Bg(s_0)^\delta $, so that \[  s_ j\leq s_0+2B g(s_0)^\delta \sum _{i=0}^\infty 2^{-i\delta }=C \qquad 	ext{for every }j.  \] If the construction stops because $g(s_ j)=0$ for some $j$, then $g(C)\leq g(s_ j)=0$. u (E_ s)\leq I/s$. Taking $t=1$ in the sublevel estimate and using the measure inequality on $E_ s$, we find \[  g(s+1)^ n\leq \mu _ u(E_ s)\leq  rac{
u (E_ s)}{1-a} \leq  rac I{(1-a)s}.  \] Choose $s=1+I(2B)^{n/\delta }/(1-a)$ and $s_0=s+1$. Since $(1-a)s>I(2B)^{n/\delta }$, we get $g(s_0)^ n\leq (2B)^{-n/\delta }$, that is, $2Bg(s_0)^\delta \leq 1$. Thus $s_0$ satisfies the condition imposed on it above, and the constant in ( 17.33 ) is at most $s_0+(1-2^{-\delta })^{-1}$. Since $(2B)^{n/\delta }= igl (2(A/(1-a))^{1/n} igr )^{n/\delta }$, this is the right side of ( 17.31 ). Let $u\in \mathcal E^1(X,	heta ,\phi )$ with $u\leq \phi $, and let $A>0$ and $\delta >0$ be such that \[  \mu _ u(E)\leq A\operatorname {Cap}_{	heta ,\phi }(E)^{1+\delta } \quad 	ext{for every Borel set }E\subset X.  \] If $L\geq 0$ and $E_	heta ^\phi (u)\geq -L$, then \[  \phi -\left(2+(n+1)L(2A^{1/n})^{n/\delta } + rac1{1-2^{-\delta }}ight)\leq u\leq \phi .  \] Proof. u =\mu _ u$. Proof. Since $\sup _ Xu=0$, lemma 16.4.2 gives $u\leq \phi $; recall also that $\sup _ X\phi =0$, by definition 16.3.1 . Let $q=p/(p-1)$ be the conjugate exponent. u =f\omega ^ n$ satisfies the capacity bound in ( 17.30 ) with $\delta =1$ and $A=B_2\| f\| _{L^ p}/m^2$, where $B_2$ depends only on $X,	heta ,\omega ,p$. (If $f=0$ almost everywhere, take $A=1$ instead.) With $\delta =1$, the constant ( 17.31 ) equals $4+2^ nAI/(1-a)^2$. u (E_ s)}{1-a} \leq  rac I{(1-a)s}.  \] Choose $s=1+I(2B)^{n/\delta }/(1-a)$ and $s_0=s+1$. Since $(1-a)s>I(2B)^{n/\delta }$, we get $g(s_0)^ n\leq (2B)^{-n/\delta }$, that is, $2Bg(s_0)^\delta \leq 1$.
