title: Positive mass and bigness
text:
17.4.4 Positive mass and bigness So far the background class has been big, and big classes have positive volume by proposition 15.8.2 . The equations solved above give the converse for pseudo-effective classes. In this subsection $	heta $ denotes an arbitrary smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form on $X$; its class need not be big, and no model potential is fixed. Let $\alpha =\{ 	heta \} $ be a pseudo-effective class whose volume, in the sense of definition 15.8.1 , is positive. The classes $\alpha +\varepsilon \{ \omega \} $, $\varepsilon >0$, are big, and in each of them we solve the Monge–Ampère equation whose right-hand side is a fixed smooth measure rescaled to the total mass $\operatorname {vol}(\alpha +\varepsilon \{ \omega \} )$, which is at least $\operatorname {vol}(\alpha )$. A pointwise inequality between traces, integrated against these solutions, yields lower bounds for the pairings $\int _ X	heta \wedge 	au $ with strictly positive $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closed $(n-1,n-1)$-forms $	au $, uniformly in $\varepsilon $. Lamari's duality criterion, which we prove first, turns such bounds into a Kähler current in $\alpha $. Recall from section 7.2 that weak and strong positivity coincide for real $(n-1,n-1)$-forms, so that we speak simply of positive forms, and that such a form is strictly positive if at every point it lies in the interior of the cone of positive forms. For instance, $\omega ^{n-1}$ is strictly positive: at a point $x$, choose linear coordinates on the tangent space in which $\omega (x)$ is the standard form $ eta $; then $\omega (x)^{n-1}= eta ^{n-1}$ is an interior point of the cone by proposition 7.2.1 , and complex-linear isomorphisms preserve positivity. For real $(n-1,n-1)$-forms we write $\eta \leq 	au $ if $	au -\eta $ is positive. Lemma 17.4.18 (Lamari's criterion) . Let $	heta $ be a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form on $X$. Then $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )
eq \varnothing $ if and only if 17.34  egin{equation} \label{eq:lamari-positive-tests} \int _ X	heta \wedge 	au \geq 0 \end{equation} for every smooth strictly positive real $(n-1,n-1)$-form $	au $ on $X$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}	au =0$. Consequently, the class $\{ 	heta \} $ is big if and only if there is $\delta >0$ such that every such form $	au $ satisfies 17.35  egin{equation} \label{eq:lamari-strict-tests} \int _ X	heta \wedge 	au \geq \delta \int _ X\omega \wedge 	au . \end{equation} Proof. Necessity. If $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$, then $T=	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq 0$. For $	au $ as in the statement, the definition of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ as a current gives $\int _ X\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\wedge 	au =\int _ Xu\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}	au =0$, hence $\int _ X	heta \wedge 	au =\int _ XT\wedge 	au $, which is nonnegative by the definition of a positive current, since $	au $ is positive, hence strongly positive. Sufficiency. Conversely, assume ( 17.34 ) for all forms $	au $ as in the statement. We extend the functional $	au \mapsto \int _ X	heta \wedge 	au $ from $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closed forms to a positive linear functional on all smooth real $(n-1,n-1)$-forms, regard the extension as a positive $(1,1)$-current $T$, and show that $T-	heta $ is $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ of a distribution. A positive extension. Let $F$ be the real vector space of smooth real $(n-1,n-1)$-forms on $X$, let $S=\{ 	au \in F:\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}	au =0\} $, and put $e=\omega ^{n-1}$, with $e=1$ if $n=1$. Since $\omega $ is closed, $e\in S$, and $e$ is strictly positive. Define $\ell _0(	au )=\int _ X	heta \wedge 	au $ for $	au \in S$. By hypothesis $\ell _0(	au )\geq 0$ when $	au \in S$ is strictly positive. If $	au \in S$ is merely positive, then $	au +te\in S$ is strictly positive for every $t>0$. Indeed, at each point $x$ the cone of positive forms contains a ball about $e(x)$, for some norm; since the cone is stable under sums and positive multiples, it also contains the ball of $t$ times that radius about $	au (x)+te(x)$. Hence $\ell _0(	au )+t\ell _0(e)\geq 0$, and letting $t\downarrow 0$ gives $\ell _0(	au )\geq 0$. We next compare the forms in $F$ with $e$. Fix finitely many holomorphic charts $U_1,\ldots ,U_ N$ and compact sets $K_ a\subset U_ a$ with $ igcup _ aK_ a=X$. In $U_ a$ write $\eta \in F$ as $\eta =\sum _{I,J}\eta ^ a_{IJ}\, \mathrm dz_ I\wedge \mathrm d ar z_ J$, the sum running over increasing multi-indices of length $n-1$, and put \[  \| \eta \| =\max _{1\leq a\leq N}\  \max _{I,J}\  \sup _{K_ a}|\eta ^ a_{IJ}|.  \] We claim that there is a constant $M>0$ such that 17.36  egin{equation} \label{eq:lamari-uniform-domination} -M\| \eta \| e\leq \eta \leq M\| \eta \| e\qquad 	ext{for every }\eta \in F. \end{equation} Let $Z$ be the finite-dimensional real vector space of real $(n-1,n-1)$-forms with constant coefficients on $\mathbb C^ n$, normed by the maximum modulus of the coefficients, and let $P\subset Z$ be the closed convex cone of positive forms (proposition 7.2.1 ). For $x\in U_ a$, the differential of the chart is a complex-linear isomorphism from the tangent space at $x$ onto $\mathbb C^ n$, under which $\mathrm dz_ j$ corresponds to the $j$th coordinate form. Since complex-linear isomorphisms preserve positivity, a real $(n-1,n-1)$-form $\eta $ is positive at $x$ if and only if its coefficient form $\eta ^ a(x)=\sum _{I,J}\eta ^ a_{IJ}(x)\, \mathrm dz_ I\wedge \mathrm d ar z_ J\in Z$ lies in $P$. Because $e$ is strictly positive, the continuous map $x\mapsto e^ a(x)$ sends the compact set $K_ a$ into the interior of $P$; the complement of this interior is closed and disjoint from the compact image, so it has positive distance $r_ a$ from it. Put $r= rac12\min _ ar_ a$. If $\eta \in F$ satisfies $\| \eta \| \leq r$ and $x\in K_ a$, then $e^ a(x)\pm \eta ^ a(x)$ lies within distance $r<r_ a$ of $e^ a(x)$, hence in $P$; thus $e\pm \eta $ is positive at $x$. Since the sets $K_ a$ cover $X$, the forms $e\pm \eta $ are positive. Applying this to $r\eta /\| \eta \| $ for $\eta 
eq 0$ proves ( 17.36 ) with $M=1/r$. For $\eta \in F$, a form $	au \in S$ with $	au \geq \eta $ is called an $S$-majorant of $\eta $, and we put \[  p(\eta )=\inf \{ \ell _0(	au ):	au 	ext{ is an $S$-majorant of }\eta \} .  \] Let $\eta \in F$ and $C=M\| \eta \| $, so that $-Ce\leq \eta \leq Ce$ by ( 17.36 ). The form $Ce$ is an $S$-majorant of $\eta $, so $p(\eta )\leq C\ell _0(e)$. If $	au $ is an $S$-majorant of $\eta $, then $	au +Ce\geq \eta +Ce\geq 0$, so $	au +Ce\in S$ is positive and $\ell _0(	au )\geq -C\ell _0(e)$. Thus $p$ is finite. It is sublinear: the sum of $S$-majorants of $\eta _1$ and $\eta _2$ is an $S$-majorant of $\eta _1+\eta _2$, and for $\lambda >0$ the $S$-majorants of $\lambda \eta $ are $\lambda $ times those of $\eta $. If $\eta \in S$, then $\eta $ is its own $S$-majorant, and every $S$-majorant $	au $ of $\eta $ satisfies $\ell _0(	au )-\ell _0(\eta )=\ell _0(	au -\eta )\geq 0$ because $	au -\eta \in S$ is positive. Hence $p=\ell _0$ on $S$. Next we extend $\ell _0$ to a linear functional on $F$ dominated by $p$; this is the Hahn–Banach theorem, whose proof we recall. Let $\ell $ be a linear functional on a subspace $W\supset S$ which extends $\ell _0$ and satisfies $\ell \leq p$ on $W$, and let $\eta _0\in F\setminus W$. For $\eta _1,\eta _2\in W$, \[  \ell (\eta _1)+\ell (\eta _2)=\ell (\eta _1+\eta _2)\leq p(\eta _1+\eta _2)\leq p(\eta _1-\eta _0)+p(\eta _2+\eta _0),  \] so \[  \sup _{\eta _1\in W} igl (\ell (\eta _1)-p(\eta _1-\eta _0) igr ) \leq \inf _{\eta _2\in W} igl (p(\eta _2+\eta _0)-\ell (\eta _2) igr ).  \] Taking $\eta _1=\eta _2=0$ shows that the supremum is greater than $-\infty $ and the infimum is less than $+\infty $; hence both are finite, and we may choose a real number $c$ between them. Define $\ell (\eta +t\eta _0)=\ell (\eta )+tc$ for $\eta \in W$ and $t\in \mathbb R$. For $t>0$, the upper bound for $c$ with $\eta _2=\eta /t$, multiplied by $t$, gives $\ell (\eta )+tc\leq p(\eta +t\eta _0)$; for $t<0$, the lower bound for $c$ with $\eta _1=\eta /|t|$, multiplied by $|t|$, gives the same inequality. Thus the extension to $W+\mathbb R\eta _0$ is still dominated by $p$. The union of a chain of such extensions is again such an extension, so Zorn's lemma gives a maximal one, and by the step just proved its domain is $F$. We denote it again by $\ell $. The functional $\ell $ is positive: if $\eta \in F$ is positive, then $0$ is an $S$-majorant of $-\eta $, so $\ell (-\eta )\leq p(-\eta )\leq 0$. It is also bounded: by ( 17.36 ), the form $M\| \eta \| e$ is an $S$-majorant of both $\eta $ and $-\eta $, so 17.37  egin{equation} \label{eq:lamari-functional-bound} |\ell (\eta )|\leq M\ell _0(e)\| \eta \| \qquad (\eta \in F). \end{equation} We now turn $\ell $ into a current. Every smooth form on the compact manifold $X$ is a test form. For a complex form $\varphi $ of degree $2n-2$, let $\varphi '$ be its component of bidegree $(n-1,n-1)$, and put $T(\varphi )=\ell (\operatorname{Re}\varphi ')+\mathrm i\, \ell (\operatorname{Im}\varphi ')$, where $\operatorname{Re}\varphi '=(\varphi '+\overline{\varphi '})/2$ and $\operatorname{Im}\varphi '=(\varphi '-\overline{\varphi '})/(2\mathrm i)$ are real forms in $F$. This is a complex-linear functional: replacing $\varphi $ by $\mathrm i\varphi $ replaces $(\operatorname{Re}\varphi ',\operatorname{Im}\varphi ')$ by $(-\operatorname{Im}\varphi ',\operatorname{Re}\varphi ')$. Moreover, $T$ has the continuity property of a current of degree $2$. Indeed, let $Q$ be a compact subset of a chart $U$, and let $\varphi $ be supported in $Q$, with coefficients $\varphi _ J$ in real coordinates on $U$. On the compact set $K_ a\cap Q$, the coefficients of $\operatorname{Re}\varphi '$ and $\operatorname{Im}\varphi '$ in the chart $U_ a$ are linear combinations of the functions $\varphi _ J$ and $\overline{\varphi _ J}$ with coefficients that are smooth on $U\cap U_ a$, and they vanish on $K_ a\setminus Q$. Hence $\| \operatorname{Re}\varphi '\| +\| \operatorname{Im}\varphi '\| \leq C_ Q\sum _ J\sup _ Q|\varphi _ J|$ with a constant $C_ Q$ independent of $\varphi $, and ( 17.37 ) gives $|T(\varphi )|\leq MC_ Q\ell _0(e)\sum _ J\sup _ Q|\varphi _ J|$. By construction $T$ vanishes on forms of bidegree other than $(n-1,n-1)$, so it is a current of bidegree $(1,1)$. It is real, because the $(n-1,n-1)$-component of $\overline\varphi $ is $\overline{\varphi '}=\operatorname{Re}\varphi '-\mathrm i\operatorname{Im}\varphi '$, so that $T(\overline\varphi )=\overline{T(\varphi )}$. It is positive, because a strongly positive test form $\varphi $ of bidegree $(n-1,n-1)$ is real and positive, so that $T(\varphi )=\ell (\varphi )\geq 0$. Since $\ell $ extends $\ell _0$, the real $(1,1)$-current $R=T-	heta $ annihilates $S$. The current $R$ is $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-exact. We first show that $R$ is closed. If $\xi $ is a smooth form of bidegree $(n-2,n-1)$, then $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\partial \xi = rac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }\partial  ar\partial \partial \xi =- rac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }\partial \partial  ar\partial \xi =0$, and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}} ar\partial \xi '= rac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }\partial  ar\partial  ar\partial \xi '=0$ for $\xi '$ of bidegree $(n-1,n-2)$. Since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ is a real operator, the conjugate of a $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closed complex $(n-1,n-1)$-form $\sigma $ is $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closed, so the real forms $\operatorname{Re}\sigma $ and $\operatorname{Im}\sigma $ lie in $S$; as $R$ is complex-linear and annihilates $S$, it annihilates $\sigma $. In particular $R(\partial \xi )=R( ar\partial \xi ')=0$. For a smooth $(2n-3)$-form $\gamma $, the $(n-1,n-1)$-component of $\mathrm d\gamma $ is $\partial \gamma ^{n-2,n-1}+ ar\partial \gamma ^{n-1,n-2}$; since $R$ has bidegree $(1,1)$, it follows that $R(\mathrm d\gamma )=0$. Therefore $\mathrm dR=0$. Since $e\in S$, we also have $\int _ XR\wedge \omega ^{n-1}=0$. Let $\Lambda $ denote contraction with $\omega $, as in lemma 14.1.6 ; the identity $R\wedge \omega ^{n-1}=(\Lambda R)\omega ^ n/n$ shows that the trace $\Lambda R$ has mean zero. By lemma 14.1.3 (2), applied to the Laplacian $L=\mathrm d^*\mathrm d$ of section 14.1 , there is a real distribution $f$ with $Lf=-4\pi \Lambda R$. By lemma 14.1.6 , $\Lambda \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f=\Lambda R$, so $R'=R-\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$ is a closed real $(1,1)$-current with zero trace. By the last assertion of lemma 14.1.6 , $R'$ is harmonic, and by lemma 14.1.3 (1) it is smooth. If $n=1$, a $(1,1)$-form with zero trace vanishes, so $R'=0$. If $n\geq 2$, ( 14.13 ) gives $*R'=-R'\wedge \omega ^{n-2}/(n-2)!$, a smooth closed $(n-1,n-1)$-form; hence $*R'\in S$. Since $R$ annihilates $S$ and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}{*R'}=0$, \[  \| R'\| _{L^2}^2 =\int _ XR'\wedge *R' =R(*R')-\int _ Xf\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}{*R'}=0.  \] Thus $R'=0$ and $R=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$ in every dimension. Conclusion. The current $T=	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$ is closed and positive, and it lies in the class $\{ 	heta \} $, since it differs from $	heta $ by $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ of a distribution. By corollary 14.1.9 , there is $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ with $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=T$. This proves sufficiency. For the last assertion, $\{ 	heta \} $ is big exactly when $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta -\delta \omega )
eq \varnothing $ for some $\delta >0$. Indeed, if $T\geq \delta \omega $ is a Kähler current in $\{ 	heta \} $ (definition 14.3.1 ), then $T-\delta \omega $ is a closed positive current in the class $\{ 	heta -\delta \omega \} $, so $T-\delta \omega =	heta -\delta \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ with $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta -\delta \omega )$, by corollary 14.1.9 . Conversely, if $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta -\delta \omega )$, then $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq \delta \omega $ is a Kähler current in $\{ 	heta \} $. Applying the first part to $	heta -\delta \omega $ shows that this holds if and only if ( 17.35 ) holds for that $\delta $. $\square$ The proof of the bigness criterion rests on the following lower bound for the product of two trace masses of a current with prescribed Monge–Ampère measure. Lemma 17.4.19 . Let $A$ be a closed subset of $X$ of Lebesgue measure zero in every chart, and let $S$ be a closed positive $(1,1)$-current on $X$ whose local potentials are locally bounded on $X\setminus A$. Let $	au $ be a smooth strictly positive real $(n-1,n-1)$-form, and put $
u =\omega \wedge 	au $. If \[  \langle S^ nangle =m
u \qquad 	ext{for some }m\geq 0,  \] then 17.38  egin{equation} \label{eq:prescribed-density-mixed-trace} \left(\int _ X S\wedge 	au ight) \left(\int _ X\langle S^{n-1}angle \wedge \omega ight) \geq  rac mn\left(\int _ X
u ight)^2. \end{equation} For $n=1$ the second factor is $\int _ X\omega $. Proof. We prove a pointwise inequality for smooth forms, apply it to regularizations of the potentials of $S$ on small balls in $X\setminus A$, and globalize with a partition of unity. Step 1: a pointwise inequality. Let $\sigma $ be a smooth positive definite real $(1,1)$-form. At a given point, choose linear coordinates on the tangent space that diagonalize the Hermitian matrices of $\omega $ and $\sigma $ simultaneously, so that $\omega =\sum _ j\gamma _ j$ and $\sigma =\sum _ j\lambda _ j\gamma _ j$ with $\lambda _ j>0$, where $\gamma _ j=\mathrm i\, \mathrm dz_ j\wedge \mathrm d ar z_ j$, and put $\mathrm dV=\gamma _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \gamma _ n$. Since $	au $ is strictly positive (section 7.2 ), the form $	au -c\, \omega ^{n-1}$ is positive at this point for some $c>0$. The product of the strongly positive form $\gamma _ j$ with this positive form is a nonnegative multiple of $\mathrm dV$ (proposition 7.2.1 ), and $\gamma _ j\wedge \omega ^{n-1}=(n-1)!\, \mathrm dV$, so $\gamma _ j\wedge 	au \geq c(n-1)!\, \mathrm dV$; thus $\gamma _ j\wedge 	au =t_ j\, \mathrm dV$ with $t_ j>0$. Expanding the products, we obtain \[   rac{\sigma \wedge 	au }{\omega \wedge 	au } = rac{\sum _ j\lambda _ jt_ j}{\sum _ jt_ j},\qquad  rac{\sigma ^{n-1}\wedge \omega }{\sigma ^ n} = rac1n\sum _ j\lambda _ j^{-1}.  \] Since $\lambda _ j\sum _ k\lambda _ k^{-1}\geq 1$ for every $j$, the product of these two ratios is at least $1/n$. If $\sigma $ is only semipositive, we apply this to $\sigma +s\omega $ and let $s\downarrow 0$. Thus, for every smooth semipositive real $(1,1)$-form $\sigma $, as densities with respect to any fixed smooth volume form, 17.39  egin{equation} \label{eq:pointwise-mixed-trace} (\sigma \wedge 	au )(\sigma ^{n-1}\wedge \omega ) \geq  rac1n\sigma ^ n
u . \end{equation} Step 2: regularization on a ball. Since the local potentials of $S$ are locally bounded on the open set $X\setminus A$, every point of $X\setminus A$ is the center of a coordinate ball $B\Subset X\setminus A$ on which $S=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$ with $v$ plurisubharmonic and bounded. Fix such a ball, put $\eta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|z|^2$ as in section 9.7 , and write $
u =g\eta ^ n$ with $g$ smooth and positive on $B$. Since $v$ is bounded on $B$, the non-pluripolar powers of $S$ on $B$ are the Bedford–Taylor powers of $v$ (see the remark following definition 15.1.3 ); in particular $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n=mg\eta ^ n$. Let $v_\varepsilon =v*ho _\varepsilon $ be the regularizations of $v$ by the radial mollifiers of section 1.4 . On each ball $B'$ concentric with $B$ and of smaller radius, the functions $v_\varepsilon $ are defined for $\varepsilon $ smaller than the difference of the radii, and by proposition 8.2.2 (2) they are smooth and plurisubharmonic on $B'$ and decrease to $v$ as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. As recalled at the beginning of section 9.7 , $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_\varepsilon )^ n=\det \mathcal H(v_\varepsilon )\, \eta ^ n$. The last assertion of proposition 9.7.3 , applied on $B$ to $v$ and the continuous density $mg$, therefore gives \[  (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_\varepsilon )^ n=F_\varepsilon \eta ^ n, \qquad F_\varepsilon =\det \mathcal H(v_\varepsilon )\geq  igl ((mg)^{1/n}*ho _\varepsilon  igr )^ n.  \] The right side converges to $mg$ uniformly on compact subsets of $B$, by lemma 1.4.1 (1) applied to the continuous function $(mg)^{1/n}$. Hence $\sqrt{F_\varepsilon g}$ is bounded below by functions converging uniformly to $\sqrt mg$ on compact sets, and for every nonnegative $\chi \in C^\infty _ c(B)$, 17.40  egin{equation} \label{eq:mixed-trace-local-root-limit} \varliminf _{\varepsilon \downarrow 0} \int \chi \sqrt{F_\varepsilon g}\, \eta ^ n \geq \sqrt m\int \chi 
u . \end{equation} Moreover, for every $\chi \in C^\infty _ c(B)$, as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ along any sequence, \[  \int \chi \, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_\varepsilon \wedge 	au \longrightarrow \int \chi \, S\wedge 	au , \qquad \int \chi \, (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_\varepsilon )^{n-1}\wedge \omega \longrightarrow \int \chi \, \langle S^{n-1}angle \wedge \omega .  \] For the first convergence, note that $\int \chi \, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_\varepsilon \wedge 	au =\int v_\varepsilon \, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\chi 	au )$, by the definition of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ on currents (section 7.2 ); since $v_\varepsilon 	o v$ in $L^1$ on $\operatorname{Supp}\chi $ (lemma 1.4.1 (2)), this tends to $\int v\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\chi 	au )=\int \chi \, S\wedge 	au $. For the second convergence, choose a ball $B'$ as above containing $\operatorname{Supp}\chi $, and a sequence $\varepsilon _ j\downarrow 0$. By theorem 9.2.5 , applied on $B'$ to the closed positive current $\omega $ of bidimension $(n-1,n-1)$ and to $n-1$ copies of the decreasing sequence $(v_{\varepsilon _ j})$, the currents $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_{\varepsilon _ j})^{n-1}\wedge \omega $ converge weakly to the Bedford–Taylor product $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^{n-1}\wedge \omega $. By proposition 9.1.2 (1) and (4), these products are the exterior products with $\omega $ of the smooth forms $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_{\varepsilon _ j})^{n-1}$ and of the current $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^{n-1}$, which equals $\langle S^{n-1}angle $ on $B$. (For $n=1$ both sides of the second convergence equal $\int \chi \, \omega $.) Step 3: globalization. Let $\chi $ be a smooth function with compact support in $X\setminus A$ and $0\leq \chi \leq 1$. Cover $\operatorname{Supp}\chi $ by finitely many balls $B_ l$ as in Step 2, and write $\chi =\sum _ l\chi _ l$ with nonnegative $\chi _ l\in C^\infty _ c(B_ l)$; for instance, multiply $\chi $ by a partition of unity with compact supports subordinate to the cover of $X$ by the balls $B_ l$ and $X\setminus \operatorname{Supp}\chi $ (proposition 7.1.3 ). In each $B_ l$ we use the notation of Step 2 with an index $l$ and put \[  a_{l,\varepsilon }=\int \chi _ l\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_{l,\varepsilon }\wedge 	au ,\qquad b_{l,\varepsilon }=\int \chi _ l\, (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_{l,\varepsilon })^{n-1}\wedge \omega .  \] Let $\alpha _{l,\varepsilon }$ and $ eta _{l,\varepsilon }$ be the densities of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_{l,\varepsilon }\wedge 	au $ and $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_{l,\varepsilon })^{n-1}\wedge \omega $ with respect to $\eta _ l^ n$. By ( 17.39 ) with $\sigma =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_{l,\varepsilon }$, $\alpha _{l,\varepsilon } eta _{l,\varepsilon }\geq F_{l,\varepsilon }g_ l/n$, so the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality gives \[  \int \chi _ l\sqrt{F_{l,\varepsilon }g_ l}\, \eta _ l^ n \leq \sqrt n\int \chi _ l\sqrt{\alpha _{l,\varepsilon } eta _{l,\varepsilon }}\, \eta _ l^ n \leq \sqrt{n\, a_{l,\varepsilon }b_{l,\varepsilon }}.  \] Summing over $l$ and applying the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality to the finite sum $\sum _ l\sqrt{a_{l,\varepsilon }b_{l,\varepsilon }}$, we obtain \[  \left(\sum _ l a_{l,\varepsilon }ight) \left(\sum _ l b_{l,\varepsilon }ight) \geq  rac1n\left(\sum _ l \int \chi _ l\sqrt{F_{l,\varepsilon }g_ l}\, \eta _ l^ night)^2.  \] Now let $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ along a sequence. By Step 2, the two sums on the left converge to $\int _ X\chi \, S\wedge 	au $ and $\int _ X\chi \langle S^{n-1}angle \wedge \omega $. These are at most the corresponding integrals over $X$ without $\chi $, because $S\wedge 	au $ and $\langle S^{n-1}angle \wedge \omega $ are positive measures and $0\leq \chi \leq 1$. By ( 17.40 ) and $g_ l\eta _ l^ n=
u $, the lower limit of the right side is at least $(m/n)(\int _ X\chi 
u )^2$. Therefore \[  \left(\int _ X S\wedge 	au ight) \left(\int _ X\langle S^{n-1}angle \wedge \omega ight) \geq  rac mn\left(\int _ X\chi 
u ight)^2.  \] Finally, we remove the cutoff. Fix a metric $d$ inducing the topology of $X$ (lemma 7.1.4 ), and for $k\geq 1$ let $K_ k=\{ x\in X:d(x,A)\geq 1/k\} $, with $K_ k=X$ if $A=\varnothing $. These compact subsets of $X\setminus A$ increase to $X\setminus A$, because $A$ is closed. By proposition 7.1.3 there are smooth functions $\chi _ k\colon X	o [0,1]$ with compact support in $X\setminus A$ and $\chi _ k=1$ on $K_ k$. Since $
u $ has a smooth density and $A$ has Lebesgue measure zero, $
u (K_ k)	o 
u (X\setminus A)=\int _ X
u $, so $\int _ X\chi _ k
u 	o \int _ X
u $. Applying the last inequality to $\chi =\chi _ k$ and letting $k	o \infty $ proves ( 17.38 ). Both factors on its left are finite: the first is the pairing of a current with a smooth form on the compact manifold $X$, and the second is finite by theorem 15.4.3 . $\square$ Theorem 17.4.20 . A pseudo-effective class $\alpha \in H^{1,1}(X,\mathbb R)$ is big if and only if $\operatorname {vol}(\alpha )>0$. In particular, if a closed positive $(1,1)$-current $T$ satisfies $\int _ X\langle T^ nangle >0$, then its class is big. Proof. By proposition 15.8.2 , big classes have positive volume, and every closed positive $(1,1)$-current $T$ satisfies $\int _ X\langle T^ nangle \leq \operatorname {vol}(\{ T\} )$. It therefore suffices to show that a pseudo-effective class $\alpha $ with $m=\operatorname {vol}(\alpha )>0$ is big, and we do so by verifying Lamari's criterion (lemma 17.4.18 ). Write $\alpha =\{ 	heta \} $ with $	heta $ smooth and closed, choose $C>0$ such that $	heta +C\omega $ is positive definite, and put \[  C_0=\int _ X(	heta +(C+1)\omega )^{n-1}\wedge \omega >0;  \] the integrand is a positive multiple of the volume form at every point, by the positivity of mixed discriminants of positive definite matrices (lemma 7.2.2 (2),(3)). For $0<\varepsilon \leq 1$ let $	heta _\varepsilon =	heta +\varepsilon \omega $. Since $\alpha $ is pseudo-effective, there is $q\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ (corollary 14.1.9 ), and $	heta _\varepsilon +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q\geq \varepsilon \omega $; thus $\{ 	heta _\varepsilon \} =\alpha +\varepsilon \{ \omega \} $ is big. By proposition 16.3.2 (4), $P_{	heta _\varepsilon }[V_{	heta _\varepsilon }]=V_{	heta _\varepsilon }$, and the mass of $V_{	heta _\varepsilon }$ is \[  m_\varepsilon =\operatorname {vol}(\alpha +\varepsilon \{ \omega \} ) \geq m>0;  \] the inequality holds because $\operatorname {vol}(\alpha +\varepsilon \{ \omega \} )$ decreases to $\operatorname {vol}(\alpha )$ as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, by definition 15.8.1 , proposition 15.8.2 . Hence $V_{	heta _\varepsilon }$ is a model potential of mass $m_\varepsilon $. Fix a smooth strictly positive real $(n-1,n-1)$-form $	au $ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}	au =0$, normalized by $\int _ X\omega \wedge 	au =1$. The measure $m_\varepsilon \omega \wedge 	au $ has a smooth density with respect to $\omega ^ n$ and total mass $m_\varepsilon $. By corollary 17.4.17 , applied in the big class $\{ 	heta _\varepsilon \} $ with the reference $V_{	heta _\varepsilon }$, there are $u_\varepsilon \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta _\varepsilon )$ and finite constants $B_\varepsilon $ such that \[   egin{gathered} S_\varepsilon =	heta _\varepsilon +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\varepsilon \geq 0, \qquad \langle S_\varepsilon ^ nangle =m_\varepsilon \omega \wedge 	au ,\ V_{	heta _\varepsilon }-B_\varepsilon \leq u_\varepsilon \leq V_{	heta _\varepsilon }. \end{gathered}  \] The constants $B_\varepsilon $ need not be bounded uniformly in $\varepsilon $; we only use that $u_\varepsilon $ is locally bounded outside a closed set of measure zero. By lemma 16.2.3 , applied to the big class $\{ 	heta _\varepsilon \} $, there is a closed pluripolar set $A_\varepsilon \subset X$ such that $V_{	heta _\varepsilon }$ is locally bounded on $X\setminus A_\varepsilon $; being pluripolar, $A_\varepsilon $ has Lebesgue measure zero in every chart (see the remarks after definition 10.1.1 ). Hence $u_\varepsilon $, which lies between $V_{	heta _\varepsilon }-B_\varepsilon $ and $V_{	heta _\varepsilon }$, is locally bounded on $X\setminus A_\varepsilon $, and so are the local potentials of $S_\varepsilon $, which differ from $u_\varepsilon $ by smooth local potentials of $	heta _\varepsilon $ (lemma 7.3.1 ). We may thus apply lemma 17.4.19 to $S_\varepsilon $, with $A_\varepsilon $, $
u =\omega \wedge 	au $ and $m_\varepsilon $ in place of $A$, $
u $ and $m$: \[  \left(\int _ X S_\varepsilon \wedge 	au ight) \left(\int _ X\langle S_\varepsilon ^{n-1}angle \wedge \omega ight) \geq  rac{m_\varepsilon }{n}\geq  rac mn.  \] We bound the two factors on the left. Since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}	au =0$, the first factor equals the cohomological pairing $\int _ X	heta _\varepsilon \wedge 	au =\int _ X	heta \wedge 	au +\varepsilon $. If $n\geq 2$, the form $	heta _\varepsilon +C\omega $ is positive definite, so theorem 15.4.3 gives \[  \int _ X\langle S_\varepsilon ^{n-1}angle \wedge \omega \leq \int _ X(	heta +(C+\varepsilon )\omega )^{n-1}\wedge \omega \leq C_0;  \] the last inequality holds because $	heta +(C+1)\omega =(	heta +(C+\varepsilon )\omega )+(1-\varepsilon )\omega $ and products of positive $(1,1)$-forms are positive. If $n=1$, the second factor equals $\int _ X\omega =C_0$. As the first factor is nonnegative, in both cases \[  \left(\int _ X	heta \wedge 	au +\varepsilon ight)C_0\geq  rac mn.  \] Letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ gives $\int _ X	heta \wedge 	au \geq m/(nC_0)$. Removing the normalization of $	au $, we conclude that every smooth strictly positive $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closed $(n-1,n-1)$-form $	au $ satisfies ( 17.35 ) with $\delta =m/(nC_0)>0$. By lemma 17.4.18 , the class $\alpha $ is big. $\square$ If $\{ 	heta \} $ is pseudo-effective but not big, the theorem shows that every $	heta $-psh potential has zero non-pluripolar mass. This allows us to extend the contact theorems of chapter 16 from big to pseudo-effective classes. Corollary 17.4.21 . Let $	heta $ be a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form, and let $f\colon X	o [-\infty ,+\infty ]$ be a quasi-continuous Borel function. Suppose that the family $\mathcal A_	heta (f)$ of definition 16.1.3 is nonempty and uniformly bounded above. Then $u=P_	heta (f)$ satisfies \[  \mu _ u igl (X\setminus \{ u=f\}  igr )=0.  \] If $\{ 	heta \} $ is not big, then $\mu _ u=0$. Moreover, if $r\geq 1$ and $u_1,\ldots ,u_ r\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ have a rooftop $w=P_	heta (\min _{1\leq j\leq r}u_ j)$ that is not identically $-\infty $, then \[  \mu _ w\leq \sum _{j=1}^ r\mathbf1_{\{ w=u_ j\} }\mu _{u_ j}.  \] Proof. By proposition 16.1.4 (1), $u\in \mathcal A_	heta (f)$; that is, $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ and $u\leq f$ quasi-everywhere. If $\{ 	heta \} $ is not big, then $\mu _ u(X)=0$ by theorem 17.4.20 , since otherwise $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ would be a closed positive current of positive non-pluripolar mass in $\{ 	heta \} $. Hence $\mu _ u=0$, and in particular the first assertion holds. If $\{ 	heta \} $ is big, the first assertion is theorem 16.2.5 . For the rooftop, the function $\min _ ju_ j$ is quasi-continuous, as a finite minimum of potentials (see the beginning of section 16.1 ), and it is bounded above; its envelope is $w$. Since $w$ is not identically $-\infty $, the family $\mathcal A_	heta (\min _ ju_ j)$ is nonempty, and it is uniformly bounded above because the obstacle is. By the first assertion, $\mu _ w$ is carried by $\{ w=\min _ ju_ j\} \subset  igcup _ j\{ w=u_ j\} $. The obstacle is upper semicontinuous, so $w\leq u_ j$ everywhere by proposition 16.1.4 (1),(2), and lemma 16.2.2 gives $\mathbf1_{\{ w=u_ j\} }\mu _ w\leq \mathbf1_{\{ w=u_ j\} }\mu _{u_ j}$ for every $j$. Summing over $j$ proves the rooftop inequality. $\square$ Corollary 17.4.22 . Let $	heta $ be a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form with $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )
eq \varnothing $, and let $f$ be a continuous real function on $X$ with bounded metric Laplacian. Then \[  \langle (	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}P_	heta (f))^ nangle =\mathbf1_{\{ P_	heta (f)=f\} }(	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f)^ n,  \] where the right side is understood as in theorem 16.2.31 . In particular $\langle (	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V_	heta )^ nangle =\mathbf1_{\{ V_	heta =0\} }	heta ^ n$. If $\{ 	heta \} $ is not big, both sides of these two identities vanish. Proof. The potential $V_	heta +\min _ Xf$ lies below $f$, so $\mathcal A_	heta (f)$ is nonempty, and it is bounded above by $\max _ Xf$. Put $u=P_	heta (f)$. Since $f$ is continuous, $u\leq f$ everywhere by proposition 16.1.4 (1),(2). The scalar case of theorem 16.2.31 , with all $	heta _ j=	heta $, $u_ j=u$ and $f_ j=f$, gives \[  \mathbf1_{\{ u=f\} }\langle 	heta _ u^ nangle =\mathbf1_{\{ u=f\} }(	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f)^ n,  \] and corollary 17.4.21 shows that $\langle 	heta _ u^ nangle $ is carried by $\{ u=f\} $. This proves the first identity. For $f=0$ the envelope $P_	heta (0)$ is $V_	heta $, by definition 14.2.6 , which gives the second. If $\{ 	heta \} $ is not big, the left sides vanish by corollary 17.4.21 , and hence so do the right sides. $\square$

title: Lamari's criterion
text:
Lemma 17.4.18 (Lamari's criterion) . Let $	heta $ be a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form on $X$. Then $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )
eq \varnothing $ if and only if 17.34  egin{equation} \label{eq:lamari-positive-tests} \int _ X	heta \wedge 	au \geq 0 \end{equation} for every smooth strictly positive real $(n-1,n-1)$-form $	au $ on $X$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}	au =0$. Consequently, the class $\{ 	heta \} $ is big if and only if there is $\delta >0$ such that every such form $	au $ satisfies 17.35  egin{equation} \label{eq:lamari-strict-tests} \int _ X	heta \wedge 	au \geq \delta \int _ X\omega \wedge 	au . \end{equation} Proof. Necessity. If $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$, then $T=	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq 0$. For $	au $ as in the statement, the definition of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ as a current gives $\int _ X\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\wedge 	au =\int _ Xu\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}	au =0$, hence $\int _ X	heta \wedge 	au =\int _ XT\wedge 	au $, which is nonnegative by the definition of a positive current, since $	au $ is positive, hence strongly positive. Sufficiency. Conversely, assume ( 17.34 ) for all forms $	au $ as in the statement. We extend the functional $	au \mapsto \int _ X	heta \wedge 	au $ from $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closed forms to a positive linear functional on all smooth real $(n-1,n-1)$-forms, regard the extension as a positive $(1,1)$-current $T$, and show that $T-	heta $ is $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ of a distribution. A positive extension. Let $F$ be the real vector space of smooth real $(n-1,n-1)$-forms on $X$, let $S=\{ 	au \in F:\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}	au =0\} $, and put $e=\omega ^{n-1}$, with $e=1$ if $n=1$. Since $\omega $ is closed, $e\in S$, and $e$ is strictly positive. Define $\ell _0(	au )=\int _ X	heta \wedge 	au $ for $	au \in S$. By hypothesis $\ell _0(	au )\geq 0$ when $	au \in S$ is strictly positive. If $	au \in S$ is merely positive, then $	au +te\in S$ is strictly positive for every $t>0$. Indeed, at each point $x$ the cone of positive forms contains a ball about $e(x)$, for some norm; since the cone is stable under sums and positive multiples, it also contains the ball of $t$ times that radius about $	au (x)+te(x)$. Hence $\ell _0(	au )+t\ell _0(e)\geq 0$, and letting $t\downarrow 0$ gives $\ell _0(	au )\geq 0$. We next compare the forms in $F$ with $e$. Fix finitely many holomorphic charts $U_1,\ldots ,U_ N$ and compact sets $K_ a\subset U_ a$ with $ igcup _ aK_ a=X$. In $U_ a$ write $\eta \in F$ as $\eta =\sum _{I,J}\eta ^ a_{IJ}\, \mathrm dz_ I\wedge \mathrm d ar z_ J$, the sum running over increasing multi-indices of length $n-1$, and put \[  \| \eta \| =\max _{1\leq a\leq N}\  \max _{I,J}\  \sup _{K_ a}|\eta ^ a_{IJ}|.  \] We claim that there is a constant $M>0$ such that 17.36  egin{equation} \label{eq:lamari-uniform-domination} -M\| \eta \| e\leq \eta \leq M\| \eta \| e\qquad 	ext{for every }\eta \in F. \end{equation} Let $Z$ be the finite-dimensional real vector space of real $(n-1,n-1)$-forms with constant coefficients on $\mathbb C^ n$, normed by the maximum modulus of the coefficients, and let $P\subset Z$ be the closed convex cone of positive forms (proposition 7.2.1 ). For $x\in U_ a$, the differential of the chart is a complex-linear isomorphism from the tangent space at $x$ onto $\mathbb C^ n$, under which $\mathrm dz_ j$ corresponds to the $j$th coordinate form. Since complex-linear isomorphisms preserve positivity, a real $(n-1,n-1)$-form $\eta $ is positive at $x$ if and only if its coefficient form $\eta ^ a(x)=\sum _{I,J}\eta ^ a_{IJ}(x)\, \mathrm dz_ I\wedge \mathrm d ar z_ J\in Z$ lies in $P$. Because $e$ is strictly positive, the continuous map $x\mapsto e^ a(x)$ sends the compact set $K_ a$ into the interior of $P$; the complement of this interior is closed and disjoint from the compact image, so it has positive distance $r_ a$ from it. Put $r= rac12\min _ ar_ a$. If $\eta \in F$ satisfies $\| \eta \| \leq r$ and $x\in K_ a$, then $e^ a(x)\pm \eta ^ a(x)$ lies within distance $r<r_ a$ of $e^ a(x)$, hence in $P$; thus $e\pm \eta $ is positive at $x$. Since the sets $K_ a$ cover $X$, the forms $e\pm \eta $ are positive. Applying this to $r\eta /\| \eta \| $ for $\eta 
eq 0$ proves ( 17.36 ) with $M=1/r$. For $\eta \in F$, a form $	au \in S$ with $	au \geq \eta $ is called an $S$-majorant of $\eta $, and we put \[  p(\eta )=\inf \{ \ell _0(	au ):	au 	ext{ is an $S$-majorant of }\eta \} .  \] Let $\eta \in F$ and $C=M\| \eta \| $, so that $-Ce\leq \eta \leq Ce$ by ( 17.36 ). The form $Ce$ is an $S$-majorant of $\eta $, so $p(\eta )\leq C\ell _0(e)$. If $	au $ is an $S$-majorant of $\eta $, then $	au +Ce\geq \eta +Ce\geq 0$, so $	au +Ce\in S$ is positive and $\ell _0(	au )\geq -C\ell _0(e)$. Thus $p$ is finite. It is sublinear: the sum of $S$-majorants of $\eta _1$ and $\eta _2$ is an $S$-majorant of $\eta _1+\eta _2$, and for $\lambda >0$ the $S$-majorants of $\lambda \eta $ are $\lambda $ times those of $\eta $. If $\eta \in S$, then $\eta $ is its own $S$-majorant, and every $S$-majorant $	au $ of $\eta $ satisfies $\ell _0(	au )-\ell _0(\eta )=\ell _0(	au -\eta )\geq 0$ because $	au -\eta \in S$ is positive. Hence $p=\ell _0$ on $S$. Next we extend $\ell _0$ to a linear functional on $F$ dominated by $p$; this is the Hahn–Banach theorem, whose proof we recall. Let $\ell $ be a linear functional on a subspace $W\supset S$ which extends $\ell _0$ and satisfies $\ell \leq p$ on $W$, and let $\eta _0\in F\setminus W$. For $\eta _1,\eta _2\in W$, \[  \ell (\eta _1)+\ell (\eta _2)=\ell (\eta _1+\eta _2)\leq p(\eta _1+\eta _2)\leq p(\eta _1-\eta _0)+p(\eta _2+\eta _0),  \] so \[  \sup _{\eta _1\in W} igl (\ell (\eta _1)-p(\eta _1-\eta _0) igr ) \leq \inf _{\eta _2\in W} igl (p(\eta _2+\eta _0)-\ell (\eta _2) igr ).  \] Taking $\eta _1=\eta _2=0$ shows that the supremum is greater than $-\infty $ and the infimum is less than $+\infty $; hence both are finite, and we may choose a real number $c$ between them. Define $\ell (\eta +t\eta _0)=\ell (\eta )+tc$ for $\eta \in W$ and $t\in \mathbb R$. For $t>0$, the upper bound for $c$ with $\eta _2=\eta /t$, multiplied by $t$, gives $\ell (\eta )+tc\leq p(\eta +t\eta _0)$; for $t<0$, the lower bound for $c$ with $\eta _1=\eta /|t|$, multiplied by $|t|$, gives the same inequality. Thus the extension to $W+\mathbb R\eta _0$ is still dominated by $p$. The union of a chain of such extensions is again such an extension, so Zorn's lemma gives a maximal one, and by the step just proved its domain is $F$. We denote it again by $\ell $. The functional $\ell $ is positive: if $\eta \in F$ is positive, then $0$ is an $S$-majorant of $-\eta $, so $\ell (-\eta )\leq p(-\eta )\leq 0$. It is also bounded: by ( 17.36 ), the form $M\| \eta \| e$ is an $S$-majorant of both $\eta $ and $-\eta $, so 17.37  egin{equation} \label{eq:lamari-functional-bound} |\ell (\eta )|\leq M\ell _0(e)\| \eta \| \qquad (\eta \in F). \end{equation} We now turn $\ell $ into a current. Every smooth form on the compact manifold $X$ is a test form. For a complex form $\varphi $ of degree $2n-2$, let $\varphi '$ be its component of bidegree $(n-1,n-1)$, and put $T(\varphi )=\ell (\operatorname{Re}\varphi ')+\mathrm i\, \ell (\operatorname{Im}\varphi ')$, where $\operatorname{Re}\varphi '=(\varphi '+\overline{\varphi '})/2$ and $\operatorname{Im}\varphi '=(\varphi '-\overline{\varphi '})/(2\mathrm i)$ are real forms in $F$. This is a complex-linear functional: replacing $\varphi $ by $\mathrm i\varphi $ replaces $(\operatorname{Re}\varphi ',\operatorname{Im}\varphi ')$ by $(-\operatorname{Im}\varphi ',\operatorname{Re}\varphi ')$. Moreover, $T$ has the continuity property of a current of degree $2$. Indeed, let $Q$ be a compact subset of a chart $U$, and let $\varphi $ be supported in $Q$, with coefficients $\varphi _ J$ in real coordinates on $U$. On the compact set $K_ a\cap Q$, the coefficients of $\operatorname{Re}\varphi '$ and $\operatorname{Im}\varphi '$ in the chart $U_ a$ are linear combinations of the functions $\varphi _ J$ and $\overline{\varphi _ J}$ with coefficients that are smooth on $U\cap U_ a$, and they vanish on $K_ a\setminus Q$. Hence $\| \operatorname{Re}\varphi '\| +\| \operatorname{Im}\varphi '\| \leq C_ Q\sum _ J\sup _ Q|\varphi _ J|$ with a constant $C_ Q$ independent of $\varphi $, and ( 17.37 ) gives $|T(\varphi )|\leq MC_ Q\ell _0(e)\sum _ J\sup _ Q|\varphi _ J|$. By construction $T$ vanishes on forms of bidegree other than $(n-1,n-1)$, so it is a current of bidegree $(1,1)$. It is real, because the $(n-1,n-1)$-component of $\overline\varphi $ is $\overline{\varphi '}=\operatorname{Re}\varphi '-\mathrm i\operatorname{Im}\varphi '$, so that $T(\overline\varphi )=\overline{T(\varphi )}$. It is positive, because a strongly positive test form $\varphi $ of bidegree $(n-1,n-1)$ is real and positive, so that $T(\varphi )=\ell (\varphi )\geq 0$. Since $\ell $ extends $\ell _0$, the real $(1,1)$-current $R=T-	heta $ annihilates $S$. The current $R$ is $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-exact. We first show that $R$ is closed. If $\xi $ is a smooth form of bidegree $(n-2,n-1)$, then $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\partial \xi = rac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }\partial  ar\partial \partial \xi =- rac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }\partial \partial  ar\partial \xi =0$, and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}} ar\partial \xi '= rac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }\partial  ar\partial  ar\partial \xi '=0$ for $\xi '$ of bidegree $(n-1,n-2)$. Since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ is a real operator, the conjugate of a $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closed complex $(n-1,n-1)$-form $\sigma $ is $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closed, so the real forms $\operatorname{Re}\sigma $ and $\operatorname{Im}\sigma $ lie in $S$; as $R$ is complex-linear and annihilates $S$, it annihilates $\sigma $. In particular $R(\partial \xi )=R( ar\partial \xi ')=0$. For a smooth $(2n-3)$-form $\gamma $, the $(n-1,n-1)$-component of $\mathrm d\gamma $ is $\partial \gamma ^{n-2,n-1}+ ar\partial \gamma ^{n-1,n-2}$; since $R$ has bidegree $(1,1)$, it follows that $R(\mathrm d\gamma )=0$. Therefore $\mathrm dR=0$. Since $e\in S$, we also have $\int _ XR\wedge \omega ^{n-1}=0$. Let $\Lambda $ denote contraction with $\omega $, as in lemma 14.1.6 ; the identity $R\wedge \omega ^{n-1}=(\Lambda R)\omega ^ n/n$ shows that the trace $\Lambda R$ has mean zero. By lemma 14.1.3 (2), applied to the Laplacian $L=\mathrm d^*\mathrm d$ of section 14.1 , there is a real distribution $f$ with $Lf=-4\pi \Lambda R$. By lemma 14.1.6 , $\Lambda \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f=\Lambda R$, so $R'=R-\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$ is a closed real $(1,1)$-current with zero trace. By the last assertion of lemma 14.1.6 , $R'$ is harmonic, and by lemma 14.1.3 (1) it is smooth. If $n=1$, a $(1,1)$-form with zero trace vanishes, so $R'=0$. If $n\geq 2$, ( 14.13 ) gives $*R'=-R'\wedge \omega ^{n-2}/(n-2)!$, a smooth closed $(n-1,n-1)$-form; hence $*R'\in S$. Since $R$ annihilates $S$ and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}{*R'}=0$, \[  \| R'\| _{L^2}^2 =\int _ XR'\wedge *R' =R(*R')-\int _ Xf\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}{*R'}=0.  \] Thus $R'=0$ and $R=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$ in every dimension. Conclusion. The current $T=	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$ is closed and positive, and it lies in the class $\{ 	heta \} $, since it differs from $	heta $ by $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ of a distribution. By corollary 14.1.9 , there is $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ with $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=T$. This proves sufficiency. For the last assertion, $\{ 	heta \} $ is big exactly when $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta -\delta \omega )
eq \varnothing $ for some $\delta >0$. Indeed, if $T\geq \delta \omega $ is a Kähler current in $\{ 	heta \} $ (definition 14.3.1 ), then $T-\delta \omega $ is a closed positive current in the class $\{ 	heta -\delta \omega \} $, so $T-\delta \omega =	heta -\delta \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ with $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta -\delta \omega )$, by corollary 14.1.9 . Conversely, if $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta -\delta \omega )$, then $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq \delta \omega $ is a Kähler current in $\{ 	heta \} $. Applying the first part to $	heta -\delta \omega $ shows that this holds if and only if ( 17.35 ) holds for that $\delta $. $\square$

Lemma 17.4.19 . Let $A$ be a closed subset of $X$ of Lebesgue measure zero in every chart, and let $S$ be a closed positive $(1,1)$-current on $X$ whose local potentials are locally bounded on $X\setminus A$. Let $	au $ be a smooth strictly positive real $(n-1,n-1)$-form, and put $

We prove a pointwise inequality for smooth forms, apply it to regularizations of the potentials of $S$ on small balls in $X\setminus A$, and globalize with a partition of unity. Step 1: a pointwise inequality. Let $\sigma $ be a smooth positive definite real $(1,1)$-form. At a given point, choose linear coordinates on the tangent space that diagonalize the Hermitian matrices of $\omega $ and $\sigma $ simultaneously, so that $\omega =\sum _ j\gamma _ j$ and $\sigma =\sum _ j\lambda _ j\gamma _ j$ with $\lambda _ j>0$, where $\gamma _ j=\mathrm i\, \mathrm dz_ j\wedge \mathrm d ar z_ j$, and put $\mathrm dV=\gamma _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \gamma _ n$. Since $	au $ is strictly positive (section 7.2 ), the form $	au -c\, \omega ^{n-1}$ is positive at this point for some $c>0$. The product of the strongly positive form $\gamma _ j$ with this positive form is a nonnegative multiple of $\mathrm dV$ (proposition 7.2.1 ), and $\gamma _ j\wedge \omega ^{n-1}=(n-1)!\, \mathrm dV$, so $\gamma _ j\wedge 	au \geq c(n-1)!\, \mathrm dV$; thus $\gamma _ j\wedge 	au =t_ j\, \mathrm dV$ with $t_ j>0$. Expanding the products, we obtain \[   rac{\sigma \wedge 	au }{\omega \wedge 	au } = rac{\sum _ j\lambda _ jt_ j}{\sum _ jt_ j},\qquad  rac{\sigma ^{n-1}\wedge \omega }{\sigma ^ n} = rac1n\sum _ j\lambda _ j^{-1}.  \] Since $\lambda _ j\sum _ k\lambda _ k^{-1}\geq 1$ for every $j$, the product of these two ratios is at least $1/n$. If $\sigma $ is only semipositive, we apply this to $\sigma +s\omega $ and let $s\downarrow 0$. Thus, for every smooth semipositive real $(1,1)$-form $\sigma $, as densities with respect to any fixed smooth volume form, 17.39  egin{equation} \label{eq:pointwise-mixed-trace} (\sigma \wedge 	au )(\sigma ^{n-1}\wedge \omega ) \geq  rac1n\sigma ^ n
u . \end{equation} Step 2: regularization on a ball. Since the local potentials of $S$ are locally bounded on the open set $X\setminus A$, every point of $X\setminus A$ is the center of a coordinate ball $B\Subset X\setminus A$ on which $S=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$ with $v$ plurisubharmonic and bounded. Fix such a ball, put $\eta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|z|^2$ as in section 9.7 , and write $
u =g\eta ^ n$ with $g$ smooth and positive on $B$. Since $v$ is bounded on $B$, the non-pluripolar powers of $S$ on $B$ are the Bedford–Taylor powers of $v$ (see the remark following definition 15.1.3 ); in particular $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n=mg\eta ^ n$. Let $v_\varepsilon =v*ho _\varepsilon $ be the regularizations of $v$ by the radial mollifiers of section 1.4 . On each ball $B'$ concentric with $B$ and of smaller radius, the functions $v_\varepsilon $ are defined for $\varepsilon $ smaller than the difference of the radii, and by proposition 8.2.2 (2) they are smooth and plurisubharmonic on $B'$ and decrease to $v$ as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. As recalled at the beginning of section 9.7 , $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_\varepsilon )^ n=\det \mathcal H(v_\varepsilon )\, \eta ^ n$. The last assertion of proposition 9.7.3 , applied on $B$ to $v$ and the continuous density $mg$, therefore gives \[  (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_\varepsilon )^ n=F_\varepsilon \eta ^ n, \qquad F_\varepsilon =\det \mathcal H(v_\varepsilon )\geq  igl ((mg)^{1/n}*ho _\varepsilon  igr )^ n.  \] The right side converges to $mg$ uniformly on compact subsets of $B$, by lemma 1.4.1 (1) applied to the continuous function $(mg)^{1/n}$. Hence $\sqrt{F_\varepsilon g}$ is bounded below by functions converging uniformly to $\sqrt mg$ on compact sets, and for every nonnegative $\chi \in C^\infty _ c(B)$, 17.40  egin{equation} \label{eq:mixed-trace-local-root-limit} \varliminf _{\varepsilon \downarrow 0} \int \chi \sqrt{F_\varepsilon g}\, \eta ^ n \geq \sqrt m\int \chi 
u . \end{equation} Moreover, for every $\chi \in C^\infty _ c(B)$, as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ along any sequence, \[  \int \chi \, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_\varepsilon \wedge 	au \longrightarrow \int \chi \, S\wedge 	au , \qquad \int \chi \, (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_\varepsilon )^{n-1}\wedge \omega \longrightarrow \int \chi \, \langle S^{n-1}angle \wedge \omega .  \] For the first convergence, note that $\int \chi \, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_\varepsilon \wedge 	au =\int v_\varepsilon \, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\chi 	au )$, by the definition of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ on currents (section 7.2 ); since $v_\varepsilon 	o v$ in $L^1$ on $\operatorname{Supp}\chi $ (lemma 1.4.1 (2)), this tends to $\int v\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\chi 	au )=\int \chi \, S\wedge 	au $. For the second convergence, choose a ball $B'$ as above containing $\operatorname{Supp}\chi $, and a sequence $\varepsilon _ j\downarrow 0$. By theorem 9.2.5 , applied on $B'$ to the closed positive current $\omega $ of bidimension $(n-1,n-1)$ and to $n-1$ copies of the decreasing sequence $(v_{\varepsilon _ j})$, the currents $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_{\varepsilon _ j})^{n-1}\wedge \omega $ converge weakly to the Bedford–Taylor product $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^{n-1}\wedge \omega $. By proposition 9.1.2 (1) and (4), these products are the exterior products with $\omega $ of the smooth forms $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_{\varepsilon _ j})^{n-1}$ and of the current $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^{n-1}$, which equals $\langle S^{n-1}angle $ on $B$. (For $n=1$ both sides of the second convergence equal $\int \chi \, \omega $.) Step 3: globalization. Let $\chi $ be a smooth function with compact support in $X\setminus A$ and $0\leq \chi \leq 1$. Cover $\operatorname{Supp}\chi $ by finitely many balls $B_ l$ as in Step 2, and write $\chi =\sum _ l\chi _ l$ with nonnegative $\chi _ l\in C^\infty _ c(B_ l)$; for instance, multiply $\chi $ by a partition of unity with compact supports subordinate to the cover of $X$ by the balls $B_ l$ and $X\setminus \operatorname{Supp}\chi $ (proposition 7.1.3 ). In each $B_ l$ we use the notation of Step 2 with an index $l$ and put \[  a_{l,\varepsilon }=\int \chi _ l\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_{l,\varepsilon }\wedge 	au ,\qquad b_{l,\varepsilon }=\int \chi _ l\, (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_{l,\varepsilon })^{n-1}\wedge \omega .  \] Let $\alpha _{l,\varepsilon }$ and $ eta _{l,\varepsilon }$ be the densities of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_{l,\varepsilon }\wedge 	au $ and $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_{l,\varepsilon })^{n-1}\wedge \omega $ with respect to $\eta _ l^ n$. By ( 17.39 ) with $\sigma =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_{l,\varepsilon }$, $\alpha _{l,\varepsilon } eta _{l,\varepsilon }\geq F_{l,\varepsilon }g_ l/n$, so the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality gives \[  \int \chi _ l\sqrt{F_{l,\varepsilon }g_ l}\, \eta _ l^ n \leq \sqrt n\int \chi _ l\sqrt{\alpha _{l,\varepsilon } eta _{l,\varepsilon }}\, \eta _ l^ n \leq \sqrt{n\, a_{l,\varepsilon }b_{l,\varepsilon }}.  \] Summing over $l$ and applying the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality to the finite sum $\sum _ l\sqrt{a_{l,\varepsilon }b_{l,\varepsilon }}$, we obtain \[  \left(\sum _ l a_{l,\varepsilon }ight) \left(\sum _ l b_{l,\varepsilon }ight) \geq  rac1n\left(\sum _ l \int \chi _ l\sqrt{F_{l,\varepsilon }g_ l}\, \eta _ l^ night)^2.  \] Now let $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ along a sequence. By Step 2, the two sums on the left converge to $\int _ X\chi \, S\wedge 	au $ and $\int _ X\chi \langle S^{n-1}angle \wedge \omega $. These are at most the corresponding integrals over $X$ without $\chi $, because $S\wedge 	au $ and $\langle S^{n-1}angle \wedge \omega $ are positive measures and $0\leq \chi \leq 1$. title: Positive nonpluripolar mass bigness
text: Theorem 17.4.20 . A pseudo-effective class $\alpha \in H^{1,1}(X,\mathbb R)$ is big if and only if $\operatorname {vol}(\alpha )>0$. In particular, if a closed positive $(1,1)$-current $T$ satisfies $\int _ X\langle T^ n\rangle >0$, then its class is big. Proof. By proposition 15.8.2 , big classes have positive volume, and every closed positive $(1,1)$-current $T$ satisfies $\int _ X\langle T^ n\rangle \leq \operatorname {vol}(\{ T\} )$. It therefore suffices to show that a pseudo-effective class $\alpha $ with $m=\operatorname {vol}(\alpha )>0$ is big, and we do so by verifying Lamari's criterion (lemma 17.4.18 ). Write $\alpha =\{ \theta \} $ with $\theta $ smooth and closed, choose $C>0$ such that $\theta +C\omega $ is positive definite, and put \[  C_0=\int _ X(\theta +(C+1)\omega )^{n-1}\wedge \omega >0;  \] the integrand is a positive multiple of the volume form at every point, by the positivity of mixed discriminants of positive definite matrices (lemma 7.2.2 (2),(3)). For $0<\varepsilon \leq 1$ let $\theta _\varepsilon =\theta +\varepsilon \omega $. Since $\alpha $ is pseudo-effective, there is $q\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ (corollary 14.1.9 ), and $\theta _\varepsilon +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q\geq \varepsilon \omega $; thus $\{ \theta _\varepsilon \} =\alpha +\varepsilon \{ \omega \} $ is big. By proposition 16.3.2 (4), $P_{\theta _\varepsilon }[V_{\theta _\varepsilon }]=V_{\theta _\varepsilon }$, and the mass of $V_{\theta _\varepsilon }$ is \[  m_\varepsilon =\operatorname {vol}(\alpha +\varepsilon \{ \omega \} ) \geq m>0;  \] the inequality holds because $\operatorname {vol}(\alpha +\varepsilon \{ \omega \} )$ decreases to $\operatorname {vol}(\alpha )$ as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, by definition 15.8.1 , proposition 15.8.2 . Hence $V_{\theta _\varepsilon }$ is a model potential of mass $m_\varepsilon $. Fix a smooth strictly positive real $(n-1,n-1)$-form $\tau $ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\tau =0$, normalized by $\int _ X\omega \wedge \tau =1$. The measure $m_\varepsilon \omega \wedge \tau $ has a smooth density with respect to $\omega ^ n$ and total mass $m_\varepsilon $. By corollary 17.4.17 , applied in the big class $\{ \theta _\varepsilon \} $ with the reference $V_{\theta _\varepsilon }$, there are $u_\varepsilon \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta _\varepsilon )$ and finite constants $B_\varepsilon $ such that \[  \begin{gathered} S_\varepsilon =\theta _\varepsilon +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\varepsilon \geq 0, \qquad \langle S_\varepsilon ^ n\rangle =m_\varepsilon \omega \wedge \tau ,\\ V_{\theta _\varepsilon }-B_\varepsilon \leq u_\varepsilon \leq V_{\theta _\varepsilon }. \end{gathered}  \] The constants $B_\varepsilon $ need not be bounded uniformly in $\varepsilon $; we only use that $u_\varepsilon $ is locally bounded outside a closed set of measure zero. By lemma 16.2.3 , applied to the big class $\{ \theta _\varepsilon \} $, there is a closed pluripolar set $A_\varepsilon \subset X$ such that $V_{\theta _\varepsilon }$ is locally bounded on $X\setminus A_\varepsilon $; being pluripolar, $A_\varepsilon $ has Lebesgue measure zero in every chart (see the remarks after definition 10.1.1 ). Hence $u_\varepsilon $, which lies between $V_{\theta _\varepsilon }-B_\varepsilon $ and $V_{\theta _\varepsilon }$, is locally bounded on $X\setminus A_\varepsilon $, and so are the local potentials of $S_\varepsilon $, which differ from $u_\varepsilon $ by smooth local potentials of $\theta _\varepsilon $ (lemma 7.3.1 ). We may thus apply lemma 17.4.19 to $S_\varepsilon $, with $A_\varepsilon $, $\nu =\omega \wedge \tau $ and $m_\varepsilon $ in place of $A$, $\nu $ and $m$: \[  \left(\int _ X S_\varepsilon \wedge \tau \right) \left(\int _ X\langle S_\varepsilon ^{n-1}\rangle \wedge \omega \right) \geq \frac{m_\varepsilon }{n}\geq \frac mn.  \] We bound the two factors on the left. Since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\tau =0$, the first factor equals the cohomological pairing $\int _ X\theta _\varepsilon \wedge \tau =\int _ X\theta \wedge \tau +\varepsilon $. If $n\geq 2$, the form $\theta _\varepsilon +C\omega $ is positive definite, so theorem 15.4.3 gives \[  \int _ X\langle S_\varepsilon ^{n-1}\rangle \wedge \omega \leq \int _ X(\theta +(C+\varepsilon )\omega )^{n-1}\wedge \omega \leq C_0;  \] the last inequality holds because $\theta +(C+1)\omega =(\theta +(C+\varepsilon )\omega )+(1-\varepsilon )\omega $ and products of positive $(1,1)$-forms are positive. If $n=1$, the second factor equals $\int _ X\omega =C_0$. As the first factor is nonnegative, in both cases \[  \left(\int _ X\theta \wedge \tau +\varepsilon \right)C_0\geq \frac mn.  \] Letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ gives $\int _ X\theta \wedge \tau \geq m/(nC_0)$. Removing the normalization of $\tau $, we conclude that every smooth strictly positive $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closed $(n-1,n-1)$-form $\tau $ satisfies ( 17.35 ) with $\delta =m/(nC_0)>0$. By lemma 17.4.18 , the class $\alpha $ is big. $\square$

title: Pseudoeffective obstacle contact
text: Corollary 17.4.21 . Let $\theta $ be a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form, and let $f\colon X\to [-\infty ,+\infty ]$ be a quasi-continuous Borel function. Suppose that the family $\mathcal A_\theta (f)$ of definition 16.1.3 is nonempty and uniformly bounded above. Then $u=P_\theta (f)$ satisfies \[  \mu _ u\bigl (X\setminus \{ u=f\} \bigr )=0.  \] If $\{ \theta \} $ is not big, then $\mu _ u=0$. Moreover, if $r\geq 1$ and $u_1,\ldots ,u_ r\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ have a rooftop $w=P_\theta (\min _{1\leq j\leq r}u_ j)$ that is not identically $-\infty $, then \[  \mu _ w\leq \sum _{j=1}^ r\mathbf1_{\{ w=u_ j\} }\mu _{u_ j}.  \] Proof. By proposition 16.1.4 (1), $u\in \mathcal A_\theta (f)$; that is, $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and $u\leq f$ quasi-everywhere. If $\{ \theta \} $ is not big, then $\mu _ u(X)=0$ by theorem 17.4.20 , since otherwise $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ would be a closed positive current of positive non-pluripolar mass in $\{ \theta \} $. Hence $\mu _ u=0$, and in particular the first assertion holds. If $\{ \theta \} $ is big, the first assertion is theorem 16.2.5 . For the rooftop, the function $\min _ ju_ j$ is quasi-continuous, as a finite minimum of potentials (see the beginning of section 16.1 ), and it is bounded above; its envelope is $w$. Since $w$ is not identically $-\infty $, the family $\mathcal A_\theta (\min _ ju_ j)$ is nonempty, and it is uniformly bounded above because the obstacle is. By the first assertion, $\mu _ w$ is carried by $\{ w=\min _ ju_ j\} \subset \bigcup _ j\{ w=u_ j\} $. The obstacle is upper semicontinuous, so $w\leq u_ j$ everywhere by proposition 16.1.4 (1),(2), and lemma 16.2.2 gives $\mathbf1_{\{ w=u_ j\} }\mu _ w\leq \mathbf1_{\{ w=u_ j\} }\mu _{u_ j}$ for every $j$. Summing over $j$ proves the rooftop inequality. $\square$

title: Pseudoeffective regular obstacle density
text: Corollary 17.4.22 . Let $\theta $ be a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form with $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )\neq \varnothing $, and let $f$ be a continuous real function on $X$ with bounded metric Laplacian. Then \[  \langle (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}P_\theta (f))^ n\rangle =\mathbf1_{\{ P_\theta (f)=f\} }(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f)^ n,  \] where the right side is understood as in theorem 16.2.31 . In particular $\langle (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V_\theta )^ n\rangle =\mathbf1_{\{ V_\theta =0\} }\theta ^ n$. If $\{ \theta \} $ is not big, both sides of these two identities vanish. Proof. The potential $V_\theta +\min _ Xf$ lies below $f$, so $\mathcal A_\theta (f)$ is nonempty, and it is bounded above by $\max _ Xf$. Put $u=P_\theta (f)$. Since $f$ is continuous, $u\leq f$ everywhere by proposition 16.1.4 (1),(2). The scalar case of theorem 16.2.31 , with all $\theta _ j=\theta $, $u_ j=u$ and $f_ j=f$, gives \[  \mathbf1_{\{ u=f\} }\langle \theta _ u^ n\rangle =\mathbf1_{\{ u=f\} }(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f)^ n,  \] and corollary 17.4.21 shows that $\langle \theta _ u^ n\rangle $ is carried by $\{ u=f\} $. This proves the first identity. For $f=0$ the envelope $P_\theta (0)$ is $V_\theta $, by definition 14.2.6 , which gives the second. If $\{ \theta \} $ is not big, the left sides vanish by corollary 17.4.21 , and hence so do the right sides. $\square$

title: Mixed masses and concavity
text:
17.4.5 Mixed masses and concavity We now compare the mixed non-pluripolar mass of $n$ closed positive currents, which may lie in different classes, with their individual masses. The idea is to replace each current by a solution of a Monge–Ampère equation with one and the same smooth right-hand side. Since singularity envelopes preserve mixed masses (proposition 16.3.2 (3)), such a replacement does not change the mixed mass, and for the solutions the pointwise mixed lower bound of proposition 15.4.5 integrates to the desired inequality. The equations can be solved because, by theorem 17.4.20 , every current of positive mass lies in a big class. Theorem 17.4.23 . Let $X$ be a connected compact Kähler manifold of dimension $n\geq 1$, and let $T_1,\ldots ,T_ n$ be closed positive $(1,1)$-currents on $X$. Then 17.41  egin{equation} \label{eq:ordinary-mixed-mass-geometric-mean} \int _ X\langle T_1\wedge \cdots \wedge T_ nangle \geq \prod _{i=1}^ n\left(\int _ X\langle T_ i^ nangle ight)^{1/n}. \end{equation} Consequently the functions \[  T\longmapsto \left(\int _ X\langle T^ nangle ight)^{1/n}, \qquad T\longmapsto \log \left(\int _ X\langle T^ nangle ight)  \] are concave on the convex cone of closed positive $(1,1)$-currents on $X$, with the convention $\log 0=-\infty $ for the second function. Proof. All the masses involved are finite by theorem 15.4.3 . If one of the masses $\int _ X\langle T_ i^ nangle $ vanishes, the right side of ( 17.41 ) is zero and there is nothing to prove. Otherwise put $m_ i=\int _ X\langle T_ i^ nangle >0$. Both sides of ( 17.41 ) are positively homogeneous of degree one in each $T_ i$, by the multilinearity of non-pluripolar products (proposition 15.1.5 ), so after replacing $T_ i$ by $m_ i^{-1/n}T_ i$ we may assume $m_ i=1$ for all $i$. By theorem 17.4.20 , the class of each $T_ i$ is big. Let $	heta _ i$ be a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form in the class of $T_ i$ (definition 14.1.8 ). By corollary 14.1.9 we can write $T_ i=	heta _ i+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ i$ with $u_ i\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta _ i)$. Set $\phi _ i=P_{	heta _ i}[u_ i]$. By the mass preservation in proposition 16.3.2 (3) and by theorem 16.4.7 , $\phi _ i$ is a model potential of mass one. Let $
u =\omega ^ n/\int _ X\omega ^ n$. This smooth probability measure is non-pluripolar, as noted after definition 17.4.1 . In each big class $\{ 	heta _ i\} $, theorem 17.4.13 gives \[  w_ i\in \mathcal E(X,	heta _ i,\phi _ i),\qquad S_ i=	heta _ i+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ i\geq 0,\qquad \langle S_ i^ nangle =
u .  \] By proposition 16.4.10 , $P_{	heta _ i}[w_ i]=P_{	heta _ i}[\phi _ i]=\phi _ i$. Applying the mixed mass preservation of proposition 16.3.2 (3) first to the tuple $(w_1,\ldots ,w_ n)$ and then to the tuple $(u_1,\ldots ,u_ n)$, we obtain \[  \int _ X\langle S_1\wedge \cdots \wedge S_ nangle =\int _ X\left\langle  igwedge _{i=1}^ n (	heta _ i+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\phi _ i)ightangle =\int _ X\langle T_1\wedge \cdots \wedge T_ nangle .  \] On the other hand, proposition 15.4.5 , with all densities equal to one, gives $\langle S_1\wedge \cdots \wedge S_ nangle \geq 
u $. Hence the common value of these mixed masses is at least $
u (X)=1$, which is the normalized inequality. Undoing the scalings proves ( 17.41 ). For the concavity, let $T,S$ be closed positive $(1,1)$-currents and $0<t<1$; for $t=0,1$ there is nothing to prove. Put $a=\int _ X\langle T^ nangle $ and $b=\int _ X\langle S^ nangle $. By multilinearity, \[  \int _ X\langle ((1-t)T+tS)^ nangle =\sum _{k=0}^ n inom nk(1-t)^ kt^{n-k} \int _ X\langle T^ k\wedge S^{n-k}angle .  \] For $1\leq k\leq n-1$, ( 17.41 ) with $k$ factors $T$ and $n-k$ factors $S$ gives $\int _ X\langle T^ k\wedge S^{n-k}angle \geq a^{k/n}b^{(n-k)/n}$; the terms with $k=n$ and $k=0$ are $a$ and $b$, also when one of them vanishes. The binomial formula therefore yields \[  \int _ X\langle ((1-t)T+tS)^ nangle \geq  ig ((1-t)a^{1/n}+tb^{1/n} ig )^ n.  \] Taking $n$th roots proves that the function $T\mapsto (\int _ X\langle T^ nangle )^{1/n}$ is concave. If $a$ and $b$ are both positive, then, since the logarithm is increasing and concave, \[   egin{aligned}  \log \Big(\int _ X\langle ((1-t)T+tS)^ nangle \Big) & \geq n\log  ig ((1-t)a^{1/n}+tb^{1/n} ig )\ & \geq (1-t)\log a+t\log b. \end{aligned}  \] If one of them is zero, the right side is $-\infty $ for $0<t<1$, so there is nothing to prove. $\square$ The connectedness of $X$ cannot be omitted when $n\geq 2$. Let $X$ be the disjoint union of two compact Kähler manifolds $X',X''$ of dimension $n\geq 2$, with Kähler forms $\omega '$ and $\omega ''$. Let $T_1$ equal $\omega '$ on $X'$ and zero on $X''$, let $T_2$ equal zero on $X'$ and $\omega ''$ on $X''$, and let $T_3,\ldots ,T_ n$ equal $\omega '$ on $X'$ and $\omega ''$ on $X''$. Every mass $\int _ X\langle T_ i^ nangle $ is positive, but $\langle T_1\wedge \cdots \wedge T_ nangle =0$. The theorem applies separately on each connected component.

text:

u .  \] By proposition 16.4.10 , $P_{	heta _ i}[w_ i]=P_{	heta _ i}[\phi _ i]=\phi _ i$. u $. Hence the common value of these mixed masses is at least $
u (X)=1$, which is the normalized inequality. Undoing the scalings proves ( 17.41 ). For the concavity, let $T,S$ be closed positive $(1,1)$-currents and $0<t<1$; for $t=0,1$ there is nothing to prove. Put $a=\int _ X\langle T^ nangle $ and $b=\int _ X\langle S^ nangle $. By multilinearity, \[  \int _ X\langle ((1-t)T+tS)^ nangle =\sum _{k=0}^ n inom nk(1-t)^ kt^{n-k} \int _ X\langle T^ k\wedge S^{n-k}angle .  \] For $1\leq k\leq n-1$, ( 17.41 ) with $k$ factors $T$ and $n-k$ factors $S$ gives $\int _ X\langle T^ k\wedge S^{n-k}angle \geq a^{k/n}b^{(n-k)/n}$; the terms with $k=n$ and $k=0$ are $a$ and $b$, also when one of them vanishes. title: Ordinary mixed mass geometric mean
