This proves $K_{F+G}=K_ F+K_ G$. Finally, if $K_ F=P$ and $K_ G=P'$, then $F\preceq h_ P$ and $G\preceq h_{P'}$ by the first part, and $h_ P+h_{P'}=h_{P+P'}$; hence $F+G\in \mathcal P(N_{\mathbb R},P+P')$ and $K_{F+G}=P+P'$, so that $F+G\in \mathcal E(N_{\mathbb R},P+P')$. $\square$

title: Convex mollification
text: Lemma 18.3.3 . Let $A$ be a finite convex function on $N_{\mathbb R}$, and let $\rho _\varepsilon (y)=\varepsilon ^{-n}\rho (y/\varepsilon )$ be the mollifiers of section 1.4 , in the coordinates of a basis of $N$. Then the functions $A*\rho _\varepsilon $, $\varepsilon >0$, are smooth and convex, $A*\rho _\varepsilon (x)$ is a nondecreasing function of $\varepsilon >0$ with $A*\rho _\varepsilon \geq A$ for every $x$, and $A*\rho _\varepsilon \to A$ locally uniformly as $\varepsilon \to 0$. Proof. If $n=0$, then $A*\rho _\varepsilon =A$ and there is nothing to prove; let $n\geq 1$. Recall that $\rho $ is smooth, nonnegative, even, supported in the unit ball, and has integral one. Since $A$ is continuous, being locally Lipschitz by proposition 18.1.3 , the functions $A*\rho _\varepsilon $ are smooth by section 1.4 , and they converge to $A$ locally uniformly by lemma 1.4.1 (1). They are convex, because $A*\rho _\varepsilon (x)=\int A(x-y)\rho _\varepsilon (y)\, \mathrm dy$ and the convexity inequalities of the functions $x\mapsto A(x-y)$ can be integrated against $\rho _\varepsilon (y)\, \mathrm dy\geq 0$. For fixed $x$, consider the function \[  g(\varepsilon )=\int A(x-\varepsilon y)\rho (y)\, \mathrm dy\qquad (\varepsilon \in \mathbb R),  \] which is finite because $A$ is continuous and $\rho $ has compact support. The substitution $y\mapsto \varepsilon y$ shows that $g(\varepsilon )=A*\rho _\varepsilon (x)$ for $\varepsilon >0$, and $g(0)=A(x)$. For each $y$, the function $\varepsilon \mapsto A(x-\varepsilon y)$ is convex, so $g$ is convex; and $g$ is even, because $\rho $ is even. A convex even function on $\mathbb R$ is nondecreasing on $[0,+\infty )$: if $0\leq a<b$, then $a=\lambda b+(1-\lambda )(-b)$ with $\lambda =(a+b)/(2b)\in (0,1]$, so that $g(a)\leq \lambda g(b)+(1-\lambda )g(-b)=g(b)$. Hence $A*\rho _\varepsilon (x)$ is nondecreasing in $\varepsilon >0$ and bounded below by $g(0)=A(x)$. $\square$

title: Convex decreasing smooth growth approximation
text: Proposition 18.3.4 . Let $P\subset M_{\mathbb R}$ be a convex body. Every $F\in \mathcal P(N_{\mathbb R},P)$ is the pointwise limit of a decreasing sequence of smooth functions $F_ j\in \mathcal E^\infty (N_{\mathbb R},P)$, and the convergence is locally uniform. If functions $F_ j\colon N_{\mathbb R}\to (-\infty ,+\infty ]$ decrease pointwise to a function $F$, then the conjugates $F_ j^*$ increase pointwise to $F^*$. A sequence of finite convex functions on $N_{\mathbb R}$ converges pointwise to a finite function if and only if it converges locally uniformly. Proof. Let $A_ j=\max \{ F,h_ P-j\} $. These are convex functions, decreasing in $j$, with $A_ j\sim h_ P$, and $A_ j=F$ on every compact set on which $h_ P-F\leq j$; hence $A_ j\to F$ locally uniformly. With the mollifiers $\rho _\varepsilon $ of lemma 18.3.3 , choose $\varepsilon _ j\downarrow 0$ and set $F_ j=A_ j*\rho _{\varepsilon _ j}$. By that lemma, these functions are smooth and convex, and the monotonicity in $\varepsilon $ together with $A_{j+1}\leq A_ j$ gives $F_{j+1}=A_{j+1}*\rho _{\varepsilon _{j+1}}\leq A_ j*\rho _{\varepsilon _{j+1}}\leq A_ j*\rho _{\varepsilon _ j}=F_ j$, and $F_ j\geq A_ j\geq F$. By proposition 18.3.2 , $F$ and $h_ P$ are Lipschitz with constant $\max _{p\in P}|p|$, hence so is $A_ j$, and therefore $|F_ j-A_ j|\leq C\varepsilon _ j$ with $C=\max _{p\in P}|p|\int |y|\rho (y)\, \mathrm dy$. Consequently $F_ j\sim A_ j\sim h_ P$, so $F_ j\in \mathcal E^\infty (N_{\mathbb R},P)$, and $F_ j\to F$ locally uniformly. If $F_ j\downarrow F$ pointwise, then \[  \sup _ jF_ j^*(p)=\sup _ j\sup _ x\bigl (\langle p,x\rangle -F_ j(x)\bigr )=\sup _ x\sup _ j\bigl (\langle p,x\rangle -F_ j(x)\bigr )=F^*(p),  \] and the conjugates $F_ j^*$ increase, because conjugation reverses inequalities. Finally, if a sequence of finite convex functions on $N_{\mathbb R}$ converges pointwise to a finite function, it converges locally uniformly by proposition 18.1.4 , applied with $\Omega $ and the dense subset both equal to $N_{\mathbb R}$, and conversely local uniform convergence implies pointwise convergence. $\square$

title: Convex degenerate full mass sum
text: Example 18.3.5 . The hypotheses $K_ F=P$ and $K_ G=P'$ in the last assertion of proposition 18.3.2 cannot be replaced by $F\in \mathcal E(N_{\mathbb R},P)$ and $G\in \mathcal E(N_{\mathbb R},P')$: when $P$ has empty interior, membership in $\mathcal E(N_{\mathbb R},P)$ does not force a function to use every slope in $P$. Let $N_{\mathbb R}=M_{\mathbb R}=\mathbb R^2$ with the standard pairing, $P=[0,1]\times \{ 0\} $ and $P'=\{ 0\} \times [0,1]$. Both bodies have empty interior, and the zero function belongs to $\mathcal P(N_{\mathbb R},P)=\mathcal E(N_{\mathbb R},P)$ and to $\mathcal E(N_{\mathbb R},P')$, since $0\leq h_ P$ and $0\leq h_{P'}$. The sum of the zero function with itself is zero, whose slope body is $\{ 0\} $, whereas $P+P'=[0,1]^2$ has nonempty interior. Hence the zero function does not belong to $\mathcal E(N_{\mathbb R},P+P')$.

title: Monomial growth convex hull
text: Lemma 18.3.6 . Let $m\geq 1$ and $\beta _1,\ldots ,\beta _ m,\alpha \in M_{\mathbb R}$. The function \[  x\longmapsto \log \sum _{i=1}^ m\mathrm e^{\langle \beta _ i,x\rangle } -\langle \alpha ,x\rangle  \] is bounded below on $N_{\mathbb R}$ if and only if $\alpha $ belongs to the convex hull of $\beta _1,\ldots ,\beta _ m$. Suppose that all $\beta _ i$ and $\alpha $ lie in $M$, identify $M$ with $\mathbb Z^ n$ by a basis and $N_{\mathbb R}$ with $\mathbb R^ n$ by the dual basis, and write $z^\alpha =z_1^{\alpha _1}\cdots z_ n^{\alpha _ n}$. Then this condition is also equivalent to the boundedness on $(\mathbb C^*)^ n$ of \[  \frac{|z^\alpha |^2}{\sum _ i|z^{\beta _ i}|^2}.  \] Proof. If $\alpha =\sum _ i\lambda _ i\beta _ i$ is a convex combination, then $\langle \alpha ,x\rangle \leq \max _ i\langle \beta _ i,x\rangle \leq \log \sum _ i\mathrm e^{\langle \beta _ i,x\rangle }$, so the function is nonnegative. Conversely, suppose that $\alpha $ is not in the convex hull. The hull is compact, being the image of the standard simplex under the linear map $(\lambda _ i)\mapsto \sum _ i\lambda _ i\beta _ i$, and convex, so lemma 18.1.2 (1), applied in $M_{\mathbb R}$, gives $v\in N_{\mathbb R}$ with $\langle \alpha ,v\rangle >\max _ i\langle \beta _ i,v\rangle $. Since the logarithmic sum differs from $\max _ i\langle \beta _ i,x\rangle $ by a number in $[0,\log m]$, the value of the function at $x=tv$ is at most $t(\max _ i\langle \beta _ i,v\rangle -\langle \alpha ,v\rangle )+\log m$, which tends to $-\infty $ as $t\to +\infty $. For the last assertion, put $x_ j=\log |z_ j|^2$. Then $|z^\gamma |^2=\mathrm e^{\langle \gamma ,x\rangle }$ for every $\gamma \in \mathbb Z^ n$, including exponents with negative entries, so the displayed quotient equals the exponential of minus the function above; and $z\mapsto x$ maps $(\mathbb C^*)^ n$ onto $\mathbb R^ n$. $\square$

title: The real Monge–Ampère measure
text:
18.4 The real Monge–Ampère measure Let $F$ be a finite convex function on $N_{\mathbb R}$. Following Alexandrov, we measure a set $E\subset N_{\mathbb R}$ by the volume of the set $\partial F(E)$ of supporting slopes of $F$ at points of $E$. For a smooth $F$ with positive definite Hessian, $\partial F(E)=
abla F(E)$, and the change of variables formula gives $\operatorname {vol}(
abla F(E))=\int _ E\det (D^2F)\, \mathrm dx$, so this is a weak form of the real Monge–Ampère operator (see proposition 18.4.4 ). Two difficulties arise in general: the subgradient map is multivalued, and it is not clear a priori that $\partial F(E)$ is measurable. Both are resolved by looking at the inverse map. By duality, a slope $p$ belongs to $\partial F(E)$ if and only if $E$ meets $\partial F^*(p)$, and $\partial F^*(p)$ is a single point for almost every $p$ in the domain of $F^*$. Theorem 18.4.1 . Let $F$ be a finite convex function on $N_{\mathbb R}$, let $G=F^*$, and let $D$ be the set of points of the interior of $\operatorname {dom}G$ at which $G$ is differentiable. For every Borel set $E\subset N_{\mathbb R}$, the set $\partial F(E)$ is measurable for the completed Lebesgue measure, and \[  \operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F)(E)=n!\operatorname {vol}(\partial F(E))  \] defines a positive Radon measure on $N_{\mathbb R}$, the real Monge–Ampère measure of $F$. It is given by \[  \operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F) =(
abla G)_*(n!\mathbf1_ D\, \mathrm dp).  \] If $\operatorname {dom}G$ has empty interior and $n>0$, then $\operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F)=0$. In every case \[  \operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F)(N_{\mathbb R}) =n!\operatorname {vol}(K_ F).  \] Proof. The set $\operatorname {dom}G$ is convex, and its difference from its interior is a null set: if the interior is nonempty, this difference lies in the relative boundary, which is null by lemma 18.1.2 (4); otherwise $\operatorname {dom}G$ lies in a proper affine subspace. By proposition 18.1.3 (4), applied to the finite convex function $G$ on the interior of its domain, $D$ is a Borel set, the gradient $
abla G\colon D	o N_{\mathbb R}$ is a Borel map, and the complement of $D$ in the interior of $\operatorname {dom}G$ is a null set. Therefore the complement of $D$ in $\operatorname {dom}G$ is a null set; it is a Borel set, because $\operatorname {dom}G= igcup _ k\{ G\leq k\} $ is a countable union of closed sets, $G$ being lower semicontinuous. Let $p\in D$. Then $\partial G(p)=\{ 
abla G(p)\} $. Indeed, $\partial G(p)$ is nonempty by proposition 18.1.3 , and every subgradient of $G$ at $p$ is also a subgradient at $p$ of the restriction of $G$ to the interior of $\operatorname {dom}G$, whose only subgradient at $p$ is $
abla G(p)$ by proposition 18.1.3 (3). Hence theorem 18.2.2 gives, for every $E\subset N_{\mathbb R}$, \[  p\in \partial F(E)\quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad 
abla G(p)\in E.  \] Every subgradient of $F$ lies in $\operatorname {dom}G$, so $\partial F(E)$ differs from the Borel set $(
abla G)^{-1}(E)\cap D$ by a subset of the fixed null set $\operatorname {dom}G\setminus D$. Hence $\partial F(E)$ is measurable for the completed measure, and $\operatorname {vol}(\partial F(E))=\operatorname {vol}((
abla G)^{-1}(E)\cap D)$. This proves the pushforward formula, which in turn shows that $E\mapsto n!\operatorname {vol}(\partial F(E))$ is countably additive on Borel sets. If $K$ is compact, $\partial F(K)$ is bounded by proposition 18.1.3 (1), and it is closed, since the graph of $\partial F$ is closed and $K$ is compact; so $\partial F(K)$ is compact and has finite volume. Thus the measure is finite on compact sets, and it is a Radon measure by proposition 1.1.2 . If $\operatorname {dom}G$ has empty interior and $n>0$, then $D=\varnothing $ and the measure vanishes. In general, the total mass is $n!\operatorname {vol}(D)=n!\operatorname {vol}(\operatorname {dom}G)$, and $\operatorname {vol}(\operatorname {dom}G)=\operatorname {vol}(K_ F)$ because $K_ F\setminus \operatorname {dom}G$ lies in the relative boundary of $\operatorname {dom}G$, or in a proper affine subspace. In dimension zero, $F$ is a constant, $D$ is the single point of $M_{\mathbb R}$, and the formula gives unit mass, with $0!=1$. $\square$ Theorem 18.4.2 . Let $F_ j$ and $F$ be finite convex functions on $N_{\mathbb R}$ such that $F_ j	o F$ locally uniformly. Then $\operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F_ j)	o \operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F)$ vaguely. Moreover, let $P\subset M_{\mathbb R}$ be a convex body. A function $F\in \mathcal P(N_{\mathbb R},P)$ belongs to $\mathcal E(N_{\mathbb R},P)$ if and only if \[  \operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F)(N_{\mathbb R})=n!\operatorname {vol}(P).  \] If $F$ and $H$ are finite convex functions with $F\preceq H$, then $K_ F\subset K_ H$, and the total mass of $\operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F)$ is at most that of $\operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(H)$. Proof. Write $\mu _ j=\operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F_ j)$ and $\mu =\operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F)$. Steps 1 and 2 compare the masses of compact and of open sets, and Step 3 deduces vague convergence. Step 1: compact sets. Let $K$ be compact. If $x\in K$ and $0
eq p\in \partial F_ j(x)$ (in particular $n\geq 1$), choose $e\in N_{\mathbb R}$ with $|e|=1$ and $\langle p,eangle =|p|$; the subgradient inequality at $x$, evaluated at $x+e$, gives $|p|\leq F_ j(x+e)-F_ j(x)\leq 2\sup \{ |F_ j(y)|:\operatorname {dist}(y,K)\leq 1\} $. By local uniform convergence, the sets $\partial F_ j(K)$ are therefore contained in a fixed ball for all large $j$. If $x_ j\in K$, $p_ j\in \partial F_ j(x_ j)$, $x_ j	o x$ and $p_ j	o p$, then letting $j	o \infty $ in the subgradient inequalities gives $p\in \partial F(x)$. The set $\partial F(K)$ is compact, being bounded and closed by proposition 18.1.3 (1), since $K$ is compact. Consequently, for every $\varepsilon >0$, the set $\partial F_ j(K)$ lies in the closed $\varepsilon $-neighborhood $(\partial F(K))^\varepsilon $ of $\partial F(K)$ for all large $j$. Otherwise, for infinitely many $j$ there would be points $x_ j\in K$ and $p_ j\in \partial F_ j(x_ j)$ at distance at least $\varepsilon $ from $\partial F(K)$; as $K$ is compact and the $p_ j$ are bounded, a subsequence of $(x_ j,p_ j)$ would converge to some $(x,p)$ with $p\in \partial F(x)$, which is impossible. As $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, these neighborhoods decrease to $\partial F(K)$, and continuity from above of Lebesgue measure on sets of finite measure gives \[  \varlimsup _ j\mu _ j(K)\leq \mu (K).  \] Step 2: open sets. Let $U$ be open and let $G=F^*$, with $D$ as in theorem 18.4.1 . For $p\in \partial F(U)\cap D$, the point $x=
abla G(p)$ lies in $U$ and is the only point with $p\in \partial F(x)$, so $x$ is the unique minimum point of $F-\langle p,\cdot angle $. Choose $r>0$ with $\overline{B(x,r)}\subset U$. Since the sphere $\{ y:|y-x|=r\} $ is compact, $F-\langle p,\cdot angle $ exceeds its minimum by some $\delta >0$ on it. For large $j$ we have $|F_ j-F|<\delta /3$ on $\overline{B(x,r)}$, so the minimum of $F_ j-\langle p,\cdot angle $ on $\overline{B(x,r)}$ is attained at a point $x_ j\in B(x,r)$. A local minimum of a convex function is a global minimum, because the function is convex along each segment starting at that point; hence $p\in \partial F_ j(x_ j)\subset \partial F_ j(U)$ for all large $j$. Since $\partial F(U)\setminus D$ is a null set, Fatou's lemma, applied to the indicator functions of the sets $\partial F_ j(U)$, gives \[  \mu (U)\leq \varliminf _ j\mu _ j(U).  \] Step 3: vague convergence. Let $f\geq 0$ be continuous with compact support $S$. By Step 1 there is $C$ with $\mu _ j(S)\leq C$ for all large $j$. For $t>0$, the set $\{ f\geq t\} $ is compact and $\{ f>t\} $ is open. By Tonelli's theorem, $\int f\, \mathrm d
u =\int _0^\infty 
u (\{ f>t\} )\, \mathrm dt=\int _0^\infty 
u (\{ f\geq t\} )\, \mathrm dt$ for every positive measure $
u $. Hence Step 2 and Fatou's lemma give \[   egin{split}  \int f\, \mathrm d\mu & =\int _0^\infty \mu (\{ f>t\} )\, \mathrm dt\ & \leq \varliminf _ j\int _0^\infty \mu _ j(\{ f>t\} )\, \mathrm dt=\varliminf _ j\int f\, \mathrm d\mu _ j, \end{split}  \] and Step 1 and Fatou's lemma, applied to the nonnegative functions $t\mapsto C-\mu _ j(\{ f\geq t\} )$ on $(0,\max f]$, give \[   egin{split}  \varlimsup _ j\int f\, \mathrm d\mu _ j& =\varlimsup _ j\int _0^{\max f}\mu _ j(\{ f\geq t\} )\, \mathrm dt\ & \leq \int _0^{\max f}\mu (\{ f\geq t\} )\, \mathrm dt=\int f\, \mathrm d\mu . \end{split}  \] Hence $\int f\, \mathrm d\mu _ j	o \int f\, \mathrm d\mu $. A general continuous function with compact support is the difference of its positive and negative parts, which proves vague convergence. Full mass. Let $F\in \mathcal P(N_{\mathbb R},P)$. Then $K_ F\subset P$ by proposition 18.3.2 , and the total mass of $\operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F)$ is $n!\operatorname {vol}(K_ F)$ by theorem 18.4.1 . Suppose that $P$ has nonempty interior. If $K_ F=P$, the two masses agree. If $K_ F
eq P$, choose $p\in P\setminus K_ F$ and a ball $B(p,r)$ disjoint from the closed set $K_ F$. Since $P$ is the closure of its interior by lemma 18.1.2 (4), there is an interior point $q$ of $P$ in $B(p,r/2)$, and a small ball about $q$ lies in $P\setminus K_ F$. Hence $\operatorname {vol}(K_ F)<\operatorname {vol}(P)$. This proves the equivalence when $P$ has nonempty interior. If $P$ has empty interior, then $n>0$, both $\operatorname {vol}(K_ F)$ and $\operatorname {vol}(P)$ vanish, and $\mathcal E(N_{\mathbb R},P)=\mathcal P(N_{\mathbb R},P)$ by definition, so the equivalence holds as well. Finally, if $F\leq H+C$, then $F^*\geq H^*-C$, so $\operatorname {dom}F^*\subset \operatorname {dom}H^*$ and $K_ F\subset K_ H$. The inequality between the total masses follows from theorem 18.4.1 . $\square$ Example 18.4.3 . In theorem 18.4.2 , vague convergence cannot be replaced by narrow convergence without a condition that prevents mass from escaping to infinity. Let $n=1$, identify $N_{\mathbb R}$ and $M_{\mathbb R}$ with $\mathbb R$ so that $N=M=\mathbb Z$, and put \[  F_ j(x)=\max \{ 0,x-j\} \longrightarrow 0, \qquad \operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F_ j)=\delta _ j.  \] Indeed, $\partial F_ j(x)$ is $\{ 0\} $ for $x<j$, $\{ 1\} $ for $x>j$, and $[0,1]$ for $x=j$. All slopes lie in $[0,1]$, and $F_ j	o 0$ locally uniformly. As in example 1.5.4 , the measures $\delta _ j$ converge vaguely to $\operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(0)=0$, while their total masses remain equal to one. Here each $F_ j$ has full mass for $P=[0,1]$, but the limit does not. If the functions and their limit all have full mass for one fixed body, the measures converge narrowly by lemma 18.5.2 below. Proposition 18.4.4 . Let $F$ be a convex function on $N_{\mathbb R}$ of class $C^{1,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}$, that is, differentiable with locally Lipschitz gradient. Then the distributional Hessian $D^2F$ of $F$, computed in the coordinates of a basis of $N$, is a locally bounded measurable matrix-valued function, and \[  \operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F) =n!\det (D^2F)\, \mathrm dx.  \] Moreover, there is a unique way to assign to every $n$-tuple $(F_1,\ldots ,F_ n)$ of finite convex functions on $N_{\mathbb R}$ a positive Radon measure $\operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F_1,\ldots ,F_ n)$, the mixed real Monge–Ampère measure , which is symmetric in its arguments, additive and positively homogeneous in each argument, and satisfies $\operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F,\ldots ,F)=\operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F)$. It is continuous for the vague topology under local uniform convergence of each argument. Proof. Smooth functions. Let $F$ be smooth with positive definite Hessian. For $x
eq y$, \[  \langle 
abla F(y)-
abla F(x),y-xangle =\int _0^1D^2F(x+s(y-x))(y-x,y-x)\, \mathrm ds>0,  \] so $
abla F$ is injective, and it is a local diffeomorphism by the inverse function theorem. Since $\partial F(E)=
abla F(E)$ by proposition 18.1.3 (3), the change of variables formula gives the asserted identity. Now let $F$ be smooth and convex; its Hessian is positive semidefinite, because the second derivatives of $F$ along lines are nonnegative. Apply the identity just proved to $F+\varepsilon |x|^2/2$, where $|x|$ is the Euclidean norm in the lattice coordinates. As $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, these functions converge to $F$ locally uniformly and their densities $n!\det (D^2F+\varepsilon I)$ converge to $n!\det (D^2F)$ locally uniformly; comparing the two vague limits, by theorem 18.4.2 , proves the identity for $F$. Functions of class $C^{1,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}$. We work in the coordinates of a basis of $N$. Fix $k$ and $l$, and let $g=\partial _ kF$, which is locally Lipschitz. Let $B=B(x_0,r)$ be a ball, and let $L_ B$ be a Lipschitz constant of $g$ on $\overline{B(x_0,2r)}$. For a nonnegative test function $\chi $ supported in $B$ and $0<|h|<r$, the substitution $x\mapsto x-he_ l$ in one of the two terms gives \[  \int g(x) rac{\chi (x+he_ l)-\chi (x)}h\, \mathrm dx=\int  rac{g(x-he_ l)-g(x)}h\, \chi (x)\, \mathrm dx,  \] and the right side is at most $L_ B\int \chi \, \mathrm dx$ in absolute value. As $h	o 0$, the difference quotients of $\chi $ converge uniformly to $\partial _ l\chi $, with supports in a fixed compact set, so the left side tends to $\int g\, \partial _ l\chi \, \mathrm dx=-\langle \partial _ lg,\chi angle $. Hence $|\langle \partial _ l\partial _ kF,\chi angle |\leq L_ B\int \chi \, \mathrm dx$, and corollary 1.7.2 (2), applied to Lebesgue measure, gives a Borel function $H_{kl}$ that represents the distribution $\partial _ l\partial _ kF$ and satisfies $|H_{kl}|\leq L_ B$ almost everywhere on each such ball $B$. Covering $N_{\mathbb R}$ by countably many such balls and setting $H_{kl}=0$ on the null set of points of some ball of the cover at which the bound fails, we may assume that $H_{kl}$ is bounded on every compact set. This proves that $D^2F=(H_{kl})$ is a locally bounded Borel matrix-valued function. Since distributional derivatives commute, $H_{kl}=H_{lk}$ almost everywhere, by the uniqueness in corollary 1.7.2 . Next, $D^2F(x)$ is positive semidefinite for almost every $x$. Indeed, let $v\in \mathbb R^ n$ and let $\chi $ be a nonnegative test function. Taylor's formula shows that the second difference quotients $h^{-2}(\chi (x+hv)+\chi (x-hv)-2\chi (x))$ converge uniformly to $\sum _{k,l}v_ kv_ l\partial _ k\partial _ l\chi $ as $h	o 0$, so the substitutions $x\mapsto x\mp hv$ give \[  \Bigl \langle \sum _{k,l}v_ kv_ l\partial _ k\partial _ lF,\chi \Bigr angle =\lim _{h	o 0}\int  rac{F(x-hv)+F(x+hv)-2F(x)}{h^2}\, \chi (x)\, \mathrm dx\geq 0,  \] because $F$ is convex. Thus the function $\sum _{k,l}v_ kv_ lH_{kl}$ defines a positive distribution, so its mollifications are nonnegative by proposition 1.4.3 (3); since they converge to it at its Lebesgue points (theorem 1.7.3 ), it is nonnegative almost everywhere. Applying this to a countable dense set of vectors $v$, and using the continuity of the quadratic form in $v$, we see that $D^2F(x)$ is positive semidefinite for almost every $x$. We now obtain the formula by mollification. With the mollifiers $ho _\varepsilon $ of lemma 18.3.3 , in the same coordinates, the functions $F_\varepsilon =F*ho _\varepsilon $ are smooth and convex, and they converge to $F$ locally uniformly, by that lemma. By proposition 1.4.3 (1), their second derivatives are $\partial _ k\partial _ lF_\varepsilon =H_{kl}*ho _\varepsilon $. Hence, for $\varepsilon \leq 1$, the Hessians $D^2F_\varepsilon $ are bounded on each compact set $K$ by the bound of $D^2F$ on the set of points at distance at most $1$ from $K$, and by theorem 1.7.3 they converge to $D^2F(x)$ at every point $x$ that is a Lebesgue point of all the entries $H_{kl}$, that is, almost everywhere. By the smooth case, $\operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F_\varepsilon )=n!\det (D^2F_\varepsilon )\, \mathrm dx$. Let $\varepsilon $ run through a sequence tending to zero. For $f\in C_ c(N_{\mathbb R})$, dominated convergence gives $n!\int f\det (D^2F_\varepsilon )\, \mathrm dx	o n!\int f\det (D^2F)\, \mathrm dx$, while $\operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F_\varepsilon )	o \operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F)$ vaguely by theorem 18.4.2 . This proves the formula. Mixed measures. For smooth convex $F_1,\ldots ,F_ n$ define \[  \operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F_1,\ldots ,F_ n)=n!\, D(D^2F_1,\ldots ,D^2F_ n)\, \mathrm dx,  \] where $D$ is the mixed discriminant of section 7.2 , applied to the real symmetric, hence Hermitian, Hessian matrices. This measure is positive, because the mixed discriminant of positive semidefinite matrices is nonnegative (lemma 7.2.2 (3)), and it is symmetric and multilinear, with $D(A,\ldots ,A)=\det A$ (lemma 7.2.2 (1)). Expanding $\operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(\sum _{j\in J}F_ j,\ldots ,\sum _{j\in J}F_ j)$ by multilinearity and using symmetry, we obtain the polarization identity 18.7  egin{equation} \label{eq:real-mixed-polarization} \operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F_1,\ldots ,F_ n)= rac1{n!}\sum _{J\subset \{ 1,\ldots ,n\} } (-1)^{n-|J|}\operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R} \left(\sum _{j\in J}F_ jight), \end{equation} where the empty sum is the zero function, whose measure is zero for $n>0$ (its only slope is $0$). Indeed, after the expansion, a term $\operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F_{\sigma (1)},\ldots ,F_{\sigma (n)})$ with $\sigma \colon \{ 1,\ldots ,n\} 	o \{ 1,\ldots ,n\} $ appears with total coefficient $\sum _{J\supset \sigma (\{ 1,\ldots ,n\} )}(-1)^{n-|J|}$, which vanishes unless $\sigma $ is a bijection, and the $n!$ bijections all give $\operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F_1,\ldots ,F_ n)$ by symmetry. Any symmetric, multilinear assignment with the given diagonal values satisfies ( 18.7 ), by the same expansion; this proves uniqueness. Now let $F_1,\ldots ,F_ n$ be arbitrary finite convex functions, and let $F_{j,\varepsilon }=F_ j*ho _\varepsilon $ be their mollifications, which are smooth and convex by lemma 18.3.3 . For every $J$, $\sum _{j\in J}F_{j,\varepsilon }	o \sum _{j\in J}F_ j$ locally uniformly as $\varepsilon 	o 0$ (lemma 1.4.1 (1)). Let $\varepsilon $ run through a sequence tending to zero. By ( 18.7 ) for the smooth functions $F_{j,\varepsilon }$ and by theorem 18.4.2 , for every $f\in C_ c(N_{\mathbb R},\mathbb R)$ the integrals $\int f\, \mathrm d\operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F_{1,\varepsilon },\ldots ,F_{n,\varepsilon })$ converge to \[  \Lambda (f)= rac1{n!}\sum _{J\subset \{ 1,\ldots ,n\} }(-1)^{n-|J|}\int f\, \mathrm d\operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}\Bigl (\sum _{j\in J}F_ j\Bigr ).  \] The functional $\Lambda $ is linear, and it is positive as a limit of integrals against positive measures. By theorem 1.2.2 , there is a unique Radon measure $\operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F_1,\ldots ,F_ n)$ with $\int f\, \mathrm d\operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F_1,\ldots ,F_ n)=\Lambda (f)$ for every $f$; for smooth $F_ j$ it agrees with the previous definition, by ( 18.7 ). It is symmetric, because $\Lambda $ is a symmetric function of $F_1,\ldots ,F_ n$. Additivity and positive homogeneity in each argument hold for the smooth mixed measures; since mollification is linear, they pass to the vague limit. For $F_1=\cdots =F_ n=F$, the smooth mixed measures are $n!\det (D^2F_\varepsilon )\, \mathrm dx=\operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F_\varepsilon )$, which converge vaguely to $\operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F)$; hence $\operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F,\ldots ,F)=\operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F)$. Finally, if $F_ j^{(k)}	o F_ j$ locally uniformly as $k	o \infty $ for each $j$, then $\sum _{j\in J}F_ j^{(k)}	o \sum _{j\in J}F_ j$ locally uniformly for every $J$, and the formula for $\Lambda $ together with theorem 18.4.2 shows that $\operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F_1^{(k)},\ldots ,F_ n^{(k)})	o \operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F_1,\ldots ,F_ n)$ vaguely. In dimension zero the mixed measure has no arguments, and it is the unit mass at the point. $\square$

title: Alexandrov measure construction
text:
Theorem 18.4.1 . Let $F$ be a finite convex function on $N_{\mathbb R}$, let $G=F^*$, and let $D$ be the set of points of the interior of $\operatorname {dom}G$ at which $G$ is differentiable. For every Borel set $E\subset N_{\mathbb R}$, the set $\partial F(E)$ is measurable for the completed Lebesgue measure, and \[  \operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F)(E)=n!\operatorname {vol}(\partial F(E))  \] defines a positive Radon measure on $N_{\mathbb R}$, the real Monge–Ampère measure of $F$. It is given by \[  \operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F) =(
abla G)_*(n!\mathbf1_ D\, \mathrm dp).  \] If $\operatorname {dom}G$ has empty interior and $n>0$, then $\operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F)=0$. In every case \[  \operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F)(N_{\mathbb R}) =n!\operatorname {vol}(K_ F).  \] Proof. The set $\operatorname {dom}G$ is convex, and its difference from its interior is a null set: if the interior is nonempty, this difference lies in the relative boundary, which is null by lemma 18.1.2 (4); otherwise $\operatorname {dom}G$ lies in a proper affine subspace. By proposition 18.1.3 (4), applied to the finite convex function $G$ on the interior of its domain, $D$ is a Borel set, the gradient $
abla G\colon D	o N_{\mathbb R}$ is a Borel map, and the complement of $D$ in the interior of $\operatorname {dom}G$ is a null set. Therefore the complement of $D$ in $\operatorname {dom}G$ is a null set; it is a Borel set, because $\operatorname {dom}G= igcup _ k\{ G\leq k\} $ is a countable union of closed sets, $G$ being lower semicontinuous. Let $p\in D$. Then $\partial G(p)=\{ 
abla G(p)\} $. Indeed, $\partial G(p)$ is nonempty by proposition 18.1.3 , and every subgradient of $G$ at $p$ is also a subgradient at $p$ of the restriction of $G$ to the interior of $\operatorname {dom}G$, whose only subgradient at $p$ is $
abla G(p)$ by proposition 18.1.3 (3). Hence theorem 18.2.2 gives, for every $E\subset N_{\mathbb R}$, \[  p\in \partial F(E)\quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad 
abla G(p)\in E.  \] Every subgradient of $F$ lies in $\operatorname {dom}G$, so $\partial F(E)$ differs from the Borel set $(
abla G)^{-1}(E)\cap D$ by a subset of the fixed null set $\operatorname {dom}G\setminus D$. Hence $\partial F(E)$ is measurable for the completed measure, and $\operatorname {vol}(\partial F(E))=\operatorname {vol}((
abla G)^{-1}(E)\cap D)$. This proves the pushforward formula, which in turn shows that $E\mapsto n!\operatorname {vol}(\partial F(E))$ is countably additive on Borel sets. If $K$ is compact, $\partial F(K)$ is bounded by proposition 18.1.3 (1), and it is closed, since the graph of $\partial F$ is closed and $K$ is compact; so $\partial F(K)$ is compact and has finite volume. Thus the measure is finite on compact sets, and it is a Radon measure by proposition 1.1.2 . If $\operatorname {dom}G$ has empty interior and $n>0$, then $D=\varnothing $ and the measure vanishes. In general, the total mass is $n!\operatorname {vol}(D)=n!\operatorname {vol}(\operatorname {dom}G)$, and $\operatorname {vol}(\operatorname {dom}G)=\operatorname {vol}(K_ F)$ because $K_ F\setminus \operatorname {dom}G$ lies in the relative boundary of $\operatorname {dom}G$, or in a proper affine subspace. In dimension zero, $F$ is a constant, $D$ is the single point of $M_{\mathbb R}$, and the formula gives unit mass, with $0!=1$. $\square$

title: Real monge ampere vague continuity
text:
Theorem 18.4.2 . Let $F_ j$ and $F$ be finite convex functions on $N_{\mathbb R}$ such that $F_ j	o F$ locally uniformly. Then $\operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F_ j)	o \operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F)$ vaguely. Moreover, let $P\subset M_{\mathbb R}$ be a convex body. A function $F\in \mathcal P(N_{\mathbb R},P)$ belongs to $\mathcal E(N_{\mathbb R},P)$ if and only if \[  \operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F)(N_{\mathbb R})=n!\operatorname {vol}(P).  \] If $F$ and $H$ are finite convex functions with $F\preceq H$, then $K_ F\subset K_ H$, and the total mass of $\operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F)$ is at most that of $\operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(H)$. Proof. Write $\mu _ j=\operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F_ j)$ and $\mu =\operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F)$. Steps 1 and 2 compare the masses of compact and of open sets, and Step 3 deduces vague convergence. Step 1: compact sets. Let $K$ be compact. If $x\in K$ and $0
eq p\in \partial F_ j(x)$ (in particular $n\geq 1$), choose $e\in N_{\mathbb R}$ with $|e|=1$ and $\langle p,eangle =|p|$; the subgradient inequality at $x$, evaluated at $x+e$, gives $|p|\leq F_ j(x+e)-F_ j(x)\leq 2\sup \{ |F_ j(y)|:\operatorname {dist}(y,K)\leq 1\} $. By local uniform convergence, the sets $\partial F_ j(K)$ are therefore contained in a fixed ball for all large $j$. If $x_ j\in K$, $p_ j\in \partial F_ j(x_ j)$, $x_ j	o x$ and $p_ j	o p$, then letting $j	o \infty $ in the subgradient inequalities gives $p\in \partial F(x)$. The set $\partial F(K)$ is compact, being bounded and closed by proposition 18.1.3 (1), since $K$ is compact. Consequently, for every $\varepsilon >0$, the set $\partial F_ j(K)$ lies in the closed $\varepsilon $-neighborhood $(\partial F(K))^\varepsilon $ of $\partial F(K)$ for all large $j$. Otherwise, for infinitely many $j$ there would be points $x_ j\in K$ and $p_ j\in \partial F_ j(x_ j)$ at distance at least $\varepsilon $ from $\partial F(K)$; as $K$ is compact and the $p_ j$ are bounded, a subsequence of $(x_ j,p_ j)$ would converge to some $(x,p)$ with $p\in \partial F(x)$, which is impossible. As $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, these neighborhoods decrease to $\partial F(K)$, and continuity from above of Lebesgue measure on sets of finite measure gives \[  \varlimsup _ j\mu _ j(K)\leq \mu (K).  \] Step 2: open sets. Let $U$ be open and let $G=F^*$, with $D$ as in theorem 18.4.1 . For $p\in \partial F(U)\cap D$, the point $x=
abla G(p)$ lies in $U$ and is the only point with $p\in \partial F(x)$, so $x$ is the unique minimum point of $F-\langle p,\cdot angle $. Choose $r>0$ with $\overline{B(x,r)}\subset U$. Since the sphere $\{ y:|y-x|=r\} $ is compact, $F-\langle p,\cdot angle $ exceeds its minimum by some $\delta >0$ on it. For large $j$ we have $|F_ j-F|<\delta /3$ on $\overline{B(x,r)}$, so the minimum of $F_ j-\langle p,\cdot angle $ on $\overline{B(x,r)}$ is attained at a point $x_ j\in B(x,r)$. A local minimum of a convex function is a global minimum, because the function is convex along each segment starting at that point; hence $p\in \partial F_ j(x_ j)\subset \partial F_ j(U)$ for all large $j$. Since $\partial F(U)\setminus D$ is a null set, Fatou's lemma, applied to the indicator functions of the sets $\partial F_ j(U)$, gives \[  \mu (U)\leq \varliminf _ j\mu _ j(U).  \] Step 3: vague convergence. Let $f\geq 0$ be continuous with compact support $S$. By Step 1 there is $C$ with $\mu _ j(S)\leq C$ for all large $j$. For $t>0$, the set $\{ f\geq t\} $ is compact and $\{ f>t\} $ is open. By Tonelli's theorem, $\int f\, \mathrm d
u =\int _0^\infty 
u (\{ f>t\} )\, \mathrm dt=\int _0^\infty 
u (\{ f\geq t\} )\, \mathrm dt$ for every positive measure $
u $. Hence Step 2 and Fatou's lemma give \[   egin{split}  \int f\, \mathrm d\mu & =\int _0^\infty \mu (\{ f>t\} )\, \mathrm dt\ & \leq \varliminf _ j\int _0^\infty \mu _ j(\{ f>t\} )\, \mathrm dt=\varliminf _ j\int f\, \mathrm d\mu _ j, \end{split}  \] and Step 1 and Fatou's lemma, applied to the nonnegative functions $t\mapsto C-\mu _ j(\{ f\geq t\} )$ on $(0,\max f]$, give \[   egin{split}  \varlimsup _ j\int f\, \mathrm d\mu _ j& =\varlimsup _ j\int _0^{\max f}\mu _ j(\{ f\geq t\} )\, \mathrm dt\ & \leq \int _0^{\max f}\mu (\{ f\geq t\} )\, \mathrm dt=\int f\, \mathrm d\mu . \end{split}  \] Hence $\int f\, \mathrm d\mu _ j	o \int f\, \mathrm d\mu $. A general continuous function with compact support is the difference of its positive and negative parts, which proves vague convergence. Full mass. Let $F\in \mathcal P(N_{\mathbb R},P)$. Then $K_ F\subset P$ by proposition 18.3.2 , and the total mass of $\operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F)$ is $n!\operatorname {vol}(K_ F)$ by theorem 18.4.1 . Suppose that $P$ has nonempty interior. If $K_ F=P$, the two masses agree. If $K_ F
eq P$, choose $p\in P\setminus K_ F$ and a ball $B(p,r)$ disjoint from the closed set $K_ F$. Since $P$ is the closure of its interior by lemma 18.1.2 (4), there is an interior point $q$ of $P$ in $B(p,r/2)$, and a small ball about $q$ lies in $P\setminus K_ F$. Hence $\operatorname {vol}(K_ F)<\operatorname {vol}(P)$. This proves the equivalence when $P$ has nonempty interior. If $P$ has empty interior, then $n>0$, both $\operatorname {vol}(K_ F)$ and $\operatorname {vol}(P)$ vanish, and $\mathcal E(N_{\mathbb R},P)=\mathcal P(N_{\mathbb R},P)$ by definition, so the equivalence holds as well. Finally, if $F\leq H+C$, then $F^*\geq H^*-C$, so $\operatorname {dom}F^*\subset \operatorname {dom}H^*$ and $K_ F\subset K_ H$. The inequality between the total masses follows from theorem 18.4.1 . $\square$

title: Real mass escaping to infinity
text: Example 18.4.3 . In theorem 18.4.2 , vague convergence cannot be replaced by narrow convergence without a condition that prevents mass from escaping to infinity. Let $n=1$, identify $N_{\mathbb R}$ and $M_{\mathbb R}$ with $\mathbb R$ so that $N=M=\mathbb Z$, and put \[  F_ j(x)=\max \{ 0,x-j\} \longrightarrow 0, \qquad \operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F_ j)=\delta _ j.  \] Indeed, $\partial F_ j(x)$ is $\{ 0\} $ for $x<j$, $\{ 1\} $ for $x>j$, and $[0,1]$ for $x=j$. All slopes lie in $[0,1]$, and $F_ j\to 0$ locally uniformly. As in example 1.5.4 , the measures $\delta _ j$ converge vaguely to $\operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(0)=0$, while their total masses remain equal to one. Here each $F_ j$ has full mass for $P=[0,1]$, but the limit does not. If the functions and their limit all have full mass for one fixed body, the measures converge narrowly by lemma 18.5.2 below.

title: Smooth and mixed real monge ampere
text:
Proposition 18.4.4 . Let $F$ be a convex function on $N_{\mathbb R}$ of class $C^{1,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}$, that is, differentiable with locally Lipschitz gradient. Then the distributional Hessian $D^2F$ of $F$, computed in the coordinates of a basis of $N$, is a locally bounded measurable matrix-valued function, and \[  \operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F) =n!\det (D^2F)\, \mathrm dx.  \] Moreover, there is a unique way to assign to every $n$-tuple $(F_1,\ldots ,F_ n)$ of finite convex functions on $N_{\mathbb R}$ a positive Radon measure $\operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F_1,\ldots ,F_ n)$, the mixed real Monge–Ampère measure , which is symmetric in its arguments, additive and positively homogeneous in each argument, and satisfies $\operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F,\ldots ,F)=\operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F)$. It is continuous for the vague topology under local uniform convergence of each argument. Proof. Smooth functions. Let $F$ be smooth with positive definite Hessian. For $x
eq y$, \[  \langle 
abla F(y)-
abla F(x),y-xangle =\int _0^1D^2F(x+s(y-x))(y-x,y-x)\, \mathrm ds>0,  \] so $
abla F$ is injective, and it is a local diffeomorphism by the inverse function theorem. Since $\partial F(E)=
abla F(E)$ by proposition 18.1.3 (3), the change of variables formula gives the asserted identity. Now let $F$ be smooth and convex; its Hessian is positive semidefinite, because the second derivatives of $F$ along lines are nonnegative. Apply the identity just proved to $F+\varepsilon |x|^2/2$, where $|x|$ is the Euclidean norm in the lattice coordinates. As $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, these functions converge to $F$ locally uniformly and their densities $n!\det (D^2F+\varepsilon I)$ converge to $n!\det (D^2F)$ locally uniformly; comparing the two vague limits, by theorem 18.4.2 , proves the identity for $F$. Functions of class $C^{1,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}$. We work in the coordinates of a basis of $N$. Fix $k$ and $l$, and let $g=\partial _ kF$, which is locally Lipschitz. Let $B=B(x_0,r)$ be a ball, and let $L_ B$ be a Lipschitz constant of $g$ on $\overline{B(x_0,2r)}$. For a nonnegative test function $\chi $ supported in $B$ and $0<|h|<r$, the substitution $x\mapsto x-he_ l$ in one of the two terms gives \[  \int g(x) rac{\chi (x+he_ l)-\chi (x)}h\, \mathrm dx=\int  rac{g(x-he_ l)-g(x)}h\, \chi (x)\, \mathrm dx,  \] and the right side is at most $L_ B\int \chi \, \mathrm dx$ in absolute value. As $h	o 0$, the difference quotients of $\chi $ converge uniformly to $\partial _ l\chi $, with supports in a fixed compact set, so the left side tends to $\int g\, \partial _ l\chi \, \mathrm dx=-\langle \partial _ lg,\chi angle $. Hence $|\langle \partial _ l\partial _ kF,\chi angle |\leq L_ B\int \chi \, \mathrm dx$, and corollary 1.7.2 (2), applied to Lebesgue measure, gives a Borel function $H_{kl}$ that represents the distribution $\partial _ l\partial _ kF$ and satisfies $|H_{kl}|\leq L_ B$ almost everywhere on each such ball $B$. Covering $N_{\mathbb R}$ by countably many such balls and setting $H_{kl}=0$ on the null set of points of some ball of the cover at which the bound fails, we may assume that $H_{kl}$ is bounded on every compact set. This proves that $D^2F=(H_{kl})$ is a locally bounded Borel matrix-valued function. Since distributional derivatives commute, $H_{kl}=H_{lk}$ almost everywhere, by the uniqueness in corollary 1.7.2 . Next, $D^2F(x)$ is positive semidefinite for almost every $x$. Indeed, let $v\in \mathbb R^ n$ and let $\chi $ be a nonnegative test function. Taylor's formula shows that the second difference quotients $h^{-2}(\chi (x+hv)+\chi (x-hv)-2\chi (x))$ converge uniformly to $\sum _{k,l}v_ kv_ l\partial _ k\partial _ l\chi $ as $h	o 0$, so the substitutions $x\mapsto x\mp hv$ give \[  \Bigl \langle \sum _{k,l}v_ kv_ l\partial _ k\partial _ lF,\chi \Bigr angle =\lim _{h	o 0}\int  rac{F(x-hv)+F(x+hv)-2F(x)}{h^2}\, \chi (x)\, \mathrm dx\geq 0,  \] because $F$ is convex. Thus the function $\sum _{k,l}v_ kv_ lH_{kl}$ defines a positive distribution, so its mollifications are nonnegative by proposition 1.4.3 (3); since they converge to it at its Lebesgue points (theorem 1.7.3 ), it is nonnegative almost everywhere. Applying this to a countable dense set of vectors $v$, and using the continuity of the quadratic form in $v$, we see that $D^2F(x)$ is positive semidefinite for almost every $x$. We now obtain the formula by mollification. With the mollifiers $ho _\varepsilon $ of lemma 18.3.3 , in the same coordinates, the functions $F_\varepsilon =F*ho _\varepsilon $ are smooth and convex, and they converge to $F$ locally uniformly, by that lemma. By proposition 1.4.3 (1), their second derivatives are $\partial _ k\partial _ lF_\varepsilon =H_{kl}*ho _\varepsilon $. Hence, for $\varepsilon \leq 1$, the Hessians $D^2F_\varepsilon $ are bounded on each compact set $K$ by the bound of $D^2F$ on the set of points at distance at most $1$ from $K$, and by theorem 1.7.3 they converge to $D^2F(x)$ at every point $x$ that is a Lebesgue point of all the entries $H_{kl}$, that is, almost everywhere. By the smooth case, $\operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F_\varepsilon )=n!\det (D^2F_\varepsilon )\, \mathrm dx$. Let $\varepsilon $ run through a sequence tending to zero. For $f\in C_ c(N_{\mathbb R})$, dominated convergence gives $n!\int f\det (D^2F_\varepsilon )\, \mathrm dx	o n!\int f\det (D^2F)\, \mathrm dx$, while $\operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F_\varepsilon )	o \operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F)$ vaguely by theorem 18.4.2 . This proves the formula. Mixed measures. For smooth convex $F_1,\ldots ,F_ n$ define \[  \operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F_1,\ldots ,F_ n)=n!\, D(D^2F_1,\ldots ,D^2F_ n)\, \mathrm dx,  \] where $D$ is the mixed discriminant of section 7.2 , applied to the real symmetric, hence Hermitian, Hessian matrices. This measure is positive, because the mixed discriminant of positive semidefinite matrices is nonnegative (lemma 7.2.2 (3)), and it is symmetric and multilinear, with $D(A,\ldots ,A)=\det A$ (lemma 7.2.2 (1)). Expanding $\operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(\sum _{j\in J}F_ j,\ldots ,\sum _{j\in J}F_ j)$ by multilinearity and using symmetry, we obtain the polarization identity 18.7  egin{equation} \label{eq:real-mixed-polarization} \operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F_1,\ldots ,F_ n)= rac1{n!}\sum _{J\subset \{ 1,\ldots ,n\} } (-1)^{n-|J|}\operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R} \left(\sum _{j\in J}F_ jight), \end{equation} where the empty sum is the zero function, whose measure is zero for $n>0$ (its only slope is $0$). Indeed, after the expansion, a term $\operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F_{\sigma (1)},\ldots ,F_{\sigma (n)})$ with $\sigma \colon \{ 1,\ldots ,n\} 	o \{ 1,\ldots ,n\} $ appears with total coefficient $\sum _{J\supset \sigma (\{ 1,\ldots ,n\} )}(-1)^{n-|J|}$, which vanishes unless $\sigma $ is a bijection, and the $n!$ bijections all give $\operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F_1,\ldots ,F_ n)$ by symmetry. Any symmetric, multilinear assignment with the given diagonal values satisfies ( 18.7 ), by the same expansion; this proves uniqueness. Now let $F_1,\ldots ,F_ n$ be arbitrary finite convex functions, and let $F_{j,\varepsilon }=F_ j*ho _\varepsilon $ be their mollifications, which are smooth and convex by lemma 18.3.3 . For every $J$, $\sum _{j\in J}F_{j,\varepsilon }	o \sum _{j\in J}F_ j$ locally uniformly as $\varepsilon 	o 0$ (lemma 1.4.1 (1)). Let $\varepsilon $ run through a sequence tending to zero. By ( 18.7 ) for the smooth functions $F_{j,\varepsilon }$ and by theorem 18.4.2 , for every $f\in C_ c(N_{\mathbb R},\mathbb R)$ the integrals $\int f\, \mathrm d\operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F_{1,\varepsilon },\ldots ,F_{n,\varepsilon })$ converge to \[  \Lambda (f)= rac1{n!}\sum _{J\subset \{ 1,\ldots ,n\} }(-1)^{n-|J|}\int f\, \mathrm d\operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}\Bigl (\sum _{j\in J}F_ j\Bigr ).  \] The functional $\Lambda $ is linear, and it is positive as a limit of integrals against positive measures. By theorem 1.2.2 , there is a unique Radon measure $\operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F_1,\ldots ,F_ n)$ with $\int f\, \mathrm d\operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F_1,\ldots ,F_ n)=\Lambda (f)$ for every $f$; for smooth $F_ j$ it agrees with the previous definition, by ( 18.7 ). It is symmetric, because $\Lambda $ is a symmetric function of $F_1,\ldots ,F_ n$. Additivity and positive homogeneity in each argument hold for the smooth mixed measures; since mollification is linear, they pass to the vague limit. For $F_1=\cdots =F_ n=F$, the smooth mixed measures are $n!\det (D^2F_\varepsilon )\, \mathrm dx=\operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F_\varepsilon )$, which converge vaguely to $\operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F)$; hence $\operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F,\ldots ,F)=\operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F)$. Finally, if $F_ j^{(k)}	o F_ j$ locally uniformly as $k	o \infty $ for each $j$, then $\sum _{j\in J}F_ j^{(k)}	o \sum _{j\in J}F_ j$ locally uniformly for every $J$, and the formula for $\Lambda $ together with theorem 18.4.2 shows that $\operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F_1^{(k)},\ldots ,F_ n^{(k)})	o \operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F_1,\ldots ,F_ n)$ vaguely. In dimension zero the mixed measure has no arguments, and it is the unit mass at the point. $\square$

title: Real mixed polarization
text: 18.7 \begin{equation} \label{eq:real-mixed-polarization} \operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F_1,\ldots ,F_ n)=\frac1{n!}\sum _{J\subset \{ 1,\ldots ,n\} } (-1)^{n-|J|}\operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R} \left(\sum _{j\in J}F_ j\right), \end{equation}

title: Compact convex envelopes and full-mass limits
text:
18.5 Compact convex envelopes and full-mass limits We add two complements. First, the convex envelope of finitely many closed convex functions whose effective domains lie in a common compact set, such as the conjugates of finitely many functions in $\mathcal P(N_{\mathbb R},P)$, is closed, and the infimum defining it is attained. Second, vague convergence of real Monge–Ampère measures improves to narrow convergence when the total masses converge, as they do for functions of full mass. Lemma 18.5.1 . Let $G_1,\ldots ,G_ r$, with $r\geq 1$, be closed proper convex functions on a finite-dimensional real vector space, whose effective domains lie in a common compact set $K$, and let $H$ be the largest convex function below $\min _ iG_ i$, given by the formula of proposition 18.2.3 (2). Then $H$ is closed and proper, and at every point $x$ with $H(x)<+\infty $ the infimum defining $H(x)$ is attained. Consequently $H=(\max _ iG_ i^*)^*$. In particular, if $P\subset M_{\mathbb R}$ is a convex body and $F_1,\ldots ,F_ r\in \mathcal P(N_{\mathbb R},P)$, then the convex envelope of $F_1^*,\ldots ,F_ r^*$ is closed and equals $(\max _ iF_ i)^*$. Proof. Each $G_ i$ is bounded below: the increasing open sets $\{ G_ i>-k\} $, $k\in \mathbb N$, cover the compact set $K$, because $G_ i$ is lower semicontinuous and does not take the value $-\infty $, so one of them contains $K$; and $G_ i=+\infty $ outside $K$. Let $B$ be a common lower bound. In a combination $\sum _ j\lambda _ jG_{i_ j}(x_ j)$ as in proposition 18.2.3 (2), the terms with the same function $G_ i$ can be merged: if $\Lambda _ i$ is the sum of their weights, the convexity of $G_ i$ gives $\sum _{j:i_ j=i}\lambda _ jG_ i(x_ j)\geq \Lambda _ iG_ i(y_ i)$ with $y_ i=\Lambda _ i^{-1}\sum _{j:i_ j=i}\lambda _ jx_ j$, and the barycenter is unchanged. Hence it suffices to consider combinations $\sum _{\lambda _ i>0}\lambda _ iG_ i(x_ i)$ with one point $x_ i\in \operatorname {dom}G_ i$ for each $i$ and weights $\lambda _ i\geq 0$ summing to one; for an index $i$ with $\lambda _ i=0$ we let $x_ i$ be a fixed point of $\operatorname {dom}G_ i$, and the corresponding term is omitted. Let $x_

Thus $H(x)\leq L$, which proves that $H$ is lower semicontinuous. Moreover $B\leq H\leq G_1$, so $H$ is proper. Applying the same argument to the constant sequence $x_
u =x$ and admissible combinations whose values tend to $H(x)<+\infty $, we see that the infimum defining $H(x)$ is attained. By proposition 18.2.3 (2), $H^*=\max _ iG_ i^*$, and since $H$ is closed and proper, theorem 18.2.2 gives $H=H^{**}=(\max _ iG_ i^*)^*$. For the last assertion, the conjugates $F_ i^*$ are closed proper convex functions whose effective domains lie in the compact set $P$, by theorem 18.2.2 , proposition 18.3.2 . Since $F_ i^{**}=F_ i$, the first part gives the formula $(\max _ iF_ i)^*$ for their convex envelope. $\square$ Lemma 18.5.2 . Let $\mu _ j$ and $\mu $ be finite positive Radon measures on a finite-dimensional real vector space $W$ such that $\mu _ j	o \mu $ vaguely and $\mu _ j(W)	o \mu (W)$. Then $\int h\, \mathrm d\mu _ j	o \int h\, \mathrm d\mu $ for every bounded continuous function $h$ on $W$, that is, $\mu _ j	o \mu $ narrowly (section 1.5 ). In particular, if $P\subset M_{\mathbb R}$ is a convex body, $F_ j,F\in \mathcal E(N_{\mathbb R},P)$ and $F_ j	o F$ locally uniformly, then $\operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F_ j)	o \operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F)$ narrowly. Proof. Let $\varepsilon >0$. By inner regularity there is a compact set $S$ with $\mu (W\setminus S)<\varepsilon $; let $\eta $ be a continuous function with compact support, $0\leq \eta \leq 1$ and $\eta =1$ on $S$. Since $\int \eta \, \mathrm d\mu _ j	o \int \eta \, \mathrm d\mu $ and the total masses converge, we have \[  \lim _ j\int (1-\eta )\, \mathrm d\mu _ j =\int (1-\eta )\, \mathrm d\mu <\varepsilon ,  \] so that $\mu _ j(W\setminus \operatorname{Supp}\eta )\leq \int (1-\eta )\, \mathrm d\mu _ j<\varepsilon $ for all large $j$. Thus the sequence $(\mu _ j)$ is eventually uniformly tight, and proposition 1.5.3 gives narrow convergence. (If $W$ is a point, every function on $W$ has compact support, and vague and narrow convergence coincide.) For the real Monge–Ampère measures, theorem 18.4.2 gives vague convergence and the common total mass $n!\operatorname {vol}(P)$. $\square$

title: Compact domain finite convex envelope
text:
Lemma 18.5.1 . Let $G_1,\ldots ,G_ r$, with $r\geq 1$, be closed proper convex functions on a finite-dimensional real vector space, whose effective domains lie in a common compact set $K$, and let $H$ be the largest convex function below $\min _ iG_ i$, given by the formula of proposition 18.2.3 (2). Then $H$ is closed and proper, and at every point $x$ with $H(x)<+\infty $ the infimum defining $H(x)$ is attained. Consequently $H=(\max _ iG_ i^*)^*$. In particular, if $P\subset M_{\mathbb R}$ is a convex body and $F_1,\ldots ,F_ r\in \mathcal P(N_{\mathbb R},P)$, then the convex envelope of $F_1^*,\ldots ,F_ r^*$ is closed and equals $(\max _ iF_ i)^*$. title: Full mass real measure bounded testing
text: Lemma 18.5.2 . Let $\mu _ j$ and $\mu $ be finite positive Radon measures on a finite-dimensional real vector space $W$ such that $\mu _ j\to \mu $ vaguely and $\mu _ j(W)\to \mu (W)$. Then $\int h\, \mathrm d\mu _ j\to \int h\, \mathrm d\mu $ for every bounded continuous function $h$ on $W$, that is, $\mu _ j\to \mu $ narrowly (section 1.5 ). In particular, if $P\subset M_{\mathbb R}$ is a convex body, $F_ j,F\in \mathcal E(N_{\mathbb R},P)$ and $F_ j\to F$ locally uniformly, then $\operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F_ j)\to \operatorname {MA}_{\mathbb R}(F)$ narrowly. Proof. Let $\varepsilon >0$. By inner regularity there is a compact set $S$ with $\mu (W\setminus S)<\varepsilon $; let $\eta $ be a continuous function with compact support, $0\leq \eta \leq 1$ and $\eta =1$ on $S$. Since $\int \eta \, \mathrm d\mu _ j\to \int \eta \, \mathrm d\mu $ and the total masses converge, we have \[  \lim _ j\int (1-\eta )\, \mathrm d\mu _ j =\int (1-\eta )\, \mathrm d\mu <\varepsilon ,  \] so that $\mu _ j(W\setminus \operatorname{Supp}\eta )\leq \int (1-\eta )\, \mathrm d\mu _ j<\varepsilon $ for all large $j$. Thus the sequence $(\mu _ j)$ is eventually uniformly tight, and proposition 1.5.3 gives narrow convergence. (If $W$ is a point, every function on $W$ has compact support, and vague and narrow convergence coincide.) For the real Monge–Ampère measures, theorem 18.4.2 gives vague convergence and the common total mass $n!\operatorname {vol}(P)$. $\square$

title: Lattice points and volume
text: 18.6 Lattice points and volume By theorem 18.8.5 below, the dimension of a space of sections on a projective toric manifold is the number of lattice points in a dilated polytope. We show that $k^{-n}$ times the number of lattice points in $kK$ tends to the volume of the convex body $K$, and that this remains true if the lattice points are prescribed only up to a sublinear distance from $kK$. The reason is that the boundary of a convex body has volume zero. In this section we fix a basis of $M$. Its coordinates identify $M_{\mathbb R}$ with $\mathbb R^ n$ and $\operatorname {vol}$ with Lebesgue measure; we use the Euclidean norm of these coordinates on $M_{\mathbb R}$ and the dual norm on $N_{\mathbb R}$. For a convex body $K\subset M_{\mathbb R}$, $k>0$ and $\varepsilon >0$ put $kK=\{ kp:p\in K\} $ and \[  K^\varepsilon =\{ p:\operatorname {dist}(p,K)\leq \varepsilon \} , \qquad K_\varepsilon =\{ p:\overline{B(p,\varepsilon )}\subset K\} ,  \] and $K^0=K$. Since the distance to the compact set $K$ is attained, the outer parallel body $K^\varepsilon $ equals $K+\overline{B(0,\varepsilon )}$, the image of the compact convex set $K\times \overline{B(0,\varepsilon )}$ under addition; so it is a convex body. The inner set $K_\varepsilon =\bigcap _{|y|\leq \varepsilon }(K-y)$ is compact and convex but may be empty; it is empty whenever $K$ has empty interior and $n>0$, because a closed ball of positive radius has interior points. Definition 18.6.1 . The Hausdorff distance between convex bodies $K,L\subset M_{\mathbb R}$ is \[  d_{\mathrm H}(K,L)=\max \left\{ \sup _{p\in K}\operatorname {dist}(p,L), \sup _{q\in L}\operatorname {dist}(q,K)\right\} .  \] Proposition 18.6.2 . If $n>0$, then for convex bodies $K,L\subset M_{\mathbb R}$ \[  d_{\mathrm H}(K,L)=\max _{|x|=1}|h_ K(x)-h_ L(x)|.  \] If convex bodies $K_ j$ converge to a convex body $K$ in this distance, then $\operatorname {vol}(K_ j)\to \operatorname {vol}(K)$. In particular, \[  \lim _{\varepsilon \downarrow 0}\operatorname {vol}(K^\varepsilon ) =\operatorname {vol}(K)= \lim _{\varepsilon \downarrow 0}\operatorname {vol}(K_\varepsilon ).  \] In dimension zero the only convex body is the point, which has volume one. Proof. Let $n>0$. If $d_{\mathrm H}(K,L)\leq \varepsilon $, then every $p\in K$ has a point $q\in L$ with $|p-q|\leq \varepsilon $, and for $|x|=1$ we get $\langle p,x\rangle \leq \langle q,x\rangle +\varepsilon \leq h_ L(x)+\varepsilon $; hence $h_ K\leq h_ L+\varepsilon $ on the unit sphere, and by symmetry $|h_ K-h_ L|\leq \varepsilon $ there. Conversely, suppose that $|h_ K-h_ L|\leq \varepsilon $ on the unit sphere. The support function of the convex body $L+\overline{B(0,\varepsilon )}$ is $h_ L(x)+\varepsilon |x|$. If some $p\in K$ were outside $L+\overline{B(0,\varepsilon )}$, lemma 18.1.2 (1) would give a unit vector $x$ with $\langle p,x\rangle >h_ L(x)+\varepsilon \geq h_ K(x)$, which is impossible. Hence $K\subset L+\overline{B(0,\varepsilon )}$, and by symmetry $d_{\mathrm H}(K,L)\leq \varepsilon $. This proves the formula. It shows that $d_{\mathrm H}$ satisfies the triangle inequality, and by lemma 18.1.2 (1) a convex body is determined by its support function; thus $d_{\mathrm H}$ is a metric. Let $\varepsilon _ j=d_{\mathrm H}(K_ j,K)\to 0$. For large $j$ all $K_ j$ lie in the bounded set $K+\overline{B(0,1)}$. A point $p$ outside $K$ has positive distance from $K$, so $p\notin K_ j$ once $\varepsilon _ j<\operatorname {dist}(p,K)$. If $p$ is an interior point of $K$, choose $r>0$ with $\overline{B(p,r)}\subset K$. Then, for $|x|=1$, \[  h_{K_ j}(x)\geq h_ K(x)-\varepsilon _ j \geq \langle p,x\rangle +r-\varepsilon _ j.  \] If $\varepsilon _ j<r$ and $p\notin K_ j$, strict separation would give a unit vector $x$ with $\langle p,x\rangle >h_{K_ j}(x)$, contradicting this inequality; hence $p\in K_ j$ for large $j$. Thus $\mathbf1_{K_ j}\to \mathbf1_ K$ outside the boundary of $K$. If $K$ has nonempty interior, its boundary is a null set by lemma 18.1.2 (4); if $K$ has empty interior, it lies in a proper affine subspace and is itself a null set, and $\mathbf1_{K_ j}\to 0=\mathbf1_ K$ almost everywhere by the outside-point argument. In either case dominated convergence, with the dominating function $\mathbf1_{K+\overline{B(0,1)}}$, gives $\operatorname {vol}(K_ j)\to \operatorname {vol}(K)$. The outer parallel bodies $K^\varepsilon $ have finite volume and decrease to the compact set $K$ as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, so continuity of measure from above gives the first limit. The inner sets $K_\varepsilon $ increase, as $\varepsilon $ decreases, to the interior of $K$, which differs from $K$ by a null set, as we saw in the previous paragraph; monotone convergence gives the second limit. In dimension zero both $K^\varepsilon $ and $K_\varepsilon $ equal the single point for every $\varepsilon $. $\square$ Theorem 18.6.3 . Let $K\subset M_{\mathbb R}$ be a convex body, let $a_ k\in M_{\mathbb R}$ be arbitrary, and let $r_ k\geq 0$ satisfy $r_ k/k\to 0$. Then for every continuous function $f\colon M_{\mathbb R}\to \mathbb R$, \[  \lim _{k\to \infty }\frac1{k^ n} \sum _{m\in (kK)^{r_ k}\cap (M+a_ k)}f(m/k) =\int _ K f(p)\, \mathrm dp.  \] In particular $k^{-n}\# (kK\cap M)\to \operatorname {vol}(K)$. Here the exponent $n$ and the measure are those of the ambient space, also when $K$ has empty interior. The convergence is uniform with respect to the translations $a_ k$. Proof. For $n=0$ every set in question is the single point, and both sides equal its value under $f$. Suppose that $n>0$, and let $Q=[0,1)^ n$ be the half-open unit cube in the chosen coordinates. The cells \[  \frac mk+\frac1k Q,\qquad m\in M+a_ k,  \] partition $M_{\mathbb R}$; each has volume $k^{-n}$, and its points lie within distance $c/k$ of its anchor $m/k$, where $c=\sqrt n$. Let $U_ k$ be the union of the cells whose anchors $m/k$ occur in the sum, that is, with $m/k\in K^{r_ k/k}$. Then \[  K_{c/k}\subset U_ k\subset K^{(r_ k+c)/k}.  \] For the first inclusion, if $p\in K_{c/k}$, the anchor of the cell containing $p$ lies within $c/k$ of $p$, hence in $K$, so the cell is selected. For the second, every point of a selected cell lies within $c/k$ of its anchor, which lies within $r_ k/k$ of $K$. Since $K_{c/k}\subset K\subset K^{(r_ k+c)/k}$ and $(r_ k+c)/k\to 0$, proposition 18.6.2 gives $\operatorname {vol}(U_ k\mathbin \triangle K)\to 0$, and the volumes $\operatorname {vol}(U_ k)$ stay bounded. For large $k$ the selected cells lie in the fixed compact set $K^1$. Let $\omega _ f$ be the modulus of continuity of $f$ on $K^1$. Since $k^{-n}f(m/k)$ is the integral of the constant $f(m/k)$ over the cell of $m$, we obtain \[  \left|k^{-n}\sum _ m f(m/k)-\int _{U_ k}f(p)\, \mathrm dp\right| \leq \omega _ f(c/k)\operatorname {vol}(U_ k)\longrightarrow 0.  \] Since $f$ is bounded on $K^1$, the symmetric-difference estimate gives $\int _{U_ k}f\, \mathrm dp\to \int _ Kf\, \mathrm dp$. Taking $f=1$, $r_ k=0$ and $a_ k=0$ proves the counting formula. All the estimates depend only on the size of the cells, and not on their position, so they hold uniformly in the translations $a_ k$. $\square$ Corollary 18.6.4 . Let $K\subset M_{\mathbb R}$ be a convex body, and suppose that subsets $S_ k\subset M$ satisfy \[  kK\cap M\subset S_ k\subset (kK)^{r_ k}\cap M, \qquad r_ k\geq 0,\quad r_ k/k\to 0.  \] Then $k^{-n}\# S_ k\to \operatorname {vol}(K)$. In particular, a boundary error of bounded size does not affect the leading term of the count, even when $K$ has zero volume. Proof. By theorem 18.6.3 with $f=1$ and $a_ k=0$, both $k^{-n}\# (kK\cap M)$ and $k^{-n}\# ((kK)^{r_ k}\cap M)$ tend to $\operatorname {vol}(K)$, and $\# S_ k$ lies between these two counts. $\square$

In either case dominated convergence, with the dominating function $\mathbf1_{K+\overline{B(0,1)}}$, gives $\operatorname {vol}(K_ j)\to \operatorname {vol}(K)$. title: Bounded boundary error lattice count
text: Corollary 18.6.4 . Let $K\subset M_{\mathbb R}$ be a convex body, and suppose that subsets $S_ k\subset M$ satisfy \[  kK\cap M\subset S_ k\subset (kK)^{r_ k}\cap M, \qquad r_ k\geq 0,\quad r_ k/k\to 0.  \] Then $k^{-n}\# S_ k\to \operatorname {vol}(K)$. In particular, a boundary error of bounded size does not affect the leading term of the count, even when $K$ has zero volume. Proof. By theorem 18.6.3 with $f=1$ and $a_ k=0$, both $k^{-n}\# (kK\cap M)$ and $k^{-n}\# ((kK)^{r_ k}\cap M)$ tend to $\operatorname {vol}(K)$, and $\# S_ k$ lies between these two counts. $\square$

title: Smooth lattice polytopes and projective charts
text:
18.7 Smooth lattice polytopes and projective charts So far a convex body $P\subset M_{\mathbb R}$ has served as a bound for the slopes of convex functions. When $P$ is a lattice polytope, it also determines a compactification of the complex torus with character group $M$. If $P$ is smooth, the primitive edge directions at each vertex form a basis of $M$, and the corresponding characters become holomorphic coordinates on a chart isomorphic to $\mathbb C^ n$, which reaches across the boundary of the torus. Definition 18.7.1 . A lattice polytope in $M_{\mathbb R}$ is the convex hull of finitely many points of $M$. A face of a lattice polytope $P$ is a set of the form $\{ m\in P:\langle m,xangle =\min _{m'\in P}\langle m',xangle \} $ with $x\in N_{\mathbb R}$; faces are nonempty, and $P$ itself is the face for $x=0$. Vertices , edges and facets are the faces of dimension zero, of dimension one and of codimension one, respectively. A nonzero vector of a lattice is primitive if it is not of the form $ky$ with $y$ in the lattice and an integer $k\geq 2$. Let $P$ have nonempty interior. Its vertices are lattice points, each edge is a segment $[v,v']$ between two vertices, and a vertex contained in an edge is one of its endpoints (lemma 18.7.2 ). Thus an edge $[v,v']$ containing a vertex $v$ determines the primitive edge direction at $v$, the unique primitive vector of $M$ that is a positive multiple of $v'-v$ (see below). The polytope $P$ is smooth , or Delzant , if at each vertex its primitive edge directions form a basis of $M$. In dimension zero the single point is smooth, with the empty basis. Every nonzero vector $y$ of a lattice is a positive multiple of exactly one primitive vector. Indeed, if $d$ is the greatest common divisor of the coordinates of $y$ in a basis of the lattice, then $y/d$ is primitive, since its coordinates are coprime. If $y'$ and $y''$ are primitive and $y'=cy''$ with $c>0$, then $c$ is a quotient of integer coordinates, say $c=a/b$ with coprime positive integers $a$ and $b$, and $by'=ay''$ shows that $b$ divides all coordinates of $y''$ and $a$ all those of $y'$; hence $a=b=1$. The cone $\operatorname {cone}(S)$ generated by a set $S$ consists of its finite nonnegative linear combinations. A ray is a half-line $\mathbb R_{\geq 0}y$ with $y
eq 0$, and a ray contained in a cone $C$ is extreme if, whenever a vector of the ray is the sum of two vectors of $C$, both summands lie on the ray. An affine function $\ell $ that is nonnegative on a convex set $C$ and vanishes at a point $b\in \operatorname {ri}C$ vanishes on $C$. Indeed, for $y\in C$ the point $b-\varepsilon (y-b)$ lies in $C$ for small $\varepsilon >0$, and $0=\ell (b)$ is a convex combination, with positive weights, of the nonnegative numbers $\ell (y)$ and $\ell (b-\varepsilon (y-b))$; hence $\ell (y)=0$. Lemma 18.7.2 . Let $P\subset M_{\mathbb R}$ be a lattice polytope; in (2)–(4) assume moreover that $P$ has nonempty interior. The vertices of $P$ are lattice points, $P$ is their convex hull, every face of $P$ is the convex hull of the vertices it contains, and $P$ has finitely many faces. Every edge of $P$ is a segment $[v,v']$ between two distinct vertices, and a vertex contained in an edge is one of its endpoints. $P$ has an irredundant facet presentation \[  P=\{ m:\ell _ho (m)=\langle m,u_ho angle +a_ho \geq 0 	ext{ for every facet }ho \} ,  \] where, for each facet $ho $, the normal $u_ho \in N$ is primitive and inward pointing, $a_ho \in \mathbb Z$, and $ho =\{ m\in P:\ell _ho (m)=0\} $. At a vertex $v$, the tangent cone \[  C_ v=\{ y:\langle y,u_ho angle \geq 0 	ext{ for the facets }ho 
i v\}  =\operatorname {cone}(P-v)  \] is generated by its extreme rays, and these are the rays spanned by the edge directions at $v$. If $P$ is smooth and $v$ is a vertex with primitive edge basis $e_1,\ldots ,e_ n$, then exactly $n$ facets contain $v$, and their normals $u_1,\ldots ,u_ n$ form the dual basis of $N$, that is, $\langle e_ i,u_ jangle =\delta _{ij}$. Thus \[  m-v=\sum _ i t_ i e_ i,\qquad t_ i=\ell _ i(m)\geq 0\quad (m\in P),  \] and $v+e_ i\in P\cap M$ for each $i$. Proof. (1) Let $P$ be the convex hull of a finite set $S\subset M$, and discard points of $S$ one at a time as long as some point lies in the convex hull of the others; this does not change $P$. If only one point remains, $P$ is that point, it is the only face, and all assertions hold. Otherwise, for a remaining point $s$, lemma 18.1.2 (1) gives $x\in N_{\mathbb R}$ with $\langle s,xangle <\langle s',xangle $ for all $s'$ in the convex hull of $S\setminus \{ s\} $. Every point of $P$ is a convex combination $\lambda s+(1-\lambda )s''$ with $s''$ in that hull, so $\langle \cdot ,xangle $ attains its minimum on $P$ only at $s$, and $\{ s\} $ is a vertex. Conversely, let $Q$ be any face, the set where $\langle \cdot ,x'angle $ is minimal for some $x'\in N_{\mathbb R}$, and write a point $m\in Q$ as a convex combination of points of $S$: all points with positive coefficient minimize $\langle \cdot ,x'angle $, hence lie in $Q$. Thus $Q$ is the convex hull of the points of $S$ it contains. Applied to a vertex $\{ v\} $, this shows $v\in S$. Hence the vertices are exactly the remaining points of $S$, and in particular lattice points. Every face is the convex hull of the vertices it contains, so there are only finitely many faces. Let $\{ v\} $ be a vertex, the set where some $\langle \cdot ,xangle $ is minimal on $P$. Then $v$ is not of the form $(1-t)a+tb$ with $a
eq b$ in $P$ and $0<t<1$: the values $\langle a,xangle $ and $\langle b,xangle $ are at least $\langle v,xangle $, and their weighted mean equals it, so $a$ and $b$ would also be minimum points, that is, $a=b=v$. An edge is the convex hull of the finitely many vertices it contains, which lie on a line, so it is the segment between the two outermost ones; a vertex in the edge is not an interior point of the segment, hence it is an endpoint. (2) We first show that every boundary point $b$ of $P$ lies in a facet. By lemma 18.1.2 (2), $b$ lies in a face $Q$ where some $x

Suppose that $Q$ has dimension $d<n-1$, and let $c$ be the minimum of $\langle \cdot ,xangle $ on $P$. The linear functionals vanishing on the directions of $Q$ form a space of dimension $n-d\geq 2$, which contains $x$; choose $y$ in it, independent of $x$, and put $x_ s=x+sy$. On $Q$ the functional $\langle \cdot ,yangle $ is constant, say equal to $c'$, and for each vertex $w
otin Q$ consider the gap $g_ w(s)=\langle w,x_ sangle -(c+sc')=(\langle w,xangle -c)+s(\langle w,yangle -c')$, which is positive at $s=0$. Some vertex $w

The new face contains $Q$ and $w$, and $w$ does not lie in the affine span of $Q$, because $\langle \cdot ,xangle $ equals $c$ on that span and is larger at $w$. So the dimension of the face has increased, and after finitely many steps we reach a facet containing $b$. A facet $ho $ contains $n$ affinely independent vertices, which are lattice points by (1). The linear functionals vanishing on the differences of these points form a line, which is defined by linear equations with integral coefficients in the coordinates of bases of $M$ and $N$; Gaussian elimination over $\mathbb Q$ produces a nonzero rational solution, and clearing denominators gives a nonzero vector of $N$ on the line. Then $a_ho =-\langle v,u_ho angle $, for any vertex $v\in ho $, is an integer, $\ell _ho \geq 0$ on $P$, and $ho =\{ m\in P:\ell _ho (m)=0\} $. Next we show that $P$ is the intersection of the half-spaces $\{ \ell _ho \geq 0\} $. Let $q
otin P$ and let $p$ be an interior point of $P$. The set of $s\in [0,1]$ with $p+s(q-p)\in P$ is an interval $[0,s_0]$ with $s_0<1$, and $b=p+s_0(q-p)$ is a boundary point of $P$, hence lies in some facet $ho $. The affine function $s\mapsto \ell _ho (p+s(q-p))$ is positive at $s=0$, because the nonconstant affine function $\ell _ho $, which is nonnegative on $P$, cannot attain its minimum at the interior point $p$. It vanishes at $s_0<1$, so $\ell _ho (q)<0$. For irredundancy, let $b$ be a point of the relative interior of a facet $ho $, which exists by lemma 18.1.2 (4). If $\ell _{ho '}(b)=0$ for another facet $ho '$, then $\ell _{ho '}$, which is nonnegative on $ho $, vanishes on $ho $ by the observation preceding the lemma. Then $u_{ho '}$ is constant on $ho $, whose differences span a hyperplane, so $u_{ho '}$ lies on the line of $u_ho $, and $u_{ho '}=\pm u_ho $, because both vectors are primitive. If $u_{ho '}=-u_ho $, then $\ell _{ho '}=-\ell _ho $, since both vanish on $ho $; as both are nonnegative on $P$, $\ell _ho $ would vanish on $P$, which is impossible at an interior point. Hence $\ell _{ho '}=\ell _ho $ and $ho '=ho $. Thus all other facet functions are positive at $b$, and a point near $b$ on the side where $\ell _ho <0$ violates only the inequality of $ho $. (3) If $m\in P$ and $v\in ho $, then $\langle m-v,u_ho angle =\ell _ho (m)\geq 0$; hence $\operatorname {cone}(P-v)\subset C_ v$. Conversely, if $y\in C_ v$, then $v+sy\in P$ for all small $s>0$, because the inequalities of the facets containing $v$ hold along this half-line and the finitely many other facet functions are positive at $v$; hence $y\in \operatorname {cone}(P-v)$. The cone $C_ v$ contains no line: if $y
eq 0$ and $\pm y\in C_ v$, then $v\pm sy\in P$ for small $s>0$, and $v$ would be the midpoint of two points of $P$, which is impossible for a vertex. Let $u$ be the sum of the normals $u_ho $ of the facets containing $v$. If $y\in C_ v$ and $\langle y,uangle =0$, then $\langle y,u_ho angle =0$ for all these facets, so $-y\in C_ v$ and $y=0$. Consequently, the slice $\Sigma =\{ y\in C_ v:\langle y,uangle =1\} $ is bounded (otherwise a limit of normalized unbounded points would give a nonzero $y\in C_ v$ with $\langle y,uangle =0$), and $C_ v=\operatorname {cone}(\Sigma )$. Induction on the codimension of this span therefore proves the claim, because a point $y\in \Sigma $ whose active normals together with $u$ span $N_{\mathbb R}$ is basic: its active normals annihilate $y
eq 0$, so they span a space of dimension at most $n-1$, and at least $n-1$, since adding $u$ raises the dimension by at most one. Next, $y\in \Sigma $ is basic if and only if $\mathbb R_{\geq 0}y$ is an extreme ray. If $y$ is basic, its active normals annihilate exactly the line $\mathbb Ry$; if $y=y_1+y_2$ with $y_1,y_2\in C_ v$, then for each active normal both pairings $\langle y_ k,u_ho angle $ are nonnegative with sum zero, hence zero, so $y_1,y_2\in \mathbb Ry\cap C_ v=\mathbb R_{\geq 0}y$. Conversely, if $\mathbb R_{\geq 0}y$ is extreme, write $y$ as a convex combination of basic points; extremality forces each of them to lie on the ray, hence to equal $y$. Therefore $C_ v$ is generated by its extreme rays. It remains to identify the extreme rays with the edges at $v$. If $y\in \Sigma $ is basic, the set $\{ m\in P:\ell _ho (m)=0	ext{ for the active facets of }y\} $ is a face, namely the set where the sum of the corresponding functionals $\langle \cdot ,u_ho angle $ is minimal; it contains $v+sy$ for small $s>0$ and is contained in $v+(C_ v\cap (\mathbb Ry))=v+\mathbb R_{\geq 0}y$. Hence it is an edge at $v$ with direction $y$. Conversely, let $E$ be an edge at $v$ with direction $y$, so $y\in C_ v$. If $y=y_1+y_2$ with $y_1,y_2\in C_ v$, then for small $s>0$ the point $v+sy\in E$ is the midpoint of $v+2sy_1$ and $v+2sy_2$, which lie in $P$. Since $E$ is the set where some linear functional is minimal on $P$, both points lie in $E\subset v+\mathbb R_{\geq 0}y$, and so $y_1,y_2\in \mathbb R_{\geq 0}y$. Thus the ray of $y$ is extreme. (4) Let $P$ be smooth and $v$ a vertex. By (3), $C_ v=\operatorname {cone}(e_1,\ldots ,e_ n)$. Let $e_1^*,\ldots ,e_ n^*\in N$ be the dual basis, so that $C_ v=\{ y:\langle y,e_ i^*angle \geq 0	ext{ for all }i\} $. If $ho $ is a facet containing $v$, then $u_ho \geq 0$ on $C_ v$, so $u_ho =\sum _ ic_ ie_ i^*$ with $c_ i=\langle e_ i,u_ho angle \geq 0$. The set $ho -v$ lies in $C_ v\cap u_ho ^\perp =\operatorname {cone}\{ e_ i:c_ i=0\} $ and spans a space of dimension $n-1$, so exactly one coefficient $c_ i$ is positive. Since $u_ho $ and $e_ i^*$ are primitive, $u_ho =e_ i^*$. Distinct facets have distinct normals, because a facet is the set where its normal is minimal; so at most $n$ facets contain $v$. If some $e_ i^*$ were not the normal of a facet through $v$, the vector $-e_ i$ would satisfy all the inequalities defining $C_ v$, although $-e_ i
otin \operatorname {cone}(e_1,\ldots ,e_ n)$. Hence exactly $n$ facets contain $v$, and numbering them suitably, $u_ i=e_ i^*$. For $m\in P$ this gives $m-v=\sum _ i\langle m-v,u_ iangle e_ i=\sum _ i\ell _ i(m)e_ i$, because $\ell _ i(v)=0$. Finally, the edge in direction $e_ i$ is a segment $[v,v']$ with $v'$ a lattice point, so $v'-v=ke_ i$ for a positive integer $k$, and $v+e_ i\in [v,v']\subset P$. In dimension zero there are no facets and no edges, and the assertions are empty. $\square$ For the rest of the chapter we fix a smooth lattice polytope $P\subset M_{\mathbb R}$, which by definition has nonempty interior, with the notation $\ell _ho $, $u_ho $ and $a_ho $ of lemma 18.7.2 , and we put $A=P\cap M$, a finite set containing the vertices. Let $T=\operatorname {Hom}(M,\mathbb C^*)$ be the group of homomorphisms from $M$ to the multiplicative group $\mathbb C^*$, and $T_ c=\operatorname {Hom}(M,S^1)$ its compact subgroup, where $S^1=\{ \zeta \in \mathbb C:|\zeta |=1\} $. Each $m\in M$ defines a character $\chi ^ m\colon T	o \mathbb C^*$, $\chi ^ m(t)=t(m)$, so that $\chi ^{m+m'}=\chi ^ m\chi ^{m'}$. A basis $m_1,\ldots ,m_ n$ of $M$ identifies $T$ with $(\mathbb C^*)^ n$ through $t\mapsto (\chi ^{m_1}(t),\ldots ,\chi ^{m_ n}(t))$, since a homomorphism on $M$ is determined by its values on a basis, which may be arbitrary. The resulting structure of complex manifold on $T$ does not depend on the basis, because a change of basis acts on the coordinates by a monomial map whose inverse is again monomial. In these coordinates $\chi ^ m$ becomes the Laurent monomial $z_1^{c_1}\cdots z_ n^{c_ n}$ for $m=\sum _ jc_ jm_ j$, and $T_ c$ becomes $(S^1)^ n$, acting on $T=(\mathbb C^*)^ n$ by multiplication, that is, by separate rotations of the coordinates. The tropicalization map $\operatorname {Trop}\colon T	o N_{\mathbb R}$ is defined by \[  \langle m,\operatorname {Trop}(t)angle =\log |\chi ^ m(t)|^2\qquad (m\in M);  \] in the coordinates above, with $N_{\mathbb R}$ identified with $\mathbb R^ n$ by the dual basis, it is $z\mapsto (\log |z_1|^2,\ldots ,\log |z_ n|^2)$. By corollary 18.1.6 , the $T_ c$-invariant plurisubharmonic functions on $T$ are exactly the functions $F\circ \operatorname {Trop}$ with $F$ finite and convex on $N_{\mathbb R}$. (In dimension zero, $T$ and $N_{\mathbb R}$ are points, and by definition 8.1.1 both classes consist of the real constants.) Let $\mathbb P^{|A|-1}$ be the complex projective space of lines in $\mathbb C^ A$, with homogeneous coordinates $Z=[Z_ m]_{m\in A}$. By example 14.5.5 , with homogeneous coordinates indexed by the finite set $A$, it is a compact complex manifold of dimension $|A|-1$, with the affine charts $\{ Z_{m_0}
eq 0\} $, $m_0\in A$, and the coordinates $Z_ m/Z_{m_0}$, $m
