title: Complex spaces and modifications
text: A Complex spaces and modifications Analytic sets enter pluripotential theory as the pole sets of potentials with analytic singularities, as the zero sets of the ideals that describe these poles, and as the exceptional divisors of modifications. This appendix collects the facts about analytic sets, reduced complex spaces and modifications that are used from chapter 12 on: for multiplier ideals and Lelong numbers along divisors in chapter 12 , for analytic singularities and their log resolutions in chapter 13 , for currents supported on analytic sets in chapter 14 , and for the non-Kähler locus in chapter 16 . It can be consulted when these tools first appear. Besides results of the earlier chapters, such as the Weierstrass preparation theorem (theorem 7.4.2 ), only two existence theorems are used without proof: the resolution of singularities and the principalization of coherent ideals, stated as theorem A.5.4 , theorem A.5.5 . The local theory rests on the Weierstrass division theorem. It shows that the ring of germs of holomorphic functions is Noetherian and, through Oka's theorem, that the sheaf of holomorphic functions is coherent, so that statements about one stalk extend to a neighborhood. The local parametrization theorem (theorem A.2.3 ) presents an irreducible germ of an analytic set as a finite branched covering of a polydisc. From it we deduce the analytic Nullstellensatz, the basic properties of dimension, Cartan's theorem on the coherence of the ideal sheaf of an analytic set, and the decomposition of an analytic set into irreducible components. We also show that a closed real $(1,1)$-current with measure coefficients supported on a nowhere dense analytic set is a combination of currents of integration along hypersurfaces (theorem A.2.17 ). One phenomenon requires care: an irreducible analytic set can have several local branches at one point. The normalization (theorem A.3.6 ) separates these branches; its holomorphic functions are the weakly holomorphic functions, that is, the functions that are holomorphic on the regular locus and locally bounded near the singular locus. The cusp shows that a space with only one branch at each point need not be normal (example A.3.10 ). For modifications, explicit charts describe blowups along submanifolds and the transformation of ideals under them (proposition A.5.2 , proposition A.5.3 ); together with the two existence theorems they give log resolutions of coherent ideals. Remmert's theorem, proved together with the Remmert–Stein extension theorem, shows that images of analytic sets under proper holomorphic maps, in particular the images of exceptional divisors, are analytic (theorem A.6.2 ). We then prove a relative principalization theorem, which controls an ideal and its restriction to a submanifold simultaneously (theorem A.6.5 ), show that proper bimeromorphic maps onto spaces with one local branch at each point have connected fibers (theorem A.7.1 ), and prove that every prime divisor over a compact complex space appears on a model obtained by finitely many blowups with smooth centers (theorem A.7.6 ). The last section defines plurisubharmonic functions on reduced complex spaces by local extension to an ambient space, proves that they are constant on compact connected spaces, and shows that they are locally bounded above near analytic subsets of codimension at least two. Holomorphic curves through singular points, constructed in section A.4 , reduce these statements to the maximum principle in one variable. These results on reduced spaces are used in [ XiaSampleBook ] . Historical remarks and references for this appendix are collected in section B.21 .

title: Division and finite analytic modules
text:
A.1 Division and finite analytic modules Let $n\geq 0$. We write $\mathcal O_ n$ for the ring of germs at $0\in \mathbb C^ n$ of holomorphic functions; two functions defined near $0$ have the same germ if they agree on some neighborhood of $0$, and identities between germs are understood in this sense. By the iterated Cauchy formula of section 7.1 , every germ is given near $0$ by its Taylor series ( 7.1 ), which converges normally on a small polydisc. Conversely, a power series $\sum _\alpha c_\alpha z^\alpha $ with $\sum _\alpha |c_\alpha |r^{|\alpha |}<\infty $ for some $r>0$ defines a holomorphic function on the polydisc $\{ |z_ j|<r\} $: since $|c_\alpha |\leq Cr^{-|\alpha |}$, the series of partial derivatives of each order converge normally on every polydisc $\{ |z_ j|\leq s\} $ with $s<r$, so the sum is smooth, may be differentiated termwise, and satisfies the Cauchy–Riemann equations. Thus germs are the same as convergent power series, $\mathcal O_ n=\mathbb C\{ z_1,\ldots ,z_ n\} $, and $\mathcal O_0=\mathbb C$. The ring $\mathcal O_ n$ is an integral domain: if $fg=0$ near $0$ and $f
eq 0$, then $g$ vanishes on the nonempty open subset $\{ f
eq 0\} $ of a connected neighborhood of $0$, so $g=0$ by the identity theorem. A germ that does not vanish at the origin has a holomorphic reciprocal near the origin; hence $\mathcal O_ n$ is a local ring, whose maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$ consists of the germs vanishing at the origin. The order $\operatorname {ord}_0f$ of a nonzero germ $f$ is the degree of the first nonzero homogeneous term of its Taylor expansion. The order of a product is the sum of the orders. Indeed, if $P_ s$ and $Q_ t$ are the first nonzero homogeneous terms of $f$ and $g$, then $P_ sQ_ t$ is the homogeneous term of degree $s+t$ of $fg$. It is not zero: a polynomial vanishing on a nonempty open set is zero, so the sets $\{ P_ s
eq 0\} $ and $\{ Q_ t
eq 0\} $ are open and dense, and therefore meet. Hence every element of the $k$th power $\mathfrak m^ k$ has order at least $k$. Conversely, let $f=\sum _ eta c_ eta z^ eta $ have order at least $k$. Assign to each $ eta $ with $| eta |\geq k$ the first multi-index $\alpha \leq  eta $ with $|\alpha |=k$ in the lexicographic order, and let $f_\alpha =\sum c_ eta z^{ eta -\alpha }$, the sum over the $ eta $ assigned to $\alpha $. These series converge normally wherever the series of $f$ does, so $f_\alpha \in \mathcal O_ n$, and $f=\sum _{|\alpha |=k}z^\alpha f_\alpha \in \mathfrak m^ k$. Thus $\operatorname {ord}_0f\geq k$ if and only if $f\in \mathfrak m^ k$. A holomorphic change of coordinates fixing $0$ induces a ring automorphism of $\mathcal O_ n$ that preserves $\mathfrak m$ and its powers; so the order does not depend on the coordinates. For a holomorphic function $f$ near a point $a$ of a complex manifold whose germ at $a$ is nonzero, $\operatorname {ord}_ af$ is the order of its germ in local coordinates centered at $a$. This is the order used for Lelong numbers in proposition 12.1.4 ; chapter 12 also defines the order of a coherent ideal at a point and the order along a prime divisor (definition 12.6.3 ). Write points of $\mathbb C^ n$, $n\geq 1$, as $(z',w)$ with $z'\in \mathbb C^{n-1}$. A Weierstrass polynomial of degree $m\geq 0$ in $w$ is a polynomial \[  P(z',w)=w^ m+a_1(z')w^{m-1}+\cdots +a_ m(z'),\qquad a_ j\in \mathcal O_{n-1},\quad a_ j(0)=0.  \] We shall often use the following bound for the roots $t$ of a monic polynomial with complex coefficients: A.1  egin{equation} \label{eq:monic-root-bound} t^ m+d_1t^{m-1}+\cdots +d_ m=0\quad \Longrightarrow \quad |t|\le 2\max _{1\leq j\leq m}|d_ j|^{1/j}. \end{equation} Indeed, otherwise $|d_ j|<(|t|/2)^ j$ for all $j$, and dividing the equation by $t^ m$ gives $1\le \sum _{j=1}^ m|d_ j/t^ j|<\sum _{j=1}^ m2^{-j}<1$. In particular, the roots of $P(z',\cdot )$ tend to $0$ as $z'	o 0$. A germ $f\in \mathcal O_ n$ is distinguished in $w$ if $f(0,w)$ is not identically zero. If $f(0,w)$ vanishes to order $m\geq 1$ at $w=0$, the Weierstrass preparation theorem (theorem 7.4.2 ) writes $f$ as a unit times a Weierstrass polynomial of degree $m$; if $f(0)
eq 0$, then $f$ is itself a unit, which is the case $m=0$. Every nonzero germ becomes distinguished in the last coordinate after a linear change of coordinates. Indeed, let $P_ s$ be the first nonzero homogeneous term of $f$ and choose $v$ with $P_ s(v)
eq 0$; in linear coordinates whose last basis vector is $v$, we have $f(0,w)=P_ s(v)w^ s+O(w^{s+1})$, which vanishes to order exactly $s$, the order of $f$. Since $P_ s
eq 0$, the admissible vectors $v$ form a dense open set. Hence the new coordinates can be chosen arbitrarily close to given ones, and finitely many nonzero germs become distinguished simultaneously if $v$ avoids the zero set of the product of their first homogeneous terms. Proposition A.1.1 (Weierstrass division) . Let $n\geq 1$ and $m\geq 0$, and let $P$ be a Weierstrass polynomial of degree $m$ in $w$. Then every germ $f\in \mathcal O_ n$ can be written uniquely as \[  f=Pq+R,\qquad q\in \mathcal O_ n,\quad R\in \mathcal O_{n-1}[w],\quad \deg _ w R<m.  \] Moreover, let $\Delta '\subset \mathbb C^{n-1}$ be a polydisc centered at $0$ and $\Delta =\{ |w|<r\} $ a disc such that the coefficients of $P$ are holomorphic near $\overline{\Delta '}$ and all roots of $P(z',\cdot )$, $z'\in \Delta '$, lie in $\{ |w|\leq ho \} $ for some $ho <r$; such polydiscs $\Delta '	imes \Delta $ exist with arbitrarily small radii. Then every holomorphic function $f$ on $\Delta '	imes \Delta $ can be written uniquely as $f=Pq+R$, where $q$ is holomorphic on $\Delta '	imes \Delta $ and $R$ is a polynomial in $w$ of degree less than $m$ with holomorphic coefficients on $\Delta '$; for every $s\in (ho ,r)$, $z'\in \Delta '$ and $|w|<s$, A.2  egin{equation} \label{eq:weierstrass-division-integrals}  egin{aligned}  q(z',w)& = rac1{2\pi \mathrm i}\int _{|\zeta |=s}  rac{f(z',\zeta )}{P(z',\zeta )(\zeta -w)}\, \mathrm d\zeta ,\  R(z',w)& = rac1{2\pi \mathrm i}\int _{|\zeta |=s}  rac{f(z',\zeta )}{P(z',\zeta )}\,   rac{P(z',\zeta )-P(z',w)}{\zeta -w}\, \mathrm d\zeta . \end{aligned} \end{equation} Division is a bounded linear operation on bounded holomorphic functions on $\Delta '	imes \Delta $: there is a constant $C$, independent of $f$, with \[  \sup _{\Delta '	imes \Delta }|q|+\sup _{\Delta '	imes \Delta }|R|\le C\sup _{\Delta '	imes \Delta }|f|.  \] Proof. Polydiscs as in the statement exist with arbitrarily small radii, because the roots of $P(z',\cdot )$ tend to $0$ as $z'	o 0$, by ( A.1 ). Let $\Delta '	imes \Delta $ be such a polydisc and $f$ a holomorphic function on it. For $ho <s<r$ and $|w|<s$ define $q$ and $R$ by ( A.2 ). For fixed $z'$ and $w$, both integrands are holomorphic in $\zeta $ on the annulus $\{ ho <|\zeta |<r\} $, except for the pole of the first one at $\zeta =w$; by Cauchy's theorem the integrals do not depend on $s$ as long as $|w|<s$, and the second one does not depend on $s\in (ho ,r)$ at all. Hence $q$ and $R$ are defined on $\Delta '	imes \Delta $, and they are holomorphic by differentiation under the integral sign. The difference quotient $(P(z',\zeta )-P(z',w))/(\zeta -w)$ is a polynomial in $w$ of degree $m-1$ whose coefficients are polynomials in $\zeta $ and in the $a_ j(z')$; hence $R$ is a polynomial in $w$ of degree less than $m$ with holomorphic coefficients on $\Delta '$. Adding the two integrals, we obtain $Pq+R=(2\pi \mathrm i)^{-1}\int _{|\zeta |=s}f(z',\zeta )(\zeta -w)^{-1}\, \mathrm d\zeta =f$ by Cauchy's formula. For the estimate, let $f$ be bounded, and fix $s_0=(ho +r)/2$. For $|\zeta |\geq s_0$ we have $|P(z',\zeta )|=\prod _ l|\zeta -\lambda _ l(z')|\geq (s_0-ho )^ m$, where $\lambda _ l(z')$ are the roots, and the coefficients of the difference quotient are bounded for $z'\in \Delta '$, $|\zeta |=s_0$ and $|w|<r$, since the $a_ j$ are bounded on $\Delta '$. The integral over $|\zeta |=s_0$ therefore gives $|R|\leq C_1\sup |f|$ on $\Delta '	imes \Delta $. For $s_0\leq |w|<r$ we have $|q|=|f-R|/|P|\leq (1+C_1)(s_0-ho )^{-m}\sup |f|$, and the maximum principle for the holomorphic functions $q(z',\cdot )$ on the discs $\{ |w|\leq s\} $, $s_0\leq s<r$, extends this bound to all of $\Delta '	imes \Delta $. For uniqueness, suppose that $Pq+R=0$ on a polydisc as above, with $R$ a polynomial in $w$ of degree less than $m$. For each $z'$, the polynomial $R(z',\cdot )=-P(z',\cdot )q(z',\cdot )$ vanishes at the $m$ roots of $P(z',\cdot )$, counted with multiplicity, all of which lie in $\Delta $. Its degree is less than $m$, so $R(z',\cdot )=0$. Then $P(z',\cdot )q(z',\cdot )=0$, and since $P(z',\cdot )$ has only finitely many zeros, the continuous function $q(z',\cdot )$ vanishes on a dense set, hence everywhere. Finally, every germ is represented by a bounded holomorphic function on some polydisc as above, and an identity between germs holds on some such polydisc; so the assertions for germs follow. $\square$ The first consequence of division is the Noetherian property of $\mathcal O_ n$. Proposition A.1.2 . Every ideal of $\mathcal O_ n$ is finitely generated, and every submodule of $\mathcal O_ n^ r$, $r\geq 1$, is finitely generated. Consequently, every increasing sequence of ideals of $\mathcal O_ n$, or of submodules of a finitely generated $\mathcal O_ n$-module, is eventually constant. Proof. We first recall three algebraic facts about a commutative ring $\Lambda $ all of whose ideals are finitely generated. Every submodule $N$ of $\Lambda ^ r$ is finitely generated, by induction on $r$: the projection of $N$ to the last coordinate is an ideal; choose elements of $N$ whose last coordinates generate it, and add generators of $N\cap (\Lambda ^{r-1}	imes \{ 0\} )$, which exist by the induction hypothesis. A finitely generated module is a quotient of some $\Lambda ^ r$, and the inverse image of a submodule is a submodule of $\Lambda ^ r$; hence submodules of finitely generated modules are finitely generated. Finally, the union of an increasing sequence of submodules is a submodule; its finitely many generators already lie in one member of the sequence, which is therefore stationary from then on. It remains to prove that the ideals of $\mathcal O_ n$ are finitely generated, which we do by induction on $n$. The ring $\mathcal O_0=\mathbb C$ is a field. Let $n\geq 1$ and let $I\subset \mathcal O_ n$ be an ideal. If $I=0$ or $I$ contains a unit, it is generated by one element. Otherwise choose a nonzero germ in $I$, and coordinates in which it is distinguished in $w$. By the preparation theorem it is a unit times a Weierstrass polynomial $P$ of some degree $m\geq 1$, and $P\in I$. Divide every $f\in I$ by $P$ using proposition A.1.1 ; the remainder $R_ f=f-Pq$ again belongs to $I$. The remainders of degree less than $m$ that lie in $I$ form an $\mathcal O_{n-1}$-submodule of $\mathcal O_{n-1}[w]$, which we identify, through their coefficients, with a submodule of $\mathcal O_{n-1}^ m$. By the induction hypothesis and the first paragraph, it is generated by finitely many remainders $R_1,\ldots ,R_ k$. Then $P,R_1,\ldots ,R_ k$ generate $I$. $\square$ Division also factors a monic polynomial near each of its roots. Lemma A.1.3 . Let $n\geq 1$, let $P(z',w)=w^\mu +a_1(z')w^{\mu -1}+\cdots +a_\mu (z')$ be a monic polynomial in $w$ whose coefficients are holomorphic near a point $x'\in \mathbb C^{n-1}$, and let $w_0$ be a root of multiplicity $\mu '\geq 1$ of $P(x',\cdot )$. Then, near $x=(x',w_0)$, \[  P=P_ xQ_ x,  \] where $P_ x$ is a Weierstrass polynomial of degree $\mu '$ in $w-w_0$ with respect to the coordinates $(z'-x',w-w_0)$, and $Q_ x$ is a monic polynomial of degree $\mu -\mu '$ in $w$ with coefficients holomorphic near $x'$ and $Q_ x(x)
eq 0$. Proof. In the coordinates $(z'-x',w-w_0)$ centered at $x$, the function $w\mapsto P(x',w)$ has a zero of order $\mu '$ at $w_0$. By the Weierstrass preparation theorem (theorem 7.4.2 ), $P$ is, near $x$, a nowhere vanishing holomorphic function $U$ times a Weierstrass polynomial $P_ x$ of degree $\mu '$ in $w-w_0$. Since $P_ x$ is monic in $w$, Euclidean division of the polynomial $P$ by $P_ x$, with coefficients holomorphic near $x'$, gives $P=P_ xQ+R$, where $Q$ is a monic polynomial of degree $\mu -\mu '$ in $w$ and $R$ is a polynomial in $w$, equivalently in $w-w_0$, of degree less than $\mu '$. The identities $P=P_ xQ+R$ and $P=P_ xU+0$ are two divisions of the germ of $P$ at $x$ by $P_ x$; by the uniqueness in proposition A.1.1 , applied in the coordinates centered at $x$, we get $Q=U$ near $x$ and $R=0$. Hence $Q_ x=Q$ has the required properties, with $Q_ x(x)=U(x)
eq 0$. $\square$ We use sheaves in the following elementary form. A sheaf $\mathcal F$ of modules on a topological space assigns to each open set $U$ a module $\mathcal F(U)$ of sections, with restriction maps, such that sections that agree locally are equal and compatible local sections glue. The stalk $\mathcal F_ x$ consists of the germs at $x$ of sections defined near $x$. Kernels and images of morphisms of sheaves are defined stalkwise, and a sequence of morphisms is exact if it is exact on every stalk; in particular, a section of the image of a morphism is, near each point, the image of a section of the source. Similarly, the quotient $\mathcal S/\mathcal F$ of a sheaf of modules by a subsheaf has the stalks $\mathcal S_ x/\mathcal F_ x$, and its sections are the families of classes that are, near each point, the classes of a section of $\mathcal S$; so sections of $\mathcal S/\mathcal F$ can be lifted locally to sections of $\mathcal S$. The cokernel of a morphism is the quotient of its target by its image. Let $\mathcal A$ be a sheaf of rings and $\mathcal F$ a sheaf of $\mathcal A$-modules. We say that $\mathcal F$ is locally finitely generated if every point has a neighborhood $U$ and finitely many sections $s_1,\ldots ,s_ p\in \mathcal F(U)$ whose germs generate $\mathcal F_ y$ over $\mathcal A_ y$ for every $y\in U$. This requires one family of generators on a whole neighborhood, not merely finite generation of each stalk. The sheaf of relations of sections $s_1,\ldots ,s_ p\in \mathcal F(U)$ is the kernel of the morphism $\mathcal A^ p|_ U	o \mathcal F|_ U$, $(a_ i)\mapsto \sum _ ia_ is_ i$. The sheaf $\mathcal F$ is coherent if it is locally finitely generated and the sheaf of relations of every finite family of sections over every open set is locally finitely generated. Lemma A.1.4 . Let $\mathcal A$ be a sheaf of rings. Kernels, images and cokernels of morphisms between coherent $\mathcal A$-modules are coherent. If two of the three sheaves in an exact sequence $0	o \mathcal F	o \mathcal S	o \mathcal G	o 0$ of $\mathcal A$-modules are coherent, so is the third. Finite direct sums of coherent sheaves are coherent. If $\mathcal A$ is coherent as a module over itself, every locally finitely generated $\mathcal A$-submodule of $\mathcal A^ r$ is coherent. Proof. A locally finitely generated submodule of a coherent sheaf is coherent, because its sections have the same relations when they are regarded as sections of the larger sheaf. The image of a morphism from a coherent sheaf is locally generated by the images of local generators of the source, so the image of a morphism between coherent sheaves is coherent. For the kernel of a morphism $\phi \colon \mathcal F	o \mathcal G$ between coherent sheaves, choose local generators $F_1,\ldots ,F_ p$ of $\mathcal F$ and local generators $R_ j=(R_{j1},\ldots ,R_{jp})$ of the relations of $\phi (F_1),\ldots ,\phi (F_ p)$. If $\sum _ ia_ iF_ i$ lies in the kernel, then $(a_ i)$ is a relation of the $\phi (F_ i)$, hence a combination of the $R_ j$; so the sections $\sum _ iR_{ji}F_ i$ generate the kernel, which is therefore coherent. Let $\mathcal F\subset \mathcal S$ be coherent sheaves and consider $\mathcal G=\mathcal S/\mathcal F$; this covers cokernels, because images are coherent. Local generators of $\mathcal S$ map to local generators of $\mathcal G$. Given sections $G_1,\ldots ,G_ p$ of $\mathcal G$, lift them locally to sections $S_1,\ldots ,S_ p$ of $\mathcal S$, and choose local generators $F_1,\ldots ,F_ k$ of $\mathcal F$. A tuple $(a_ i)$ is a relation of the $G_ i$ exactly when $\sum _ ia_ iS_ i\in \mathcal F$, that is, when $(a,b)$ is a relation of $(S_1,\ldots ,S_ p,F_1,\ldots ,F_ k)$ in $\mathcal S$ for some $b$. Hence the projections to the first $p$ coordinates of local generators of the latter relations generate the relations of the $G_ i$, and $\mathcal G$ is coherent. Now let $\mathcal F$ and $\mathcal G$ be coherent. Local lifts of generators of $\mathcal G$, together with local generators of $\mathcal F$, generate $\mathcal S$. Given sections $S_1,\ldots ,S_ p$ of $\mathcal S$, let $R_1,\ldots ,R_ l$ generate the relations of their images in $\mathcal G$. The combinations $H_ j=\sum _ iR_{ji}S_ i$ lie in $\mathcal F$; let $Q_1,\ldots ,Q_ k$ generate their relations. Every relation $(a_ i)$ of the $S_ i$ is first a relation of their images, so $a=\sum _ jc_ jR_ j$, and then $\sum _ jc_ jH_ j=\sum _ ia_ iS_ i=0$, so $c$ is a combination of $Q_1,\ldots ,Q_ k$. Hence the tuples $\sum _ jQ_{
u j}R_ j$, $1\leq 
u \leq k$, which are relations of the $S_ i$, generate all of them, and $\mathcal S$ is coherent. The remaining case of the exact sequence, with $\mathcal S$ and $\mathcal G$ coherent, is the kernel case. A finite direct sum is an extension $0	o \mathcal F	o \mathcal F\oplus \mathcal G	o \mathcal G	o 0$. Finally, if $\mathcal A$ is coherent, so is $\mathcal A^ r$, and the last assertion follows from the first sentence of the proof. $\square$ Theorem A.1.5 (Oka's coherence theorem) . The sheaf $\mathcal O_ M$ of holomorphic functions on a complex manifold $M$ is coherent. In particular, the kernel of the morphism $\mathcal O_ U^ q	o \mathcal O_ U^ p$ defined by a $p	imes q$ matrix of holomorphic functions on an open set $U\subset M$ is locally finitely generated. Proof. The sheaf $\mathcal O_ M$ is generated by the constant $1$, and the statement is local, so we must show that the relations of finitely many holomorphic functions $F_1,\ldots ,F_ q$ near a point of $\mathbb C^ n$, which we take to be the origin, are locally finitely generated. We argue by induction on $n$: we reduce to relations that are polynomials in one variable of bounded degree, and apply the induction hypothesis to their coefficients. For $n=0$ the assertion is finite-dimensional linear algebra. Let $n\geq 1$. If the germ of some $F_ j$ at $0$ is zero, then $F_ j$ vanishes on a connected neighborhood, and the relations of the $F_ i$ are those of the remaining functions, with an arbitrary $j$th coordinate; so we may assume that no germ $F_ j$ is zero (if all are zero, every tuple is a relation). Choose coordinates $(z',w)$ in which all $F_ j$ are distinguished in $w$. By the preparation theorem, on a small polydisc each $F_ j$ is a holomorphic unit $u_ j$ times a Weierstrass polynomial; since $(g_ j)$ is a relation of the $F_ j$ exactly when $(u_ jg_ j)$ is a relation of the Weierstrass polynomials, we may assume that each $F_ j$ is a Weierstrass polynomial in $w$ whose coefficients are holomorphic on a polydisc $\Delta '\subset \mathbb C^{n-1}$. Renumbering, let $F_ q$ have the maximal degree $\mu $. We claim that at every point $x=(x',w_0)$ of the polydisc, the stalk of relations is generated by relations whose coordinates are polynomials in $w$ of degree at most $\mu $ with coefficients holomorphic near $x'$. If $F_ q(x)
eq 0$, then for a relation $g=(g_1,\ldots ,g_ q)$ we have $g_ q=-\sum _{j<q}g_ jF_ j/F_ q$, so $g=\sum _{j<q}(g_ j/F_ q)(F_ qe_ j-F_ je_ q)$ is a combination of the elementary relations $F_ qe_ j-F_ je_ q$, which are polynomial of degree at most $\mu $. Suppose that $F_ q(x)=0$, and let $\mu '\geq 1$ be the order of the root $w_0$ of $F_ q(x',\cdot )$. By lemma A.1.3 , near $x$ the monic polynomial $F_ q$ is the product of a Weierstrass polynomial $P_ x$ of degree $\mu '$ in $w-w_0$ and a monic polynomial $Q_ x$ in $w$ of degree $\mu -\mu '$: \[  F_ q=P_ xQ_ x,\qquad Q_ x(x)
eq 0.  \] Let $g$ be a relation at $x$. Dividing each $g_ j$, $j<q$, by $P_ x$ (proposition A.1.1 ) and writing $P_ x=F_ qQ_ x^{-1}$, we obtain $g_ j=F_ qt_ j+r_ j$ with $\deg _ wr_ j<\mu '$. Subtracting $\sum _{j<q}t_ j(F_ qe_ j-F_ je_ q)$ from $g$, we obtain a relation whose first $q-1$ coordinates are $r_1,\ldots ,r_{q-1}$; we call its last coordinate $r_ q$. Then \[  P_ xQ_ xr_ q=-\sum _{j<q}F_ jr_ j.  \] The right-hand side is a polynomial in $w$; dividing it by $P_ x$ as a polynomial and comparing with the uniqueness of division at $x$, we find that $Q_ xr_ q$ is a polynomial of degree less than $\mu $. Each $Q_ xr_ j$, $j<q$, is also a polynomial of degree at most $(\mu -\mu ')+(\mu '-1)<\mu $. Thus $(Q_ xr_1,\ldots ,Q_ xr_ q)$ is a polynomial relation of degree less than $\mu $, and $(r_ j)$ is its product with the unit $Q_ x^{-1}$. This proves the claim. A tuple of polynomials $g_ j=\sum _{k=0}^{\mu }c_{jk}(z')w^ k$ is a relation exactly when the $2\mu +1$ coefficients of the polynomial $\sum _ jF_ jg_ j$ vanish. These coefficients are given by a holomorphic matrix acting on the coefficient vectors $(c_{jk})$, with entries formed from the coefficients of the $F_ j$. By the induction hypothesis and lemma A.1.4 , the kernel of this matrix is coherent, so it has finitely many generators on a smaller polydisc $\Delta '_1$, generating its stalk at every point of $\Delta '_1$. The corresponding polynomial tuples are relations of the $F_ j$, and they generate, over the rings of germs on the base, all polynomial relations of degree at most $\mu $ at every point over $\Delta '_1$. By the claim, they generate all relations at every point of the polydisc over $\Delta '_1$. This proves that $\mathcal O_ M$ is coherent. The last assertion follows from lemma A.1.4 , since the kernel of a morphism between the coherent sheaves $\mathcal O_ U^ q$ and $\mathcal O_ U^ p$ is coherent. $\square$ We now turn to the zero sets of holomorphic functions. An analytic subset of a complex manifold $M$ (definition 7.1.1 ) is a closed subset $A\subset M$ such that every point of $M$ has a neighborhood $U$ and finitely many holomorphic functions $g_1,\ldots ,g_ k$ on $U$ with $A\cap U=\{ g_1=\cdots =g_ k=0\} $. It is proper if $A
eq M$. Lemma A.1.6 . Let $A$ be a proper analytic subset of a connected complex manifold $M$. Then $A$ is nowhere dense in $M$. Moreover, if $U\subset M$ is a nonempty connected open set and $g_1,\ldots ,g_ k$ are holomorphic functions on $U$ with $A\cap U=\{ g_1=\cdots =g_ k=0\} $, then some $g_ i$ is not identically zero on $U$. In particular, every point of $A$ has a connected open neighborhood $U$ with a holomorphic function $g
ot\equiv 0$ on $U$ such that $A\cap U\subset \{ g=0\} $. Proof. The interior of $A$ is open, and we show that it is closed in $M$. Let $a\in M$ be a limit of interior points of $A$, and choose a connected coordinate neighborhood $U$ of $a$ and functions $g_1,\ldots ,g_ k$ with $A\cap U=\{ g_1=\cdots =g_ k=0\} $. Each $g_ i$ vanishes on a nonempty open subset of $U$, hence on $U$ by the identity theorem; so $U\subset A$, and $a$ is an interior point. Since $M$ is connected and $A
eq M$, the interior of $A$ is empty. In the second assertion, if all $g_ i$ vanished identically on $U$, the nonempty open set $U$ would lie in $A$, contradicting the first. For the third, take for $U$ a connected coordinate ball on which $A$ is the common zero set of finitely many holomorphic functions, and for $g$ one of them that is not identically zero, which exists by the second assertion. $\square$ We recall some algebraic terminology. The field of fractions $\operatorname {Frac}(R)$ of an integral domain $R$ consists of the formal quotients $b/c$ with $b,c\in R$ and $c
eq 0$, where $b/c=b'/c'$ if $bc'=b'c$, with the usual addition and multiplication; it contains $R$ through $b\mapsto b/1$. More generally, the total ring of fractions of a commutative ring $R$ is defined in the same way, with denominators restricted to the nonzerodivisors of $R$. An element of a commutative ring containing $R$ is integral over $R$ if it is a root of a monic polynomial with coefficients in $R$, and $R$ is integrally closed if every element of $\operatorname {Frac}(R)$ that is integral over $R$ belongs to $R$. Lemma A.1.7 . Let $A$ be a proper analytic subset of a connected complex manifold $M$. Every holomorphic function on $M\setminus A$ which is locally bounded near $A$ extends uniquely to a holomorphic function on $M$, and $M\setminus A$ is connected. Moreover, let $b,c\in \mathcal O_ n$ with $c
eq 0$, and suppose that representatives satisfy $|b|\leq C|c|$ on a neighborhood of $0$ for a constant $C$. Then $b\in c\, \mathcal O_ n$. In particular, the ring $\mathcal O_ n$ is integrally closed. Proof. Let $f$ be holomorphic on $M\setminus A$ and locally bounded near $A$. If $\dim M=0$, then $A=\varnothing $ and there is nothing to prove. Fix $a\in A$. By lemma A.1.6 there is a holomorphic function $g
ot\equiv 0$ on a connected neighborhood of $a$ vanishing on $A$; choose linear coordinates $(z',w)$ centered at $a$ in which $g$ is distinguished in $w$. By the Weierstrass preparation theorem and ( A.1 ), there is a polydisc $\Delta '	imes \Delta $ centered at $a$, with $\Delta =\{ |w|<r\} $, on which $g$ is a unit times a Weierstrass polynomial $W$ and $f$ is bounded off $A$, such that all roots of $W(z',\cdot )$, $z'\in \Delta '$, have modulus at most some $ho <r$. For fixed $z'\in \Delta '$, the function $f(z',\cdot )$ is holomorphic on $\Delta $ outside the finitely many points of $A$ in the fiber, which are roots of $W(z',\cdot )$, and it is bounded near them; by the removable singularity theorem in one variable it extends holomorphically to $\Delta $. For $ho <s<r$ the function \[  F(z',w)= rac1{2\pi \mathrm i}\int _{|\zeta |=s} rac{f(z',\zeta )}{\zeta -w}\, \mathrm d\zeta ,\qquad z'\in \Delta ',\  |w|<s,  \] is holomorphic, by differentiation under the integral sign, since $f$ is holomorphic near $\Delta '	imes \{ |\zeta |=s\} $, a set disjoint from $A$. By Cauchy's formula for the extended functions $f(z',\cdot )$, it agrees with $f$ outside $A$. Letting $s\uparrow r$, we obtain a holomorphic extension of $f$ to $\Delta '	imes \Delta $. Since $A$ is nowhere dense, two holomorphic extensions on overlapping open sets agree, being continuous functions that coincide on a dense subset; so the local extensions glue to a holomorphic function on $M$, and this extension is unique. If $M\setminus A$ were disconnected, the function equal to $0$ on one nonempty union of its connected components and to $1$ on the others would be bounded and holomorphic on $M\setminus A$. Its holomorphic extension is continuous and takes values in $\{ 0,1\} $ on the dense set $M\setminus A$, hence everywhere; since $M$ is connected, it is constant, a contradiction. Now let $b,c\in \mathcal O_ n$, $c
eq 0$, with $|b|\leq C|c|$ on a connected neighborhood $U$ of the origin on which both are defined. The set $\{ c=0\} $ is a proper analytic subset of $U$, and the holomorphic function $b/c$ on $U\setminus \{ c=0\} $ is bounded by $C$. By the first part it extends to a holomorphic function $h$ on $U$, and $ch=b$ on the dense set $U\setminus \{ c=0\} $, hence on $U$; so $b\in c\, \mathcal O_ n$. Finally, let $b/c\in \operatorname {Frac}(\mathcal O_ n)$, with $c
eq 0$, satisfy a monic equation $(b/c)^ m+a_1(b/c)^{m-1}+\cdots +a_ m=0$ with $a_ j\in \mathcal O_ n$. Multiplying by $c^ m$, we obtain the identity $b^ m+a_1b^{m-1}c+\cdots +a_ mc^ m=0$ between germs, which holds on a connected neighborhood of $0$ on which the $a_ j$ are bounded. At the points of this neighborhood where $c
eq 0$, the number $b/c$ is a root of a monic polynomial with bounded coefficients, so $|b/c|$ is bounded there by ( A.1 ); at the points where $c=0$ the identity gives $b^ m=0$. Hence $|b|\leq C|c|$ on this neighborhood for some constant $C$, and by what we have just proved, $b/c\in \mathcal O_ n$, which proves that $\mathcal O_ n$ is integrally closed. $\square$

title: Monic root bound
text: A.1 \begin{equation} \label{eq:monic-root-bound} t^ m+d_1t^{m-1}+\cdots +d_ m=0\quad \Longrightarrow \quad |t|\le 2\max _{1\leq j\leq m}|d_ j|^{1/j}. \end{equation}

title: Weierstrass division
text: Proposition A.1.1 (Weierstrass division) . Let $n\geq 1$ and $m\geq 0$, and let $P$ be a Weierstrass polynomial of degree $m$ in $w$. Then every germ $f\in \mathcal O_ n$ can be written uniquely as \[  f=Pq+R,\qquad q\in \mathcal O_ n,\quad R\in \mathcal O_{n-1}[w],\quad \deg _ w R<m.  \] Moreover, let $\Delta '\subset \mathbb C^{n-1}$ be a polydisc centered at $0$ and $\Delta =\{ |w|<r\} $ a disc such that the coefficients of $P$ are holomorphic near $\overline{\Delta '}$ and all roots of $P(z',\cdot )$, $z'\in \Delta '$, lie in $\{ |w|\leq \rho \} $ for some $\rho <r$; such polydiscs $\Delta '\times \Delta $ exist with arbitrarily small radii. Then every holomorphic function $f$ on $\Delta '\times \Delta $ can be written uniquely as $f=Pq+R$, where $q$ is holomorphic on $\Delta '\times \Delta $ and $R$ is a polynomial in $w$ of degree less than $m$ with holomorphic coefficients on $\Delta '$; for every $s\in (\rho ,r)$, $z'\in \Delta '$ and $|w|<s$, A.2 \begin{equation} \label{eq:weierstrass-division-integrals} \begin{aligned}  q(z',w)& =\frac1{2\pi \mathrm i}\int _{|\zeta |=s} \frac{f(z',\zeta )}{P(z',\zeta )(\zeta -w)}\, \mathrm d\zeta ,\\  R(z',w)& =\frac1{2\pi \mathrm i}\int _{|\zeta |=s} \frac{f(z',\zeta )}{P(z',\zeta )}\,  \frac{P(z',\zeta )-P(z',w)}{\zeta -w}\, \mathrm d\zeta . \end{aligned} \end{equation} Division is a bounded linear operation on bounded holomorphic functions on $\Delta '\times \Delta $: there is a constant $C$, independent of $f$, with \[  \sup _{\Delta '\times \Delta }|q|+\sup _{\Delta '\times \Delta }|R|\le C\sup _{\Delta '\times \Delta }|f|.  \] Proof. Polydiscs as in the statement exist with arbitrarily small radii, because the roots of $P(z',\cdot )$ tend to $0$ as $z'\to 0$, by ( A.1 ). Let $\Delta '\times \Delta $ be such a polydisc and $f$ a holomorphic function on it. For $\rho <s<r$ and $|w|<s$ define $q$ and $R$ by ( A.2 ). For fixed $z'$ and $w$, both integrands are holomorphic in $\zeta $ on the annulus $\{ \rho <|\zeta |<r\} $, except for the pole of the first one at $\zeta =w$; by Cauchy's theorem the integrals do not depend on $s$ as long as $|w|<s$, and the second one does not depend on $s\in (\rho ,r)$ at all. Hence $q$ and $R$ are defined on $\Delta '\times \Delta $, and they are holomorphic by differentiation under the integral sign. The difference quotient $(P(z',\zeta )-P(z',w))/(\zeta -w)$ is a polynomial in $w$ of degree $m-1$ whose coefficients are polynomials in $\zeta $ and in the $a_ j(z')$; hence $R$ is a polynomial in $w$ of degree less than $m$ with holomorphic coefficients on $\Delta '$. Adding the two integrals, we obtain $Pq+R=(2\pi \mathrm i)^{-1}\int _{|\zeta |=s}f(z',\zeta )(\zeta -w)^{-1}\, \mathrm d\zeta =f$ by Cauchy's formula. For the estimate, let $f$ be bounded, and fix $s_0=(\rho +r)/2$. For $|\zeta |\geq s_0$ we have $|P(z',\zeta )|=\prod _ l|\zeta -\lambda _ l(z')|\geq (s_0-\rho )^ m$, where $\lambda _ l(z')$ are the roots, and the coefficients of the difference quotient are bounded for $z'\in \Delta '$, $|\zeta |=s_0$ and $|w|<r$, since the $a_ j$ are bounded on $\Delta '$. The integral over $|\zeta |=s_0$ therefore gives $|R|\leq C_1\sup |f|$ on $\Delta '\times \Delta $. For $s_0\leq |w|<r$ we have $|q|=|f-R|/|P|\leq (1+C_1)(s_0-\rho )^{-m}\sup |f|$, and the maximum principle for the holomorphic functions $q(z',\cdot )$ on the discs $\{ |w|\leq s\} $, $s_0\leq s<r$, extends this bound to all of $\Delta '\times \Delta $. For uniqueness, suppose that $Pq+R=0$ on a polydisc as above, with $R$ a polynomial in $w$ of degree less than $m$. For each $z'$, the polynomial $R(z',\cdot )=-P(z',\cdot )q(z',\cdot )$ vanishes at the $m$ roots of $P(z',\cdot )$, counted with multiplicity, all of which lie in $\Delta $. Its degree is less than $m$, so $R(z',\cdot )=0$. Then $P(z',\cdot )q(z',\cdot )=0$, and since $P(z',\cdot )$ has only finitely many zeros, the continuous function $q(z',\cdot )$ vanishes on a dense set, hence everywhere. Finally, every germ is represented by a bounded holomorphic function on some polydisc as above, and an identity between germs holds on some such polydisc; so the assertions for germs follow. $\square$

title: Analytic noetherian
text: Proposition A.1.2 . Every ideal of $\mathcal O_ n$ is finitely generated, and every submodule of $\mathcal O_ n^ r$, $r\geq 1$, is finitely generated. Consequently, every increasing sequence of ideals of $\mathcal O_ n$, or of submodules of a finitely generated $\mathcal O_ n$-module, is eventually constant. Proof. We first recall three algebraic facts about a commutative ring $\Lambda $ all of whose ideals are finitely generated. Every submodule $N$ of $\Lambda ^ r$ is finitely generated, by induction on $r$: the projection of $N$ to the last coordinate is an ideal; choose elements of $N$ whose last coordinates generate it, and add generators of $N\cap (\Lambda ^{r-1}\times \{ 0\} )$, which exist by the induction hypothesis. A finitely generated module is a quotient of some $\Lambda ^ r$, and the inverse image of a submodule is a submodule of $\Lambda ^ r$; hence submodules of finitely generated modules are finitely generated. Finally, the union of an increasing sequence of submodules is a submodule; its finitely many generators already lie in one member of the sequence, which is therefore stationary from then on. It remains to prove that the ideals of $\mathcal O_ n$ are finitely generated, which we do by induction on $n$. The ring $\mathcal O_0=\mathbb C$ is a field. Let $n\geq 1$ and let $I\subset \mathcal O_ n$ be an ideal. If $I=0$ or $I$ contains a unit, it is generated by one element. Otherwise choose a nonzero germ in $I$, and coordinates in which it is distinguished in $w$. By the preparation theorem it is a unit times a Weierstrass polynomial $P$ of some degree $m\geq 1$, and $P\in I$. Divide every $f\in I$ by $P$ using proposition A.1.1 ; the remainder $R_ f=f-Pq$ again belongs to $I$. The remainders of degree less than $m$ that lie in $I$ form an $\mathcal O_{n-1}$-submodule of $\mathcal O_{n-1}[w]$, which we identify, through their coefficients, with a submodule of $\mathcal O_{n-1}^ m$. By the induction hypothesis and the first paragraph, it is generated by finitely many remainders $R_1,\ldots ,R_ k$. Then $P,R_1,\ldots ,R_ k$ generate $I$. $\square$

title: Monic weierstrass factor
text: Lemma A.1.3 . Let $n\geq 1$, let $P(z',w)=w^\mu +a_1(z')w^{\mu -1}+\cdots +a_\mu (z')$ be a monic polynomial in $w$ whose coefficients are holomorphic near a point $x'\in \mathbb C^{n-1}$, and let $w_0$ be a root of multiplicity $\mu '\geq 1$ of $P(x',\cdot )$. Then, near $x=(x',w_0)$, \[  P=P_ xQ_ x,  \] where $P_ x$ is a Weierstrass polynomial of degree $\mu '$ in $w-w_0$ with respect to the coordinates $(z'-x',w-w_0)$, and $Q_ x$ is a monic polynomial of degree $\mu -\mu '$ in $w$ with coefficients holomorphic near $x'$ and $Q_ x(x)\neq 0$. Proof. In the coordinates $(z'-x',w-w_0)$ centered at $x$, the function $w\mapsto P(x',w)$ has a zero of order $\mu '$ at $w_0$. By the Weierstrass preparation theorem (theorem 7.4.2 ), $P$ is, near $x$, a nowhere vanishing holomorphic function $U$ times a Weierstrass polynomial $P_ x$ of degree $\mu '$ in $w-w_0$. Since $P_ x$ is monic in $w$, Euclidean division of the polynomial $P$ by $P_ x$, with coefficients holomorphic near $x'$, gives $P=P_ xQ+R$, where $Q$ is a monic polynomial of degree $\mu -\mu '$ in $w$ and $R$ is a polynomial in $w$, equivalently in $w-w_0$, of degree less than $\mu '$. The identities $P=P_ xQ+R$ and $P=P_ xU+0$ are two divisions of the germ of $P$ at $x$ by $P_ x$; by the uniqueness in proposition A.1.1 , applied in the coordinates centered at $x$, we get $Q=U$ near $x$ and $R=0$. Hence $Q_ x=Q$ has the required properties, with $Q_ x(x)=U(x)\neq 0$. $\square$

title: Coherent sheaf algebra
text: Lemma A.1.4 . Let $\mathcal A$ be a sheaf of rings. Kernels, images and cokernels of morphisms between coherent $\mathcal A$-modules are coherent. If two of the three sheaves in an exact sequence $0\to \mathcal F\to \mathcal S\to \mathcal G\to 0$ of $\mathcal A$-modules are coherent, so is the third. Finite direct sums of coherent sheaves are coherent. If $\mathcal A$ is coherent as a module over itself, every locally finitely generated $\mathcal A$-submodule of $\mathcal A^ r$ is coherent. Proof. A locally finitely generated submodule of a coherent sheaf is coherent, because its sections have the same relations when they are regarded as sections of the larger sheaf. The image of a morphism from a coherent sheaf is locally generated by the images of local generators of the source, so the image of a morphism between coherent sheaves is coherent. For the kernel of a morphism $\phi \colon \mathcal F\to \mathcal G$ between coherent sheaves, choose local generators $F_1,\ldots ,F_ p$ of $\mathcal F$ and local generators $R_ j=(R_{j1},\ldots ,R_{jp})$ of the relations of $\phi (F_1),\ldots ,\phi (F_ p)$. If $\sum _ ia_ iF_ i$ lies in the kernel, then $(a_ i)$ is a relation of the $\phi (F_ i)$, hence a combination of the $R_ j$; so the sections $\sum _ iR_{ji}F_ i$ generate the kernel, which is therefore coherent. Let $\mathcal F\subset \mathcal S$ be coherent sheaves and consider $\mathcal G=\mathcal S/\mathcal F$; this covers cokernels, because images are coherent. Local generators of $\mathcal S$ map to local generators of $\mathcal G$. Given sections $G_1,\ldots ,G_ p$ of $\mathcal G$, lift them locally to sections $S_1,\ldots ,S_ p$ of $\mathcal S$, and choose local generators $F_1,\ldots ,F_ k$ of $\mathcal F$. A tuple $(a_ i)$ is a relation of the $G_ i$ exactly when $\sum _ ia_ iS_ i\in \mathcal F$, that is, when $(a,b)$ is a relation of $(S_1,\ldots ,S_ p,F_1,\ldots ,F_ k)$ in $\mathcal S$ for some $b$. Hence the projections to the first $p$ coordinates of local generators of the latter relations generate the relations of the $G_ i$, and $\mathcal G$ is coherent. Now let $\mathcal F$ and $\mathcal G$ be coherent. Local lifts of generators of $\mathcal G$, together with local generators of $\mathcal F$, generate $\mathcal S$. Given sections $S_1,\ldots ,S_ p$ of $\mathcal S$, let $R_1,\ldots ,R_ l$ generate the relations of their images in $\mathcal G$. The combinations $H_ j=\sum _ iR_{ji}S_ i$ lie in $\mathcal F$; let $Q_1,\ldots ,Q_ k$ generate their relations. Every relation $(a_ i)$ of the $S_ i$ is first a relation of their images, so $a=\sum _ jc_ jR_ j$, and then $\sum _ jc_ jH_ j=\sum _ ia_ iS_ i=0$, so $c$ is a combination of $Q_1,\ldots ,Q_ k$. Hence the tuples $\sum _ jQ_{\nu j}R_ j$, $1\leq \nu \leq k$, which are relations of the $S_ i$, generate all of them, and $\mathcal S$ is coherent. The remaining case of the exact sequence, with $\mathcal S$ and $\mathcal G$ coherent, is the kernel case. A finite direct sum is an extension $0\to \mathcal F\to \mathcal F\oplus \mathcal G\to \mathcal G\to 0$. Finally, if $\mathcal A$ is coherent, so is $\mathcal A^ r$, and the last assertion follows from the first sentence of the proof. $\square$

title: Oka's coherence theorem
text: Theorem A.1.5 (Oka's coherence theorem) . The sheaf $\mathcal O_ M$ of holomorphic functions on a complex manifold $M$ is coherent. In particular, the kernel of the morphism $\mathcal O_ U^ q\to \mathcal O_ U^ p$ defined by a $p\times q$ matrix of holomorphic functions on an open set $U\subset M$ is locally finitely generated. Proof. The sheaf $\mathcal O_ M$ is generated by the constant $1$, and the statement is local, so we must show that the relations of finitely many holomorphic functions $F_1,\ldots ,F_ q$ near a point of $\mathbb C^ n$, which we take to be the origin, are locally finitely generated. We argue by induction on $n$: we reduce to relations that are polynomials in one variable of bounded degree, and apply the induction hypothesis to their coefficients. For $n=0$ the assertion is finite-dimensional linear algebra. Let $n\geq 1$. If the germ of some $F_ j$ at $0$ is zero, then $F_ j$ vanishes on a connected neighborhood, and the relations of the $F_ i$ are those of the remaining functions, with an arbitrary $j$th coordinate; so we may assume that no germ $F_ j$ is zero (if all are zero, every tuple is a relation). Choose coordinates $(z',w)$ in which all $F_ j$ are distinguished in $w$. By the preparation theorem, on a small polydisc each $F_ j$ is a holomorphic unit $u_ j$ times a Weierstrass polynomial; since $(g_ j)$ is a relation of the $F_ j$ exactly when $(u_ jg_ j)$ is a relation of the Weierstrass polynomials, we may assume that each $F_ j$ is a Weierstrass polynomial in $w$ whose coefficients are holomorphic on a polydisc $\Delta '\subset \mathbb C^{n-1}$. Renumbering, let $F_ q$ have the maximal degree $\mu $. We claim that at every point $x=(x',w_0)$ of the polydisc, the stalk of relations is generated by relations whose coordinates are polynomials in $w$ of degree at most $\mu $ with coefficients holomorphic near $x'$. If $F_ q(x)\neq 0$, then for a relation $g=(g_1,\ldots ,g_ q)$ we have $g_ q=-\sum _{j<q}g_ jF_ j/F_ q$, so $g=\sum _{j<q}(g_ j/F_ q)(F_ qe_ j-F_ je_ q)$ is a combination of the elementary relations $F_ qe_ j-F_ je_ q$, which are polynomial of degree at most $\mu $. Suppose that $F_ q(x)=0$, and let $\mu '\geq 1$ be the order of the root $w_0$ of $F_ q(x',\cdot )$. By lemma A.1.3 , near $x$ the monic polynomial $F_ q$ is the product of a Weierstrass polynomial $P_ x$ of degree $\mu '$ in $w-w_0$ and a monic polynomial $Q_ x$ in $w$ of degree $\mu -\mu '$: \[  F_ q=P_ xQ_ x,\qquad Q_ x(x)\neq 0.  \] Let $g$ be a relation at $x$. Dividing each $g_ j$, $j<q$, by $P_ x$ (proposition A.1.1 ) and writing $P_ x=F_ qQ_ x^{-1}$, we obtain $g_ j=F_ qt_ j+r_ j$ with $\deg _ wr_ j<\mu '$. Subtracting $\sum _{j<q}t_ j(F_ qe_ j-F_ je_ q)$ from $g$, we obtain a relation whose first $q-1$ coordinates are $r_1,\ldots ,r_{q-1}$; we call its last coordinate $r_ q$. Then \[  P_ xQ_ xr_ q=-\sum _{j<q}F_ jr_ j.  \] The right-hand side is a polynomial in $w$; dividing it by $P_ x$ as a polynomial and comparing with the uniqueness of division at $x$, we find that $Q_ xr_ q$ is a polynomial of degree less than $\mu $. Each $Q_ xr_ j$, $j<q$, is also a polynomial of degree at most $(\mu -\mu ')+(\mu '-1)<\mu $. Thus $(Q_ xr_1,\ldots ,Q_ xr_ q)$ is a polynomial relation of degree less than $\mu $, and $(r_ j)$ is its product with the unit $Q_ x^{-1}$. This proves the claim. A tuple of polynomials $g_ j=\sum _{k=0}^{\mu }c_{jk}(z')w^ k$ is a relation exactly when the $2\mu +1$ coefficients of the polynomial $\sum _ jF_ jg_ j$ vanish. These coefficients are given by a holomorphic matrix acting on the coefficient vectors $(c_{jk})$, with entries formed from the coefficients of the $F_ j$. By the induction hypothesis and lemma A.1.4 , the kernel of this matrix is coherent, so it has finitely many generators on a smaller polydisc $\Delta '_1$, generating its stalk at every point of $\Delta '_1$. The corresponding polynomial tuples are relations of the $F_ j$, and they generate, over the rings of germs on the base, all polynomial relations of degree at most $\mu $ at every point over $\Delta '_1$. By the claim, they generate all relations at every point of the polydisc over $\Delta '_1$. This proves that $\mathcal O_ M$ is coherent. The last assertion follows from lemma A.1.4 , since the kernel of a morphism between the coherent sheaves $\mathcal O_ U^ q$ and $\mathcal O_ U^ p$ is coherent. $\square$

title: Proper analytic nowhere dense
text: Lemma A.1.6 . Let $A$ be a proper analytic subset of a connected complex manifold $M$. Then $A$ is nowhere dense in $M$. Moreover, if $U\subset M$ is a nonempty connected open set and $g_1,\ldots ,g_ k$ are holomorphic functions on $U$ with $A\cap U=\{ g_1=\cdots =g_ k=0\} $, then some $g_ i$ is not identically zero on $U$. In particular, every point of $A$ has a connected open neighborhood $U$ with a holomorphic function $g\not\equiv 0$ on $U$ such that $A\cap U\subset \{ g=0\} $. Proof. The interior of $A$ is open, and we show that it is closed in $M$. Let $a\in M$ be a limit of interior points of $A$, and choose a connected coordinate neighborhood $U$ of $a$ and functions $g_1,\ldots ,g_ k$ with $A\cap U=\{ g_1=\cdots =g_ k=0\} $. Each $g_ i$ vanishes on a nonempty open subset of $U$, hence on $U$ by the identity theorem; so $U\subset A$, and $a$ is an interior point. Since $M$ is connected and $A\neq M$, the interior of $A$ is empty. In the second assertion, if all $g_ i$ vanished identically on $U$, the nonempty open set $U$ would lie in $A$, contradicting the first. For the third, take for $U$ a connected coordinate ball on which $A$ is the common zero set of finitely many holomorphic functions, and for $g$ one of them that is not identically zero, which exists by the second assertion. $\square$

title: Bounded holomorphic removal
text:
Lemma A.1.7 . Let $A$ be a proper analytic subset of a connected complex manifold $M$. Every holomorphic function on $M\setminus A$ which is locally bounded near $A$ extends uniquely to a holomorphic function on $M$, and $M\setminus A$ is connected. Moreover, let $b,c\in \mathcal O_ n$ with $c
eq 0$, and suppose that representatives satisfy $|b|\leq C|c|$ on a neighborhood of $0$ for a constant $C$. Then $b\in c\, \mathcal O_ n$. In particular, the ring $\mathcal O_ n$ is integrally closed. Proof. Let $f$ be holomorphic on $M\setminus A$ and locally bounded near $A$. If $\dim M=0$, then $A=\varnothing $ and there is nothing to prove. Fix $a\in A$. By lemma A.1.6 there is a holomorphic function $g
ot\equiv 0$ on a connected neighborhood of $a$ vanishing on $A$; choose linear coordinates $(z',w)$ centered at $a$ in which $g$ is distinguished in $w$. By the Weierstrass preparation theorem and ( A.1 ), there is a polydisc $\Delta '	imes \Delta $ centered at $a$, with $\Delta =\{ |w|<r\} $, on which $g$ is a unit times a Weierstrass polynomial $W$ and $f$ is bounded off $A$, such that all roots of $W(z',\cdot )$, $z'\in \Delta '$, have modulus at most some $ho <r$. For fixed $z'\in \Delta '$, the function $f(z',\cdot )$ is holomorphic on $\Delta $ outside the finitely many points of $A$ in the fiber, which are roots of $W(z',\cdot )$, and it is bounded near them; by the removable singularity theorem in one variable it extends holomorphically to $\Delta $. For $ho <s<r$ the function \[  F(z',w)= rac1{2\pi \mathrm i}\int _{|\zeta |=s} rac{f(z',\zeta )}{\zeta -w}\, \mathrm d\zeta ,\qquad z'\in \Delta ',\  |w|<s,  \] is holomorphic, by differentiation under the integral sign, since $f$ is holomorphic near $\Delta '	imes \{ |\zeta |=s\} $, a set disjoint from $A$. By Cauchy's formula for the extended functions $f(z',\cdot )$, it agrees with $f$ outside $A$. Letting $s\uparrow r$, we obtain a holomorphic extension of $f$ to $\Delta '	imes \Delta $. Since $A$ is nowhere dense, two holomorphic extensions on overlapping open sets agree, being continuous functions that coincide on a dense subset; so the local extensions glue to a holomorphic function on $M$, and this extension is unique. If $M\setminus A$ were disconnected, the function equal to $0$ on one nonempty union of its connected components and to $1$ on the others would be bounded and holomorphic on $M\setminus A$. Its holomorphic extension is continuous and takes values in $\{ 0,1\} $ on the dense set $M\setminus A$, hence everywhere; since $M$ is connected, it is constant, a contradiction. Now let $b,c\in \mathcal O_ n$, $c
eq 0$, with $|b|\leq C|c|$ on a connected neighborhood $U$ of the origin on which both are defined. The set $\{ c=0\} $ is a proper analytic subset of $U$, and the holomorphic function $b/c$ on $U\setminus \{ c=0\} $ is bounded by $C$. By the first part it extends to a holomorphic function $h$ on $U$, and $ch=b$ on the dense set $U\setminus \{ c=0\} $, hence on $U$; so $b\in c\, \mathcal O_ n$. Finally, let $b/c\in \operatorname {Frac}(\mathcal O_ n)$, with $c
eq 0$, satisfy a monic equation $(b/c)^ m+a_1(b/c)^{m-1}+\cdots +a_ m=0$ with $a_ j\in \mathcal O_ n$. Multiplying by $c^ m$, we obtain the identity $b^ m+a_1b^{m-1}c+\cdots +a_ mc^ m=0$ between germs, which holds on a connected neighborhood of $0$ on which the $a_ j$ are bounded. At the points of this neighborhood where $c
eq 0$, the number $b/c$ is a root of a monic polynomial with bounded coefficients, so $|b/c|$ is bounded there by ( A.1 ); at the points where $c=0$ the identity gives $b^ m=0$. Hence $|b|\leq C|c|$ on this neighborhood for some constant $C$, and by what we have just proved, $b/c\in \mathcal O_ n$, which proves that $\mathcal O_ n$ is integrally closed. $\square$

title: Analytic sets and their local branches
text:
A.2 Analytic sets and their local branches The local study of an analytic set rests on the parametrization of an irreducible germ as a branched covering of a polydisc (theorem A.2.3 ). From it we derive the Nullstellensatz, the dimension theory, Cartan's coherence theorem, the structure of the singular locus and the irreducible components. The section ends with hypersurfaces and the currents supported on analytic sets. Let $M$ be a complex manifold and $x\in M$. Two subsets of $M$ define the same germ at $x$ if they agree on a neighborhood of $x$; an analytic germ at $x$ is the germ $(A,x)$ of an analytic subset $A$ of a neighborhood of $x$. Holomorphic coordinates identify the ring $\mathcal O_{M,x}$ of germs of holomorphic functions at $x$ with $\mathcal O_ n$. For an analytic germ $(A,x)$ let $I_{A,x}\subset \mathcal O_{M,x}$ be the ideal of germs vanishing on $(A,x)$. Conversely, for an ideal $I\subset \mathcal O_{M,x}$ let $V(I)$ be the germ at $x$ of the common zero set of finitely many generators of $I$, which exist by proposition A.1.2 ; it does not depend on the choice of generators. Both operations reverse inclusions, and $V(I_{A,x})=(A,x)$, because local defining functions of $A$ belong to $I_{A,x}$. Finite unions and finite intersections of analytic subsets are analytic: they are defined locally by the products of the defining functions and by the union of the families of defining functions, respectively. A nonempty analytic germ is irreducible if it is not the union of two analytic subgerms different from it. A point $a$ of an analytic subset $A\subset M$ is regular if $A$ is a complex submanifold of $M$ near $a$; the dimension of this submanifold is the dimension of $A$ at the regular point $a$. The regular points form an open subset $A_{\mathrm{reg}}$ of $A$, the regular locus , and $A_{\mathrm{sing}}=A\setminus A_{\mathrm{reg}}$ is the singular locus . Proposition A.2.1 . Every analytic germ is the union of finitely many irreducible analytic germs, and this decomposition is unique up to order if none of its members is contained in another. A nonempty analytic germ is irreducible if and only if its ideal is prime. The members of the decomposition are called the irreducible branches , or local branches , of the germ. Proof. A decreasing sequence of analytic germs is eventually constant, because the corresponding ideals increase and are eventually constant by proposition A.1.2 , and $V(I_{A,x})=(A,x)$. Split a reducible germ into two analytic subgerms different from it, split each reducible piece again, and so on. If this process did not terminate, the resulting tree, in which every vertex has at most two children, would be infinite, and choosing at each level a child with infinitely many descendants would produce a strictly decreasing infinite sequence of analytic germs, which is impossible. Hence a finite decomposition into irreducible germs exists; removing members contained in others, we may assume that no member is contained in another. An irreducible germ contained in a finite union of analytic germs is contained in one of them, since it is the union of its intersections with them. Now let $ igcup _ iA_ i= igcup _ jB_ j$ be two such decompositions. Each $A_ i$ is contained in some $B_ j$, which in turn is contained in some $A_ k$; then $A_ i\subset A_ k$ forces $k=i$ and $A_ i=B_ j$. By symmetry the two decompositions agree. Let $(A,x)$ be irreducible. Its ideal is proper, since $x\in A$. If $fg$ vanishes on $(A,x)$, then $(A,x)$ is the union of its intersections with $\{ f=0\} $ and $\{ g=0\} $, so one of them is all of $(A,x)$, and $f$ or $g$ belongs to $I_{A,x}$; thus $I_{A,x}$ is prime. Conversely, suppose that $(A,x)$ is the union of two analytic subgerms $(B,x)$ and $(C,x)$ different from it. Since $V(I_{B,x})=(B,x)
eq (A,x)$, there is a germ $f\in I_{B,x}\setminus I_{A,x}$, and similarly $g\in I_{C,x}\setminus I_{A,x}$. Then $fg$ vanishes on $(A,x)$ while neither factor does, so $I_{A,x}$ is not prime. $\square$ Multiple roots of polynomials are detected by the discriminant, which we define by a polynomial formula in the coefficients. For a monic polynomial $P(T)=T^ q+a_1T^{q-1}+\cdots +a_ q$, $q\geq 1$, with coefficients in a commutative ring, let $C_ P$ be its companion matrix , the $q	imes q$ matrix with entries $1$ just below the diagonal, last column $(-a_ q,\ldots ,-a_1)^{\mathsf T}$ and zeros elsewhere. Put $S_ k=\operatorname {tr}(C_ P^ k)$ for $k\geq 0$, and define the discriminant $\operatorname {Disc}(P)=\det (S_{j+l})_{0\leq j,l\leq q-1}$, a polynomial with integer coefficients in $a_1,\ldots ,a_ q$. If the $a_ j$ are complex numbers and $	au _1,\ldots ,	au _ q$ are the roots of $P$, counted with multiplicity, then A.5  egin{equation} \label{eq:discriminant-roots} \operatorname {Disc}(P)=\prod _{i<k}(	au _ i-	au _ k)^2; \end{equation} in particular $\operatorname {Disc}(P)
eq 0$ if and only if the roots of $P$ are distinct.
