text: A.13 \[\begin{aligned}\begin{align}  (\mathfrak a\mathcal O_ W)\mathcal O_{W'} & =\mathcal O_{W'}(-H|_{W'}). \label{eq:relative-restricted-ideal} \end{align}\end{aligned}\]

title: Connected fibers and resolution models
text:
A.7 Connected fibers and resolution models A proper bimeromorphic map can contract analytic sets, so its fibers may have positive dimension. Over a unibranch space they are nevertheless connected (theorem A.7.1 ). Consequently a finite bimeromorphic map onto a normal space is an isomorphism, and a proper bimeromorphic map between manifolds is an isomorphism outside a set of codimension at least two. We then introduce smooth models and prime divisors over a complex space, and show that every prime divisor over a compact space is realized after finitely many blowups with smooth centers. Theorem A.7.1 . Let $f\colon Y	o X$ be a proper bimeromorphic holomorphic map between complex spaces, and let $x\in X$ be a point at which the germ $(X,x)$ is irreducible. Then the fiber $f^{-1}(x)$ is connected. In particular, if $X$ is unibranch, every fiber of $f$ is connected. Proof. Choose a nowhere dense analytic subset $A\subset X$ such that $f^{-1}(A)$ is nowhere dense and $f$ is an isomorphism over $X\setminus A$. Suppose that the compact fiber over $x$ is disconnected, and write it as the union of two disjoint nonempty compact sets. Since $Y$ is Hausdorff, they have disjoint open neighborhoods $V_1$ and $V_2$. Since $f$ is proper, hence closed, $U=X\setminus f(Y\setminus (V_1\cup V_2))$ is an open neighborhood of $x$ with $f^{-1}(U)\subset V_1\cup V_2$. As $(X,x)$ is irreducible, corollary A.3.9 allows us to shrink $U$ so that $U\setminus A$ is connected. Each set $V_ i\cap f^{-1}(U)$ is open and nonempty, so it meets the dense set $Y\setminus f^{-1}(A)$. Therefore $V_1$ and $V_2$ split $f^{-1}(U\setminus A)$ into two disjoint nonempty open sets. This contradicts the connectedness of $U\setminus A$, which is isomorphic to $f^{-1}(U\setminus A)$. $\square$ Corollary A.7.2 . A finite bimeromorphic holomorphic map to a normal complex space is an isomorphism. Let $\phi \colon S	o X$ be a holomorphic map from a normal complex space to a complex space such that $\phi ^{-1}(X_{\mathrm{sing}})$ is nowhere dense in $S$. Then $\phi $ factors uniquely through the normalization $
u \colon \widetilde X	o X$: there is a unique holomorphic map $\psi \colon S	o \widetilde X$ with $
u \circ \psi =\phi $. Proof. Let $f\colon Y	o X$ be finite and bimeromorphic, with $X$ normal, and let $A\subset X$ be a nowhere dense analytic subset such that $f$ is an isomorphism over $X\setminus A$ and $f^{-1}(A)$ is nowhere dense. Normal spaces are unibranch, so the finite fibers of $f$ are connected by theorem A.7.1 , hence consist of at most one point. The image of $f$ is closed, because $f$ is proper, and contains the dense set $X\setminus A$; so $f$ is a continuous closed bijection, that is, a homeomorphism. Let $x\in X$ and $y=f^{-1}(x)$. Choose a neighborhood $V$ of $y$, relatively compact in the domain of a local model of $Y$, so that the coordinate functions of the model are bounded on $V$. Composed with $f^{-1}$, they are bounded holomorphic functions on $f(V)\setminus A$, where $f^{-1}$ is holomorphic, and $f(V)$ is an open neighborhood of $x$. By lemma A.3.4 they extend holomorphically to $f(V)$, and the extensions are the continuous functions $(	ext{coordinates})\circ f^{-1}$. Hence $f^{-1}$ is holomorphic. For the second assertion, over the dense open set $S\setminus \phi ^{-1}(X_{\mathrm{sing}})$ there is a unique lift $\psi _0=
u ^{-1}\circ \phi $, because $
u $ is an isomorphism over $X_{\mathrm{reg}}$. We extend it by the argument used for the uniqueness in the proof of theorem A.3.6 . Let $s\in S$ and $x=\phi (s)$, choose disjoint neighborhoods $W_ l$ of the finitely many points of $
u ^{-1}(x)$, relatively compact in domains $W'_ l$ of local models of $\widetilde X$, and a neighborhood $U$ of $x$ with $
u ^{-1}(U)\subset  igcup _ lW_ l$, which exists by properness. Since $S$ is normal, hence unibranch, corollary A.3.9 gives a neighborhood $V$ of $s$ with $\phi (V)\subset U$ such that $V\setminus \phi ^{-1}(X_{\mathrm{sing}})$ is connected. Then $\psi _0$ maps this set into a single $W_ l$. The coordinate functions of $W'_ l$ composed with $\psi _0$ are bounded and extend holomorphically to $V$, by lemma A.3.4 ; the extended map takes values in $\overline{W_ l}\subset W'_ l$, and it satisfies the equations of the local model, which hold on a dense subset of $V$. This gives a holomorphic lift on $V$, with $
u \circ \psi =\phi $ by density. Lifts agree on the dense set where $\psi _0$ is defined, so these local lifts glue, and the lift is unique. $\square$ Proposition A.7.3 . A proper bimeromorphic holomorphic map $f\colon M'	o M$ between complex manifolds is an isomorphism outside an analytic subset $S$ of $M$ of codimension at least two. In particular, every irreducible hypersurface $D$ in $M$ has a well-defined strict transform in $M'$, namely the closure $D'$ of $f^{-1}(D\setminus S)$, which does not depend on the choice of $S$; it is an irreducible hypersurface, $f(D')=D$, and $f$ maps $D'$ isomorphically onto $D$ over the dense open subset $D\setminus S$ of $D$. Proof. We take for $S$ the image of the critical set of $f$; the main point is that a component of $S$ of codimension one would contain a point over which $f$ is finite, hence an isomorphism by corollary A.7.2 . Step 1: the set $S$. We may work over each connected component of $M$, of dimension $n$ say; every connected component of its inverse image has dimension $n$ as well, because it contains a nonempty open set mapped isomorphically onto an open subset of $M$, by lemma A.3.1 . The map $f$ is surjective, since its image is closed and dense. The critical set of $f$, where the Jacobian determinant vanishes in local coordinates, is analytic, and its image $S$ is analytic by theorem A.6.2 . Over $M\setminus S$ the map $f$ is proper and, by proposition 7.1.2 (1), a local biholomorphism, so its fibers are discrete and finite. They are connected by theorem A.7.1 , and nonempty; so they are single points, and $f$ is a bijective local biholomorphism, hence an isomorphism, over $M\setminus S$. Since $f$ is an isomorphism over a dense open subset of $M$, it has no critical points over this set, so $S$ does not meet it and is nowhere dense. Step 2: $S$ has codimension at least two. Suppose that $S$ has an irreducible component $D_0$ of codimension one. Choose a point of $(D_0)_{\mathrm{reg}}$ outside the other components of $S$, and a coordinate polydisc $U$ centered at it in which $D_0\cap U=S\cap U=\{ h=0\} $ for one of the coordinate functions $h$; then $D_0\cap U$ is a connected manifold. Let $A\subset M$ be a nowhere dense analytic subset such that $f^{-1}(A)$ is nowhere dense and $f$ is an isomorphism over $M\setminus A$. The function $h\circ f$ does not vanish identically on any connected component $V$ of $f^{-1}(U)$: otherwise $f$ would map the nonempty open set $V\setminus f^{-1}(A)$ isomorphically onto an open subset of $M$ contained in the hypersurface $D_0$, which is impossible. By proposition A.4.6 , $E=f^{-1}(D_0\cap U)$ is pure of dimension $n-1$. Let $K\subset D_0\cap U$ be a compact neighborhood of the chosen point in $D_0$. Only finitely many irreducible components $E_1,\ldots ,E_ k$ of $E$ meet the compact set $f^{-1}(K)$, and by theorem A.6.2 each image $f(E_ j)$ is an analytic subset of $D_0\cap U$. If its dimension is $n-1$, then $f(E_ j)$ contains an open subset of the connected manifold $D_0\cap U$ and therefore equals it, since proper analytic subsets of connected manifolds are nowhere dense (lemma A.1.6 ); we then call $E_ j$ dominating. Otherwise $f(E_ j)$ has dimension at most $n-2$. For a dominating $E_ j$, the maximal rank of $f$ restricted to the connected manifold $(E_ j)_{\mathrm{reg}}$, as a map into the coordinate hyperplane $D_0\cap U$, is $n-1$. Otherwise $f((E_ j)_{\mathrm{reg}})$ would be $\mathcal H^{2n-2}$-null by lemma A.2.12 (1); so would $f((E_ j)_{\mathrm{sing}})$, by the same lemma, since $(E_ j)_{\mathrm{sing}}$ has dimension at most $n-2$ by corollary A.2.10 (1) and is therefore, by (2) of the same corollary, a finite union of complex submanifolds of dimension at most $n-2$; and $f(E_ j)$ would have dimension at most $n-2$ by lemma A.2.12 (2). Let $R_ j$ be the union of $(E_ j)_{\mathrm{sing}}$ and of the regular points where this rank is less than $n-1$. It is analytic. Indeed, near a point of $E_ j$, let $e$ be a local equation of the irreducible hypersurface $E_ j$ as in lemma A.2.16 , and let $f'$ be the map formed by the $n-1$ coordinates of $f$ in the coordinate hyperplane $D_0\cap U$. At a regular point $p$ of $E_ j$ we have $\mathrm de(p)
eq 0$ and $T_ pE_ j=\ker \mathrm de(p)$, so the rank of $f'|_{E_ j}$ at $p$ is $n-1$ exactly when the Jacobian determinant of $(e,f')$ does not vanish at $p$. Hence $R_ j$ is, near this point, the union of the analytic set $(E_ j)_{\mathrm{sing}}$ and of the zero set in $E_ j$ of this Jacobian determinant. It is different from $E_ j$, because the rank $n-1$ is attained on $(E_ j)_{\mathrm{reg}}$; so it is nowhere dense in the irreducible set $E_ j$ and has dimension at most $n-2$, by corollary A.2.14 (2), and $f(R_ j)$ is analytic of dimension at most $n-2$, by theorem A.6.2 and lemma A.2.12 (3). Choose a point $a$ in the interior of $K$ outside the finitely many sets $f(E_ j)$, $E_ j$ not dominating, and $f(R_ j)$, $E_ j$ dominating. Let $p\in f^{-1}(a)$. Since $f^{-1}(a)\subset E\cap f^{-1}(K)$, the point $p$ lies on some of the components $E_1,\ldots ,E_ k$. Each of them that contains $p$ is dominating, and $p
otin R_ j$, so $f|_{E_ j}$ is a local biholomorphism at $p$ onto an open subset of $D_0$, by proposition 7.1.2 (1) in charts, and $p$ is isolated in $f^{-1}(a)\cap E_ j$. The components of $E$ not containing $p$ form a locally finite family of closed sets, so near $p$ the set $f^{-1}(a)$ lies in the union of the components containing $p$, and $p$ is isolated in $f^{-1}(a)$. Thus $f^{-1}(a)$ is discrete, and being compact, it is finite. Let $p_1,\ldots ,p_ l$ be the points of $f^{-1}(a)$, and choose disjoint coordinate balls $B_1,\ldots ,B_ l$ around them. By properness there is a neighborhood $U_0$ of $a$ with $f^{-1}(U_0)\subset  igcup _ iB_ i$. The fibers of $f$ over $U_0$ are compact analytic subsets of these balls, hence finite by corollary A.4.3 . Thus $f$ is finite and bimeromorphic over the manifold $U_0$, which is normal, and it is an isomorphism over $U_0$ by corollary A.7.2 . In particular $f$ has no critical points over $U_0$, which contradicts $a\in S$. Therefore $S$ has codimension at least two. Step 3: strict transforms. Let $D$ be an irreducible hypersurface. Then $S\cap D$ has dimension at most $n-2$, so $D\setminus S$ is dense in $D$ by corollary A.2.14 (2). The closure $D'$ of $f^{-1}(D\setminus S)=f^{-1}(D)\setminus f^{-1}(S)$ is analytic by lemma A.2.5 , and $f$ is an isomorphism from $D'\setminus f^{-1}(S)=f^{-1}(D\setminus S)$ onto $D\setminus S$. The set $f(D')$ is closed, because $f$ is proper, it contains the dense subset $D\setminus S$ of $D$, and it is contained in the closed set $D$; so $f(D')=D$. The set $Q=f^{-1}(D_{\mathrm{reg}}\setminus S)$ is a connected manifold of dimension $n-1$, because $D_{\mathrm{reg}}\setminus S$ is connected by lemma A.1.7 ; it is open in $D'$ and dense in $D'$, since $D_{\mathrm{reg}}\setminus S$ is open and dense in $D\setminus S$. Hence $Q$ consists of regular points of $D'$ and lies in a single connected component of $(D')_{\mathrm{reg}}$, whose closure, an irreducible component of $D'$ by corollary A.2.13 , contains $\overline Q=D'$; so $D'$ is irreducible, of dimension $n-1$. Finally, if $S_1$ is another analytic subset of codimension at least two off which $f$ is an isomorphism, then $D\setminus (S\cup S_1)$ is dense in $D\setminus S$ and in $D\setminus S_1$, by corollary A.2.14 (2), so $f^{-1}(D\setminus (S\cup S_1))$ is dense in both $f^{-1}(D\setminus S)$ and $f^{-1}(D\setminus S_1)$, and the two closures agree. $\square$ A smooth model of a complex space $X$ is a proper bimeromorphic holomorphic map $M	o X$ with $M$ a complex manifold; resolutions (theorem A.5.4 ) are smooth models. Two smooth models $f_1\colon M_1	o X$ and $f_2\colon M_2	o X$ have a common smooth model, that is, a smooth model $M_3$ with proper bimeromorphic maps $M_3	o M_1$ and $M_3	o M_2$ commuting with the maps to $X$. To construct it, let $E_1,E_2\subset X$ be nowhere dense analytic subsets as in the definition of bimeromorphic maps for $f_1$ and $f_2$, and put $U=X\setminus (E_1\cup E_2)$. Both $f_ i$ are isomorphisms over $U$, and $f_ i^{-1}(U)$ is dense in $M_ i$ by lemma A.3.1 . Let $\Gamma \subset M_1	imes _ XM_2=\{ (p_1,p_2):f_1(p_1)=f_2(p_2)\} $ be the closure of the graph of $f_2^{-1}\circ f_1$ over $U$. The fiber product is analytic in $M_1	imes M_2$, since the equality of the two images is expressed by coordinate equations in local embeddings of $X$. Over $U$ the fiber product is the graph, so $\Gamma $ is the closure of the complement in the fiber product of the analytic set of points lying over $E_1\cup E_2$, and it is analytic by lemma A.2.5 . The projections of $\Gamma $ are proper: over a compact subset of $M_1$, the second coordinates lie in the compact inverse image under $f_2$ of its image in $X$, and $\Gamma $ is closed. Their images are closed and contain the dense sets $f_ i^{-1}(U)$, so they are surjective; they are isomorphisms over $f_ i^{-1}(U)$, and the inverse images of the complements $f_ i^{-1}(E_1\cup E_2)$ are nowhere dense in $\Gamma $, because the graph over $U$ is dense in $\Gamma $; hence they are bimeromorphic. Resolving $\Gamma $ by theorem A.5.4 and composing with the projections, we obtain the common smooth model; the composites are proper and bimeromorphic by corollary A.6.3 . When $X$ is compact and the two smooth models are themselves obtained from $X$ by finite sequences of blowups with smooth centers, there is also a common refinement of the same kind. Let $X=X_0\leftarrow X_1\leftarrow \cdots \leftarrow X_ k=M_1$ be the first sequence, where $X_ j$ is the blowup of $X_{j-1}$ along the ideal of a smooth center $C_ j\subset X_{j-1}$. We start from a resolution of $X$, which is such a sequence because $X$ is compact, and lift it through the first sequence one center at a time. Suppose that the current smooth model $N$, obtained from $X$ by a finite sequence of blowups with smooth centers, has been constructed with a map to $X_{j-1}$ over $X$. The maps $N	o X$ and $X_{j-1}	o X$ are proper and bimeromorphic by corollary A.6.3 ; let $U\subset X$ be the complement of a nowhere dense analytic subset over which both are isomorphisms. The pullback of the ideal of $C_ j$ to $N$ is not identically zero on any component of $N$. Indeed, its zero set is the inverse image of $C_ j$, which is nowhere dense in $X_{j-1}$ because the ideal of $C_ j$ is not identically zero on any branch of $X_{j-1}$ (definition A.5.1 ). Over $U$ the map $N	o X_{j-1}$ is an isomorphism, so this inverse image meets the dense open part of $N$ over $U$ in a nowhere dense set, and its part over $X\setminus U$ is nowhere dense by lemma A.3.1 . Principalizing it by theorem A.5.5 , we obtain a sequence of blowups $N'	o N$ with smooth centers, finite because $N$ is compact, on which the pulled-back ideal is invertible, and proposition A.5.2 lifts $N'	o X_{j-1}$ to a map $N'	o X_ j$. Repeating this for the finitely many centers of the first sequence and then of the second, we obtain a finite sequence of blowups with smooth centers over $X$ that dominates both models. All three models are proper and bimeromorphic over $X$, by proposition A.5.2 , corollary A.6.3 ; by lemma A.3.1 there is a complement $U\subset X$ of a nowhere dense analytic subset over which all three are isomorphisms. The maps from the new model to the two given ones commute with the maps to $X$, so they are isomorphisms over the parts lying over $U$. The complements of these parts are nowhere dense analytic subsets of the three models, again by lemma A.3.1 ; so the two maps are bimeromorphic, and they are proper because the source is compact. (For general proper bimeromorphic models we only have the common smooth model constructed above.) Definition A.7.4 . Let $X$ be a complex space. A prime divisor over $X$ is represented by a pair consisting of a smooth model $M	o X$ and an irreducible hypersurface $F\subset M$; two pairs are identified if the strict transforms of their hypersurfaces, in the sense of proposition A.7.3 , agree on a common smooth model. The prime divisor is exceptional if the image of $F$ in $X$ has codimension at least two. Lemma A.7.5 . Let $X$ be a complex space. The identification of pairs in definition A.7.4 is an equivalence relation, and the image in $X$ of the hypersurface $F$ of a representative $(M,F)$ depends only on the prime divisor. Let $(M,F)$ represent a prime divisor over $X$, and let $g\colon M'	o M$ be the composite of the principalization of $\mathcal I_ F$ given by theorem A.5.5 with the empty divisor. Then $g$ is proper and bimeromorphic, the strict transform $F'$ of $F$ is a smooth irreducible hypersurface of $M'$, and $(M',F')$ represents the same prime divisor. In particular, every prime divisor over $X$ has a representative $(M,F)$ with $F$ smooth. Proof. We begin with two remarks used in the proof of (1). First, two maps from a smooth model $M_3$ to a smooth model $M_1$ that commute with the maps to $X$ agree. Indeed, let $U\subset X$ be the complement of a nowhere dense analytic subset over which both models are isomorphisms; the two maps agree over $U$, and the part of $M_3$ over $U$ is dense, by lemma A.3.1 . Second, strict transforms are compatible with composition. Let $g\colon P	o N$ and $h\colon N	o M$ be proper bimeromorphic maps between complex manifolds, so that $h\circ g$ is proper and bimeromorphic by corollary A.6.3 , and let $D\subset M$ be an irreducible hypersurface, with strict transform $D^ N$ in $N$. We claim that the strict transform of $D^ N$ under $g$ is the strict transform $D^ P$ of $D$ under $h\circ g$. Let $S_ h,S_{hg}\subset M$ and $S_ g\subset N$ be analytic subsets of codimension at least two as in proposition A.7.3 for $h$, $h\circ g$ and $g$, and let $T=S_ h\cup S_{hg}\cup h(S_ g)$, which is analytic of codimension at least two by theorem A.6.2 and lemma A.2.12 (3). The set $O=D^ N\cap h^{-1}(M\setminus T)=h^{-1}(D\setminus T)$ is open in $D^ N$, nonempty, and does not meet $S_ g$; its complement $D^ N\cap h^{-1}(T)$ is an analytic subset of the irreducible set $D^ N$ different from $D^ N$, hence nowhere dense by corollary A.2.14 (2). So $O$ is dense in $D^ N\setminus S_ g$, and since $g$ is an isomorphism over $N\setminus S_ g$, the strict transform of $D^ N$ under $g$ is the closure of $g^{-1}(O)=(h\circ g)^{-1}(D\setminus T)$. By the independence of the choice of $S_{hg}$ in proposition A.7.3 , applied with $T$, this closure is also $D^ P$. Now let $(M_ i,F_ i)$, $i=1,2,3$, be pairs such that $(M_1,F_1)$ and $(M_2,F_2)$ are identified on a common smooth model $N_{12}$, and $(M_2,F_2)$ and $(M_3,F_3)$ on $N_{23}$. Let $P$ be a common smooth model of $N_{12}$ and $N_{23}$, and let $p_ i\colon P	o M_ i$ be the composite maps; by the first remark, the two composite maps $P	o M_2$, through $N_{12}$ and through $N_{23}$, coincide. By the second remark, the strict transforms of $F_1$ and $F_2$ under $p_1$ and $p_2$ are the strict transforms in $P$ of their strict transforms in $N_{12}$, which agree; similarly for $F_2$ and $F_3$. Hence $F_1$ and $F_3$ have the same strict transform in $P$, and the identification is transitive; it is reflexive, with $M_1$ itself as common smooth model, and symmetric by definition. Since $p_ i$ maps the strict transform of $F_ i$ onto $F_ i$ (proposition A.7.3 ), the images of $F_1$ and $F_3$ in $X$ both equal the image of their common strict transform in $P$; so the image of $F$ in $X$ depends only on the prime divisor. We now prove (2). Let $(M,F)$ represent a prime divisor. The ideal $\mathcal I_ F$ is coherent by theorem A.2.8 , and it is not identically zero on any component of $M$, because $F$ is nowhere dense. Let $g\colon M'	o M$ be as in (2), so that $\mathcal I_ F\mathcal O_{M'}=\mathcal O_{M'}(-H)$ with $H$ an effective divisor whose support has simple normal crossings; $g$ is proper, it is an isomorphism off $g^{-1}(F)$, and $g^{-1}(F)$, the support of $H$, is nowhere dense, so $g$ is bimeromorphic. The strict transform $F'$ of $F$ is an irreducible hypersurface contained in the support of $H$, so by corollary A.2.14 (4) and (3) it is one of its irreducible components, which are smooth. The pair $(M',F')$ represents the same prime divisor, as we see on the common smooth model $M'$, which is a smooth model of $X$ by corollary A.6.3 . $\square$ Theorem A.7.6 . Let $X$ be a compact complex space. Every prime divisor over $X$ is represented on a smooth model obtained from $X$ by a finite sequence of blowups with smooth centers. Its representative may also be chosen smooth. Proof. After reducing to the case of a manifold, we blow up the image of the divisor in $X$ as long as it has codimension at least two; each step lowers the order of vanishing along the divisor of the Jacobian determinant of the model. Step 1: reduction to a manifold. Let $\widehat X	o X$ be a resolution given by theorem A.5.4 , a finite sequence of blowups with smooth centers, since $X$ is compact. Let the prime divisor be represented by $(M_0,F_0)$, and let $M$ be a common smooth model of $M_0$ and $\widehat X$, with $E\subset M$ the strict transform of $F_0$ (proposition A.7.3 ); then $(M,E)$ represents the same divisor, as we see on the common smooth model $M$. A finite sequence of blowups with smooth centers over $\widehat X$, composed with $\widehat X	o X$, is such a sequence over $X$, and smooth models of $\widehat X$ are smooth models of $X$, by corollary A.6.3 . Hence we may assume that $X$ is a compact complex manifold, and we are given a proper bimeromorphic map $f\colon M	o X$ from a compact manifold and an irreducible hypersurface $E\subset M$. Since $E$ is irreducible, hence connected, it lies in a connected component $M_ E$ of $M$, and $f(M_ E)$ lies in a connected component $X_ E$ of $X$. These components have the same dimension $n$, because $M_ E$ contains a nonempty open set mapped isomorphically onto an open subset of $X$ (lemma A.3.1 ); moreover $n\geq 1$ and $\dim E=n-1$, since $E$ is a nonempty hypersurface. If $n=1$, the center $f(E)$ considered below is a point of $X_ E$, hence a hypersurface. Step 2: the order of the Jacobian. The Jacobian determinant $J_ f$ of $f$ in local coordinates is holomorphic and determined up to multiplication by holomorphic units. It does not vanish identically near any point, because $f$ is an isomorphism over a dense open subset of $X$ whose inverse image is dense in $M$ (lemma A.3.1 ). Its order of vanishing $\operatorname {ord}_ EJ_ f$ along $E$ is the largest $k$ such that $J_ f$ is divisible by the $k$th power of a local equation of $E$ near points of $E_{\mathrm{reg}}$; definition 12.6.3 uses the same notion of order along a hypersurface. It is a finite nonnegative integer $k$, since a function divisible by all powers of a local coordinate $y$ has vanishing Taylor coefficients in $y$ and vanishes near the point. It does not depend on the point of $E_{\mathrm{reg}}$, which is a connected manifold by corollary A.2.14 : for each integer $j$, the set of points of $E_{\mathrm{reg}}$ at which the order is at least $j$ is open, and it is closed by the identity theorem on $E_{\mathrm{reg}}$, since a holomorphic function vanishing on $E$ near a regular point is divisible by a local equation of $E$. For composable maps the chain rule gives A.14  egin{equation} \label{eq:divisor-jacobian-order-chain} \operatorname {ord}_ E J_{g\circ h} =\operatorname {ord}_ E J_ h+ \operatorname {ord}_ E(J_ g\circ h), \end{equation} because orders of vanishing along $E$ add under multiplication. Replacing $M$ by a common smooth model $h\colon M'	o M$ and $E$ by its strict transform $E'$ does not change $k$: by proposition A.7.3 , $h$ is an isomorphism near generic points of $E'$, so $\operatorname {ord}_{E'}J_ h=0$ and $\operatorname {ord}_{E'}(J_ f\circ h)=k$. Step 3: one principalization lowers the order. The center $Z=f(E)$ is an analytic subset of $X$ by theorem A.6.2 , of dimension at most $\dim E=n-1$ by lemma A.2.12 (3). It is irreducible: if $Z=Z_1\cup Z_2$ with analytic subsets $Z_1,Z_2$, then the irreducible set $E$ is the union of its analytic subsets $E\cap f^{-1}(Z_1)$ and $E\cap f^{-1}(Z_2)$, so it lies in one of them, and $Z$ equals $Z_1$ or $Z_2$. The same argument shows that images of irreducible analytic sets under proper holomorphic maps are irreducible. Suppose first that $Z$ is a hypersurface, and let $S\subset X$ be as in proposition A.7.3 for $f$. The strict transform $Z^ M$ of $Z$ in $M$ is an irreducible hypersurface containing $f^{-1}(Z\setminus S)$. The set $E\cap f^{-1}(Z\setminus S)$ is open in $E$, and it is nonempty, because $f(E)=Z$ is not contained in $S$, which has codimension at least two. So $E\cap Z^ M$ is an analytic subset of $E$ with interior points in $E$, and $E\subset Z^ M$ by corollary A.2.14 (2); then $E=Z^ M$ by corollary A.2.14 (3). Hence $(X,Z)$ represents the given divisor, as we see on the common smooth model $M$. Suppose now that $Z$ has codimension at least two. Its ideal $\mathcal I_ Z$ is coherent by theorem A.2.8 , and it is not identically zero on any component of $X$, since $Z$ is nowhere dense. Let $\sigma =\sigma _1\circ \cdots \circ \sigma _ t\colon X'	o X$ be the finite sequence of blowups with centers $C_ i\subset X_{i-1}$ and transformed ideals $\mathfrak a_ i$, $\mathfrak a_0=\mathcal I_ Z$, given by theorem A.5.5 ; it is proper and bimeromorphic by corollary A.6.3 , so $X'$ is a smooth model of $X$. Let $h\colon M'	o M$ and $f'\colon M'	o X'$ be the maps from a common smooth model of $M$ and $X'$, so that $f\circ h=\sigma \circ f'$, let $E'$ be the strict transform of $E$, let $ho _ i\colon M'	o X_ i$ be the induced maps, and let $Z_ i=ho _ i(E')$; thus $Z_0=Z$. Let $r\geq 2$ be the codimension of $Z$, which is pure by corollary A.2.14 (1). We claim that for some $i$ the center $C_ i$ contains $Z_{i-1}$, and that the connected component of $C_ i$ containing $Z_{i-1}$ has codimension $r$. The sets $Z_ j$ are irreducible, as images of the irreducible set $E'$, and $\sigma _{j+1}(Z_{j+1})=Z_ j$. Put $	au _ j=\sigma _1\circ \cdots \circ \sigma _ j$. Suppose that $Z_{l-1}
ot\subset C_ l$ for all $l\leq j$. We show by induction on $j$ that there are a nowhere dense analytic subset $A_ j\subset Z$ and an open set $N_ j\subset X\setminus A_ j$ containing $Z^\circ _ j=Z\setminus A_ j$ such that $	au _ j$ is an isomorphism over $N_ j$ and, on $	au _ j^{-1}(N_ j)$, \[  Z_ j=	au _ j^{-1}(Z^\circ _ j),\qquad \mathfrak a_ j=\mathcal I_ Z\mathcal O_{X_ j}.  \] For $j=0$ take $A_0=\varnothing $ and $N_0=X$. Assume the assertion for some $j<t$, and suppose that $Z_ j
ot\subset C_{j+1}$. On $	au _ j^{-1}(N_ j)$ we have $C_{j+1}\subset V(\mathfrak a_ j)=	au _ j^{-1}(Z^\circ _ j)\subset Z_ j$. By corollary A.2.14 (2), $C_{j+1}\cap Z_ j$ is nowhere dense in $Z_ j$. Its image $	au _ j(C_{j+1}\cap Z_ j)\subset Z$ is analytic by theorem A.6.2 , and it is nowhere dense in $Z$: its part in $Z^\circ _ j$ corresponds under the isomorphism $	au _ j$ to the nowhere dense part of $C_{j+1}\cap Z_ j$ in the open subset $	au _ j^{-1}(Z^\circ _ j)$ of $Z_ j$, and $A_ j$ is nowhere dense. Let $A_{j+1}=A_ j\cup 	au _ j(C_{j+1}\cap Z_ j)$ and $N_{j+1}=N_ j\setminus A_{j+1}$. Then $	au _ j^{-1}(N_{j+1})$ does not meet $C_{j+1}$, so $\sigma _{j+1}$ is an isomorphism over it and does not change the ideal there: $\mathfrak a_{j+1}=\mathcal O_{X_{j+1}}(E_{j+1})\mathfrak a_ j\mathcal O_{X_{j+1}}=\mathcal I_ Z\mathcal O_{X_{j+1}}$ on $	au _{j+1}^{-1}(N_{j+1})$. Moreover $Z_{j+1}\cap 	au _{j+1}^{-1}(N_{j+1})=\sigma _{j+1}^{-1}(Z_ j\cap 	au _ j^{-1}(N_{j+1}))=	au _{j+1}^{-1}(Z^\circ _{j+1})$, because $\sigma _{j+1}(Z_{j+1})=Z_ j$ and $\sigma _{j+1}$ is injective there. This completes the induction. Since $A_ j$ is nowhere dense in $Z$, the set $Z^\circ _ j$ is nonempty, and so is $	au _ j^{-1}(Z^\circ _ j)$. If $Z_{l-1}
ot\subset C_ l$ held for all $l\leq t$, the induction would reach $j=t$, and $\mathfrak a_ t$ would be the ideal of the nonempty set $	au _ t^{-1}(Z^\circ _ t)$ on $	au _ t^{-1}(N_ t)$, whereas $\mathfrak a_ t$ is the unit ideal. So there is a least index $i$ with $Z_{i-1}\subset C_ i$, and the assertion holds for $j=i-1$. On $	au _{i-1}^{-1}(N_{i-1})$ we have $Z_{i-1}\subset C_ i\subset V(\mathfrak a_{i-1})=	au _{i-1}^{-1}(Z^\circ _{i-1})\subset Z_{i-1}$, so $C_ i$ coincides there with a copy of the open subset $Z^\circ _{i-1}$ of $Z$, which is pure of codimension $r$. The set $Z_{i-1}$ is connected, being the closure of the connected manifold $(Z_{i-1})_{\mathrm{reg}}$, so it lies in one connected component of the manifold $C_ i$, and this component has codimension $r$. By ( A.8 ) and proposition A.5.3 , near points over this component the Jacobian determinant of $\sigma _ i$ is, in any local coordinates, a unit times the $(r-1)$st power of a local equation of the exceptional divisor $E_ i=\sigma _ i^{-1}(C_ i)$. Since $Z_ i=ho _ i(E')$ lies over $Z_{i-1}\subset C_ i$, the function $J_{\sigma _ i}\circ ho _ i$ vanishes on $E'$; it does not vanish identically near any point, because $J_{\sigma _ i}$ vanishes only on $E_ i$, and $ho _ i^{-1}(E_ i)$ is nowhere dense, $ho _ i$ being proper and bimeromorphic as the composite of $f'$ with $\sigma _{i+1}\circ \cdots \circ \sigma _ t$ (corollary A.6.3 ). Hence it has positive order along $E'$. The Jacobians of the other blowups composed with the corresponding maps $ho _ j$ are holomorphic, so they have nonnegative order, and by the chain rule $J_\sigma \circ f'=\prod _ j(J_{\sigma _ j}\circ ho _ j)$. Thus \[  \operatorname {ord}_{E'}(J_\sigma \circ f')\geq 1.  \] Applying ( A.14 ) to $f\circ h=\sigma \circ f'$ and using Step 2, we obtain \[  0\leq \operatorname {ord}_{E'}J_{f'} =k-\operatorname {ord}_{E'}(J_\sigma \circ f')\leq k-1.  \] Step 4: conclusion. The pair $(M',E')$ represents the given prime divisor, as we see on the common smooth model $M'$, and $X'$ is a compact manifold. We repeat Step 3 with $X'$, $f'$ and $E'$ in place of $X$, $f$ and $E$. Each repetition in which the center has codimension at least two lowers the nonnegative integer $k$ by at least one, so after at most $k$ repetitions the center is a hypersurface on the current model, which is obtained from $X$ by a finite sequence of blowups with smooth centers, and it represents the given prime divisor. Finally, by lemma A.7.5 (2), principalizing the ideal of this hypersurface by theorem A.5.5 gives a further sequence of blowups with smooth centers, finite because the model is compact, on which the strict transform of the hypersurface is smooth and represents the same prime divisor. $\square$

title: Unibranch connected fibers
text: Theorem A.7.1 . Let $f\colon Y\to X$ be a proper bimeromorphic holomorphic map between complex spaces, and let $x\in X$ be a point at which the germ $(X,x)$ is irreducible. Then the fiber $f^{-1}(x)$ is connected. In particular, if $X$ is unibranch, every fiber of $f$ is connected. Proof. Choose a nowhere dense analytic subset $A\subset X$ such that $f^{-1}(A)$ is nowhere dense and $f$ is an isomorphism over $X\setminus A$. Suppose that the compact fiber over $x$ is disconnected, and write it as the union of two disjoint nonempty compact sets. Since $Y$ is Hausdorff, they have disjoint open neighborhoods $V_1$ and $V_2$. Since $f$ is proper, hence closed, $U=X\setminus f(Y\setminus (V_1\cup V_2))$ is an open neighborhood of $x$ with $f^{-1}(U)\subset V_1\cup V_2$. As $(X,x)$ is irreducible, corollary A.3.9 allows us to shrink $U$ so that $U\setminus A$ is connected. Each set $V_ i\cap f^{-1}(U)$ is open and nonempty, so it meets the dense set $Y\setminus f^{-1}(A)$. Therefore $V_1$ and $V_2$ split $f^{-1}(U\setminus A)$ into two disjoint nonempty open sets. This contradicts the connectedness of $U\setminus A$, which is isomorphic to $f^{-1}(U\setminus A)$. $\square$

title: Finite bimeromorphic normal target
text:
Corollary A.7.2 . A finite bimeromorphic holomorphic map to a normal complex space is an isomorphism. Let $\phi \colon S	o X$ be a holomorphic map from a normal complex space to a complex space such that $\phi ^{-1}(X_{\mathrm{sing}})$ is nowhere dense in $S$. Then $\phi $ factors uniquely through the normalization $
u \colon \widetilde X	o X$: there is a unique holomorphic map $\psi \colon S	o \widetilde X$ with $
u \circ \psi =\phi $. Proof. Let $f\colon Y	o X$ be finite and bimeromorphic, with $X$ normal, and let $A\subset X$ be a nowhere dense analytic subset such that $f$ is an isomorphism over $X\setminus A$ and $f^{-1}(A)$ is nowhere dense. Normal spaces are unibranch, so the finite fibers of $f$ are connected by theorem A.7.1 , hence consist of at most one point. The image of $f$ is closed, because $f$ is proper, and contains the dense set $X\setminus A$; so $f$ is a continuous closed bijection, that is, a homeomorphism. Let $x\in X$ and $y=f^{-1}(x)$. Choose a neighborhood $V$ of $y$, relatively compact in the domain of a local model of $Y$, so that the coordinate functions of the model are bounded on $V$. Composed with $f^{-1}$, they are bounded holomorphic functions on $f(V)\setminus A$, where $f^{-1}$ is holomorphic, and $f(V)$ is an open neighborhood of $x$. By lemma A.3.4 they extend holomorphically to $f(V)$, and the extensions are the continuous functions $(	ext{coordinates})\circ f^{-1}$. Hence $f^{-1}$ is holomorphic. For the second assertion, over the dense open set $S\setminus \phi ^{-1}(X_{\mathrm{sing}})$ there is a unique lift $\psi _0=
u ^{-1}\circ \phi $, because $
u $ is an isomorphism over $X_{\mathrm{reg}}$. We extend it by the argument used for the uniqueness in the proof of theorem A.3.6 . Let $s\in S$ and $x=\phi (s)$, choose disjoint neighborhoods $W_ l$ of the finitely many points of $
u ^{-1}(x)$, relatively compact in domains $W'_ l$ of local models of $\widetilde X$, and a neighborhood $U$ of $x$ with $
u ^{-1}(U)\subset  igcup _ lW_ l$, which exists by properness. Since $S$ is normal, hence unibranch, corollary A.3.9 gives a neighborhood $V$ of $s$ with $\phi (V)\subset U$ such that $V\setminus \phi ^{-1}(X_{\mathrm{sing}})$ is connected. Then $\psi _0$ maps this set into a single $W_ l$. The coordinate functions of $W'_ l$ composed with $\psi _0$ are bounded and extend holomorphically to $V$, by lemma A.3.4 ; the extended map takes values in $\overline{W_ l}\subset W'_ l$, and it satisfies the equations of the local model, which hold on a dense subset of $V$. This gives a holomorphic lift on $V$, with $
u \circ \psi =\phi $ by density. Lifts agree on the dense set where $\psi _0$ is defined, so these local lifts glue, and the lift is unique. $\square$

title: Smooth bimeromorphic divisor locus
text: Proposition A.7.3 . A proper bimeromorphic holomorphic map $f\colon M'\to M$ between complex manifolds is an isomorphism outside an analytic subset $S$ of $M$ of codimension at least two. In particular, every irreducible hypersurface $D$ in $M$ has a well-defined strict transform in $M'$, namely the closure $D'$ of $f^{-1}(D\setminus S)$, which does not depend on the choice of $S$; it is an irreducible hypersurface, $f(D')=D$, and $f$ maps $D'$ isomorphically onto $D$ over the dense open subset $D\setminus S$ of $D$. Proof. We take for $S$ the image of the critical set of $f$; the main point is that a component of $S$ of codimension one would contain a point over which $f$ is finite, hence an isomorphism by corollary A.7.2 . Step 1: the set $S$. We may work over each connected component of $M$, of dimension $n$ say; every connected component of its inverse image has dimension $n$ as well, because it contains a nonempty open set mapped isomorphically onto an open subset of $M$, by lemma A.3.1 . The map $f$ is surjective, since its image is closed and dense. The critical set of $f$, where the Jacobian determinant vanishes in local coordinates, is analytic, and its image $S$ is analytic by theorem A.6.2 . Over $M\setminus S$ the map $f$ is proper and, by proposition 7.1.2 (1), a local biholomorphism, so its fibers are discrete and finite. They are connected by theorem A.7.1 , and nonempty; so they are single points, and $f$ is a bijective local biholomorphism, hence an isomorphism, over $M\setminus S$. Since $f$ is an isomorphism over a dense open subset of $M$, it has no critical points over this set, so $S$ does not meet it and is nowhere dense. Step 2: $S$ has codimension at least two. Suppose that $S$ has an irreducible component $D_0$ of codimension one. Choose a point of $(D_0)_{\mathrm{reg}}$ outside the other components of $S$, and a coordinate polydisc $U$ centered at it in which $D_0\cap U=S\cap U=\{ h=0\} $ for one of the coordinate functions $h$; then $D_0\cap U$ is a connected manifold. Let $A\subset M$ be a nowhere dense analytic subset such that $f^{-1}(A)$ is nowhere dense and $f$ is an isomorphism over $M\setminus A$. The function $h\circ f$ does not vanish identically on any connected component $V$ of $f^{-1}(U)$: otherwise $f$ would map the nonempty open set $V\setminus f^{-1}(A)$ isomorphically onto an open subset of $M$ contained in the hypersurface $D_0$, which is impossible. By proposition A.4.6 , $E=f^{-1}(D_0\cap U)$ is pure of dimension $n-1$. Let $K\subset D_0\cap U$ be a compact neighborhood of the chosen point in $D_0$. Only finitely many irreducible components $E_1,\ldots ,E_ k$ of $E$ meet the compact set $f^{-1}(K)$, and by theorem A.6.2 each image $f(E_ j)$ is an analytic subset of $D_0\cap U$. If its dimension is $n-1$, then $f(E_ j)$ contains an open subset of the connected manifold $D_0\cap U$ and therefore equals it, since proper analytic subsets of connected manifolds are nowhere dense (lemma A.1.6 ); we then call $E_ j$ dominating. Otherwise $f(E_ j)$ has dimension at most $n-2$. For a dominating $E_ j$, the maximal rank of $f$ restricted to the connected manifold $(E_ j)_{\mathrm{reg}}$, as a map into the coordinate hyperplane $D_0\cap U$, is $n-1$. Otherwise $f((E_ j)_{\mathrm{reg}})$ would be $\mathcal H^{2n-2}$-null by lemma A.2.12 (1); so would $f((E_ j)_{\mathrm{sing}})$, by the same lemma, since $(E_ j)_{\mathrm{sing}}$ has dimension at most $n-2$ by corollary A.2.10 (1) and is therefore, by (2) of the same corollary, a finite union of complex submanifolds of dimension at most $n-2$; and $f(E_ j)$ would have dimension at most $n-2$ by lemma A.2.12 (2). Let $R_ j$ be the union of $(E_ j)_{\mathrm{sing}}$ and of the regular points where this rank is less than $n-1$. It is analytic. Indeed, near a point of $E_ j$, let $e$ be a local equation of the irreducible hypersurface $E_ j$ as in lemma A.2.16 , and let $f'$ be the map formed by the $n-1$ coordinates of $f$ in the coordinate hyperplane $D_0\cap U$. At a regular point $p$ of $E_ j$ we have $\mathrm de(p)\neq 0$ and $T_ pE_ j=\ker \mathrm de(p)$, so the rank of $f'|_{E_ j}$ at $p$ is $n-1$ exactly when the Jacobian determinant of $(e,f')$ does not vanish at $p$. Hence $R_ j$ is, near this point, the union of the analytic set $(E_ j)_{\mathrm{sing}}$ and of the zero set in $E_ j$ of this Jacobian determinant. It is different from $E_ j$, because the rank $n-1$ is attained on $(E_ j)_{\mathrm{reg}}$; so it is nowhere dense in the irreducible set $E_ j$ and has dimension at most $n-2$, by corollary A.2.14 (2), and $f(R_ j)$ is analytic of dimension at most $n-2$, by theorem A.6.2 and lemma A.2.12 (3). Choose a point $a$ in the interior of $K$ outside the finitely many sets $f(E_ j)$, $E_ j$ not dominating, and $f(R_ j)$, $E_ j$ dominating. Let $p\in f^{-1}(a)$. Since $f^{-1}(a)\subset E\cap f^{-1}(K)$, the point $p$ lies on some of the components $E_1,\ldots ,E_ k$. Each of them that contains $p$ is dominating, and $p\notin R_ j$, so $f|_{E_ j}$ is a local biholomorphism at $p$ onto an open subset of $D_0$, by proposition 7.1.2 (1) in charts, and $p$ is isolated in $f^{-1}(a)\cap E_ j$. The components of $E$ not containing $p$ form a locally finite family of closed sets, so near $p$ the set $f^{-1}(a)$ lies in the union of the components containing $p$, and $p$ is isolated in $f^{-1}(a)$. Thus $f^{-1}(a)$ is discrete, and being compact, it is finite. Let $p_1,\ldots ,p_ l$ be the points of $f^{-1}(a)$, and choose disjoint coordinate balls $B_1,\ldots ,B_ l$ around them. By properness there is a neighborhood $U_0$ of $a$ with $f^{-1}(U_0)\subset \bigcup _ iB_ i$. The fibers of $f$ over $U_0$ are compact analytic subsets of these balls, hence finite by corollary A.4.3 . Thus $f$ is finite and bimeromorphic over the manifold $U_0$, which is normal, and it is an isomorphism over $U_0$ by corollary A.7.2 . In particular $f$ has no critical points over $U_0$, which contradicts $a\in S$. Therefore $S$ has codimension at least two. Step 3: strict transforms. Let $D$ be an irreducible hypersurface. Then $S\cap D$ has dimension at most $n-2$, so $D\setminus S$ is dense in $D$ by corollary A.2.14 (2). The closure $D'$ of $f^{-1}(D\setminus S)=f^{-1}(D)\setminus f^{-1}(S)$ is analytic by lemma A.2.5 , and $f$ is an isomorphism from $D'\setminus f^{-1}(S)=f^{-1}(D\setminus S)$ onto $D\setminus S$. The set $f(D')$ is closed, because $f$ is proper, it contains the dense subset $D\setminus S$ of $D$, and it is contained in the closed set $D$; so $f(D')=D$. The set $Q=f^{-1}(D_{\mathrm{reg}}\setminus S)$ is a connected manifold of dimension $n-1$, because $D_{\mathrm{reg}}\setminus S$ is connected by lemma A.1.7 ; it is open in $D'$ and dense in $D'$, since $D_{\mathrm{reg}}\setminus S$ is open and dense in $D\setminus S$. Hence $Q$ consists of regular points of $D'$ and lies in a single connected component of $(D')_{\mathrm{reg}}$, whose closure, an irreducible component of $D'$ by corollary A.2.13 , contains $\overline Q=D'$; so $D'$ is irreducible, of dimension $n-1$. Finally, if $S_1$ is another analytic subset of codimension at least two off which $f$ is an isomorphism, then $D\setminus (S\cup S_1)$ is dense in $D\setminus S$ and in $D\setminus S_1$, by corollary A.2.14 (2), so $f^{-1}(D\setminus (S\cup S_1))$ is dense in both $f^{-1}(D\setminus S)$ and $f^{-1}(D\setminus S_1)$, and the two closures agree. $\square$

title: Prime divisor model
text: Definition A.7.4 . Let $X$ be a complex space. A prime divisor over $X$ is represented by a pair consisting of a smooth model $M\to X$ and an irreducible hypersurface $F\subset M$; two pairs are identified if the strict transforms of their hypersurfaces, in the sense of proposition A.7.3 , agree on a common smooth model. The prime divisor is exceptional if the image of $F$ in $X$ has codimension at least two.

title: Prime divisor well defined
text: Lemma A.7.5 . Let $X$ be a complex space. The identification of pairs in definition A.7.4 is an equivalence relation, and the image in $X$ of the hypersurface $F$ of a representative $(M,F)$ depends only on the prime divisor. Let $(M,F)$ represent a prime divisor over $X$, and let $g\colon M'\to M$ be the composite of the principalization of $\mathcal I_ F$ given by theorem A.5.5 with the empty divisor. Then $g$ is proper and bimeromorphic, the strict transform $F'$ of $F$ is a smooth irreducible hypersurface of $M'$, and $(M',F')$ represents the same prime divisor. In particular, every prime divisor over $X$ has a representative $(M,F)$ with $F$ smooth. Proof. We begin with two remarks used in the proof of (1). First, two maps from a smooth model $M_3$ to a smooth model $M_1$ that commute with the maps to $X$ agree. Indeed, let $U\subset X$ be the complement of a nowhere dense analytic subset over which both models are isomorphisms; the two maps agree over $U$, and the part of $M_3$ over $U$ is dense, by lemma A.3.1 . Second, strict transforms are compatible with composition. Let $g\colon P\to N$ and $h\colon N\to M$ be proper bimeromorphic maps between complex manifolds, so that $h\circ g$ is proper and bimeromorphic by corollary A.6.3 , and let $D\subset M$ be an irreducible hypersurface, with strict transform $D^ N$ in $N$. We claim that the strict transform of $D^ N$ under $g$ is the strict transform $D^ P$ of $D$ under $h\circ g$. Let $S_ h,S_{hg}\subset M$ and $S_ g\subset N$ be analytic subsets of codimension at least two as in proposition A.7.3 for $h$, $h\circ g$ and $g$, and let $T=S_ h\cup S_{hg}\cup h(S_ g)$, which is analytic of codimension at least two by theorem A.6.2 and lemma A.2.12 (3). The set $O=D^ N\cap h^{-1}(M\setminus T)=h^{-1}(D\setminus T)$ is open in $D^ N$, nonempty, and does not meet $S_ g$; its complement $D^ N\cap h^{-1}(T)$ is an analytic subset of the irreducible set $D^ N$ different from $D^ N$, hence nowhere dense by corollary A.2.14 (2). So $O$ is dense in $D^ N\setminus S_ g$, and since $g$ is an isomorphism over $N\setminus S_ g$, the strict transform of $D^ N$ under $g$ is the closure of $g^{-1}(O)=(h\circ g)^{-1}(D\setminus T)$. By the independence of the choice of $S_{hg}$ in proposition A.7.3 , applied with $T$, this closure is also $D^ P$. Now let $(M_ i,F_ i)$, $i=1,2,3$, be pairs such that $(M_1,F_1)$ and $(M_2,F_2)$ are identified on a common smooth model $N_{12}$, and $(M_2,F_2)$ and $(M_3,F_3)$ on $N_{23}$. Let $P$ be a common smooth model of $N_{12}$ and $N_{23}$, and let $p_ i\colon P\to M_ i$ be the composite maps; by the first remark, the two composite maps $P\to M_2$, through $N_{12}$ and through $N_{23}$, coincide. By the second remark, the strict transforms of $F_1$ and $F_2$ under $p_1$ and $p_2$ are the strict transforms in $P$ of their strict transforms in $N_{12}$, which agree; similarly for $F_2$ and $F_3$. Hence $F_1$ and $F_3$ have the same strict transform in $P$, and the identification is transitive; it is reflexive, with $M_1$ itself as common smooth model, and symmetric by definition. Since $p_ i$ maps the strict transform of $F_ i$ onto $F_ i$ (proposition A.7.3 ), the images of $F_1$ and $F_3$ in $X$ both equal the image of their common strict transform in $P$; so the image of $F$ in $X$ depends only on the prime divisor. We now prove (2). Let $(M,F)$ represent a prime divisor. The ideal $\mathcal I_ F$ is coherent by theorem A.2.8 , and it is not identically zero on any component of $M$, because $F$ is nowhere dense. Let $g\colon M'\to M$ be as in (2), so that $\mathcal I_ F\mathcal O_{M'}=\mathcal O_{M'}(-H)$ with $H$ an effective divisor whose support has simple normal crossings; $g$ is proper, it is an isomorphism off $g^{-1}(F)$, and $g^{-1}(F)$, the support of $H$, is nowhere dense, so $g$ is bimeromorphic. The strict transform $F'$ of $F$ is an irreducible hypersurface contained in the support of $H$, so by corollary A.2.14 (4) and (3) it is one of its irreducible components, which are smooth. The pair $(M',F')$ represents the same prime divisor, as we see on the common smooth model $M'$, which is a smooth model of $X$ by corollary A.6.3 . $\square$

title: Divisor smooth blowup realization
Divisor jacobian order chain
text: A.14 \begin{equation} \label{eq:divisor-jacobian-order-chain} \operatorname {ord}_ E J_{g\circ h} =\operatorname {ord}_ E J_ h+ \operatorname {ord}_ E(J_ g\circ h), \end{equation}

title: Plurisubharmonic functions on reduced spaces
text:
A.8 Plurisubharmonic functions on reduced spaces At a singular point of a complex space there is no intrinsic complex Hessian, so we define plurisubharmonic functions on a complex space as local restrictions of plurisubharmonic functions on ambient domains. Their compositions with holomorphic discs are then subharmonic, and together with the curves of section A.4 this gives a maximum principle on compact spaces and local upper bounds near analytic subsets of codimension at least two. Definition A.8.1 . Let $X$ be a complex space. A function $u\colon X	o [-\infty ,+\infty )$ is locally plurisubharmonic if every point of $X$ has a local model, which identifies a neighborhood of the point with an analytic subset of a domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ N$, and a ball $V\subset \Omega $ around the point such that $u$ is the restriction to $X\cap V$ of a function on $V$ that is plurisubharmonic or identically $-\infty $. Let $X$ be a complex space. Let $u$ be locally plurisubharmonic on $X$. For every local model of a neighborhood of a point of $X$, there is a ball $V$ around the point in the ambient domain such that $u$ is the restriction to $X\cap V$ of a function on $V$ that is plurisubharmonic or identically $-\infty $. text: Proposition A.8.3 . A locally plurisubharmonic function on a compact connected complex space is constant, possibly equal to $-\infty $. Proof. title: Historical and bibliographical notes
text: B Historical and bibliographical notes These notes give the sources of the results in this book. For each chapter we indicate where the main results were first proved or where they can be found in the literature, compare our statements, proofs and normalizations with those of the sources, and point to alternative presentations. The sections follow the order of the book: each concerns one chapter, except that the notes on chapter 17 occupy three sections, and the last section concerns chapter A . A few ideas recur throughout the book: a function is recovered from its distributional derivatives, exceptional sets are controlled by capacities, nonlinear measures are constructed by approximation with bounded potentials, and singular potentials are compared through their envelopes. These ideas have different origins, and their formulation has changed as the theory moved from domains in Euclidean space to compact complex manifolds. When the book is compared with another source, the conventions of that source matter as much as its hypotheses. We use $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}=\mathrm i\partial \bar\partial /(2\pi )$; Lelong numbers are normalized so that $\log |z|^2$ has Lelong number $1$ at the origin, and multiplier ideals are defined with the weight $\mathrm e^{-\varphi }$. Several of the sources cited below use the operator $\mathrm{dd^ c}=\mathrm i\partial \bar\partial /\pi $, measure Lelong numbers against $\log |z|$ and use the weight $\mathrm e^{-2\varphi }$. A source with the last two conventions assigns to $\varphi =u/2$ the Lelong numbers and multiplier ideals that we assign to $u$. If the operator is multiplied by a constant $c>0$, then at fixed potentials a product of $p$ factors of the form $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ is multiplied by $c^ p$. We record these conversions where they matter. Theorem and page numbers refer to the cited version of a work. When this version is a preprint rather than the published article, whose numbering or scope may differ, we say so. Two existence theorems are used without proof, namely the resolution and principalization theorems (theorem A.5.4 , theorem A.5.5 ); their source is given in section B.21 .

title: Measures and distributions
text: B.1 Measures and distributions The representation of positive linear functionals by measures, theorem 1.2.2 , is the Riesz representation theorem. For its formulation on locally compact, $\sigma $-compact spaces compare [ Theorem 24 , Tao09Radon ] ; on open subsets of Euclidean space our proof constructs the measure from a metric outer measure and identifies the functional by slicing functions into level sets. The regularity and density statements in proposition 1.1.2 , proposition 1.2.3 correspond to [ Theorem 21, Exercise 22 and Proposition 10 , Tao09Radon ] . For the measurability part of the outer-measure construction compare [ Theorem 5 , Tao10Products ] . The assertions on product measures and the interchange of integrals in proposition 1.1.7 form the Tonelli–Fubini theorem for $\sigma $-finite measures; compare [ Theorem 36 and its proof , Tao10Products ] , where the monotone class lemma (Lemma 35 there) is applied to the Boolean algebra of finite disjoint unions of rectangles. We instead apply Dynkin's $\pi $–$\lambda $ theorem, lemma 1.1.6 , to the rectangles themselves. For the local order bound, regularization by mollifiers and the fact that positive distributions are measures (definition 1.3.1 , proposition 1.4.3 , theorem 1.4.5 ) compare [ Section 1, Exercises 4–5; Section 2, Definition 1, Exercise 15 and Lemma 2 , Tao09Distributions ] . That source writes the test function first and gives the space of distributions the conjugate complex structure. Our pairing $\langle u,\chi \rangle =\int u\chi \, \mathrm d x$ is complex linear in both variables, the convention used for currents later in the book; with this pairing the derivative of a distribution is defined with the same sign as in that source. The selection theorem for sequences of measures, theorem 1.5.5 , is proved by a diagonal argument over countably many test functions. The compactness theorem for nets, theorem 1.6.3 , rests instead on Tychonoff's theorem for a product of intervals, which we prove with ultrafilters (lemma 1.6.2 ); this is where the axiom of choice enters. Subnets are Willard subnets throughout the book, and proposition 1.6.1 characterizes compactness in these terms. The Arzelà–Ascoli theorem, proposition 1.6.4 , is proved in the usual way, by showing that an equicontinuous and pointwise bounded family is uniformly bounded and totally bounded for the uniform metric. For the differentiation of integrals compare [ Section 2, Theorems 32 and 36, Exercise 38 and Lemma 39 , Tao10Differentiation ] . In theorem 1.7.3 we use cubes instead of balls. The covering argument is the same: a finite disjoint subfamily of the cubes covers the original cubes after enlargement by the factor three, and the constant in the maximal inequality becomes $3^ d$. The Poincaré-type inequality lemma 1.7.4 follows by integrating the fundamental theorem of calculus along segments parallel to the coordinate axes. For the Radon–Nikodym theorem compare [ Corollary 1, following Theorem 2 , Tao09RN ] . The book uses only the case of a Borel measure that is dominated, at least locally, by a constant multiple of a Radon measure, lemma 1.7.1 . We prove it by an $L^2$ argument on half-open dyadic cubes, so that no assumption on the measure of cube boundaries is needed. This lemma provides, for instance, the densities of the coefficient measures in lemma 9.13.1 .

title: Harmonic functions and boundary values
text: B.2 Harmonic functions and boundary values Fundamental solutions, the regularity of distributional solutions of the Laplace equation, the Poisson formula and Harnack's inequality are treated in [ Theorems 3.1.2–3.1.7, pp. 117–123 , Hor07 ] . As there, the fundamental solution $E$ of proposition 2.2.1 satisfies $\Delta E=\delta _0$, whereas our Green functions are positive and satisfy $-\Delta G=\delta _ x$. Our proof of Weyl's lemma, theorem 2.1.4 , uses radial averaging and convolution; Theorem 3.1.3 of that book contains in addition a statement on analytic continuation. The Poisson formula and Harnack's inequality (theorem 2.3.1 , proposition 2.3.2 ) are stated with the explicit Poisson kernel and its two-sided bounds, and they include the case of dimension one. Perron's method, barriers and the solution of the Dirichlet problem for continuous boundary data are developed in [ Section 3.3, pp. 171–174, especially Theorem 3.3.3, Definition 3.3.4 and Theorem 3.3.5 , Hor07 ] . In theorem 2.4.2 , theorem 2.4.4 we work with continuous subsolutions. For the characterization of regular boundary points by barriers compare also [ Theorem 3.4.17, pp. 219–220 , Hor07 ] . Our local barrier criterion, proposition 2.4.7 , uses a positive continuous supersolution near the given boundary point whose continuous extension to the nearby boundary vanishes only at that point; the theorem in Hörmander's book allows more general exceptional sets. The Green function of theorem 2.5.2 is constructed only on bounded regular domains; within this class the theorem also shows that Green functions increase with the domain and converge along increasing sequences of domains whose union is again bounded and regular.

title: Subharmonic functions and polar sets
text: B.3 Subharmonic functions and polar sets The characterizations of subharmonic functions by comparison with harmonic functions and by mean values, their local integrability, the Riesz decomposition and the distributional characterization are developed in [ Theorem 3.2.3, Corollary 3.2.8 and Theorems 3.2.9–3.2.11, pp. 143–148 , Hor07 ] ; see theorem 3.1.3 , proposition 3.1.5 , theorem 3.2.3 , theorem 3.2.2 . Since a subharmonic function is the limit of its means at every point, the canonical representative of a distribution with positive Laplacian is determined by the distribution at every point, not only almost everywhere. Our Riesz measure is $\Delta u$, without a factor $1/(2\pi )$; thus a logarithmic pole in the plane has Riesz mass $2\pi $. For the compactness theorem and Hartogs' lemma (theorem 3.3.2 , theorem 3.3.3 ) compare [ Theorems 3.2.12–3.2.13, pp. 149–151 , Hor07 ] . Theorem 3.2.13 there also contains convergence statements in Sobolev spaces and against measures; the latter are discussed in the next section. Choquet's lemma and the regularized upper envelope (lemma 3.4.1 , theorem 3.4.2 ) correspond to [ Proposition 3.4.4, pp. 205–206 , Hor07 ] ; theorem 3.4.2 also asserts that the pointwise supremum of an arbitrary family is Lebesgue measurable. For the local definition of polar sets and the removable singularity theorem (definition 3.5.1 , theorem 3.5.2 ) compare [ Definition 3.4.1 and Theorem 3.4.3, pp. 203–205 , Hor07 ] . Our proof works directly with the local subharmonic functions of the definition, and the connectedness of the complement of a closed polar set in a domain follows from the maximum principle.

title: Energy, capacity and exceptional sets
text: B.4 Energy, capacity and exceptional sets The continuity principle and the restriction of a measure to compact sets on which its potential is continuous (theorem 4.2.2 ) follow the argument of [ Theorems 3.4.6–3.4.7, pp. 207–208 , Hor07 ] ; the approximation lemma of Lusin type used there is lemma 4.2.1 . The criterion for polarity of compact sets is [ Theorem 3.4.5, pp. 206–208 , Hor07 ] . Our relative capacity of a compact set is the total mass of the Riesz measure $\Delta u$ of its regularized relative extremal function $u$, and our Green functions are positive with $-\Delta G=\delta $; the numerical values of the capacity depend on these normalizations. Strong subadditivity, outer regularity and capacitability are developed in [ Section 3.4, pp. 209–216, especially Theorems 3.4.9 and 3.4.12 and Proposition 3.4.13 , Hor07 ] . Choquet's capacitability theorem, theorem 4.4.1 , which underlies the capacitability assertion of that section, is proved here by approximating continuous images of countable intersections of countable unions of compact sets from inside by compact sets. The convergence of integrals against measures with continuous potentials in lemma 4.4.3 is part of [ Theorem 3.2.13, pp. 150–151 , Hor07 ] , and the fact that the exceptional sets of the limit theorems are polar, theorem 4.4.4 , corresponds to [ Theorem 3.4.14, pp. 216–217 , Hor07 ] . This polarity strengthens the equality almost everywhere of an upper envelope and its regularization in theorem 3.4.2 . For the identity between Green energy and Dirichlet energy and for quasi-continuity compare [ Propositions 3.4.19 and 3.4.21, pp. 221–223 , Hor07 ] . In proposition 4.5.1 we work with the explicit, symmetric Green function of a ball. The positivity of the Newtonian energy and of the logarithmic energy (proposition 4.1.2 ) is proved by expressing the kernels as integrals of Gaussians. For the logarithmic kernel, positivity and the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality are proved, and used, only for signed measures of total mass zero. The equilibrium measure is obtained by minimizing the energy, and proposition 4.4.5 describes its potential (Frostman's theorem) with our normalization of the kernels. The example [ Example 6.1.3 , XiaSampleBook ] uses an atom-free measure on a polar Cantor set and refers to [ p. 31 , Car83 ] for the Cantor set. Such a measure $\mu $ is constructed explicitly in proposition 4.2.4 : the Cantor set $K$ is built from a rapidly decreasing sequence of lengths, so that the subharmonic function $p(z)=\int _ K\log |z-a|^2\, \mathrm d\mu (a)$ equals $-\infty $ at every point of $K$. The remaining ingredients of that example, namely the potential on the projective line, its integrability and the computation of its mass in degree one, are proposition 15.3.7 , corollary 12.3.2 , example 15.3.8 .

title: Fine topology and balayage
text: B.5 Fine topology and balayage Fuglede attributes the classical fine topology to Cartan and the quasi-Lindelöf principle to Doob in [ Introduction, p. 227 , Fug71Fine ] . His preliminaries [ Section 1, pp. 228–230 , Fug71Fine ] are formulated in an axiomatic harmonic space satisfying the domination axiom and admitting a positive potential, and they assume the general duality theory of sweeping before fine connectedness is studied. In the Euclidean setting of this book the quasi-Lindelöf principle, theorem 5.4.1 , follows directly from Choquet's lemma and the polarity of the exceptional set of an upper envelope. By example 5.1.7 , the fine topology is not Lindelöf, so a countable subfamily can only be expected to cover the union of a family of finely open sets up to a polar set. Reduction and balayage (theorem 5.2.5 , theorem 5.3.1 , theorem 5.3.2 ) are treated only on a ball, where the Green function is explicit and symmetric and Green energy is a Dirichlet integral by proposition 5.2.2 . In this setting the swept measure is determined by an orthogonality relation for the energy, which also gives additivity, and the general duality of sweeping recalled by Fuglede is not required. Example 5.3.3 expresses the swept potential of a Dirac measure through harmonic measure, for a compact set whose complement in the ball is a regular domain. Proposition 5.5.1 is proved directly from the definitions; it shows that for $n\geq 2$ the classical fine topology of $\mathbb C^ n=\mathbb R^{2n}$ differs from the topology generated by the upper semicontinuous functions that are subharmonic or identically $-\infty $ on complex lines, which is the plurifine topology of chapter 10 (example 10.3.4 ).

title: Fourier analysis and complex-line incidence
text: B.6 Fourier analysis and complex-line incidence For Fourier inversion on the Schwartz space and Plancherel's theorem (lemma 6.1.1 , theorem 6.1.2 ) compare [ Exercises 38–42, formula (11), Theorem 43 and Exercise 44 , Tao09Fourier ] . Our Fourier transform uses the character $\mathrm e^{-2\pi \mathrm i x\cdot \xi }$. Gaussian integration gives the exact constant in the Fourier expression of the Riesz energy, theorem 6.1.4 ; the kernel there is $|x-y|^{-s}$, without the normalization of a fundamental solution. For the dyadic decomposition compare [ Proposition 4.3 and proof, pp. 23–24 , Tao06Fourier3 ] ; for the weak type $(1,1)$ estimate and its consequences by interpolation and duality compare [ Lemma 2.7, Corollaries 2.9–2.10 and proofs, pp. 7–9 , Tao06Fourier4 ] . We treat only the Hessian multipliers $-\xi _ a\xi _ b/|\xi |^2$ (lemma 6.2.1 ), whose kernels are obtained by differentiating the heat kernel. Their weak type $(1,1)$ bound and their $L^ p$ bounds are lemma 6.2.2 , theorem 6.2.3 ; the exponents $p>2$ are obtained by duality. The interpolation inequality lemma 6.2.5 and Morrey's inequality lemma 6.2.6 are used for metric Laplacians in chapter 16 . The star-shaped annular sets, the projections onto complex hyperplanes and the incidence argument follow [ Lemmas 1.3–1.5, pp. 2–4 , PSHD ] ; this manuscript carries no author's name and no publication data. The Borel selection required by the argument is lemma 6.4.1 : the sets of high values on circles are closed and, by the submean inequality, have positive length, so a median with respect to arc length gives a Borel choice, and no general measurable selection theorem for compact-valued maps is needed. The unitarily invariant measures are constructed from the Gaussian measure on matrices, and volumes in projective space are controlled by an explicit estimate for projective balls instead of volume charts. In corollary 6.5.4 the function is assumed to be Borel; in the proof of theorem 8.1.3 this measurability is established before the corollary is applied.

title: Differential forms, currents and holomorphic divisors
text: B.7 Differential forms, currents and holomorphic divisors For positive forms and currents, the characterization of weak positivity by restriction to complex subspaces and the fact that positive currents have order zero, compare [ Chapter III, Section 1.A–B, pp. 129–134, especially (1.4), (1.6) and (1.14) , DemBook ] . In addition, proposition 7.2.1 shows that $\beta ^ p$ lies in the interior of the cone of strongly positive forms, which gives the trace bounds for positive currents; the proof averages over sign changes and permutations of the coordinates. Our currents are indexed by bidegree, whereas Demailly's subscripts there refer to bidimension. Pushforward and pullback of currents (proposition 7.5.1 , proposition 7.5.2 ) correspond to [ Chapter III, (1.17), p. 134 , DemBook ] ; for the pushforward the map need only be proper on the support of the current. The mixed Hodge–Riemann theorem of linear algebra, due to Timorin, is recorded in [ Proposition 2.1, p. 4 , DN2005mixedv2 ] (second arXiv version). Lemma 7.2.3 is its case of real $(1,1)$-forms, written with mixed discriminants of Hermitian matrices; we prove it by induction on principal minors and deformation to identity matrices, where the form is given by an explicit trace formula. For local potentials of closed positive $(1,1)$-currents compare [ Chapter III, Section 1.18 and (1.19), p. 135 , DemBook ] . Our proof of theorem 7.3.2 is different: we subtract the complex Hessian of the potential of the trace measure, and the remainder, which has trace zero and therefore harmonic coefficients, is $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-exact by the smooth local result lemma 7.3.1 . In proposition 7.3.3 the composition with a holomorphic map is taken pointwise, for the canonical representative; it is proved by radial regularization. Our proof of the Weierstrass preparation theorem, theorem 7.4.2 , is the proof by contour integrals in [ Chapter II, Section 2.A, pp. 79–80, Theorem (2.1) , DemBook ] , where it is attributed to Siegel. The Poincaré–Lelong formula, theorem 7.4.5 , is [ Chapter III, (2.15), pp. 143–144 , DemBook ] . The expression $(\mathrm{i}/\pi )\partial \bar\partial \log |f|$ appearing there equals our $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |f|^2$, while the operator $\mathrm{dd^ c}$ used subsequently in that book is twice ours. In our proof, slicing by coordinate lines and lemma 7.4.4 show that $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |f|^2$ puts no mass on the singular locus of the divisor, so that it equals the current of integration over the regular part, weighted by multiplicities. Example 7.4.6 gives the corresponding identity in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ for quotients of holomorphic functions.

title: Plurisubharmonic functions and invariant minima
text: B.8 Plurisubharmonic functions and invariant minima The theorem that a function which is subharmonic or identically $-\infty $ on complex lines is automatically upper semicontinuous is proved in the unsigned manuscript [ Theorem 1.1 and its proof, pp. 1–6 , PSHD ] , and our proof of theorem 8.1.3 completes the argument given there. In that manuscript, Lemma 1.2, pp. 1–2, proves measurability by induction on the dimension, using means over bounded fibers; Proposition 2.1, pp. 4–5, identifies a finite function that is subharmonic on lines with the canonical representative; and the final proof, p. 6, uses truncation. The incidence results needed for this argument are proved in chapter 6 , and proposition 7.3.3 describes the restrictions of the canonical representative to complex lines without using the theorem. We keep the usual definition of plurisubharmonic functions (definition 8.1.1 ), which requires upper semicontinuity; theorem 8.1.3 , proved shortly afterwards, shows that this condition is redundant. The distributional characterization, upper envelopes and compactness of plurisubharmonic functions (theorem 8.2.1 , theorem 8.3.2 , theorem 8.3.4 ) are deduced from the corresponding results for subharmonic functions in chapter 3 , chapter 4 . At this stage the set where an upper envelope differs from its regularization is only known to be real polar, that is, polar as a subset of $\mathbb R^{2n}$ in local charts; its pluripolarity is proved in chapter 10 . The extension theorem (theorem 8.4.3 ) gives both local boundedness and extension across a relatively closed set that is locally $\mathcal H^{2n-3}$-null; to apply it to analytic sets of codimension at least two (corollary A.2.15 ) one needs the local estimate for the Hausdorff measure of analytic sets in terms of their dimension. For $L^ p$ integrability and convergence in $L^ p_{\mathrm{loc}}$ compare [ Theorem 1.48, parts 1–2 and proof Steps 1–2, pp. 30–32 , GZ17 ] . As there, we pass from discs to polydiscs (lemma 8.3.5 , proposition 8.3.6 , theorem 8.3.7 ), but we use the Riesz decomposition with a compactly supported measure instead of the Poisson–Jensen formula on the boundary. Since our Riesz measure is $\Delta v$, its logarithmic potential carries the factor $1/(2\pi )$. The bound ( 8.6 ) gives uniform estimates on smaller polydiscs, and convergence in $L^ p_{\mathrm{loc}}$ then follows from Hölder's inequality. The identity with the factor two in the truncation display of [ p. 32 , GZ17 ] is incorrect, as is also noted in an unofficial list of errata for that book. The local exponential integrability estimates (lemma 8.3.8 , proposition 8.3.9 ) are proved with the same compactly supported Riesz decomposition and Jensen's inequality (lemma 1.1.4 ), with an exponent that depends only on a local $L^1$ bound; a finite covering by charts then gives the uniform estimate for normalized quasi-plurisubharmonic functions on a compact manifold, corollary 14.2.3 . The partial Legendre transform is due to Kiselman [ Kis78 ] . For his minimum principle and the regularization argument in its proof compare [ Chapter I, Section 7.B, Theorem (7.5) and its proof, p. 57 , DemBook ] . In theorem 8.5.1 the existence of an invariant exhaustion is a hypothesis, and the smooth case is proved with a Schur complement. Such an exhaustion is constructed for product tubes over open convex sets in corollary 8.5.2 ; the case of general pseudoconvex tubes, corollary 11.2.6 , uses in addition the plurisubharmonicity of $-\log $ of the boundary distance.

title: Bounded products and nonlinear capacity
text: B.9 Bounded products and nonlinear capacity The recursive definition of products of currents $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ with $u$ locally bounded and plurisubharmonic, the Chern–Levine–Nirenberg estimates and continuity along decreasing sequences are developed in [ Chapter III, Section 3, (3.1)–(3.11), pp. 144–150 , DemBook ] ; see theorem 9.1.3 , theorem 9.2.5 . In our proof of decreasing continuity, the integration by parts formula lemma 9.2.1 for functions that coincide near the boundary of a ball is combined with an induction on the number of factors, which also gives the symmetry of the product at each stage. The weighted estimate theorem 9.3.1 concerns only the measures $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q\wedge \beta ^{n-q}$; a version relative to a closed positive current, for one factor at a time, is lemma 15.3.1 . For continuity along increasing sequences, the behavior of products under maxima and the comparison principle (theorem 9.5.1 , proposition 9.2.7 , theorem 9.2.8 ) compare [ Theorem 3.23, pp. 89–91, and Theorems 3.27 and 3.29, pp. 93–94 , GZ17 ] . The domination principle corollary 9.2.9 is [ Proposition 1.2.10 , XiaSampleBook ] ; we prove it by a strictly plurisubharmonic quadratic perturbation and the comparison principle, applied on the given bounded open set itself. The Monge–Ampère capacity, quasi-continuity and convergence in capacity (definition 9.3.2 , theorem 9.4.2 , theorem 9.4.8 ) appear in [ Proposition 4.19, Theorem 4.20 and Lemma 4.21, pp. 110–112, and Theorem 4.26, pp. 114–115 , GZ17 ] . Our capacity is defined with competitors taking values between zero and one, whereas the competitors in [ Definition 4.16, p. 108 , GZ17 ] take values between $-1$ and $0$; since adding a constant does not change Monge–Ampère measures, the two normalizations give the same capacity. Both Demailly's book and [ GZ17 ] use the operator $\mathrm{dd^ c}=(\mathrm{i}/\pi )\partial \bar\partial $, twice ours, so their Monge–Ampère measures and capacities are $2^ n$ times ours. The estimate of proposition 9.3.5 is attributed to Błocki in [ Proposition 3.21, pp. 88–89 , GZ17 ] . The power $M^{n+1}$ of the oscillation printed there should be $M^ n$: the proof uses $n$ integrations by parts, and the left-hand side is homogeneous of degree $n$ in $v$. We prove the estimate with $M^ n$, under the assumption that $u=h$ near the boundary of the ball, first for smooth functions and then, by regularization and corollary 9.2.6 , for bounded ones. Corollary 9.5.2 shows that the set where an upper envelope differs from its regularization has capacity zero; this is used in chapter 10 to show that such sets are pluripolar. The solution of the homogeneous Dirichlet problem on the ball, theorem 9.6.3 , goes back to [ BT76 ] . Averaging over automorphisms that move the center exactly to a prescribed point is carried out for polydiscs in [ Section 2.3, Theorem 2.3.2 and Proposition 2.3.3, pp. 50–52 , Blo02Pluripotential ] ; lemma 9.6.1 provides the corresponding automorphisms of the ball. Compare also [ Theorems 5.13–5.14, pp. 143–149 , GZ17 ] . In Step 3 of the proof of theorem 9.6.3 , the determinant of the complex Hessian of the solution is shown to vanish almost everywhere by comparing the solution with its second-order Taylor polynomial at points where this expansion holds. For functions with bounded real Hessian, the expansion holds almost everywhere by proposition 1.7.5 , which is proved with the differentiation of integrals and the Poincaré inequality on cubes. The homogeneous balayage of corollary 9.6.4 , together with the comparison principle, shows that a locally bounded plurisubharmonic function is maximal if and only if its Monge–Ampère measure vanishes (theorem 9.6.6 ); in particular, maximality is a local property for locally bounded functions. The characterization of the inequality $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n\geq f\eta ^ n$, where $\eta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|z|^2$, by upper test functions and the linearization of the determinant (proposition 9.7.3 ) are proved in [ Proposition 1.5 and Lemma 1.7, pp. 5–7 , EGZ10ViscosityV1 ] , the first arXiv version of the later article by Eyssidieux, Guedj and Zeriahi. The passage from upper test functions to distributional inequalities, which the proof in that preprint quotes from Hörmander, is lemma 9.7.2 . The trace matrices used there have determinant $n^{-n}$; multiplying them by $n$ gives our matrices of determinant one. The inequality for mixed products of smooth functions and its extension to bounded functions whose Monge–Ampère measures have densities with respect to Lebesgue measure are stated in [ Theorems 1.1–1.2, pp. 1–2 , Din07MixedV1 ] , the first arXiv version of Dinew's article; the extension is attributed there to Kołodziej and Błocki. We prove the case of continuous densities, corollary 9.7.4 , by linearization and decreasing convolution, and the case of a common measure in corollary 9.11.2 . At fixed potentials, the smooth measure displayed by Dinew is $(4\pi )^ n$ times ours. The Dirichlet problem on a ball with continuous density, theorem 9.8.2 , follows the argument of [ Theorems 5.13–5.14 and Corollary 5.15, pp. 143–149 , GZ17 ] . Since the automorphisms of lemma 9.6.1 move the center exactly to a prescribed point, the preliminary Lipschitz comparison with translations used there is not needed. Under such an automorphism $S$ the $n$-th root of the density transforms into $(f^{1/n}\circ S)|\det _{\mathbb C}DS|^{2/n}$; on p. 145 this factor is written first without the absolute value and later without the derivative. The symmetric error is quadratic, and the half-sum is taken only once; this corrects the formulas printed on pp. 145–146. The stability estimate ( 9.33 ) contains a term for the boundary data, which is omitted on p. 149, and its proof does not require monotone approximation of the boundary data and of the density. Densities are taken with respect to $\eta ^ n=(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|z|^2)^ n$; at fixed potentials, the operator of [ GZ17 ] gives $2^ n$ times our measures. The extension to bounded densities (lemma 9.9.1 , theorem 9.9.2 ) corresponds to [ Theorem 5.17 and Lemma 5.18, pp. 150–151 , GZ17 ] . In lemma 9.9.1 the comparison is made on strict sublevel sets, and only the shifted sublevel set is required to be relatively compact. In the proof of theorem 9.9.2 the approximating densities have an explicit common bound. Convergence in capacity of the approximating solutions is proved without assuming that the solution for a bounded measurable density is continuous inside the ball, by applying Hartogs' lemma on compact sets outside the exceptional sets of quasi-continuity. Approximating the $n$-th roots of the densities by convolution extends the stability estimate ( 9.33 ) to bounded densities. The class $\mathcal E_0(B)$ of definition 9.10.1 is due to Cegrell: its definition on hyperconvex domains is recalled in [ Section 3, p. 161 , Ceg04 ] , where the class is said to have been introduced in [ Ceg98 ] , and it is also recalled in [ Section 2, p. 3 , Din07MixedV1 ] . The moment condition used in Dinew's article to approximate a measure by its averages over cubes is stated in Theorem 2.2, pp. 4–5, whose conclusions on approximation and stability are quoted from other sources. Theorem 9.10.2 establishes the moment condition for measures dominated by the Monge–Ampère measure of a bounded plurisubharmonic function; it follows from Błocki's estimate proposition 9.3.5 by integration over level sets, after truncating the function with zero boundary values and passing to a smaller ball. The constants depend explicitly on the mass of the measure and on the oscillation of the subsolution, and the estimate also holds in dimension one. By proposition 9.10.3 , which combines this estimate with the local $L^ p$ bound proposition 8.3.6 , the cube averages satisfy the moment condition uniformly. Applied to the solutions with zero boundary values, this gives uniform bounds for their local energy moments, and applied to the measure $\eta ^ n$, a constant multiple of Lebesgue measure, it gives compactness in $L^1$ along subsequences. At fixed potentials, Dinew's operator multiplies measures and local energy moments by $(4\pi )^ n$; because of the power of the mass on its right-hand side, both sides of ( 9.43 ) are multiplied by the same factor.
